en: The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume One, the first part of the first section,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kasmīra and Zhu Fonian et al. during the Yao Qin dynasty.
In the first section, I prostrate my head before all Buddhas, As well as the Dharma and the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus;
I now expound the Vinaya teachings To cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
With Upāli at their head, as well as the others who have realized the body;
now I shall speak the essential meaning of the precepts—let all the virtuous ones listen together.
Now I wish to proclaim the profound precepts for those who delight in upholding them.
For those who are able to recite and chant, it brings benefit to all the elders.
Now I shall speak the meaning of these ten verses, the precepts and Dharma of all Buddhas:
to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice in eternal peace, and for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha together.
It causes those without faith to believe, and increases the faith of those who already believe;
it causes those who break the precepts to abandon them, and leads those on wrong paths into the right path;
it brings peace to those with a sense of shame and modesty, and ensures that the Buddha-dharma endures for a long time.
Therefore, the World-Honored One of Supreme Excellence expounds this Sūtra of the Prohibitory Precepts.
Among all mountains, Sumeru is supreme; among all flowing waters, the ocean is supreme.
Among hundreds of thousands of millions of sūtras, the precepts are the foremost and most supreme.
Those who seek the foremost excellence in this world and the next, Should maintain these precepts and never violate them throughout their lives.
By removing the fetters, one becomes free from obstruction; Through this, all bonds and attachments are liberated.
Examine yourself by means of the precepts, as a mirror reflects the image of one's face.
Those who wish to cultivate wholesome dharmas should fully equip themselves with the three types of action;
they must carefully examine their intentions, as taught in the *Rāhulovāda Sūtra*.
The reason a king is established is due to the disputes and litigation of the world;
he is one raised up by the multitude, according to the constant laws of antiquity.
Those who commit offenses know the law, while those who follow the law achieve fulfillment.
The precepts are likewise: like a king governing by the True Dharma, or like a physician examining various ailments to ensure that movement and stillness are appropriate;
he administers medicine where it can be cured, but abandons those for whom it cannot.
As stated in the medical treatises, there are four conditions that cannot be cured;
thirteen are salvageable, while the remainder need not be saved.
It is like a corpse: the great ocean will not accept it.
Driven by a violent wind, it was cast upon the shore.
Those who perform evil deeds are like that corpse;
rejected by all people, for this reason one should maintain the precepts.
As when a gatekeeper is firm and reliable, one need not fear the loss of wealth;
yet if the walls and fences are broken and ruined, the possessor of wealth is filled with anxiety and dread.
So too, when the Buddha’s precepts are without flaw or omission, those who uphold them have no cause for worry.
When the prohibitive precepts are not firm, those who violate them harbor sorrow.
As clay vessels have many cracks and leaks, the potter harbors grief;
but if the vessels are complete and intact, all members of his family rejoice.
One whose observance of the precepts has flaws and who commits evil is constantly filled with anxiety;
one who does not violate the prohibitions always harbors joy in their heart.
Just as a spark of fire, though minute, should not be disregarded as small;
All the grasses and trees it passes through are burned away until nothing remains.
Though the evil one commits may be slight, be careful not to deem it trivial;
like the breaking of an *elā* leaf, one will always remain among the dragons.
As the roar of a lion or a tiger does not terrify the intoxicated,
yet the faint cry of a small beast strikes fear into the sober; so too,
those possessed by the three defilements feel no dread of any evil.
The wise person harbors constant fear toward even the slightest evil.
Just as one compiles various medicines and selects away those that are unsalutary;
when the patient takes them, they are cured, and with a healthy body, they attain peace and happiness.
Thus, by mindfully cultivating ethical discipline, one can avoid all evil conduct;
having eliminated the afflictions of the fetters, one enters nirvana in peace and security.
If one wishes to travel a long road, one must protect one's own feet.
If one's feet are destroyed, one cannot travel a long road;
Seeking heaven or nirvana, one should guard the precepts through skillful means.
Thus, being free from destruction, one will surely be able to cross the perilous path.
Just as one who wishes to cross a river uses their hands and a flotation bag;
though the water be deep, they have no fear of drowning and can reach the further shore.
So too do these sons of the Buddhas, practicing the foundation of the prohibitive precepts.
Never turning back toward the flow of heterodoxy, they do not drown in the ocean of birth and death.
Like the hall of Śakra, adorned and fashioned from various jewels;
with stairways made of the seven treasures, it is the place where devas and humans travel.
Such is the Hall of the True Dharma, adorned with the seven factors of enlightenment;
with the prohibitive precepts as its steps, it is the practice of the noble and holy ones.
Just as one who has well studied all worldly arts and crafts, [so too is this hall].
Being cherished by the king, one thereby attains peace and happiness.
Those who are able to skillfully practice the prohibitions and precepts taught by the Buddha will never fall into the evil realms, but will forever attain a place of security and tranquility.
Just as one first makes one's own ranks firm and then breaks the enemy army;
so too, when the assembly of the noble ones is firm, they then break the army of Māra.
When the assembly of the noble ones is in harmony, they are praised by the World-Honored One.
Because the community is in harmony, the Buddha-dharma shall endure for a long time.
Like a compassionate nurse who nurtures and protects her child,
[the Sangha] guards against all dangers of water and fire so that no harm may come.
The precepts are like a compassionate mother, protecting the practitioner;
one shall never fall among animals, hungry ghosts, or in the hells.
Just as a valiant general is well-trained in the arts of combat;
Having subdued those enemies, they face death without regard for their own lives.
So too is it with the sons of the Buddha: having trained well in the prohibitions and precepts, they never fear the end of life when the five aggregates dissolve and perish.
Born from the Buddha’s precepts, you are truly born;
just as Aṅgulimāla was, so the Tathāgata has prophesied.
If one abandons the precepts, for the Buddha-dharma they are as dead.
Maintain the precepts as you would protect your life, guarding them without any breach or loss.
Just as one who possesses a royal seal encounters no obstacles wherever they go;
so too, those who violate or break them will face censure, and those who lose them entirely will be bound.
One who fully possesses the seal of the precepts encounters no obstacles wherever they go;
if they slightly violate them, their state is uncertain, but if they greatly violate them, they enter the three evil realms.
For the sake of all people, they subdue all demons and malevolent spirits.
The divine seers possessing the five supernormal powers devised these incantations;
for the sake of those who possess a sense of shame, they were intended to restrain those who lack it.
Thus the Tathāgata established the prohibitions and precepts, reciting them every half-month.
Having already explained the benefits of the precepts, I prostrate and pay homage to all Buddhas.

This verse was not composed by those present at the time of the assembly of the thousand followers of Kāśyapa to compile the Vinaya; rather, it was created later by the members of the five schools as they divided and each relied upon their own traditions.

This refers to one who stands at the head of a community; wishing to explain and interpret the characteristics of the Vinaya for the sake of the assembly, he first offers praise in verse and then speaks upon it. The Four Pārājika Dharmas, Part One. At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the country of Sūrabhava with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. Gradually proceeding on his journey, he arrived at Piḷañña and stayed there overnight beneath a maṇḍala tree on the bank of the Nerañjarā River.

The brahmin Vairaṇya heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, a son of the Śākya clan, had left the Śākyas to go forth into the religious life; having departed from the country of Sūrabhu with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus, he was traveling by stages until he arrived here at Vairaṇya and was staying beneath a mandāra tree on the bank of the Nairañjanā River.
This śramaṇa Gautama possesses such a great reputation:
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.

Among the assemblies of devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, he has attained supernormal powers and realized them; he constantly proclaims the True Dharma—excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its end—with pure meaning and phrasing, naturally and fully endowed with the practice of the holy life.
"How wonderful!
We have been able to see such a person free from attachment; we should now go to pay our respects to the śramaṇa Gautama.
At that time, the brahmin Vairaṇyā went to where the World-Honored One was, and having arrived, they exchanged greetings and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached the Dharma for them, transforming and enlightening them so that they attained joy.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching and attained joy, they immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"Please, out of compassion for me, accept my invitation for you and the community of bhikṣus to observe the three-month summer retreat.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus accepted the invitation by remaining silent.

When the brahmin Vairaṇyā saw that the World-Honored One had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, he rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed; the World-Honored One then entered the three-month summer retreat with a community of five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a horse merchant from the country of Vārāṇasī who drove five hundred horses to stay at Pīlava for the ninety days of the summer retreat.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were starving; white bones lay scattered everywhere, and it was difficult to obtain anything through begging.
At that time, although the Brahmin Vairaṇyā had invited the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus for three months, he provided them with no offerings or necessary supplies whatsoever. Why was this?
"All of this was the doing of Māra Pāpīyān.
At that time, the bhikṣus were unable to obtain alms while begging in the Ārāmavatī grove; they then proceeded to the place where the horse-dealer was to beg for food.
At that time, the horse dealer thought to himself:
"Nowadays, in this region, the price of grain is high and the people are starving; it is difficult for them to obtain even alms-food, and white bones lie scattered everywhere."
"Those bhikṣus have come here simply because they could not obtain alms-food there!
I should now rather give five *śīrṣa* of horse-barley daily to each bhikṣu, and one *dōng* to the World-Honored One!"
Just as he had thought, each day he gave five *śīrṣas* of horse-barley to the bhikṣus and one *droṇa* to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the portion of barley obtained by the Buddha was given to Ānanda; Ānanda had a person grind it and prepare dry rice (*śuṣka-bhakta*) to offer to the Buddha, and the Buddha ate the dry rice.
The bhikṣus each obtained cooked barley and ate it, whereas the food consumed by the Buddha and the bhikṣus was different.

Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “Bhadanta!...”
At present, grain is expensive here; the people are starving and it is difficult to obtain food through begging. The bhikṣus eat coarse and poor-quality food and have all become emaciated.
If the World-Honored One would permit the bhikṣus with supernormal powers to go to Uttarakuru and take the naturally grown non-glutinous rice for their food, we should go there.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Those bhikṣus who possess supernormal powers may go there and take the polished rice for food; but what shall those who lack supernormal powers do?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“Those who possess supernormal powers may go there as they please; those who do not possess supernormal powers, I shall take by means of my own supernormal power.”
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana: “Stop! Stop!”
Do not speak such words.
Why is this? While it may be possible for you, O great men, who possess supernormal powers, what will become of the bhikṣus of future ages?
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, while in a secluded place, had this thought:
"Which of the Buddhas, the Perfectly Awakened Ones, has practiced the holy life such that their Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time?"
"What causes the Tathāgata’s practice of the holy life and the Buddha-dharma to not endure for long?

Then Śāriputra rose from his secluded dwelling, adjusted his robes, and approached the Blessed One. He prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet, sat to one side, and after a short while withdrew slightly and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Just now, as I was sitting in my secluded dwelling, this thought occurred to me:"
"Which Tathāgatas, having practiced the holy life, cause the Buddha-dharma to endure for a long time?
Which Tathāgatas, having practiced the holy life, cause the Buddha-dharma not to endure for a long time?
We pray that you will reveal this to us."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“The Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Krakucchanda, and Kāśyapa—through these Buddhas, the Dharma of practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) has remained for a long time.”
"Under the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda, and Kāśyapa, the Dharma did not remain for long.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By what causes and conditions did the practice of the holy life under the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Krakucchanda, and Kāśyapa endure for a long time?"
"For what reason did the Dharma of the practice of pure conduct under the Buddhas Vipasyin and Kanakamuni not endure for long?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The Buddhas Kanakamuni and Vipasyin did not extensively teach the Dharma to their disciples."

The *sūtra*, *geya*, *vyākaraṇa*, *gāthā*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *jātaka*, *vaipulya*, *adbhutadharma*, *avadāna*, and *upadeśa*—he does not extensively expound these, from the *sūtra* up to the *upadeśa*, nor does he establish the precepts or proclaim the precepts; consequently, his disciples become weary and disheartened, and for this reason the Dharma does not abide long.
At that time, because the World-Honored One perceived that his disciples were weary and disheartened, he gave them this instruction:
"This should be brought to mind; this should not be brought to mind. This should be contemplated; this should not be contemplated. This should be abandoned; this should be fully cultivated."
"Śāriputra, in the past, the Buddha Anupama dwelt in the Bhīṣaṇa Forest together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, Śāriputra!"
If there are those who have not yet abandoned desire, their body hairs will all stand on end upon entering that forest; therefore, it is named the Forest of Fear.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kanakamuni Buddha and the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Vipaśyin Buddha, observing that the hearts of a thousand bhikṣus were weary and exhausted, preached the Dharma for them, saying:

"This matter should be recollected; this matter should not be recollected. This matter should be contemplated; this matter should not be contemplated. This should be abandoned; this should be fully cultivated."
“Śāriputra, you should know that while that Buddha and his śrāvakas were still in the world, the Buddha-dharma was widely disseminated.

However, after that Buddha and his śrāvakas had entered parinirvāṇa, people of various names, various clans, and various families went forth from the household life; for this reason, the Buddha-dharma quickly declined and did not remain long.”
Why is this? Because they are not gathered by means of the sūtras and the Dharma. Śāriputra!
It is like various kinds of flowers scattered upon a table; when the wind blows, they are dispersed.
Why is this? Because they have not been strung together with a thread. Such is the case here.
Śāriputra! As long as that Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas remain in the world, the Buddha-dharma will continue to spread.

However, after that Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas have passed away, those who leave the household life from various names, various clans, and various families will cause the Dharma to perish quickly and not endure for long.
"Why is this? It is because they do not grasp it by means of the sūtras and dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:

“Vipaśyin Buddha, Śikhin Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha extensively expounded the Dharma for their disciples, from the Sūtras up to the Upadeśas; they also established the precepts and recited the precepts, until the assembly of disciples became weary in heart.”
At that time, the Buddha, knowing their minds were weary and disheartened, gave them this instruction:
"This should be contemplated; this should not be contemplated. This should be reflected upon; this should not be reflected upon. This should be abandoned; this should be fully cultivated."
"In this way, Śāriputra!
As long as those Buddhas and their assemblies of śrāvakas remain in the world, the Buddha-dharma will continue to spread.

However, after those Buddhas and their assemblies of śrāvakas have passed into parinirvāṇa, people of various names, various clans, and various families from throughout the world may go forth into homelessness, thereby preventing the Buddha-dharma from quickly perishing."
Why is this? Because they are well-sustained by the Dharma of the sutras. Śāriputra!
It is like various kinds of flowers placed upon a table; when strung together with thread, they do not scatter even when blown by the wind.
Why is this? Because they are well-strung and held together by the thread.
Thus it is, Śāriputra!
As for that Buddha and his assembly of śrāvakas remaining in the world, the extensive teaching of the Buddha-dharma was as described above. Śāriputra!
For this reason, the teachings of the Buddhas from Vipaśyin down to Kāśyapa remained for a long time.
For this reason, the teachings of Kanakamuni Buddha and Śikhin Buddha did not remain for a long time.
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Now is precisely the time; I only pray that the Great Sage, together with the bhikṣus, will establish the precepts and recite them, so that the practice of the Brahma-faring may endure for a long time.
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Stop! Wait!"
The Buddha himself knew the proper time. Śāriputra,
the Tathāgata had not yet established the precepts for the bhikṣus.
Why is this? Because among the bhikṣus, there has as yet been no one who has committed an outflowing dharma (āsrava-dharma).
Only when someone has committed an outflowing dharma does the World-Honored One establish precepts for the bhikṣus in order to sever that outflowing dharma.
Śāriputra! As long as a bhikṣu has not yet obtained gain and offerings, the outflowing dharmas do not arise;
once he obtains gain and offerings, the outflowing dharmas then arise.
If tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) arise, the World-Honored One then establishes precepts for the bhikṣus, desiring that they sever those tainted phenomena. Śāriputra!
As for a bhikṣu who has not yet given rise to tainted phenomena, he is recognized by others by his name alone, because he possesses great learning and abundant wealth and merit.
If a bhikṣu acquires fame and even great wealth, then tainted phenomena (āsrava-dharma) arise within him.
Once these tainted phenomena have arisen, the World-Honored One will then establish a precept for his sake, desiring to cause him to sever those tainted phenomena.
“Śāriputra, you should desist; the Tathāgata himself knows the proper time.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in Vaiśālī. Then, in the village of Kalandaka, there was a son of Sūdena who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures; with firm faith, he left the household life to practice the Way.
At that time, grain was expensive and alms were difficult to obtain. Then, the son of Sudinna reflected thus:
"Now that grain is expensive in the world, it is difficult for the bhikṣus to obtain alms."
"I should now take these bhikṣus to the village of Kalandaka to beg for alms.

Because of me, the bhikṣus will obtain great gains and offerings, enabling them to practice the holy life; furthermore, it will allow my own kinsmen to joyfully practice giving and perform various meritorious deeds."
Having formed this thought, he immediately took the bhikṣus and went to the village of Kalandaka.
When Sūdena’s mother heard that her son was returning to his native village with the bhikṣus, she went at once to meet him.
Arriving at his son's location, he said to him:
"You should now abandon the Way and return to being a layperson. Why is this?"
"Your father has already died and I am now alone; I fear that our family property will be confiscated by the authorities.

Since your father's wealth was already vast, let alone the immeasurable riches inherited from his grandfather and ancestors, it is truly precious. Therefore, you should now renounce the path and return to secular life."
He immediately replied to his mother, saying, "I cannot abandon the Way to practice this unrighteousness; I now take great delight in the holy life and cultivate the unsurpassed path.
Thus he spoke three times, and his son likewise replied:
"He cannot abandon the Path to return to lay life.
His mother then left him and went to her daughter-in-law's place, saying to her:
"When your menstrual period arrives, come and tell me."
When the wife knew that her time had come, she went to speak to her mother-in-law:
"Mistress, you should know that my period has arrived.
Her mother-in-law said to her daughter-in-law:
“Take the garments and ornaments you wore when you were first married and come here wearing them all.
She then adorned herself exactly as instructed and went together with her mother to her son’s place, saying:
“Now is the very time; you may abandon the path and return to secular life.”
"Why is this? If you do not renounce the Way, my property shall be confiscated by the government.
The son replied to his mother:
"I cannot abandon the Path.
His mother spoke thus to her son a second and a third time:
"Your wife has now reached her fertile season; you should father a child so that your lineage shall not be severed."
The son said to his mother, "This matter is very easy; I am capable of doing it.

At that time, before the Buddha had yet established the precepts, Kalandaka’s son perceived no impurity in desire; he then took his wife by the arm, led her to a secluded spot within the park, and committed the three types of unwholesome sexual acts.

At that time, a ghost in the garden whose life had ended was immediately conceived in her womb; after nine months in the womb, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was so upright and handsome that he was peerless in the world, and they named him Bījaka.

With his faculties complete, he gradually grew up, shaved his hair, donned the *kāṣāya*, and out of firm faith left the household life to study the Path. Through diligent and tireless effort, he attained *arhatship*. Possessing supernormal powers, transformations, and immeasurable majestic virtue, he was therefore called the Venerable Bījaka.
Sudinna practiced the dignified deportment of a śramaṇa; there was nothing he did not know, and he engaged in every practice, even being able to teach others in turn.
At that time, since Sudinna had committed an act of impurity, he constantly harbored sorrow and anxiety. When his fellow students saw this, they asked, "Why are you so sorrowful and anxious?"
“You have long cultivated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and there is no aspect of your deportment or etiquette that you do not know; why are you sorrowful, as if you find no joy in the holy life?

Sūpannaya replied, “I truly delight in the holy life, but recently, in a secluded place, I committed an evil deed by engaging in impure conduct with my former wife; it is for this reason that I am sorrowful.”
The bhikṣus said: "Sudinna! How could you commit such an evil deed?

Within the pure Dharma of the Tathāgata—where there is desirelessness within desire and stainlessness within defilement; where one can sever craving, destroy the nest, eliminate all fetters and bonds, and attain nirvāṇa through the extinction of craving—how could you do this?"
"How is it that you now, within this pure Dharma, engage in unchaste conduct with a former wife?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus. The World-Honored One asks when he knows [the answer], and does not ask when he does not know; he asks at the proper time, and does not ask when it is not the proper time; he asks when it is consistent with the meaning, and does not ask when it is inconsistent with the meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the proper moment and the appropriateness of the situation, asked Sudinna:
"Is it true that you engaged in unchaste conduct with your former wife?
"It is so, World-Honored One! he replied.
"I have committed an impure act.
At that time, the World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"Upatiṣya! How can you practice within this pure Dharma, even unto the nirvana where craving is exhausted, while engaging in impure conduct with your former wife?"
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"It would be better to take one's male organ and place it in the mouth of a venomous serpent than to place it within the female organ. Why is this?"
One will not fall into the evil realms on account of this.
However, if one commits an offense against a woman, at the dissolution of the body after death, one will fall into the three evil realms. Why is this?

Through countless skillful means, I have taught the Dharma for severing desire: to sever the perception of desire, to extinguish thoughts of desire, to dispel the fever of desire, and to transcend the fetters of craving.

Through countless skillful means, I have taught that desire is like fire, like holding a torch of straw, like the fruit of a tree, like a loan, like a dry bone, like a piece of meat, like what is seen in a dream, like treading upon the edge of a blade, like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun, like the head of a venomous snake, like a whirling wheel-blade, like standing upon a sharp spear-point, or like being pierced by a sharp halberd—it is utterly loathsome and censured by the Buddha.
“Sudinna! Within my pure Dharma, even unto the Nirvana that is the exhaustion of craving, you have committed the impure act with a former wife.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked him through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Sudinna, you foolish man!
You have committed the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows.
From this day forward, I shall establish a rule of training for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning:”

First, to be embraced by the Saṃgha; second, to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice; third, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; fifth, to increase the faith of those who already believe; sixth, to bring those difficult to discipline into submissiveness; seventh, to grant peace and happiness to those possessed of a sense of shame and remorse; eighth, to sever the outflows (āsrava) of the present; ninth, to sever the outflows of the future; tenth, to ensure that the True Dharma endures for a long time.
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak thus:
"If a bhikṣu commits an impure act by engaging in sexual intercourse, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a Bhadrayānīya bhikṣu who, distressed and finding no joy in the pure life, returned home and engaged in unchaste conduct with his former wife.
He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu commits an impure act, engaging in sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in communion.'"
"However, out of grief and lack of joy in the pure life, I returned home and engaged in unchaste conduct with my former wife. Will I not have committed a *pārājika* offense? What shall I do?"
He then said to his fellow students:
"Venerable sirs!

The Blessed One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: if a bhikṣu commits an impure act by engaging in sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and may no longer live in community."
"However, I was distressed and unhappy with my pure conduct; I returned home and engaged in unchaste conduct with my former wife. Will I not have committed a pārājika offense?"
"What shall I do now? Excellent, Elder!
Please inform the Buddha of this matter for me; I shall practice according to whatever the Buddha instructs."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣu Vatsīputra:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, you fool!
Not delighting in pure conduct, you have returned home to engage in impure conduct with your former wife?
Upon the very first entry [into that act], it is a *pārājika*; you fool, having committed a *pārājika*, you are no longer to live in communion."
Therefore, monks, if there are others who do not delight in the pure practice, you should permit them to relinquish the precepts and return to lay life.
If they later wish to go forth again within the Buddha-dharma to cultivate the pure practice, you should ordain them, allowing them to go forth and receive the full precepts.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu who shares the same precepts with other bhikṣus does not renounce the precepts, or if his precepts have become weak and he does not repent, yet commits an impure act by engaging in sexual intercourse, that bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went on almsround and resided in a forest grove; a female macaque had previously lived in that grove.

At that time, the bhikṣu who went for alms returned to the forest to eat after begging in the village; having finished eating, he gave the remaining food to this macaque. In this way, it gradually became tamed and obedient, following behind the bhikṣu until it finally reached the point of holding onto his hand and refusing to leave.
This bhikṣu then seized the monkey and committed an impure act with it.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were inspecting their lodgings and arrived in succession at that grove.
There, the monkey stood before the bhikṣu, turned its body away from him, and displayed its sexual organs.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"This monkey has turned its body before us and displayed its sexual organs; could it be about to engage in unchaste conduct with another bhikṣu?"
They all informed one another and waited for him in a secluded place.

When that bhikṣu returned from his almsround and was in the forest, having finished eating, he gave the remaining food to the macaque; once the macaque had eaten it, they immediately engaged in unchaste conduct together.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they immediately came to him and said:
"Has the Tathāgata not prohibited [this], saying:
'A bhikṣu must not engage in unchaste conduct'?"
That bhikṣu replied, “The Tathāgata has prescribed that men may not commit offenses with women, but he has not prescribed such for animals.
When the other bhikṣus heard these words, they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet in salutation, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked that alms-seeking bhikṣu, saying: "How can this be, bhikṣu!"
"Did you engage in unchaste conduct with a monkey?
This constitutes the first *pārājika* offense.
One who intends to recite the precepts should speak as follows:

If a bhikṣu, while living together with other bhikṣus under the same precepts, does not return the precepts and, though his precepts are weak, does not repent, and commits an impure act even as far as with an animal, this bhikṣu is defeated (pārājika) and shall not live in community.

"Regarding 'a bhikṣu': there is the bhikṣu by name, the bhikṣu in appearance, the self-proclaimed bhikṣu, the bhikṣu who has been invited to come (svāgata-bhikṣu), the bhikṣu who lives by begging, the bhikṣu who wears the cut-and-sewn robes (khaṇḍa-cīvara), the bhikṣu who has destroyed the fetters (āsrava-kṣaya), and the bhikṣu who has received the full ordination through a formal act of fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma and has thereby attained his status."

Among these, a bhikṣu is one who has received the full ordination through the formal procedure of the fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma, has attained his standing, and dwells within the dharma of a bhikṣu; this is the meaning of "bhikṣu."

Among these, "a bhikṣu who is in common" refers to one who has received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) through a formal act of motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) that is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma; having attained the status of a resident bhikṣu within the Dharma, this is the meaning of "being in common."
What is meant by "identical precepts"?

After I have established the precepts for my disciples, they would rather die than violate them; within this assembly, sharing the same precept, the same precept, and the equal precept with other bhikṣus is called "identical precepts."

What is meant by "not abandoning the precepts"? Abandoning the precepts while insane; abandoning the precepts before one who is insane; abandoning the precepts while mentally deranged; abandoning the precepts before one who is mentally deranged; abandoning the precepts while in pain; abandoning the precepts before one who is in pain; abandoning the precepts while mute; abandoning the precepts while deaf; abandoning the precepts while both mute and deaf; abandoning the precepts before one who is mute; abandoning the precepts before one who is deaf; abandoning the precepts before one who is both mute and deaf; abandoning the precepts before a person from the central lands who is from the borderlands; abandoning the precepts before a person from the borderlands who is from the central lands; abandoning the precepts while not being in a state of tranquility yet perceiving it as tranquility; abandoning the precepts while in a state of tranquility yet perceiving it as non-tranquility; and abandoning the precepts in jest.

Whether it be a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, a preta, a sleeping person, a dead person, an ignorant person, one who does not speak for oneself, or one who speaks but is not understood by the other person—in such cases as these, it is not called the relinquishing of the precepts.
What is the relinquishing of the precepts?

If a bhikṣu takes no delight in practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*), desires to return to the household life, and feels weary of the bhikṣu-dharma; if he constantly harbors shame and remorse while craving the pleasures of the household life, craving the dharma of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or perhaps longing for the dharma of a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), or delighting in the dharma of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), or delighting in the dharma of followers of non-Buddhist paths, or delighting in that which is neither the dharma of a śramaṇa nor the dharma of a son of the Śākya, he then speaks as follows:

"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus; I renounce my preceptor, my co-preceptors, my ācārya, and my co-ācāryas; I renounce all fellow practitioners of the holy life, the precepts, the Vinaya, and the training. I accept the way of the householder: I shall become a lay servant, I shall become a lay follower (upāsaka), I shall become a novice (śrāmaṇera), I shall become a follower of external paths, I shall become a disciple of external paths, and I shall no longer be a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya."
If, moreover, one speaks thus: "I shall stop!
There is no need for a Buddha; what benefit would a Buddha be to me?"
Having departed from the presence of the Buddha, and so on, even regarding the matters of training it is likewise.

If he further speaks other words, disparaging the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, even the matters of training, and instead praises household affairs, even saying they are not śramaṇas and not sons of the Śākya.
To speak such words with full clarity is called "abandoning the precepts.
Regarding the weakening of the precepts (*śīla-kaśāya*), there are cases where the precepts are weakened but not abandoned, and there are cases where the precepts are weakened and abandoned.
What constitutes being weak in morality yet not relinquishing the precepts?

If a bhikṣu is distressed and finds no joy in the holy life (brahmacarya), desiring to return home and grow weary of the bhikṣu-dharma; if he constantly harbors a sense of shame and takes pleasure in living as a householder, even to the point of desiring to perform the practices of those who are neither śramaṇas nor sons of the Śākya; and if he then speaks thus:
"I long for my father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, villages, towns, gardens, fields, and bathing pools; I wish to abandon the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha, as well as the training."
He then wishes to take up his household affairs, even to the point of no longer being a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya; this is called "being weak in morality but not relinquishing the precepts.
What is meant by "being weak in morality and relinquishing the precepts"?
If one thinks, "I wish to relinquish the precepts," and then relinquishes them,
this is called relinquishing the precepts while they are already weakened.
"Unwholesome conduct" refers to the practice of sexual desire.
"Down to even with an animal" refers to any place where sexual intercourse may be performed.
Why is this called a *pārājika*?
For example, just as a person whose head is severed cannot be raised up again, so it is with a bhikṣu: one who commits this offense no longer becomes a bhikṣu; therefore, it is called a pārājika.
What is meant by "not living together"?
There are two forms of living together:
performing the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) in common and reciting the *prātimokṣa* (code of precepts) in common.
One must not abide in these two matters; therefore, it is called "not dwelling together.
There are three types of committing impure acts that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
with a human, a non-human, or an animal.
Furthermore, there are five types of committing unchaste acts that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
with another's wife, an unmarried girl, a hermaphrodite, a eunuch, or a man. To commit an unchaste act with respect to these five objects constitutes a *pārājika*.
To engage in unchaste conduct with three kinds of women constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
What are the three?
A human woman, a non-human woman, and an animal female; to engage in unchaste conduct with these three types of beings constitutes the commission of a *pārājika*.
If one commits the act of impurity with three kinds of girls, three kinds of hermaphrodites, three kinds of eunuchs, or three kinds of men, it is likewise a *pārājika* offense.
If one commits [sexual intercourse] with three parts of a human female—namely, the anus, the urinary tract, and the mouth—it is a *pārājika* offense.

It is likewise for non-human females, female animals, human girls, non-human girls, female animals, human hermaphrodites, non-human hermaphrodites, and female animal hermaphrodites; for these as well, all three parts are treated in the same manner.
If one commits an act of impurity with a human eunuch in two places—
the anus and the mouth— it is a *pārājika*.
It is the same for non-human eunuchs and animal eunuchs.
The same applies to two cases involving a human male, a non-human male, or a male animal.

If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, directs himself toward the anus, the urethra, or the mouth of a human woman, he commits an offense if [the organ] enters even slightly; if it does not enter, there is no offense.
Whether there is a barrier or no barrier, whether the barrier exists on one side or both sides, or whether there is no barrier at all—this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.

If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, directs his attention toward a non-human female, a female animal, a human girl, a non-human girl, a female animal, a human hermaphrodite, a non-human hermaphrodite, or a female animal hermaphrodite—the same applies to the three orifices.
Human eunuchs, non-human eunuchs, and animal eunuchs; human males, non-human males, and animal males—the same applies to these two locations as well.

If a bhikṣu, with a lustful intention, approaches a sleeping woman—whether her body is dead but not yet decomposed or mostly undecomposed—at the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth, he commits an offense if it enters even slightly; if it does not enter, he commits no offense.
The same detailed explanation applies to whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, and so on up to the case of a male.

If a bhikṣu is led by an enemy to a woman’s dwelling and is forcibly made to insert his male organ into one of the three orifices, and he experiences pleasure at the initial entry, pleasure once it has entered, and pleasure at the time of withdrawal, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If there is pleasure upon first entering, pleasure after having entered, but no pleasure at the time of exiting, it is a *pārājika*.
If there is pleasure upon first entering, no pleasure after having entered, but pleasure at the time of exiting, it is a *pārājika*.
If one does not take pleasure at the initial entry, does not take pleasure after having entered, and does not take pleasure upon exiting, it is a *pārājika*.
If one does not take pleasure at the initial entry, takes pleasure after having entered, and takes pleasure upon exiting, it is a *pārājika*.
If one experiences displeasure upon first entering, displeasure while inside, but pleasure upon exiting, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense;
the same applies whether there is a partition or no partition,
and likewise for women who are non-humans, up to and including men.
If a bhikṣu is led by an enemy to a sleeping woman, whether her body is dead and not yet decomposed or mostly undecomposed, the experience of pleasure is likewise;
whether there is a barrier or no barrier, it is likewise;
and from a non-human female down to a male, it is likewise.
If an enemy forcibly seizes a bhikṣu and performs an impure act through the anus, if he perceives pleasure upon entry, it is a pārājika offense;

if he perceives pleasure after entry and also perceives pleasure at the time of exit, it is likewise as stated above; this applies even to cases where there is an obstruction or no obstruction, as described above.
Entering through a path, entering through a path into what is not a path, or entering through what is not a path into a path;
whether by partial entry, full entry, whether spoken or unspoken, or with a lustful mind—even if the entry is as small as a hair-tip—it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs the means but does not enter, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu employs the means with the intent to commit an impure act, if it is accomplished, it is a *pārājika*; if it is not accomplished, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu instructs another bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, if that bhikṣu carries it out, the instructor commits a thullaccaya;
if he does not carry it out, the instructor commits a dukkaṭa.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, if the bhikṣu performs it, the bhikṣuṇī commits a sthūlātyaya;
if he does not perform it, the bhikṣuṇī commits a duṣkṛta.
Excluding the cases of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, if other members of the community instruct one another to engage in unchaste conduct, whether they perform it or not, all commit a duṣkṛta.
If one performs the act of impurity upon a corpse that is half-decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is mostly decomposed or entirely decomposed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one performs the act of impurity between the bones, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one pierces the ground to make a hole, or kneads clay to make a hole, or if it is within the mouth of a *kuṇḍikā* (water flask), one commits a *sthūlātyaya*;
if there is the perception of a path, or if there is doubt—in all such cases, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a path as a path, it is a *pārājika*;
if one suspects it is a path, it is a *pārājika*;
if one perceives what is not a path as a path, it is a *pārājika*.
If it is not a path, yet one perceives it as a path, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is not a path, yet one suspects it to be so, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *pārājika*; for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* leading to expulsion. This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one was asleep and unconscious; if one did not experience pleasure and had no intention of sexual misconduct at all, there is no offense.
There is no offense if it occurred before the precept was established, or if one was insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The first section ends. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Rājagṛha named Dhaniya the Potter, who was dwelling in a secluded place in a single grass hut.
That bhikṣu entered a village to beg for food. Later, a wood-gatherer tore down his grass hut and carried it away.
When the bhikṣu returned from begging, he thought to himself:
"I am now alone in this secluded place; I gathered grass and wood myself to build this hut, yet after I went into the village to beg, a wood-gatherer came and tore my hut down, carrying it off."
"I myself possess the necessary skills; I can certainly mix mud and build a complete house of baked bricks.
Thereupon, that bhikṣu mixed the mud and built a complete house of baked bricks; he took firewood and cow dung to burn it, and when the house was finished, its color was as red as fire.

At that time, the World-Honored One descended from Vulture Peak Mountain and saw from afar that this house was red as fire. Having seen it and knowing [the reason], he asked intentionally: "O bhikṣus!"
"What kind of red color is this?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
There was a bhikṣu named Dhaniya Kumbhakāraputra who lived alone in seclusion in a grass hut. After he had finished his almsround, some wood-gatherers broke open his hut and carried it away.
Upon returning and seeing that his house was ruined, he thought to himself:
"I possess my own skills; I should now build a complete, finished tile-roofed house and dwell within it."
He then did exactly so, and thus the color of his hut became red like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you do this, bhikṣu Tāṇḍika, son of a potter?"
"Why have you built this house yourself and set it ablaze with a great heap of firewood and cow dung?
I have constantly taught through countless skillful means the practice of compassion for all sentient beings.
How can you be so foolish, you man!"
"Why do you build a mud house yourself and then burn it after piling up firewood and cow dung?
From this day forward, you must not build houses entirely of red-baked bricks; whoever does so commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the bhikṣus:
"All of you, assemble together and go quickly in a group to the house of Dhanika to break it open.
Then the bhikṣus, following the Buddha's instruction, went there and broke it open.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had finished demolishing the hut, Cunda saw it and spoke these words:
"What fault have I committed that you have demolished my hut? The bhikṣus replied:
"You have committed no fault, nor do I harbor any ill will toward you.
It was only because I had received the instruction of the World-Honored One that I came to break down your hut! The bhikṣu Dhanika said:
"If the World-Honored One gives such instruction, it would be most appropriate.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha had a timber-guard who was a close friend and acquaintance of this bhikṣu, Dhanika, from their youth.
Then the bhikṣu Cunda went to the timber-guard and said to him:
"Do you know? King Bimbisāra has granted me timber; as I now require timber, you may give it to me."
The man said, "If Your Majesty grants them, you may take as much as you wish, whether good or bad, much or little.
The bhikṣus then took the essential timber left by the king, hewing it and carrying it away.

At that time, there was a high minister in charge of city affairs who went to the timber yard and saw the essential timber reserved for the king cut and scattered in disarray. Having seen this, he immediately questioned the timber guards, saying:
"Who has taken these essential timbers reserved for the king, having cut them up?"
The timber-guard said:
"This is the bhikṣu Dhanika; he came to me and spoke these words:
'The King has granted me timber; if you have need of it now, you may give it to me.'"
I immediately replied, "The King has granted you timber; take as much as you desire.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu entered the timber yard, cut what he needed, and departed with it.
When the minister heard these words, he immediately took offense at the king’s speech, saying:
“Why do you give such essential timber to a bhikṣu?
Fortunately, there are other remaining timbers that can be given to him; why instead allow this bhikṣu to cut away and carry off the essential timber?”
Then the minister went to the king’s presence and said: “Great King!
Why have you given the essential timber previously reserved for this purpose to the bhikṣu, allowing him to cut it up and take it away?”
"Fortunately, there is still more timber remaining that can be given to him; for what reason have you ruined this fine timber?
The king replied, "I do not recall at all giving timber to anyone; if there is someone who remembers it, let them speak to me."
Then the minister immediately had the timber-guard seized and brought before the king.
When the timber-guard saw the bhikṣu Dhanika from afar, he said to him:
"Venerable Sir!"
“Because you seek timber, I have now taken you away; you should come and resolve this for me out of compassion. The bhikṣu replied, “Just go!”
"I am indeed going there.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhanika went later to the king's location and stood silently before him.
The king then asked:
"Venerable sir!
Did I truly give you timber?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I truly gave you timber.
The king said, "I do not recall giving you timber; you may act as my reminder for me."
The bhikṣu replied,
"Does Your Majesty not remember?
When you first ascended the throne, you spoke these words yourself:"

"If, during my reign, there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas within my realm who possess a sense of shame and take pleasure in training in the precepts, they may take what is given and not take what is not given; they may use what is given and not use what is not given."
"From this day forward, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are permitted to use grasses, woods, and water as they please; they need not refrain from using them without having been given permission.
From now on, it is permitted for śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to use grasses, woods, and water according to their own will."
The King said: "Virtuous One!
When I first ascended the throne, I indeed spoke such words."
The King said, "Venerable Sir!
I speak of things that have no owner; I do not speak of things that have an owner."
“The Venerable One ought to die!
The King thought to himself:
“I am a Kṣatriya king of the consecrated lineage; how can I, on account of such a trifle, take the life of one who has left the household life?”
"This is improper.

At that time, after the king had rebuked the bhikṣu with countless skillful means, he commanded his ministers to release the bhikṣu; they then released him immediately according to the king's instructions.
Thereafter, all the ministers raised their voices in loud protest,
saying, "What is the King’s intention?
Regarding such a matter of death, is he merely to reprimand him and then release him?"
At that time, there were among the laypeople in the city of Rājagṛha those who did not have faith in or delight in the Buddha-dharma, all of whom spoke with derision and disdain:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have neither shame nor remorse and possess no sense of dread; they take what is not given, yet outwardly they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"If this is so, what Dharma of the True Teaching remains?
They even take timber from the royal forest, let alone from others.

From this day forward, we shall no longer associate with these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas; we shall not prostrate to them, inquire after their health, make offerings to them, or show them respect. Do not allow them to enter the village, and do not provide them with lodging."

When the bhikṣus heard this, those who were few in desire, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, possessed of a sense of shame and dread of blame, and who delighted in training in the precepts, censured Dhanika:
"How could you have stolen King Bimbisāra’s timber?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat down to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked him intentionally:
"Bhikṣu Dhanika, is it true that you took timber without the king granting it?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣu Dhanika, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not a compliant practice, and something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that King Dhanika took timber without giving it?
I have, by countless skillful means, praised those who give when one should take, and those who take when they have been given.
Why, then, do you now take timber from the king without his having given it?"

At that time, there was also a bhikṣu named Gāla, who had formerly been a high minister of the king and was well-versed in worldly affairs; he sat among the assembly not far from the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing yet intentionally questioning the bhikṣu Kāla, said:
"According to the royal law regarding taking what is not given, for how much amount of property should one be put to death?
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one takes five coins, or property worth five coins, one should be put to death.
"How is it, Bhikṣu Dhanika, that you took timber when the king had not given it to you?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣu Dhanika with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:

“The foolish bhikṣu Dhanika has committed the first offense among the many bases for the outflows. From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu, whether in a village or in a secluded place, takes what is not given with a thieving mind, according to the nature of taking what is not given, and is consequently seized by a king or a king’s minister, or is executed, bound, or driven out of the country, [the king] saying: “You are a thief! You are a fool! You have no sense!”’”
"Such a bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with us.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are four kinds of villages: [text continues].
First, those with surrounding walls; second, those with fences; third, those with incomplete fences or walls; fourth, those with buildings on all four sides.
As for a "secluded place," it refers to an empty and quiet location outside a village; this is called a secluded place.
"Not giving" means that the other person does not relinquish it.
"Stealing" means taking with a thieving mind.
"Taking what is not given" refers to either five coins or something worth five coins.
A "king" is one who has attained sovereignty and is not subject to others.
"Ministers" refers to various ministers who assist the king.
Regarding "expulsion and non-residence," it is as explained above.
There are three ways of taking what is not given that constitute a *pārājika*:
taking with one's own hand, taking by watching for an opportunity, or taking by sending another person.
Furthermore, there are three other ways of taking that constitute a *pārājika*: [taking by force, taking by stealth, and taking by deception].
Taking what is not one's own while perceiving it as such, taking it without intending temporary use, and taking it without consent.
Furthermore, there are three factors for taking:
another's property, the perception that it is another's property, and the act of lifting it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of taking:
taking what belongs to another, taking with the perception that it belongs to another, and lifting it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of taking:
Taking what belongs to another, with the perception that it belongs to another, if one lifts it and removes it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are four ways of taking what is not given that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
taking with one's own hand, taking by watching over it, taking by sending another person, or lifting it and removing it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of taking that constitute a *pārājika* offense:

taking what one perceives as not being one's own property; taking it without intending to return it temporarily; taking it without the owner's consent; or lifting it and moving it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of taking:
another's property, the perception that it is another's property, the object being of significant value, and its removal from its original location.
There are again four kinds:
There is an owner, the perception that there is an owner, it is a heavy object, and one lifts it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are four types:
another's possession, the perception that it is another's possession, it is a heavy object, and one lifts it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are five types of taking what is not given that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
taking with one's own hand, watching another take it, sending someone to take it, taking an object of value, or lifting it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are five factors:

taking what is not one's own with the perception that it is not one's own; not taking it temporarily; taking it without consent; if it is a heavy object; or lifting it and moving it from its original place.
Furthermore, there are five factors:
[taking] another's property, the perception that it is another's property, [the object being] of significant value, the intention to steal, and moving it from its original location.
Furthermore, there are five factors:
There is an owner, the perception that there is an owner, it is a valuable object, there is the intent to steal, and one moves it from its original location.
Furthermore, there are five factors:
it is protected by another, the perception that it is protected by another, it is a valuable object, there is the intent to steal, and one moves it from its original location.
Furthermore, there are six types of taking what is not given that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
taking with one's own hand, taking by watching over it, sending another to take it, if it is a heavy object, with a thieving mind, and moving it from its original place.

There are six kinds of taking what is not one's own while perceiving it as not one's own; these are likewise [to be understood]. These constitute the six types of *pārājika* offenses involving taking. Regarding "places":

whether on the ground, above the ground, in a vehicle, on a shoulder-pole, in the air, in a tree, in a village, in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), in a field, at a site, on a boat, in the water; or if one crosses a frontier pass privately without paying taxes; or if one takes another’s entrusted goods;
or if one takes water, willow twigs, fruits from trees, grasses, or wood.
Sentient beings without feet, those with two feet, four feet, or many feet;
those who share in wealth and industry, those who wait for an opportunity, those who guard, or those who patrol the main roads—these are called "locations."

Regarding the location: within the earth there are hidden treasures, as yet unextracted, consisting of the seven jewels—gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, and *śaṅkha-śilā*—as well as raw gold, precious gems, and garments.
Furthermore, if there are other items required for the grounds that belong to an owner, and one takes them with a thieving mind—whether they are five coins or more than five coins;
whether by dragging them away or by burying them; [one commits an offense].
If one lifts [an object] and removes it from its original place, at the moment of first removal, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs the means to lift it but does not actually lift it, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Regarding objects situated on the ground—such as gold, silver, the seven treasures, or even clothing and bedding that have not been buried—if there are other items required for use on the ground that belong to an owner, and one takes them with a thieving mind for five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, whether by dragging them away, burying them, or lifting them from their original place, at the moment of first removal, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs the means to lift [the object] but does not lift it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "riding," there are four kinds of riding:
riding on elephants, riding on horses, riding in carriages, and riding on foot.
Furthermore, if there are other vehicles that are all termed "vehicles," and upon these vehicles there are gold,

silver, the seven treasures, or even clothing and bedding, or any other requisite items belonging to an owner— if one takes them with a thieving mind for five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, whether by pulling them away, burying them, or taking them so they leave their original place— the initial act of moving them from that place constitutes a *pārājika*.
If one employs the means to lift them but does not actually lift them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one takes a vehicle from a path to a path, from a path to a non-path, from a non-path to a path, from a pit to dry land, or from dry land to a pit—thus taking it away from its original place—the first moment it leaves the place constitutes a *pārājika* offense;
if one employs the means to take it but does not actually take it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "places of carrying": whether carried on the head, on the shoulders, on the back, or held in the arms, or any other manner of carrying—should there be gold, silver, the seven treasures, or even clothing and bedding upon these loads, or any other necessary items belonging to another, if one takes them with a thieving mind for five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—whether by dragging or pulling them away, or by burying them—if they are taken and removed from their original location, at the moment of the first removal, it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs the means to lift them but does not actually lift them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one who takes up a burden moves it from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from a pit to dry land, or from dry land to a pit—if, with the intent to steal, they take it and move it from its original place, at the first movement, it is a *pārājika*;
if they employ means to take it but do not actually take it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "empty places": if one takes with a thieving mind five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*—whether it be wind-blown wool, cotton, *koccha*, *carapaṇi*, *kūśa* grass, hemp, silk-cotton, *pattalaṃbha*, *tūtūra*, or the property of others such as geese, cranes, peacocks, parrots, or mynas—and moves it from its original location, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense at the moment of the first displacement.
If one employs means to take it but does not actually take it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "objects in high places": if one takes with a thieving mind objects worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—such as gold, silver, or other necessary items like clothing and bedding—that are situated on a tree, a wall, a fence, a stake, a "dragon-tooth" stake, a clothes rack, a rope bed, a wooden bed, a large or small mat, a table, or a floor covering; whether by pulling them down, burying them, or lifting them from their original location, the offense of *pārājika* is incurred at the moment they are first moved.
If one employs the means to lift them but does not actually lift them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "inhabited places," there are four types as mentioned above.

If there are gold, silver, or even clothing and other necessary items within a village that have an owner, and one takes five *kārsāpaṇa* coins or more with the intent to steal—whether by pulling them away, burying them, or lifting them and moving them from their original location—the offense of *pārājika* is incurred at the moment they are first moved.
If one employs the means to lift them but does not actually lift them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one attacks and destroys a village by means of mechanical devices, or floods it with water, or relies on intimacy and force, or takes it through the deception of eloquent speech, one incurs a *pārājika* offense upon first acquiring it;
if one employs the means to take it but does not actually acquire it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the "aranyaka" (wilderness) location: it refers to an unoccupied space outside a village that has an owner. If there are gold, silver, the seven treasures, clothing, or other necessary items belonging to an owner within that vacant space, and one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with the intent to steal—whether by picking them up or burying them—and moves them from their original place, at the moment they are moved away, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs the means to pick them up but does not actually pick them up, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one uses skillful means to destroy another's vacant land, or pours water upon it, or relies on intimacy or force, or takes it by deceiving them through eloquent speech, one incurs a *pārājika* offense upon first obtaining it;
if one employs skillful means with the intent to take it but does not succeed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding fields: rice fields, wheat fields, sugarcane fields, or whatever other fields there may be; if within those fields there are gold, silver, the seven treasures, clothing, or other necessary items that have an owner, and one, with the intent to steal, takes five coins or more than five coins—whether by lifting them up, burying them, or moving them from their place—the first moment they are moved constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs the means to lift them but does not actually lift them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one destroys another's field through expedient means—whether by flooding it with water, relying on intimacy or force, or by deceiving them with eloquent speech—one incurs a *pārājika* offense upon first obtaining [the property].
If one employs expedient means with the intent to take but does not actually obtain it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the location: whether it be a house, a marketplace, a fruit orchard, a vegetable garden, a pond, a courtyard, the area behind a dwelling, or any other place; if there is gold, silver, the seven treasures, clothing, or other necessary items belonging to an owner, and one takes five coins or more with the intent to steal—whether by picking them up, burying them, or removing them from their place—the moment they are moved from that location, it constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs the means to move them but does not actually move them, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If one destroys another's dwelling place, or relies on powerful kin or intimates, or takes [the property] by means of deceptive speech and sophistry, one incurs a *pārājika* offense upon first obtaining it;
if one employs the preparatory effort but does not obtain it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "places on water": small boats, large boats, platform boats, single-log boats, *fang* (double-decker) boats, oar-boats, tortoise-shaped boats, turtle-shaped boats, leather boats, gourd-buoy boats, fruit-boats, suspended boats, rafts, or any other such vessels; if there are gold, silver, the seven treasures, clothing, or other necessary items upon them that have an owner, and one takes five *kārsāpaṇa* or more with the intent to steal—whether by burying them or moving them from their original location—the first moment they are moved constitutes a *pārājika*.
If one employs means to take them but does not succeed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one goes from this shore to the other shore, or from the other shore to this shore; whether going against the current, with the current, sinking into the water, or moving onto the bank; or if one releases [the object] at the place of movement, it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs the means to take it but does not succeed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "in water": if one conceals gold, silver, the seven treasures, or various garments and bedding, and sinks them into the water; or if there are otters, fish, turtles, *śiśumāra* crocodiles, or *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, as well as other aquatic objects that have an owner—if, with the intent to steal, one takes five *kārsāpaṇa* or more, whether by pulling them out or burying them, and they are moved from their original location, it is a *pārājika* offense at the moment of first displacement.
If one employs means to take them but does not succeed, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a stratagem to take water from another's source, it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense as described above.

Regarding the non-payment of taxes: monks have no obligation to pay taxes. If there is an item subject to tax belonging to a layperson (*avadātavasana*), and a monk, with a thieving intent, causes it to pass through a checkpoint for another—whether by throwing it outside the barrier, whether the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five, whether by burying it and then digging it up, by using eloquent speech and arguments to deceive, or by passing it through the use of incantations—it constitutes a *sthūlātyaya* offense through such stratagems, as described above.

Regarding one who takes another’s entrusted property: having received the entrusted property and departed, if with the intent to steal they take five *māṣakas* or more than five *māṣakas*, moving it from the head to the shoulder, from the shoulder to the head, from the right shoulder to the left shoulder, from the left shoulder to the right shoulder, or from the right hand to the left hand, from the left hand to the right hand, or if holding it in their arms or placing it on the ground—whenever it is lifted and separated from its original place, at that first separation, it is a *pārājika*;
if it was merely an attempt (*upakrama*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding water: if one takes with a thieving mind five *māṣakas* or more than five *māṣakas* from various water vessels such as large or small basins, or other kinds of water containers, whether it be scented water or medicinal water—whether by pulling it out or by discarding it—it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the preparatory means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding *yāñcī* (tooth-sticks): whether one, two, many, a handful, a bundle, an armful, or a load; whether scented with incense or smeared with medicine—if one takes them with a thieving mind for five *māṣaka* coins or more, and by pulling or dragging them away from their original place, at the moment they leave that place, it is a *pārājika*;
if there was an attempt (*upakrama*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "gardens": if there are various grasses, trees, thickets, flowers, or fruits belonging to an owner, and one takes them with a thieving mind—whether they are worth five māsakas or more than five māsakas—by pulling them, dragging them, lifting them, or burying them, such that they are moved from their original location, at the moment of the first displacement, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the preparatory means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "footless sentient beings": if one, with the intent to steal, takes from snakes, fish, or other footless sentient beings that have an owner, an amount worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means [to do so], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding two-legged beings: if one takes with a thieving mind five *kārsāpaṇas* or more from humans, non-humans, birds, or other two-legged beings who have an owner, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means for such an act, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding four-footed sentient beings—such as elephants, horses, oxen, camels, donkeys, deer, sheep, and other four-footed sentient beings that have an owner—if one takes them with a thieving mind for a value of five māsakas or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the preparatory means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding those with many legs: bees, *urucungas*, centipedes, and other many-legged sentient beings that have an owner—if one takes them with a thieving mind for a value of five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means [to take them], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding those who share in wealth: when wealth is obtained through joint labor, it shall be shared together. If one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means [to do so], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "making a mutual agreement": it refers to making a mutual agreement with another by instructing them, saying, "Go at such a time; come back at such a time. Whether they break through a wall to take property, whether they plunder on the road, or whether they set fire [to a place], if one takes for oneself five *kārsāpaṇas* or more in value from the wealth obtained from that person with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika*;
if it is an attempt (*prayoga*), it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "waiting upon": I shall go to observe that village, whether it be a town, a city, a ferry crossing, a mountain valley, a place where people dwell, a marketplace, or a workshop. Whatever goods are obtained there, if one takes them with a thieving mind—whether they are worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means [to take them], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the "guardian": if wealth is obtained from outside and one thinks, "I shall guard it," and if all the goods so acquired are shared [with the owner], yet one takes five *kārsāpaṇas* or more with a thieving mind, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means [to take it], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding those who observe the Path: "I shall observe the Path. If an army of kings, an army of bandits, or an army of elders should come, one must inform them; whatever wealth or goods are obtained shall be shared by all. If, with a thieving mind, one takes property worth five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs the means for such theft, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs skillful means to seek more than five *māṣaka* coins and obtains more than five *māṣaka* coins, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs skillful means to seek more than five *māṣaka* coins and obtains exactly five *māṣaka* coins, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs means to seek more than five *māṣakas* and obtains less than five *māṣakas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs means to seek more than five *māṣakas* and does not obtain them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs means to seek five coins and obtains more than five coins, it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs means to seek five coins and obtains exactly five coins, it is a *pārājika*.
