If one employs means to seek five coins and obtains less than five coins, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs means to seek five coins but does not obtain them, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs means to seek less than five coins but obtains more than five coins, it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs means to seek less than five coins but obtains exactly five coins, it is a *pārājika*.
If one employs a stratagem to seek to acquire less than five *kārsāpaṇas* and succeeds in acquiring less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs a stratagem to seek to acquire less than five *kārsāpaṇas* but does not succeed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another through skillful means to seek more than five coins and obtains more than five coins, both are guilty of a *pārājika* offense.
If one instructs another through skillful means to seek more than five coins and obtains exactly five coins, both are guilty of a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek more than five *māṣaka* coins, and less than five coins are obtained, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek more than five *māṣaka* coins, and none are obtained, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek five coins, and more than five coins are obtained, both are guilty of a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek five coins, and exactly five coins are obtained, both are guilty of a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas*, and they obtain less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas*, and they do not obtain them, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek less than five *māṣaka* coins, but obtains more than five *māṣaka*, the one who takes it commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek less than five *māṣaka* coins, but obtains exactly five *māṣaka*, the one who takes it commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek less than five *māṣakas*, and they obtain less than five *māṣakas*, both are guilty of a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one employs skillful means to instruct another to seek less than five *māṣakas*, but they do not obtain them, both are guilty of a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one uses skillful means to instruct another to seek five coins, and if it exceeds five coins, and the person instructed takes a different object, the taker commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one uses skillful means to instruct another to seek five coins or more than five coins, and the person so instructed takes the object from a different location, the person who was instructed commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one uses skillful means to instruct another to seek five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five *kārsāpaṇas*, and the person so instructed, thinking they are being sent to fetch goods and lacking the intent to steal, takes them—whether it be five *kārsāpaṇas* or more—the instructor commits a *pārājika* offense, while the person who was instructed incurs no offense.

If one instructs another to take an object, and the person receiving the instruction intends it as an act of theft, then if the object is obtained—whether its value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or exceeds five *kārsāpaṇas*—the person who received the instruction commits a *pārājika* offense, while the instructor incurs no offense.
If there is an owner and one perceives there is an owner, and one takes what is not given—whether it be five coins or more than five coins—it is a *pārājika*.
If there is an owner but one has doubt, and one takes five coins or more than five coins, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes what belongs to no owner while perceiving it as belonging to an owner, and the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes an object belonging to no owner while doubting its ownership, and the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes property belonging to another while perceiving it as such, and the value is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one takes property belonging to another while being in doubt about its ownership, and the value is less than five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes what belongs to another while perceiving it as belonging to another, and the value is less than five *māṣakas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one takes an object that does not belong to another while suspecting it may belong to another, and the value is less than five *māṣakas*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense resulting in expulsion; this is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

taking what is intended [as one's own], perceiving it as one's own property, perceiving it as refuse, perceiving it as a temporary loan, or perceiving it through a sense of intimacy. In all such instances, there is no offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain. These are called non-offenses.
End of Section Two.

The Second of the Four Pārājika Dharmas. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Kalandakanivāpa Hall on the banks of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī. By means of countless skillful means, he taught the bhikṣus the practice of impurity, praised the practice of impurity, and praised the contemplation of impurity. The bhikṣus then thought:
“Now the Blessed One has taught us the practice of impurity, praised the practice of impurity, and praised the contemplation of impurity.”

At that time, the bhikṣus practiced the contemplation of impurity through countless skillful means. Having awakened from their meditative concentration, they felt revulsion toward their bodies and lives, becoming sorrowful and discontented.
It was like a self-indulgent man or woman who has a dead snake, a dead dog, or a dead human tied around their neck; they find it utterly loathsome and foul-smelling.

The bhikṣus were likewise; through countless skillful means they practiced the contemplation of impurity, becoming weary of their bodies and lives, filled with sorrow and discontent, and thus sought out blades to take their own lives, praising death, extolling death, and encouraging death.
While staying in a grove by the side of the Vaggumudā River, the bhikkhus thought to themselves:
“The Blessed One has, by means of countless skillful methods, taught the practice of impurity, praised the practice of impurity, and praised the contemplation of impurity.”

Employing countless skillful means, he practiced the contemplation of impurity, becoming weary of his body and life; filled with grief and discontent, he sought a blade to commit suicide, lamenting death, praising death, and exhorting others toward death.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Vṛjikadanti—“Vṛjikadanti” being his clan name, as the term *śramaṇa-gotra* refers to a family lineage—and he entered the Pārileyyaka grove carrying a sharp sword in his hand. There he saw a certain bhikṣu who, weary of his own life and body as filthy and impure, saw the bhikṣu Vṛjikadanti approaching from afar and said to him:
“Venerable sir!...”
"Come and take my life; I shall give you my robes and bowl.
Having accepted the payment of the robes and bowl, he then took his life.
He washed his knife by the riverbank and, feeling remorse in his heart, said:
"I have now gained neither profit nor merit; that bhikṣu is without fault or transgression, yet I have been hired to sever his life-root.

At that time, a certain heavenly Māra, knowing the thoughts in the bhikṣu’s mind, immediately arrived by means of his supernormal power and stood upon the water before the bhikṣu Dhavallaka Nandika without sinking. He spoke words of praise and encouragement:
"Excellent, excellent! [It is well done!]"
“Good son! You have now attained great merit and have delivered those who were not yet delivered.
When the bhikṣu Nandi heard the Māra’s praise, his regret and remorse were immediately extinguished, and he thought to himself:
"I have now attained great merit; I shall deliver those who have not yet been delivered.
He then took up his sword again and entered the park, asking:
"Who has not yet been delivered? I wish to deliver them now."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had not yet abandoned desire; upon seeing the bhikṣu Vulligga Nandiya, he became extremely terrified, and his hair stood on end.
When Vulligga Nandiya saw this, he said to the bhikṣus, "Do not be afraid!"
"Those whose faculties are not yet mature and who are not yet fit to receive transformation must wait until they have reached maturity;
then we shall transform them. Among those bhikṣus, those whose craving was exhausted saw Vṛjika Nandika’s mind without fear and their body hairs did not stand on end.
At that time, the bhikṣu Mūlaka-nandi would sometimes kill one bhikṣu, or two, three, four, five, and even up to sixty people.
At that time, corpses were strewn about in that garden, its foul stench and impurity resembling a cemetery.

Then, some lay devotees (*gṛhapati*), while paying homage to various monasteries, gradually arrived at that garden. Having seen it, they were all struck with wonder and astonishment, and spoke with reproach:
"Such a transformation has occurred in this garden! These śramaṇa sons of the Śākya lack compassion and have killed one another, yet they claim for themselves:..."
"I cultivate the True Dharma.
How can there be such a True Dharma that involves mutual killing?
These bhikṣus kill one another; how much more so would they toward others?
"From this day forward, we shall no longer show respect to, serve, or make offerings to these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
They then announced to all the villages and towns that they were not to be tolerated or allowed to come and go.
At that time, when the lay devotees saw such filth and impurity within this garden, they no longer frequented it.

Then, on account of some minor matter, the bhikṣus of Vaiśālī gathered in one place. At that moment, the World-Honored One observed that the assembly of bhikṣus had diminished and that those great virtuous bhikṣus of renown were nowhere to be seen.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing yet intentionally asking Ānanda, said:
"For what reason has the assembly of monks diminished?
Where are those renowned and virtuous ones now; they are nowhere to be seen!"
At that time, Ānanda, recounting the previous circumstances, addressed the Buddha in full:

“World-Honored One, previously, by means of countless skillful means, you extensively taught the bhikṣus the practice of impurity, praised the practice of impurity, and praised the contemplation of impurity.”
When the bhikṣus heard this, they became weary of their own bodies and lives and sought someone to end their lives; for this reason, there were so few remaining!

We only pray that the World-Honored One will employ further skillful means to preach the Dharma for the bhikṣus, so that their minds may be opened and understood, and they may forever be free from doubt.
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"You may now assemble the bhikṣus in the lecture hall.
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, immediately assembled the bhikṣus in the lecture hall.
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The assembly of monks has now gathered; may the Holy One know that it is time."
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the lecture hall and sat among the assembly, addressing the bhikṣus:
"There is a samādhi called ānāpāna, which is tranquil and blissful; when unwholesome dharmas arise, it can immediately extinguish them, ensuring they never arise again."
For example, in autumn, after the rain has fallen, there is no longer any dust or filth.
Again, just as heavy rain can stop a violent wind, so too is the *ānāpāna-samādhi*: it is tranquil and blissful, and whenever unwholesome dharmas arise, it is able to extinguish them.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, expounded for the bhikṣus the samādhi of ānāpāna; he praised the samādhi of ānāpāna and extolled the cultivation of the samādhi of ānāpāna.
Those bhikṣus then had this thought:

"Today, the World-Honored One has used countless skillful means to teach us the ānāpāna-samādhi, to praise the ānāpāna-samādhi, and to praise the cultivation of the ānāpāna-samādhi; we should diligently practice it."
Then the bhikṣus, employing various skillful means and through contemplation, entered the ānāpāna-samādhi.
Having awakened from the ānāpāna-samādhi, they knew for themselves that they had attained a superior and sublime dharma and were abiding in the realization of the fruit.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣus in the Veṇuvana Grove:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
“How is it that these foolish bhikṣus in the Pāvārika Garden have taken their own lives together?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“These foolish bhikṣus in the Pāvārika Garden have committed the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, provides a weapon to another, praises death, or encourages death, saying: 'Ho!'"
"O man! What is the use of this wretched life?
It would be better to die than to live."
If, having formed such a thought, one uses various means to praise death, extol it, and urge others toward it, that bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and is not to live in community.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. Regarding "a person," it refers to the taking of life from the initial consciousness up to the final consciousness.

As for "killing," it includes: killing by oneself; inciting another to kill; sending a messenger to kill; using a messenger who goes and returns to kill; using a messenger sent in succession to kill; seeking out a man to kill; instructing someone to seek out a man to kill; seeking out a man with a sword to kill; instructing someone to seek out a man with a sword to kill; manifesting signs through the body; speaking through the mouth; manifesting signs through both body and mouth; sending a letter; instructing someone to send a letter; digging a pitfall; setting a trap; administering poison; or providing the means for execution.
Regarding one who commits suicide: if one kills oneself by means of the hand, or with a tile, stone, knife, staff, or other objects, the killer commits a *pārājika* offense;
if one employs the means but does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding one who instructs another to kill: if at the time of killing they personally observe it, or instruct another person to throw [the victim] into water or fire, or push them off a mountain into a valley, or cause an elephant to trample them to death, or cause a predatory beast to devour them, or cause a snake to bite them, or employs various other such methods to instruct the killing—the killer commits a *pārājika* offense;
if they employ the preparatory means but do not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "sending a messenger to kill": if a bhikṣu sends a messenger to take the life of a certain person, and that messenger goes according to his instructions and takes the life, it is a pārājika offense;
if he employs the means but does not take the life, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.

Regarding messengers who go and return: if a bhikṣu dispatches a messenger to take the life of a certain person, and the messenger goes according to his instructions with the intent to kill, but returns before the killing is accomplished, and then, acting upon the previous instruction, goes again to kill; if he kills, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs the means but does not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding "repeatedly sending a messenger": a bhikṣu sends a messenger, saying, "Go and take the life of so-and-so.
He then sends another messenger, and continues in this manner up to four or five times; that messenger then goes and kills him. As for the killer, it is a pārājika offense.
If one attempts to kill through an expedient means, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Regarding successive messengers: a bhikṣu sends a messenger, saying, "Go and take the life of so-and-so."
If that messenger further dispatches another messenger—whether a hundred or a thousand times—to go and take his life, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs the means but does not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Those seeking a man thought, "Who among these knows of such a person who can wield a blade, who possesses skill through long practice, who is without fear, does not retreat, and is able to take the life of so-and-so?"
If that messenger goes and takes his life, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if he employs the means but does not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the instruction to seek out a man: one instructs another to seek someone who knows such a person capable of using a knife, who possesses the skill, who has practiced for a long time, who is not terrified, who does not retreat, and who can take the life of so-and-so.
If that messenger goes and takes his life, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs a means but does not kill him, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If he seeks out someone to wield a knife, seeking them himself:
"Who is brave and strong enough to take up a blade and sever the life of so-and-so?
If the person thus directed goes and kills him, it is a *pārājika*;
if they do not kill him, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to instructing another to seek out someone with a knife.

Regarding manifesting bodily signs: if one manifests a bodily sign to kill—such as causing another to fall into water or fire, to fall from a height into a valley, to be trampled by an elephant, or to be eaten by a predatory beast or stung by a venomous snake—and that person commits suicide because of this manifested bodily sign, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if one employs the means but does not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
As for those who speak with their mouths, some say this:
"The evil you have committed is devoid of benevolence and compassion; you harbored poisonous intent and did not perform any virtuous deeds.
You provided no protection or refuge; having been born, you have already incurred much suffering, so it would be better to die."
If, moreover, one should say this:
"You have not committed evil or violence; you are compassionate and do not harbor malicious intent.

You have performed many virtuous deeds, you have cultivated merit, and you have provided protection. Although you have been born to undergo manifold sufferings, if you die, you shall be reborn in heaven."
If, because of these words, he commits suicide, it is a *pārājika*;
if he employs the means but does not kill him, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The same applies to manifesting signs through body or speech.
If one sends a messenger, or sends a messenger to that person saying:
"The good and evil you have committed are as described above," and the recipient,
upon hearing these words from the messenger's mouth, utters a cry of despair at death and commits suicide, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs a stratagem to cause death, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sends a letter to kill someone and, upon receiving the letter, says:
"Such are the good and evil deeds you have committed."
The detailed exposition is also as above.
The same applies to sending a messenger or a letter.

Regarding "trapping in a pit": having ascertained that the person will certainly travel by a certain path, one should dig a deep pit along that road and place within it fire, or a blade, or a venomous snake, or a sharp stake, or coat a spike with poison. If the person falls into it and dies, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one employs a means to cause death but the person does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding "setting a trap": knowing that a person will certainly pass by a certain place—whether it be a tree, a wall, or a fence—and if one places fire, a blade, a stake, a venomous snake, or a poisoned needle outside of it, and by means of a mechanical device causes them to fall into it and die, it is a *pārājika*;
if one employs a means but the person does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding medicine: if one knows the illness of another person and gives them non-medicine, or medicine mixed with poison, or gives various medicines in excessive amounts with the intent to cause death, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if they give medicine but the person does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Regarding the preparation of the means of killing: if one first knows that a person has long been weary of their own life and loathes this body as filthy and base, and then provides a knife, poison, a rope, or other instruments of death and places them before them; if that person uses any one of these items to commit suicide, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if they employ the means but do not kill, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one employs such means or other expedients to kill a sentient being who dies as a result, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if one employs the expedient but the being does not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If it is a son of a deva, a son of a nāga, a son of an asura, a son of a gandharva, a yakṣa, or a preta; or if it is an animal that possesses the intelligence to understand human speech, or one capable of transforming its shape—if one seeks to kill such a being through an expedient and kills it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one attempts to kill [a human] but fails, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one kills an animal that is unable to change its form, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
if one attempts to kill it but does not succeed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives a human being as a human being and kills them, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if one suspects they are a human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one perceives a non-human being as a human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If it is not a human being, yet one perceives it as a human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if there is doubt as to whether it is a human being or not, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pārājika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense resulting in formal expulsion (*pravāsanīya*). This is an offense.
There is no offense if, while throwing a blade, a staff, a tile, or a stone, one inadvertently strikes their body and they die.
If one is engaged in construction work on a dwelling and, by accident, causes a person to fall into a ditch or onto stones, timber, rafters, or pillars, resulting in death, there is no offense.

If one supports a gravely ill person while helping them rise, or while helping them lie down; or during bathing, or while taking medicine; or when moving from a cool place to a warm place, or from a warm place to a cool place; or when entering or leaving a room, or walking to and from the latrine—if the person dies in all such cases without any harmful intent, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The third section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Gabled Lecture Hall on the bank of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī. At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine, making it difficult to obtain almsfood.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"Let all the bhikṣus who are in Vaiśālī assemble in the lecture hall.
Ānanda immediately received the Buddha’s instruction and command, and the bhikṣus gathered in the lecture hall.
When the assembly of monks had gathered, they prostrated with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The bhikṣus of Vaiśālī have already assembled in the lecture hall; may the Holy One know the proper time.”
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the lecture hall and sat among the great assembly. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should know this! At present, the price of grain in the world is high and the people are suffering from famine; it is difficult to obtain almsfood."

"Whosoever among you has the same preceptor, the same teacher, or is a close friend or acquaintance, each of you should enter the rains retreat here in the vicinity of Vaiśālī as is appropriate; I, too, shall enter the rains retreat at this very place."
"Why is this? Because food and drink are difficult to obtain, it would cause the assembly to suffer exhaustion and hardship.

When the bhikṣus had heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, they each went to dwell in retreat in the vicinity of Vaiśālī, following their respective upādhyāyas, ācāryas, and close friends and acquaintances; the World-Honored One himself dwelt in retreat within the city of Vaiśālī.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat in a monastery by the side of the Vālukā River, and they thought to themselves:
"At present, grain is expensive in this country; the people are starving, and it is difficult to obtain almsfood."
"What skillful means can we employ so that we do not suffer from hunger and thirst?
They immediately thought to themselves:
"We should now go to the houses of the lay devotees and say:"
"I have attained the state of a superior person!

I am an Arhat; I have attained dhyāna, attained supernormal powers, and know the minds of others. Furthermore, I praise that certain person as having attained Arhatship, having attained dhyāna, having attained supernormal powers, and knowing the minds of others."
Among them, there will be lay devotees with faith and joy who, not daring to eat their own food or give it to their wives and children, shall instead offer it as an act of worship to us.
Those lay devotees will also praise us, saying:
"These bhikṣus are truly fields of merit worthy of veneration."
"In this way, we shall be able to obtain excellent and delicious food and drink, dwell in peace and happiness, and not be distressed by the need for alms.
Having had this thought, the bhikṣus on the banks of the Bālukā River then went to the houses of the lay devotees and said of themselves:
"We have attained the state of a superior person; we are arhats who have attained dhyāna, attained supernormal powers, and know the minds of others."
Furthermore, he praised a certain bhikṣu, saying that he had attained arhatship, attained the dhyānas, attained the supernormal powers, and possessed the knowledge of others' minds.

At that time, the faithful lay devotees accepted his words and, from then on, withheld all food and drink as well as their own portions for wives and children, offering them entirely to the bhikṣus, saying:
"These are those who are worthy of veneration in the world."
These bhikṣus, having received the offerings of the householders, had radiant complexions, cheerful countenances, and were fully endowed with physical strength.
However, the other bhikṣus who had observed the rains retreat at Vaiśālī had haggard complexions, emaciated bodies, and tattered robes.
When the rains retreat was concluded, they took up their robes and bowls and went to where the World-Honored One was; prostrating with their heads at his feet, they sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One greeted the bhikṣus, saying:
"Have you been dwelling together in harmony and living in peace?"
"Do you not find it difficult to subsist on food and drink?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha,
"We dwell together in harmony and peace."

At that time, the price of grain was high and the people were suffering from famine; it was difficult to obtain alms, which was a source of hardship. Yet, the bhikṣus who were observing the rains retreat in the saṃghārāma by the Vālukā River had complexions that were radiant and serene, and their physical strength was fully restored.

When the *varṣā* retreat had concluded, they gathered their robes and bowls and went to where the World-Honored One was. Upon arrival, they prostrated with their heads at his feet and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One greeted the bhikṣus, asking:
"Have you been living together in harmony and in peace?"
"Do you not find it difficult to obtain food and drink?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha, "We dwell in harmony and live in peace; we do not find it difficult to obtain food and drink."

The Buddha asked, "In this world, grain is expensive and the people are suffering from famine; it is difficult to obtain almsfood. By what skillful means do you not find it a hardship to go without food?"
The bhikṣus then reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, explaining that for this reason they did not consider food and drink to be suffering.
The World-Honored One asked the bhikṣus: "Is this true of you?"
He replied, "Some are real, and some are unreal.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“You foolish people, you should not speak even of what is real to others, much less speak of what is unreal.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In the world there are two kinds of thieves:”

First, one who is not actually of pure conduct yet claims to be of pure conduct; second, for the sake of food and clothing, one who speaks falsely in the midst of the great assembly regarding what is untrue and not one's own possession, claiming:
"I have attained the state of a superior person."

"In this regard, for the sake of food and clothing, one utters false speech within the great assembly—claiming what is untrue and not one's own possession—by saying of oneself, 'I have attained the state of a superior person. Such a person is the greatest of thieves."
"Why is this? Because they have stolen the food and drink offered by others.
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣus who were observing the rainy-season retreat in the monastery by the Pārileyyaka River through countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man has committed the first offense among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, while truly possessing no knowledge, declares of himself:'"
"I have attained the state of a superior person. I know this; I see this.
At a later time, whether questioned or not, desiring to purify himself, he makes this statement:
“I truly did not know and did not see, yet I said that I knew and saw; this was a false and deceptive lie.
Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in communion.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a monk of overweening pride who said to others,
"I have attained the Way.
Later, he applied himself with unremitting diligence and zealously sought skillful means to realize the most supreme and excellent Dharma.
He thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no knowledge, claims of himself:
"I have attained the state of a superior man; I know this; I see this. "
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he says:
"I truly did not know and did not see; to say that I knew and saw was a false and deceptive lie."
"Such a bhikṣu commits a pārājika offense and shall not dwell in communion.
Yet, with a mind of pride, I said of myself:
"I have attained the Way."
Thereafter, through diligent application of skillful means and unremitting vigor, he realized the most supreme and excellent Dharma.
"I wonder if I have committed a pārājika offense?
What should I do now?"
He then addressed the like-minded bhikṣus:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus:
'If a bhikṣu, while actually possessing no knowledge, declares of himself:'"
"I have attained the state of a superior person; I know this; I see this.
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he says:
"In truth, I neither knew nor saw; my claims that I knew and that I saw were false, deceptive, and a lie."
"An offense of defeat (pārājika); one may not dwell together [with such a person].
Because of overweening pride (adhimāna), I falsely claimed for myself:
'I have attained the Path.'"
"Later, through diligent application of skillful means and unremitting vigor, I realized the most supreme and excellent Dharma.
Might I not have committed a pārājika offense?
How wonderful, O Great Virtuous One!"
"Please inform the Buddha on my behalf; I shall carry out whatever the Buddha instructs.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs. Through countless skillful means, he praised the dhūta practices, extolling those who are upright and dignified, who have few desires and are content, and who delight in renunciation.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"One who possesses overweening pride does not commit an offense.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, while having no actual knowledge, claims for himself:
'I have attained the state of a superior person; I have entered the noble wisdom and the supreme Dharma; I know this; I see this. "
At another time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to purify himself, he makes this statement:
"I truly did not know and did not see; to say that I knew and saw was a false and deceptive lie."
"Except in the case of overweening pride, this bhikṣu has committed a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Not knowing and not seeing" means that in reality, there is no knowledge or vision.
"Self-proclamation" refers to proclaiming for oneself that one possesses faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, and eloquence.
"Personal phenomena" refers to the aggregates of a person, the elements of a person, and the sense bases of a person.
The "state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) refers to those dharmas capable of leading to liberation and accomplishment.

It includes claiming: mindfulness is established in oneself; claiming right mindfulness; claiming observance of the precepts; claiming the presence of desire [for the goal]; claiming non-negligence; claiming diligence; claiming attainment of concentration; claiming attainment of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*); claiming the possession of the Path; claiming cultivation; claiming the possession of wisdom; claiming vision; claiming attainment; and claiming the fruit.

Regarding the statement "one who is mindful of the body": there is mindfulness that can lead one to transcendence. By becoming familiar with, attending to, cultivating, and expanding this dharma—like a well-trained vehicle—and by guarding it, observing it, and attaining perfect equanimity, one reaches certainty; being free from further difficulty, one attains mastery. This is what is meant by saying, "one has attained the foundation of mindfulness of the body."

To say that one is "rightly mindful" means there is mindfulness capable of leading one to transcendence; one becomes familiar with and closely attached to this Dharma, cultivating and expanding it like a well-trained vehicle, guarding and observing it until attaining perfect equanimity. Having attained certainty, one is free from further difficulty and achieves mastery; this is what is meant by saying one is rightly mindful.

He himself declares that he has attained the precepts; he himself declares that he has desire; he himself declares that he is not negligent; he himself declares that he is energetic—all as explained above.

Regarding his own declaration that he has attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*): there are the *savitarka-savicāra* samādhi, the *avitarka-vicāramātra* samādhi, the *avitarka-avicāra* samādhi, and the emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) samādhis. He frequents, associates with, and contemplates these concentrations, while the rest is as explained above.

Regarding those who claim to have attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*): they claim to have attained the absorption of perception, the absorption of non-perception, the absorption conforming to the Dharma, the absorption of mental ideation, the absorption of removing the perception of form, the absorption of not removing the perception of form, the absorption of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the absorption of the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). They become familiar with, closely attached to, and contemplate these absorptions; the rest is as explained above.

One who claims to possess the path—from the path with one factor up to the path with eleven factors—becomes habituated to and closely attached to this path through contemplation; the rest is as explained above.

Regarding those who say they practice: they practice the precepts, practice concentration, practice wisdom, practice the wisdom of liberation, and practice the wisdom of the vision of liberation; they associate with and remain close to them, as described above for the rest.

One who claims to possess wisdom—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), and knowledge of the minds of others (*paracitta-jñāna*)—should cultivate and dwell intimately with these forms of wisdom through reflection; the rest is as explained above.
One who speaks of their own vision sees suffering, sees its origin, sees its cessation, and sees the path. Furthermore, they might say:

"With the purified divine eye, I observe all sentient beings—those being born and those passing away, those of beautiful form and those of ugly form, those in fortunate realms and those in unfortunate realms."
He knows beauty and ugliness, nobility and lowliness, and understands them as they truly are according to the karmic retribution of sentient beings.
As for his intimacy and close association, it is as described above.

Regarding those who claim to have attained [the fruits], he knows those who have attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; as for his intimacy and close association with them, it is as described above.

Regarding the fruits of one's own realization: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship—associating with and drawing close to these is as explained above.
Thus, being empty and unreal, yet neither knowing nor seeing [the truth], one says to others:
"I have attained the state of a superior person.
If one speaks this oneself to another and that person understands it, it is a *pārājika* offense.
If one speaks [of it] and does not know [the truth], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sends a hand-sign, or dispatches a messenger, or writes a letter, or makes a sign of knowledge, if the other knows [it], it is a *pārājika*;
if the other does not know [it], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one dwells in a secluded place while perceiving it as not secluded, and says with their own mouth,
"I have attained the state of a superior person," it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one perceives what is not a secluded place as a secluded place and says with their own mouth,
"I have attained the state of a superior person," it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one speaks to devas, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, pretas, or animals who are capable of transforming their forms and possess intelligence, claiming to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*), it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense if the listener knows [the claim to be false];
it is a *duṣkṛta* offense if the listener does not know [it to be false].
If one uses hand gestures as a messenger, or writing, or makes signs to make another understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the other does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To speak of having attained the qualities of a superior person (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*) to an animal that cannot transform its shape is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a person who has truly attained the Path says to a monk of great standing with whom they do not share mutual agreement,
"I have attained the state of a superior person," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one explains to others the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, intentions, liberations, samādhis, and meditative attainments, and we claim to have attained these, it is a pārājika offense.
If one perceives a human being as a human being, it is a *pārājika* offense;
if one suspects a human being [to be so], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
if one perceives a human being as a non-human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If it is not a human being, yet one perceives it as a human being, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if there is doubt as to whether it is a human being or not, it is also a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pārājika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring formal suspension (*pravāsanīya*).
This is considered an offense.
One who is not guilty of an offense is a person of overweening pride (*adhimānika*) who says of themselves:
"This is due to the causal conditions of karmic retribution, not something attained through cultivation.

If one speaks of superhuman states (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*) to a like-minded great bhikṣu, or speaks to others of the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), mindfulness (*manasikāra*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), yet does not claim for oneself, "I have attained these."
If one speaks while joking, or speaks hurriedly, or speaks alone in a private place, or speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Section Four, Part Two: The Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in Śrāvastī.
Then, Kālodāyin’s lustful desires were so intense that his complexion grew haggard and his body became emaciated.

"How is it that you have attained such a state?
He replied, "I abide in peace and happiness; I do not regard food and drink as a hardship."
He asked again: "By what means do you dwell in peace and happiness, such that food and drink do not become a source of suffering? He replied:
"Venerable Sir!
Previously, my desire was intense; my complexion was haggard and my body was emaciated.

Within this True Dharma, it is taught that desire is removed by desire, pride is removed by pride, craving is extinguished, all fetters are severed, and with the exhaustion of craving, there is Nirvana.
"How is it that your lustful mind is so intense that, following your thoughts and recollections, you play with and discharge impurity?

He replied, "It is indeed so!

Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may long endure. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his own organ and emits semen, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a distracted mind, fell asleep and emitted semen during a dream. Having become mindful of it, upon waking he thought:

He then related everything in detail to the bhikṣu who shared his view, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'To emit semen by manipulating one's own organ constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.'"

On account of this matter, the World-Honored One immediately assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"There are five faults in sleeping with a distracted mind:
first, having evil dreams;..."
Second, the devas do not protect them;

fourth, they do not contemplate the signs of light.
Fifth, the emission of semen during sleep.
These are the five faults.
There are five merits in sleeping with a virtuous mind:
One does not see evil dreams;
one is protected by the devas;

Fixing the mind on the sign of light;
not emitting semen during dreams—

If one emits semen in a dream, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally manipulates his organ and emits semen, except in a dream, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Blue, yellow, red, white, black, the color of curd, and the color of curd-liquor.
What is the color of the essence?

The *srotāpanna* is the essence.

It is the essence of the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
At that time, there was a brahmin living in a secluded and quiet place who recited and maintained incantations.

If, with intentional recollection, one manipulates [the organ] desiring to emit blue semen and it is emitted, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If it is for the sake of medicine, for the sake of self-testing, for the sake of merit, for the sake of sacrifice, for the sake of rebirth in heaven, for the sake of giving, for the sake of seeds, for the sake of one's own arrogance and indulgence, for the sake of testing one's own strength, or for the sake of a pleasant countenance, it is likewise so.
If one regards internal form, external form, internal-external form, water, wind, and space:
internal form refers to appropriated form;
external form refers to non-appropriated form.
Regarding internal and external forms, these are forms that are either perceived or not perceived.
Regarding water, it is whether one follows the current, goes against the current, or sprinkles with water.
Regarding wind, it is whether one follows the wind, goes against the wind, or blows with the mouth.

It is likewise regarding external forms, and likewise regarding internal and external forms; it is likewise regarding water, wind, and space. If one intentionally plays with and emits impurity, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is not emitted, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.

If a woman bows and grasps one’s feet, and one perceives the pleasure of the touch without moving the body, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, touches his robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, grass mat, or even his own body, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is a human female and one has doubt, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is a human female and one perceives her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a non-human female as a human female, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if one has doubt regarding a non-human female, it is a sthūlātyaya.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pārājika.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if there is contact during the act of taking or giving something, contact during playful joking, or contact while assisting one another.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[End of Section Two] *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Volume II.
