Part Two of the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Kālodāyin heard of the precepts established by the World-Honored One: that one must not play with the genitals to cause the emission of semen, nor touch another’s body. He then took his house keys and stood outside the gate, waiting for women—specifically the women of householders’ families—to come, and spoke to them, saying:
"Sisters! You may enter my room and look.
Having led them into the room, he addressed them with coarse and evil words born of lustful intent.
The female musicians laughed at what he said; those who were displeased became angry and reviled him, then left the room and said to the bhikṣus, "Venerable sirs, you should know this!"
"What I have now observed is not good, not in accordance with the Dharma, not appropriate, and ill-timed.
I always considered this place to be secure, free from affliction, free from calamity, and free from fear; yet today, fear has arisen once more and my hair stands on end."
"We originally thought that water could extinguish fire, yet now fire has emerged from the water.
How do we know this? Kāḷodāyin saw us being led into the room and, with lustful intent, addressed us with coarse and evil words."
"When I was at home, even when my husband spoke harsh and abusive words to me, I could not endure them; how much less can I now endure such foul speech from one who has left the household life?"

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked Kālodāyin, having explained the matter at length as above, and then went to where the World-Honored One was. Prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet, they sat to one side and reported the entire incident to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, in the midst of the great assembly,
knowing the matter yet asking deliberately: "Kāḷudāyin, is it true that you have actually done this?"
He replied, “It is so.
Then the World-Honored One rebuked him:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus: "This foolish Kālodāyin!..."
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.
From now on, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may long endure.
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, utters coarse and lewd words of sexual desire toward a woman, for every such coarse and lewd word of sexual desire spoken, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as stated above.
The meaning of "with lustful intent" is as stated above.
"A woman" is also as stated above.
"Coarse and wicked" refers to non-celibate conduct.
"Sexual speech" refers to speaking of the merits or defects of the two [sexual] organs.
Whether seeking it for oneself, or instructing another to seek it; whether asking, answering, explaining, speaking, teaching, or reviling.
"Seeking" means saying to another, "Do such and such a thing for me," or speaking other similar words.
"Instructing another to seek" means saying, "May the gods, Brahmā, the water deities, or Maheśvara assist me to do such and such a thing with you," or speaking other similar words.
The questioner asked: "What are your passages for excrement and urine like?
How do you conduct yourself with your husband, and how is it that you also consort with outsiders?"
If she speaks further words, the respondent says:
"Your anus and vagina are such; you have common intercourse with outsiders, even with your husband, in such a manner. If she speaks further words, [the same applies].
The same applies to the one who understands and the one who explains.

As for the teacher, I instruct you thus: "Treat these two paths in such a way that you may cause your husband and other people to respect and love you; if you speak otherwise, [the result will be different]."
"Abusive speech" refers to saying:
"You are ruined, putrid, scorched, fallen, and fit only for a donkey," or using other such words to revile.
If a bhikṣu addresses a woman with coarse and wicked speech even once, it is one saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
According to the number of such coarse and wicked words spoken, if they are clearly understood, each constitutes a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
if they are not clearly understood, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one conveys a message by means of a hand-seal, a letter, or by dispatching a messenger, such that the woman understands it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if she does not understand it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the passages for excrement and urine, if one speaks of the good or bad qualities of other places, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one uses coarse and wicked speech toward a goddess, an asura-woman, a yakṣa-woman, a nāga-woman, or a female animal capable of transforming her shape, or toward a eunuch or a hermaphrodite, such that they understand the meaning, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if they do not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one uses a hand gesture, a written message, a messenger, or displays a sign to make it known to another, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the other does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks harsh words toward an animal that cannot change its form, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one speaks harsh words toward a man, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu, with lustful intent, utters coarse and wicked speech while perceiving it as such, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
if he utters coarse and wicked speech while entertaining doubt about it, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If it is not harsh speech, yet one perceives it as harsh speech, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if there is doubt whether it is harsh speech or not, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If it is a human female, and one perceives her as a human female, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If one suspects a human woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one perceives a human woman as a non-human woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a non-human woman as a human woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one suspects a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, for the sake of a woman, one explains the contemplation of the impurities and foul secretions:
"Sister, you should know!..."
"This body has nine sores, nine apertures, nine leakages, and nine flows.
As for the "nine apertures," they are the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils, the mouth, and the passages for feces and urine.
When speaking of this impurity, that woman may think one is uttering coarse and wicked words;
when speaking of the Vinaya in its proper sequence, she may likewise think one is uttering coarse and wicked words.

There is no offense in any of the following cases: when receiving the scriptures, when two people receive them together, when questioned by her, when reciting together, when speaking in jest, when speaking to oneself, when speaking rapidly, when speaking in a dream, or when intending to speak of one thing but mistakenly speaking of another. All such instances constitute no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The third section is concluded. While the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī, at that time Kāḷodāyin had already heard the World-Honored One establish the precepts: that one must not play with one's own genitals to cause the emission of semen, must not touch the body of a woman, and must not speak coarse or wicked words toward a woman.
He then took the door keys and stood outside the gate, waiting for the women—specifically the women of the householders—to come, and said to them:
"Sisters! You may enter my room and look around."
Having entered her quarters, she praised herself, saying:
"Sisters, do you know?
I am the foremost among those who train; I am one who practices the holy life, maintains the precepts, and cultivates the Dharma of wholesome qualities."
"You may offer me sexual gratification.
At that time, he who was delighted remained silent and laughed at what was said; he who was not delighted reviled him and departed, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs, you should know!"
"What we have just witnessed is neither good, nor appropriate, nor righteous, nor timely.
We always believed that this place was free from affliction, free from calamity, and free from fear."
"Why is it that today I have once again given rise to fear and dread, such that the hairs on my body stand on end?
I originally thought that water could extinguish fire, yet now fire emerges from within the water."
"When I was at home, my husband spoke to me in such a manner that I could not even endure it; how much more so for one who has left the household life to speak in such a way!

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked Kāḷodāyin:

"How can you, having heard the World-Honored One establish the precepts—prohibiting the manipulation of the genitals to cause the emission of semen, the physical contact of the body with a woman, and lewd or coarse speech—[still act in this way]?"

Having finished this extensive rebuke as described above, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Kālodāyin: "Is it truly so?
He replied: [It is.]
“Yes,” he replied.
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked Kāḷodāyin: “What you have done is improper;
it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done.”
After the Blessed One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Kāḷudāyin is a fool! This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such bases for the outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, with a lustful mind, in the presence of a woman, praises his own body, saying:
'O Great Sister!'"

"I practice the holy life, uphold the precepts, and diligently cultivate wholesome dharmas; you may offer this dharma of sexual desire to me as an offering, for such an offering is the foremost and supreme."
“Saṃghāvaśeṣa. The meaning of “bhikṣu” is as explained above.
The meaning of “with lustful intent” is as explained above.
"Women" is as described above.
"Praising one's own body" means praising one's own physical form as being upright and handsome, or one's complexion, and claiming, "I am of the Kṣatriya, householder, layperson, or Brahmin caste."
The practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) diligently cultivates freedom from defilement and turbidity.
The upholder of the precepts (*śīlavant*) is without deficiency, without breach or leakage, and free from contamination.

The one of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharmin*) delights in secluded places; he goes for alms at the proper time, wears rag-robes (*pāṃsukūla*), practices the ritual of leftover food (*vighasa-dharma*), eats in a single sitting, eats in a single mouthful, dwells among graves, dwells in the open air, dwells under trees, dwells constantly seated, and dwells wherever he happens to be. He maintains the three robes, recites the *geya*, is widely learned, is able to preach the Dharma, upholds the Vinaya, and practices meditation.
Having thus praised oneself, if one comes to make an offering to me but does not speak of sexual desire, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one speaks of sexual desire, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If, in the presence of a human woman, one praises one's own body, it constitutes one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for each instance.
According to how much and how clearly one praises one's own body, for every distinct instance, there is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if one speaks but does not do so clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one makes oneself known by means of a hand gesture, a letter, a messenger, or by manifesting a sign, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense if the other person understands;
it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense if they do not understand.
If, excluding the two paths, one further seeks another place for offerings, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one speaks to a celestial woman, an asura woman, a naga woman, a yakṣa woman, a preta woman, or a female animal capable of transforming her shape, praising one's own body and making oneself understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one uses a hand gesture, a written letter, a messenger, or the manifestation of a sign to praise or describe one's own body so that another comes to know it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one speaks but the other does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one praises one's own body to an animal that cannot change its form, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one praises one's own body to a man, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is a human female and one perceives her as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is a human female but there is doubt, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is a human female but one perceives her as a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a non-human female as a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one suspects a non-human female [to be a human female], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if a bhikṣu says to a woman:

"In this place, this Exalted One is supreme; this bhikṣu is diligent, observant of the precepts, and cultivates wholesome dharmas. You should honor him with kindness through bodily action, kindness through verbal action, and kindness through mental action."
The women thought that the bhikṣu was praising his own body for their sake;
however, when he was reciting the Vinaya, his speech sounded similar [to such praise], and they believed he was praising himself.

There is no offense in the following cases: if receiving or reciting the sūtras from another; if two people receive or recite them together; if asking questions or reciting along with someone; if speaking in jest; if speaking rapidly; if speaking in a dream; or if intending to speak of one thing but mistakenly speaking of another.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[Section Four ends. The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Kāla in the city of Rājagṛha who had formerly been a high minister to the king and was well-versed in worldly affairs.
He acted as a matchmaker in this manner, speaking of women to men and speaking of men to women.
At that time, whenever the laypeople in the city of Rājagṛha wished to arrange a marriage, they would all go to Kāla to consult him.
Kāla replied, "I must first go to that house and observe it. Having observed it,
he went to the houses of various lay devotees and said:
"If you wish to marry such-and-such a person, do as you please.
Then the householders acted according to their words and arranged the marriages.
At that time, those men and women who had found a suitable match through marriage were filled with joy; they made offerings and offered praise, saying:
“May Kāla always enjoy happiness just as I do today. Why is this?
It is because of Kāla that I have obtained such happiness; may Kāla and the other bhikṣus also receive offerings.”
If those men and women who have married are not satisfied with their spouses, they will say:
"May Kāla always suffer affliction just as we do today."

Why is this? It is because of Kāla that I have been forced into marriage and am undergoing such suffering; it is because of Kāla that the bhikṣus also experience distress and are unable to receive offerings.
At that time, the laypeople in the city of Rājagṛha who did not have faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha said to one another:

"If you wish to obtain a marriage with those of great wealth, abundant property, and many treasures, you should go among the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, and inquire; by providing them with offerings at the proper times and attending upon them with reverence, you may obtain your desires."
"Why is this? This śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is skilled at acting as a matchmaker, saying, 'This man may marry that woman; that woman may be given to this man.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the bhikṣu Kāla:
"What is meant by acting as a matchmaker for a man to give him to a woman, or acting as a matchmaker for a woman to give her to a man?
Having rebuked them, they went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Kāla:
"Is it true that you have acted as a matchmaker?
He replied: [Yes.]
"It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"I have used countless skillful means to teach the monks the matter of renouncing desire; why do you now engage in the act of sexual union?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the monks: "This foolish Kāla!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu acts as a go-between, traveling back and forth between two parties, conveying a man’s intent to a woman, or conveying a woman’s intent to a man—whether for the purpose of arranging a marriage or for illicit intercourse—even for a mere moment, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "those who come and go," these are those whom one should cause to be reconciled.
There are twenty kinds of women:

A slave protected by her mother; a slave protected by her father; a slave protected by both parents; a slave protected by her brother; a slave protected by her sister; a slave protected by both brother and sister; a slave protected by herself; a slave protected by the Dharma; a slave protected by her clan; a slave protected by her kinsmen; a slave who has become a servant of her own accord; a slave given as clothing; a slave given as wealth; a slave who works alongside [the master]; a slave rescued from being swept away by water; a slave exempt from paying taxes; a slave set free; a slave hired for labor; a slave protected by another; and a slave obtained from a border region.
"Protected by the mother" means protected by the mother's care.
"Protected by the father" means protected by the father's care.
The same applies to being protected by both parents, protected by an elder brother, protected by an elder sister, or protected by both an elder brother and an elder sister.
Self-protection means attaining mastery over the body.
Dharma-protection means practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Lineage-protection means not associating with those of low birth.
"Protected by kinsmen" means being safeguarded by one's relatives.
"One who delights in being a slave" means delighting in serving as a slave for others.
"One to whom clothing is given" means that clothing is provided as the price [for the transaction].
"One who gives wealth" refers to one who provides even a single coin as a price.
"A fellow laborer" refers to one who works together with another before the rites of marriage have been performed.
"One swept away by water" refers to one rescued from the water.
"Not paying taxes" means not taking the taxes that are due.
"Releasing a female slave" refers to one who was purchased or born in the household.
"A hired laborer" refers to one made to work for wages, such as a domestic servant.
"Obtained from another" means receiving a flower garland from another as a gift.
"Obtained from a border region" means obtained through plunder or robbery.
These are called the twenty kinds [of flowers].
There are likewise twenty kinds of men, as previously described.
Regarding a man protected by his mother—whether it be a man protected by his mother or a woman protected by her mother—if one sends a bhikṣu as a messenger to say to him:
"Become my wife" or "Have illicit relations with me."

If it is said that "in a moment," or "in the space of a single thought-instant," and a bhikṣu, having personally received a message from another, goes in person to speak to the other party and receives their reply to report back, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, goes in person to deliver it to the other party, and sends a messenger back with a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, sends a messenger to deliver it to the other party, and returns with a reply himself, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message in person, sends a messenger with a message to the other party, and has the messenger bring back a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message in person, writes a letter himself and takes it to the other party, and brings back a reply letter himself, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, writes a letter himself, takes it to the other person, and sends a messenger back with a reply letter, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, sends a messenger to take the letter to the other person, and returns with the reply letter himself, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, sends a messenger with a letter to the other party, and sends a messenger back with a reply, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The same applies to using a signet ring (*aṅgulipratyaya*) or making gestures (*nimitta*), each of which constitutes four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
If a bhikṣu personally receives a letter, carries it to the other person, and personally carries a reply back, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a letter, carries it to the other person, and dispatches a messenger to carry a reply back, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, sends a messenger to deliver it to the other party, and returns with a reply letter that he carries himself, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, sends a messenger to deliver it to the other party, and sends a messenger to return with a reply letter, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, goes to the other person with a signet-ring seal himself, and returns with a report using a signet-ring seal himself, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, goes to the other person with a signet-ring seal himself, and dispatches a messenger with a signet-ring seal to return with a report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, sends a messenger with a signet ring to the other party, and returns with a signet ring himself to report [the result], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a letter himself, sends a messenger with a signet ring to the other party, and sends another messenger with a signet ring to return the report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The fourfold set of manifested signs is also thus; the fourfold set of verbal expressions is also thus.
The sixteenfold set of finger-seals is also thus; the sixteenfold set of manifested signs is also thus.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a message, personally carries a letter to that person, and personally carries a signet-ring back as a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a message, personally carries a letter to that person, and dispatches a messenger with a signet-ring back as a reply, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message in person, sends a messenger with a letter to the other party, and returns with a report using a signet seal in person, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message in person, sends a messenger with a letter to the other party, and sends a messenger with a signet seal to return with a report, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, carries a letter himself to the other party, and returns with a report by means of a sign himself—there are four permutations, which are likewise as such.
If a bhikṣu receives a message himself, carries a finger-seal himself to the other party, and returns with a report by means of a sign himself—there are four permutations, which are likewise as such.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a letter, personally carries a signet seal to that person, and personally carries a signal back to report [the result], the four permutations are likewise.
If a bhikṣu personally receives a verbal message, goes to that person, and returns with a report, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if he personally receives a verbal message, goes to that person, and does not return with a report, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one hears the words, goes to that person to speak them, but does not return with a report, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one speaks to the person but they do not accept [the message], yet one nevertheless goes to that person to speak it and returns with a report, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one hears the words but does not go to the person to speak them, nor returns with a report, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one hears the words but does not go to the person to speak them, nor returns with a report, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not accept the message, goes to deliver it, but fails to return with a report, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one says she has already been married to another, or says she has gone elsewhere, or says she is dead, or says she has been carried off by bandits, or says she does not exist—at all these, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one reports back such words as: "I have leprosy," "an ulcer," "white leprosy," "consumption," "insanity," "hemorrhoids," "a sore in the [sexual] organ," or "pus that flows out incessantly," it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu acts as a matchmaker for a woman once, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
For every instance of matchmaking, according to how many times he speaks and whether his words are clearly understood, there is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense for each;
if he speaks but the words are not clearly understood, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one communicates by means of written signs, finger-seals, or gestures, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one uses gestures to make the other understand, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if the other does not understand, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the two [sexual] paths, if one acts as a matchmaker for the various parts of the body or limbs, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one acts as a matchmaker for celestial women, *asura* women, *nāga* women, *yakṣa* women, *preta* women, or female animals capable of transforming their shape; or for eunuchs, those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), or those who act as matchmakers—if the speech is clear and intelligible, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if it is not clear, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one writes a signet seal or manifests a physical gesture to make another understand [the intent], it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the other does not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts as a matchmaker for animals that cannot transform their shape, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To act as a matchmaker for men is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu engages in matchmaking and perceives it as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if he engages in matchmaking while harboring doubt about it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one acts as a matchmaker when not acting as a matchmaker, yet perceives it as such, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one acts as a matchmaker when not acting as a matchmaker, yet perceives it as such, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one acts as a matchmaker when not acting as a matchmaker, yet is uncertain of it, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one acts as a matchmaker for a human woman while perceiving her as a human woman, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if there is doubt regarding whether she is a human woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if one perceives a human woman as a non-human woman, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives a non-human female as a human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if there is doubt regarding a non-human female, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣu carries another's letter and does not look at it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one performs other services for a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

This constitutes an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if a man and woman have already had sexual relations and later separate only to reunite; if it is for the sake of one's parents who are ill; if one goes to see a prisoner and brings them a letter; if it is for the sake of a faithful and diligent upāsaka who is ill; if one goes to see a prisoner and brings them a letter; if it is for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, or a stūpa; or if one goes to see a sick bhikṣu and brings him a letter—in such cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu from the country of Āṭavī who heard that the World-Honored One had permitted the bhikṣus to build private dwellings. He immediately built a large private dwelling for himself.
Because the labor required to build the large dwelling was so great and arduous, he made it his constant business to go about begging, saying:
"Give me skilled craftsmen; provide me with vehicles and drivers; give me timber, bamboo, grass, and ropes."

Because the bhikṣus were so numerous in their begging, the laypeople, seeing them from afar, would turn their carriages to avoid them; some would enter the lanes and alleys, some the market stalls, some their own homes, or others would simply walk straight on with heads bowed, refusing to look at the bhikṣus.
Why was this? For fear that the bhikṣus might have some desire for gain.
At that time, there was another bhikṣu in the wilderness who wished to build a dwelling and began cutting down a tree himself.
At that time, the tree deity had many children and grandchildren, and he thought to himself:
"I now have many descendants; this tree is my refuge and provides me with protection."
"This bhikṣu has cut, severed, and destroyed [my body]; I should now surely strike this bhikṣu.
That ghost then thought again:

"If I strike him now without first investigating the matter, I fear it will violate the principles of propriety. I should instead go to the World-Honored One and report these circumstances in detail to him."
"If the Blessed One has any instruction or command, I shall carry it out.

Having thought this, he immediately went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and reported the aforementioned matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Excellent! You were indeed able not to strike a bhikṣu who upholds the precepts; had you struck him, you would have incurred immeasurable guilt."
"You should now go quickly to the banks of the Ganges River. There is a great tree there named Śāla, where a deity has just passed away.
You may take up residence there!
At that time, the deity prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times, and then vanished from sight.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus from the kingdom of Magadha, arrived at the city of Khaṇḍava and stayed there for the night.

When morning dawned, he put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; his gait was dignified and his gaze was not cast askance, and his movements—bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—were distinct from those of the multitude.

At that time, the laypeople within the city, seeing the bhikṣus from afar, would avoid them; they entered the lanes and alleys or went into the marketplaces, or else retreated into their own homes or walked straight on with heads bowed, so as not to encounter the bhikṣus.
Having witnessed this event, Kāśyapa asked one person, saying:
"For what reason do these lay devotees see the bhikṣus and each flee from them, rather than meeting with them?"
That person replied: "Kāśyapa!
The World-Honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to build private dwellings; because the begging for materials is so burdensome, people are therefore fleeing."
When Kāśyapa heard these words, he was despondent and unhappy.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from Rājagṛha with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and proceeded to the city of Khaṇḍava, where they each spread out their seats and sat down.

Then Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Just now, when I entered the city to beg for alms, I saw that whenever the laypeople saw the bhikṣus from afar, they each fled and avoided meeting them.”
Having spoken at length as above, he prostrated himself at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed from the city of Āṭavī. Why was this?
For fear that the bhikṣus of Āṭavī might give rise to a mind of malice.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"I recall that in the past, when I was staying here on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, a deity came to me, prostrated with his head at my feet, and stood to one side, saying to me:
'Blessed One, you have permitted the bhikṣu Āṭavika to build a private dwelling. [The deity] requested much more, as described above."
"I now ask you: is it true that you have privately constructed these dwellings and solicited many things?
They replied, "It is indeed so."
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣus:

"How is it that you, having been permitted by me to build private dwellings, have instead built large monasteries? You have made many requests and solicited in an unrighteous manner; such things are difficult to accept."
Having rebuked that bhikṣu, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, by the side of this Ganges River, there was a śramaṇa with a conch-shell topknot who constantly dwelt on this riverbank; his complexion was haggard and his body was emaciated."
At that time, I went to him and met with him, asking:
"Why is your body so emaciated and your countenance so haggard?
He then replied to me, saying:
"In the waters of this river there is a nāga king named Maṇibhadra; he has come forth from his palace to my presence and, coiling his body around my head, covers me from above."
At that time, I had this thought:
"The nature of nāgas is violent and impetuous; I fear they might take my life.
It was because of this anxiety and distress that my body became emaciated and my countenance grew haggard.
Then I said to that brahmin:
"Do you wish for this nāga to remain constantly within the water, never coming out to your place?"
The brahmin replied,
“I truly wish to prevent this nāga from coming to my place.
I then asked the brahmin:
"Does that dragon have any necklaces?
The brahmin replied,
"Beneath his throat, he wears a fine pearl necklace."
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"If this dragon emerges from the water and comes to where you are, you should rise to meet him and say:
'O Dragon King, please wait! "
"Take the pearl necklace from beneath your neck and give it to me.
And he spoke this verse for him:
"I now require such a thing: The pearl necklace from beneath your neck."
"With a heart of faith and joy, you have given me this exquisite, beautiful pearl.
At that time, having received my words, the brahmin later saw the dragon king emerge from the water and approach him. Seeing him from afar, he rose immediately to welcome him and said:
"Stop, stop! Dragon King!
I pray that you grant me the pearl necklace from beneath your neck."
And he spoke in verse:
"I now require such a pearl necklace for my neck;
with a heart of faith and joy, you should give me this exquisite jewel."
At that time, the Dragon King again replied to the Brahmin in verse:
"The wealth and treasures I possess Are all due to this jewel;
Since you are but a seeker, I shall not come to see you again."
"You were so upright and pure that you used a pearl to startle me;
since you no longer come to meet me, why should I give you the pearl?
Thereupon, the Dragon King immediately returned to his palace and ceased coming back.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Excessive seeking brings no love; Seeking too much invites resentment and hatred.
The brahmin sought the dragon's pearl, And so they were never seen again."

The World-Honored One again addressed the bhikṣus:

"In the past, at one time, while I was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, a certain bhikṣu came to where I was, prostrated with his head at my feet, and sat down to one side."
I comforted and inquired after them, saying:
"Are you all dwelling in peace and happiness?
Does the practice of begging for food not cause you hardship?"
He replied to me, saying:
"We dwell in peace and happiness, and we do not consider begging for food to be a hardship.
However, what we suffer from in this forest is the many birds; after midnight, they call out to one another with mournful cries, disturbing our meditative concentration, and this is our affliction."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying,
"Would you wish for these birds not to return to the forest to dwell and rest there?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
We truly do not wish for this bird to return to the forest to roost.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“When that bird returns to the forest to roost, you should say to it:
‘Give me both your wings; I have an urgent need for them now. The bhikṣu replied:
"Yes. Then, having received my instruction, that bhikṣu waited for the bird to return to its dwelling in the forest; when the night was nearly half over, he went to where the bird was and said:
"I now urgently require both your wings; give them to me."
At that time, the birds thought to themselves:
"This bhikṣu has begged such things from us.
They immediately departed from the forest and never returned again.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know that even birds and beasts do not delight in begging; how much less could one who seeks much from others not be loathed?"
“O foolish wilderness monk!
You have built a large dwelling for yourself and made many requests.
Having spoken at length as above, [he continued:]...
Again, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a son of noble family named Rāṣṭrapāla who left the household life to pursue the Way; even when returning to his parents' home, he never begged for anything."
Then the father said to Rataupala: "Do you know?
I have reflected within myself that there is rarely anyone who does not beg from me; you are my own son—why do you not beg from me?"
Then Ratakhara spoke these verses to his father:
"Many desires are not loved by people; If one does not obtain them, one should harbor no resentment.
Therefore, I do not beg, Fearing that it would give rise to increase or decrease."

“Bhikṣus, you should know that even at his own parents’ home, Rāṭṭhapāla did not beg for anything; how much less, O bhikṣus, should you seek many things from the houses of householders, causing them displeasure?”
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣus for begging at improper times, begging with lack of gentleness, and begging in an improper manner.
The Blessed One, having praised through countless skillful means seeking at the proper time, seeking with gentleness, and seeking rightly,
addressed the bhikṣus:
“This bhikṣu of the wilderness is a fool!
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu seeks to build a house for himself, where there is no patron and it is for his own use, he must build it according to the prescribed measurements."
Regarding the measurements therein: it shall be twelve spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and seven spans in internal width.
One should lead another monk to point out the site; that monk shall indicate a location that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.

If a bhikṣu, in a place that is dangerous or obstructed, seeks to build a house for himself, without an owner and for his own use, and does not have another bhikṣu point out the location, or if he builds it in excess of the prescribed measure, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"To beg for oneself" means to solicit from various places.
"House" refers to a dwelling.
"Without an owner" means that there is no person—whether one, two, or many—who possesses it.
"For oneself" means seeking it for oneself and making it for oneself.
"Of proper measure" means it is twelve spans long according to the Buddha's span and seven spans wide on the inside.
"A difficult location" refers to places where there are tigers, wolves, lions, and various other predatory beasts, down to even ants.
If a bhikṣu is not troubled by these insects and beasts, he should level the ground; if there are stones, tree stumps, or thorns, he should have them excavated by others.
If there are ditches, pits, ponds, or pools, one should have them filled.
If one fears they may be flooded by water, one should establish embankments in advance.
If the land is claimed by others, one should resolve the matter together so that no further disputes arise; these are called difficult locations.
A "place of obstruction" refers to a location where a grass-covered cart cannot pass, turn around, or travel back and forth; this is called a place of obstruction.

Having inspected that the site is free from difficulties and free from obstructions, the bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, remove his leather sandals, bare his right shoulder, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
I, the bhikṣu [Name], am personally begging for materials to build a dwelling, which is ownerless and intended for my own use.
I now request from the Saṃgha that they recognize a site that is free of difficulties and free of obstacles.
Thus he should speak a second and a third time.
At that time, the community of monks should examine whether this bhikṣu is trustworthy or not;
if he is trustworthy, they should immediately grant permission for him to act.
If it cannot be trusted, the entire Saṃgha should go to that place to investigate.
If the Saṃgha does not go, they should dispatch a trustworthy person from among the monks to go to that place and investigate.
If that place is subject to danger and involves an obstruction, one should not grant permission;
if it is free from danger but involves an obstruction, one should not grant permission;
if it involves danger but is free from obstruction, one should not grant permission.
If there is no obstacle and no impediment, one should grant the authorization; it should be granted in this manner.

Among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether an elder (*sthavira*), a junior monk, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not—should be appointed. He should then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

A certain bhikṣu is personally soliciting materials to build a dwelling for himself; as there is no patron, he is acting on his own behalf. He now requests the Saṃgha to designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent and bestow upon this bhikṣu a site that is free from obstructions and free from difficulties.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to build a dwelling for himself; it has no owner and is for his own use. He requests from the Saṃgha a site that is free of difficulties and free of obstructions."
The Saṃgha now grants a location free from difficulties and obstacles to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting a location free from difficulties and obstacles to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
“The Saṃgha has already consented to grant the bhikṣu so-and-so the assignment of a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”

Regarding the construction of a hut, it should be understood that the initial laying of the foundation—whether of stone, brick, or lumps of clay—and continuing until the final plastering is complete, constitutes the act.

If the site has not been formally assigned by the Saṃgha, or if it exceeds the prescribed dimensions, or if there are obstacles or obstructions, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, it exceeds the proper measure, there is an obstacle, and there is no space free from hindrance, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and one *dukkaṭa*.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, it exceeds the proper measure, there is no obstacle, but there is space with hindrances, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and one *dukkaṭa*.
If the Sangha has not authorized it, it is not of excessive size, there are difficulties, and there is an obstructive site, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Sangha has not authorized it, it is not of excessive size, there are difficulties, but there is no obstructive site, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Sangha has not authorized it, it is excessive in size, there are no difficulties, and there is an obstructive site, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the Sangha has authorized it, it is excessive in size, there are difficulties, and there is an obstructive site, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and two *dukkaṭa* offenses.

If the site has been formally assigned by the Saṃgha, exceeds the prescribed dimensions, presents difficulties, and yet lacks a space free from obstacles, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *dukkaṭa* offense.

If the site has been formally assigned by the Saṃgha, exceeds the prescribed dimensions, presents no difficulties, but lacks a space free from obstacles, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the Sangha has assigned the site, it is not excessive in size, there are obstacles, and there is interference, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Sangha has assigned the site, it is not excessive in size, there are obstacles, but there is no interference, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, it exceeds the proper measure, there is no danger, yet it is in a place that causes obstruction, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, it exceeds the proper measure, there is no danger, and it is in a place that does not cause obstruction, it is two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized it, if it is of excessive size, and if there is no difficulty or hindrance, it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the Saṃgha has authorized it, if it is of excessive size, and if there is no difficulty or hindrance, it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu builds a house for himself that has not been authorized by the Saṃgha, exceeds the prescribed dimensions, is situated in a dangerous location, or is in an obstructed place, and it is completed, he commits two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and two duṣkṛta offenses;
if it is commenced but not completed, he commits two sthūlātyaya offenses and two duṣkṛta offenses.
If he causes another to complete it, there are two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses;
if it is attempted but not completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one builds a house for another and it is completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and two *duṣkṛta* offenses;
if it is built but not completed, there are four *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one marks out the ground with a cord according to the prescribed measurement while building a house, and the builder exceeds that measurement, the builder commits an offense.

If a bhikṣu instructs another to build according to a measuring line, and the one who receives the instruction builds it according to the Dharma but exceeds the prescribed dimensions, that person who received the instruction commits an offense.

If the one who instructed the person to build according to the measuring line does so exactly as prescribed by the Dharma, yet fails to inform [the supervisor] of this, the builder commits an offense.
If one instructs another to work according to the marking line, and the worker acts accordingly, yet the instructor does not ask,
"Is it being done according to the Dharma?",
the instructor commits an offense.
If the Saṃgha has not made a formal decision, yet one perceives it as such, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if the Saṃgha has not made a formal decision, yet one suspects it, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the Saṃgha has not made a formal decision, yet one perceives it as having been so decided, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one perceives that the Saṃgha has made a formal decision when it has not, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if one has doubt regarding whether the Saṃgha has made a formal decision, it is a sthūlātyaya.
The same applies to exceeding the prescribed dimensions.
If there is a danger and one perceives it as such, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if there is a danger and one has doubt about it, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if there is a danger and one perceives no danger, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is no obstacle but one perceives it as such, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if there is no obstacle but one suspects it to be so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
The same applies to obstructed locations.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases:
making it according to the prescribed measurement; making it less than the prescribed measurement;
The Saṃgha shall authorize its construction;
it shall be built in a location free from difficulties and free from obstructions;
and it shall be constructed according to the Dharma.
Whether it be for the sake of the Sangha;
for a Buddhist temple, a lecture hall, a grass hut, or a leaf hut;
or if one builds a small shelter sufficient to house oneself;
If one builds a dwelling for many people to reside in, there is no offense in such a case.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

The sixth section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. King Udayana, who was a close friend and acquaintance of the Venerable Chanda, said to him:
"I wish to build a dwelling for you; let it be as you please. Wherever there is good land suitable for constructing a residence, you may build it as you see fit."
He replied, "Very well. At that time,
there was a nyagrodha spirit-tree near the city of Kauśāmbī, where many people came and went, and elephants, horses, and carriages would halt beneath it.
At that time, the Venerable Channa went to fell this tree to build a large house.
When the householders saw it, they all reviled him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they take the lives of living beings, yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma. How can there be such a True Dharma?
Here is a fine tree, under which many people come and go, and where elephants, horses, and carriages rest; yet it is cut down to build a great house.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Chanda, saying:
"There was such a fine tree, beneath which many people traveling back and forth on elephants, horses, and carriages used to rest; how could you cut it down to build a large house?"

At that time, after the bhikṣus had finished their reprimand, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Chanda:
"Is it true that you did so? He replied: [Yes].
"It is indeed so.
With countless skillful means, the World-Honored One rebuked him:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"There is such a fine tree, beneath which many people pass by and elephants, horses, and carriages rest. Why would you cut it down to make a large house?
You must not cut down a sacred tree; if you do so, you commit a *duṣkṛta* offense."
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"The foolish man Chanda has committed the first offense among the many bases for the outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu wishes to construct a large dwelling, and there is a patron who builds it for his own sake, he should take other bhikṣus to designate the site; those bhikṣus should designate a site that is free from difficulties and free from obstructions."

If a bhikṣu builds a large dwelling in a place that is difficult or obstructive, for himself, with a patron providing the materials, and does not take other bhikṣus along to inspect and designate the site, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Large" means using a great deal of wealth and materials.
"Room" (房) refers to a building.
"Having an owner" means there is one, two, or many people who own it.
"For oneself" means making it for one's own person.
"A dangerous place" refers to lions, tigers, wolves, bears, and brown bears, down to even ants.

If a bhikṣu is not disturbed by those [local inhabitants], he should level the ground; if there are tree stumps, stones, or thorny brambles, they should be removed; if there are pits, ditches, mud, or water, they should be filled and leveled; if there is fear of water, embankments should be constructed; and if anyone claims ownership of the site, it should first be settled. This is called a place free from difficulties.
A "place free from obstruction" is one where there is sufficient space for a grass cart to turn around; this is called a place free from obstruction.

Once that bhikṣu has completed the site preparation so that it is free from difficulties and obstructions, he should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the senior monks, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], wish to construct a large dwelling for myself with a patron; I now request from the Saṃgha that a location free from difficulties and obstructions be assigned.
Thus he speaks a second and a third time.
The assembly of monks should examine that person: is he trustworthy?
Does he possess wisdom?
If he possesses both faith and wisdom, they should trust him and grant him the *karmavācanā*.
If there is no one with faith or wisdom, the entire assembly should go together.
If one sends someone who possesses both faith and wisdom, they should be instructed to point out the location.
However, if that place is difficult to access or obstructed, one should not provide such instructions.
If there is danger or no space free from obstruction, one should not assign the location;
if there is no danger but there is a space with obstructions, one should also not assign it;
only if there is neither danger nor any obstructed space should one assign it.
One should perform the instruction in this manner.
From within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, wishes to construct a large dwelling for himself, with a patron providing the materials; he now requests from the Saṃgha that a site free from difficulties and obstructions be assigned to him.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant this bhikṣu, so-and-so, the assignment of a site free from difficulties and obstructions.
The motion is thus made: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is constructing a large dwelling for himself with a patron; he requests from the Sangha the assignment of a site that is free of difficulties and obstructions."
Now the Saṃgha grants a place free from difficulty and free from obstruction to the bhikṣu [Name].
Whichever Venerable Ones approve that the Saṃgha grant a place free from difficulty and free from obstruction to the bhikṣu [Name], let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.

“The Sangha has already granted its consent for the bhikṣu so-and-so to designate a site that is free from difficulties and obstructions; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”

The one who builds the hut should know that it begins with the laying of stones, the laying of earthen bricks, and the application of mud-clods; this constitutes the completion of the hut, up until the final smoothing of the mud.
If the Sangha has not appointed someone to direct the work, and there is a difficulty or an obstructed location, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the Sangha has not assigned the task, but there is no difficulty and the location is unobstructed, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized the site, there is no danger, but there is an obstruction: one saṃghāvaśeṣa and one duṣkṛta.
If the Saṃgha has authorized the site, but there is danger and an obstruction: two duṣkṛtas.
If the Saṃgha has made a formal decision, there is a difficulty, and there is no place free from obstruction, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If the Saṃgha has made a formal decision, there is no difficulty, but there is a place with obstruction, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If a monk builds a large dwelling where the Saṃgha has not authorized it, where there is no danger, and where there is no obstruction, it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a bhikṣu builds a large dwelling where the Saṃgha has not authorized it, where there is danger, and where there is obstruction, for himself and with a patron, and completes it, it is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and two *duṣkṛtas*.
If he builds it but it is not completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya* and two *duṣkṛtas*.
If one instructs another to construct it, there is one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense;
if it is constructed but not completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense and one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has completed building a room for another, there is one *sthūlātyaya* and one *duṣkṛta*;
if one has built it but not completed it, there are three *duṣkṛtas*.
If the Saṃgha has not authorized [the construction] and one perceives it as unauthorized, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If the Saṃgha has not made a formal disposition, yet one entertains doubt [regarding its validity], it is a sthūlātyaya;
if the Saṃgha has not made a formal disposition, yet one perceives it as having been formally disposed of, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if the Saṃgha has made a formal disposition, yet one perceives it as not having been formally disposed of, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a monk entertains doubt regarding a formal act of the Saṃgha, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If there is an obstacle and he perceives it as such, or if there is an impediment and he perceives it as such, each of these five cases is likewise treated.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a sthūlātyaya.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the Saṃgha has authorized it, or if it is made in a place free from danger and free from obstruction.
If one builds for the Sangha, for a Buddhist temple, a lecture hall, a grass hut, a leaf hut, or a small shelter for the body;
or if one builds a house for many people, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The seventh section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha. Then the Venerable Trapuṣa Malla, having attained arhatship, was reflecting in a quiet place and thought to himself:
"This body is not firm; by what skillful means should I now seek the Dharma of firmness?"
He further thought: "I should now provide offerings according to my ability; I shall distribute bedding and seating for the Saṃgha and assign the order of those who receive invitations to meals.

Then, at the time of the afternoon meal, Ṭhapassamāla rose from his place of seclusion, adjusted his robes, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"While staying in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind:
'This body is not firm; by what means may I seek that which is firm?
I should now perhaps offer service with my own strength, distribute bedding and seats for the Saṃgha, and take turns accepting invitations for meals!'"
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:

"Appoint Upāli to distribute the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha, and to assign the order for receiving invitations to meals. This was to be done by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the motion (*jñapti*) should be made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let it appoint Upatiṣya (Tapassu) to distribute the bedding and furniture of the monks, and to assign the order of receiving invitations for meals."
The motion is thus made. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now appoints Ṭhapamāra-putta to distribute the bedding and seating of the Saṃgha, and to assign the order for receiving invitations to meals."

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of Daṇḍapālamātāputra to distribute the bedding and seating of the Saṃgha and to assign the order for receiving invitations to meals, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to appoint Trapusa-māra-putra to distribute the bedding and seating of the Sangha and to assign the order for receiving invited meals; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Then the Venerable Trapusa immediately distributed the bedding for the Saṃgha:
those of like mind shared together;
those who were forest-dwellers (āraṇyaka) shared with other forest-dwellers.
They share in the practice of begging for alms;
they share in the practice of wearing robes made of discarded rags;
they share in the practice of not performing the ritual of leaving over food.
Eating in a single sitting is shared with those who eat in a single sitting; eating in a single mouthful is shared with those who eat in a single mouthful;
sitting at the base of a tree is shared with those who sit at the base of a tree.
Sitting in the open air together with those who sit in the open air;
sitting under a tree together with those who sit under a tree;
always sitting together with those who always sit.
They share sitting places;
they share the three robes;
they share the recitation of the *bhāṇaka* texts.
Those who are learned share with those who are learned;
Dharma-preachers share with Dharma-preachers;
those who uphold the Vinaya share with those who uphold the Vinaya.
While they were practicing meditation together, a visiting bhikṣu arrived in Rājagṛha; Upavāna Mālava then assigned him a portion of bedding according to the established order of seniority.
At that time, an elder bhikṣu ascended Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain toward evening. Then the Venerable Trapusa, emitting a flame from his hand, assigned him bedding and spoke to him, saying:

"This is the room; this is the corded bed, this is the wooden bed, these are the large and small mats, this is the pillow, this is the ground covering, this is the spittoon, this is the vessel for holding urine, this is the place for defecation, this is the pure area, and this is the impure area."
Then the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Among my disciples, Tapassu Bharadvaja is the foremost in distributing monastic bedding.

At that time, a bhikṣu named Maitrāyaṇīputra arrived in the city of Rājagṛha. Then Tapassu Bharadvāja distributed bedding for the visiting bhikṣu, giving him a place according to the seniority of the elders and as was appropriate for his station.
At that time, among the assembly of bhikṣus, the junior monk Maitrībala, having received a poor room and inferior bedding, became resentful and said:
"Dravyamāla has favoritism; he gives good rooms and fine bedding to those he likes, while he gives poor rooms and inferior bedding to those he does not like."
"Because they do not love us, they have given us a poor room and poor bedding.
How can the Sangha appoint such biased individuals to distribute the Sangha's bedding?"
When the night had passed and the following day arrived, the Venerable Trapusa was assigned by the Saṃgha to accept an invitation for a meal.
At that time, there was a donor in the city of Rājagṛha who regularly provided the Saṃgha twice a year with rich and delicious food.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrībala was assigned by rotation to visit that household.
When the donor heard that the bhikṣu Maitrībala was next in line to receive food, he spread out a worn-out sitting mat outside the gate and prepared coarse food.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrībala, having received this poor food, became even more resentful and said:
"Dravyamāla has favoritism; he gives fine rooms and bedding to those whom he likes."
Those whom we do not like are given inferior rooms and inferior bedding.
Because they do not love us, they are given inferior rooms and inferior bedding.
Today, because they do not love us, they have again been assigned to give us poor food.
"How is it that the Saṃgha has appointed such a bhikṣu, full of craving, to distribute bedding for the Saṃgha and to assign the order of invitations?
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī in the city of Rājagṛha named Maitrā, who was the sister of the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra.
Hearing that the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra had arrived in the city of Rājagṛha, he went immediately to where the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra was and stood before him, greeting him:
"Are you weary from your long journey?"
"Are you not exhausted?
Thus he inquired with these kind words.
At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrakanyaka remained silent and did not answer.
The bhikṣuṇī said: "Venerable sir!
What fault have I committed that you do not answer me?"
He replied, "Why should I speak with you?
You were harassed by Ṭhapassamāla, yet you did not assist me. The bhikṣuṇī said:
“What kind of expedient means do you wish me to employ so that Trapuṣa Māra will not harass the Venerable One?
The bhikṣu Maitrībala said:
“When you observe that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus are assembled, go into the midst of the assembly and speak these words:”
"Venerable Sir!
This is not good, not appropriate, not excellent, not in accordance with the Dharma, improper, and untimely.
Previously, that upon which I relied was free from fear and affliction; why then has fear and affliction arisen anew today?"
"How can fire arise from within water?
This Ta-pa-mo-lo-tzu (Dravyamāla) has come to offend me!
The community of monks should immediately assemble in harmony to carry out a formal act of expulsion against him; in this way, he will no longer come to harass us.
The bhikṣuṇī said: "What difficulty is there in this? You may do it."
Then the bhikṣuṇī Maitrā went before the Saṃgha and related what had been said above.
(The Fourth Part of the First Division of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Four).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Part Three of the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas. At that time, the Venerable Trapuṣabhadrika was not far from the Buddha; the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked him:
“Did you hear what this bhikṣuṇī said? He replied,
“I heard it.”
"Only the World-Honored One should know this.
The World-Honored One said:
"Now you should not report to me in such a manner; if it is true, you should say it is true, and if it is not true, you should say it is not true."

Then, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, Trapusa Māra-putra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Since my birth, I have never even dreamed of engaging in impurity, much less doing so while awake!”
The World-Honored One replied:
"Excellent, excellent, Ṭhapussa! Māluṅkyaputta!"
"You should speak thus.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"You should interrogate this bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra; do not slander him with groundless charges of unchaste conduct. This bhikṣu Dharmaruci is a pure person; if one slanders him with groundless charges of unchaste conduct, one incurs a grave and heavy offense."
The bhikṣus replied, “So be it,
World-Honored One! Having received the instruction from the Buddha,
the bhikṣus immediately went to the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra and interrogated him regarding the beginning and end of the matter.
"What is this matter? Is it truly so?

Do not slander him with groundless charges of unchaste conduct; this Dharmaruci is a pure practitioner of the holy life. To slander a pure practitioner of the holy life with groundless charges of unchaste conduct brings about a grave offense."
When the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra had been questioned by the bhikṣus, he replied:
"I know that Ṭaṃpāmaṭhīputra is a practitioner of pure brahmacarya; such a thing did not happen."
I arrived at the city of Rājagṛha, and there the Saṃgha was distributing rooms and bedding; they gave us inferior rooms and inferior bedding.
I immediately felt resentment and said:
"The Sthavira Upavāna has favoritism; he gives good rooms and good bedding to those he likes, while he gives inferior rooms and inferior bedding to those he does not like."
"Because he does not love me, he has given me a poor room and poor bedding.
He was assigned to places where he received poor food during invitations; because of this, his resentment increased manifold as he said:
"Why do the Saṃgha appoint such a person who has attachments to divide rooms and bedding for the Saṃgha, and to assign him to invitations for meals?"
"Yet this Ṭhapassī Māṇava is a practitioner of pure brahmacariya; such a thing does not exist for him.

When the bhikkhus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta-guṇas, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing.
They censured the bhikkhu Mettiya: "How can you, with groundless charges of non-brahmacariya, slander the practitioner of brahmacariya, Ṭhapassī Māṇava?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it that one slanders a pure practitioner of the holy life with groundless claims of non-celibacy?
The Blessed One told the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of persons who invariably enter hell."
What are the two?

If one who does not lead the holy life claims to lead the holy life, or if one who truly leads the holy life is slandered with groundless charges of not leading the holy life—these are the two who invariably enter hell.
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This bhikṣu Maitrībala is a foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, being overcome by anger, should defame a bhikṣu who is not guilty of a pārājika offense with groundless charges of a pārājika offense, desiring to destroy that person’s pure conduct."
If at another time, whether questioned or not questioned, he knows that this matter was spoken without foundation and says,
"I spoke those words out of anger," if a bhikṣu makes such a statement, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The meaning of “bhikṣu” is as explained above.
Regarding “resentment and anger”: one becomes resentful due to the ten unwholesome factors, and within those ten matters, resentment arises from each one individually.
As for the “roots,” there are three roots:
The root of seeing, the root of hearing, and the root of doubt.
Regarding the root of seeing: one actually sees the commission of a breach of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), sees the theft of five coins or more than five coins, or sees the taking of human life.
If one sees another person and hears from them [the report], this is called the root of seeing (*darśana-mūla*).

Regarding the root of hearing (*śravaṇa-mūla*): if one hears that [another] has violated the holy life (*brahmacarya*), heard that they have stolen five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five, heard that they have taken a human life, or heard that they have praised themselves for having attained the state of a superior person (*uttara-manuṣya-dharma*), and if one hears it from the person who spoke it, this is called the root of hearing.
Regarding the root of doubt, there are two ways in which doubt arises:
arising from what is seen and arising from what is heard.

That which arises from what is seen refers to seeing [the practitioner] entering a forest or leaving a forest with a woman, being naked and unclothed, or having the male organ impure and defiling his hands and body.
Holding a blood-stained blade and associating with evil companions—this is called doubt arising from what one has seen.

Doubt arising from what one has heard occurs when, whether in a dark place, or hearing the sound of a bed, or hearing the sound of turning over on a grass mat, or hearing the sound of bodily movement, or hearing the sound of conversation, or hearing the sound of sexual union, or hearing the claim "I have violated the holy life," or hearing the claim "I stole five coins or more than five coins," or hearing the claim "I killed a person," or hearing the claim "I have attained the state of a superior man"—this is called doubt arising from what one has heard.
Apart from these three grounds, to slander another by means of other matters is called groundless.
If that person is not pure, yet they have not seen, heard, or suspected that he has committed a *pārājika* offense, and they nevertheless say:
"I have seen, heard, or suspected that he has committed a *pārājika* offense."
If one slanders another with groundless charges, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*. This applies even if that person is not actually impure;

that is, if one has not seen him commit a *pārājika*, nor heard of him committing a *pārājika*, nor suspected him of committing a *pārājika*, yet one gives rise to the perception that he has seen, heard, or suspected such an offense.
Later, having forgotten this thought, one says:
"I have seen, heard, or suspected that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.
To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and he has neither seen, heard, nor suspected that the other committed a *pārājika* offense, yet after having had doubts, he then says:
"I have no doubt regarding this matter."
"I have seen, heard, or suspected [him].
To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If that person is not pure, and one has not actually seen, heard, or suspected him of committing a *pārājika* offense, yet after having entertained such doubt, he subsequently forgets that doubt and says:
"I have seen, heard, or suspected [the offense].
To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
