If that person is not pure, and one slanders them for a *pārājika* offense without having seen, heard, or suspected such a transgression—yet being certain within oneself that this is the case—one then says:
"I have doubt regarding the intermediate state; having seen, heard, or doubted [the offense], I have committed a *pārājika*.
To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and one has not seen, heard, or doubted their commission of a *pārājika*, yet later—having no such doubt and subsequently forgetting it—one says:
"I have seen, heard, or suspected that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.
To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not actually impure, and one has not seen him commit a *pārājika*, yet one nevertheless says:
"I have heard and suspect that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.
To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not actually impure, and one does not see him commit a *pārājika*, yet at that time possesses the perception that one sees it, but later forgets this perception and says:
"I have heard and suspect that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.
To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and one does not see him commit a *pārājika*, yet harbors doubt therein and says:
“There is no doubt in this matter;
I heard that he had committed a *pārājika* offense.
To slander another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and one does not see them committing a *pārājika* offense, but has a doubt regarding it, and later forgets that doubt, one then says:
"I heard that I suspected him of committing a *pārājika* offense."
To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and one has no doubt that they have not committed a *pārājika* offense, yet one says: "I have doubts."
"I have heard and suspect that he has committed a *pārājika* offense.
To defame another with groundless charges constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If that person is not pure, and one does not see him commit a *pārājika* offense, there is no doubt in this matter.
Later, having forgotten this and being without doubt, he said:
"I heard him suspected of committing a *pārājika* offense.
Because he slandered him with groundless charges, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The same applies to hearing what is doubtful. Furthermore, there are other clauses herein, which are not included due to the prolixity of the text.
If a bhikṣu slanders another bhikṣu with the four baseless matters, and his speech is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one sends a messenger with a finger-seal or a written message, or makes a sign that is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, if one further slanders another by means of other non-monastic practices, saying:

"You have committed a bordering offense; you have violated a bhikṣuṇī; you received the precepts with a thieving mind; you have broken [the community of] internal and external paths; you are a eunuch; you have killed your father, killed your mother, killed an arhat, or caused a schism in the Saṃgha; you have shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind; you are a non-human, an animal, or one with two sexual organs."
If one speaks and it is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a signet ring, a letter, or a messenger, or makes a gesture of understanding, and it is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Apart from these non-monk-like acts, if one further slanders a monk with other groundless charges, it constitutes the offense previously specified. If one slanders a nun with eight groundless *pārājika* offenses, if the speech is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a hand gesture, a written message, or makes a clear sign to communicate, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense if it is clearly understood;
it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense if it is not clearly understood.
Apart from these eight *pārājika* offenses, if one further slanders another with groundless charges of conduct unbecoming a *bhikṣuṇī*, and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if the meaning is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a finger-seal to write a letter or makes a sign that is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

This excludes the case of a nun; if one further slanders a nun with other groundless charges, it is according to the offense previously committed. Excluding monks and nuns, if one slanders others with groundless charges, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: speaking the truth based on what was seen, heard, or suspected; speaking in jest; speaking rapidly; speaking alone; speaking in a secluded place; speaking in a dream; or intending to speak of one thing but mistakenly speaking of another. There is no offense in these instances.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The eighth section concludes. While the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Mātṛceṭa descended from Vulture Peak. He saw a large ram engaging in sexual intercourse with a ewe. Having seen this, he said to himself:
"This ram is none other than Ṭhapassamāla-putta, and the ewe is the bhikṣuṇī Mātṛ."
"I shall now say to the bhikṣus:

'Previously, I slandered the Venerable Trapusa on the basis of groundless charges; we have now seen with our own eyes that the Venerable Trapusa has indeed engaged in unchaste conduct with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrā.'"
They immediately went to where the bhikṣus were and said:
"Previously we heard that you had groundlessly slandered Dharmaruci with a pārājika offense; now we have seen with our own eyes Dharmaruci engaging in sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrā."
The bhikṣus said: "What is this matter?
Do not slander the practitioner of the holy life, Dharmaruci, with groundless charges; to slander a practitioner of the holy life with groundless charges constitutes a grave offense."
At that time, having been interrogated by the bhikṣus, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra spoke thus:
"The Venerable Trapusa does not possess such things; he is a person of pure conduct."
"Previously, as we were descending from Vulture Peak, we saw several rams engaging in sexual intercourse with ewes.
We then said to one another: 'This ram is Ṭhapanaka, and the ewe is the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī.'"
"Today we have seen it with our own eyes.
We shall say to the bhikṣus:
'Previously, based on hearing groundless charges, I slandered Dharmaruci; now I have seen with my own eyes that he committed sexual misconduct with the bhikṣuṇī Maitrāyaṇī.'"
"However, this Dharmaruci is a person of purity; in truth, such a thing did not occur.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse.
They censured the bhikṣu Maitrībala, saying: "How can you falsely accuse the pure person Dharmaruci with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense involving a different matter?"
The bhikṣus immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Tapassī the son of Māra practices the holy life; how can you falsely accuse this pure person of an unfounded *pārājika* offense involving a different category?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra is a fool!
Among the many bases for outflows, this is his first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, out of anger, takes a fragment from a matter belonging to a different category and, though the bhikṣu is not guilty of a pārājika offense, slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge, desiring to destroy his pure conduct."
At another time, whether questioned or not, he knows that this is a partial extraction from a different matter;
that bhikṣu says of himself: "I spoke these words out of anger."
"One who speaks these words commits a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Malice and anger" are as described above.

Regarding "a different category": if a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense, yet claims to have seen him commit a pārājika offense, and thus slanders him with groundless charges of a different category, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
If a bhikṣu has not committed a pārājika offense, yet another claims he has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense,
and slanders him with a groundless pārājika charge based on a different category [of offense], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣu who has not committed a pārājika offense is seen by another to have committed a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, a sthūlātyaya, a duṣkṛta, or a wrong speech, and he slanders him with a groundless charge of a pārājika dharma based on a matter belonging to a different category, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If a bhikṣu has committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, and another says he has committed a pārājika, thereby slandering him with a groundless pārājika charge based on a different matter, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, and he claims it is a pāyattika, pratideśanīya, sthūlātyaya, duṣkṛta, or dubbhāsita; yet he slanders another with a groundless charge of a pārājika offense based on matters belonging to a different category, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If one who is impure, resembling an impure person—sharing the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance—slanders that person with a groundless *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a person who is not pure, being similar to one who is pure—sharing the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance—accuses that person with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense based on a different matter, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If a pure person is similar to an impure person—having the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance—and one slanders that person on account of another, using a groundless accusation of a pārājika offense belonging to a different category, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.

If a pure person, being similar to a pure person—sharing the same name, the same clan, and the same appearance—slanders that person by means of a groundless accusation involving a *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one sees that when he was formerly a householder, he committed sexual misconduct, stole five coins or more than five coins, or killed a human being, and then says to others:
"I saw a bhikṣu commit sexual misconduct, steal five coins or more than five coins, or kill a human being."
If one slanders another with a groundless *pārājika* offense that belongs to a different category, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

Suppose one hears that [the accused], while formerly living as a layperson, committed sexual misconduct; or hears that he stole five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five; or hears that he took human life; or hears that he claimed to have attained superhuman states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*). He then says: "I heard that he committed sexual misconduct;
I heard that he stole five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five; I heard that he took a human life; I heard that he claimed to have attained superhuman states."
If one slanders another with a groundless *pārājika* offense based on a different category, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu says of himself:

"I heard a rumor that I committed sexual misconduct; I heard that I stole five *kārsāpaṇas* or more than five; I heard that I took a human life; I heard that I claimed to have attained superhuman states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*)."
If one slanders [a bhikṣu] with a groundless *pārājika* offense belonging to a different category, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If a bhikṣu slanders another bhikṣu with a groundless charge of any of the four matters belonging to a different category, if the statement is clear and distinct, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if the statement is not clear and distinct, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a finger-seal, a written message, a messenger, or makes a sign of understanding, and it is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, one slanders another with other unfounded matters that do not constitute the status of a monk, saying:
"You have committed an offense bordering on defeat," and so forth, up to "you possess both sexual organs," as described above.
If she speaks and it is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If by means of a sign with the finger, or by writing, or by a messenger, or by making a gesture of understanding, and it is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Excluding the aforementioned cases, if one further slanders a bhikṣu with another groundless charge of a different category, it is according to the offense previously committed.
If a bhikṣu slanders a bhikṣuṇī with a groundless charge of one of the eight *pārājika* offenses belonging to a different category, and the speech is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If it is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Whether by sign, or by letter, or by messenger, or by making a sign of understanding—if it is clear, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

Excluding the eight *pārājika* offenses, if one slanders another by means of other unrelated matters that are not the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī, and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one uses a hand gesture, a written message, a messenger, or makes a sign that is clearly understood, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*;
if it is not clearly understood, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
Unless it concerns the *bhikṣuṇī*-dharma, if one further slanders a *bhikṣuṇī* with a groundless charge based on a different category of offense, the penalty is according to what was committed.
Except for the case of slandering a *bhikṣu* or a *bhikṣuṇī*, if one slanders another person with a groundless charge based on a different category of offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one speaks truthfully based on what was seen, heard, or suspected; if speaking in jest; if speaking rapidly; if speaking alone; if speaking in a dream; or if intending to speak of one thing but mistakenly speaking of another. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The ninth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Mithilā, within the territory of Ānupiya. At that time, many sons of the Śākya nobility, whose faith was firm and steadfast, sought ordination from the World-Honored One.
At that time, there were two brothers among the Śākya clan:
the first was named Aniruddha, and the second was named Mahānāman.

As for Aniruddha, his mother cherished him so deeply that she never let him out of her sight. She provided him with palaces for the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—and sent him with various court ladies to indulge freely in the five desires and enjoy themselves together.
Then Mahānāma, the son of the Śākya clan, said to Aniruddha:

"Now all the noble descendants of the Śākya clan have, with firm faith, sought to go forth from home under the World-Honored One; yet in my own family, there is not a single person who has gone forth."
"Brother, you know the family business; I entrust all matters, both public and private, to you. I wish to leave the household life.
If you cannot do so, I shall maintain the family business, and you may leave the household life."
Anuruddha said, "I cannot go forth into homelessness now; you may do so.
Mahānāma spoke thus a second and a third time, and Anuruddha likewise replied a second and a third time:
“I cannot go forth into homelessness,” Mahānāma said to Anuruddha.

“If you cannot go forth, I shall now inform my elder brother to take charge of the family estate; he should oversee the laborers and maintain the house, attend to our noble relatives and kinsmen, observe the proper decorum and etiquette when entering or leaving the royal presence, and attend to the work of plowing and sowing in accordance with the seasons.”
Aniruddha replied: "What you have said is far too prolix; it is more than I can bear!
Why do you not speak instead of how we may enjoy ourselves together amidst the five desires?"
"As for the affairs of our household and livelihood, you may attend to them yourself; I wish to follow the World-Honored One in faith and seek to leave the home life.
Mahānāman replied, "Brother, you should go and take leave of your mother."
Then Aniruddha went to his mother’s quarters and said to her:

“Listen to what your son has to say: you should know that all the Śākya clansmen have gone forth together as renunciants, yet in our family alone there is no one who has done so. I now wish to go to the World-Honored One and seek to go forth.”
"If my mother grants her permission, I shall immediately leave the household life to cultivate pure conduct.
His mother replied, "I have only you two children;
my affection for you is so deep that I do not wish to have you out of my sight for even a moment."
"Now, how can I allow you to leave the household life?
Even unto death I would not wish to be parted from you, much less at the time of birth.
At that time, Anuruddha addressed his mother thus a second and a third time, seeking permission to go forth.
His mother also replied twice and thrice:
"I will never let you go!
At that time, Anuruddha repeatedly requested his mother for permission to leave the household life, whereupon his mother thought to herself:
"What skillful means can I employ to prevent my son from leaving the household life?
He then reflected further:
"Bhadrika, the son of the Śākyas, is dearly beloved by his mother; she will certainly not permit him to leave the household life."
"You should say to Anuruddha:
'If the mother of Bhaddiya releases her son to leave the household life, I shall likewise release you to leave the household life.
Having thought this, he immediately spoke to Anuruddha.
When Aniruddha had heard these words from his mother, he went to where Bhadrika was and said to him:
"Do you know what has happened?
All the Śākyas have gone forth into homelessness, yet among us there is no one who has done so. The two of us should go forth together."
Bhadrika replied, "I am not fit for the homeless life; you may go forth as you please.
Although Anuruddha exhorted him thus two or three times, Bhadrika likewise replied two or three times:
"I shall not leave the household life," Anuruddha replied.
"The matter of my leaving the household life today depends entirely upon you."
He replied, "How is it that you have come to this state of renunciation? Anuruddha replied:
"When I took leave of my mother to go forth, she replied to me, saying:
'If you can cause Bāhīka to go forth as well, then I shall allow you to go forth.
It was for this reason that it came about through mutual dependence."
Bhadrika replied, "Wait a moment!
I must go inform my mother."
Then the Śākya son Bhadrika went to his mother’s place, knelt down, and said to her:

"Mother, do you know? All the sons of the Śākyas have gone forth [into homelessness], yet our family alone remains without one. I now have faith and joy, and wish to seek the going-forth from the World-Honored One; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
His mother replied,
“I will not permit you to go forth. Why is that?

I have only you, my one son; I cherish you with all my heart and do not wish to be separated from your presence for even a moment. Even unto death I would not wish to part from you, much less during life.
Bhadrika thus entreated his mother three times, seeking only her permission; his mother likewise replied to her son three times that she would not allow him to leave home.
Seeing her son’s resolve, the mother thought to herself:
"What skillful means might I employ to prevent my son from leaving home?"
At that time, his mother thought to herself:
"Anuruddha’s mother loves her son dearly; she will never permit him to go forth into homelessness.
However, if she were to grant permission for him to go forth, I too would let my son leave home."
Having thought this, he spoke to Bhadrika, saying:
"If Aniruddha’s mother permits her son to go forth, I shall release you.
Then the Śākya youth Bhadrika went to Aniruddha and said:

"Our mother has already granted us permission to leave the household life; therefore, let us first remain here for another seven years, enjoying ourselves to our heart's content with the five sensual pleasures, and only then go forth."
Anuruddha replied, "Seven years is an extremely long time; human life is impermanent.
Bhaddiya spoke again:
"If one cannot do so for seven years, would it not be better to spend six, or five, four, three, two, or even one year at home, amusing oneself with the five desires?
Anuruddha replied, "Even one year is far too long; I cannot endure it, for human life is impermanent."
Bhadrika said, "If you cannot endure it for one year, may you instead enjoy the five desires for seven months! Anuruddha replied:
"Seven months is an extremely long time; I cannot endure it, for human life is impermanent.
Vaddha said, "If you cannot endure seven months, could we enjoy each other's company for six, five, four, three, two, or even one month?"
Aniruddha said, "A month is an excessively long time; I cannot endure it, for human life is impermanent. Bhadrika said:
"If you cannot do so for one month, might we enjoy each other's company for seven days?
Anuruddha replied, "Seven days is not long;
it would be well if, at the end of those seven days, you were able to go forth."
"If we do not go forth [into homelessness], we shall all go forth together.
Then, during those seven days, the Śākya youths indulged themselves to their heart's content in the five objects of desire.

When the seven days had passed, the Śākya youth Aniruddha, the Śākya youth Bhadrika, the Śākya youth Nanda, the Śākya youth Kapphiṇa, the Śākya youth Ānanda, the Śākya youth Upananda, the Śākya youth Ānanda, the Śākya youth Devadatta, and the barber Upāli as the ninth—each having bathed thoroughly, anointed their bodies with perfumes, groomed their hair and beards, and put on pearl necklaces and ornaments—mounted great elephants and horses and departed from the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the people of the kingdom, seeing the Śākyas, said to one another:
"These Śākyas previously bathed their bodies, adorned themselves with necklaces and ornaments, and entered the park riding great elephants and horses for sightseeing, just as they do today."

Then the Śākya sons, riding upon great elephants and horses, dismounted from their mounts within the boundary and removed their garments, necklaces, and ornaments, as well as the elephants, saying to Upāli:
"You have always relied upon us for your livelihood; we are now going forth into homelessness, so we give these precious garments and the great elephants to you to provide for your own sustenance."
Then the Śākyas proceeded forward to the country of Āmrapālī.
Upāli remained behind, thinking to himself:

"It was by means of these Śākyas that I originally obtained my livelihood; today, out of faith and devotion, they have abandoned me to go forth under the World-Honored One. I would now rather follow them and go forth as well, so that whatever they attain, I too shall attain."
Then Upāli took the precious robes and necklaces he had obtained, wrapped them in white cotton cloth, and hung them on a tall tree, thinking:
"Whoever comes to take these, let them have them."
Thereupon, he went to where the Śākyas were and said to them:
"After you had departed, this thought immediately arose in me:

'I have always relied upon the Śākyas for my livelihood; today, since these Śākyas have with faith and joy sought to go forth from the world under the World-Honored One, how much more so should I not follow them and go forth! "
"Whatever the sons of the Śākyas have attained, I too shall attain.
Then the sons of the Śākyas and Upāli went together to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Our parents have already granted us permission to go forth; we pray that the Venerable One will allow us to go forth.
We only wish that the World-Honored One would ordain Upāli first. Why is this?"
"We have much pride; we wish to eliminate this pride.

At that time, the World-Honored One first ordained Upāli, followed by Aniruddha, then Bāḍhī the son of Śākya, then Nandika the son of Śākya, then Kapphiṇa the son of Śākya, and then Nanda the son of Śākya. Among them, Upāli, having received the full precepts, was the most senior elder (sthavira).
At that time, there was a great elder named Vīradatta who ordained the Śākya son Ānanda; the other senior elders ordained Upananda and Devadatta.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had ordained the Śākyan sons, he sent them to the kingdom of Campā.

Having received the instructions of the World-Honored One and the senior elders, the Śākyan sons departed for that country; each reflected upon and realized the higher stages (*abhibhvāyatana*), and Devadatta attained the realization of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
At that time, the Śākya son Bhadrika was alone in a forest hermitage, beneath a tree, among the graves, engaged in contemplation; when the night had passed, he cried out in a loud voice:
"How wonderful! How blissful!"
"How wonderful!
Hearing this, the monks nearby thought to themselves:

"When this monk Bhaddiya was formerly a layman, he constantly amused himself with the five desires. Having renounced that glory and pleasure to leave the household life for the sake of the Path, he now dwells alone in an araṇya, beneath trees, or among burial mounds; yet when the night has passed, he proclaims for himself:"
"Extremely joyful! Extremely joyful!
Does this son of the Śākya, Vādi, perhaps think of the five sensual pleasures with which he amused himself when he was formerly at home, and thus exclaim to himself, "It is extremely joyful"?
Then, at dawn, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One commanded a bhikṣu:
"You may quickly summon the bhikṣu Bhadrika.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣu immediately went to call the bhikṣu Bhadrika, saying:
“The World-Honored One summons you.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu Bhadrika went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side.
Knowing [the answer], the World-Honored One asked him nonetheless:
“Bhadrika, is it true that you, while staying alone in a forest hermitage, among the charnel grounds, or at the foot of a tree until midnight, have declared to yourself, ‘How joyful! How joyful!’?”
Bhadrika replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said,
“Bhadrika! Upon observing what meaning do you declare to yourself, ‘It is most pleasant, it is most pleasant’?”
Bhadrika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When I was formerly at home, I constantly protected myself both internally and externally with swords and staves.
Even with such protection, I still experienced fear, apprehending that external enemies or bandits might come to invade and take my life."
"Now, when I am alone in an araṇya, among burial mounds, or beneath trees, reaching the middle of the night, I have no fear and my body hairs do not stand on end,
O Venerable One!"
"I contemplate the bliss of renunciation; for this reason, I declare, 'How joyful! How joyful!
The World-Honored One said, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Noble son! This is what you ought to do: leave the household life out of faith and delight in pure conduct.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha. King Bimbisāra had no son; the king immediately assembled the Brahmins skilled in physiognomy and ordered them to examine the features of his various wives, saying to them:
“You must examine these ladies and determine which one shall give birth to a son.
The Brahmin, having performed the divination, said:
“This youthful lady shall bear a son, but he will be an enemy to the king.”
Having heard these words, the king united with his consort that very night, and she immediately became pregnant.
Later, a son was born, handsome and of perfect countenance. Before the child was born, a brahmin had prophesied, saying:
"He shall be the king's enemy."
For this reason, he was given the name Ajātaśatru.
As the prince gradually grew older, Devadatta used his supernormal powers to inspire faith and devotion in him.
Devadatta thought to himself, "I wish to maintain a following of disciples.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. There was a man in that country named Kāśyapa Kula-putra who, not long after his death, was reborn in the Heaven of Sovereign Transformation.

At that time, during the middle of the night, the devaputra Kakuda came to where Mahāmaudgalyāyana was, prostrated with his head at the elder’s feet, and stood to one side. He addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Devadatta intends to do evil; he has conceived the thought, 'I wish to maintain a following of disciples.'"
When the devaputra Kāśyapa had spoken these words, he prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, circumambulated him, and then vanished from sight.

When the night had passed, Maudgalyāyana went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported this entire matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked Maudgalyāyana: "What do you think?
Is it truly as the devaputra Kakuda has said, without any error?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One told Maudgalyāyana:

"Do not speak thus. Among all devas, worldlings, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, I see none whose speech is as true and without contradiction as that of the Tathāgata alone; his words are never false."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana: “In the world there are five things that are most venerable,” as will be explained below.

At that time, Devadatta went to the place where Prince Ajātaśatru was; by means of his supernormal powers, he flew through the air, sometimes manifesting his body to preach the Dharma, sometimes concealing his body to preach the Dharma, sometimes manifesting half his body to preach the Dharma, or not manifesting half his body to preach the Dharma. Sometimes smoke issued from his body, or fire issued from his body; sometimes he transformed his body into that of an infant, wearing jeweled necklaces as he rolled about in the Prince’s arms and sucked at the Prince’s finger. When Prince Ajātaśatru saw these transformations, he was struck with such terror that the hair on his body stood on end.
At that time, Devadatta, knowing that the prince was terrified, immediately said to him:
"Do not harbor fear! Do not harbor fear!"
The Prince asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am Devadatta. The Prince said, "If you are truly Devadatta, then restore yourself to your original body."
He immediately restored his body.
Having seen this, his faith and joy increased; once his faith and joy had increased, his offerings grew even greater.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru daily led five hundred chariots to pay his respects morning and evening, while also providing five hundred cauldrons of food and drink.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that King Ajātaśatru was visiting Devadatta morning and evening with five hundred chariots to pay his respects and providing him with offerings of food and drink from five hundred cauldrons, they immediately went to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you should restrain your own minds; do not give rise to greedy attachment toward Devadatta’s offerings. Why is this?"

Even if Ajātaśatru were to visit him every day with five hundred chariots, making inquiries morning and evening and providing five hundred cauldrons of food and drink, it would only serve to increase Devadatta’s evil intent.
For example, it is like a man striking a vicious dog on the nose, which only causes that dog to become even more ferocious.

Bhikṣus, you should know that this case is exactly the same: even if Ajātaśatru were to visit Devadatta every day with five hundred chariots morning and evening to pay his respects, and provide him with offerings of food and drink from five hundred cauldrons, it would only serve to increase Devadatta’s evil intent.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha heard that Ajātaśatru was daily sending five hundred chariots morning and evening to inquire after Devadatta’s health and provide him with food and drink from five hundred cauldrons.

At that time, King Bimbisāra was daily accompanied by seven hundred chariots as he went morning and evening to pay his respects to the World-Honored One and provide offerings of seven hundred cauldrons of food and drink.

When Devadatta heard that King Bimbisāra was accompanying seven hundred chariots morning and evening to pay his respects to the World-Honored One and provide seven hundred cauldrons of food and drink, he conceived a heart of jealousy for the sake of gain and honor, and immediately lost his supernormal powers. He then thought to himself:
"I shall now wait for the time when the Buddha and the great assembly have gathered, go to the Buddha's presence, and beg him with these words:"

“The World-Honored One is already advanced in years and his lifespan exceeds that of ordinary men; he has long practiced the Way and should now dwell in quiet seclusion, maintaining himself in silent composure.
The World-Honored One is the sovereign of all dharmas; it would be fitting to entrust the Saṃgha to me, for I shall protect and sustain it.”
At that time, Devadatta, waiting for the great assembly to gather, reported everything exactly as he had intended to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told him:
"I would not even entrust the Saṃgha to Śāriputra or Maudgalyāyana; how much less could I entrust it to you, a foolish man whose body is like spit and snot?"
At that time, Devadatta had this thought:
"Now, in the midst of the great assembly, the World-Honored One has called me a foolish body, like spit and snot.
Immediately, he gave rise to a mind of intolerance.
This was the first instance in this life that Devadatta gave rise to an attitude of intolerance toward the World-Honored One.
At that time, Devadatta went to Ajātaśatru and said:

"A king who rules by the True Dharma attains long life. You shall become king only after your father dies; he is already old and decrepit and will not be able to enjoy himself for long amidst the five desires."
"You may kill your father, and I shall kill the Buddha; with a new king and a new Buddha in the realm of Magadha, would it not be joyful to rule the kingdom and transform the people?"
The prince replied, "So be it," and immediately questioned Devadatta:
"What do you require? He replied,
"I require a multitude of people."
He then gave it to them. At that time, Devadatta immediately sent two men to kill the Buddha, instructing them:
"After you have killed the Buddha, return by a different path."
After sending those two away, he sent four more, saying: "Go and intercept those two;
if you catch them, kill them immediately, and then return by another route."
Later, he again dispatched eight men, saying to them:
"Go against those four men; if you encounter them on the road, kill them immediately and return by a different route."
In this manner, he successively sent out twice as many people until there were sixty-four.
Thus, the root was severed and destroyed; it could not be distinguished, and no one knew who had harmed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was sitting in the Sūkara-khanda cave; emerging from this cave, he walked up and down beneath a mountain crag.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"The karmic conditions I established in the past are destined to bear fruit this very day."
At that time, the two men, having received Devadatta’s instructions, donned armor and took up swords and staves, proceeding toward the World-Honored One with the thought in their hearts:
"We wish to kill the Buddha."
As soon as this thought arose, they were immediately unable to move forward and reflected:
"The World-Honored One possesses great spiritual merit and immeasurable power; even though his disciples likewise possess supernatural powers, how could we possibly harm the World-Honored One?"

As soon as this thought arose, he was able to go there. From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One, whose countenance was upright and handsome, whose faculties were tranquil and stilled, having attained supreme self-mastery and the highest quiescence; his faculties were as firm as a tamed dragon-elephant, his mind undisturbed, like water that is clear and transparent both within and without.

Having seen this, he gave rise to a heart of joy; he immediately cast away his sword and staff, set them aside in one place, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.

The World-Honored One gradually taught the subtle and wonderful Dharma to the two men, inspiring them with joy and exhorting them to cultivate goodness; he spoke of generosity, of ethical discipline, and of the merit of rebirth in heaven, censuring the impurity of sensual desire and praising renunciation.

At that very moment, while sitting upon their seats, all defilements were cleansed from them and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, we accept the three refuges—taking refuge in the Buddha, taking refuge in the Dharma, and taking refuge in the Sangha—and become lay followers (upāsakas)."
"From this day forward, for as long as life lasts, you shall not kill living beings, nor shall you drink intoxicants.
Then the World-Honored One said to the two men:
"If you wish to return, go by that path again; do not take this path."
He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Arriving at Devadatta’s location, he said to him:
“The World-Honored One possesses great spiritual power and majesty, and his immeasurable disciples likewise possess supernatural powers; how could we possibly harm the World-Honored One?”
Then Devadatta replied: "Get out! Be gone!"
"What use are you?
Why can these two men not kill one man?
Driven by this surge of malice, Devadatta went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa himself and, seizing a large rock with his own hands, hurled it from afar at the World-Honored One.

At that time, a deva immediately caught the stone and placed it atop the mountain; from the edge of that stone, a small fragment splintered off and came striking the Buddha’s toe, wounding the skin and drawing blood.
Then the World-Honored One turned his gaze to the right like a great dragon and spoke these words:
"It has never happened that Gautama would do such a thing.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered the cave once more; he folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers and lay on his right side like a lion, with one foot resting upon the other. Though suffering extreme pain, he endured it with single-minded concentration.
At that time, when the many bhikṣus heard that Devadatta had sent men to harm the Buddha, each of them took up sticks and stones and circumambulated the cave, shouting loudly.
The Buddha emerged from the cave and said to the bhikṣus,
"Why are you taking these sticks and stones to circumambulate the cave and shout so loudly?"
"It is like the cry of a fisherman who has caught a fish.

The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, "We heard earlier that Devadatta intended to come and harm the Buddha; therefore, we came to this cave carrying staves and stones in our hands, fearing that an enemy might come to harm the World-Honored One."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Each of you should return to your respective dwellings and cultivate the Path with single-minded devotion; it is the constant law of all Buddhas that there is nothing to conceal or protect. Why is this?"
Because he has already conquered all enemies, you bhikṣus should know that it is impossible for a wheel-turning sage king to be harmed by external foes.
The Tathāgata is likewise; it is impossible for any evils to come and harm him.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are five kinds of venerable persons in the world.
What are the five?
There may be a venerable one whose precepts are not pure, yet he claims for himself: "My precepts are pure.
His disciples, having approached him and knowing the truth of the matter, say:
"Now my teacher's precepts are not pure, yet he claims his own precepts are pure; if I were to speak of this to the laypeople, they would be displeased.
If they are displeased, I should not speak of it; let him remain receiving the offerings of others, for he shall know for himself in the end."

"In this way, O bhikṣus, regarding that Dharma honored by the world, the disciples provide protection through their observance of the precepts, and the teacher seeks the protection of the disciples. Second, O bhikṣus!"
There are some whose livelihood is impure, yet they claim for themselves:
"My livelihood is pure," as described above.
Third, monks, there may be one whose vision and wisdom are not pure, yet claims of himself:
"My vision and wisdom are pure."
As stated above.
Fourth, there may be one whose speech is not pure, yet who claims of themselves: "My speech is pure."
As stated above. Fifth, there may be those who stand outside the Dharma and Vinaya, yet claim for themselves:
"I am pure within the Dharma and Vinaya."
As stated above. Thus, O bhikṣus!
There are these five things in the world that constitute the honored dharmas.
"O bhikṣus! I now maintain the precepts with purity, and I also declare of myself:
'I maintain the precepts with purity.'"
"I do not require my disciples to protect me, nor do I seek protection from my disciples. Thus, O bhikṣus!
My life is pure; I declare of myself:"
"My life is pure," as was said above. Thus it is, O bhikṣus!
With the purification of his vision and wisdom, he declares of himself:
"My vision and wisdom are purified," as described above.
"O monks! My speech is pure; I declare of myself: 'My speech is pure.'"
As stated above: "O bhikṣus!
While within my Dharma and Vinaya, I declare of myself:"
"I am within the Dhamma," as has been said above.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
"You all should appoint Śāriputra as a messenger to inform the assembly of laypeople: 'Whatever is done by Devadatta is not a matter of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṅgha; it is the doing of Devadatta.'"
A formal motion with a second (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) should be made; one capable of performing the karman should be appointed as described above, and the following motion should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Bhikṣu Śāriputra now be appointed to speak before the assembly of laypeople regarding the deeds of Devadatta, declaring that they are not the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, but should be known as the actions of Devadatta."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu Śāriputra to go before the assembly of laypeople and declare that the deeds performed by Devadatta are not the affairs of the Buddha, Dharma, or Saṃgha, but are the deeds of Devadatta himself."

"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha appointing Śāriputra to explain before the assembly of laypeople that what Devadatta has done is not the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Sangha, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to appoint Śāriputra to relate before the assembly of laypeople the deeds committed by Devadatta, which are not the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Teaching of the Buddha.
Since the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held thus."

When Śāriputra heard these words, doubt arose in his mind. He immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
How could I possibly speak of his faults among the assembly of laypeople?
For what reason?

It was because I had previously praised his virtues to the laypeople, saying that he was one who has left the household life from a great clan, who is intelligent, possesses great supernormal powers, and is handsome in appearance.
The Buddha said to Śāriputra:
“Is it true, as you have previously praised, that Devadatta is clever, possesses great supernormal power, and has gone forth from a noble family?”
He replied, "Venerable sir,
it is indeed so."
"Therefore, Śāriputra! You should now go among the assembly of laypeople and say:
'Devadatta was such in the past, and he is such today.'"
"You should know that what Devadatta has done is not the work of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; it is the work of Devadatta.
At that time, having received the Buddha's instruction, Śāriputra went among the assembly of laypeople and said to them:
"Devadatta was such in the past, and he is such today."
"You should know that what Devadatta has done is not the work of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; it is the work of Devadatta.
At that time, those in the great assembly who approved of Devadatta immediately said:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have given rise to a mind of jealousy because of the offerings [received by Devadatta]. Because they do not rejoice in Devadatta receiving offerings, they have spoken these words in the midst of the great assembly:"
“Whatever Devadatta has done is not the work of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; it is merely the work of Devadatta.
Among them, those who had faith and devotion to the Buddha then said:
“Devadatta may have already done it, or he may yet do it.”
At that time, Ajātaśatru secretly wrapped a sword in his robes and entered the palace in haste, intending to harm his father.
Then, the gatekeepers detected him and searched his person, finding the sword;
they asked, "What do you intend to do with this sword?"
He replied, "I wish to enter the palace to harm the king.
The gatekeeper asked him:
"Who taught you to give rise to such a thought?
He replied, "Devadatta taught me."
Then the gatekeeper immediately led him to the place where the ministers were and said to them,
"Ajātaśatru wishes to harm the King.
At that time, the ministers asked:
"Who taught you? He replied, "Devadatta taught me."
Among the assembly, a minister said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, all do such things; they should all be killed.
Another minister said:
"Not all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are evil; they should not all be killed. It was only Prince Devadatta who did this; he alone shall now be put to death."
Some ministers said:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are not all evil-doers; however, although what Devadatta and Ajātaśatru have done deserves death, they should not be killed."
"Why is this? Your Majesty is a Dharma King; upon hearing this, he will surely not be pleased.
Thereupon, the commander of the guard went to King Bimbisāra and addressed the king, saying:
"This Ajātaśatru wishes to harm the King.
The King asked,
"Who has instructed you?"
He replied, "It was Devadatta. Among them, a minister said:
"All the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are utterly evil; they all ought to be killed.
When the king heard these words, his heart was deeply displeased.
Among them, a minister said:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are not all evil; they should not all be killed.
It was only Devadatta and Ajātaśatru who acted [wrongly], and it is you, O King, who should kill them."
Upon hearing these words, the king was also displeased.
Among them, a minister said:
"Not all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are evil; they should not all be killed."
"These were the deeds of Devadatta and Ajātaśatru; although they ought to die now, you must not kill them.
Why? Because you are a Dharma King, and I fear that upon hearing this, you would surely be displeased."
At that time, King Bimbisāra was pleased with these words and addressed his ministers, saying:
"Not all these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are necessarily evil; therefore, they should not all be killed."
These were the deeds of Devadatta and Ajātaśatru, and they too should not be killed.
Why is this? For the Buddha previously commanded Śāriputra to speak among the great assembly, saying:
"What Devadatta has done is not the work of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; it is merely the work of Devadatta. Thus, he should not be killed.
Having thus rebuked Prince Ajātaśatru, the father-king addressed the ministers:
"May Prince Ajātaśatru be forgiven.
He was immediately released.
At that time, all the ministers raised their voices together and said:
“King Ajātaśatru has committed a grave offense for which he ought to die; why then, after merely reprimanding him so lightly, have you released him?

At that time, Devadatta had already incited others to harm the Buddha and further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father; consequently, his ill repute spread far and wide, and his offerings and gains were cut off.
At that time, Devadatta, together with four others, went from house to house to beg for alms;
the first was named Śāṇakavāsin, the second Khaṇḍadravya, the third Koṭikarṇa, the fourth Kālodāyin, and his own self made five.

At that time, the bhikṣus heard that Devadatta had instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited Ajātaśatru to kill his father; consequently, his ill repute spread abroad and his offerings were cut off. He then went with his five followers from house to house to beg for food, and having approached the World-Honored One, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the great assembly and, knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, addressed Devadatta:
"Is it true that you went from house to house with four people to beg for alms? He replied:
"So it is, World-Honored One!
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked Devadatta with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you separately go to four households for alms?"
"I have taught through countless skillful means that one should show compassion toward the households of laypeople; why do you now go separately to four families to beg for alms?
Having thus rebuked Devadatta with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not eat apart from the community; it is permitted to eat in groups of up to three."
The reason for this is that there are two benefits:
it is for the sake of gathering those who are difficult to discipline, and it is out of compassion for the households of laypeople. Why is this so?
"Fearing that person who is difficult to subdue, he has formed a separate faction to trouble the Saṃgha.
Devadatta then had this thought: "How extraordinary!..."
"The śramaṇa Gautama has cut off the food from people's mouths.
I should rather break his monastic wheel; after my death, I shall be renowned by the name:
'The śramaṇa Gautama possessed great supernormal powers and unimpeded wisdom, yet Devadatta was able to break his monastic wheel.'"
Then Devadatta went to his fellow bhikṣus and said to them:
"We should now join together to break that Saṃgha-wheel. After we have died, our reputation will be such that people will say:
'The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal powers and unimpeded wisdom, yet Devadatta was able to break his Saṃgha-wheel.'"
At that time, Devadatta’s companion, named Śāṇakavāsin, who was of high intelligence and great talent, replied:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great supernormal power, and his disciples and followers are likewise so; how could we possibly break his monastic wheel?"

Devadatta said: “The Tathāgata has always praised the dhūta practices—those who have few desires, are content, and delight in renunciation. I now possess five dharmas that are likewise superior dhūta practices for those with few desires, contentment, and a delight in renunciation:

begging for food for as long as life lasts; wearing rag-robes for as long as life lasts; sitting in the open air for as long as life lasts; not eating ghee or salt for as long as life lasts; and not eating fish or meat for as long as life lasts.”
"Now that I uphold these five dharmas, I shall instruct the bhikṣus so as to inspire in them sufficient faith and joy. I shall say to the bhikṣus:
'The World-Honored One has, by means of countless skillful expedients, praised the dhūta practices for those who have few desires, are content, and delight in renunciation.'"
We now have five dharmas which are also the superior dharmas of dhūta practice:
begging for alms for as long as life lasts, and so forth, up to not eating fish or meat; these may be practiced together.

"Young bhikṣus will surely accept many instructions, whereas elder bhikṣus may fearfully refuse to believe and accept them; by this expedient means, you shall succeed in breaking their monastic wheel."
Then Svāgata said to Devadatta, "If you act in this way,
it will be sufficient to break that wheel of the Saṃgha.
Thereupon, Devadatta immediately taught the five points to the bhikṣus, saying:
“The World-Honored One has praised through countless skillful means the dhūta practices, those who have few desires and are content, and those who delight in renunciation.
We now possess five dharmas that are likewise dhūta, superior dharmas of having few desires, contentment, and delight in renunciation:

we shall beg for food for as long as we live; we shall wear rag-robes for as long as we live; we shall sit in the open air for as long as we live; and we shall abstain from consuming ghee, salt, fish, and meat for as long as we live.”
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus heard that Devadatta was thus teaching the bhikṣus with five points to lead them to faith and delight, as explained in detail above.
Having heard this, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"Devadatta today wishes to sever the four noble lineages. What are these four? [They are: being content with any kind of robe, being content with any kind of alms-food, being content with any kind of bedding, and delighting in seclusion and cultivation."

I have always, through countless skillful means, taught that one should find contentment with clothing; I have also praised and spoken of finding contentment with clothing. I have likewise, through countless skillful means, taught that one should find contentment with food, drink, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick; I have also praised and spoken of finding contentment with food, drink, bedding, seats, and medicine for the sick.
“Bhikṣus, you should know that today Devadatta intends to sever the four noble lineages.
Then the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he addressed Devadatta, saying:
“Is it true that you wish to instruct the bhikṣus with five rules?”
The detailed account is as above. He replied: "It is so."
“World-Honored One!

Section Four of the Thirteen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas: At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked them with countless skillful means:
“How is it that you teach the bhikṣus with five dharmas?
[The rest] is explained at length as above. “Devadatta!...”
Do not sever the four noble lineages.
What are the four?
They are as described above.

Devadatta! Do not now employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not persistently uphold and refuse to relinquish such means for causing a schism in the Saṃgha. You should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha, free from contention, and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma, like water and milk blended as one.
Therefore, Devadatta!

You should know that breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha is an extremely evil and difficult transgression that incurs a grave and heavy offense; one who breaks the harmony of the Saṃgha shall suffer punishment in the hells for one kalpa, from which there is no salvation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, caused Devadatta’s intention to split the Saṃgha to momentarily cease.
Having rebuked Devadatta with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“I authorize the Saṃgha to issue a formal admonition to Devadatta so that he may relinquish this matter; this shall be done by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).”
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Devadatta intends to use expedient means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha and stubbornly persists in not relinquishing his course."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this formal admonition so that he may relinquish this matter: "Devadatta!

Do not cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha by persistently refusing to abandon it. Devadatta, you should live in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without dispute, as one milk blends with water, dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma."
The motion is made thus: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This Devadatta wishes to adopt the practice of schisming the harmonious Saṃgha and persists in it without relinquishing it. Now the Saṃgha shall reprove and admonish him so that he may abandon this matter: [the formula of the admonition follows]."

"Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha by persistently refusing to relinquish it. Devadatta, you should instead be in harmony with the Saṃgha; rejoicing and without dispute, like water and milk mixed together, may you dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s granting of this formal admonition to Devadatta to relinquish this matter, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already granted its assent to the formal admonition of Devadatta to abandon this matter; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld."
"One should issue such a formal reprimand.

The Saṃgha performed this formal reprimand consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against Devadatta. On account of this matter, the bhikṣus informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If any other bhikṣu should attempt by means of various stratagems to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, he too shall be admonished with this *jñapti-caturtha-karman*."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu seeks to cause a schism in a harmonious Saṃgha, employs means to adopt the methods for causing a schism, and obstinately maintains his position without relinquishing it."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying: "Venerable sir! Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not employ means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; do not accept the principles that cause a schism and persist in holding to them without relinquishing them."
"Venerable One!

You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha; being in harmony with the Saṃgha, you should rejoice without dispute. Being of one teacher and one training, like water and milk mixed together, you will find increase in the Buddha’s Dharma and dwell in peace and happiness."
If that bhikṣu, when thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [his position], those bhikṣus should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"In harmony" means performing the same *karmavācanā* (formal act) and reciting the same *prātimokṣa* (code of discipline).
"Saṃgha" refers to four bhikṣus, or five, or ten, up to an indefinite number.

Regarding "refutation," there are eighteen matters by which one refutes: what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma; what is Vinaya and what is non-Vinaya; what is an offense and what is not an offense; whether it is light or heavy; whether it is with remainder or without remainder; whether it is grossly evil or not grossly evil; what is customary practice and what is not customary practice; what is prescribed and what is not prescribed; and what is spoken and what is not spoken—these constitute the eighteen.
Regarding those who abide in the practice of schism within the Saṃgha, it refers precisely to those who abide in these eighteen matters.

If a bhikṣu, through skillful means, desires to cause a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha and accepts the practice of schism, persisting in it without relinquishing it, other bhikṣus should admonish that bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
Do not employ means to break the harmony of the Saṃgha; do not accept the methods for breaking the Saṃgha and persistently hold to them without relinquishing them.
Venerable one!
You should be in harmony with the Saṃgha, rejoicing without dispute, as one with water and milk, so that there may be increase and peaceful dwelling within the Buddha-dharma.
"Venerable one!
You should abandon this matter; do not cause the Saṃgha to carry out a formal reprimand and thereby commit a grave offense.
If he follows these words, it is well.
If they do not employ words, one should further cause bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various heterodox śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to seek [the truth].
If monks from other regions hear that this person is one who trusts and acts upon their words, they should come.
If he acts upon their words, it is well; if he does not act upon their words, they should perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having performed the announcement, they should further request:
"Venerable sir!..."
I have finished the motion; the formal ritual (kamma) remains.
You should now relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform the ritual against you and you further commit a grave offense.
"If they accept the words, it is well; if they do not accept the words, one should perform the first *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"I have already announced the motion and completed the first *karmavācanā*; two *karmavācanās* remain.
You should abandon this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform further *karmas* against you and cause you to commit a grave offense."
"If they accept this proposal, it is well; if they do not accept it, one should perform the second *karmavācanā*.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should again request:
'Venerable Sir!'"
I have already completed the first of the two *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal procedures consisting of a motion and one proclamation); only one *karman* remains.
You should relinquish this matter, lest the Saṃgha perform another *karman* against you and cause you to incur a grave offense.
"If she is able to relinquish it, that is well; if she does not relinquish it, once the third *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If she relinquishes it after the second *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) has been completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s."
If one relinquishes [the object] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā* have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one relinquishes it after the formal motion has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one relinquishes it before the initial formal motion has been completed, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one has not yet made a formal announcement (*jñapti*), yet employs skillful means with the intent to split a harmonious Saṃgha, and accepts the method for splitting a harmonious Saṃgha, persisting in it without relinquishing it, it is entirely *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If, while the Saṃgha is performing the formal act of censure and admonition against a person who has caused a schism in the community, there is a bhikṣu who instructs him,
saying, "Do not relinquish [your position]," that bhikṣu commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one does not reprove or admonish them, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs [the other], saying:
"Do not abandon [it]."
For a nun, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If she has not yet been formally admonished and she instructs others not to relinquish [the offense], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Apart from monks and nuns, if there are other persons who instruct her not to relinquish it, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if, upon the first admonition, one abandons [the course]; or if the censure-admonition is performed by an illegal separate assembly; or if the censure-admonition is performed by an illegal united assembly; or if it is performed by a legal separate assembly, a legal-like separate assembly, or a legal-like united assembly; or if it is something that is neither Dharma, nor Vinaya, nor the teaching of the Buddha.

If one has not yet performed a formal reprimand; if one has estranged evil companions or evil associates; if one prevents those who employ expedient means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha from succeeding; if one uses the *karmavācanā* of two or three people to prevent those who employ expedient means to assist in causing a schism; if one intends to perform an illegal or non-Vinaya *karmavācanā*; or if one causes harm or creates a state of instability for the sake of the Saṃgha, a stūpa, one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*), a co-preceptor, one’s teacher (*ācārya*), a co-teacher, or a spiritual friend—these are called non-offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The first section ends. The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha. At that time, Devadatta persistently adhered to these five practices and went to teach the bhikṣus, saying:

"The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has always praised the dhūta ascetic practices—those who have few desires, know contentment, and delight in renunciation: namely, begging for food for as long as life lasts, wearing rag-robes, sitting in the open air, abstaining from butter and salt, and abstaining from fish and meat."
Then the bhikṣus said to Devadatta: "Do not cause a schism in the Saṃgha;
do not persist in the practices that cause a schism and refuse to relinquish them. Why is this?"
"When the Sangha is in harmony, joyful, and without dispute—like water and milk mixed together—they will find increase and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
At that time, Devadatta’s faction used skillful means to assist the bhikṣus who were breaking the harmony of the Sangha, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Do not criticize what Devadatta says; Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya. We accept and approve of what Devadatta says."

When the monks heard this, among them were those who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;

they censured the monks who were the companions of Devadatta, saying: "How can you say: 'Devadatta is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya; we approve of what Devadatta says'?"

After the bhikṣus had finished censuring him with resentment, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣus who were partisans of Devadatta:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
How could one say to the bhikṣus:
"Do not criticize what Devadatta says; Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya; we accept and approve what Devadatta says"?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the monks who were the companions and partisans of Devadatta through countless skillful means, addressed the monks:

"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal admonition against the monks who are the companions and partisans of Devadatta, so that they may abandon this practice; this shall be done by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations)."
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus who are the companions and partisans of Devadatta follow Devadatta and speak as follows:"
“O bhikṣus, do not revile Devadatta. Why is this?
Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya; what Devadatta has spoken, we accept and approve.”

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now carry out a formal admonition against the bhikṣus who are the companions and partisans of Devadatta, for the purpose of making them abandon this matter:
'You must not say: "Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya; we approve of what Devadatta says. "

"However, Devadatta is not a monk who speaks according to the Dharma, nor is he a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya. You must not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead support the harmony of the Saṃgha."
"Venerable Sir!
May there be harmony with the Saṃgha, joy, and no contention; may we be as one, like water and milk, so that within the Buddha-dharma there may be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness.
Thus he should speak.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus who are the companions and partisans of Devadatta follow Devadatta and speak thus:
'You bhikṣus, do not revile Devadatta; Devadatta is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma and a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Vinaya.'"
"We accept and approve what Devadatta has said.
The Saṃgha now issues a formal admonition to the monks who are Devadatta’s companions and partisans, in order that they may relinquish this matter:

Do not speak these words:
"Devadatta is a monk who speaks according to the Dharma, a monk who speaks according to the Vinaya; we approve of what Devadatta has said."

"Venerable sirs!
May there be harmony with the Saṃgha, joy, and freedom from dispute, like water and milk blended as one; thus may there be progress and a dwelling in peace within the Buddha’s Dharma.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s admonition of the bhikṣus who are partisans of Devadatta, urging them to abandon this matter, should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to the admonition of the bhikṣus who are companions of Devadatta, commanding them to abandon this matter. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"You should perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to rebuke and admonish the monks who are Devadatta’s faction in this manner.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha told the monks:

"From now on, if there are such factions that assist one another in destroying the harmony of the Saṃgha, they too shall be rebuked and admonished through a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* in this same way."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has a faction of companions—whether one, two, three, or even countless—and that bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!'"
"Do not admonish this bhikṣu; this bhikṣu is a speaker of Dharma and a speaker of Vinaya. We delight in what this bhikṣu says; we approve of what this bhikṣu says."
That bhikṣu said: "Venerable sir! Do not speak thus:..."
"This bhikkhu is one who speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and speaks in accordance with the Vinaya; what this bhikkhu says we delight in, and what this bhikkhu says we approve of."
"But these bhikṣus do not speak according to the Dharma, nor do they speak according to the Vinaya.
Venerable sirs!
Do not seek to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; you should instead desire harmony within the Saṃgha."
"Venerable Sir!

Be in harmony with the Saṃgha, joyful and without dispute; let us study under the same teacher like water and milk blending together, so that there may be increase and a dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma."
If that bhikṣu, when thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [the matter], those bhikṣus should admonish him up to three times so that he may relinquish it.
If he relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
There are two kinds of compliance:
compliance regarding the Dharma and compliance regarding robes and food.
Regarding compliance with the Dharma: one instructs through the Dharma, increasing virtue, concentration, and wisdom, so that they may recite, receive, and uphold it.
Regarding compliance with material needs: one provides clothing, bedding, food, seats and mats, and medicines for the sick and infirm.
The faction consists of four or more than four persons.
Those who assist the faction with their speech consist of one, two, three, or many persons.
If a monk forms an illegal faction and says to the other monks,
"Venerable sirs,
do not admonish this monk; this monk is one who speaks according to the Dharma and speaks according to the Vinaya."

If one abandons it after the motion has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya*.

With the exception of monks and nuns, if one instructs any other person [to do so], [it is likewise an offense]."

He performed such unrighteous acts as these: he planted flowering trees himself and taught others to plant them; he irrigated them himself and taught others to irrigate them; he plucked flowers himself and taught others to pluck them; he made flower garlands himself and taught others to make them; he strung them with thread himself or taught others to string them; he carried flowers himself or taught others to carry them; and he gave flower garlands to others himself or taught others to give them to others.

If there are women or young girls in that village who sit and rise upon the same bed, eat and drink from the same vessel, converse and laugh together; or who sing, dance, or perform as entertainers themselves, or join in singing when others perform; or who engage in comic recitations, play drums and reed organs, blow conch shells, or imitate the calls of peacocks or various birds; or who run about, or pretend to limp, or whistle, or perform contortions of the body, or perform for hire in jesting and laughter.

At that time, that bhikṣu went begging in Vairaṇyā and obtained food only with great difficulty. He thought to himself:

Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having dressed and taken up their bowls, set out from the kingdom of Kāśi with a community of five hundred great bhikṣus and traveled to Veṇugrāmaka.

'If a bhikṣu, residing in a village or a town, defiles families and engages in evil conduct—such that his defiling of families is both seen and heard of, and his engagement in evil conduct is both seen and heard of.'"
The monks should say to that monk: "Venerable sir!
You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to have defiled families, and you have been seen and heard to have committed evil deeds."
"Venerable one!

When that bhikṣu spoke these words to the other bhikṣu:

The bhikṣus replied: "Venerable sir,

Venerable Sir!

If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well;
