The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
As for "village," there are four kinds, as described above.
"Settlements, towns, and cities" belong to the king.
A "family" consists of both men and women.
There are four ways of defiling a family:

defiling a family by relying on the household itself, defiling a family by relying on material gain, defiling a family by relying on relatives and friends, and defiling a family by relying on the monastery.
What is meant by "defiling a family" based on a household?
It is when one receives goods from one family and gives them to another.
Those from whom the goods were received are displeased upon hearing of it, while those to whom they were given think they should be repaid for the favor, and thus say: [as follows].
"If someone gives to me, I shall repay them; if they do not give to me, why should I give?
This is defiling a family by relying on the household.
What is defiling a family by relying on gain?

If a bhikṣu receives gains in accordance with the Dharma—even down to the remnants in his alms bowl—and gives them to one layperson while not giving them to another, the one who receives them will immediately form this thought:
"I shall repay his kindness; to those who give to me, I shall repay them, but as for those who do not give to me, why should I give?"
This refers to defiling families for the sake of gain.
What is defiling families for the sake of kinsmen and friends?
If a bhikṣu relies upon a king or a high minister, or on one lay devotee or several lay devotees, he thinks that whatever they do for him must be repaid.
"To those who act for my benefit, I shall offer support; to those who do not act for my benefit, I shall not offer support.
This is defiling a household by relying on friends and associates.
What is defiling a household by relying on a monastery?
If a bhikṣu takes flowers or fruits belonging to the Saṃgha and gives them to one layperson while not giving them to another, he then forms this thought:
"I shall provide offerings for those who give to me, but I shall not provide offerings for those who do not give to me."
This refers to defiling families by relying on monasteries.
It is for these four reasons that one defiles families; therefore, it is called "defiling the families of others.

Regarding those who practice evil conduct: they personally plant flowering trees or instruct others to plant flowering trees, even going so far as to accept employment for entertainment and jesting, as described above.

If a bhikṣu dwells in dependence upon a village and defiles the families there, engaging in evil conduct; and if his defiling of the families is both seen and heard of, and his engagement in evil conduct is also both seen and heard of.

we have both seen and heard that you defile families, and we have both seen and heard that you engage in evil conduct."
"Venerable one!

"Venerable one!
You should abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after being rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he complies with these words, it is well; if he does not comply, a second *karmavācanā* (formal act) should be performed.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
"Venerable Sir!
The second *karmavācanā* has been performed; only one *karmavācanā* remains."
"Venerable one!
You should abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after being rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he complies with these words, it is well; if he does not comply, the third *karmavācanā* is performed.
Once the third *karmavācanā* has been performed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one relinquishes it after the second *karmavācanā*, there are three *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one relinquishes it after the first *karmavācanā*, there are two *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one relinquishes it after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya*.
If one relinquishes it before the initial announcement is completed, there is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, prior to the announcement, one says:
"If the Saṃgha has attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion," all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta*.
If, while the Saṃgha is performing a formal admonition (*prativādana*), another bhikṣu instructs [the monk] not to relinquish [his position], this bhikṣu commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one has not yet issued a formal reprimand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, while the Saṃgha is issuing a formal reprimand, there is a bhikṣuṇī who instructs [the offender], saying:
"Do not relinquish [your position]."
If [she says this], it is a *sthūlātyaya* for a nun.
If she instructs [others] before the formal admonition has been carried out, it is a *duṣkṛta* for the nun.
With the exception of monks and nuns, if she instructs others not to relinquish [the matter], whether they are formally admonished or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
If one takes it away without having read the book, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts as a messenger for a layperson, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense. There is no offense for one who desists at the first utterance;

If one plants flowering trees and further teaches others to plant them as an offering to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; teaches others to gather flowers to offer to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; personally fashions flower garlands and teaches others to fashion them as offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; personally strings flowers with thread and teaches others to string them as offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; personally holds flowers and teaches others to hold flowers as offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; or personally strings flower garlands with thread and teaches others to string and hold them as offerings to the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—in all these cases, there is no offense.

If a person raises their hand intending to strike, or if one encounters thieves, elephants, bears, brown bears, lions, tigers, or wolves in a place of perilous difficulty, or if one carries thorns and brambles while running to take refuge among them, there is no offense.
If one leaps over a river, ditch, canal, or pit while crossing, there is no offense.
If a companion is walking behind and one calls out with a whistle because they cannot be seen upon looking back, there is no offense.

If one carries letters back and forth for the sake of a parent’s illness, or for one imprisoned in jail, or for the sake of a devout upāsaka who is ill or imprisoned, or for the sake of a stūpa, the Saṃgha, or a sick bhikṣu, there is no offense in any such case.

At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Gośīrṣa Garden in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Chanda was of a wicked nature and would not accept the words of others.
He spoke to the bhikṣus, saying: "Do not speak to me of what is good or bad; nor shall I speak to the venerable ones of what is good or bad."

Do not say anything further.
What is the use of instructing me?"
I should instruct the venerable ones! Why is this? Because my noble Lord has attained perfect enlightenment.

It is just as when a great flood first comes and sweeps away various grasses and trees, piling them together in one place; so too it is with the venerable ones, who have gone forth from various clans, various names, and various families, and have gathered together in one place.

the Saṃgha should appoint a competent person to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) as described above, making the following motion:

Venerable sirs, please desist; there is no need for you to instruct me."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now carry out a formal admonition against the bhikṣu Chanda for the purpose of making him abandon this matter:
'You, Chanda, must not act as one who is uncommunicative; you must act as one who is communicative.'"

Cunda, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus should likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma. In this way, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples will flourish, as they instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent before one another.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Chanda is of an evil nature and will not accept the words of others. Although the bhikṣus have instructed him according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, he has made himself unapproachable for conversation, saying to the bhikṣus:"
"Venerable sirs!
Do not speak to me of what is good or bad, nor shall I speak to you venerable sirs of what is good or bad.
Venerable sirs, please desist; there is no need for you to instruct me."
Now the Saṃgha, for the purpose of making the bhikṣu Channa abandon this matter, issues this formal admonition:
"You, Channa, must not act as one who is uncommunicative; you must act as one who is communicative."
"You should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus should also admonish you in accordance with the Dharma.
In this way, the Saṃgha of the Buddha’s disciples will flourish, instructing one another, admonishing one another, and confessing to one another."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu Chanda to relinquish this matter, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:

"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal admonition against the bhikṣu Chanda to make him abandon this matter; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld."
"One should reprove and admonish him in this manner.

After the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprove the bhikṣu Chanda, commanding him to relinquish this matter, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there be another bhikṣu who is of evil character and refuses to accept the words of others, the Saṃgha shall likewise perform for him this formal act of censure (*tajjanīya-karman*) consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

From this day forward, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

'If a bhikṣu is of evil character and refuses to accept the words of others, and after the bhikṣus have admonished him according to the Dharma regarding the rules of training, he himself does not accept the admonition and says:'"
"Venerable sirs! Do not speak to me of what is good or what is evil, nor shall I speak to you venerable sirs of what is good or what is evil.
Venerable sirs, please desist; do not admonish me."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Do not yourself refuse to accept admonition. Venerable sir!"
One should personally accept words of admonition.
"Venerable sir, you should admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, and the bhikṣus shall likewise admonish you in accordance with the Dharma!
In this way, the Saṅgha of the Buddha’s disciples will attain increase, admonishing one another, instructing one another, and confessing to one another."
If this bhikṣu, when thus admonished, persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu should admonish him three times to relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it by the third admonition, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
One of "evil character who does not accept instruction" is one who is intolerant and does not receive the teachings and admonitions of others.
Regarding those who instruct according to the Dharma through the Vinaya, there are seven groups of offenses:
Pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, sthūlātyaya, duṣkṛta, and dubbhāsita.
"In accordance with the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.

If a bhikṣu is of evil character and does not accept the words of others, and the bhikṣus attempt to instruct him in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, he himself makes himself unapproachable for conversation, saying:
"Venerable sirs, do not speak to me whether it be good or bad; I likewise shall not speak to you venerable sirs whether it be good or bad."
"Venerable sir!
Stop; there is no need to admonish me.
That bhikṣu then spoke to this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, do not make yourself one who is not to be spoken with; rather, be one who is to be spoken with.
Venerable sir, as you admonish the bhikṣus in accordance with the Dharma, so too should the bhikṣus admonish you in accordance with the Dharma!"
In this way, the community of the Buddha’s disciples attains increase; they instruct one another, admonish one another, and repent before one another.
"Venerable sir, you should abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after having been censured by the Saṃgha."
"If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, one should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having performed the announcement, one should further request:
'Venerable One!'"
I have already completed the formal announcement (*jñapti*); three further *karmas* remain.
Venerable sir, you should desist from this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a grave offense once again.
"If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) shall be performed.
Once the first *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should further request:
'Venerable Sir!'"
The first *karmavācanā* has been completed; two *karmavācanās* remain.
Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and commit a grave offense once again.
"If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, the second *karmavācanā* (formal proclamation) shall be recited.
Having recited the second *karmavācanā*, one should further request:
'Venerable sir!'"
I have completed the first proclamation and the second *karmavācanā*; only one *karmavācanā* remains.
Venerable sir, you should relinquish this matter; do not be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a grave offense once again.
"If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, the third *karmavācanā* is to be recited.
When the third *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense."
If one relinquishes through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, there are three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one relinquishes through a *jñapti-prathama-karman*, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one relinquishes after the *jñapti* has been made, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one abandons the proposal before it has been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, prior to the formal announcement, one of a wicked nature refuses to accept the words of others, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
If, while a formal reprimand is being made for such a wicked person, another bhikṣu should instruct him, saying:
"Do not abandon [this course].
This bhikṣu commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If he speaks thus before the formal admonition has been carried out, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs her, saying,
"Do not abandon it," this bhikṣuṇī commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one has not yet rebuked or admonished [the offender], it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
With the exception of monks and nuns, if others instruct [the offender] not to relinquish [the offense], whether they are rebuked or not rebuked, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one desists at the first utterance; or if [the assembly] is an illegal separate assembly, an illegal united assembly, a legal separate assembly, a legal-like separate assembly, or a legal-like united assembly; or if it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and not taught by the Buddha; or if nothing has been done prior to the formal admonition of censure. There is no offense in these cases.
If one is rebuked and admonished by an ignorant person, one should say to them:
"The conduct of your own preceptor and ācārya is also like this; you should further study and recite the sūtras."
"If the matter is such that one speaks while joking, speaks rapidly, speaks to oneself, speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that, this is called non-offense."

There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain. The Thirteenth [Section] concludes. The Two Indeterminate Rules (Aniyata-dharma).

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. During his lay life, Kālodāyin had a close female friend, a laywoman named Ciñcā Māṇavikā, who was beautiful in appearance; Kālodāyin was also handsome in appearance.
Kāḷudāyin fixed his mind upon her, and that female lay follower likewise fixed her mind upon Kāḷudāyin.

Then, when it was time, Kāḷudāyin dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the house of that female lay follower who was observing the fast; there he sat with her alone in a secluded and concealed place.
At that time, Kālodāyin was conversing with a female lay follower (upāsikā).
There was then a mother of the Vaiśyāyana clan who, having some minor business, went to a neighboring house and heard from afar the voice of Kālodāyin speaking.
This upāsikā possessed a heart of faith and devotion; hearing the voice of an inner bhikṣu, she thought to herself, "He might be preaching the Dharma.
She immediately leaned against the wall to listen, but heard only the sound of speech that was not the Dharma.
He further thought to himself:
"I heard the voice of a bhikṣu speaking words that are not in accordance with the Dharma; a bhikṣu should not speak such words.
He then peered inside and saw Kālodāyin sitting on the same bed with the laywoman Ciñcā, speaking improper words.
Having seen this, she thought to herself:
"This bhikṣu sits in an improper place and speaks improper words.
If her husband sees him, he will surely scold and revile his wife, and she will lose his trust."

Then the upāsikā immediately left her house and went quickly to where the World-Honored One was. She prostrated herself at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Having addressed the Blessed One in this way, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the answer, asked Kālodāyin intentionally:
"Did you indeed sit alone with the upāsikā Cailā in a secluded and concealed place?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One rebuked him with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why are you now sitting alone in a secluded, private place with the laywoman Ciñcā?
Having thus rebuked Kālodayin through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The foolish Kālodayin has committed the first transgression of the precepts among many such bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed place, a screened place, or a place suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words."
There is a female lay follower established in faith who, regarding each of the three categories of offenses, speaks of them as either a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *pāyattika*.
The bhikṣu seated there says of himself:
"I have committed this offense.
Among the three categories of dharma, he should be dealt with according to each one: whether it be a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika.
As stated by the female lay follower who abides in faith, this bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the Dharma; this is called an undetermined rule (aniyata-dharma).
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"A woman" refers to a human female who possesses intelligence and has not yet died.
"Alone" means one bhikṣu and one woman.
"A secluded place" is of two kinds:
The first is concealment by sight; the second is concealment by hearing.
Regarding concealment by sight: it refers to cases where one does not see another due to dust, mist, or darkness.
"Sound is heard when screened" refers to places where one does not hear the sound of ordinary speech.
"Obstructed by a covering" refers to being blocked by trees, walls, fences, clothing, or other such objects.
"A place suitable for sexual intercourse" refers to a space capable of accommodating sexual acts.
"Speaking unrighteous words" refers to speaking of the dharma of lustful desire.

"A laywoman who has faith and delight" is one who believes in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; who takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; and who abstains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants—one who skillfully maintains these matters, does not err in what she says, and is truthful rather than deceptive.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place toward which he is heading, declares the place where he has arrived, declares that he is sitting, declares that he is lying down, or declares that he is performing an action, he should be disciplined exactly according to what the bhikṣu has said.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place toward which he was heading, declares the place he reached, declares that he sat, or declares that he lay down, but does not declare that he committed the act, he should be dealt with according to the rule prescribed for an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place he was heading toward, himself declares the place he reached, and himself declares that he sat, but does not himself declare that he lay down or that he acted, he should be dealt with according to what was stated regarding an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place he was heading toward, himself declares the place he reached, but does not himself declare that he sat, did not himself declare that he lay down, and does not himself declare that he acted, he should be dealt with according to what was prescribed for an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the destination toward which he is heading, but does not declare where he has arrived, nor that he is sitting, nor that he is lying down, nor that he is performing an action, he should be dealt with according to the rule prescribed for an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu does not himself declare where he is going, does not himself declare where he has arrived, does not himself declare that he is sitting, does not himself declare that he is lying down, and does not himself declare what he is doing, he should be dealt with according to the rule prescribed for an upāsikā.
In this matter, there is no fixed rule; therefore, it is called "indeterminate.
[End of Chapter One. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Kālodāyin had a female friend from his days as a layman, a laywoman named Ciñcā Māṇavikā, who was of beautiful appearance; Kālodāyin was also of beautiful appearance.
Kālodāyin constantly fixed his mind upon the upāsikā Śikhaṇḍinī, and the upāsikā Śikhaṇḍinī likewise fixed her mind upon Kālodāyin.
Then, when it was time, the Venerable Kālodāyin dressed, took his bowl, and went to the home of the upāsikā Śikhaṇḍinī; there, the two of them sat together in an exposed place and conversed.
At that time, Viśākhā Mātṛ went to Vaiśālī on some minor business; hearing the voice of Kālodāyin from afar, she thought to herself:
"He might be preaching the Dharma."
He immediately went to lean against the wall and listen; he heard only the sound of unrighteous speech being uttered within. He then thought to himself:
"I hear the voice of a bhikṣu speaking unrighteous words; a bhikṣu should not speak such words."
He immediately peered inside and saw Kālodayin sitting together with the laywoman Ciñcā Mānavikā in a secluded place, speaking improper words.
Having seen this, he thought:
"This bhikṣu sits in an improper place and speaks improper words; if her husband were to see him, he would surely scold and revile his wife, thereby giving rise to a lack of faith."

Then the upāsikā immediately left her home and went quickly to where the World-Honored One was. She prostrated herself at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Having addressed the World-Honored One in this way, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the situation, intentionally asked Kālodāyin:
"Did you indeed sit and converse with the laywoman Ciñcā Māṇavikā in an exposed place?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it that you, Kāḷudāyin, are now sitting with the laywoman Ciñcā Mānavikā in an exposed place, discussing matters contrary to the Dharma?
Having thus rebuked Kāḷudāyin through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Kāḷudāyin is a foolish man; this is the first transgression of the precepts among many such occasions for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sits with a woman in an exposed place, where sexual intercourse is not possible, and utters coarse and wicked words."
There was a female lay follower (upāsikā) established in faith who spoke of each of two matters: either a saṃghāvaśeṣa or a pāyattika.
The bhikṣu sitting there said of himself:
"I have committed this offense."
"Among these two matters, each should be dealt with according to its respective rule—whether it be a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*.
As described by the faithful female lay follower (*upāsikā*), that bhikṣu should be dealt with according to the law; this is called an *aniyata-dharma*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"An open place" refers to a location without walls or trees, and without fences or any other obstructions.
"A place unfit for sexual intercourse" refers to a location where sexual intercourse cannot be performed.
Harsh speech refers to speaking of sexual practices and praising the merits or defects of the two paths.

A laywoman who has faith and joy is one who believes in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; she takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; she abstains from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants; she maintains these matters well without error, and her words are truthful and not deceptive.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place he is heading toward, declares the place he has reached, declares that he is sitting, or declares that he is lying down, he should be dealt with according to what the bhikṣu has said.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place toward which he was heading, declares the place where he arrived, and declares that he sat, but does not declare that he lay down, he should be dealt with according to what was stated regarding the upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the place toward which he was heading and the place he reached, but does not himself declare that he sat or lay down, he should be dealt with according to what was stated regarding an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu himself declares the destination toward which he was heading, but does not declare the place he reached, nor that he sat, nor that he lay down, he should be dealt with according to what was stated regarding an upāsikā.

If a bhikṣu does not himself state where he has gone, does not himself state where he has arrived, does not himself state that he is sitting, and does not himself state that he is lying down, he should be dealt with according to what the upāsikā has said.
In this matter, there is no fixed rule; therefore, it is called "undetermined.
The two undetermined rules are concluded.

4. The Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. Part One: The First of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. The World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣus to possess the three robes (*tricīvara*), but they must not exceed the prescribed length.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept extra robes—whether robes for early morning, robes for midday, or robes for late afternoon—and they constantly busied themselves with adorning, storing, and maintaining such garments.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"The Buddha has permitted the keeping of the three robes, but not in excess. Whose robe is this?"
He replied, "This is our extra robe. When the monks heard this,

those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six monks, saying:
“The Tathāgata has permitted the wearing of the three robes; why then do you keep extra robes—a morning robe, a midday robe, and an afternoon robe?
The bhikṣus immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣus!
The Tathāgata has permitted the wearing of the three robes; why do you keep extra robes?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“The foolish group of six bhikṣus has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.’”
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, Ānanda obtained from someone a high-priced discarded robe (pāṃśukūla) which he wished to offer to Mahākāśyapa, because Mahākāśyapa constantly practiced the dhūta austerities and wore such garments.
Kāśyapa being absent, Ānanda thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"
"I have now obtained these precious rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) which I wish to offer to Mahākāśyapa.
However, Mahākāśyapa is currently away on his dhūta-penance wearing such robes; I do not know what to do."
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One, you have established a precept for the bhikṣus: if a bhikṣu keeps an extra robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.”
"I have now obtained a highly valuable *pāṃśukūla* robe, which I wish to offer to Mahākāśyapa.
Mahākāśyapa constantly practices the *dhūta* austerities and wears robes made of discarded rags.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"When will Kāśyapa return?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying,
"He shall return ten days hence."

For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs. Through countless skillful means, he taught the dharma of having few desires and being content, practicing the dhūta austerities, and delighting in renunciation. Having done so, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit you to keep extra robes for a period of up to ten days."
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak thus:
"If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina has been relinquished, he may keep an extra robe for ten days; provided it has not been formally assigned to another, he may keep it."
"If it exceeds ten days, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"The robes are finished" means that the three robes and the *kaṭhina* robe have already been relinquished.
There are ten kinds of robes:

cotton cloth robes, *kappāsa* (cotton) robes, *kambala* (wool) robes, *kṣauma* (flax) robes, *śāṇa* (hemp) robes, *sāṇa* (coarse hemp) robes, *māṣa* (bean-cloth) robes, *kāyīra* robes, *kauśeya* (silk) robes, and *kṣomapaṭṭa* (fine silk) robes.
Regarding "extra robes": if they are eight fingers long according to the measurement of the Tathāgata, or four fingers wide, these qualify.

If a bhikṣu acquires a robe on the first day and keeps it, and acquires another robe on the second day, continuing in this manner until he acquires one on the tenth day and keeps them, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all [the robes] become *niḥsargika* (subject to forfeiture).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, does not obtain one on the second, obtains one on the third, and obtains one on the fourth, and continues in this manner until he obtains a robe on the tenth day, such that when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during those nine days become *niḥsargika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third day and obtains one on the fourth day—in this manner, descending by days until he does not obtain a robe for ten days—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second or third days, and then obtains robes from the fourth day up to the tenth day, such that the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during those eight days become *niḥsargika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third or fourth day, and then obtains one on the fifth day—following this descending sequence until he does not obtain a robe on the ninth or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, does not obtain one on the second, third, or fourth day, and then obtains one on the fifth day, continuing in this manner until he obtains one on the tenth day, such that the dawn of the eleventh day appears, then all the robes obtained during those seven days constitute *niḥsargika* offenses.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, or fifth day, and then obtains one on the sixth day—following this descending sequence until he does not obtain a robe on the eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, or fifth day, and then obtains a robe on the sixth day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, all the robes obtained during those six days constitute *niḥsargika* offenses.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day; or if he obtains them in such a descending sequence until he does not obtain a robe on the seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, and does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day, but obtains one on the seventh day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and then the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during those five days become *niḥsargika* (subject to forfeiture).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, and then obtains a robe on the eighth day—following this pattern of decreasing intervals down to not obtaining a robe for six, seven, eight, nine, or ten days—the formulation of the sentence is as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, and then obtains a robe on the eighth day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, all the robes obtained during those four days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day, and then obtains a robe on the ninth day—thus decreasing in sequence until he does not obtain a robe for five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten days—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, and does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, or eighth day, but obtains robes on the ninth and tenth days, then all the robes obtained during those three days become *niḥsargika* (subject to forfeiture) when the dawn of the eleventh day appears.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, obtains a robe on the second day, and does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day, but obtains a robe on the tenth day.

In this manner, the sequence continues in descending order until the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth day; if one does not obtain a robe, the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, and does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day, but obtains a robe on the tenth day, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during that period constitute *niḥsargika* offenses.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day and obtains a robe on the second day, but does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—and thus the sequence descends in this manner until he does not obtain a robe on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day, and when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during that period of ten days become *niḥsargika* (relinquishable).

If a bhikṣu obtains a robe on the first day that has not been formally offered (apariśuddha-datta), obtains a robe on the second day that has been formally offered (pariśuddha-datta), and obtains robes on the third day up to the tenth day such that they have not been formally offered, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the robes obtained during those nine days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu receives a robe on the first day, receives a robe on the second day without having made it a formal gift (apariśuddha-dāna), receives a robe on the third day having made it a formal gift (pariśuddha-dāna), and receives a robe on the fourth day without having made it a formal gift—thus alternating and decreasing in this manner down to the tenth day, whether receiving a robe with or without it being a formal gift—the formulation of the cases is as above.

Likewise, if one sends it to another person, the case is as above; if the robe is lost, the case is as above; if it is intentionally damaged, the case is as above; if it is made into something that is not a robe, the case is as above; if it is taken with the intention of treating it as a gift for a friend, the case is as above; if it is forgotten and left behind, the case is as above—in all these instances, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), yet retains the garment without relinquishing it and instead exchanges it for another, there is one *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *dukkaṭa*.

This forfeited garment must be relinquished to the Saṃgha—whether to a large group or to a single person—and may not be relinquished to a separate faction; if relinquished in such a manner, the relinquishment is invalid and constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate to the senior monk (upādhyāya), kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak these words:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have intentionally kept this surplus robe for more than ten days; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having finished relinquishing the robe, he should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then accept the confession, making the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept such an extra robe and committed an offense involving forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, he should then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind!
To which they reply:
"Yes. If it is difficult for the community of monks to assemble, and this bhikṣu has a reason to travel far away, one should ask him:
"To whom will you give this robe?"
"Once he has spoken thus, [the Sangha] shall grant it.
The Sangha should then return this robe to the bhikṣu; it should be granted by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
Within the Sangha, one capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept such a surplus robe and committed an offense of relinquishment (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to that bhikṣu, so-and-so, who shall then return it to this bhikṣu."
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept such an excess robe and has committed an offense involving forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Sangha."
The Saṃgha shall take this robe and give it to that bhikṣu named so-and-so; that bhikṣu named so-and-so shall then return it to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha taking this robe and giving it to that bhikṣu named so-and-so, for him to then return it to this bhikṣu, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent; this matter is thus upheld.
If that bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the robe within the Sangha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone says, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one makes it a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), or gives it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), or intentionally damages it, or burns it, or makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if, within ten days, one transfers it as a pure gift (*pariṣkāra-dāna*), or gives it away to another; or if one perceives it as being stolen by thieves, lost, burned, or swept away; or if one does not transfer it as a pure gift or give it away to another. In these cases, there is no offense.
If his robes are stolen, lost, burned, or carried away by water; or if he takes them for use, or another gives them to him for use, or another makes them for him, he commits no offense.

If that person who has received the entrusted robe dies, departs for a distant place, abandons the path, is forcibly taken away by bandits, is harmed by wild beasts, or is swept away and drowned by water—in such cases, it does not constitute an offense if one does not perform the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddhi-dāna*) nor dispatch it to another person.
There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.
[The first case concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took their robes and entrusted them to a bhikṣu who was a close friend, departing to travel through the human world.
Having received this entrustment, the entrusted bhikṣu repeatedly exposed the robes to the midday sun to dry them.
When the bhikṣus saw it, they asked,
"The Buddha has permitted bhikṣus to keep three robes,
but not in excess. Whose robe is this?"

He replied: "These robes belonging to the group of six bhikṣus were entrusted to me by a close friend while he was traveling through the countryside; I am merely sun-drying them for fear that insects might damage them."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you entrust your robes to a bhikṣu who is a friend and then travel through the countryside separated from your robes?"
Having reproached themselves, they went to the place where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of this, the Blessed One assembled the community of monks and rebuked the group of six monks, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
“How can they entrust their robes to fellow monks and wander through the human world separated from their robes?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“The group of six bhikṣus are foolish men; this is the first transgression among many such bases for outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu has finished making his robes and has relinquished the *kaṭhina* robe, and he stays overnight apart from any one of his three robes in a different location, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu who suffered from the disease of consumption and possessed a saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags that was heavy and burdensome.
This bhikṣu had business requiring him to travel among the people; unable to carry his robes with him, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus that we must not sleep apart from our robes."
"To stay overnight separated from one's robe constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

However, I am currently suffering from a wasting disease, and my *pāṃśukūla-saṃghāṭī* is extremely heavy; because of certain circumstances, I wish to travel among the people, yet I am unable to carry it with me."
"What shall I do now? He then said to his fellow bhikṣu:

"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu has finished preparing his three robes and the kaṭhina cloth has been withdrawn, should he remain apart from any one of these three robes overnight, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
"I have contracted the disease of consumption, and these robes are extremely heavy. Having business that requires me to travel among the people, I am unable to carry them while traveling.
What should I do now?"
"Venerable sirs, please go and inform the Blessed One on my behalf; whatever the Blessed One instructs, I shall carry out.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:

"From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to establish the 'non-loss of robes' for this sick bhikṣu."
It should be granted in this manner.

That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, and prostrating toward the elder; then, kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

I, bhikṣu [name], am afflicted with the disease of consumption; this saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags is heavy, and though there is a necessary reason for me to travel among the people, I am unable to carry it while traveling.
"I now request from the Saṃgha the authorization for the practice of not losing one's robe.
One should make this request in this manner, repeating it up to three times.
Within the Saṃgha, a capable person for performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has contracted the disease of consumption. He possesses a heavy *kaṭhina* robe made of discarded rags (*pāṃśukūla-saṃghāṭī*), and because he wishes to travel among the people for a necessary reason, he is unable to carry it with him. He requests from the Saṃgha the authorization to maintain the 'non-loss of robes' (*acchinna-cīvara*) rule."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha establish for this bhikṣu the rule regarding the non-loss of robes.
The motion is as follows. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

A certain bhikṣu has contracted the disease of consumption; he possesses a saṃghāṭī robe made of discarded rags that is heavy, and because of certain necessary circumstances he wishes to travel among the people, yet he is unable to carry it while traveling. He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal authorization for the "non-loss of robe" (acchinna-cīvara) rule.

Now the Saṃgha grants the *akopya-cīvara-dharma* (the rule of not losing one's robe) to the bhikṣu so-and-so. Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting the *akopya-cīvara-dharma* to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to establish the 'non-loss of robe' rule for the bhikṣu so-and-so; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:

If a bhikṣu, having finished his robes and having had the kaṭhina cloth removed, should stay overnight separated from any one of his three robes in a different location, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃgha-kamma), it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"The robes are finished" refers to the three robes (*tricīvara*), once the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.
The three robes are the *saṃghāṭī*, the *uttarāsaṅga*, and the *antarvāsaka*.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as explained above.
Regarding "the Sangha," it refers to those who share a single recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and a single *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "not losing the robe," within a monastery there is a single boundary (*sīmā*).
Regarding the loss of one's robes: within a monastery, there are several distinct boundaries.
Regarding the non-loss of one's robes: under a tree, there is a single boundary;
regarding the loss of one's robes: under a tree, there are several distinct boundaries.
For one who does not lose their robe, the threshing floor constitutes a single boundary;
for one who loses their robe, the threshing floor constitutes multiple boundaries.
For one who does not lose their robe, the cart constitutes a single boundary.
Regarding the loss of robes: for a vehicle, there are several boundaries;
for one who does not lose their robes, a boat has a single boundary;
for one who loses their robes, a boat has several boundaries.
For one who does not lose his robe, the village constitutes a single boundary;
for one who loses his robe, the village constitutes several boundaries.
For one who does not lose his robe, the house constitutes a single boundary.
Regarding one who has lost his robe, there are several boundaries within the dwelling;
regarding one who has not lost his robe, there is a single boundary within the hall;
regarding one who has lost his robe, there are several boundaries within the hall.
For one who does not lose their robe, the storehouse constitutes a single boundary;
for one who loses their robe, the storehouse constitutes multiple boundaries.
For one who does not lose their robe, the granary constitutes a single boundary.
Regarding "one who has lost his robe," there are various boundaries within the storehouse.
Regarding "a saṃghārāma," there are four types, as described above.
Regarding "a tree," it is one that provides sufficient shade for a person to sit cross-legged beneath it.
A "field" (*kṣetra*) refers to a place where the five grains are cultivated.
A "cart" (*śakaṭa*) refers to a place where a cart turns around.
A "boat" (*nau*) refers to a place where a boat turns around.
Regarding "village," there are four types as mentioned above.
A "hall" is mostly open and exposed.
A "storehouse" is where vehicles, litters, and goods for sale are stored and accumulated.
A "granary" refers to the storage of rice and grain.

Regarding the "boundary of a saṃghārāma": it is the boundary of this saṃghārāma and not that saṃghārāma; it is the boundary of this saṃghārāma and not the boundary of its trees, and so on, up to the boundary of the storehouse and not the boundary of that storehouse—it is likewise in all such cases.
This is the boundary of a tree, not that tree’s boundary; the same applies up to the boundaries of storehouses and monasteries.
This is the boundary of a threshing floor, not that threshing floor’s boundary; the same applies up to the boundaries of monasteries and trees.
The formulation of the remaining [categories] is also as above.

Regarding the boundary of a monastery (*saṃghārāma-sīman*): it is located at the edge of the monastery; the area reached by a person of average height throwing a stone or a brick is called the boundary.
The same applies up to the boundary of the storehouse.

If a bhikṣu places his robe within a monastery and stays overnight under a tree, and before the dawn has appeared, he either relinquishes the robe, holds the robe in his hand, or goes to a place where a stone could be thrown;

if he does not relinquish the robe, does not hold the robe in his hand, and does not go to a place where a stone could be thrown, and the dawn appears, he commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense according to the distance he has stayed apart from the robe.
Except for the three robes, if one is separated from any other robe, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣu leaves his robe within a monastery and goes to stay at a threshing floor, if the dawn has not yet appeared, he may either relinquish the robe, hold the robe in his hand, or go to a place where a stone can be thrown;

if he does not relinquish the robe, does not hold the robe in his hand, and does not go to a place where a stone can be thrown, and the dawn appears, then according to the distance he was separated from the robe while staying overnight, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This applies even to staying overnight in a storehouse; every single phrase is likewise.
If a bhikṣu leaves his robe under a tree and goes to stay overnight in a threshing floor, it is likewise for staying overnight in a storehouse or a monastery.
Regarding "not losing one's robe": if there is no boundary in an araṇya (wilderness) location, the distance between eight trees is such that there are seven *dhanus* (bows) between each tree.
According to the method for making a *dhanus* in the country of Cāmara, its length is four *madhyama-hasta* (middle cubits).

If a bhikṣu, in a forest hermitage where there is no village, leaves his robe among these eight trees and stays overnight in another location, and if at the appearance of dawn he has not relinquished the robe, nor taken hold of it with his hand, nor gone to a place within reach of a thrown stone, then at the appearance of dawn, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one sets aside the three robes and remains apart from other miscellaneous robes, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
These robes subject to forfeiture must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; they must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monk (*upādhyāya*), kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!..."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for sleeping apart from my robe; I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, he should then perform confession (*pratideśana*).
The person receiving the confession shall first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then accept the confession, making the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture involving separation from his robe while staying overnight; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that I accept the confession of this bhikṣu, so-and-so."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
One should speak to that person as follows:
“Reprove your own mind. He replied, “I shall.”
The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu, and it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
A competent person for the *karman* should be appointed from within the Saṃgha as described above, and he should make the following proclamation:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
"Venerable Saṃgha, this bhikṣu [Name] has committed an offense of forfeiture for sleeping apart from his robe; he now relinquishes this robe to the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, may the Saṃgha return this robe to that bhikṣu [Name]."
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* for sleeping apart from his robe; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha shall return this robe to that bhikṣu, [named] So-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to that bhikṣu, [named] So-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
“The Sangha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it is silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Sangha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone says,
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), or sends it to another person, or takes it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes it into miscellaneous robes (*pārihārika-cīvara*), or intentionally damages it, or burns it, or makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if the Saṃgha has performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for him; or if, before the dawn has appeared, he holds the robe in his hand, or discards the robe, or reaches a place where a stone could be thrown; or if he has the thought that it is being plundered, lost, burned, swept away, or destroyed; or if the path is cut off by water, or is dangerous and difficult to traverse; or if there is danger from bandits, danger from wild beasts, or if the irrigation ditches are overflowing; or if he is held by forceful persons, or is bound, or faces danger to life, or danger to his holy life (*brahmacarya*); if, under such circumstances, he does not discard the robe, does not hold the robe in his hand, and does not reach a place where a stone could be thrown, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(End of Section Two. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose saṃghāṭī robe was old, worn out, and tattered. He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'When the robes have been finished and the kaṭhina period has ended, it is permitted to keep an extra robe for ten days; if one exceeds this limit, they commit a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
"However, this saṃghāṭī of mine is old, tattered, and worn out; I cannot manage to have a new one made within ten days. What shall I do now?
He then said to the bhikṣu who shared his views:
"Excellent, Venerable One!"
"Please inform the Blessed One on my behalf: if the Blessed One has any instruction, I shall carry it out.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep extra robes (cīvara) for the purpose of fulfilling their requirements."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had permitted them to keep extra robes for the purpose of fulfilling their requirements. They possessed some *pāṃsukūla* robes and other kinds of robes, but as they were insufficient in size, they took one of medium quality from among the *pāṃsukūla* robes, washed it, dyed it, and marked the four corners with dots to perform the ritual of purification (*kappiya*). Having entrusted it to a bhikṣu who was a relative or friend, they set out on their travels through the human world.
At that time, because the monk to whom the robes had been entrusted had not returned after a long absence, the other monks took them out to dry.
When the monks saw this, they asked:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept permitting one to keep three robes, but not more than that."
"Whose robe is this? He replied,
"This is the robe of the group of six bhikṣus."
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts allowing us to keep extra robes until they are full.

Now, we have some *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) materials and other kinds of cloth; since those of the same quality are insufficient, we took a medium-quality *pāṃśukūla*, washed it, dyed it, and marked the four corners with dots to purify it. We then entrusted it to you to take to the human world, and we merely dried it for fear that it might become moldy or damaged."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How can you say that the World-Honored One permitted the keeping of extra robes for the purpose of fulfilling one's needs, yet because your own robes were insufficient, you took a refuse-rag from among the middling ones, washed and dyed it, marked the four corners with dots to perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi), and entrusted it to a bhikṣu friend to take into the human world?"
The bhikṣus immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice that conforms to the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣus!

The Blessed One has permitted bhikṣus to keep extra robes for the purpose of fulfilling their requirements; yet, while your own robes are insufficient, you take a discarded rag from the refuse heap, wash it, dye it, and mark its four corners to purify it, then entrust it to a bhikṣu friend and depart for the human world?"
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu’s robes are finished and the kaṭhina cloth has been relinquished, and that bhikṣu obtains an out-of-season robe, he may accept it if he needs it; having accepted it, he must quickly have it made into a robe."
If it is sufficient, that is well; if it is insufficient, one may keep it for one month in order to fulfill it.
If one keeps it beyond that period, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"The robes are finished" means that the three robes have been completed and the *kaṭhina* robe has been relinquished.
"At the proper time" means one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if there is no *kaṭhina*, or five months after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony if there is a *kaṭhina*.
"Untimely" means if it exceeds this limit.
"Robe" refers to the ten kinds of robes as mentioned above.

If within ten days the robe-material is sufficient, one should cut it, or sew it together with thread, or stitch it into a robe, or perform a formal act of dedication (*śuddhaka-dāna*), or give it away to another person.

If one does not cut and sew it into a robe, nor join it with thread, nor perform the ritual of impure giving (*aśuddha-dāna*), nor give it away to another, then at the appearance of the dawn on the eleventh day, for however many robes there may be, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If the robes are insufficient until the eleventh day, one must cut, sew, and make a robe from them, or join them with strips of cloth, on that very eleventh day. If one does not cut, sew, and make a robe; nor joins them with strips of cloth; nor performs a formal relinquishment (*viśuddhi-dāna*); nor gives them away to another; and they reach the appearance of dawn on the twelfth day, then according to the number of robes [involved], there is an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This applies likewise up to the twenty-ninth day.

If the robes are sufficient for thirty days, whether they are sufficient or insufficient, whether they are the same robes or different robes, one must on that very day cut, sew, and make them into a robe; or join them with thread; or perform a *pariṣkāra-dāna* (purification-gift); or give them away to another. If one does not cut, sew, and make them into a robe; or does not join them with thread; or does not perform a *pariṣkāra-dāna*; or does not give them away to another, then when the dawn of the thirty-first day appears, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it should not be relinquished to a separate faction.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go into the midst of the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monk (upādhyāya), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], have possessed this many robes for more than this many days and have thus committed an offense involving forfeiture.
I now relinquish them to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished them, one should then perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, possesses such-and-such robes and has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) after exceeding such-and-such days."
I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
The motion is thus made.
Having made this formal announcement, one should then accept the confession and say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind. He shall reply:
"Yes. The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) as follows.
A competent person capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed from within the Saṃgha as described above, and he should make the following announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, possesses such-and-such robes; having exceeded the permitted number of days, he has committed an offense involving forfeiture. He now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha take these robes and return them to the bhikṣu, so-and-so."
The motion is thus made.
"Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, possesses such-and-such robes; having exceeded the permitted number of days, he has committed an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). He now relinquishes them to the Sangha."
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it is silent; this matter is thus upheld.
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Sangha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
saying, "Do not return," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one does not return it, but instead transfers it as a pure gift (*śuci-dāna*), sends it to another person, uses it to make the three robes (*tricīvara*), makes it into miscellaneous articles (*pārikkhārika-cīvara*), intentionally damages it, burns it, makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if, within ten days, the requisite robes are sufficient; or if they are cut, or joined with thread, or sewn into a robe; or if the requisite robes are insufficient until the eleventh day, at which point the requisite robes must be cut, or joined with thread, or sewn into a robe, or formally given away (*viśuddha-dāna*), or sent to another person; this applies likewise up to the twenty-ninth day.

By the thirtieth day, whether the robe-material is sufficient or insufficient, whether it is of the same cloth or of different cloths, one should on that very day cut it, or sew it together with thread, or stitch it into a robe, or perform a formal relinquishment (*viśuddha-dāna*), or give it away to another; doing so, one does not commit an offense.

If there is the perception that it has been taken away, the perception that it has been lost, the perception that it has been burned, or the perception that it has been washed away; or if one does not cut it, does not join it with thread, does not sew it to make a robe, does not perform the formal act of relinquishment (pariṣkāra-dāna), and does not send it to another person, there is no offense.
If one's robes have been taken away, lost, burned, or swept away by water, and one takes and wears them, or another gives them to wear, or makes them into a cloak, there is no offense.

If the monk who has received a deposited robe dies, or travels far away, or ceases his religious practice, or is robbed by thieves, or is harmed by wild beasts, or is swept away by water; and if he does not cut it, nor sew it with thread, nor stitch it into a robe, nor send it to another person, he commits no offense.
There is no offense for one who was acting before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The third section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there was a woman named Utpalavarṇā, whom her parents had married off to a man from the country of Ujjayinī. Later, she became pregnant; wishing to give birth, she returned to her parents' home, where she gave birth to a daughter of beautiful and upright countenance.
While Utpalavarṇā was inside the house with her daughter, her husband had a secret affair with her mother.
At that time, a maidservant of Utpalavarṇā saw them and immediately informed Utpalavarṇā.
Having heard this, Utpalavarṇā thought to herself: "Alas!
How can a woman and her mother share the same husband? Of what use is a woman's body?"

He immediately released his embrace, placed the woman inside the house, and departed. He went to the city of Vārāṇasī and stood outside the city gate, his body covered in dust and his bare feet torn and wounded.

At that time, there was an elder in the city whose wife had passed away. He mounted a carriage with his attendants and departed from the city of Vārāṇasī to visit a park for recreation. There he saw this woman, Puṣpavarṇā, standing outside the gate; she was of upright and beautiful countenance, yet her body was covered in dust and her feet were bare and wounded. He immediately fixed his mind upon her.
He immediately went before the woman and asked,
"To whom do you belong? Padmāvatī replied:
"I have no one to whom I belong.
The elder asked again,
"If you have no one to whom you belong, could you become my wife?"
He replied, "So be it.
He immediately called her to mount the carriage, took her along with him, and returned home to take her as his wife.

Later, at another time, the husband of Utpalavarṇā gathered a great amount of wealth and traveled from Vārāṇasī to the kingdom of Ujjayinī to conduct business. At that time, it happened to be the day of the festival for young maidens, a time of merriment and laughter; the daughter born of Utpalavarṇā, dressed in fine garments, was also among them.
This girl was beautiful; upon seeing her, the elder immediately fixed his mind upon her and asked those nearby, "Whose daughter is she? They replied:
"This is the girl so-and-so.
He asks again:
"Where does she reside?"
He replied, “In such-and-such a place.
He asked again:
"In which street or lane?
He replied, "In such-and-such a street or lane."
The householder asked again:
"In which direction does the entrance to that house face? He replied:
"Go to such-and-such a place.
He then went to that house and asked her father,
"Is this your daughter?"
He replied, "She is my daughter.
He asked again:
"Could you give me in marriage?
She replied, "That may be so."
The elder asked, "How much wealth do you require? His father replied:
"If you give me one hundred thousand taels of gold, I shall grant it to you.
Her father then adorned his daughter and returned from the kingdom of Ujjayinī to Vārāṇasī.

At that time, Utpalavarṇā saw her from afar and looked upon her with the thought that she was her own daughter; the girl, seeing Utpalavarṇā, likewise regarded her with the intention that she was her mother, and so they became intimately acquainted over a long period.
Utpalavarṇā combed the girl's hair and asked,
"From which country do you come? Whose daughter are you?"
He replied, “I am a native of Ujjayinī.
He asked again:
“Where is your home? In which lane or alley does it stand?
And in which direction does its gate face?”
"Who is your father? The girl replied, "My home is at such-and-such a place;
my street and lane are at such-and-such a place; my gate faces such-and-such a direction; and my father's name is So-and-so."
He asked again,
"What is your mother's clan?
The girl replied:
"I do not know my mother," he said.
"I have only heard people say:
'Her name was Utpalavarṇā; she abandoned me when I was young.'"
At that time, Utpalavarṇā thought to herself,
"This is indeed my daughter," and she reproached herself:
"Alas! Of what use is this female body?
Why is it that today mother and daughter must share a single husband?"
He immediately left that house and went to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an immeasurable great assembly as he preached the Dharma.
