From afar, [the man] saw the World-Honored One, whose countenance was upright and handsome, whose faculties were tranquil and stilled, who had attained supreme self-mastery like a tamed dragon-elephant, and who was as clear and pure as water, free from all dust and defilement.
Having seen him, he conceived a heart of joy and approached the World-Honored One, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and standing to one side.

Then the World-Honored One gradually expounded for him the subtle and wondrous Dharma: he spoke of generosity, of observing the precepts, and of the merit of rebirth in heaven; he censured the impurity of desire and praised renunciation; furthermore, he fully analyzed the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

At that moment, Utpalavarṇā attained the purity of the Dharma-eye while still upon her seat; just as a fresh, clean white cloth, free from dust and grime, easily takes on color, so too was the purification of the Dharma attained by Utpalavarṇā.
Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, realized the fruit, and achieved the realization, he approached the Buddha and said:
"May the World-Honored One grant me permission to go forth, so that I may cultivate the pure conduct within the Buddha's Dharma."
The Buddha said to Ānanda,
"Take this woman, Pāṭalavarṇā, to Mahāprajāpatī and have her ordained.
Ānanda immediately accepted the Buddha’s instruction and went to Mahāprajāpatī, saying to her:
"The World-Honored One has given this command: 'You must ordain this woman.
" She was immediately ordained and allowed to leave the household life.
At another time, through diligent reflection and daily progress, she attained arhatship and possessed great supernormal powers.
At that time, there were many bhikṣuṇīs dwelling in a secluded place. The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was sitting separately in a grove, practicing meditation.

A bandit leader habitually resided in Utpalavarṇā’s dwelling; when he saw her maintaining her dignified deportment and observing the decorum of ritual etiquette, he immediately conceived a virtuous mind.
Later, on another occasion, a bandit leader obtained a large amount of pork; having eaten most of it, he wrapped the remainder and hung it from a tree branch, saying:
"If there is any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in this forest who possesses great supernormal power, let him take it."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā heard the sound with her divine ear and saw with her purified divine eye that the pork was wrapped in white cotton cloth and hung upon a tree branch.
When the night had passed, he said to the śikṣamāṇā and the śrāmaṇerī:
"Go to that tree in such-and-such a place; there is white cotton cloth wrapped around pork—bring it here!"
She immediately went to fetch it and gave it to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā instructed her to cook it; then, when it was time for the meal, she went herself to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain and ate it together with the elder bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu wearing a worn-out saṃghāṭī patched with rags. Having seen him, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā gave rise to a heart of compassion and immediately asked the bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Why have you put on this worn-out saṃghāṭī? She replied, "Sister!"
"This is merely because this dharma is subject to exhaustion and decay.
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wearing an expensive saṃghāṭī, said to the bhikṣu:
"Venerable Sir!"
"I offer this robe to you, Venerable Sir; may you give me the robe you are currently wearing?
The bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
She immediately took off her saṃghāṭī and gave it to the bhikṣuṇī, who took it and put on the bhikṣu’s worn-out, old garment.
Later, at another time, Utpalavarṇā, wearing this worn-out garment, went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated with her head at his feet, and stood to one side.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Why is the robe you are wearing so tattered?
The bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā then related the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"You should not act in this way, Utpalavarṇā!"
"I permit you to keep and wear five robes that are complete and sturdy; as for other robes, you may give them away as pure gifts or bestow them upon others as you wish. Why is this?
Even when women wear fine garments, they are still not considered beautiful, let alone worn-out clothes."
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked that bhikṣu intentionally:
"Is it true that you took a robe from the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the precepts—it is something that should not be done.
How could you take a robe from a bhikṣuṇī?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for the outflows (āsrava), this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
After the Blessed One had thus laid down the precept for the bhikṣus, all the bhikṣus were cautious and fearful, not daring to accept robes from bhikṣuṇīs who were their relatives.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to receive robes from bhikṣuṇīs who are their relatives.
For what reason? Because..."
If they are not relatives and do not deliberate, they will be unable to discern what may be taken and what may not be taken, nor whether it is good or bad, old or new.
If it is a relative who deliberates, they will know whether [the items] exist or not, whether they may be taken or not, and whether they are good or bad, new or old.
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu receives a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a training rule for the bhikṣus.

At that time, within the Jeta Grove, the two communities of monks received donated robes and divided them together; however, the bhikṣuṇīs' robes were mistakenly received by the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus' robes were mistakenly received by the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī took a robe to the saṃghārāma and said to a bhikṣu:
"I bring this robe to give to you, Venerable Sir; please give me your robe."
The bhikṣus replied, "The Buddha has not permitted us to take the robes of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the exchange of robes.
Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu takes a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relatives" refers to those who are not relatives of one's parents, extending back through seven generations;
"relatives" refers to those who are relatives of one's parents, extending back through seven generations.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as mentioned above.

Regarding "exchanging," it means exchanging robe for robe; exchanging a robe for what is not a robe; or exchanging what is not a robe for a robe; or exchanging a robe for such things as a needle, a tube, a knife, thread, small pieces of material, or even a single pill of medicine.
If a bhikṣu receives a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* article must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate toward the elder (*sthavira*), kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], having taken the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, have committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one must perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal motion (jñapti):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, took the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should accept the confession and say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind. He replied, "So be it."
The Sangha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
The Sangha should appoint a person capable of performing the *karman* as described above, and he should make the following proclamation:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
The bhikṣu so-and-so has taken the robe of a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant that this robe be returned to this bhikṣu.
The motion is thus made. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense involving the taking of a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, which constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
“The Sangha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If, after having relinquished the robe within the Sangha, one refuses to return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs one not to return it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), or sends it to another person, or makes it into one's own three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes it into a *pārihārika* robe, or intentionally destroys it, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined—in all these cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in taking a robe from a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative; nor is there an offense in exchanging robes, or in taking them for the sake of the Saṃgha or the Buddha’s shrine.
There is also no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The fourth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin was handsome and of pleasing appearance, and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was likewise handsome and of pleasing appearance.
Kālodāyin fixed his thoughts on Thullanandā, and Thullanandā likewise fixed her thoughts on Kālodāyin.

When it was time for Kālodāyin to go begging for alms, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to where the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was; he sat down before her with his body uncovered, and the bhikṣuṇī also sat down with her body uncovered, each gazing at the other with lustful intent.
Kāḷudāyin soon discharged semen, staining his lower robe (antarvāsaka). When Sthūlanandā saw this, she said to him:
"Venerable sir, bring this robe here; I wish to wash it for you."
She immediately took off her garment and gave it to her.

Having received this garment, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā went to a secluded place, where she used her fingernails to take up some impurity and placed it in her mouth; she then put a small amount into her urinary tract, and subsequently became pregnant.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they said to her, "You are shameless; you have committed an impure act. She replied:
"Sister! It is not that I lack a sense of shame or dread of blame;
I have not committed an impure act. The bhikṣuṇīs said:
"If you have not committed an act of impure conduct, why are you pregnant?
Why is it that the other bhikṣuṇīs who do not commit acts of impure conduct are not pregnant?"
Then Thullanandā recounted the circumstances in full.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
because of these circumstances, they censured Kālodāyin: "How could you, Venerable One, have done such a thing with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha, for this reason, assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned Kāḷodāyin:
"Is it true that you have had such dealings with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha, employing countless skillful means, rebuked Kālodāyin, saying:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you perform such an act toward the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“This foolish man! Among the many bases for the outflows (āsrava), this is the first transgression of the precepts.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī wash an old garment, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus; subsequently, the bhikṣus were each filled with apprehension and caution, not daring to have their relatives, the bhikṣuṇīs, wash old clothes, nor dye them, nor beat them.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to have their relatives, the bhikṣuṇīs, wash their old robes, or dye them, or beat them.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relatives" is as explained above;
"relatives" is also as explained above.
"Old cloth" refers to that which has been worn on the body even once.
Regarding robes, there are ten kinds as mentioned above.
If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash an old robe, or dye it, or beat it, it constitutes three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.
If she instructs [a person] to wash, dye, and beat [the cloth], and that person washes and dyes it but does not beat it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If she instructs [a person] to wash, dye, and beat [the cloth], and that person washes and beats it but does not dye it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to wash, dye, and beat [a robe], and that person does not wash but dyes and beats it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to wash, dye, and beat, and that person does not wash, dye, or beat it, there are three *dukkaṭas*.
If a bhikṣu causes a śrāmaṇerī or a śikṣamāṇā who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat old robes, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat new robes, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate faction.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the Elder, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, Bhikṣu [Name], having caused a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat my old robes, have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"Venerable Sangha, this bhikṣu so-and-so has caused a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat his old robes; he has thus committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I now relinquish these robes to the Sangha.
If it is the proper time for the Sangha and the Sangha permits me, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu so-and-so."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one then accepts the confession and should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind."
He replies, "So be it.
The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu; the formal act of authorization (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) for giving it to the Saṃgha should be performed as follows.
An appointed capable *karmadāna* (officer) shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti*) as follows:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having caused a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat his used robes, has committed an offense of forfeiture and downfall (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: I shall take this robe and return it to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having caused a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or beat his old robes, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
The Sangha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha returning this robe to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent; this matter is thus upheld.
If, after the bhikṣu has finished relinquishing the robe within the Sangha, he refuses to return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
"Do not return," and they do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one does not return [the robe], but instead transfers it as a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into the three robes oneself, makes it into a *pārikkāra* robe, burns it, intentionally damages it, or wears it until it is worn out, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one washes, dyes, or beats an old garment belonging to a relative nun; or if one washes, dyes, or beats it because of illness; or if one washes, dyes, or beats it for the sake of the Sangha or a Buddhist monastery; or if one washes, dyes, or beats a garment borrowed from another. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(The fifth section concludes. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Six. [Volume Seven begins. Section Seven of the First Division.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Part Two of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī who, having prepared his carriage at dawn and accompanied by attendants, went to a park for sightseeing. Having finished his tour, he turned his chariot back toward the Jetavana Monastery. He parked the carriage outside the gate of Jetavana and entered on foot to see the Śākya son Upananda. After paying his respects and inquiring after his well-being, he sat before him to listen to the Dharma.

The Śākya son Upananda, possessing eloquence and wisdom and being skilled at preaching the Dharma, employed various skillful means to teach the elder, transforming him through instruction and exhorting him until he was filled with joy.
Having heard the Dharma, he immediately said to Baddhālinda, "What do you require?
I pray that you will tell me."
He replied, "I require nothing; this itself constitutes my full offering.
The elder spoke again:
"I pray you will instruct me; if there is anything you require, do not hesitate or find it difficult to speak.
Upananda said, "Enough!"
Stop! There is no need to say more.
Even if I were in need of something, you would be unable to give it to me in any case.
The householder spoke again:
"Please simply tell me what you require, and I shall provide it.
At that time, the householder was wearing an expensive, wide, and long white cotton cloth garment, and Upāli (Bhadanta) said:
"You may give me that which you are wearing; I have need of it.
The elder replied, "Come to my house tomorrow; I shall give it to you then."
Bhadanta said, "I told you before that even if you had what was required, you would not give it to me;
now it has indeed turned out exactly as I said."
The householder replied, "I am giving it to you;
it is not that I refuse to give it. However, come tomorrow.
If I give you this robe, I may have others that are even better to give."
"If I were to take off this robe and give it to you right now, I would not be able to enter the city of Śrāvastī without a robe.
Upananda said, "Stop! Do not do so!"
"Stop! I have no further need of it.
At that time, the elder was filled with resentment and displeasure; he immediately took off his garment, folded it, and handed it to Upananda, saying:
"I previously said to the Venerable One, 'Come tomorrow; I shall give you this robe, or perhaps one even better.
But you did not believe me, and now you have made me enter the city of Śrāvastī wearing only a single robe."
At that time, the elder immediately departed from the Jetavana Monastery, mounted his carriage, donned a single robe, and entered the city.
When the gatekeeper saw him, he said to the elder:
"From where have you come? Who has robbed you?"
The householder replied,
"Just now, while inside Jetavana, I was plundered by bandits. Thereupon,
the gatekeeper immediately took up his sword and staff, intending to go to Jetavana, whereupon the householder said:
"Stop! Stop! There is no need to go."
Then the gatekeeper asked, "For what reason? At that time,
the elder explained the circumstances in detail.
When the lay devotees heard this, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are insatiable in their many requests and lack any sense of shame; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:
'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
Why do you seek the upper garment from the elder's body?
Although a donor may give without weariness, the recipient ought to know contentment."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the Śākya son Upananda, saying: "How could you have requested such an expensive garment from the householder for your own body?"
Then the bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked Upananda:
"Is it true that you requested an upper garment from the householder?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked Baddhananda, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
How could you have asked the householder for the upper garment from his own body?"
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“The foolish man, Upananda!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such sources of outflows.”
From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a layperson, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus; all the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to ask for robes from their own kinsmen, the lay devotees (gṛhapati).
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to ask for robes from their own kinsmen, the lay devotees; there is no offense."
From this day forward, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu solicits a robe from a householder who is not a relative, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat in the kingdom of Kośala and performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day, took up their robes and bowls on the sixteenth day and set out for the place where the Blessed One was staying. Because it was too hot to travel during the day, they traveled by night; consequently, they lost the correct path and proceeded along a wrong road.
At that time, some bandits who had returned with a great amount of plundered wealth encountered the bhikṣus on a bypath.
The bandits said to the bhikṣus,
"Have you come seeking us?"
The bhikṣus replied, "We did not come for your sake.

Having completed our summer retreat in the kingdom of Kosala and performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day, we set out on the sixteenth day with our robes and bowls, intending to go and see the World-Honored One; it is from there that we have come."
"The heat during the day was unbearable for travel, and because we lost our way while traveling at night, we came here; it was not for the sake of you that we came.
The bandits spoke again:
"If you do not intend to seek us out, why did you travel along this path? Do you not wish to harm us?"
He then struck the bhikṣu until he died and seized his robes and bowl.
The bhikṣus went away naked and stood outside the gate at Jetavana.
When the other bhikṣus saw them, they said:
“You naked Nigaṇṭhas, you are not worthy to enter the Jeta Grove.
The bhikṣus replied, “We are not Nigaṇṭhas; we are merely śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas.”
At that time, Upāli was walking up and down not far from there. The bhikṣus went to him and said, "There are now many naked ascetics standing outside the gate.
We told them, 'You are Nirgranthas; do not enter the Jeta Grove Monastery.'"
That man replied, "I am not a Nirgrantha; I am a Śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas! Then the bhikṣus said to Upāli:
"You should go and see who this person is.
Thereupon, he immediately went out the door and asked: "Who are you?"
He replied, "I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas! He asked again:
"How old are you? They replied, "I am so many years old."
He asked again,
"When did you receive the precepts? They replied:
“I was such-and-such at that time.
“Who was your teacher and preceptor? He replied:
"Preceptor and Upādhyāya, [I am] so-and-so. "Why are you naked?
The bhikṣus then explained the circumstances in detail.
Then Upāli returned to where the bhikṣus were and said to them, "These are not Nirgranthas;
they are all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya! Upāli spoke thus to the bhikṣus:
"You should temporarily borrow robes to wear; do not let your bodies be exposed before the Buddha.
The bhikṣus then borrowed robes and went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrating themselves at his feet and sitting to one side.
Then the World-Honored One comforted the bhikṣus, saying:
"Are you all physically well?
Are you living together in harmony and peace?"
"Do you not find food and drink to be a hardship?
The bhikṣus replied, "Venerable Sir!"
We have dwelt in physical ease, living in harmony and happiness, without suffering from lack of food or drink.

Having completed our summer retreat in the kingdom of Kosala and performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, we took up our robes and bowls, intending to come and pay our respects to the World-Honored One. However, the daytime heat was unbearable for travel, and traveling by night caused us to lose our way; we encountered bandits who robbed us.
He reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One as above.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, you foolish man!
Why do you walk about naked?
If one walks about naked, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."

If such a situation arises, one should cover the body with soft grass or tree leaves and proceed to the vicinity of the monastery; if there is a long robe (atirekacīvara) already available, one should take it and wear it.
If there is none, the bhikṣus who are his friends should take and wear any extra robes they possess.
If his friends have no robes, he should ask the Saṃgha: "What kind of robes are available here that may be distributed?"
If there is one, it should be given;
if there is not, one should ask:
"Are there bedding and furnishings?"
"If there is [any cloth], it should be given.

If not, one should personally open the storehouse and look; if there are mattress covers, floor mats, woolen rugs, or blankets, one should tear them apart and take them, cutting them into robes to cover one's body, and then go outside to beg for clothing."
At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to take items from this place to that place.
The Buddha said:
"I permit it."
The bhikṣus had their robes confiscated, lost their robes, had their robes burned, or had their robes washed away; fearing transgression, they did not dare to wear the robes belonging to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear them."
After he had received the robe, the monastic robe was not returned to its original place.
The Buddha said,
"One should not do so."

"Once you have obtained the robe, you should return it; wash, dye, sew, and repair it, and place it securely back in its original location. If it is not placed back in its original location, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose robes were seized, lost, burned, or carried away by water. Fearing and being cautious, he did not dare to ask for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who was not a relative.
The Buddha said:
“If one’s robes are lost, stolen, burned, or carried away by water, it is permitted to ask for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative.”
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu requests a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate time, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
"Other times" refers to when a bhikṣu has had his robes taken away, lost them, had them burned, or had them carried away by water; these are called "other times.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Relatives and non-relatives are as described above.
Laymen and laywomen are as explained above.
As for robes, there are ten kinds, as described above.
If a bhikṣu asks for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This forfeiture must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, pay homage to the elder (*sthavira*), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], have committed the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* by begging for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative; I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession makes the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having begged for a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, has committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture; he now forfeits it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits me, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession and say to that bhikṣu:
“Reproach your own mind. He replied, “I shall.”
The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu. It should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
A capable person for the *karman* should be appointed from within the Saṃgha as described above, and he should make the following proclamation:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) by begging for robes from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative; he now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to take these robes and return them to the bhikṣu, so-and-so.
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having requested a robe from a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative, has committed an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). He now relinquishes it to the Sangha."
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu, [named] So-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to give the robe to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
Having relinquished the robe within the Saṃgha, if one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
"Do not return," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one does not return it, but instead makes it a pure gift (*śuci-dāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into one's own three robes (*tricīvara*), makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), intentionally damages it, burns it, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if: one's robes have been seized, lost, burned, or carried away by water; or if one begs from a householder or housewife who is not a relative, or from a householder or housewife who is a relative, or from a fellow renunciant; or if one begs on behalf of another, or another begs for one's sake; or if one obtains them without having sought them. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The sixth section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus who had encountered bandits and lost their robes arrived at the Jetavana Monastery.

A certain upāsaka, hearing that the bhikṣus had encountered bandits and lost their robes upon arriving at the Jetavana Monastery, brought many fine robes and went to where the bhikṣus were, asking them:
"I have just heard that there are bhikṣus who have lost their robes; which ones are they?"
They replied, "We are they; why do you ask? He answered:

"We have heard that some bhikṣus encountered bandits and lost their robes while coming to Jetavana; therefore, we have brought these robes here for the sake of those venerable ones who require robes—take them as you please."
He replied: "Stop! Stop!"
"They have already performed the offering.
We have our own three robes ourselves; we do not need them.
The group of six bhikṣus said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs! Since you have sufficient three robes, why do you not take these and give them to us, or to others?

At that time, because the bhikṣus had lost their robes, the lay devotees gave them robes; yet, although the bhikṣus already possessed a complete set of the three robes, they took the robes from the lay devotees and gave them to the group of six bhikṣus and to others.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the bhikṣus, saying:

"The laypeople of Śrāvastī gave these robes because the bhikṣus had lost theirs; yet you yourselves already possess a full set of the three robes. Why did you take these other robes to give to the group of six bhikṣus and to others?"
Having rebuked him, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked them:
"Bhikṣus, is it true that you, while possessing a complete set of three robes, took another’s robe and gave it to the group of six bhikṣus or others?"
He replied: “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."

The lay devotees of Śrāvastī gave robes because the bhikṣus had lost theirs; how is it that you, though already fully provided with the three robes, took those robes to give them to the group of six bhikṣus and to others?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!
Among the many bases for the outflows, this is the first violation of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu has lost his robes, had them stolen, burned, or carried away by water, and a householder or householder’s wife who is not a relative should of their own accord invite him and offer many robes, that bhikṣu should receive the robes with contentment."
"If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "non-relative" and "relative," these are as explained above.
"Householder" and "householder’s wife" are as explained above.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as above.

If one robe is lost, he should not take another; if two robes are lost and only one remains—whether it be double-layered, triple-layered, or quadruple-layered—he should tear it down [to the required size]. Whether it be a *saṃghāṭī*, an *uttarāsaṅga*, or an *antarvāsaka*, if all three robes are lost, that bhikṣu should receive robes with a sense of contentment.
Contentment is of two kinds:
contentment for laypeople and contentment for renunciants.
Regarding contentment for laypeople, they accept whatever clothing is given by white-robed householders.
For a renunciant, contentment consists of the three robes.

If a layperson, out of their own volition, offers many robes to a bhikṣu, and if the robes are fine, thin, or not durable, he should take them and make them into double, triple, or quadruple layers; he should provide borders for the shoulders, apply patches to areas prone to dirt and grease, and install hooks and fasteners.
If there is any remainder, he says to the householder:
"What shall this remaining robe-material be cut and made into? If the donor says:
"I do not give this to you because you have lost your robe; we are giving it to the Venerable ourselves.
If he wishes to accept it, he may do so.
If a bhikṣu accepts a robe beyond what is sufficient for his needs, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate assembly.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe], one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate toward the senior monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], having taken clothing beyond what is sufficient, have committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal motion (jñapti):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu [Name] has committed an offense of forfeiture by taking more clothing than is necessary for his needs; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that I accept the confession of the bhikṣu [Name]."
"Recite thus. Having made this announcement, one may then accept the confession and should say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind."
He replies, “Yes. The Saṃgha should then return this robe to the bhikṣu;
it should be given by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as follows.
Within the Saṃgha, one should appoint a capable person to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) as described above, making the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) by taking clothing beyond what is sufficient; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let the Sangha now take this robe and return it to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion. "Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) by accepting robes beyond what is necessary for his contentment;
he now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha now returns these robes to this bhikṣu.
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved and given the robe to the bhikṣu [Name]. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus settled."
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, at the time of returning it, someone instructs them, saying:
"Do not return it."
If [one does not return it], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not return it, but instead makes it a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), or sends it to another person, or makes it into one's own three robes (*tricīvara*), or makes it into a *pārikkāra* robe, or intentionally damages it, or burns it, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined—it is in all such cases a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one takes what is sufficient; or if one takes less than what is sufficient; or if a householder gives much cloth; or if the cloth is fine, thin, or not durable; or if one makes a robe of two, three, or four layers; or if one adds borders, patches, or reinforcements for soiled areas, and attaches buttons and hooks; or if there is leftover cloth remaining and one says to the householder: "What shall I do with this?"
If a householder says,
"I am not giving this because you have lost your robe; we wish to give it to you,
Venerable Sir," and one accepts it with such intent, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The seventh section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went for alms; when it was time, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī. Arriving at the house of a lay devotee to beg for food, he overheard the husband and wife of that layman discussing together:
"The śramaṇa Nanda is an old acquaintance of ours; we shall take this price for cloth and purchase such a garment to give to that bhikṣu."
Having finished his almsround, he returned to the monastery and saw the Śākya son Upananda, to whom he said:
"It is unprecedented, Gautama; you are a person of great merit."
He then asked, "What have I done that you say I am a person of merit? He replied:
"I entered the city to beg for alms and heard a householder and his wife discussing together, saying:
'The Śākya son Upananda is an old acquaintance of ours; we shall take this price for cloth and buy such a garment to give him.'"
He then asked, "Is this truly so? The bhikṣu replied:
"It is indeed so. He asked again:
"In what place does that householder live?"
"In which direction does the gate face?
The bhikṣu replied, "The house of the lay devotee is at such-and-such a place; the gate faces such-and-such a direction."
Bhadananda immediately said to the bhikṣu, "This is an old donor whom I have known for a long time; he has always supported me, just as you have said.
The next morning, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, entered the city of Śrāvastī, went to the house of the lay devotee, and spoke to him:
"Do you truly wish to give me a robe?
He replied, "I was speaking these words while in a secluded place."
Bhadanta said to the householder:
"If you wish to give me a robe, it should be made broad, large, new, fine, and sturdy so that I may accept and wear it;
if it is not suitable for me to accept and wear, what is the use of it?"
At that time, the householder spoke with derision, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they seek much and are never satisfied. Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
Yet he forcibly demands fine garments from others; how can such conduct be considered the True Dharma?
Although the donor may never grow weary of giving, the recipient ought to know contentment; why then does he immediately seek out a secluded place to converse in private?
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard this, he censured the Śākya son Upananda, saying:
"How can you thus forcibly demand fine robes from people?
The bhikṣu then immediately returned to the city, went to the saṃghārāma, and related these circumstances to the other bhikṣus.
Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame;
they reproached the Śākya son Upananda, saying: "How can you thus forcibly solicit fine robes from others?"
Having reproached him, he went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of monks and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How can he thus forcibly demand fine robes from others?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife intends to provide the price for robes for a bhikṣu..."
"Take this price for robes and buy such a robe to give to such-and-such a bhikṣu.
That bhikṣu then goes to the householder's home and says:
"Buy such a robe and give it to me."
"For the sake of [its] beauty.
If one obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
A lay devotee personally invited a bhikṣu and asked him,
"Venerable sir, what kind of robe do you require?
The bhikṣu, harboring doubts in his mind, did not answer.
If a householder offers to provide whatever a bhikṣu may request, he should respond accordingly.
Suppose a householder wishes to make an expensive robe for a bhikṣu, but that bhikṣu is one who has few desires and is content, not needing a robe of great value but desiring something less costly.
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to seek what they desired at their own discretion.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus who have few desires and are content to seek that which is inferior."
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:
"If a householder or a householder’s wife provides the price for robes for a bhikṣu, intending to purchase such a robe and give it to a certain bhikṣu."
If a bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to a householder’s home and says:
"Excellent, householder!
Buy such and such a robe for me and give it to me."
"For the sake of [personal] preference.
If one obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Householder" and "householder's wife" are as defined above.
"Price of robes" refers to money, gold, pearls, lapis lazuli, shells, jade, necklaces, or wrought and unwrought gold.
Regarding "robes," there are ten types as mentioned above.
Regarding "requesting," there are two kinds:
first, requesting the price; second, requesting the robe itself.
Regarding the seeking of price: when a donor provides a garment of great value, one may seek even as much as an increase of one-sixteenth of a coin.
Regarding the seeking of cloth: one says to the householder, "Make a garment of such width and length," even increasing it by a single thread.
If a bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to seek a costly and wide robe, and if he obtains such a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If one seeks [an item] and does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, baring the right shoulder, removing one's leather sandals, prostrating toward the Elder, and with the right knee on the ground, join the palms and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

I, Bhikṣu [Name], having previously not received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, went to seek out and obtain a robe of high value; I have thus committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having not previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, went to seek a high-priced robe; he has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, he should then accept the confession and say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind.
That bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
The Saṃgha should immediately return this robe to the bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) as follows.
A competent person for the formal act should be appointed from within the Saṃgha as described above, and he should make the following announcement:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, previously not having received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, went with a robe to seek a robe of high value; he has committed an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now returns this robe to the bhikṣu, so-and-so.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so, having previously not received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, went to seek a garment of high value and thereby committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to give that robe to such-and-such a person; because the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If that bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the robe within the Sangha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs him, saying,
"Do not return," it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one does not return it, but instead makes it a pure gift (*śuci-dāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into the three robes (*tricīvara*) oneself, makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), deliberately damages it, burns it, or wears it until it is worn out through frequent use—in all such cases, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one goes to seek [food] after having previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā*; if one seeks with moderation and in reduced measure; if one seeks from relatives; if one seeks from those who have left the household life; if one seeks on behalf of another; if another seeks on one's own behalf; or if one obtains it without having sought it at all. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The eighth section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when it was time for alms, a bhikṣu who went begging for food dressed himself, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Proceeding from house to house, he came to the residence of a layman and heard the husband and wife of that layman discussing together:
"The śramaṇa Upāli, son of the Śākyas, is an old acquaintance of ours; we should buy such a robe and give it to him."
Furthermore, he heard two laypeople, a husband and wife, discussing in another place:
"Bhadanta Nanda is an old acquaintance of ours; we should buy such a robe and give it to him."
Then, having finished his almsround, that bhikṣu who subsists on alms returned from Śrāvastī to the monastery. There he saw the Śākya son Upananda and said to him:
"Venerable one, you are a person of great merit."
Bhadanta asked, "On what grounds do you call me a person of great merit? He replied:
"Recently, when I entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms, I went from house to house in due order until I reached the home of a certain layman, where I heard a husband and wife discussing together:
'The śramaṇa Vāṣpa-nanda is an old acquaintance of ours; we should buy such a robe and give it to him.'"
Furthermore, he heard another householder and his wife discussing together:
"Bhadananda is an old acquaintance of ours; we should buy such a robe and give it to him. Bhadananda asked:
"Is it truly so? He replied, "It is truly so."
He asked again:
"Where is the house of the householder?
In which direction does its gate face?"
He replied, "It is at such-and-such a place, with its entrance facing such-and-such a direction.
Then, Bhadanta said to that bhikṣu:
"These householders are truly my donors; they constantly provide for me with offerings.
The next morning, having dressed and taken his bowl, he entered the city of Śrāvastī and went to the houses of those two householders, saying to them:
"Do you people truly intend to make robes for me?"
The householder replied,
"In a secluded place, such words were spoken.
Then the Śākyan son Upananda said:
"If you wish to make a robe for me, you may make a single robe together; it must be made extremely large, vast, and sturdy so that I may accept and wear it.
If it does not meet these requirements for acceptance, it is not what I need."
When the householders heard this, they immediately began to criticize and disparage him, saying:
"The Śākya son Upananda knows no contentment and lacks a sense of shame; yet he proclaims to others of himself:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
Thus, seeking with greed and not knowing contentment—how can there be the True Dharma?
Although the giver may never grow weary, the receiver ought to know sufficiency.
They come to seek and beg, speaking in private places.
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard this, he rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"How can you forcibly demand a robe from a person?
Then that bhikṣu returned to the saṃghārāma outside the city and recounted these circumstances to the other bhikṣus.

Among the bhikṣus who heard this, there were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the Śākyaputra Upananda, saying: "How can you forcibly demand robes from others?"
Having rebuked him, he went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How can he forcibly demand a robe from another person?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man, Baddhananda!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If two laymen and a laywoman wish to provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣu..."
"We have prepared the price for such robes and are giving it to a certain bhikṣu.
When that bhikṣu arrives at the houses of the two lay devotees, he speaks thus: "Excellent!"
"Procure such and such a price for a robe and give it to me, so that we may make a single robe together," [saying this] for the sake of obtaining something fine.
If she obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus. At that time, a householder invited the bhikṣus at their own discretion and asked them, "What kind of robe do you require?
The bhikṣu, being in doubt, did not answer.
If a householder invites a bhikṣu to accept robes at his own discretion, the bhikṣu should respond accordingly.

Suppose a householder wishes to provide a bhikṣu with a robe of high value, but that bhikṣu is of few desires and contented, not requiring a robe of high value, but rather one of inferior quality; the bhikṣu, being hesitant, does not dare to request it as he wishes.
The Buddha said:
“I permit the bhikṣus who have few desires and know contentment to seek one that is inferior.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:”
If two laymen or two laywomen provide the price for a robe for a bhikṣu, saying:
"With this price for a robe, buy such a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
This bhikṣu, having not previously received an invitation from the householders for the *pravāraṇā*, went to the houses of two householders and spoke thus: "Excellent!
Householders, provide such and such an amount for the price of cloth and give it to me; let us together make one robe."
"Because he desires it.
If he obtains a robe [in this manner], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
The layman and the wife of the layman are as described above.
The price of the robe is as described above.
As for the robe, there are ten kinds, as described above.
There are two kinds of seeking, as mentioned above.

If a bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation for a self-indulgent gift, seeks and obtains a costly robe or a large robe, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika).
If one goes to seek it and does not obtain it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This *naiḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate group.

"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.

Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
One should say to that bhikṣu:
"Reprove your own mind.
That bhikṣu then says:
"Yes. The Saṃgha should then immediately return the robe to that bhikṣu. The formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* should be performed as follows.
A competent person capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent; the Saṃgha shall return this robe-cloth to this bhikṣu.

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. This bhikṣu so-and-so, having previously not accepted an invitation to the *pravāraṇā*, went and sought it, obtaining a robe-cloth of high value. He has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."

If someone instructs another, saying,
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Whether one makes a formal relinquishment (*pariśuddhi*), gives it away to another, makes it into the three robes oneself, makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), or intentionally damages it—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one goes to seek [an item] because another person has previously received an invitation for *pravāraṇā*; if one seeks something inferior among expensive, high-quality garments; if one seeks from a relative; if one seeks from a renunciant; if one seeks on behalf of another; if another seeks for oneself; or if one obtains it without having sought it at all. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

At that time, there was a high minister in the city of Rājagṛha who was a close friend of the Śākya son Upananda; they frequented one another, and the minister sent a messenger with the price for a robe, saying:
"The Śākya son Upananda is an old acquaintance of mine whom I have always held in high esteem; take this price for a robe and purchase such a garment as this to give to him."
Then that messenger, carrying the price for the robes, went to the monastery and, arriving at the place where Upananda was, spoke thus:
"Excellent! You are a person of great merit."
He asked, "On what grounds do you say that I am a person of merit? He replied:
"In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a high minister who sent me with this price for clothing to purchase such a garment as this to give to you.
He asked again, "Is it truly so?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Then, Vāḍananda asked:
"Where is the minister's residence?
In which direction is its entrance? He replied:
"The house is in such-and-such a place, and the door faces such-and-such a direction.
Bhaṇḍana said, "It is exactly as you say;
this is an old donor of mine with whom I have long been acquainted, who constantly makes offerings to and serves me."
At that time, there was another householder in the city of Śrāvastī who was an old friend of Upananda and with whom he frequently socialized.
Upananda the Śākyaputra then took this messenger into the city of Śrāvastī and went to that householder’s home, saying:
"A high minister in the city of Rājagṛha has sent this messenger with the price for robes to have me make a robe; please accept it on my behalf."
The householder then took charge of it for him.
At another time, the minister asked the messenger, "Previously, I sent a messenger with the price for robes to be given to Baddhananda; once the robes were made, did he give them to me to wear?"
The messenger replied,
"He will not wear it.
The minister then sent another messenger to say to Bāṣpananda:
"I previously sent a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to you, yet you did not purchase one. Of what use is my robe to me?
You should send it back now.
When Baddhananda heard these words, he immediately hurried to the house of that elder and said:
"The robe-fund I previously entrusted to you—I now require a robe; please make one for me.
At that time, the elders of Śrāvastī had assembled, and there was a prior regulation that anyone who did not attend would be fined five hundred coins.
The elder replied, “There is a regulation for this great assembly: anyone who fails to attend shall be fined five hundred coins.
I am going there now for a moment; Venerable Sir, please wait briefly until I return from the assembly, so that I do not have to pay the fine of five hundred coins.”
Bhadanta replied, "That will not do;
first take this price for the robes and have them made for me.
When the elder had finished having the robes made with that price, the assembly adjourned. Because he had not arrived, the crowd fined him five hundred coins.
At that time, the elder spoke with reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have caused the multitude to fine me five hundred coins.
Then, among the householders in the city of Śrāvastī, those who did not believe in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha all joined together in reproach, saying:
“O śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya!
You know no contentment and possess no sense of shame or remorse; yet you claim of yourselves:
‘We know the True Dharma.’”
"In this way, what kind of True Dharma is there that causes a householder not to attend the assembly and instead pay five hundred coins?
From this day forward, one should not associate with, prostrate to, inquire after, serve, or make offerings to such persons."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they rebuked Upananda, saying: "How could you cause the multitude to fine the elder five hundred coins?"
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked Upananda, saying:
“What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done.”
"How is it, Bāḷhika, that you have caused this householder to be fined five hundred coins by the assembly?
Having thus rebuked Bāḷhika with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“O fool! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If a bhikṣu, having been sent by a king, a great minister, a brāhmaṇa, a householder, or a householder’s wife as a messenger, is given the price for a robe with these words:
"Take this price for a robe and give it to such-and-such a bhikṣu."
That messenger went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"Venerable Sir!
These robe-funds have been sent for your sake; please accept them."
That bhikṣu should speak to that messenger as follows:
"I should not accept this price for robes; if I require a robe, I shall accept one that is timely and pure."
The messenger said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir,
is there anyone who manages affairs for you?"
The monk who needs robes should say: "There are.
Whether they be monastery attendants or lay devotees (upāsaka), these are the attendants for the monks who constantly perform services for them."
Then that messenger went to the person in charge, gave him the price for the robe, and returned to where the bhikṣu was, speaking to him thus:
"Venerable One!..."
"Regarding the attendant named so-and-so whom you have mentioned, I have already given him the price for the robe.
Venerable sir!
You should know the time and go there; you shall obtain the robe."
A bhikṣu who needs robes should go to the person in charge of robes affairs and, after reminding them two or three times, should say: "I need robes."
"If, after being reminded two or three times, he obtains the robe, that is well;
if he does not obtain the robe, he should stand silently before him four, five, or six times."
If he stands silently before [the donor] for four, five, or six times, and obtains the robe, it is well;
if he does not obtain the robe, and yet seeks to obtain it beyond that number of times, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he does not obtain the robe, he should go himself or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was received and say:

The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "king" is one who has attained sovereignty and is not subject to anyone else.
A "great minister" is one who stands at the king's side.
"Brahmins" refers to those born into the brahmin caste.
"Householders" refers to all those living at home, excluding kings, royal ministers, and brahmins.
"A householder’s wife" refers likewise to a woman living at home.
"The price of the robe" is as described above.
"Robes" are of ten kinds, as described above.
Regarding "recalling": if the person in charge of affairs is at home, in the market, or at a place of work, one should go to that location two or three times and say:
"I now require robes; please make robes for me."
One who acts as a reminder is as follows:
if one reminds them two or three times and obtains the robe, it is well;
if the robe is not obtained, one should go before them four, five, or six times and stand silently.
Standing before him is that attendant, whether he be at home, in the marketplace, or at his place of work;
one should stand silently before him. If the attendant asks:
"For what reason are you standing here?
The bhikṣu replied,
"You should know for yourself."
If that person says, "I do not know," and there is another person who does know, the bhikṣu should say to them:
“That person knows it.
If a bhikṣu makes one statement, he breaks two periods of silence;
if he makes two statements, he breaks four periods of silence.
If he makes three requests and remains silent for six turns,
and if a bhikṣu goes beyond two or three requests and stands silently for more than six turns, and if he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group, a number of individuals, or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate faction.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the object] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the Elder, and with the right knee touching the ground and palms joined, make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], having requested a robe three times by speaking and having stood silently six times, have obtained a robe and committed an offense of forfeiture; I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The one receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, [named] So-and-so, having requested a robe three times and having stood silently for six turns, has obtained a robe and committed an offense of forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
You should say to that bhikṣu:
"Reprove your own mind.
He shall reply:
"Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that bhikṣu’s robe; it should be given by performing a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) in this manner.
A competent person for the *karman*, as described above, should be appointed from within the Saṃgha to make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having spoken three times and stood silently for six times to solicit a robe, has obtained a robe and committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let this bhikṣu’s robe be returned to him.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having requested a robe three times and having stood silently for six turns, has obtained a robe and committed an offense of forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.

If that bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the robe in the midst of the Saṃgha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
saying, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (pariśuddha-dāna), or makes it into one's own three robes (tricīvara), or makes it into a miscellaneous robe (pārihārika-cīvara), or sends it to another person, or wears it repeatedly until it is ruined, in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one obtains a robe after requesting it three times; or if one obtains a robe by standing silently for six times.
If one does not obtain a robe, one should go in person or send a messenger to the place where the price for the robe was received and say:

If he says, "I do not need it;

I shall give it to you as a gift," that bhikṣu should, at the proper time and with gentle speech and skillful means, request the robe. If it is given for the sake of a *pārihārika* (extra) item, and he requests it at the proper time, with gentle speech, and by skillful means, there is no offense in receiving it.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were making new bedding from mixed wild silkworm cotton. They went to the houses of sericulturists and said, "We require cotton."
He replied, "Wait a moment;
you must come when the cocoons are ready.

The group of six bhikṣus stayed nearby waiting and watching. While the cocoons were being boiled, the silkworm pupae made a noise. When the householders saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying: [text continues]

among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding by mixing wild silk cotton with [other materials], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
