if it is made but not completed, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to make [an article], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense;
if it is made but not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This should be discarded; as for discarding it therein, one should chop it finely with an axe or a hatchet, mix it with clay, and apply it to walls or to earthen platforms.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one obtains something already completed; or if one uses an axe or hatchet to chop and hack it into pieces to mix with mud, or applies it to a wall or a plastered mound—there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.

"Why have you made such bedding out of pure white wool?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of significance so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding, he should use two parts of pure black wool, three parts of white, and four parts of variegated wool."
"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"White" refers to that which is naturally white or has been dyed white.
"Variegated color" refers to hair on the head, hair on the ears, hair on the legs, or any other variegated-colored hair.
If a bhikṣu wishes to make a woolen bedding mat of forty *pala*, it shall consist of twenty *pala* of pure black wool, ten *pala* of white wool, and ten *pala* of variegated wool.
If one wishes to make a bedding of thirty *patra*, fifteen *patra* shall be pure black and fifteen *patra* half-white and half-spotted.
If one wishes to make a bedding of twenty *patra*, ten *patra* shall be pure black, five *patra* white, and five *patra* spotted.
If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding for himself using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to make it and it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate faction.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate toward the Elder, and with the right knee on the ground and palms joined, make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture by making a new bedding with two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated.
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, [named] So-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) by making a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated.
He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience as I accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, he should then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind. The bhikṣu replies:
"Yes. The Sangha shall immediately return the bedding and requisites to that bhikṣu. The formal authorization (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) should be granted as follows.
A competent person for the formal act should be appointed from within the Sangha, as described above, and the following motion (jñapti) should be made:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) by making a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated."
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to return these bedding requisites to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion.
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense involving forfeiture by making a new bedding without using two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated wool.”
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha shall now take these bedding materials and return them to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning these bedding materials to this bhikṣu, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to the return of these bedding and requisites to this bhikṣu so-and-so; because the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If that bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the bedding and requisites within the Sangha, does not return them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs another, saying,

"Do not return it," or if the object is transformed into a pure gift (pariśuddha-dāna), or if it is sent to another person, or if it is repeatedly spread out and damaged, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta; for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.

This is what constitutes an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one makes a new bedding with two parts black, three parts white, and four parts variegated; if white is insufficient and one uses variegated material to complete it; if one makes it entirely variegated; if one obtains one that is already finished; if it has been cut into pieces; if it has been dyed a discolored color (kāṣāya); if it is made into a pillow; if it is made into a mattress; if it is made into a lying mat; if it is made into a small square sitting mat; if it is made into a cushion to wrap a bowl; if it is made into a case for a razor; or if it is made into socks, a hot-weather towel, or a cloth to wrap leather sandals—in all these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The thirteenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were dissatisfied with their bedding—whether it was too heavy or too light, or whether they disliked it for being too thin or too thick—and without giving up their old bedding, they made new ones. Thus constantly seeking out bedding, they accumulated a great quantity of it.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you, out of dislike for your old bedding—whether it be light or heavy, thin or thick—not discard the old and instead make new bedding, resulting in such a great abundance of bedding?"
Having reproached themselves, they went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of this, the Blessed One assembled the community of monks and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the group of six monks:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"O Group-of-Six Bhikṣus!
Why do you take offense at bedding—whether it be light or heavy, thin or thick—and make new bedding while hoarding up such large quantities?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These foolish men of the group of six!
Among the various bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this time forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat and keeps it for six years, or less than six years, and without relinquishing the old one makes another new bedding or mat, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu afflicted with consumption who possessed a very heavy refuse-rag bedding. Having a minor reason to travel among the people, he thought to himself:

"The Blessed One has laid down a rule: 'If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding and keeps it for six years, or less than six years, and without having discarded his old bedding makes another new one, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"
"I have now contracted the disease of dry consumption; these bedding materials are heavy, and I wish to travel through the human world for a minor matter.
What should I do? He spoke thus to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!"

"I am currently suffering from the disease of consumption, and my rag-robe bedding is extremely heavy; there is a minor matter requiring me to travel among the people, yet I am unable to carry it with me."
"Venerable sirs, inform the Blessed One on my behalf; whatever instructions the Blessed One may give, I shall carry them out.
Having heard these words, the bhikṣus went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for that bhikṣu.

This bhikṣu shall go before the Saṃgha, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, prostrating toward the elders, placing his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, make the following announcement:”
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am afflicted with the disease of consumption. Having a minor matter to attend to, I wish to travel among the people; however, I possess a refuse-rag bedding that is extremely heavy and cannot be carried on my journey."
"I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for making new bedding.
Thus he should repeat this up to three times.
Then, a person capable of performing the formal act should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and he should make the following motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has contracted the disease of consumption and wishes to travel through the human world; however, his refuse-rag bedding is heavy. He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the manufacture of new bedding."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of providing new bedding and seating for this bhikṣu.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so by name, suffers from the disease of consumption; his discarded bedding is heavy, and he wishes to travel through the human world. He now requests the Saṃgha to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for him to prepare a new set of bedding.
Now the Saṃgha is performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for that bhikṣu, so-and-so, to provide him with new bedding.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha providing that bhikṣu, so-and-so, with new bedding, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.

"The Sangha has already consented to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so to have a new bedding set made; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:

If a bhikṣu makes a new bedding or mat and uses it for six years, or less than six years, yet does not discard the old one before making another new one—unless by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu, having less than six years remaining [until his robes must be renewed], does not discard his old bedding but instead makes new bedding, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he makes it but it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to make it and it is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate assembly.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the Elder (upādhyāya), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!..."

"I, bhikṣu [name], having less than six years remaining [in my seniority], have not discarded my old bedding and have instead made new bedding; I have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, being less than six years [in seniority], did not relinquish his old bedding but instead made new bedding; he has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession and say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind.
The bhikṣu replied, "I shall."
The Sangha should then return the bedding and requisites to that bhikṣu. It should be granted by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) as follows.
A competent person for the *karman* should be appointed from within the Sangha as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu, named So-and-so, being less than six years [in seniority], has not discarded his old bedding but has instead made new ones; he has thus committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant that this bedding be returned to this bhikṣu.
The motion is thus stated.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, being less than six years [senior], has not discarded his old bedding but has instead made new ones; he has committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha."
The Sangha now returns this bedding to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha returning this bedding to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Sangha has already consented to the return of that bhikṣu’s bedding; the Sangha consents by remaining silent, and thus this matter is so upheld.
If that bhikṣu, having relinquished the bedding within the Sangha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs another,
saying, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one converts it into a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), or sends it to another person, or repeatedly spreads it out and damages it, or uses it for something other than bedding, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

when the Sangha has granted permission; when six years have elapsed; when one discards an old [robe] and makes a new one within less than six years; or if none are available, one makes it oneself, or someone else makes one for one, or one obtains one that is already finished. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the fourteenth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One sent someone to invite him for a meal.

It is the constant custom of the Buddhas that after the bhikṣus have accepted an invitation, they go from room to room. They saw old sitting mats left in disorder in various places: in the heated hall, in the teaching hall, on the walking path, on the stone for washing feet, or on the raised mounds before the doors; or on pegs, or on dragon-tooth stakes, or on clothing racks, or on rope beds and wooden benches, or on pillows, or on floor coverings—scattered everywhere with no one to collect them.
Having seen this, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"The bhikṣus find their sitting mats either too heavy or too light, or say they are too thick or too thin; yet they do not discard the old ones to make new ones. Consequently, there are many sitting mats scattered about everywhere, with no one to collect them."
"How can I now allow the bhikṣus to use old sitting cloths? He further thought:

"I shall permit the bhikṣus to make new sitting cloths, provided they take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and patch it onto the new one for the purpose of discoloring it."
After the World-Honored One had finished eating, he assembled the community of bhikṣus for this reason and said to them:

"Just now, after the community of monks had accepted my invitation, I went on a round through the various rooms and saw that the old sitting mats were scattered everywhere in disarray, with no one to collect them."
Having seen this, I thought to myself:
"Some of the bhikṣus say my sitting mat is heavy; some say it is light; some say it is thin; and some say it is thick."
Because they did not discard their old sitting mats to make new ones, the old ones lay scattered everywhere with no one to collect them.
I thought to myself:
"How can I cause the bhikṣus to use old sitting mats?"
He further thought to himself:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to make new sitting mats; they should take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one in order to spoil its color."

"Therefore, I permit the bhikṣus to make new sitting mats; however, they must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one in order to achieve a discolored appearance."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had permitted bhikṣus to make new sitting mats, provided they take a piece of old material one span in length and breadth and patch it onto the new material in order to spoil its color.
When making a new sitting mat, one does not take a piece of old material—one span in length and breadth—and patch it onto the new material for the purpose of discoloring it.

When the monks heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six monks, saying:

"How is it that while the World-honored One has permitted the monks to make new sitting mats, he also instructed that one must take a piece of old material—one span in length and breadth—and patch it onto the new material for the purpose of discoloring it?"
"Yet when you make new ones, why do you not attach a patch, even one span in length and breadth, from the old ones onto the new?

Having thus rebuked them, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is what should not be done."

How is it that I have established a training rule for the bhikṣus: "If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth and attach it to the new one, in order to spoil its color."
"Why do you, sirs, make new sitting mats without taking a piece of one *vitasti* (span) from an old one to patch it upon the new?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣus are foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of transgressing the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, he must take a piece from an old one, measuring one span in length and breadth, and patch it onto the new one in order to spoil its color."

If one makes a new sitting mat and does not attach a piece from an old one measuring one span in length and breadth to the top of the new one for the purpose of discoloring it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

When that bhikṣu makes a new sitting mat, if his old sitting mat has not yet deteriorated or developed holes, he should take it to be washed, dyed, and treated; he should stretch it out by pulling and tugging, and cut from it a piece one span (vitasti) in length and breadth to be applied either to the edge or to the center of the new mat for the purpose of discoloring it.
If a bhikṣu does not take an old [mat] and patch it onto a new one for the purpose of discoloring it, but instead makes a new sitting mat that is completed, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one causes another to make [an article] and it is completed, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate assembly.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monk (upādhyāya), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."

I, Bhikṣu [Name], have made a new sitting mat without patching the old one over the new one for the purpose of discoloring it; thus I have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should first make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, made a new sitting mat without patching the old one onto the new one for the sake of discoloration; thus he has committed an offense involving forfeiture.
He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, he should then accept the confession.
You should say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind. The bhikṣu replies:
"Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that bhikṣu’s sitting mat to him, granting it by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
It should be granted in this manner.
The Saṃgha shall appoint a capable person to perform the formal act (karmavācanā) as described above, making the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu so-and-so has made a new sitting mat without patching the old one over the new one for the sake of discoloration; he has thus committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika)."
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent that this sitting mat be returned to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has made a new sitting mat without patching the old one over the new one for the sake of discoloration; he has thus committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this sitting mat to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this sitting mat to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Sangha has already consented to grant that certain bhikṣu his sitting mat; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If a bhikṣu, having relinquished his sitting mat within the Sangha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs:
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddhaka-dāna*), or accepts it for oneself, or sends it to another person, or if it is damaged by repeated sitting, in all such cases there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one cuts up old [material] and patches it onto new material to change its color;

or if the person has nothing else and makes a new one themselves; or if someone else makes it for them; or if one obtains one that is already finished; or if one makes it using purely old material. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the fifteenth [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was traveling on a road and obtained a great deal of wool; he threaded it onto the end of a staff and carried it along the road.
When the lay devotees saw this, they looked upon him with disdain and reproached him, saying:
"How can a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, engage in the trade of selling wool?"
He then asked, "Venerable sir!
Would you sell this wool?"

When the bhikṣus heard these words, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they reproached Upananda, saying:
"How could you take wool, thread it onto the end of a staff, and carry it along the road?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that should not have been done."
"How could he carry a load of wool on his own back while traveling on the road, only to be ridiculed by a householder?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!..."
Among the various bases of outflows (*āsrava*), this was the first transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu traveling on a road obtains wool and there is no one to carry it, he may carry it himself for up to three *yojanas*."
"If no one else carries it, and one carries it oneself for more than three *yojanas*, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu is traveling on a road, or if he obtains wool while at a residence, he may take it if he requires it.
If there is no one to carry it, one may carry it oneself for up to three yojanas.
If there is someone to carry it, one should say to that person:
"I now have this object; you should assist me in carrying it."
"Furthermore, in that case, a bhikṣu must not assist in carrying [the goods] during this interval.
If he assists in carrying them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he causes a bhikṣuṇī to carry them for more than three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If one causes a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to carry [wool] beyond three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
With the exception of wool, if one carries other items—such as milk, leaves, grass, kusa grass, hemp, or *cīrapaṇi*—beyond three yojanas, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
Furthermore, if one carries other items on the head of a staff while walking, it is also a *dukkaṭa*.
This *niḥsargika* offense must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monk (*sthavira*), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], having carried wool for a distance exceeding three yojanas, have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture; I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having carried wool for more than three *yojanas*, has committed an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
You should say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind. The bhikṣu replies:
"Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that wool to the bhikṣu by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
It should be given in this manner.
Within the Saṃgha, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has traveled three *yojanas* carrying wool, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
“If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the wool of bhikṣu so-and-so be returned to him.
This is the motion. “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having carried wool for a distance exceeding three yojanas, has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha now take this wool and return it to this bhikṣu.
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha holding this wool and returning it to this bhikṣu, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has already approved of giving the wool to the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If a bhikṣu has relinquished [an object] within the Saṃgha and does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
Furthermore, if someone instructs him, saying:
"Do not return it," [he likewise commits an offense].
To say this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Furthermore, if one subsequently makes it a pure gift (*śuddhaka-dāna*), or sends it to another person, or uses it repeatedly, all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.

For a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense; this is what is called an offense. There is no offense if one carries it for three *yojanas*, or less than three *yojanas*;

or if someone else carries it for them, or instructs another to carry it, such that they do not assist in carrying it further along the way; or if they cause a bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī to carry it for three *yojanas*; or if they carry wool, woolen cloth, or woolen cords; or if they carry hair from the head, hair from the neck, or hair from the legs; or if they are making a cap, a sunshade, or wrapping leather sandals—in all these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Section sixteen concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Kapilavastu in the Nyagrodha Park of the Śākyas.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took sheep’s wool to make new sitting mats, having bhikṣuṇīs wash, dye, and card it for them.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, while dyeing the wool, stained her hands with the dye. She went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the reason, asked intentionally:
"For what reason, Gautamī, do your hands have dye upon them, as if you were a dyer?
She immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The group of six bhikṣus wished to make new sitting mats; they brought wool and asked us to wash, dye, and card it, which is why our hands are soiled.
Having said this, they prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet and returned to their respective dwellings.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking on purpose, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly have new sitting mats made, and cause bhikṣuṇīs to wash, dye, and tear them?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How can you cause bhikṣuṇīs to wash, dye, and card wool?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The group of six bhikṣus are fools!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has a bhikṣuṇī wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*."
After the Blessed One had thus laid down the precept for the bhikṣus, the bhikṣus each harbored doubts and did not dare to have their relatives, the bhikṣuṇīs, wash, dye, or card wool.
The Buddha said:
"I permit those who are relatives to wash, dye, and card [the wool].
From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus:..."
"If a bhikṣu causes a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding those who are not relatives and those who are relatives as described above:
if a bhikṣu washes, dyes, or card wool for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it constitutes three *niḥsargika-pāyattikas*.
If one instructs [a person] to wash, dye, and tear [the cloth], and that person washes and dyes it but does not tear it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs [a person] to wash, dye, and tear, and that person washes and tears it but does not dye it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to wash, dye, and tear [the robe-material], and that person does not wash, dye, or tear it, there are two *niḥsargika-pāyattikas* and one *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to wash, dye, and tear, and that person does not wash, dye, or tear it, there are three *dukkaṭas*.
If one causes a *śrāmaṇerī* or a *śikṣamāṇā* who is not a relative to wash, dye, or tear [the robe], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This [robe] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monks (*sthavira*), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have had a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, had a bhikṣuṇī who was not a relative wash, dye, and card wool; he has thus committed an offense involving forfeiture and expiation."
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I accept the confession of this bhikṣu, [Name].
Thus is the formal announcement (jñapti).
After he has made this request, one should then accept his confession and say to that bhikṣu:
"Reprove your own mind."
The bhikṣu replied, “So be it.
The Saṃgha shall then return that wool to the bhikṣu by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman).
It should be granted in this manner.
The Saṃgha shall appoint a capable person for the formal ritual (karmavācanā) as described above, and make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense involving forfeiture by having a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative wash, dye, or card wool; he now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this wool back to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
The motion is thus made: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has caused a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative to wash, dye, or card wool; he has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika)."
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha shall now take these woolen fibers and return them to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning these woolen fibers to this bhikṣu, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."
"The Saṃgha has already consented to give the wool to that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
Once the wool has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, if one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs:
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), or sends it to another person, or uses it repeatedly, or intentionally damages it, in all such cases there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is likewise entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one causes a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative to wash, dye, or card [the wool]; or if one washes, dyes, or cards it for the sake of a sick person; or if one washes, dyes, or cards it for the sake of the Saṃgha, the Buddha, or a stūpa.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The seventeenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a high minister within the city who was a close friend and acquaintance of Upananda.
On another occasion, he obtained a large quantity of pork and immediately instructed his wife:
"The Śākya son Upananda is my dear friend; set aside a portion for him."
The wife then gave him his share.
At that time, on a day of public festival in Rājagṛha, the people performed various musical entertainments and did not sleep all night.
The minister’s son was also among them and did not sleep all night; being exhausted with hunger, he asked his mother:
"Is there any meat remaining?
His mother replied, "The meat is exhausted; only the flesh of the Śākya son Upananda remains."
The boy immediately gave the money to his mother and said, "Take this money and buy more meat for Baddhananda; give this meat to me.
The mother then took the money and bought the meat.
The Śākya son Upananda, having dressed in the morning and taken his bowl, went to the house of a high minister and sat down upon a seat.
At that time, the minister’s wife said to him:
"Recently I obtained a great quantity of meat; the elder instructed me, saying:"
“Bāḷhika, the son of the Śākyas, is an old acquaintance of mine; I shall set aside a portion for him.
I immediately accepted this instruction and reserved a portion for the Venerable One.
On the day of a festival, my son played until midnight without sleeping; exhausted by hunger, he came to me asking for meat, so I gave him five coins and said to him:
“Go to the market and buy some meat for me; give this meat to me.
I immediately gave it to him.
Now that I have this money and am about to buy meat, Venerable Sir, you might wait a moment.
Bhadanta asked, "Did he give me the money for my sake? He replied:
"Yes," [he replied].
"If you would give me money for my sake, there is no need for meat.
At that moment, he placed the money on the ground and gave it to him.
When Upāli (Baddhalita) had obtained this money, he took it and left it at a marketplace stall before departing.
When the lay devotees saw this, they all reproached him, saying:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya are trafficking in wealth; they take money and leave it at a stall before going away."

When the monks heard this, among them were those who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Upananda, saying:
"How could you take money yourself and place it on a shop counter before departing?"
Then the king and his ministers assembled and spoke thus:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, may take hold of gold, silver, or coin; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not renounce gold, silver, coins, precious treasures, pearls, necklaces, or raw and wrought gold."
At that time, there was another great minister in the assembly named Muktika, who addressed the other ministers, saying:
"Do not speak such words as:
'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, may handle gold, silver, or coins, and do not relinquish precious treasures, pearls, or necklaces.'"

Why is this? I have heard from the Tathāgata himself that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, must not handle gold, silver, or money; the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, must renounce precious treasures, pearls, and necklaces.
At that time, the minister Maṇicūḍa, who was powerful, capable, and skilled in eloquent speech, caused all people to rejoice, believe, and understand.
He then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One:
"Was what I have just said not in contradiction with the Dharma?"
The Buddha told the great minister:
"What you have said is highly beneficial for the True Dharma and contains no error or contradiction. Why is this so?"

A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, must not handle gold, silver, or money; a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, renounces precious gems, pearls, and necklaces, and does not wear ornaments for the sake of beauty.

You should know this now: if one were permitted to handle gold, silver, or money, and were not to renounce pearls, necklaces, and precious gems, then one would likewise have to accept the five objects of sensual desire.
If one indulges in the five desires, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākyas.
Great Minister!

You should know now that if you see a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākyas who takes me as his teacher yet grasps gold, silver, coins, or precious gems, you may know with certainty that this is not the dharma of a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākyas.
I have spoken these words:
"If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of building a dwelling, seeks timber, bamboo, grass, or tree bark, he may accept them; however, he should not accept them for his own personal use."
"Great Minister, you should know that the sun and moon have four afflictions:
they are not bright, not pure, unable to illuminate anything, and devoid of majestic power.
What are these four?"

Asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist are the great afflictions of the sun and moon; when encountering these afflictions, they are neither bright nor pure, unable to illuminate anything, and devoid of majestic power.
Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas likewise have four afflictions; being without clarity, without purity, unable to illuminate anything, and lacking majestic spiritual power, they are also like this.
What are the four?

If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa does not renounce drinking alcohol, does not renounce sexual desire, does not renounce holding gold and silver in hand, and does not renounce wrong livelihood for their own sustenance—these are called the four great afflictions of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, which cause them to be without clarity, without purity, unable to illuminate anything, and devoid of majestic power.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured Upananda, they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, by means of countless skillful methods, rebuked Upananda:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How could he take money in his own hand, place it upon the stall, and depart?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu takes money, gold, or silver with his own hand, or instructs another to take it, or accepts it when placed on the ground, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "money," it refers to that which bears inscribed images.
If a bhikṣu takes gold, silver, or money with his own hand, instructs another to take it, or accepts it when it is placed on the ground, it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This should be relinquished. Regarding this relinquishment: if there is a faithful and devoted park-keeper or an upāsaka, one should say to them, "This is not for me to keep; you should know this."
If that person takes it back and gives it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should accept it for the sake of that person's property and instruct a *kappiya-kāraka* (a steward) to take charge of it.
If he obtains pure robes, alms bowls, needle cases, or sitting mats (*niṣīdana*), he should trade for them and then formally accept and keep them.
If that upāsaka, having taken it, gives a pure robe, an alms bowl, a sitting mat, or a needle case to a bhikṣu, it should be accepted and kept.
If he takes it and does not return it, another bhikṣu should be told:
"The Buddha has given this instruction: 'It was given to you for the sake of purification; you must return this item to that bhikṣu.'"
If other bhikṣus say, "He has not returned," one should go there in person and say:

“The Buddha has taught that for the sake of purification, this was given to you; you may now give it to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to your preceptor (upādhyāya), to your co-preceptor, to your teacher (ācārya), to your co-teacher, to your relatives, friends, or acquaintances, or return it to its original owner.”
Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause them to lose the merit of that faithful offering.
If one does not speak to that person to let them know, "Look at this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, this constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one says: "Know this; look at this.
Or if there is a faithful lay follower (*upāsaka*) or a park-keeper who has confidence and devotion, one should speak to that person, saying:
"This object is not for me to accept; you should know this.
If that person, having accepted it, returns it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should accept it on their behalf and entrust it to a *śucika* (a pure person) to hold.
If later one obtains pure robes, an alms bowl, a needle case, or a sitting mat (niṣīdana), one may accept them in exchange for what was held [previously] and keep them.
If that person, having taken [the items], gives back pure robes, a sitting mat, or a needle case, one should accept and keep them.
If that person is unwilling to give it back, the other bhikṣus should say to him:
"The Buddha has given an instruction: 'We gave this to you for the sake of purification; you must return this object to that bhikṣu.'"
If that person does not give it, one should go there oneself and say:
"The Buddha taught that a bhikṣu may purify [the gift] by giving it to you.

Whether you give it to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to your preceptor (upādhyāya), to your co-preceptor, to your teacher (ācārya), to your co-teacher, or to your kinsmen and acquaintances; or if you are instructed to give it back to the original donor—it is so that the faithful offering of that person shall not be lost."
All such cases are without offense. Those without offense are:
when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The eighteenth [chapter] concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.
Then, Baddhananda went to the marketplace and exchanged money for more money, taking it away with him.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, exchange money for money; they are truly skilled at buying and selling.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured Upananda, saying:
“How can one carry away money after exchanging it for coins?
The bhikṣus went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can one exchange money for money?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. Regarding "various kinds of buying and selling":

this refers to exchanging finished gold for finished gold, exchanging it for unrefined gold, or exchanging it for both finished and unrefined gold; exchanging it for finished silver, exchanging it for unrefined silver, exchanging it for both finished and unrefined silver, or exchanging it for coins. It also refers to exchanging unrefined gold for finished gold, exchanging it for unrefined gold, or exchanging it for both finished and unrefined gold; or exchanging it for finished silver, exchanging it for unrefined silver, exchanging it for both finished and unrefined silver, or exchanging it for coins.

One exchanges finished gold for unfinished gold, unfinished gold for finished gold, or finished and unfinished gold for finished gold; one exchanges it for finished silver, unfinished silver, finished and unfinished silver, or for coinage.
Exchanging wrought silver for gold, and likewise exchanging it for money, is also like this.
Exchanging unwrought silver for gold, and likewise exchanging it for money, is also like this.
Exchanging both wrought and unwrought silver for gold, and likewise exchanging it for money, is also like this.
Exchanging money for gold, and likewise exchanging it even for more money, is treated in the same manner.
There are eight kinds of money:
gold coins, silver coins, iron coins, copper coins, white tin coins, lead-tin coins, wooden coins, and coins made of foreign resin.
If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of buying and selling of precious objects, exchanging finished gold for finished gold, or even exchanging it for coin, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This must be relinquished. Regarding this relinquishment: if there is a monastery attendant or a faithful lay follower (*upāsaka*), one should say to that person:
"This object is not something I ought to accept; you should know this."
If that person, having accepted it, returns it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should accept it for that person's sake and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure" person) take charge of it.
Later, if he obtains a pure robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, he may trade them for it and keep them.
If that person, having accepted it, gives the bhikṣu a pure robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, he should accept and keep them.
If that person, having accepted it, does not give them to the bhikṣu, he should instruct another bhikṣu to say:
"The Buddha has given this instruction: 'It was given to you for the sake of purification; you should return these items to that bhikṣu.'"
If another bhikṣu still does not respond when spoken to, one should go to him personally and say:

"The Buddha has given this instruction: 'I gave this to you for the sake of purification; you may now give it to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to your upādhyāya, to your fellow upādhyāya, to your ācārya, to your fellow ācārya, to your relatives, friends, or acquaintances, or return it to the original donor.'"
Why is this? Because one does not wish to cause the donor's gift of faith to go to waste.
If a bhikṣu does not speak to that person, saying:
"To look at it and know it" constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one says to that person:
"Having seen it, one knows it.
If there is a park-keeper who is a faithful lay follower (*upāsaka*), one should say to him: "This is not for me; you should know this."
If that person, having received it, returns it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should accept it for that person’s sake and have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) take charge of it.
If he obtains a pure robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, he may trade them and keep them as his own.
If that person, having received it, gives the bhikṣu a pure robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, he may accept and keep them.
If that person, having received it, does not return it to the bhikṣu, the bhikṣu should instruct another bhikṣu to say:
"The Buddha has a teaching: 'I gave this to you for the sake of purification; you should return it to this bhikṣu.'"
If he does not return it, [the monk] should go to him in person and say:
"The Buddha has given this instruction: 'Give this to you for the sake of purification.

You should give it to the Saṃgha, to a stūpa, to your preceptor (upādhyāya), to the preceptor's fellow-student, to your teacher (ācārya), to the teacher's fellow-student, to your relatives, friends, or acquaintances; or else return it to the original donor.'"
Why is this? It is because one does not wish to cause the loss of faith regarding the gift of material things.
If one uses money to purchase ornaments for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, or exchanges ornaments for money for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The nineteenth section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was traveling on a road in the kingdom of Kośala when he went to an uninhabited village. Having arrived at the village, he exchanged fresh ginger for food; after eating it, he departed.

At that time, Śāriputra was also wandering among the people in the kingdom of Kośala. He arrived at the village of Anāthapiṇḍada, and when it was time, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village to beg for food. Gradually approaching the house where food was being sold, he stood there in silence.
Having seen him, the rice-seller asked:
"Venerable sir! What do you seek?"
He replied, "Householder! I require food."
That person said, "Bring the price. He replied:
"Householder! Do not speak such words; this is not for us to do. That person said:
"Previously, Bhaṇḍa exchanged ginger for food and left after eating it.
Venerable Sir,
why do you not accept it?"
When Śāriputra heard these words, he was filled with shame and remained silent.
Having finished his almsround, he returned to the saṃghārāma and related these circumstances to the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a non-Buddhist ascetic in the city of Śrāvastī who obtained a costly garment and thought to himself:
"What use have I for this expensive garment?"
"I would rather exchange these for other robes.
He further thought:
"Where shall I trade for robes?"
"Only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, delight in wearing fine robes; they will surely be able to exchange them.
He then took the robe to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus, "I wish to trade this robe;
whoever wishes to trade, let us exchange it together."
Having seen this, Upāli said to him, "Come tomorrow; I shall exchange robes with you.
Upāli was skilled at mending clothes; that very night he washed his old robe and pressed it until it shone like a new one.
In the early morning, those non-Buddhists took their robes and went to the monastery, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Who wishes to exchange robes?
Let us trade together."
Then, Vāṇa took out his robe and showed it to him, saying to the outsider, "I will give this robe to you; will you give me yours? He replied:
"I give it to you.
Thereupon, they immediately exchanged their robes.
Having received the robe, the non-Buddhist returned to the park where he resided and showed it to the other non-Buddhists, saying:
"You should know that the robes I am currently wearing are easily obtained compared to these robes.
Among the non-Buddhists, one who possessed wisdom said:
"You have been deceived by another."
For what reason?
The garment you wear is new, fine, vast, and sturdy; this garment is actually an old one, merely beaten and polished until it has a luster that resembles something new.
The non-Buddhist practitioner then took the robe and returned to the monastery, saying to Upananda:
"I am returning the robe to you; you must return it to me."
Bhadanta said, "I have already finished trading with you; it cannot be returned.
The outsider said:
"My robe is new, fine, vast, and sturdy; your robe is worn and old, merely polished and smoothed to look as if it were new.
Baddhālita replied, "Once I have traded with you, I shall never give it back."
Those non-Buddhists criticized him, saying:
"Is it that this is one's own robe, yet though sought it cannot be obtained?
My robe is new, fine, vast, and sturdy; yours is tattered and worn."
"How is it that we have gone forth together, yet having traded clothes with one another, you do not allow for a reversal of the transaction?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Upananda: "How can you exchange ginger for food, and then trade clothing with an outsider while refusing to permit a reversal?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"Why is it that while ginger is easy to consume, you trade clothing with non-Buddhists yet do not permit a reversal?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I permit the five groups of renunciants to engage in mutual trade among themselves. They should examine and determine the value for themselves; they must not engage in haggling or bargaining like the methods of merchants. They must not trade with others [of different categories]; they should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) conduct the trade. If there is regret, a reversal is permitted."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu engages in various kinds of trade and commerce, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. Regarding "various kinds of trading": exchanging what is timely for what is timely; exchanging what is timely for what is untimely; exchanging what is timely for what is permitted for seven days; exchanging what is timely for what is permitted for life; exchanging what is timely for a *pālikāla* [robe]; exchanging what is untimely for what is untimely; exchanging what is untimely for what is permitted for seven days; exchanging what is untimely for what is permitted for life; exchanging what is untimely for a *pālikāla* robe; exchanging what is untimely for what is timely; exchanging what is permitted for seven days for what is permitted for seven days; exchanging what is permitted for seven days for what is timely—and so on, including the case of the untimely, which is likewise.
Exchanging for as long as one lives what lasts for as long as one lives, and so on up to exchanging for seven days, is likewise.
Exchanging for a *parikalpa* what lasts for a *parikalpa*, and so on up to exchanging for as long as one lives, is likewise.
Regarding "selling": the price is one *kārsāpaṇa*, yet it is repeatedly raised and lowered.
Regarding "selling at an increased price": the price is one *kārsāpaṇa*, but one says it is worth three *kārsāpaṇas*.
Regarding "selling at a further increased price": the price is one *kārsāpaṇa*, but one says it is worth five *kārsāpaṇas*; the same applies to buying.
If a bhikṣu acquires anything through various kinds of trade, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he does not acquire it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This *niḥsargika* article must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At the time of abandoning it, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], having acquired wealth through various kinds of trading, have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense involving forfeiture by engaging in various kinds of trade to acquire wealth; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement in this manner, one should thereafter accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reprove your own mind.
That bhikṣu will then reply:
"Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that object to the bhikṣu, granting it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) as follows.
A competent person capable of performing the *karman* within the Saṃgha should be appointed to make this proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed an offense involving forfeiture through various acts of trading; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to return this object to that bhikṣu, so-and-so."
The motion is thus stated.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so has committed an offense involving forfeiture by acquiring wealth through various kinds of trade; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this object to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this object to this bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Saṃgha has already granted the object to that bhikṣu; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If, after having relinquished [the object] within the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
saying, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one converts it for the purpose of pure giving, or sends it to another person, or intentionally damages it, or uses it repeatedly, or keeps it for other purposes, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one exchanges goods with members of the fivefold assembly of renunciants, provided one personally ascertains that there is no disparity in value as in the practice of market trade; nor is there an offense if one does not exchange with others, or if one causes a *kappiya-kāraka* (a "pure person") to conduct the exchange; furthermore, there is no offense if one repents and returns the item, or if one exchanges ghee for oil, or oil for ghee.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian and others.
[Chapter on] the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas, Part Four. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept alms bowls; they would keep those that were fine and set aside those that were not. In this manner, they constantly sought out fine bowls, and the number of bowls they kept eventually became many.
At that time, several laypeople came to visit the dwelling and saw that the group of six bhikṣus possessed many alms bowls. Having seen this, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are insatiable in their desire and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim of themselves:
'We understand the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what is there of the True Dharma?
You have accumulated so many bowls that you are like a potter’s shop selling earthenware.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"Why is it that you keep alms bowls, retaining those that are fine while setting aside those that are not, constantly seeking out fine bowls so that the number of bowls you keep has become so great?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it that he keeps alms bowls, retaining those that are fine while setting aside those that are not, constantly seeking out fine bowls so that the number of bowls he keeps has become so great?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"The foolish man, Upananda!..."
Among the various bases for outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms bowl beyond the permitted limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, Ānanda obtained a precious bowl from the kingdom of Soma and wished to give it to Mahākāśyapa, because Kāśyapa habitually used bowls from this country.
As Kāśyapa was not present, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu keeps an extra bowl, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
"I have now obtained a precious bowl from the kingdom of Soma and intend to give it to Mahākāśyapa.
However, he is not here; I do not know what to do.
At that time, Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: ‘If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
I have now obtained a precious bowl from the kingdom of Soma and wish to give it to Mahākāśyapa.”
"But he is not here; we do not know what has become of him.
The Buddha asked Ānanda, "In how many days will Mahākāśyapa return?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "Ten days from now he shall return.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma accordingly. By means of countless skillful methods, he praised those who practice the dhūta austerities, who are disciplined and orderly, who have few desires and are content, and who delight in renunciation. He then addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep an extra alms-bowl for up to ten days.
The precept should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu keeps an extra alms-bowl, provided it has not been formally dedicated to another, he may do so for a maximum of ten days.'"
If one exceeds [the limit], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
As for the "bowl," there are six kinds:
There are iron bowls, bowls from the country of Soma, bowls from the country of Uggara, bowls from the country of Ugasa, black bowls, and red bowls.
In brief, there are two main types:
iron bowls and clay bowls.

The large size is three *dōng* (pecks), and the small size is one and a half *dōng*; these are the measurements for a bowl. One should maintain them in this manner and should perform the ritual of pure giving (*śuddhaka-dāna*).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, or even up until the tenth day, and keeps it until the dawn of the eleventh day, all the bowls obtained during those ten days constitute a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, does not obtain one on the second day, obtains one on the third day, and obtains one on the fourth day, and continues in this manner until he obtains a bowl on the tenth day, such that at the appearance of the dawn on the eleventh day, all the bowls obtained during those nine days constitute *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offenses.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, obtains one on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third day—and thus continues in descending order until he does not obtain a bowl on the tenth day—the formulation of the rule is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, does not obtain one on the second or third days, but obtains one on the fourth day, and continues in this manner until obtaining a bowl on the tenth day, such that the dawn of the eleventh day appears, then all the bowls obtained during those eight days become subject to the *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains a bowl on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third or fourth day, and then obtains a bowl on the fifth day—thus alternating in descending order, even until he does not obtain a bowl on the ninth or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, does not obtain a bowl on the second, third, or fourth day, and obtains a bowl on the fifth day—continuing in this manner until he obtains a bowl on the tenth day—and then the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the bowls obtained during those seven days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains a bowl on the second day, but does not obtain a bowl on the third, fourth, or fifth day—and thus continues to decline in this manner until he does not obtain a bowl on the eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the phrasing of the rule is also as stated above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, or fifth day, and then obtains a bowl on the sixth day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, all the bowls obtained during those six days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains one on the second day, but does not obtain a bowl on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day—and thus continues in descending order until he does not obtain a bowl on the eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth day, and then obtains a bowl on the seventh day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and until the dawn of the eleventh day, all the bowls obtained during those five days become *niḥsargika* (requisites for forfeiture).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains one on the second day, but does not obtain a bowl on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, and then obtains a bowl on the eighth day—thus descending in sequence until he does not obtain a bowl on the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day, and then obtains a bowl on the eighth day—or even if he obtains it on the tenth day—and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, all the bowls obtained during those four days become *niḥsargika* (relinquishable).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains one on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day—thus descending in this manner—and continues until he does not obtain one on the fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day, the formulation of the sentence is likewise.
