If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, but does not obtain one on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day, and then obtains a bowl on the tenth or eleventh day, then all the bowls obtained during those three days become subject to forfeiture (*niḥsargika*) when the dawn of the eleventh day appears.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains a bowl on the second day, but does not obtain a bowl on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—following this descending sequence down to four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, or ten days without obtaining a bowl—the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, and does not obtain a bowl on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, or ninth day, but obtains a bowl on the tenth day, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the bowls obtained during those two days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day and obtains one on the second day, but does not obtain one on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day—the sequence of decline continues in this manner down to the case where he does not obtain a bowl on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day; the formulation of the sentence is also as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, but does not obtain a bowl on the second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, or tenth day, and the dawn of the eleventh day breaks, the bowl obtained during that first day becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu receives an alms-bowl on the first day that is not formally offered (apariśuddha-datta), receives an alms-bowl on the second day that is formally offered (pariśuddha-datta), and receives alms-bowls on the third day through the tenth day that are not formally offered, then when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, all the bowls received during those nine days become subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains a bowl on the first day, obtains a bowl that has not been formally offered (*apariśuddha-datta*) on the second day, obtains a bowl that has been formally offered (*pariśuddha-datta*) on the third day, and obtains a bowl that has not been formally offered on the fourth day—and so on, descending in this manner until he obtains bowls both not formally offered and formally offered on the tenth day—the formulation of the sentences is also as above.

The phrases regarding giving it away to another are as above; the phrase regarding losing it is as above; the phrase regarding intentionally damaging it is as above; the phrase regarding making it into something other than a bowl is as above; the phrase regarding taking it with the intent of treating it as a personal possession is as above; and the phrase regarding forgetting it and leaving it behind is as above—all constitute *niḥsargika* offenses.
If one commits an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika*) but, without relinquishing the bowl, trades it for another, there is one *niḥsargika-pāyattika* and one *duṣkṛta*.
This forfeited bowl must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At the time of abandoning it, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], have kept an extra bowl for more than ten days and have thus committed an offense of forfeiture; I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, he should then perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has kept an extra bowl for more than ten days and has committed an offense of forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should accept his confession and speak to that bhikṣu as follows:
“Reproach your own mind. The bhikṣu replied, “Yes.”
The Saṃgha should immediately return the bowl to that bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
A person capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and he should make the following proclamation:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
This bhikṣu, [name], has kept an extra alms bowl for more than ten days and has thus committed an offense involving forfeiture; he now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to return this bowl to this bhikṣu, [name].
The announcement is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has kept an extra bowl for more than ten days and has thus committed an offense involving forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this bowl to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this bowl to the bhikṣu so-and-so should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Sangha has already consented to the return of this bowl to the bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If, after the bowl has been relinquished within the Sangha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs another, saying,
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transfers it as a pure gift, or sends it to another person, or intentionally destroys it, or makes it into something other than a bowl, or uses it repeatedly, in all such cases there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if, within ten days, one has performed a formal act of relinquishment (*visuddhi-dāna*), or given it away to another, or if one perceives it as having been stolen, lost, destroyed, or carried away by water; in these cases, there is no offense.

If the bowl is stolen, lost, burnt, or washed away; if it is taken for use or used because another gave it; or if the bhikṣu who was entrusted with the bowl dies, travels far, abandons the path, is robbed by bandits, is harmed by a wild beast, or is swept away by water—provided he does not give it to anyone else—he commits no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-first section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda’s bowl broke; he entered the city of Śrāvastī and said to a householder, “Do you know?
My bowl has broken; please provide one for me.”
Then that householder immediately purchased a bowl and gave it to him.
He then went to another householder's home and said, "My bowl is broken; please provide one for me."
Those householders then purchased bowls and gave them to him.
He broke one bowl and sought out many more bowls to keep.
At another time, those householders gathered together in one place.
A certain householder said to the other householders,
"I have now obtained immeasurable merit!
The householders asked:
“How does one obtain immeasurable merit?
He replied, “Venerable Sir, Venerable Upananda’s bowl was broken; I purchased a bowl and gave it to him, and for this reason I have obtained immeasurable merit.”
Each of the laypeople said to one another,
"We too shall obtain immeasurable merit.
Then other laypeople asked:
"For what reason have you obtained such immeasurable merit?
The lay devotees replied,
"Bhadanta Upananda’s bowl was broken, so we also purchased a bowl and gave it to him."
The laypeople all spoke with derision, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they pursue their desires without satiety, yet outwardly they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
To break one bowl and seek many bowls for the sake of accumulation—
though the donor may give without weariness, the recipient ought to know contentment."

When the monks heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta-austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the Śākyan son Upananda, saying:
"How can you break one bowl and seek to possess many bowls?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teachings]. It is something that should not have been done."
"How can he destroy one bowl and seek to keep many bowls?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man, Upananda!..."
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu possesses an alms bowl with fewer than five patches that is not leaking, yet seeks a new bowl for the sake of its appearance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."

That bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha and relinquish it; they should then pass it around until the lowest-ranking bowl is obtained and given to him to keep, and he should continue to keep it until it breaks—this is the proper time.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "five mends": a mend is made at intervals of two finger-widths apart.
If a bhikṣu’s bowl is broken but has less than five mends and does not leak, yet he seeks a new bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bowl that has reached five mends and is not leaking is discarded to seek a new one, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha; as for this relinquishment, it is to be relinquished within the Saṃgha at this residence.

One should go before the Saṃgha, baring the right shoulder, removing one's leather sandals, prostrating toward the senior monk, placing the right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], have a bowl that is broken with fewer than five mends and is not leaking; yet I have sought a new bowl, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, whose bowl was broken with fewer than five patches and not leaking, sought a new bowl and thereby committed an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now relinquishes it to the Sangha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu, [Name].
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement and accepted his confession, one should say to that person:
“Reproach your own mind. That bhikṣu replied, “I will.”
“If this bhikṣu’s bowl is expensive and of fine quality, it should be set aside; one should take the lowest and most inferior one and give it to him.
A formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) should be performed, and it should be given in this manner.”
Within the Saṃgha, one should appoint a capable person to perform the *karmavācanā* as described above, making the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has a bowl that is broken with fewer than five patches and is not leaking; yet he sought a new bowl, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, listen:
I announce that this almsbowl is given to the bhikṣu so-and-so. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, whose bowl has been broken and repaired fewer than five times yet remains leak-free, has sought a new bowl and thereby committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha. The Saṃgha now grants this bowl to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha giving this bowl to this bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to give this bowl to this bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
That bhikṣu, having made a formal motion (jñapti), should question the Saṃgha as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let this bowl be questioned in turn with the Elder."
"Thus is the announcement.
Having made this announcement, one should hold the bowl and present it to the senior monk (sthavira).
If the senior monk wishes to take this bowl, one should give it to him.
One should take the bowl of the senior monk and give it to the next in rank.

If it is given to that bhikṣu, he should accept it; he should not refuse to accept it out of a desire to protect the Saṃgha, nor should he, on this account, keep the very lowest bowl. If he does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If the second senior monk takes this bowl, he should take the bowl of the second senior monk and give it to the third senior monk; if he gives it to that bhikṣu, that bhikṣu should accept it. He should not refuse to accept it out of regard for the Saṃgha, nor should he accept the very lowest bowl on account of such a reason. If he accepts it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
In this manner, proceeding in turn until reaching the lowest-ranking monk, if one holds the bowl of this monk, one should return it to this monk.

If one holds the bowl of the very lowest-ranking monk and intends to give it [to another], at the time of giving, one should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), and it should be given in this way.
Within the Saṃgha, one should appoint a capable person to perform the *karmavācanā* as described above, making the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now bestow this bowl of the lowest-ranking monk upon the bhikṣu [Name] to be used until it breaks."
The motion is thus: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now bestows this bowl of the lowest-ranking monk upon the bhikṣu so-and-so to be used until it breaks."
"Whichever elders among you consent to giving this bowl to this bhikṣu, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to give this bowl to this bhikṣu. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

That bhikṣu must guard this bowl: he must not place it where tiles or stones might fall upon it; he must not place it beneath a leaning staff or beneath a leaning sword; he must not place it beneath a suspended object; he must not place it on a path; he must not place it on a stone; he must not place it beneath a fruit tree; and he must not place it on uneven ground.
A bhikṣu must not hold two bowls with one hand, except when the fingers are separated by the middle [of the bowls].
He must not hold two bowls with one hand while opening a door, except when he is exercising careful mindfulness.
One must not place [the bowl] inside the threshold or beneath the door leaf; one must not hold the bowl and place it under a corded bed or a wooden bed, except for temporary placement.
One must not place it between a corded bed and a wooden bed, nor at the corner of a corded bed or a wooden bed, except for temporary placement.
One must not stand and shake the bowl, nor even let it fall to the ground, so as to cause it to break.
That bhikṣu should not intentionally damage the bowl, nor should he intentionally cause it to be lost.
If he should intentionally damage it, he must not use it for anything other than a bowl.
If, after having relinquished the bowl among the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one instructs another not to return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one makes a formal gift of purification (viśuddhi-dāna), or sends it to another person, or intentionally loses it, or intentionally destroys it, or uses it for purposes other than a bowl, or uses it repeatedly [after relinquishment], in all such cases it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if the bowl has five patches or fewer; if one seeks a new bowl because the current one has fewer than five patches; if one asks for it from a relative; if one asks for it from a renunciant;

if one seeks it on behalf of another; if another seeks it for one's sake; if one obtains it without having asked for it; if one receives it in due order when bowls are being distributed to the Sangha; or if one purchases and keeps one by means of one's own funds—all these are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-second [section] concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Baddhānanda wished to sew a saṃghāṭī robe; he entered the city and went to the houses of various lay devotees, saying: "Do you know?
I wish to sew a saṃghāṭī robe and require thread."
The householder immediately gave him thread.
He then went to another householder's home and said, "I wish to sew a saṃghāṭī; I require thread."
Thus, as he begged here and there, he obtained a great deal of thread.
He thought to himself:
"I might seek thread from other places at another time to sew my saṃghāṭī."
"Robes are difficult for a bhikṣu to obtain; he ought to provide himself with the three robes. I shall now take this thread and have a weaver weave it into the three robes.
He then took the thread and went to give it to a weaver, who personally wound the bobbins and personally supervised the weaving.
When the laypeople saw this, they spoke with derision and reproach:
"Look at this Śākyaputra Bāḍananda! He has spun the thread with his own hands and personally supervised the weaver as he wove the three robes."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Upananda, saying: "How can you seek out so much thread and have weavers weave three robes for you, while you yourself roll the silk and personally supervise the weavers as they weave?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why do you seek thread so extensively, spin it yourself by hand, and personally supervise the weavers as they weave the three robes?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu personally solicits thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave it into a robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Begging for oneself" means begging for one's own sake in various places.
"Threads" refers to ten kinds, namely the ten kinds of threads for robes mentioned above.
If the weaver is not a relative and the one who provides the thread is not a relative, it is an offense for the one who is not a relative.
If the weaver is not a relative and the one who provides the thread is either a relative or not a relative, it is an offense for the one who is not a relative.
If the weaver is not a relative but the one who provides the thread is a relative, there is an offense for the one who is not a relative.
Or, whether the weaver is a relative or not, if the one who provides the thread is not a relative, there is an offense for the one who is not a relative.
Whether the weaver is a relative or not a relative, and whether the one who provides the thread is a relative or not a relative—it is an offense for the one who is not a relative.
Whether the weaver is a relative or not a relative, if the one who provides the thread is a relative, there is no offense; if the one who provides the thread is not a relative, there is an offense.
If the weaver is a relative, but the one who provides the thread is not a relative, the one who is not a relative commits an offense.
If the weaver is a relative, but the one who provided the thread is either a relative or not a relative—should it be someone who is not a relative—the offense is incurred.
If a bhikṣu personally begs for thread and has a weaver weave it into a robe, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
Whether one watches others weave, weaves for oneself, or makes skeins for oneself, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
This *naiḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], having personally requested much thread and had a weaver weave it into a robe, have committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, he performs confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having personally requested much thread and sent a weaver to weave a robe for him, has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (jñapti).
Having made this request, he should receive the confession and say to that bhikṣu:
"Reproach your own mind.
The bhikṣu shall reply:
"Yes. The Saṃgha should then return this robe to the bhikṣu by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), and it should be given in this manner.
From within the assembly, a person capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having sought much thread, had a weaver who was not a relative weave a robe for him; he has thus committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now return this robe to this bhikṣu.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having requested much thread, had a weaver who was not a relative weave a robe for him; he has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha returning this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to returning that robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If, after the robes have been relinquished within the Saṃgha, one does not return them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs them, saying,
"Do not return them," [it is likewise an offense].
To do so [with such intent] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Whether one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into one’s own three robes (*tricīvara*), makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), destroys it, burns it, makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly—all these constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if the weaver is a relative, or if the one who provides the thread is a relative; or if one weaves for oneself a bowl bag, a leather sandal bag, or a needle-cushion; or if one makes a meditation belt, a waistband, a cap, socks, a heat-retaining cloth, or a cloth for wrapping leather sandals. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-third [section] concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in the city of Śrāvastī who was a close friend and acquaintance of the Śākya son Upananda. He provided high-quality thread and had a weaver weave a robe of such and such a kind for the Śākya son Upananda.
Having given the thread to the weaver, he went to another village.
At that time, the weaver came to the monastery and said to the Śākya son Upananda:
"Venerable sir!..."
"It is unprecedented; this person possesses merit.
He asked, "By what means do you know that I am a person of merit?"
He replied: "A certain lay devotee gave me this thread, saying:
'The Śākya son Upananda is my close friend and spiritual mentor; weave such and such a robe for him and give it to him.'"
"For this reason, we know that you, Venerable One, are a person of great merit.
He asked again: "Is it truly so?"
The weaver replied, "It is indeed so. Then, Bhadanta said:
"If you wish to weave a robe for me, let it be vast and excellent, woven with such firmness and density that it may be fit for my use.
If it is not fit for my use, then it is unnecessary."
The weaver replied, "As the Venerable One has said, this thread is too little; it will not suffice to make a robe. Upananda said:
"You need only continue weaving; I shall seek out more thread to supplement it.

Then, in the morning, Upananda dressed himself, took his bowl, went to the householder’s home, sat down on a seat, and said to the householder’s wife, "The householder previously provided thread for a weaver to make a robe for me, but now the thread is insufficient."
Then the householder’s wife immediately took a thread box and placed it before him,
saying, "Take as much as you wish. Thereupon,
Upananda selected the finest threads at his leisure and, taking them with him, went to the weaver's house and said:
"I have obtained this much thread; please weave it for me into a robe.
The weaver replied, "The robe you are now having made, Venerable Sir, is being provided with insufficient payment."
Bhadananda replied, "Simply weave it for me, and I shall give you the payment.
When the weaver had finished the garment, he immediately delivered it to the householder's wife.
At that time, the householder returned from elsewhere and asked his wife, "I previously gave thread to a weaver to make a robe for the Śākya son Upananda; is it finished now?"
His wife replied, "The robe you were weaving is finished; it is here now.
The householder said:
"Bring the robe here so I may see it.
He immediately opened the chest, took out the robe, and showed it to him. The householder said to his wife, "This robe is not the one for which I previously gave instructions to be woven."
The wife replied,
"This very garment is it! The householder said:
"This garment is not the one for which you previously gave me the instructions to weave using this thread.
At that time, the wife explained the circumstances in detail.
The householder and his wife then put on the garment together to examine it. Just then, the Śākya son Upananda arrived at the householder's home and asked the householder:
"Is this the robe that you previously had woven for me? He replied, "It is."
He said, "If it is so, you may give it to me.
The householder then spoke with reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, accept gifts without satiety and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim of themselves:
'We know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such as these?"
"When begging for robes from others, although the donor may never grow weary of giving, the recipient should know contentment; one must not even speak of it in private.
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard these words, he censured the Śākya son Upananda, saying:
"How can you be so greedily attached to begging robes from others?"
Having rebuked him, he returned to the monastery and spoke of these matters to the bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked Upananda, saying:
"How can you be so greedily attached as to beg for robes from others?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can one be greedily attached to robes obtained by begging from others?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows (*āsrava*), this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when a householder or a householder’s wife has sent a weaver to weave a robe for a bhikṣu, goes to that person's house and says to the weaver:"
"Do you know? This robe is being made for me; weave it well so that it is wide, long, and sturdy, and I shall give you some price for it.
If that bhikṣu gives him a price down to the value of a single meal, and he obtains the robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, various householders invited the bhikṣus to accept robes at their own discretion, saying:
"Venerable sirs, what kind of robe do you require?"
The bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to answer.
The Buddha said:
"If one has previously been invited to accept robes through the *pravāraṇā*, one should answer according to one's own inclination."

If a householder wishes to give a monk a garment of high value, yet the monk—being of few desires and contented—desires something of lesser quality, he may hesitate out of apprehension and not dare to ask for it.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit those who are of few desires and know contentment to answer as they wish when asked about something that is not as it should be.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited in this manner:"
If a monk, when a householder or a householder’s wife has employed a weaver to weave a robe for that monk, goes to the weaver’s place before having been invited to do so and says:
"This robe is being made for me; weave it for me very well, making it wide, large, and firm, and I shall give you a small amount of payment."
"If that bhikṣu gives a price, even as much as the value of a single meal, and obtains a robe [thereby], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
The layman and the wife of the layman are as described above.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds of robes, as described above.
Regarding "one who requests," there are two kinds, as described above.
If a bhikṣu, without having previously received an invitation for a formal robe-offering, goes to seek robes and obtains them, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
if he does not obtain robes, it is a duṣkṛta.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single individual; it may not be relinquished to a separate assembly.
If the relinquishment is performed but is not validly accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe], one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monks, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"I, bhikṣu [Name], having previously not received an invitation for a self-invitation (pravāraṇā), went and obtained a fine robe; I have committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). I now forfeit it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus forfeited it, one must perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so previously went to seek a fine robe without having received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); he now relinquishes it to the Sangha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind.
That bhikṣu shall reply:
"Yes. The Saṃgha should then return the robe to that bhikṣu, granting it through a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as follows.
Within the Saṃgha, a person capable of performing the karman should be appointed as described above, and the following motion should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, previously went to seek fine robes without having received an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, previously went to seek fine robes without having first accepted an invitation for the *pravāraṇā*, thereby committing an offense of forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); he now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now returns these robes to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Whichever elders approve of returning this robe to this bhikṣu, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved the return of this robe to this bhikṣu. Since the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If that bhikṣu, having finished relinquishing the robe within the Saṃgha, does not return it, he commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs him, saying: "Do not return it," [he likewise commits an offense].
To say this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Whether one transfers it as a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), sends it to another person, makes it into one's own three robes (*tricīvara*), makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), intentionally destroys it, burns it, makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one has previously accepted an invitation for a *pravāraṇā* (self-invitation) and goes to seek [food], seeking only what is sufficient and avoiding excess; or if one requests from a relative, or requests from a renunciant, or does so for another's sake, or if another obtains it for one's sake, or if one obtains it without having requested it. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-fourth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda’s disciple was skilled at exhortation and conversion. To him, Upananda said:
“Come now and travel through the human world with me; I shall give you a robe.”
He replied, "So be it.
Then, before the others had even given their robes, Bhaddali gave his robe first. The other bhikṣus said to him:
"For what purpose did you travel among the people with the foolish Baddhālaka?
This fool does not know how to recite the precepts, does not know how to proclaim the precepts, does not know the poṣadha, and does not know the poṣadha-karman."
That bhikṣu then replied:
"If that is truly so, I shall no longer follow you.
Later, at another time, Upananda said to him:
"You may go together with those among humans.
He replied immediately, saying, "You may go by yourself; I cannot follow you."
Bhadanta said to him: "The reason I previously gave you this robe was that we intended to travel together through the human world.
Since you now do not wish to go, return my robe to me."
The bhikṣu said, "Since you gave me this robe, I shall not return it to you.
At that time, Upananda became enraged and stepped forward to forcibly seize the robe. The bhikṣu cried out in a loud voice:
“Do not! Do not! Hearing this sound, the bhikṣus in the various rooms all came together and gathered, asking the bhikṣu:
"Why did you shout so loudly?
At that time, the bhikṣu related the circumstances in detail to the other bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Upananda, saying:
"How could one give a robe to a bhikṣu and then, out of anger, take it back?
Having thus reproached him, she went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teaching]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How can one, out of anger and resentment, take back another's robe?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu has previously given a robe to another bhikṣu, and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or instructs another to take it away, saying, 'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
"If a bhikṣu returns a robe and the one who takes it accepts it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Robe" refers to the ten kinds of robes, as described above.
If a bhikṣu first gives a robe to another bhikṣu and later, out of anger, either takes it back himself or instructs another to take it back and conceal it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*;
if he takes it back but does not conceal it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If it is placed upon a tree, a wall, a fence, a stake, a "dragon-tooth" peg, a clothes rack, a rope bed, a wooden bed, a small cushion, a large cushion, a pillow, or a mat spread on the ground, and one takes it away from its place, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; if one takes it without removing it from its place, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate faction.
If the relinquishment is performed but is invalid, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the assembly, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the Elder, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], having already given a robe to a bhikṣu, later, out of anger and resentment, took it back; thus I have committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one must perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, later regretted it out of anger and resentment and took it back; he has thus committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of this bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
Having made this announcement, one should thereafter accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reprove your own mind. The bhikṣu replies:
“Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that bhikṣu’s robe by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), and it should be given in this manner.
From within the assembly, a person capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following proclamation:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having already given a robe to another bhikṣu, later, out of anger, took it back; he has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now return this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having given a robe to another bhikṣu, later, out of anger, took it back; he has thus committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. He now forfeits it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to the bhikṣu, so-and-so.
"Whichever elders approve of returning this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
"The Sangha has approved the return of this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so. Since the Sangha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If someone instructs them, saying,
"Do not return it," [it is likewise an offense].

To do so is a *dukkaṭa*. Whether one transfers it as a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*), makes it into one's own three robes (*tricīvara*), sends it to another person, makes it into a miscellaneous robe (*pārikkāra-cīvara*), intentionally destroys it, burns it, makes it into something that is not a robe, or wears it repeatedly—all these constitute *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if one says without anger:
"I regret it; I will not give you the robe; bring my robe back.
Or if that person, knowing the other's heart has changed, returns the robe.
If another person says, "This bhikṣu wishes to repent and return the robe to you," and if one borrows another's robe to wear,
and that other person wears it improperly, then taking it back is not an offense.

If one fears losing the robe, or fears it will be damaged, or if that person has violated the precepts, violated right view, or violated proper conduct; or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or have been expelled (*pabbājanīya-kamma*), or are subject to expulsion; or if for these reasons there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—in all such cases, taking [the robe] away without hiding or storing it is not an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.
[The twenty-fifth section ends. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Nine.
[End of] *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Ten, Part One, Section Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
[This is] the fifth section of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus were afflicted by wind-related ailments during the autumn months; their bodies became withered and they developed malignant sores.
While staying in a secluded place, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"These bhikṣus are now afflicted by wind-related ailments during the autumn months; their bodies are withered and they have developed malignant sores. I should now find a suitable method to enable the bhikṣus to take various medicines, such that these medicines may be consumed as if they were food—like rice or parched grain—without appearing coarse."
He further thought: "There are five kinds of medicines known to the people of the world—clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
I shall permit the bhikṣus to consume these five kinds of medicine; they may be used as food or as medicine, just like rice or parched rice, provided they do not appear coarse."
Then the World-Honored One arose from his quiet chamber and, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus, saying:
"While in my quiet chamber, I had this thought:

'Now that the autumn winds have disturbed the bodily humors of these bhikṣus, their bodies are withered and they have developed malignant sores. I should now find a skillful means to enable the bhikṣus to take various medicines; these should be treated as food or medicine, appearing no coarser than ordinary rice or parched grain.'"

I had this thought: "There are five kinds of medicine known to the world—clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar—which I permit the bhikṣus to consume. They should be treated as food or medicine, just like cooked rice or parched grain, so that they do not appear coarse."
"Therefore, I permit the consumption of the five kinds of medicine; when a bhikṣu is ill, he should take them.

At that time, the bhikṣus obtained rich and delicious food, yet even when they obtained meat or meat broth, they were unable to eat it in a timely manner; how much more so would this be the case for these five kinds of medicine?
Although they stored much medicine, their illnesses did not subside; their bodies became withered and dry, and foul sores broke out.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason have these bhikṣus' bodies become withered and dry, and foul sores broken out?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“These sick bhikṣus have obtained fine, rich food and meat and meat broth, yet they are unable to eat them in a timely manner; how much less could they possibly take the five kinds of medicine at the appropriate times?”
"Although he has stored many medicines, his illness does not improve; for this reason, his body has become withered and foul sores have broken out.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus, at the proper time or otherwise, to take these five kinds of medicine when there is a cause for illness."
At that time, the sick bhikṣus received rich and delicious food, including meat and meat broth, but being unable to eat it in time, they gave it all to their attendants.
After the attendants had eaten their fill, they did not eat the remainder themselves and simply discarded it; consequently, flocks of crows scrambled for the food, clamoring and calling out.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the reason yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are the crows crying out?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:
"When various sick bhikṣus receive rich and delicious food, such as meat and meat broth, they are unable to eat it in time and give it all to their attendants.
Once the attendants have eaten their fill, they do not eat the remainder themselves but discard it; consequently, the crows scramble for the food and cry out."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I permit those who are ill to eat leftovers; the attendant of the sick person may eat as much as they wish, whether they have already had enough or not."
At that time, after the bhikṣus had received their morning light meal, they entered the village to beg for food.
Having eaten their fill, they returned to the saṃghārāma and gave the food they had received in the morning to the other bhikṣus.
After the bhikṣus had finished their meals, they did not eat what remained and simply discarded it; the flocks of crows then clamored as they vied for the food.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the flocks of crows clamoring?"
Ānanda related the preceding circumstances in detail, explaining why the crows were crying out.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, whether you have already received the morning meal or have finished eating to fullness, you are permitted to eat by performing the *yavāśeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual."
One who performs the ritual for leftover food says:
"Venerable sir!
I have already eaten my fill; you may look at this and recognize it as such."
This constitutes the ritual for leftover food.
He should say to him:
"Restrain your greedy mind."
"One should eat according to this *khalupaścādbhakti* (remaining-food) procedure.

There are further circumstances and matters that are no different from what is explained in the *pāyattika* section regarding the *khalupaścādbhakti* procedure; therefore, to avoid tedious text, they are not set forth here again.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra was afflicted by a wind disorder;
his physician instructed him to consume five kinds of fat—bear fat, fish fat, donkey fat, pig fat, and makara fish fat—and permitted him to take these five kinds of fat.

If one receives [the oil] at the proper time, cooks it at the proper time, and strains it at the proper time according to the rules for consuming oil, yet receives it at an improper time, cooks it at an improper time, or strains it at an improper time, and then consumes it, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the countryside from Śrāvastī, accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine, making it difficult to obtain almsfood. There were then five hundred beggars who followed behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to sit beneath a tree. Then there was a mahout named Sīhavalāha, who was coming along that road with five hundred wagons carrying black honey-cake (śarkarā).
At that time, the elephant trainer saw upon the road the footprint of the Tathāgata, marked with a thousand-spoked wheel, complete with radiant signs, pure, bright, and beautiful.

Having seen it, he followed the tracks to seek him out and saw from afar the World-Honored One sitting beneath a tree. His countenance was upright and handsome; his faculties were tranquil and settled; he had attained supreme self-mastery and freedom, like a tamed dragon-elephant, or like a clear deep pool, pure both within and without. Having seen this, he gave rise to a heart of joy. He went before the World-Honored One at the place where the Tathāgata was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the elephant trainer, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy.
Having heard the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma and having given rise to a heart of joy, the elephant trainer made offerings to the bhikṣus, providing each person with one vessel of rock honey.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, saying:
"The Tathāgata has not yet permitted bhikṣus to accept black stone honey.
They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
“From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept black stone honey.
The Buddha spoke to the elephant trainer:
"Simply give one measure of stone honey to the bhikṣus.
Having received the Tathāgata’s instruction, the elephant trainer gave one measure of stone honey to the bhikṣus, yet there was still a remainder.
The Buddha said to the elephant trainer,
"Give him more as you wish, until he is fully satisfied. Then,
following the Buddha's instruction, the trainer did so three times, and thus there was still some left over.
The Buddha said to the elephant trainer,
"You may now take this remaining candied honey and give it to that beggar.
He gave it to him, yet there was still a remnant left over.
The Buddha spoke again to the elephant trainer:
"You may take this remaining stone honey and distribute it two or three times to the beggars until they are satisfied.
He then distributed it two or three times, yet there was still some left over.
The Buddha said to the elephant trainer:
"Now take this remaining honey-cake and place it on clean ground or in water free of insects. Why is this?"
I do not see any among the devas, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, or worldly people who can digest this residual rock-honey, except for the Tathāgata alone.

Then the elephant trainer took this remaining candied sugar and placed it in pure water free of insects; immediately, the water roared and shook, smoke issued forth, and fire blazed up, just like when a large red-hot iron is cast into water—the roar and shaking are fierce, and smoke issues and fire blazes—and so it was when the remaining candied sugar was poured into the water.

When the elephant trainer had witnessed this transformation, the hair on his body stood on end and he was filled with terror. He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the elephant trainer was terrified, immediately preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma to him: the merit of giving, observing the precepts, and rebirth in heaven; he censured the impurity of desire and praised renunciation.

Immediately upon his seat, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, and having attained the fruit of realization, he addressed the Buddha, saying:

"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. I pray only that the World-Honored One will grant me the status of an upāsaka; for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, and so forth, up to refraining from drinking alcohol."

At that time, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma and having attained joy and understanding, the elephant trainer rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.

Meanwhile, as the bhikṣus entered the village for alms, they saw stone honey being made by mixing it with various other substances; all of them had doubts and did not dare to eat it outside of the proper time.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I permit eating at improper times. The ritual procedure should be performed in this manner.”
When there was doubt regarding unrefined sugar that had not yet been fully processed, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat it.
When there was doubt regarding thin sugar that had not yet been fully processed, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat.
When he obtained thick stone honey (*phāṇita*), the Buddha said:
"I allow you to eat."

If white candied sugar is obtained, it is permitted to eat; if mixed water-candied sugar is obtained, it is permitted to drink; if sugarcane juice that is not yet fermented is obtained, it is permitted to drink, but if it is fermented, it is not permitted to drink; if one drinks it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
When sugarcane was obtained, the Buddha said,
"I allow it to be eaten at the proper time.
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from the realm of Magadha through the human world to the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, Pindola Bharadvaja was residing in this city; he had many acquaintances and a large following of disciples, and he received abundant offerings of ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar, which he shared with his disciples.

The disciples, upon receiving them, accumulated and stored them until the large jars, *kuṇḍikās*, cups, bowls, large and small alms-bowls, or even net-bags and water-strainers were filled. They hung them everywhere—on pegs, on ivory curved hooks, or between the windows and doors—until they overflowed and spread out, making the dwellings foul and stinking.
At that time, several householders entered the room and saw such a heap of various medicines scattered about in disorder; they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and seek much without satiety; yet outwardly they claim, 'We understand the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what is there of the True Dharma?
To thus hoard various medicines is no different from the treasury of King Bimbisāra.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the disciples of Piṅgalavatsa:
"How is it that they hoard various medicines, even to the point of hanging them everywhere so that they overflow and spill?
Having rebuked them, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the disciple of Pilindavatsa, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice. It is something that should not have been done."
"How can he store up such a multitude of medicines until they overflow and spread out, no different from the treasury of King Bimbisāra?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu is ill, he may consume leftover medicines—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—for up to seven days. If he consumes them beyond the seventh day, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "sick person" refers to one who has been instructed by a physician to take a specific kind of medicine.
"Medicine" refers to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.

If a bhikṣu acquires medicinal substances on the first day and keeps them, and acquires medicinal substances on the second, third, fourth, up to the seventh day, and when the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicinal substances acquired during those seven days constitute a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, does not obtain it on the second day, obtains it on the third day, and obtains it on the fourth day, and continues in this manner until he obtains medicine on the seventh day, such that when the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those six days becomes *niḥsargika*.

If a bhikṣu receives medicine on the first day, receives it on the second day, but does not receive it on the third day, and so on in descending order until he does not receive medicine on the seventh day—the formulation of the sentence is likewise for each case.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, but does not obtain it on the second or third days, and then obtains it from the fourth day up to the seventh day, such that when the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those five days becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and on the second day, but does not obtain it on the third or fourth day, and then obtains it on the fifth day—following this descending sequence until he does not obtain it on the sixth or seventh day—the formulation of the sentence is likewise.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, but does not obtain it on the second, third, or fourth day, and then obtains medicine on the fifth day, continuing until he obtains it on the seventh day, such that by the time the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those four days constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and obtains it on the second day, but does not obtain it on the third, fourth, or fifth day—thus descending in sequence—and continues until he does not obtain it on the fifth, sixth, or seventh day, the formulation of the sentence is as above.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, but does not obtain it on the second, third, fourth, or fifth day, and then obtains it on the sixth or seventh day such that the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those three days becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and on the second day, but does not obtain it on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day; and then obtains it again on the seventh day—following this descending sequence down to the case where he does not obtain it on the fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day—the formulation of the sentence is likewise.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, but does not obtain it on the second, third, fourth, fifth, or sixth days, and then obtains it on the seventh day such that the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those two days becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and obtains it on the second day, but does not obtain it on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day—thus descending in this manner down to the case where he does not obtain it on the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, or seventh day—the formulation of the sentence is likewise.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day, but does not obtain it on the second, third, or even up to the seventh day, and when the dawn of the eighth day appears, the medicine obtained during that first day becomes *niḥsargika*.

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and does not perform the formal act of relinquishment (apariśuddha-dāna), obtains medicine on the second day and performs the formal act of relinquishment, and then obtains medicine on the third day up to the seventh day without performing the formal act of relinquishment, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, all the medicine obtained during those six days becomes subject to forfeiture (niḥsargika).

If a bhikṣu obtains medicine on the first day and does not perform the formal act of relinquishment (apariśuddha-dāna), and on the second day he obtains medicine and performs the formal act of relinquishment, and on the third day he obtains medicine and does not perform the formal act of relinquishment—thus alternating in descending order—up until the seventh day when he obtains medicine and either performs or does not perform the formal act of relinquishment; the formulation of the offense is as stated above. The formulation regarding sending it to another person is also as stated above. Whether it is lost, intentionally destroyed, transformed into something that is not medicine, taken with the intention of treating it as a gift for a friend, or forgotten and carried away—the formulation of the offense is likewise the same in all these cases, and it constitutes a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If one has committed an offense involving forfeiture (niḥsargika-pāyattika) and does not relinquish the medicine, but instead exchanges it for other medicine, there is one *niḥsargika* and one *dukkaṭa*.
This forfeited item must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one relinquishes [the robe] but the relinquishment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the senior monk (*sthavira*), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!..."
"I, bhikṣu [name], have intentionally kept extra medicine beyond the seven-day limit; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, he should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept extra medicine beyond seven days, thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reprove your own mind. The bhikṣu replies:

"Yes. The Saṃgha shall then return that medicine to the bhikṣu. Whatever ghee or oil belonging to that bhikṣu has exceeded seven days, he shall smear it on the door-sill; the honey and rock sugar he shall give to the park-keeper.
If it reaches the seventh day, that which was relinquished should be given to a bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu should accept and eat it.
If it is less than seven days, it should be returned to this bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation) as follows.
Within the Saṃgha, one should appoint a capable person to perform the formal act (karmavācanā) as described above, making the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept surplus medicine and has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of patience, listen as I restore this medicine to this bhikṣu.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, intentionally kept extra medicine and thereby committed an offense involving forfeiture; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now returns this medicine to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this medicine to this bhikṣu, so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Saṃgha has consented; the medicine for this bhikṣu so-and-so has been returned, as the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent. This matter is thus upheld.
Having taken it, this bhikṣu shall use it to anoint his feet or to light a lamp.
If one discards [an item] among the Sangha and does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If someone instructs them, saying:
"Do not return it," [it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*].
To say this constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Whether one transforms it into a pure gift (*śuddhadāna*), gives it away to another, intentionally destroys it, burns it, makes it into something that is not medicine, or consumes it repeatedly—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if it is medicine kept for more than seven days; or if clarified butter or oil is used to smear a door hinge; or if honey or rock sugar is given to a park keeper; or if, upon reaching the seventh day, it is discarded and given to a bhikṣu to eat.
If he returns the robe to that bhikṣu before seven days have passed, and the latter uses it to anoint his feet or to light a lamp, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-sixth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, Viśākhā, the Mother, invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for a meal on the following day; that very night, she prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink.
The next morning, a maidservant was sent to the monastery to announce that the time had come; at that moment, it was raining heavily, with drops falling like elephant urine.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"All of you go out today to bathe in the rain. This is the last rain; as it rains here in Jambudvīpa today, you should know that the rain throughout the four continents is likewise."
When the bhikṣus had heard the Buddha’s instruction, they each went out from their dwellings and bathed naked in the rain.
At that time, the maidservant went outside the gate of the saṃghārāma and saw from afar that all the bhikṣus were bathing naked. Having seen this, she thought to herself:
“There are no śramaṇas here; these are all naked heretics.”
The maidservant returned and informed Vaisākha, saying:
"Mistress, you should know that those in the monastery are all naked ascetics; there are no śramaṇas there."
Viśākhā Mātṛ was clever and wise; she immediately thought to herself:
"Just now it rained, and some of the bhikṣus may have removed their robes and bathed naked in the rain."
The maidservant, being ignorant, thought they were naked ascetics.
He further commanded her, "Go quickly to the monastery and inform the bhikṣus:
'The time has now arrived.'"
She immediately went outside the gate of the saṃghārāma.
At that time, the bhikṣus had finished bathing, put on their robes, and returned to sit in meditation within the quiet chambers.
The maidservant stood outside the gate; seeing that the saṃghārāma was empty and silent with no one there, she again thought to herself:
"Now the saṃghārāma is empty and there are no bhikṣus here.
He immediately returned home and said to the Mother Viśākhā:
"Madam, you should know that the saṃghārāma is empty and there are no bhikṣus."
At that time, Viśākhā Mātṛ was wise and intelligent; she immediately thought to herself:
"The bhikṣus, having finished their bath, will surely enter a quiet room for meditation, yet this ignorant maidservant thinks there are no bhikṣus in the saṃghārāma."
He further instructed her again, saying, "Go quickly to the saṃghārāma and announce in a loud voice:
'The time has now arrived.
The maidservant immediately went to the saṃghārāma and announced in a loud voice:
"The time has now arrived.
Then the World-Honored One emerged from his private chamber and said to the maidservant, "You go on ahead; I shall follow immediately."
The Blessed One said to the bhikṣus, “Put on your robes and take up your bowls; the time has now come.

The bhikṣus, having received the Blessed One’s instruction, each took up their robes and bowls. Then the Blessed One, together with a great saṃgha of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, suddenly vanished from the Jeta Grove Monastery in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and appeared at the residence of Viśākhā, where he sat down upon a seat. His robes remained dry, and those of the bhikṣu-saṃgha were likewise all dry.

At that time, the maidservant arrived at the house late in the evening; she saw that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus had already arrived and were seated in order, their robes not even dampened by the rain. Having seen this, she thought to herself:
"How extraordinary is the World-Honored One!
"How extraordinary!
You possess such great supernatural power!
Having come after me, you have arrived before me."

Then Viśākhā, the Mother, provided the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus with various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink. When they had finished eating and set aside their bowls, she took a low seat and sat before them, saying to the Buddha:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me my wish."
The Buddha told Visākhā: “The Tathāgata does not refuse the requests of others.
Visākhā then spoke again to the Buddha:
“Venerable One!
If it can be prepared with purity, I pray that you grant it to me.
The Buddha told him:
“As you wish,” the World-Honored One replied. Visākhā, Mother of Migāra, then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“There may be visiting bhikṣus who come from afar and do not know where to go; I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide food for visiting bhikṣus for as long as I live.”
Again, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“There may be monks traveling on a long journey who, for the sake of food, are unable to keep pace with their companions. I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide lifelong offerings of food to these monks traveling on long journeys.”
He addressed the World-Honored One again, saying:

"If sick bhikṣus do not receive food appropriate to their illnesses, they may pass away; if they receive food appropriate to their illnesses, they may recover. I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide food for sick bhikṣus for as long as I live."
He further addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“If sick bhikṣus do not obtain medicine appropriate to their ailments, they may pass away; yet if they obtain medicine appropriate to their ailments, their illnesses can be cured. I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide sick bhikṣus with medicine appropriate to their ailments for as long as I live.”
He addressed the World-Honored One again, saying:

"If a monk who attends to the sick seeks food for himself, he will consequently neglect his nursing duties. I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide food for the nurse throughout my entire life."
He again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, may you permit the bhikṣus of the country of Aṇāpinḍada to eat gruel. If the World-Honored One would permit the bhikṣus to eat gruel, I shall provide it for them for as long as I live."
She addressed the World-Honored One again, saying:

"This morning I sent a maidservant to the saṃghārāma to announce that the time had come. I saw that all the bhikṣus were bathing naked in the rain. I pray that the World-Honored One will permit me to provide the bhikṣus with rain-bathing robes for as long as I live."
Again, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I had some minor business that led me to the banks of the Ajiravatī River, where I saw several bhikṣuṇīs bathing naked. At that time, some female thieves and courtesans went to the bhikṣuṇīs and said:

'You are young and your features are beautiful; you have no hair yet under your arms and you are in the prime of youth. Why do you not indulge in sensual desires? You may practice the holy life once you are old. In this way, you will lose nothing of either. "
Among them, some young bhikṣuṇīs felt a sense of dissatisfaction and wished:
"May the World-Honored One permit us to wear bathing robes for as long as we live.
At that time, the Buddha spoke to the Mother of Viśākhā:
“For what benefit or purpose do you seek these eight vows?
Vimalā, the mother of Viśākhā, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If a bhikṣu should arrive from afar, he would say to the World-Honored One:”
"Where has the bhikṣu named so-and-so been reborn after passing away?

At that time, the World-Honored One would immediately provide a prediction, stating that among the four fruits of the path, he will certainly realize the fruit of srotāpanna, or the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, or the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat.
I shall ask: "Did that deceased bhikṣu ever come to this Śrāvastī?
If I hear that he did indeed come, I shall further think thus:

"This visiting bhikṣu may have previously accepted my food for visiting bhikṣus, or food for bhikṣus traveling from afar, or food for sick bhikṣus; or he may have accepted medicine for a sick bhikṣu, or food for one who nurses the sick, or gruel, or a rain-bathing robe."
