Having heard these words, I immediately gave rise to a heart of joy; having given rise to a heart of joy, I abandoned all evils. Once physical evils were removed, I attained physical happiness; having attained physical happiness, my mind then attained concentration. With my mind thus concentrated, I was able to cultivate the faculties, the powers, and the factors of enlightenment throughout the long night.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"Vishakha, this matter is indeed as you say. Why is that?
You are an intelligent and wise donor who possesses faith and joy."
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of Visākhā:
"Rejoicing, one gives food and drink; The disciples of the Buddha uphold the precepts.
Bestowing gifts upon all people, One subdues the mind of stinginess and envy."
Relying on pleasant feelings and pleasant retribution, one attains eternal peace and happiness;
one obtains a dwelling in the heavens and attains the untainted noble path.
With a mind that delights in merit, its joy is beyond compare.
"One shall be born in the heavens, Long-lived and always at peace.

At that time, the World-Honored One used various skillful means to preach the Dharma to Vimalakīrti’s mother, exhorting her until she was filled with joy. He then rose from his seat and returned to the monastery. On account of this matter, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma accordingly. Using countless skillful means, he praised those who practice the dhūta austerities, who are dignified and pure, and who delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"From this day forward, I authorize the giving of food to visiting bhikṣus, food for bhikṣus traveling on long journeys, food for sick bhikṣus, medicine for sick bhikṣus, and food for those attending to the sick. I authorize the eating of gruel, the acceptance of rain-bathing robes (varṣāśāṭī), and the giving of bathing robes to bhikṣuṇīs."

At that time, having heard that the World-Honored One had permitted the bhikṣus to accept food from visiting bhikṣus, and even to provide rain-bathing robes for the bhikṣuṇīs, the Mother of Viśākhā immediately provided food for visiting bhikṣus for as long as she lived, and even provided rain-bathing robes for the bhikṣuṇīs.

When the Mother of Viśākhā heard that the Blessed One had granted permission, she immediately had many *vassikasīva* (rain-bathing robes) made and sent people to carry them to the monastery to give to the bhikṣus, who then divided them among themselves.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it shall be given according to the order of the senior monks.
If it does not suffice for all, one should remember the sequence of the distribution; if more robes are obtained later, they should be distributed in turn until everyone has received their share."
He gave the expensive robes according to their sequence. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should ask from the senior monk downward in order.
If they do not require them, only then should you give them according to the sequence."
"If it is not sufficient for all, you should take robes from among the Sangha that can be distributed and give them so that everyone may have enough.

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted bhikṣus to keep rain-bathing robes, they immediately sought rain-bathing robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter. They did not relinquish their rain robes but used them for other purposes; even while possessing rain robes, they would bathe naked.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"Although the Tathāgata permitted bhikṣus to keep rain-bathing robes, why do you constantly seek rain-bathing robes throughout spring, summer, and winter? Why do you fail to relinquish your rain robes when you have other uses for them, and even while possessing rain robes, bathe naked?"
Then, having rebuked him, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why do you constantly seek rain-bathing robes during the spring, summer, and winter?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!..."
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when one month of the spring season remains, seeks a rain-bath robe, he should use it for bathing for the remaining half-month."
"If a bhikṣu seeks a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance, or uses it for bathing more than half a month in advance, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the rain-bathing robe: it is for a bhikṣu to bathe in the rain.
There are ten kinds of robes, as mentioned above.
That bhikṣu should seek a rain-bathing robe on the sixteenth day of the third month and should use it on the first day of the fourth month.
If a bhikṣu seeks rain-clothing before the sixteenth day of the third month and uses it before the first day of the fourth month, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This article of forfeiture must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When one wishes to abandon it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, pay homage to the elder (*sthavira*), place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], having sought a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance, and having used it more than half a month in advance, have committed an offense involving forfeiture. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, requested a rain-bathing robe more than one month ago and used it more than half a month ago, thereby committing an offense of expiation involving forfeiture."
I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I accept the confession of that bhikṣu.
Thus is the formal announcement (jñapti).
After the formal announcement has been made, one should then accept the confession and say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind."
The bhikṣu replied, “So be it.
The Saṃgha shall then return the rain-cloak to that bhikṣu; it should be given by performing a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) in this manner.
Within the Saṃgha, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so, having sought a rain-bath robe more than one month prior [to its need], used it more than half a month prior [to its allowance], and has thus committed an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)."
I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let us return this rain-cloak to that bhikṣu, so-and-so.
The motion is as follows.
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, requested a rain-bath robe more than one month in advance and used it more than half a month before the prescribed time; he has committed an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).”
"I now relinquish this to the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha shall now return this rain-bathing robe to this bhikṣu, so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this rain-bathing robe to that bhikṣu, so-and-so, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."
"The Saṃgha has already consented to the return of this rain-bathing robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If, after the rain-bathing robe has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs them,
"Do not return," and they do so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (śuddhadāna), or sends it to another person, or makes it into one’s own three robes (tricīvara), or makes it into a miscellaneous robe (pārikkhārika-cīvara), or intentionally damages it, or burns it, or uses it repeatedly, in all such cases it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one requests [the rain-cloth] on the sixteenth day of the third month and uses it on the first day of the fourth month; or if, having relinquished the rain-cloth, one subsequently makes other use of it; or if one wears a bathing robe for the purpose of bathing; or if there is no rain-cloth; or if one makes a bathing robe; or if one washes or dyes it; or if one dyes it at the place where it was kept. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-seventh section ends. At that time, the Buddha was observing the summer retreat at Piraṇḍu.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Go and tell the brahmin Vairaṇyā: 'I have completed my summer retreat with you; now I wish to travel through the human world.'"
Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to the brahmin of Veḷukaṇṭaka and said to him:
“The Tathāgata says to you:
‘I have completed my summer retreat at your invitation and now wish to travel through the human realm.’”
When the brahmin Vairaṇyā heard these words of the Blessed One, he immediately reflected:
"I have gained no profit! I have gained no wholesome benefit!"
I have no attainment!
No wholesome attainment! Why is this?
"I invited the śramaṇa Gautama and the Saṅgha for a period of ninety days, yet I have not provided them with offerings at all.
Then the brahmin Verañjā, together with Ānanda, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the World-Honored One gradually taught the subtle Dharma to the Brahmin Vairaṇyā, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will once again accept my invitation for ninety days at Vairaṇyā."
The Buddha said to the brahmin:
"I have already accepted your invitation for the ninety-day summer retreat, which has now concluded; I now wish to travel among the people.
The brahmin spoke again, saying:
"May the Blessed One and the Saṃgha accept my invitation for tomorrow.
The Blessed One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the Blessed One had accepted by silence, the brahmin rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Upon returning home, he prepared various kinds of excellent food that very night and informed the Buddha the following morning that the time had come.
The World-Honored One, having donned his robes and taken up his bowl, went to the house together with five hundred bhikṣus; having arrived, they took their seats.

Then the brahmin prepared various kinds of excellent food and served it to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus until they were all fully satisfied. When the meal was finished, each person put away their bowl.
The brahmin offered three robes to the Buddha and two robes to each of the bhikṣus, as an offering for the summer retreat.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not accept the robes and said to the donors:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted us to receive summer robes.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I allow you to accept summer robes.

When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had allowed the acceptance of summer robes, they began begging for robes at all times—during spring, summer, and winter—and they begged for and accepted robes even before their period of retreat (vassa) was completed.

At that time, after the Śākya son Upananda had completed his rains retreat at one location, he heard that the bhikṣus who had observed the summer retreat at another location had received a great deal of offerings and robes.
He immediately went to that retreat site and asked the people there, "Have you already divided the robes obtained from the summer retreat?"
He replied, “Not yet. [The other said,] “Bring it here; I shall give you my share.”
Again, he went to other places, not just once, and in each case asked:
"Have you received your share of the *varṣāśāṭī* (rainy-season robe)? They replied:
"No. "Bring it here; I shall give you my share.
Then, as he distributed the robes everywhere, Baddhananda obtained a large portion of robes, which he brought back and entered the Jetavana Monastery.

When the bhikṣus saw this, they said to Upananda, "The World-Honored One has permitted the keeping of the three robes; apart from these three robes, he has not permitted the keeping of extra robes. Whose robe is this?"
Bhadananda replied, "There are places where one may obtain robes during the summer retreat; I have come here with my share from one such place.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
“Vāḷanada the Śākyaputra!

Why does the Tathāgata permit the acceptance of robes for the summer retreat, yet also allow for the constant begging of robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and even accept and beg for robes when the retreat has not yet concluded?”
“O Vāḷananda, son of the Śākyas!
You have entered the rains retreat in one place and received your robes in another.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter to the World-Honored One in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and reprimanded the group of six bhikṣus in various ways: "O Śākyaputra Baddhananda!

I have permitted bhikṣus to accept robes for the summer retreat; how is it that you constantly beg for robes at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and even beg for and accept robes before the retreat has concluded?"
“Venerable Upāli! Did the son of the Śākyas, Nanda, observe the rains retreat in one place and receive his robes in another?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus and the son of the Śākyas, Nanda, by means of countless skillful expedients, addressed the bhikṣus:

"One must not constantly beg for robes at all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter; nor may one beg for or accept robes before the rainy-season retreat has concluded; nor may one reside in one location for the retreat while receiving the share of summer robes in another location."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī. At that moment, there were rebels among the people within the realm of King Prasenajit.
The king then dispatched two high ministers named Liśadatta and Pūrṇa, commanding them to lead an expedition against them.
At that time, the two ministers thought to themselves:
"We are now about to go on a military expedition; we do not yet know whether we shall return safely or not.
We have always provided meals and offered robes for the Sangha upon the conclusion of their summer retreat."

"The current retreat has not yet concluded; would it not be appropriate to prepare food and various garments, and offer them to the Sangha as an offering of robes according to the rules of the retreat?
The elders went in person to the monastery and addressed the bhikṣus with these words:
"Tomorrow we wish to provide a meal and offer robes for the retreat; we pray that you will each deign to accept our invitation."
The bhikṣus replied to the householder:
"Please provide only food; there is no need for a gift of robes. Why is this?"
"Until the summer retreat is concluded, one may neither receive robes nor beg for robes.
The elder said: "We have now been dispatched by King Prasenajit to go on a military expedition. We thought to ourselves:"
"I do not yet know whether I shall return or not;
however, as was the custom previously, once the summer retreat has concluded, I wish to provide a meal for the community of monks and offer them robes.
Now, I likewise wish to provide a meal and offer robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept *ātyayika-cīvara* (emergency robes).
If the bhikṣus know it to be an emergency robe, they should accept it."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If, during the final ten days of the three-month summer retreat, the bhikṣus receive an urgent offering of robes, and the bhikṣu knows it is an urgent offering of robes, he should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it until the time for robes."
"If one keeps it beyond [the prescribed period], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "urgent gift-clothing" (*ātyayika-cīvara*), if one accepts it, one acquires it; if one does not accept it, one loses it.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as described above. Regarding "the time for robes":

after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, there is one month when the *kāṭhina* robe is not spread, and five months when the *kāṭhina* robe is spread. If ten days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk obtains an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), knowing it to be such an urgent gift, he should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for ten days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

There is one month when the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, and five months when the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread. If there are nine days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for those nine days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months plus one additional day, if there are eight days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for those eight days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and two additional days have passed—if seven days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for seven days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and three additional days have passed—if there remain six days until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for those remaining six days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and four additional days have elapsed—if there are five days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), that monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he may keep it for those five days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and an additional five days have passed, if there are four days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), that monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he should keep it for those four days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months with an additional six days, if three days remain until the *pravāraṇā*, a bhikṣu may receive an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*). Knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, he should accept it; having accepted it, he should keep it for those three days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and seven days have been added, if there are two days remaining until the *pravāraṇā*, and a monk obtains an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), the monk, knowing it to be an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he should keep it for those two days until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and eight days have further elapsed—if the *pravāraṇā* is to be held tomorrow and a monk receives an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*), that monk, knowing it is an urgent gift of robes, should accept it; having accepted it, he should keep it from this very day until the conclusion of the *pravāraṇā*.

When the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread for one month, or when it has been spread for five months and nine additional days, if a bhikṣu obtains an urgent offering of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) and keeps it beyond the preceding or subsequent limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This robe should be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a partial assembly.
If it is relinquished in such a manner that the relinquishment is invalid, it constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.

If one wishes to relinquish it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, prostrate toward the Elder, kneel with the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"I, bhikṣu [name], having received an urgent gift of robes, have either exceeded the prior limit or exceeded the subsequent limit and thus committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika). I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should then perform confession.
The person receiving the confession shall first announce this, and only then accept the confession, making the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having received an urgent gift of robes, either kept it beyond the prescribed time before or after [the distribution], thereby committing an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement.
Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
The one receiving the confession says to that person:
"You must reproach your own mind.
The bhikṣu replies:
"So be it. The Saṃgha shall then return that bhikṣu’s robe and grant it to him by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
From within the assembly, one capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having received an urgent gift of cloth, has committed an offense involving forfeiture by exceeding the prior limit and the subsequent limit; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to return this cloth to this bhikṣu, so-and-so."
The motion is thus made: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having obtained an urgent gift of robes, has committed an offense of forfeiture by exceeding the prior limit and the subsequent limit; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
The Saṃgha now returns this robe to this bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha returning this robe to the bhikṣu named so-and-so should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to return this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
If, after the robe has been relinquished within the Saṃgha, it is not returned, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one instructs,
"Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift (śuddhadāna), or accepts it to make it into the three robes or other garments, or sends it to another person, or wears it repeatedly, all such acts constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one obtains an urgent gift of robes (*ātyayika-cīvara*) that is neither received before nor after the prescribed time, there is no offense.
Furthermore, if robes are seized by thieves, lost, burned, or swept away by water, it is not an offense to receive them even beyond the prescribed time.

If one forms the perception that [the robe] has been stolen, lost, burned, or carried away; or if there are dangerous obstacles such that the road is impassable; or if there are many thieves and robbers, the danger of wild beasts, or if a river is in high flood; or if one is detained and imprisoned by a king; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if the bhikṣu to whom the robe was entrusted has died, gone abroad, renounced the precepts, been plundered by thieves, been harmed by a wild beast, or been swept away by water—then if [the robe] is used after these circumstances have passed, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the bhikṣus had completed their summer retreat and were staying in an araṇya for the final month of the kārttika period,
many bandits plundered the bhikṣus' robes, bowls, sitting mats, needle-cases, and various requisites, while also beating and striking the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus, fearing bandits, all came to the Jeta Grove Monastery and stayed there gathered together.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason have these bhikṣus come to the Jeta Grove Monastery and stayed there gathered together?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The bhikṣus have completed their summer retreat and were staying in an araṇya for the final month of the kārttika period when they were robbed of their robes, bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and various requisites by bandits. Furthermore, the bandits beat the bhikṣus; out of fear and dread, all the bhikṣus have come to stay at the Jetavana Monastery.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to dwell in araṇyas that are suspicious or full of fear.
While dwelling in such an araṇya, if a bhikṣu wishes to leave his robes behind, he may leave any one of his three robes within the village.”

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted staying in forest hermitages where there was cause for suspicion or fear; while staying in such places, they wished to leave their robes behind, placing one or another of the three robes within the village.
Even though he had left his robes inside the dwelling and departed after entrusting them to a fellow bhikṣu, that fellow bhikṣu later took the robes out to dry in the midday sun.
When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said to one another, "The World-Honored One has established a precept permitting bhikṣus to possess three robes and no more; whose robes are these?"

That bhikṣu said: "The group of six bhikṣus are my acquaintances and close friends; they left their robes here and have gone out to wander among the people. For this reason, we were drying the robes."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing; they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How is it that the World-honored One has permitted the bhikṣus to dwell in forest hermitages where there is suspicion and fear, yet [you] leave one of the three robes behind and wear it inside the village?"
"How is it that you now travel through the human world with many robes entrusted to acquaintances and friends, and spend the night apart from your robes?
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, Group of Six Bhikṣus!
I have permitted the bhikṣus to dwell in an araṇya where there is suspicion or fear; when a bhikṣu dwells in such a place, he may leave one of his three robes behind in a dwelling."
"How is it that you now entrust many robes to your friends and travel through the human world, staying overnight apart from your robes?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These group-of-six bhikṣus are foolish men!"
Regarding the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, at the end of the three months of the summer retreat, when the month of Kārttika has concluded, should reside in an araṇya that is a place of suspicion and fear, and while residing in such a place, should wish to leave one of his three robes behind in a village dwelling."
"If there is a legitimate reason, monks may stay apart from their robes for up to six nights.
Should they exceed this limit, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "monk" is as explained above.
Regarding the "araṇya" location: it is five hundred bows' distance from a village.
In the kingdom of Cāmara, a bow is four cubits long; the measurement should be taken using the medium cubit.
A "place of doubt" refers to a place where there is suspicion of thieves or robbers.
"Fearful" refers to the presence of fearsome thieves and bandits within.
"Inside the house" refers to a village settlement.
"The three robes" are the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka.
Regarding robes, there are ten kinds, as explained above.

If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason to stay apart from his robes overnight, then at the end of those six nights, before the dawn of the seventh night has appeared, he must either relinquish the three robes, hold them in his hand, or go to a place within reach of a stone’s throw.

If a bhikṣu, after the six nights have passed, during the seventh night before the appearance of dawn, does not relinquish his three robes, does not hold the robes in his hand, and does not stay within the range of a stone's throw, and thus spends the night separated from the robes when the dawn of the seventh night appears, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense in every case.
If, having set aside the three robes, one stays overnight separated from the remaining robes, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate group.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one wishes to abandon it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, place the right knee on the ground, prostrate at the feet of the senior monks, and then kneel with palms joined, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"I, Bhikṣu [Name], having stayed apart from my robe for more than six nights, have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one must perform confession.
The person receiving the confession shall first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), and only after that announcement may they accept the confession. The announcement should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has stayed apart from his robe for more than six nights and has committed an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya). He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that I accept the confession of this bhikṣu, so-and-so."
"I announce it thus.
Having made this announcement, one may then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind.
The bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
The Saṃgha should then return the robe to that bhikṣu; it should be given by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* as follows.
A competent person for performing the *karman* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and he should make the following formal motion:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has stayed apart from his robe for more than six nights and has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to return this robe to that bhikṣu.
The motion is thus made. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has stayed apart from his robe for more than six nights and has committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika); he now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha."
"Monks, the robe is now returned to that bhikṣu.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha returning this robe to that bhikṣu should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to the return of that bhikṣu’s robe. Since the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If a bhikṣu has finished relinquishing his robe and does not return it to that bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he instructs another not to return it, it is also a duṣkṛta offense.

Whether it be a pure gift, or something sent to another person, or if one accepts it to make the three robes, or makes a *pārikkāra* robe, or repeatedly takes it up and wears it—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if, after six nights have passed, one arrives at the location of the robe before the light of dawn appears on the seventh night; or if one relinquishes the robe, or takes hold of it with the hand, or reaches a place where a stone could be thrown. There is no offense.

There is no offense if there is the perception of being robbed, the perception of loss, the perception of being swept away, or the perception of being burned; nor if one does not relinquish the robe, does not grasp the robe with the hand, or does not go to a place reachable by the throw of a stone.

If a boat cannot provide passage, if the road is perilous and difficult, if there are many bandits, if there are fierce beasts, if a river is in flood, if one is held by force, or if one is imprisoned, or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya)—in such cases, if one does not relinquish the robe, does not hold the robe, and does not go as far as a stone could be thrown, there is no offense whatsoever.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-ninth [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a lay devotee who had long been accustomed to giving alms; he intended to provide a meal for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, as well as to bestow fine robes upon them.
When the śramaṇa Vāḍananda heard that this lay devotee wished to feed the Buddha and the bhikṣu-saṃgha and also give fine robes, he immediately went to the lay devotee’s house and asked him:
“Is it true that you wish to feed the Buddha and the bhikṣu-saṃgha and also bestow fine robes?”
The householder replied,
"Yes. Then the Śākya son Upananda said to the householder:
“The Sangha possesses great benefit, great power, and great merit; those who give to the Sangha receive much in return.
You should now give your food to the Sangha, and you may give your robe to me alone.”
The householder replied, "So be it.

Thereupon, the elder no longer provided robes for the Saṃgha; instead, that very night he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, and on the following day, he informed the Saṃgha that the time had come.
The community of bhikṣus, having put on their robes and taken up their bowls, went to the house of a lay devotee and sat down in their assigned seats.
At that time, seeing the elder bhikṣu’s perfect deportment, the lay devotee cried out in a loud voice:
"How could I have created an obstacle for such a well-disciplined assembly of monks by withholding their robes?"
Then the bhikṣus asked the householder,
"Why did you speak these words?
At that time, the householder answered them according to the facts.

At that time, there were among the assembly those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they reproached the Śākya son Upananda, saying: "How can you appropriate for yourself the benefits of the Saṃgha?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How can one appropriate for oneself the gains of the Saṃgha by cutting them off?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the Śākya son Upananda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu appropriates property belonging to the Saṃgha for his own personal use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether it was property belonging to the Saṃgha or not, nor whether it had been granted to the Saṃgha or not; only later did they realize it was property belonging to the Saṃgha and had already been granted to the Saṃgha. Some performed the confession for a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense, while others felt shame. If one did not know [the nature of the object], there was no offense.
"From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that an object belongs to the Saṃgha, seeks it for himself and takes possession of it, he commits a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already been given to the Saṃgha for the sake of the Saṃgha.
"Property of the Saṃgha" also refers to that which has already been promised to the Saṃgha.
"Regarding those things belonging to the Saṃgha: 'for the sake of the Saṃgha' means one acts for the sake of the Saṃgha, though it has not yet been granted to the Saṃgha.
'Already given to the Saṃgha' means it has already been granted to the Saṃgha and already relinquished to them.
'Property of the Saṃgha' refers to robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, and so on, down to drinking vessels."
If a bhikṣu knows that an item belongs to the Saṃgha and seeks it for himself, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If an item intended for the Saṃgha is diverted to a stūpa, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one permits a stūpa to be diverted to the Saṃgha, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If an object permitted for the Saṃgha of the four directions is diverted to the present Saṃgha, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If an object permitted for the present Saṃgha is diverted to the Saṃgha of the four directions, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one consents for an object to be transferred from the community of bhikṣus to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one consents for it to be transferred from the community of bhikṣuṇīs to the community of bhikṣus, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one promises [to give] from one place but gives from another, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one has already promised and perceives it as having been promised, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one has already promised but the mind harbors doubt, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one perceives that permission has been granted when it has not been granted, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one suspects that permission has not been granted, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This *naiḥsargika* article must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a partial assembly.
If one abandons [the robe] but the abandonment is not valid, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one wishes to abandon it to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, place the right knee on the ground, pay homage to the senior monks, and then kneel with palms joined, making this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

"I, Bhikṣu [Name], knowing that this object had already been assigned to the Saṃgha, have taken it for myself; I have committed an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) and now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, one should perform confession.
After the person receiving the confession has made the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one should then accept the confession by making the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, knowing that these items had already been promised to the Saṃgha, took them for himself; he has committed an offense of forfeiture and downfall (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) and now relinquishes them to the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession and say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind. That bhikṣu replied, "Yes."
The Saṃgha should immediately return the items relinquished by that bhikṣu; it should grant them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
A competent person for the *karman* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and he should make the following formal motion:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, knowing that these items had already been assigned to the Saṃgha, took them for himself; he has thus committed an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. He now forfeits them to the Saṃgha.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant permission to return these forfeited items to that bhikṣu.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu, so-and-so..."
Having recognized this object as such, he requested it from the Saṃgha and intended it for himself;
thus he committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
He now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha. May the Saṃgha now return this relinquished object to that bhikṣu.
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha returning the items relinquished by that bhikṣu, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved the return of the items relinquished by that bhikṣu. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If, after having relinquished [the object] and given it away, one does not return the relinquished item to that bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one instructs another not to return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

If one transforms it into a pure gift, sends it to another person, accepts it to make the three robes, makes it into a *pārikkāra* robe, or uses it repeatedly, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if one does not know; or if one has already consented but perceives it as not having consented; or if one has consented to a small amount but encourages giving a large amount; or if one has consented to a few people but encourages giving to many; or if intending to consent to something inferior, one encourages giving something superior; or if speaking in jest; or if speaking by mistake; or if speaking while alone; or if speaking in a dream; or if intending to say this but saying that instead—there is no offense in these cases.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain. [The thirty rules are concluded.
*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume 14, Section 11 of the First Part of Volume 11.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty. 5.
The Ninety Dharmas of the Single Confession (Naiḥsargika-pāyattika). Part One: At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, Śākyaśvī.

At that time, among the Śākyas there was a son of the Śākya clan named Hastibala, who was skilled in debate. He would frequently engage in discussions with non-Buddhist brahmins; whenever he was unable to prevail, he would contradict his previous statements. When questioned about these matters within the Saṃgha, he again contradicted his previous words, knowingly uttering falsehoods in the midst of the assembly.
The various brahmins criticized them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or remorse and constantly speak falsehoods, yet they claim for themselves:
'I practice the True Dharma.'"
"What right Dharma exists now?

Your discourse was untimely and thus contradicted your previous words; when questioned among the assembly of monks, you again contradicted your previous words, knowingly speaking falsehoods in the midst of the community."

When the monks heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of shame and remorse, rebuked the Śākya son Elephant Strength (Hastibala):

"How could you, when debating with a brahmin, contradict your own previous words if you were not successful; and how could you, when questioned by the Saṃgha, again contradict your previous words, knowingly speaking falsehoods in the midst of the Saṃgha?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Hastibala:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, Bhikṣu Hastika-bala!

When you debated with the brahmin, if you were not as good as him, you immediately contradicted your own previous words; when questioned by the Saṃgha, you again contradicted your previous words. Do you knowingly speak falsehoods in the midst of the assembly?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Hastibala with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu knowingly speaks falsehood, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. To speak falsely while knowing the truth means:

to say one has seen what one has not seen; to say one has heard what one has not heard; to say one has touched what one has not touched; to say one knows what one does not know; or conversely, to say one has not seen what one has seen; to say one has not heard what one has heard; to say one has not touched what one has touched; and to say one does not know what one knows.
As for "seeing," it is the visual consciousness that sees.
As for "hearing," it is the auditory consciousness that hears.
As for "touching," it is three consciousnesses that touch: the olfactory consciousness, the gustatory consciousness, and the tactile consciousness.
That which knows is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna).
That which does not see refers to the other five consciousnesses, excluding visual consciousness.
That which does not hear refers to the other five consciousnesses, excluding auditory consciousness.
"Non-contacting" refers to those other than the three consciousnesses; it consists of the remaining eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, and mental-consciousness.
"Not knowing" refers to those other than the mental-consciousness; it consists of the remaining five consciousnesses.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet speaks thus:
"I have seen, heard, touched,
and known," and speaks falsely despite knowing the truth, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not see, does not hear, does not touch, and does not know, yet within that state there arise perceptions of seeing, hearing, touching, and knowing, one would say:
"I do not see, I do not hear, I do not touch, and I do not know."
To speak falsely while knowing [the truth] is a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet harbors doubt in one's mind, and then says:
"I have no doubt; I have seen, I have heard, I have touched, and I have known."
To speak falsely while knowing [the truth] is a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet harbors doubt in one's mind, one should say:
"I have no doubt regarding this," and then say: "I have not seen, heard, touched, or known."
To speak falsely while knowing the truth constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, heard, touched, or known, yet in one's mind there is no longer any doubt, and one says:
"I have doubts; I have seen, I have heard, I have touched, I have known."
To speak falsely while knowing the truth is a *pāyattika*.
If one has not seen, has not heard, has not touched, and does not know, yet has no doubt in one's mind, but then says: "I have doubts; I have not seen, heard, touched, or known."
To speak falsely while knowing the truth constitutes a *pāyattika*.
This should be explained in detail: one forms the initial thought, "I shall speak falsely."
When one speaks a falsehood while knowing it is a falsehood, and having known it is a falsehood, one deliberately speaks that falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.
This is when one first forms the thought:
"I shall speak a falsehood."
When one speaks a falsehood, knowing it to be a falsehood, yet after having spoken the falsehood does not recall having done so, and thus speaks the falsehood, it is a *pāyattika*.
This applies when one has not previously formed the thought: "I shall speak a falsehood."
If one knows it is a lie at the time of speaking the lie, and after having spoken the lie, one knows it was a lie, and thus speaks the lie intentionally, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one did not originally intend to speak a lie, but at the time of speaking knows it is a lie, and after having spoken the lie does not recall it was a lie, yet speaks the lie intentionally, it is a *pāyattika*.

If one’s perception differs, one’s tolerance differs, one’s original desire differs, one’s contact differs, one’s conception differs, and one’s mind differs—such matters are all false speech. To knowingly speak falsely in the midst of the great assembly constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one speaks but is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
When the precepts are being recited, if one remembers an offense even after being asked three times and does not confess it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who, not having seen, says they have not seen; not having heard, says they have not heard; not having touched, says they have not touched; or not having known, says they have not known; and who, having seen, says they have seen; having heard, says they have heard; having touched, says they have touched; or having known, says they have known—provided that what they say is in accordance with their mental perception and conception. There is no offense in such a case.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The first section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus interrupted the proceedings of a dispute and reviled the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus were so ashamed and abashed that they forgot what had come before or after and were unable to speak.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How can you, group of six bhikṣus!"
"When one interrupts a matter being settled by rebuking a bhikṣu with various insults, causing him shame and making him forget what came before and after so that he cannot speak?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teaching—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, you group of six bhikṣus!
Why do you interrupt a matter of dispute by reviling a bhikṣu, causing him shame and making him forget his words so that he cannot speak?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"In a past age, there was a bull belonging to a brahmin in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, whom he tended day and night, grooming, rubbing, and stroking.
At that time, there was also a householder in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā who went through the cities and streets, proclaiming aloud:
'Who has a strong bull? Let him yoke his bull with mine to pull a hundred carts; I will wager a thousand pieces of gold!'"
At that time, having heard the sound of the chanting, the Brahmin’s ox thought to himself:
"This Brahmin has fed me day and night, groomed me, and stroked me; I should now exert all my strength and give my utmost to obtain those thousand ounces of gold to repay this man's kindness."
Then that ox spoke to the Brahmin, saying:
"You should know this now: In the kingdom of Kāśi, there is an elder who has made this proclamation:
'Whoever has an ox, let them yoke it with my ox to pull a hundred carts; I shall wager a thousand pieces of gold.'"
"Master, you should now go to that householder's home and say:
'I have oxen; let them pull a hundred carts together with your oxen, and I shall wager one thousand taels of gold.'"
Then the brahmin went at once to the house of the elder and said to him:
"I have oxen that can be yoked together with yours to pull a hundred carts; I will wager one thousand pieces of gold."
The elder replied,
"Now is precisely the right time.
The Brahmin immediately led his own oxen to yoke them together with the elder's oxen to pull a hundred carts, wagering one thousand taels of gold.
At that time, as many people looked on, the brahmin spoke disparaging words before the crowd, saying, "Only one horn can be pulled.
When the ox heard these disparaging words, it immediately felt ashamed and refused to exert its strength to compete with him; thus, the elder’s ox was victorious.
The Brahmin’s ox was no match for the other, and he forfeited a thousand taels of gold.
At that time, the Brahmin said to his ox:
"Day and night I have fed you, stroked you, and groomed you, hoping that you would exert all your strength for me to defeat that other ox."
"Why do you now, on the contrary, require me to pay a thousand pieces of gold?
The ox said to the brahmin:
"In the presence of the multitude, you reviled me, saying:"
"One horn can be pulled.
This caused me great shame before the assembly, and therefore I was unable to exert further strength to compete with him in the race.
If you could change your past words and no longer disparage me by name or appearance, you may go and say this to that elder: [text continues]
"If you can pull a hundred carts together with me once more, I shall give you another two thousand pieces of gold.
The Brahmin said to the ox,
"Do not make me have to pay another two thousand pieces of gold again."
The ox replied to the brahmin, saying:
"Do not again revile me before this assembly, saying:
'One horn can be pulled.'"
"In the presence of the multitude, you should praise me, saying:
'Excellent for its fine lead-rope, magnificent horns!
Then the brahmin went to the house of that elder and said:
"If you can further yoke my oxen to pull a hundred chariots, I will bet you two thousand taels of gold.
The elder replied,
"Now is precisely the right time."
Then the Brahmin’s ox and the householder’s ox harnessed a hundred carts together, wagering two thousand taels of gold, while many people gathered to watch.
In front of the crowd, the Brahmin praised his ox, saying:
"It pulls well, it is magnificent, and its horns are beautiful."
Upon hearing these words, the ox immediately exerted its strength and contended for the lead with the other; the Brahmin’s ox prevailed.
The householder’s ox was no match for it, and the Brahmin obtained two thousand taels of gold.
At that time, the Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"When anyone wishes to speak, they should speak wholesome words and should not speak unwholesome words; wholesome words are beneficial, while unwholesome words cause one's own distress."
Therefore, monks! Even when animals are reviled by humans, they still feel shame and are unable to exert their strength;
how much more so for a human being—when subjected to the insults and humiliation of others, how could one not feel shame?

These six groups of foolish bhikṣus, by interrupting the proceedings of a dispute and reviling the other bhikṣus, cause them such shame that they forget what precedes and what follows, rendering them unable to speak.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
Among the various bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu speaks words of disparagement regarding another's lineage, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "one who disparages others by their kind": this refers to one born into a low-caste family, whose occupation is also low, and whose skills and crafts are likewise low; or one who says:
"You are a person who has committed an offense."
Some said: "You employ many bound persons. Others said:
"You are a blind man," or he says,
"You are a bald and sightless man."
"Lowly" refers to those of the Caṇḍāla caste, the scavenger caste, the bamboo-worker caste, and the carriage-maker caste.

"Low-born families" refers to the Kauṇḍinya, Kausika-Vāśiṣṭha, Kāśyapa, Ātreya, and Bhāradvāja; or, if one is not originally of low birth but practices low arts, they are likewise considered low-born.

Those of low occupations include those who trade in pigs and sheep, slaughter oxen, release hawks and falcons, hunt, net fish, commit robbery, capture robbers, guard cities, and administer criminal justice.
"Lowly crafts" refers to smithing, carpentry, pottery, leatherwork, barbering, and wickerwork. Regarding the offenses:
they include *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *sthūlātyaya*, *duṣkṛta*, and *durbhāṣita*.
"Bonds" refers to the bonds ranging from ill-will up to the five hundred bonds.
"The blind and the sightless" refers to those who are blind or sightless, hunchbacked or lame, deaf or mute, and those afflicted by other various ailments.
If a bhikṣu reviles another bhikṣu, saying:
"You were born into a low and base family; your occupation is base, your craft is base; you have committed offenses; you are bound by the fetters; you are bald and blind."
In this manner, there are insults delivered face-to-face, insults by way of metaphor, and insults by way of self-comparison.
As for insults delivered face-to-face, one says:
"You are born of a *caṇḍāla* family, born of a scavenger family, of the bamboo-worker caste, of the carriage-maker caste, or of the Kauṭa, Kauśīvasu-dyu, Kāśyapa, Ātreya, or Bhāradvāja lineages."

"If one is originally of low birth and practices low arts, they are indeed of low birth. You are a merchant; you are a butcher of oxen, pigs, and sheep; you are a thief or a pursuer of thieves; you are a city guard or a judicial official; you are a smith, a carpenter, a potter, a leatherworker, or a barber."

"You are one who has committed a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or an *adhikaraṇa-śamatha*; you are one possessed by the fetter of hatred, even up to being possessed by five hundred fetters; you are blind, squint-eyed, bald, lame, mute, deaf, and afflicted by all manner of maladies."
Regarding the metaphor of verbal abuse: "You resemble the Caṇḍāla caste; you resemble the Mātaṅga (scavenger) caste;
you resemble the Veṇukāra (bamboo-worker) caste; you resemble the Rathakāra (chariot-maker) caste; you resemble the Kauṣītakas;
you resemble the Kauśīlavaśyāyas; you resemble the Kāśyapas; you resemble the Ātreya caste; you resemble the Vā..."
O Vatsa, you resemble a seller of pigs and sheep; you resemble a butcher of oxen; you resemble a falconer;
you resemble a fisherman or a hunter; you resemble a thief or a pursuer of thieves;
you resemble a city guard or a judge; you resemble a blacksmith; you resemble a carpenter.
"O man, you resemble a potter; you resemble a leather-worker; you resemble a barber;
you resemble one who has committed a *pārājika* offense; you resemble one who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense;
you resemble one who has committed a *pāyattika* offense; you resemble one who has committed a *pratideśanīya* offense."
"You resemble one who has committed a *sthūlātyaya*; you resemble one who has committed a *duṣkṛta*;
you resemble one who has committed a *durbhāṣita*; you resemble one bound by a messenger; you resemble one who is blind; you resemble one who is sightless;
you resemble one who is lame; you resemble one who is crippled; you resemble one who is mute and deaf."
Regarding those who revile themselves by comparison: "I am not of the *caṇḍāla* caste; I am not of the sweepers' caste;
I am not of the bamboo-workers' caste; I am not of the cartwrights' caste;
I am not a *kauṭa*, a *kuśīlava*, a *vasu*, a *vatsa*, a *kāśyapa*, an *atithi*, a *naya*, a *brāhmaṇa*, nor one who trades in pigs and sheep or slaughters oxen."
I am not one who hunts deer, nor one who releases hawks and falcons, nor one who nets fish, nor a hunter, nor a thief,
nor a pursuer of thieves, nor a city guard, nor a judicial official, nor a blacksmith, nor a carpenter,
nor a bamboo-worker, nor a wheelwright, nor a potter, nor a leather-worker, nor a barber. I have committed no such offense.
I am not one who has committed a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *durbhāṣita*. I am not bound by the fetters;
I am neither blind nor sightless, nor am I bald, lame, crippled, mute, or deaf.
If a bhikṣu, as described above, reviles another by means of their lineage, it is a pāyattika.
If the words of the revilement regarding the lineage are clear, it is a pāyattika;
if they are not clear, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one reviles another by praising virtuous qualities— whether through direct verbal abuse, through metaphorical abuse, or through self-comparison—

regarding those who praise virtuous qualities, such as forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), alms-seekers (*piṇḍapātika*), wearers of rag-robes (*paṃsukūlika*), and even practitioners of meditation (*dhyāyin*).
Regarding those who revile by speaking of virtuous qualities: they say, "You are an araṇyaka," up to "you are a practitioner of dhyāna.
Regarding those who revile by way of analogy: they say, "You resemble an araṇyaka," up to "you resemble a practitioner of dhyāna."
Regarding "insulting by comparison": [saying] "I am not a forest-dweller," up to "I am not a practitioner of meditation.
If a bhikṣu speaks of the wholesome Dharma and insults him face-to-face, insults him with metaphors, or insults him by comparison, and does so clearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
if he does so unclearly, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: speaking for the sake of mutual benefit; speaking for the sake of the Dharma; speaking for the sake of the Vinaya; speaking for the sake of instruction; speaking out of affection for a friend; speaking in jest; speaking inadvertently due to the flow of conversation; speaking while in private; speaking in a dream; or intending to say one thing but mistakenly saying another. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(End of section two. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spread rumors from one side to another; they took private words from this person and spoke them to that person, and took private words from that person and spoke them to this person. Thus they did not cease, until eventually quarrels arose among the assembly where none had existed before, and quarrels already present were not extinguished.
The bhikṣus each had this thought:
"For what reason and by what cause has the Saṃgha, which previously had no strife, now come to have this dispute, and having already had such a matter of strife, is unable to extinguish it?"

The bhikṣus knew for themselves that these six groups of bhikṣus were passing words back and forth, leading eventually to quarrels and disputes within the Saṃgha; thus, they caused disputes to arise where none had existed before, and they were unable to extinguish disputes that already existed.

At that time, there were among the assembly those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you transmit words back and forth, such that disputes arise within the Saṃgha where none previously existed, and existing disputes cannot be extinguished?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How is it that you transmit words back and forth, such that disputes arise within the Saṃgha where none previously existed, and existing disputes are not extinguished?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"Listen, you all! In ancient times there were two wicked beasts who were companions; one was named Good-Tusked Lion and the other was named Good-Spotted Tiger. Day and night they waited and hunted for herds of deer."
At that time, there was a jackal who followed behind those two beasts, sustaining its own life by eating their leftover meat.
Then the jackal secretly thought to itself:
"I cannot continue to follow them for long; by what skillful means might I cause discord between these two beasts so that they no longer follow one another?"
Then the jackal went to where the lion Suprabuddha was and spoke thus to him:
"The tiger Subhadra has spoken these words:
'My birthplace is superior, my lineage is superior, my physical form is superior to yours, and my power and majesty are superior to yours.'"
Why is this? Day after day I obtain fine and delicious food.
The lion Śānakhāda follows behind me, consuming my leftover meat to sustain his own life.
He then spoke in verse:
"In physical form and birth, he is powerful and superior;
Sudanta cannot match him."
Śubhaṅkara spoke these words. Śubhadanta asked the jackal,
"By what means did you come to know this?"
He replied, "You two beasts may gather in one place and see each other for yourselves.
At that time, after the jackal had spoken secretly to Śunaḥśepa, he went and spoke to the tiger Śubhaṅga:
"Do you know? Sudaṃta has spoken these words:
'As for my lineage and place of birth today, they are both superior to yours, and my power and influence are likewise superior.'"
Why is this? I always eat choice meat.
This clever tiger eats the remains of my meat to sustain its own life.
Then he spoke in verse:
"Physical form and its origins, Great power and further excellence— Though one may be skilled in debate,
one cannot be truly good."
Śubhadanta spoke thus. Subhūṣita asked:
"By what means did you come to know this?"
He replied, "You two beasts shall gather together in one place; you will know each other upon seeing one another.
Later, when the two beasts gathered in one place and glared at each other with eyes of wrath, the lion with excellent tusks thought to himself:
"I ought not to strike him first without having asked.
At that time, the lion Supuṣpita addressed the tiger Subāhu with a verse, asking:
"Regarding your form and your birth, Your great strength and your excellence; [How did you attain this?]"
"Is Śubhavyūha not my equal?
Is he truly one who speaks thus? He thought to himself:
"Surely it must be a jackal causing discord among us.
Then, the tiger Suparṇa spoke this verse in reply to the lion Sudanta:
"Suparṇa does not speak of this: Neither his form and color, nor his birth;..."
Though one possesses great strength and is superior, if one’s teeth are not well-guarded, one cannot act rightly.
If one accepts harmful words and believes the speech of others regarding this or that,
one will destroy one's own close kin and thus become an enemy.
If one knows reality as it truly is, one should extinguish hatred and affliction;
now speak with sincerity so that the body may attain benefit.
Now one should skillfully subdue and eliminate evil associates.
"One should kill this jackal who incites strife and discord among us.
They then killed the jackal, and the two beasts returned to their harmony.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"If even these two beasts, having been defeated by him, gather together in one place and find no joy upon seeing one another;
how much more so for a human being—having been defeated by another, how could the mind not be troubled?"
"How is it that the group of six bhikṣus incite strife between one another, creating disputes where none previously existed and failing to extinguish those already present?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this is the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu engages in double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "divisive speech": it refers to a bhikṣu who incites strife among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings and their ministers, non-Buddhists, heterodox śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.

A bhikṣuṇī returns to incite strife among bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings and their ministers, as well as non-Buddhist practitioners, heterodox śramaṇas, brahmins, and bhikṣus.

A śikṣamāṇā incites others to fight and create discord among other śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings and ministers, non-Buddhist practitioners, heterodox śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs.

The śrāmaṇeras further incite quarrels and disturbances among other śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings and ministers, followers of external paths and heterodox teachers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, and śikṣamāṇās.

The śrāmaṇerikās further incite strife among śrāmaṇerikās, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings and ministers, non-Buddhists and heterodox practitioners, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerikās.

An upāsaka incites others to quarrel and create discord among other upāsakas and upāsikās, kings and ministers, followers of external paths and heterodox teachers, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs.

The upāsikā incites quarrels and discord among other upāsikās, as well as kings and ministers, non-Buddhists and heterodox teachers, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and upāsakas.

Furthermore, the king incites strife against other kings, as well as ministers, non-Buddhists, heterodox śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

The minister returned to contend with and disturb other ministers, as well as non-Buddhist practitioners, heterodox teachers, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and kings.

Various heterodox practitioners, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas will further incite strife among various heterodox practitioners, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, as well as among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, and ministers.
Regarding those who cause strife and discord, someone says these words:

"You are of the Caṇḍāla caste, the scavenger caste, the bamboo-worker caste, the chariot-maker caste, the Kauṭa, the Kauśīlava, the Sūdha caste, the Kāśyapa, the Ātreya, or the Bhr̥gu; you are a seller of pigs and sheep, a butcher of oxen, a falconer, a fisherman, a hunter, a thief, a captor of thieves, a city guard or jailer, a blacksmith, a potter, a leather-worker, or a barber; you have committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, a pāyattika, a pratideśanīya, a sthūlātyaya, a duṣkṛta, or an improper speech."
"Bonds" refers to everything from ill-will up to the five hundred bonds; [those who possess them] are like the bald, the blind, the one-eyed, the lame, the crippled, the deaf, and the mute.
If a bhikṣu incites others to break their monastic unity and causes strife among the bhikṣus, if he speaks clearly, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he speaks unclearly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
