There is no offense in the following cases: when one breaks away from evil associates; when one breaks away from an evil faction; when one breaks away from those who employ expedient means to destroy the Saṃgha; when one breaks away from those who assist in destroying the Saṃgha; or when one breaks away from two or three people performing a formal ritual (karmavācanā).

If one breaks [the Sangha] by performing an illegal *karmavācanā* or an un-disciplinary *karmavācanā*, there is no offense if the person being broken is a member of the Sangha, or a stupa, or a temple, or an upādhyāya, or a co-upādhyāya, or an ācārya, or a co-ācārya, or a spiritual friend, or a relative, or someone who speaks repeatedly; or if it is without meaning or benefit, and one intends to act without meaning or benefit through skillful means when breaking such a person. There is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Part Three concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha was traveling from Śrāvastī toward the kingdom of Kośala; along the way, he arrived at a village where no bhikṣus resided and asked, "Who will give me a place to stay?"
Hearing that there was a courtesan’s house where guests were always accommodated and stayed under the portico,
Anuruddha went to that courtesan’s house and said, “Sister!
"I wish to stay for one night; would that be possible?
The courtesan replied, "You may stay;
the gateway is spacious, so you may rest there as you please."

Anuruddha immediately entered the gate and descended, spreading out a mat of grass as his seat and sitting down cross-legged with his mind focused in single-minded contemplation, binding his mindfulness before him.

At that time, several elders from the kingdom of Kosala, having business to attend to, also arrived at that village seeking a place to stay for the night. They heard that the courtesan’s house was accustomed to hosting guests, so they went to her home to request lodging, saying:
"Would it be possible to stay here for one night?"
The courtesan replied, "I have already invited a śramaṇa to stay overnight; you may ask that śramaṇa whether he can accommodate you, and if so, you may stay."
The man then went to Ānanda and said, "I spoke to the master earlier requesting lodging and was granted permission; would it not be inconvenient for me to stay with you tonight?"
Anuruddha replied, "I have finished spreading my grass mat; the porch is spacious and large, so you may stay there as you please without hesitation.
Thereupon, the elders entered the porch; as the company of elders was large, they sat down close together.

Upon seeing him, the courtesan immediately felt compassion and said, "This Aniruddha is the descendant of a noble and wealthy family; having been accustomed to pleasure for so long, he cannot endure such suffering."
"Now these householders are crowding together.

He then went to Ānanda and said, "Venerable sir, you have long been accustomed to comfort and cannot endure hardship. Now that these householders are crowding together, would you be able to stay overnight in my house?"
He replied, "Very well. Thereupon,
the Venerable Aniruddha entered the house and sat cross-legged at his seat, fixing his mindfulness before him.
At that time, oil lamps were burning in the courtesan’s chamber throughout the entire night without ceasing. During the first watch of the night, the courtesan came to Ānanda and said to him:
"Recently, many elders and brahmins of great wealth have all come to me and said:
'You should become my wife.'"
I then said to those elders: "You are all ugly;
I cannot become your wives. If you were handsome and upright, I would now become your wives."
“I observe that the Venerable One’s appearance is upright and handsome; would you be willing to be my husband?
At that time, although the Venerable Anuruddha heard these words, he remained silent and gave no answer, nor did he even look at her.
Why is this? It is because the Venerable One has attained the supreme liberation of both parts.
When the end of the night had arrived and the light of dawn was about to appear, he spoke again to Aniruddha, saying:
“Many Brahmins and householders of great wealth and treasure all spoke to me, saying:
‘Become our wife. I immediately refused them.”
"However, Aniruddha’s countenance is so handsome and upright; could he serve as my husband?
Aniruddha again remained silent and gave no answer, nor did he even look at her.
Why is this? It is because by means of this, the Venerable One has attained the unsurpassed twofold liberation.
At that moment, the courtesan immediately removed her clothes, came forward, and seized him; then, Āniruddha, by the power of his supernormal faculties, leaped into the air.

Upon seeing him, the courtesan was filled with shame and crouched down naked; she then quickly took her clothes and put them on. With palms joined in reverence, she looked up into the air and said to Anuruddha, "I repent!
I confess my transgression!"
"I confess!
Thus he said up to three times.
"I pray that the Venerable One will return and sit in his original place."
Anuruddha then descended and sat down in his place.

After this woman had paid homage at Anuruddha’s feet, she withdrew to sit on one side. Anuruddha taught her various subtle and sublime dharmas: namely, the meaning of generosity, the meaning of ethical discipline, and the meaning of rebirth in heaven; he censured the impurity of sensual desire and the bonds of outflows (*āsrava*), and praised renunciation as bliss and the increase of liberation.
At that moment, the courtesan, while still seated, was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, she said:

"I pray that you will grant me permission to become a lay follower (*upāsikā*). I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; from this day forth, for as long as I live, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants."
"I pray that the Venerable One will accept my invitation for a meal today.
Anuruddha accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that Anuruddha had silently accepted her invitation, the courtesan prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink to offer him. When he had finished eating, she took a small stool and sat before Anuruddha.
Aniruddha taught him various dharmas, exhorting and encouraging him until his heart was filled with joy. Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
Returning to the saṃghārāma, he related this incident in detail to the bhikṣus.

At that time, among the assembly there were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Aniruddha, saying: "How can it be, Aniruddha!"
"Did you sleep in the same room as women?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed Aniruddha, saying:
"Is it true that you stayed overnight alone in the same room with a woman?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The Buddha, through countless skillful means, rebuked Aniruddha, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done.
How could this be, Anuruddha!"
"Sleeping in the same room as a woman?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked Anuruddha with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu sleeps in the same room as a woman, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Woman" refers to a human female who is of sound mind and whose life-force is not severed.

A "room" (śālā) is that which has walls on all four sides with a roof covering above; or it may have an open front without walls; or it may have walls on all four sides but no roof; or it may have a roof though not covering the entire structure; or it may have a roof covering the whole yet contain openings—this is called a room.

If a bhikṣu arrives first and a woman arrives later; or if a woman arrives first and the bhikṣu arrives later; or if both arrive at the same time—if he lies down half-stretched with his side touching the ground, it is a pāyattika offense.
If she turns over onto her side, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one sleeps in the same room as a celestial maiden (*devī*), an asura maiden, a naga maiden, a yakṣa maiden, or a preta maiden, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one sleeps in the same room as an animal female, whether she possesses the power of transformation or not, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one sleeps in the same room as a *paṇḍaka* or a person with both sexual organs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a woman stands during the day while a bhikṣu lies down, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if a bhikṣu stays overnight in a room without knowing that a woman is there;
or if the bhikṣu arrives first and the woman arrives later, such that the bhikṣu was unaware [of her presence].

If a building has a roof but lacks enclosures on four sides; or if it is fully roofed but half-enclosed; or if it is fully roofed but slightly enclosed; or if it is fully enclosed but lacks a roof; or if it is fully enclosed but has a small roof; or if it is half-roofed and half-enclosed; or if it is slightly roofed and slightly enclosed; or if it is neither roofed nor enclosed, such as an open space—there is no offense.
Whether walking or sitting within this room, there is no offense.
If one falls to the ground due to dizziness or lies down because of illness, there is no offense.
Or if one is seized by force, bound by others, or faces a threat to life or a threat to pure conduct, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been promulgated; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Four concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Khaṇḍava.

The group of six bhikṣus were staying together with several elders in the lecture hall. At that time, one among the group of six fell asleep with a distracted mind and became unaware of his surroundings; as he slightly shifted his position, his body was exposed.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who covered himself with his robe; however, he turned over again and remained naked. Another bhikṣu covered him with his robe once more, but he immediately turned over again and his body was exposed.
When the householders saw this, they immediately gave rise to derision and laughed in mockery.
At that time, the sleeping bhikṣu felt ashamed and lost face, and the other bhikṣus also felt ashamed.
Among them were those who had few desires and were content, who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame, who practiced the dhūta austerities, and who delighted in training in the precepts;
they censured these bhikṣus, saying: "How can the group of six bhikṣus stay overnight together with these householders?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice of compliance—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, O group of six bhikṣus!
Do you dwell together with householders?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These six groups of bhikṣus are foolish men!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.
Thus did the Blessed One establish a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, and the bhikṣus spoke as follows:
“The Buddha has not permitted us to stay overnight with those who have not received the full precepts; we must send Rāhula out.
At that time, Rāhula had no place to stay and went to sleep in the latrine. When the Buddha knew of this, he went to the latrine and made a coughing sound.
At that time, Rāhula also cleared his throat. The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"Who is in here? Rāhula replied:
"I am Rāhula. He asked again, "What are you doing here?"
He replied: "The bhikṣus said:
'One must not stay overnight with a person who has not received full ordination.'"
"He drove me out!
The World-Honored One then said:
"How can a foolish bhikṣu, lacking any heart of compassion, drive a small child out?"
"Is this son of the Buddha not protecting my wishes?
He then immediately extended his finger for him to grasp, and taking him with him, he entered his own quarters and stayed there together for one night.
The next morning at dawn, he assembled the bhikṣus and said to them:
"You lack a heart of compassion; you have driven out a young boy. Is he not a son of the Buddha? Do you not protect my intention?"

From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to stay together with those who have not yet received the full precepts for two nights; if they reach the third night, they should rise and depart before the dawn has appeared.
If one reaches the fourth night, whether one goes oneself or sends another person who has not received the precepts,
from this day forward the precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu stays overnight with a person who has not received the full ordination, exceeding two nights and reaching the third night, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "a person who has not received the precepts," this refers to anyone other than bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs—namely, those who have not yet received the full ordination (mahā-śīla).
Regarding sleeping in the same room, it is as previously explained.

If a bhikṣu arrives first and a person who has not yet received full ordination arrives later; or if the unordained person arrives first and the bhikṣu arrives later; or if both arrive at the same time—if he places his side against the ground, he commits an offense; even if he merely turns slightly over, he also commits an offense.

If one stays together for more than two or three nights with a male deva, a male asura, a male gandharva, a male yakṣa, a male preta, or any among the animals—whether capable of transformation or incapable of transformation—it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if: the bhikṣu did not know beforehand that someone was staying there when a person who has not yet received the precepts arrived later; or if the person who has not yet received the precepts arrived first and the bhikṣu arrived later; or if the dwelling has a roof but lacks four sides, or is entirely roofed but half-enclosed, or is entirely enclosed but has little roofing, or is half-enclosed and half-roofed, or has little enclosure and little roofing; or if they sit or practice walking meditation in the open air. In these cases, there is no offense.
If one falls to the ground due to dizziness, or lies ill, or is seized by force, or is imprisoned, or faces a threat to life or a threat to one's pure conduct, these constitute no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the fifth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Khāṇumata.

The group of six bhikṣus were reciting Buddhist scriptures together with various elders in the lecture hall; their voices were so loud that they were no different from the sound of Brahmins reciting their texts, disturbing those who were practicing meditation.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you recite the sūtras together with the elders in the lecture hall, making a sound like that of Brahmins reciting their scriptures?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"How is it that you were in the lecture hall with the householder, reciting the sūtras with voices no different from those of brahmins?"
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These deluded men!
Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu recites together with one who has not received the full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Those who have not received the precepts are, with the exception of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, all others.

[This concerns] the meaning of phrases and what is not the meaning of phrases, the flavor of phrases and what is not the flavor of phrases, and the meaning of syllables and what is not the meaning of syllables.
Regarding the meaning of the phrases: reciting them together with others, neither ahead of nor behind them, [one says]: "Commit no evil, practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas."

Regarding "non-sentential meaning" (*apada-artha*): it is as when one person has not yet finished saying, "Commit no evil," and a second person repeats the preceding words, "Commit no evil. Regarding "sentential flavor" (*pada-rasa*):
it is when two people recite together, neither before nor after the other, [saying], "The eye is impermanent, the ear is impermanent, and so on, up to: the mind is impermanent."

Regarding "non-sequential phrasing" (*apada-rasa*): for example, when one person has not yet uttered that "the eye is impermanent," a second person repeats the preceding words, "the eye is impermanent.
Regarding "meaning of the syllables" (*akṣara-artha*): two people recite together, neither before nor after the other, [saying] "A-ra-pa-ca-na."
Regarding "non-literal meaning": it is like when one person has not yet uttered the word "A," and a second person anticipates the preceding word and says "A. Regarding "syntactic structure":
it consists of that which is spoken by the Buddha, that which is spoken by the śrāvakas, that which is spoken by the ṛṣis, and that which is spoken by the devas.

If a bhikṣu recites together with a person who has not yet received the precepts—whether by oral transmission or by written transmission—and does so once, twice, or thrice, if it is clearly understood, it is a pāyattika;
if it is spoken but not clearly understood, it is a duṣkṛta.

If a son of a deva, a son of an asura, a son of a yakṣa, a son of a nāga, a son of a gandharva, or an animal capable of transformation speaks once, twice, or thrice—whether the speech is clear or not clear—it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If the teacher does not instruct by saying, "When I have finished speaking,
you may speak," the teacher commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when you have finished speaking and I speak; when one person has finished reciting and another writes it down; when two people share the same task and recite together; or when speaking in jest, or speaking rapidly, or speaking to oneself, or speaking in a dream, or intending to say this but saying that instead—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Six concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were bhikṣus undergoing *pārivāsika* and *mānatva* penances sitting in the lower seats; the group of six bhikṣus then said to the laypeople:
"Do you know who these people are sitting in the lower seats?"
The laypeople replied, "We do not know.
The group of six bhikṣus said to them:
"Because these individuals have committed such offenses, and because they have committed such offenses, the Saṃgha shall punish them by making them sit in the lower row.
When the bhikṣus who have committed the transgressions hear this, they feel shame; when the other bhikṣus hear it, they also feel shame.

Among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu, having committed a gross and evil offense, go on to speak of it to laypeople?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you, knowing a bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, go on to tell a layperson about it?"
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for the outflows (āsrava), this is the first violation of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu reveals a grave offense committed by another bhikṣu to a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, some bhikṣus did not know what was coarse and offensive, nor what was not coarse and offensive; only later did they realize it was coarse and offensive. Some then performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were filled with apprehension and caution.
The Buddha said:
"If you did not know, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination (anupasampanna), it is a pāyattika.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, Śāriputra was appointed by the assembly to speak of Devadatta’s transgressions among the royal retinue and the multitude of common people:
"Regarding what Devadatta has done, do not say it is the work of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; you should know that this is the work of Devadatta."
Having heard this, Śāriputra felt a sense of fear and apprehension. When the bhikṣus learned of this, they went and informed the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One told them:
"If one is appointed by the Saṃgha, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Those who have not received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) are, with the exception of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, all others.
A grave offense (sthūlātyaya) refers to the four pārājikas and the saṃghāvaśeṣas.
The Sangha consists of a single *karma* and a single recitation of the precepts.
If a bhikṣu knows that another has committed a grave offense and speaks of it to one who has not received full ordination, except by formal authorization of the Sangha, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Apart from a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*), if one speaks of any other offense to a person who has not received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one confesses a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) that one has committed oneself to a person who has not received the full ordination, it is a duṣkṛta.
With the exception of monks and nuns, if one confesses a grave offense committed by another person to a person who has not received the full ordination, it is a duṣkṛta.
If there is a grave offense and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is a grave offense but one suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If there is no grave offense but one perceives it as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it is not coarse or malicious speech, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one does not know, or if one has been appointed by the Sangha, or if what is coarse and evil is perceived as not coarse and evil, or if a layperson has already heard of this coarse and evil offense. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in these cases: for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts; or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The seventh section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Gabled Hall on Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī. On account of this matter, he assembled the community of monks. Knowing [the answer] already, the Buddha asked intentionally: "Monks of the Bākravana Grove!"
“Is this truly so?
He replied to the Buddha,
“It is truly so.”
“World-Honored One.
The Buddha said: “You foolish people!”
"If one cannot even speak of what is true to others, how much less so that which is untrue?
Having rebuked the bhikṣu of the Bhārgava Garden with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma) to a person who has not received full ordination, saying:"
"I have seen this; I know this. To speak such a truth constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Those who have not received the full precepts" refers to all others except for bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs.
"Human phenomena" refers to the human realm, the human aggregates, and the human sense bases.
Regarding the "state of a superior person" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*): it refers to the essential deliverance from all phenomena, wherein one claims:

"I have attained mindfulness of the body and wholesome reflection; I possess morality, aspiration, heedfulness, diligence, concentration, right concentration, the Path, cultivation, wisdom, vision, attainment, and fruition."
If he truly has such a thing and speaks of it to one who has not yet received full ordination, and the meaning is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he speaks of it but the meaning is not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

If one conveys [the claim of having attained] superior human states (*uttarimanussadhamma*) by means of a hand-seal, a written message, or by sending someone with a clear sign, it is an *pāyattika* offense if the meaning is understood;
it is a *dukkaṭa* offense if it is not understood.

If one speaks thus to a son of a deva, a son of an asura, a son of a yakṣa, a son of a gandharva, a son of a nāga, a son of a preta, or a beast—whether capable of transformation or incapable of transformation—it is a *dukkaṭa* offense whether the meaning is understood or not.

If one truly attains the qualities of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) and speaks of them to a person who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) but is not of like mind, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one claims for oneself:

"I have attained the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of awakening (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*), the path (*magga*), meditative concentration (*jhāna*), liberation (*vimokkha*), and entry into samādhi," [it is likewise an offense].
To speak of this to others constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if it is due to overweening pride; if one says for oneself that this is the result of karmic retribution rather than saying it was attained through cultivation; if one truly attains a state superior to that of ordinary men and speaks of it to a fellow bhikṣu who is of like mind; if one speaks of the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, the path, the liberations, the entrances, or the samādhis, but does not say to others "I have attained these"; or if speaking in jest, speaking to oneself, speaking in a dream, or intending to speak of one thing but speaking of another instead—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The eighth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin, when the hour had come, put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of a certain great householder; there, in the presence of his mother-in-law, he spoke the Dharma in whispers with her daughter-in-law.
Upon seeing him, the mother-in-law immediately asked her daughter-in-law,
"What did you say to that bhikṣu just now?
The daughter-in-law replied:
"Preach the Dharma to us.
The mother-in-law said to her daughter-in-law:
"If you are to preach the Dharma, you should speak aloud so that we may hear; why do you speak only into your own ears?"
His wife replied, "What she said just now was no different from the words of a brother; there was no other fault.
When the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard this, he immediately rebuked Kālodāyin, saying:
“How is it, Venerable One? Did you speak the Dharma in whispers to your daughter-in-law in front of your mother-in-law?
At that time, the mendicant bhikṣu returned to the monastery and related these circumstances in detail to the other bhikṣus.

Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Kāḷudāyin, saying:
"How can this be, Venerable One!"
"Did you whisper the Dharma in the presence of your father-in-law for the sake of his daughter-in-law?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the answer, asked Kālodāyin intentionally:
"Is it true that you spoke in private with another’s daughter-in-law in the presence of her mother-in-law while preaching the Dharma?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Kālodāyin:
"What you have done is improper; it is not decorous, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the rules—it is something that should not have been done.
How could you, in the presence of your paternal aunt, whisper and preach the Dharma to another’s daughter-in-law?"
Having rebuked Kālodayin, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish Kālodayin, in many ways a source of outflows,
has committed the first breach of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there were women who invited the bhikṣus, saying:
"We pray, Venerable Sirs, that you will preach the Dharma to us."
At that time, the bhikṣus each felt apprehensive and cautious; for the World-Honored One had established a precept stating that a bhikṣu must not preach the Dharma to women.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to preach the Dharma to women using five or six sentences.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman and exceeds five or six words, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus, however, became apprehensive; fearing that there might be no man present who understood the teaching, they ceased preaching the Dharma to women altogether.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, it is permitted for a man who possesses understanding to speak the Dharma to a woman using more than five or six words.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman and speaks more than five or six words, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, there were women who requested the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!"
"I wish to receive the five precepts.
At that time, the bhikṣus felt apprehensive and hesitant; because there was no man present who understood [the procedure], they did not confer the precepts upon him.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted for a woman to receive the five precepts from a man who does not possess full knowledge.
At that time, a certain woman requested of the bhikṣus:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
"Please explain the Dharma of the five precepts to me.
At that time, there was no man who knew [the rules], and the bhikṣu, feeling apprehensive and cautious, did not explain the Dharma of the five precepts to him.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to teach the five precepts to women even in the absence of a man who understands [the Dharma].

At that time, there were women who wished to receive the eightfold fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), but the bhikṣus, being apprehensive and cautious, did not grant them the fast because no man who understood [the Dharma] was present.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to receive the eightfold precepts for lay practitioners from women when no man capable of understanding them is present."
Then the women requested the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
Please explain the eightfold precepts of the fast for us."
At that time, as there was no man present who understood [the matter], the bhikṣus, out of a sense of caution and apprehension, did not explain the Eightfold Precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) to the woman.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to explain the Eightfold Precepts to women even when no man who understands [the matter] is present."
At that time, the women said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
We wish to hear the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path."
At that time, as there was no man present who understood [the Dharma], the bhikṣu felt apprehensive and did not explain the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path to the woman.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I allow bhikṣus to explain the Dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path to women even when no man who understands [the Dharma] is present."
At that time, some women said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Please explain the ten unwholesome paths of action to us."
At that time, as there was no man present who understood [the matter], the bhikṣus felt apprehensive and hesitant, and did not explain the ten unwholesome paths of action to the woman.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to explain the ten unwholesome paths of action to women even when no man who understands [the matter] is present."
At that time, some women said to the bhikṣus:
"Virtuous ones!
Please teach us the ten wholesome dharmas."
The bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious; because there was no man present who understood [the teachings], they did not explain the ten wholesome dharmas to women.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to explain the ten wholesome dharmas to women even when no man who understands [them] is present."

At that time, there were women who came to ask the bhikṣus about the meaning of the Dharma; however, because they lacked the confidence and caution required and because no man capable of understanding was present, the bhikṣus did not answer the questions posed by the women.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit a man who does not understand [the doctrine] himself to answer the questions of women regarding its meaning.
If he does not understand, he should explain it extensively for her."
From this day forward, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu teaches the Dharma to a woman and speaks more than five or six words, except in the presence of a man capable of understanding, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above;
"woman" is also as explained above.
Regarding the "five phrases," they are: form is non-self, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self.
The six statements are: "The eye is impermanent; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are impermanent.
A man of knowledge understands matters that are coarse and evil, as well as those that are not coarse or evil.
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma to a woman for more than five or six sentences, except when a man capable of understanding is present, it is a pāyattika offense if he speaks clearly;
it is a dukkaṭa offense if he does not speak clearly.

If a celestial maiden, an asura maiden, a naga maiden, a yaksha maiden, a gandharva maiden, a preta maiden, or a beast maiden who is capable of transformation speaks more than five or six words—whether clearly or indistinctly—it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one speaks more than five or six words to an animal that is incapable of transformation, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for all.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one speaks five or six words; if one speaks more than that in the presence of a man who understands;

or if, in the absence of a man who understands, one bestows the five precepts upon a laywoman (upāsikā), explains the dharma of the five precepts, gives the eightfold fasting precepts (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), explains the dharma of the eight fasts, explains the dharma of the Eightfold Noble Path, explains the ten unwholesome dharmas and the ten wholesome dharmas, or answers questions on the meaning of the dharma posed by a woman—provided there is no man present who understands to whom she should respond. If she does not understand, she may explain it at length.
There is no offense if one speaks while joking, speaks rapidly, speaks to oneself, speaks in a dream, or intends to say one thing but says another.
There is no offense for those who acted before the precept was established, or those who were insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The ninth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Khāṇumata.
Then the group of six bhikṣus, while assisting the Buddha in repairing a lecture hall, dug up the ground all around the perimeter of the hall themselves.
At that time, the householders saw this and spoke with derision:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they sever the life-root of others, yet outwardly they claim, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
"Looking at this now, what righteous Dharma is there in this?
To dig the earth oneself and sever the life-root of another!

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that the Buddha, while preparing the lecture hall, has dug up the ground himself, causing the elders to criticize and resent him?
The bhikṣus immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in conformity [with the teachings]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that they dig up the ground themselves, causing the elders to criticize and despise them?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were repairing a lecture hall and instructing people to dig the earth, saying:
"Dig here; place it there."
When the householders saw this, they reviled him, saying:
"How can these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame? They instruct people to dig the earth and take the lives of others, possessing not even a heart of compassion."
They claim for themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
Yet, observing it now as it is, what True Dharma is there?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you repair the Buddha’s lecture hall by instructing people to dig the ground, saying:
'Dig here! Place it there!'?"
"Will this cause the elder householders to criticize and disparage us?
Having rebuked him thus, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
How can you prepare the lecture hall by instructing people to dig the earth, saying,
"Dig here; place it there," thereby causing the elders to criticize and find fault with you?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus:
if a bhikṣu digs the earth with his own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "ground," it refers to ground that has already been excavated or ground that has not yet been excavated.

If ground that has been excavated for four months or more becomes saturated with rainwater and returns to its original state, and one then uses a hoe, a pickaxe, a mallet, or a sickle to strike or pierce it—even down to scratching it with a fingernail—it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
To drive a stake into the ground, it is a *pāyattika*.
To kindle a fire upon the ground, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is ground and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not instruct them by saying,
"Look at this; know this," it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one says: "Know this; look at this. Or if one drags timber or bamboo; or if one rights what has fallen over;

or if one turns over bricks or stones, takes cow dung, or takes earth from a collapsed bank; or if one takes earth from a rat hole; or if one removes earth from a walking path (*caṅkrama*) or removes earth from within a building; or if one walks back and forth on a path; or if one sweeps the ground; or if one strikes the ground with a staff; or if one does not intentionally dig—none of these constitute an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[End of Section Ten. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Eleven.
*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Twelve, Part One, Section Twelve.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Ninety Dharmas of the Pāyattika, Part Two. At that time, the Buddha was in the city of Khānumata; for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
“Did the wilderness bhikṣu cut down trees himself in order to repair his dwelling?
He replied, “I indeed did.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked him, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why do you cut down trees yourself for the sake of repairing your dwelling?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu destroys a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Ghosts" refers to non-human beings.
"Villages" refers to all grasses and trees; because they are cut down and felled, they are said to be "destroyed."
There are five kinds of seeds:
root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, node-seeds, and seed-seeds.
As for root-seeds, these include the *harītakī*, ginger, *uśīra*, *mūlaka*, *tālukaṇṭha*, and other seeds produced from roots.
As for those propagated from cuttings, these include the willow, *śamāra*, *bhalīta*, and other such species propagated from cuttings.
As for those produced from joints, these include the *sumana* flower, *surapa*, *pūṣkara*, coriander, sorrel, and other such species produced from joints.
Those that grow from slips include sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, lotus roots, and other species that propagate by means of slips.
Those that grow from seeds are those in which the seed itself gives rise to another seed.

If one perceives something as living and cuts it oneself, or instructs another to cut it; or roasts it oneself, or instructs another to roast it; or cooks it oneself, or instructs another to cook it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

If one harbors doubt, or cuts [the plant] oneself or instructs another to cut it; or fries it oneself or instructs another to fry it; or cooks it oneself or instructs another to cook it—these constitute a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is living as not living, yet cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, or even cooks it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is not living as living, yet cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, or even cooks it, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is not a case of harboring doubt; if one cuts them oneself, instructs another to cut them, or even cooks them, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are seven colors of plants and trees: blue, yellow, red, white, black, pale green, and purple.
If one perceives living plants as living plants, and either cuts them oneself, instructs another to cut them, or even cooks them, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one suspects that living plants are present and either cuts them oneself, instructs another to cut them, or even cooks them, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one perceives what is not a living plant as a living plant, and if one cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, or even cooks it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one perceives what is not a living plant as a living plant, and if one cuts it oneself, instructs another to cut it, or even cooks it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one suspects that plants or trees are living and, whether cutting them oneself or instructing another to cut them, even to the point of boiling them, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrongdoing).
If one strikes a wooden stake into a living tree, it is a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If one sets fire to growing grass or trees, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one cuts more than half of growing grass or trees, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one cuts grass or trees that are half-dry and half-growing, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one does not say,
"Look at this; know this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: saying, "Look at this; know this"; cutting withered or dry grass and wood;

dragging timber or bamboo across living plants for the purpose of erecting a fence or screen; nudging away bricks or stones; taking cow dung; clearing a path covered by living grass by pushing it aside with a staff; blocking or cutting living plants with tiles or pillars; removing [obstructions] from a walking path (*caṅkrama*); or accidentally nudging and cutting living plants while sweeping the ground where one walks or travels. There is no offense in nudging living plants and cutting them while striking the ground with a staff.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the eleventh [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Kausāmbī in the Ghosira Park.
At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Channa committed an offense. When the other bhikṣus asked him,
"Do you know that you have committed an offense?",
he replied to the bhikṣus with some other matter.
"To whom did you speak?
What matter did you explain?
What principle did you discuss?"
Are you speaking to me, or to whom? Who has committed the offense?
From what does the offense arise?
"I see no fault! Why do you say that I am guilty?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:
"How can you, knowing for yourself that you have committed an offense, when questioned by other bhikṣus, instead answer them with some other matter, saying:
'To whom did you speak? About what matter were you speaking?'?"
To discuss what principle?
Is it for my sake that you speak, or for the sake of others?
Who has committed the offense?
"From what does sin arise?
I do not see any sin!
How can you say that I have committed a sin?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity with the path—something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, Bhikṣu Chanda!
When you have committed an offense and the bhikṣus ask you, 'Do you recognize your offense? [do you acknowledge it?]"
He then answered the bhikṣus with evasive words:
"To whom were you speaking?
What matter were you discussing?"
To discuss what principle?
Is this being said for my sake, or for the sake of others?
Who has committed the offense?
"From what does transgression arise?
I do not perceive any transgression!
Why do you speak such words?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Channa through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, it is permitted that once the formal announcement has been made, one shall be designated as 'one who speaks evasively'."
The formal announcement should be made as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense. When the bhikṣus questioned him, [he said:]..."
"Do you yourself know that you have committed an offense?
He then replied to the bhikṣus with a different matter,
saying, "To whom were you speaking just now?"
What matter do you speak of?
What principle do you discuss?
Is it for my sake that you speak, or for the sake of others?
Who commits an offense?
From what does an offense arise?
I do not perceive an offense!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the bhikṣu Chanda be designated as one who speaks evasive words.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this motion, he is designated as one who speaks evasive words.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu uses evasive speech, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Venerable Channa, against whom the Saṃgha had established a rule prohibiting him from using evasive speech, subsequently began to harass the Saṃgha: when summoned he would not come, and when not summoned he would come; when he was told to rise he would not rise, and when told not to rise he would rise; when he was told to speak he would not speak, and when told not to speak he would speak.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires, were contented, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:

"How can it be that after the Saṃgha has designated you as one who speaks evasively, you subsequently continue to harass the Saṃgha? When summoned, you do not come; when not summoned, you come. When you ought to rise, you do not rise; when you ought not to rise, you rise. When you ought to speak, you do not speak; when you ought not to speak, you speak?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, Bhikkhu Channa!

The Saṅgha has imposed upon you the formal act of 'speaking otherwise' (ukkhepanīyakamma). Yet you still intentionally harass the Saṅgha: when summoned, you do not come; when not summoned, you come; when you ought to rise, you do not rise; when you ought not to rise, you rise; when you ought to speak, you do not speak; and when you ought not to speak, you speak."
After the Blessed One had rebuked the bhikṣu Channa with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, having made a formal announcement, one shall designate the bhikṣu Channa as 'one who causes provocation.'"
One should make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

The bhikṣu Chanda, after the Saṃgha has pronounced against him the *anyavāda* (charge of speaking otherwise), has harassed the assembly of monks: when summoned he does not come, yet comes when not summoned; when he ought to rise he does not rise, yet rises when he ought not to rise; when he ought to speak he does not speak, yet speaks when he ought not to speak."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let it be decreed that the bhikṣu Chanda shall be designated as 'the Troublemaker.
This is the formal motion.
Having made this motion, he is designated as "the Troublemaker."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsely to vex another, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "speaking irrelevantly": before the Sangha has even made the formal motion (*jñapti*), one speaks irrelevantly, saying: "To whom were you speaking?
What matter were you discussing?"
To discuss what principle?
Is it for my sake that you speak, or for the sake of others?
I do not see this offense.
If one speaks in such a manner [before the formal motion], it is entirely a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one speaks in such a manner after the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, it is entirely a *pāyattika* offense.

Regarding causing annoyance: if before the formal motion, one calls for someone to come and they do not come, or does not call for them and they come; if one should rise and does not rise, or should not rise and rises; if one should speak and does not speak, or should not speak and speaks—all of these are entirely *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If, after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, one speaks in this manner, all incur a *pāyattika*.
If an elder summons someone and they do not come, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one did not understand because they were hard of hearing, if there was confusion in the preceding speech, or if one says, "To whom did you speak? up to "I do not see this offense."

If one intends to perform an illegal *karma* or a non-disciplinary (*aviniya*) *karma*, or if one intends to perform a *karma* that is unbeneficial toward the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, an upādhyāya, a co-upādhyāya, an ācārya, a co-ācārya, or a close friend or acquaintance—and thus refuses to grant them reconciliation; if they do not come when summoned, there is no offense.

If one intends to perform an illegal *karmavācanā* or a non-disciplinary *karmavācanā*—whether against the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, an upādhyāya, a co-upādhyāya, an ācārya, a co-ācārya, or a close friend or acquaintance—and wishes to perform an act that is unbeneficial, if one wishes to know [of this], one should instruct them, saying:
"Do not come."
If he comes immediately, there is no offense.
If one eats while remaining seated, or if one eats without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food), or if one is ill and does not rise when called, there is no offense.

If the dwelling collapses or is burned; if a venomous snake enters the dwelling; if one encounters bandits; if one encounters tigers, wolves, or lions; if one is taken away by force; if one is bound by others; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya)—if one is instructed not to rise but rises nonetheless, there is no offense.
If one asks with an evil intent, or if one asks about the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma),
saying, "Do you say this is so?", and one answers him, there is no offense.

If a formal act (karmavācanā) is performed that is contrary to the Dharma or contrary to the Vinaya; or if it concerns the Saṃgha, a stūpa or monastery, one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), a co-preceptor, an instructor (ācārya), a co-instructor, or a close friend and acquaintance; and if one wishes to cause them harm, there is no offense in speaking even when instructed not to speak.
If one speaks in a low voice, speaks very rapidly, speaks while dreaming, or speaks to oneself; or if, intending to say this, one says that by mistake—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The twelfth section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Then, the Venerable Trapusa-māra-putra was appointed by the community of monks to oversee the seating arrangements for the Saṃgha and to assign the distribution of food.

At that time, the bhikṣus Maitrāyaṇīputra and Pṛthivībandhu, standing at a distance from one another such that they could see each other with their eyes but could not hear each other’s voices, said to one another:
"This Trapusa-Mālava has affection, hatred, fear, and delusion."
Other bhikṣus said to them:
"This Trapuṣabhadra has been appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee the seating arrangements for the monks and to assign the monks' meals; you must not say of him:
'He has favoritism, he has ill will, he has fear, or he has delusion.'"
The bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra replied, "We did not speak to their faces; we merely criticized them in private!

When the other bhikṣus heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, spoke in disapproval of the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying:
"This Trapusa-māra-putra has been appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee the seating arrangements for the monks and to assign their meals.
How can you say of him:
'He possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion'?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the teachings—it is what should not be done."
"How is it, Bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra!
Since Ṭhapassamala was appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee the seating arrangements for the Saṃgha and to assign the food to the monks, why do you all find fault with him, saying:
'He has attachment, he has aversion, he has fear, and he has delusion'?"
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“The bhikṣu Maitrībala is a fool!
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu reviles or disparages [another], it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
Later, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra again employed a stratagem; he went to a place where the bhikṣu Ṭhapassamallaputta could hear him but not see him, and they said to one another:
"This Ṭhapassamallaputta has attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion."
The bhikṣus said to him,
"Has the Buddha not established a precept stating that disparaging others is a pāyattika offense?
The bhikṣu Maitrībala replied:
"We do not resent this; it is merely an insult!

At that time, some bhikṣus heard this. Among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse.
They censured the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra, saying: "This Trapusa was appointed by the Saṃgha to manage the seating arrangements for the monks and to assign their meals. Why do you revile him?"

After the bhikṣus had finished their reprimand, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Maitrībala:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice; it is that which should not be done."
“Tapassamallaputta has been appointed by the Saṃgha to oversee the seating arrangements for the monks and to assign their meals; why do you revile him?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Māluṅkyaputra with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus: if a bhikṣu reviles another out of resentment, it is a pāyattika.”
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
This refers to either reviling someone face-to-face or scolding them behind their back.
Regarding "reviling face-to-face," this refers to speaking within the range of sight but outside the range of hearing.
"There is lust, there is hatred, there is fear, and there is delusion.
To revile from behind means to speak in a place where one's ears can hear but one cannot see, saying:
"There is lust, there is hatred, there is fear, and there is delusion."
If a bhikṣu reviles another bhikṣu and his words are clearly understood, it is a pāyattika;
if they are not clearly understood, it is a duṣkṛta.
If an elder instructs you to revile someone, and you, having received that instruction, proceed to revile them, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if the person actually committed the act, yet—possessing attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion and fearing future regret—speaks so as to cause them to confess according to the Dharma, saying:
"I have attachment, I have aversion, I have fear, and I have delusion."
There is no offense.
There is no offense if one speaks in jest, speaks to oneself, or speaks in a dream; nor is there an offense if, intending to say this, one mistakenly says that instead.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The thirteenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Śrāvastī who wished to invite the Saṃgha for a meal. There were seventeen groups of bhikṣus who took the monastic sitting mats and spread them out in the open air, pacing back and forth while waiting for the time of the meal to arrive.
When the time arrived, they did not gather up their monastic sitting mats before departing for that meal;
consequently, the monks' sitting mats were immediately covered in wind-blown dust and soil, damaged by insects and birds, and became filthy and impure.

After the bhikṣus had finished eating, they returned to the saṃghārāma and saw that the monastic mats were covered in wind-blown dust and soil, damaged by insects and birds, and defiled and impure. They immediately asked:
"Who has spread out the monastic mats and departed without gathering them up?"
Consequently, it was subjected to wind, dust, and soil; it was pecked at and damaged by insects and birds; it became filthy and impure.
He replied, “The group of seventeen bhikṣus took the matting.”

When the monks heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of seventeen monks, saying:

"How is it that you spread out the monastic sitting mats and do not gather them up, allowing wind, dust, and soil to settle upon them, letting insects and birds peck at and damage them, and leaving them filthy and impure?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this incident and rebuked the seventeen groups of bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, group of seventeen bhikṣus!

Having spread out the saṃgha’s sitting mats, you departed without gathering them up, allowing wind, dust, and soil to settle upon them, letting insects and birds peck at and damage them, and leaving them defiled and impure?"
Having rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu takes a rope bed, a wooden bed, a bedding mat, or a sitting cushion belonging to the Saṃgha, and spreads it out on an open space himself or instructs another to spread it, and then departs without putting it away himself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to that which belongs to the Saṃgha for the sake of the Saṃgha.
"Saṃgha property" refers to that which has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.
"Belonging to the Saṃgha" means that which has been made for the Saṃgha but not yet relinquished to the Saṃgha.
"Appropriated by the Saṃgha" means that which has already entered the Saṃgha and has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.
There are five kinds of rope beds:
There are rope beds with curved legs, straight-legged rope beds, curved-legged rope beds, those with steps, and those without legs; wooden beds are likewise.
"Reclining requisites" refers to those used for sitting or lying down.
"Cushions" are used for sitting.

If a bhikṣu spreads out a monastic corded bed, a wooden bed, a reclining mat, or a sitting cushion on an open space, or instructs another to spread them, when he departs, if there is a resident bhikṣu, a *māmāte*, or a steward present, he should speak to them as follows:
"I now entrust this to you; you must guard and look after it.
If there is no one at all present, one should lift it to a secluded place and depart.
If there is no secluded place, and one knows for certain that this spot will not be damaged and will remain secure, one should cover the fine items with the coarse ones and depart.

If he can return immediately upon arriving, he should go; if it rains heavily but he can return quickly without damaging his sitting mat, he should go; if it rains moderately and he can travel through it and return, he should go; if it rains lightly and he can travel a short distance and return, he should go. That bhikṣu should depart by employing such expedients in this sequence.
If a bhikṣu proceeds without having made such preparations, at the moment he first steps out the door, it is a pāyattika.
If one foot is outside the door and one foot is inside the door, and though he intends to go he does not go but instead turns back in regret, it is entirely a duṣkṛta.
If two people sit together on a single rope bed or wooden bed, the junior person should clear it away before departing.

If the junior person intends that the senior person will clear it away, yet the senior person fails to do so and the junior person nevertheless commits a *pāyattika* offense, they also commit a *dukkaṭa* offense due to improper conduct.
The Elder’s intention was that the Junior should collect [the items], yet the Junior did not collect them; thus, the Elder commits a *pāyattika* offense.
If the two are neither before nor after one another and both fail to collect them, both commit a *pāyattika* offense.

Furthermore, if one leaves behind other items such as empty rope beds, wooden beds, squatting stools, tables, or bathing benches; or the outer and inner linings of bedding; or floor coverings; or takes up ropes, cords, or wool and places them in the open air without putting them away before departing, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one spreads bedding for the Saṃgha in an open space and fails to put it away before entering a room to sit in meditation, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one takes a monastic rope bed, wooden bed, squatting stool, table, bedding, or sitting cushion, spreads it oneself in an open space or instructs another to spread it, and upon departing, speaks to the resident monks, the *māmādika*, or the manager, saying:
"Guard this; I entrust it to you."
If there is no one present, he should collect them and place them in a secluded spot before departing;

if there is no secluded place where they can be set down, and he knows for certain that they will not be lost nor feared to be damaged in that location, he may cover the finer items with the coarser ones before departing;
or he may depart and immediately return.
If one returns quickly due to a violent wind and heavy rain;
or if one travels at a moderate pace during moderate rain and returns at a slow pace when the rain is light;
or if one proceeds by employing such expedient means in succession—there is no offense.
If one is constrained by force, or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), it is not an offense if one does not depart in the proper sequence.
If two people sit together on a single rope-couch, the junior person should withdraw.

If there are various other empty wooden beds, rope beds, squatting stools, or tables, bathing benches, or the outer and inner covers of bedding, or ropes and woolen mats spread upon the open ground, and one collects them and departs; or if—
If one spreads a monastic sitting mat on open ground and, having gathered it up, enters a room for contemplation, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain.
The fourteenth [section] is finished. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu said to a resident bhikṣu:
"I have spread out bedding and stayed overnight in a peripheral monk's cell."
Later, at another time, he departed without informing the resident bhikṣus. Consequently, the Sangha’s bedding and furniture became moldy, ruined, infested with insects, and faded in color.
At the times of the morning meal, the midday meal, the night Dharma discourse, and the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the resident bhikṣus did not see the visiting bhikṣu.
The resident bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Why is it that we do not see the visiting bhikṣus?

Have they perhaps passed away? Or have they gone far away? Or have they renounced the precepts to become laypeople? Or have they been robbed by bandits? Or have they been devoured by wild beasts? Or have they been swept away by water?"
He immediately went to the dwelling and saw that the monks' sitting mats were rotted, gnawed by insects, and discolored. Having seen this, he censured the visiting bhikṣu for his conduct:

"How could you, visiting bhikṣu, tell me to spread out the monks' bedding in the peripheral room for the night, yet depart without telling me, causing the monks' sitting mats to become rotted, gnawed by insects, and discolored?"

When the monks heard this, among them were those who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta-austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing;

they censured the visiting monks, saying: "How can these visiting monks, having told an established monk that they would stay overnight after spreading the bedding belonging to the Saṃgha in a peripheral room, depart without informing him, thereby causing the Saṃgha's bedding to become moldy, infested with insects, and discolored?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the visiting bhikṣu:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
