Why did you spread out bedding for the community of monks in a peripheral room, stay there overnight, and then depart without informing the resident bhikṣus, thereby causing the community’s bedding to become moldy and discolored?
Having rebuked the visiting bhikṣu with countless skillful means, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu spreads bedding belonging to the Saṃgha within a monastic dwelling—whether spreading it himself or instructing another to do so—and sits or lies upon it, yet when departing does not himself remove it nor instruct another to remove it, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Property of the Saṃgha" is as explained above.
"Bedding and furniture" refers to rope beds, wooden beds, mattresses, sitting mats, pillows, floor coverings, and down to woolen blankets.

If that bhikṣu, within the monastic quarters, spreads bedding for the community of monks—whether spreading it himself or instructing another to do so—and then sits or lies upon it, yet upon departing does not lift it up himself nor instruct another to lift it, then if there is a resident bhikṣu, a steward (*karmadāna*), or a *māmaka* (superintendent) present, he should say to them:
"Take charge of this and lift it up securely."

If there is no one to whom it can be entrusted therein, and he does not fear losing it, he should move his bed away from the wall and prop the legs high; he should place his pillows, mattresses, and bedding inside, cover them with another bedding, and then depart.
If one fears that [the bedding] might be damaged or ruined, one should take the bedding, rugs, and pillows, place them upon a clothing rack or a standing bed, and then depart.
That bhikṣu should act in this manner before departing; if a bhikṣu departs without acting in this way and crosses the boundary, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one foot is outside the boundary and one foot is inside the boundary, yet one regrets the action and does not proceed, it is entirely *duṣkṛta*.
If one intends to go but does not go, it is *duṣkṛta*.

If he returns before long, having stayed outside the boundary for two nights, and on the third night before the dawn has appeared, he either goes to his own quarters himself or sends a messenger to say to the *māmakya* (steward) or the person in charge:
"Please take charge of and protect this item."
If a bhikṣu stays outside the boundary for two nights, and upon reaching the third night before the dawn has broken, he neither goes to his own quarters himself nor sends a messenger to say:
"Please take charge of and protect this item."
[If one] says this, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one spreads bedding for the Sangha, whether spreading it oneself or instructing another to spread it, or if one sits or lies down upon it.
If, while he is departing, there is among them an original resident, a *karmadāna*, or an administrator who says to him:
"Guard these items; act as the *karmadāna* therein."

If there is no one to whom it may be entrusted, one should ensure that nothing is damaged or ruined. One should lift the bed away from the wall, take the bedding, pillows, and mats, place them upon the bed with a heavy cover over them, and then depart;
or, if one fears they might be damaged, one should place the bedding on a clothing rack and stand the bed upright before departing.
Departing in such a manner constitutes no offense.
If the dwelling is dilapidated, collapsing, or burning with fire;
if there is a venomous snake within;
or if one is seized by thieves, tigers, wolves, lions, or those of powerful force;
If one is bound in fetters, or faces danger to life, or danger to the holy life;
or if the time for returning is not long;
or if one stays outside the boundary for two nights, and on the third night before the dawn has appeared, one should depart by oneself, or send a messenger to say to those formerly residing there:
"Take charge of these items and act as their steward (māmadhi).
[This applies] if there are obstacles on the way to the water source;
or if there are bandits, tigers, wolves, or lions on the road.
If there is a great flood;
if one is held by force;
or if one is bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya);
If one has stayed outside the boundary for two nights and the dawn of the third night appears, one may neither go there oneself nor dispatch a messenger to say to someone:
"Take charge of these items and act as my *māmādhi* (steward)."
There is no offense.
One for whom there is no offense is one to whom the precept has not yet been promulgated, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The fifteenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were traveling along a road in the kingdom of Kosala toward another village, arriving at a place where no other bhikṣus resided.
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus said to the group of six bhikṣus,
"You should go first to seek a place to stay.
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"You go yourself; what business is it of yours?
The group of six bhikṣus were the seniors of the group of seventeen bhikṣus, so the group of seventeen bhikṣus said to the group of six:
"You are our seniors; as seniors, you should seek lodging first, and we shall seek it afterwards."
The group of six bhikṣus replied, "You may go;
we do not seek a place to stay. Thereupon, the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to seek a dwelling, where they themselves spread out bedding and stayed the night.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the group of seventeen bhikṣus had sought out a place to stay and finished arranging their bedding, went to them and said:
"Arise; you must dwell according to the order of seniority."
He said, "I will not rise for you.
The group of six asked:
"How old are you now? The group of seventeen replied, "The elders are truly our seniors; we have already spoken to the elders previously."
"We should first seek a place to stay, and only then shall we seek a place for ourselves;
now that you have already settled here, we can certainly no longer move.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus forcibly spread out bedding and stayed among the seats. The group of seventeen bhikṣus called out in a loud voice:
"Venerable sirs, do not do this!
Venerable sirs, do not do this!

When the monks heard this, among them were those who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six monks, saying:
"How is this, Group of Six Bhikṣus!
The Group of Seventeen Bhikṣus had already obtained a dwelling place; have you come later and forcibly spread out bedding within it to stay the night?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, Group of Six Bhikṣus!
The Group of Seventeen Bhikṣus had already obtained a dwelling place; have you come later and forcibly spread out bedding within it to stay there?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six bhikṣus are foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, when another bhikṣu has already occupied a dwelling, later comes and forcibly spreads bedding within it to stay the night, thinking to himself:"
"If that person finds it cramped, they shall depart of their own accord.
By making such a pretext, which is neither otherwise nor in accordance with proper decorum, it is a *pāyattika*.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether it was a previously inhabited dwelling or not. Later, when they realized it was a previously inhabited dwelling, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive.
The Buddha said: "For those who did not know, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precept shall be established as follows:
If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu already occupies a dwelling, comes later and forcibly spreads out bedding within it to stay the night, thinking to himself:
"If he finds it too cramped, he will naturally avoid me and leave."
"By acting with such causes and conditions, and not otherwise, nor in accordance with proper decorum, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"In between" refers to either beside the head, beside the feet, or beside both sides of the body.
Regarding bedding: this refers to mats of grass or leaves, down to ground-covering cloths or sleeping blankets.

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has already obtained a dwelling place, later comes and forcibly spreads his bedding within it to stay the night, such that even as he turns over on his side he comes into contact with the bed, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if one did not know it beforehand; or if, after speaking, one remains stationary;
or if one has previously granted an opening;
or if the opening is so wide that there is no obstruction.
If there is an acquaintance, and that acquaintance instructs [the monk], saying,
"Simply spread it out upon it; I myself shall speak to its owner," yet he falls to the ground,
or due to illness turns over and falls onto it;
There is no offense if one is held by force;
or if one is imprisoned;
or if there is danger to life; or if there is danger to the holy life.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Section sixteen concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of seventeen bhikṣus were traveling on the road through the wilderness of Kosala and arrived at a small resting place.
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus said to the group of six bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Go first to spread out the bedding.
The group of six replied, "You go yourself; why should we concern ourselves with your affairs?"
The group of six bhikṣus were the senior monks of the group of seventeen; they spoke thus:
"Venerable sir, you are our senior; you go first and spread out the bedding, and we shall spread it out in succession."
The group of six replied, "You may go ahead; we will not spread out [the bedding].

The group of seventeen bhikṣus, who took pride in their cleanliness, entered the monastery and swept and sprinkled the rooms until they were clean, spreading fine bedding upon which they stayed for the night.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the group of seventeen had entered the monastery and had already swept and sprinkled the rooms until they were clean and pure and had spread out fine bedding, went immediately into the rooms and said:
"Elders, rise and sit according to your seniority."
They replied, "We shall not rise.
The group of six then asked:
"How old are you now? The seventeen groups of bhikṣus replied, "Venerable sir, you are truly our senior;
we have already told the senior that we would spread [the bedding] first, and we shall spread it afterwards in succession."
"Now that we are already seated and cannot rise, and as it is now close to dusk, we shall simply stay together for the night.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus forcibly pulled [the others] out of the room, driving them away with anger and displeasure.
Then the group of seventeen bhikṣus cried out in a loud voice:
"Do not do this, worthy sirs!
Do not do this, worthy sirs!"
At that time, the bhikṣus in the neighboring rooms heard this and immediately asked,
"For what reason are you shouting so loudly?
Then the seventeen groups of bhikṣus explained the matter to them in full detail.

Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you, out of anger and displeasure, forcibly drag the group of seventeen bhikṣus out of the monastic quarters?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the proper course of action—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, Six Group Bhikṣus!
Out of anger and displeasure, did you forcibly drag the Seventeen Group Bhikṣus out of the monastic quarters?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the Six Group Bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If a bhikṣu, out of anger toward another bhikṣu, does not wish for him to dwell in the communal monastery quarters,
and either drags him out himself or instructs another to drag him out, it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Monastery" (saṃghārāma) is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu, being angry with another bhikṣu and displeased with him staying in the monastery, either drags him out himself or instructs another to drag him out, for every step he is dragged, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one drags many people out through many doors, there are multiple pāyattikas.
If one drags many people out through one door, there are multiple pāyattikas.
If one drags one person out through many doors, there are multiple pāyattikas.
If one drags a person out through a single door, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one carries another's belongings out, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one throws an object outside the door, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one closes another inside and leaves them outside the door, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one departs in due order without a mind of resentment;
or if, after staying together for two nights up to three nights, one sends away a person who has not yet received the precepts.
If one has broken the precepts, broken the views, or broken the deportment; if they have been formally accused by another, or expelled by another, or are subject to expulsion;
and for these reasons there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life—there is no offense in expelling such persons as these.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The seventeenth section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Some bhikṣus were staying on an upper story of a multi-storied building. Sitting on a bed with removable legs, they sat without composure; a bhikṣu who was staying overnight below the gallery had the bed’s leg detach and fall onto him, injuring his body and causing blood to flow.
At that time, the bhikṣu looked up and reviled him in anger: "How can you, O bhikṣu!
While staying atop a multi-storied pavilion, sit upon a bed with removable legs and fail to remain composed, causing the legs of the bed to slip out and strike my body until it bleeds?"

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They reproached that bhikṣu, saying:

"How could a bhikṣu, while on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sit upon a bed with removable legs and sit so unsteadily that the legs of the bed slip out from beneath and strike another bhikṣu’s body, causing blood to flow?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."

"How is it, bhikṣu? While on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sitting on a bed with removable legs, did you sit without composure, causing the legs of the bed to slip out and strike that other bhikṣu’s body, wounding him and drawing blood?"
After the Blessed One had rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for the outflows (āsrava), this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, in a room or on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"House" (śālā) refers to either a monastic dwelling or a private room.
A "multi-storied building" (kūṭāgāra) is one where, when standing at the bottom, the head does not reach the upper level.
Regarding "a bed with removable legs": this refers to a bed whose legs are inserted into sockets.
If a bhikṣu sits or lies down on a bed with removable legs while staying on an upper story of a multi-storied building, and his side touches the bed as he turns over, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Excluding beds with detachable legs, if one uses a single-seated chair, a plank bed, or a bathing bench, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

if one sits on a rope bed with curved legs, a rope bed with straight legs, a bed with curved legs, or a legless bed; if the supports of the bed are large; if it is a bed with removable legs fitted with a narrow waistband; if there is a wooden board covering the upper level of a multi-storied building; if there is a carved wooden floral canopy; if there is a heavy, thick covering; if one sits by turning the bed around; or if one sits after removing the legs of the bed. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the eighteenth [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the Venerable Bhikṣu Chanda was building a large house; he mixed mud with water containing living creatures and instructed his laborers to do so. When the local elders saw this, they reproached him, saying:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and lack compassion; they harm the lives of sentient beings while outwardly claiming, 'I practice the True Dharma.'"
“Looking at it now, what righteous Dharma is there?
To teach people to mix water with insects and mud for the purpose of harming the lives of many sentient beings!

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Chanda, saying:
“How can one construct a dwelling by mixing mud with water containing insects and instructing others to do so, thereby harming the lives of many sentient beings?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Chanda, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, Chanda!
Did you instruct people to mix mud with water containing living creatures to build a house?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked Chanda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu mixes water containing living beings with mud, or instructs another to mix it, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not yet know which water contained living beings and which was free of them; only later did they realize there were living beings present. Consequently, some offered confession for a pāyattika offense, while others remained fearful and apprehensive. The Buddha said:
"If one does not know, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu knows that water contains living beings, and he himself pours it over mud or grass, or instructs another to pour it, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If one knows that water contains insects and throws grass or earth into it, it is a *pāyattika*.
Excluding water, if one pours insect-infested curd-milk (*takrapāna*), clear curd-milk, vinegar, or malt-water onto mud or grass, or instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places soil or grass into clear buttermilk containing living insects, or into vinegar, water, or malt-infused liquid, or if one instructs another to do so, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If there are insects in the water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are insects in the water but one suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If there are no insects in the water but one perceives them as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one suspects that water contains insects, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one does not know there are insects and perceives them as being absent; or if the insects are large and one touches the water with the hand to make them leave; or if one strains the water and sprinkles it on the ground; or if one instructs another to sprinkle it—in all such cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the nineteenth [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the country of Kauśāmbī, in the Gośṛṅga Park.

At that time, the Venerable Channa was building a large dwelling; after it had been roofed, there was still some grass remaining, so he roofed it again, and there was still more grass, so he roofed it a third time, yet there was still grass remaining.
Then he thought to himself:
"I cannot constantly beg for grass from my donors; if I continue to add heavy coverings, the house will eventually collapse.
When the householders saw this, they looked upon his conduct with disdain.
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they beg without satiety.
Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"Looking at it now, what righteous Dharma is there?
Why did you construct this great hall with such heavy roofing without ceasing, causing it to break, snap, and collapse?
Although the donor gave it, the recipient ought to have known contentment."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:
"How could you build a large dwelling with such heavy roofing without ceasing, causing it to collapse and break apart?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Candana, why have you built this large hall with such excessive roofing that it has caused it to collapse and crumble?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Candana through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Chanda the bhikṣu is a fool!
This is the first instance of transgression among many sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”

If a bhikṣu constructs a large dwelling, including its doors, windows, and other decorative fittings, he may direct that the roofing and thatching be completed in two or three layers; if he exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
A "large dwelling" (mahāśaya) refers to one that uses many materials and is further adorned with carvings, engravings, and colorful paintings.
Regarding the "roof," there are two kinds:
Whether covering lengthwise or crosswise,
once that bhikṣu has directed the covering of two joints and the third joint is not yet finished, he must depart to a place where he is neither seen nor heard.

If a bhikṣu has covered two sections and the third section is not yet finished, and he does not go to a place where he is neither seen nor heard, then upon the completion of the third section, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one abandons the place of hearing and goes to the place of seeing, or abandons the place of seeing and goes to the place of hearing, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one has assigned the work for two sections of roofing and, before the third section is finished, goes to a place where one is neither seen nor heard;

or if the path by water or land is cut off; or there is danger from bandits, danger from various predatory beasts, or the waters have risen high; or if one is held by force, or is bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya); in such cases, having assigned the work for two sections and being on the verge of the third section before it is finished, if one does not go to a place where one is neither seen nor heard, there is no offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain. [The twentieth section concludes.

At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus. They were observing the summer retreat during the middle months of the year, and all were renowned throughout the world, such as: the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Kapphiṇa, the Venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Revata, the Venerable Ānanda, the Venerable Nanda, the Venerable Nadi—these and others, numbering five hundred, were present together.

At that time, five hundred bhikṣuṇīs—including Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī, Kṣemā Bhikṣuṇī, Utpalavarṇā Bhikṣuṇī, Tiṣyā-Gautamī Bhikṣuṇī, Pāṭalīcārī Bhikṣuṇī, Sūmī Bhikṣuṇī, Śuklā Bhikṣuṇī, Sulā Bhikṣuṇī, Cārī Bhikṣuṇī, Vācārī Bhikṣuṇī, Śīlavācanā Bhikṣuṇī, Ārāpā Bhikṣuṇī, Mālāpī Bhikṣuṇī, Cunī Bhikṣuṇī, and Vanī Bhikṣuṇī—with Mahāprajāpatī at their head, entered the rains retreat within the royal park at Śrāvastī.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and sat to one side. Having sat down, she addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will permit the bhikṣus to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs."
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"I now permit the bhikṣus to provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs and to preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī bowed her head at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“From this day forward, it is permitted to appoint senior bhikṣus in turn to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them.”
At that time, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda went to where the bhikṣu Panthaka was and said to him: "Elder,
provide instruction and preach the Dharma for the bhikṣuṇīs."
Paṇḍa replied to Ānanda, "I have recited only a single verse!
How can I instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?"
"How do you preach the Dharma?
Ānanda spoke again to Panthaka: "Elder!..."
"Exhort the bhikṣuṇīs by preaching the Dharma to them.
Paṇḍaka replied again to Ānanda,
"What I have recited is but a single verse!"
"How should one instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them?
Ānanda spoke for a third time to the bhikṣu Panthaka:
"The World-Honored One has given an instruction, appointing the elder bhikṣus to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them."
"Elder! You should instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma to them.
At that time, the Venerable Panthaka accepted the command in silence.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs heard that the Venerable Bandhaka Bhikṣu was scheduled to come the following day to provide instruction, and they said to one another:
"This foolish and ignorant Bandhaka knows only a single verse!"
"Having spoken thus, you should remain silent; what more is there to say?

Then, on the following morning at dawn, the Venerable Panthaka put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished his begging, he returned to the saṃghārāma, adjusted his garments, and taking a certain bhikṣu with him, went to the place where the bhikṣuṇīs were observing the rains retreat in the Royal Garden.

At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs saw the Venerable Panthaka approaching from afar, they each went forward to meet him; some brushed his robes, some took up his bowl and prepared his sitting mat, and some set out pure water and vessels for washing his feet.
At that time, the Venerable Panthaka took his seat and sat down. After the bhikṣuṇīs had come forward and prostrated at his feet, they sat to one side.
Then Mahāprajāpatī addressed the Venerable Panthaka, saying:
"Now is the right time; you should provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs."
At that time, Panthaka spoke these verses:
"The one who has entered into tranquility rejoices; seeing the Dharma, they attain peace and happiness.
In this world, freedom from anger is the greatest joy; it consists in not harming living beings."
"There is no pleasure in the world like the renunciation of sensual desire;
if one subdues the conceit of 'I am,' this is the supreme happiness.
When the Venerable Panthaka had spoken this verse, he immediately entered the fourth dhyāna.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs said to one another in jest:
"I have already said this: the foolish bhikṣu Paṇḍaka only recites a single verse; once he has come and preached it for us, what else will there be left for him to say?"
"Now that you remain silent, it is indeed as you have said.
At that time, all the bhikṣuṇīs who were arhats, hearing what Paṇḍaka had spoken, were filled with great joy and knew that Paṇḍaka possessed great supernormal powers.
Then Mahāprajāpatī spoke again to the Venerable Panthaka:
"Exhort the bhikṣuṇīs and preach the Dharma for them.
Thereupon, the Bhikṣu Panthaka repeated the verses he had previously spoken; having done so, he entered the fourth dhyāna and remained silent without uttering a word.
Then Mahāprajāpatī again requested the Venerable Panthaka to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣu Panthaka then repeated the verses he had previously spoken, after which he returned to enter the fourth dhyāna and remained there in silence.
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs said to one another:
"The Venerable Panthaka is dull-witted; he knows only a single verse. If he comes to preach to us, he will have finished his teaching after reciting it just once."
"Now that he remains silent, it is indeed as you have said.
Only the Arhat Bhikṣuṇī knew that Paṇḍaka was an Arhat possessed of great supernormal powers. At that time, the Venerable Paṇḍaka formed this thought:
"I shall now observe the minds of these people; will they rejoice upon hearing what I have just said?"
At that time, the Venerable Panthaka observed the minds of the bhikṣuṇīs; some were joyful, while others were not. He then thought further:
"I should now manifest a sign of remorse for them."

He immediately ascended into the void, sometimes manifesting his body to preach the Dharma, sometimes concealing his form to preach the Dharma, sometimes manifesting half his body to preach the Dharma, or sometimes not manifesting half his body to preach the Dharma; at times smoke and flames issued from his body, and at other times they did not appear.
At that time, after the Venerable Panthaka had manifested these various transformations in mid-air for the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs and preached the Dharma, he immediately departed from the air.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sent a messenger to say to the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"It is now our turn to provide instruction and preach the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs."
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs addressed the community of bhikṣuṇīs, saying, "The group of six bhikṣus is next in turn to provide instruction and preach the Dharma.

When the night had passed, on the following morning at dawn, the group of six bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished their alms-round, they returned to the saṃghārāma, readjusted their garments, composed their deportment, and proceeded to the Royal Garden to the place where the bhikṣuṇīs were observing the rains retreat, whereupon they took their seats.
When the bhikṣuṇīs had prostrated at his feet, they each took their seats. At that time, the group of six bhikṣus,
while instructing the bhikṣuṇīs, spoke of other matters instead of discussing morality,
concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, fewness of desires and contentment, and the essential path to deliverance.
They advance in their practice, abandon [unwholesome paths] to incline toward the good, and do not dwell in noisy turmoil.
They discourse on the twelve links of dependent origination, yet they speak only of treatises concerning kings,
subjects, armies and horses, strife and contention, ministers, riding and chariots, women, flower garlands, drinking parties, and courtesans.
Discourses on beds and bedding, discourses on clothing, discourses on fine food and drink, discourses on bathing pools and recreation,
discourses on visiting kinsmen, discourses on various distinctions, discourses on contemplating worldly affairs, and discourses on entering the sea— they frequently engage in such discourses,
sometimes laughing, sometimes dancing, or puffing their lips and playing lutes and drums.
They whistle, or puff their mouths to produce the sound of a conch shell; some imitate the cry of a peacock, others the call of a crane;
some run side by side, some limp on one leg, and some engage in mock combat.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, seeing such a thing, were exceedingly joyful and said:
"The group of six bhikṣus teaches in this manner; it is most appropriate."
The Arhat Bhikṣuṇīs remained silent out of a heart of reverence.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side. After a short while, she addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"It is now the turn of the group of six bhikṣus to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, yet they speak of other matters instead."

Nor did he discourse on the treatises of precepts or concentration, nor even dwell amidst the clamor of the twelvefold chain of dependent origination; instead, he spoke only of royal affairs, even discussing mundane matters such as contemplating the sea, and would further engage in jesting, singing, dancing, or even limping on one leg in battle.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, having reported this matter to the World-Honored One, prostrated herself at his feet and departed.
Then the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"Is it true that you have instructed the bhikṣuṇīs in such a manner?"
Then the group of six bhikṣus replied,
“It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you instruct the bhikṣuṇīs in such a manner?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the Saṃgha shall appoint a person from among its members to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal motion with one subsequent proclamation) should appoint a capable person to perform the *karman*, as described above, making the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let it appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs."
"Whichever elders approve of appointing this bhikṣu to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has finished appointing the bhikṣu so-and-so to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs. Since the Saṃgha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said:
"The Saṃgha has not appointed us to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

They then went outside the boundary and appointed one another to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, sending a messenger to tell the group of six bhikṣuṇīs: "Speak on our behalf to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, saying:"
"The group of six bhikṣus has been appointed by the Saṃgha to come and instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.

When the other bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-observances, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"The Saṃgha has not appointed you to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; why then do you, while outside the boundary, appoint one another to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs and send a messenger to tell the bhikṣuṇīs: [and so forth].
"Has the Saṃgha already appointed us to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs?
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs immediately informed the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, saying:
“The Saṃgha has already appointed the group of six bhikṣus to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
When Mahāprajāpatī heard these words, she went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, and stood to one side.
Having reported these matters in detail to the World-Honored One, he prostrated himself at his feet and departed.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the answer, intentionally asked the group of six bhikṣus:
"Did you truly go outside the boundary and appoint one another to instruct the community of bhikṣuṇīs?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
How can you, foolish man!..."

Without being appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, they went outside the boundary and appointed one another to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, sending a messenger to say to the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"The Saṃgha has appointed us to admonish the bhikṣuṇīs; we shall now proceed to instruct them."
After the World-Honored One had finished his reprimand, he addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, if a bhikṣu is endowed with ten qualities, he may then instruct the bhikṣuṇīs:

being fully possessed of the precepts; having heard much and being able to recite the two sets of precepts; being decisive and free from doubt; being skilled in preaching the Dharma; having left the household life from a noble family; having a handsome countenance; causing the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs to rejoice upon seeing him; being capable of preaching the Dharma to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs and exhorting them to joy; not having donned the dharma-robes as one who has gone forth for the sake of the Buddha and yet committed a grave offense; and being either twenty years of age or more than twenty years of age. Those who possess such qualities may provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, not having been appointed by the Saṃgha, instructs a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Saṃgha" refers to those who perform a single *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) and a single *karmavācanā*.
"Appointed" means one appointed from within the Saṃgha by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
Regarding the instructors, there are eight rules that must not be transgressed. What are the eight?

If a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years' seniority sees a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, she should rise to meet him, inquire after his well-being, prostrate to him, and invite him to sit. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed.

A bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor must she slander him by saying that he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, one must not violate it.
A bhikṣuṇī must not expose the offenses of a bhikṣu by saying:
"What you have done is such! or "What you have done is not such!"

One may not make a self-accusation; one may not obstruct another’s search for an offense; one may not obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Pravāraṇā*; a bhikṣuṇī may not speak of the faults of a bhikṣu, whereas a bhikṣu may speak of the faults of a bhikṣuṇī. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised, and it must not be violated for as long as one lives.

Having already trained in the precepts as a śikṣamāṇā, one should seek to receive the full ordination from the Saṃgha; this rule should be respected, honored, and praised, and must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month within both communities of monks and nuns. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

Every half-month, a bhikṣuṇī must seek out a person for instruction from among the community of monks; this rule should be respected, honored, and praised, and it must not be violated for as long as life lasts.
A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where no bhikṣus reside; this rule should be honored, revered, and praised, and must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

When a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat, she should go before the assembly of monks and request the *pravāraṇā* regarding the three matters of what has been seen, heard, or suspected. This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as one lives.
At the time of the recitation of the precepts, the senior monk (upādhyāya) should ask the community of bhikṣuṇīs:
"Who has been sent? If there is someone present, she should immediately rise and inform the Saṃgha, saying:
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is in harmony; it bows at the feet of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha and requests a person to provide instruction.
At the time of the recitation of the precepts, the Elder (Upādhyāya) should further ask:
"Who will act as the instructor for the bhikṣuṇīs?"
If there is someone available, they should be appointed.
If those who instruct the bhikṣuṇīs are many, a messenger should be sent to speak to the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha:
"There are many instructors here; whom do you choose to invite?"
If that nun says, "I invited this person," and she replies again:
Regarding the statement, "I shall follow the community's instructions," the Saṃgha should assign [the preceptor] according to the sequence of those regularly authorized to instruct bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣu-saṃgha should arrive at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇīs should also go out to meet them at the appointed time.
If a bhikṣu does not arrive at the appointed time, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not go out to meet [the instructor] when the time arrives, it is also a *duṣkṛta*.

Upon hearing that the instructor is coming, a bhikṣuṇī should go out half a *yojana* to welcome him, provide whatever is required, prepare bathing implements, and make various kinds of porridge and meals; if she fails to provide such offerings, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one goes when not appointed by the Saṃgha, or on a day other than the designated day for instruction, and expounds the eight dharmas that must not be transgressed, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one goes when not appointed by the Saṃgha and expounds the Dharma, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the community of bhikṣus is ill, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health.
If the community of bhikṣus is not in harmony or is incomplete, one should send someone to pay respects and inquire after their health.
If one does not do so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the community of bhikṣuṇīs is ill, they should likewise send someone to pay homage and inquire after the health of the community of bhikṣus.
Even if the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs is not in harmony or not fully constituted, they should still send someone to pay homage and inquire; if they do not, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the Sangha has appointed a monk to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, and at the time of the recitation of the precepts, the senior monk asks:
"Who sent these bhikṣuṇīs here?
If there is such a person, he should immediately rise and inform the Sangha, saying:
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is in harmony; she bows at the feet of the Bhikṣu Saṃgha and requests a person to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
The Elder should then ask:
"Who ought to provide instruction to the bhikṣuṇīs?"
If there is someone who should be appointed as an instructor,
and if there are many candidates for the instruction, the presiding elder (upādhyāya) should ask:
"Whom have you invited to provide the instruction?"
If a bhikṣuṇī says, "I specifically request such-and-such a person," the Saṃgha should appoint her according to what she has said.
If a bhikṣuṇī says, "I entrust myself entirely to the disposition of the Saṃgha," then at that time,
one should immediately appoint her from among those regularly assigned to provide instruction, according to the order of seniority.
The community of monks shall go at the appointed time, and the bhikṣuṇīs shall also go out to meet them at the appointed time.

When the bhikṣuṇīs hear that the instructor has arrived, they should go out half a yojana to welcome him, prepare a place for him to sit, and provide bathing requisites as well as various kinds of gruel and food.
If the Saṃgha has appointed her to go on the day of the assembly to recite the eight rules that are not to be transgressed, she should proceed in due order to preach the Dharma.
If the Saṃgha is ill, the bhikṣuṇī shall send a messenger to pay respects to the Saṃgha.
If the assembly of monks is incomplete or if a separate faction is not in harmony, one should send a messenger to pay respects.
If a bhikṣuṇī is ill, or if the assembly is incomplete or not in harmony, she likewise sends a messenger to pay respects and inquire after the well-being of the assembly of monks.

If there are obstacles on the waterway, if the road is perilous, or if there are robbers, tigers, wolves, lions, or a sudden rise in river waters; or if one is held by force, imprisoned, or faces a threat to life or to one's holy life (*brahmacarya*), such that it is impossible to send someone to pay respects and inquire after one’s welfare—in these circumstances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-first section concludes. *The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Volume Twelve.

Section Three of the Ninety *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Nanda had been appointed by the community of monks to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs; having finished instructing them, he remained silent.
Then Mahāprajāpatī said to him: "Venerable Nanda!"
"We wish to hear the Dharma; we pray that you will speak further for us.
At that time, after the Venerable Nanda had finished preaching the Dharma, he remained silent.
Mahāprajāpatī again entreated him, saying:
"We wish to hear the Dharma; we pray that you will speak for us.
Then the Venerable Nanda, with his melodious voice, preached the Dharma for them; the listeners were so delighted by what they heard that it continued until sunset.

At that time, a bhikṣuṇī departed from the Jetavana Monastery and headed for the city of Śrāvastī; however, as the city gates were already closed, she was unable to enter. She then took up residence for the night outside the gate within the moat, and when the gates opened at dawn, she entered the city ahead of them.
When the elders saw this, they all said:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have no sense of shame and no pure conduct; yet they claim for themselves:
'We practice the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what righteous Dharma is there?
All of you observe that this bhikṣuṇī spends the entire night sleeping with a bhikṣu, only to release him back in the daytime.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among the assembly who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, spoke with reproach:
"How is it that Nanda instructs the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset, causing the householders to feel resentment and reproach?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked the Venerable Nanda:
"Is it true that you gave instructions to the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Nanda, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
How is this so, Nanda?"
“Did he preach the Dharma and give instructions to the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset?
Having rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This foolish man, Nanda!”
Among the many bases of outflows, this is the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, having been appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs, continues until sunset, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the "Saṃgha," it consists of those who share the same instruction (*śikṣā*) and the same formal ritual (*karmavācanā*).
As for "instruction," it refers to the appointment of a person from among the assembly of monks through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation).
That bhikṣu appointed by the Saṃgha to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs should return by the time the sun has set.
If a bhikṣu instructs the bhikṣuṇīs until sunset, it is a pāyattika offense.
Except when giving instruction, if one receives a sutra, recites a sutra, asks questions, or engages in other matters until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
With the exception of a bhikṣuṇī, if one recites a sutra for any other woman, or receives a sutra from her, or asks questions, or engages in other matters until sunset, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is evening and one perceives it as evening, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is evening and one suspects it is so, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it is evening but one does not perceive it as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it is not evening, but one perceives it as evening, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If there is doubt as to whether it is evening, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.
There is no offense if, while instructing a bhikṣuṇī, one stops before sunset.
Except for women, if one does so for others—whether teaching them to recite or receive the scriptures, answering their questions, or for any other purpose—it is not an offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī listens while he is preaching at a ferry crossing; or if he preaches at night while traveling together with merchants; or if he preaches within a bhikṣuṇī monastery; or if she comes into the assembly on the day of the *poṣadha* and listens when the instructor happens to be preaching—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The twenty-second [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the bhikṣuṇī heard that the instructor was coming, she went out half a yojana to welcome him, provided him with a dwelling, prepared gruel or food and drink, and arranged for beds, seats, and bathing facilities.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Those other bhikṣus have not appointed us to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs.
Giving rise to a heart of jealousy, they said:
"Those bhikṣus who instruct bhikṣuṇīs lack sincerity; they instruct bhikṣuṇīs to recite the sūtras, receive the sūtras, or ask questions about them solely for the sake of food and drink."

When the monks heard this, among them were those who possessed few desires, were contented, practiced the dhūta-austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the group of six monks, saying: "How can you speak such words as:
'The monks have not appointed us to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs'?"
He then gave rise to a mind of jealousy, thinking:

"Those bhikṣus teach the bhikṣuṇīs without any sincerity; they teach the bhikṣuṇīs, whether for reciting the sūtras, receiving the sūtras, or answering questions, solely for the sake of food and drink."
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done.
How is this, O group of six bhikṣus!"
They then spoke these words:
"Those bhikṣus did not appoint us to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs," and they gave rise to a mind of jealousy.

"Those bhikṣus who instruct bhikṣuṇīs do so without sincerity; they instruct bhikṣuṇīs—whether for reciting the sūtras, receiving the sūtras, or answering questions—merely for the sake of food and drink."
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“These foolish men!
Among the many bases of outflows, this is the first offense regarding the breaking of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
If a bhikṣu speaks to other bhikṣus and says these words:
"If a bhikṣu instructs a bhikṣuṇī for the sake of food or drink," it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
That bhikṣu spoke thus:
"The bhikṣus instruct the bhikṣuṇīs for the sake of food and drink; they teach them to recite the sūtras, receive the sūtras, or answer their questions for the sake of food and drink."
If she speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the matter is actually as described.
If one instructs a bhikṣuṇī for the sake of providing food and drink;
if, for the sake of food and drink, one teaches her to recite the sūtras, receives them from her, or questions her;
or if one speaks jokingly, speaks in private, or speaks in a dream; or if, intending to say this, one mistakenly says that—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-third section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu in the city of Śrāvastī who was fully endowed with dignified deportment. A certain bhikṣuṇī, upon seeing him, conceived a virtuous mind and repeatedly invited the bhikṣu [to her home], but the bhikṣu did not accept.

Later, at another time, when the community of monks at Jetavana was distributing robes, this bhikṣu took his share of the robes and was exiting the gate of Jetavana, while that bhikṣuṇī was just then entering Jetavana. The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This bhikṣuṇī has repeatedly invited me, yet I did not accept. Now, I would rather take this portion of robes to invite her; she will surely not take them, and it will suffice as a gift for her."
Then that bhikṣu said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! This robe is my portion; if you need it, you may take it."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī accepted it immediately.
This bhikṣu reprimanded the bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"I have repeatedly said to others:"
"That bhikṣuṇī repeatedly invited me and offered me the leftovers from her alms-bowl, yet I did not accept them.
I thought to myself: "That bhikṣuṇī repeatedly invited me and offered me the leftovers from her alms-bowl, yet I did not accept them."
"I would rather take this portion of my robe and give it to that bhikṣuṇī; she will certainly not accept it, and that will suffice as a gift. Yet, she accepted it.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they reproached that bhikṣu, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu give a robe to a bhikṣuṇī and, without relinquishing it, invite her [to use it]?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, bhikṣu, that you give a robe to a bhikṣuṇī and, without relinquishing it, invite another?
Having rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who, out of caution and apprehension, did not dare to give robes to their own relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs, and they informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted to give robes to a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative. If one gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, within the Jeta Grove, the two divisions of the Saṃgha shared their robes: the portion of robes belonging to the bhikṣus was received by the bhikṣuṇīs, and the portion of robes belonging to the bhikṣuṇīs was received by the bhikṣus.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī brought the robe she had obtained to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Would you like to trade for this robe?"
The bhikṣus replied, "Sisters!
We are not permitted to give robes to bhikṣuṇīs who are not our relatives."
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if there is an exchange, I permit you to give robes to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relative" is as explained above.
"Relative" is also as explained above.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as explained above.

Regarding "exchanging," this refers to exchanging robe for robe; exchanging robe for what is not a robe; exchanging what is not a robe for a robe; exchanging a needle for a knife; or exchanging thread and yarn, down to a single piece of medicine.
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, except in exchange for goods, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a dukkaṭa; for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a dukkaṭa.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for those who trade robes with a relative nun,
or who give [robes] to a stūpa, to the Buddha, or to the Saṃgha.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Twenty-four concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who wished to make a saṃghāṭī; for the purpose of making the robe, she came to the monastery and said to the Venerable Kālodāyin:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I have this cloth and wish to make a saṃghāṭī; I pray that you, Venerable Sir, will make it for me.
Kālodāyin replied, "I cannot make it."
He asked, "For what reason do you not work for me? He replied:
"You come here so frequently to urge me, that I am unable to do it.
The bhikṣuṇī replied, "I do not come frequently to urge you; once it is finished, give it to me."
Kāḷudāyin replied, "So be it.

Then the bhikṣuṇī gave him the cloth and departed. Kāḷudāyin, being well-versed in the methods of tailoring, immediately cut and sewed it into the likeness of a man and a woman engaged in sexual intercourse.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī came to the saṃghārāma and asked Kālodāyin,
"Venerable sir,
have you finished making the robe for me?"
He replied, “The robe is finished. The bhikṣuṇī said:
"If the robe is finished, you may give it to me now.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin folded the robe and handed it to her,
saying, "Sister!..."

You should know that this robe must not be removed or worn for inspection, nor should it be shown to others; when the time for the announcement arrives, you shall put on this robe and walk behind the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī followed her instructions; she neither opened the robe to look at it nor told anyone else.
Later, at another time when the time for the meal had arrived, she immediately put on this robe and walked behind the community of bhikṣuṇīs.
When the laypeople saw this, they all mocked her together; some clapped their hands toward one another, some struck wooden blocks or whistled, and some laughed loudly, saying:
"Look at the robes worn by these bhikṣuṇīs! Look at the robes worn by these bhikṣuṇīs!"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, having seen this, said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Quickly unfold and spread out this robe."
She then folded it and placed it upon her shoulder.
Later, after her meal, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī returned to the saṃghārāma and said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Bring me the garment you had with you earlier; I wish to examine it."
He immediately took it out and showed it to him, asking,
"Who made this robe for you? He replied:
"It was Kāḷudāyin who did this.
He said, "Why did you not open it to look at it and show it to your fellow students?"
"Is the sewing and cutting not done well?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī related in detail everything she had been instructed by Kālodāyin.

Among the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, there were those who possessed few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Kālodāyin, saying:
"How could one make such a robe for a bhikṣuṇī?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus immediately went to inform the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he said to Kālodāyin:
"Is it true that you made such a robe for a bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, employing countless skillful means, rebuked Kālodāyin, saying:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the precepts—it is something that should not have been done.
Why have you made such a robe for a bhikṣuṇī?"
Having rebuked Kālodayin, he addressed the bhikṣus: "This foolish man!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such occasions for the outflow of impurities."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious, not daring to make robes for their own relatives who were bhikṣuṇīs. They went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus to make robes for their own bhikṣuṇī relatives."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Non-relative" and "relative" are as defined above.
"Robe-cloth" refers to ten kinds, also as defined above.
If a bhikṣu makes a robe for a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative, for every amount of cloth cut according to the blade's stroke, it is a pāyattika offense.
To sew even a single stitch is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, to open and inspect it, to pull and stretch it, to iron it, or to rub and stroke it with the hand; or to grasp the corners and pull them to make it square and smooth; or to seek out the threads, to search for the yarn, or to join the yarn—all these are *dukkaṭa* offenses.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one acts for a bhikṣuṇī who is a relative, or for the Saṃgha, or for a stūpa; or if one borrows [an item] to wash, dye, or repair it and then returns it to the owner, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-fifth section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin was handsome in appearance, and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was likewise handsome in appearance, both being extraordinary among people.
Kāḷudāyin had lustful thoughts toward the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā also had lustful thoughts toward Kāḷudāyin.
At that time, Kāḷodāyin, having dressed in the early morning and taken his bowl, went to the place where Thullanandā was and sat together with her outside the door.
When the laypeople saw this, they all felt resentment and said to one another:
"Look at these two sitting together; they are like a husband and wife, or like a pair of mandarin ducks."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Kāḷodāyin, saying: "How could you sit together with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in one place outside the gate?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kālodāyin:
"Is it true that you were sitting together with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in a single place outside the gate?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked Kāḷodāyin, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you sit together with the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā in one place outside the gate?"
Having rebuked Kālodayin, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the various bases for the outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"In one place" means there is one bhikṣu and one bhikṣuṇī.
"A secluded place" refers to a place where one can see in private or hear in private.
"To see in a concealed place" means not seeing due to dust, mist, smoke, clouds, or darkness.
"To hear in a concealed place" means not even hearing the sound of ordinary speech.
"Obstructed" means: whether by a tree, a wall, a fence, a garment, or by any other object acting as a screen.
If a bhikṣu sits alone in a secluded place with a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one stands still, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense. There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion;

or if there is a wise person present; or if there are two people who are neither blind nor deaf; or if he falls while walking due to sudden force; or if he turns over because of illness; or if he is held by force; or if he is imprisoned; or if there is danger to life or danger to his brahmacarya. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-sixth section ends. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through the human settlements of Kosala. When the householders saw them, they all spoke with reproach:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and do not cultivate the holy life; yet outwardly they claim, 'We practice the True Dharma.'"
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To travel through the human world with bhikṣuṇīs, and if there is any desire, to leave the path.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
“How is it that you travel among the people together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, O group of six bhikṣus!
Are you wandering together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through the human realm of Kośala?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu travels together with a bhikṣuṇī from one village to another village, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, some bhikṣus did not first make an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī, but encountered her unexpectedly on the road; fearing and being cautious, they did not dare to travel together.
The Buddha said:
"If you did not make an appointment, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precept should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel along the same road, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī, and at that same time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs were also traveling from Śrāvastī to Vaiśālī.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir,
where do you wish to go?"
The bhikṣus replied, “We wish to go to Vaiśālī. The bhikṣuṇī said:
“Venerable sir!
I also wish to go. The bhikṣus replied:
“Sister! If you wish to go, you should go in front and we shall follow behind;
if we go in front, you, sister, should follow behind.”
"Why is that? Because the World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not travel along the same path as a bhikṣuṇī. The bhikṣuṇīs said:
“Venerable One! You are our most honored superior and should go ahead; we shall follow behind.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went behind and were plundered by bandits, losing their robes and alms bowls.
