The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, if you travel with merchants, or if there is suspicion, fear, or dread, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu agrees with a bhikṣuṇī to travel along the same road from one village to another, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense."
"An unusual time" refers to when one travels with merchants, or when there is suspicion, fear, or dread; this is called "an unusual time.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Appointment" means saying that they will go together to a certain village, city, or country.
A place of doubt is one where there is suspicion that thieves may commit robbery or theft.
A place of fear is one where there is apprehension that thieves may commit robbery or theft.
A path is a designated route for travel between villages.

If a bhikṣu agrees with a bhikṣuṇī to travel along the same path, even as far as the boundary of a village, for each instance according to the number of boundaries involved, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one travels outside a village or in an open space for even ten *li*, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one travels less than a village or less than ten *li*, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one travels through the same boundary between many villages, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes preparations and agrees to go together, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense. There is no offense if there was no prior agreement; if traveling with a large group;

if traveling through a place of suspected danger or fear where going there would bring safety; if one is held by those possessing forceful power; or if one is bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The twenty-seventh section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were traveling upriver and downriver together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke of it with disdain, saying to one another:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and do not cultivate the holy life; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I practice the True Dharma.
How can this be called practicing the True Dharma?
To board a boat with a bhikṣuṇī and travel upstream or downstream, and when there is a desire, to stop by the riverbank as one pleases.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame;
they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "How can you travel together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs on a boat, going upriver and downriver?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can you travel together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs on a boat, going upriver and downriver?
Having rebuked them, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These people of the group of six bhikṣus are fools!"
Among the various bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels on board a boat with a bhikṣuṇī, whether going upstream or downstream, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive even when they had not made an appointment. The Buddha said:
"If there was no appointment, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together on the same boat, whether upstream or downstream, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus wished to cross the Ganges River from this bank to the other; at that same time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs also wished to cross the Ganges River from this bank to the other.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to her and asked,
"Venerable One,
where do you wish to go?"
The bhikṣus replied,
"We wish to cross the Ganges. The bhikṣuṇī said:
“Can we cross together with you as companions?
The bhikṣus replied, “Sisters, you go ahead; we shall follow behind.”
"If it were not so, sisters, you would be behind and we would be ahead. Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One has established a precept that one must not cross a body of water in the same boat as a bhikṣuṇī; therefore, it is not permitted."
The bhikṣuṇīs said, “Venerable Sir, you are our honored one and should go first; we shall follow behind.

At that time, during the summer months, there was a great torrential rain, and the river water swelled so high that when the boat reached the opposite bank, the sun had already set before they could return.
The bhikṣuṇīs stayed overnight on the bank and were robbed by wicked bandits at night.
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"If one crosses directly to the other shore, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precept shall be established as follows:
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to board the same boat to travel upstream or downstream, except in the case of crossing directly across, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Agreeing together" is also as explained above. "Boat" is as described above.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a bhikṣuṇī to travel together on the same boat upstream or downstream—except for crossing directly across—and if he enters the boat, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one foot is on the boat and one foot is on the ground; or if one makes an effort to enter but does not enter; or if one makes an appointment to adorn oneself—in all such cases, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if there was no prior agreement; or if one crosses directly to the other shore; or if one boards a boat and the boatman loses control while going upstream or downstream; or if one goes to the other shore but cannot find safety; or if one is seized by those with forceful power; or if one is bound; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Twenty-Eight concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in the city of Śrāvastī who invited Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana for a meal. That very night, he prepared various kinds of fine food; on the following day, having spread excellent mats in the open air, he announced that the time had come.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was formerly a member of a lay family.
One morning, Thullanandā put on her robes, took her bowl, and went to that lay family’s home. Seeing the layman spreading many fine seats in the open air, she asked him:
“Layman, have you spread these many seats intending to invite the bhikṣus?”
She replied, "I wish to invite them.
The bhikṣuṇī then asked:
"Which bhikṣus do you invite? He replied,
"I invite Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana."
The bhikṣuṇī said: "The people you have invited, householder, are all of lowly birth. Had you told me beforehand, I would have invited for you the 'Dragon among Dragons'."
The householder asked,
"Who is the dragon among dragons? The bhikṣuṇī replied:
“They are the Venerable Devadatta, Samudradatta, Dakṣaṇada, Dabba-Gopāli, and Kālodāyin.”
While these words were still being spoken, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had already arrived.
Upon seeing them, the bhikṣuṇī said to the householder,
"The dragon among dragons has arrived."
The householder then said to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Just now you called me a person of low birth; how is it that you now call me a 'dragon among dragons'?
From this day forward, do not come to my house again."
At that time, the householder addressed Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana regarding their seats, and they immediately took their places and sat down.

The householder then provided various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink as an offering. When they had finished eating, he removed the serving vessels, prostrated at their feet with his head and face, and taking a small seat, sat to one side and said:
"I wish to hear the Dharma."
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana taught them various subtle and wonderful dharmas, exhorting them to rejoice; having finished preaching the Dharma, they rose from their seats and departed.
Returning to the saṃghārāma, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Did you receive sufficient food today at the invitation?"
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:
“Although the food was sufficient, we were treated as lowly persons in the householder’s home; yet, we are also the dragons among dragons.”
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason? At that time,
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
“Devadatta has dispatched his faction of bhikṣuṇīs to solicit offerings on his behalf, and they have accepted food and drink.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing the answer, he nevertheless asked the bhikṣus who were Devadatta’s faction:
“Is it true that you dispatched bhikṣuṇīs to go and praise him, solicit donors, and obtain food?”
He replied, "It is indeed so. Then,
the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣus who were followers of Devadatta, saying:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you send bhikṣuṇīs to exhort donors to accept food from them?"
Having rebuked the bhikṣus who were followers of Devadatta’s faction, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“This foolish man has committed the first transgression of the precepts among the many sources of outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sends a bhikṣuṇī to solicit alms-food, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether there had been solicitation or no solicitation; only later did they come to know it. Consequently, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
"Previously, there was no offense because it was not known.
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu knows that he has received food through the teaching of a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a great elder in the city of Rājagṛha who was a close friend and acquaintance of Upatiṣya. He said:
"If the Venerable Upatiṣya comes to the city of Rājagṛha, we shall provide offerings to the Saṃgha on account of his being the first to arrive."
The bhikṣuṇī from the householder’s family heard these words and kept them silently in her heart.
At another time, when the Venerable Likhita entered the city of Rājagṛha, the bhikṣuṇī, having heard that the Venerable Likhita had entered the city, went to speak with the householder, saying:
“Do you wish to know?”
"Having arrived at Rājagṛha, the Licchavis have entered the city.
The householder immediately dispatched a messenger to the saṃghārāma to invite them:
"I pray that tomorrow at dawn, the Venerable One and the assembly of monks will deign to accept my meal."
At that time, the householder prepared various kinds of sweet and delicious food and drink during that very night. At dawn, he went to inform [the monks] that the time had arrived.
Then the bhikṣus put on their robes, took their bowls, and went to the householder’s home, where they sat down in their assigned seats.
Then the householder went to where Rṣidatta was and said,
"It is specifically for the sake of the Venerable One that I am providing food for the assembly of monks. Then Rṣidatta asked the householder:
"How did you know that I had come here?
The householder replied,
"The bhikṣuṇī whom our family supports told me."
The Licchavi addressed the householder, saying,
"If this is truly so, I ought not to eat this food.
The householder replied:
"I did not prepare this meal because of what this bhikṣuṇī said; rather, I had previously made a vow that if Liśadatta were to come, I would provide food and make offerings to the Saṃgha."
The Licchavi further said to the elder,
"Even though you say this, I still ought not to eat this food.
At that time, the Licchavi immediately desisted and did not eat.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter in full to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
"If it was the intention of the donor from the outset, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, knowing that he has received food as a result of being praised and exhorted by a bhikṣuṇī, eats it—except when there was a prior intention on the part of the donor—he commits a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "those who teach and transform": these are forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), alms-seekers (*piṇḍapātika*), wearers of rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*), those who practice the rule of refusing further food (*khalupaścādbhaktika*), those who eat in a single sitting (*aikāsanika*), those who eat from a single morsel (*prāptapiṇḍika*), those who dwell among graves (*śmāśānika*), those who sit in the open air (*ābhyavakāśika*), those who sit under trees (*vṛkṣamūlika*), those who remain seated constantly (*naiṣadyika*) or follow their posture wherever they go (*yathāsaṃstarika*), those who maintain the three robes (*traicīvarika*), those who praise verses and are learned Dharma-preachers (*dharmabhāṇaka*), those who uphold the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*), and those who practice meditation (*dhyāyin*).
Regarding "food": one may eat from dawn until midday.
If a bhikṣu knowingly eats food obtained through the solicitation of a bhikṣuṇī, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.
Apart from this meal, if he obtains other items such as undergarments, lamp oil, or foot ointment through her solicitation, it is all a duṣkṛta offense.
If one knows that they have been instructed and perceives them as having been instructed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one suspects that they have been instructed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one has not instructed them but perceives them as having been instructed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one fails to instruct and transform those who harbor doubts, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense if one does not know; or if it was the intention of the donor beforehand; or if there was no thought of teaching when one was actually teaching; or if the bhikṣuṇī acted on her own initiative; or if the donor had the bhikṣuṇī manage the matter; or if she did not intentionally teach but was given almsfood [as a result]. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a woman from Vaiśālī who had married a man from Śrāvastī was returning to her native country after having a dispute with her mother-in-law.
Then, as Ānanda was traveling from Śrāvastī toward Vaiśālī, the woman asked the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, where are you going?"
He replied, "I wish to go to Vaiśālī. The woman then said:
"Can you go and fetch it? He replied, "I can."
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha traveled along the same road with this woman.
At that moment, the woman’s husband had gone out earlier and was not at home; when he returned home the following day and did not see his wife, he asked her mother, "Where is my wife?"
Her mother replied, "After fighting with me, she fled and ran away; we do not know where she is.
Thereupon, her husband quickly went in pursuit and found his wife on the road. He took her with him and went to Ānanda, saying:
"Why have you fled with my wife?
At that time, Anuruddha replied, "Stop!"
"Stop! Do not speak such words; we do not act in that way.
The householder said:
"How can you say it is not so?
You are currently walking along with those who follow the same path.
The wife then said to her husband:
"I have been traveling with this venerable one like brothers; there has been no other fault or evil between us.
Her husband replied, "This man has fled with you today; how could he not say such a thing!"
At that time, the man struck Ānanda so violently that his life-force was on the verge of being severed.

Thereupon, the Venerable Ānanda descended from the path and sat cross-legged in a secluded spot; with body erect and mind upright, he focused his mindfulness before him and entered the fire-light samādhi.
When the elder saw this, a virtuous mind arose within him, and he thought to himself:
"If this Anuruddha were to arise from his samādhi, I would pay him homage and repent."
Then, when the Venerable Aniruddha had awakened from samādhi, the elder immediately confessed:
"I only pray, Great Virtue,
that you will accept my confession."
Aniruddha accepted his confession.

Then the householder, having prostrated at his feet, sat to one side. At that time, Aniruddha taught the householder various subtle and wondrous Dharma teachings to inspire a heart of joy. Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, after Anuruddha had finished eating, he went to the monastery and related these circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Anuruddha:
"How is it, Anuruddha, that you traveled alone with a woman along the same path?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter to the World-Honored One in full detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus; though he already knew the situation, he asked Āniruddha:
"Is it true that you traveled along the same road as a woman?"
He replied, "It is truly so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked Aniruddha, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Why have you now traveled along the same road as a woman?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked Aniruddha through countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"In many ways, this Aniruddha has committed various outflows; this is his first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same path with a woman, even as far as the vicinity of a village, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, when bhikṣus encountered one another on the road without having made a prior appointment, they were apprehensive and did not dare to travel together. The Buddha said:
"If there was no prior appointment, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same path, even as far as a village, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Woman" is as explained above.
"Making an appointment together" is also as explained above.
The meaning of "road" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu makes an appointment with a woman to travel along the same road, even for the distance between villages, it constitutes a pāyattika offense for each successive boundary segment traversed.
If one travels ten *li* from a village or through an uninhabited area, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is less than a village or less than ten *li*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one travels within a single boundary inside a village, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one intends to go by means of an expedient but does not go, or if one has made a mutual appointment for a formal adornment but does not depart, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one did not previously make a mutual appointment; if it was necessary to go there for the sake of obtaining safety; or if one was held by force, or imprisoned, or faced a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The thirtieth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a village without a permanent residence in the kingdom of Kosala. A householder built a dwelling for the bhikṣus and regularly provided them with food and drink, stipulating that those who stayed there should observe the practice of eating only one meal a day.

At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who wished to go to an uninhabited village in the kingdom of Kośala. Upon arriving at that dwelling, they stayed for one night and obtained excellent food and drink; therefore, they stayed for a second night and again obtained excellent food and drink.
Those six groups of bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The sole reason we wander is for the sake of food, and now we have obtained it.
They ate repeatedly at that dwelling place, whereupon the lay devotees all joined in criticizing and disparaging them:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are insatiable and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim of themselves, 'We know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma could there be for such as these?"

"To repeatedly receive food at this residence is exactly as if we were constantly providing meals for these śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas; originally, I intended it only to provide for those staying for a single night."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "How can the group of six bhikṣus repeatedly accept meals at this residence?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, O group of six bhikṣus!
Why do you repeatedly accept food at this residence?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu eats at a single dwelling place, he should accept only one meal; if he exceeds one meal, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, Śāriputra was traveling through the kingdom of Kośala; he went to this village of No-Abode and stayed there for one night, obtaining excellent food at dawn the following morning.
While Śāriputra was ill there, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept that a bhikṣu should eat only one meal at a single lodging; if one exceeds this, it is a pāyattika offense."
He immediately supported himself as he left with his illness, but the ailment subsequently worsened.
At that time, a bhikṣu went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to receive food after the meal has been distributed."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"At a place where a single meal is offered, a bhikṣu who is not ill should take only one meal; if he accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Residence" refers to staying overnight in such a place. "Eating" extends even to eating at the proper time.
"One who is ill" refers to one whose condition worsens upon leaving that village.
If a monk who is not ill stays overnight at that same lodging and consumes food again, for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
Apart from food, if he receives other items such as undergarments, lamp oil, or oil for rubbing the feet, it is all a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: receiving food for one night; receiving food while ill;
or when laypeople invite a Venerable One to stay, saying, "We shall provide you with food;

we have prepared this lodging and supplied these meals for the sake of the Śramaṇa Śākyaputras, and even if we do not obtain [the presence of] the Śramaṇa Śākyaputras, we shall still give them to others."
If a donor invites one to eat in succession;
or if a son, daughter, sister, or daughter-in-law invites one to eat in succession, there is no offense.
Or if one accepts food from a person today;
Or perhaps one receives that person's food only on the following day;
or perhaps there is a sudden flood of water, making the road difficult and treacherous;
or there may be robbers, tigers, wolves, or lions.
If one is held by those with power and influence;
or is imprisoned and confined;
or faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), there is no offense in exceeding the limit of a single meal.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the thirty-first [section]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of the Kalandakas.
The World-Honored One departed from the city of Rājagṛha to travel among the people, accompanied by a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, within the borders of the kingdom, the crops had failed to ripen and grain was exceedingly scarce; it was difficult to obtain almsfood, and all the people bore the appearance of hunger. At that time, there were five hundred beggars who followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, there was a brahmin named Sātī who had five hundred wagons filled with food and drink; throughout the winter and summer, he followed behind the World-Honored One, waiting for a day when there would be no meal provided so that he might offer a供养 (dāna).

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually traveled from the borders of the kingdom of Magadha, teaching and transforming beings as he went, until he reached the borders of the kingdom of Aṇāpinḍada.
The people of that country vied with one another to provide offerings, providing meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus without a single day of interruption.
At that time, the brahmin watched for an entire day and night without finding a single lapse in the schedule where he could provide offerings. He then went to Ānanda and said to him:

"I, Śāṭa, have five hundred carts filled with food and drink. Having followed the World-Honored One through winter and summer, I have been watching for a lapse in the schedule—a day when there is no meal provided—so that I may present these offerings."

However, we are currently unable to provide our offerings in turn, as we live as laypeople beset by many difficulties. We are subject to official service and must attend whenever legal matters are decided; furthermore, we must manage our household affairs and supply grain and wealth to the government. Thus, we are driven back and forth between public and private duties without a moment’s rest.
I only pray that the Venerable One will inform the Buddha on my behalf; if the Buddha instructs me, I shall carry out his teaching.

If the Buddha and the Saṃgha are unable to receive food in turn, I shall spread the provisions from these five hundred chariots along the road so that the Buddha and the Saṃgha may pass over them with their feet, thereby accepting my offerings.
Ānanda replied, "Wait a moment! I shall now go and inform the Buddha."
Then Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"The brahmin Sāṭu came to me and said:

'I have five hundred chariots filled with food and drink; throughout the winter and summer, I shall follow the World-Honored One, waiting for a day when he is without food, so that I may provide him with offerings.'"

"However, we have not been able to receive our turn for offerings today. As laypeople, we face many difficulties; we are subject to official service and must attend when legal cases are being adjudicated. Furthermore, we must manage our household affairs, with neither public nor private duties ever ceasing. We only pray that the Venerable One will inform the Buddha on our behalf. If the Buddha instructs us, we shall respectfully carry out his teachings."

"If I do not receive the opportunity to provide my offerings in due order, I shall instead spread the food and drink from these five hundred chariots along the road so that the Buddha and the Sangha may walk upon them as they pass; in this way, they will have accepted my offerings."
I previously replied, saying:
"Please wait a moment; I shall presently inform the Buddha on your behalf.
For this reason, I have now addressed Your Honor.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda:
"You should go and tell the brahmin: 'Tomorrow morning, prepare this food and drink into porridge and give it to the bhikṣus to eat; afterwards, they shall receive their meal at the proper time.'"
At that time, Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, went to where the brahmin was and said to him:
"You may prepare this food and drink into porridge and give it to the bhikṣus to eat; afterwards, you shall receive [your own] meal at the proper time."

At that time, the brahmin observed that among all those providing offerings, none had any cakes. That very night, he prepared various delicious foods—ghee, sesame seeds, milk, pure water, ginger, pepper, and long pepper—and made various kinds of porridge and cakes.
When the night had passed, he offered this rice porridge to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
However, the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it and said to the brāhmaṇa:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted bhikṣus to receive ghee, oil, or even the three kinds of medicinal substances used to make various types of porridge."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept ghee and oil, and even the three kinds of medicinal substances, to prepare various gruels and eat them."
There are five benefits to eating congee:
it effectively relieves hunger, relieves thirst, digests food remaining from previous meals, regulates the flow of feces and urine, and alleviates ailments caused by wind.
One who eats congee possesses these five beneficial qualities.
Then the brahmin proceeded to offer some cakes, but the bhikṣu did not dare to accept them and said to the brahmin:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted bhikṣus to receive cakes."
He immediately went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "From this day forward,
I allow the bhikṣus to accept cakes and food. At that time,
the lay devotees of the country of Aṇāpinḍada, hearing that the World-Honored One had permitted the bhikṣus to eat congee and cakes, were all greatly delighted and said to one another:
"We have truly gained the opportunity to perform meritorious offerings.
Then, there was another minister of little faith who, seeing that the Buddha and the Saṃgha had received such great offerings, spoke thus:
"These are no small fields of merit; for even amidst this famine, the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus receive such offerings as these."
"I would now rather prepare various kinds of rich and delicious food and meat, one vessel for each person.
At that time, he immediately sent a messenger to the saṃghārāma, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha! [Please come]."
"I pray that you will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.

That very night, he prepared various kinds of rich and delicious food and drink. At dawn the next day, he went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had arrived; at that moment, the World-Honored One remained within the monastery and sent someone to request the meal.

At that time, the lay devotees of Ānāpindika, having previously heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to eat gruel, prepared various kinds of gruel that night as described above and sent it to the saṃghārāma the following day to give to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus had already accepted invitations for meals elsewhere, yet they ate this various thick gruel first, and only afterwards went to that minister’s house to eat.
At that time, the minister of little faith provided the community of bhikṣus with various kinds of food and drink, to which the bhikṣus said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Stop! Lay donor, put it on gradually.
The minister said to the community of bhikṣus:
"I have therefore prepared rich and delicious food for the community of bhikṣus, with a portion of meat for each individual; do not eat insufficiently because you think my faith is slight."
"Venerable sirs!
Just eat; I have faith. The bhikṣus replied:

"It was not for this reason that he did not eat. When the people of the city heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to eat congee and parched grain, they immediately prepared various kinds of ghee, sesame seeds, milk, pure water, ginger, pepper, and long pepper to make congee that very night. The next morning, they delivered it to the saṃghārāma to give to the bhikṣus.
"Because we have already eaten that porridge earlier, we are simply unable to eat much more now; do not be offended!
Then the Minister of Minor Faith spoke with resentment:
"I intentionally prepared these various kinds of fine food for the assembly of monks, including a vessel of meat for each person, intending for the monks to consume it all."
"Why have you eaten thick gruel first before receiving my food?

At that time, the minister, filled with resentment, immediately withheld various kinds of parched grain, meat, and delicacies, and prepared only soup and rice. He then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Having sat down, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding the offerings I previously prepared for the assembly of monks, would the merit be great?"
"Is the transgression great?
The Buddha told the minister:

"The merit you have gained from providing this offering is exceedingly great; it is indeed a cause for rebirth in heaven. As for the bhikṣus, even those who receive but a single morsel of food from you will obtain immeasurable merit."

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught him the Dharma: the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in the heavens; he censured the faults and evils of sensual desire as well as the outflows of the higher realms, and praised renunciation for the increase of liberation.

Having been taught this Dharma, while still seated upon his mat, he was cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, he practiced the True Dharma and attained the superior fruit.

He addressed the Buddha, saying: "From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Please accept me as a lay follower (upāsaka); for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, and so forth, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants."
At that time, after his meal, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Knowing [the situation] yet asking on purpose, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Did you all eat another’s thick gruel early in the morning, and only afterwards accept the invitation of the great minister?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not have been done.
Why were you so foolish as to eat that thick gruel first and only afterwards accept the invitation?"
Having already accepted an invitation, one must not eat thick gruel first.
Regarding "thick gruel": if one draws a line with a blade of grass and it does not hold together, it is not permitted to eat; if one eats it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering through the human realm among the people of Ānāpindika, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, rice and grain were extremely scarce within the kingdom, making it difficult to obtain alms; all the people had the appearance of hunger. Nevertheless, there were five hundred beggars who constantly followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling gradually through the kingdom of Magadha and returned to the city of Rājagṛha. At that time, the Buddha and the community of monks received abundant offerings.

In the city of Rājagṛha, there was a certain master of the arts who had little faith or devotion; seeing that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus were receiving such great offerings, he thought to himself:
"These are no small fields of merit, for even amidst this famine, the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus receive such abundant offerings."
"What if I were now to take all the produce of one year and prepare various kinds of rich and delicious food, providing each person with a vessel of meat to offer to the Buddha and the Sangha?"
Thereupon, he went himself to the monastery and addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "Tomorrow at dawn,
please accept my invitation for a meal offering. That very night,
having prepared various kinds of excellent food, he went again at dawn the following day to announce that the time had arrived.

At that time, on the day of a festival in the city of Rājagṛha, various householders vied with one another to carry rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat to the saṃghārāma to offer to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus would then eat what they had received before accepting formal invitations.
At that time, the musician personally served various kinds of food and drink with his own hands, whereupon the bhikṣus said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Layman, do not eat too much.

The musician replied, "Whatever wealth I have produced over the past year, I have specifically used it to prepare various kinds of rich and delicious food for the community of bhikṣus. Each person has a vessel of meat; do not, because of my slight faith, fear that a lack of faith might arise and thus fail to eat much."
"I pray that you simply eat; I have faith and devotion.
At that time, the bhikṣus replied to the musician:
"It is not for this reason that we do not eat; rather, because we previously accepted food from various people in Rājagṛha, we have eaten only a little today."
"There is no other intention; do not be offended.
At that time, the minor master of ceremonies, having heard these words, immediately gave rise to contempt and said:

"How is it that from all the goods I have produced throughout the entire year, you have intentionally prepared various kinds of rich and delicious food and drink for the Sangha, with a bowl of meat for each person?"
"How is it that these bhikṣus first accept other offerings of rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat, and only afterwards receive my food?
The musician, filled with resentment, immediately withheld various kinds of rich and delicious foods and gave them only soup and plain rice.
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side. Having sat down, he asked the Buddha:
"Was the merit of the food and drink I prepared earlier great?"
"Is the transgression great?
The Buddha told him:

"The food you have now offered is a cause for rebirth in heaven; even if the bhikṣus were to eat but a single morsel, their merit would be immeasurable, let alone now having provided such an extensive offering as this—the merit of this is beyond measure."

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma for him, explaining the causes for rebirth in heaven through generosity and the observance of precepts, and censuring the faults of desire as well as the outflows of the higher realms.

Upon hearing these words, the musician immediately attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, with all defilements and impurities vanishing while seated; he saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, practiced the True Dharma, and attained the superior fruit. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I pray that you will accept me as an upāsaka; for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from killing, and so forth, up to refraining from drinking alcohol."
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the situation] yet asking deliberately, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you first accepted invitations for the five kinds of food from others, and only afterwards accepted this invitation to a meal?"
He replied, “It is truly so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
How can you, foolish man!..."
"Having first accepted five kinds of food from another, do you then accept an invitation?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should not first accept an invitation to eat five kinds of food from another, and only thereafter accept an invitation."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats by taking turns [between meals], it is a pāyattika offense."
In this way, the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there were sick bhikṣus who had been invited to a place where food suitable for their illnesses or medicine suitable for their illnesses was not available.

If there were wholesome food and medicine suitable for a specific illness, yet a monk, out of apprehension and caution, did not dare to eat it for fear of committing the offense of "successive eating" (paryuṣita-bhakta), the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha told them:
"From this day forward, I permit a sick bhikṣu to engage in successive eating."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats in succession, except at the proper times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The 'proper times' are: when one is ill."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a householder who invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, wishing to provide them with a meal as an offering.
Furthermore, there was another householder who also invited the Buddha and the Sangha, desiring to provide offerings of food, drink, and clothing. He went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"I wish to invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to receive offerings of food and drink."
The bhikṣus replied,
“We have already accepted an invitation.
The householder said:
"Venerable Sir!
I wish to offer fine food, drink, and clothing; I only pray that the community of monks will accept my invitation.
At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to eat by successive rounds when robes are being distributed as alms.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu eats in succession (at multiple meals), except at the appropriate times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
The "appropriate times" are: when one is ill, and when robes are being distributed; these are called the appropriate times.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Successive eating" refers to being invited.
There are two kinds of invitations:
If one partakes of food— whether through an invitation by the monastic order (*saṃgha*) or a private invitation— consisting of rice, parched grain, solid rice, fish, or meat;
and if one is ill such that one cannot eat a sufficient amount of fine food while remaining seated in a single posture.
Regarding the giving of robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, if there is no *kāṭhina* robe in place, it is for one month; if a *kāṭhina* robe is in place, it is for five months.
Furthermore, regarding other gifts of food or robes: if one receives many invitations for meals on the same day, one should accept only one invitation.
The remainder should be given to others, and when giving it, one should say:
"Venerable sir!
I ought to go there; I now give this to you."
If a bhikṣu does not relinquish a previous invitation but accepts a later invitation for a meal, there is a pāyattika offense for every swallow.
If he does not relinquish a later invitation but accepts a previous invitation for a meal, there is a dukkaṭa offense for every swallow.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when it is the time for receiving robes;
if there are many invitations within a single day, one may accept one invitation oneself and give the others away to others;

if the invitation is for non-food, or if the food is insufficient, or if there is no food provided at the invitation, or if one obtains food after having already eaten, or if there is both a morning meal and an afternoon meal at the same location—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The thirty-second section ends. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Thirteen. [Volume Fourteen, Part One, Section Fourteen]
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Section Four of the Ninety Dharmas of Saṃghāvaśeṣa. At that time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha.
At that time, Devadatta incited others to harm the Buddha and further incited King Ajātaśatru to kill his father; consequently, his evil reputation spread and his offerings were cut off.
He then went from house to house to beg for alms together with five bhikṣus: Traipusa, Bhallika, Daśabala, Kapphiṇa, and Kolita.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that Devadatta had instructed others to harm the Buddha and further incited King Ajātaśatru to kill his father, his ill repute spread abroad and his offerings were cut off; consequently, he went together with five bhikṣus from house to house to beg for food.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed Devadatta, saying:
"Is it true that you, along with five bhikṣus, have been begging for alms from house to house?"
He replied: "It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!"
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked Devadatta, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, Devadatta? Do you go from house to house for alms with the five bhikṣus?
"Devadatta! [he replied.]
"I have used countless skillful means to benefit and show compassion for the families of laypeople.
How can it be, you foolish Devadatta,
that you go on alms-rounds from only five households?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Devadatta with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"This Devadatta is a foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there were sick bhikṣus who had been invited to a meal, yet they were unable to obtain food and medicine suitable for their illnesses;

furthermore, when excellent food and medicine suitable for their illnesses were available, they feared and hesitated to accept them, dreading that they might commit the offense of eating separately from the community.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to accept food from a separate assembly.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, except during the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The remaining times are: when one is ill.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, after the bhikṣus had completed the *pravāraṇā*, during the month of Kārttika when robes were being made, the upāsakas thought to themselves:
"These bhikṣus have finished the *pravāraṇā* and are making robes during the month of Kārttika; it would be appropriate for me now to provide food for the Saṃgha."
"Why is this? I fear that the bhikṣus will be unable to obtain food and will suffer from exhaustion.
He then went to the saṃghārāma and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"May the Venerable Ones accept our invitation for a meal tomorrow.
The bhikṣus replied:
"Please invite only three of us; we may not eat apart from the community."
Those upāsakas said to the bhikṣus: "Each of us has had this thought:

'Venerable sirs, once the *pravāraṇā* ceremony is concluded, you will be making robes during the month of Kārttika; we fear that the bhikṣus may not obtain sufficient food and will suffer from exhaustion.'"
"Therefore, today we have invited the Saṃgha for a meal.
The bhikṣus replied again, saying:
"Invite only three people; we should not eat separately from the assembly."
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to accept food from a separate group when it is the time for making robes."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except during the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The remaining times are: when one is ill, and when making robes; these are called the remaining times."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a householder who wished to offer food and robes; he came to the saṃghārāma and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I wish to give food; I pray that the Saṃgha will accept my meal for tomorrow."
The bhikṣus replied, “We request only three people to provide us with food; we may not eat separately from the group.
The householder said:
"Venerable sir!
I wish to offer you food and robes; please accept my invitation. That bhikṣu said:
"We request only three people; we may not eat in a group apart from the community.
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One declared:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to eat in a separate group when receiving donated robes."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
'Other times' refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of receiving robes."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling together with several lay devotees (gṛhapati) on the road toward the kingdom of Kośala.
When it was time for almsround, they said to the lay devotees, "We wish to go into the village for alms; please wait for us a moment, and we shall return together."
The laypeople replied,
"Just follow us and we shall provide you with food and drink. The bhikṣus replied:
"But we may not eat separately from the group if we give [alms] to only three people.
The lay devotees said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"This path is perilous and difficult, filled with uncertainty and fear. Come here alone and I shall provide you with food and drink; do not come later, for you are few in number.
The bhikṣus said, "Give it to three of us; we may not eat separately from the community."

Then the bhikṣus entered the village to beg for food, while their companions proceeded ahead; the bhikṣus lagged behind and were unable to keep up, whereupon they were plundered of their robes by bandits.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if you are traveling on a dangerous road, I permit the bhikṣus to eat separately from the community."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
'Other times' refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, the time of receiving robes, and the time of traveling on a journey."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling downstream by boat with some lay devotees. When it was time for almsround, they said to the lay devotees, "Stop the boat for a moment!"
"We wish to enter the village to beg for alms; we shall return together.
The householders said, "Go, and we shall provide you with food and drink."
The bhikṣus replied, "Give it to only three people; we may not eat separately from the assembly.
The lay devotees said:

"On this bank there are many bandits and places of suspected danger; since your companions are few, do not stay behind lest you be plundered by thieves. Just go, and I shall provide you with food and drink."
The bhikṣus replied, "We shall give it to only three people; we may not eat separately from the group.
The bhikṣus then went ashore to beg for food while their boat companions moved on ahead. When the bhikṣus arrived later, they were all plundered of their robes by bandits.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"From now on, I allow you to eat separately from the community when traveling by boat."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, except at the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The remaining times are: when one is ill, when making robes, when robes are being offered, when traveling on a road, and when traveling by boat."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling from the kingdom of Kośala and arrived at a small village. The local householders thought to themselves:
"The community of monks is large, yet this village is small; would it not be well for us to provide food for the community of monks?"
"Do not cause the community of monks to suffer exhaustion.
He then went to the monastery and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs!"
"Please accept our meal tomorrow.
The bhikṣus replied, "Please invite only three people; we may not eat separately from the assembly."
The laypeople said, "We thought to ourselves:
'Since the Sangha is so numerous and the village is small, we fear they will not obtain food and drink, which would cause the Sangha to suffer from exhaustion!'"
The bhikṣus replied, “Please invite only three people; we may not eat separately from the group.
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One declared:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to eat separately from the community when there is a great assembly.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu eats separately from the community, except at the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The remaining times are: when one is ill, when making robes, when robes are being offered, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, and when the great assembly gathers.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, Kāla, the nephew of King Bimbisāra, had provided food for the śramaṇas and wished to go forth among the heterodox followers of other schools; he went to King Bimbisāra and said:
"I have already provided food for the śramaṇas, and now I wish to go forth."
The King asked, "In what place do you wish to go forth? He replied:
"I wish to go forth among the Nirgranthas.
The king asked again,
"In the end, will you provide food and drink for us śramaṇas?"
Kāla replied, “Great King, who is a śramaṇa?”
The king replied,
"They are the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
Kāla reported this, saying:
"I have not yet provided food for them. The king said,
"Go now and provide food for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas."
He immediately went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"I now wish to provide a meal for the community of bhikṣus; I pray that you will accept my invitation. The bhikṣus replied:
"We should not eat separately from the group; we shall give [the food] only to three people.
Then Kāla said to the bhikṣus:
"I have prepared this meal for the śramaṇas because I wish to go forth among the non-Buddhists."
I immediately went to King Bimbisāra and said to him:
"I have already provided food for the śramaṇas; now I wish to leave the household life.
The king asked me:
"Where do you wish to go forth? I replied,
"I wish to go forth among the Nirgranthas."
The King asked me again,
"Have you yet provided food for us, the śramaṇas?
At that time, I asked him:
"Great King! Who is a śramaṇa? The king replied to me, saying:
“They are the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.
At that time, I replied to the king, saying:
“I have not yet provided food for the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya.”
The king said to me:
"Go now to that place and provide food for the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas; only after that shall you be permitted to depart.
It was for this reason.
He came to the monastery and requested the virtuous elders, saying, "I pray that you will accept my invitation.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit śramaṇas to receive food separately from the community when it is being distributed.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu eats in a separate group, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.

"Other times" refers to: when one is ill; when making robes; when robes are being offered; when traveling on a road; when traveling by boat; when a great assembly has gathered; and when śramaṇas offer food—these are the [permitted] times.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Eating in a separate group" refers to four or more than four people.
"Food" refers to rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat.
"Those who are ill" refers to those down to those with foot ulcers or lameness.

"When making robes" means during the month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony when there is no *kaṭhina* robe in force, or during the five months when the *kaṭhina* robe is in force, up until the point of making even a single "horse-tooth" stitch upon the robe.

Regarding the giving of robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, there is a period of one month if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, and five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread; this also includes other gifts of food and robes.
Regarding those who travel by land: it includes anyone coming or going within a distance of half a yojana.
Regarding those who travel by boat: it includes those traveling up or down by boat within a distance of half a yojana.

Regarding the gathering of a great assembly: when four people have gathered for a meal, having one person in excess constitutes a fault; with five, ten, or even up to a hundred people, having one person in excess constitutes a fault.
As for those who give food to śramaṇas, this refers to those other renunciants outside of these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, as well as those who have gone forth from among the non-Buddhist paths.
If a bhikṣu has no cause or condition for eating separately from the group, that bhikṣu should immediately rise and say:
"I have no cause or condition regarding this separate meal; I wish to leave."
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to go out.
If others have no other business, they are also permitted to go out; then two or three people may eat as they please.
If there are four or more than four people, they should divide into two groups and enter for the meal in turns.
If a bhikṣu has a reason for eating separately from the group and wishes to enter, he should immediately rise and announce:
"I have a reason for eating separately from the group; I wish to enter."
The Buddha said:
"They should be permitted to enter according to the order of seniority.
If a bhikṣu eats apart from the community, for every swallow there is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not speak [the truth] when there is a cause or condition for doing so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

when one is ill; when making robes; when robes are being distributed as gifts; when traveling on a road; when traveling by boat; when a great assembly has gathered; or when śramaṇas are distributing food. Furthermore, there is no offense if three or four people eat in mutual exchange, or if one departs for a stated reason.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The thirty-third section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a woman named Gañjā who had previously lived in a large village; she came to the kingdom of Uddiyāna to become a wife to someone, and after several months had passed, she became pregnant and returned to her parents' home.
Whenever there were bhikṣus who came to her house to beg for alms, she would personally take food or fruit and offer it to them.
Later, at another time, her husband sent a messenger to call his wife back home. When the wife went out to meet the messenger, she said to him:
"Please wait a moment; I am just now preparing food and drink and dressing myself, after which we shall go together."
At that time, several bhikṣus came to her house to beg for alms.
When the girl saw them, she immediately gave away all the food and drink she had prepared to those bhikṣus.
He said: "Venerable sir,
please eat this food."
At that time, the bhikṣus took all the food and left nothing remaining.
While his wife was still behind him, busy with her adornments, before she had returned, her husband had already taken another wife. He sent a messenger to tell her:
"I have now taken another wife; whether you wish to come back or not is entirely up to your own will."
When Gaja’s father heard this, he went to the monastery; upon seeing him, the bhikṣus said to him, “Your daughter Gaja is deeply faithful.”
"I take great delight in giving.
His father replied, "As the venerable ones have said, you truly possess firm faith; however, today you have obtained that which is disliked by women."
The bhikṣus asked, "What have you obtained? His father replied:
“Her husband has already taken another wife.
At that time, outside the city gates of Vārāṇasī, a large caravan of merchants was staying overnight together.
Then, a certain bhikṣu who lived on alms, having dressed in his robes and taken up his bowl at the proper time, entered this encampment of merchants to beg for food.
At that time, as that bhikṣu went on his alms-round in succession, he gradually approached a merchant who was full of faith and stood silently before him.
The merchant asked, "Venerable sir, for what reason are you standing here now?"
The bhikṣu replied, “I am begging for alms.
She then said to him:
"Bring me your bowl. At that time, the bhikṣu immediately handed over his bowl, and the merchant took the bowl, filled it with excellent food and drink, and gave it to him.

Then, as the bhikṣu carrying the food was leaving the caravan camp, he had not gone far when another bhikṣu seeking alms arrived at the caravan camp to beg for food and asked the bhikṣu who had obtained food:
"Can alms be obtained? He replied, "They can."
He asked again,
"From whom did you receive it?
and [the other] replied:
"I obtained it from a certain merchant.
At that time, the bhikṣu who was begging for alms went before the merchant and stood there in silence.
The merchant asked:
"Why are you here? The bhikṣu replied,
"I am now begging for alms."
The merchant said, "Pass the bowl over here.
At that time, the bhikṣu immediately handed the bowl to him; the merchant took the bowl, filled it with excellent food and drink, and presented it to the bhikṣu.
After the bhikṣu had received [the food] and returned from the wagon camp, before he had gone far from the camp, another bhikṣu seeking alms arrived at the wagon camp to beg for food and asked:
"Can alms be obtained?"
He replied, “It can be obtained.
He asked again:
"From whom did you obtain it? He replied,
"I obtained it from a certain merchant."
Thus they informed one another until the others had finished eating.
Only then did the merchant leader enter the city of Vārāṇasī to purchase more provisions; his companions had already departed, leaving him behind, and he was plundered by bandits on the road.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured those bhikṣus, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu eat the food of a woman returning from her husband's home or the food of merchants on the road, and cause it all to be consumed without any remainder?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked them, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, not a compliant practice, and is something that should not have been done."
"What do you think, monks?
How can one eat the food of a woman who has returned home from her husband, or the provisions for a merchant on the road, until nothing remains?
Having thus rebuked that monk with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the monks:
“O foolish bhikṣus! This is the first transgression of the precepts among many bases for the outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”

If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson who invites him for a meal—whether it be rice or roasted flour—the bhikṣu may accept two or three bowls if he requires them. Having accepted them, he should return to the saṃghārāma and distribute the food among the other bhikṣus.
"If one accepts more than two or three bowls [of food] and, upon returning to the monastery, does not distribute it to the other bhikṣus for them to eat, it is a pāyattika.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the sick bhikṣus, being fearful and cautious, did not dare to accept food beyond the prescribed limit and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the sick bhikṣus to accept food beyond the limit."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:

If a bhikṣu goes to the home of a layperson and is invited by that layperson to receive food, whether it be rice or flour, and the bhikṣu desires it, he may accept two or three bowls. Upon returning to the saṃghārāma, he should divide it and give it to the other bhikṣus to eat.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls [of food] and, upon returning to the monastery, does not share it with the other bhikṣus, it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Lay households" refers to those with both men and women.
"Illness" means being unable to sit in one place and finish eating fine food.
If a bhikṣu goes to the house of a layperson who invites him to eat cakes and parched grain, he should ask the host:
"Is this food for a newly married bride returning home?
Or is it provisions for merchants on a journey?"
If one says, "This is food for a woman returning home,
or provisions for a merchant on a journey," then one should eat it and depart immediately, returning to the saṃghārāma to inform the bhikṣus:
“Such-and-such a household has food for a newly arrived wife, and merchants have provisions for their journey. If you wish to eat, you may do so; having eaten, you should depart.
If you wish to take food back with you, take no more than two or three bowls. I shall not bring any food here.”
If one wishes to take a bowl of food back to the monastery to share it with the other bhikṣus, one should say to the other bhikṣus:

"In such-and-such a house there is food for a newly arrived wife and provisions for merchants on the road; if any of you go to that house, eat there. If you take food back, you should take two bowls, while I shall return with one."
"If you return carrying two alms bowls, you should share the food with the other bhikṣus.
He further addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If there is food from a woman returning home at such-and-such a house, or provisions for travelers on the road at a merchant's house, and if you wish to go to that house to beg for food, you may eat there."
"Those who wish to take [food] back should take one bowl and return; I have now already taken two bowls back.
If he takes all three bowls back, upon returning to the monastery, he shall divide them among the bhikṣus for a communal meal and say to the other bhikṣus:

"Now, at such-and-such a house there is food from a woman returning home and provisions for merchants on the road. Those who wish to go to that house to beg for food may eat there immediately; those who wish to take it back, be careful not to take it back, as I have already brought three bowls."
If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts more than two or three bowls of food from that household and, having returned, passes through its gate, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, and he makes a movement to leave but then stops, it is entirely a duṣkṛta offense.
If one takes food without asking whether it was prepared for a returning wife or as provisions for a merchant on the road, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one carries it to a monastery and eats it alone without distributing it to the other bhikṣus, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not inform other bhikṣus, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for one who accepts food in two or three bowls;
nor for one who accepts more than that due to illness.

If one asks returning women or traveling merchants for provisions for the road and, upon returning to the saṃghārāma, shares them with the bhikṣus to eat, one should inform the other bhikṣus so they may know the location of the village;
if they personally deliver it to the saṃghārāma, it may be accepted, and if they further deliver it to the bhikṣuṇī-vihāra, it may likewise be accepted—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the bhikṣus the practice of eating a single meal and praised the practice of eating a single meal.

When the bhikṣus heard the World-Honored One teach the practice of eating a single meal and extol its virtues, they would eat *khajjaka* foods, or the five kinds of formal meals, or drink gruel, or take medicine, yet they would then observe the rule of eating only once and not eat again, causing their bodies to become emaciated and their complexions to grow haggard.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing yet intentionally questioning Ānanda, said:
"For what reason are these bhikṣus so emaciated in body and withered in complexion?
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught the bhikṣus the practice of eating a single meal and praised the practice of eating a single meal. Yet, having heard this, the bhikṣus immediately consume khajjaka food, or eat the five kinds of cooked food, or drink gruel, or take medicine while remaining on a single seat; they then observe the rule of eating only once and do not eat again. For this reason, their bodies have become withered and their complexions emaciated.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to eat until they are fully satiated while remaining on a single seat.
When the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had authorized eating until full on a single seat, [they rejoiced].

At that time, whether the bhikṣus were eating khādanīya (hard food), the five kinds of cooked food, drinking gruel, or taking medicine, they would satisfy themselves and eat no more; consequently, the bodies of the bhikṣus became withered and their complexions grew haggard.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are these bhikṣus so withered in body and so haggard in countenance?
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

When the bhikṣus heard that the Blessed One had permitted them to eat until they were fully satiated while remaining on a single seat—whether eating khādanīya (solid food), the five kinds of cooked food, drinking beverages, or taking medicine—they would eat until they were full and then refuse to eat further; for this reason, their bodies became emaciated and their complexions grew haggard.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:

"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to eat five kinds of food—whether it be boiled rice, parched grain, dry rice, fish, or meat—to their full satisfaction. Among these five kinds of food, they may eat each one individually as obtained, until they are satisfied."

At that time, although the sick bhikṣus obtained fine food—cooked rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat—they were unable to eat it all in a single sitting; their bodies became withered and their complexions grew haggard.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asking deliberately, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are the bodies of these sick bhikṣus withered and their complexions emaciated?
