Then Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Although this sick bhikṣu has received the five kinds of food, he is unable to eat them all in a single sitting; therefore, his body is withered and his complexion is emaciated.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to eat repeatedly; for a sick person, there is no rule regarding 'having had enough' (paryāpta-bhakta)."

At that time, when the sick bhikṣus received fine and delicious food, they were unable to finish it all and gave it to their attendants. Having already eaten their fill, the attendants did not dare to eat it and threw it away; flocks of birds vied with one another to scramble for the food, clamoring and calling out.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are the birds crying out?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"These sick monks received excellent and delicious food, but they could not finish it all; they gave the leftovers to their attendants. Having already eaten their fill, the attendants did not dare eat the remainder and simply threw it away. For this reason, the birds are quarreling over the food and crying out."
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"From this day forward, I permit those who attend to the sick to eat the remains of the food of the patient; when eating the remains of the patient's food, there is no requirement for the *atireka-bhojana* (leftover food) procedure."

At that time, the bhikṣus received their morning meal, set it aside, and entered the village to beg for food. After they had eaten, they returned to take the food they had set aside and gave it to the other bhikṣus.
Since those bhikṣus had already eaten their fill, they did not dare to eat it and simply discarded it; consequently, flocks of crows scrambled for the food, cawing and clamoring.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asked intentionally, said to Ānanda: "Why is this crow cawing?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

“On the morning of the day, the bhikṣus accepted food, set it aside, and entered the village to beg for alms. Having eaten, they returned with the food they had set aside and gave it to the other bhikṣus.
Since those bhikṣus had already finished their meals, they did not dare to eat it and simply discarded it; therefore, the crows quarreled over the food and clamored.”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I allow you to take the food you have received and perform the *yūṣa-karma* (the rite for leftover food) before eating it. You should speak these words for the *yūṣa-karma*:
'Venerable One!'"
"I have finished my meal; I know this and see this.
This constitutes the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (the ritual for leftover food).
That bhikṣu, having taken a small amount of food, should say to that other bhikṣu:
"Take as much food as you wish. This is how one should perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the formal procedure for leftover food) before eating.

Later, there was an elder monk with many acquaintances who entered a village to beg for alms. Having obtained a great amount, he gathered it in one place and ate together with others. He then took the leftovers back to the monastery and gave them to the monks. Since the monks had already finished their meals, they did not dare to eat them and consequently discarded them; flocks of birds then scrambled for the food, clamoring and crying out.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the reason yet asking anyway, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are the birds crying out?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"The Elder has many acquaintances; when a bhikkhu enters a village for alms, he obtains a great quantity of food and drink, which he gathers in one place and eats together, then brings back the leftovers to give to the other bhikkhus."
"Since the bhikṣus have already finished their meals, they did not dare to eat [the leftovers] and instead discarded them; the crows are clamoring because they are competing for that food.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to take food from there back [to the monastery], and they shall eat it by performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food)."
One should perform the ritual for leftover food (*khalupaścādbhakti*) by saying:
"Venerable sir, I have finished my meal; I know this and I see this."
This is the procedure for the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (remaining-food) rite.
Having taken a small portion of that food, he should say to the other bhikṣu:
"I have finished; you may take and eat it."
"That bhikṣu should eat according to this *khalupaścādbhaktika* (leftover-food) procedure.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu in Śrāvastī who, being gluttonous and lacking moderation, did not know what constituted sufficient food or insufficient food, nor what constituted leftover food or non-leftover food; whenever he obtained food, he would simply eat it.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured that bhikṣu, saying:
"How can you be so gluttonous, not knowing whether food is sufficient or insufficient, nor whether it is leftover or not leftover, yet eat it as soon as you receive it?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally asked that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you were so gluttonous as to not know whether food was sufficient or insufficient, nor whether it was leftover or not leftover, yet ate it as soon as you obtained it?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The Buddha then rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
How is this so, bhikṣu?"
"Is your greed for food such as this?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. To assemble the ten points of meaning and so forth, until the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, having finished his meal, should at any time accept an invitation and eat without performing the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Food" refers to five kinds of food:
boiled rice, parched grain, dry rice, fish, and meat.
Among these five kinds of food, whether one eats each type individually—be it boiled rice, parched grain, dry rice, fish, or meat—one should eat until fully satiated.

There are five factors that constitute having finished one's meal: knowing it is rice, knowing it has been brought, knowing the prohibition [of further food], knowing the proper deportment, and knowing the relinquishing of that deportment. If, after having finished one's meal and relinquished the deportment, one obtains and eats it without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), there is an offense of *pāyattika* for every swallow.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In how many places must a practicing bhikṣu be considered to have had sufficient food?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
“There are five instances where one should consider oneself to have had enough food. What are these five?

Upāli! When a bhikṣu knows the proper time for eating, he knows the food, he knows its bringing, he knows the restrictions, he knows the deportment, and he knows the relinquishing of deportment. Having known that he has eaten his fill and relinquished his deportment, he may eat what he obtains without performing the ritual of leaving food remaining.
For every swallow, it is a *pāyattika*. In this regard, Upāli!

If a bhikṣu knows it is the time for walking, knows roasted flour, parched rice, fish, and meat; knows they have been brought, knows the prohibition, knows the proper deportment, and knows the relinquishing of deportment—if, having finished eating and relinquished the deportment, he obtains and eats food without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leaving food), for every swallow it is a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu who knows the proper time for eating, knows the meal of parched grain, knows what has been brought, knows what is prohibited, knows the rules of decorum, and knows when to relinquish those rules—having finished his meal and relinquished the rules of decorum—if he obtains and eats food without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu knows the time for eating, knows dry rice, knows fish and meat-rice, knows when it has been brought, knows what is prohibited, knows proper deportment, and knows when to abandon deportment. Once he has finished eating and abandoned his deportment, if he obtains and eats food without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leaving no remainder), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu knows the time for eating, knows dry rice as food, knows what has been brought, knows prohibitions, knows proper deportment, and knows the relinquishing of deportment. Having finished eating and relinquished his deportment, if he obtains and eats it without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leftover food), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu knows the proper time for eating, knows fish, meat, rice, and parched grain; he knows when food has been brought, knows what is prohibited, knows the rules of decorum, and knows when to relinquish those rules. Having finished eating and relinquished the rules of decorum, if he obtains and eats food without performing the *kṛtya-śeṣa* (the ritual for leftover food), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu knows the time for eating, knows the fish-food, knows its bringing, knows the prohibitions, knows the proper deportment, and knows the relinquishing of deportment. Having finished eating and relinquished his deportment, if he obtains food and eats it without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual for leftover food), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, Upāli! A bhikṣu knows the time for eating;

he knows meat, rice, parched grain, and dry rice; he knows when food has been brought, he knows what is prohibited, he knows proper deportment, and he knows when to abandon deportment. Once he has finished eating and abandoned his deportment, if he obtains and eats it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
In this regard, Upāli!

A bhikṣu who knows the proper time for eating, knows [the rules regarding] meat-eating, knows what has been brought, knows prohibitions, knows the proper deportment, and knows the relinquishing of deportment—having finished eating and relinquished his deportment—if he obtains food and eats it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (remaining-food) rite, for every swallow he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
In this regard, Upāli! A bhikṣu knows the proper time for eating;

he knows rice, parched grain, dry rice, and fish; he knows when food has been brought; he knows what is prohibited; he knows proper deportment; and he knows the relinquishing of deportment. Once he has finished eating and relinquished his deportment, if he obtains and eats food without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food), there is a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow.
"Upāli! These are the five ways for a practicing bhikṣu to be satisfied with food; it is the same when standing, sitting, or lying down.
Regarding "solid food" (khādaniya):
There are solid foods consisting of roots;
solid foods consisting of stalks, leaves, flowers, and fruits;
and solid foods consisting of oil, sesame, and finely ground powder of black honey.

If that bhikṣu, having already finished his meal, accepts and eats food without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite for leftover food), he commits a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful swallowed.
If, having already finished his meal, he performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* for another person but the *khalupaścādbhakti* is not properly accomplished, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one knows that another has already finished eating, and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) procedure when it is not validly performed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu takes food with his own hand and performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* procedure when it is not validly performed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one places food on the ground and attempts to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (leftover-food) rite, the rite is not validly performed; it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu has a *śrāmaṇera* or lay attendant carry food and attempts to perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite, the rite is not validly performed; it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu performs the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the ritual of leftover food) in the presence of a *kappiyakāraka* (a lay attendant), it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one covers good food with inferior food and performs the *khalupaścādbhakti*, the ritual is not established as a valid *khalupaścādbhakti*; it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu accepts the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (leftover-food) procedure from another and carries it all away, the *khalupaścādbhaktika* procedure is not established; this is a *duṣkṛta*.
If he has eaten his fill and perceives that he has eaten his fill, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has eaten enough but there is doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu perceives that he has not eaten enough when he has actually eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is doubt as to whether he has eaten enough, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one eats while perceiving food as non-food; if one performs the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual for food, but does not perform the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual for non-food;

if one takes it oneself and performs the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual; if one performs the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual without placing it on the ground, even when it reaches the hand; if one gives it to another, or if another has given it, and then performs the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual;
or if one is ill and does not perform the *kṛta-śeṣa* ritual.

If one consumes the leftover food of a sick person without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food), it is an offense; however, if the *kṛtapiṇḍa* has already been performed, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept had not yet been promulgated, or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[Chapter] Thirty-Five concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were two brothers in Śrāvastī who had become bhikṣus. One of these bhikṣus was gluttonous and fond of food; he did not know the difference between having eaten enough and not having eaten enough, nor between what was leftover and what was not leftover, and he would eat whatever he obtained.
Another bhikṣu said to him:

"Never before have I seen anyone as gluttonous and fond of food as you are, who does not know the difference between having had enough and not having had enough, or between what is leftover and what is not leftover, yet eats whatever he obtains."

When that monk heard these words, he harbored resentment in his heart. Later, seeing that other monk having finished his meal, he earnestly invited him to accept food without having performed the *atirittaka* (remaining-food) ritual; the latter then accepted and ate it.
The gluttonous bhikṣu said:

"Never before have I seen one as gluttonous as you—thus lacking contentment with food, not knowing when enough has been eaten, not knowing what constitutes leftover food, not knowing when there is no more, eating whatever is obtained without ever knowing satiety."
That bhikṣu replied, "Although I have eaten, I am not yet satisfied.
That other bhikṣu said:
"You have already finished your meal. That bhikṣu asked,
"Do you know that I have had enough?"
He replied, "I know. That bhikṣu asked:
“Did you do this intentionally, knowing [the consequences]? He replied, “I knew.”
At that time, those bhikṣus reproached that bhikṣu, saying:
"How can you, knowing that another bhikṣu has already finished his meal, earnestly invite him to eat, intending to cause him to commit an offense?"

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured that bhikṣu, saying:
"How can you, knowing that another has already finished eating, insistently invite him to eat, desiring to cause him to commit a transgression of the precepts?"
Then that bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, intentionally questioned that bhikṣu:
"Is it true that you, knowing another had already finished eating, earnestly invited him to eat, desiring to cause him to commit an offense against the precepts?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
At that time, the Blessed One rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can you know that another has already finished his meal, yet persistently invite him to eat, wishing to cause him to transgress the precepts?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of significance and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished eating, persistently invites him to eat, saying, 'Venerable sir, please eat this food,' and does so for no other reason than with the desire to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what had been eaten or what had not yet been eaten, nor did they know what constituted having eaten enough or not having eaten enough. Later, when they realized they had already eaten or had already eaten enough, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were apprehensive and cautious.
The Buddha said:
"If one did not know, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited in this manner:"

If a bhikṣu, knowing that another bhikṣu has finished his meal, and having been invited, does not perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite of leftover food), yet persistently invites him to eat, saying, "Venerable sir, please take this food," and does so for no other reason than with the desire to cause the other to commit an offense, it is a *pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Food" is of five kinds, also as explained above.
"Invitations" are also of five kinds, also as explained above.
When that bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has finished his meal and has not performed the *khalupaścādbhaktika* rite, he earnestly invites him to eat, saying:
"Venerable sir, please eat this."
If he accepts and eats it, both incur a *pāyattika* offense for every mouthful.
If he gives it to him to eat and the former bhikṣu does not eat it but discards it, the giver incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣu gives food to someone, and that person receives it but does not eat it, setting it aside instead, the giver commits a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣu gives food to someone, and that person, having received it, transfers it to another, the giver commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If a bhikṣu gives food to another person without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of "leftover food"), and that person performs the *kṛtapiṇḍa* and eats it, the giver commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he gives food to a sick person with the intent to cause the other to commit an offense, the giver commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one gives leftover food from a sick person to another with the intent to cause that other to commit an offense, the giver commits a *duṣkṛta*.
If, after performing the ritual for "leftover food" (*atiriktapiṇḍapāta*), one gives it to another with the intent to cause that other to commit an offense, the giver commits a *duṣkṛta*.
If one has eaten to full satisfaction and perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one has eaten to full satisfaction but suspects it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one has not eaten to full satisfaction but perceives it as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one eats when there is insufficient food and harbors doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one did not previously know it was sufficient food yet had the perception that it was insufficient;

or if one gave it [to another] with the instruction to discard it and then ate it; or if one gave it [to another] with the instruction to set it aside and then ate it; or if one sent it to someone else to take and eat.
If one has not performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual for leftover food) and gives it to another to perform that ritual before eating, yet the other eats it without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa*;
or if one gives the leftovers of a sick person and does not cause the other to commit an offense;
or if one gives after having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* and does not cause the other to commit an offense—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Thirty-Six concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the people of Rājagṛha were holding a festival and performing various musical entertainments. Then the two Śākyan sons, Nanda and Upananda, went there to watch the performances. Because the Śākyan sons Nanda and Upananda were handsome and of upright appearance, the multitude all gathered together to gaze upon them.
At that time, there was a man who said to the crowd:
"You all look upon these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas in vain; why do you not first provide them with food and drink as offerings before you gaze upon them?"
Then the crowd immediately provided them with food and drink.
Having finished eating, the two Śākya sons, Nanda and Upananda, continued to watch the performance. As evening approached, they returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain. When the bhikṣus saw them, they asked:
"For what reason are you traveling so late at night?"
At that time, Nanda and Upananda related these circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.

Then, as evening fell, Kālodāyin put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. As the sky grew dark and overcast, he went to the house of a pregnant woman to beg. When the woman came out with food, she encountered a flash of lightning and caught a brief glimpse of his face; terrified, she cried out, "A ghost!"
“Demon! At that, she miscarried. Kālodāyin said to her:
“Elder sister! I am not a ghost;
I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākya!”
The woman spoke in anger:
"A śramaṇa son of the Śākyas would rather burst his own belly than go begging for alms at night.
When Kālodāyin heard these words, he returned to the saṃghārāma and recounted this incident to the bhikṣus.

Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured and rebuked Nanda, Upananda, and Kālodāyin, the sons of the Śākyas, saying:
"How is it that Nanda, Upananda, and Kālodāyin go begging for food at an improper time and watch performances of music and dance?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked Nanda, Upananda the Śākyas, and Kāḷodāyin:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"Nanda, Upananda the Śākyan, and Kāḷudāyin, how is it that you beg for food at an improper time and watch performances?
Having rebuked Nanda, Upananda the Śākyan, and Kāḷudāyin with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not watch performances.
To watch a performance is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning and so forth, until the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, he commits a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Proper time" refers to the period from the appearance of the dawn light until midday; according to this rule, the same applies to eating throughout the four continents.
"Improper time" refers to the period from midday until the appearance of the morning light.
"Food" is of two kinds: *khādaniya* (solid food), as described above; and *bhojaniya* (soft food), the five kinds of which are as described above.
If a bhikṣu eats food at an improper time, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he eats after the improper time has passed, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If he keeps [medicines] for seven days or beyond seven days, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one consumes medicine for life without a valid reason, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one consumes it at an improper time while perceiving it as such, it is a *pāyattika*. If one consumes it at an improper time while doubting whether it is so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If it is not the proper time, but one perceives it as the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense. If it is the proper time, but one perceives it as not the proper time, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is not the proper time, but one is uncertain, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following case: Suppose there was a bhikṣu who went on almsround and saw that another person had made black stone honey containing *kṛtani* (curdled milk); out of caution and apprehension, he did not dare to eat it at an improper time.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to eat; there is no offense.
The ritual procedure should be performed in this manner."

At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who had taken emetic and purgative medicine. While the bhikṣu was cooking rice gruel, the time for his meal had already passed; he should therefore cook barley so that the husks do not break, strain the juice, and drink it—there is no offense.
If one spits out from the throat and swallows it back again, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The thirty-seventh [chapter] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Kāla was dwelling there, constantly sitting in meditation and contemplation.
When the time for alms-round arrived, Kāla put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food.
At that time, alms were easy to obtain in the city of Rājagṛha, and Kāla thought to himself:
"Why do I weary myself by entering the city to beg for food every single day?"
"I would rather eat what I obtain first; as for what I obtain later, I shall take it back.
Later, he did exactly as he had thought.
At that time, the bhikṣus could not see Kāla at either the morning meal or the midday meal.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"We have not seen Kāla at either the morning meal or the midday meal; could it be that his life has come to an end?"
Have you not traveled too far?
Have you not rested on the road?
Have you not been robbed by bandits?
“Were you not harmed by wild beasts?
Were you not swept away by water?
Later, at another time, he saw Kāla and asked him:
“Where have you come from lately?
We did not see you at either the morning meal or the midday meal.
We thought you had passed away, or had gone on a long journey, or had left the monastic life, or had been harmed by a wild beast.”
At that time, Kāla related these circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.

Among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Kāla, saying:
"How can you store up food overnight and then eat it?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kāla intentionally:
"Is it true that you ate food kept overnight? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful means, rebuked Kāla:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is this, Kāla? Do you eat food that has been kept overnight?
Although your intention is to have few desires and be content, your subsequent conduct follows the ways of the common folk."
After the Blessed One had rebuked Kāla, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This foolish man Kāla has committed the first offense regarding the many bases for outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "stale food": having received it on this day and kept it until the next day, it is entirely impure for all śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, who have received full ordination.
There are two kinds of food:
proper food and improper food.
Improper food refers to food from roots up to fine flour-based foods.
"Proper food" refers to rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, and meat.
If a bhikṣu eats food that has been kept overnight, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.
To eat at an improper time when it is past the proper time is a *pāyattika* offense.
To consume seven-day medicine after the seven days have passed is a *pāyattika* offense.
To take lifetime medicine without the presence of a cause or condition of illness is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one perceives it as having been prepared overnight, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one suspects it has been prepared overnight, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it has not been prepared overnight, but one perceives it as such, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If it was not a pre-existing doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one has food remaining from a previous meal and gives it to one's parents, to those working for the stupa, or to those working on the dwelling, providing them with the value of the food as wages.

At another time, a bhikṣu seeking alms obtained food from a laborer; as he was eating from his bowl, there were holes and cracks in it, and the food fell through them. He picked out the broken pieces and washed them. If, after washing according to the rule, no further fragments emerge, there is no offense.

If one has previously received medicinal ghee or oil for nasal irrigation, and if the ghee or oil comes out with the saliva when pinching the nose, it should be discarded; in other cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following circumstances: when the precept had not yet been established, or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The Thirty-Eight [Rules] Concluded. The Vinaya in Four Parts, Volume Fourteen.
Part One, Fifteen: The Vinaya in Four Parts, Volume Fifteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others;
the fifth section of the Ninety *Pācittiya* Rules. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu in the city of Śrāvastī who had this thought:
"I would rather now always beg for food and wear robes made of discarded rags.
He then acted exactly according to what he had thought.

At that time, the laypeople of Śrāvastī, for the sake of deceased parents, brothers, sisters, or husbands, prepared food and drink as offerings for sacrifice at crossroads, or beneath gateways, or by the banks of rivers, or under trees, or beside rocks, or within shrines.
Then that mendicant bhikṣu took the food for himself and ate it. When the lay devotees saw this, they all reproached him together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they commit theft by taking what is not given, yet outwardly they claim, 'We practice the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what righteous Dharma is there?

We prepare food and drink as offerings for the sake of deceased parents, brothers, and sisters, and we eat it ourselves; yet it is as if we were intentionally providing food and drink to the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas and placing it in such a location, while we ourselves then consume these offerings of food and drink set out for the sake of deceased parents, brothers, and sisters."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse.

They censured the bhikṣu who had gone for alms, saying: "How can a bhikṣu who goes for alms take food for himself when laypeople in Śrāvastī have prepared a meal as a sacrificial offering and供养 (offering) for deceased parents, brothers, and sisters?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked that bhikṣu:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"What do you think, mendicant bhikṣu!
How can you take for yourself the sacrificial food of the householders of Śrāvastī and eat it?
Having rebuked that mendicant bhikṣu with countless skillful means, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“This foolish bhikṣu who begs for alms has committed the first offense among many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu receives food or medicine and places it in his mouth without having first accepted it, it is a pāyattika.’”
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus became doubtful in this matter and did not dare to take tooth-sticks or pure water themselves. The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, it is no offense for you to take tooth-sticks and pure water yourselves."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, except for water and tooth-sticks, places food or medicine into his mouth without having received it [from another], it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Not given" refers to that which has not yet been received.
There are five kinds of receiving: [the five types of formal acceptance].
Giving with the hand and receiving with the hand;
or giving with the hand and receiving with an object;
or giving with an object and receiving with the hand.
If one gives by holding an object and receives by holding an object;

or if one gives by passing an object from a distance, such that both the giver and the receiver know it has reached the recipient's hand without being touched or obstructed in the interim—these are called the five ways of receiving.
Furthermore, there are five ways of receiving food:

receiving from body to body, receiving from robe to robe, receiving from the crook of one arm to the crook of another, receiving from vessel to vessel, or, when there is a specific reason, receiving by placing it on the ground; these are the five ways of receiving food.
Khaḍaniya food refers to food from roots up to fine ground flour.
Bhojya food refers to parched grain, boiled rice, solid rice, fish, and meat.
Sāyāniya food refers to ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, and rock sugar.
If a bhikṣu takes food and puts it into his own mouth without it being given to him—except for water and tooth-sticks—he commits a pāyattika offense for every swallow.
If he eats at an improper time or consumes food past the proper time, he commits a pāyattika offense.
If one consumes a seven-day medicine after the seven days have passed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one consumes a lifetime medicine without having formally accepted it when there is no valid reason to do so, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one does not receive [an offering] while perceiving that one has not received it, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one suspects that one has not received it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one receives it while perceiving that one has not received it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one receives [the precepts] with doubt, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: taking water or tooth-sticks; or if, upon receiving clarified butter, oil, or nasal medication, it comes out together with saliva; in all other instances, there is no offense.

If food is dropped into the bowl of a bhikṣu seeking alms by a bird, or if it is blown into the bowl by the wind, he may remove that food even if it requires the use of a fingernail; regarding the remainder, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The thirty-ninth [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the merchant leader Sāḷha was a donor to the Śākya son Upananda. When it was time, the Śākya son Upananda put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the merchant’s house, saying these words:
"I now wish to have some mixed food!"
The merchants asked,
"What trouble do you have now that you think of this food? He replied:
"I have no illness or suffering; I simply wish to obtain some mixed food.
The merchants replied, "We are mere traders who live by buying and selling, yet even we cannot obtain mixed food; how much less so can those who have left the household life?"
At that time, the bhikṣu who was begging for alms heard these words and reproached the Śākya son Upananda, saying:
"How can you, for your own sake, beg for such fine food?"
Then, having finished his meal, the bhikṣu who had gone for alms returned to the monastery and recounted these circumstances to the other bhikṣus.
Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the śākyaputra Upananda, saying: "How can you beg for such fine food for yourself?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
“Vāṣpa, son of the Śākyas! Why do you beg for such fine food for yourself?
After the Blessed One had rebuked Vāṣpa, the son of the Śākyas, with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Bhadanta, you foolish man!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If there are such delicacies as milk, curd, fish, and meat, and if a bhikṣu seeks such delicacies for his own sake, it is a pāyattika offense.
Thus the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

When the sick bhikṣus heard these words, they all became fearful and cautious; they did not dare to beg for themselves, nor did they dare to beg on behalf of sick bhikṣus, and having obtained food, they did not dare to eat it.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit a sick bhikṣu to beg for food, and I also permit another person to beg on behalf of that sick bhikṣu; once it has been obtained through begging, I permit him to eat it."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If one obtains fine and delicious food and drink—such as milk, curd, fish, or meat—and a bhikṣu, being free from illness, seeks such fine food and drink for his own sake, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Delicious food" refers to milk, curd, fish, and meat.
"Illness" refers to being unable to finish eating even during a single sitting session.
If a bhikṣu who is not ill begs for such fine food for his own sake and eats it, for every swallow he commits a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the sick person begs for themselves, or if one begs on behalf of the sick person and eats what was obtained;
or if one acts for another's sake, or another acts for one's own sake.
If one obtains something without having asked for it, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

The fortieth [chapter] concludes. At that time, the Buddha, leading one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, traveled from the kingdom of Kosala and arrived at Śrāvastī. At that time, the various donors made offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks, obtaining a great quantity of cakes and food.
Then the World-Honored One said to Ānanda, “Divide these cakes among the assembly of monks.
Ānanda immediately received the instruction and divided the cakes to give to the assembly; having finished dividing them, some still remained.
The World-Honored One again addressed Ānanda:
"Give these remaining cakes to the beggars.
Ānanda immediately followed this instruction and gave one cake to each person.

At that time, among the crowd of beggars, there was a naked ascetic woman who was beautiful in appearance. As Ānanda was distributing the cakes, they became stuck together; he thought it was a single cake and gave it to this woman.
This woman then asked those standing nearby,
"How many cakes did you receive?
At that time, they replied:
"I have obtained one cake.
He then asked him in return:
"How many cakes did you obtain?"
She replied, "I have obtained two cakes.
Then that woman spoke to this girl, saying:
"He had an illicit affair with you; how could he not give you two cakes?
When Ānanda heard these words, he was immediately filled with sorrow, and when the bhikṣus heard them as well, they were likewise displeased.

At that time, there was a brahmin in that assembly who, having finished his meal there, set out for the kingdom of Kosala. On the road, he encountered a devout brahmin who practiced physiognomy, and he asked him:
"Where have you come from?"
He replied, "I have come from Śrāvastī.
He asked again:
"How can one obtain food and drink by begging within the city of Śrāvastī?
Furthermore, will it be possible to carry them away? He replied:
"What you seek can be obtained.
He asked again, "From whom can it be obtained?"
He replied, "I obtained it from the shaven-headed householder.
He asked again:
"Who is this bald-headed householder?
He replied, "It is the śramaṇa Gautama."
The brahmin asked, "Who are you that,
having eaten another's food, utters such evil words?"
That brahmin went to the monastery and related to the bhikṣus exactly what he had heard.
Then the bhikṣus reported these two matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣu gives food to a naked ascetic, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
All the other non-Buddhists and others voiced complaints, saying:
"If one or two non-Buddhists have committed an offense, what fault have we committed that we are not permitted to receive food?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, if any bhikṣus wish to give food, they should place it on the ground to give, or have someone else give it."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a male follower of another sect or a female follower of another sect, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Tīrthika" refers to those who follow the heterodox teachings of the naked ascetics (nirgranthas).
"Pāśiparājaka" refers to those who have gone forth from within these [heterodox] groups.
Solid food (*khādaniya*) refers to foods consisting of roots up to fruits, and foods consisting of oils up to finely ground powders.
Edible food (*bhojya*) refers to rice, roasted flour (*saktu*), boiled rice, fish, and meat.
If a bhikṣu gives food with his own hand to a naked ascetic, whether male or female, it is a pāyattika.
If he accepts food given [by such a person], it is a pāyattika.
To offer [something] and not accept it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To employ means with the intent to give but then fail to give and subsequently change one's mind and regret it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.
There is no offense if one gives it after setting it down on the ground.
If one causes another person to give [the food],
or gives it to parents, to those working for the stupa, or to those working in a separate room, providing them with the calculated price for their labor;
or if it is forcibly seized by means of power or influence— there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The forty-first [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a prominent householder in the city of Śrāvastī who was a long-standing friend of the Śākya son Upananda. He thought to himself:
"If the Śākya son Upananda should enter this city, I shall provide a meal for the community of monks on behalf of Upananda."
On another occasion, when the Śākya son Upananda entered the city, the elder, hearing that he had arrived, immediately sent a messenger to the saṃghārāma to tell the bhikṣus:
"I invite you for a meal tomorrow."
That very night, he prepared various kinds of delicious food and drink. At dawn the next day, he went to inform them that the time had arrived.
When the bhikṣus reached the time for the meal, they put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house of the elder, where they sat down in their assigned seats.
The bhikṣus said to the elder, "The Saṃgha has assembled; since the food and drink are prepared, you may serve them at this time."
The householder replied,
"Venerable sirs, please wait a moment until Subhadra, the son of the Śākyas,
arrives. The bhikṣus replied:
“The assembly of monks has already gathered; if the food and drink are prepared, you may now serve them.
Why must you wait?
The time is passing late, and I fear the bhikṣus will not receive a full and complete meal.”
Then the householder said to the bhikṣus:

"I previously made a vow that if the Śākya son Upananda were to enter this city, I would provide a meal for the Saṃgha on behalf of the Śākya son Upananda. I pray that the Venerable Ones will wait a short while for Upananda."
At that time, during the morning meal, Upāli’s younger brother, Upananda, went to yet another family and did not return until the time for the meal was nearly past.
When the monks saw that the time was passing and, although they had received food and drink, it was ultimately insufficient, [they were distressed].
Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse;

they censured the Śākya son Upananda, saying: "How can the Śākya son Upananda go to another household during the morning meal and only arrive when the time is nearly past, causing the bhikṣus to be unable to eat their fill?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, Vāḍiśaputra Bāṇanda!
When the time for the morning meal has almost passed, you have only now arrived, causing the bhikṣus to be unable to eat their fill?"
After the Blessed One had rebuked the Śākya son Upananda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such sources of outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu has previously accepted an invitation and then goes to another household at the time of the morning meal, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a high minister in the city of Rājagṛha who was an old friend and close associate of the Śākya son Upananda.
At another time, that minister obtained some large, sweet fruits. He immediately commanded a man, saying:
"The Śākya son Upananda is an old friend and acquaintance of mine. You should take these fruits to the monastery and show them to him, saying:
'I am an old acquaintance of yours; you may distribute these fruits among the community of monks.'"
Then that messenger took the fruit and went to the saṃghārāma, saying to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
This is new fruit for the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣus said to him,
"If it is for the Saṃgha, you may distribute it. The man replied:
"A minister in the city of Rājagṛha commanded me, saying:
'Take these fruits to the saṃghārāma and show them to the Śākya son Bhadanta, so that he may distribute them among the monks.'"
"Now that Śubhānanda the Śākya son has arrived, it shall be assigned to the Saṃgha.
At that time, after his meal, Śubhānanda went to other households and did not return until the time had passed, causing the community of monks to be unable to eat the fresh fruit.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Upananda, saying:
"How can you go to another house only after having finished your meal, returning only when the time has passed, thereby causing the bhikṣus to be unable to eat fresh fruit?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. They reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, Vāḷananda the son of the Śākyas!
Having finished your meal, you go again to other households and only return when the time has passed, causing the bhikṣus to be unable to eat fresh fruit."
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, goes to other households before or after the meal, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a great occasion for invitations to the Saṃgha within the city of Rājagṛha; yet all the bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious, not daring to enter the city to accept the invitations.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to enter the city after having entrusted one another with their care.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom they should entrust themselves.
The Buddha said:
"One should entrust oneself to a bhikṣu; if one dwells alone in a single room, one should entrust oneself to a neighboring resident.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal without having informed [another bhikṣu], it is a pāyattika.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, a sick bhikṣu had previously instructed a donor’s household to prepare soup, porridge, and rice; however, out of fear and caution, he did not dare enter the city, for he feared committing the offense of eating at another house after the proper time.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow a sick bhikṣu to enter without having made a formal entrustment.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, having previously accepted an invitation, goes to another household before or after the meal without informing another bhikṣu, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika offense.
"In this context, 'time' refers to the time of illness.
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, when the bhikṣus reached the period for making robes, they required either large cauldrons, small cauldrons, jars, ladles, water-pots, axes, basins, bowls, small cups, pans, ropes, cloth-hangers, *aineyanta* (a type of netting), or woolen mats.
The bhikṣus were all fearful and cautious, not daring to enter the city, for they feared violating the rule against entering a village without having informed [a fellow monk].
They reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to enter a village without informing [another] while they are making robes."
From this day forward, the precept shall be established as follows:

If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation from another, visits other households before or after the meal without having informed another bhikṣu, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"The exceptions are: when one is ill, or when one is making robes.
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, when the season for receiving robes arrived, some bhikṣus had already found places where robes were to be given, while others were still seeking them. Fearing and being cautious, they did not dare enter the city, dreading that they might commit the offense of entering a town without having informed another.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to enter the city without having made a formal entrustment when giving away robes.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, visits other households before or after the meal without having entrusted his affairs to another bhikṣu, except during the special times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the time of illness, the time of making robes, and the time of receiving robes; these are called "other times.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Before the meal" means from the appearance of the dawn light until the time for the meal.
"Having already eaten" refers to the period from the time of the meal until midday.
"A household" refers to a place where men and women reside.
"Other bhikṣus" refers to those who dwell together within the same boundary.
The "sick person" is as described above.

Regarding the "time for making robes": after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, it is one month if there is no *kaṭhina* robe in effect, and five months if there is a *kaṭhina* robe in effect; this continues until one has made even a single "horse-tooth" seam upon the robe.

Regarding the time for giving robes: after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, it is one month if the *kaṭhina* robe is not spread, and five months if the *kaṭhina* robe is spread. Excluding these periods, the remaining time is when one encourages others to prepare food and give robes.
If a bhikṣu has given his consent (*chandadāna*) intending to go to a village, but returns on the way, he loses that prior consent;
if he later wishes to go, he must give his consent again.
If a bhikṣu has given his consent intending to go to a village, but does not reach the place to which he gave his consent and instead goes to another house, he loses that prior consent.
If one wishes to go, one should receive further formal authorization (*anuśāsti*) before departing.

If, after receiving authorization, one goes to the house of a layperson, then further to a storehouse or a dwelling on the outskirts of a village, or enters a *bhikṣuṇī* monastery, or even returns directly from the layperson’s house, the previous authorization is lost;
one must receive further authorization before proceeding.

If a bhikṣu, having already accepted an invitation, visits other households before or after the meal without having informed another bhikṣu of his entry into the village, except at other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one has one foot inside the gate and one foot outside the gate, and though prepared and adorned with the intention to depart, does not actually go, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one is ill; when making robes; when robes are being offered; or when one has entrusted the matter to a bhikṣu.

If there is no bhikṣu to whom one can entrust it, and one goes to another storehouse, a village, a peripheral dwelling, or to a bhikṣuṇī monastery; or if one goes to the house of a layperson to whom one had entrusted the matter; or if many people have spread out sitting mats and invited the bhikṣus; or if one is held by force; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya)—in these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-second section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the Venerable Kālodāyin was formerly a layman, he had a female friend from among the white-robed householders named Ciñcā, who was of upright and beautiful countenance; Kālodāyin, too, was of upright and beautiful countenance.
At that time, Kālodāyin fixed his mind upon the upāsikā Ciñcā, and Ciñcā likewise fixed her mind upon Kālodāyin.

When the time arrived, Kālodāyin dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the home of the upāsikā Ciñcā, where he sat down upon a seat. Meanwhile, the upāsikā Ciñcā bathed and adorned her body; her husband loved and respected her deeply, never being apart from her.
The husband asked Kālodayin, "What do you require? He replied:
"I must eat. Her husband then said to his wife,
"Go out and give him some food."
The wife immediately gave him food as she had been told.
After Kāḷodāyin had finished eating, he remained seated and did not leave.
Her husband said to Kāḷodāyin, "You said earlier that you needed food; now that you have been given food, why do you not go?"
At that time, the laywoman Śikṣā made a sign to indicate that he should not leave.
Her husband then rebuked Kālodāyin in anger, saying: "This bhikṣu is hindering me!
You said earlier that you needed food; now that you have eaten, why do you not depart? What else do you intend to do?"
"I am now leaving you; follow behind me and do whatever you wish.
Having spoken these words in anger, the husband then departed.
At that time, a bhikṣu who was begging for alms came to his house; the begging bhikṣu then reproached Kālodāyin, saying:
"Why are you sitting comfortably inside a house where food is being prepared?"
At that time, the bhikṣu who had gone for alms returned to the saṃghārāma in Śrāvastī and related these circumstances to the bhikṣus.

Among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Kālodāyin, saying:
"How could you sit at ease inside a house where food is being prepared?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kālodāyin:
"Did you indeed sit at ease in the house where food was being served?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Kāḷodāyin:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that should not have been done.
How could you sit down and remain at ease in a house where food is being served while treasure is present?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked Kālodāyin with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the various sources of outflows, he has committed the first breach of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sits down insistently where there is treasure in a household that is eating, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "food": men take women as their food, and women take men as their food; this is what is meant by "food.
Regarding "household": it is as explained above.
"Jewels" refers to musaragalva, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver.
If a bhikṣu is in a household where food is being served and there are jewels within reach of his outstretched hand, he should sit;
if a bhikṣu sits down by force in a household where food is being served and there are jewels present, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one is blind but not deaf, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is deaf but not blind, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one stands rather than sits, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one enters a house where food is being served while there is wealth present, provided that one sits within arm’s reach of the door; or if there are two bhikṣus as companions; or if there is a person capable of recognizing [the situation]; or if there is a guest in the same place who is neither blind nor deaf; or if one passes through from the front without stopping; or if one suddenly falls to the ground due to an outbreak of illness; or if one is held by those with forceful power; or if one is imprisoned; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The forty-third [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the Venerable Kālodāyin was still a layman, he had a female friend from among the white-robed householders named Jyotiṣkī; she was of beautiful appearance, and Kālodāyin was likewise of beautiful appearance.
At that time, Kālodāyin fixed his mind upon the upāsikā Cailā, and the upāsikā Cailā likewise fixed her mind upon Kālodāyin.
Then, when the time had come, the Venerable Kālodāyin put on his robes, took his bowl, and went to the home of the upāsikā Cailā, thinking to himself:
"The World-Honored One has spoken these words:"
"One should not sit cross-legged when eating in a house where there are treasures; one should sit in a place where one can reach out with the hand or near the door.
He then sat behind the door panel.
At that time, Kāḷudāyin was conversing with a female lay follower (*upāsikā*). A bhikṣu who was wandering for alms arrived at that house and, hearing Kāḷudāyin’s voice, reproached him, saying:
"How can you sit in a secluded place within a house where food is being prepared, so that we do not know what you are doing?"
At that time, the bhikṣu who had gone for alms returned to Śrāvastī and went to the saṃghārāma, where he related these circumstances in detail to the bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Kāḷodāyin, saying:
"How could you sit in a secluded place with valuables present in a layperson's home?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side. They reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the facts, asked Kālodāyin intentionally:
"Is it true that you were sitting and conversing in a secluded place with a woman in a family home where there were valuables?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Kāḷodāyin:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can he sit in a screened-off place within a family's home where there are treasures?
Having rebuked Kālodayin, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of a transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of significance and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place within a household where food is being served while precious objects are present, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "food": women are the food of men, and men are the food of women.
Regarding "jewels": cat's-eye, agate, pearl, amber, gold, and silver.
A "secluded place" refers to a spot screened by a tree, a wall, a fence, a cloth screen, or other such objects.

If that bhikṣu enters the house of a donor and sits in a secluded place where there is treasure, he should position himself so that his outstretched hand can reach the door, allowing the bhikṣu who is begging for alms to see him.
If a bhikṣu sits in a secluded place within a family home where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika.
If he is blind but not deaf, it is a dukkaṭa.
If he is deaf but not blind, it is a dukkaṭa.
To stand without sitting down constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, while in a household where food is being served, there is a seat with valuables and it is within arm's reach of the door so that a bhikṣu seeking alms may see it;
or if there are two bhikṣus as companions.
If there is a discerning person nearby;
or if there is a guest in the same place who is neither blind nor deaf;

or if one passes through without staying; or if one suddenly falls to the ground due to illness; or if one is held by a person of forceful power; or if one is imprisoned; or if there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life—there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-fourth case concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the Venerable Kālodāyin was formerly a layman, he had a female friend among the white-robed laity named Cailā, who was beautiful in appearance; Kālodāyin was likewise handsome in appearance.
At that time, Kālodāyin’s mind was fixed upon the female lay follower (upāsikā) Ciñcā, and Ciñcā’s mind was likewise fixed upon Kālodāyin.

Then, when the time had come, the Venerable Kālodāyin dressed himself, took his bowl, and went to the home of the female lay follower Ciñcā, where he sat together with her in an open space and conversed.

A certain bhikṣu who was begging for alms came to that house and saw Kālodāyin sitting and conversing in an open space with a female lay follower (upāsikā) who had received the fast-day precepts (upoṣadha). He immediately censured the Venerable Kālodāyin, saying:
"How can you sit and converse in an open space in one place with a female lay follower who has received the fast-day precepts?"
At that time, after the bhikṣu who was begging for alms had finished his meal in the city of Śrāvastī, he returned to the saṃghārāma and related these circumstances to the other bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached Kālodayin, saying:
"How could you sit and converse in one place with a laywoman in the open air during the fast-day?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked Kāḷudāyin intentionally:
"Is it true that you sat and conversed in a secluded place with the upāsikā Cīrā?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked Kālodāyin:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not compliant conduct, and is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, Kāḷudāyin! Are you sitting and conversing in one place in the open air with a laywoman who has undertaken the uposatha?
Having thus rebuked Kāḷudāyin, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Woman" refers to a human female who possesses intelligence and whose life-faculty is not severed.
"Alone" means one woman and one bhikṣu.
"A secluded place" means a place where one can see in seclusion or hear in seclusion.
A "place where one can see in seclusion" refers to a place where faces cannot be seen due to dust, mist, or darkness.
"Regarding 'hearing from a screened place': one does not hear the sound of ordinary conversation.
If that bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in an open space in the same location, it is a pāyattika offense.
If he is blind but not deaf, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
If one is deaf but not blind, it is a duṣkṛta.
If one stands rather than sits, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one has two bhikṣus as companions.
If there is a discerning person nearby;
or if there is a guest in one place who is neither blind nor deaf;
or if [the object] has passed by previously and does not remain;
Or they may suddenly fall to the ground from illness;
or they may be seized by forceful power;
or they may be bound and imprisoned.
There is no offense in cases of danger to life or danger to the holy life.
There is also no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Forty-five. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda had been quarreling with another bhikṣu; although he sought to offer an apology, Upananda harbored resentment in his heart.
Later, at another time, the Śākya son Upananda said to that bhikṣu:
"Follow me to the village; I shall give you food.
The bhikṣu replied:

"So be it. Then, at the proper time, Upananda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and together with that bhikṣu, entered the city of Śrāvastī; leading him to a place where there was no food, he walked about everywhere.
With only a short time remaining, Bāḷhika thought to himself:
"If this bhikṣu goes out from the city of Śrāvastī to the Jetavana, the time for the meal will have already passed."
Bhadanta said to that bhikṣu, "It is unprecedented that you are such a wicked person. The bhikṣu asked:
"What fault have I committed?
Vāḍananda replied, "It is because of you that I am now unable to obtain food."
"Elder, go quickly!
I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting alone and speaking alone.
Having spoken thus to that bhikṣu, Upananda entered the city of Śrāvastī and ate at a place where food was available.
Then that bhikṣu left the city of Śrāvastī and arrived at the Jeta Grove Monastery; as the time for the meal had already passed, he was unable to eat and was extremely exhausted.

Hearing of this, those bhikṣus among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the son of the Śākyas, Upananda, saying:
"How could you have spoken to the other bhikṣus thus?"
"I will take you to a village and give you food," he said;
yet in the end, he did not give the bhikṣu any food, but instead spoke to him:
"Go away quickly!"
"I find no pleasure sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.
Having sent that bhikṣu back to the Jeta Grove, the time for the meal passed, and he was unable to obtain any food at all, becoming utterly exhausted.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
How is it that, having said to other bhikṣus,
"I will give you food," he ultimately does not give them any food and instead says:
"Go quickly! I find no pleasure sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure sitting and speaking alone.
Would he not cause that bhikṣu to enter the Jeta Grove, so that the time for the meal would pass and he would be left utterly exhausted by hunger?
