At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the Śākya son Upananda with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for outflows, this is his first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu says to another bhikṣu:
'Venerable sir!'"
"We shall go together to the village and give you food.
Yet that bhikṣu did not ultimately instruct anyone to give food to this bhikṣu, but instead said to him: "Go away!"
‘I do not find pleasure sitting or speaking with you in one place; I find pleasure sitting and speaking alone.
If, for this reason and by no other means, he sends him away, it is a *pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Village" refers to the four kinds of villages, as described above.
"Food" refers to food taken at the proper time (*kālabhojana*).
That bhikṣu said to this bhikṣu:
"I will go into the village and give you food.
But he ultimately did not give the bhikṣu any food, and then spoke to him, saying:
"Go away! I do not find pleasure in sitting or speaking with you; I find pleasure in sitting and speaking alone.
By such means, he sends her away and abandons her from sight and hearing; this is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one leaves the place where one sees [the object] and goes to the place where one hears [of it], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one leaves the place where one hears [of the object] and goes to the place where one sees [it], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one uses a stratagem to have [the person] go away and then personally leaves both the place where one sees and the place where one hears, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one abandons the place of seeing to go to the place of hearing, or abandons the place of hearing to go to the place of seeing, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one gives food and sends [the person] away;
or if [the person] is ill; or if they lack dignified deportment such that people see them and are displeased, and one says to them:
"Go! I shall send food to the saṃghārāma.
Even if he has broken his precepts, broken his views, or broken his proper conduct;
If one is nominated by the assembly;
if one has been expelled or is subject to expulsion;
or if, seeing a threat to life or a threat to pure conduct, one employs skillful means to send them away.
If one does not dismiss [the person] out of resentment or hatred, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-sixth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Kapilavastu in the Śākya country.

At that time, Mahānāma of the Śākya clan invited the Saṃgha to provide them with medicine. He respectfully offered the best quality to the elders; he gave it to those who asked for it, and he also gave it to those who did not ask.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"This Mahānāma, a son of the Śākya clan, has invited the Saṃgha to provide medicinal supplies.

He shows respect to the elders by giving them the best items, yet he lacks any heart of respect for us; he gives us only the inferior things. Even when we ask for them, he does not give, let alone obtain them without asking."
They said to one another,
"We should go to his house and seek out that rare medicine which he does not possess.
Thereupon, they went to his house and spoke, saying:
"We require such-and-such medicines.
Mahānāma replied, "If there is anything of the sort in my house, I shall give it to you; if not, I shall go to the market to seek and purchase them for your supply."
The group of six bhikṣus replied,
“Does your household not have such-and-such medicines? Mahānāman replied:
"Whatever we have at home, we shall give to you; whatever we do not have, we shall go to the market to seek it out and give to you.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke again, saying:
"You invited the Saṃgha to provide medicine; you showed respect to the elders by giving them the best, and you gave to those who asked as well as to those who did not ask."

"You associate with those of low station and evil character, and you are neither diligent nor respectful. When you seek something, it is not given to you; how much less could you obtain it without asking?
Although there is nothing in your home, you invite the Saṃgha to give them medicine; thus, you possess both attachment and falsehood."
Mahānāman replied, “I have previously made a solemn vow:
I shall provide whatever my household possesses to the Saṃgha; if I lack anything, I shall go to the market to seek it out and give it.”
"Why do you now say:
'I have attachment; I am a speaker of falsehoods and lack sincerity'? Elder, depart!"
"From this day forward, I shall no longer be able to provide medicine for the community of monks!

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"O Mahānāma, son of the Śākyas!..."
With faith, joy, and reverence, you provided him with excellent medicine and constantly gave alms of medicine to the Sangha.
How is it that you revile him, saying,
"He speaks false words out of attachment"?
"Would you cause the medicine of the Saṃgha to be cut off?
Then those bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity with the path—it is something that should not be done."
Mahānāman, how is it that you, a son of the Śākya clan who possesses faith and delights in giving, constantly providing medicine to the Saṃgha, are reviled by you with the words:
"He speaks falsehoods out of attachment"?
"Did you cause the community of monks to be deprived of their medicine?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These six bhikṣus are foolish men!"
Among the various bases of outflows, this was the first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for four months or an invitation for medicinal requisites based on a specific cause, and should he accept beyond that limit, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, some sick bhikṣus, out of a sense of apprehension and caution, did not dare to accept medicine beyond the prescribed limit.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I permit sick bhikṣus to accept medicine beyond the limit.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts an invitation for medicine for four months, and accepts it beyond that limit, it is a pāyattika offense.’”
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, lay devotees frequently invited the bhikṣus to accept regular offerings of medicine; however, the bhikṣus, being apprehensive and cautious, did not dare to accept these regular invitations for the provision of medicine.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to accept regular invitations for the provision of medicine.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts an invitation for medicine for four months, and if he accepts beyond that period—except in the case of a regular invitation—it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.
Then Mahānāma the Śākya son again had this thought:
"How could I, for the sake of just one or two people, cut off the medicine for the Saṃgha?
Now, I must instead invite the Saṃgha once more to provide them with medicine."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the monastery and invited the bhikṣus, saying:
"I pray that the venerable Saṃgha will accept my invitation to receive medicinal provisions."
The bhikṣus each felt apprehensive and dared not accept further invitations for medicine.
They informed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept further invitations for the provision of medicine."
The bhikṣus then calculated the number of days from the previous day and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not calculate from the previous day; rather, one should count from the day the medicine was resumed after the suspension."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts an invitation for four months' supply of medicine, and accepts it beyond that limit—excepting regular invitations and special invitations—it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, lay devotees invited the bhikṣus to share their medicinal herbs with them, but the bhikṣus, out of fear and caution, did not dare to accept them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to receive their allotted portion of medicine.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu who is not ill accepts an invitation for four months' supply of medicine, and accepts it beyond that limit—excepting invitations for regular meals, special invitations, or invitations for specific portions of medicine—it is a pāyattika offense.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, various householders invited the bhikṣus to accept medicines for life, but the bhikṣus, being fearful and cautious, did not dare to accept medicines for life.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to accept medicines for as long as they live.
From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus:"
If a bhikṣu accepts an invitation for medicinal requisites for a period of four months, a bhikṣu who is not ill may accept such an invitation.
If he accepts it beyond that limit—excepting invitations for regular supply, special invitations, invitations for specific portions, or lifelong invitations—it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Four months" refers to the four months of the summer retreat.
"Circumstance" refers to an invitation for medicine.
The "sick person" is one who is instructed by a physician to take medicine.
The "one who constantly requests" is a person who speaks thus:
"I shall always provide the medicine."
"Regarding 're-invitation' (punar-yācanā): after [the invitation] has been terminated, one requests it once again.
Regarding 'giving a portion of medicine' (bhājana-bhaiṣajya): taking the medicine to the monastery, one distributes it.
Regarding 'a lifetime invitation' (yāvaj-jīva-yācanā): that person says:"
"I shall provide medicine for as long as my life lasts.
There are four types of invitations:

some invitations have a limit on the duration of the night but no limit on the medicine; some invitations have a limit on the medicine but no limit on the duration of the night; some invitations have a limit on both the medicine and the duration of the night; and some invitations have no limit on either the duration of the night or the medicine.
What is meant by requesting medicine with a limit for the night but no limit for the substance?
One sets a limit for the night but does not set a limit for the medicine, saying:
"I shall give you medicine for this many nights."
This is called "requesting a limit for the night, but no limit for the medicine.
What is "requesting a limit for the medicine, but no limit for the night"?
One establishes a limit for the medicine but does not establish a limit for the night, speaking as follows:
"I give you such-and-such medicine.
This refers to a request for medicine that has a limit regarding the substance but no limit regarding the time of night.
What is a request for medicine that has limits both regarding the time of night and regarding the substance?
He establishes a limit for the night and a limit for the medicine, saying:
"For such a duration of the night, give such medicine.
This is called a request with a limit for the night and a limit for the medicine.
What is the invitation for medicine without a limit of time and without a limit of substance?
One does not establish a limit for the night nor a limit for the medicine, but speaks thus:
"I invite you to give me medicine."
This refers to an invitation for the night and medicine both being without a fixed limit.

Within this, there may be a fixed limit for the night but no fixed limit for the medicine, or a fixed limit for the night and a fixed limit for the medicine; in such cases, one should accept the invitation during the four months of the summer retreat.

Among these medicines, there are those with a fixed duration and those without a fixed duration; for medicines without a fixed duration, one should accept them according to the time of their offering.

A bhikṣu who is not ill may accept medicines provided during the four months of the summer retreat; if he accepts them beyond that period—except in cases of a regular invitation, a renewed invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation—he commits a *pāyattika* offense for every swallow.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: receiving an invitation for four months and being given medicine; a sick person accepting an invitation beyond that limit; or receiving a regular invitation, a repeated invitation, a partial invitation, or a lifelong invitation—there is no offense in these instances.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The forty-seventh [rule] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the subjects of King Prasenajit’s realm rose in rebellion; the king personally led his sixfold army to suppress them, and at that moment, the group of six bhikṣus went to the midst of the army to observe the military formations.
Then King Prasenajit said: "Venerable sirs!
What do you intend to do here within this army?"
The group of six replied, "We have done nothing;
we merely came to observe the military formations!
When King Prasenajit heard this, he was deeply displeased and asked again:
"Where do you intend to go now?
The group of six replied,
"We wish to go to the kingdom of Śrāvastī to see the Buddha."
Then the king spoke, saying:
"If you reach the kingdom of Śrāvastī, take my name and pay homage to the World-Honored One, inquiring after him, saying:
'Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your walking about robust and strong? Are you not fatigued by the toil of teaching and transforming others?'"
"I now bring this parcel of stone honey to offer to the World-Honored One.
I shall relate these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to Śrāvastī and approached the Jetavana Monastery. Having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, they sat to one side and, addressing King Prasenajit by name, said:

"I pay homage to the World-Honored One and inquire after his well-being: Are you light and at ease in your movements? Is your health robust? Have you not been weary in your work of teaching and transforming others?
I offer this parcel of rock honey to the World-Honored One."
He then reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One.
At that time, on account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice of compliance—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that you foolish men look upon the military power of a king's army?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu goes to observe a military array, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the people within the territory of King Prasenajit rose in rebellion. There were two brothers among his high ministers:
the elder was named Liśudra, and the younger was named Pūraṇa.

The king dispatched these two men to lead an army on a punitive expedition; these two, however, were filled with longing to see the bhikṣus, so they immediately sent a messenger to invite the bhikṣus, saying:
"Venerable sirs, please come!"
"I wish to see you.
All the bhikṣus, feeling apprehensive and cautious, said:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept: if a bhikṣu goes to view a military array, it is a pāyattika offense."
Then the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"If there is a need, something to report, or an invitation, you are permitted to go."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣu goes to view an army formation, except for other special circumstances, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"An array" refers to either a performance or a battle.
"An army" may consist of one army, two armies, three armies, or four armies.
One army consists of one elephant corps, one cavalry corps, one chariot corps, and one infantry corps.
There may be an army consisting solely of cavalry, an army consisting solely of elephant corps, infantry, or chariot corps.

As for "two armies," this refers to two [units] each of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; or there may be elephants and horses together, or elephants and chariots, or elephants and infantry, or horses and chariots, or horses and infantry, or chariots and infantry.

The "three armies" consist of three types of elephants, three types of cavalry, three types of chariots, and three types of infantry; that is, either elephants, cavalry, and chariots; or elephants, cavalry, and infantry; or cavalry, chariots, and infantry.
The "fourfold army" consists of four elephants, four horses, four chariots, and four infantry; alternatively, it may refer to elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry.

If that bhikṣu goes to observe the military array—moving from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from low ground to high ground, or from high ground to low ground—and sees it while departing [from the monastery], it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not look [at the army], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes preparations with the intention of observing it but does not go, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu is already traveling on the road and the military array arrives later, the bhikṣu should step off the road to avoid it; if he does not avoid it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if the bhikṣu goes because he has business;
or if he is invited to go;
or if he is taken away by force.
If one travels ahead while the army arrives later, one should leave the road to avoid them;
or if the paths by water or land are cut off;
or if there is danger from bandits, danger from wild beasts, or if the waters have risen in great flood.
If one is led away by being bound by force;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and one does not descend the path, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The forty-eighth [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had a reason to stay overnight within a military camp. When the lay devotees saw them, they said to one another:
"It is only because of our affection that we are staying here tonight!"
"And what is this śramaṇa doing here?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one may enter an army only when there is a specific cause and condition; how is it that you have stayed overnight within an army?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, you group of six bhikṣus!
Is there ever a time or circumstance that allows one to enter among the military, that you would stay overnight within the army?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first offense against the precepts among many bases for the outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu has a legitimate reason, he is permitted to stay within an army for two or three nights; if he exceeds this limit, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣu has a reason to go among an army, he may stay for two nights; upon reaching the third night, before the first light of dawn has appeared, he must leave a place where he can see or hear the army.

When that bhikṣu has stayed among the army for two nights, if he does not remain within sight or hearing distance until the third night when the dawn light has not yet appeared, and the dawn light appears, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one leaves the place of seeing and goes to the place of hearing, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one leaves the place of hearing and goes to the place of seeing, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.
There is no offense if, having stayed for two nights, by the time of the third night before the dawn has appeared, they have moved to a place beyond the range of sight or hearing.
If the path by water or land is cut off;
if there is the danger of fierce beasts, the danger of bandits, or the rising of great waters; if one is detained or held captive by those with power;
or if one is imprisoned;

If there is danger to one's holy life (*brahmacarya*) or danger to one's life, it is not an offense to stay for two nights, or to remain within an army for three nights, provided that the dawn has not yet appeared and one does not depart from the range of sight or hearing.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-ninth section ends. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Fifteen.
[End of Volume Fifteen] *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
This is the sixth of the ninety *pācittika* rules. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting bhikṣus to stay within an army for two or three nights due to specific circumstances. While staying in the army, they watched military formations and battles, and observed the various people, elephants, and horses from all directions.
At that time, one among the group of six bhikṣus was struck by an arrow while observing a military formation; his companions then wrapped him in their robes and carried him back.
When the laypeople saw this, they asked the bhikṣu,
"What is this man suffering from? He replied:
“Ānanda! Previously, while observing an army formation in battle, he was struck by an arrow.
At that time, the lay devotees all spoke in derision, saying:
“We have raised this military array for the sake of our loved ones; what business do you renunciants have going into the midst of an army?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting bhikṣus to stay in an army for two or three nights when there is a timely cause or condition. Now that you have already stayed in the army for two or three nights, why did you go to observe the military array and the battle, only to be struck by arrows?”
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the path]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣus!

The World-Honored One has permitted bhikṣus to go to an army on account of specific circumstances and stay for two or three nights; yet you have gone to an army to stay for two or three nights only to observe military formations and battles, being struck by arrows?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These deluded men!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such occasions for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu stays within an army for two or three nights, and at any time observes the military formations and combat, or observes the strength and power of the marching troops, elephants, and horses, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Fighting" refers to either playful fighting or actual combat.
"Army" refers to an army of one type up to an army of four types; it may be a royal army, a bandit army, or a householder's army.
As for "power and momentum," it refers to the foremost strength of elephants, the foremost strength of horses, the foremost strength of chariots, and the foremost strength of infantry.

As for "formations," these include the square formation, the circular formation, the crescent-moon formation, the *jang-jin* (spreading-screen) formation, or the *giam-sang* (diminished-appearance) formation; as well as the formations of elephant-kings, horse-kings, and human-kings.

If that bhikṣu goes to observe military arrays and battles, or the prowess of elephants and horses—whether proceeding from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from high ground to low ground, or from low ground to high ground—and sees them upon arriving, it is a pāyattika offense.
To go and not see [the army] constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
To prepare the means and intend to go but not go constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense in all such cases.
If a bhikṣu is already traveling on the road and the military array arrives later, he should avoid it; if he does not avoid it, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in cases where there is a specific cause and condition: if one has something to report; or if summoned; or if led away by force; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
or if one has already set out on the road while the army arrives later and one takes a side path to avoid it;
or if the way by water or land is cut off.
If one encounters bandits, wild beasts, or a great flood;
or if one is seized and bound by force;
or if there is danger to life or danger to one's pure conduct—there is no offense if one does not avoid the path.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The fifty rules are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Cīda with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus. At that time, the Venerable Sāgata served as the attendant who provided offerings for the Buddha.
At that time, Sāgata left the road and went to the dwelling of a matted-hair brahmin, saying to him:
"This first cell of your dwelling, I now wish to stay there for one night; could you allow me to stay?"
The brahmin replied, “I do not begrudge it;
you may stay the night, but there is a venomous dragon within this place, and I fear he might harm you!
The bhikṣu said:
"I see only that you have granted me leave to stay, or perhaps you will not harm me.
The matted-hair brahmin replied, "This chamber is vast; you may dwell here as you please."
At that time, the Elder Sāgata entered the room, spread out a mat of grass, and sat down cross-legged with his mindfulness fixed before him.
When the venomous dragon saw Sāgata sitting cross-legged, it immediately emitted fire and smoke; Sāgata also emitted fire and smoke.
The venomous dragon, enraged by this, again released flames from its body, and Sāgata likewise released flames from his body.
At that time, the chamber blazed as if with a great conflagration. Sāgata thought to himself:
"Should I now extinguish these dragon-flames so as not to harm the dragon's body?"
Thereupon, he immediately extinguished the dragon’s fire so that it would not cause harm.
At that time, the poisonous dragon’s flames were colorless, whereas Sāgata’s flames grew increasingly intense and displayed various colors: blue, yellow, red, white, green, azure, and crystal.

At that time, during that very night, Sāgata subdued this venomous dragon and placed it within his alms-bowl. On the following morning at dawn, he took it with him and went to the dwelling of the matted-hair brahmin, saying:
"As for the venomous dragon you spoke of, I have already subdued it and placed it in my bowl; therefore, I bring it here to show you."
At that time, the Lord of Kauśāmbī was staying overnight in the house of a matted-hair brahmin.
He thought to himself: "How extraordinary!
The disciples of the World-Honored One possess such great supernormal powers; how much more so must the Tathāgata himself!"
He then addressed Sāgata, saying,
"If the World-Honored One comes to Kauśāmbī, I pray that you will inform me so that I may pay him my respects. Sāgata replied:
"Excellent! At that time, the World-Honored One traveled through the human realm from the country of Cīna to the country of Kauśāmbī.

When the ruler of that country heard that the World-Honored One was approaching this land with one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples, he immediately mounted his carriage to go out and welcome him. From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One’s countenance, which was upright and dignified; his faculties were tranquil and settled, his mind was extinguished, and he had attained supreme self-mastery, like a tamed dragon-elephant or a clear, still pool.

Having seen him, a deep faith arose within him; with a mind of reverence, he immediately alighted from his carriage and approached the World-Honored One. Having prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached the Dharma to exhort and transform him, causing him to attain joy.

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching through countless skillful means and being exhorted and transformed by it, the Lord of Kauśāmbī was filled with great joy. Looking around at the assembly of monks, he did not see Sāgata, and so he asked the bhikṣus: "Where is Sāgata now?"
The bhikṣus replied, "We are behind; we shall arrive shortly.
At that time, Sāgata arrived behind, accompanied by the group of six bhikṣus.
When the ruler of Kauśāmbī saw Sāgata approaching, he went forth to meet him, bowed his head at his feet in salutation, and stood to one side.
Then Sāgata, employing various skillful means, preached the Dharma to him, exhorting and transforming him until his heart was filled with joy.
At that time, the ruler of Kauśāmbī, having heard Sāgata’s various skillful means of preaching the Dharma and his exhortations, attained great joy and said:
"What do you require?"
"You may speak. Sagata replied, "Stop!"
"Stop! This itself constitutes my worship.
He spoke again, saying:
"Please tell us what you require or desire.
The group of six bhikṣus said to him,
"Do you not know?"
"A bhikṣu’s robe, alms bowl, sitting mat, and needle case—these are items that are easy to obtain!
There are other things even more difficult for a bhikṣu to acquire; give those to him."
He then asked, "Among the bhikṣus, what is most difficult to obtain?
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"I wish for black liquor.
He replied, "If you wish for it, you may come tomorrow to take as much as you desire."
Then he prostrated at Sāṅgharakṣita’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

The next morning at dawn, Sāṅgharakṣita put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of the lord of Kauśāmbī, where he sat down upon a seat. Then the lord of Kauśāmbī brought forth various kinds of sweet foods and drinks, as well as black liquor, and served them until he was thoroughly satiated.

At that time, after Sāgata had finished eating and drinking to his satisfaction, he rose from his seat and departed. On the way, he became intoxicated by alcohol, fell to the ground, and vomited; thereupon, various birds cried out in confusion.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the reason] yet asked intentionally, said to Ānanda:
"For what reason are the various birds crying out?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

This Sāgata accepted an invitation from the lord of Kauśāmbī for various foods and drinks, including black liquor; having become intoxicated, he lay by the roadside vomiting profusely, which is why the birds are crying out in such confusion."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"This bhikṣu Sagata is a fool!
If he cannot subdue a small dragon even now, how much less could he subdue a great dragon?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are ten faults for those who drink alcohol.
What are these ten?
First, the complexion is unsightly;
second, one has little strength; third, vision is unclear.
Fourth, manifesting signs of anger;
fifth, destroying the means of livelihood such as fields and property;
sixth, increasing and bringing about illness.
Seventh, they increase litigation and disputes;
eighth, they lack renown while ill repute spreads abroad;
ninth, their wisdom diminishes.
Tenth, at the dissolution of the body after death, one falls into the three evil realms. Ānanda!
These are called the ten faults of one who drinks alcohol.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"From this day forward, those who take me as their teacher must not, even so much as place the tip of a blade of grass or wood into alcohol and put it into their mouths."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Sagada with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣu Sagada is a foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu drinks intoxicants, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "alcoholic liquor": it refers to liquor made from wood, rice wine made from non-glutinous rice, rice wine made from other types of rice, barley wine, or any other substance that has been processed according to the methods for making wine.
Wood-based liquors include pear juice wine, jambu fruit wine, sugarcane wine, śāluka fruit wine, bael fruit juice wine, and grape wine.
Regarding pear-juice wine: if it is prepared by mixing honey or rock sugar, and even grape wine is likewise mixed in this way;
as for "wine," that which has the color, fragrance, and taste of wine should not be drunk.
There may be an intoxicant that lacks the color of an intoxicant, yet possesses the fragrance and taste of an intoxicant; this should not be drunk.
There may be an intoxicant that lacks both the color and the fragrance of an intoxicant, yet possesses the taste of an intoxicant; this should not be drunk.
There may be that which is alcohol, yet lacks the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol; this should not be drunk.
There may be that which is not alcohol, yet possesses the color, fragrance, and taste of alcohol; this should be drunk.
That which is not liquor, nor has the color of liquor, yet possesses the fragrance and taste of liquor, may be drunk.
That which is not liquor, nor has the color of liquor, nor the fragrance of liquor, yet possesses the taste of liquor, may be drunk.
If it is not liquor, nor has the color of liquor, nor the fragrance of liquor, nor the taste of liquor, it may be drunk.
If that bhikṣu eats or drinks that which is liquor, that which has been boiled with liquor, or that which is mixed with liquor, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one drinks sweet-flavored liquor, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one drinks vinegar-flavored liquor, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one eats yeast or dregs of wine, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If it is liquor and one perceives it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is liquor and one suspects it to be so, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is liquor and one does not perceive it as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is no wine, but one perceives it as wine, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is no wine, but one suspects it may be so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one has such-and-such an illness, and because other medicines fail to cure it, wine is used as medicine.
If one applies alcohol to a wound, there is no offense whatsoever.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Fifty-one [cases] concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus were playing in the waters of the Ajiravatī River; they went from this bank to that bank, sometimes with the current and sometimes against it, or submerged here and emerged there, or traced patterns in the water with their hands, or splashed one another with water.

At that time, King Prasenajit and Queen Mallikā were atop a multi-storied pavilion. From afar, they saw the group of seventeen bhikṣus sporting in the waters of this river, going from this bank to that bank, sometimes with the current and sometimes against it, sometimes submerging here and surfacing there, sometimes drawing patterns in the water with their hands, and sometimes splashing one another with the water. Having seen this, the King immediately said to Queen Mallikā:
"Look at those whom you serve!"
Then Queen Mallikā replied to the king:
"These bhikṣus are young men who have only recently left the household life; they have not long been in the Buddha-dharma, or perhaps they are elders who are dull-witted and know nothing."
Then Lady Mallikā immediately hurried down from the upper story and said to the brahmin Nālaka:
"Go on my behalf to the Jeta Grove and inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being, asking:
'Are you walking with vigor and strength? Is your work of teaching and transforming laborious yet fruitful?'"
"Having offered this package of stone honey to the World-Honored One, report the circumstances of this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the brāhmaṇa followed the lady's instructions, went to where the World-Honored One was, and after exchanging greetings, sat down to one side.
The brāhmaṇa Nālaka addressed the Blessed One, saying:
"Lady Mallikā has sent me specifically to inquire after the Blessed One:
'Are you walking with vigor and strength? Are your daily activities light and easy? Is your work of teaching and transforming laborious?'"
"I now offer this parcel of stone honey.
He then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of these events and, employing countless skillful means, rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you do this, monks of the group of seventeen?"

They played and sported in the waters of the Ajitavatī River, going from this bank to the other, sometimes with the current and sometimes against it; they would dive here and surface there, or draw patterns in the water with their hands, or splash one another with the water.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of seventeen bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
Among the various bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu sports or plays in water, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding "playing in the water," this refers to acting with unrestrained license: going from this shore to the other shore, either with or against the current; diving here and surfacing there; drawing patterns in the water with the hands; splashing one another with water; or even playing by filling a bowl with water—all such acts constitute a *pāyattika* offense.
Once water has been removed, if one plays with curd-milk, clear curd-milk, fermented grain wine, or barley gruel in a vessel, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one is traveling on a road and crossing water;
or if one goes from this shore to the other shore;
or if one is dragging timber through the water.
Whether it be bamboo or reeds floating up and down with the current;
whether it be picking up stones or picking up sand;
or whether an object lost sinks to the bottom of the water, disappearing here and reappearing there.
Or, if one wishes to learn the art of swimming and, while floating, raises their arms and splashes or splatters water, there is no offense in any of these cases.
There is no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or for those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Fifty-two [cases] concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, among the group of six bhikṣus, there was one person who tickled one person from the group of seventeen bhikṣus until he died.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How could you provoke the group of seventeen bhikṣus to such an extent as to cause their deaths?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat down to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"What do you think, group of six bhikṣus!
Did you provoke the group of seventeen bhikṣus until they reached their end?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“O foolish group of six bhikṣus!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
As for "fingers," there are ten on the hands and ten on the feet.
If a bhikṣu strikes or tickles another with his fingers or toes, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika) in all cases.

Excluding the fingers and toes, if he strikes or tickles another with a staff, a door-key, the handle of a fly-whisk, or any other object whatsoever, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) in all cases.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if one does not intentionally poke or tickle;
if one touches another while sleeping to wake them;
or if one comes and goes or walks about.
If one accidentally touches [the ground] while sweeping, or accidentally touches it with the tip of a staff, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Fifty-three [cases] concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the country of Kauśāmbī, in the Gośṛṅga Park.
At that time, Chanda intended to violate the precepts, and the bhikṣus admonished him, saying:
"Do not harbor such thoughts; you ought not to do so."
At that time, Chanda did not follow the admonitions of the bhikṣus and immediately violated the precepts.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they reproached Chanda, saying:
"How is it that Chanda, wishing to violate the precepts, does not follow the words of the bhikṣus when they admonish him, but instead commits the offense?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Chanda, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
“Chanda, how is it that the bhikṣus admonish you and yet you do not follow their words, thereby committing an offense?
Having rebuked Chanda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Does not accept admonition" means that if another person should interpose, saying:
"Do not do this; you should not act thus. If one intentionally commits a fundamental offense by refusing to comply with such instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows that what one has done is wrong, yet intentionally commits a fundamental offense by refusing to comply with such instruction, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if an ignorant person comes to admonish one, and one replies:
"You should first ask your teacher or preceptor about learning and reciting the scriptures; once you know the method of admonition, then you may admonish."
"If one is admonishing, it should be done [seriously];
if spoken in jest, or spoken while alone, or spoken in a dream;
or if intending to say this but mistakenly saying that—in all such cases, there is no offense."
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The fifty-fourth case ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. At that time, the Venerable Nāgapāla Bhikṣu constantly attended upon the World-Honored One, providing him with whatever he required.
The Buddha said to Nāgapāla, "Bring me the rain-cloak;
I wish to go to the place for walking meditation to practice walking.
He immediately followed the instruction, took the rain-cloak, and presented it to the World-Honored One.
At that time, having accepted the rain-cloak, the Blessed One went to his place for walking meditation and began to walk.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, manifested a golden hall for walking meditation and, with palms joined before the Blessed One, said:
"My Blessed One walks; my Sugata walks. It is the constant law of all Buddhas that when they are walking, those who wish to make offerings stand at the head of the path."
At that time, the bhikṣu Nāgapāla was standing at the head of the walking path; knowing that the first watch of the night had already passed, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"The first watch has passed; you may now return to your chamber."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.

Then Nāgapāla, perceiving that the middle watch and the latter watch of the night had passed and the dawn signs had appeared, and seeing that the birds were awakening as the sky was about to grow bright, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“The first, middle, and last watches of the night have already passed; the dawn signs have appeared, the birds are awakening, and the sky is about to grow bright. We pray that the World-Honored One will return to his chamber.”
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent.
Then Nāgapāla thought to himself:
"I should now terrify the Buddha and cause him to enter the room!"
At that time, Nāgapāla was immediately seized and brought before the Buddha, who let out a terrifying, non-human voice:
"Śramaṇa! I am a ghost!"
The World-Honored One replied,
"You should know that the mind of this foolish person is likewise evil.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Is there also such a person among the assembly?
The Buddha told Śakra Devānām Indra:
“There is such a person in the assembly.”
He said to Śakra Devānām Indra,
"This person shall attain the pure Dharma within this very life.
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra praised the Buddha with a verse:
The Noble One walks alone in heedfulness; whether reviled or praised, he remains unmoved.
Hearing the lion’s roar, he is not startled; like the wind passing over grass, he is unimpeded.
He guides all multitudes and brings certainty to all humans and devas.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Does the Lord of Devas say this because he thinks I am afraid?
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and vanished from sight.
Then, when the night had passed, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus at dawn and recounted this matter in detail to them, saying:
"This foolish man, Nāgapāla!"
"He wishes to terrify me.
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣu Nāgabala with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This deluded man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu causes fear in another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "frightening": it refers to frightening people by means of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is frightening by means of form?
Or taking the form of an elephant, a horse;
or the form of a ghost, a bird—using such forms and colors to terrify people so that they see them.
Whether they are terrified or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such forms and colors to frighten another person, yet that person does not see them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

What is meant by using sounds to frighten another person? Whether it be the sound of a conch, a drum, a *bherī* drum, an elephant, a horse, a camel, or the sound of weeping—if one uses such sounds to frighten another person so that they hear them, whether they are actually frightened or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such sounds to frighten another person, and that person does not hear them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
What constitutes using fragrance to frighten another?

If one uses root-fragrance, *sāla* tree-fragrance, resin-fragrance, bark-fragrance, pith-fragrance, leaf-fragrance, flower-fragrance, fruit-fragrance, or pleasant scents, or odors, and uses these various fragrances to frighten another person—if that person smells the fragrance, whether they become frightened or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such fragrances to terrify another person, and that person does not smell them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
What is meant by using flavors to terrify another?

If one gives a flavor to another—whether sour, sweet, bitter, astringent, salty, or the taste of *kāṣāya* (monastic robe)—and uses such a flavor to terrify that person, causing them to taste it, whether they are terrified or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such flavors to frighten another person, and that person does not taste them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

What is meant by using touch to frighten another? Whether by means of heat, or cold, or lightness, or heaviness, or subtlety, or coarseness, or smoothness, or roughness, or softness, or hardness—using such touches to frighten another person and causing that person to experience the fear, whether they actually become afraid or not, constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such physical contact to frighten another person, and that person is not touched, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
How does one frighten another by means of the Dharma?
One says to the person before them:
“I have seen such signs: either you will die in a dream, or you will lose your robes and bowl, or you will abandon the path;
likewise, your preceptor and ācārya will also die, or lose their robes and bowls, or abandon the path;
or your parents will fall gravely ill, or pass away.”
If one uses such a teaching to frighten another person, whether that person perceives the fear or not, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one uses such a teaching to frighten another person and that person does not perceive it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣu terrifies another person by means of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, if he speaks and is understood, it is a pāyattika;
if he speaks but is not understood, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if one is sitting in a dark place without a lamp, or in a place for defecating or urinating, and seeing something from afar, says:
"This is an elephant, or a thief, or a wild beast."
He becomes terrified;

if he enters a dark room where there is no lamp or fire, or a place for defecation and urination, he is struck with fear upon hearing the sound of footsteps, the rustling of grass or trees, or the sound of coughing.
However, if he shows forms to others, he does not harbor a sense of terror; likewise, if he presents sounds, odors, tastes, or tactile objects to others, he does not harbor a sense of terror.
If such a thing were actually to occur;
or if one sees such signs;

or if one sees them in a dream—whether it be that one will die, or will renounce the path, or lose one’s robes and bowl; or if one’s preceptor or teacher will die, lose their robes and bowl, or renounce the path; or if one’s parents are gravely ill and will die—one should then speak these words to them, saying:
"I have seen you in such various transformed states.
Whether spoken in jest, in haste, while talking to oneself, or in a dream; or if one intended to say this but mistakenly said that—there is no offense in any of these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The fifty-fifth case concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda. There was a pond there, and King Bimbisāra of Magadha permitted the bhikṣus to bathe in the pond at all times.

At that time, during the latter part of the night before the dawn light had appeared, the group of six bhikṣus entered a pond to bathe. At that same time, King Bimbisāra, during the latter part of the night before the dawn light had appeared, went to the pond with his court ladies, intending to bathe. Hearing the sound of the group of six bhikṣus bathing in the pond, he immediately asked those around him, "Who is bathing here?"
He replied, “It is a bhikṣu. The king said:
"Do not make a great noise, lest the bhikṣus depart before they have had time to bathe.
Those six groups of bhikṣus used various fine medicinal powders to bathe one another until the first light of dawn appeared; at that time, King Bimbisāra was unable to bathe and departed.
At that time, all the ministers collectively censured him and said to one another:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; though they claim to themselves, 'We practice the True Dharma,' [they act otherwise]."
"How can there be any True Dharma in this?

During the final watch of the night, they led one another into the pool to bathe with various fine medicinal powders until the first light of dawn appeared, so that the king was unable to bathe at all before they departed."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How could you enter the pool water to bathe during the final watch of the night, using various fine medicinal powders to wash one another until the appearance of the dawn, thereby preventing the king from bathing?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the teachings—it is what should not be done."

Why did you enter the pool water during the latter part of the night, bathe one another with various fine medicinal powders, and remain there until the appearance of dawn, so that the King was unable to bathe and depart?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many such occasions of outflows. From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus."
For the sake of compiling the ten points of meaning and so forth, until the long endurance of the True Dharma, one who wishes to recite the precepts should speak thus:
"If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, yet exceeds this interval, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, during the intense heat, blisters and rashes broke out on the bodies of the bhikṣus, becoming soiled and foul-smelling; yet, out of fear and caution, they did not dare to bathe, lest they violate the rule against bathing more than once every half-month.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow sick bhikṣus to bathe frequently during the heat.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month except during other times, and does so beyond that limit, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
'Other times' refers to the hot season.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.

Among them were many sick bhikṣus whose bodies were covered with blisters and rashes, becoming filthy and foul-smelling; some were defiled by excrement, urine, or vomit. Fearing that they might violate the rule against bathing more than once every half-month, they did not dare to bathe.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow sick bhikṣus to bathe repeatedly.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month and does not exceed this interval, except during other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the hot season and the time of illness.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bodies of the bhikṣus became soiled and foul-smelling while they were working; yet, out of a sense of apprehension and caution, the bhikṣus did not dare to bathe.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow the bhikṣus to bathe frequently while working.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu bathes more than once every half-month, except during the special times, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
The special times are: the heat of the season, the time of illness, and the time of labor.
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, as the bhikṣus were traveling through wind and rain, their bodies became covered in blisters and rashes, and they were soiled with dust and filth; yet, out of fear and scrupulousness, they did not dare to bathe.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to bathe frequently during times of wind and rain.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month and does not exceed this frequency, except during other times, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the heat of summer, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind, and the time of rain.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, while traveling on the road, the bodies of the bhikṣus became covered with heat-induced blisters and rashes, and were soiled with grime and dust, becoming filthy and impure; yet, out of fear and caution, they did not dare to bathe.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to bathe frequently while traveling on the road.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
If a bhikṣu bathes every half-month, a bhikṣu who is not ill must accept this and may not exceed it, except during other times; otherwise, it is a pāyattika offense.
"Other times" refers to the time of heat, the time of illness, the time of labor, the time of wind and rain, and the time of traveling on a road; these are the other times.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "the hot season," it refers to the forty-five days of spring and the first month of summer.
Regarding "illness," it includes all ailments down to the foul odor and impurity of the body.
"An agent" refers to one who goes as far as sweeping the ground before a house.
"In wind or rain" refers to when even a single whirlwind or a single drop of rain touches the body.
"On a journey" refers to traveling as little as half a *yojana*, whether coming or going.
If a bhikṣu bathes once every half-month, except during the permitted times, and if he exceeds this by pouring water over his body even once, it is a pāyattika.
If he washes half of his body with water, it is a pāyattika.
If one intends to bathe as part of a preparatory adornment but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for all [monastics].
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: bathing once every half-month;
bathing frequently during the heat of summer, when ill, while working, during windy weather, during rainy weather, or while traveling on a road.
If one is compelled by force or power to bathe, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Fifty-sixth [Section] concluded. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Kalandaka. Then the group of six bhikṣus said to one another:
"We are not permitted to speak as we please in the presence of the elder."
He immediately went outside the room into the open air, gathered various twigs, grass, and large tree stumps, and lit a fire to warm himself.

At that time, there was a venomous snake inside an empty tree trunk; driven by the heat of the fire's energy, it emerged from a hole in the tree. When the bhikṣus saw this, they were all struck with terror and cried out, "A venomous snake!"
"A poisonous snake!
he cried, immediately taking the wood intended for burning and scattering it here and there; the flying sparks then set fire to the Buddha’s lecture hall.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you say among yourselves,
'We may not speak as we please in the presence of the Elder,' yet go outside the room to gather grass,

wood, and large tree stumps, lighting a fire in the open air toward the sky? When a venomous snake emerged from a hollow in a tree, were you so terrified that you grabbed the burning fuel and scattered it here and there, causing sparks to fly and set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, group of six bhikṣus!
You say among yourselves:
'We may not speak as we please in the presence of the elders.'"

"Having gone outside the room, he gathered various grasses, wood, and large tree stumps, and while lighting a fire in the open air, a venomous snake emerged. Terrified, he seized the burning fuel and scattered it in all directions; might he not have caused the sparks to leap and set the Buddha’s lecture hall on fire?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
Among the various bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, for the purpose of warming himself, lights a fire on open ground, or instructs another to light one, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a sick bhikṣu, out of fear and caution, did not dare to kindle a fire himself nor instruct another to do so.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow sick bhikṣus to light a fire in the open air and to instruct others to light one.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, when not ill, lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of warming himself, or instructs another to light one, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to cook gruel, or soup and rice, for the sick bhikṣus—whether in a heated chamber, a kitchen, or a bathhouse—or when they wished to fumigate their bowls, dye their robes, light lamps, or burn incense—all the bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to do these things.
The Buddha said:
"Such matters are permitted to be done.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu, being free from illness, lights a fire on open ground for the purpose of warming himself, or instructs another to light one, except when there is a specific reason, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika).
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "the sick," it refers to one who requires fire to warm the body.

If a bhikṣu, being not ill, lights a fire on open ground for the sake of warming himself—whether lighting grass, wood, branches, leaves, ramie, hemp, cow dung, husks, chaff, or sweepings—if he burns any such thing, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one places fire among grass, wood, branches, leaves, hemp, ramie, cow dung, chaff, manure, or sweepings and sets them ablaze, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika) in every case.
If one throws something that has been half-burnt by fire into the flames, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one burns charcoal, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one does not speak to the person before them, saying:
If one says, "Look at this; know this," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense for a monk and a *pāyattika* offense for a bhikṣuṇī.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for one who says to the person in question:
"To look is to know. Whether the patient does it themselves or instructs another to do so;
at times, due to circumstances, the caregiver may cook congee, soup, or rice for the patient.
If one is in a kitchen, in a warm room, or in a bathhouse; or if one is fumigating a bowl, boiling dye for robes, lighting a lamp, or burning incense—in all such cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The fifty-seventh [rule] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a householder invited the community of monks for a meal on the following day; he immediately prepared various kinds of rich and delicious food and drink during that night, and went to inform them at dawn on the next morning that the time had arrived.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus placed their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases to one side, and while walking up and down, they waited for the mealtime to arrive.

Then, when the group of six bhikṣus saw them walking with their backs turned, they took their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases and hid them away. When the group of seventeen heard it announced that the time had come, they looked around and said:
"Our robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases are right here; who has taken them?"
The other bhikṣus asked,
"Where have you come from? They replied:
"We shall remain here, setting aside our robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, and practice walking meditation while awaiting the arrival of the mealtime.

The group of six bhikṣus went ahead to play tricks; the other bhikṣus observed them and, seeing the group of six playing tricks, concluded that it must be those people who had taken and hidden their robes and bowls.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you have taken the robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases of the group of seventeen bhikṣus and hidden them?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this incident and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, you group of six bhikṣus!
While the group of seventeen bhikṣus were walking back and forth with their backs turned, did you take their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases and hide them?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robe, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case—whether hiding it himself or instructing another to hide it—even if done in jest, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu hides another bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, or needle case, or instructs another to hide them—even if done merely in jest—it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if: one takes up and secures the property after having correctly identified its characteristics and substance;
or if it is taken up and secured because it was being blown away or soaked by wind and rain while in an open space;

or if the owner is habitually negligent in storage, and the items—robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases—are scattered in disorder, and one takes them up and stores them for the purpose of admonishing that person.
If one borrows another's clothing and that person does not take care of it, one may take it up out of fear that it will be lost;
or, if because of these robes, bowls, or other belongings there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya), one may take them and hide them—in all such cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The fifty-eighth case concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after the group of six bhikṣus had truly given robes as gifts to bhikṣus who were their close friends, they later took them back and wore them without informing the owners.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you first took robes and gave them as gifts to bhikṣus who were your close friends, and afterwards took them back and wore them without informing the owners?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teachings]. It is something that should not have been done."
“What do you think, Group-of-Six Bhikṣus!
Having first taken a robe and given it to a bhikṣu who was a close friend, did you later take it back and wear it yourself without informing the owner?
