Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the Group-of-Six Bhikṣus with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If a bhikṣu gives a robe to a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, and later takes it back and wears it without informing the owner, it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds, as described above.
"Gives robes" refers to giving robes through the ritual of formal dedication (*viśuddha-dāna*).
There are two kinds of pure giving of robes:
first, true pure giving; second, indirect pure giving.
Regarding true pure giving, one says:

"This is my extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), which has not yet been purified (*apariśuddha*). Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir, so that it may become a true purification (*bhūta-pariśuddhi*).

Regarding the successive transfer of purification (*paramparā-pariśuddhi-dāna*): "This is my extra robe, which has not yet been purified. Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable Sir."
He should speak thus: "Venerable sir, listen!
You have this long robe which has not yet been made *pariṣkāra*; now, for the sake of making it *pariṣkāra* for me, I accept it."
Having received it, one should ask:
"To whom do you wish to give it?
One should reply:
"Give it to so-and-so. He should speak as follows:

"Venerable sir, you have this long robe which has not yet been formally purified (*pariśuddhi*). Now that you give it to me for the sake of purification, I accept it; having accepted it, I shall give it to the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"This robe belongs to so-and-so; for the sake of so-and-so, you shall guard and maintain it, using it as you please.
Regarding this true purification through gift (viśuddhi-dāna), one should inquire of the owner before taking and wearing it.
Regarding "successive pure giving" (*pariśuddha-dāna*): whether one informs the donor or not, one may take and wear [the robe] as one pleases.
If a bhikṣu takes and wears a robe that has been truly given as a pure gift without informing the owner, it is a *pāyattika*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, regarding a truly pure gift, one takes possession after speaking to the donor;
or if, regarding a gift purified through transfer, one takes possession whether or not one has spoken to the donor. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The fifty-ninth [rule] concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were walking about wearing white robes. When the laypeople saw them, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty and are insatiable in their receiving; yet outwardly they claim, 'We practice the True Dharma.'"
“Looking at it now, what true Dharma is there?
Why do you go about wearing new white robes, appearing just like a king or a great minister?

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"Why do you all go about wearing new white robes?
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter to the World-Honored One in full detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant conduct—it is something that should not be done."
"What is this, Six Groups of Monks!
Why do you go about wearing white robes?
Having thus rebuked the Six Groups of Monks with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the monks:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among many sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he should apply one of the three kinds of discoloration according to his preference from among these colors: blue, black, or madder-brown.
If a bhikṣu wears any other new robe without discoloring it with one of the three [prescribed] colors—blue, black, or madder—he commits a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "new": whether it be a new garment or something first obtained from another person, all such items are termed "new.
Regarding "garment": there are ten types of garments, as described above.
"Discolored" means dyed blue, black, or madder-brown.
If a bhikṣu obtains a new robe and does not dye it in one of these three colors—blue, black, or madder-brown—and instead wears another new robe, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one possesses heavy robes without having performed the ritual of *pariśuddhi* (purification), it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one possesses light robes without having performed the ritual of *pariśuddhi*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one possesses items that are not robes—such as a bowl bag, a sandal bag, a needle-and-thread bag, a meditation belt, a waistband, a hat, socks, a heat-retaining cloth, or a cloth for wrapping sandals—without having performed the ritual of *pariśuddhi*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one leaves un-dyed robes with a householder’s family, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one obtains a white cloth and dyes it into three colors—blue, black, or madder;
or if one keeps a heavy robe after having performed the ritual of purification (*kappiya-kāraka*).
If it is light clothing, one may also keep it after performing the ritual of purification (*śuddhi*);
if it is not clothing, but items such as a bowl-bag, or even a cloth for wrapping leather sandals, all may be kept after performing the ritual of purification;
or if dyed robes are entrusted to the home of a layperson (*avadātavasana*).
If the color of the robe fades and it is dyed again, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty [cases] are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin took no pleasure in seeing crows; he made a bow and shot at them. Shooting them without ceasing, he killed a great many crows, until they formed a massive heap within the saṃghārāma.
At that time, several lay devotees came to the monastery to pay their respects; seeing this great pile of dead crows, they were all disgusted and said to one another:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and lack compassion, yet they take the lives of many creatures. While outwardly claiming, 'We practice the True Dharma,' they act in such a manner."
"Looking at this now, what 'True Dharma' is there?
He shot and killed a multitude of crows, creating nothing but a great heap.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Kālodāyin, saying:
"How is it that you have shot and killed so many crows that they have formed such a great heap?
Then the bhikṣus went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew, asked Kāḷudāyin intentionally:
"Is it true that you did not like seeing crows, but instead shot and killed many crows with a bamboo bow until they formed a great heap?"
He replied, “It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One rebuked Kālodayin with countless skillful means:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done. Why, Kālodāyin!"
"Did he shoot and kill the many crows so as to form a great heap?
Having rebuked Kāḷudāyin, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the World-Honored One established a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, as the bhikṣus sat, rose, walked, and moved about, they killed many small insects; among them, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were filled with apprehension and caution.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who did not know does not commit an offense.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu intentionally kills the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

Regarding animals: if one who cannot transform [into another form] takes their life—whether by killing them oneself, instructing another to kill them, sending a messenger, sending a messenger back and forth, sending a messenger repeatedly, sending messengers in succession, seeking out a messenger oneself, instructing another to seek out a messenger, seeking out a person with a blade oneself, instructing another to seek out a person with a blade, by means of bodily gestures, by verbal speech, by both body and speech, by sending a messenger with instructions, by sending a letter with instructions, by sending a messenger with a letter containing instructions, by setting a pitfall to trap them, by placing a blade where they habitually lean or stay, by using poison, or by placing instruments of death before them—if one employs such means, or if there are other ways one desires to kill an animal and kills it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one intends to kill through skillful means but does not actually kill, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one does not kill intentionally; or if one throws tiles, stones, knives, or clubs elsewhere and by mistake causes death;
or if a bhikṣu, while engaged in building a dwelling, accidentally kills someone because a tile or stone escapes from his hand.
If, while handling earthen bricks, timber, or house components such as pillars, bracket-rafters, ridgepoles, or purlins, one fails to exercise restraint and they fall, killing [the person];
or if one assists a sick person in rising and they die;
or if they die after being laid back down again.
If one dies while bathing;
if one dies while taking medicine;
or if one dies when about to enter a room;
If one dies while about to leave the room;
or if one dies while sitting at midday;
or if one dies while in the shade—should such various circumstances occur, there is no offense for one who dies without having harbored a harmful intent.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty-first [case] concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took water containing various insects and drank it.
When the laypeople saw this, they all expressed their reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking any heart of compassion, they kill the lives of insects while outwardly claiming,
"I practice the True Dharma.
Observing them now, what True Dharma could there possibly be?
They then took water containing various insects and used it.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
“How can you lack a heart of compassion, as to drink water containing insects and thus harm their lives?”
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you drink water containing various insects and thereby harm their lives?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These deluded men!"

Regarding the many bases of outflows and the initial transgression of the precepts: from this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu drinks water containing insects, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether there were insects or not; only later did they find out, and some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others were filled with apprehension and caution.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who did not know.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu knowingly drinks water containing insects, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣu knowingly drinks water mixed with insects, it is a pāyattika.
If, after removing the water, one drinks a mixture of insects with gruel, fermented sorghum wine, clear curd-liquor, or clear wheat-juice, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there are insects in the water and one perceives them as such, it is a *pāyattika*.
If there is water with insects and one suspects it so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is water without insects but one perceives it as having insects, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If there is water without insects and one suspects it so, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one was previously unaware of the presence of insects;
or if there are coarse insects that touch the water and cause it to flow away;
or if one drinks water after filtering it—there is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The sixty-second section ends. *Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Volume 16. [Volume 17, Part 17 of the First Division.]
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
This is the seventh of the ninety *pācittiya* rules. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to the group of six bhikṣus and said,
"Venerable sirs!
How do you enter the first dhyāna, the second, the third, and the fourth dhyānas?"
How does one enter emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness?
How does one attain the fruit of a stream-enterer, the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, and the fruit of an arhat?
Then the group of six bhikṣus replied,
"If you have spoken as you have, you have already committed a pārājika offense and are no longer bhikṣus.
Thereupon, the group of seventeen bhikṣus went to where the elder bhikṣus were and asked them:
"If there are bhikṣus who ask such questions as:
'How does one enter the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, up to the fourth dhyāna; the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness [samādhis]; and the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhatship?'"
"For what offense have you committed?
The senior bhikṣu replied,
"I have committed no offense."
The group of seventeen bhikṣus said:
"A while ago, we went to the place where the group of six bhikṣus were and asked them:
'How does one enter the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does one attain the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship?'"
He immediately replied, "You yourselves claim to have attained the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma), yet you have committed a pārājika offense; you are no longer bhikṣus.
That bhikṣu then perceived that these six groups of bhikṣus were causing suspicion and distress for the seventeen groups of bhikṣus.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they reproached the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "How is it that you have caused doubt and distress for the group of seventeen bhikṣus?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that you have caused doubt and distress for the group of seventeen bhikṣus?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six bhikṣus are foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu causes another to feel doubt or distress, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus gathered in one place to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya, and one bhikṣu withdrew.
The one who had departed felt doubt in his mind and said:
"Those bhikṣus have caused me doubt.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense for one who acts unintentionally.
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣu intentionally harasses another bhikṣu so that he is made unhappy for even a moment, it is a pāyattika.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "doubt and vexation": it may concern birth, or age, or the reception of the precepts, or the *karmavācanā*, or an offense, or the Dharma.
To those who were doubtful about when they had been born, he asked:
"How long has it been since you were born? They replied:
"I have been born for such a duration. He replied:
"You were not born for such a duration; you were born like other people, not for such a duration."
This is called doubt arising when asking about one's birth.
What is doubt arising when asking about one's age?
One asks, saying:
"How old are you? He replied, "I am so many years old."
He said: "You are not of such an age as other persons who have received the precepts; you have not yet reached that age.
This is called the arising of doubt when inquiring about one's age.
What is meant by "inquiring about the reception of precepts and giving rise to doubt"?
It refers to asking:
"Since you have received the precepts while being under twenty years of age, and furthermore, the assembly within the boundary was divided."
This is called raising a doubt regarding the time of receiving the precepts.
What is meant by raising a doubt regarding the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual)?
It is asked as follows:
"When you received the precepts, the proclamation was not valid and the *karmavācanā* was not valid; it was an illegal act performed by a separate assembly.
This is called "arising doubt regarding the *karmavācanā*.
What is meant by "arising doubt regarding an offense"? It refers to speaking as follows:
"You have committed a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, a *sthūlātyaya*, a *duṣkṛta*, or a *durbhāṣita*."
This is called having doubt regarding an offense.
What is meant by having doubt regarding the Dharma?
"The Dharma about which you have asked refers to one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer a bhikṣu."
This is called giving rise to doubt regarding the Dharma.
If a bhikṣu intentionally causes doubt for another bhikṣu—whether by means of the time of birth, the age, or even the time of the Dharma—and speaks so as to be clearly understood, it is a pāyattika;
if he speaks but is not clearly understood, it is a dukkaṭa.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the fact is truly so and not intentionally misrepresented;
or if the person was not born at such a time, yet one fears that they might later feel doubt or regret, and thus accepts their offerings and the veneration of other great bhikṣus, saying:
"You were not born at such a time, but were born like others are; I know you were not born at such a time, for the fact is indeed as it is."

Since he did not have that many years [of seniority], fearing that others might later harbor doubts or regrets regarding his unwarranted acceptance of offerings and the prostrations of other great bhikṣus, he spoke to him, saying:
"You do not have that many years; as for the seniority of other bhikṣus, you have not yet reached such a number of years."

"It is indeed so. If one is less than twenty years of age and the assembly is separate within the boundary, fearing that there may later be doubt or regret regarding the groundless acceptance of offerings from others and the reception of prostrations from great bhikṣus, one should speak to let them know and have them return to their original place to receive the precepts again; therefore, one says to them:
"You are less than twenty years of age and the assembly within the boundary was separate; it is indeed so."

"The *jñapti* was not accomplished, and the *karman* was not accomplished; it was an illegal separate assembly (*adharmika pṛthag-saṃgha*). Fearing that you might later have doubts or regrets regarding the groundless acceptance of offerings from others and the reception of salutations and respect from great bhikṣus, we spoke to you so that you would know this. You must return to your original place and receive the precepts again. Thus he spoke to him:
"The *jñapti* was not accomplished, and the *karman* was not accomplished; it was an illegal separate assembly. This matter is indeed so."

If one has committed a *pārājika*, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, *sthūlātyaya*, *duṣkṛta*, or *durbhāṣita*, and fearing future doubt or regret, accepts the offerings of others without cause or receives the salutations and respect of a monk who upholds the precepts—desiring to make that person know how to perform a confession according to the Dharma—one should say:
"You have committed a *pārājika* offense, up to and including a *durbhāṣita*."
Furthermore, if that person is by nature coarse and ignorant of speech, one says:
"As you have spoken, claiming for yourself the state of a superior person, you have committed a *pārājika* offense; this is not the conduct of a bhikṣu."
There is no offense if one speaks while joking, speaks hurriedly, speaks to oneself, speaks in a dream, or intends to say one thing but mistakenly says another.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The sixty-third [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Baddhālita was on intimate terms with a certain bhikṣu; however, as the Śākya son Baddhālita repeatedly committed offenses, he said to that bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"I have indeed committed such and such an offense;
do not tell anyone. That bhikṣu replied, "So be it."
On another occasion, the Śākya son Upananda quarreled with that bhikṣu.
Then, that bhikṣu spoke to other bhikṣus, saying:
"The Śākya son Upananda has committed such and such an offense."
The monks asked that monk, "How do you know this? The monk replied:
“Venerable Upāli, the son of the Śākyas, spoke thus to me.
The bhikṣus asked him, “Why did you not speak of this to the other bhikṣus?”
The bhikṣu replied, "Previously I endured and did not speak; now, because I cannot endure it, I speak.

When the other bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"Why have you, sirs, concealed the offense of the Śākya son Upananda?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
“What do you think, bhikṣus!
Should the offense of the Śākya son Upananda be concealed?
Having thus rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
"If a bhikṣu conceals a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) committed by another bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣus.

Later, those bhikṣus did not know whether they had committed a grave offense or not; only after they later realized it was a grave offense did some perform the pāyattika confession, while others remained doubtful. The Buddha said:
"If you did not know, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) and conceals it, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "grave offenses" (sthūlātyaya), these refer to the four *pārājika* and the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules.
If a bhikṣu knows that another bhikṣu has committed a grave offense, and he speaks of it after the morning meal when he learned of it, he commits a *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows [the time] after a meal and speaks until the first watch of the night, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows [the time] during the first watch and speaks until the middle watch, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows [the time] during the middle watch and continues until the last watch, intending to speak but not yet having spoken, when the dawn light appears, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one conceals other offenses while excluding grave offenses (sthūlātyaya), it is a duṣkṛta.
To conceal a grave offense for oneself is a duṣkṛta.
Excluding monks and nuns, to conceal the grave offenses of other persons is a duṣkṛta.
If it is a grave offense (sthūlātyaya) and one perceives it as such, it is a pāyattika.
If there is doubt regarding a grave offense, it is a duṣkṛta.
If it is not a grave offense but one perceives it as such, it is a duṣkṛta.
If there is no doubt regarding a grave offense, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one did not previously know it was a grave offense and speaks to another while perceiving it as not grave;
or if there is no one toward whom one may speak.
Having resolved to say, "I shall speak," if the dawn has already appeared while he has not yet spoken; or if, were he to speak,
there would be danger to his life or danger to his holy life (brahmacarya), then not speaking is without offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, there were seventeen groups of youths in the city of Rājagṛha who were formerly close friends. The eldest was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve. The wealthiest possessed eight million [kārsāpaṇas], while the poorest possessed eighty thousand.
Among them was a young boy named Upāli, who was the only son of his parents; they loved him so dearly that he was never out of their sight.
His parents thought to themselves:
"What craft should we teach this child so that, after we have passed away, he may live in comfort and lack for nothing?"
He then thought to himself:
"I shall first teach them to learn writing; after we have died, they will easily find a livelihood, lacking nothing and not exhausting their physical strength."
Again, he thought to himself:
"Teaching my son to read and write also involves physical exhaustion and suffering.
What other craft or skill should I learn so that after we have died, my son may live comfortably, lacking nothing and without physical exhaustion?"
He thought to himself:
"I shall now teach my son the arts of calculation and technical skills, so that after we have passed away, he may live happily, lacking nothing and without physical exhaustion or suffering."
The parents thought to themselves:
"Now, even teaching our son to study arithmetic involves physical exhaustion and hardship.
What craft should we now teach this boy so that after we have died, he may live happily, lacking nothing and without physical fatigue?"
"We shall now teach this child the art of painting so that, after we have passed away, he may live comfortably and lack for nothing.
Then he thought again:
"If I teach him painting now, I fear it will cause his eyesight to become fatigued."
"What further craft should we teach this boy so that after we have died, he may easily make a living without lack or want, and his eyes shall not suffer from toil?
Then they thought to themselves:
"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!"

We shall maintain ourselves well, living in peace and happiness free from all suffering and distress; if we should instruct this child to leave the household life and enter the path as a śramaṇa among the sons of the Śākyas, then after our deaths he will be able to live comfortably, without lack or deficiency, and his body will not suffer exhaustion or pain.
At a later time, the group of seventeen youths said to the youth Upāli,
"You should follow us and leave the household life to practice the Way."
He replied, "What use would I have for going forth?
You go forth yourself."
The group of seventeen youths spoke to Upāli for a second and a third time, saying:
"Come, let us go forth together into the religious life. Why is this?"
"Just as we are now enjoying ourselves together, so too shall we enjoy ourselves and play together there.
Then the youth Upāli said to the other youths, "Wait a moment!"
"I must go and inform my parents.
The youth Upāli then went to his parents and said, "I now wish to leave the home life to practice the Way; I pray that my parents will grant me their permission."
The parents replied, "We have only you, our one son;
we cherish you with all our hearts, to the point that we do not wish for even death to cause us to part, much less a separation while still alive."
The youth Upāli addressed his parents in this way a second and a third time, saying:
"I only pray that you will grant me permission to go forth.
His parents likewise replied:
“We have only you, our one son; we cherish you deeply in our hearts and do not wish for you to die and part from us, much less to live apart.
At that time, having received Upāli’s repeated and earnest entreaties, his parents thought to themselves:
“We already had this intention previously:”
"What craft should we teach this child so that after we have passed away, he may live easily, without lack of anything, and his physical strength shall not be exhausted by toil?"
He then thought to himself:

"If we teach them writing and even painting, after our deaths they will live comfortably with no lack of anything, and their physical strength will not be exhausted by toil; yet I fear that it will exhaust the children's physical and visual energy, leading to weariness and suffering."
He thought to himself:
"Only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas,
truly nourish their bodies well, free from all suffering and affliction."
"If we allow this child to renounce the world within this [order], he will live happily and be free from all suffering.
Then the parents replied to the child, "Now is precisely the right time; we grant you permission to renounce the world."

Then the youth Upāli returned to where the group of seventeen youths was and said to them, "My parents have already granted me permission to go forth; if you wish to leave as well, now is the very time."
Then the youths went at once to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
We wish to leave the household life to study the Way; we pray that you, honored ones, will ordain us as practitioners."
Then those bhikṣus immediately ordained them, allowing them to go forth and receive full ordination.

At that time, the youths, having been accustomed to music since childhood, were unable to endure eating only once a day; by midnight, they suffered from hunger and cried out loudly, wailing: "Give us food! Give us food!"
The bhikṣus said to him, "Child, wait until daybreak;
if the Saṃgha has food, we shall eat together, and if there is no food, we shall go on almsround together."
"Why is this? Because in this place there has never before been a place for preparing food.
At that time, the World-Honored One was meditating in a quiet place during the night; hearing the sound of a child crying, he knew the cause but asked Ānanda intentionally:
"What was the sound of that infant crying at midnight?
At that time, Ānanda related these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"One should not confer the full precepts upon one who is less than twenty years of age. Why is this?
If one is less than twenty years of age, they are unable to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, violent winds, mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects, nor can they endure harsh words."
If one's body experiences various pains that cannot be endured, and furthermore, if one is unable to maintain the precepts or observe the practice of eating only once a day—
Ānanda, you should know that those who have reached twenty years of age are capable of enduring all such matters as these.
At that time, when the night had passed, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, for this reason, addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

'If a bhikṣu is twenty years of age, he shall receive the full ordination (upasampadā). If one receives the full ordination before reaching twenty years of age, that person does not obtain the precepts; that bhikṣu is to be censured for his folly, and it is a pāyattika offense.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

A certain bhikṣu did not know whether [a candidate] was twenty years of age or less than twenty; later, he learned that he was less than twenty. Some then performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained doubtful. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who did not know."
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:

One who has reached twenty years of age should receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). If a bhikṣu knows that one is less than twenty years of age and yet confers the full ordination upon them, that person does not obtain the precepts; because that bhikṣu is blameworthy for his folly, he commits a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.

If a person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, and the upādhyāya knows they are less than twenty, and both the Saṃgha and the candidate for ordination also know they are less than twenty, yet [the upādhyāya] asks within the assembly:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

The person seeking ordination replies that they are either twenty years old, or not yet twenty, or they are uncertain, or they do not know their age, or they remain silent, or the Saṃgha does not inquire; in these cases, the preceptor commits a pāyattika offense, and the Saṃgha commits a duṣkṛta offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, and the preceptor knows they are under twenty, while the Sangha and the candidate for ordination believe they are twenty, the Sangha asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or that they are not, or that they are uncertain, or that they do not know, or remains silent, and the Sangha does not inquire further, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense, while the rest of the Sangha is without offense.

If the candidate for ordination has not yet reached twenty years of age, and the preceptor knows they have not yet reached twenty, while the Sangha and the candidate themselves are in doubt, someone among the assembly asks:
"Have you reached twenty years of age?"

If the person who has not yet received the precepts replies that they are twenty years old or more, or less than twenty, or is doubtful, or does not know, or remains silent, and the Saṃgha does not inquire further, the Upādhyāya commits a *pāyattika* offense and the assembly of monks commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is not yet twenty years of age, and the preceptor also knows they are not yet twenty, while the assembly of monks and the person receiving the precepts do not know it, and someone among the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person seeking ordination replies that they are twenty years of age, or that they are not yet twenty, or that they are uncertain, or that they do not know, or remains silent; and if the Saṃgha does not inquire [further], the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense, while the assembly of monks incurs no offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, yet the preceptor claims they are twenty, and both the assembly of monks and the person receiving the precepts know that they are less than twenty, the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person who has not yet received the precepts replies that they are either twenty years of age or not twenty, or if they are uncertain, or do not know, or remain silent, and the Sangha does not inquire further, the preceptor commits no offense, but the assembly of monks commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If the person receiving the precepts is not yet twenty years of age, but the preceptor says they are twenty, and both the assembly of monks and the person receiving the precepts also say they are twenty, and someone within the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or has not yet reached twenty, or is uncertain, or does not know, or remains silent, and the Saṃgha does not inquire further, there is no offense for the preceptor, nor is there any offense for the assembly of monks.

If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, yet the preceptor claims they are twenty, and the assembly of monks as well as the candidate themselves have doubts, someone in the midst of the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or that they are less than twenty, or that they are uncertain, or that they do not know, or remains silent, and the assembly does not inquire, the preceptor commits no offense, but the Sangha commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If the person receiving the precepts is not yet twenty years of age, but the preceptor claims they are twenty, and neither the assembly of monks nor the person receiving the precepts knows otherwise, the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

The person seeking ordination may reply that they are twenty years of age, or that they are not yet twenty, or they may be uncertain, or unaware, or remain silent; if the Saṃgha does not inquire further, the preceptor and the Saṃgha are not at fault.
If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, and the upādhyāya is doubtful, while both the assembly of monks and the candidate know they are under twenty, the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person seeking ordination replies that they are twenty years of age—or that they are not, or that they doubt it, or that they do not know, or that they remain silent—and the assembly does not inquire further, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense and the community of monks commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, and while the preceptor doubts this, the assembly of monks and the candidate themselves believe he has reached twenty, the assembly asks him:
"Have you reached twenty years of age?"

The person who has not yet received the precepts may reply that [the number] is complete, or incomplete, or express doubt, or remain ignorant, or remain silent; or the assembly may fail to inquire. In such cases, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense, while the community of monks incurs no offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, and the preceptor is in doubt, while the community of monks and the candidate for ordination are also in doubt, someone among the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or that they are not yet twenty, or that they are doubtful, or that they do not know, or if they remain silent, and the assembly does not inquire further, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense and the community of monks commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, and the preceptor suspects it, while the assembly of monks and the candidate themselves do not know, someone in the midst of the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or that they are not yet twenty, or that they are doubtful, or that they do not know, or remains silent, and the assembly does not inquire further, the preceptor commits a *pāyattika* offense, while the Sangha is not at fault.

If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, and the preceptor does not know this, while the assembly of monks and the candidate for ordination themselves know that he is less than twenty years of age, someone in the midst of the assembly asks him:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person not yet ordained replies that they are twenty years old, or have not yet reached twenty, or is doubtful, or does not know, or remains silent, and the assembly does not inquire, the preceptor commits no offense, but the Saṃgha commits a *duṣkṛta*.

If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, yet the *upādhyāya* does not know this, and both the assembly of monks and the person receiving the precepts believe he is twenty, the assembly asks him:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

The person seeking ordination may reply that they are twenty years old, or that they are not yet twenty, or that they are uncertain, or that they do not know, or remain silent; or the assembly may fail to inquire. In such cases, the preceptor and the Sangha are not at fault.

If the person receiving the precepts is under twenty years of age, and the preceptor is unaware of this while the assembly of monks and the candidate themselves are in doubt, someone within the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person seeking ordination replies that they are twenty years old—or that they are not yet twenty, or are doubtful, or do not know, or remain silent—and the assembly does not inquire, the preceptor commits no offense, but the Saṃgha incurs a duṣkṛta.

If the person receiving the precepts is less than twenty years of age, and the preceptor does not know it, nor do the assembly of monks or the candidate themselves know it, and someone among the assembly asks:
"Are you twenty years of age?"

If the person seeking ordination replies that they are twenty years old—or if they have not yet reached twenty, or are uncertain, or do not know, or remain silent—and the assembly does not inquire further, the preceptor and the Sangha are without offense.

If that bhikṣu knows that the candidate is less than twenty years of age, yet completes the three *karmavācanās* for conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*), the preceptor commits a *pāyattika*.
If he has completed the formal motion (*jñapti*) and two *karmavācanās*, the preceptor commits three *duṣkṛta*s.
When the motion has been made and one *karmavācanā* (formal act) is completed, the preceptor incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
When the motion is completed, the preceptor incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense.
While the motion is not yet completed, the preceptor incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one performs the preparatory act of shaving the hair before the formal announcement (*jñapti*), or if one intends to assemble the community for the sake of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), it is all *duṣkṛta*.
If the community of monks has assembled, the preceptor incurs *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerikā, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.
There is no offense if one did not know beforehand; or if one accepted the words of a person who had received the precepts;
or if there was testimony from a bystander; or if one trusted one's parents; or if, after receiving the precepts, one had doubts. The Buddha said:
"In such cases, one should be permitted to count the months of the pregnancy and to count the intercalary months."
If one counts every fourteen-day *poṣadha* ceremony as a full year, there is no offense. There is no offense in the following cases:
when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty-fifth [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, after a dispute had been settled according to the Dharma, later reopened it and said:

"You did not observe well, so your observation was not established; you did not understand well, so your understanding was not established; you did not settle well, so your settlement was not established. You have caused a dispute to arise where none existed before, and you have failed to eliminate a dispute that already exists."
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"For what reason does a dispute arise among the Saṃgha when none yet exists, and why is a dispute not resolved once it has arisen?"
Then the bhikṣus investigated and discovered that the six group of bhikṣus had re-aroused a dispute after it had already been settled in accordance with the Dharma. They spoke thus:

"You did not observe well and thus your observation was not accomplished; you did not understand well and thus your understanding was not accomplished; you did not settle well and thus your settlement was not accomplished."
Thus, they caused disputes to arise where none had existed before, and failed to extinguish those that had already arisen.

When the monks heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six monks, saying:
"How is it that after you have settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, you later raise it up again, saying:..."
"You have not observed correctly and have failed to achieve observation, up to and including failing to achieve cessation.
Thus, you cause disputes to arise where none existed in the Saṃgha, and you fail to eliminate disputes that already exist.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
How is it that after a matter of dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, one later raises it again, saying:
"You have not observed well, you have not achieved observation, and so on, up to: you have not achieved cessation"?
"...causing disputes to arise where none existed before, and failing to resolve those that already exist?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These deluded men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, after a dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, should later re-ignite it, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether a legal dispute had been settled according to the Dharma or not; it was only later that they realized it had been settled according to the Dharma. Consequently, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who did not know.
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣu, knowing that a matter of dispute has already been settled according to the Dharma through confession, should later raise it again, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"According to the Dharma" means in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.
There are four kinds of disputes:
disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning searching, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning matters.
If a monk, knowing that a dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, later re-ignites it and speaks as follows:

"If one does not contemplate well, contemplation is not accomplished; if one does not understand well, understanding is not accomplished; if one does not extinguish well, extinction is not accomplished.
To speak these words clearly constitutes a *pāyattika*;
to speak them unclearly constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
Once this dispute has been settled, if one engages in further quarreling or verbal abuse, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing) for every instance of such instigation.
If one initiates a dispute oneself, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
Except for monks and nuns, if one initiates a dispute, quarrel, or verbal abuse with others again after it has already occurred, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one perceives what is not as being so, it is a *pāyattika*.
To observe with doubt is a *duṣkṛta*.
To have the perception of observing when it is not actually observed is a *duṣkṛta*.
To have the perception of doubt when it is not actually doubted is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one did not know it beforehand;
if one perceives something as not being what it appears to be;
or if the fact is actually so.

Not skillfully contemplating, one does not achieve contemplation; not skillfully understanding, one does not achieve understanding; not skillfully extinguishing, one does not achieve extinction. Then one says:
"From lack of skillful contemplation up to lack of skillful achievement of extinction."
There is no offense if one speaks while joking, if one speaks hurriedly, if one speaks in a dream, or if, intending to say this, one says that by mistake.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty-sixth [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

A large number of bhikṣus were traveling from Śrāvastī toward Vaiśālī. At that time, there was a caravan of merchants who intended to cross a customs post in secret without paying the king’s taxes. Then the merchants asked the bhikṣus, saying:
“Venerable Sirs!...”
"Where do you wish to go?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I wish to go to Vaiśālī."
The merchants said,
"May we travel as companions with your reverences? The bhikṣus replied:
"So be it. At that time, the bhikṣus traveled as companions with these bandit merchants and crossed the frontier gate in secret.
When the gatekeepers caught them, they took them to King Prasenajit and addressed the king, saying:
"These people crossed the pass in secret and did not pay the tax.
The king then asked, "These merchants crossed the pass in secret and did not pay the tax; what further matter is there with these śramaṇas?"
The gatekeeper replied, "Be a companion to this man.
The King then questioned the bhikṣus again, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Are you truly traveling as a companion with these merchants? He replied:
"It is indeed so. He asked again:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Do you know whether this person pays the king's taxes or not? He replied, "I know."
The king said,
"If you truly know this, according to the law you ought to die.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"I am now a consecrated king of the royal lineage; how could I possibly kill a śramaṇa son of the Śākyas?
Having thus rebuked the bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the king then commanded his attendants in front of the multitude to release the bhikṣu and let him go.
Having received these instructions, he was immediately released.
At that time, those in the king’s assembly all cried out in a loud voice:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has violated the king’s grave law; his crime deserved death, yet the king merely reprimanded him lightly and set him free."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "How can you travel as companions with bandit merchants?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked them, saying:
"How is it that you travel as companions with bandit merchants?"
Having rebuked the bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many occasions for the outflow of impurities."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu travels along the same road with a band of thieves, even for the distance between one village and another, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.

Some bhikṣus, not knowing they were with thieves, traveled as companions with those who were not thieves; later, when they realized they were traveling with a band of thieves, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
The Buddha said:
"One who does not know is not guilty.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited in this manner:"
"If a bhikṣu knows that he is traveling along the same road with a band of thieves, even for as far as the distance between two villages, it is a pāyattika.
Thus did the Blessed One lay down this precept for the bhikṣus.
That bhikṣu did not make a formal agreement; there was doubt.
The Buddha said:
"Since he did not make a formal agreement, there is no offense."
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, knowing he is traveling with a band of thieves, makes an agreement to travel together along the same road for even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Criminal companions" refers to those who have returned from committing a robbery or are about to go out to do so.
"Making a pact" means they agree together to go to a city or to a village.
"Road" refers to any road leading from place to place within a village.

If a bhikṣu, knowing he is traveling with a band of thieves, agrees to travel along the same road with them, proceeding from one place to another toward various roads within a village, for each such road reached, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one travels together for ten *li* through a desolate area where there are no villages and no defined boundaries, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one travels together halfway through a village, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one shortens the distance by ten *li*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one travels along a single path between villages, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one employs the means to go but does not go, or if one intends to go together with others but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one was previously unaware of it; if one did not travel in company with [the offender];
if one traveled separately for the sake of safety to a certain destination;
or if one was held by force.
If one is bound and led away;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or those who are insane, mentally deranged, or oppressed by intense pain.
The sixty-seventh [chapter] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ariṣṭa who gave rise to such a pernicious view:
“I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One: for one who commits sexual misconduct, it is not an obstacle to the path.”
At that time, the bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa had conceived such an evil view:
"I understand the Dharma taught by the Blessed One such that committing sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path."

When the bhikṣus heard this, wishing to remove the evil view of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, they went to where Ariṣṭa was. After paying their respects and exchanging greetings, they sat to one side. The bhikṣus said to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa:
"Do you truly know that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One holds that committing sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path?"
Ariṣṭa replied, "I truly know that the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One holds that committing sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path.
Then, the bhikṣus, wishing to eliminate Ariṣṭa’s evil view, earnestly questioned him:
“Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the Blessed One. It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak thus.”

Āḷavaka! The Blessed One, through countless skillful means, teaches the Dharma to instruct on the severing of sensual desire and the understanding of sensual perceptions; he teaches the removal of craving for sensual desires and the abandonment of the perception of sensual desires, so that one may remove being consumed by sensual craving and cross beyond the fetter of sensual attachment.

The World-Honored One has taught through countless skillful means that desire is like a great pit of fire; desire is like a torch; it is also like fruit that has ripened; desire is like a loan; desire is like a dry bone; desire is like a piece of meat; it is like what is seen in a dream; desire is like a sharp blade; desire is like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun; desire is like the head of a venomous snake; desire is like grasping a sharp sword; desire is like a sharp halberd.
The Blessed One has spoken thus regarding desire: "Āḷavaka! Thus has the Blessed One well-expounded the Dharma:

cutting off desire and being free from desire, removing defilement and being free from defilement, subduing craving, destroying the nesting place, emerging from all fetters and bonds—the extinction of craving, which is Nirvāṇa."
"The Buddha has taught the Dharma in this way; how can you say, 'The commission of sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path'?
When the bhikṣus thus questioned Ariṣṭa earnestly, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa stubbornly maintained his evil view and spoke with firm conviction:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.

At that time, the bhikṣus were unable to eliminate the evil views of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, so they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed a certain bhikṣu:
"Go, take my word and quickly summon the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa.
Having received these instructions, that bhikṣu went at once to where the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was and said to him:
“The Blessed One summons you.

When the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa heard that the Blessed One was calling him, he went at once to where the Blessed One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and sat down to one side. The Buddha asked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa:
“Is it true that you spoke these words:”
"Do you know, Āḷavaka, that I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha to mean that engaging in sexual desire is not an obstacle to the path? Āḷavaka replied:
“Venerable One!
It is indeed true that such words were spoken.
The Buddha said to Ariṣṭa:
"How do you know that what I have said is thus?
I have taught the method for severing sensual desire through countless skillful means, as described above.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

“Listen, O Saṃgha! For the sake of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) shall be performed as a reprimand so that he may abandon this matter.
The reprimand should be conducted as follows: from among the assembly, a competent person for the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
‘May the venerable Saṃgha listen!’”
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa has spoken thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now issues a formal reprimand to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa so that he may relinquish this matter.
“Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One. The Blessed One does not speak thus;
rather, the Blessed One has taught by means of countless skillful methods that sensual desire is an obstacle to the path.”
"If one commits sexual misconduct, it is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
Thus he speaks. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa has spoken thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha that the commission of sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path.
The Saṃgha now issues a formal reprimand against him for the purpose of making him abandon this matter.

“Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One. To slander the Blessed One is unwholesome. The Blessed One does not say such things. By means of countless skillful methods, the Blessed One has taught that sensual desire is an obstacle to the path; if one commits sexual misconduct, it is indeed an obstacle to the path.”
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to relinquish this matter, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner:
"The Saṃgha has finished admonishing the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld."
"One should reprimand the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa in this manner; having abandoned this matter, a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) shall be performed.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there be other bhikṣus who speak in this way:"
"I know what the Buddha has taught: engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path.
The Sangha should likewise reprimand him with a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of significance so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
If a bhikṣu should speak thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not a dharma that obstructs the path," that bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One, for to slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome.
The World-Honored One does not say such things; rather, through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One has taught that engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path."
When that bhikṣu exhorts this bhikṣu, if he persists and does not relinquish [his position], that bhikṣu may exhort him up to three times so that he might relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it after the third exhortation, it is well; if he does not relinquish it, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. That bhikṣu speaks thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstructive factor for the path."
That bhikṣu should admonish this bhikṣu, saying:
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus. By means of countless skillful expedients, the Blessed One has said:..."
"Engaging in sexual intercourse is a dharma that obstructs the path.
You should now abandon this matter; do not be rebuked by the Sangha and commit a further grave offense.
If he accepts these words, it is well; if he does not follow these words, one should make a formal announcement (jñapti).
Having made the motion, one should say:
"I have finished the motion; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) remains.
You should abandon this matter so that you do not incur the censure of the Sangha nor commit a further grave offense."
"If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) shall be performed.
Once the first *karmavācanā* has been completed, one should say:
'I have finished the first proclamation; two further *karmavācanās* remain.'"
"You should abandon this matter; do not allow yourself to be censured by the Saṃgha and commit a further grave offense.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, a second *karmavācanā* (formal motion) shall be performed.
Having performed the second *karmavācanā*, one should say:
"The first of the two *karmavācanās* has been completed; one *karmavācanā* remains.
You should relinquish this matter so that you do not incur further offense by being censured by the Saṃgha."
"If one complies with these words, it is well; if one does not comply, then after the three *karmavācanās* have been recited, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one desists after the *jñapti* has been made and two *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is three *duṣkṛtas*."
If one abandons [the object] after the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been made and the first *karmavācanā* (motion) is completed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one abandons it after the announcement has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one abandons it before the announcement is completed, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one has not yet made the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and says:
"I know what the Buddha has taught: engaging in sexual desire is not an obstructive factor for the path," it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
When that bhikṣu is admonishing this bhikṣu, if another bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, or anyone else should intervene, saying:
"Do not abandon this matter."
If the community of monks has finished their admonition and yet [the offender] does not desist, those who obstruct [the process] all commit a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *pāyattika*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one relinquishes [the position] at the first word;

or if the admonition is by an illegal separate assembly; or if the admonition is by an illegal united assembly; or if it is by a legal separate assembly; or if it is by a legal-similar separate assembly; or if it is by a legal-similar united assembly.
This is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha;
if there is no one to admonish, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty-eighth [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa held a pernicious view; although the Saṃgha admonished him with reproof, he nevertheless did not relinquish it.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, saying:
"How is it that you, with such evil views, do not relinquish them even though the Saṃgha has admonished and exhorted you?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not be done."
“Venerable Āḷavaka! What kind of evil view is it that you do not relinquish even after the Saṃgha has admonished and exhorted you?
Having rebuked the bhikṣu Āḷavaka with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

“From this day forward, the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations) for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, for his refusal to relinquish an evil view.

It should be performed in this manner: one shall perform the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīya*) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa; having performed the suspension, one shall perform the act of calling to mind (*smṛti*); and having performed the calling to mind, one shall impose the penalty.”
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Ariṣṭa holds an evil view; although the Saṃgha has admonished him with reproach, he still does not relinquish it."

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepa-karman*) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not relinquishing his evil view.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa holds an evil view; although the Saṃgha has admonished and exhorted him, he still does not relinquish it.
The Saṃgha now performs the formal act of suspension for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa on account of his refusal to relinquish an evil view.

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha now performing the formal act of suspension for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa on account of his refusal to relinquish evil views, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are to be recited in the same manner.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the formal act of suspension for the monk Ariṣṭa on account of his refusal to relinquish a wrong view; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld."
At that time, the Saṃgha performed the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa-karman*) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not relinquishing his evil views.
Nevertheless, the group of six bhikṣus provided him with his necessities, participated in formal acts together with him, and stayed and conversed with him.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing; they rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, the Saṃgha has performed the *karma* of suspension against him for not relinquishing his evil view."
"How should one provide for their necessities, dwell together with them, and converse?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, group of six bhikṣus!

While the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of suspension (*utkṣepa-karman*) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not relinquishing his evil view, how can you provide him with what he requires, allow him to stay overnight, and converse with him?"
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“These group-of-six bhikṣus are foolish men!”
Among the many sources of outflows (*āsrava*), this is the first offense regarding the violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu provides for the needs of, performs formal acts (*karmavācanā*) with, shares a dwelling, or converses with a person who speaks in such a manner and who has not yet performed the formal act of renouncing such an evil view, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether such words had been spoken or whether they had not been spoken; later, when they learned that such words had indeed been spoken, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who did not know.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣu knows that such a person has not performed the formal act of reconciliation, yet persists in this wrong view without relinquishing it, and he provides them with their necessities, performs *karmavācanā* together with them, or stays and converses with them, it is a *pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above. One who speaks thus says:
"I have heard the World-Honored One teaching the Dharma that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path."
"Regarding those for whom the formal act has not been performed: if they have been subject to suspension (*ukkhepana*) and it has not yet been revoked;
such persons hold this view, maintaining this view, and recognize that the Dharma taught by the Blessed One is not a factor that obstructs the path."
