"If a bhikṣu carves or scrapes a needle-case made of bone, ivory, or horn, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣu himself carves or scrapes bone, ivory, or horn to complete such a work, it is a pāyattika.
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another to do it and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts on behalf of another, whether the act is completed or not, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one uses iron, copper, lead or tin, white tin, bamboo, wood, reeds, or *śara* grass to make a needle case.
If one makes a point for the head of a mendicant’s staff;
or if one makes a point for a parasol or for the head of a ladle;
or if one makes a curved hook.
Whether it be made as a scraping knife,
or as a wish-fulfilling gem,
or as a jeweled ring;
Whether it be made into a spoon, or a ladle,
or a hook for hanging clothes;
Whether it be for making an eye-salve applicator,
or for making a tongue-scraper,
or for making a dental pick;
If one makes an ear-scraper,
a meditation weight,
or a nose-irrigation tube— such as these, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[Section Eighty-Six ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One did not accept the invitation; it is the constant law of all Buddhas that if they do not accept an invitation, they shall walk through the dwellings. He saw that in another place, the bedding and mats belonging to the Sangha had been spread out in the open air and defiled by impurities.
At that time, there was a great downpour of rain, and the World-Honored One used his supernormal powers to ensure that the bedding and seats of the monks were not soaked by the rain.
When the bhikṣus returned, the World-Honored One assembled the community of monks for this reason and addressed them, saying:
"Just now, as I was walking through the various rooms, I saw that in certain places the bedding and seats of the monks had been spread out in the open air and defiled by impurities."
At that time, it rained heavily; by my supernormal power, I caused the rain not to soak [me].

You should know that this defilement belongs to one who possesses desire, not to one free from desire; to one who possesses hatred, not to one free from hatred; and to one who possesses delusion, not to one free from delusion.
If even non-Buddhist seers who have abandoned desire do not possess such a thing, how much less so an Arhat?
If even a bhikṣu who maintains undistracted mindfulness while sleeping does not possess such a thing, how much less so an Arhat?
"From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to make *niṣīdana* mats for the purpose of protecting the body, the robes, and the bedding.
Once the World-Honored One had permitted the making of *niṣīdana* mats, the group of six bhikṣus then made many that were excessively large and long.
At that time, the bhikṣus saw them and asked, "The World-Honored One has established a precept permitting the keeping of three robes, but not exceeding [the prescribed length].
What kind of robe is this? The group of six bhikṣus replied:

"This is our *niṣīdana*. When the monks heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the *dhūta* austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six monks, saying:
"How is it that you have made so many large and wide *niṣīdana*s?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice; it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that you have made such a wide and long sitting mat (niṣīdana)?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat), he must make it according to the prescribed measurement."
Regarding the measurements herein: the length shall be two spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width one and a half spans.
Should it exceed these dimensions, once the excess has been cut off, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Thus did the Blessed One establish this precept for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Venerable Kālodāyin was large of body, while his sitting mat (niṣīdana) was small, so he could not sit upon it. Knowing that the World-Honored One was coming along this path, he stood by the roadside and pulled at the sitting mat with his hands, wishing to make it wider.
When the World-Honored One saw Kāḷudāyin pulling at his sitting mat (niṣīdana), he, knowing the reason, asked him intentionally:
"For what reason are you pulling this sitting mat?"
He replied, “I pulled it because I wished to make it vast.

At that time, the World-Honored One, based on this matter, preached the Dharma in accordance with the needs of the bhikṣus, praising those who practice dhūta, who have few desires and know contentment, and who delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to increase the length and width by half a vitasti each.
From this day forward, the precept should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣu makes a niṣīdana, he must make it according to the prescribed measure. The measure herein is: two vitastis in length and one and a half vitastis in width; it may be increased by an additional half a vitasti in both length and width.’”
"If one exceeds the prescribed dimensions, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Naiṣadyika" (seating mat) refers to that which is spread beneath the seat.
If a bhikṣu makes a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat) that exceeds the prescribed measurement in length but not in width;
or exceeds it in width but not in length;
or exceeds it in both length and width.
If one completes it oneself, it is a *pāyattika*;
if one does not complete it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to have it completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts on behalf of another, whether it is completed or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who makes [the robe] according to the prescribed measure, or makes it less than the measure; or if one obtains a finished garment from another and cuts it to the proper measure; or if one folds it double, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acts before the precept has been established, or for one who is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh [rule]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from boils, sores, scabies, and various other skin ailments; pus and blood flowed out, defiling their bodies, their robes, and their bedding.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep wound-covering robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus' wound-covering robes were coarse and hairy; when they applied them to their wounds and lifted the robes, it caused them pain.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to cover their sores with expensive, fine, soft garments and wear the nivāsana over them."
When one arrives at the house of a layperson and is invited to sit, one should say: "I am ill. If the host says:
"Simply sit down.
"You should pull up your *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* and sit while covering the wound with this cloth.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had permitted the making of a wound-covering cloth, they then made many wound-covering cloths that were excessively large and long.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they immediately asked, "The World-Honored One has established a precept that one may possess no more than three robes and they must not exceed the prescribed length;
what kind of robe is this? The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"This is our 'wound-covering cloth.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you have made so many large and long wound-covering cloths?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"Why do you all make such numerous, wide, and long garments for covering sores?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣu makes a cloth for covering sores, it must be made according to the proper measure. The measure herein is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width. If he exceeds these dimensions after cutting it out, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the "wound-covering cloth": it refers to various types of sores or ailments for which one uses [this cloth] to cover the body.

If it is of proper measurement in length but not of proper measurement in width; or of proper measurement in width but not of proper measurement in length; or if both the width and length are not of proper measurement—if one makes it oneself and completes it, it is an *pāyattika* offense.
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another to complete it, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts on behalf of another, whether the act is completed or not, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, and a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure, or makes it less than the measure; or if one obtains it from another and cuts it to the proper measure; or if one folds it double—there is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The eighty-eighth [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when Viśākhā Mātṛ heard that the Tathāgata had permitted the bhikṣus to make rain-bathing robes, she immediately had many rain-bathing robes made and sent someone to take them to the saṃghārāma to give to the bhikṣus.
When the bhikṣus received it, they immediately divided it. The Buddha said:
"This robe should not be divided. From now on, if a rain-bath robe is obtained, it shall be assigned according to the order of seniority."
"If it is insufficient, one should recall the next [monk] in order; having obtained more, one should continue the sequence and distribute it until it reaches everyone.
At that time, he obtained a robe of high value and continued the sequence to give it away. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should exchange it with the Elder."
When the senior monk has first received [the portion], he shall pass it on in turn to those of lower rank.
If it is not distributed to all, the community should provide him with shareable monastic robes and clothing so that everyone may receive their full allotment.

At that time, having heard that the Tathāgata had established the precepts and permitted the bhikṣus to make rain-bathing robes, the group of six bhikṣus immediately made many rain-bathing robes for themselves that were excessively large.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they immediately asked, "The Tathāgata has established a precept that one may keep three robes but they must not exceed a certain length; whose robes are these?
The group of six bhikṣus replied:
"These are our rain-bathing robes.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you have made so many large rain-bathing robes?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why do you all make so many large rain-bathing robes?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe, it must be made according to the prescribed measurements."
Regarding the measurements herein: the length shall be six spans of the Buddha’s hand, and the width two and a half spans.
Should one exceed these dimensions after the cutting is finished, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding the rain-bathing robe: if various bhikṣus wear it while bathing in the rain;

and if a bhikṣu makes a rain-bathing robe that is of improper length but proper width, or of improper width but proper length, or of improper length and width in both respects—if he completes it himself, it is a *pāyattika*;
if he does not complete it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one instructs another to make it and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one makes it for another, whether it is completed or not, it is entirely a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measurement, or makes it less than the measurement; or if one obtains it from another and cuts it to the proper measurement; or if one folds it double—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the eighty-ninth [case]. At that time, the Buddha was staying in the Nyagrodha Park at Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Venerable Nanda was four finger-widths shorter than the Buddha. When the bhikṣus saw Nanda approaching from afar, they all thought it was the Buddha coming; they immediately rose to welcome him, only realizing it was Nanda once he had arrived.
All the bhikṣus felt shame and remorse, and at that time Nanda also felt shame and remorse.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I decree that the bhikṣu Nanda shall wear black robes."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, or even exceeding that size.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame;
they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying: "How can you make robes equal in size to those of the Tathāgata, or even exceeding that size?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance; it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, you group of six bhikṣus!
Do you make robes equal in measure to the Tathāgata’s, or even exceeding that measure?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“O foolish man! This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many bases for the outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”
If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in measure to that of the Tathāgata, or exceeding that measure, it is a pāyattika offense.
Herein, the measure of the Tathāgata’s robe is ten spans in length and six spans in width; this is called the measure of the Tathāgata’s robe.
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "robes," there are ten kinds of robes, as described above.

If a bhikṣu makes a robe equal in size to the Tathāgata’s robe—whether it is appropriate in length but not in width, or appropriate in width but not in length, or inappropriate in both width and length—and completes it himself, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one instructs another to complete it, it is a *pāyattika*;

"One must not walk into the house of a layperson while swaying the body; this is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"House of laypeople" is as explained above.
"Swinging the body" means walking while swaying the body from side to side.
If a bhikṣu intentionally sways his body, twists his body to the left and right, or runs while entering the house of a layperson, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct;
if it was not intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; when one is struck by another and turns the body to avoid a blow; when a rogue elephant approaches; when one is threatened by bandits; when one is encountered by lions or other fierce beasts; or when meeting someone carrying thorns—one turns the body to avoid these things; or when crossing a ditch, a canal, or a place of mud and water, one moves the body through them;
or when putting on a robe, one turns the body to check whether it is properly adjusted.
Is there an offense regarding high or low [postures]?
Is it not [the case] with the "elephant-trunk," the "tāla-leaf," or the "fine pleats"?
One who turns the body in this manner to look incurs no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

The fourteenth rule concludes: "One must not enter the house of a layperson walking with the body swaying and sit down; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya* [training rule], and it is likewise [for other related behaviors]."
Fifteen [rules] concluded. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus walked into the houses of laypeople with their arms swinging.
At that time, the laypeople saw this and all reviled them, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:
'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what righteous Dharma is there?
Now, walking with arms swinging as one enters the house of a layperson, you resemble kings, ministers, elders, or householders."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you walk into the houses of laypeople with your arms swinging?"
Having rebuked them, they went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of monks and rebuked the group of six monks, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant conduct—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you all enter the houses of laypeople with your arms flung out?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You foolish men!..."
Among the various bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of significance and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One must not walk into the house of a layperson with arms swinging; this is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Swinging the arms" means swinging the arms forward and backward.
If a bhikṣu intentionally walks into the house of a layperson while swinging his arms, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for improper conduct;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

when one has such an illness; when raising a hand to ward off someone who is striking one; when encountering a rogue elephant approaching; when encountering lions, wild beasts, or thieves; when encountering someone carrying thorns and raising a hand to ward them off; when crossing a river by swimming; when leaping across a ditch or moat; when there is mud or water; or when traveling with a companion and unable to call out to them with the hand. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The section on] the sixteenth [offense] concludes. Sitting [in violation] is also as described above.
[The section on] the seventeenth [offense] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople while failing to properly cover their bodies.
When the householders saw this, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they enter the houses of laypeople wearing robes that do not properly cover their bodies, appearing just like brahmins."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you do not properly cover your bodies when entering the houses of laypeople?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"Why is it that you, wearing your robes poorly and failing to cover your bodies, enter the houses of laypeople?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You foolish men!"
Among the various bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"Entering the house of a layperson with one's body well-covered is a *śikṣākaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"A layperson's house" refers to a village.
"Not properly covering the body" means being exposed in various places.
If a bhikṣu intentionally enters the house of a layperson with his body improperly covered, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*).
Because it was intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*asamudācāra*);
if it was not intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; when one is bound; or when the wind blows the robe away from the body.
There is no offense for those who acted before the precept was established, or for those who were insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The eighteenth [section] concludes; sitting is also like this.
The nineteenth [section] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus walked into the houses of laypeople while looking around to the left and right.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they receive and take without satiety.
Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
It is like a thief who, looking left and right, enters the house of a layperson.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you walk into the houses of laypeople while looking here and there?"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you, looking here and there as you walk, enter the houses of laypeople?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These foolish men!..."
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One must not walk into the house of a layperson while looking left and right; this is a śikṣākaraṇīya."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"The house of a layperson" refers to a village.
"Looking around here and there" means gazing about in various directions.
If a bhikṣu intentionally walks into the house of a layperson while looking repeatedly to the left and right, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; or if one is observing the time and season;
or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), and one seeks a way to escape by looking for a convenient path on all sides, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by illness.
[The rule concerning] sitting is also the same.
[The twenty-first section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople shouting and clamoring loudly.
When the householders saw this, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they receive and take without satiety."
Externally, they claim for themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is there in such a case?
They raised their voices and called out loudly, as if they were a multitude of Brahmins.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; these reproached the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you enter the houses of laypeople making such loud noises?"
The bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not the practice of compliance, and is something that ought not to be done."
"Why do you enter the houses of laypeople with such loud voices?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this is the first offense of transgressing the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"Entering the house of a layperson in silence is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
In this context, "not remaining silent" refers to shouting loudly, calling out, giving instructions, or making loud noises while offering food.
If one intentionally makes such loud noises or calls out, one commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* for violating the rules of decorum;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense. There is no offense if, at times, one has such an illness;

or if being deaf, one does not hear sounds and must call out loudly; or if one gives instructions loudly; or if one distributes food loudly; or if, due to danger to life or danger to the brahmacarya, one runs away while shouting loudly. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
This concludes the twenty-second [section]. The same applies to sitting.
The twenty-third section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus entered the houses of laypeople while laughing and joking.
At that time, the lay devotees saw this and all spoke in derision, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they receive and take without satiety.
Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
Entering the homes of laypeople with frivolous laughter is like a monkey.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you enter the houses of laypeople while joking and laughing?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, not a compliant practice, and is something that should not be done."
"How can you, sirs, enter the homes of laypeople in a playful and laughing manner?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!..."

Regarding these various sources of outflows, this was the first instance of a transgression of the precepts. From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One must not enter the houses of laypeople while laughing or playing; this is a śikṣākaraṇīya."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"Laughing in jest" means laughing with the teeth exposed.
If a bhikṣu intentionally enters the house of a layperson while laughing in jest, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; when the lips are painful and the teeth are not covered; or when one smiles out of joy while contemplating the Dharma. These are non-offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been promulgated; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
This concludes the twenty-fourth [section]. The same applies to sitting.
[The twenty-fifth section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, a householder invited the community of monks to provide them with food and drink; he prepared various kinds of fine foods that very night and went in the morning to announce that the time had arrived.

At that time, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the house of a lay devotee, where they sat down upon prepared seats; the lay devotee then personally served them various kinds of food and drink with his own hands.
The group of six bhikṣus did not mindfully receive their food, but instead cast away the soup and rice.
When the lay devotees saw this, they said to one another, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they take and accept without satiety."
Externally, they claim for themselves:
"I know the true Dharma.
What kind of true Dharma is there in such a case?
"What is meant by eating without mindfulness?
It is receiving food with a greedy mind in great quantities, as if during a time of high grain prices.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"Why do you not receive your food with mindfulness?
The bhikṣus went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, not a compliant practice, and something that ought not to be done."
"Why is it that you do not eat with mindfulness, but instead cast away the soup and rice?
Having rebuked them through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this is the first offense regarding the violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"Eating with deliberate intent constitutes a *śaikṣakaraṇīya* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
Regarding "receiving food without care," this refers to discarding the soup and rice while eating.
If a bhikṣu intentionally receives food without care, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for violating the rules of decorum;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or where, because the bowl is small, one discards rice while eating, or where it falls back onto the table. These are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Chapter Twenty-Six concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a householder invited the community of monks to a meal. That very night he prepared the food and drink, and at dawn he went to inform them that the time had arrived.
Then, when the time came, the bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to the householder’s home, where they sat down in their assigned seats.

At that time, a lay devotee personally served the soup and rice with his own hands; however, the group of six bhikṣus received food until their bowls overflowed, causing them to spill and discard the soup and rice.
When the lay devotee saw this, he criticized and disparaged them all, saying, "These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they accept food without satiety."
Externally, they claim for themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such a case?
"They receive food until their bowls overflow, as if they were hungry people greedy for more.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you receive food until your bowls overflow and then discard the soup and rice?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not a compliant practice, and something that should not have been done."
"Why do you all receive food until your bowls overflow and then discard the soup and rice?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"These foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first instance of violating the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One should receive food with a level bowl; this is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
"An uneven bowl" means one that is overflowing.
If a bhikṣu intentionally accepts food with an uneven bowl, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa* for improper conduct;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, it is an offense of *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, at times, there is such an illness; or if, at times, the bowl is small; or if, at times, it falls back onto the table. These cases involve no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The twenty-seventh section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder who invited the community of monks, intending to provide them with a meal. That very night, he prepared the food and utensils; on the following day, he went to inform them that the time had arrived.
Then the bhikṣus, having dressed and taken their bowls, went to the householder’s home and sat down in their assigned seats.

At that time, the lay devotees personally served various kinds of food, including soups and rice. The group of six bhikṣus took such excessive amounts of rice that there was no room left for the soup.
When the lay devotees saw this, they all spoke in derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they accept and take without satiety."
Externally, they claim for themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be such a thing as the True Dharma?
"He has taken such an excessive amount of rice that there is no room for the soup; he looks like a person who, being hungry, greedily devours his food.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They reproached the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you have taken such an excessive amount of rice that there is no room for the soup?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"Why is it that you all have taken such an excessive amount of rice that there is no room for the soup?
After the Buddha had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You foolish men!"
Among the many bases of outflows, this was the first transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the tenfold purpose up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One should receive soup with a level bowl; this is a *śaikṣakaraṇīya*."
The meaning of "bhikṣu" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣu intentionally receives soup in a bowl that is unevenly balanced, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession (*sāntika*).
Because it was done intentionally, he also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If one does not do so intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus as described above, and having reached the point of the initial transgression of the precept, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten points of meaning, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not eat by grasping scattered grains of rice in the hand; this is a *śaikṣa-āpatti*.'"
"Scattering the rice" means to scatter and discard the rice.
If a bhikṣu intentionally eats by scattering the rice with his hand, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If one does not do so intentionally, one commits a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣuṇī, down to a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; when there is grass or insects in the food; when it is defiled by impurities; or when one discards food that has not yet been formally accepted. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-sixth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder who invited the bhikṣus to provide them with various kinds of excellent food. He prepared everything that night and went the next morning to inform them that the time had arrived.
The bhikṣus put on their robes, took up their bowls, and went to his house where they sat down in their assigned seats. The householder then personally served them food and drink with his own hands.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who, with hands soiled by impure grease, grasped drinking vessels and ate.
When a householder saw this, he spoke with reproach:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; how can they even be said to possess the True Dharma?"
As described above, they held their drinking vessels with unclean hands, appearing like kings or royal ministers.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the behavior and went to the World-Honored One. They prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. As previously, he rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, and having concluded with the original transgression of the precept, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten points of meaning, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not grasp a drinking vessel with dirty hands; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
Regarding "defiled hands" herein, it refers to hands that have greasy rice adhering to them.
If a bhikṣu intentionally grasps a drinking vessel with unclean, greasy hands, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; or when receiving [food] from grass, or from leaves, or having washed one's hands;
or when there is no offense because the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Forty-seven. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who, having finished eating at the house of a lay devotee, washed their bowls and discarded the bowl-washing water and leftover food in a messy heap upon the ground.
Having seen this, the laypeople spoke with derision and reproach:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; how can there even be true Dharma?
They consume such vast amounts of food and drink as if they were starving, yet they discard it in such a messy and wasteful manner, like kings or high ministers."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured [the offender], they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus as previously described, and having concluded with the initial transgression of the precept, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten points of meaning, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not discard bowl-washing water inside the dwellings of laypeople; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.'"
Regarding "washing-bowl water" herein, it refers to water mixed with rice.
If a bhikṣu intentionally discards washing-bowl water inside the residence of a layperson, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of improper conduct);
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when one has a certain illness, or when one uses a vessel or a basin to catch water while pouring it out and discards it outside.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The forty-eighth rule concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus defecated, urinated, and spat upon living grass and vegetables.
When a householder saw this, he spoke with reproach:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma"— how can there be such a True Dharma?
[For you] discharge excrement, urine, mucus, and spittle upon living grasses and vegetables, just like pigs, dogs, camels, oxen, and donkeys.

At that time, among the bhikṣus there were those who possessed few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having heard of this, they censured [the offender] and went to the World-Honored One. Prostrating themselves at his feet, they sat to one side and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus as described above, and having concluded with the initial transgression of the precept, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten benefits, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so in this way:
'One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon living grass or vegetables; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
After the Blessed One had thus established the precept for the bhikṣus,
a sick bhikṣu was unable to avoid living grass and vegetables and became utterly exhausted.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for a sick bhikṣu.
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
'One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate upon living grass or vegetables, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣādharmā*.'"
If a bhikṣu, being not ill, intentionally voids excrement or urine upon living grass or vegetables, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, down to a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense. There is no offense in cases such as these: when one has such an illness;

or when, being in a place devoid of grass or vegetables, one’s excrement or urine flows and falls upon living grass or vegetables; or when it is blown there by the wind; or when it is carried there by a crow and dropped into living grass or vegetables. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical suffering.
Thus ends the forty-ninth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus defecated, urinated, spat, and sneezed in the water.
When a householder saw this, he spoke with reproach:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be such a thing as the True Dharma?
To defecate and urinate in water is like the behavior of pigs, dogs, oxen, donkeys, and camels.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured the group of six bhikṣus, they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. Having rebuked the group of six as before, and having addressed the bhikṣus regarding the original transgression of the precept, he said:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten benefits, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water; this is a *śaikṣādharmā* offense.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, a sick bhikṣu became utterly exhausted by avoiding places where there was water.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense for one who is ill.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
‘One must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in pure water unless one is ill; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense.’”
If a bhikṣu intentionally voids excrement, urine, nasal mucus, or spits into water, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*).
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*ācāra-duṣkṛta*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is what is called an offense.

There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness; or where, while defecating or urinating on the bank, the excrement or urine flows and falls into the water; or where it is blown by the wind or carried off by a bird and falls into the water. These are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The fiftieth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stood while urinating and defecating.
When a householder saw this, he spoke with reproach:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma"— how can there be such a True Dharma?
He stands while defecating and urinating, just like oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, and camels.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. He rebuked the group of six bhikṣus as described above, even regarding their initial transgression of the precepts. Having addressed the bhikṣus, he said:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so in this way:
'One must not stand while defecating or urinating; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, some sick bhikṣus were so exhausted that they were unable to remain in a squatting position.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense for one who is ill.
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
'One must not stand while defecating or urinating, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.'"
If a bhikṣu intentionally stands while urinating or defecating, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, down to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, at times, one has such an illness, or is bound [in restraint], or if the feet or calves are covered in grease or soiled by mud.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The fifty-first section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who preached the Dharma to people who were disrespectful and had their robes tucked up behind.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured the six groups of bhikṣus, they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus. As previously stated, he rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, even down to their initial transgression of the precepts. Having addressed the bhikṣus, he said:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not preach the Dharma to a person who has tucked up their robe and is disrespectful; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense.'"
At that time, the bhikṣus were hesitant to preach the Dharma to those who were ill and had folded their robes over one shoulder.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense for one who is ill."
"From this day forward, one must not preach the Dharma to a person who has their robe draped over one shoulder and lacks respect, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣāpada*.

If a bhikṣu intentionally preaches the Dharma to a person who has their robe draped over one shoulder and lacks respect, provided that person is not ill, he commits an offense of *duṣkṛta* requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of improper conduct);
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; or if acting for the sake of a king or a royal minister;
or in the case of no offense, such as when the precept has not yet been established, or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Fifty-two [rules] concluded. It is a *śikṣāpada* offense for one who is not ill to preach the Dharma to someone with a cloth wrapped around their neck;
as stated above.
Three: it is a *śikṣāpada* offense for one who is not ill to preach the Dharma to someone with their head covered; as stated above.
As above. Fourth:
One must not preach the Dharma to those who have wrapped their heads, except in cases of illness; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense.
As above, fifth.
One must not preach the Dharma to someone with hands on hips, except in the case of illness; this is a *śikṣāpada*.
As above. Six:
one must not preach the Dharma to someone wearing leather sandals, except in the case of illness; this is a *śikṣāpada*.
As above. Seventh:
One must not preach the Dharma to one wearing wooden clogs, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*. As above.
8. One must not preach the Dharma to those riding on vehicles, except when they are ill; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*, as stated above.
9. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stayed overnight in a Buddhist stūpa.

When other bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How can you stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa?"
He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat to one side, reporting the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this incident and, as previously stated, rebuked the group of six up to the point of their initial transgression of the precepts.

“From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘One must not stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.’”
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, out of doubt, did not dare to stay overnight in a Buddhist stūpa for the sake of guarding it.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense for the purpose of guarding [the stupa].
From this day forward, the precept should be recited as follows:
‘One must not stay overnight within a Buddha-stūpa, except for the purpose of guarding it; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.’”
If a bhikṣu intentionally stays overnight in a Buddhist stūpa, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, or even for a śrāmaṇera or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in cases where one stays overnight due to such an illness, or for the sake of protection, or if one is seized by those using force, or if one stays overnight because of danger to life or danger to the brahmacarya.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The sixty rules are concluded. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who concealed their property and placed it within the Buddha’s stūpa.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the six groups of bhikṣus. "From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus. For the sake of the ten benefits, up to the long endurance of the True Dharma, those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not conceal wealth or property by placing it within a Buddhist stūpa; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"

from this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"One must not conceal wealth or goods within a Buddha-stūpa, except for the purpose of securing them; this is a *śaikṣa-dharma*.

This is called an offense. In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The sixty-first [case] concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, down to a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣus.

"I allow you to eat while seated; however, you must not leave grass or food to defile the ground.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who ate while seated, yet he did not eat if the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) procedure had not been performed.
If a bhikṣu is ill, he may not dare to leave leftover food on the grass to soil the ground.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to gather it and place it by your side; when you depart, take it away and discard it."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"One must not sit beneath a stūpa to eat, nor leave grass or food waste that defiles the ground; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
If a bhikṣu intentionally eats beneath a stūpa and leaves grass or leftover food that defiles the ground, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs the *dukkaṭa* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; or when one carries it out from a place where many are gathered at the time of departure and discards it;
or when one is among those for whom the rule was not yet established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
The seventh section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried a corpse past the base of a stūpa, and the deity who protected the stūpa became angry.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣus, saying:
"How is it that you carry a corpse past the base of a Buddha-stūpa?"
Having finished his reprimand, he went to where the Buddha was staying, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this incident and, as before, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, [proceeding] up to the point of their original transgression of the precepts.

“From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘One must not carry a corpse past a stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.’”
If a bhikṣu intentionally carries a corpse past a stūpa, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct;
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, or even for a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or when it is necessary to travel by this path, or when one is led away by forceful persons.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The eighth rule is concluded. One must not bury a corpse within a stūpa; this constitutes a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti* (an offense requiring training).
As above. Ninth:
One must not burn a corpse beneath a stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*. As above.
Seventy: One must not burn a corpse facing a stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As above. Seventy-one:
One must not burn a corpse within four paces of a Buddha-stūpa so that its foul odor enters [the sacred precinct]; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As above. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who, carrying the clothes and the bed of a deceased person, passed beneath a stūpa; the deity residing in that place became angry.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured [the offender], they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus as described above, up to the point of their original transgression of the precepts.

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not carry a corpse's garment or a bed past a stūpa; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇa* offense.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus who wore refuse rags were doubtful and did not dare to pass beneath a stūpa while carrying such garments.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to wash, dye, and perfume it, and then bring it inside.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"One must not carry a corpse's garment or bed beneath a stūpa, except when they have been washed, dyed, or perfumed with incense; this is a *śaikṣa-kaulaitya* offense.
If a bhikṣu intentionally carries a discarded garment from a corpse beneath a stūpa without having washed, dyed, or perfumed it, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* for violating the rules of decorum;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, down to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; or when one washes, dyes, or perfumes [the robes];
or when there is no offense because the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
3. One must not defecate or urinate beneath a Buddha stūpa; this is a *śikṣāpada*.
As above. 4.
One must not defecate or urinate facing a Buddha stūpa; this is a *śikṣāpada*.
As above. Fifth:
one must not defecate or urinate on all four sides of a Buddha-stūpa such that a foul odor enters [the interior];
this is a *śaikṣāpada*. As above.
Sixth: One must not carry an image of the Buddha to places for defecation or urination; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense, as explained above.

There are three circumstances under which there is no offense: if one has such an illness; if the path necessarily passes through those areas; or if one is being taken away by force by another person. In these cases, there is no offense.
7. One must not chew a tooth-stick beneath a Buddha-stūpa; this is a *śaikṣādharmā*.
As above. 8.
One must not chew a tooth-stick facing a Buddha-stūpa; this is a *śaikṣādharmā*.
As above. Ninth:
One must not chew tooth-sticks within four cubits of a Buddha stupa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense. As above.
80. One must not spit or sneeze beneath a Buddha-stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
As above. 81.
One must not spit or sneeze toward a Buddha-stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
As above. Second:
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spat on all four sides of the Buddha’s stūpa.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they reproached them, saying:
"How can you spit on all four sides of the stūpa?
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, as described above regarding their initial transgression of the precepts.
He addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not spit or snot on the four sides of a stūpa; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
If a bhikṣu intentionally spits on the four sides of a stūpa, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, or even for a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where there is such an illness, or when a large bird carries [the object] and places it near a stūpa, or when it is blown away by the wind.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stretched out their legs toward the stūpa.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked them. They then went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, up to the point of their initial transgression as described above. Having done so, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
A certain bhikṣu, being doubtful, did not dare to stretch out his legs toward the interior of a stūpa.
