"If there is an intervening partition, it is permitted.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
One must not sit with legs extended toward a stūpa; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense."
If a bhikṣu intentionally extends his legs toward a stūpa, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, down to a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or if there is an intervening barrier, or if one is held by force.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kosala toward the brahmin village of Todeyya.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus placed the Buddha’s stūpa in a lower room and resided in an upper room.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six. They then went to the World-Honored One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, [recounting their faults] down to their initial transgression of the precepts.

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the tenfold benefits and so forth, until the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'One must not reside in an upper room while having placed a Buddha-stūpa in a lower room; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense.'"
If a bhikṣu intentionally causes a Buddha-stūpa to be placed in a lower room and then resides in an upper room, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣuṇī, down to a śrāmaṇera or śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, at a time when such an illness occurs, one places the Buddha-stūpa in a lower room and stays in an upper room.
There is no offense in cases of danger to life or danger to the holy life.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was promulgated, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
If five people are seated while one is standing, one must not preach the Dharma to them; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As stated above, because of such uncertainty, they did not dare to preach the Dharma to the sick.
The Buddha said:
"I permit it.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"One must not preach the Dharma while standing to a person who is seated, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense.
If a bhikṣu intentionally preaches the Dharma while standing to a person who is seated, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense for violating the rules of decorum;
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when one has such an illness; or when one is seized and detained by a king or a royal minister.
There is also no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
If six persons are lying down and one is sitting, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As stated above:
if seven persons are seated and one is not seated, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As stated above:
if eight persons are seated on high seats while one is seated on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense.
As above. If nine people are walking ahead and one is behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense. As above.
If ninety people are on a high walking path and one is on a lower walking path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇa* offense.
As stated above:
if there are ninety-one persons on the path while one is not on the path, one should not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti*.
As above. Second:
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus walked along the road holding hands, or they obstructed men and women.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; though they claim for themselves, 'We know the True Dharma,' [they act otherwise]."
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
Walking along the road hand-in-hand like kings, royal ministers, or wealthy and noble elders.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus. They then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with their heads at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, [proceeding] up to the original transgression of the precepts:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should speak thus:
'One must not walk along a road with hands joined; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense.'"
If a bhikṣu does so intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
because it was intentional, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If he does not do so intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, down to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where there is such an illness, or when a bhikṣu suffers from impaired vision and requires assistance; in these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was observing the summer retreat atop a large tree; he would descend from the tree to relieve himself.
At that moment, the tree deity became enraged and, watching for an opportunity, sought to sever his life-faculty.
At that time, the bhikṣus heard of this and, having censured him with disapproval, went to inform the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, as before, rebuked that one bhikṣu, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the precepts]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How can you defecate and urinate upon a tree?
Having rebuked them, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must not observe the rainy-season retreat upon trees, nor may you defecate or urinate around a tree."
"If there was already a place for excrement and urine previously, there is no offense in voiding excrement or urine [there].
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man!"

Regarding various instances of outflows (*āsrava*), this is the first offense of transgressing the precepts. From this day forward, I shall establish a training rule for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One must not climb a tree higher than a person; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmāpatti* (an offense requiring training)."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣus.
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling through the country of Kośala when they encountered wild beasts on the road. Terrified, they climbed trees as high as a man and thought to themselves:
"The Blessed One has established a precept forbidding us from climbing trees higher than a man."
"If one does not dare to go higher than that, one will immediately be harmed by wild beasts.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to climb trees higher than a person's height in cases of danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya)."
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
"One must not climb a tree higher than a person, except when there is a specific reason; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
If a bhikṣu intentionally climbs a tree higher than a person, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense that requires confession.
If committed intentionally, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of improper conduct);
if not committed intentionally, one incurs a *dukkaṭa*.
For bhikṣuṇīs, as well as śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases such as when one has such an illness, or when there is danger to life or danger to the holy life; climbing a tree higher than a person's height is not an offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Baddhananda placed his bowl inside a netted bag, fastened it to the head of a staff, and carried it upon his shoulder.
When the lay devotees saw him, they thought he was a government official; they all stepped off the road to avoid him and watched from a secluded spot, only then realizing it was Baddhananda.
At that time, the laypeople all spoke with reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; how can they carry their bowls in netted bags slung over their shoulders as they walk along the road?"
"It is as if an official were here, making me leave the road to avoid him.
At that time, a bhikṣu heard this, rebuked him, and went to inform the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Upananda, saying:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you carry a net-bag containing your bowl suspended from the head of your staff over your shoulder as you walked, causing the laypeople to leave the road to avoid you?"
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This foolish man! Among the many bases for outflows, this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"One must not carry a bowl placed in a net-bag, suspended from the head of a staff over one's shoulder while walking; this is a *śaikṣādharmā*."
If a bhikṣu does so intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense requiring confession;
because it was done intentionally, he also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense of improper conduct (*anācāra*).
If he does not do so intentionally, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, down to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or is coerced by those using force, or is bound, or faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya).
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus preached the Dharma to those who were disrespectful and carrying staves.
When the other bhikṣus heard of this, they rebuked them as described above and went to inform the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, having rebuked them as above, addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣus, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a person is carrying a staff, one should not preach the Dharma to them; this is a śaikṣa-dharmā.'"
He was hesitant and did not dare to preach the Dharma to a sick person who was holding a staff.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense in preaching to a sick person."
From this day forward, I establish a precept for the bhikṣus:
one must not preach the Dharma to a person who carries a staff and shows no respect, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā*.
If a bhikṣu intentionally preaches the Dharma to one who carries a staff, he commits a *tūlīyā* offense requiring confession (*pratideśanīya*).
Because it was done intentionally, he commits a *tūlīyā* offense of improper conduct (*adharma-vinaya*);
if it was not done intentionally, he commits a *tūlīyā* offense.
For bhikṣuṇīs, down to śrāmaṇeras and śrāmaṇerīs, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in cases where one has such an illness, or when acting for the sake of a king or a high minister.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
One should not preach the Dharma to six types of people who carry swords, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇa* (an offense requiring training).
As above. One should not preach the Dharma to seven persons holding spears, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣādhikaraṇīya* offense. As above.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a knife, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense, as stated above.
One should not preach the Dharma to a person holding a parasol, except in the case of illness; this is a *śaikṣa-dharmā* offense.

As above, the hundred [rules] are concluded. These seven methods for settling disputes are as follows; these seven methods for repentance are recited every half-month during the recitation of the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.

If any matter of dispute arises, it should be immediately extinguished: if the *saṃmukha-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties) should be applied, then the *saṃmukha-vinaya* shall be applied.
Where the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted, the *smṛtivinaya* shall be granted;
where the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) should be granted, the *amūḍhavinaya* shall be granted;
where the *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by confession) should be granted, the *pratijñākāraka* shall be granted.
If one should be granted the *tassapāpiyasikā* (formal act for the worse), one should grant the *tassapāpiyasikā*;
if one should be granted the *yebhuyyasika* (formal act by a majority), one should grant the *yebhuyyasika*;

Second Division: 1. The Dharma of the Bhikṣuṇī Precepts; The Eight Pārājika Dharmas. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Gabled Lecture Hall on the banks of the Monkey River in Vaiśālī.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, compiled from ten points of significance:

first, to bring the Saṃgha together; second, to cause the Saṃgha to rejoice; third, to cause the Saṃgha to dwell in peace and happiness; fourth, to inspire faith in those who have not yet believed; fifth, to increase the faith of those who already believe; sixth, to bring those who are difficult to discipline into submissiveness; seventh, to grant peace and happiness to those who possess a sense of shame and remorse; eighth, to sever the outflows (āsrava) of the present; ninth, to sever the outflows of the future; and tenth, to ensure that the True Dharma endures for a long time."
One who wishes to recite the precepts should speak thus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī commits sexual misconduct and engages in impure conduct, even with an animal, this bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense and is no longer in communion."

Regarding "a bhikṣuṇī": this refers to one who is a bhikṣuṇī by name, a bhikṣuṇī in appearance, a bhikṣuṇī by self-claim, a bhikṣuṇī by the "Welcome" (Svāgata) formula, a bhikṣuṇī by begging for alms, a bhikṣuṇī who wears the cut-and-sewn robes (khaṇḍa-cīvara), a bhikṣuṇī who has destroyed the fetters (āsrava-kṣaya), and a bhikṣuṇī who has received the full ordination (upasaṃpadā) through a formal act of fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma and attained her status.

Among these, a bhikṣuṇī is one who has received the full ordination through the formal procedure of the fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman) in accordance with the Dharma, has attained her standing, and abides within the discipline of a bhikṣuṇī; this is the meaning of "bhikṣuṇī."
Regarding the commission of unchaste conduct or impure acts, even with an animal: the "place where sexual intercourse can be performed" refers to such locations.

As for *pārājika*, it is like a person whose head has been severed who cannot rise again; a bhikṣuṇī is likewise. Once she has committed a *pārājika* offense, she no longer remains a bhikṣuṇī; therefore, it is called *pārājika*.
What is meant by "not living together"? There are two forms of not living together:
first, regarding formal acts (*kamma*);
second, regarding the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). That bhikṣuṇī is not permitted to participate in these two matters; therefore, it is called "not living together."
There are three locations for engaging in sexual intercourse that constitute a *pārājika* offense:
a human, a non-human, or an animal. To engage in sexual intercourse with any of these three constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
Furthermore, one commits a *pārājika* offense by engaging in sexual intercourse with three kinds of males:
a human male, a non-human male, or a male animal; by engaging in sexual intercourse with these three types of beings, one commits a *pārājika*.

If one engages in sexual intercourse with those possessing the two sexual organs (ubhatovyañjanaka) of three types—human ubhatovyañjanakas, non-human ubhatovyañjanakas, or animal ubhatovyañjanakas—one commits a *pārājika* offense; engaging in sexual intercourse with those possessing the two sexual organs in these three locations constitutes a *pārājika*.
If one engages in sexual intercourse with three kinds of eunuchs, one commits a *pārājika* offense:
with a human eunuch, a non-human eunuch, or an animal eunuch; engaging in sexual intercourse in these three instances constitutes a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with lustful intent, grasps a human male organ and places it in three locations—
the anus, the urinary tract, or the mouth— it constitutes an offense if it enters;
if it does not enter, there is no offense.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, whether there is an obstruction on one side and not on the other, or no obstruction on either side—in all such cases, it is a *pārājika*.
The same applies to non-human males, male animals, hermaphrodites, and eunuchs.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, takes hold of a sleeping man or a dead man whose body is not yet decomposed or is only slightly decomposed, and inserts his male organ into her three orifices—if it enters, she commits an offense;
if it does not enter, she does not commit an offense.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, whether there is an obstruction on one side and not on the other, or no obstruction on either side—this constitutes a *pārājika*.
The same applies as above for non-human males, male animals, hermaphrodites, and eunuchs.
If a bhikṣuṇī is seized by bandits and taken to a man, and he inserts his male organ into her three places—
experiencing pleasure upon initial entry, pleasure after entry, and pleasure at the time of withdrawal— she commits a pārājika offense.
If there is pleasure upon first entry, pleasure after entry, but no pleasure at the time of exit, it is a *pārājika*.
If there is pleasure upon first entry, no pleasure after entry, but pleasure at the time of exit, it is a *pārājika*.
If one finds pleasure at the initial entry, but finds no pleasure once inside and finds no pleasure upon exiting, it is a *pārājika*.
If one finds no pleasure at the initial entry, finds no pleasure once inside, but finds pleasure upon exiting, it is a *pārājika*.

If at the beginning there is no pleasure, during entry there is pleasure, and at the time of exit there is pleasure, it is a *pārājika*; this is the sixth case.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, and whether there is no obstruction or no obstruction, it is also as stated above.
For non-human males, male animals, hermaphrodites, and eunuchs—whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, and whether there is no obstruction or no obstruction—it is also as stated above.

If a bhikṣuṇī is seized by bandits and brought before a sleeping man, or before a dead body that is either uncorrupted or slightly corrupted, and he inserts his male organ into her three places—the anus, the vagina, and the mouth—such that there is pleasure upon first insertion and pleasure after insertion, or even if there is no pleasure upon first insertion or pleasure after insertion, yet there is pleasure at the time of withdrawal, it is also as described above.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, up to neither obstruction nor non-obstruction, it is also as stated above.
This applies even to eunuchs, as stated above;
whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, up to neither obstruction nor non-obstruction, it is also as stated above.

If a bhikṣuṇī is seized by bandits and engages in sexual intercourse at the three locations—whether there is pleasure upon entry, pleasure after entry, and pleasure at the time of exit; or even if there is no pleasure upon entry, no pleasure after entry, but pleasure at the time of exit—the cases are all as described above.
Whether there is an obstruction or no obstruction, up to the case of neither obstruction nor non-obstruction, it is also as stated above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, through expedient means, intends to commit an impure act, if she carries it out, it is a pārājika;
if she does not carry it out, it is a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣu uses skillful means to instruct a bhikṣuṇī to commit sexual misconduct, the one who carries it out commits a sthūlātyaya;

If a bhikṣuṇī instructs a bhikṣuṇī to commit sexual misconduct, the one who carries it out commits a sthūlātyaya.
If one does not perform it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
With the exception of monks and nuns, if one instructs others, whether they perform it or not, it is entirely a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a pārājika offense;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense resulting in expulsion.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one is asleep and unconscious; if one knows and does not experience pleasure; or if one has a mind entirely free from desire—there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who has not yet had the precept formulated, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.

"This refers to physical contact.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"With a defiled mind" means that the mind is characterized by passionate attachment.
The same applies to a man with a defiled mind.
"Below the armpits" refers to the parts of the body below the armpits;
"above the knees" refers to the parts of the body above the knees.
The body extends from the toes up to the hair of the head.

"Pushing" means to push away.

"Downward stroking" (*anumardana*) means from the top to the bottom.
"Lifting" means to lift up by embracing.
"Lowering" means to embrace from below, or to sit together, or to stand together.

If a man, perceiving another as a man, touches a nun’s body with his own body, clothing, or ornaments, and with a mind of lustful attachment experiences the pleasure of touch without moving his body, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If a man perceives a man and, with a mind of lustful attachment, touches his body and experiences the pleasure of touch though not moving his body, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.

If it is a male and one suspects [it to be so], it is a *duṣkṛta*.

"If they comply with these words, it is well;

"Do not abandon [your position]," [it is likewise an offense].
If the Saṃgha carries out a formal reprimand against her, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if they do not carry out the reprimand, it is a duṣkṛta. If a bhikṣuṇī says:
"Do not abandon [the offense].
If the Saṃgha pronounces a formal reprimand (tarjanīya-karman), it is a sthūlātyaya;
if they do not pronounce a reprimand, it is a duṣkṛta.

saying, "Do not abandon [the robe]," whether they are rebuked or not rebuked, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;

There is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

When the bhikṣuṇī heard of this, she thought to herself:
"While I was away on my travels, they have immediately given away my vihāra to another."
Then that bhikṣuṇī immediately returned to the vihāra and said to the brahmin maiden,
"Keep away from me!
Do not stay in my vihāra."
The brahmin woman replied:
"This is indeed your vihāra, built for you by a donor;
yet when you went forth to wander among the people, you took it and gave it to me, so that I am now unable to leave."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī became angry and immediately dragged her out.
Thereupon, the female brahmin went to the magistrate and spoke.
The magistrates then summoned the bhikṣuṇī; however, the bhikṣuṇī hesitated and would not go, thinking to herself:
"The Blessed One has established a precept that one must not go to a judge to engage in litigation.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, if anyone calls for you, you should go.
At that time, those bhikṣuṇīs went to the place of the judges. The judges asked them:
“Sister! What is this matter? Please explain it well.”
The bhikṣuṇī replied: "All this land belongs to the king;
domestic affairs belong to the householder; the dwelling belongs to the donor; and the same applies to the beds, seats, and bedding."
To repair and maintain dwellings so that the Saṃgha may reside therein brings great merit. Why is this?
Because by such an act, they enable me to dwell in peace.
The judges replied, "As the noble lady has said:
all land belongs to the king, household affairs belong to the householder, the dwelling belongs to the donor, and the same applies to the beds, seats, and bedding."
To repair and maintain dwellings so that the Sangha may reside there brings great merit. Why is this?
Because by such giving, they enable me to dwell in peace.
"Now this vihāra should be given to the female brahmin so that she may dwell there.
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has spoken incorrectly, and the judge has also answered incorrectly. Why is this?
What was given previously is the Dharma; what was given subsequently is not the Dharma."

At that time, when King Prasenajit heard the bhikṣuṇī speak thus, the judges answer thus, and the World-Honored One speak thus, the king punished the judges, and their wealth and property were all confiscated by the state.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, the precepts should be recited in this manner:..."

If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the authorities and accuses a householder, a householder’s son, a slave, or a hired laborer, whether by day or by night, for even a single moment, a snap of the fingers, or a brief instant, that bhikṣuṇī commits an offense of the first category requiring relinquishment, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"To quarrel" means to go before government officials to dispute right and wrong together.
A "householder" (gṛhapati) is one who has not left the household life.
A "son" is one born to a householder;
a "slave" is one either purchased or born into the household;
a "hired laborer" is one employed for work by means of payment.
The female brahmin is one who has gone forth outside of this Dharma.

If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a person—whether a householder, a householder’s son, a slave, or a hired laborer—and whether by day or by night, for the duration of a single thought-moment, a finger-snap, or a brief interval, it is as when the female brahmin went to the authorities and proclaimed her case.
If a judge commits an act by hand, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If he speaks it verbally without specifying the name [of the person], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*. This is called an offense. There is no offense if one is summoned;

or if one wishes to make a report; or if one is taken away by force; or if one is taken away while being bound; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Even if one speaks aloud but does not inform the authorities, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the fourth [section]. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī on the bank of the Monkey River, in the Gabled Hall.

At that time, there was a Licchavi woman who went out to play; she was accompanied by a female thief from among the crowd, who waited for the moment they were enjoying themselves to steal their belongings and flee.
Then the women sent a messenger to inform the Licchavis:
"A female thief has taken our property and fled; we pray that you will seek her out for us.
Thereupon, the Licchavis dispatched men to search for her, with the instruction that she was to be killed as soon as she was found.
When the female bandit heard these words—
"Send people to search for her and kill her as soon as you find her"—
she immediately abandoned Vaiśālī and fled. She went to the city of Rājagṛha and arrived at the nunnery of the bhikṣuṇīs, where she spoke to the nuns, saying:
"I have faith and a longing for the life of renunciation.
Upon hearing this, the nuns immediately ordained her, granting her the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
When the Licchavis heard that this female thief had fled and gone to Rājagṛha, they went at once to inform King Bimbisāra of Magadha.
"There is a female thief here who has taken my women and property and fled to this place; I pray that Your Majesty will assist me in searching for her.
King Bimbisāra immediately commanded his attendants to conduct a search.
The attendants said to the King:
"There is a female thief who has already gone forth in the nuns' monastery to practice the Way.
When King Bimbisāra heard that a female thief had come there and that a bhikṣuṇī had ordained her to go forth and practice the Way, he was informed.
He immediately sent a messenger to say to the Licchavis:
"I have heard that there is a female thief in the nunnery who has already left the household life to practice the Way; I cannot speak of her."
At that time, all the Licchavis collectively reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they are all female thieves who outwardly claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"

"How can there be the True Dharma in this? You have ordained a female thief who should have been put to death and was known by many, allowing her to leave the household life and receive full ordination."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How could you ordain a female bandit and cause her to leave the household life to practice the Way?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not a compliant practice, and is something that should not be done."
“Knowing her to be a female thief, how could you allow her to go forth and receive full ordination?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked that bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This bhikṣuṇī has committed many sources of outflows; this is the first breach of the precepts.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains another woman who is a thief deserving of death and well-known to many, causing her to leave the household life and receive full ordination, that bhikṣuṇī commits an initial offense requiring forfeiture, a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, thieves from within the city went out to the villages, and thieves from the villages entered the city.

The bhikṣuṇīs did not know whether they were thieves or not, whether they deserved death or not, or whether they were known to others or not; only later did they realize they were thieves, that they deserved death, and that they were known to others. Some said they had committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, while others were doubtful.
The Buddha said:
"One who does not know is not at fault.
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing beforehand that a woman is a thief, one whose crime deserves death, and known to the public, should ordain her as a renunciant and grant her full ordination without having inquired of the king or his ministers, nor having inquired about her lineage, this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense entailing the first rule, which must be relinquished, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
A "thief" refers to one who steals five coins or more than five coins.
One "deserving death" is one who stands in the midst of execution.
"Known by many" means known by the king, known by the ministers, and known by the common people.
As for the king, he does not depend on others for his sustenance.
As for the ministers, they receive high positions from the king to assist in governing the affairs of state.
Regarding the clans: the Śākyas, the Koliyas, the Vṛjis, and the Malla-Somas.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is a thief, one whose crime deserves death, or one widely known to the public, ordains her into the religious life without first consulting the king, the ministers, or the clan, [she commits an offense].
If the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense for the preceptor;
if the second *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) has been completed, it is three *sthūlātyaya* offenses;
if the first *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-ekavācika-karman*) has been completed, it is two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If the formal announcement (*jñapti*) has been completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, prior to the announcement, one shaves the hair, grants the going-forth (*pravrajyā*), or grants the full ordination (*upasampadā*) while assembling the community of monks, all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If the assembly is full, it is likewise a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense if one does not know; or if it concerns the lineage of a king or a high minister; or if the crime would merit death but the king permits the person to go forth; or if there is a crime but permission to go forth is granted; or if one releases someone from bondage to allow them to go forth; or if one rescues and enables them to escape [bondage]—in these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The fifth section concludes. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Wei-ci had been formally censured by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions; yet she did not comply, and having committed an offense, she did not repent, so the Saṃgha had not yet granted her formal reintegration.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, without having informed the community of bhikṣuṇīs and without being authorized by the community, went outside the boundary on her own initiative and performed the *karmavācanā* for the absolution of offenses for Ucchya.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta ascetic virtues, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Steyānanandā, saying:

"How is it that when the community of nuns has, in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching, formally charged the bhikṣuṇī Ucchya, you do not comply, do not repent for your offense, and the Saṃgha has not yet granted you leave to dwell together?"
"The bhikṣuṇīs did not give instructions, yet you arbitrarily went outside the boundary to resolve their offenses?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Steunronanda:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, Thullanandā!

The community of nuns, acting in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as instructed by the Buddha, has formally censured the bhikṣuṇī Uttarā; yet she does not comply, does not repent for her offense, and the Saṃgha has not yet granted her leave to live together with them."
“Nun, you did not receive an appointment or instruction, yet you arbitrarily went outside the boundary to perform a *karmavācanā* for her to resolve her offense.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“In many ways, this is a source of outflows; this is the first instance of Steālanaṃdā’s transgression of the precepts.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, yet she does not comply, has not confessed her offense, and the Saṃgha has not yet performed the *karmavācanā* for her restoration to communal life."

Out of affection, if she does not consult the Saṃgha nor receive instructions from the Saṃgha, but instead goes outside the boundary to perform a *karmavācanā* to grant absolution for an offense, this nun commits an initial offense requiring forfeiture, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as stated above.

"Saṃgha" is as explained above. "Accused" (ud-dhṛta) refers to one who has been formally charged by the Saṃgha through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations).
The Dharma is that which accords with the Dharma, accords with the Vinaya, and accords with what the Buddha has taught.
One who does not comply with it does not practice the methods for the punishment of offenses established by the Buddha.
One who does not repent does not confess their offense to others.
"Those with whom one has not yet established communal residence" refers to those who have been formally accused by the Saṃgha but whose offenses have not yet been absolved.

Out of favoritism, one does not consult the Saṃgha, nor does the Saṃgha issue an injunction; instead, one goes outside the boundary and performs a formal ritual (kamma) to grant absolution for the offense. When the three proclamations (ñatti) are completed, it constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
When the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (motion with one proclamation) is completed, there are three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
When the *jñapti-ekakaraṇa-karman* (motion with one motion) is completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
When the *jñapti* (motion) alone is completed, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the assembly has gathered before the announcement but the quorum is not yet reached, all are guilty of a *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who has informed the Saṃgha, or if they have been enjoined by the Saṃgha, or if they can humble their mind and repent for the original offense; or if the Saṃgha, out of anger, does not grant absolution from the offense while that person grants it—there is no offense.

If the original community has already performed the *karmavācanā* for him, and that community subsequently moves away, dies, travels far, abandons the path, is taken away by bandits, or is swept away by water, and he is then released from his offense, there is no transgression.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the sixth [section]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, alone, lifted her robe high as she crossed from this bank to the other.
This bhikṣuṇī was of beautiful appearance; at that time, a bandit saw her and set his mind upon her. Once she had finished crossing the water, he seized her and attempted to violate her.
When the laypeople saw this, they all reproached her together, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame or modesty; she practices impure conduct, yet outwardly she claims, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
“Thus, she travels alone, lifting her robes high as she crosses the water, no different from a courtesan.
How can such a person possess the True Dharma?

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Cāmā had many disciples. Not far from that monastery was a village where she had relatives; on account of some minor business, she left the community and entered the village alone. When the laypeople saw her, they said to one another:
"The reason this Bhikṣuṇī Kṣema wanders alone is simply because she desires a man.
That bhikṣuṇī then stayed overnight alone in that village and did not return. The laypeople spoke again:
"The reason she stays overnight alone is precisely because she needs a man."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, along with Thullanandā and a large number of other bhikṣuṇīs, were traveling through the wilderness of the Kosalā country.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā were constantly walking alone behind [the others] along the side of the road.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw them, they said: "Sisters!..."
"Why do you walk behind us instead of accompanying us?
They replied, "You should simply go on your own way; what concern is this of yours?"
They immediately asked,
"Have you not heard that the Buddha has established a precept that we should travel together in groups?
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs and Steya-nandā replied:
"Do you not know me? They replied, "We do not."
They replied, “The reason we walk behind is that we wish to obtain a man. When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this,

those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured those bhikṣuṇīs.
“How is it that a bhikṣuṇī crosses water with her robes hitched high, travels alone to a village, stays overnight alone, or walks behind her companion?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked that bhikṣuṇī:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"What is this, bhikṣuṇī? Why do you cross water alone with your robes hitched high, travel alone to a village, stay overnight alone while traveling with companions, or walk behind alone?
Having thus rebuked that bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed many things that are sources of outflows; this is her first offense against the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī crosses water alone, enters a village alone, stays overnight alone, or walks behind alone, she commits an initial offense requiring forfeiture, a saṃghāvaśeṣa.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above. Regarding "water":

if it is a river that one cannot cross alone, that bhikṣuṇī must seek out another bhikṣuṇī to cross with her; the bhikṣuṇī should gradually lift her robes, enter the water, and wait for her companion.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the water hurriedly so that her companions cannot catch up, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If, upon entering the water, she raises her robe according to the depth of the water to wait for her companions, there is no offense; however, if she enters the water hurriedly without waiting for her companions, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one reaches the opposite bank and gradually lowers one's robes to wait for later companions, there is no offense.
However, if one intends to proceed quickly and does not gradually lower one's robes to go ashore, nor waits for later companions, it is a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
That bhikṣuṇī must seek out another bhikṣuṇī to accompany her when going to a village.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes alone to a village, wherever that village may be, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one goes alone to a desolate place where there is no path and travels for the duration of a single drum-beat, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one travels alone but has not yet reached a village, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one drum-beat is reduced [in duration], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
To walk alone within a single village boundary is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one seeks the means to go but does not go, or if one forms a group with the intent to go but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If that bhikṣuṇī sleeps together with another, they must remain within reach of each other’s outstretched hands; if that bhikṣuṇī sleeps alone such that her side touches the ground [without another being within reach], it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If she turns over, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

If two bhikṣuṇīs stay together overnight in a village, if they lie down such that their outstretched hands can reach one another, or if their outstretched hands cannot reach one another, for every single turn-over, there is a separate *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.

When those bhikṣuṇīs travel together on a road, they must not travel beyond the range of sight or hearing; if a bhikṣuṇī travels on a road beyond the range of sight or hearing, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If one leaves the place where [the act] was seen but does not leave the place where it was heard, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If one leaves the place where it was heard but does not leave the place where it was seen, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
For the bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if two bhikṣuṇīs cross a body of water together; when entering the water, they gradually lift their robes according to the depth of the water and wait for their companion to enter.
When departing, do not go too hurriedly, but wait for your companions; when stepping onto the shore, gradually lower your robes and wait for those who follow.
One may cross by means of supernormal power, or by boat;
one may cross by bridge, or by treading upon the beams.

If the companion bhikṣuṇī passes away, or leaves the religious life, or travels far away, or is taken away by bandits; or if there is danger to her life, or danger to her brahmacarya, or danger from wild beasts; or if she is taken away by those using force, or taken away while bound, or is swept away by water—there is no offense.

If two bhikṣuṇīs enter a village, and while they are in the midst of the village one companion bhikṣuṇī dies, or leaves the religious life, or travels far away, or is carried off by bandits, or is even swept away by water as described above, there is no offense.
If one stays overnight with two bhikṣuṇīs within reach of each other’s outstretched hands;

or if one bhikṣuṇī goes out to relieve herself of excrement or urine, or to receive or recite the scriptures, or for the sake of quietude to dwell alone and practice walking meditation (caṅkrama), or to cook soup, porridge, or rice for a sick bhikṣuṇī; or if she passes away, or leaves the monastic life, or travels far away, or is carried off by bandits, or even if she is swept away by water—in all these cases, as stated above, there is no offense.
If one travels together with two bhikṣuṇīs, remaining within sight and hearing of one another, there is no offense.
If one bhikṣuṇī goes out to relieve herself, or passes away, or leaves the monastic life, or is carried off by bandits, or even is swept away by water—as in the cases above—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The seventh section concludes. *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle 22. [Fascicle 23, Part 2 of 2: Clarifying the Rules of Discipline for Bhikṣuṇīs.]
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian and others, following the remainder of the Seventeen Saṃghāvaśeṣa Dharmas:
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī; at that period, grain was extremely scarce and expensive, making it difficult to obtain almsfood.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who entered the city to beg for food and returned with an empty bowl.

Then, at the proper time, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā-Nandā put on her robes, took up her bowl, and entered the city to beg for food; she gradually arrived at the house of a merchant and stood there in silence.
The bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā was of handsome appearance; when a merchant saw her, his mind became attached to her, and he immediately went up to her and asked, "Auntie!..."
"What do you seek? He replied,
"I wish to beg for food."
He said, "Give me the bowl. He then gave him the bowl.
He filled his bowl to the brim with rice and stew and gave it to the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā.
Thereafter, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā repeatedly went to the houses of merchants, putting on her robes and carrying her bowl, and stood there in silence.
He asked again: "Venerable lady! What do you seek?"
He replied, "I wish to beg for food.
The other immediately filled his bowl to the brim with rice and soup and handed it to him.

other bhikṣuṇīs should admonish those bhikṣuṇīs,
saying: "Sisters!..."
"You all should not associate with one another, engage in evil conduct together, spread an evil reputation together, or conceal each other's offenses.
If you do not associate with one another, engage in evil conduct together, or spread an evil reputation together, you will attain increase, benefit, and dwell in peace within the Buddha-dharma."
"You should all abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after being rebuked and admonished by the Saṃgha.
If they comply with these words, it is well; if they do not comply, a formal announcement (jñapti) shall be made.
Having made the announcement, one should say: "Sister!
I have finished the announcement; there remains the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). You should desist from this matter, lest you be rebuked by the Saṃgha and again commit a grave offense."
"If she complies with these words, it is well; if she does not comply, the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) shall be performed.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should speak to her again: 'Sister!'"
The first *karmavācanā* has already been completed; two remain. You should relinquish this matter, lest you be censured and exhorted by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
"If she complies with these words, it is well; if she does not comply, you should perform two *karmavācanās*.
Having performed the two *karmavācanās*, you should say to her: 'Sister!'"

The second *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* has been completed; there remains only one *karman*. You should relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked and exhorted by the Saṃgha and again commit a grave offense.
If she complies with what is said, it is well; if she does not comply, and after the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If she desists after the *jñapti* has been made and two *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is three *sthūlātyaya*s.
If one abandons [the offense] after the motion has been made and the first *karmavācanā* (formal act) is completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one abandons it after the motion has been made, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one abandons it before the motion is completed, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If, before having announced [the offense], they associate with one another and commit evil deeds such that an evil reputation spreads, it is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) for all.
For a bhikṣu, it is an offense according to what was committed;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense if, at the first instance of speaking, one desists; or if the admonition and exhortation is carried out by an illegal separate assembly; or by an illegal united assembly; or by a legal separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-law separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-law united assembly; or if the admonition and exhortation is illegal, contrary to the Vinaya, and not taught by the Buddha; or if no admonition or exhortation is performed at all. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The fourteenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, after the bhikṣuṇī Soma-Pāpīyā had been admonished by the Saṃgha, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā instructed her, saying:
"You should all live together!"

Why is this? I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, associating with one another, committing evil deeds together, spreading an evil reputation together, and concealing each other’s offenses; because of their anger toward you, the Saṃgha has instructed you to live separately.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, saying:
"The Saṃgha has already issued a formal reprimand against the bhikṣuṇī Somā Bhāradvājī; why do you instruct her to say:
'Do not live separately!'"?
Why is this? I have also seen that these bhikṣuṇīs associate closely with one another, commit evil deeds, spread an evil reputation, and cover for each other’s offenses.
Out of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to live separately.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"The Saṃgha has issued a formal admonition against the bhikṣuṇī Somā Bhāradvājī; why did you instruct her to speak in such a manner?"
"You all must not dwell apart;
you should dwell together. Why is this?"

"I also see that these bhikṣuṇīs live together, engage in evil conduct, and spread an evil reputation, while mutually concealing their offenses; therefore, out of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to live separately."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs to perform a formal act of censure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against the group of six and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā."
One should reprimand them in this manner.
Among the community of nuns, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!..."
The Saṃgha has issued a formal admonition to these six groups of bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, instructing them to say:
"Do not live separately!
You should dwell together. Why is this?
For I have also seen various bhikṣuṇīs associating with one another, engaging in evil conduct together, spreading an evil reputation together, and covering for each other’s offenses.
"Because of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you all to dwell separately.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant a formal reprimand to the group of six bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā for the sake of relinquishing this matter:
"Do not speak such words as these:"
"Do not dwell apart!
You should dwell together! Nor should you say:
"I also see that these bhikṣuṇīs associate with one another, commit evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation, and cover for each other's offenses.
Out of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to live separately."

"Now there are precisely these two bhikṣuṇīs who are close associates, who together commit evil deeds, whose evil reputation has spread abroad, and who conceal each other's offenses; there are no others."

If these bhikṣuṇīs do not associate with one another and do not engage in evil conduct that causes an evil reputation to spread, they will experience growth and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
These Bhikṣuṇīs of the group of six, together with the Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, have been admonished by the Sangha regarding the Bhikṣuṇī Somā Babbhī, yet they instruct her to speak in this manner:..."
“Do not live separately! You should live together.
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs who, living in close association with one another, engage in evil conduct, spread an evil reputation, and cover for each other’s offenses.”
"Because of anger, the Saṃgha instructed you all to live separately.
The Saṃgha now performs a formal reprimand against the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā for the purpose of making them abandon this matter:
'You must not live separately!'"
"You should dwell together! Do not say:
'I have also seen the bhikṣuṇīs associating with one another, committing evil deeds together, and spreading an evil reputation, while covering for each other's offenses.'"
"Because of anger, the Saṃgha instructed you all to live separately.
Now there are precisely these two bhikṣuṇīs who remain close to one another, commit evil deeds, spread an evil reputation, and conceal each other's offenses; there are no others besides them.
"If these bhikṣuṇīs do not associate with one another, there will be increase in the Buddha-dharma and they will dwell in peace and happiness.
Sisters, those of you who consent to the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā to abandon this matter, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise spoken.

"The Saṃgha has finished admonishing the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, commanding them to relinquish this matter. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such."
The Saṃgha completed the formal ritual of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprimand the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If there are other bhikṣuṇīs who act in this manner, the Saṃgha should likewise perform for them the formal ritual of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of reprimand to cause them to abandon this matter."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is formally admonishing her, instructs another bhikṣuṇī to say:
'Do not live separately from them!'"
We shall dwell together.
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs not dwelling apart, but dwelling together, engaging in evil conduct, having an evil reputation spread abroad, and mutually concealing their offenses.
"The Sangha has instructed you to live separately because of their anger.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that other bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!..."
Do not instruct other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"You should not live separately!
For I have seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, engaging in evil conduct together, and having their evil reputations spread abroad while covering for one another's offenses."
"Because of anger, the Saṃgha instructed you to live separately.
Now there are exactly these two bhikṣuṇīs who live together, commit evil deeds together, spread an evil reputation together, and conceal each other's offenses; there are no others besides them.
"If this bhikṣuṇī lives separately, she will find increase and dwell in peace and happiness within the Buddha-dharma.
When these bhikṣuṇīs admonish that bhikṣuṇī, if she persists and does not relinquish her position, those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times to cause her to relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes [the offense] after up to three admonitions, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, this bhikṣuṇī has committed a third offense that must be relinquished, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Saṃgha" is as defined above.
When the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha is performing a formal reprimand and admonition, if other bhikṣuṇīs instruct them to say:
"Do not live separately!"
"You should dwell together.
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs dwelling in close association with one another, engaging in evil conduct together, spreading an evil reputation together, and covering for each other's offenses."
"Because of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to dwell separately.
That bhikṣuṇī then admonished the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "Sisters!..."
Do not instruct other bhikṣuṇīs by saying:
"You should not live separately;
you should live together."
I have also seen other bhikṣuṇīs who associate with one another, engage in evil conduct together, spread an evil reputation among themselves, and conceal their offenses from one another.
Out of anger, the Saṃgha has instructed you to live separately.
"Now there are only these two bhikṣuṇīs and no others.

You have been associating with one another, committing evil deeds together, spreading an evil reputation together, and covering for each other's offenses. If these bhikṣuṇīs were to live separately, there would be increase and peaceful dwelling within the Buddha-dharma."
"You should now abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after being rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, a formal announcement (jñapti) shall be made.
Having performed the formal announcement (*jñapti*), one should say: "Sister!
I have finished the announcement; there remains the formal act (*karman*). You should relinquish this matter."
"If you comply with these words, it is well; if you do not comply, the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) shall be performed.
When the first *karmavācanā* has been completed, you should be told:
'The first formal motion has been concluded; two more remain. You should abandon this matter, lest you be censured and exhorted by the Saṃgha and again commit a grave offense.'"
"If she complies with what is said, it is well; if she does not comply, you should perform two *karmas*.
Having performed the two *karmas*, you should say to her: 'Sister!'"

The second *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* has been completed; there remains only one *karman*. You should relinquish this matter, lest you be rebuked and exhorted by the Saṃgha and further commit a grave offense.
"If one complies with the instruction, it is well; if one does not comply, once the three *karmavācanās* are completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If one desists after the second *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) is completed, it is three *sthūlātyayās*."
If one relinquishes after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā* have been completed, there are two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one relinquishes after the motion has been made, there is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one relinquishes before the motion is completed, there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
Before she had announced it, he said:
"Do not live separately!
I too have seen other bhikṣuṇīs living together, engaging in evil conduct, having their ill repute spread abroad, and mutually concealing their offenses."
"The Saṃgha, out of anger, has instructed you to live separately.
This constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense for all involved.
If there is such a bhikṣuṇī, and while the Saṃgha is performing the formal admonition against her, if there is a bhikṣu who instructs [the others] to say:
"Do not abandon it.
If one reprimands [the offender], it is a sthūlātyaya;
if one does not reprimand, it is a duṣkṛta.
If a bhikṣuṇī instructs,
"Do not abandon it," or if she rebukes [the offender], it is a sthūlātyaya.
If one has not yet rebuked them, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

This is called an offense. There is no offense if one desists at the first word; or if the censure is carried out by an illegal separate assembly; or by an illegal united assembly; or by a legal separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-dharma separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-dharma united assembly; or if the censure is contrary to the Dharma and the Vinaya and not taught by the Buddha; or if there is no censure at all. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the fifteenth [section]. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, on account of some trivial matter, became angry and displeased, and spoke these words:
"We renounce the Buddha; we renounce the Dharma; we renounce the Saṃgha."
"It is not only we, the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life; we may also practice the holy life under them."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you, for the sake of such a trivial matter, become so angry and displeased as to speak these words:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha'?"
"It is not only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life (brahmacarya); we may also practice the holy life under them."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you, for the sake of a mere trifle, out of anger and displeasure, speak such words as this?"
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, and I renounce the Saṃgha.
It is not only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life; we may also practice the holy life under them."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) to reprimand the group of six bhikṣuṇīs for the purpose of making them abandon this matter."
One should issue such a reprimand.
Among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs, on account of even a minor matter, became resentful and displeased, and immediately spoke these words:
"We renounce the Buddha, we renounce the Dharma, we renounce the Saṅgha."
"It is not only these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, that exist!
There are also other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life; we may also practice the holy life under them."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now reprove the group of six bhikṣuṇīs regarding this matter: 'Sisters!
Do not, on account of some minor matter, become angry and displeased, and then speak such words.'"
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, and I renounce the Saṅgha.
It is not only these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
There are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life; we may also practice the holy life under them."
Thus it was announced.

"Whichever of you sisters approves of the Saṃgha’s censure of the group of six bhikṣuṇīs for this matter and their relinquishing of it, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak."

The second and third are to be recited in the same manner.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal act of censure against the group of six bhikṣuṇīs for the relinquishing of this matter; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

After the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to rebuke the group of six bhikṣuṇīs for abandoning this matter, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is such a bhikṣuṇī, the Saṃgha shall perform a formal act of censure (*tajjanīya-karman*) consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).

From this day forward, I establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:"
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure over even a minor matter, should speak thus:
"I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṃgha.
There are not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya!"
"Furthermore, there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life (brahmacarya); we may also practice the holy life under them.
That bhikṣuṇī should then admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!..."
"Do not, out of anger and displeasure over a mere trifle, speak thus:
'I renounce the Buddha, I renounce the Dharma, I renounce the Saṅgha.
There are not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!'"
"Furthermore, there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who practice the holy life; we may also practice the holy life under them.
If, when these bhikṣuṇīs are admonishing that bhikṣuṇī, she persists and does not relinquish her position, those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times to make her relinquish this matter.
If she desists after up to three admonitions, it is well;
if she does not desist, this bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving the three rules that must be relinquished, which is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

There are not only these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!"

You should abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense again after having been rebuked by the Saṃgha.
"If you comply with these words, it is well; if you do not comply, a formal motion (jñapti) shall be made.

"If [the monk] complies with these words, it is well; if he does not comply, the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) shall be performed.
Once the first *karmavācanā* has been performed, one should say to him:

"If you comply with these words, it is well; if you do not comply, a second *karmavācanā* shall be performed.
Once the second *karmavācanā* has been performed, you should be addressed again:
'I have completed the first of the two *karmavācanās*; one remains. You should abandon this matter, lest you be censured by the Sangha and further commit a grave offense.'"
"If she complies with what is said, it is well; if she does not comply, and the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
If she relinquishes [the offense] after the second *karmavācanā* has been completed, it is three *sthūlātyaya*s."
If one renounces [the offense] after the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the single proclamation (*karma-vācanā*) have been completed, it is two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one renounces it after the motion has been completed, it is one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If one renounces it before the motion has been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If the Saṃgha issues a formal reprimand, it is a sthūlātyaya;
