Part Two of the Thirty *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* Dharmas. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā had a donor; in the morning, she dressed, took her bowl, and went to his house, saying:
"I need ghee. He replied, "So be it."
He immediately bought it and gave it to him.
Having purchased the ghee and given it to him, he said:
"I do not need ghee; I need oil."
He replied, "It can be obtained.
He then went to a butter merchant's house and said:
“I do not need ghee; I need oil.
The man replied, “I shall take your ghee according to the procedure for purchasing ghee, and I shall give you oil according to the procedure for selling oil.”
That donor then spoke with reproach:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of satiety and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim for themselves, 'We understand the True Dharma.'"
"To seek ghee while asking for oil, or to seek oil while asking for ghee—how can such a thing be the True Dharma?
If one needs ghee, one should simply ask for ghee; if one needs oil, one should ask for oil; and if one needs anything else, one should ask for that very thing."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Steunānanandā, saying:
"How can you seek ghee while asking for oil, and seek oil while asking for ghee?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Stevanandā, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How can you seek ghee while asking for oil, or seek oil while asking for ghee?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā has committed many things that lead to outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī seeks this and then seeks that [in addition], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Wishing to seek this, yet seeking that" means that having sought ghee, one further seeks oil; having sought oil, one further seeks ghee.
If she seeks other items, it is likewise.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having sought this, then seeks that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

This *naiḥsargika* article must be relinquished to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, or to many individuals, or to a single person; it must not be relinquished to a separate group. If it is relinquished [in such a manner], the relinquishment is invalid, and it is a *duṣkṛta*.

When one wishes to relinquish [the robe], one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, and after prostrating at the feet of the Saṃgha, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], having sought this and further sought that, have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*. I now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having relinquished it, one should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*), and only then accept the confession, making the announcement as follows:
“Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

This Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so requested this [item], and having requested it, further requested that other [item]; she has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: I shall accept the confession of the Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.”
The announcement is made as follows.
Having thus made the announcement, one should accept their confession and say to them:
"Reproach your own mind!"
She replied, “Yes.

The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha should then return the items relinquished by that Bhikṣuṇī; they should grant them by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) as follows.
Within the Saṃgha, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"May the noble Saṃgha listen!
This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so requested this [item] and then requested that other; she has committed an offense involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), and now she forfeits it to the Saṃgha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: I shall take this relinquished object and return it to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the motion.
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so requested this [item], and then requested that other; she has committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and now relinquishes it to the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha take these relinquished items and return them to the Bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
"Whichever sisters approve of the Sangha returning the items relinquished by the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
"The Sangha has approved the return of the items relinquished by the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so. Since the Sangha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If, after having relinquished an object, one does not return it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If, at the time of returning it, someone instructs one saying, "Do not return it," it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If one does not return it and instead makes it a pure gift (*pariśuddha-dāna*), or sends it to another person, or intentionally destroys it, or burns it, or converts it into something that is no longer the original object, or uses it repeatedly, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if: one requests ghee when ghee is needed, or oil when oil is needed; or if one requests other items when those other items are needed; or if one requests from a relative; or if one requests from a renunciant; or if one requests on behalf of another for their own sake; or if one obtains something without having requested it. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The nineteenth section concludes. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs were reciting the precepts in the open air. A lay follower saw them and asked, "Aunties!
Why are you reciting the precepts in the open air? Is there no hall for reciting the precepts?"
He replied, “No. [The Buddha asked,] “If you were given the funds for the hall, would you be able to build it?”
He replied, "I can.
He then provided him with materials for constructing a hall for the recitation of the precepts.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"When it is time for us to recite the precepts, we simply take our seats and sit down to recite them.
Since bhikṣuṇī robes are difficult to obtain and one should possess the five robes, we might as well use these items to purchase clothing and share it among ourselves."
They immediately traded for the robes and divided them between them.
Later, on another occasion, while the bhikṣuṇīs were still reciting the precepts in the open air, a layperson saw them and asked:
"Why are you reciting the precepts in the open air? Is there no hall?"
He replied, "No. The householder said:
"What shall I do with the items for the *poṣadha* hall that I previously gave you?
He replied, "I have done nothing with them."
He asked again, "Why did you not do it? The bhikṣuṇī replied:

"We had this thought: 'Once we have reached our seats, we shall recite the precepts. Since it is difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain robes and they ought to possess the five robes, we might as well use these items to trade for robes.'"
"Immediately, they bartered these goods for clothing and divided them among themselves.
At that time, those laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they receive gifts without satiety, yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
What True Dharma is there in such a thing?
By trading the property of my monastery for cloth and sharing it out, do you mean to say that I did not know clothing is difficult to obtain and that one must possess the five robes?
"As the Buddha has taught, those who can create the foremost merit are they who build fine dwellings and offer them to the Sangha of the four directions.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you, having received material for a hall for the recitation of the precepts from a lay devotee, traded it for robes and divided them among yourselves?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it, bhikṣuṇīs! That you trade the materials for a hall belonging to a layperson for robes and divide them among yourselves?
Having rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a gift intended by a donor for the Saṃgha is for a specific purpose, diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

Regarding the specific case of a gift intended for the Saṃgha that is diverted: giving it to be used for a *poṣadha* hall when it was meant to be used for robes; giving it to be used for robes when it was meant to be used for a *poṣadha* hall; or giving it to be used for one place when it was intended for another.
The property of the Saṃgha is for the Saṃgha and belongs to the Saṃgha.
"Property of the Saṃgha" refers to that which has already been assigned to the Saṃgha.
"For the Saṃgha" refers to that which is being prepared for the Saṃgha but has not yet been assigned to them.
"Belonging to the Saṃgha" means it has already been promised to the Saṃgha or has already been relinquished to the Saṃgha.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a donor’s gift intended for the Saṃgha is for a specific purpose, diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha, whether it be a large group, a small group, or a single person; it may not be relinquished to a separate assembly. If it is relinquished [to such a group], the relinquishment is invalid, and there is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

When relinquishing [the robe] to the Saṃgha, one should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, and after prostrating at the feet of the monks, place the right knee on the ground and join the palms, speaking these words:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], have diverted for personal use the property designated by the Saṃgha for a specific purpose; I have committed an offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* and now relinquish it to the Saṃgha.
Having thus relinquished it, she should perform confession.
The person receiving the confession should first make a formal announcement (*jñapti*) and then accept the confession, making the announcement as follows:
"May the noble Sangha listen!

This bhikṣuṇī so-and-so, having received a gift intended for the Sangha, diverted it for other uses; she has committed an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*), and now she relinquishes it to the Sangha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall accept the confession of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement, one should then accept the confession.
One should say to that person:
"Reproach your own mind.
They will reply:

"Yes. The Saṃgha should then return this robe to the bhikṣuṇī by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), and it should be given in this manner.
Within the Saṃgha, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following proclamation (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, misappropriated a gift intended for the Sangha for another purpose; she has committed an offense entailing forfeiture and confession, and now she forfeits it to the Sangha."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent to return the robe to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so.
This is the formal motion.
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, having received a specific gift from the Saṃgha, diverted it for other uses; she has thus committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
She now forfeits it to the Saṃgha. Whichever of you, sisters, approves of the Saṃgha returning this robe to this Bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
“The Saṃgha has already consented to return the robe to the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If, after having relinquished the robe within the Saṃgha, one does not return it, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, upon returning, someone instructs one saying,
"Do not return," it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If one accepts [the robe] to make it into the five robes, or transforms it into a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*), or uses it for another purpose, or sends it to someone else, or intentionally destroys it, or burns it, or makes it into something other than a robe, or wears it repeatedly, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one asks the owner for permission and uses it according to the portion assigned;
or if, when giving the object, one says:
"Use it as you please."
"No offense. There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
[The twentieth section ends. At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā intended to come to Śrāvastī.

When the bhikṣuṇīs who had resided there for a long time heard that the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā was coming, they went from house to house to beg for alms and obtained a great quantity of wealth, food, and drink. When the appointed day arrived, however, that bhikṣuṇī did not arrive at all.
The resident bhikṣuṇīs said to one another:
"We had made an appointment with the bhikṣuṇī Anvaya to go together to Śrāvastī, yet she did not arrive."
"Robes for bhikṣuṇīs are difficult to obtain; we ought to prepare the five robes. We would rather take these goods, trade them for cloth, and share them.
They then made the five robes and divided them among themselves.
Later, at another time, the bhikṣuṇī Anvaya arrived in Śrāvastī.
When the night had passed and it was time, she put on her robes, took her bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food. Then the lay devotees saw her and asked:
"Auntie, what are you seeking?"
He replied, "I am begging for alms.
He asked again:
"Does the Sangha have no food? He replied,
"There is none."

On a later day, the lay devotee went to the former bhikṣuṇī and asked, "We previously each contributed goods for the purpose of providing for and supporting the bhikṣuṇī Ānanda; have you prepared food with them?"
He replied, "I have not. He asked again:
"Why did you not do so? He replied, "I had previously made an appointment with the bhikṣuṇī An-yin (Kṣemā) to come together to Śrāvastī, but she did not arrive."
We thought to ourselves:
"We had made an appointment with An-yin to go together to Śrāvastī, yet he did not arrive.
It is difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain robes; they ought to provide themselves with the five garments."
"We would rather trade these items for clothing and share them.
They then traded the items for clothing and shared it.
At that time, the householders all spoke in derision and reproach, saying: [text continues]
"These bhikṣuṇīs lack a sense of shame and remorse, and they receive gifts without satiety. Yet they claim for themselves externally:
'I know the True Dharma.
How can they first provide for the comfort of the bhikṣuṇīs by each contributing goods to prepare food and drink, and afterwards trade those items for robes to be shared among themselves?"
"In this way, what 'True Dharma' is there?

We also know that it is difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain clothing and that they ought to possess the five robes; however, the reason we give these is precisely to provide for their comfort and to supply them with food and drink as they travel afar."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:
"How is it that you, when a householder offers goods intended for the provision and comfort of bhikṣuṇīs by making food, instead trade them for robes and divide them among yourselves?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, bhikṣuṇīs! When a householder provides goods for the support and comfort of bhikṣuṇīs to prepare food, how can you instead trade them for robes and share them?
Having rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a nun receives a gift intended for one purpose but seeks it for herself or for the Saṃgha, and then diverts it for another use, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

Regarding the specific difference in what is given: if one gives food intended for clothing, or gives clothing intended for food, or if what was intended for one place is instead used for another place.
"Seeking for oneself" means seeking in various places.
"Property of the Saṃgha" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, for whom a gift was intended for one purpose, seeks it out for herself and diverts it for other uses belonging to the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha according to the aforementioned procedure; having relinquished it, one must confess as previously described.
The Saṃgha shall then return that relinquished robe to him through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, as detailed above.
If one does not return [the robe], but instead makes it into five robes or even into non-robes and wears them repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* as described above.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one says to a layperson, "Use it as you please," or if the layperson has already given the object and says, "Use it as you please. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-first section concludes. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder who was the patron (*dānapati*) of the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā. When the time arrived, she put on her robes, took her bowl, went to his house, spread out her seat, and sat down.
Then the householder greeted her, asking:
"Are you dwelling in peace and comfort?"
He replied, "I am not at ease. He asked:
"Why is that? He replied, "The place where I reside is noisy and bustling; therefore, I find no peace or happiness."
He then asked, "Is there no separate room? He replied:
"No. "If you were given the price for a house, would you be able to build one? He replied:
"Yes," she replied,
and immediately gave him the price for the house.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I were to build a house, there would be many affairs to attend to, and it would be difficult for a bhikṣuṇī to obtain robes; she ought to provide herself with the five robes.
Might I not now trade the value of this house for robes?"
She then purchased the robe.
Later, on another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī An-yin (Anvaya) put on her robes, took her bowl, went to the house of a lay devotee, and sat down upon a seat.
The layperson asked,
"Venerable lady!
Are you dwelling in peace and comfort?"
He replied, "I am not at ease. He asked:
"Why are you not at ease? He replied,
"Because the place where I stay is noisy and bustling, I am not at ease."
He then asked, "Is there no separate room? He replied:
"No. He asked again, "Did you not ultimately build the house for which you previously received the payment?"
He replied, "I did not. He asked again:
"Why did you not do it? He replied:
"I had this thought to myself:"
"If one uses these goods to build a dwelling, there will be many affairs to attend to; it is difficult for a bhikṣuṇī to obtain clothing, so she must provide the five robes.
She then used those goods to trade for robes.
At that time, the laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are insatiable; yet outwardly they claim for themselves, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what is there of the True Dharma?
I provided the materials for building a house, yet you used it to trade for clothing.
Do I not know that a bhikṣuṇī’s robes are difficult to obtain and she ought to possess the five garments?"
"But we have heard what the World-Honored One has said: 'The foremost merit is to build a dwelling and offer it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.

" When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked An-yin, saying:
"How could you take the goods a donor gave for the purpose of building a dwelling and instead use them to make robes?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Anurādha:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of conformity—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that a donor gives material for a house, yet you use it to make robes?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"The nun Ānanda has committed the first offense regarding the many bases of outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī diverts material goods given by a donor for one purpose to use them for another, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

Regarding the difference in the objects offered for donation: if one intends to build a separate room with the gift but uses it to make robes, or intends to make robes with the gift but uses it to build a separate room, or if it was donated for one place but used for another, [it constitutes an offense].
If a bhikṣuṇī, having received a gift intended for a specific purpose, diverts it to build a separate room or uses it for another purpose, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *naiḥsargika* article must be relinquished to the Saṃgha according to the procedure described above.
Having completed the relinquishment, the confession is as described above.
The Saṃgha should immediately return that relinquished robe to him; the formal act of returning it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is as described above.

If they do not return it, and he accepts it to make it into one of the five robes, or even uses it for something other than a robe, or wears it repeatedly, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one asks the donor and uses the item according to the donor's instructions; or if, when the gift is being given, one says:
"Use it as you please";
or if one says so to a close friend.
"You may use it as you please.
If I inform the owner, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-second [section] is concluded. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs were begging among the people to build a dwelling for themselves; they solicited from place to place and obtained much wealth and property.
The bhikṣuṇīs then thought to themselves:

"If we build a house with this property, there will be many complications; it is difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain the robes they require, and we must provide the five types of garments. We would now rather use this property to purchase cloth and share it among ourselves."
Having thought this, they traded their garments and divided them between them.
Later, at another time, some lay devotees asked,
"Has the house that was previously intended for the gift of goods been built yet?"
He replied, "I did not. He asked:
"Why do you not do so? They replied,
"We thought to ourselves:"
"Since there are many complications involved in building a house, it will be difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain their robes; they ought to possess the five requisite robes.
We would rather exchange these goods for robes so that we may share them."
Having thought this, she immediately traded it for cloth and shared it with them.
When the laypeople heard of this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are insatiable in their receiving; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be such a thing as the True Dharma?
For we have abandoned our integrity to trade for robes and share them among ourselves.
"Do we not know that it is difficult for bhikṣuṇīs to obtain robes and that they ought to possess the five robes?
However, we have heard what the World-Honored One has said:
'The foremost merit is to construct a dwelling and offer it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters.'"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you exchange the value of another's house for robes and then divide them among yourselves?"
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not be done."
"What do you think, bhikṣuṇīs!
How can donors give money for a house and trade it for robes to be shared among yourselves?
Having rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Those bhikṣuṇīs are foolish people!
This is the first transgression of the precepts among many bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:”

"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the donor has designated a specific object for a particular purpose, seeks it out for herself and diverts it for other uses intended for the Saṃgha, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

Regarding the difference in the objects given: if one gives for the purpose of constructing a monastery but uses it to make robes, or gives for the purpose of making robes but uses it to construct a monastery, or if what was given for one place is used for another place.
"Seeking for oneself" means begging for things for one's own use.
"For the Saṃgha" refers to property belonging to the Saṃgha as described above.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a gift intended for one purpose but, having sought it for herself, diverts it for the Saṃgha or uses it for another purpose, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha according to the aforementioned procedure; having relinquished it, one must perform confession as previously described.
The Saṃgha shall then return that relinquished robe to him, performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) as previously described.
If one does not return [the robe], but instead makes it into five robes or even into non-robes and wears them repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing) as described above.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one uses the object after asking the owner and acting according to the owner's instructions, or if, when giving the object, one says:
"Use it as you please."
If it is someone with whom one is closely acquainted, one may say:
"Use it as you wish.
I shall inform the owner; in this case, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-third section concludes. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs possessed bowls of fine color; they kept their old ones aside and accumulated many bowls without washing or cleaning them, leaving them in disarray upon the ground.
When several laypeople went to the monastery to visit and saw this, they spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are insatiable in receiving gifts; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what 'True Dharma' is there?
By hoarding many fine-colored bowls, these bowls lie scattered and disheveled on the ground, no different from a pottery shop.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"How is it that you keep so many bowls of fine color, yet leave your old bowls unwashed and neglected, scattered in disarray upon the ground?
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
Why do you keep fine-colored bowls, yet leave the old ones unwashed and untended, lying in disarray upon the ground?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of faulty actions; this was their first transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, compiled from the ten points of meaning up until the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms-bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

That bhikṣuṇī, on the very day she obtains a bowl, should accept and maintain one bowl that same day; the others she must either give away through a formal act of purification (pariṣkāra-dāna) or hand them over to another person.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra bowl, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This forfeiture should be relinquished to the Saṃgha according to the aforementioned rule; once relinquished, she must perform confession as previously described.
The Saṃgha should immediately return that relinquished bowl to him, performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) as described above.
If it is not returned, even down to the point where it is no longer used as a bowl, all [offenses] are *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), as described above.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one obtains a bowl on that very day and accepts only one bowl on that very day; or if the remaining bowls are given as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) or sent to another person;
or if one has the thought that they have been seized, lost, broken, or swept away; or if they were not given as a pure gift or not sent to another person—there is no offense.
There is no offense if the bowl is taken away, lost, broken, or carried off by water; or if one uses it oneself, or if another gives it to one for use.

There is no offense if the person to whom the bowl was entrusted has died, has gone on a long journey, has left the religious life, or has been carried off by bandits; or if one encounters the danger of wild beasts, is swept away by water, has not performed the ritual of *pariṣkāra-dāna*, or has not sent it to someone else.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth [section]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs kept many fine-colored vessels and retained those that were not fine; they accumulated such a multitude of vessels that they failed to wash, clean, or maintain them, leaving them in a state of disarray upon the ground.
At that time, many laypeople went to visit the various monasteries to look around; having seen [the nuns], they spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs are insatiable in receiving and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim of themselves:
'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what Dharma is there?
You keep many vessels scattered in disarray upon the ground, no different from a pottery shop.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"Why do you all keep so many vessels that they lie scattered and in disarray on the ground?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
Why do you keep so many vessels that they lie scattered in disorder upon the ground?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed various offenses that lead to outflows; this is the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī keeps many fine-colored vessels, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

That bhikṣuṇī, having obtained a bowl on that very day, should accept it on that same day. Of those she requires for use, there may be sixteen; the remainder should be given away as a pure gift (*viśuddha-dāna*) or sent to others.

Sixteenth: large cauldrons, their lids, large basins and ladles; small cauldrons, their lids, small basins and ladles; water jars, their lids, basins and ladles; rinsing jars, their lids, basins and ladles.
If a bhikṣuṇī keeps many vessels, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished and given to the Saṃgha as described above.
Once relinquished, the confession is performed according to the method described above.
The Saṃgha should immediately return that discarded vessel to him; the procedure for returning it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is as described above.
If the Saṃgha does not return it, and [the offender] uses it repeatedly, all instances constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses as described above.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, on that very day, one obtains the bowl and accepts sixteen [measures], while the remainder is to be given away as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) or sent to another;
or if one has the thought that it has been seized, lost, broken, or swept away, and thus does not perform the ritual purification (*pariṣkāra-karaṇa*) nor send it to another, there is no offense;
or if the bowl is seized, lost, broken, or swept away; or if one takes it for one's own use; or if another gives the bowl for use.

If the bhikṣuṇī to whom the item was entrusted passes away, or ceases her religious practice, or travels far away, or is carried off by bandits, or faces danger from wild beasts, or is swept away by water, then it is not an offense if one does not perform the ritual purification (pariśuddhi) nor send it to another person.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-fifth section ends. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs had their menstrual blood flow, which soiled their bodies, robes, and sitting mats.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear a menstrual cloth; if it slips out, I allow you to fasten it with a band."
If menstrual blood still flows from both sides and soils the garment, it is further permitted to make a double-layered sick-cloth, wearing the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* over it.
When entering the house of a layperson, one should say: "I am ill."
If a layperson says, "Just sit;
there is no harm," that bhikṣuṇī should lift up her undergarment (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī) and sit while shielding her body with this sick-cloth.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Candanasunā who constantly claimed to herself that she had no thoughts of desire. She said to another bhikṣuṇī:
"When your menstrual flow occurs, you should take this robe from me."
She replied, "So be it.
The other bhikṣuṇīs,
constantly looking forward to this robe, did not prepare any further robes themselves.
At another time, the bhikṣuṇī Cāndanīśunā experienced her menstrual flow, as did other bhikṣuṇīs.
Then, those other bhikṣuṇīs sent a messenger to the bhikṣuṇī Cāndanīśunā, saying:
"Previously you promised us sick-clothing; you may give it to us now."
She replied, "Sister!
I too am currently experiencing my menses; I cannot give it to you."
That bhikṣuṇī reproached the bhikṣuṇī Candanasūna, saying:
"Previously you said to me:
'If my menstrual flow occurs, take a sick-cloth from me.'"
"I have always hoped to receive robes and did not provide for them myself; now that I go to ask for them, will you not give them to me?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the bhikṣuṇī Candanasūna:
"How could you promise a sick robe to that bhikṣuṇī while causing her to fail to provide for one herself, and now, when she asks for it, refuse to give it?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Candanasūnā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, Bhikṣuṇī Candanāśūna! Having consented that he would not provide the robe for his illness himself, why do you now demand it and refuse to give it?
After rebuking the Bhikṣuṇī Candanāśūna with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“The nun Cāndanī, in many ways, was the first to commit an offense regarding the sources of outflows (*āsrava*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī promises a sick-nun’s robe to another bhikṣuṇī and later does not give it, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "sick-clothing," it refers to that which covers the body when menstrual blood flows; one wears the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (inner robe) over it.
As for "clothing," there are ten types of clothing, as described above.
If that bhikṣuṇī promises a robe for illness to another but does not give it, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
Apart from robes for illness, if she promises other robes but does not give them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If, after setting aside the extra robes, one does not give other necessary items that have been promised, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī promises a sick robe to another bhikṣuṇī and later does not give it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] should be relinquished to the Saṃgha as described above.
Having relinquished it, one should confess as described above.
The Saṃgha shall then immediately return the relinquished robe to him as described above.
If one does not return [the robe], but accepts it as five robes and uses them repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing) as described above.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one has agreed to give a robe for illness, or if there is no robe for illness, or if one is making a robe for illness, or if one has washed, dyed, beaten, or stored it in a secure place and, upon being asked, refuses to give it. There is no offense in these cases.

If that bhikṣuṇī has violated the precepts, or violated the views, or violated the dignified conduct; or if she has been subject to formal suspension (ukkhepana), or has been expelled (pabbājana), or is subject to expulsion; or if, due to these circumstances, there is a threat to her life or a threat to her holy life (brahmacariya)—if, in such cases, she does not give the robe for the sick even though it was promised, she commits no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-sixth section concludes. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs accepted out-of-season robes to make into seasonal robes.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they said to them, "The World-Honored One has permitted bhikṣuṇīs to possess five robes; whose robes are these?"
He replied, "This is our seasonal robe. He then said:
"Sister! Now is the time, not the wrong time.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
“How is it that you have accepted out-of-season robes and treated them as in-season robes?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
How can you accept an out-of-season robe and treat it as an in-season robe?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of faulty actions; this is the first breach of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī receives a non-seasonal robe and treats it as a seasonal robe, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above. Regarding "time":
after the completion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), it is one month if the *kaṭhina* robe has not been spread, and five months if the *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
"Out of season" means that, excluding this [specific case], one obtains an extra robe at other times.
"Robe" refers to the ten kinds of robes as mentioned above.
If a bhikṣuṇī accepts an out-of-season robe and treats it as a robe for the [specified] season, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] should be relinquished to the Saṃgha as described above.
Having completed the relinquishment, the confession is performed as described above.
The Saṃgha shall then return the relinquished robe to him; the formal procedure (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for its return is as described above.
If one does not return [the robe], but accepts it as five robes and wears them repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* as described above.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: receiving an out-of-season robe and making it into an out-of-season robe; receiving an in-season robe and making it into an in-season robe—these are not offenses.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who acted before the precept was first established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The twenty-seventh [case] concludes. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā exchanged robes with another bhikṣuṇī; later, out of anger, she seized them back, saying:
"Sister!..."
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
Your robe belongs to you, and my robe belongs to me.
You take your own robe, and I shall take my own."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Steunānandā:
"How could you, after exchanging robes with a bhikṣuṇī, later become angry and take them back yourself, saying:
'Sister!'"?
"Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
Your robe belongs to you; my robe belongs to me.
Take your own robe yourself; I shall take my own robe myself."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is this, Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā! Having traded a robe with a bhikṣuṇī, you later seize it back out of anger?
After rebuking the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the first offense of the many leaky (āsava) matters committed by Thullanandā.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī exchanges a robe with another bhikṣuṇī, and later, out of anger, takes it back herself or causes another to take it back...'"
"Sister! Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.
Your robe belongs to you, and my robe must be returned to me."
"Whoever [does so], it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Robe" refers to the ten kinds of robes as described above.

Regarding trade: one may exchange clothing for clothing, or clothing for what is not clothing, or what is not clothing for clothing, or what is not clothing for other items that are not clothing—such as needles, knives, thread, scraps of material, or even a single pill of medicine.
If that bhikṣuṇī, having traded robes with another bhikṣuṇī, later becomes angry and seizes them herself, or instructs another to seize them, or hides them, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes [the robe] and does not conceal it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.

If that person obtains the robe and places it upon a tree, a wall, a fence, a stake, an ivory peg, a clothing rack, a rope bed, a wooden bed, a large or small mat, or upon a ground-covering, and then takes it away from its place, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one takes it and does not leave the place, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha as described above.
Having relinquished it, one must perform confession as described above.
The monk shall immediately return that robe to him; the procedure for returning it by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is as described above.
If he does not return it, whether he accepts it to make it into the five robes or wears it repeatedly, all such acts constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses as described above.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one speaks conciliatorily: "Sister!
I repent; give me back my robe."
Knowing that she has the intention to repent, he returns the robe.
If another bhikṣuṇī says to him:
"This bhikṣuṇī wishes to repent; you should return the robe."
Alternatively, if he returns it because its borrowing was improper; or if he knew beforehand that it would be lost; or if he feared it would be damaged;

or if that person has broken the precepts, broken the view, or broken the decorum; or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or have been expelled (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), or are subject to expulsion; or if, for the sake of this matter, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacariya*)—if he does not conceal it under such circumstances, he commits no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The twenty-eighth section ends. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Upper Story Lecture Hall on the bank of the Monkey River.
At that time, there was a need for a Licchavi of Vaiśālī to obtain wealth from a certain householder.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālā who frequently went to and from this householder’s home, serving as his donor.
Then Liśa said to Kālī, "I wish to discuss a matter concerning property with you,
my aunt. She replied:
“Very well,” he replied,
and immediately arranged for the matter.
Having obtained the wealth and goods, the man was delighted and asked:
“Sister! What do you require? She replied:
"Stop! This itself shall suffice as an offering to me.
He then asked again:
“Sister! If you have anything you require, please speak. She replied:
"Stop! Why must you speak?
Even if I had something I required, you would not grant it to me in any case."
The householder replied, "Speak freely;
whatever you require, I shall provide it.
He then pointed to a robe worth a thousand pieces of fine cloth and said:
"I must have such a robe.
At that time, the householders all spoke in reproach, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs receive gifts without satiety; yet they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be such a thing as the True Dharma?
Why then do you demand a price of a thousand pieces of fine cloth? Even if a donor were to bestow them upon you, you should still practice contentment.
She immediately gave it to her and spoke these words:
"If I go there myself, I am capable of managing this matter; thus, you need not lose this robe.
Then, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilā went to the home of her relatives and sat down upon a seat.
The laypeople asked,
"Venerable lady! What do you require?"
He replied, "Stop; you have already made an offering to me.
He spoke again, saying:
"Simply tell me, what do you require?
He replied, "What need is there to say?"
"Even if you wish to have something, it will not be given to you at all.
He replied, "It shall be given; it is not that it will not be given."
"Tell me simply, what do you require?
He then pointed to a garment worth a thousand pieces of fine cloth and said, "I need this robe."
At that time, the laypeople criticized them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs accept gifts without satiety, yet they claim of themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what constitutes the True Dharma?
To demand the price of a thousand pieces of fine cotton cloth—even if a donor were to give it to you—you should still practice contentment.
Having said this, he gave him the robe and spoke further:
"What use does a bhikṣuṇī have for such an expensive robe?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilā, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī demand from him a robe worth a thousand pieces of cloth?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kālāvadaka-pilā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How could she demand the price of a thousand pieces of fine cloth from him?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Kālavatī Kāpilā has committed many kinds of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, comprising ten points of meaning, even unto the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī requests a heavy robe, its value should not exceed four *paṭa* cloths; should she exceed this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Heavy clothing" refers to garments for warding off the cold.
"Clothing" refers to the ten types mentioned above.
When a bhikṣuṇī seeks a heavy robe, it may have at most sixteen strips.
If a bhikṣuṇī seeks the price for a heavy robe exceeding four *paṭa* cloths, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] must be relinquished to the Saṃgha as described above.
Once the robe has been relinquished, the confession is performed according to the method described above.
The Saṃgha should then immediately return the robe to that bhikṣuṇī, granting it by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), as described above.
If the monk does not return it, or if he accepts it and makes it into the five robes, or even wears them repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* as described above.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one requests four pieces of cloth that are equal or fewer in size; or if one begs from a renunciant; or if the other person acts for one's sake or one acts for their sake; or if one obtains them without having requested them. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth [section]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, there was a matter in Vaiśālī for which a Licchavi should obtain wealth from a certain householder.
There was a Kālī bhikṣuṇī who frequently entered and left that household, serving as its patron (dānapati).
Then Liśā said to the bhikṣuṇī Kālī: "Auntie!
I wish to attend to a certain matter regarding wealth; can you manage it for me?"
He replied, “I can,” and immediately prepared it for him.
Having obtained the wealth and goods, he said with joy,
"Auntie! What do you wish to have?"
He replied, "Stop! This itself shall suffice as my offering."
He spoke again, saying:
"If you have anything you require, please speak. He replied:
"Stop! Even if I had something I required, you would not grant it to me in any case. He replied:
"It must be given; it is not that it is not to be given, but simply spoken of.
He then pointed to a light robe worth five hundred pieces of cotton cloth and said, "I require such a garment as this."
At that time, the householders all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs accept gifts without satiety, yet they claim of themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what constitutes the True Dharma?
To demand a price of five hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth—even if a donor were to offer such a gift—one should still know contentment."
She then took the robe and gave it to her, saying:
"If I were to go there myself, I would have been able to accomplish the task; thus, you shall not lose this robe.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Bhadrakāpilā, who returned to her relatives' home and sat down upon a seat.
Then the householder asked,
"Auntie! What do you require?"
He replied, "Stop! You have already made an offering to me."
He spoke again:
"I say only that there is no suffering; what do you require? He replied:
He replied, "Stop; there is no need to speak. Even if you wish to have something, it will not be granted to you.
The other said, "It shall be given;
it is not that it will not be given. What do you require?"
He then pointed to a light robe made of five hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth and said, "I require this robe.
At that time, the householder spoke with derision:
"This bhikṣuṇī accepts gifts without satiety, yet outwardly proclaims:
'I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?"
She then asked for five hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth for a light garment, saying, "Even if a donor were to give this to you, you should still know contentment.
Having given her the robe, she immediately said,
"What use has a bhikṣuṇī for such an expensive garment?"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the bhikṣuṇī Kālabhadrikā Kapilā, saying:
"How could you have requested from her the value of five hundred pieces of fine cotton cloth?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kālāvadaka-pilā:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it, bhikṣuṇīs, that you have requested from him a light garment worth five hundred pieces of cotton cloth?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Kālāvadaka-Kapilā has committed the first offense among the various bases of outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to beg for light clothing, the maximum value allowed is two and a half bolts of cloth; should she exceed this, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Light clothing" refers to clothing that wards off heat.
"Clothing" refers to the ten types mentioned above.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests light clothing, it may extend at most to ten strips; if a bhikṣuṇī requests light clothing exceeding two and a half bolts of cloth, it is a *niḥsargika-pāyattika*.
This *niḥsargika* [offense] should be relinquished to the Saṃgha as described above.
Having completed the relinquishment, the confession is performed according to the method described above.
The Saṃgha shall then return that relinquished robe to him; the formal act (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for its return is as described above.

If one does not return it, or accepts it to make into five robes or even into something that is not counted as a robe, and wears it repeatedly, all constitute *duṣkṛta* (offenses of wrong-doing) as described above.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who begs for the price of two and a half bolts of cloth or less than two and a half bolts; or if begging from one who has left the household life; or if begging on behalf of another; or if another begs on one's behalf; or if obtaining it without having begged. These cases do not constitute an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

[The thirty rules conclude. 4. The One Hundred and Seventy-eight *Pācittiya* Dharmas for Bhikṣuṇīs. Part One of the One Hundred and Seventy-eight *Pācittiya* Dharmas. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Anupiya in the Nyagrodha Garden near Kapilavastu in the kingdom of Śākya.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī speaks intentionally false words, it is a pāyattika.'"
1. "If a bhikṣuṇī speaks disparagingly, it is a pāyattika.
2. If a bhikṣuṇī speaks with double-tongued speech, it is a pāyattika."
3. "If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika offense.
4. "If a bhikṣuṇī sleeps in the same room as a woman who has not yet received the precepts, and stays for more than three nights, it is a pāyattika offense."
5. "If a bhikṣuṇī recites the Dharma together with a person who has not received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.

6. "If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), speaks of it to a person who has not received the higher ordination, except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma), it is a pāyattika."
7. "If a bhikṣuṇī speaks of a superhuman state (uttarimanussa-dhamma) to a person who has not received the full ordination, saying:
'I know this; I have seen this,' and it is true, it is a pāyattika."
8. “If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, except when a wise woman is present, it is a pāyattika.
9. “If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth herself or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.”
"Should a bhikṣuṇī destroy a village of spirits, it is a pāyattika.
(11) Should a bhikṣuṇī speak falsely and maliciously to annoy another, it is a pāyattika."
12. "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of resentment, reviles [another], it is a pāyattika. 13.

"If a bhikṣuṇī takes a monastic corded bed, a wooden bed, or bedding and cushions, spreads them out in the open air herself or instructs another to spread them, and then departs without herself putting them away or instructing another to put them away, it is a pāyattika."

14. “If a bhikṣuṇī takes bedding belonging to the Saṃgha from within a monastic dwelling, spreads it herself or instructs another to spread it, and then sits or lies upon it there, and subsequently departs from that place without putting it away herself or instructing another to put it away, it is a pāyattika.”
15. "If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī is already residing in a dwelling, later arrives and spreads out bedding in the space between them to stay overnight, thinking:
'If she finds it cramped, she will naturally move away from me.'"
If one acts with such motives and not otherwise, nor as part of proper decorum, it is a *pāyattika*.

16. "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger toward another bhikṣuṇī and being displeased with her, personally drags her out of the communal monastery quarters, or instructs another to drag her out, it is a *pāyattika*."
17. “If a bhikṣuṇī, while on an upper story of a multi-storied building, sits or lies down upon a rope bed or a wooden bed with removable legs, it is a pāyattika.”
18. "If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living organisms, uses it herself to sprinkle on mud or grass, or instructs another to do so, she commits a pāyattika offense."

19. "If a bhikṣuṇī constructs a large dwelling, including doors, panels, windows, and other decorative fittings, she must direct that the roofing and thatching be limited to two or three layers; if she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika."
20. “If a bhikṣuṇī, at a place where a single meal is offered, being free from illness,
should accept more than one meal, it is a pāyattika offense.”
21. “If a bhikṣuṇī eats apart from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika offense.

The ‘appropriate times’ are: when one is ill, when making robes, when robes are being offered, when traveling on a journey, when on a boat, during a great assembly, or when food is being offered by śramaṇas; these are the appropriate times.”

22. "If a bhikṣuṇī goes to a donor’s house where she is earnestly invited to receive cakes and parched grain, and the bhikṣuṇī wishes to accept them, she may accept two or three bowls; she must then carry them to the monastery and distribute them among the other bhikṣuṇīs for their meal.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, accepts more than three bowls and carries them to the monastery without distributing them among the other bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika."
23. “If a bhikṣuṇī eats at an improper time, it is a pāyattika offense.
24. “If a bhikṣuṇī consumes food that has been kept overnight, it is a pāyattika offense.”
25. “If a bhikṣuṇī, without having received food or medicine, places it in her mouth—except for water and tooth-sticks—it is a pāyattika. 26.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having already accepted an invitation, goes to another house before or after the meal without informing another bhikṣuṇī—except during other [permitted] times—it is a pāyattika.”
The exceptions are: when one is ill, when making robes, or when robes are being distributed; these are the appropriate times.
Twenty-seven: "If a bhikṣuṇī sits down forcefully in a family home where there is wealth, it is a pāyattika."
28. “If a bhikṣuṇī sits in a secluded place within a household where there is treasure, it is a pāyattika offense.
29. “If a bhikṣuṇī sits alone with a man in one place on open ground, it is a pāyattika offense.”
30. "If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī: 'Sister!'"
"I will go with you to the village and give you food.
Yet that bhikṣuṇī did not actually provide food for this bhikṣuṇī, but instead spoke thus: "Sister, go!"
"I do not find pleasure sitting and conversing with you; I find pleasure sitting and conversing alone.
For this reason, and by no other means, he sends her away; this is a *pāyattika* offense.
31. “If a bhikṣuṇī accepts medicine offered for four months, she should do so only if she is not ill.
If she accepts it beyond that period—except in the case of a regular invitation, a special invitation, an invitation to share, or a lifelong invitation—it is a pāyattika.”
32. “If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view a military array, except when there is a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.
33. “If a bhikṣuṇī has a reason to go into a military camp and stays for two or three nights, exceeding that limit, it is a pāyattika.”

34. "If a bhikṣuṇī stays among an army for two or three nights, or at any time observes military arrays and battles, or observes the strength of the marching troops' elephants and horses, it is a pāyattika."
35. “If a bhikṣuṇī drinks alcohol, it is a pāyattika.
36. “If a bhikṣuṇī plays in mud or water, it is a pāyattika.”
37. "If a bhikṣuṇī tickles another bhikṣuṇī with her finger, it is a pāyattika. 38. "If a bhikṣuṇī does not accept admonition, it is a pāyattika."
39. “If a bhikṣuṇī causes another bhikṣuṇī to feel afraid, it is a pāyattika.
40. “If a bhikṣuṇī bathes every half-month, she who is free from illness must accept [the invitation].”
If one accepts [food] beyond this limit, except during the remaining times, it is a pāyattika offense.
The remaining times are: the time of heat, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of high winds, the time of rain, and the time of traveling from afar; these are the [permissible] times.
41. “If a bhikṣuṇī, when not ill, lights a fire on the open ground for the purpose of warming herself, or instructs another to light one, except at other times, it is a pāyattika.”

42. “If a bhikṣuṇī conceals another bhikṣuṇī’s bowl, robe, sitting mat, or needle case—whether she conceals it herself or instructs another to conceal it—even down to doing so in jest, it is a pāyattika.”
