One hundred and seventy-eighth *Naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rule, Part Two: "If a bhikṣuṇī, having given a robe as a pure gift (*śuci-dāna*) to a bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī, subsequently takes it back and wears it without asking the owner, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
44. “If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she must dye it one of three kinds of discolored hues: blue, black, or mūlāna.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe and does not dye it one of these three kinds of discolored hues—blue, black, or mūlāna—but keeps the new robe as it is, it is a pāyattika.”
45. “If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes the life of an animal, it is a pāyattika. 46.
“If a bhikṣuṇī knows that water contains living beings and drinks it, it is a pāyattika.”
47. “If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally harasses another bhikṣuṇī, even to the extent of causing her momentary displeasure, it is a pāyattika.
48. “If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense (sthūlātyaya), conceals it, it is a pāyattika.”
49. "If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a matter of dispute has already been settled according to the Dharma through confession, should later raise it again, it is a pāyattika. 50."
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that someone is a companion of thieves, travels along the same road with them for even as far as a single village, it is a pāyattika. (51) 'If a bhikṣuṇī speaks thus:
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path."'"
Those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the World-Honored One, for to slander the World-Honored One is unwholesome."

"The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, the Blessed One has taught through countless skillful means that sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path, and that one who commits sexual misconduct is obstructed by that dharma.

When those bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī, she stubbornly maintains her position and does not relinquish it. Those bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times to make her relinquish this matter.
If she relinquishes [the view] upon being admonished up to three times, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, it is a *pāyattika*. 52.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that such a person has not undergone the formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) and has not relinquished such evil and heterodox views, yet keeps her in common ritual action (*ekakarma*) or shares a lodging with her (*ekavihāra*), it is a *pāyattika*."
53. “If a śrāmaṇerikā should speak thus:
‘I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha; practicing sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path,’ that bhikṣuṇī should admonish this śrāmaṇerikā, saying:”
"Do not speak such words; do not slander the World-Honored One, for it is unwholesome to slander the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One does not say such things, O śrāmaṇerī!"
"The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught that sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path, and that one who commits sexual misconduct is obstructed by this dharma.
When that bhikṣuṇī exhorts this śrāmaṇerī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should admonish and exhort her up to three times so that she may abandon this matter.
If she relinquishes [the practice] by the time of the third admonition, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, that bhikṣuṇī should say to this śrāmaṇerikā:

"From this day forward, you are no longer a disciple of the Buddha. You may not follow other bhikṣuṇīs. While other śrāmaṇerikās are permitted to stay with bhikṣuṇīs for two nights, you no longer have this privilege. Depart, go away! You need not remain here."
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a śrāmaṇerī has been thus expelled, should keep her as a companion and share a lodging with her, it is a pāyattika.
(54) “If a bhikṣuṇī, when being admonished in accordance with the Dharma, speaks as follows:
‘I will not study these precepts now; I shall wait until I have questioned those who possess wisdom and uphold the Vinaya, and then I will raise my objections.’”
[This constitutes] a *pāyattika*.
If one wishes to seek clarification, one should pose questions.
55. "If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), speaks thus:"
"Sister! What is the use of reciting these minor precepts?
When these precepts are recited, they cause people distress, shame, and doubt."
Because she disparages the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
56. "If a bhikṣuṇī, at the time of reciting the precepts, speaks as follows: 'Sisters!'"
"I have only now learned that this precept—the Biyue-banyue Shoujie Jing (Bhikṣuṇī-Prātimokṣa Sūtra)—is recited every half-month.
Other bhikṣuṇīs know that this bhikṣuṇī has sat through two or three such recitations, let alone more!

That bhikṣuṇī was ignorant and lacked understanding; if she has committed an offense, she should be dealt with according to the Dharma, and furthermore, the rule regarding ignorance shall be applied more strictly:
"Sister! You have gained no benefit and have acquired what is unwholesome."
"When you were reciting the precepts, you did not apply your mind, nor did you listen to the Dharma with single-minded attention.
Because of this lack of understanding, it is a *pāyattika*.
57. "If a bhikṣuṇī, after a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed together [with others], later speaks thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of favoritism toward those she is close to, gives property belonging to the Saṃgha to them," it is a pāyattika.
(58) "If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha is engaged in formal business, rises and departs without having given her consent (chanda), it is a pāyattika."
59. “If a bhikṣuṇī, having already given her consent (*chanda*), later revokes it, it is a pāyattika. 60.
“If a bhikṣuṇī, after two bhikṣuṇīs have been quarreling, listens to their words with the intention of reporting them to the other party, it is a pāyattika.”
61. "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika. 62.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes a bhikṣuṇī with her hand, it is a pāyattika."
63. "If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, slanders another with a groundless saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, it is a pāyattika."
64. “If a bhikṣuṇī enters the palace of a Kṣatriya king—anointed with water—who has not yet come forth nor hidden his treasures, and she crosses the threshold, it is a pāyattika.”

65. "If a bhikṣuṇī takes hold of treasure or articles adorned with treasure, whether she takes them herself or instructs another to take them, except within a monastery or at a lodging place, it is a pāyattika."

Whether in a monastery or at a lodging place, if there is treasure or something adorned with treasure, whether one takes it up oneself or instructs another to take it, it should be taken only if the owner is known; such is the cause and condition, and no other.
66. "If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time and does not inform another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika offense. 67.
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be no higher than eight fingers of the Buddha’s span."
If one inserts [cotton] into the joints or holes above the steps, and it exceeds the limit after being cut, it is a *pāyattika*.
Sixty-eight: "If a bhikṣuṇī uses tūla-cotton as stuffing to make a rope bed, a wooden bed, or bedding or seating mats, it is a *pāyattika*."
69. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Gabled Hall on the bank of the Monkey River at Vaiśālī.
At that moment, there was a garlic garden in another location; the nun Thullanandā was walking not far from it when the owner of the garden asked her: "Auntie!"
"Do you require garlic? He replied,
"I require garlic."
She then took the garlic and gave it to her.
Having received the garlic, that bhikṣuṇī went there again and again.
As she walked not far from his place, the man saw her and spoke to her once more:
“Sister, do you need more garlic? She replied, “I do.”
"If I obtain garlic, I shall be able to eat it.
He then gave him the garlic.
Having given the garlic, he commanded the garden keeper, saying:
"From this day forth, let each bhikṣuṇī be provided with five cloves of garlic.
At that time, the owner of the garden left one person to guard it and went himself to Vaiśālī to sell the garlic.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā returned to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Do you know? A certain donor at such-and-such a place provides each bhikṣuṇī with five cloves of garlic daily; you may go there to collect them."
Then, Stūlanandā took the śrāmaṇerikās and śikṣamāṇās and went directly to the garlic grove, asking the guardian of the garlic:
"Where is the owner of this grove?"
He replied, "I am going to Vaiśālī to sell garlic.
At that time, the person guarding the garlic said:
"Why do you ask? She replied, "The owner of this garden provides each bhikṣuṇī with five cloves of garlic daily; you may now take some from me."
The garlic keeper said: "Wait a moment!
You must wait for the garden master to arrive; I have no autonomy, for my duty is merely to guard and watch over it."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "The mistress has offered it as alms, but the slave is unwilling to give it.

Thereupon, Steunānandā commanded a śrāmaṇerikā to pull up the garlic and count how much there was, saying, "This is for the elder, the next elder, the upādhyāya, and the ācārya; this is for those with the same upādhyāya, those with the same ācārya, and our close friends and acquaintances."
"This is for today's meal; this is for tomorrow's meal; this is for the day after.
Thus, they immediately took all the garlic from the garden.
When the owner of the garlic returned and saw that it was gone, he asked the gardener:
"Why has the garlic been completely consumed? He replied, "O Master!"

Because she had previously developed faith and joy, she provided five cloves of garlic daily for each member of the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha. Recently, some śrāmaṇerīs and śikṣamāṇās came to me and said to me, "Where is the owner of the garlic now?"
I replied, "I entered Vaiśālī to sell garlic. I then asked:
"Why do you ask? he replied to me, "The owner of the garlic gives each person five cloves daily; you may have some now."
I replied: "Wait a moment! Until the owner of the garden returns, I am merely guarding it; I have no autonomy."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "My mistress gave me garlic, but the slave was unwilling to give it to me.
At that time, she immediately commanded a śrāmaṇerikā to pull up the garlic, count how much there was, and say:

"This for the Elder; this for the Sub-elder; this for the Preceptor; this for the Teacher; this for those with the same Preceptor and the same Teacher; this for close friends and acquaintances; this for today's meal; this for tomorrow's meal; this for the day after tomorrow's meal."
“They ate them all up at once; for this reason, the garlic in the garden has been completely consumed.
The owner of the garden immediately spoke with reproach and disdain:
“These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or modesty and know no satiety in what they receive. Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:”
"I know the True Dharma"—if this is so, what kind of True Dharma is there?
Even when a donor bestows a gift, one should still practice contentment; how much more so when one takes everything without even seeing the owner?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Steunānanda:
"How could you all uproot all the garlic belonging to others, eat it and carry it away, leaving nothing behind?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the discipline]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How could you not see your master and yet pluck all the garlic belonging to another?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the past, there was a brāhmaṇa who was one hundred and twenty years old and whose body was emaciated. This brāhmaṇa’s wife was incomparably beautiful, and they had many sons and daughters."

This brahmin fixed his mind upon his wife and their children, never letting go of them; because his attachment was so profound, he passed away and was reborn among the geese, with the feathers of his body entirely golden in color.
Due to the causes and conditions of past merit, he recollected his former lives and reflected within himself:
"By what means shall I provide for these children so that they do not fall into poverty and suffering?"
Day after day he came to his house, and at sunset a single golden feather would fall and depart.
Upon receiving it, the man and woman reflected to themselves:
"By what cause and condition does this king of geese come daily and leave us a single golden feather?"
"We would rather wait for him to come and find a way to seize him and take all his golden feathers.
Following their plan, they immediately seized him and plucked out the golden feathers; once they were removed, white feathers grew back in their place.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that brāhmaṇa was who died and became a goose at that time, could it be anyone else?
Do not view it otherwise; he was none other than the owner of the garden."
The woman of upright conduct who gave birth to many sons and daughters was none other than the bhikṣuṇī Steunānanda.
Those sons and daughters were none other than the śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇerīs, and others.
"Because of her original craving, she caused the golden feathers to be exhausted and white feathers to grow in their place.
Now, because of her renewed attachment, she has caused the garlic to be consumed and has instead incurred poverty.
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This nun has committed the first offense among many such bases for the outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, it is a pāyattika.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī eats raw garlic, cooked garlic, or garlic that is mixed with other things, for every swallow she commits a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness that one must eat garlic wrapped in a cake;
or if it cannot be cured by other medicines and one is permitted to take garlic for recovery;
or if one applies it to a wound—none of these constitute an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
The seventieth [case] concludes. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā shaved the hair from three areas of her body; she then went to the house of a donor and sat down before the women, failing to cover herself and leaving her body exposed.
Then that woman, having seen her, said: "Auntie!
Come and bathe together."
He replied, "Stop! Having thus received the offering, he spoke again:
"Come, let us bathe together.
She replied, "I have no need for a bath."
Then the women forcibly removed her clothes and saw the place where she had shaved, and they said to her:
"Auntie! The reason people in the world shave their hair is for the sake of sexual desire; for what reason have you shaved it?"
Stūlanandā replied, "I have practiced this method since I left the secular life; it is not only now.
Thereupon, the laywomen immediately spoke with derision and reproach:
“Bhikṣuṇīs who lack shame and remorse practice impure conduct, yet outwardly they claim,
‘I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
She then shaved the hair of three places, appearing just like a courtesan or a female thief.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Steunānandā, saying:
"How could you shave the hair of three places?"
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
On account of these circumstances, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Steyānanandā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, Thullanandā! Why have you shaved the hair from three places?
Having thus rebuked Thullanandā with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“This nun Thullanandā has committed many acts of defilement; this is her first breach of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair from the three places, it is a pāyattika offense.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding the "three places of hair": these are the areas of the anus, the vagina, and the armpits.
If a bhikṣuṇī shaves the hair from these three places, for each stroke of the razor, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one pulls it out, cuts it off, or burns it, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *sthūlātyaya*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; if there is a sore that requires shaving [the hair] to apply medicine; or if one is seized by someone using force. These are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(71) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Anupiya in the Nyagrodha Park near Kapilavastu in the Śākyas' territory.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“The female body is foul-smelling, filthy, and impure.
Having spoken these words, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to perform the ritual purification with water.

When Steyānanandā heard this regulation, she immediately performed the purification with water; however, with a lustful mind, she inserted her finger into the vaginal canal. The finger was so deep that it wounded the interior with her fingernail, causing blood to flow and defile her body, robes, and bedding.
The bhikṣuṇīs immediately asked,
"What is your affliction?
She then related the circumstances in detail.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Steunānanda:
"How could you perform the ritual purification with water by inserting your finger into the vaginal canal and injuring the interior, causing blood to flow that stained your body, robes, and bedding?"
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Steyanandā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you, having performed purification with water, used a desire-filled mind to insert your fingernail deep inside, causing blood to flow and defiling your body, robes, and bedding?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked Thullanandā with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Thullanandā has committed many kinds of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs the purification with water, it should be limited to two fingers, each at one joint; if she exceeds this, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "purifying with water," this means washing the interior with water.
If that bhikṣuṇī, having purified it with water, inserts more than one joint of two fingers into the [vagina], it is a pāyattika offense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if [the fingernails] are level with two finger-joints each, or less than one joint; or if there is such an illness; or if there is grass inside; or if there is an insect inside that has been pulled out. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(72) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣuṇīs, their lustful desires burning intensely, became haggard in countenance and emaciated in body; they went into the palace of King Prasenajit.
When the women within the palace saw them, they asked, "Aunties, what affliction or suffering do you have?"
He replied, "I have a physical ailment.
The other then asked:
"What kind of affliction do you have regarding form? He replied,
"My desire-mind is burning intensely."
The women said: "When we are within the palace, we obtain men only from time to time.

When we do not obtain a man, we sometimes fashion a male organ out of lac resin and insert it into the female organ; since this brings us satisfaction, it is not called engaging in sexual misconduct."
"Auntie, it may also be done in this way; since one has attained what is pleasing to the mind, it is not called 'committing sexual misconduct.

At that time, there were two bhikṣuṇīs from the group of six who, having fashioned such a male organ, engaged in sexual intercourse together. Other bhikṣuṇīs saw them and thought they were engaging in sexual intercourse with a man; only after the act was finished did they realize it was not a man.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you have fashioned male organs out of lacquer resin and engaged in sexual intercourse?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
That you use this animal glue to fashion a male organ and engage in sexual intercourse?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One then addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of taintful offenses; this is the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī makes a male organ out of lacquer resin, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "one who makes a male organ," this refers to making one using various materials—whether made of lacquer resin, or rice, or flour, or wax.
If a bhikṣuṇī uses these various objects to insert into the female organ, it is a pāyattika offense in all cases.
If she inserts them into the female organ without having polished or prepared them, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is what is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; if one is wearing medicinal fruits or medicinal pills; if one is blocking the menstrual flow with clothing; or if one is seized by someone using force. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(Seventy-three) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣuṇīs, their lustful desires burning intensely, became haggard in countenance and emaciated in body as they went to the palace of King Prasenajit.
When the women of the palace saw them, they asked, "Aunties,
what ailment or suffering do you have?"
He replied, “Because my wishes were not fulfilled. He asked:
"What wish do you have that has not been granted? He replied,
"My lustful mind is burning intensely."
The women said, "When we are within the palace, we only occasionally obtain men.

When we do not obtain them, we take substances mixed with resin to create a male organ and insert it into the female organ; since this satisfies our lustful desires, it does not constitute actual sexual intercourse. Why, O Venerable Ones, do you not act in this same way?"
The bhikṣuṇīs replied, "Sisters!
The World-Honored One has established a precept that does not permit such a thing."
He then spoke again: "Auntie!
While we were in the palace, we only obtained a male child from time to time."
"If one does not obtain a man, is it not called engaging in sexual intercourse when two people beat each other to satisfy lustful pleasure? Aunt, why do you not do so?

At that time, two bhikṣuṇīs of the group of six beat each other; the other bhikṣuṇīs saw them and thought they were engaging in sexual intercourse with a man, but only after they had risen did they realize it was not a man.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you all slap one another like this?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can you all be slapping one another?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the first transgression among the many bases for outflows of these bhikṣuṇīs."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, comprising the ten points of meaning, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī slaps another, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Patting" refers to patting with the palm of the hand, or patting with the foot, or patting the female organ against the female organ, or bhikṣuṇīs patting one another.
To strike [another] is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
for the one who receives the strike, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If two female organs strike each other, both commit a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; if one is coming or going; if one is walking up and down (caṅkrama); if one is sweeping the ground; if one touches it with a staff unintentionally; or if one touches it with the hand while washing—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(74) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elder who had gone forth from the household life with his wife to practice the Path. When it was time for the meal, he went to the village to beg for food; having obtained it, he returned to the nuns' monastery.
As they were about to eat, his former wife, now a bhikṣuṇī, stood before him holding water and fanned him with a fan.
The bhikṣu said: "Move aside!
I am ashamed before people; do not stand in front of me."
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Venerable sir, why do you feel ashamed before me?
He replied again:
"Why do you not leave quickly?
I am ashamed. The bhikṣuṇī replied:
"I told you it was shameful when I stood before you; why are you not ashamed that you have actually done such and such things?
The bhikṣuṇī wife became enraged and struck him with the handle of a fan, doused his head with water, and then left to enter her room.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How can you, out of anger, strike a bhikṣu?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that bhikṣuṇī:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, bhikṣuṇī! Why do you strike a bhikṣu?
Having thus rebuked this bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed the first offense among many such bases for outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī provides water or fans a bhikṣu while he is eating, it is a pāyattika.'"
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs were filled with doubt; they did not dare to attend to sick bhikṣus, and when there was no one to give them water, they did not dare to ask.
The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to inquire after the sick bhikṣus; if there is no water, they are permitted to ask.
From this day forward, the precept should be established as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī provides water or fans a bhikṣu with a fan during a meal when he is not ill, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, when a bhikṣu is not ill, provides him with water at mealtime or stands before him fanning him with a fan, it is a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for one who, while attending to a sick bhikṣu, does not ask for water.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
75. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs begged for raw grain, sesame, rice, or large and small beans, and large and small wheat.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs never tire of begging; they have no sense of shame. Yet outwardly they claim, 'We understand the True Dharma.'"
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To beg for various kinds of raw grain and rice like this is no different from a courtesan or a female thief.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Why have you all begged for these various kinds of raw grains and rice?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"Why do you all beg for these various kinds of raw grains and rice?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In many ways, this constitutes a source of outflows for these six bhikṣuṇīs; it is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī begs for raw grain, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣuṇī begs for raw grain, including even large and small wheat, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika) in all cases.
For a bhikṣu, it is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one begs from a relative, or begs from one who has left the household life, or if another acts on one's behalf, or if one acts on behalf of another, or if one obtains it without begging.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(76) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Not far from the bhikṣuṇī’s vihāra, there grew a fine kind of *jālī-grass*.

At that time, several laypeople (gṛhapati) would frequently come there to sit and lie down, engaging in flirtatious play; they would sometimes chant, sing, or dance, while at other times they would make sounds of weeping. These disturbances troubled the bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing meditation.
After the lay devotees had departed, they placed their excrement and urine upon the grass.
When the lay devotees returned and were playing therein, their bodies and clothes became defiled by these impurities, and as the grass was thus stained with filth, it subsequently withered and died.
At that time, the laypeople, on account of this matter, all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs are insatiable in receiving gifts and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim for themselves:
'We understand the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what kind of True Dharma is there?
We have frequently come here to play, laugh, sing, and dance; why has a bhikṣuṇī defiled and ruined the pure grass with excrement and urine, and furthermore defiled our bodies and clothing?"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse.

They rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "How can you, in a place where laypeople amuse themselves, defile them with the impurities of excrement and urine placed upon living grass, thereby soiling their bodies and clothing, and causing the living grass to wither and die?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
Thereupon, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, bhikṣuṇī? Why do you place excrement and urine upon living grass in places where laypeople enjoy themselves, thereby defiling your body and your robes?"
Having rebuked this bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
“This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many sources of outflows for these bhikṣuṇīs.”

From this day forward, I establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine upon living grass, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
This is what is called an offense.

There is no offense if one has such an illness, or if one urinates or defecates in a place without grass and the waste flows onto the grass, or is blown there by the wind, or carried there by birds, thereby defiling the grass. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(77) At that time, the Blessed One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī from the group of six who, having voided excrement and urine into a vessel during the night, discarded it outside the wall the following morning without looking.
At that moment, a minister who lacked faith and devotion was driving his carriage at dawn, intending to pay his respects to King Bimbisāra, when his route passed by the side of the bhikṣuṇīs’ vihāra.
The excrement and urine discarded by a nun fell upon the head of this great minister, defiling his body and clothing.
At that time, the minister thought to himself:
"I shall report this matter to the judicial officials."
At that time, a devout Brahmin who was skilled in reading signs asked,
"Where do you wish to go?
The minister replied:
"The bhikṣuṇī has defiled and insulted me with excrement and urine; I wish to speak to the officials who adjudicate legal matters.
The Brahmin Jñānadarśin admonished him, saying:
"Desist! Do not do so!"
"Do not speak of this matter to the authorities; otherwise, the matter may fail and you will incur further punishment.
At these words, the minister immediately returned.
That Brahmin who knew the signs then went to the bhikṣuṇī monastery and asked:
“Which bhikṣuṇī is it that, at night, fills a vessel with excrement and urine and discards it outside the wall without looking? The bhikṣuṇīs replied, “We do not know.”
The bhikṣuṇīs asked, "Why do you ask about this matter?
Then the brahmin related the circumstances in detail to the bhikṣuṇīs.
"I have already rebuked this minister and made him desist, telling him: 'From this day forward, do not act like this again.
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇīs immediately examined one another to see who had done this.
They immediately knew that one among the group of six bhikṣuṇīs had committed this act.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How could you, at night, place your excrement and urine in a vessel and, when morning came, discard it outside the wall without looking?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
At night, how can you discharge excrement and urine into a vessel and discard it outside the wall without looking?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of taintful offenses; this is the first breach of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī disposes of a vessel for excrement or urine at night outside a wall during the daytime without first inspecting it, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
That bhikṣuṇī, having discharged excrement or urine into a vessel at night, must look out over the wall during the daytime before discarding it.
If one rises at night, one must first snap one's fingers and clear one's throat.
If a bhikṣuṇī disposes of excrement or urine in a vessel at night and does not look outside the wall before discarding it during the day, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one discards [the refuse] at night without coughing or snapping one's fingers, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one voids excrement or urine into a vessel at night and discards it outside the wall during the day;
or if one snaps one's fingers or coughs at night [before disposing of it].
If there are tiles, stones, tree stumps, thorns, or other impure places where it may be discarded;
or if there is a pool of water, a ditch or embankment, or a heap of refuse, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(78) At that time, the Blessed One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.
At that time, on a day of national custom and festival, there were performances of music and games. The group of six bhikṣuṇīs went to watch them.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or modesty and practice impure conduct; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?
To watch such various performances together—how is this any different from being with courtesans or female thieves?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you all go together to watch such spectacles?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On that occasion, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you all go together to watch performances?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This group of six bhikṣuṇīs has committed many things that lead to outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to watch performances of music and dance, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "watching": she watches various kinds of performances and laughter.
That bhikṣuṇī, whether going from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from high to low, or from low to high, goes to watch such musical performances.
If one sees [the offense], it is a *pāyattika*;
if one does not see it, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one forms the intention to go but does not go, or if one intends to go but returns midway, in all such cases it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has something to report; if one is summoned and passes by on the side of the path; if it is the place where the other person is staying; if one is taken away by force; if one is bound and taken away; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(79) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs entered a village and stood conversing with men in a secluded place.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they commit impure acts while outwardly claiming: [we are pure]."
"I know the True Dharma"—
what kind of True Dharma is this?
To enter a village and converse in private with men is no different from being a courtesan or a female thief.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you enter a village and stand conversing with men in a secluded place?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
“How is it that you enter a village and stand in a secluded place to converse with men?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“This group of six bhikṣuṇīs has committed many kinds of outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village and stands or converses with a man in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Village" refers to the residence of laypeople.
"A secluded place" refers to a location where one cannot see or hear.
A "place out of sight" refers to a place obscured by dust, mist, or darkness.
A "place out of hearing" refers to a place where even the sound of ordinary speech cannot be heard.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village and stands in a secluded spot with a man to converse with him, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the companion is blind but not deaf, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If they are deaf but not blind, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If they stand but do not speak, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if two bhikṣuṇīs are her companions; or if she has a reliable person as a companion; or if she stands together with many women; or if she is neither blind nor deaf; or if she is walking and not standing still; or if she falls to the ground due to illness; or if she is seized by those using force; or if she is bound and led away; or if there is danger to life or danger to her brahmacarya. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Section Eighty concludes. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs entered a secluded place together with men.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they commit impure acts while outwardly claiming for themselves:..."
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?
How can a bhikṣuṇī enter a secluded place together with a man, no different from a courtesan or a female thief?

At that time, among the bhikṣuṇīs, those who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, heard of this and censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you all enter a secluded, screened place together with men?"
The bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"What is this, O group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
Entering a secluded place together with a man?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many points of outflow; this is their first transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters a secluded place together with a man, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
A "screened place" refers to one that is concealed by a tree, a wall, a fence, a cloth, or any other object.
If that bhikṣuṇī enters a secluded place together with a man, it is a pāyattika offense.
If her companion is blind but not deaf, or deaf but not blind, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If one stands [and obstructs], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if there are two bhikṣuṇīs as companions,
or if there is a person capable of being known [as a witness] as a companion.
If there is another woman as a companion;

if she is not blind or deaf; if she is walking and not stationary; if she has fallen to the ground due to illness; or if she is being led away by force, or is bound, or faces a threat to her life, or a threat to her celibacy—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
81. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs stood together and conversed with men in secluded places within the streets and alleys of a village; or, having sent their companions far away, they whispered alone with men.
At that time, the laypeople saw this and all together reviled her, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame or modesty; she violates the pure conduct (brahmacarya), yet outwardly she claims, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
"What kind of true Dharma is this?

How can a bhikṣuṇī enter the secluded lanes within a village and stand or converse with a man, or send her companions far away to whisper alone with a man, no different from a courtesan or a bandit woman?"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you enter a village and stand in secluded places within the lanes and streets to whisper with men?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that ought not to be done."
"What is this, bhikṣuṇīs! Entering into the narrow alleys within the village, how can you stand alone in a secluded place and whisper with a man?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of unwholesome acts; this is the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having entered the lanes and alleys within a village, sends her companion far away and stands in a secluded place whispering with a man, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
A "village" refers to the lanes and streets of the dwellings of laypeople.
A "secluded place" refers to a place where one is hidden from sight or a place where one is hidden from hearing.
"Hidden from sight" refers to smoke, clouds, mist, dust, and darkness, which are not seen by the eye.
"Hidden from hearing" refers to even ordinary speech whose sound is not heard.
"Whispering" means speaking beside the ear.

If that bhikṣuṇī, having entered a village lane or street, sends her companion away to a place where she is neither seen nor heard, and stands together with a man in a secluded spot whispering in his ear, it is a pāyattika offense.
To go from a place where one cannot see to a place where one can hear, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
To go from a place where one cannot hear to a place where one can see, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense.

There is no offense if she is accompanied by two bhikṣuṇīs, or by a woman whose [mental] capacity is known, or by other persons; or if her companions are not blind or deaf; or if a companion falls to the ground due to a sudden illness; or if she is seized by a person of superior force, or bound and taken away; or if there is danger to life or danger to the brahmacarya; or if someone gives her something and sends her companions far away; or if a companion is ill; or if a companion lacks proper decorum, and she says: [“I am going alone”].
“Sister, you go! I shall send food for you.

There is no offense if [the recipient] has broken the precepts, broken the view, or broken the decorum; or if they have been formally censured (*ukkhepanīya*); or if they are subject to expulsion (*pabbājanīya*); or if, on account of this matter, there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(82) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, when the time had come, put on her robes, took up her bowl, and went to the house of a lay devotee. Having arrived, the laywoman spread out a single seat for her to sit upon; once she was seated, the woman left and entered the inner room.
This bhikṣuṇī sat for a short while; without speaking to the host, she abandoned her seat and departed.
Just as she had stepped out the door, a māṇava entered the house. Looking around and seeing no one, he thought to himself:
"This bed and seat will be of benefit to me."
She immediately took it and departed.
When the householder’s wife came out, she did not see the bhikṣuṇī, nor did she see the solitary sitting bench. She immediately sent a messenger to inquire of the bhikṣuṇī:
“Where is the solitary sitting bench?”
The bhikṣuṇī replied, “I do not know.
When I went out, a māṇava came into your house; perhaps he took it away—you should inquire of him.”
She immediately went to search for it and returned with the bed and seat.
At that time, the laypeople all criticized her, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame; she claims for herself externally:"
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?
How can you sit upon the master’s bed and depart without a word, no different from a prostitute or a thief?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī sit upon a master’s bed or seat and then depart without speaking?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked these bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that should not have been done."
"What do you think, bhikṣuṇī!
How could you sit upon the master’s bed or seat and then depart without speaking to the master?
Having thus rebuked this bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed the first offense among many such bases for taints.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sits inside the house of a layperson and departs without informing the host, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the house of a layperson and sits down, and then departs through the door without informing the host, it is a pāyattika offense.

If one foot is inside the gate and one foot is outside the gate, and if one intends to leave through skillful means but does not go, or if one has made an appointment to go but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one speaks to the host and departs; or if there is another person sitting on the seat; or if, when departing, one entrusts the matter to a neighbor-sitter, and that neighbor-sitter says:
"You may go; there is no harm."

If one sits upon a stone, a piece of wood, a brick, a grass mat, or a straw mat; or if the house is about to collapse, or is on fire, or there are venomous snakes, wild beasts, or thieves; or if one is seized by force, bound, or faces a threat to life or a threat to one’s holy life (brahmacarya), and departs without informing the host, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(83) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a minister in the city of Rājagṛha who lacked faith and devotion; he possessed a solitary seat upon which no one dared to sit.
The bhikṣuṇī Sthūlanandā frequently entered and left his house, serving as his patron (dānapati).
When Thullanandā arrived, she put on her robes, took up her bowl, and went to that house; without speaking, she sat down upon the minister’s couch.
When the minister saw this, he asked:
"Who allowed this bhikṣuṇī to sit upon my bed?"
He replied, "There is no one speaking; he has simply come and sat down himself.
At that time, the minister spoke with derision, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā is devoid of shame and remorse, yet she claims of herself:
'I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is there in such a person?"
"How is it that this bhikṣuṇī sits upon another's seat without informing the owner, no different from a female thief or a courtesan?
When Steunānadā sat upon the bed, her menstrual blood flowed and defiled the bedding; she then abandoned it and departed.
Having seen this, the minister became even more enraged and said:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame; outwardly she claims for herself, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To sit upon another’s seat without informing her owner—how does this differ from a prostitute or a thief?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires, were contented, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Steyānanandā.
"How is it that a bhikṣuṇī sits upon another's bed without first informing the owner?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā: "What you have done is improper;
it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teachings]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"What is this, Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā!
How could you sit upon another's bed without first informing the owner?
Having thus rebuked the Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun Thullanandā has committed many acts of outflow; this is her first transgression of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and sits upon a bed without informing the host, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and sits upon a bed or seat without first informing the host, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one speaks to the host and sits down; or if there is a customary place to sit; or if they are close friends; or if there is a close friend who says:
"You may simply sit down without concern; I shall inform the host."

If one is sitting on a stone, a piece of wood, a mound of earth, or a grass mat; or if one falls to the ground due to a fit of insanity; or if one is seized by someone using force; or if there is a threat to life or a threat to one’s brahmacarya—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(84) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs were traveling along a road toward the kingdom of Kośala, intending to go to a certain village without permanent dwellings.
Having arrived, they did not inform the host, but instead spread out their own sitting mats and stayed there for the night.
When the laypeople saw them, they asked,
"Who has settled these bhikṣuṇīs here to stay overnight? They replied:
"There is no one here to provide security; come and stay yourself.
At that time, the laypeople criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?
How can a bhikṣuṇī enter another's house and settle herself there at will without first informing her master?
"How is this any different from being with a prostitute or a bandit woman?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame;
they censured those bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "How can a bhikṣuṇī, without informing the host, enter another's house and sit, lie down, or stay overnight there?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"What is this, bhikṣuṇī? How can you enter another's house to stay, sit, or lie down without first informing the host?
Having thus rebuked this bhikṣuṇī with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These various points of leakage among the bhikṣuṇīs constitute the first breach of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters the home of a layperson and, without informing the host, spreads out a seat for herself and stays overnight, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "spreading a seat": it means spreading grass, or spreading leaves, or even spreading a bedding mat.

If that bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson's house and, without informing the host, spreads out her own seat and stays there to sleep, then for every side of her body that touches the ground, or for every turn she makes, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one informs the host of one's intention to stay; or if it is an empty house, a merit-dedicated shelter, or the residence of an acquaintance or a close friend, and one says:
"You simply sit here; I shall speak with the host on your behalf."
There is no offense if one is coerced by force, bound, or faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
There is also no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precept, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
85. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs entered a dark room together with men.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or modesty; they commit impure acts.
Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma. How can this be called knowing the True Dharma?
How can a bhikṣuṇī enter a dark room together with a man, no different from a courtesan or a female thief?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you enter a dark room together with men?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it, O group of six bhikṣuṇīs,
that you enter a dark room together with men?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of taintful offenses; this is the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī enters a dark room together with a man, it is a pāyattika offense.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
A "dark room" is one that has no lamps or fire, no windows or openings, and no light.
If a bhikṣuṇī enters such a dark room together with a man, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if there is light from a lamp or the radiance from a window; or if one is led inside by force; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical suffering.
