One hundred and seventy-eight rules on the *Pratideśanīya-dharmas*, Part Three. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyānandā, who was a disciple of the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā.
Her teacher said to her:
"Bring me your robe, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, having received her teacher’s instruction without careful scrutiny, said to the other bhikṣuṇīs:
“My teacher instructed me to steal robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases.”
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard these words, they immediately asked the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā:
"Is it true that you instructed your disciple to steal the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case?"
She replied, "Sisters!
How could I ever have such an intention as to instruct my disciples to steal robes, alms-bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases?"
"I was simply telling her to bring the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case; I did not instruct her to steal.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Nandā, saying:
"How could you receive your teacher's words without careful discernment?"
She spoke to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"The teacher instructed me to steal the robes, the bowl, the sitting mat, and the needle case.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Nandā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How could you have received your teacher's words without careful examination, and then said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
'My teacher instructed me to steal robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases'?"
At that time, having rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Nandā with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā Nandā has committed many things that lead to outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having carefully verified what she has heard, speaks it to others, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
That bhikṣuṇī, having not received the words with careful attention, spoke to the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"My teacher instructed me to steal robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases."
If one speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the matter is actually so and one says: [the truth].
"Go and steal the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case and bring them here.
She said to the bhikṣuṇīs,
"My teacher instructed me to steal the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case and bring them here."
There is no offense if one speaks while joking, or speaks hurriedly, or speaks to oneself, or speaks in a dream, or intends to say one thing but mistakenly says another.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh [rule]. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs became angry over a minor matter and together uttered curses, saying:
"May we fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma if I do this;
may you also fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma if you do this."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you, upon having such a minor matter, become so enraged as to utter such curses, saying:
'May I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma'—if I have committed such an act, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma?"
"If you possess such things, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the precepts—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
Because of some trivial matter, you become angry and utter such curses, saying: 'May I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma:
if I have committed such an act, may I enter the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma;'"
"If you possess such things, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born into the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This group of six bhikṣuṇīs has committed many sources of outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, on account of some minor matter, should utter a curse that one might fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma, saying:
'If I have such a thing, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma;'"
"If you possess such things, you too shall fall into the three evil realms and not be born into the Buddha-dharma.
This constitutes a *pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to invoke 'Namo Buddha. If I encounter such a situation, I shall say 'Namo Buddha';
if you encounter such a situation, you too shall say 'Namo Buddha.'"
That bhikṣuṇī, on account of a minor matter, cursed herself that she would fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma, saying:
"If I have committed this act, may I fall into the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma;
if you have committed this act, may you likewise enter the three evil realms and not be born within the Buddha-dharma."
If one speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one says "Namo Buddha," or speaks in jest, or speaks rapidly, or speaks to oneself, or speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that. These are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(88) At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Kuśinagara in the Gośṛṅga Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālā engaged in a quarrel with another; unable to properly recall the details of the dispute, she began to beat her breast with her own hands and weep.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this—among whom were those who possessed few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse—they rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kālā:
"How can you, having quarreled with another, beat your breast with your own hands and weep?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kālā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teaching]. It is something that ought not to be done."
"What is this, Bhikṣuṇī Kālā! Why do you quarrel with another and beat your breast with your hand while weeping?
Having thus rebuked the Bhikṣuṇī Kālā through countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This Bhikṣuṇī Kālā has committed the first offense among many such sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the Bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a Bhikṣuṇī engages in quarreling and strife, and failing to properly keep the matter of the dispute in mind, beats her breast and weeps, it is a Pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding that bhikṣuṇī who engages in quarreling with others, there are four kinds of disputes as mentioned above.
If a bhikṣuṇī quarrels and, unable to properly recall the matter of the dispute, beats her breast and weeps, for each instance of beating her breast, it is a pāyattika offense.
For every single drop of tears that falls, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *dukkaṭa*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

when one has such an illness; when one strikes oneself because of a choking sensation while eating; when tears flow due to urination or defecation; when tears flow due to wind, cold, or heat; when tears flow from being smoked by fumes; when tears flow from a mind of weary detachment upon hearing the Dharma; or when tears flow from applying medicine for an eye ailment—in these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(89) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in the kingdom of Vṛji.

At that time, two bhikṣuṇīs of the group of six lay together on one bed; when the other bhikṣuṇīs saw them, they thought they were lying with a man, but upon seeing them rise, they realized it was not a man.

At that time, there was a great general—valiant, wise, and fully equipped with all manner of skills—who was highly proficient in combat. Having recently married and not long ago received an official decree to go on campaign, he had this thought:
"Now that I am going on a distant expedition, to whom shall my wife be entrusted?"
Just as he was about to entrust [his wife] to the householder, the householder had many men in his home and could not accept the entrustment.
The general had previously been acquainted with the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilānī and thought to himself:
"I would rather entrust my wife to the bhikṣuṇī Kapilā first, and only then set out on campaign."
She then handed her over.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kāpilā accepted the woman as a wife; for the sake of protection, they shared a bed and stayed together overnight.
This bhikṣuṇī Kāpilā had a body that was delicate and soft, and when the woman’s body touched hers, she gave rise to a mind of lustful attachment.

At that time, the general returned from his campaign and went to meet his wife at home; however, the wife, having become attached to the fine and soft body of a bhikṣuṇī, fled back to where that nun was staying.
This general thought to himself:
"I desired to do good, yet I have instead obtained evil; why is it that my wife no longer loves me, but has become infatuated with a bhikṣuṇī and fled back to her place?"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the six group of bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilānī, saying:
"How is it that you two lie together on the same bed?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs and the bhikṣuṇī Kāpilā:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you two lie together on the same bed?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣus and the bhikṣuṇī Kāpilā with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This group of six and the bhikṣuṇī Kāpilā have committed the first offense regarding many such bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī lies on the same bed with another, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
At that time, those who were uncertain did not dare to lie on the same bed with a sick bhikṣuṇī, nor did they dare to sit together or lie down together with one another.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to lie on the same bed as one who is ill.
I allow you to change positions by sitting and lying down."
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill lies on the same bed with another, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "beds," there are five types as mentioned above.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is not ill lies down on a bed together with another person, for every side of her body that comes into contact with the bedding, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
For each instance of following along, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one lies on the same bed with a sick person, or sits and lies down alternately with them; or if the sick person falls to the ground, or is seized by those using force, or is bound, or there is danger to life, or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Ninety: At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in the kingdom of Vṛji.
At that time, two bhikṣuṇīs from the group of six lay together on the same mat and under the same blanket.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw them, they thought they were lying with a man; it was only upon rising that they realized it was not a man.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you two lie together on one mat and under one blanket?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you two lie together on the same mat and under the same blanket?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"In many ways, this constitutes a source of outflows for these six bhikṣuṇīs; it is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī lies down to sleep on the same mat and under the same blanket with another, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
A certain bhikṣuṇī had a single mat made either of grass or of tree leaves; the other bhikṣuṇīs, being doubtful, did not dare to lie down with her.
The Buddha said:

"I permit the bhikṣuṇīs to each spread out their own sleeping mats. If there is only one blanket during the cold season, they are permitted to each wear an undergarment beneath it and then lie down together."
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same mat and under the same blanket with another, except at other times, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If those bhikṣuṇīs lie down on the same mat and under the same blanket, with their sides resting against the bed, it is a pāyattika offense.
For each instance of following along [in such conduct], there is one *pāyattika* offense.
If they share the same mat but use separate covers, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If they share the same cover but use separate mats, it is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if there is only one mat, or if one is lying on grass or leaves, each having spread out their own separate bedding;

or if it is during the cold season and they are under the same blanket but each wearing an inner garment; or if one has fallen to the ground due to illness; or if one is seized by someone using force; or if one is bound; or if there is danger to life; or if there is danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
91. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, for the sake of causing annoyance, would—whether they had arrived after those already residing there or had arrived before them—take precedence in reciting the sūtras, inquiring about their meaning, and providing instruction.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"How is it that for the sake of causing disturbance, you—whether arriving after those already settled or having arrived first—recite the sūtras, inquire about their meaning, and provide instruction in front of others?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On that occasion, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"How is it that you, out of a desire to cause trouble, [allow those who] arrived later to [displace those who] were already residing there, or [allow those who] arrived later to [displace those who] were already residing there; and how is it that you recite the sūtras, inquire about their meaning, or provide instruction while standing in front [of them]?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This group of six bhikṣuṇīs has committed many kinds of outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of a desire to cause annoyance, [approaches] one who was already residing first by arriving later, or one who arrived later by being the first resident, and recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or provides instruction in their presence, it is a pāyattika."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.

Those bhikṣuṇīs did not know whether they had arrived first or not, nor whether they had arrived later or not; it was only afterwards that they realized it. Among them, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
"If one does not know, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she arrived after those who were already residing, or that those who arrived later were already residing before her, for the sake of causing annoyance, recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or instructs them while standing in front of them, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that she arrived later than those who were already residing there, or that they arrived earlier than she did, for the sake of causing annoyance, recites the sūtras, inquires about their meaning, or provides instruction while standing in front of them, it constitutes a pāyattika offense if she is clearly understood;
if she is not clearly understood, it is a dukkaṭa offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one does not know [the fault], or if it was previously permitted, or if the person is a close relative or friend, or if a close relative or friend says:
"You need only provide instruction; I shall speak for you."

If one who was already residing there receives the sutra from one who arrives later; or if one who arrives later recites it from one who was already residing there; or if both receive it together from another; or if the other asks and this person answers; or if they recite it together; or if they speak jokingly; or if they speak very rapidly; or if they speak in a dream; or if they intended to say this but mistakenly said that—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(92) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā did not tend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī living with her who was ill.
Other bhikṣuṇīs said to her, "A fellow bhikṣuṇī living with you is ill; why do you not look after her?"
She still did not look after her, and because she failed to look after her, the nun eventually passed away.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Steyānanandā:
"How could you fail to look after a fellow co-resident bhikṣuṇī who was ill?"
"The bhikṣuṇīs exhorted you, yet you did not follow their words in providing care, and consequently caused her life to end.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice; it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā! Why did you not tend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī living with you who was ill?
When the other bhikṣuṇīs urged you to look after her, you did not follow their words, and consequently caused her life to end."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā through countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā has committed many things that are sources of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not tend to a fellow bhikṣuṇī with whom she lives when that bhikṣuṇī is ill, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Living together" refers to two bhikṣuṇīs living their lives in common.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not tend to another bhikṣuṇī with whom she lives when that bhikṣuṇī is ill, it is a pāyattika offense.

Except in the case of a fellow resident who is ill, if one does not nurse any other bhikṣuṇī who is ill—whether it be one’s preceptor (upādhyāya), one’s teacher (ācārya), a fellow preceptor, a fellow teacher, a disciple, or a close friend or acquaintance—it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one is tending to a fellow resident who is ill; or if one is oneself ill and unable to tend to the patient; or if, due to such circumstances, there is a danger to life or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya) and one does not attend to them. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(93) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having initially permitted another bhikṣuṇī to arrange a bed within her room during the summer retreat, became enraged during the retreat and dragged the bed out, driving her away.
At that time, that bhikṣuṇī, feeling ashamed and fearing she would lose her lodging, immediately abandoned the path.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Steunānanda:

"How could you, at the beginning of the retreat, allow another bhikṣuṇī to set up a bed in your room, yet during the retreat, out of anger, pull the bed away and drive her out, causing her to feel ashamed and abandon the path?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not the practice of conformity—it is something that should not be done."
How is this, Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā!

At the beginning of the rainy season retreat, you permitted other bhikṣuṇīs to place their beds in the rooms; yet during the retreat, out of anger, you pulled their beds and drove them out, causing them to feel ashamed and abandon the path?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā through countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā has committed many things that are sources of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having initially permitted another bhikṣuṇī to place a bed in her room during the rainy season retreat, subsequently drives her out out of anger, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"During the rainy season retreat" means having entered the retreat.
"Beds" refers to the five kinds of beds as described above.

If that bhikṣuṇī, at the beginning of the rainy-season retreat, permits another bhikṣuṇī to place a bed in her room, but later, out of anger, drives her out by employing various means, for every step she takes toward the door, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
If one employs a means to drive many people out of many doors, there are many *pāyattikas*.
If one employs a means to drive many people out of a single door, there are many *pāyattikas*.
If one employs a stratagem to drive a single person out of many doors, there are many *pāyattikas*.
If one employs a stratagem to drive a single person out of one door, there is one *pāyattika*.
If one brings out other clothing or articles, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one closes the door so that [the person] cannot enter, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, without anger, one drives out a junior seat-holder according to the order of seniority.
If one stays overnight with a person who has not received the full ordination (upasampadā), after the second night, they must be expelled on the third night;
or if one causes a sick person to go out to a place for defecation or urination to relieve themselves;

or if [the person] has broken the precepts, broken their views, or broken their deportment; or if they have been subject to formal censure (ukkhepanīyakamma), or have been suspended (pabbājaniyakamma), or are subject to suspension.
If, due to this matter, there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), and one expels [the person] in all cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.
94. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs traveled through the human settlements during all seasons—spring, summer, and winter.
At that time, encountering heavy rain, the river overflowed its banks, causing her to lose her robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case, and to trample and kill living grass.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame; she takes the lives of living beings, yet outwardly claims for herself:"
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?

How can a bhikṣuṇī travel through human settlements at all times—during spring, summer, and winter—and encounter torrential rains that cause rivers to overflow, resulting in the loss of various belongings, as well as treading upon living grass and cutting off the lives of sentient beings?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"How is it that you all travel through human settlements at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and upon encountering rain, the river waters overflow, causing you to lose your belongings and trample and kill living grasses, thereby inciting the reproach and suspicion of the laypeople?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it, group of six bhikṣuṇīs!

You wander through human settlements at all times—spring, summer, and winter—and when encountering rain, the river waters overflow, causing you to lose your belongings and trample and kill living grass, leading householders to criticize and despise you?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This group of six bhikṣuṇīs has committed many forms of outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels among the people at any time—whether in spring, summer, or winter—it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs:
"If that bhikṣuṇī [is absent] for the sake of affairs concerning the Buddha, affairs concerning the Dharma, affairs concerning the Saṃgha, or affairs concerning a sick bhikṣuṇī..."
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive the seven-day rule and go beyond the boundary.
From this day forward, the precepts should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī wanders through human settlements at all times—during spring, summer, and winter—except for other valid reasons, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣuṇī wanders among people at all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter—and enters the boundary of a village, it is a pāyattika for each instance.
If she travels ten *li* in a place where there is neither a village nor a defined boundary, it is a pāyattika.
To reduce [the distance] by one village or ten *li* constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
To travel within a single boundary between two villages also constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes preparations to go but does not go, or if one has agreed with others to go but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if it is for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha; for the sake of a sick bhikṣuṇī; or if one has received the seven-day rule and travels outside the boundary;
or if one is seized by force, or bound and led away, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life—there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.
(95) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the lay devotees of Śrāvastī invited the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā to establish a formal regulation together:
"We shall collectively provide offerings to the Saṃgha until the end of the rainy season retreat."
When the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā had finished her rainy-season retreat, she remained there and did not depart.
At that time, the lay devotees all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"We previously established a regulation to invite the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā to come so that we might together provide offerings to the Saṃgha until the end of the retreat."
"The bhikṣuṇī Śamā has now completed her *varṣā* retreat, yet she still does not depart.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Śamā, saying:
"The lay devotees collectively established a regulation, inviting the bhikṣuṇī Śamā to come so that they might together provide offerings to the Saṃgha until the end of the *varṣā*."
"Now that the summer retreat has concluded, we remain here and do not depart.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went to inform the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done."
“How is it that the lay devotees provided you with offerings for the summer retreat, which has now concluded, yet you still remain here, causing the lay devotees to criticize and disparage you?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first transgression among the many bases of outflows.”

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat, does not depart, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
When a bhikṣuṇī has completed the rainy-season retreat (varṣā), she should go forth on a journey for at least one night.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy-season retreat, does not go forth on a journey, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: having completed the summer retreat (varṣā), one departs; or if that householder further invites one to stay, thinking, "I shall provide further offerings";

or if there is the practice of receiving food from various households; or if male or female relatives invite one for a meal today or tomorrow; or if one encounters illness and lacks an attendant to look after them; or if there is danger from water, danger from wild beasts, or danger from bandits; or if the river is in flood; or if one is seized by forceful persons, or is bound in fetters; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In such circumstances, if one does not go forth after the summer retreat has ended, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the people in the border regions of King Prasenajit’s realm had rebelled.
Then the group of six bhikṣuṇīs wandered through those human settlements in places where there was suspicion and fear.
When the bandits saw them, they said:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs are all supported by King Prasenajit; we should collectively harass them."
When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or modesty; they have all violated the holy life (brahmacarya).
Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I practice the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
To wander through frontier human settlements and places of terror is no different from being with bandit women or courtesans.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying: "How is it that you wander through fearful places in the human world?"
They immediately went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
At that time, for this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not compliant conduct—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you all wander through fearful places in the human world?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī travels among the people in a border region that is suspicious and dangerous, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Border region" refers to a place far from a city.
"Having suspicion" means suspecting the presence of thieves or robbers.
"Fear" refers to the apprehension of thieves or robbers.
If that bhikṣuṇī wanders through a border region where such suspicion and fear exist, for every boundary she enters while traveling from village to village, there is a pāyattika offense for each.
If one travels ten *li* through a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) that is not a village, it is one *pāyattika*.
If one travels less than a village’s distance or less than ten *li*, it is one *dukkaṭa*.
If one travels within a single boundary inside a village, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one intends to go by making an appointment but does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense in all cases.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, and a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one is summoned, invited, or has something to report; or if one is seized by those using force, bound, or faces a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacarya*); or if, having arrived first, a subsequent suspicion or fearful incident arises. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.

Then, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs wandered through that realm in places where there was suspicion and fear.

"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs are all supported by King Prasenajit; we should collectively harass them."

"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or remorse and have all violated the holy life (brahmacarya). Yet outwardly they claim for themselves:

"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To wander within the boundaries of the monastic precincts in places of doubt and fear is no different from being a female thief or a prostitute.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs.
"How is it that you wander through places in the human world that are full of fear?
They immediately went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"Why do you, sirs, wander within the boundaries among humans in places of fear?
Having thus rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of outflows; this is their first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī wanders through inhabited areas within a boundary where there is suspicion or fear, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Within the boundary" refers to the area surrounding the four sides of the city wall.
"One who has doubt" refers to one who suspects the presence of thieves or robbers.
"Fear" refers to the apprehension of thieves or robbers.

If a bhikṣuṇī wanders among people within that boundary in a place where such fear and suspicion exist, for every single boundary she enters while traveling from village to village, it constitutes a pāyattika offense.
In a forest hermitage where there is no village, if one travels ten *li*, it is one *pāyattika*.
If it is less than a village or less than ten *li*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one walks within a single boundary inside a village, it is one *dukkaṭa*.
If one intends to go by means of an expedient but does not go, or agrees to go with another but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one has something to report, or is summoned, or is invited to go, or is seized by those using force, or is bound, or faces a threat to life, or a threat to the holy life (brahmacarya); nor is there an offense if, having arrived first, a subsequent matter of doubt or fear arises.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is deluded, insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who associated with laymen and lived together with the sons of laymen, engaging in improper conduct.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying:
"Do not associate with laymen or the sons of laymen and engage in improper conduct."
"Sister, you should live separately; if you live separately, you will attain increase, benefit, and dwell in peace within the Buddha-dharma.
Yet she still did not live separately.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How can you associate with householders and live together with the sons of householders, engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice; it is something that should not have been done."
"How can she associate with and dwell together with laymen and the sons of laymen, engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma?
Having rebuked her, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against that bhikṣuṇī, in order to cause her to abandon this matter."

One should thus reprove her and cause her to relinquish this matter; among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!..."
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so by name, associates with laymen and the sons of laymen, living with them and engaging in conduct that is not in accordance with the Dharma.
Other bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying: "Sister!..."
"Do not associate with householders or the sons of householders by engaging in improper conduct.
You, sister, should dwell apart;
if you dwell apart, there will be progress in the Buddha’s Dharma and you will abide in peace and happiness."
That bhikṣuṇī still does not reform.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha,
may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant that such-and-such bhikṣuṇī a formal reprimand so that she may relinquish this matter.
“Sister, do not associate with householders or the sons of householders, nor dwell with them in conduct that is unwholesome.
Sister, [do not do so].”
"You may live separately; if you live separately, there will be increase in the Buddha-dharma and you shall dwell in peace and happiness.
[The motion] is thus announced.
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so by name, associates with laymen and the sons of laymen, dwelling with them and engaging in improper conduct.
Other bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying:
"Sister!..."
Do not associate with or dwell together with householders or the sons of householders, practicing what is discordant [with the Dharma].
Sister, you should now dwell apart; if you dwell apart, there will be progress in the Buddha’s teaching and you will abide in peace and happiness.
Yet she still does not desist.
Now the Saṃgha shall carry out a formal reprimand against this bhikṣuṇī so that she may abandon this matter: "Sister!..."
Do not associate with or dwell together with householders or the sons of householders, engaging in conduct that is discordant.
Sister, you should dwell apart;
if you dwell apart, there will be growth in the Buddha’s Dharma and you will abide in peace and happiness.
"Which of you, sisters, approves of the Saṃgha’s censure of that bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for the relinquishing of this matter? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak."
Thus it was said a second and a third time:

"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal act of censure against that bhikṣuṇī for the purpose of making her abandon this matter; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld."
"One should issue such a reprimand.

After the community of bhikṣuṇīs had performed the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to reprimand that bhikṣuṇī and cause her to relinquish this matter, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If there is such a bhikṣuṇī, the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha shall also perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to reprove her and cause her to abandon this matter.

From now on, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī associates with a layman or the son of a layman, dwelling together and engaging in improper conduct.’”
Other bhikṣuṇīs admonished this bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Sister!
Do not associate with laymen or the sons of laymen, nor dwell with them in conduct that is improper."
"Sister!
You should live separately; if you live separately, there will be growth and a peaceful dwelling within the Buddha's Dharma.
When that bhikṣuṇī exhorts this bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], that bhikṣuṇī should exhort her up to three times to relinquish this matter.
"Up to three admonitions, it is well if she abandons this matter;
if she does not abandon it, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"To associate with" means to speak repeatedly, laugh repeatedly, and engage in playful banter repeatedly.
"Householder" refers to one who has not yet gone forth as a renunciant.
"Son" likewise refers to one who has not yet gone forth as a renunciant.
That bhikṣuṇī associates with that householder and his son, dwelling with them and engaging in improper conduct.
Another bhikṣuṇī admonishes this bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister!..."
Do not associate with householders or the sons of householders by engaging in conduct that is discordant.
You should dwell apart; if you dwell apart, there will be progress and a dwelling in peace and happiness within the Buddha’s Dharma.
"You should now abandon this matter; do not commit a grave offense by being censured by the Saṃgha.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, a formal announcement (jñapti) shall be made.
Having made the announcement, one should say:
"Sister! I have already made the announcement; there remains the formal ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*)."
"You may abandon this matter; do not commit further offenses after having been rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, the first *karmavācanā* (formal motion) shall be performed.
Having performed the first *karmavācanā*, one should say:
"Sister! The motion has been made and the first *karmavācanā* has been performed; two *karmavācanās* remain."
"You should abandon this matter; do not commit further offenses after having been rebuked by the Saṃgha.
If he follows these words, it is well; if he does not follow them, a second *karmavācanā* is performed.
After performing the second *karmavācanā*, one should say:
"The motion (*jñapti*) and the first *karmavācanā* have been performed; only one *karmavācanā* remains.
You should relinquish this matter, lest you be censured by the Saṃgha and commit further offenses."
"If they comply with what was said, it is well; if they do not comply, once the three *karmavācanās* have been completed, it is a *pāyattika*.
If the second *karmavācanā* (the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) has been completed, there are three *dukkaṭas*."

When the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) has been completed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses. Once the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.

Before the motion has been completed, and prior to the making of the motion, if one associates with a layperson (*gṛhapati*) or the son of a layperson and performs actions that are not in accordance with the Dharma, all such instances constitute *duṣkṛta* offenses.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one desists at the first word; or if the censure is carried out by an illegal separate assembly; or by an illegal united assembly; or by a legal separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-dharma separate assembly; or by a semblance-of-dharma united assembly; or if it is neither according to the Dharma nor the Vinaya nor taught by the Buddha; or if none of these forms of censure are performed at all, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Ninety-nine: At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs went to view the painted halls, gardens, and bathing pools of the royal palace.
When the laypeople saw them, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame and have violated their pure conduct; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma. What kind of True Dharma is this?
To go and gaze upon royal palaces, painted halls, gardens, and bathing pools is no different from being a thief or a courtesan.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you go to view the royal palace, the painted halls, the gardens, and the bathing pools?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
Thereupon, the Buddha, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣuṇīs!
Why have you gone to view the royal palace, the painted halls, the gardens, and the bathing pools?
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This nun has committed the first offense among many such sources of outflows.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view the ornate decorations, painted halls, gardens, or bathing pools of a royal palace, it is a pāyattika.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view the royal palace, ornamental decorations, painted halls, gardens, groves, or bathing pools—moving from path to path, from path to non-path, from non-path to path, from high to low, or from low to high—and is seen while departing, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not go, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes preparations to go but does not go, or if one has made an appointment to go but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one enters a royal palace to report a matter; if summoned or invited; if passing through on the way; if staying overnight; if seized by those using force; if being led away in bonds; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*);
or if one goes to view a painted hall for the sake of monastic affairs or stūpa affairs, desiring to take its measurements as a model—there is no offense.

If one enters a monastery to receive instruction or listen to the Dharma; or if one passes through it while being invited elsewhere; or if one stays there as a guest; or if one is seized by those using force, or bound and taken away; or if one goes to observe gardens, groves, or bathing pools for the sake of monastic affairs or stūpa affairs, desiring to grasp the formal rules—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were bathing naked in river water, spring water, pond water, and deep water.
There were some female thieves and courtesans who went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said to them:
"You are young and the hair has not yet grown under your arms; why have you gone forth to study the Path and practice the holy life?"
"Just as one is young now, one may enjoy oneself together with sensual desires; when old, one may practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). In this way, both matters can be accomplished.
Upon hearing this, the youths among them immediately felt a sense of displeasure.
At that time, the laypeople saw this and all together reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves, 'We know the True Dharma. "
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To expose one's body and bathe in deep waters of rivers, springs, and ponds is no different from a courtesan or a female thief.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who had few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Why do you, sirs, bathe naked in rivers, springs, ponds, and deep waters?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha.
At that time, for this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"What is this, bhikṣuṇīs?
Are you bathing naked in rivers, ponds, springs, and deep waters?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many types of faulty actions; this is the first violation of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī bathes with her body exposed in river water, spring water, deep water, or pond water, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

That bhikṣuṇī should bathe while covering her body with four things: if she is on the bank of a flowing stream at a bend or a turn; or if there is a place covered by the shade of trees; or if there is a barrier of water; or if she covers her body with a robe.
Regarding the three aforementioned matters, one must not exchange vessels or utensils with others;
however, if they are shielded by a robe, all such lawful activities may be performed.
If that bhikṣuṇī bathes her body in a river, pond, spring, or deep water while naked, immersing herself entirely, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not soak [the robe] thoroughly, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one intends to wash it through preparatory means but does not actually wash it, or if one makes an appointment to go [to the washing place] but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta. This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases:

at a place where a riverbank curves back on itself, in a place covered by the shade of trees, when obstructed by water, when the body is shielded by a garment, or when one is seized by force. These are not offenses.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One permitted the bhikṣuṇīs to make bathing robes.
When the group of six bhikṣuṇīs heard that the World-Honored One had permitted the bhikṣuṇīs to make bathing robes, they then made many large and expansive bathing robes.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī saw it and asked,
"The Buddha has permitted the bhikṣuṇīs to keep five robes.
What kind of robe is this?"
They replied, "These are our bathing robes. When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this,

those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
“The Blessed One has permitted the keeping of bathing robes.
Why, then, have these been made so large and wide?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
“What do you think, bhikṣuṇīs?
Do you frequently make vast bath-garments?
Having thus rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"These six groups of bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of taintful offenses; this is the first breach of the precepts.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bathing robe, she must make it according to the prescribed measurement.'"
Regarding the measurement of the garment: it shall be six spans long and two and a half spans wide according to the Buddha’s span; if it exceeds these dimensions, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
A bathing robe (*udakasāṭikā*) is that which covers the body for the purpose of bathing.

If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bathing robe that is excessive in length but sufficient in width, or sufficient in length but excessive in width, or excessive in both dimensions, and she cuts and sews it herself, it is a *pāyattika* offense;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one instructs another to cut [cloth] and it is completed, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one acts on behalf of another, whether it is completed or not, it is in all cases a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is what constitutes an offense.

There is no offense if one makes it according to the prescribed measure or less; if one obtains a pre-made garment, one should cut it to conform to the Dharma; if it is made by layering pieces together, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who wished to sew a saṃghāṭī. Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said:
"Sister, bring it here!"
"I will sew it for you. He then gave her the cloth for the robe.
That bhikṣuṇī was intelligent and possessed great knowledge; she was skilled in teaching and transforming others.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, with this intention—to cause that other bhikṣuṇī to provide her with offerings for a long time—cut out the cloth for a robe but did not immediately sew it together.
At that time, a fire broke out in the vihāra where the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā resided; her robes and possessions were consumed by the flames, and others were scattered and blown away by the wind.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke with derision and reproach:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame or modesty; outwardly she claims for herself:"
"I practice the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
How can a bhikṣuṇī cut another's cloth yet fail to sew it immediately, so that it is consumed by fire or blown away by the wind?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Steyanandā, saying:
"How could you have made a robe for another and not sewn it to completion, so that it was consumed by fire and blown away by the wind?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not be done."
"What do you think, bhikṣuṇīs?
Did you cut the cloth for a robe but fail to sew it immediately, so that it was consumed by fire or blown away by the wind?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This nun has committed the first offense among many such bases for taints.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a nun sews a saṃghāṭī robe beyond five days, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs: when they seek a saṃghāṭī robe and the kaṭhina cloth has been suspended, six difficult circumstances may arise that cause doubt.
The Buddha said:
"If such a matter occurs, there is no offense.
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:"

If a bhikṣuṇī sews a saṃghāṭī for more than five days, except when she is seeking a saṃghāṭī, when the kaṭhina robes have been suspended, or when the six difficult circumstances arise, it is a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"How could you leave your saṃghāṭī robe in the room, failing to look after it, dry it, or repair it, such that it became infested with worms, rotted, and its color faded?"
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.

With the exception of the *saṃghāṭī*, if one does not inspect other robes every five days, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
With the exception of other robes, if one does not inspect other necessary items every five days such that they are lost, infested by insects, or their color fades, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if: one leaves the *saṃghāṭī* robe in the dwelling and inspects it every five days;
or if the place where it is stored is secure;
