'I shall cause the Saṃgha not to release the kaṭhina robe now, but to release it later,' desiring that the five privileges be maintained for a long time."
"An *pāyattika* offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as stated above.
"Saṃgha" is as stated above.
The Dharma is that which accords with the Dharma, accords with the Vinaya, and accords with the Buddha’s instruction.
That bhikṣuṇī formed this thought:
"I shall cause the Saṃgha to suspend the formal act of disrobing the kaṭhina robe according to the Dharma, desiring that the five privileges be maintained for a long time."
...so saying, it is a pāyattika.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.

This is called an offense. There is no offense in the following cases: if one departs at an improper time; if the assembly is improperly divided; if the assembly is improperly united; if the assembly is properly divided; if the assembly is improperly united in a manner resembling the Dharma; if it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what was taught by the Buddha; or if, at the time of departure, there is fear of loss, or if one prevents another from departing because they are obstructed or would be ruined. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs wished to perform the formal act of relinquishing the kaṭhina robe.
Then, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs conceived this thought:

"Now that the community of bhikṣuṇīs is performing the formal act of relinquishing the kaṭhina in accordance with the Dharma, we shall obstruct it so that it is not performed, desiring that they continue to enjoy the relaxation of the five privileges for a long time."
The bhikṣuṇīs knew that the group of six bhikṣuṇīs intended this:
"We shall obstruct the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha from rightfully disrobing the kaṭhina, desiring that the five privileges be retained for a long time."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta-austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you harbor such an intention:
'We shall obstruct the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha from rightfully extending the kaṭhina robe, desiring that the five privileges be maintained for a long time'?"
They went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the rules—it is something that should not have been done.

The community of bhikṣuṇīs wishes to perform the formal act of releasing the kaṭhina according to the Dharma; why do you obstruct them so that it is not released, desiring that they remain deprived of the five privileges for a long time?"
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among many such bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī forms such an intention:
'I will obstruct the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha from releasing the kaṭhina robe, desiring that they remain deprived of the five privileges for a long time.'"
"A *pāyattika*. The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as stated above.
"Saṃgha" is as stated above.
The Dharma is that which accords with the Dharma, accords with the Vinaya, and accords with the Buddha’s instructions.
That bhikṣuṇī formed this intention:
"I shall obstruct the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha from rightfully disrobing the kaṭhina robe, desiring to cause them to retain the five privileges for a long time."
If one speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who, when the kaṭhina robe is being removed at an improper time, does so because the assembly is unrighteous and divided, or the assembly is unrighteous but united, or the assembly is righteous but divided, or the assembly is similar to the righteous but divided, or the assembly is similar to the righteous and united; or if it is something that is neither Dharma nor Vinaya nor taught by the Buddha; or if one removes it because they fear it will be lost or destroyed—such obstructions constitute no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were some bhikṣuṇīs who were quarreling together; they went to the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā and said, "Please help us settle this dispute.
The bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was clever and wise, capable of extinguishing disputes as soon as they arose, yet she ultimately made no effort to settle this particular dispute.
At that time, because of those matters of dispute, that bhikṣuṇī was unable to reach reconciliation; overcome with grief and anxiety, she subsequently abandoned the path.

When the community of bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse.
They censured Steyānanandā, saying: "How can a bhikṣuṇī speak thus?"
"Please settle this dispute for me!
Yet you ultimately failed to employ skillful means to resolve this dispute, causing that bhikṣuṇī to remain unreconciled over the matter and consequently abandon the religious life. Is this so?
She immediately went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Steunānanda:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"Why have you not finally reconciled with her regarding this matter of dispute, thereby allowing her to cease her practice?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"This bhikṣuṇī Steunānanda has committed many instances of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."
From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma.
Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows: "If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī, 'Settle this dispute for me!'"
"If one does not employ skillful means to bring about its cessation, it is a *pāyattika*.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "quarrels," there are four kinds, as described above.
If that bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī,
"Extinguish this dispute for me!
but does not employ skillful means to extinguish that dispute, it is a pāyattika.
Once the dispute has been settled, if there are further minor matters of contention that one does not strive to extinguish, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one’s own personal matter of dispute, one does not strive to extinguish, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Except for monks and nuns, if other persons engage in quarrels and disputes and one does not employ skillful means to extinguish them, it is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
For a monk, it is a *duṣkṛta*;
for a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one acts to extinguish [the dispute], or provides the means for its extinction, or if one is ill, or if the other party refuses to act upon the instruction, or if they have broken their precepts, broken their views, or broken their conduct; or if they have been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), or have been expelled (*pabbājaniya-kamma*), or are subject to expulsion; or if, on account of this matter, there is a threat to life or a threat to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), and one does not provide the means for its extinction. In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
11. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the Śākya son Baddhālita had two śrāmaṇeras:
one named Karṇa and the other named Madhu; one of them abandoned the religious life, while the other donned the kashaya robe and entered the assembly of non-Buddhist outsiders.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs took food and gave it to laypeople and those who had entered other paths.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you take food and give it to laypeople and those who have entered other paths?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it that you take food and give it to laypeople and those who have entered other paths?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is one of the many bases for outflows (āsrava) for this bhikṣuṇī; it is her first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, comprising the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who would recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives food that is fit to be eaten to a layperson or one who has entered a non-Buddhist sect, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
They were hesitant and did not dare to place it on the ground to give it, nor did they dare to have someone else give it.
The Buddha said:
“Listen: one may give by means of another person or place it on the ground.
From this day forward, the precept shall be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī gives food with her own hands to a layperson or enters among the food of non-Buddhists, it is a pāyattika.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Laypeople" (avadātavasana) refers to those who have not gone forth from the household life.
"Non-Buddhists" (tīrthika) refers to those who have gone forth outside of the Buddha-dharma.
"Edible food" is as defined above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hands, gives food to a layperson or enters among those of external paths to give it, and that person receives it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one does not accept it, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one employs a stratagem intending to give but does not give, or if one promises to give but then regrets it and does not give, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if [the object] is placed on the ground for them, or if one causes another to give it, or if it is given to one's parents, or to those working for a stūpa, or if it has been seized by forceful persons. There is no offense in these cases.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense physical pain.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs managed domestic affairs: they pounded grain, ground flour, cooked rice, parched wheat, boiled food, spread out beds and bedding, swept the floors, fetched water, or performed errands for others.
When the laypeople saw this, they all laughed together and said:
"Just as my wife manages the household affairs—pounding grain, grinding flour, cooking rice, and even receiving the commands of others—so too do these six groups of bhikṣuṇīs."
At that time, the laypeople all gave rise to feelings of contempt and no longer showed them respect.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you manage household affairs, perform tasks such as pounding and grinding, and even accept the commands of others, being no different from worldly people?"
They went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How can she manage her household affairs, performing tasks such as pounding grain and grinding, and even receiving errands, no differently from a layperson?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a messenger for a layperson, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
To act as a messenger for a layperson refers to performing tasks such as pounding grain, grinding, or even receiving commissions on their behalf.
If that bhikṣuṇī manages a household’s affairs, performing tasks such as pounding grain, grinding, or receiving commissions and orders, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in every instance.
For a bhikṣu, it is an offense according to what was committed;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one's parents are ill or imprisoned, and one provides them with bedding and mats, sweeps the floor, fetches water, or performs whatever service they require;
if a faithful upāsaka is ill or imprisoned, and one provides him with bedding and mats, sweeps the floor, fetches water, or performs service for him;
or if one is seized by those who exercise force—in all such instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
Thirteen. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were spinning yarn with their own hands.
When the laypeople saw this, they all mocked them together, saying:
"Just as my wives spin yarn, so too do these bhikṣuṇīs."
The laypeople immediately conceived feelings of pride and lacked any sense of reverence.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you spin yarn with your own hands?"
They went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How can she spin and weave with her own hands, no different from a layperson?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread with her own hands, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding "thread," there are ten kinds as described above.
If a bhikṣuṇī spins thread with her own hands, for every single pull [of the spindle], it constitutes one pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one seeks the thread oneself and joins it, or if one is coerced by force.
There is also no offense for those for whom the precept has not yet been established, or for those who are insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
14. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having dressed and taken her bowl at the proper time, went to the house of a lay devotee and sat down on a prepared seat.
At that time, the householder’s wife removed her jewelry and garments and entered the rear garden to bathe.
Thereupon, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā took the other's jewelry and garments and lay down upon the householder’s bed.

At that time, the householder had previously gone out and was not at home; later, upon returning home, he suddenly saw Thullanandā and, thinking she was his own wife, immediately lay down with her, grasping her hand to caress her and kissing her mouth.
When he felt him, he realized his head was bald, and only then asked:
"Who are you? He replied:
“I am the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā. The householder said to her,
“Why have you put on my wife’s jewelry and clothes?”
"Lying upon my bed, you caused me to see you and think you were my wife.
Depart at once! From this day forward, do not enter my house again."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta-austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached Steya-nandā, saying:
"How could you lie down on a bed wearing the jewelry and garments of another woman?"
She immediately went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Steunānanda, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can she enter the house of a layperson, put on the jewelry and clothes of another's wife, and lie down upon the bed, causing the layperson to feel resentment and suspicion?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"This is one of the many bases for outflows (āsrava) for a bhikṣuṇī; it is the first offense against the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, comprising the ten points of meaning, even unto the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson's house and sits or lies down upon a small bed or a large bed, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Layperson's house" refers to a village.
"Small bed" refers to a sitting bench.
"Large bed" refers to a bed for reclining.

If that bhikṣuṇī enters the interior of a layperson’s house and sits or lies down upon a small bed or a large bed, and her side touches the bed, each time she turns over once, it constitutes one *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; if one is sitting alone on a seat; if one has spread out many seats for the community of bhikṣuṇīs; if one falls to the ground due to illness; if one is seized by those using force; if one is imprisoned; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these instances, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were many bhikṣuṇīs traveling along the road toward the kingdom of Kośala who arrived at an uninhabited village. They spoke to the owner of the house, requesting to spread out bedding within the dwelling for the night.
When the next morning dawned, she departed without bidding farewell to her host; subsequently, a fire broke out in the village hut and consumed the dwelling.
At that time, the lay devotee whose house was burning assumed there were people inside, so he did not go to extinguish the fire.
Once the house was completely burnt down, he asked, "Where is the bhikṣuṇī?"
He replied, "They have already departed.
The lay devotees all joined together in criticism and disparagement, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or modesty; they claim of themselves that 'we practice the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is there in such as this?"
"How could the master of the house stay overnight within the dwelling and depart the next day without taking leave?
We thought there was someone inside the house and did not extinguish the fire, allowing it to burn the entire structure."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta ascetic practices, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, reproached those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How could you have told your host to stay overnight in another's house, yet upon leaving fail to inform the host, thereby causing fire to burn that other's house to the ground?"
She immediately went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How could you have told your host to stay overnight in another's house and then depart without informing him, thereby causing a fire to burn that house to the ground?"
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the house of a layperson and asks the host to prepare a seat for her to stay overnight, yet departs the following day without taking leave of the host, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"A layperson's house" refers to a village.
"To stay overnight" means to remain and lodge within it.
Regarding "spreading out": it refers to spreading out either grass or leaves, down to one's own bedding mat.
That bhikṣuṇī, having gone inside the house of a layperson, tells the host to spread out a seat for her to stay the night.
If one departs without taking leave the following day, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one foot is inside and one foot is outside, or if one makes preparations to depart but does not do so, or if one has agreed to go with others but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one departs after taking leave of the host; or if there is already someone else residing within the dwelling; or if the dwelling was previously empty; or if it was previously designated as a house for merit; or if the person is a close friend, and that close friend says:
"You may simply go; I shall speak to the host on your behalf."

If the dwelling collapses, or is consumed by fire, or if there are venomous snakes or predatory beasts within it, or if thieves enter, or if one is seized by those using force, or if one is imprisoned, or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya), there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
16. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣuṇīs who recited various miscellaneous incantations and arts: some chanted spells for the limbs and joints, some for the Kṣatriyas, some for spirits, and some for auspiciousness and misfortune; some practiced the divination of the revolving deer-wheel, while others practiced interpreting the sounds of voices.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the Ṣaḍvargika bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you practice and recite such various spells for the limbs and joints, even down to the spells for interpreting all sounds?"
Having rebuked them, they went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
On account of these causes and conditions, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the group of six bhikṣuṇīs:

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they reproached those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"The World-Honored One has established the precept that for a girl of eighteen years, one should grant her two years of training in the precepts; once she has fulfilled the six rules, at twenty, she shall be granted full ordination."
"How is it that you did not instruct him in the six rules of conduct before conferring full ordination, such that he has violated the celibate life, stolen five coins, or even drunk alcohol?
He then informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that should not have been done."

"You bhikṣuṇīs, when a girl is eighteen years of age, you should grant her two years of training in the precepts and the six rules; once she has completed [these], at twenty years of age, you should confer upon her full ordination."
"Why then did you not prohibit the six dharmas, such as committing sexual misconduct up to drinking alcohol?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among many sources of outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to a girl of eighteen years who has completed two years of training in the precepts but has not been granted the six rules, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a śikṣamāṇā commits sexual misconduct, she should be expelled.
If she has physical contact with a man who possesses a defiled mind while she herself also possesses a defiled mind, her precepts are deficient and she must receive the precepts again.
If one steals five coins or more than five coins, they should be expelled.
If it is less than five coins, the precepts are deficient and the precepts should be conferred again.
If one takes the life of a human being, they should be expelled.
If one takes the life of an animal, the precepts are deficient; the precepts should be conferred again.
If one claims for oneself the attainment of superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), one should be expelled.
If one intentionally utters a falsehood within the assembly, the precepts are deficient; the precepts should be conferred again.
If one eats at an improper time, the precepts are deficient and should be conferred again.
If one drinks alcohol, the precepts are deficient and should be conferred again.

If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to an eighteen-year-old maiden who has completed two years of training in the precepts, yet has not been granted the six rules, and she reaches twenty years of age before the full ordination is conferred—once the three *karmavācanās* have been recited—the preceptor bhikṣuṇī commits a *pāyattika*.
When the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (formal act with one motion and one proclamation) is completed, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
When the *jñapti-ekakarma* (formal act with one motion and no proclamation) is performed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Once the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is one *duṣkṛta*.
If, before the announcement, the assembly has gathered or the quorum has been reached, it is entirely *duṣkṛta*.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense in the case of a girl of eighteen years who has studied the precepts for two years; having been given the six rules, she receives full ordination—this is not an offense.
There is no offense for one who was not yet subject to the formulated precepts at the outset, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(23) At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the World-Honored One had established the precepts—stipulating that a girl who has reached the age of eighteen must train in the six rules for two years, and once she has completed them, at twenty, she shall be granted full ordination—they [acted accordingly].
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs ordained those who were blind, sightless, humpbacked, crippled, lame, deaf, mute, and others afflicted with various diseases, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Saṅgha.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who possessed few desires, were content, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"The World-Honored One has established the precept that a girl of eighteen years shall undergo two years of training in the precepts and the six rules; only when she is twenty years old shall she be granted full ordination."
"How can you have gone so far as to ordain those who are blind, sightless, and afflicted with various diseases, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Saṃgha?
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"A bhikṣuṇī should receive eighteen-year-old girls as trainees for two years; when they have completed those twenty years, she may confer the full ordination upon them.
Why, then, do you ordain those who are blind, sightless, and various other types of sick people?"
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you shall perform the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of bhikṣuṇīs."
One should grant it in this manner.

Once the candidate for ordination has been established at a place where they can see [the assembly] but cannot hear [the proceedings], the preceptor therein should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) to appoint an instructor (*śikṣācārya*).
One should make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so."
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent that so-and-so shall serve as the preceptor for instruction.
This is the formal motion.
That person should then go to the place where the candidate for ordination is and say to them:
"Sister! This is the antaravāsaka; this is the uttarāsaṅga; this is the saṃghāṭī; this is the saṃkakṣikā; this is the kakṣapuṭa; and this is the pātra."
"Is this robe and bowl yours?
Sister, listen!
Now is the time for truth, the time for speaking the actual fact. As I now question you, you should speak what is true as true and what is not true as not true."
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor?
Have you reached twenty years of age?"
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given their permission?
Has your husband given his permission?
Are you not in debt? Are you not a slave? Are you a woman?

Women have such various ailments as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption, insanity, hermaphroditism, the confluence of the two channels, narrowness of the birth canal, and the constant discharge of urine and feces, as well as the constant flow of mucus and saliva; do you have any such ailment?
If they say, "No," one should further say to them:
"Just as I have just now questioned you, so shall I question you among the assembly; and just as you have answered me just now, so shall you answer within the community of monks."

When the instructor has finished questioning her, he returns to the midst of the assembly with his usual dignified demeanor and stands at a distance where their hands can reach one another, making this formal announcement:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
That person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, I have finished instructing him; please allow him to come forward.
"Thus it is declared. He should then say to him: "Come here!"
Once she has arrived,

the preceptor should take hold of her robe and bowl, instruct her to prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣuṇīs, and then have her stand before the precept-teacher with her right knee on the ground and palms joined.
The preceptor shall instruct her to make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], am seeking to receive full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name]."
I, [Name], now request from the Sangha the conferral of full ordination; with [Name] Bhikṣuṇī as my preceptor, may the Sangha, out of compassion, deliver me.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.
The preceptor should then make the formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the noble assembly of nuns listen!
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
This [person], so-and-so, now requests the Sangha for full ordination, with the nun so-and-so acting as preceptor.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, I shall ask about matters concerning obstacles.
This is the formal announcement. He should then say to them:
"Sister, listen attentively!
Now is the time for truth. I now question you: you must speak what is true as true, and what is not true as not true.
What is your name?"
What is the name of your preceptor?
Are you twenty years of age?
Are your robes and bowl complete?
"Do your parents permit you?
Does your husband permit you?
Are you not in debt?"
Are you not a slave?
Are you a woman? Women have such various ailments as these:
Leprosy, carbuncles, leucoderma, consumption, insanity, hermaphroditism, conjoined genitals, narrow genitalia, constant discharge of urine and feces, and the constant flow of mucus and saliva.
"Do you have such an illness? If he says, "No."
The formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Sangha the full ordination, with the nun [Name] acting as preceptor.
[Name] has personally declared that she is pure and free from all obstacles, that she is twenty years of age, and that her robes and bowl are complete.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let [the name] receive the full ordination, with [Name] Bhikṣuṇī as the preceptor.
This is the formal motion.
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This [name], from the preceptor nun [name], seeks to receive full ordination.

This [name] now requests the Sangha for full ordination; [name] is her preceptor. [Name] herself declares that she is pure and free from all obstacles, that she is twenty years of age, and that her robes and bowl are complete.
Now the Sangha confers full ordination upon [Name], with Nun [Name] acting as preceptor.
Which of you, Venerable Sisters, approves of the Sangha conferring full ordination upon [Name], with Nun [Name] as preceptor? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to confer full ordination upon [Name], with Nun [Name] acting as preceptor; the matter is concluded. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, it shall be held thus."
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume Twenty-seven and Volume Twenty-eight, Part Two, Section Seven: Clarifying the Rules of Discipline for Bhikṣuṇīs.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
