Part Five of the One Hundred and Seventy-eight Dharmas of the *Prātimokṣa*: "At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs should take the candidate for ordination to the midst of the community of bhikṣus. Having bared her right shoulder and prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, she should place her right knee on the ground, join her palms, and speak these words:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
I, [Name], seek to receive the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name].
I, [Name], now request the Saṃgha of Nuns to grant me the full ordination, with [Name] Nun as my Preceptor. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, deliver me!
The second and third times he should speak in the same manner.
He should then ask: "What is your name?"
What is the name of your preceptor? ...
[and so on] ... as above regarding the constant flow of mucus and saliva.
Have you trained in the precepts with purity?
If she says, "My training in the precepts is pure," one should further question the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"Is this person pure in their training in the precepts?
If they say, "I am pure in my training in the precepts."
The preceptor shall then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor nun [Name]."
This [person], so-and-so, now requests from the community of nuns the conferral of full ordination, with the nun so-and-so as preceptor.
So-and-so has already trained in the precepts and is pure.

If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent; the Sangha shall now confer full ordination upon so-and-so, with the nun so-and-so as preceptor. This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so.
This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with the nun so-and-so acting as preceptor.”
So-and-so has already trained in the purity of the precepts.
Now the Saṃgha confers full ordination upon So-and-so, with the nun So-and-so acting as preceptor.
Which elders who consent to the Saṃgha conferring full ordination upon So-and-so, with the nun So-and-so as preceptor, remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise recited.
'The Saṃgha has granted full ordination to so-and-so, with nun so-and-so as preceptor; since the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.'"
“Listen, daughter of good family!
These are the eight *pārājika* rules taught by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. One who violates them is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
One must not engage in impure conduct or practice the dharma of sexual desire.
If a bhikṣuṇī, out of desire, should engage in impure conduct or practice the dharma of sexual desire—even with an animal—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say so."
“Yes. “One must not steal even as much as a blade of grass.

If a bhikṣuṇī steals five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether she takes it herself or causes another to take it, whether she cuts it herself or causes another to cut it, whether she breaks it herself or causes another to break it, or burns it, buries it, or destroys its color—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say so."
“Yes. “One must not intentionally take the life of any living being, even so small as an ant.

If a bhikṣuṇī intentionally takes a human life with her own hand, or provides a weapon to another, or instructs someone to die, praises death, encourages death, or administers non-medicinal substances; or if she causes an abortion, performs incantations or curses for the purpose of killing—whether she acts herself or instructs another to do so—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say: [Yes]."
“Yes. “One must not speak falsely, even in jest.

If a bhikṣuṇī, being untrue and possessing nothing herself, claims for herself, ‘I have attained the state of a superior man; I have attained dhyāna, I have attained liberation, I have attained samādhi and right reception, I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhat; devas, nāgas, and spirits come to make offerings to me’—this woman is no bhikṣuṇī, no daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"You must not do this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say so."
“Yes. “One must not touch the body [of a man], even down to that of an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, touches the body of a man with a defiled mind—from below the armpits and above the knees—if she grasps him, rubs him, pulls him, pushes him, strokes him upward, strokes him downward, lifts him up, lowers him, seizes him, or presses him, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say so."
"Yes. "She must not commit eight things, even [acting] with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, accepts the hand-grasping or robe-grasping of a man with a defiled mind; if she enters a secluded place, stands together in a secluded place, speaks together, walks together, touches his body, or makes an appointment with him—if she commits these eight things, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has committed these eight offenses."
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say so."
“Yes. “One must not conceal the offenses of others, even down to a *duṣkṛta* or a minor transgression.

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense, yet does not herself raise it, nor inform the Saṃgha or a group of many people, and at a later time—whether that bhikṣuṇī has left the order, been expelled, been barred from participating in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha, or has entered among the heretics—she then speaks as follows:”
"I previously knew that such and such a thing existed.
She is not a bhikṣuṇī, nor a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has concealed a grave offense.
You must not do this for as long as you live.
"Are you able to uphold it?
If you are able, you should say:
'I am able.'"
"One must not comply with the words of a monk who has been suspended, including even a park-keeper or a novice.

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a monk has been suspended by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s teaching, does not comply and does not repent, yet continues to comply with him before the Saṃgha has granted him reintegration."
That bhikṣuṇī should admonish the other bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Sister, do you know?

The Saṃgha has now censured this bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha's teaching; he does not comply and does not repent, and the Saṃgha has not yet granted him leave to dwell together. You must not comply with him."

When that bhikṣuṇī is being admonished by another bhikṣuṇī and persists in her refusal to relinquish [the position], that bhikṣuṇī must be formally admonished up to three times so that she may abandon this matter.
If she relinquishes it after being admonished up to three times, it is well;
if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she has followed the censurable course.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live.
Can you uphold it?
If you can, you should say: [Yes]."
“Yes. “Listen, daughter of good family!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; by relying upon these, a bhikṣuṇī may go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī.”
Relying on rag-robes, one may go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣuṇī.
Are you able to maintain this for as long as life lasts?
If you are able, you should say: "I am able."
“Yes. “If one obtains long-term benefits, such as robes offered by a donor or robes made from discarded cloth, these may be accepted.
By relying on alms-gathering, one may go forth and receive full ordination, thereby accomplishing the status of a bhikṣuṇī.”
"Can you maintain this throughout the rest of your life?
If you can, you should say: 'I can.'"

"If one obtains long-term benefits—such as food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day, food on the fourteenth or fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the Saṃgha, or food offered at the invitation of a donor—one should accept it."
"By sitting beneath a tree, one attains the status of a bhikṣuṇī through going forth and receiving full ordination.
Are you able to maintain this for as long as life lasts?"
One who is able should say, "I am able.
If one obtains additional benefits, such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed house, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door, one should accept them.
"By relying on the medicine of putrefaction, one may go forth and receive full ordination to become a bhikṣuṇī.
Are you able to maintain this for as long as life lasts?"
One who is able should say, "I am able.
If one obtains long-term benefits such as clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar, these should be accepted.

"You have already received the full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, accomplished in accordance with the Dharma and having obtained the proper standing. Your preceptor is in accordance with the Dharma, your ācārya is in accordance with the Dharma, and the Saṃgha of the two assemblies is complete and in accordance with the Dharma. You should properly receive the teachings; you ought to exhort and transform others, cultivate merit, repair stupas, and make offerings to the Saṃgha."

If you do not disobey any instruction given by your preceptor or teacher in accordance with the Dharma, and instead diligently seek skillful means through study, questioning, and recitation of the sutras, you shall attain the fruit of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, or arhatship within the Buddha-dharma; thus, the merit of your initial resolve to leave the household life will not be in vain, and its karmic fruition will never cease.
"Whatever else you do not know, you should ask the Upādhyāya or Ācārya.
Having thus instructed them, he had the person receiving the precepts go in front and the other nuns follow behind.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should speak as follows:

If a bhikṣuṇī grants full ordination to an eighteen-year-old girl who has completed two years of training in the precepts and the six rules, and who has reached twenty years of age, yet the Saṃgha has not granted its permission, it is a pāyattika offense.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as stated above;
"the Saṃgha" is as stated above.

If a bhikṣuṇī who is twenty years of age has completed two years of training in the precepts and has been granted the six rules (ṣaḍ-dharma), yet the Saṃgha does not grant permission, and she is nevertheless conferred full ordination (upasampadā)—once the third *karmavācanā* is concluded, the preceptor bhikṣuṇī commits a *pāyattika* offense.
In a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
In a *jñapti-ekakāra-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and no further proclamation), there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Once the motion has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the assembly has gathered and the quorum is reached before the announcement, everyone incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the person is twenty years of age, has studied the precepts for two years, and the Sangha grants permission for them to receive full ordination. This is not an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(24) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, although the World-Honored One had established the precepts and permitted bhikṣuṇīs to bestow full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, they nevertheless ordained young women and bestowed full ordination upon them.

Having bestowed the full ordination, they did not discern whether a man possessed a defiled mind or was free from a defiled mind; they stood together with, spoke together with, and flirted together with men who possessed defiled minds.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta ascetic practices, fond of training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the other bhikṣuṇīs:

"How is it that you, though the World-Honored One has established the precepts permitting bhikṣuṇīs to ordain others and grant them full ordination (upasampadā), nevertheless ordain other young women who have previously been married and grant them full ordination; and once they have received full ordination, they do not know whether a man has a defiled mind or an undefiled mind, yet they stand together with, speak together with, and engage in mutual flirtation with men who possess defiled minds?"
They went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the Blessed One.
On account of this matter, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."

How is it that you confer the full ordination upon young women who have previously been married, yet after they have received the full ordination, you do not know whether a man has a defiled mind or an undefiled mind, and you allow them to stand together with, speak together with, and engage in mutual flirtation with men who possess defiled minds?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, if you wish to ordain others and grant them full ordination, you must first inform the Saṃgha and have their hair shaved, up to the granting of the ten precepts, according to the aforementioned rules."

From this day forward, it is permitted to ordain women who have been married for ten years and grant them two years of training in the precepts; once they have reached twelve years of age, they shall be granted full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The formal procedure of the motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) is as described above.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a woman who has previously been married and is ten years of age, she must grant her two years of training in the precepts; when she has reached twelve years of age, she may then be granted full ordination."
"If one bestows full ordination upon a person who is less than twelve years of age, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

If that bhikṣuṇī, knowing the candidate is less than twelve years of age, bestows full ordination upon her and the three *karmavācanās* are completed, the preceptor bhikṣuṇī commits a pāyattika offense.
When the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) is completed, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
When the *jñapti-ekakarmavācana* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) is completed, there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Once the motion (*jñapti*) has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If the assembly has gathered before the announcement but the quorum is not yet reached, all are *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, when she is ten years old, she is ordained and given two years of training in the precepts, and at twelve, she is granted full ordination. This is not an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(25) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting them to ordain women who had previously been married for ten years, provided them with two years of training in the precepts, and then confer full ordination upon them once they reached twelve years of age, they proceeded to ordain others who were blind, one-eyed, lame, crippled, deaf, or afflicted by various other ailments, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Saṃgha.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"The World-Honored One has established a rule that women who have been married for ten years or more may be received as novices; after two years of training in the precepts, when they have completed twelve years, they shall be granted full ordination."
"How can you go so far as to deliver others who are blind, deaf, and afflicted by various other ailments, thereby bringing disgrace upon the community of monks?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teaching—it is something that should not be done."

Why did the Blessed One establish the precept permitting bhikṣuṇīs to ordain women who have been married for ten years, requiring them to undergo two years of training in the precepts, and then conferring the full ordination upon them once they have completed twelve years?
"And yet you have gone so far as to ordain others who are blind, sightless, lame, crippled, deaf, and afflicted with various other ailments, thereby bringing disgrace upon the Sangha!
After rebuking them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the bestowal of full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal motion followed by three proclamations)."
One should act in this manner:

leading the candidate for ordination to a place out of earshot but within sight, and so forth, until one has finished the instruction; then, having signaled for them to come, they should do so as described above.

Once she has come and joined the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, the preceptor should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*), inquire regarding the obstacles to ordination, and proceed through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* as described above; this continues until the conferral of the precepts within the assembly of bhikṣus, each of these procedures being identical to the eighteen rules for a maiden (*kumārikā*).

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains a young woman who has previously been married, and after she has completed two years of training and reached the age of twelve, bestows the full ordination upon her without having informed the community of monks, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

If that bhikṣuṇī ordains a young woman who has previously been married, and after she has completed two years of training in the precepts and reached the age of twelve, bestows the full ordination (upasampadā) upon her without having informed the community of monks, then at the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, the preceptor bhikṣuṇī commits a *pāyattika* offense.
With a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses;
with a *jñapti-ekakara-karman*, two *duṣkṛta* offenses;
and after the motion (*jñapti*) alone, one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the announcement has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the assembly has gathered and the quorum is reached before the announcement, everyone incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the case of ordaining a woman who has been married and is over twelve years of age, provided she receives full ordination after informing the community of monks; this is not an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(26) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs ordained a courtesan and conferred full ordination upon her. Those who had previously been intimate with this woman saw her and said to one another:
"This courtesan formerly did such and such things to us."
When the bhikṣuṇīs who had been ordained and the other bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they were all filled with shame.

At that time, among the bhikṣuṇīs who heard of it, there were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How is it that you have ordained a courtesan and conferred the full ordination upon her?"
They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How can you all ordain a courtesan and grant her full admission?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon such a person, it is a pāyattika offense."
Thus the Blessed One established a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.

The bhikṣuṇīs did not know whether such a person was indeed such a person or not; only later did they realize it was so. Consequently, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
“There is no offense for one who did not know.
From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly confers full ordination upon such a person, it is a pāyattika.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Such a person is a courtesan; she may have a husband, or a husband’s brother, or even someone with whom she has had a long-standing illicit affair.
If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon such a person, she should lead them away for five or six yojanas.
If she does not do so, she must hide them securely in a secluded place.

If that bhikṣuṇī, having ordained such a person and conferred the full precepts upon them, does not take them away for five or six yojanas, or does not conceal them securely, it is a pāyattika offense.
Monks, this is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
this is what is called an infraction.

There is no infraction if one did not know such a person beforehand and then conferred the full ordination upon them; or if one leads them for five or six *yojanas*, or instructs another to lead them for five or six *yojanas*, or if they are hidden away securely. In these cases, there is no infraction.
There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
(27) At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā ordained many disciples but failed to instruct or admonish them. Because they were not provided with instruction, they did not maintain dignified deportment; their robes were not properly arranged, they begged for food improperly, accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they shouted loudly at small and large meal assemblies, like the gathering customs of the brahmins.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs saw them and said: "Sisters! Why do you not maintain proper deportment?

Why are your robes not worn neatly? Why do you beg for food in an improper manner? Why do you accept impure food from various places, or accept food in an impure bowl? Why do you raise your voices and shout loudly at the small and large meals, like the assembly customs of the brahmins?"
The bhikṣuṇīs replied: "We are the disciples of the bhikṣuṇī An-yin; she has many disciples, yet she does not instruct us, and it is precisely because we have not been instructed."

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī An-yin, saying:
"How is it that you have ordained many disciples yet fail to instruct them?"
"Because they do not provide instruction, the communal affairs are not conducted according to the Dharma.
Having rebuked them, he went and informed the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus then went and informed the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī An-yin, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."

Why is it that you ordain many disciples but do not instruct them, such that they do not observe the rules of decorum, their robes are not properly arranged, they beg for food improperly, they accept impure food from various places, or they accept food in impure bowls, and they shout loudly at small and large meals like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains many disciples but does not instruct them in the two years of training in the precepts, nor takes them under her care by means of the two dharmas, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
Regarding the "two things," the first is the Dharma and the second is food and clothing.

As for "gathering through the Dharma," it means teaching [them] to increase in higher morality (*adhiśīla*), higher mind (*adhicitta*), and higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), as well as to engage in study and recitation of the sūtras.
Regarding the inclusion by means of food and clothing: one should provide food, clothing, bedding, seats, and medicine, supplying whatever is necessary according to one's ability.

If a bhikṣuṇī ordains many disciples and grants them full ordination (*upasampadā*), yet does not instruct them in the two years of training in the precepts (*śikṣamāṇā*) or include them through the two methods of care, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Monks, this is a *dukkaṭa* offense;
this is what is called an infraction.
There is no infraction if one ordains someone after they have completed two years of training in the precepts and has been sustained by these two things: [the instruction and the exhortation].
First is the Dharma, and second is food and clothing;
if, after receiving full ordination, one departs from the community of harmonious monks;
or if one violates the precepts, violates right view, or violates proper decorum.
If one has been suspended, or is undergoing banishment, or is subject to banishment;
or if, on account of this matter, there is danger to life or danger to the holy life—there is no offense.
There is no offense in the case of one for whom the precept was not yet promulgated, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
28. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, many bhikṣuṇīs were ordaining disciples, but later those disciples all departed from their preceptors and teachers. They did not receive instruction, they did not observe the rules of decorum, their robes were not properly arranged, they went for alms in an improper manner, they accepted impure food in various places, or they accepted food in impure bowls, and in both small and large meals they shouted loudly, like the assemblies of brahmins.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs saw them and asked, "Sisters! Why do you not maintain proper decorum?

Your robes are not properly arranged, your alms-round is not according to the Dharma, you accept impure food in various places, or you accept food in an impure bowl, and you shout loudly at the small and large meals like the assembly of Brahmins?"
The bhikṣuṇīs replied, “It is simply because we have left our preceptors after receiving full ordination and have not received instruction. When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard this,

those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"How is it that you, having received full ordination, have departed from your preceptors; that you do not receive instruction, do not maintain proper decorum, wear your robes in a disordered manner, beg for food improperly, accept impure food at various places, or accept food in an impure bowl, and that you raise your voices and shout loudly during the morning and midday meals, like the assembly customs of the Brahmins?"
After the bhikṣuṇīs had finished their reprimand, they went to inform the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the Buddha.
On account of this incident, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the teachings—it is something that should not have been done."

What is it like for one who, having received full ordination (*upasampadā*), departs from their preceptor and teacher, fails to receive instruction, does not observe the rules of decorum, begs for food improperly, accepts impure food at various places, or accepts food in an impure bowl, and while at small or large meals, raises their voice and shouts loudly, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed many bases for outflows; this is the first breach of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not follow her preceptor nun (upādhyāyinī) for two years, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣuṇī does not follow her preceptor-ni for two years, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for one who, having received full ordination, has remained for two years under a bhikṣuṇī upādhyāyī.
If the upādhyāya permits it, one may go;

or if the upādhyāya has broken the precepts, broken the view, or broken the decorum; or if he has been subject to formal censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), or has been expelled (*pabbājanīyakamma*), or is subject to expulsion;
or if, due to such circumstances, there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (*brahmacariya*), then to depart after two years is not an offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(29) At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One established the precepts and permitted the ordination of others and the bestowal of full ordination (*upasampadā*). However, some foolish bhikṣuṇīs, having ordained others, did not know how to instruct them.

Because they failed to provide instruction, [the disciples] did not maintain dignified deportment; their robes were not properly arranged; they begged for food improperly; they accepted impure food in various places, or accepted food in impure bowls; and in the small and large dining halls, they raised their voices and shouted loudly, like the assemblies of brahmins.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, delighting in training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the other bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"How is it that although the World-Honored One established the precepts and permitted you to ordain others, you, being foolish, have immediately ordained people without knowing how to instruct them? Because you do not instruct them, they do not maintain dignified deportment, even to the point of shouting loudly at the small and large meals, like the manner of a gathering of Brahmins?"
They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teaching]. It is something that should not have been done."

"How is it that although the World-Honored One has established the precepts and permitted you to ordain others, you, being foolish, have haphazardly ordained people without knowing how to instruct them? Because you do not instruct them, they do not maintain proper deportment; they beg for food improperly, accepting impure food in various places, or accepting food in an impure bowl; and in both small and large meals, they shout and clamor loudly, as if at a Brahmin assembly?"
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I allow the Saṃgha to confer full ordination through the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation)."
One who wishes to ordain others should go among the community of monks and seek [permission] in this manner.

Having gone into the midst of the community of bhikṣuṇīs, they should bare the right shoulder, remove their leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣuṇīs, place the right knee on the ground, join their palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!..."
"I, Bhikṣuṇī [Name], seek the Saṃgha of Bhikṣuṇīs to request the conferral of full ordination upon this person.
Thus she should speak a second and third time.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha should then examine whether this person is capable of being instructed in the two-year training in the precepts and whether she can be sustained by the two forms of support.
First is the Dharma; second is food and clothing.
Thus it is permitted.
If one is unable to provide instruction, or cannot provide the two years of training in the precepts, the two methods of inclusion, and food and clothing, one should say to them:
"Sister, stop! Do not ordain others.

If she possesses wisdom and is capable of providing instruction, and if she has trained in the precepts for two years and has embraced [the candidate] with the two methods, then one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* among the assembly should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, now requests from the community of nuns the authorization to bestow full ordination upon others.
If the time is right for the Sangha and the Sangha consents, let it grant so-and-so the authorization to bestow full ordination upon others."
[The motion] is thus stated.
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, now requests from the community of nuns the conferral of full ordination upon another person."
The Saṃgha now intends to confer full ordination upon the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so for another person.
Those of you, venerable sisters, who consent to the Saṃgha conferring full ordination upon so-and-so for another person, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for the full ordination of such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī by such-and-such a person; since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon another person without the consent of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.'"
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
"Saṃgha" is as explained above.
"To grant permission" means that the Saṃgha grants permission through a formal motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
If that bhikṣuṇī, without the consent of the Saṃgha, bestows full ordination upon another, it is a pāyattika.
If she grants dependence [to a novice] or keeps a śrāmaṇerikā or a śikṣamāṇā without the consent of the community of monks, it is a duṣkṛta.
Monk, this is a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the Saṃgha has authorized one to bestow full ordination (*upasampadā*), or when one receives dependence (*niśraya*) from a bhikṣuṇī, or when one maintains a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*) or a probationary nun (*śikṣamāṇā*). This is called no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
[The thirty rules are concluded. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting bhikṣuṇīs to request from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination upon others.
Those newly ordained young women, having requested from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination upon others, were unable to provide instruction.

Because they did not receive instruction, they did not observe the rules of decorum: their robes were worn untidily, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly at small and large meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"How is it that you, having heard that the World-Honored One established the precepts permitting the ordination of others, have now—after newly initiated young women have requested and received full ordination from you—failed to instruct them? Because they receive no instruction, they do not maintain dignified deportment, their robes are not properly arranged, and they even shout loudly at the morning and midday meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?"
At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had expressed their disapproval and reprimand, they went and told the bhikṣus, who in turn went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these circumstances, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣuṇīs:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that you new initiates and youths, having requested and received the full ordination from others, are unable to provide instruction?

Because they do not receive instruction, they do not maintain proper decorum; their robes are not properly arranged, their alms-round is not according to the Dharma, and they even shout and clamor loudly, like the assemblies of brahmins?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked these bhikṣuṇīs with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"This is the first transgression of the precepts among the many sources of outflows for these bhikṣuṇīs."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is less than twelve years of age confers full ordination upon another, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is less than twelve years of age confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another, it is an offense of expiation (*pāyattika*).
If she is less than twelve years of age and provides dependence (*niśraya*), keeps a *śikṣamāṇā*, or keeps a *śrāmaṇerikā*, in all such cases it is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monk, this is a *duṣkṛta* offense;
this is what is called an infraction.

There is no infraction if one who has reached twelve years of age is granted full ordination (*upasampadā*), or if one provides dependence (*niśraya*), or keeps a *śikṣamāṇā* or a *śrāmaṇerī*; in these cases, there is no infraction.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(31) At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting those who were twelve years of age to bestow full ordination upon others, they all claimed for themselves:

Being foolish, they hastily confer the full ordination upon others without knowing how to instruct them.

Because they do not receive instruction, they do not observe the rules of decorum: their robes are not worn properly, they beg for food improperly, they accept impure food from various places, or they accept food in an impure bowl; furthermore, at small or large meals, they shout and clamor loudly, like the assemblies of Brahmins.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse, reproached those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"You have heard that the World-Honored One established the rule that one who is twelve years old may bestow full ordination upon others; yet how is it that you yourselves claim to be twelve years of age and seek to bestow full ordination upon others, being so foolish as not to know how to provide instruction?"

Because he has not received instruction, he does not maintain dignified deportment; his robes are not properly adjusted, and he goes for alms in an improper manner, even as if following the assembly customs of the Brahmins.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance—it is something that should not have been done."

"How is it that you yourselves claim to have completed twelve years [of training], yet when requested to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*), you are so foolish as not to know how to provide instruction?

Because they do not receive such instruction, they do not maintain proper deportment; their robes are not worn in an orderly fashion, and they beg for food improperly—even like the assembly customs of the Brahmins?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is twelve years of age grants full ordination to another person without the permission of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī who is twelve years of age or older confers the full ordination upon another person without the permission of the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika offense.
If the community of monks does not grant permission, yet one grants dependence (*niśraya*), keeps a *śikṣamāṇā*, or keeps a *śrāmaṇerī*, it is all a *duṣkṛta* offense.
For a *bhikṣu*, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense for one who is twelve years of age, or when the Sangha permits the conferring of full ordination upon another, or when providing dependence (niśraya) to another, or when maintaining a śikṣamāṇā or a śrāmaṇerī; in these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.

"These bhikṣuṇīs have committed many kinds of outflows; this is the first transgression of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning and leading to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon a woman whose parents or husband have not given their permission, it is a pāyattika offense."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

In the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal motion followed by one proclamation), there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
In the case of a *jñapti-ekakara-karman* (a formal motion followed by a single proclamation), there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
Once the motion has been made, there is one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the formal motion (*jñapti*) has not yet been completed, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If, prior to the formal motion, one prepares the proposal and formally proposes to the Saṃgha to grant the tonsure and assemble the community, and the assembly is complete, all [involved] incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.

There is no offense if one has the permission of one’s parents or husband; or if there are no parents or husband, there is no offense.

They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.

How could she have conferred full ordination upon a woman who was grieving, joyful, or angry because of her mutual affection for a young man or another man,

Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

In the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation), there are three *duṣkṛta* offenses. In the case of a *jñapti-prathama-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and no further proclamation), there are two *duṣkṛta* offenses.

This is called an offense. There is no offense if one was previously unaware; or if one acted based on the words of a trustworthy person; or if one acted based on the words of one's parents; or if the illness arose after one had already received full ordination. In these cases, there is no offense.

If that bhikṣuṇī confers full ordination upon another person before one year has passed, it is a pāyattika offense.

Monk, this is a *dukkaṭa* offense;
this is what is called an infraction.

There is no offense for one who, having completed twelve months, confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another, completes twelve months before providing dependence (*nissaya*) to another, confers the two-year training in the precepts upon a *śikṣamāṇā*, or ordains a *śrāmaṇerī*. Thus the Blessed One laid down a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs were hesitant and did not dare to enter a monastery that lacked a community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said:
“Listen and enter.
From this day forward, the precept should be formulated as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī enters a saṃghārāma where bhikṣus are present, it is a pāyattika.”
Thus the Blessed One laid down this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs did not know whether there was a bhikṣu present or not; it was only later that they realized a bhikṣu was there. Consequently, some performed the *pāyattika* confession, while others remained in doubt.
"There is no offense for one who does not know.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the precept shall be formulated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly enters a monastery where bhikṣus reside, it is a pāyattika.
Thus the Blessed One established this precept for the bhikṣuṇīs.
They wished to seek instruction but did not know from whom they should seek it.
Having a doubt he wished to ask, but not knowing from whom to ask,
he did not dare enter the monastery.
The Buddha said:
“From this day forward, it is permitted to enter the monastery only after making an announcement.
When they wished to pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpa and the śrāvakas’ stūpas, the Buddha said:
“If one wishes to pay homage to the Buddha’s stūpa or the śrāvakas’ stūpa, it is permitted to enter at will; for all other matters, one must enter only after making an announcement.”
From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a bhikṣu-saṃghārāma, enters it without having announced her presence, it is a pāyattika.
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a bhikṣu-saṃghārāma, enters its gate without having announced her presence, it is a pāyattika offense.
With one foot inside the gate and one foot outside the gate, while intending to enter through skillful means, if one intends to enter but does not do so, it is all *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one was unaware beforehand; or if there were no other bhikṣus present when entering;
or if one enters after having informed others while paying homage to a stūpa of the Buddha or a stūpa of a śrāvaka;

or if one comes to receive instruction; or if one comes to enter for the purpose of asking about the Dharma; or if one has been invited; or if one passes through on the way; or if one stays overnight there; or if one is led away by force; or if one is taken away after being imprisoned; or if there is danger to life or danger to the holy life (brahmacarya). In these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
(44) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the night had passed, the Elder Kapphiṇa put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī for alms in the early morning.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw Kapphiṇa, they immediately reviled him, saying:
"This wicked, lowly man of a craftsman's caste has destroyed our stūpas and cast them away outside the saṃghārāma!"

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured them, saying: "How is it that you have reviled the Elder Kapphiṇa?"
Having rebuked her, she went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How could she revile Kapilavastu?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed many things that are sources of outflows; this is her first transgression of the precepts."
From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

To "revile" means to say that she was born of a lowly station, that her lineage is lowly, that her craft is lowly, or that her occupation is lowly; or to speak of her committing an offense, or to say that she possesses such-and-such fetters (saṃyojana), or to touch upon what is a taboo for her.
If that bhikṣuṇī reviles a bhikṣu according to his class, or even speaks of what he holds dear,
if she speaks clearly, it is a pāyattika;
if she does not speak clearly, it is a duṣkṛta.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one speaks in jest, speaks rapidly, speaks to oneself, speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that instead.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.
(45) At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kālā delighted in quarreling and was unskilled at putting such disputes out of her mind; subsequently, she became angry and resentful, reproaching the community of bhikṣuṇīs.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those among them who were of few desires, contented, practitioners of the dhūta austerities, fond of training in the precepts, and possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, censured the bhikṣuṇī Kālā, saying:
"How could you, having delighted in quarreling, continue to harbor resentment after the dispute had been settled, and spend the night reviling the community of bhikṣuṇīs?"
He immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked Kāla, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not compliant conduct—it is something that should not have been done."
"How could she, having already ceased her fondness for quarreling, harbor resentment overnight and then employ such means as to revile the assembly of nuns?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first transgression among the many bases of outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī delights in quarreling and, having failed to properly remember the matter of the dispute, subsequently becomes angry and displeased, and reviles the community of bhikṣuṇīs, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
There are four kinds of disputes, as explained above.
"Assembly" refers to either four or more than four persons.
If that bhikṣuṇī, delighting in quarreling, reviles the community of bhikṣuṇīs after spending the night [in dispute], it is a pāyattika offense if she speaks clearly;
it is a dukkaṭa offense if she does not speak clearly.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if one speaks in jest, speaks rapidly, speaks to oneself, speaks in a dream, or intends to say this but mistakenly says that instead.
There is no offense for one who acted before the precept was established, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense pain.
(46) At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, in the kingdom of Śākya.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakāpilā had an abscess on her body that required a man to lance it.

This bhikṣuṇī’s body was so delicate and soft that it was no different from a celestial body; when the man’s hand touched her skin, he felt its exquisite smoothness and gave rise to lustful attachment. He then stepped forward, seized her, and intended to violate her, whereupon she cried out in a loud voice: “Do not do this!”
"Do not do so! At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs standing nearby heard her cry and all came to ask,
"Why did you just shout so loudly?"
She then recounted the circumstances in detail.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Bhadrakāpilā, saying: "How can a bhikṣuṇī have a man break open her abscess?"
She immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrakapilā, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How can she cause a man to break open the abscesses on his body?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed many things that lead to outflows; this is the first breach of the precepts."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, encompassing the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī has a boil or various kinds of sores arising on her body, and she does not inform the assembly or others, but instead arbitrarily employs a man to lanced them or bandage them, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above;
the meaning of "saṃgha" is also as explained above.

If that bhikṣuṇī has a boil or various kinds of sores on her body and, without informing the community, causes a man to break them open—even if he applies the blade but once—it is a pāyattika offense.
If, while wrapping it, one wraps it once, it is a pāyattika for the bhikṣu;
it is a duṣkṛta for the bhikṣuṇī;
and it is a duṣkṛta for the śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, and śrāmaṇerī.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense for one who informs the Sangha to have a man lanced a boil or an ulcer, or to bandage it; nor is there an offense if one is seized by those using force.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(47) At that time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a lay devotee who wished to prepare food and drink to invite the community of bhikṣuṇīs. That very night, he prepared many kinds of delicious food and drink; when the night had passed, at dawn, he went to inform them that the time had arrived.

At that time, on a day of secular festival in the city of Śrāvastī, various householders each brought rice, parched grain, flour, fish, and meat, coming to the saṃghārāma to give them to the bhikṣuṇīs.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had received and eaten this offered food, they then proceeded to the house of a lay devotee to eat.
At that time, the lay devotee personally served the soup and rice with his own hands to the bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣuṇīs said: "Stop! Stop!"
“Householder, there is no need for such abundance.
The householder replied,
“The reason I have prepared these various kinds of delicious food and a separate vessel of meat for each person is precisely for the sake of the Āryā!”
"Do not say that you do not eat because you lack faith.
Auntie, simply eat; I truly have faith. The bhikṣuṇī replied:

"We do not do this because today is a festival day; various laypeople each bring rice, parched grain, dry rice, fish, meat, and various kinds of soups and meals to the monastery to give to the bhikṣuṇīs."
"We have already eaten; for this reason, we have received only a little.
At that time, the lay devotees all spoke together in derision, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs do not know contentment; yet they claim of themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma. How can this be considered the True Dharma?
Why is it that after first accepting my invitation, you then accept various kinds of food from others, and only afterwards accept my meal?

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They reproached those bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"How can you, having first accepted an invitation from a layperson, subsequently accept other food?"
They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the teaching]. It is something that should not have been done."
"How can she first accept an invitation from a lay devotee and later accept further food?
Having rebuked her with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This bhikṣuṇī has committed the first offense among the many bases for outflows."

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for the bhikṣuṇīs, gathering the ten points of meaning up to the long endurance of the True Dharma. Those who wish to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has previously accepted an invitation and, having finished her meal, subsequently eats rice, parched grain, boiled rice, fish, or meat, it is a pāyattika."
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.

If that bhikṣuṇī has previously accepted an invitation and has already finished her meal, yet afterwards eats another's rice, parched flour, boiled rice, fish, or meat, for every swallow she commits one *pāyattika* offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense if one accepts an invitation for non-food, or an invitation for food that is not sufficient, or if one has not previously been invited, or if one receives more food while already at the meal, or if one accepts the "forenoon" and "afternoon" meals at that same house; in these cases, there is no offense.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
(48) At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Tiṣyā, who was a disciple of the bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā. She had an old acquaintance, a family of lay donors.
The bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā said to the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, "We should go together to the house of the donor."
He replied, "If you wish to go, so be it.
The two of them went together.

The bhikṣuṇī Ānanda was neatly dressed and maintained her dignified deportment; when the donors saw her, they gave rise to a heart of joy, and because of this joyful heart, they immediately provided her with offerings.
Then, after her meal, the bhikṣuṇī An-yin returned to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣuṇī Ti-she:
"This donor is deeply faithful, joyful, and fond of giving offerings."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, harboring a jealous mind, spoke these words:
"The donor is deeply faithful and fond of giving; he provides offerings for you.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta ascetic virtues, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, saying:
"How can you give rise to a jealous mind and speak such words as:
'This donor is sincere in faith and fond of giving, and he makes offerings to you'?
He then informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Tiṣyā, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can you give rise to a mind of jealousy and say:
'The donor, with sincere faith and a love for giving, provides offerings to you'?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“This nun has committed the first offense among many such bases for taints.

From this day forward, I shall establish a precept for nuns, gathering the ten points of meaning so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. One who wishes to recite the precepts should do so as follows:
‘If a nun harbors a mind of jealousy toward a household, it is a *pāyattika*.’”
The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
That bhikṣuṇī conceives a mind of jealousy toward a household and says:
"This donor is deeply faithful and fond of giving; he provides offerings for you."
If one speaks and is clearly understood, it is a *pāyattika*;
if not clearly understood, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if the matter is actually so, or if that donor is deeply faithful and fond of giving, and while making offerings to them, says these words:
"If this donor has placed deep faith in you," there is no offense [if one speaks] jokingly,
or speaks rapidly, or speaks to oneself, or speaks in a dream, or intends to say one thing but mistakenly says another.
There is no offense for one who has not yet been subject to the formulation of the precepts, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

"If a bhikṣuṇī applies fragrant unguents to her body, it is a pāyattika."

For a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.
There is no offense if, at some time, such an illness occurs, or if one is seized by force.
There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense suffering.

The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained above.
If that bhikṣuṇī smears or rubs sesame dregs upon her body, it is a pāyattika offense.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta offense.

For every village boundary she traverses while walking in leather sandals and carrying a parasol, it constitutes a separate pāyattika offense.
In an uninhabited forest hermitage, for every ten *li* traveled, there is one *pāyattika*.
For traveling less than the boundary of a village, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
For traveling less than ten *li*, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
If one walks within a single boundary, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one makes the effort to go but does not go, or if one has made an appointment to go together but does not go, in all such cases it is a *duṣkṛta*.
For a bhikṣu, it is a duṣkṛta;
for a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, it is a duṣkṛta.
This is called an offense.

There is no offense in the following cases: if one has such an illness; or if, for the sake of protecting the body, the robes, or the bedding, one makes a canopy of tree bark, leaves, or bamboo within the monastery;
or if, for the sake of protecting the body, the robes, or the bedding, one wears sandals within the monastery—there is no offense.

when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

There is no offense in the following cases: when the precept has not yet been established; or when one is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
