There he saw a pure site, level, well-proportioned, and magnificent, most delightful to behold; the living grass was soft and all curled to the right, the bathing pools were cool and the flowing streams were pure, and the groves and gardens were lush and beautiful.
He surveyed the area all around and saw that there were many people in the villages to the left and right; having seen this, he thought to himself:
"For a son of noble family who wishes to seek the place where fetters are severed, this is an excellent location."
"I now seek the place where the fetters are severed; this very spot is it.
I would rather sit here and sever the underlying tendencies.
At that time, five men pursued the Bodhisattva, thinking to themselves:
"If the Bodhisattva attains the Way, he shall preach the Dharma for us.
At that time, Uruvilvā had four daughters— first named Prabhāvatī,
second named Uruvilvā, third named Sundarī, and fourth named Kāpilānī— all of whom fixed their hearts upon the Bodhisattva.
"If the Bodhisattva leaves home to study the Way, we shall become his disciples.
If the Bodhisattva does not leave home to study the Way, but remains at home following worldly customs, we shall become his wives and concubines."
Then the Bodhisattva practiced asceticism at that place for six years; yet even so, he did not realize the supreme noble wisdom and sublime Dharma.
At that time, the Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"In the past, while staying under a jambu tree in my father the king's field, I removed desire and unwholesome states, and with directed thought and evaluation, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, I sported in the first dhyāna."
At that time, the Bodhisattva again thought to himself:
"Is there perhaps such a path by which one may attain the exhaustion of the source of suffering?
He then further thought:
"This path is able to bring an end to the source of suffering.
At that time, the Bodhisattva cultivated this wisdom through the power of diligence; by means of this path, he attained the exhaustion of the source of suffering.
Then the Bodhisattva again had this thought:
"Is it possible to obtain the Dharma of bliss by means of unwholesome dharmas of desire?
He then further had this thought:
"One does not attain the state of happiness through unwholesome states characterized by desire. He further reflects:
"Is there perhaps a cultivation of non-desire that abandons unwholesome states and attains the state of happiness?"

"However, I do not attain the Dharma of happiness by thus afflicting my own body. Might it not be better for me now to eat a small amount of rice and parched grain so that I may restore my physical strength?
At that time, the Bodhisattva at another occasion ate a small amount of rice and parched grain, whereby he regained his strength.
At that time, when the Bodhisattva was eating a meager meal, the five men each grew weary and abandoned him, saying to one another:
"This Śramaṇa Gautama is deluded and has lost the Way; how could there be any true path in him?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva’s physical strength having been fully restored, he went once more to the banks of the Nairañjanā River; having entered the water to bathe his body and emerged onto the bank, he proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree.
At that time, not far from the tree, there was a man named Kṣema cutting grass.
The Bodhisattva approached this man and said to him:
"I now require some grass; please grant me a small portion."
Jixian replied, "Very well! I shall not begrudge it."
He then handed the grass to the Bodhisattva.

Taking the grass, the Bodhisattva went further to the foot of another auspicious tree, where he spread it out and sat down; with his body straight and his mind upright, he fixed his mindfulness before him.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having removed sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, joy, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind, dwells sporting in the first dhyāna; this is called the Bodhisattva’s initial attainment of the supreme wholesome dharmas.
Why is this? It is because his mind is bound in single-minded mindfulness and he is not negligent.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, having eliminated directed thought and sustained examination, attains internal confidence, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind, being without directed thought or sustained examination; he sports in the second dhyāna. This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of these two supreme wholesome dharmas.
Why is this? It is because he fixes his mind with single-minded attention and remains free from negligence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva eliminates joy and experiences physical bliss; he attains the bliss of being protected by the vision of noble wisdom and sports in the third dhyāna. This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the three supreme dharmas.
Why is this? It is because he binds his mind with single-minded mindfulness and remains free from negligence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva has already abandoned suffering and pleasure, and having previously cast off sorrow and joy, he dwells in the purity of equanimity, free from both suffering and pleasure, sporting in the fourth dhyāna. This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of these four supreme dharmas.
Why is this? It is because his mind is bound in single-minded mindfulness and he is free from negligence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva attains this concentrated state of mind; all fetters and latent tendencies are completely eliminated, becoming pure and free from blemish. His conduct becomes supple, and dwelling in a state of firm stability, he realizes the knowledge of past lives.
He recollects his own past lives: one birth, two births, three births, four births,
five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births, a hundred births, a thousand births,
a hundred thousand births, countless hundreds of births, countless thousands of births, and countless [births].
Throughout hundreds of thousands of births, through the formation and destruction of kalpas, through the formation of countless kalpas and the destruction of countless kalpas,
and through the formation and destruction of countless kalpas, I have been born in such-and-such a place, with such-and-such a name and such-and-such a clan;
I was born in this manner, ate such-and-such food, had such-and-such a lifespan, lived for such-and-such a duration, and remained in the world for such-and-such a length of time.
Thus, experiencing such suffering and pleasure, passing away from there to be born there, passing away from there to be born again there,
and passing away from there to be born here— he thus perceives the countless events of his past lives in their various characteristics.

At that time, during the first watch of the night, the Bodhisattva attained this first clarity: ignorance was exhausted and wisdom arose; darkness was extinguished and light appeared—namely, the realization of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives. Why was this so?
Due to his diligence and heedfulness, the Bodhisattva further attained the purity of samādhi;

his mind was stainless and free from fetters, all defilements were exhausted, his conduct was gentle, and he dwelt in a state of firm stability, knowing those among the living beings who are born and those who die.

With the purified divine eye, they behold sentient beings—those being born and those dying, those of beautiful appearance and those of ugly appearance, those in happy realms and those in miserable realms, whether noble or lowly—and they know them all according to the actions performed by each sentient being.

He immediately examines and realizes: "This sentient being has practiced evil with the body, evil with speech, and evil with the mind; holding wrong views, they have slandered the noble ones and created the karmic retribution of wrong views. When their body perishes and life ends, they will fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts."

Furthermore, he observes sentient beings who practice wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; who possess right view and do not revile the noble ones; and who, having performed karma based on right view, at the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn among gods or humans.

With such purified divine eye, he observes sentient beings being born and dying according to their respective actions; this is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of the second clarity during the middle watch of the night.
When ignorance is exhausted, clarity arises; when darkness is exhausted, light arises. This is called the divine eye-knowledge that perceives sentient beings.
Why is this? It is because of diligence and non-negligence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva attained such a pure state of meditative concentration; all fetters were completely eliminated, becoming pure and flawless. His conduct was supple and his dwelling firm, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows manifested before him.

With the mind taking the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows as its object, one knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin of suffering, knows the cessation of suffering, and knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering; thus, one attains the Noble Truths.
Knowing it as it truly is, he knows the taints as they truly are; he knows the origin of the taints, and he knows the path leading to the cessation of the taints as it truly is.

By knowing and contemplating in this way, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, his mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and his mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.

Having attained liberation, he gains the knowledge of liberation: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of these three knowledges during the latter part of the night.
When ignorance is exhausted, clarity arises; when darkness is exhausted, light arises. This is called the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
Why is this? Because it is by means of this knowledge that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has attained unimpeded liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One, at that very place, exhausted all outflows and eliminated all fetters and latent tendencies.
He sat cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree for seven days without moving, experiencing the bliss of liberation.
At that time, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One arose from his meditative concentration; during those seven days, he had not partaken of any food.

At that moment, there were two merchant brothers, one named Trapusa and the other named Bhallika, who were traveling with five hundred wagons laden with treasures, passing not far from the Bodhi tree.

At that time, the tree spirit had deep faith in the Buddha and was an old acquaintance of these two merchants; wishing to enable them to attain liberation, she went to where the merchants were and said to them, "Do you know?"
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has fully realized all dharmas within seven days.
During these seven days he has not yet partaken of any food; you should offer honey-gruel to the Tathāgata, so that you may obtain benefit, virtue, peace, and happiness for a long night.
At that time, having heard the words of the tree deity, the two brothers were filled with joy. They immediately took honeyed parched grain and went to the Bodhi tree.

From afar they beheld the Tathāgata’s countenance, which was extraordinary; his faculties were tranquil and perfectly subdued, like a tamed elephant free from all violence, or like clear, still water devoid of any turbidity. Having seen him, they gave rise to a heart of great joy.
They approached the presence of the Tathāgata, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and stood to one side.
Then the two men said to the World-Honored One:
"We now offer this honey-gruel; please accept it out of your compassion."
Then the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"Now these two persons offer honey and parched grain; with what vessel shall I receive them?
He further spoke these words:
“What did the Buddhas of the past—the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas—use to receive their food?
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not receive food with their hands.”

At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings stood at his left and right; knowing what the Buddha was thinking, they went to the four directions and each took a stone bowl, offering them to the World-Honored One and saying:
"We pray that you will accept the flour and honey from those merchants with these bowls."
Then, out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted the bowls from the Four Heavenly Kings, causing them to be joined into one, and accepted the flour and honey from those merchants.
Having accepted the flour and honey from those merchants, he instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with this teaching.
He then uttered this prayer of blessing:
"Whoever practices giving shall surely obtain its benefit and purpose;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, they will surely attain peace and joy hereafter."
"O merchants! You should now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
They then accepted the Buddha's teaching and said:
“Venerable Sir!
We now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
This was the first instance of receiving the two refuges among the upāsakas, with these two merchant brothers as the leaders.
Then the two merchants said to the Buddha:
"We now wish to return from here to our native land; once we arrive there, how should we cultivate merit?
What should we venerate and offer?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their sincere intention, immediately gave them his hair and nails, saying:
"Take these and go there to perform meritorious acts of veneration and offering."
At that time, although the merchants obtained the hair and nail-clippings, they were unable to make offerings with a sincere heart, saying:
"These hair and nail-clippings are things despised and discarded by the people of the world; why has the World-Honored One taken them and given them to us for our worship?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the merchants' minds, spoke to them, saying:
"Do not harbor even a hair’s breadth of negligence toward the hair and nails produced from the Tathāgata, nor say: 'How can the Tathāgata cause us, who are despised by the world, to make offerings?'"
"O Merchant, you should know!

Throughout the world—including the hosts of Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans—those who offer worship and reverence to the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata cause all these devas, worldly people, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas to obtain merit that is beyond measure."
The merchant addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one makes offerings to these hairs and nails, what signs of verification will there be?
The Buddha told the merchant:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Jayasena who ruled over Jambudvīpa.
At that time, within Jambudvīpa, rice and grain were abundant, the population was flourishing, and the land was exceedingly blissful."
There were eighty-four thousand walled cities, five hundred and fifty million villages, and sixty thousand minor kingdoms.

At that time, the capital city where King Vijitāvin resided was named Padmā; it measured twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north. The land was fertile and abundant, grain was cheap and plentiful, and the population was vast and flourishing. The kingdom was peaceful and happy, with lush gardens and groves, secure walls and moats, cool bathing pools, and every necessity fully provided; its streets and lanes were laid out in perfect symmetry.
"O Merchant, you should know!
At that time, King Jayasena had a brahmin who served as his chief minister, named Dīrghayava.
This man had been a companion to the king since their youth, and they were extremely close and affectionate."
Later, at another time, the king divided half of his kingdom and gave it to this great minister.

Thereupon, within the portion of the kingdom he received, the minister established a city with walls and moats; it was twelve yojanas long from east to west and seven yojanas wide from south to north. Rice and grain were abundant and cheap, and the population was flourishing. The land was peaceful and joyful, with lush forests; the city walls and moats were secure, the bathing pools were cool and refreshing, all necessities were provided in abundance, and the streets and lanes were well-proportioned.
The city is named Devavatī; it surpasses that city of Padmāvatī.
"O merchants, you should know!
That king has no heir."

Because he had no heir, he prayed to various deities at springs, streams, mountain sources, rivers, and bathing pools; to the Pūrṇabhadra and Maṇibhadra spirits; to the sun and moon, Śakra, Brahmā, Agni, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Maheśvara, the deity of the garden, the deity of the forest, the deity of the marketplace, the deity of the crossroads and alleys, the deity of the city of Hārītī, and the deities of the celestial shrines and merit-bestowing altars. Everywhere he sought and entreated them, saying:
"I pray that a son may be born."
At another time, the king’s principal queen became pregnant. Women possess three kinds of wisdom that are true and not false:
first, knowing for herself that she is pregnant; second, knowing for herself from whom she conceived; and third, knowing that the man has feelings of love for her.
Then that lady went to address the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know!
I am now pregnant."
The king replied, "Excellent!
He immediately commanded his attendants to provide the most superior food, drink, clothing, and bedding, ensuring that all necessities were increased by one-and-a-half times.
When the tenth month was completed, a son was born, of incomparable beauty and a rarity in this world.
As soon as he was born upon the ground, without anyone to support him, he walked seven steps by himself and spoke these words:
"I am the most supreme and most honored in the heavens and the world; I shall deliver all living beings from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death."
"He was immediately named Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara.
O merchants, you should know that at that time,
the king summoned a Brahmin who was highly proficient in the methods of physiognomy and addressed him, saying:"

"You all should know that my wife has given birth to a son whose countenance is upright and handsome, a rarity in this world. As soon as he emerged from the womb, without anyone to support him, he walked seven paces by himself and spoke these words:
'I am the most supreme and most honored in the heavens and the world; I can deliver all sentient beings from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death.'"
"You are all experts in the science of physiognomy; please examine the marks of this child for me.
At that time, the physiognomists addressed the king, saying, "We pray that Your Majesty bring forth this child so that we may examine his marks."
The king immediately entered the palace himself, took the child in his arms, and brought him out to show him to the physiognomists.
After the physiognomists had examined him, they said to the king:
"Your Majesty, this child you have fathered possesses great majestic power and great merit; he is fully endowed with blessings and vows."

If this prince remains at home, he shall become a Kṣatriya anointed-turning-wheel king (cakravartin) with the seven treasures complete, ruling over the four continents; he will have a full thousand sons who are vigorous, heroic, and fierce, capable of repelling all enemies, governing by means of the Dharma without the use of weapons or staffs.

If one goes forth from the household life, they will become a Tathāgata, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, one endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons, a trainer of men, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, and a World-Honored One. Among gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, they will personally realize this for themselves and dwell therein at ease. They shall preach the Dharma—excellent in its beginning, excellent in its middle, and excellent in its end—possessing both meaning and flavor, and fully embodying the holy life.
“O Merchant, you should know!
At that time, after the king had bestowed his rewards upon the brahmin, he appointed four nurses to attend to and look after the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara:
first, the nurse for his limbs; second, the nurse for his bathing; third, the nurse for providing milk; and fourth, the nurse for his play.”
The wet-nurse for the limbs and joints is one who holds the child, massages the limbs, and turns them to ensure they are properly aligned.
The wet-nurse for bathing is one who washes the body and cleans the clothes.
The wet-nurse who provided milk gave him milk at the appropriate times.

The playmate-nurse attended to the various children as they rode on elephants, horses, chariots, and litters; with various precious vessels, musical instruments, and rotating mechanical toys—using such diverse articles of worship and entertainment—they made offerings to and delighted the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara, holding peacock-feather parasols while following him.
“O Merchant, you should know!

When the Bodhisattva Dīpaṃkara was eight or nine years old, the King instructed him in various arts and skills: writing, arithmetic, seal-engraving, painting, comedy, song and dance, stringed instruments, riding elephants, riding horses, driving chariots, archery, horsemanship, and wrestling. There were no technical skills in which he was not thoroughly proficient.”
“Merchant, you should know!
When Dīpaṃkara reached the age of fifteen or sixteen, the king provided him with a three-season palace and assigned twenty thousand court ladies to entertain him during winter, summer, and spring.”

He created a garden and pond twenty yojanas in length and breadth, wherein he planted every kind of flower tree, fruit tree, and fragrant tree found throughout Jambudvīpa, as well as all manner of rare and extraordinary trees.
“Merchant, you should know!
The gods of the Śuddhāvāsa heaven come daily to attend upon him, thinking to themselves:
‘The Bodhisattva has now lived at home for a long time; we should now cause him to develop world-weariness.’”
"Will the Bodhisattva, having attained weary detachment, soon leave the household life, shave off his hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and cultivate the unsurpassed path?
While waiting for the Bodhisattva to enter the rear garden, he immediately went there and manifested four figures:
first, an old man; second, a sick man; third, a dead man; and fourth, one who had left the household life to become a śramaṇa.

At that time, having seen these four men, the Bodhisattva was filled with profound sorrow and weariness toward the suffering of the world. He contemplated the world, thinking: "What is there in such a state as this to be craved?
O merchants, you should know!"
At that time, having attained weary detachment, the Bodhisattva left the household life on that very day and attained the Unsurpassed Way on that very day.
Merchant, you should know!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara surveyed all beings and did not see anyone who was ready to be delivered and for whom he could turn the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma.

At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, not far from the city of Devavatī, manifested a great city—lofty, vast, and exquisite—adorned with suspended silken banners and streamers, and carved everywhere with the forms of various birds and beasts.

The surrounding pure and wondrous bathing pools and garden fruits were superior to those of the city of Devavatī; he further transformed the appearance and features of his people so that they surpassed those of the inhabitants of that country, causing the people of his own land to interact with and form friendships with them.
“Merchant, you should know!
The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, observing that the faculties of the people of the city of Devavatī were fully matured, caused the illusory city to suddenly burst into flames.”
When the people of the city of Devavatī saw this, they were filled with profound sorrow and gave rise to a mind of weary detachment.
Within seven days, Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara liberated sixty-six *nayuta* of people and five hundred and fifty million *śrāvakas*.
"O Merchant, you should know!
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara possessed great renown that spread throughout the ten directions; there were none who did not hear and know of it, and all together proclaimed:

'The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara—Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—within the entire world, including Māras, Māra-devas, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, gods, and humans, has realized for himself and dwells in bliss; he teaches the Dharma to others, with words that are excellent in the beginning, middle, and end, possessing both meaning and flavor, fully cultivating the holy life.'"
“O merchant, you should know!

While the ordinary body-light of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara illuminates one hundred yojanas, it is the constant law for all Buddha-Bhagavāns that their light shines immeasurably; they then withdraw that light so that only seven feet of radiance remain.”
"O Merchant, you should know!

At that time, King Vijitāvin heard that a crown prince had been born in the palace of King Tiyanbati, who was endowed with merit, majestic power, and all the marks of excellence; that on the very day of his birth he left the household life, and on that same day attained the path of unsurpassed, right, and true enlightenment, his fame spreading far and wide, such that all together proclaimed:
'The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara... [and so forth]... fully practicing the holy life.'"
King Jayasena immediately dispatched a messenger to King Dīrghāyu with this message:

"I have heard that you have given birth to a prince who is endowed with merit, majestic power, and all the auspicious marks; that on the very day he left home, he attained enlightenment, and has even now fully cultivated the holy life until his great fame has spread throughout the ten directions. You should now send him here, for I wish to see him."
"If you do not send someone here, I shall go there myself.
When King Tiyanbati heard these words from the messenger, he was immediately filled with sorrow and anxiety. He assembled his ministers and said to them:
"Consider this: how should we respond, and what expedient means should we employ that would be acceptable to his wishes?"
The ministers replied, "We shall inquire of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara; according to whatever instructions the Buddha gives, we shall comply and act accordingly.

Thereupon, King Tiyaṃbati, together with his retinue of ministers, went to the place where the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported the entire matter to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said to the king:
"Cease for now! Do not harbor grief or anxiety; I myself shall go there."
“O merchants, you should know!

At that time, King Tiyanbati personally provided offerings for seven days to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the community of bhikṣus—providing robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicines for the treatment of illness—ensuring they lacked for nothing.”
“O Merchant, you should know!
Seven days after the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had departed, he traveled among the people with his bhikṣus and proceeded directly to the edge of the Dragon King’s Pond on Mount Bhaiṣajya.”
"O merchant, you should know!
This palace of the Dragon King is five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the community of bhikṣus resided there."

At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara emitted a great radiance that universally illuminated the trichiliocosm; day and night were no longer distinguished. When the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers closed and the birds and beasts ceased their cries, it was known to be night;
when the *utpala* and other flowers blossomed and the various birds and beasts cried out, it was known to be day.
Thus, as twelve years passed, there was no distinction between day and night.
King Jayasena then assembled his ministers and said to them:
"I recall that in former days there were both days and nights; why is it that now there are neither days nor nights?"
If the various *utpala* flowers bloom and the various birds and beasts cry out, one knows it is day;
if the flowers close and the birds do not cry out, one knows it is night.
"Is there unrighteousness in the world? Is there a deficiency in my own conduct?
Or is it that you yourselves have committed a fault? Tell me the truth."
The ministers replied:
"The King is not at fault, nor is there any unrighteousness in the kingdom, nor have we committed any transgression.

It is because the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara is now in the palace of the Dragon King at Mount Hālida, emitting a great radiance that universally illuminates the trichiliocosm, that his majestic spiritual power causes day and night to be indistinguishable."
If you wish to know whether it is day or night: when the flowers close and the birds do not sing, you know it is night;
if the flowers bloom and the birds sing, you know it is day.

You, O King, shall incur no blame, and there shall be no unrighteousness in the kingdom; nor do I have any fault. This is the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara; there is no need for fear.
The king asked his attendants:
"How far is the palace of the Nāga King Elāpattra on Mount Ahalya from here?
The ministers replied to the king:
"It is not far from here, about thirty *li*.
The King commanded his attendants:
'Prepare the carriage adorned with precious feathers; I now wish to go there to pay homage to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.'"
The attendants immediately followed these instructions; having prepared the carriage adorned with precious feathers, they went before the King and said:
"The carriage is ready; Your Majesty knows the time."
“O merchants, you should know!
The king immediately mounted his carriage, with his ministers attending as his retinue, and proceeded to the palace of the Dragon King at Mount Halidda.
Upon arrival, they stopped at a place where it was not permitted to ride the carriage; there they alighted and advanced on foot until they reached the Dragon King’s palace.”
"O merchant, you should know!

At that time, the king saw from afar the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, whose countenance was upright and whose faculties were tranquil and composed. Having seen him, he gave rise to a heart of joy and immediately approached the place where the Buddha Dīpaṃkara was; having prostrated his head at the Buddha’s feet, he sat down to one side."
Then the World-Honored One gradually expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the king, exhorting him until he was filled with joy.
Having heard the Buddha’s exposition of the subtle and wondrous Dharma and having been exhorted until he was joyful, the king came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying: “Tathāgata!...”
"Now is precisely the time; you should enter the city of Padma.
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara silently accepted the King's invitation.
When King Jayasena knew that the Buddha had silently accepted the invitation, he rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet with his head and face, and departed.
Upon returning to the borders of his kingdom, he issued a decree to the people:

"From this Lotus City to Mount Medicine, you shall dig the earth knee-deep and compact it with pestles until it is firm. Sprinkle the ground with fragrant liquid and plant various kinds of flowers along both sides of the road. Construct railings by the roadside and place fine oil lamps upon them; fashion incense burners of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal."
When the people had received the king’s command as previously described, the king immediately assembled his ministers and said to them:

"You must adorn this great city of Padma; remove all filth, earth, stones, sand, and impurities; smear the ground with fine, excellent clay; hang silk banners and canopies; burn various kinds of fine incense; further spread various kinds of woolen rugs; and scatter various beautiful flowers over the ground."
Then the ministers immediately received the king’s command and adorned [the city] according to his instructions.
At that time, King Jayasena again addressed his great ministers:
"Proclaim throughout the lands and to the people: let there be no one who sells incense or flowers."
If there are those who sell, let there be no one who buys.
If there are those who buy or sell, they shall be severely punished. Why is this?
"It is because I myself wish to make offerings to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara.

At that time, there was a great minister and brāhmaṇa in that country named Yajñadatta, who possessed abundant wealth and treasures—pearls, amber, musāragalva, agate, crystal, gold, silver, and lapis lazuli—with rare and extraordinary jewels beyond measure.
At that time, that brahmin performed sacrificial offerings for twelve years.

If among those present at his sacrifices there was one who possessed the greatest wisdom, he would give him a golden bowl filled with silver grain, or a silver bowl filled with golden grain, along with a golden water-pitcher, an exquisite parasol, sandals, two fine pieces of woolen cloth, a staff inlaid with various jewels, and a well-adorned, beautiful woman named Sulopati. He would bestow these upon such a person.
At that time, among the assembly at the sacrifice, there was a preeminent senior Brahmin who was a high minister of the king and possessed twelve deformities:

he was blind, hunchbacked, with a protruding back, a goiter, yellow-skinned, with yellow hair, blue eyes, saw-toothed, black teeth, crooked hands and feet, a twisted body that did not stand level with others, and a protruding pelvis.
"Merchant, you should know!
That brahmin who performs the sacrifice thinks thus:
'Now this senior elder has twelve deformities and is moreover a royal minister.'"
"Why should I give my treasures and my daughter to this man?
He then thought further:
"I would rather postpone the sacrificial day; if there should be another Brāhmaṇa who is handsome, intelligent, and wise, I shall give [my daughter] to him."
“Merchants, you should know!

To the south of the Snowy Mountains there is a seer named Ratna. Having few desires and delighting in solitude, his mind is free from greed; he practices meditative concentration and has attained the five supernormal powers, and he instructs five hundred brahmins, causing them to recite and study.”

At that time, the rishi with five supernatural powers had a foremost disciple named Mijue; his parents were of pure lineage for seven generations back, and he likewise instructed five hundred disciples.
"O Merchant, you should know!
At that time, the disciple Māyujja went to the seer Ratnaka and said to him:
'That which I have studied has been mastered; what more should I study?'"
Then that Rishi Ratnaka, having composed further scriptures such as none of the other brahmins could understand, said to his disciples:
"You should study and recite these; such books do not exist among the śramaṇas or brahmins."
"If one studies and recites it, one may attain the most excellent and foremost status among all brāhmaṇas.
Merchant, you should know that at that time,
the disciple, having mastered this book through study and recitation, went to the presence of the seer Ratnaka and said:
"Once you have finished what you were to learn, what should you practice next?
The teacher replied, "If you have completed your recitation, as a disciple you ought to repay the kindness of your teacher; you should now do so."
He then asked, "How should one repay the kindness of the teacher?
The teacher replied:
"I require five hundred gold coins.

When Māṭhara heard his teacher’s words, he took five hundred disciples and traveled through the human realms south of the Snowy Mountains, going from country to country and village to village, until they gradually reached the city of Puṣpapura.
I heard from various people say:
"The Brahmin Yajñadatta has been performing sacrifices to the heavenly deities for twelve years.

To whoever is foremost in intelligence, he shall give a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain, together with a golden water-pitcher, an excellent parasol, a most fine cotton cloth, a staff inlaid with the seven precious gems, and the well-adorned, beautiful, and virtuous daughter Sulabhā."
"I should now enter among that crowd; perhaps I might obtain those five hundred gold coins.
"O merchant, you should know!
Mṛgāra then entered that sacrificial assembly. As he was entering, there was a great majesty and radiance of light."
Then the brahmin Yajñadatta thought to himself:
"This man has entered the sacrificial ground with great majesty and radiance; he must surely displace the one in the seat of honor and install this young brahmin (māṇava) in that place."

"If this Māṇava takes the seat of the Elder, you all should act as I have done: together raise your voices in praise, perform various musical performances, scatter flowers, burn incense, and pay him respectful homage."
Then those people immediately accepted the instruction, saying, "So be it.
While they were acting according to the instructions, Makhādeva entered the assembly and questioned them from the bottom up:
"What scriptures do you recite? How much have you mastered?
To each, he replied according to the extent of what they had recited:
"I have recited this much," [he said];
yet compared to what the Māṇava has recited, it is not even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousand-millionth part—it cannot be compared and is not equal to that of the Māṇava.
Next, he asked two, three, or even up to a hundred thousand people:
"What do you recite? What sūtras and books do you know?"
"How much have you recited?
They replied according to what they had recited,
saying, "We have recited this much."
"Compared to what the Māṇava recites, [my knowledge] is a hundredfold, a thousandfold, even a hundred billionfold greater; it cannot be compared to his.
Next, he asked the foremost Elder:
'What scriptures do you know?'"
"How much have you been able to recite?
The man replied according to the amount he had recited:
"I have recited this much."
"Upatiṣya the Māṇava was even more eminent than him.
At that time, Upatiṣya the Māṇava said:
'What I have recited and mastered surpasses yours.'"
He then said to that person:
"Go! I shall sit in your place."
The Elder replied, "Do not make me move;
even if I were to receive excellent offerings and gold and jewels here, I would give you twice as much."
Migala the young brahmin replied:
"Even if the entire Jambudvīpa were filled with the seven treasures and given to me, I would never accept them; you may simply move away."
"And why is that? Because I possess this Dharma, I ought to sit upon this seat.
"O merchants, you should know this!"
Then, that Māṭhara youth moved the seat of the elder and sat upon it himself.
As he was moving the seat, the earth shook in six ways; immediately, they raised their voices together in praise, performing various musical performances and making offerings of flowers and incense.
"O merchant, you should know!

That Yajñadatta was filled with extreme joy and felt immeasurable self-congratulation. He brought a golden bowl filled with silver grain, a silver bowl filled with golden grain, a golden parasol, a staff inlaid with the seven precious gems, a golden and silver water-pot, exquisite fine cotton cloth, and a beautifully adorned maiden; he went before the young brahmin Māṅkuka and said:
'I pray that you will accept these various precious objects as well as this beautiful maiden.'"
Migala replied, "I have no need for this. He then asked:
"What do you require?
he asked. He replied, "I require five hundred gold coins."
He then gave him five hundred gold coins.
"O merchant, you should know!
At that time, the young brahmin Māṭhara, having taken these five hundred gold coins, rose from his seat and departed."
At that time, the woman Sulabhā also followed after him.
Then Makkhali the young brahmin looked back and said to her,
"For what reason do you follow behind me?"
The girl replied,
"My parents have sent me to be your wife. Mṛkṣa-māṇava replied:
"I am now practicing the holy life (brahmacarya) and have no need for you; it is only those who possess lustful desire that would require you.

At that time, the woman returned to her father’s garden. Within the garden was a pure bathing pool, and in the pool were seven stalks of lotuses; five flowers grew from each stalk, their fragrance was exquisite and their colors were most wonderful.
Furthermore, there were two flowers on a single stalk, their fragrance and color exceptionally wondrous. Upon seeing them, he immediately had this thought:
"I now observe that these flowers are most exquisite; I should surely gather these flowers and give them to Māgha the young brahmin, so as to bring joy to his heart."
He immediately gathered flowers and placed them in a water jar, then went outside the garden to search everywhere for the young brahmin Māṅka.

At that time, the young brahmin Māṅka had returned to the great kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. There he saw the people of the country sweeping the roads and removing impurities, filling and leveling the ground with fine soil, scattering flowers upon it and sprinkling it with fragrant liquid, hanging silk banners and canopies, and spreading out fine woolen rugs. Having seen this, he asked the travelers in the city:
"Observing how this city is so magnificently adorned, is this for a seasonal festival, or is it for an auspicious day determined by the stars that you have prepared it in such a manner?"
The traveler replied, "The Buddha Dīpaṃkara is about to enter the city; it is for this reason that we are repairing it in such a manner.
Then the young brahmin Māyā thought to himself:

"I should now use five hundred gold coins to purchase fine flower garlands, excellent incense, beautiful musical instruments, banners and streamers, and fine parasols; first I shall offer these as worship to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, and afterwards I shall seek further wealth for my teacher."
"Consequently, whatever he sought to purchase in that country of Padma was entirely unobtainable.
Why was this? Because King Jayavijaya had established such strict prohibitions."
At that time, the woman Sulabhā saw the young brahmin Māṭhara approaching from afar and said to him:
"Young man! Why do you walk so swiftly? Do you have some need?"
He then replied to the woman,
"I require fine flowers. She asked:
"Monaka, what will you do with these flowers? He replied,
"I wish to create the unsurpassed root-planting for the lineage of the Buddha."
The girl asked: "These flowers have already withered, their color has changed, and they can no longer be planted.
How can you use them to create the unsurpassed root-planting for the seed of Buddhahood?"
The Māṇava replied to the woman, “This field is excellent and fertile;
even if these flowers were withered, their color changed, and their seeds scorched and rotten, they would still grow from being sown therein.”
The girl replied, "You may take these flowers and use them as the unsurpassed root-plants for the seed of the Buddha.
The māṇava replied:
"If you accept my price and sell me to me, I shall take you.
The girl replied, "Māṇava, why do you begrudge my wealth?"
"My father's name is Yaññadatta, and he possesses abundant wealth and treasures.
O Māṇava, if you wish to buy flowers, make this vow with me: 'In whatever place we may be born, will you always be my husband?'"
The Māṇava replied:

"I practice the path of the Bodhisattva; I have nothing for which I cherish anything. If someone comes to beg, I would not begrudge even my own flesh and bones, with the sole exception of my parents, fearing only that you might constantly create obstacles for me."
The girl replied: "The place from which you were born must possess great majestic power.
I too possess majestic power; I wish to give myself to you as a gift, to be bestowed according to your will."
At that time, he purchased five stalks of lotuses for five hundred gold coins; giving two remaining stalks to the young brahmin Māyā, he said:
"These are my flowers; entrust them to you to present to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara."
"Why is this? Because I vow that wherever you are born, we shall never be separated.
"O merchant, you should know!"
At that time, having received these seven flowers, Makhādeva was filled with such immense joy that he could not contain himself; he immediately proceeded to the eastern gate of the city.

At that very moment, countless billions of sentient beings, all carrying flowers and incense, suspending silken banners and canopies, and performing various musical performances, were waiting for Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.
Then the young brahmin Mṛgala wished to step forward to scatter flowers, but he was unable to do so; he immediately turned back and asked King Jayasena:

"For what reason have you renovated the interior of the city? Is it for a seasonal festival, or for an auspicious day determined by the stars, that you have adorned the land with such exquisite beauty?"
The king replied, "The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara is now about to enter the city; that is why it is being prepared.
The māṇava asked the king:
"How is it known that the Tathāgata possesses the thirty-two marks?
The king replied,
"It is known through what is recorded in the prophetic texts of the various Brahmins."
The Māṇava replied, “If that is so,
I have recited this scripture and clearly understand this matter.
The king said:
"If you truly know this, you should first go and observe his thirty-two marks; only then shall I see him.
"O merchant, you should know!"
At that time, having heard the king’s words, the young brahmin (māṇava) was so overcome with joy that he could not contain himself; he immediately went to the eastern gate outside the city.
When the great multitude of people saw the young brahmin approaching, they were filled with joy and all made way for him.
For what reason? Because they have received the King's command.
Merchant, you should know this!
At that time, the Māṇava saw the Tathāgata from afar and felt great joy in his heart; he immediately took seven stalks of flowers and scattered them over the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, these were instantly transformed into a flower-canopy in mid-air, twelve yojanas in width, with the stalks above and the petals below. Its fragrance was so rich and pervasive that it covered the entire kingdom, reaching everywhere so that one could never tire of beholding it. As the Buddha traveled, the flower-canopy followed him.
At that time, all the men and women of the city stripped off their new garments and spread them upon the ground.
As for the two deerskin robes worn by the Māṇava, he took off one and spread it on the ground.
At that time, the people of the city seized this leather garment and cast it away.
Then the Māṇava thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara does not take pity on me."
At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, knowing the thoughts in his mind, transformed the ground into mud such that no one was able to spread his robe upon it.
"O merchant, you should know this! [he said.]
The Mānava thought again:
"The people within the city are foolish and lack discernment; they have not spread [seats] where they ought to be spread.
He then took his deerskin garment and spread it upon that mud, yet he did not cover the mud entirely.
"O Merchant, you should know!
For five hundred years, this young man (māṇava) has always worn his hair in a topknot and has never loosened it. The young man then asked the Tathāgata:
'I wonder, World-Honored One, would you be able to step upon my hair and pass over it?'"
He replied, "I can.
The Māṇava then untied his topknot and spread the hair upon the clay, making this aspiration:
"If the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara does not grant me this prediction, I shall wither away here and end my life; I will never rise again.

At that time, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, knowing that this māṇava had cultivated roots of goodness with utmost sincerity over many lifetimes and was fully endowed with manifold virtues, stepped upon his hair with his left foot and passed by, saying:

"Māṇava, rise! In the future, after incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall be named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān."
Having heard this distinction, he immediately leaped into the air to a height of seven *tāla* trees above the ground, yet his hair remained spread upon the earth as before.
"O merchants, you should know!
At that time, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara turned his gaze to the right like a great elephant king and addressed the bhikṣus:
"None of you shall tread with your feet upon the hair of this māṇava."
"Why is this? These are the hair of a Bodhisattva; no Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha should ever tread upon it.
At that time, many thousands of millions of people all scattered flowers and burned incense as an offering to his hair.
“Merchant, you should know!

At that time, the twelve ugly ministers of King Jitaśatru, having heard that the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara had conferred the designation of ‘maṇava’ upon [the youth], immediately went to King Jitaśatru and said:

‘I am capable of providing for twenty thousand years the offerings of robes, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the assembly of monks.’”
The King replied to the brahmin, saying:
"Your intention is most excellent!
You should know that now is the time."

At that time, this brahmin, having for twenty thousand years provided the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the community of bhikṣus with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm, made this vow, saying:
"I have now, for twenty thousand years, provided the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara and the community of bhikṣus with robes, food and drink, bedding and seats, and medicinal requisites for the sick and infirm."

However, since this Māṇava has moved me from my seat, seized my offerings, and destroyed my reputation, by virtue of these karmic conditions for merit, I shall constantly humiliate and insult this man in every place where I am born, until he attains the Way, never abandoning him until the end.
"Merchants, you should know!
As for that Brahmin Yaññadatta at that time, was he anyone else?
Do not view him as another; he is none other than this Śākya of the Staff now."
At that time, who else could the woman Sulopati have been?
She is none other than the Śākya maiden Gopī today.
At that time, who else could the twelve ugly Brahmins who were ministers of King Jayasena have been? They are none other than [the present assembly].
Do not view this otherwise; he was none other than the present Devadatta.
As for the seer Ratna at that time, could he have been anyone else?
Do not view this otherwise; he was none other than the present Bodhisattva Maitreya.
At that time, was the young brahmin Māgha anyone else?
Do not view him as another; he is none other than my own self.
O merchants, you should know this!

Those who study the bodhisattva path and are able to make offerings of their nails and hair will certainly achieve the unsurpassed path; beholding the world with the Buddha-eye, there is none who does not enter the realm of nirvana without remainder and attain parinirvāṇa.
How much more so for one who is free from desire, free from hatred, and free from delusion—this is the foremost among acts of giving and the most honored of merits.
It is the foremost among receiving, yet it is without karmic retribution!
At that time, the two merchant brothers rose from their seats and returned by the same path they had come.

Then, having finished eating the merchants' parched grain and honey, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged beneath a tree for seven days without moving, dwelling in the liberation-samādhi and enjoying himself therein.
After seven days, he arose from samādhi; because he had consumed parched grain and honey, the winds within his body were stirred.

As for why this land is named Jambudvīpa: there is a tree called Jambu, and not far from it is a harītakī tree. The deity of that tree was devotedly faithful to the Buddha; she took a harītakī fruit and came to offer it to the World-Honored One. Having prostrated herself with her head at his feet, she stood to one side.
The tree deity addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Because of eating parched grain with honey, the winds within my body have been stirred."
"I pray that you may now eat this fruit; it shall serve as both food and medicine to eliminate your internal wind.
Out of compassion for him, the World-Honored One accepted it and said:
"You should now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma."
He replied, “So be it,” and immediately took refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma.
Among the deities who received refuge, the deity of the harītakī tree was the first.

At that time, having eaten the harītakī fruit, the World-Honored One sat cross-legged beneath the tree for seven days, remaining unmoving in contemplation, sporting and delighting himself in the samādhi of liberation.

After seven days, he arose from samādhi; when the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village of Uruvilvā to beg for food, eventually arriving at the courtyard of a brahmin’s house in Uruvilvā, where he stood silently.
Seeing that the World-Honored One remained silent, the brahmin felt great joy and immediately brought forth food to offer to the World-Honored One.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One accepted the food and said to him:
"Now you take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma."
He replied: “So be it, World-Honored One!
I now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.”

Then, having accepted this food from the brahmin, the World-Honored One proceeded to the foot of another tree, a *nīpa* tree, where for seven days he sat in the full lotus posture, contemplating without moving, sporting and delighting himself in the samādhi of liberation.

Then, seven days later, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi. When the time came, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the village of Uruvelā to beg for food. Gradually approaching the courtyard of a brahmin’s house in Uruvelā, he stood there in silence.

At that time, the wife of that brahmin—a daughter of the great general Sujāta—saw the Tathāgata standing silently in the middle of the courtyard; having seen him, she gave rise to a heart of joy and immediately went out to offer food to the World-Honored One.
Out of compassion for him, the World-Honored One accepted his food; having eaten, he said to him:
"Now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma. He replied:
"In this way, I now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
Among those female lay disciples (*upāsikā*) who received the refuges in the Buddha and the Dharma, this wife of Uruvilvā, the female lay disciple Sujātā, the chief of the army, was the first.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having finished eating that food, immediately returned to the foot of the Nyagrodha tree. There he sat cross-legged for seven days, contemplating without moving, sporting in and delighting himself within the samādhi of liberation.

Then, after seven days had passed, the World-Honored One dressed in his robes and took up his bowl at the proper time, entering the village of Uruvelā to beg for food. Proceeding by stages, he arrived at the courtyard of the brahmin’s house in Uruvelā and stood there in silence.

At that time, when the men and women of the Uruvilvā brahmins saw the Tathāgata, they gave rise to a heart of joy; they immediately brought forth food to offer to the Tathāgata, and out of compassion for them, he accepted their food.
After they had eaten, he said to them:
"Now you should take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
They replied:
“Excellent! We now take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
Then, having finished that meal, the World-Honored One proceeded to the palace of the Nāga King Manasvin on Mount Manasvin.
Having arrived there, he sat cross-legged for seven days, contemplating without moving, delighting himself by dwelling in the liberation-samādhi.

At that time, it rained heavily during the seven-day period and was extremely cold; the Dragon King Manasvin emerged from his palace and, encircling the Buddha’s head with his body, sheltered him from above, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Are you neither cold nor hot?"
"Are you not buffeted by the wind or scorched by the sun, nor tormented by mosquitoes and gadflies?

At that time, after seven days had passed, the rain ceased and all became clear and bright. Seeing that the rain had stopped and clarity had returned, the Dragon King untied his body and no longer coiled around the Buddha; he immediately transformed himself into a young Brahmin, stood before the Tathāgata with palms joined and kneeling on his heels, and prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata.
Then, seven days later, the World-Honored One arose from samādhi and praised it with these verses:
"Delight in the joy of freedom from desire, And in the joy of contemplating the Dharma;
Joy in the world is the absence of hatred, Not causing affliction to sentient beings."
"In this world there is no pleasure like that of transcending the realm of desire;
for one who can subdue the conceit of 'I am,' this is the foremost happiness.
At that time, the Dragon King Manasvin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The reason I encircle the Tathāgata’s body and shade his head is not because I wish to disturb the Tathāgata.
Rather, I fear that the Tathāgata’s body might be afflicted by cold or heat, wind or sun, or troubled by mosquitoes and gadflies."
"For this reason, I have circled the Buddha’s body so that my head provides shade over him.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"You now take refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma."
He replied, "So be it.
I now take refuge in the Buddha and the Dharma."
This is called receiving the two refuges among the animals, with the Dragon King as their leader.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had stayed beneath the tree of the Utpalaka Dragon King, he proceeded to the Nyagrodha tree at Āyupāla. Having arrived, he spread his sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, and reflected thus: "I have now attained this Dharma, which is exceedingly profound, difficult to understand, and difficult to know;

it is eternally quiescent, peaceful, subtle, and supreme. It can be known by the wise, but is not practiced by the foolish. Sentient beings have diverse views, diverse tolerances, diverse desires, and diverse livelihoods; relying on these diverse views, they delight in their own nests and lairs. Because sentient beings delight in such nests and lairs, the Dharma of Dependent Origination is exceedingly profound and difficult to understand."
Furthermore, there is a profound and difficult-to-understand state: the extinction of all desire and craving, which is nirvana.
Because this state is also difficult to perceive, if I were now to preach the Dharma and others did not understand it, my efforts would be in vain and merely a source of weariness and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these two verses, which had not been heard before nor previously taught:
“The attainment of the Way is exceedingly difficult; I preach it while dwelling in the thicket of the world.
Those possessed by greed, anger, and delusion Cannot enter this Dharma.”
Turning back against the current of birth and death, it is profound, subtle, and extremely difficult to understand;
those attached to desire see nothing, for they are shrouded by the body of ignorance.
*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Fascicle 31.
The Four-Part Vinaya, Volume Thirty-two, Part Two, Section Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty,
together with Zhu Fonian and others.
The Second Part of the *Prātimokṣa-vastu*: At that time, having reflected thus, the World-Honored One remained silent and did not preach the Dharma.
Then, from the Brahma Heaven, the Brahmā King, knowing from afar what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, thought:
"The world is utterly ruined! The Tathāgata has today attained this wondrous Dharma; why does he remain silent, causing the world not to hear it?"

At that time, Brahmā, like a strong man bending or extending his arm, came from there to the presence of the Tathāgata. Having prostrated with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, he stood to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that the Tathāgata will preach the Dharma; I pray only that the Sugata will preach the Dharma."

“Among the sentient beings of the world, there are also those whose defilements are thin, who possess wisdom and intelligence, and who are easy to deliver; they are able to extinguish unwholesome dharmas and accomplish wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the Brahma King: “So it is, so it is!”
Brahmā King! As you have said, while I was in a secluded place, this thought arose in me:

"I have now attained this Dharma; it is profound, difficult to know, and difficult to understand. It is eternally tranquil, quiescent, subtle, and supreme. It is known by the noble ones and is not practiced by the foolish. Sentient beings have different views, different tolerances, different desires, and different livelihoods; relying on their differing views, they delight in their own nests and caves."
Because sentient beings delight in their nests and burrows, they find the profound and difficult-to-understand nature of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) hard to grasp.

Furthermore, there is another point that is profound and difficult to understand: the nirvāṇa that results from the total extinction of all desire and craving; this state is likewise difficult to perceive.
"I now wish to preach the Dharma, but if others do not understand it, my efforts will be in vain and merely a source of weariness and suffering.
At that time, the World-Honored One had previously seen these two verses, which he had neither heard before nor ever spoken:
"The attainment of the Way was exceedingly difficult; I shall preach it while dwelling in a mountain cave."
Those possessed by greed, hatred, and delusion cannot enter this Dharma.
It flows against the current, turning back birth and death; it is profound, subtle, and extremely difficult to understand.
Those attached to desire see nothing, for they are shrouded by the darkness of ignorance.
"Therefore, Brahmā, I remain silent and do not preach the Dharma.
At that time, Brahmā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The world is in great ruin and decay; now that the Tathāgata has attained this True Dharma, why do you remain silent and not preach it, so that the world does not hear it?"
I only pray that the World-Honored One will, at this time, expound the True Dharma so that it may spread throughout the world.
There are also beings in the world whose defilements are thin and who are intelligent and easy to deliver; they are capable of extinguishing unwholesome dharmas and accomplishing wholesome dharmas.
At that time, after the Brahmā had spoken these words, he further spoke in verse:
“Within the Magadha land, amidst various defilements and impurities, the Buddha has been born therein;
I pray that you open the gate of the ambrosia and preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.”

At that time, having accepted the exhortation of the Brahmā, the World-Honored One immediately surveyed the sentient beings of the world with his Buddha-eye. He saw those born in the world and growing in the world—some with few defilements and some with many; those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties; those easy to deliver and those difficult to deliver; those who fear the retribution of future lives and are able to extinguish unwholesome dharmas and accomplish wholesome dharmas.
It is like a pool of *utpala*, a pool of *padma*, a pool of *kumuda*, or a pool of *puṇḍarīka*.

Among the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers, some have just emerged from the ground but have not yet risen above the water; some have already emerged from the ground and are level with the water; and some have risen above the water so that dust and water do not adhere to them.
The Tathāgata is likewise; with his Buddha-eye he observes the sentient beings of the world— those born into the world and grown within the world— who have few defilements or many defilements,
sharp faculties or dull faculties,
and who are easy to deliver or difficult to deliver.
Fearing the offenses of future lives, one is able to extinguish unwholesome dharmas and accomplish wholesome dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke this verse to Brahmā:
"Brahmā, I tell you: Now the gate of the Deathless is opened."
"Those who hear it shall believe and accept it; it is not spoken for the sake of causing affliction.
This is the subtle Dharma of Brahmā, the Dharma attained by the Muni.

At that time, knowing that the World-Honored One had accepted his exhortation, Brahmā prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed, immediately vanishing from sight.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"With whom should I first preach the Dharma now, so that upon hearing it, they will immediately understand?
He then reflected:
“Ārāḍa Kālāma was of little defilement, of sharp faculties, intelligent, and wise; I should now first teach him the Dharma.
Having thought this, further knowledge arose in me: “It has already been seven days since Ārāḍa Kālāma passed away. Moreover, various devas came and said to me:
‘Seven days have passed since Ārāḍa Kālāma passed away.’”
At that time, the Buddha thought to himself:
"How bitter it is! You have suffered a great loss;
how is it that you have not heard this most sublime Dharma?"
"If they hear it, they will quickly attain understanding.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"To whom should I first preach the Dharma so that they may quickly attain understanding?"
He thought to himself: “Udraka Rāmaputra has thin defilements; he is of sharp faculties, intelligent, and wise. I should now first preach the Dharma to him.
Having formed this thought, further knowledge arose in him: Udraka Rāmaputra passed away yesterday, and the devas also came to inform me, saying: [he has died].
“Udraka Rāmaputra passed away yesterday,” [the disciples] said.
The Buddha remarked, “How tragic! How painful!”
"You have suffered a great loss; why have you not heard this subtle and wondrous Dharma?
Had you heard it, you would have swiftly attained liberation.
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"I should now first teach the Dharma to whom? Who, upon hearing my Dharma, will quickly attain liberation?
He thought to himself:

"These five bhikṣus have performed their duties with diligent toil, never shunning cold or heat as they attended and made offerings to me; would it not be fitting for me to first teach them the Dharma?"
Then the World-Honored One again thought to himself:
"Where are the five bhikṣus currently residing?

With his pure divine eye, which surpasses that of gods and humans, he observed the five bhikṣus and saw them in the Deer Park of the Sages at Vārāṇasī. Having seen them, he immediately proceeded to that Deer Park of the Sages.
At that time, he saw the brahmin Udāyin also walking along the road; seeing the World-Honored One from afar, he approached and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Gautama! Your faculties are tranquil and your countenance is serene and joyful. Who is your teacher?"
"From whom did you study?
What Dharma did you study?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Omniscience is supreme; all craving for desire is liberated.
Having attained spontaneous realization, how could I learn from others?
I have no teacher, nor do I have any equal."
The sole Buddha in the world, serene and ever at peace;
I am the one without attachment in the world, I am the foremost in the world;
among all devas and humans, there is none who is my equal.
"I wish to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī;
for the world is entirely blind and dark, I shall beat the drum of the Deathless.
The brahmin asked:
“I wish to hear the meaning of what you, Gautama, have said regarding the supreme state of being unattached.
The Buddha replied in verse:
“I am liberated from all fetters, And have attained the exhaustion of all outflows;”
"I have conquered all evil dharmas; Oudāyin, I am the most supreme.
At that time, the brahmin remained silent.
Then the World-Honored One departed and went to the Deer Park of the Sages.
When the five bhikṣus saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar, they each cautioned one another, saying:
"This śramaṇa Gautama has lost his way on the road; he is wandering in confusion and has lost his resolve."
"If he comes here, you must not speak with him, nor pay him homage; instead, provide him with a separate small seat for him to sit upon.

At that time, as the World-Honored One gradually approached the five bhikṣus, the five bhikṣus were unaware of his arrival; they all rose to meet him and pay their respects. Some prepared a seat for him, some took up his robe and bowl, and some brought water to wash his feet.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "This foolish person!
Unable to make his resolve firm, he has established a restriction together with others and then broken it himself."
Why is this? Because they cannot endure the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
I shall now simply take my seat and sit down.
When the five bhikṣus saw the Tathāgata seated, they all addressed him by name, saying, "You, O Tathāgata.
Then the Buddha spoke to the five bhikṣus, saying:
"Do not address me by name, saying:
'You are the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The majestic power of the Tathāgata is immeasurable and supreme; if you were to address me by name:..."
"You, O Tathāgata, have suffered immeasurable pain throughout the long night.
Then the five men spoke, saying:

"Gautama! Previously, when you practiced austerities and maintained your dignified deportment, you were still unable to attain the state of a superior person, nor did you gain any increase in supernormal powers, wisdom, or insight to enjoy for yourself; how much less so now, when you travel along improper paths, wandering lost and having forfeited your resolve?"
The Buddha addressed the five men, saying,
"Have you ever heard me speak with double-tongued words? They replied:
“Gautama! From the past until now, I have never heard of such double-talk.
The Buddha said:
"Come, you all! I have now attained the Deathless; I shall instruct you.
Those among you who are able to accept my words will, before long, surely attain realization."

Therefore, noble son, one who, with firm faith, has gone forth from the home life into homelessness and practices the unsurpassed holy life for the sake of the Way, realizes it for himself through direct experience in this very life and dwells in its joy.
Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.

A monk who has gone forth must not associate with two extremes: indulgence in sensual pleasures, which is ignoble, worldly, and unwholesome; or self-mortification, which is painful, ignoble, and unwholesome. These do not lead to the goal of the noble ones, nor do they bring about weariness of the world, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, or Nirvana. They merely exhaust the body and weary the mind, and one cannot thereby accomplish anything significant.

Having abandoned these two extremes, the bhikṣu further follows the Middle Way, which brings clarity and wisdom to the eye, leading to eternal peace and rest; it accomplishes the superknowledges and the attainment of perfect enlightenment, and constitutes the practice of the śramaṇa’s nirvāṇa.
What is called the Middle Way?

It is the eye of wisdom that is luminous and eternally quiescent; it is the accomplishment of supernormal powers and the attainment of perfect enlightenment; it is the fulfillment of the śramaṇa’s practice of nirvāṇa. This is the Noble Eightfold Path:
right view, right action, right speech, right conduct, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This is what is called the Middle Way.
With the eye of wisdom clear and bright, forever tranquil and at rest, one achieves the superknowledges and perfect enlightenment, and accomplishes the practice of the śramaṇa’s nirvāṇa:
the Four Noble Truths. What are these Noble Truths?
The Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.

What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the disliked is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering; not obtaining what one desires is suffering; in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Furthermore, one should know the Noble Truth of Suffering: "I have known this; now I shall cultivate the Eightfold Path:
right view, right action, right speech, right effort, right livelihood, right means, right mindfulness, and right concentration."

What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is craving, which gives rise to renewed existence and is accompanied by delight and lust; this is called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.

Furthermore, this Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering must be abandoned; it has been abandoned and realized by me. One should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, from right view through to right concentration.
What is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?

It is the eternal exhaustion of that craving, its dispassion, its cessation, its relinquishment, its transcendence, its liberation, its total extinction, its stilling, and its state of being without a dwelling place; this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

Furthermore, one should take the noble truth of the cessation of suffering as the realization; having realized it myself, one should cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path, from right view up to right concentration.
What is the noble truth of the way leading to the cessation of suffering?
This Noble Eightfold Path—from right view up to right concentration—is called the Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering.
Furthermore, one should cultivate this Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering; this Noble Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering has been cultivated by me.
Regarding this Noble Truth of Suffering, which is a teaching unheard of before: knowledge arose, vision arose, awakening arose, clarity arose, penetration arose, and wisdom arose; it was realized.
Furthermore, it should be known that regarding this Noble Truth of Suffering, which is a teaching unheard of before, knowledge arose, and so on, up to wisdom arose.

Furthermore, I have known the Noble Truth of Suffering, a teaching not heard before; knowledge arose, vision arose, awakening arose, clarity arose, penetration arose, and wisdom arose—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, which was previously unheard: knowledge arose, vision arose, awakening arose, clarity arose, penetration arose, and wisdom arose.

Furthermore, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, which was previously unheard, it must be abandoned; knowledge arose, and so on, up to wisdom arose. Furthermore, regarding this noble truth of the origin of suffering, which was previously unheard, it has been abandoned by me; knowledge arose, and so on, up to wisdom arose. This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
Regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, a dharma previously unheard, knowledge arose, and so on, up to wisdom arose.
Furthermore, regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering as something to be realized, a dharma previously unheard, knowledge arose, and so on, up to wisdom arose.

Furthermore, regarding this noble truth of the cessation of suffering, which I have realized—this being a teaching unheard of before—knowledge arose, up to and including the arising of wisdom. Regarding this noble truth of the way leading to the escape from suffering, which is a teaching unheard of before, knowledge arose, up to and including the arising of wisdom.
Furthermore, one should cultivate the noble truth of the escape from suffering, a teaching not previously heard, whereby knowledge arises and even wisdom arises.
Furthermore, I have cultivated this noble truth of the escape from suffering, a teaching not previously heard, whereby knowledge has arisen and even wisdom has arisen.
These are called the Four Noble Truths.

Had I not cultivated these Four Noble Truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, and had I not known them as they truly are, I would not have now attained the unsurpassed, perfect, and true Way.

However, regarding the Four Noble Truths through their three turnings and twelve aspects, I have known them as they truly are; I have now attained unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, free from all doubt or obstruction.
If, when the Tathāgata preached these Four Noble Truths, there were none among the assembly who attained awakening, then the Tathāgata would not have turned the wheel of Dharma.
If, when the Tathāgata preached the Four Noble Truths, there were those among the assembly who attained awakening, then the Tathāgata would have turned the wheel of Dharma.
It cannot be turned back by śramaṇas, brahmins, Māra or the devas of Māra, gods, or anyone in the world; therefore, one should diligently apply skillful means to cultivate the Four Noble Truths:

the Noble Truth of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, the Noble Truth of the Cessation of Suffering, and the Noble Truth of the Path Leading to the Cessation of Suffering. One should train in this way.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, the five bhikṣus, including Ājñātakauṇḍinya, were cleansed of all defilements and attained the arising of the Dharma-eye.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing what had been realized within the mind of Ājñātakauṇḍinya, praised him with these words: “Ājñātakauṇḍinya has known!”
"Ājñātakauṇḍinya has already understood!
