From that time forth, he was named Ājñātakauṇḍinya.
At that moment, the earth deities, having heard what the Tathāgata had said, immediately informed one another:
"Now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, at the Deer Park of the Sages in Vārāṇasī, has turned the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma, which has never before been turned."
"Neither śramaṇas, brahmins, Māra or his celestial retinue, nor gods or humans, can turn it back.

The earth goddess raised this cry, which was heard by the Four Heavenly Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, who in turn informed one another, saying:
"Now the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, at the Deer Park of the Rishis in Vārāṇasī, turns the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma."
"It cannot be turned back by śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras or their celestial counterparts, nor by gods or humans.
At that moment, in the brief span of a single thought-instant, the sound of this proclamation was passed from one to another until it reached the Brahma-heaven.
At that time, the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and accomplished all dharmas, having obtained the fruit, came forward and said to the Buddha:
"I now wish to practice the holy life under the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said:
"Come, bhikṣu! In my Dharma, you shall find joyful delight; cultivate the holy life to bring an end to the source of suffering."
At that time, the Venerable Kauṇḍinya was immediately named one who had gone forth and received full ordination.
He is said to be the first among the bhikṣus to receive full ordination, with Ājñātakauṇḍinya as the foremost.
Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I now wish to enter the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for alms; I pray that you grant me leave.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus! You should know that this is the time.

Then the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to the Venerable Aśvajit and the bhikṣu Mahānāman, exhorting them until they were filled with joy.

The Dharma he taught consisted of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; he censured sensual desire as impure and a fetter of outflows, and praised renunciation as bliss. Thereupon, while still in their seats, all their defilements and dust were cleansed, and they attained the pure Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and attained the fruit, they came before the Buddha and said:
"We wish to go forth under the Tathāgata to practice the holy life."
The Buddha said:
"Come, bhikṣu! Delight yourself fully within my Dharma; cultivate the holy life to bring an end to the source of suffering. This is called going forth and receiving full ordination.
Then the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Mahānāman came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to enter the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for alms.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus! You should know that this is the time.

Then the Venerable Aśvajit and the others rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One, and donning their robes and taking up their bowls, entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the two men, Pāṭali and Pāṭikā, exhorting them to rejoice.

The Dharma he taught was that of giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; he censured sensual desire as impure and a fetter of outflows, and praised renunciation as true happiness. Thereupon, while still on their seats, they were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and perfected all dharmas, they came forward and said to the Buddha:
"We wish to practice the holy life under the Tathāgata in order to exhaust the source of suffering."
The Buddha said, “Come, bhikṣu!
Delight yourself in my Dharma; practice the holy life to bring an end to the source of suffering. This is called receiving full ordination.
Then the two, Pāṭali and Pāṭuka, came forward and said to the Buddha,
“We wish to go to the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for alms.
The Buddha said:
"It is time to know that this is the hour.

Then the Venerable Bhaṭṭika and the others rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads at the feet of the World-Honored One, adjusted their robes, took up their bowls, and entered the city of Vārāṇasī to beg for food.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma to three people, two went out to beg for food.
The food obtained by those two was sufficient for six people to eat together.
If the World-Honored One were to preach the Dharma to two among the five people, then three would go out to beg for food.
The food obtained by three people was sufficient for six to eat together.
At that time, the World-Honored One exhorted the five bhikṣus, gradually instructing them and causing them to give rise to a heart of joy.
Then, after his meal, the World-Honored One addressed the five bhikṣus: "Bhikṣus!
Form is non-self."
If form were the self, form would not increase while the self suffers.

If form were the self, one should attain mastery over it, being able to have such form as desired and not having such form as undesired; however, because form is without self, form increases, and thus one undergoes various sufferings.
Furthermore, one cannot obtain at will whatever form one desires to obtain, nor can one fail to obtain it when one does not desire such a form;
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so.
"What do you think, bhikṣu!
Is form permanent?
Or is form impermanent?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!
Form is impermanent."
The Buddha said:
"If form is impermanent, is it suffering or is it happiness?
The bhikṣus replied to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!
Form is suffering.
The Buddha said:
“If form is impermanent and suffering, and subject to change,
how could you regard form as ‘this is mine,’ ‘this is I,’ ‘this is my self,’ or ‘this belongs to me’?”
He replied, "No.
"Feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness are also like this."
Therefore, monks! Regarding all forms—whether past, future, or present;

internal or external; gross or subtle; beautiful or ugly; far or near—all forms are not-self, nor do they belong to another, nor does another belong to them, nor do they belong to self. One should apply such wisdom of correct contemplation according to reality.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
In this way, bhikṣus!

When a noble disciple has made this contemplation, he becomes weary of form; being weary, he is no longer attached; being unattached, he attains liberation; having attained liberation, he gains the knowledge of liberation: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, the minds of the five bhikṣus were liberated from all outflows (āsrava), and the knowledge of unimpeded liberation arose within them.
At that moment, there were six arhats in this world: the five disciples, with the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, as the sixth.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
In the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a son of a noble family named Yaśoda; his parents had only this one son, whom they cherished and watched over, never letting him out of their sight.
At that time, his parents provided him with palaces for the three seasons—spring, summer, and winter—and had their son constantly play within them, enjoying the pleasures of the five senses.
After the youth had fully indulged himself in the five desires, he became utterly exhausted and fell asleep.
Having awakened from sleep, he immediately observed the first palace.

He further saw that the musical instruments held by the various female entertainers were scattered in disarray; they lay propped one against another with their heads as pillows, their hair disheveled, snoring, grinding their teeth, and muttering in their sleep.

Having seen this, he was seized with terror and his hair stood on end; immediately a sense of weary detachment arose within him, and he had no desire to join the assembly, thinking, "This is suffering!
What is there to crave?"

He immediately abandoned the palace he was occupying and went to the middle palace; upon arriving there, he observed that palace and the women, which were no different than before, and his terror doubled such that the hair on his body stood on end. He conceived a sense of weary detachment and had no desire to join them, thinking, "This is suffering!"

"What is there to be craved? Thinking thus, he departed and went to the third palace. What he saw there was also as described above; his terror redoubled and the hair on his body stood on end. He conceived a sense of weary detachment (*saṃvega*) and, as before, had no desire to join the assembly. He immediately left the palace and went to the gate of the city of Śikhā.
At that time, the gatekeeper deity of Śikhin saw the youth approaching from afar; having seen him, he thought to himself:
"This youth comes surely with the desire to see the Tathāgata; there can be no other purpose."
"I shall open the gate for you to depart.
He then opened the gate for him.
When the youth had exited the city gate of Śiṅku, he went to the banks of the Vārāṇasī River.
Having arrived, he removed his golden sandals on the riverbank, crossed the Vārāṇasī River, and proceeded to the Deer Park of the Seers.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking up and down in the open air; seeing the youth approaching from afar, he immediately prepared a seat and sat down.

It is the constant law of all Buddhas that their halo of light shines everywhere. From afar, the youth Yaśoda saw that the Tathāgata’s countenance was upright and handsome; a heart of joy arose within him, and he went before the World-Honored One.
Having arrived, he addressed him, saying: "I am now in distress and have no place of refuge; I pray that you will rescue and deliver me."
The Buddha told the youth: "Come!

This place is unconditioned; this place is free from distress; this place is secure. For those who seek eternal stillness and the unconditioned, who desire the end of craving and the state of no-attachment, it is the extinction that is nirvāṇa."
At that time, the youth Yaśoda paid homage to the World-Honored One and sat to one side; the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma to him, exhorting him to give rise to a heart of joy.

The so-called Dharma consists of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; it censures sensual desires as impure and praises renunciation as bliss. At that very seat, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and accomplished all dharmas, he realized the fruit within his own person and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to practice the pure holy life under the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said: "Come, bhikṣu!
In my Dharma, you shall find joyful delight; practice the holy life to bring an end to the source of suffering."
At that time, Yaśoda immediately received full ordination.

The palace ladies and court musicians of the first chamber all woke up; having awakened, they searched for Yaśoda but did not see him. They went to the middle chamber to search for him, but did not see him there either. They then went to the third chamber to seek him out, yet once again he was not to be found.
At that time, the palace ladies and court musicians went to her mother’s quarters and said to her:
“Madam! Where is Yaśodharā now? We do not know her whereabouts.”
Then the mother immediately went quickly to her father’s place and said to him:
“Do you know? I do not know where my son is now.”
At that time, his father was in front of the central hall; having bathed and combed his hair, he quickly gathered it up and immediately commanded his attendants, saying:
"Block all the streets and alleys within the city of Vārāṇasī."
Having departed from the city gate of Śikhara and reached the banks of the Varā River, he saw his son’s golden sandals by the river's edge and thought to himself:
"My son must have crossed the river."
He immediately followed the tracks across the river and went to the Deer Park of the Seers.

At that time, the Tathāgata saw Yaśoda’s father approaching from afar and, by means of his supernormal power, caused him to see the Buddha but not his son. Upon reaching the Buddha’s presence, he said: “Great Śramaṇa!
“Have you perhaps seen my son Yaśoda?
The Buddha said, “Sit for now; you may yet see your son.”
Yaśoda’s father thought to himself:
“This Great Śramaṇa is truly marvelous and extraordinary, for he has greeted me with such consolation.
Then Yaśoda’s father prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down to one side.

The World-Honored One gradually taught him the Dharma, causing him to give rise to a heart of joy; he censured the impurity of sensual desire and praised renunciation as happiness. Thereupon, while still seated, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, he brought all dharmas to fulfillment.
Having personally examined himself and realized the fruit of attainment, he came before the Buddha and said:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha.

I pray only that the World-Honored One will allow me to become an upāsaka; from this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants."
"This was the first instance of the three refuges for lay followers (*upāsaka*), with Yaśoda’s father as the foremost.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to Yaśoda’s father; then, Yaśoda’s outflows were exhausted and his mind was liberated, and he attained the liberation of unimpeded knowledge."
At that time, there were seven arhats in the world, with six disciples and the Buddha as the seventh.
Then the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers, causing Yaśoda’s father to see his son sitting not far from the Buddha. He went immediately to where Yaśoda was and said to him:
"Your mother has lost you and, not knowing where you are, is filled with extreme grief and sorrow; she even intends to take her own life."
"You should go and visit him; do not let him harm himself.
Then Yaśoda gazed upon the countenance of the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Yaśoda’s father, saying:

“Son of good family, how does one who trains in wisdom and trains in the path attain the purity of the Dharma-eye through the exhaustion of all defilements? Having performed such contemplation, his mind with outflows attains liberation.”
"Householder, having already abandoned sensual desires, are you able to practice them again? He replied, "No."
"In this way, the noble son Yaśas, having studied knowledge and studied the Path, has exhausted all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having cultivated such contemplation, his mind with outflows (āsrava) was liberated, and he shall never again practice desire as he did formerly when he was a layman."

Now the noble son Yaśas has well attained great benefit; having studied wisdom and studied the Path, his mind is liberated from outflows (*āsrava*), all defilements are exhausted, and he has attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having performed this contemplation, his mind is liberated from outflows.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will now accept my invitation, as well as that of Yaśoda and his attendant bhikṣu.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
However, Yaśoda was unwilling to accept a separate invitation, saying, “The World-Honored One has not yet permitted me to accept separate invitations.”
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to accept individual invitations. There are two kinds of invitations: [the invitation for a group and the invitation for an individual]."
"There is the invitation by turn for the Saṅgha, and there is the special invitation.

At that time, Yaśodharā’s father, knowing that the Tathāgata had accepted the invitation by remaining silent, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed. He spoke to Yaśodharā’s mother and her former co-wife, saying: "Do you know now?"
"Yaśas is practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa.
Today I have invited the Great Śramaṇa along with Yaśas as his attendant; you should know the time has come, so please prepare whatever is required."
Yaśodharā’s mother and her former husband then prepared various kinds of food and drink as required, and went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had come.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having dressed and taken up his bowl at the proper hour, was accompanied by Yaśodhara as an attendant; after the two had been announced, they proceeded to his father’s house and sat down upon their seats.

Then Yaśodharā’s mother and her former co-wife offered the World-Honored One various kinds of food and drink as required; when he had finished eating and withdrawn his bowl, they took another small seat and sat before the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One gradually taught her the subtle and wondrous Dharma, exhorting her to give rise to a heart of joy. Immediately upon her seat, all defilements were exhausted and she attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, she was perfected in all dharmas. She then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. Please accept me as an upāsikā."
"From this day forth, for as long as life shall last, I shall refrain from taking life, up to and including refraining from drinking intoxicants.
This was called the first time a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) received the three refuges, with Yaśodharā’s mother and her two former wives at the head.
When the World-Honored One had finished preaching the Dharma to Yaśodharā’s mother and her two former co-wives, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
At that time, Yaśoda had four childhood friends living in Vārāṇasī:
the first was named Vimala, the second Subāhu, the third Pūrṇamāsa, and the fourth Gavāmpati.
Hearing that Yaśaska was practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa, they each thought to themselves:
"His virtue of precepts must not be in vain; his cultivation of the śramaṇa’s holy life as well must not be in vain."
Why is this? Because it causes this son of good family to receive instruction from him and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Since that son of good family is able to practice the holy life under him, why should we not rather practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa?
At that time, the four companions went to where Yaśas was and said to him:
"Is the practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Great Śramaṇa superior to yours?"
Yaśas replied, "I have practiced the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa; it is most subtle and wondrous.
The four men said to Yaśas:
"I, too, wish to go forth under the Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life.
Then Yaśas immediately led them to the World-Honored One; they prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"These four companions reside in Vārāṇasī and now wish to go forth under the Tathāgata to practice the holy life. We pray that you, out of compassion, will grant us permission to go forth and practice the holy life."
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent and gradually taught them the sublime Dharma.

The sublime Dharma consisted of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in the heavens; he censured sensual desire as impure and praised renunciation as bliss. Immediately upon these words, all defilements were exhausted within them, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, realized the Dharma, mastered the various dharmas, and attained the fruit of realization, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to practice the holy life under the guidance of the Tathāgata."
The Buddha said, “Come, bhikṣu!
Practice the holy life with joy within my Dharma to bring an end to the source of suffering; this is called going forth and receiving full ordination.”

He then examined what he had previously seen with renewed scrutiny, whereby he attained the exhaustion of all outflows (āsrava), his mind was liberated, and the knowledge of unimpeded liberation arose.
At that time, there were ten arhats as disciples in this world, with the Tathāgata making eleven.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
There were fifty young companions of Yaśas living outside the city of Vārāṇasī who, hearing that Yaśas was practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa, each thought to themselves:
"The holy life practiced here through the virtue of this precept is not in vain."
How do I know this? It is because this son of good family is now practicing the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa; for this reason, I know it.
Since that son of good family is able to practice the holy life there, should I not now go to the Great Śramaṇa to practice the holy life as well?
At that time, fifty companions went to where Yaśoda was and said to him:
"Is this place superior? Is the practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) excellent here?"
Yaśoda replied, "This place is excellent for cultivation, and the holy life here is sublime!
Then these fifty people said to Yaśoda:
"I, too, wish to go forth under the Great Śramaṇa and practice the holy life.
Then Yaśas immediately led him to the place where the World-Honored One was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and sat to one side.
Having sat down, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"These fifty companions of mine reside outside the city of Vārāṇasī; they now wish to go forth from the Tathāgata to practice the holy life."
“May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, grant me permission to leave the household life and practice the holy life.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent and gradually taught him the sublime Dharma.

This Dharma consisted of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; it involved censuring the impurity of sensual desires and praising renunciation as bliss. Thereupon, while still seated, he was cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye. Having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, mastered the Dharma, and realized its fruit, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We wish to go forth from the Tathāgata’s presence and practice the holy life.
The Buddha said, “Come, bhikṣus!”
"Within my Dharma, one who has swiftly cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) to exhaust the source of suffering is said to have received full ordination (upasampadā).
Having thus re-examined what was previously seen, his mind with outflows (sāsrava-citta) was liberated, and the knowledge of unimpeded liberation arose.
At that time, there were sixty arhat disciples in this world, with the Tathāgata as the sixty-first.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, there were fifty companions who came toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, intending to arrange a marriage; while wandering and sightseeing in various places outside the city of Vārāṇasī, they gradually arrived at the Ṛṣipatana Deer Park.

At that time, the fifty men saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was upright and handsome, his various marks exceptionally distinguished; having seen him, they gave rise to a heart of joy and immediately approached the Tathāgata to prostrate at his feet, then sat down to one side.
Then the World-Honored One taught him the sublime Dharma, exhorting him to give rise to a heart of joy.

This so-called sublime Dharma consisted of the merits of giving, observing the precepts, and rebirth in heaven; it censured the impurity of desire and praised renunciation as bliss. Thereupon, while still seated, all defilements were exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Having attained the Dharma, seen the Dharma, accomplished the various dharmas, and realized the fruit of realization, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"We wish to go forth from the Tathāgata’s presence to practice the holy life.
The Buddha said, "Come, bhikṣus!"
"In my Dharma, one who has swiftly cultivated the holy life (brahmacarya) to exhaust the source of suffering is said to have received full ordination.
Having thus re-examined what was previously seen, his mind with outflows was liberated, and the knowledge of unimpeded liberation arose.
At that time, there were one hundred and ten arhat disciples in the world, with the Buddha as the one hundred and eleventh.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, the Naga King Elapatra emerged from his palace situated on the banks of the Ganges River. Holding a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain, and accompanied by various naga maidens, he recited this verse on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days:
"Who is the supreme among kings?"
If the defiler and the defiled are identical, how can they be stainless?
What is called ignorance,
and who is it that is carried away by the currents?
"What must one attain to be called 'wisdom'?
How is it that there is flowing and non-flowing, yet it is called 'liberation'?
The Dragon King replied:

“If there is anyone who can fully expound the meaning of this verse, I shall give it to them, providing a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain, along with the dragon girl I have brought.”
"I seek the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

At that time, a great multitude gathered; some went to view the golden bowl with silver grain or the silver bowl with golden grain; some went to view the various nāga maidens; and some went desiring to discuss the meaning of the verses with the Nāga King.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Nārada who lived near the city of Vārāṇasī; he was one of few defilements, with sharp faculties, great wisdom, and intelligence.
Then Nārada left the city of Vārāṇasī and went to where the Dragon King was. Having arrived, he said to the Dragon King:
"Recite a verse now, and I shall expound its meaning to you in detail."
At that time, the Nāga King Elāpattra addressed Nārada with these verses:
"Who is supreme among kings?
How does one who is defiled and equal to defilement attain freedom from stain?"
What is called ignorance?
By what stream is one swept away?
What is it that constitutes wisdom?
"What is meant by 'flowing' and 'not flowing,' such that it is called liberation?

The Dragon King said, "If there is anyone who can eloquently explain and analyze the meaning of this verse, I shall offer him a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain, along with the dragon maiden I have brought; I seek [to serve] the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Then the brahmin Nārada said to the dragon king Elāpattra:
"Stop for a moment, O Dragon King;
seven days from now, I shall extensively expound the meaning of these verses."
At that time, the brahmin Nārada, having thoroughly mastered this verse through recitation, returned to the city of Vārāṇasī and thought to himself:
"Who among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas here possesses such high talent and great virtue that I should question them with this verse?"
He further thought to himself:

"This Pūraṇa Kāśyapa is a senior among the assembly and serves as a teacher and guide for others; he is venerated by the multitude, his fame is heard afar, and his knowledge is like the ocean such that many people offer him sustenance. Would it not be appropriate for me now to go to him and inquire about the meaning of this verse?"
Then the brahmin Nārada went to where Kāśyapa was and recited this verse to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa. Upon hearing this verse, Kāśyapa did not truly understand it;
he immediately knit his brows, glared with angry eyes, let out harsh sounds, and tensed his neck until the veins bulged. With such blazing fury, he remained silent and gave no answer.
He immediately departed, thinking to himself:
"Where else shall I now seek a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa to ask about the meaning of this verse?
On the way, he again thought:

“Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Kesakambalin, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra—these men stand as the foremost teachers among the assemblies; they are venerated by all, their fame is heard afar, their knowledge is like the ocean, and many offer them support. It would be fitting for me now to go to them and inquire about the meaning of this verse.”
Then the brahmin Nārada went to where Makkhali Gosāla, the Nirgrantha, and others were, and recited this verse to them.

Upon hearing this verse, they truly did not understand it; they immediately knit their brows, glared with anger, let out harsh sounds, strained their necks until their veins bulged, and, consumed by a blazing rage, were unable to respond.
Having seen him, he immediately departed again, thinking to himself:
"Where else can I seek a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa to ask about this meaning? Then he thought:

"This Great Śramaṇa Gautama is the leader among the great assembly; he is venerated by all people and his fame is heard afar. His knowledge is like the ocean and many offer him sustenance. It would be fitting for me now to go to him and inquire about the meaning of this verse."
He further thought to himself:

"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have been long ordained and have practiced for a long time are still unable to understand the meaning of this verse; how much less could this śramaṇa Gautama, who is still young and has only recently left the household life, possibly understand it?"
He further thought to himself:

"Although he is young in years, he must not be disregarded; for there are those who, having left the household life at a young age to study the Path, have attained arhatship and mastery over supernormal powers. I should now go to that śramaṇa and inquire about the meaning of this verse."

Then the brahmin Nārada departed from the city of Vārāṇasī and went to the Deer Park of the Sages. Upon arrival, he raised his hand in greeting to the Tathāgata, and sitting to one side, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I wish to ask a question; if the Śramaṇa Gautama will permit it, I shall ask."
The Buddha said:
"Brahmin! If you wish to ask a question, do so as you please."
At that time, Nārada again had this thought:

"I have seen those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who did not show me a favorable countenance, nor did they provide me with an explanation, nor did they even say 'ask whatever you wish'; yet what I see now is truly extraordinary."
At that time, the brahmin addressed the Buddha with these verses:
"Who is the supreme among kings?
How does one who is stained become equal to the unstained, and how does one attain freedom from defilement?"
What is called ignorance?
By what stream is one carried away?
What is it that constitutes wisdom?
"What is meant by 'flowing' and 'not flowing,' such that it is called liberation?
At that time, the World-Honored One replied to the brahmin Nārada in verse:
"The sixth king is supreme."
The defiler and the defilement are equal; when there is no defilement, there is no stain.
That which defiles is called ignorance.
The ignorant are carried away by the current; those who can extinguish it are wise.
One who can relinquish all taints, both celestial and worldly,
and does not associate with those taints, will not be deluded by death.
By making mindfulness the master, one attains liberation from all taints.

At that time, Nārada, having heard these verses from the Tathāgata and having recited them well, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times, and departed, returning to the city of Vārāṇasī.

Then, seven days later, the Naga King Elapatra emerged from his own palace, taking various naga maidens with him. Carrying a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain, he approached and spoke this verse:
"Who is the supreme among kings?"
Between the defiled one and the defilements, which is called stainless?
Which is called ignorant?
And which is it that is carried away by the current?
"What must one attain to be called 'wisdom'?
What is meant by 'flowing' and 'not flowing,' such that it is termed 'liberation'?

"If there is anyone who can expound the meaning of this verse, I shall give them this golden bowl filled with silver grain, this silver bowl filled with golden grain, as well as the dragon maiden I have brought along; I seek thereby the unsurpassed, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment."

At that time, a great multitude of people gathered; some were watching the golden bowl filled with silver grain, some were watching the silver bowl filled with golden grain, some were watching the dragon girl, and some wished to hear the brahmin Nārada explain the meaning of the verses.
At that time, the brahmin Nārada departed from the city of Vārāṇasī and went to the palace of the Naga King Elapatra, where he said to the Naga King:
"Recite each verse you have discussed one by one, and I shall analyze and explain its meaning for you."
Then the Dragon King addressed Nārada with this verse:
"Who is supreme among kings?
Who is the stained one and what is equivalent to the stain? What is called the stainless?"
What is called ignorance?
By what stream is one carried away?
What is attained that is called wisdom?
"How is it that one who is neither flowing nor non-flowing is called 'liberated'?
Then Nārada replied to the Dragon King in verse:
"The sixth king is supreme."
The defiled one and the defilement are equal; when there is no defilement, there is no stain.
To be defiled is called ignorance.
The ignorant are drifted by the currents; those who can extinguish [defilement] are wise.
One who can abandon all taints, both celestial and worldly,
and who does not associate with those taints, is not deluded by death.
By making mindfulness the master, one attains liberation from all taints.
Then the Naga King Elapatra asked:
"How is it, O Brahmin? Do you speak this from your own wisdom, or do you speak it having heard it from some śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa?"
He replied, "O Dragon King! I do not possess the wisdom to speak such words.

There is now a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas named Gautama, who has left the household life to study the Way and has attained unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment; it is from him that I heard this and am now speaking."
At that time, the Dragon King thought to himself:
"Has the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni already appeared in the world?"
"Has he already appeared in the world?
He then asked Nārada: "Where does the Tathāgata reside today?"
He replied, "I am currently staying nearby at the Seers' Deer Park.
Then the Nāga King spoke to Nārada:
"Let us go together to the Rishipatana Deer Park to pay homage to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.

Then Nārada and the Dragon King, surrounded by a retinue of eighty-four thousand followers, proceeded to the Rishipatana Deer Park. Upon reaching the presence of the World-Honored One, they prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and stood to one side.

Narada exchanged greetings with him and sat to one side. Among the assembly of eighty-four thousand followers, some prostrated at the Tathāgata’s feet and stood to one side; some raised their joined palms in salutation, exchanged greetings, and sat to one side; some addressed the Tathāgata by name and sat to one side; some joined their hands in reverence while gazing at the Tathāgata and sat to one side; and some remained silent and sat to one side.
When the assembly of eighty-four thousand had taken their seats, the World-Honored One gradually expounded the sublime Dharma for them, exhorting them to give rise to a heart of joy.
The Dharma he taught was that of generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in the heavens; he censured sensual desire as impure and praised renunciation as bliss.

At that time, Nārada and the assembly of eighty-four thousand beings, right there upon their seats, were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; they saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, perfected the Dharma, and attained the realization of the fruit. They came forward and said to the Buddha:

"From this day forth, we take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. We pray only that the World-Honored One will accept us as upāsakas, who for as long as life lasts shall refrain from killing, and so on, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants."
At that time, the Naga King Elapatra wept so bitterly that he could not restrain himself, and at other times he leaped about with joy.
Then Narada said to the Naga King:
"Do you weep now because you cherish the golden bowl filled with silver grain and the silver bowl filled with golden grain, as well as the Naga maidens?"
The Dragon King replied,
"It is not because of these things that I weep.
Nārada, you should know this!"
"You may now take a golden bowl filled with silver grain and a silver bowl filled with golden grain; you should take them without distress.
If you require a daughter of the kṣatriyas, brāhmaṇas, householders, or artisans from the city of Vārāṇasī, I shall exhort them to give her to you."
For what reason?
Nārada! You cannot consort with the dragon maiden.
Narada replied to the Dragon King:

"I have no need for a golden bowl filled with silver grain or a silver bowl filled with golden grain, nor does the dragon maiden have any need for them. I now wish to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) under the Tathāgata."

At that time, the brahmin Nārada, having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, and accomplished all dharmas, knowing for himself that he had realized the fruit of realization, came forward and addressed the Buddha:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"I now wish to go forth under the Tathāgata and practice the holy life.
The Buddha said, "Come, bhikṣu!"
"Within my Dharma, you have swiftly practiced the holy life to exhaust the source of suffering; this is called receiving full ordination.
Having thus re-examined what he had previously seen, his mind was liberated from outflows, and the knowledge of unimpeded liberation arose.
At that time, there were one hundred and eleven arhats in the world, with the Buddha as the one hundred and twelfth.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King, saying:
"For what reason do you weep so bitterly, unable to restrain yourself?"
At that time, the Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

I recall that in the past, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, while practicing the holy life, I committed a transgression against the precepts by damaging the leaves of an Airāvata tree. What kind of retribution should this entail?”
“World-Honored One!

Because of the retribution of this karma, I have been born among the long-lived nāgas. After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa and the Dharma has been extinguished, I shall then cast off this nāga body; yet I have lost the benefits of both sides and am unable to practice the holy life.”
"For this reason, I weep with grief, unable to restrain myself.
At that time, the World-Honored One again asked the Dragon King:
"By what cause do you now feel such joy?"
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since my own time, I have heard from Kāśyapa Buddha, who told me:
'In the future, there shall appear in the world a Śākyamuni Buddha, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.'"
"What I see now is exactly as it is and not otherwise; I have this thought:
'It is unprecedented! What the Tathāgata’s wisdom perceives is as it truly is, without duality.'"
"For this reason, I am filled with such joy and exultation that I cannot contain myself.
The Buddha told the Dragon King:
"You now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."
He replied: “So be it!
I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.”
Thus, these were the first among the animals to receive the three refuges, with the Naga King Elāpattra at their head.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus in verse:
"I have already been liberated from all things, Both from the heavens and from the world; I am the Teacher, the All-Knowing One, The Tathāgata who has attained parinirvāṇa."
"You too are liberated from all things, both gods and the world.
Then Māra Pāpīyas addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"You are bound by all bonds, both gods and the world."
"Bound by all the fetters of the multitude, the śramaṇa cannot attain liberation.
Then the World-Honored One replied to Pāpīyas with a verse:
"I am liberated from all fetters, both among the devas and in the world."
"Released from all bonds, I have now conquered you.
At that time, Pāpīyān again replied to the Buddha in verse:
"Within you there are fetters; your mind dwells in the midst of them."
"Because of this, you shall pursue me; as a śramaṇa, I cannot escape you.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied to Pāpīyas in verse: "The world has five desires, with the mental consciousness as the sixth;
I have no desire for them, and thus I have now triumphed over you."
At that time, Māra Pāpīyas thought to himself:
"The Tathāgata has scrutinized my thoughts and knows them all.
He was immediately filled with sorrow and distress, and concealing his form, he returned to his own abode.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, speaking these verses:
"I have now attained full understanding of all things, both celestial and worldly;
you too shall attain full understanding of all things, both celestial and worldly."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should travel through the human world alone, not in pairs; I now wish to go to the village of the general Uruvilvā to teach the Dharma.”
He replied: "So it is, World-Honored One!"

Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus traveled through the human world preaching the Dharma. At that time, there were those who, having heard the Dharma and gained faith, desired to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).

When the bhikṣus led those who wished to receive full ordination to the presence of the Tathāgata, they lost their original faith and resolve before reaching him, and thus were unable to receive full ordination.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to grant them the going forth and the full ordination immediately.

Those who wish to receive the full ordination should be instructed as follows: they must shave their hair and beards, don the saffron robes, remove their leather sandals, place their right knees on the ground, join their palms, and be taught to speak these words:"

"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. I now go forth in the presence of the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is my honored one."
Thus for the second and third time.

"I, [Name], have taken refuge in the Buddha, taken refuge in the Dharma, and taken refuge in the Saṅgha. I have gone forth under the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my honored one."
"In this manner, a second and a third [request shall be made].
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize three utterances; this shall be called the reception of full ordination."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling in the Uruvilvā Kāpa Grove.
Then there were fifty companions of Uruvilvā-Bhadravati who, accompanied by various women, were enjoying themselves together in this grove.
Among his companions, there was one man who had no wife; he hired a courtesan for money and brought her along to enjoy themselves together, but the courtesan then stole that man's wealth and fled.
At that time, her companions, seeing that she had lost her belongings, immediately began searching for this courtesan within the park.

Seeing from afar the Tathāgata, whose countenance was upright and whose faculties were tranquil and composed, they felt a heart of joy upon seeing him. They then approached the World-Honored One and addressed him, saying:
"Great Śramaṇa!..."
"Have you seen a woman come here?
The Buddha asked, "Who are you boys?"
"What kind of women are you seeking?
He replied, "Great Śramaṇa,
you should know that Upavartana and Bhadraka, along with fifty companions, are enjoying themselves here in this grove together with various women."

A certain companion of yours had no wife, so he hired a courtesan with money and brought her here to enjoy her company; they then stole his property and fled, and it is not known where they have gone.
"We have now come here together with our companions specifically to seek this girl.
The Buddha asked, "How is it, young man?"
"Would you rather seek yourself,
or would you seek women? The youths replied:
"It would be better to seek oneself than to seek women.
The Buddha said, "Young men, sit down; I shall teach you the Dharma."
Then the youths prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the sublime Dharma to the youths, exhorting them to give rise to a heart of joy.
As for what is called the Dharma: it is the Dharma of giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; it censures sensual desire as impure and praises renunciation as bliss.

At that very seat, their defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma, attained the Dharma, accomplished the various Dharmas, and realized the fruit, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We youths wish to go forth under the Tathāgata to practice the holy life."
The Buddha said: "Come, Bhikṣu!
Practice the holy life with joy within my Dharma to bring an end to the source of suffering; this is called receiving full ordination."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through Uruvelā.
At that time, there was a brahmin in the realm of Uruvelā named Uruvelā-Kāśyapa, who resided there.
Leading five hundred brahmacārins with conch-shell crests as his most honored and senior teachers, he was universally acclaimed as an Arhat throughout the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha.
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was staying; having arrived, he said to him:
"I wish to borrow a room to stay for one night; would this be acceptable?"
He replied, "I do not begrudge it;
however, there is an extremely wicked poisonous dragon in this chamber, and I fear he might harm you.
The Buddha said:
"No suffering!
Just let me borrow it, and the dragon will not harm me. Kāśyapa replied:
"This chamber is spacious; you may stay here as you please.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One entered the stone chamber, spread out his own sitting mat, sat down cross-legged, straightened his body, and set his mind upright.
At that time, when the venomous dragon saw that the Tathāgata sat in silence, it immediately emitted smoke; the Tathāgata also emitted smoke.
When the dragon saw that the Tathāgata had emitted smoke, it again emitted fire; the Tathāgata likewise emitted fire, and at that moment, smoke and flames rose together within the stone chamber.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw smoke and flames rising together from the stone cave and thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is exceedingly handsome; he is truly pitiable, for he will undoubtedly be harmed by the venomous dragon."
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I should now subdue this venomous dragon without harming its body. He immediately subdued it through his supernormal powers without injuring the dragon’s body.

The smoke and fire-light emitted from the dragon’s body gradually diminished, while from within the Tathāgata’s own body there issued forth countless varieties of light in colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Then the Tathāgata immediately subdued the venomous dragon and placed it within his alms bowl.
At dawn the following day, he went to where Uruvilvā Kāśyapa was and said to him:
"Do you wish to know?"
"As for the venomous dragon you spoke of, I have already subdued it; it is now within my bowl.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Only one who possesses great majestic power and mastery of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*) could subdue this venomous dragon without causing it harm.
Although this śramaṇa Gautama possesses mastery of supernatural faculties and has attained arhatship, his attainment of arhatship is not equal to my own."
Kāśyapa said, "Great Śramaṇa!
You may stay the night here; I shall provide you with food."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"If you yourself can announce that the time has come, I shall accept your invitation. Kāśyapa replied:
“Great Śramaṇa! Please stay here for the night; I shall come myself when it is time.
Then the Tathāgata, having finished his meal at Kāśyapa’s place, returned to the stone cave to stay the night.
At that time, during the silence of the night, the World-Honored One entered the fire-light samādhi, illuminating that stone cave with a brilliant and vast radiance.
Then Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw the fire-light blazing within the stone cave; having seen this, he thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is exceedingly handsome, yet he dwells in that stone cave and is being consumed by fire."
He then led his assembly to surround the stone cave and dwell there. At dawn, Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The time has now arrived; you may go to take your meal."
He asked again: "Great Śramaṇa!
For what reason was there such a great blaze of light last night?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Last night I entered the fire-light samādhi, causing this stone chamber to blaze with great brilliance.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great majestic power; at night in the stillness, he has entered the fire-light samādhi and illuminates this stone chamber.
Although the śramaṇa Gautama has attained arhatship, his attainment of arhatship is not equal to my own."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating Kāśyapa’s food, he proceeded to another grove and stayed there for the night.
On the following day, Kāśyapa went to the place where the World-Honored One was and announced, "The time has come; please go to take your meal."
The Buddha said, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly after.
At that time, having sent Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Jambū tree.
It is called Jambudvīpa because of the presence of the Jambu tree.
The Tathāgata went there, took a jambu fruit, and first proceeded to sit upon the seat of Kāśyapa.
Kāśyapa arrived later and saw that the Buddha was already seated. Having seen him, he said:
"How is this, Great Śramaṇa?
You previously sent me on ahead; how is it that you have now arrived here before me?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I sent you on ahead; I have gone to Jambudvīpa to fetch a jambu fruit and have arrived here first to sit."
"This fruit is of excellent color and fragrant flavor;
you may eat it. Kāśyapa replied, "Stop!
"Stop! Great Śramaṇa, this shall suffice as my offering.
Let the Great Śramaṇa eat for himself; this is what the Great Śramaṇa ought to eat."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained mastery as an arhat, yet he is not my equal in having attained arhatship."
Then, after the World-Honored One had finished eating Kāśyapa’s meal, he returned to his original grove to reside there.
On the following morning at dawn, Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was staying; having arrived, he said to him:
"The time has now come; you should partake of the meal."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly after.
Having sent Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One went to Jambudvīpa. Not far from that place was a harītakī tree; he took a harītakī fruit and arrived before Kāśyapa, sitting upon his seat.
At that time, Kāśyapa arrived later and saw that the Tathāgata had already arrived.
He asked, "Great Śramaṇa!
You previously sent me away, saying you would follow shortly behind; why have you now arrived first and taken my seat?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I have sent you away, you shall go to Jambudvīpa. Not far from there is a harītakī tree; I went there to fetch a harītakī fruit and have now arrived here."
"This harītakī fruit is of excellent color and fragrant aroma;
you may take it and eat it. Kāśyapa replied, "Great Śramaṇa, stop!"
"Stop! This shall suffice as an offering.
Great Śramaṇa, please eat; this is what a Great Śramaṇa ought to eat."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses mastery over supernormal powers and has attained arhatship; yet, even so, he is not equal to me in having attained arhatship."
"The *āmalaka* fruit and the *vibhītaka* fruit are also like this.
Then, after the Tathāgata had finished eating the food provided by Kāśyapa, he returned to his original grove to stay for the night.
On the following day, Kāśyapa went to where the Tathāgata was and said to him:
"The time has arrived; you may proceed to eat.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly after."

After the World-Honored One had sent Kāśyapa away, he traveled north to Uttarakuru, took some naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and returned. He arrived first and sat down on his seat; Kāśyapa arrived later, and upon seeing him, asked:
"Great Śramaṇa!..."
Previously you sent me forth, saying, "Go ahead; I shall follow shortly after.
Why have you arrived first now?
The Buddha said:
"After I have sent you away, go north to Uttarakuru to fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and return here to this seat.
This rice is of excellent color and fragrant flavor; you may take some and eat it."
Kāśyapa replied, "Stop! This itself shall suffice as my offering."
"You may take this and eat it yourself;
this is what a great śramaṇa ought to eat.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses mastery of supernormal powers and has attained arhatship; yet, even so, he does not equal my attainment of arhatship.
Then, having finished his meal, the World-Honored One returned to his original grove to stay for the night.
The next morning at dawn, Kāśyapa went to where the Buddha was and said, "The time has come; please come for the meal.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You go on ahead; I shall follow shortly after.
Having thus sent Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to fetch mandārava flowers, arriving first at the seat where Kāśyapa was to sit.
At that time, Kāśyapa arrived later; having seen him, he said:
"Great Śramaṇa, you previously sent me with the message:
'I shall follow shortly.'"
"Why have you arrived at your seat first?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I had sent you away, I went to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to fetch these flowers and arrived here first to take my seat."
"These flowers are beautiful in color and their fragrance is exquisite;
Kāśyapa, you may take them. Kāśyapa replied, "Stop!"
"Stop! Great Śramaṇa, I have already received sufficient offerings.
Great Śramaṇa, please take and use this yourself."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"There is one who has attained great supernormal powers and mastery as an Arhat; yet even so, he is not equal to my attainment of Arhatship.
Then, having finished his meal of Kāśyapa’s food, the World-Honored One returned to his original grove to stay for the night.
That night, the Four Great Kings came to the place where the World-Honored One was, bearing offerings, desiring to hear the Dharma as an act of worship.

At the time of deep darkness, they emitted a brilliant light that illuminated the four quarters like a great mass of fire; having joined their palms and prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata, they stood before him.
At that time, Kāśyapa rose during the night and saw that great radiance in the grove illuminating the four directions like a mass of blazing fire.
At dawn the following day, he went to where the Tathāgata was and said, "The time has come; you may go to take your meal."
He asked again: "Great Śramaṇa!
What was this radiance last night that illuminated the four quarters like a great mass of fire?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Last night, the Four Heavenly Kings came to my dwelling bearing offerings, desiring to hear and receive the Dharma.
It was their radiance that illuminated the four directions; it was not fire."
Kāśyapa said: "How extraordinary!
How marvelous!"
"The Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernatural power, such that he has caused the Four Heavenly Kings to come and listen to the Dharma.
The Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained Arhatship with mastery; nevertheless, even so, he is not equal to my attainment of Arhatship."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating the food provided by Kāśyapa, he returned to his original grove.

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, carrying offerings and wishing to hear the Dharma, emitted a great radiance during the darkness of night, illuminating the four quarters like a massive bonfire; this light surpassed all previous radiance, being pure and free from blemish. With hands joined in *añjali*, he prostrated at the feet of the Tathāgata and stood before him to listen to the Dharma.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw from afar a radiance illuminating the four quarters, surpassing his previous light in its purity and freedom from blemish.
Having seen this, he went the next day to the World-Honored One and said, "The time has come; please go to take your meal."
He asked again: "Great Śramaṇa!
Last night there was a great light of fire illuminating the four quarters; it was like a mass of great fire exceeding the previous light, pure and without blemish."
"What is this light?

From the *Prātimokṣa-vastu* (Section on Receiving the Precepts), Part Three. The Buddha addressed Kāśyapa:
"Last night, Śakra Devānām-indra came with offerings to make an offering to me, desiring to hear the Dharma; it was his radiance.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"How extraordinary!"
"How extraordinary!
The majesty and virtue of the Great Śramaṇa are such that he has caused Śakra, Lord of the Devas, to bring offerings and come to hear the Dharma?
Although the Great Śramaṇa possesses mastery over supernatural powers and has attained arhatship, even so, he is still not equal to my own attainment of arhatship."
Then, after the World-Honored One had finished eating that food, he returned to his original grove.

At that time, the Brahma King, wishing to offer worship, emitted a great radiance at the dark hour of night in the presence of the Tathāgata. It illuminated the four quarters like a massive conflagration; it surpassed the previous light, being pure and free from all blemish. Having joined his palms in reverence and paid homage to the Tathāgata, he stood before him.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and saw within the forest a great radiance illuminating the four quarters, like a massive mass of fire, pure and free from blemish, surpassing his previous light.
Having seen this, on the following day he went to the Tathāgata’s dwelling and said, "The time has come; you may go to take your meal.
He then asked again:
"Last night there was a great light, surpassing all previous lights;
how could this be? The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Last night the Brahmā King came to listen to the Dharma; that was his light."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great spiritual power and virtue; how extraordinary!
How marvelous!"
He is even able to cause the Brahma King to come and listen to the Dharma.
This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained mastery as an arhat; nevertheless, he is still not equal to my attainment of arhatship.
Then, after the World-Honored One had eaten that food provided by Kāśyapa, he returned to that forest grove.
At that time, Kāśyapa was about to perform a great sacrificial offering, and a vast multitude had gathered within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Many people have gathered for my sacrifice; would it not be a pleasant thing if this great śramaṇa did not come?
For what reason?"

"I am now performing a great sacrifice, and all the people of Magadha have gathered. This great śramaṇa is of such upright and handsome countenance that he is rare in the world; if the multitude see him, they will surely abandon me to take him as their teacher and no longer serve me."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Kāśyapa’s mind, immediately went to Uttarakuru to fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and sat at his daytime sitting place by the Great Anavatapta Pond.
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"Why does the Great Śramaṇa not come now to receive food?
I am performing a great sacrificial offering, and the people of the kingdom of Magadha have gathered in great numbers; would it not be appropriate to set aside a portion for him?"
He immediately commanded his attendants to set aside a portion.
At dawn the following day, Kāśyapa went to the Buddha’s dwelling and said, "The time has arrived; please know that it is now the hour."
He asked again: "Great Śramaṇa!
For what reason did you not come yesterday?"
Yesterday, I performed a great sacrifice and many people gathered; I thought to myself:
"Why has the śramaṇa not come today? I then set aside my portion of food for him.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I also knew your thoughts beforehand; you thought to yourself:
'If the Great Śramaṇa does not come today, my great sacrifice will be successful.'"

Why is this? Today I am performing a great sacrifice, and many people from the kingdom of Magadha have gathered. This great śramaṇa is handsome in appearance; when all these people see him, they will surely abandon me and take him as their teacher, no longer serving me.
Having known what was in your mind, I went to Uttarakuru to fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice, and proceeded to the Great Anavatapta Spring to sit at my daytime seat.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is truly marvelous!
Truly extraordinary!"

Possessing great divine power, he knew the thoughts within my mind; having gone as far as Uttarakuru to fetch naturally grown non-glutinous rice, he arrived at the Great Anavatapta Spring and sat upon his daytime seat.
"Although this great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained mastery as an arhat, he is not equal to me, who have attained arhatship.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating Kāśyapa’s meal, he returned to the original forest grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One obtained a precious discarded rag-robe and thought to himself, "How shall I obtain water to wash this robe?

Then Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing the thought in the Buddha's mind, immediately manifested a great pond before the Tathāgata, which was exceedingly pure and free from any turbidity. He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May the Blessed One use this water to wash his robes.
Then the Blessed One thought to himself:
"Upon what surface shall I wash my robes?"
At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing what was in the Tathāgata’s mind, went to Mount Makuṭabandhana, took a large rock from the four directions, and placed it before the Tathāgata, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One will wash his robes upon this rock.”
At that time, the World-Honored One again had this thought:
"Having washed my robes, where shall I dry them?
Śakra-devānām-indra, knowing once more what was in the World-Honored One’s mind, went again to Mount Makuṭabandhana and brought another large square stone, placing it before the Tathāgata.
"May I dry my robes upon this rock.
When the World-Honored One had finished washing and drying his robes, he further thought to himself:
"I shall now bathe in this Pond of Pointing-out-the-Earth."
He immediately removed his clothes and bathed.
The World-Honored One then thought to himself:
"What should I grasp now to emerge from this pond?"
At that time, there was a great *kaśīraka* tree by the side of the pond, its trunk originally bent outward.
Once the World-Honored One had formed this thought, the tree immediately turned toward the pond, allowing the World-Honored One to grasp it and emerge.
Then, at dawn the following day, Kāśyapa went to the place where the World-Honored One was and said:
"The time has arrived; you may go to take your meal.
He further asked:
“Great Śramaṇa! By what cause has this beautiful pond come to be?
It was never seen before.”
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"Recently, I obtained a precious discarded rag-robe.
I thought to myself:"
"How shall I obtain water to wash this robe?
At that moment, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing my thoughts, pointed his finger at the ground, and immediately this pond appeared—pure, stainless, and free from turbidity.
"I pray that the World-Honored One may wash his robes in this pond.
Kāśyapa, you should know that this pond is named Indraka; it is no different from a divine shrine.
He asked again: "By what cause has this great square stone come to be?
Originally it was not there."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I had this thought: 'In what place shall I wash my robes?'"
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra, knowing my thoughts, immediately went to Mount Makuṭabandhana, took this square stone, and brought it here, saying to me:
"You may wash your clothes upon this."
He asked again: "As for this second square stone, by what cause did it come to be?
Originally, it was not seen."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I had washed my robes, I thought to myself:
'In what place shall I dry these robes?'"
Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts in my mind, went again to Mount Makuṭabandhana, took this square stone, and brought it here, saying to me:
"I pray that you will dry your robes upon this stone."
He asked again: "The trees on this pond were originally curved outward; why are they now curved inward?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I had washed and dried my robes, I thought to myself:
'I should enter this pool to bathe.
I immediately entered the pool to bathe, and having bathed, I thought: "
"What can I grasp to emerge from here?
The tree immediately bent its trunk inward, allowing me to grasp it and emerge.
That is precisely why this happened.
He then said to Kāśyapa,
"You should know that it is no different from a divine tree.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
“Great Śramaṇa, how marvelous! How extraordinary!
You possess such great supernormal power that even Śakra Devānām-indra provides you with all necessities, and you can even cause insentient objects to act according to your will.”
Kāśyapa said: “This great śramaṇa possesses mastery over supernormal powers and has attained arhatship; yet even so, he is still not my equal in having attained arhatship.”
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished eating Kāśyapa’s food, he returned to his original grove.
Then Kāśyapa again gave rise to this thought:
"If someone comes here, I shall give them food."
Then the World-Honored One immediately manifested five hundred bhikṣus, who appeared from afar wearing their robes and carrying their alms bowls.
When Kāśyapa saw those five hundred bhikṣus from afar, wearing their robes and carrying their alms bowls as they approached, he had this thought:
"Alas! What a pity!"
"From where have these bhikṣus come?
By what means can I obtain food to give to them?
At that moment, the World-Honored One immediately withdrew his supernormal power, causing the five hundred bhikṣus to disappear.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"All of this is brought about by the supernatural power of the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"If anyone should come here, I shall give them food.
At that time, the World-Honored One again employed his supernormal powers to manifest five hundred brahmins with spiral topknots, who approached from afar holding water-pots in their hands.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw from afar five hundred brahmins with matted hair approaching, carrying water-pots in their hands, and he thought to himself: "Alas!
Now these five hundred brahmins are coming; by what means can I obtain food to give them?"
Then the World-Honored One immediately withdrew his supernormal power, causing the five hundred brahmins to disappear.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This was the doing of that great śramaṇa."
At that time, Kāśyapa again had this thought:
"If anyone comes here, I shall give them food.
Then the World-Honored One again transformed himself into five hundred fire-worshipping brahmins who, not far from the stone cave, were all together making offerings to the fire god.
When Kāśyapa saw this, he thought to himself:
"Alas! From where has this come?"
"By what means shall I obtain food to give to them?
At that moment, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal power, causing the five hundred brahmins to disappear.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This is all the doing of that great śramaṇa.
At that time, the brahmins who were disciples of Kāśyapa entered the water three times each day to bathe; they were so overcome by the extreme cold that they could not endure it.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested five hundred fire-pits, all without smoke or flames, so that the various brahmins could each warm themselves.
The brahmins thought to themselves:
"All of this is the work of the Great Śramaṇa."
At that time, all the brahmins wished to split the firewood, but they were unable to do so.
The brahmins thought to themselves,
"This is all due to the majestic power of the Great Śramaṇa."
Just as he managed to break it, he thought again:
"This is the work of the great śramaṇa’s supernatural power.
He wished to lift the axe but was unable to lift it, and so he thought:
"This must be the work of that great śramaṇa.
Just as he had managed to raise his axe, he thought again:
"This must be the work of that great śramaṇa."
The various brahmins wished to bring down the axe, but they were unable to do so;
they thought to themselves, "This is the doing of the Great Śramaṇa.
As soon as they managed to bring it down, they thought again:
"This must be the doing of that great śramaṇa.
When the brahmins wished to kindle the fire but were unable to do so, they thought to themselves,
"This is all the doing of that great śramaṇa."
Once the fire had been lit, he thought,
"This is the work of the Great Śramaṇa.
He wished to extinguish it, but was unable to do so, and he thought:
"All of this was done by that great śramaṇa.
As soon as it was extinguished, he thought to himself:
"This was done by that great śramaṇa."
He took up water from his ritual pitcher, intending to pour it away, but was unable to get it out;
he thought to himself, "This must be the doing of the Great Śramaṇa.
Once he was able to pour out the water, he thought again:
"It is the work of the Great Śramaṇa.
The brahmins, wishing to stop the water from their ritual jars, were unable to do so and thought to themselves:
"It is the work of the Great Śramaṇa."
Having attained this state of stillness, he thought to himself:
"This must be the work of the Great Śramaṇa.
At that time, great black clouds arose on all four sides, and the heavens sent down heavy rain like the urine of elephants, until the floodwaters reached his waist.
At that time, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is exceedingly handsome, the foremost among men; he might have been swept away by the water.
He then took his disciples and boarded a boat made from a tree trunk to go and seek out the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was walking in meditation in the open air outside; the ground was dry as it had been before.
When Kāśyapa saw the Buddha walking in meditation in the open air, yet the ground remained as dry as if he were inside a house, he thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa is truly marvelous!"
"How extraordinary!
He causes insentient objects to revolve according to his will.
This great śramaṇa possesses mastery over supernormal powers and has attained arhatship; yet, even so, he is still not equal to my attainment of arhatship."
On another day, Kāśyapa again went to the place where the World-Honored One was and said to him:
"The time for the meal has arrived; you may go to take your meal.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"You go on ahead; I shall follow after you.

Having thus sent Kāśyapa away, the World-Honored One, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, vanished from the place where he was walking and emerged through the bottom of Kāśyapa’s boat.
Having seen this, he spoke these words:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great supernatural power; previously he sent me on ahead with the message that he would arrive later, yet now he is already on board the ship?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"After I have sent you off, I shall vanish from my place of walking meditation and emerge through the bottom of your boat in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm."
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal power; having sent me off first, he has now emerged upon the boat from behind."
"The Great Śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained arhatship; yet, even so, he is not equal to my true Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what was in Kāśyapa’s mind, addressed him, saying: "You have always declared: [that you have attained the supreme, right, and perfect enlightenment]."
"Though the Great Śramaṇa has attained arhatship, it is not equal to my attainment of arhatship.
Now, observing you as you are, you are neither an arhat nor one progressing toward the path of arhatship.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses great majestic power; he knows what is in my mind.
This great śramaṇa possesses great supernormal powers and has attained mastery as an arhat. I should now rather practice the holy life under him."
He immediately came forward and addressed the Buddha,
saying, "I now wish to practice the holy life under the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa:
"You have five hundred disciples who study the holy life under you; you should inform them so that they may know.
If they have the aspiration, let them practice according to their own inclination."
Then Kāśyapa went to his disciples and said to them:
"Do you know? I now wish to practice the holy life under the śramaṇa Gautama."
"Whatever your hearts desire, each of you may act according to your own will.
The disciples replied, "We have long since possessed faith in that śramaṇa; we were merely waiting for our teacher."

At that time, the five hundred disciples took their conch-shell crests, fire-offering implements, pure robes, and water-pots, went to the Nairañjanā River and cast them into the water. They then came to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One gradually taught the sublime Dharma to five hundred people, exhorting them to give rise to a heart of joy.
The Dharma he taught was that of giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; he censured sensual desire as impure and praised renunciation as blissful.

At that very seat, the five hundred people were cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; they saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, perfected the various dharmas, and attained the realization of the fruit.
They then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We wish to go forth under the Tathāgata and practice the holy life."
The Buddha said: “Come, bhikṣu!
In my Dharma, practice the holy life (brahmacarya) with joy to reach the end of suffering; this is itself called receiving full ordination.”

At that time, the middle brother of Kāśyapa, named Nadī-Kāśyapa, resided downstream from the Nairañjanā River with three hundred disciples; he was the most eminent among them and served as their leader and teacher.

At that time, there was a disciple among that assembly who went to look at the waters of the Nairañjanā River; he saw there within the water the implements for fire-worship, hair, and a water-pot, as well as a clean robe being carried away by the current.
Having seen this, he went quickly to where Nadi-Kāśyapa was and said to him:
"Master, you should know that in these waters of the Nairañjanā River, there are hair, fire-offering implements, a pure robe, and a water-pot, all being carried away by the current."
"I wonder if the Great Master of the Upper Stream has perhaps been harmed by evil people?
At that time, Gayākāśyapa—the younger brother of Uruvilvākāśyapa—was dwelling on Mount Gajaśīrṣa with two hundred disciples, serving as their leader.
Then Nadi-Kāśyapa said to one of his disciples:
"Go quickly to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa; having arrived, say to Gayā-Kāśyapa: 'Do you know? "
"Now, in the waters of the Nairañjanā River, all the implements and articles for fire-worship have been swept away by the current.
Come quickly; let us go together to see whether your elder brother has not been harmed by evil persons."
Then, having received the words of Nadi-Kāśyapa, the disciple went to Gayā-Kāśyapa and said:
"Does the junior master know?
Our teacher has these words:"
"In the waters of the Nairañjanā River, there are a water-pot, pure robes, hair, and various implements for tending the sacred fire, all being carried away by the current of the Nairañjanā.
Come quickly; let us go together to see whether our elder brother has not been harmed by evil persons."
When the youngest brother heard these words, he immediately took two hundred disciples and went to where Nadī-Kāśyapa was.
Upon arrival, Nadī-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa spoke again to one of their disciples, saying:
"Go quickly to our eldest brother’s place and see whether he has not been harmed by wicked men."
Then that disciple, having received the words of his two teachers, went at once to see his elder brother.
Upon arriving, he asked:
"How is it, Great Master? Is practicing the holy life under this Great Śramaṇa superior?"
Kāśyapa replied: "You should know this!
My going forth from the world and training in the path under the World-Honored One is most excellent and sublime."
Then that disciple returned to his two teachers and said:
"Venerable masters, you should know!
My great teacher has already taken his disciples to the Great Śramaṇa to leave the household life and practice the holy life."
At that time, the two teachers thought to themselves:
"One who leaves the household life for the sake of the householdless life and trains under him in the holy life will certainly not do so in vain. Why is this?"
