"My elder brother is intelligent, with few defilements and great wisdom; he has taken various disciples to study under him because he surely considered it appropriate to do so. How much more so should we not study under him?"
Then Nadi-Kāśyapa and Gayā-Kāśyapa each led their respective disciples to the place where the elder brother was; having arrived, they addressed him, saying:
"Elder brother!..."
"Is this place superior? The elder brother replied to his two younger brothers, "This place is most excellent;
for one who leaves the household life from home to practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa, that indeed is supreme and wondrous."
The two younger brothers said to their elder brother,
"We also wish to follow the Great Śramaṇa to study and practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Thereupon, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, taking his two younger brothers along with five hundred disciples, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
Then Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa came forward and said to the Buddha:
"I have a younger brother named Nadī-Kāśyapa who dwells by the banks of the Nairañjanā River; he constantly instructs three hundred disciples and serves as their leader."
Next, the third brother dwells on Mount Gajaśīrṣa, where he instructs two hundred disciples and serves as their preceptor.
Now they have all come together, desiring to seek the practice of the holy life (brahmacarya) from the World-Honored One.
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me permission to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and practice the holy life.
The World-Honored One granted his consent and gradually taught him the sublime Dharma.
This Dharma consisted of the teachings on generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; it censured the impurity of desire and praised renunciation as true happiness.

Immediately upon their seats, all defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; seeing the Dharma and attaining the Dharma, they accomplished all dharmas and realized the fruit.
Each came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"
"We wish to go forth from within the Dharma of the Tathāgata to practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
The Buddha said, "Come, bhikṣus!"
"Within my Dharma, you have successfully practiced the holy life (brahmacarya) and attained the end of suffering; this is itself called the reception of full ordination (upasampadā).
Then the World-Honored One, having conferred full ordination upon these thousand brahmins, led them to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
On Mount Gajaśīrṣa, there was an assembly of a thousand bhikṣus who were taught by means of three methods:
first, teaching through supernormal powers; second, teaching through mindfulness; and third, teaching through the exposition of the Dharma.

Regarding those who teach through the supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*): they may transform a single person into many, or many back into one; they penetrate both internally and externally, passing through stone walls as if traveling through empty space without any obstruction;
they sit cross-legged in mid-air like a flying bird circling to and fro;
they enter the earth as if it were water, emerging and submerging with ease, and walk upon water as if on solid ground without sinking.
His body emits smoke and fire like a great mass of flames;

though the sun and moon possess great divine power and illuminate all things, he can touch them with his hand; his body reaches the Brahma Heaven, coming and going without obstruction—this is called the World-Honored One’s miraculous power in teaching and transforming a thousand bhikṣus.
Regarding the recollection of the teacher, he instructs:
"You should contemplate this; do not contemplate that.
You should be mindful of this; do not be mindful of that."
"One should extinguish this; one should accomplish that.
This is what the World-Honored One recalled and taught to the thousand bhikṣus.
Regarding the teaching and transformation through the Dharma, "all is ablaze. What is meant by "all is ablaze"?
The eye is ablaze; forms are ablaze; eye-consciousness is ablaze; eye-contact is ablaze.
Furthermore, whatever feeling arises conditioned by eye-contact—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that too is called ablaze.
What is meant by "blazing"?
Blazing refers to the fire of desire, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
Furthermore, why is it called blazing?
As for "blazing," it is blazing with birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair; I say this is the source from which suffering arises, and so it is even for the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One instructed the thousand bhikṣus with these three matters.
Having received this instruction in the three matters, those thousand bhikṣus immediately attained the outflow-free liberation of mind and the knowledge of the liberation of non-obstruction.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had transformed these thousand bhikṣus, he thought to himself:
"I previously promised King Bimbisāra that if I were to attain Buddhahood and realize all-knowledge, I would first come to the city of Rājagṛha."
"I should now go to see King Bimbisāra.

He immediately adjusted his robes and, taking with him a thousand great bhikṣus—all of whom were formerly learned śramaṇas with topknots (*śikhin*), who had all attained meditative concentration, were disciplined and gentle, and had achieved eternal liberation—he traveled through the borders of the kingdom of Magadha for the sake of teaching and transforming beings, gradually arriving at the Śiṃśapā Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One was seated beneath the king of nyagrodha trees, the Well-Situated (Susthitā), in the Śāla Grove.

King Bimbisāra heard that the śramaṇa Gautama, having gone forth from the Śākya clan to study the Way, was wandering through the realm of Magadha with a thousand disciples—all of whom were formerly learned brahmins with topknots who had attained meditative concentration, were disciplined and gentle, and had achieved eternal liberation—and that he had traveled from the realm of Magadha to the Śāla Grove, stopping beneath the king of nyagrodha trees, the Well-Situated, where he was seated.
That śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown, such that there is nothing he has not heard.

This so-called renown is: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Among the gods and the people of the world, among Māra or the gods of Māra, and among the hosts of Brahmā, śramaṇas, and brahmins, he has realized for himself the attainment of supernatural powers and wisdom, and constantly delights therein.

When preaching the Dharma to others, his words—whether superior, middling, or inferior—are all excellent; their meaning and flavor are profound, and he fully expounds them while practicing the various holy life (brahmacarya). "Excellent!"
"Only now have I been able to see such Arhats.
I should go in person to see the Great Śramaṇa Gautama.

At that time, King Bimbisāra prepared twelve thousand chariots and was surrounded by eighty-four thousand people in his retinue; with royal majesty, he departed from Rājagṛha, desiring to see the World-Honored One.
At that time, King Bimbisāra went to the Śiṃśapā Grove; having reached the point where his carriage could go, he descended from it and entered the grove on foot.

From afar, he beheld the World-Honored One, whose countenance was exceptionally sublime like purple-gold. Thereupon, a heart of joy arose within him, and having approached the Tathāgata to prostrate himself at his feet, he sat down to one side.

At that time, among the people of Magadha, some sat after prostrating at his feet; some sat after raising their hands in greeting; some sat after announcing their names; some sat with their hands joined in *añjali* toward the Tathāgata; and some sat in silence.
At that time, the people of Magadha thought to themselves:
"Is it the Great Śramaṇa who is learning the holy life under Uruvelā-Kāśyapa?
Or is it Uruvelā-Kāśyapa, together with his assembly of disciples, who is learning the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa Gautama?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of the country, spoke in verse to Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa:
"What transformation have you seen?"
"Having abandoned all implements for tending the sacrificial fire, I now ask Kāśyapa: how did you abandon these fire implements?
At that time, Kāśyapa replied to the World-Honored One in verse:
"Eating various delicious foods, Lusting after women and performing sacrifices— I see such impurities as these;
Therefore, I have abandoned the implements for tending the fire.
The World-Honored One again addressed Kāśyapa with a verse:
“Though one partakes of all manner of delicious foods, there is no true delight therein;
whether in the heavens or in the world, where now do you say that joy resides?
Kāśyapa again replied to the World-Honored One in verse: “I see the traces of rest, unimpeded throughout the three realms.”
"They are not different and cannot be made different; they do not delight in the fire sacrifice.
At that time, the people of Magadha again had this thought:
"The Great Śramaṇa has spoken two verses, and Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa has also spoken two verses. We still have not yet distinguished whether the Great Śramaṇa is receiving instruction from Kāśyapa, or..."
"Have you and your disciples come to study under the Great Śramaṇa?
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the people of Magadha, said to Kāśyapa:
"Rise and fan my back for me."
He replied, "So be it.

Having received the Buddha's instruction, Kāśyapa immediately rose from his seat, ascended into the air, and then descended again to prostrate at the feet of the World-Honored One. He rubbed the Tathāgata’s feet with his hands and kissed them, announcing his own clan and name:
“The World-Honored One is my teacher; I am his disciple.
Having said this, he took up a fan and fanned the Tathāgata from behind.
At that time, the people of Magadha said to one another:
"The Great Śramaṇa Gautama did not study the holy life under Kāśyapa; rather, Kāśyapa and his assembly of disciples study the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa Gautama."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the people of Magadha were free from doubt, gradually preached the Dharma for them, exhorting them to give rise to a heart of joy.
The Dharma he taught was that of generosity, ethical discipline, and rebirth in the heavens; he censured sensual desires as impure and praised renunciation as true happiness.

At that time, with King Bimbisāra of Magadha at their head, eighty-four thousand people and twelve nayutas of devas were cleansed of all defilements and attained the pure Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, they perfected the various dharmas and, knowing for themselves that they had attained the fruit, bore witness to it.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; please accept us as upāsakas. For as long as life lasts, we shall refrain from killing living beings, and so forth, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants."
When King Bimbisāra had seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, he approached the Buddha and said:
"I recall that in the past, when I was a crown prince, six wishes arose in my mind:
first, that when my father’s life ended, I would ascend the throne as king."
Second, may a Buddha appear in the world while I am governing the kingdom.
Third, may I personally behold the World-Honored One.
Fourth, having beheld the Buddha, may I give rise to a heart of joy toward the Tathāgata.
Fifth, having already given rise to a joyful mind, he was able to hear the True Dharma.
Sixth, having heard the Dharma, he immediately attained faith and understanding.
Now that my father, the King, has passed away, I have ascended the throne to become king.
However, while I was governing the kingdom, it happened that a Buddha appeared in the world.

Now, having seen the Buddha again, I have given rise to a heart of joy; having given rise to a heart of joy in the presence of the Buddha, I have been able to hear the Dharma; and having heard the Dharma, I have attained faith and understanding.
"Now is precisely the right time; we only pray that the World-Honored One will enter the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation and immediately rose from his seat. He donned his robes and, leading a thousand bhikṣus—all of whom were formerly learned śramaṇas with spiral-topknots (jaṭila) who had already attained meditative concentration, were disciplined and gentle, and had forever attained liberation—he entered the city of Rājagṛha by means of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, surrounded before and behind by twelve thousand chariots and eighty-four thousand followers.

At that time, it was raining; yet the World-Honored One remained clear and bright in front, behind, and in the middle, while a cloud-canopy was above him. Manifesting this miraculous transformation, the World-Honored One entered the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra transformed himself into a certain brāhmaṇa. Holding a golden staff, a golden water-pitcher, and a fan with a golden handle, he remained in mid-air at a height of four finger-widths from the ground, leading the way before the Tathāgata while praising the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha through countless skillful means.
At that time, the people of Magadha all thought to themselves:

"By whose majestic power has this form of a brahmin been conjured, holding a golden staff, a golden water-pot, and a fan with a golden handle; his body suspended in the air four finger-breadths above the ground, leading the way before the Tathāgata to clear away the crowd, and further praising the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha through countless skillful means?"
Then the people of Magadha addressed Śakra Devānām-indra with this verse:
"Who has manifested as a brahmin,
standing now before the assembly of monks?"
"Reciting the Buddha’s virtues, whom is it that you serve?
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra replied to the people of Magadha with a verse: "He who is valiant and all-knowing, Free from desire and craving for food and drink;
Modest, mindful, and content— I am his disciple."
There is none in the world equal to you; I see no one who resembles you.
You are the Tathāgata, the Truly Enlightened Buddha; I am your attendant.
You have extinguished desire and hatred, and ignorance is forever exhausted.
I am the attendant of the Arhat whose outflows are exhausted;
just as one who has crossed over those drowning, Gautama is the Dharma-ship;
having reached the further shore, the Most Victorious One, I am his attendant.
"Having crossed to the further shore of the four floods, he is able to preach the Dharma of immortality;
regarding this most supreme and unimpeded Dharma, I am his attendant.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha again thought to himself:
"If the World-Honored One, leading his disciples into the city of Rājagṛha, should first arrive at this grove, I shall immediately offer this grove to him and establish a vihāra there."
At that time, among all the gardens in the city of Rājagṛha, the Bamboo Grove of Kalanda was the most excellent.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the King of Magadha, led the great assembly to the Bamboo Grove.
The king immediately dismounted from the elephant, folded the elephant’s rug himself into four layers, spread it upon the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will sit.
The World-Honored One then took his seat and sat down.
At that time, King Bimbisāra took a golden water-pitcher and offered water to the Tathāgata for purification, then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among all the gardens in the city of Rājagṛha, this Bamboo Grove is the most excellent. I now offer it to the Tathāgata; I pray that out of compassion you will accept it."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Now you should take this Bamboo Grove and offer it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha of the four quarters.
For what reason?

If the Tathāgata possesses a garden or garden articles, a dwelling or dwelling articles, robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, or needle cases, these constitute a stūpa; they are not for the use of devas, worldlings, Māras, or Māra-devas, śramaṇas, or brahmins.
The King said,
"I now offer this Bamboo Grove to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters.
Then the World-Honored One, having accepted that grove with a heart of compassion, immediately offered a blessing:
"Those who plant various garden trees, and construct bridges, boats, and beams; who provide orchards,
fruit-bearing trees, bathing pools, and dwellings for people—
such persons as these see their merit increase day and night."
"Those who uphold the precepts and accord with the True Dharma, those people shall attain rebirth in heaven.
At that time, King Bimbisāra prostrated himself before the feet of the World-Honored One, then took another small seat and sat before the Tathāgata, desiring to hear the Dharma.
Then the World-Honored One gradually preached the Dharma for the king, exhorting him to give rise to a heart of joy.
Having given rise to a heart of joy, he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Śāṇakavāsin in the city who had two hundred and fifty disciples, with Upatiṣya and Kolita as their leaders.

At that time, the Venerable Aśvajit was attending upon the Tathāgata. When the time arrived, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. His countenance was serene and joyful, his faculties were tranquil and composed, his robes were neatly arranged, and his gait was dignified and orderly; he did not look to the left or right, nor did he lose his majestic deportment.
At that time, Upatiṣya had arrived at the park for a visit; seeing Aśvajit’s majestic deportment in such a manner, he thought to himself:
"Now, observing that this bhikṣu is fully endowed with dignified deportment, I should go and inquire about the meaning of the Dharma."
He further thought to himself:
"This is not the time for this bhikṣu to inquire about the meaning while he is begging for alms.
I shall wait until he has finished begging for alms, and then I will go to inquire about the meaning."
At that time, Upatiṣya followed closely behind him.
When the bhikṣu Aśvajit had finished his almsround in the city of Rājagṛha, he placed his bowl on the ground and folded his saṃghāṭī robe.
Upatiṣya thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu has finished his almsround; now is precisely the time to inquire about the meaning of the Dharma. I shall now ask him.
He immediately went to him and inquired about the meaning.
“Who are you? What is your teacher’s name?
What Dharma do you study?”
He replied, "My teacher is the Great Śramaṇa; he is my venerated one, and it is from him that I have studied.
Upatiṣya then asked again:
"What Dharma does your teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, teach?
He replied, "I am young in years and have been a renunciant for but a short time; I am not yet fit to expound its meaning in detail, but I shall now briefly state its essentials."
Upatiṣya said: “I desire only to hear what is essential; it matters not whether it be extensive or concise. Aśvajit replied:
“If you wish to know it, the Tathāgata teaches the dharma of dependent origination and also teaches the dharma of the cessation of dependent origination.
Whatever dharma arises through a cause, the Tathāgata calls that its cause.”
"If a phenomenon is extinguished by its cause, the Great Śramaṇa also teaches this same principle;
this is what my teacher says.
When Upatiṣya heard this, all the defilements were immediately exhausted and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
At that time, Upatiṣya thought to himself:
"To enter such a Dharma as this and reach the state of sorrowlessness—this I have never before seen, even throughout countless hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of kalpas."
Upatissa and Kolita had previously made an agreement:
"Whichever of us first attains the sublime Dharma, we shall inform the other.
At that time, Upatissa went to the place where Kolita was.
When Kolita saw Upatiṣya approaching, he spoke these words:
"Your countenance is now serene and joyful, and your faculties are tranquil and composed; it appears that you have attained something."
"Will you not see the Dharma?
He replied, "It is as you have said."
He asked, "What kind of Dharma have you attained? He replied:
"That Tathāgata teaches the dharma of dependent origination, and he also teaches the dharma of the cessation of dependent origination.
Whatever dharma arises through a cause, the Tathāgata declares that to be its cause.
Whatever dharma ceases through a cause, the Great Śramaṇa likewise teaches that principle."
Having heard these words, Kolita immediately became free from all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Kolita thought to himself:
"To enter such a Dharma as this and attain the state of sorrowlessness—this I have never seen before throughout countless billions of nayutas of kalpas."
Kulada asked, "I wonder where the World-Honored One is currently residing? He replied:
"The Tathāgata is currently residing at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
Kolita said to Upatiṣya, "Today we should go together to the place where the Tathāgata is to pay him homage and inquire after his well-being; he is our teacher."
Upatiṣya replied, "We previously had two hundred and fifty disciples who practiced the holy life under my guidance; we shall inform them of this, and they may do as they wish."
Then Upatiṣya and Kolita went to their disciples and said to them, "Do you know?
We two wish to practice the holy life under the Great Śramaṇa; each of you may do as you desire."
The disciples said, “We have all received our training from you, our teacher.
Now that even the Great Master still studies under him, how could we possibly not study under him as well?”
"If that which our teacher has attained is what we shall also attain," said Upatiṣya and Kolita,
together with their disciples, as they went forth to the Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by an assembly of countless hundreds of thousands as he preached the Dharma. Seeing from afar Upatiṣya and Kolita together with their disciples approaching, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"Those two men coming from afar are named Upatiṣya and Kolita. These two shall be the foremost among my disciples; their wisdom is immeasurable and unsurpassed, and they have attained the two kinds of liberation."
Before they had even reached the Bamboo Grove, the Tathāgata had already bestowed a prophecy upon the two friends as a pair.
When the two companions and their disciples arrived at the place where the Tathāgata was, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.
Then the World-Honored One gradually taught them the sublime Dharma to inspire in them a heart of joy.
That is to say, he taught the Dharma of giving, ethical discipline, and rebirth in heaven; he censured the impurity of sensual desire and praised renunciation as happiness.
Immediately upon these seats, all defilements were exhausted and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; they saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and became accomplished in all Dharmas.
Having personally known that they had attained the fruit of realization, they came before the Buddha and said:
"We wish to go forth from within the Dharma of the Tathāgata to practice the holy life."
The Buddha said: "Welcome, bhikṣus!
By practicing the holy life with joy within my Dharma, you shall reach the end of the source of suffering; this is called going forth and receiving full ordination."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the city of Rājagṛha.

Then the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, together with his disciples, went forth from the household life to study the Path; furthermore, there were two hundred and fifty Brahmins of the Śrṇga clan who also went forth from the household life to study the Path.
The sons of noble families within the city of Rājagṛha also left the household life to study the Path.
At that time, the elders of Rājagṛha admonished one another, saying:
"You who have sons, each of you must carefully protect them; and those wives who have husbands must also carefully protect them."
"Now this Great Śramaṇa has crossed the borders of the kingdom of Magadha bringing various brahmins with him; now that he has come here, he will surely take these people away as well.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were begging for alms, they heard what these people were saying:
"This Great Śramaṇa has brought various brahmins with him and come here; now he will surely take these people away as well."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they were all filled with shame and remorse. They went to where the World-Honored One was and reported the matter to him in detail.
The World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"While you were entering the city of Rājagṛha for alms, you heard the elders making these remarks:"
"If the Great Śramaṇa has arrived within our borders and is taking these various brahmins with him as his followers,
and now intends to take these people away as well," you should respond to them with this verse:
"The Tathāgata, possessed of great power, Is leading them away by means of the Dharma."
"Since he who leads by means of the Dharma is about to depart, why do you feel anxiety and fear?

At that time, having received the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣus entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for food. When they heard the elders speaking these words, they immediately replied to them with this verse:
"The Tathāgata, possessed of great power, departs by means of the Dharma."
"Since he departs with the Dharma, why do you feel anxiety or fear?
At that time, the elders thought to themselves:
"As we have heard, the Great Śramaṇa is departing with the Dharma; it is not for the sake of what is contrary to the Dharma."

At that time, the Venerable Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa led his disciples to leave the household life and study the Path; Śreṇika’s disciples also left the household life and studied the Path with their two hundred and fifty followers; and the sons of the prominent clans of Rājagṛha likewise left the household life and studied the Path.
The great assembly had all gathered for a tour of the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, those who had not yet received instruction did not observe the rules of decorum: their robes were not properly adjusted, they went on alms-rounds contrary to the Dharma, accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls; moreover, at both small and large meals, they shouted and clamored loudly, like the manner of a Brahmin gathering.
At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu who passed away without a disciple or anyone to attend to him. For this reason, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"From now on, I permit the existence of an upādhyāya (preceptor). An upādhyāya shall look after his disciple, caring for him as one would for a son."
Disciples should regard their preceptors as they would their own fathers.
By showing mutual respect and looking after one another with care, the True Dharma will thus endure for a long time, increasing and expanding.
One should request the preceptor in this manner.
When making the request, one should be instructed to bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, place the right knee on the ground, join the palms, and speak these words:
"I, [Name], request the Venerable One to be my preceptor. May the Venerable One act as my preceptor; I shall receive the full ordination in reliance upon the Venerable One."
The second and third times he speaks likewise.
The preceptor should reply: "So be it."
If one says: "It is so," or if one says:
"I shall instruct you. If he says:
"Be pure; do not be negligent."

The Buddha said: "From this day forward, the bestowal of full ordination by means of the three-fold formula is abolished. From this day forward, it is permitted that full ordination shall be bestowed by a group of ten fully ordained monks."
The formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for bestowing full ordination (*upasampadā*) should be conducted as follows.

One who wishes to receive the precepts shall go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the monks, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make this formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, [Name], seek to receive the full ordination from [Name].
I, [Name], now request the Sangha for the full ordination, with [Name] acting as my preceptor.
"May the Sangha deliver me, out of compassion!
Thus it should be said a second and a third time.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from such-and-one.
This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with so-and-one acting as preceptor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let [the name] receive full ordination with [the name] as the preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with [Name] acting as the preceptor (upādhyāya).
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha granting full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as preceptor should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third [announcements] are also made in this manner:
"The Sangha has already conferred full ordination upon so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor;
the Sangha consents, as it remains silent; thus this matter is upheld."
At that time, the bhikṣus knew that the World-Honored One had established the precepts and permitted the conferring of full ordination upon others.
However, newly ordained bhikṣus would immediately confer full ordination on others without being able to provide them with instruction.

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper decorum: their robes were not worn neatly, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in an impure bowl; furthermore, they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and midday meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured those bhikṣus, saying:

"The World-Honored One established the precepts and permitted the bestowing of full ordination upon others; why have you, as newly ordained bhikṣus, rashly bestowed full ordination upon others and yet failed to provide them with instruction?"

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper deportment; their robes were not worn neatly, they begged for food improperly, they accepted impure food in various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and midday meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?

At that time, the Venerable Vatsagotra was two years old; taking a disciple who was one year old, he went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"What kind of bhikṣu is this? They replied:
“World-Honored One! I am your disciple. He asked:
"How old are you now? He replied, "Two years."
He asked again, "How old is your disciple? He replied:
“One year. At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked him with countless skillful means:
“What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done.”
“Vāseṭṭha, how is it that you,
whose own milk has not yet been weaned and who ought to receive instruction from others, are instructing others?
Then the bhikṣus went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Two years ago, the bhikṣu Vatsa brought a disciple who had been his for one year to where I was; he prostrated with his head at my feet and sat to one side."
Once he had sat down on one side, I, knowing the answer, asked him intentionally: "Who is this bhikṣu? He replied:
"This is my disciple. He asked,
"How many years old are you?"
He replied, "Two years. [The other asked,] "How many years have your disciples been with you?"
He replied, "One year. I then rebuked him with countless skillful means:

"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done. Why so, Pāsa?"
"Since you yourself have not yet weaned from the mother's milk, you ought to receive instruction from others; how can you instruct others?

Although the Buddha has permitted the conferring of full ordination upon others, you, a newly ordained bhikṣu, have immediately conferred full ordination upon others without knowing how to provide instruction.

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper deportment; their robes were not worn in an orderly fashion, they begged for food improperly, accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the great and small meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus who have ten years of seniority to bestow full ordination upon others."
When those bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to confer full ordination upon others,
foolish bhikṣus of ten years' standing immediately began conferring full ordination, yet they did not know how to provide instruction.

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper deportment; their robes were not worn neatly, they begged for food improperly, accepted impure food at various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the major and minor meals, like the assembly customs of the Brahmins.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame; they rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to confer the full ordination upon others."
"How is it that you, a foolish bhikṣu of only ten years' standing, have rashly conferred full ordination upon others without knowing how to instruct them?

Because you do not instruct them, they do not maintain dignified deportment; their robes are not properly arranged, they beg for food improperly, they accept impure food from various places, or they accept food in impure bowls, and they shout loudly at the great and small meals like the gathering customs of brahmins?"
Then the bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked those bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that ought not to be done."
"How is it that the Blessed One established the precepts, permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to confer full ordination upon others?
How is it that you, a foolish bhikṣu of ten years' standing, have rashly conferred full ordination upon others without knowing how to provide instruction?"

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper deportment; their robes were not worn neatly, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food in various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the great and small meals, like the assembly customs of the Brahmins?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus who have ten years of seniority and possess wisdom to bestow the full ordination upon others."

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established the precepts, permitting bhikṣus of ten years’ standing who were wise to bestow full ordination upon others, they immediately declared of themselves:
"I am of ten years’ standing and wise; I may bestow full ordination upon others."
They would immediately confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others without knowing how to instruct them.

Because they did not provide instruction, [the novices] failed to maintain proper decorum (*īryāpatha*): their robes were not worn in a neat and orderly manner; they went for alms improperly; they accepted impure food from various places; they accepted food in impure bowls; and during the major and minor meals, they shouted and clamored loudly, like the assemblies of Brahmins.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, permitting only bhikṣus of ten years' standing and possessing wisdom to confer full ordination upon others."
How can you, claiming for yourself wisdom, hastily confer the full ordination upon others while remaining ignorant of how to instruct them?

Because you do not provide instruction, they fail to maintain dignified deportment; their robes are not worn properly, their alms-seeking is contrary to the Dharma, they accept impure food in various places, or accept food in impure bowls, and they shout loudly at the great and small meals like the practices of a Brahmin assembly?
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in conformity [with the path]. It is something that should not have been done."
The Buddha established the precepts, permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing who possess wisdom to confer full ordination upon others.
Why do you claim to be wise while arbitrarily conferring full ordination upon others, yet not knowing how to provide them with instruction?

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper decorum; their robes were not worn neatly, they begged for food improperly, accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the great and small meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?
Then the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you must establish the upādhyāya and cause him to perform the duties of an upādhyāya."
The preceptor should act toward his disciple in this manner and should conduct himself accordingly.

If the community of monks intends to perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against the disciple—whether it be a reprimand, an expulsion, a placement under dependence, a prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople, or a formal censure—the preceptor must manage the matter in accordance with the Dharma so that the Sangha does not perform such an act against the disciple; or, if they do perform it, he must ensure it is done according to the Dharma.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against a disciple—whether it be a reprimand (*tarjanīya*), a banishment (*pravāsanīya*), a requirement for dependence (*niśraya*), a prohibition from visiting the homes of laypeople (*apratisaṃkhyāna*), or a formal accusation (*utkṣepanīya*)—the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) should manage the matter in accordance with the Dharma, ensuring that the disciple complies with the Saṃgha, does not oppose them, and seeks the removal of the offense, so that the Saṃgha may swiftly grant him release from the formal act.

Furthermore, if a disciple commits an offense of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) shall attend to him according to the Dharma: if he ought to be granted *parivāsa*, he shall grant *parivāsa*;
if he ought to be granted *mūlāpakarṣa*, he shall grant *mūlāpakarṣa*;
if he ought to be granted *mānatva*, he shall grant *mānatva*.
One should grant absolution from an offense; one ought to grant absolution from an offense.
Furthermore, if a disciple falls ill, the preceptor (upādhyāya) shall attend to him, or if he causes another person to look after him, until the disciple recovers or passes away.
If a disciple does not find the dwelling place agreeable, he should move himself or instruct another to move it.
If a disciple has any matter of doubt, it should be resolved according to the Dharma and the Vinaya, as taught by the Buddha, and in accordance with the Dharma.

If wrong views arise, one should instruct them to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view; one should protect them by means of two things: protection through the Dharma and protection through food, clothing, and other necessities.

Regarding the protection of the Dharma therein, one should instruct them in the increase of virtue, the increase of concentration, and the increase of wisdom, as well as in learning and the recitation of the scriptures.
Regarding the protection of their robes and food therein, one should provide them with clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for illness according to one's capacity.
From this day forward, the rule for preceptors is established as follows: a preceptor must act accordingly; if he does not, he shall be dealt with according to the law.

At that time, the preceptor did not perform the duties of a preceptor toward his disciple, and the disciple did not perform the duties of a disciple toward the preceptor: they entered villages or the homes of laypeople without informing the preceptor; they traveled with other bhikṣus or took other bhikṣus as companions; they gave or received [gifts]; they assisted in communal affairs or accepted assistance from others; they shaved the hair of others or had their own hair shaved by others; they entered the bathhouse without informing the preceptor; they massaged the bodies of others or had their own bodies massaged by others; or they went to a lodging for the day, to a cemetery, outside the boundary, or to another region without informing the preceptor.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured those bhikṣus, saying:

"How can it be that while the upādhyāya performs the duties of an upādhyāya toward his disciple, the disciple does not perform the duties of a disciple toward his upādhyāya; and how can he enter a village or the house of a layperson without informing his upādhyāya, even going so far as to travel to another region without informing him?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."

What is it that the preceptor does not perform toward the disciple as a preceptor’s duty, and the disciple does not perform toward the preceptor as a disciple’s duty—such as entering a village or a layperson’s house without informing the preceptor, up to and including traveling to another region without informing him?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked that bhikṣu with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, you must regulate your disciples. According to the rules of conduct for disciples, you shall cause your disciples to perform the duties toward their preceptors in this manner."

If the preceptor has had a formal act (*karmavācanā*) performed against him by the community of monks—whether it be a censure, a banishment, a requirement to live under dependence, a prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople, or a formal accusation—the disciple shall manage the matter in accordance with the Dharma so that the Sangha does not perform such a formal act against the preceptor; if one is performed, he shall ensure it is made light.

Furthermore, if the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* against the preceptor—ranging from an act of censure (*tarjanīya*) up to an act of suspension (*utksepaṇīya*)—the disciple should manage the matter according to the Dharma therein, so that the preceptor becomes compliant with the Saṃgha, does not oppose it, and seeks the removal of the offense, thereby causing the Saṃgha to quickly grant him release from the *karmavācanā*.
Furthermore, if the preceptor commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, the disciple shall attend to him in accordance with the Dharma: if he ought to be granted *parivāsa*, he shall be granted *parivāsa*;
if he ought to be granted *mūlāpakarṣa*, he shall be granted *mūlāpakarṣa*;
if he ought to be granted *mānāpya*, he shall be granted *mānāpya*.
One should grant absolution from an offense; one ought to grant absolution from an offense.
Furthermore, if the preceptor is ill, the disciple shall attend to him, or have another person care for him until he recovers or passes away.
If the preceptor is dissatisfied with the dwelling place, he should move it himself or instruct another to move it.
If the preceptor has any doubts regarding a matter, one should resolve them in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the instructions of the Buddha.
If wrong views arise, one should encourage them to abandon those wrong views and abide in right view.
One should protect them with two things: with the Dharma and with food and clothing.
As for protection through the Dharma, one encourages them to increase their virtue, concentration, and wisdom, as well as their study and recitation of the scriptures.

Regarding those who provide clothing and food for protection, one should offer them the necessary items such as robes, food, bedding, mattresses, and medicinal requisites, according to one's own capacity.
"From this day forward, the rules for disciples shall be as follows; disciples must practice them.
If they do not practice them, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the disciples did not practice the duties of disciples toward their preceptors.
"A disciple must not enter a village without informing the Upādhyāya; he must not go to another's house;
he must not follow other bhikṣus, nor take other bhikṣus as companions;
he must not give, nor receive, nor assist in communal affairs, nor accept assistance from others in communal affairs."
He must have his hair shaved; he must not shave others; he must not enter a bathhouse; he must not rub another’s body;
he must not allow another to rub his body; he must not go to a lodging for the daytime;
he must not go to a cemetery; he must not go outside the boundary; he must not travel to other regions. He—
At dawn, one should enter the preceptor’s room to receive the recitation of the scriptures, the Dharma, and inquiries regarding their meaning;
one should remove the urinal vessel. When the time for the morning meal arrives, one should wash the hands thoroughly using soap-nuts or cow-dung ash.
If there is food available, one should fetch it; if there are offerings within the Sangha, one should fetch them; and one should carry the washing water.
He should offer beans and tooth-sticks to the preceptor to enable him to wash his hands and rinse his mouth;
he should offer any edible food to the preceptor; and if there is any special gain among the Sangha, he should inform the preceptor, saying:
"I have obtained such and such items; these are the preceptor’s portion."
He should ask his preceptor:
"Do you wish to enter the village?
If [the preceptor] says:
"If he does not enter," one should ask him:
"From where do you obtain food?"
If the preceptor says,
"Take it from such-and-such a place," you should go and take it according to his instructions.
If he replies,
"I wish to enter the village," you should wash your hands and then take your robe from the rack slowly, ensuring it is not inverted or misplaced.
One should take up the *antarvāsa*, spread it out, and shake it to ensure there are no insects, snakes, bees, or other harmful creatures.

Next, one should take up the belt, the *saṃkakṣikā*, and the *uttarāsaṅga*, spreading them out and shaking them to ensure there are no snakes, bees, or other harmful creatures, and then present them to the *upādhyāya*. One should fold the *saṃghāṭī* and place it upon one's head or shoulder.
Furthermore, when taking up the bowl, one should wash it with soap-nuts, ash, or cow dung, then place it inside a netted bag or wrap it in a hand-towel, and carry it away within a bowl-sack.
One should take up the preceptor’s undergarment, fold it, and set it aside; then take up the foot-washing items and the bedding for lying down and set them aside.
If the preceptor goes out, one should take hold of the preceptor’s leather sandals for walking.
When leaving the dwelling, one should look back and close the door.
Furthermore, one should push it with the hand to check whether it is secure;
if it is not secure, one should close it more firmly.

Once it is secured, one should take the cord through the hole in the door leaf; having thoroughly inspected both sides, one should place the door bolt in a concealed spot, whether out of fear that others might see it or lest it be insecure.
If it is not secure, or if people see it, one should take it away or move it to a deep and secure place.
Let the preceptor go in front.
If you encounter acquaintances on the road, you should engage them in polite conversation and maintain a mind of wholesome mindfulness.
While traveling, one should avoid the paths used by people.

When he wishes to enter a village, he should step slightly off the path, set his bowl aside on one side—either on his head or on his shoulder—and take down his saṃghāṭī robe to spread it out and inspect it, ensuring there are no snakes, scorpions, centipedes, or other harmful insects, before handing it to his preceptor.
If outside that village there is a guest house, a shop, or a workshop, one should place the leather sandals used for walking on the road inside it.
One should then ask the Upādhyāya: "May I follow after you?"
If he says, "So be it," you should immediately follow him.
If he says,
"I do not need it; I shall stay in such-and-such a place," he should stay in that place as he has said.
If the preceptor enters a village and does not emerge at the proper time, the disciple should form this thought:
"He has entered the village for alms; this portion is for the preceptor, and this portion belongs to me."

Having left the village, he returned to where his sandals were, took them off at the edge of the path, set down his bowl on the ground, and folded his saṃghāṭī robe, placing it upon his head or over his shoulder.
If you encounter someone you know on the road, you should greet them with a kind and sincere inquiry after their well-being.
If it is the dwelling or dining place of your preceptor, you should sweep it until it is clean, prepare a seat for him, and provide a pure water pitcher, bathing vessels, and food containers.
Furthermore, one should prepare for the preceptor a place for bathing and sitting, as well as a foot-washing stone, the necessary implements, and a towel for drying the feet.
If one sees the preceptor approaching from afar, one should immediately rise to welcome him.
Taking the bowl from his hand, he places it upon a bowl-stand, or on a bowl-rack, or at the corner of a corded bed, or upon his head or shoulder.
He takes up the *saṃghāṭī* robe, spreads it out, and inspects it to ensure it is not stained with grease, nor covered in dust, nor soiled by mud, nor defiled by the droppings of birds.
If there is any such stain, it should be removed; that which is suitable for washing should be washed, wrung out of water, spread out, and placed to dry upon either a wooden bed or a rope bed.

Furthermore, he should provide the preceptor with a seat, leather sandals, a foot-stone, and a foot-wiping cloth; he should also provide a water vessel for washing. Having shaken out the leather sandals, he should place them on his left side and inspect them, fearing they might be in a damp spot on the ground;
if they are in a damp spot on the ground, he should take them up and move them elsewhere.
When you have finished washing the preceptor’s feet, you should discard the water, take the foot-washing stone and the foot-wiping cloth, and return them to their original places.
Then, having washed your own hands clean, offer pure water for the preceptor to wash his hands.
From whatever food one possesses, one should take a portion and give it to the preceptor (upādhyāya), saying:
"This is my share of food; please eat it.
If he requires it, he should take it.
When the preceptor is eating, one should stand in attendance to observe and provide whatever is required.
While he eats, if there is curd-milk, boiled gruel, fermented grain-water, salt, parched barley, or vegetable greens, one should offer them to him; if they are hot, one should stir them to cool them.
If water is required, one should offer it.
If the time for the meal is about to pass, one should eat immediately at that same time.
Once the preceptor has finished eating, one should take the bowl from his hand and provide water for rinsing the mouth.

If one has finished eating oneself and there is food remaining, one should give it to a human or a non-human; or place it on clean ground where there is no grass, or place it in clean water where there are no insects.

Take the vessel for food, wash it thoroughly, and return it to its original place; take the sitting mat, the foot-washing stand, the bed, the water pitcher, and the rinsing pitcher, and return them to their respective places.
When cleaning the excrement from the dining area, he took his alms bowl and filled it with the filth to discard it. When other bhikṣus saw this, they all looked upon him with contempt.

[The Buddha declared: "From now on, one must not take an alms bowl to carry away excrement for disposal. It is permitted to use a dustpan, a broken vessel, an old bamboo basket, or a broom to remove the excrement and food."
One should maintain the alms bowl with proper care and cleanliness.
Furthermore, when entering the preceptor’s room, one should inspect it for dust and dirt.

If there is dust or dirt, one should remove the rope beds, wooden beds, sitting mats, large and small cushions, pillows, woolen blankets, bed supports, or floor coverings; having noted their original positions, one should take them outside and dry them in the sun.
When cleaning and sweeping the room, one should observe when removing excrement and soil.

If there are needles or thread, knives, or scraps of old clothing, down to even a single pill or two of medicine, one should pick them up and place them in a visible spot; if anyone recognizes them as their own, they may take them.
Furthermore, one should sweep and wipe the area above the door, or upon a wooden peg, or upon a "dragon-tooth" peg, or upon the clothing rack.

If there are damaged areas in the room, such as holes made by insects or rats, those that can be patched or filled should be repaired; those that can be plastered should be plastered; those that can be pounded should be pounded; and those that can be leveled should be leveled. One should then sprinkle it with a mud slurry to ensure it is perfectly clean and pure.
One should take up the floor-covering, dry it in the sun, shake it out, and bring it back inside the room.
If the original arrangement of the seating was uneven, one should rearrange it so that it is even; if it was originally even, one should leave it as it was.

First, one should prop up the legs of the bed and wipe them clean; then, quickly securing the rope bed and its legs, one should place it inside the room toward oneself upon the bed props. Next, one should take the large and small mats, pillows, woolen rugs, and blankets, and place them within the room.
"First spread the large mat, then spread the small mats, blankets, and covers, and place the pillows upon them.
They then took their worn clothes and unworn clothes and placed them all together in one spot; when they were taken up again, each was mixed up and disordered.
"From this day forward, you must not place the robes you are wearing together with those not being worn in one place; they should each be kept in a separate location.
He then placed his alms-bag, leather sandal bag, needle-case, and oil-container in one spot, which the bhikṣus saw and disapproved of.
The Buddha said:

"It should not be so. From this day forward, it is permitted to place the alms-bowl bag and the needle case in one location, and to place the leather sandal bag and the oil container in another location."

He should place the staff inside the room and keep watch so that it does not protrude too high or low outside the door; he should also peer through the doorway to observe the courtyard, fearing there may be dust or impurities.
If there is [dirt], one should sweep it away immediately; having taken the water jar and washed it clean, one should refill it with pure water and place it back in its original location.

Furthermore, one should provide the preceptor (*upādhyāya*) with a water jar for bathing, a jar for washing, and a vessel for drinking. If there is bathing taking place in the bathhouse, one should go and ask the preceptor:
"Do you wish to bathe?"

If one says, "I am going to bathe," one should first go into the bathhouse and inspect the floor; if there is dust, soil, grass, or debris, it should be removed. If it needs to be sprinkled with water, one should sprinkle it; if it needs to be swept, one should sweep it.

If there is impure runoff water, it should be discarded; if water is to be added, it should be added; if firewood is to be added, it should be added; if firewood is to be split, it should be split; and if it is to be placed in the hearth, it should be placed in the hearth.

One should provide the preceptor with a vessel for the warm bathhouse, as well as a sitting bench, a razor for removing sweat, water vessels, earthenware containers, cleansing powder, and all other requisites for bathing.
He should first inform his preceptor, and only then light the fire; having lit the fire, he should announce that the time has arrived.

If the preceptor is ill and weak, or extremely old, the disciple should support him by embracing him, or carry him on a rope-bench or a wooden bed, or transport him on a cloth litter, to the warm bathhouse. There, he should take the robe from the preceptor’s hands.
If there are pegs in the bathhouse, or "dragon-tooth" pegs, or clothes racks, one should take one's robes and place them in these locations.
If there is oil, one should take the oil and apply it to the body. If oil vessels are scattered about on the ground, one should pick them up and hang them upon the dragon-tooth pegs.
If the preceptor is ill, emaciated, or extremely old, one should support him and carry him into the bathhouse.
Having arrived there, one should provide him with a bathing stand, a bathing pitcher, a razor for removing sweat, a water vessel, a clay vessel, soap powder, and all other requisites for bathing.
If smoke fumes the face, one should hold a cloth to shield it; if the head or back becomes hot, one should cover them with the cloth.
One should enter the bathhouse only after having informed the *upādhyāya*.
If the preceptor has already entered first, and one fears that the bathhouse will become noisy and does not dare to enter, one should form this thought:
"I am not entering for my own sake now, but for the purpose of bathing the preceptor."
One may enter with this intention.
Having entered, one should rub and massage the body for the preceptor (upādhyāya) and stand behind him.
If one wishes to have another person rub one's body, or if one receives a body massage from another, one must inform the preceptor so that he is aware of it.
Thereafter, one should assist with the rubbing of the body.
If one receives assistance from another in rubbing the body, that person shall wash the preceptor;

having finished washing oneself, if the preceptor is ill, emaciated, or extremely old, one should support him out of the bathing room, provide a seat for him to sit upon, and take a towel for drying the body, or a face towel, or an eye-towel, and present them to the preceptor.

One should set out a foot-washing stone, provide water for washing the feet, and take up a towel for wiping the feet; one should also take up the sandals, brush them, shake them out, and present them.
Next, take the robe, spread it out to inspect it, shake it, and hand it over.
If there is eye medicine or medicinal pills, hand them over; if there is sweet syrup, honey syrup, or syrup made from black rock sugar, hand these over after the hands have been washed.
If the preceptor is ill, emaciated, or extremely old, one should carry him on a rope bed or a wooden bed; if he is too heavy for these, one should carry him on his robes back to the room.
Once he has been brought back to the room, one should feel around with the hands to locate his place of rest, spread out a mat for him, and have him lie down.
First, provide them with an undergarment; next, cover them with a robe.

Once they have left the room, return and close the door. Returning to the bathhouse, inspect thoroughly the water jars, the bathing jars, the bathing benches, the razor for removing sweat, the water containers, the vessels for holding earth, the fine medicinal powders, and the cleansing agents such as soap powder; then place each item back in its original location.

If there is impure runoff water in the bathhouse, one should remove it; if the fire needs to be extinguished, one should extinguish it; if the fire needs to be covered, one should cover it; if the door needs to be closed, one should close it; and if the door-bolt needs to be taken away, one should take it away.
He should inquire after the Master’s well-being three times each day—at dawn, midday, and dusk—and he should perform two services for the Master without declining the labor:
first, repairing the dwellings; second, mending and washing the robes.
Regarding all matters as taught by the Upādhyāya according to the Dharma, you shall fully carry them out.
If he dispatches you to various regions to conduct affairs, you must not decline or make excuses, nor may you remain there on the pretext of some circumstance.
If anyone should offer such an excuse, they shall be dealt with according to the law.

From this day forward, I establish the training rules for disciples: if a disciple does not practice the duties of a disciple toward their preceptor (upādhyāya), they shall be dealt with according to the law.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 33 [and] Volume 34,
Part 2, Section 13; translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others.
Section Four of the *Prātimokṣa-vastu*: At that time, there were many newly ordained bhikṣus whose preceptors had passed away, leaving them without anyone to instruct them.

Because they were not being instructed, they did not observe the rules of decorum; their robes were worn untidily, they begged for food improperly, accepted impure food from various places, or accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the major and minor meals, no different from the manner of a Brahmin assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the existence of ācāryas and authorize the existence of śiṣyas.

An ācārya should regard his śiṣya as a son, and a śiṣya should regard his ācārya as a father. By thus instructing one another and serving one another, the Dharma within the Buddha's teaching will increase twofold and be widely disseminated."

One should make this request to the ācārya as follows: baring the right shoulder, removing one's leather sandals, placing the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms, one should say these words:
"Virtuous One, please attend to me with a single mind!"
"I, [Name], now request the Venerable One to be my preceptor; may the Venerable One grant me his preceptorship, and I shall dwell under the Venerable One's preceptorship.
The second and third times should be spoken in the same manner.
He shall say: "So be it!
I grant you my dependence; do not be negligent!"

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established the precept permitting the granting of formal reliance (niśraya), those newly ordained bhikṣus who granted reliance to others did not know how to instruct them.

Because they were not instructed, they did not maintain proper decorum: their robes were not worn neatly, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food from various places, they accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the great and small meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts and permitted one to receive dependence from others; yet you, newly ordained bhikṣus, having received dependence from others, do not know how to provide instruction."

Because they were not instructed, they did not observe the rules of decorum; their robes were worn untidily, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food from various places, they accepted food in unclean bowls, and they shouted loudly at large and small meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly.
Having rebuked him, he went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On account of this, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, not a practice in accordance with the teaching—it is something that should not be done."

"How is it, bhikṣus? The World-Honored One has established the precepts and permitted receiving dependence from others; yet you newly ordained bhikṣus, having received dependence from others, do not know how to provide instruction?"

Because they were not instructed, they did not observe the rules of decorum: their robes were not properly adjusted, they went for alms improperly, they accepted impure food in various places, they accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and evening meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked them with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus who have ten years of standing to provide dependence for others."

When those bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to provide formal reliance (*niśraya*) to others, those bhikṣus of ten years' standing—who were foolish and lacked wisdom—proceeded to provide reliance to others, yet did not know how to instruct them.

Because they were not instructed, they did not observe the rules of decorum; their robes were not worn properly; they went for alms in an improper manner; they accepted impure food from various places; they accepted food in impure bowls; and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and evening meals, like the custom of Brahmin assemblies.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured those bhikṣus, saying:

"How is it that although the World-Honored One has established the precept permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to provide formal reliance (niśraya) to others, you yourselves, though having ten years' standing, are so foolish that you do not know how to instruct those upon whom you rely?"

Because they were not being instructed, they did not maintain proper deportment; their robes were not worn neatly, they begged for food improperly, they accepted impure food from various places, they accepted food in impure bowls, and they raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and evening meals, like the manner of a Brahmin assembly?
Having rebuked him, he went to inform the Blessed One.
On account of this incident, the Blessed One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that bhikṣu, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the discipline—it is something that should not be done."
"Why have I established the precept permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing to receive formal reliance from others?
Although you are ten years old, you are ignorant; you receive reliance from others yet do not know how to instruct them."
"Because they do not provide instruction, their robes are not worn properly, even as if following the customs of a Brahmin assembly?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I permit bhikṣus who have ten years of seniority and possess wisdom to grant formal dependence (*niśraya*) to others."

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had established a precept permitting bhikṣus of ten years' standing who possessed wisdom to provide dependence (niśraya) to others, they claimed for themselves:
"I am of ten years' standing and possess wisdom."
He then granted them formal reliance (*niśraya*).
However, having granted them reliance, he did not provide instruction.

Because he did not instruct them, they wore their robes in a disordered manner, begged for food improperly, accepted impure food from various places, accepted food in impure bowls, and raised their voices and shouted loudly during the morning and evening meals, like the custom of Brahmin assemblies.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;

they rebuked that bhikṣu, saying: "How is it that while the World-Honored One has established the precept permitting a bhikṣu of ten years' standing who possesses wisdom to grant dependence to others, you have rashly declared of yourself: 'I possess wisdom'?"
He then granted someone formal reliance (*niśraya*), but having granted it, he did not provide instruction.

Because he did not provide instruction, [the disciple] did not maintain dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*): his robes were not properly arranged, he went for alms improperly, he accepted impure food at various places, he accepted food in an impure bowl, and he shouted loudly during the morning and midday meals, like the custom of Brahmin assemblies?
Then the bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice that accords with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
How is it that I have prescribed the precept permitting a wise bhikṣu of ten years' standing to grant formal dependence to others, yet you yourself claim,
"I am wise," and grant formal dependence to others?
Having granted him formal reliance, you did not provide instruction.

Because he was not instructed, he does not maintain proper deportment: his robes are not properly adjusted, he goes for alms improperly, he accepts impure food from various places, he accepts food in an impure bowl, and he shouts loudly and clamorously during the morning and evening meals, like the custom of a Brahmin assembly?
At that time, the World-Honored One, having rebuked him with countless skillful means, addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you shall establish the rules for ācāryas and cause them to practice the duties of an ācārya."
"The ācārya should perform such a rite toward his disciple; he should act in this manner.
The ācārya’s performance of the ācārya-dharma toward his disciple is, in every detail, identical to the upādhyāya’s performance of the upādhyāya-dharma toward his disciple as described above.

The manner in which a disciple performs the duties of a disciple toward an ācārya is, in every detail, the same as the manner in which a disciple performs the duties of a disciple toward an upādhyāya; the text is identical and no different, and therefore it is not set forth here. At that time, those disciples did not serve or revere their upādhyāyas, nor did they comply with the duties of a disciple.
Then the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, you must carry out a formal reprimand against him."
Not knowing how to reprimand him, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to reprimand him by means of five matters. The preceptor should speak as follows:
'I now reprimand you; depart!'"
"Do not enter my room; do not perform services for me; do not come to where I am; I will not speak with you.
These are called the five matters by which a preceptor rebukes his disciple.
The ācārya’s reprimand of a disciple also consists of five matters, saying:
"I now reprimand you; go away! Do not enter my room;
do not perform services for me; do not rely upon me for residence; I shall not speak with you."
"These are called the five matters for which an ācārya may reprove a disciple.
Once the World-Honored One had permitted reproving, [the monks] did not know by what specific matter they should reprove him.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"There are five matters for which a preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) should administer a reprimand to a disciple:
lack of shame, lack of remorse, refusal to accept instruction, engaging in improper conduct, and lack of reverence."
If a disciple possesses these five qualities, the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the teacher (ācārya) should administer a formal reprimand.
Furthermore, there are another five:
being shameless, lacking a sense of moral dread, being difficult to speak with, associating with evil persons, and taking pleasure in visiting the houses of courtesans.
Furthermore, there are five things:
lack of shame, lack of remorse, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in visiting the homes of women.
Furthermore, there are another five things:
Lack of shame, lack of dread, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in going to the homes of unmarried girls.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
lack of shame, lack of dread, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in going to the homes of eunuchs.
Furthermore, there are five things:
lack of shame, lack of remorse, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in going to the nuns' quarters.
Furthermore, there are another five things:
Lacking shame and lacking remorse, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in going to the viharas of śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs.
Furthermore, there are five other matters:
lacking shame, lacking remorse, being difficult to speak with, befriending evil people, and taking pleasure in going to watch the catching of turtles and tortoises.
"If a disciple possesses these five matters, the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the instructor (ācārya) should administer a formal reprimand to them.
Once the Blessed One had authorized the reprimanding of disciples, they continued to reprimand them for as long as they lived. The Buddha said:
"One should not reprimand them for the duration of one's life."
He continued to reprimand him throughout the entire rainy season retreat. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
He then reprimanded the sick man, while his preceptor (upādhyāya), teacher (ācārya), and the other bhikṣus failed to look after him; consequently, the patient became critically ill. The Buddha said:
"One must not reprimand a sick person.
He did not reprimand him while he was present, but another bhikṣu said to him:
"You have already been reprimanded."
He replied, "I have not been rebuked.
The Buddha said:
"One should not reprove someone who is not present.
When he reproved them without having pointed out their transgression, the disciples said,
"What fault have we committed that we are being reproved?"
The Buddha said:
"One should not reprimand without exposing their fault.
One should expose the fault, saying:..."
"You have committed such and such an offense!
Once he had been thus rebuked, he then provided services and performed tasks for him. The Buddha said: "You should not do so."
