After he had rebuked him, [the other] accepted his provisions and performed services for him. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
Because he had been rebuked, he remained in dependence [upon that person]. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
After he had reprimanded him and granted him formal dependence (*niśraya*), the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
Having been thus rebuked, he did not repent; his preceptor and ācārya then departed. The Buddha said:
"One should not act in this way.
Having been rebuked, he then stayed with other bhikṣus, neither performing services for his preceptor and ācārya nor performing services for the other bhikṣus. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done so. After he had been rebuked, no one would comply with him, or he went away on a journey, or abandoned the path, or took no pleasure in the Buddha-dharma. The Buddha said:
"I allow another person to accept [the precepts] with such an intention, acting as his *upādhyāya* and *ācārya*, in order to cause him to repent and restore harmony."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus enticed away the disciples of others. The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not entice away the disciples of others; if one does so, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma."

When that preceptor or instructor has broken the precepts, broken the views, or broken the proper decorum; or if he has been subject to formal censure, or has been expelled, or is liable for expulsion; and when he is of no benefit to the dharma of a śramaṇa, the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to act with this intention:
'The reason we entice him and lead him away is because we wish to cause him to grow and flourish in the dharma of a śramaṇa.'"
After he had been rebuked, he did not confess to his upādhyāya and ācārya. The Buddha said:
"Once one has been rebuked, one should confess to one's upādhyāya and ācārya."
One should perform confession in this manner: baring the right shoulder, removing the leather sandals, placing the right knee on the ground, and joining the palms, one should speak these words:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I now repent and shall never do it again.
If they accept the repentance, that is well;
if they do not accept it, one should further repent at three times each day: early morning, midday, and evening.
If he accepts the confession, it is well;
if he does not accept it, the offender should immediately humble his mind and comply, seeking skillful means to resolve his transgression.
If he humbles his mind, complies, and seeks to resolve his offense without opposition, the teacher should accept it; if he does not accept it, one should deal with him according to the law.
At that time, there was a newly ordained monk who delighted in tranquility and required a formal preceptor (niśraya).
He went to inspect the dwellings and saw a cave in a forest hermitage (āraṇya). He thought to himself:
"If I obtain a preceptor, I shall dwell in this place."
He told the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, if a newly ordained bhikṣu who delights in seclusion requires a formal preceptor (niśraya), he is permitted to go to another place for such dependence and return on the very same day."
"If one does not obtain [a preceptor], it is permitted for a newly ordained bhikṣu who delights in a quiet place to dwell without relying on another.
At that time, a newly ordained bhikṣu already residing there required a formal reliance (niśraya), and he thought:
"The World-Honored One has established a rule that one must not dwell without relying on another."
He then abandoned his dwelling and departed, leaving the residence in ruins.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, when there are newly ordained bhikṣus who must rely upon a senior resident, I permit them to dwell without relying upon one for the sake of protecting the residence."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who resolved to go outside the boundary without any intention of returning.
Having gone outside the boundary, he returned on that very same day.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does this constitute a loss of reliance?
The Buddha said,
"This constitutes a loss of reliance."
The preceptor and ācārya resolved to go outside the boundary; intending not to return, they went outside the boundary, but returned on that very same day.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Has he lost his status as a *niśraya*?"
The Buddha said, "He has lost his formal reliance (niśraya).
At that time, a bhikṣu informed his upādhyāya and ācārya that he wished to go outside the boundary for a short while; having gone outside the boundary, he returned on that very same day.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Does this constitute losing one's formal dependence (niśraya)?
The Buddha said:
"Without losing the basis [of dependence].
At that time, the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the instructor (ācārya) thought to themselves:
"We shall go outside the boundary for a short while."
Having gone outside the boundary, he returned on that very same day.
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Does this constitute a loss of formal reliance?"
The Buddha said,
"The dependence [upon the preceptor] is not lost.
At that time, the bhikṣus took the candidate for ordination outside the boundary and summoned the group of six bhikṣus to confer the precepts upon him.
Those six groups of bhikṣus did not come, and thus they could not receive the precepts.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, whether one is undergoing parivāsa, mūlāpakarṣa, mānatva, ābhāṣaṇa, or performing a karmavācanā, [the candidate must be present]."

Whether it be the establishment of regulations, the reception of precepts, the appointment of personnel by the assembly, or the resolution of matters—regarding such communal affairs, those summoned must attend.
If one fails to attend, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, the bhikṣus led those who were about to receive the precepts outside the boundary and said to the elder,
"Perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman). He replied:
"I do not recite. He then spoke again to those in the middle and lower seats, saying,
"Make the formal announcement (jñapti)."
He also said, "I do not recite it," and thus created an obstacle so that he could not receive the precepts.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, a bhikṣu who has been ordained for five years must recite the *jñapti-karman*; if he does not, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having led the candidate for ordination outside the boundary, said to the elder:
"Recite the formal motion (jñapti). The elder replied:
"I have already recited it; it is not appropriate now.
He then spoke again to the middle and lower seats, saying, "Make the formal announcement (jñapti)."
He also said, "I once recited it, but now it does not come to me. Consequently,
he was unable to receive the precepts.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit bhikṣus who have been ordained for five years to recite the *jñapti-karman* until they are proficient; otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having taken one about to receive the precepts outside the boundary, heard that bandits were approaching; everyone became terrified, rose from their seats and departed, and thus the ordination could not be conferred.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, in cases of the eight difficulties or other such causes and conditions, it is permitted for two or three persons to perform a karmavācanā at one time, but not more than that."
What are called the difficult places are: first, kings; second, thieves; third, fire; fourth, water; fifth, disease; sixth, humans; seventh, non-humans; and eighth, the *śilindhra* insects.

Regarding what is called "other causes and conditions": when there is a large assembly but few sitting mats, or if there are many sick people, it is permitted for two or three persons to perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) simultaneously.
"If there is a large assembly but few dwelling places, or if it rains and the roof leaks, I allow two or three people to perform the *karmavācanā* simultaneously.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there are various urgent matters, is it permissible for more than two or three people to perform the *karmavācanā* simultaneously?"
The Buddha said:
"One must not exceed [the limit].
He sent a messenger to receive formal reliance (*niśraya*); the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He sent a messenger to provide [the student] with a formal reliance (niśraya), and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
At that time, when the preceptor and the ācārya went outside the boundary, the disciple thought to himself:
"The preceptor and the ācārya will return before long; I shall remain here in dependence upon them."
He then remained without a formal preceptor.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, it is permitted for a preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) to travel outside the boundary; on that very day, one should receive formal reliance (niśraya)."
"If you do not accept this, you shall be dealt with according to the law.
Those disciples traveled far outside the boundary, and they thought to themselves:
"We shall return before long; we will stay right here, relying upon our preceptors and teachers as our *upādhyāya*."
He then remained without a formal preceptor.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, it is permitted for a newly ordained guest bhikṣu who requires a formal preceptor not to wash his feet first, nor to drink water first; he must first receive the formal preceptor."
At that time, there was a newly ordained guest bhikṣu who required formal reliance (*niśraya*). He thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established this rule:
'A newly ordained guest bhikṣu must rely upon another; he must not wash his feet first, nor drink water first, but must first receive formal reliance.'"
"When he was receiving formal dependence (*niśraya*), he fainted and fell to the ground, whereupon he fell ill.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:

'From this day forward, it is permitted for a visiting bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts to require dependence; however, he must first wash his feet, first drink water, and rest for a short while before receiving dependence.'"

If one receives dependence (*niśraya*) from a teacher without making a careful selection, and that teacher has broken the precepts, broken the view, or broken the proper conduct; or if the teacher has been subjected to censure, formal dependence, or suspension; or if the teacher has been barred from entering the homes of laypeople; or if the teacher has been formally censured (*utkṣepaka*), there will be no long-term benefit for the practice of a śramaṇa.
The Buddha said: "From this day forward, one must not receive dependence from a teacher without having first made a careful selection."

He granted dependence without making a careful selection; consequently, the disciple may have broken the precepts, broken the view, or broken the proper conduct, or he may have been subject to censure, or expelled, or placed under dependence, or barred from entering the homes of laypeople, or formally accused.
The Buddha said:
"One must not fail to choose and rely upon a preceptor.
At that time, a newly ordained bhikṣu fell ill and required a preceptor; he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has decreed:
'One who does not rely [on a teacher] may not dwell.
That very day, he abandoned his dwelling place and departed; consequently, his illness grew more severe."
Then the bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, if a newly ordained bhikṣu is ill and requires dependence [upon another], it is permitted for him to remain without depending [on another]."
At that time, the one who was looking after the newly ordained sick bhikṣu required a formal reliance (niśraya). He thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established this rule:
'One may not dwell without a reliance.'"
After he had abandoned the sick man and departed, the patient passed away.
The bhikṣus went and informed the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted for those who attend to a newly ordained sick bhikṣu to remain without a formal preceptor."

Those bhikṣus’ preceptors and ācāryas, along with the Saṃgha, performed a formal act (karmavācanā) against them: they imposed a reprimand (tarjanīya), a banishment (pravāsanīya), a period of dependence (niśraya), a prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople (pratisaṃharaṇīya), and a formal censure (utkṣepanīya).
The bhikṣus thought to themselves,
"Has our formal dependence been lost?
The Buddha said:
"Without losing their basis of reliance.

Those disciples were subjected by the Saṃgha to formal acts (*karmavācanā*): from the act of censure (*tarjanīyakarman*) up to the act of prohibiting them from entering the homes of laypeople (*apravāsanīyakarman*), and the act of suspension (*utksepanīyakarman*).
The bhikṣus thought to themselves,
"Has our formal dependence been lost?
The Buddha said:
"Is the basis of dependence lost?
Those monks thought as follows regarding their preceptors and teachers for whom the Saṃgha had performed an act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (formal expulsion):
"Has the basis of dependence been lost?"
The Buddha said, "He has lost his formal reliance.
The monks then performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against those disciples. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Does this constitute a loss of formal reliance?
The Buddha said,
"It constitutes a loss of formal reliance."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the city of Rājagṛha.

Then Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, leading his assembly of followers, left the household life to study the Path; Śāṇavāsin’s disciples, numbering two hundred and fifty, also left the household life to study the Path; and sons of wealthy, noble, and influential families from within the city of Rājagṛha likewise left the household life to study the Path. This great multitude of people thus resided in the city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, the various ministers said to one another:
"Now, these other-worldly renunciants who study the Way wander through the human realm during spring, autumn, winter, and summer;
yet these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas dwell together in this very place and do not wander elsewhere. This must be because this location is the most excellent."
At that time, having heard this, the bhikṣus reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One then addressed Ānanda:
"Go from room to room and command the bhikṣus, saying:"
“The World-Honored One now wishes to travel south among the people; those who wish to attend upon him may do so as they please.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, went from room to room and said to the bhikṣus:
“The World-Honored One now wishes to travel south; any bhikṣus who wish to attend upon him may do so as they please.”
At that time, there was a newly ordained bhikṣu who possessed faith and devotion, who said to Ānanda:
"If our preceptors and teachers depart, we shall depart; if they do not depart, we shall not depart."

Why is this? We are newly ordained bhikṣus; if we go away, we must rely upon a preceptor for dependence, and upon returning here, we would again have to receive dependence. People would then say of us that we are fickle and lack resolve.
At that time, the World-Honored One, taking a small number of bhikṣus, traveled through the southern regions and later returned to Rājagṛha.
Then the World-Honored One, observing that the assembly of bhikṣus traveling in the south was small, though he already knew the reason, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason are there so few bhikṣus?"
Ānanda reported all these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:

"From this day forward, it is permitted for bhikṣus who have been ordained for five years and possess wisdom, as well as those who have been ordained for ten years and possess wisdom [to perform such duties]."
A bhikṣu of five years' standing should receive dependence (niśraya) from a bhikṣu of ten years' standing.
If he is foolish and lacks wisdom, he must remain in dependence for as long as life lasts.
There are five things that cause one to lose dependence:
First, reprimand by the teacher; second, departure; third, cessation of the path; fourth, not granting dependence; fifth, entering the boundary of the ordination platform (*sīmā*).
Furthermore, there are five matters:
first, death; second, departure; third, cessation of the path; fourth, not granting dependence; fifth, whether having completed five years or exceeding five years.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
if [the preceptor] dies, if he departs, if he abandons the path, if he does not grant dependence, or if one sees his original *upādhyāya*.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
Whether [the teacher] dies, departs, ceases from the path, does not grant dependence, or whether the preceptor (upādhyāya) or ācārya ceases from the path.
Furthermore, there are five other cases:
if [the teacher] dies, departs, ceases from the path, does not grant dependence, or if the disciple ceases from the path.
Furthermore, there are five circumstances:
death; departure; cessation of the path; not being granted dependence; or the passing away of the preceptor or the teacher.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
if [the teacher] dies, if he departs, if he abandons the path, if he does not grant dependence, or if the disciple passes away.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
Whether one dies, departs, abandons the path, is not granted dependence, or returns to dwell under the direct supervision of one's preceptor—
these are the five matters by which one loses dependence.
If one lacks five qualities, one is not permitted to bestow the full ordination upon others:

if one has not achieved perfection in morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; lacking these five qualities, one may not bestow the full ordination upon others.
If one accomplishes five qualities, one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; this is the reverse of the preceding statement.
Furthermore, there are five other qualities which, if accomplished, prevent one from conferring the full ordination upon others:

one’s own morality is not accomplished; one cannot teach others to abide firmly in morality; one’s own concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation are not accomplished; and one cannot teach others to abide firmly in concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. If one accomplishes these five qualities [in such a deficient manner], one may not confer the full ordination upon others.
The five qualities by whose fulfillment one may bestow the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another are the opposites of the aforementioned points.
Furthermore, there are five other qualities by whose fulfillment one may not bestow the full ordination upon another:
lack of faith, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, laziness, and forgetfulness. One who possesses these five qualities may not bestow the full ordination upon another.
There are five qualities that, when accomplished, allow one to bestow the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; these are the opposites of the aforementioned [five] points.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that, when accomplished, prevent one from bestowing the full ordination upon others:

having violated the higher morality (*adhiśīla*), having violated the higher view (*adṛṣṭi*), having violated the higher conduct (*adhicaryā*), having little learning (*alpaśruta*), and lacking wisdom (*aprajñā*). If one accomplishes these five qualities, one is not permitted to bestow the full ordination upon others.
There are five qualities that, when accomplished, permit one to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others—the reverse of the aforementioned points.
Furthermore, there are five qualities that, even if accomplished, do not permit one to confer the full ordination:

being unable to attend to a sick disciple; being unable to have another attend to them until they recover or pass away; if a disciple is dissatisfied with their dwelling place, being unable to skillfully move them to another location; if a doubt arises, being unable to resolve the disciple’s mind according to the Dharma, according to the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, nor being able to eliminate it in accordance with the Dharma; being unable to instruct the disciple to abandon evil views and abide in right views; or being less than ten years [of standing]. If one possesses these five qualities, one may not confer the full ordination upon others.
There are five qualities that, when accomplished, permit one to bestow full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; these are the opposites of the aforementioned [five].
Furthermore, there are five qualities that, when accomplished, prevent one from bestowing full ordination upon others:

not knowing what constitutes an offense, not knowing what does not constitute an offense, not knowing whether an offense is light or heavy, and being less than ten years [of standing]. One who possesses these five qualities may not bestow full ordination upon others.
If one accomplishes five qualities, one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; this is the reverse of the preceding statement.
Furthermore, there are five other qualities which, if accomplished, prevent one from conferring the full ordination:

not knowing how to instruct disciples regarding superior deportment (*ācāra*), superior pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), superior Prātimokṣa, and the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*). One who accomplishes these five qualities is not permitted to confer the full ordination upon others.
The attainment of five qualities whereby one may confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others is the reverse of the aforementioned points.
Furthermore, there are five qualities which, if not attained, prevent one from conferring the full ordination:

not knowing the higher training in morality (*adhiśīla*), not knowing the higher training in mind (*adhicitta*), not knowing the higher training in wisdom (*adhiprajñā*), not knowing the formal motion (*jñapti*), and not knowing the ritual procedure (*karman*). If one possesses these five qualities, one is not permitted to confer the full ordination upon others.
One who has accomplished five qualities may bestow the full ordination upon others:

one who knows the increase of morality, the increase of mind, the increase of wisdom, and who knows the white *karmavācanā*. One who accomplishes these five qualities may bestow the full ordination upon others.

"In this manner, [the cases of] not being permitted to grant dependence and being permitted to grant dependence, and not being permitted to keep a śrāmaṇera and being permitted to keep a śrāmaṇera, are all as stated above.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha."
At that time, there was a naked ascetic (nirgrantha) in the city named Posadha, who was skilled in debate and would constantly proclaim:
"If there is any śramaṇa son of the Śākyas here who can debate with me, let him come forth."
Then Śāriputra said, "I am capable of debating with you. At that time,
the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
“Treatises are of four kinds:

some treatises exhaust the meaning but not the phrasing; some exhaust the phrasing but not the meaning; some exhaust both the phrasing and the meaning; and some exhaust neither the phrasing nor the meaning.”

There are four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid): the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (nirukti-pratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of expression (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid).
If a master of discourse possesses these four analytical knowledges, it is impossible that his words and meanings would ever be exhausted.
"Now, it is impossible that Śāriputra, having achieved these four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), would say that both the phrasing and the meaning are exhausted.
That naked ascetic then challenged Śāriputra with a question regarding the meaning, and Śāriputra immediately replied, resolving the matter.

Then that naked ascetic challenged Śāriputra with five hundred difficult questions; Śāriputra immediately matched those five hundred challenges and further interrogated him with questions on profound meanings, until the naked ascetic was unable to resolve the questions he had posed.
At that time, the naked ascetic immediately thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! How marvelous!"
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas are exceedingly wise and intelligent; would it not be well for me now to go forth from the household life under them and study the Path?
He then went to the saṃghārāma, and seeing the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas, Upananda, from afar, he had this thought:
"If even those śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas who have little learning possess such wisdom, how much more must those with great learning possess it? How could they not?"
He went before the Śākya son Upananda and said,
"I wish to leave the household life to study the Path.
At that time, Upananda immediately ordained him as a disciple and conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
Later, at another time, he questioned Baddhala on a point of doctrine but was unable to answer.
At that moment, the naked ascetic again had this thought:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are ignorant and know nothing; I should now abandon the religious life."
He immediately donned the *kāṣāya* and entered among the assembly of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I authorize the granting of the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) for a four-month period of communal residence within the monastic community of non-Buddhists. It should be granted in this manner."
Having first shaved his hair, put on the *kāṣāya*, and removed his leather sandals, he should place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and be instructed to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

"I, [Name], a follower of external paths, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha. I seek to go forth from the household life into the path under the World-Honored One; the World-Honored One is my Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time:

"I, [Name], a follower of external paths, having taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, shall go forth under the Tathāgata to study the Path; the Tathāgata is my Truly Realized, Perfectly Awakened One."
Thus it is said a second and third time.

One should then instruct them in the receiving of the precepts: "To refrain from taking life for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept; ... up to ... to refrain from possessing gold, silver, or precious objects for as long as one lives is a śrāmaṇera precept. These are the ten śrāmaṇera precepts; they must not be transgressed for as long as one lives."

That outsider should first go among the community of monks, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, and prostrate at the feet of the monks. Then, kneeling with his right knee on the ground and joining his palms, he should be instructed to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
"I, [Name], a non-Buddhist, request from the Saṃgha a four-month period of co-residence. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me a four-month period of co-residence.

Having spoken thus a second and third time, he should be placed by the assembly in a location where he can see them but not hear them. Then, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
That outsider, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha a four-month period of co-residence.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant that outsider, so-and-so, a four-month period of co-residence.
[The motion] is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
That outsider named so-and-so has requested from the Saṃgha a four-month period of co-residence; the Saṃgha now grants him a four-month period of co-residence."
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha granting him a four-month probationary period (parivāsa) remain silent; whoever does not approve should speak.
"The Sangha has already approved granting that outsider a four-month probationary period. Since the Sangha approves by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

After those outsiders have completed their period of probationary co-residence and have caused the minds of the bhikṣus to be joyful, they shall then receive full ordination through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* within the community of monks.
Why is it that these non-Buddhists cannot gladden the hearts of the bhikṣus?

Because those non-Buddhists, by their very nature, cling to the ways of the non-Buddhist layfolk; they do not associate with the bhikṣus but associate with non-Buddhists, and instead of following the bhikṣus, they recite and study heterodox doctrines.
If they hear someone speak ill of the non-Buddhists, they give rise to anger; if they hear someone disparage the teachings of their own non-Buddhist masters, they likewise give rise to anger.
Upon hearing accounts of unrighteous matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they leap for joy;
if heterodox outsiders come and praise the excellent qualities of their own path, they leap for joy;
and if teachers of heterodox paths come and hear praise for their doctrines, they likewise leap for joy.
If one hears it said that the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are not the true Dharma, yet one still feels joy and exultation,
this is called an externalist who cannot cause the bhikṣus to rejoice.
How, then, can an externalist cause the bhikṣus to rejoice?
"The opposite of the preceding statement is true; this is called dwelling together with non-Buddhists in harmony and concord, causing the bhikṣus to rejoice.

At that time, there was a certain non-Buddhist who was granted a four-month period of probation by the Saṃgha. While undergoing this probationary stay, he attained the mind of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"If one has attained the mind of right determination, one should grant the full ordination through the rite of white-fourfold proclamation (jñapti-caturtha-karman)."
When the naked ascetic Poṣadha heard these words, he thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are wise and intelligent; would it not be better for me now to return to them, leave the household life, and train in the Path?"
He immediately went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to leave the household life to study the Path.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This one who ruins both internal and external paths will gain no benefit within my Dharma; if he has not yet received full ordination, you should not grant him full ordination."
"Those who have already received [the precepts] shall be expelled.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the city of Rājagṛha.
Then King Bimbisāra of Magadha addressed the people of the country, saying:

"Those who wish to go forth and study the Path among the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are permitted to practice the holy life well within the Dharma of the Tathāgata to bring an end to all suffering.
At that time, a certain slave came to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to go forth and become a bhikṣu."

Then the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going forth into the Way. As he gradually went among the people to beg for food, he was seized by his former master, who cried out at the top of his voice:
"Stop! Do not seize me!"
"Stop! Do not seize me!
The laypeople standing nearby asked, "Why are you calling out?"
He replied, “This man has seized me.
He then questioned that man, saying:
"Why have you seized him? He replied,
"He is my household slave."
The laypeople said to him, "Release him; you should not seize him!
You may fail to capture this man, or you may be punished by the authorities."
How is this known?

King Bimbisāra of Magadha previously issued a decree: "If there are those who can leave the household life to study the Path among the Śramaṇa sons of the Śākya, they shall be permitted to practice the holy life well within the Dharma of the Tathāgata and attain the end of suffering; let there be no obstacles."
The master immediately released him, crying out in indignation:
"How tragic! This is my slave, yet he has not attained his freedom.
Looking at it now, these śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are all nothing but a gathering of slaves!"
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not ordain slaves; if anyone ordains one, they shall be dealt with according to the law."
At that time, there was a prisoner who had broken out of jail and fled; he came to the garden and said to the bhikṣus, "I wish to leave the household life to study the Path."
At that time, the bhikṣus would arbitrarily ordain people as renunciants and confer full ordination upon them.
Then, the prison official, checking the register, asked the jailers:
"Where is the criminal prisoner so-and-so now?"
The jailer replied, "A certain criminal prisoner has broken out of prison and fled; he has gone forth as a renunciant under the śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas.
At that time, the prison officials all spoke with resentment, saying:
“Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
You have no sense of shame or modesty, yet you claim of yourselves:
‘We know the True Dharma.’”
"In this way, what true Dharma can there be?
Now, observe these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas!
They are all nothing but a gathering of thieves."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not ordain thieves; if anyone ordains one, they shall be dealt with according to the law."
At that time, there was a debtor who, having fled from his creditors, came to the garden and said to the bhikṣus,
"Ordain me so that I may leave the household life and practice the Way."

At that time, the bhikṣus would ordain people at will; once they had received full ordination, they went among the people to beg for food and were seized by householders, who cried out in a loud voice:
"Stop! Do not seize me!"
"Stop! Do not seize me!
When the laypeople nearby heard this, they immediately asked, "Why are you calling out?"
He replied, "This man has seized me.
He then questioned that man, saying:
"Why have you seized me? He replied, "I owe you wealth."
The people said to him:
"Release him; do not seize him. Since you have obtained no wealth, you may be punished by the authorities. Why is this?"

King Bimbisāra of Magadha had previously issued a decree: "If there are those who wish to leave the household life to study the Path, they shall be permitted to cultivate the holy life well and reach the end of suffering; let them do as they please without any hindrance."
The creditor immediately released him, but gave rise to anger and said:
"I lent him my wealth and yet could not recover it; judging by this, all these śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas are nothing but debtors."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, you must not ordain those who are burdened by debt. If anyone should ordain them, they shall be dealt with according to the law."
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
There were seventeen groups of youths who were close friends; the eldest among them was seventeen years old and the youngest was twelve.
The wealthiest among them possessed eight million [kārṣāpaṇas], while the poorest possessed eighty thousand.
Among them was a young boy named Upāli; his parents had only this one son and loved him so dearly that they never let him out of their sight.
His parents thought to themselves: "What craft or skill should we teach this child?"
"After we have died, we shall live happily with nothing lacking.
They then thought to themselves:
"We should first teach them to learn writing; after we have died, they will live happily with nothing lacking, and their physical strength will not be exhausted by toil."
He further thought to himself:
"Teaching my son to learn writing will also cause him physical exhaustion and suffering!
What other craft might I teach him?"
"Once we have passed away, we shall live happily without any lack or deficiency, and our physical strength will not be exhausted by suffering. They thought:

"We should now teach this child the art of calculation and technical skills; then, after we have passed away, we shall live happily without any lack or deficiency, and our physical strength will not be exhausted by suffering."
The parents thought to themselves:
"Now, teaching our son to study arithmetic has also caused him physical exhaustion and suffering!
What other craft should we now teach this boy?"
"After we have passed away, we shall live happily, lacking for nothing, and our physical strength will not be exhausted by toil.
We should now teach this child the craft of painting images; after we have passed away, we shall live happily, lacking for nothing."
He further thought to himself:
"Now, if I teach this boy the craft of painting images, I fear his eyesight will become weary and exhausted.
What other craft should I teach this boy instead?"
"After we have died, we shall live happily, lacking nothing, and our eyes will not suffer from fatigue.
They then thought: "The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas truly nourish their bodies well; they dwell in peace and happiness, free from all suffering and affliction."

"If we were to instruct this child to leave the household life and enter the path within the Dharma of the Śramaṇa Śākyaputrīyas, after our deaths we would live happily, lacking for nothing and without physical exhaustion or suffering."
Later, at another time, the seventeen young boys said to the boy Upāli:
"You should follow us and go forth from the household life to practice the Way."
He replied, "What use would I have for going forth?
You go forth yourself."
The group of seventeen youths spoke to Upāli a second and a third time, saying:
"Come, let us go forth together to follow the Way.
For what reason?"
"We shall now enjoy ourselves together, and we shall likewise sport and enjoy ourselves there as well.
Then the youth Upāli said to the other youths, "Wait a moment!"
"I must inform my parents.
The youth Upāli then went to his parents and said, "I now wish to leave the home life to follow the Way; I pray that you will grant me your permission."
The parents replied, "We have only you, our one son;
we cherish you with all our hearts. We would not wish for even death to cause us to be parted from you, much less a separation while still alive."
The youth Upāli addressed his parents in this way a second and a third time, saying:
"I pray that you will grant me permission to go forth.
His parents likewise replied:
"We have only you, our one son; we cherish you with all our hearts, even to the point that we do not wish for you to die and be separated from us, much less to be separated while still alive.
At that time, having received Upāli’s repeated and earnest entreaties, the parents thought to themselves:
"We already had this intention previously:"
"What craft should we teach this child?
After we have passed away, we wish for him to live a comfortable life without lack or deficiency, and so that his physical strength will not be exhausted by toil."
He then had this thought:

"If we teach [the children] writing and even painting, after our deaths they will easily make their living without any lack; it will not cause their physical strength to become exhausted or suffer. However, I fear that laboring the children's physical strength and eyesight might lead them to exhaustion and suffering."
He thought to himself:

"Only the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, truly nourish their bodies well and are free from manifold sufferings and afflictions. If I were to let this child go forth among them, he would live happily and be free from all suffering."
Then his parents replied to their son, saying, "Now is the very time; we grant you permission to go forth.
Thereupon Upāli returned to where the group of seventeen youths was and said to them:
"My parents have already granted me permission to go forth; if you wish to leave as well, now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, the youths went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable Sirs!"
"I wish to leave the household life to study the Way; I pray that you, the Venerable Ones, will grant me ordination as a seeker of the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going-forth and conferred the full precepts upon him.
The young boys, having been accustomed to music since childhood, could not endure even a single meal; by midnight, suffering from hunger, they cried out in loud voices, saying, "Give us food!"
"Give me some food!
The bhikṣus said to him, "Wait a moment until daybreak; if the Saṃgha has any food, we shall eat with you."
"If there were none, we would have gone for alms together with you.
Why? Because in this place, there was originally no place at all where food was prepared."
At that time, while the World-Honored One was meditating in a quiet place during the night, he heard the sound of a child crying. Knowing the cause, he intentionally asked Ānanda:
"What child is crying at this hour of midnight?"
Ānanda reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One told Ānanda:
"One should not confer the full precepts upon one who is less than twenty years of age."

Why is this? If one has not yet reached twenty years of age, they are unable to endure cold and heat, hunger and thirst, wind and rain, mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects, nor can they endure harsh words; if their body experiences various pains and they cannot endure them, or if they are unable to maintain the precepts and the practice of eating once a day, then if such a person is ordained, allowed to leave the household life, and receives full ordination (*upasampadā*), they shall be dealt with according to the law.
"Ānanda, you should know that one who has reached the age of twenty is capable of enduring the various matters mentioned above.
At that time, five kinds of diseases appeared within the borders of the kingdom of Magadha:
first, leprosy; second, carbuncles; third, white leprosy; fourth, consumption; and fifth, insanity.
Those people in that country who suffered from this illness all went to the youth Jīvaka and said:
"We pray only that you will treat us; we shall give you such and such wealth."
The youth Jīvaka replied, "I cannot treat you.
Then the patient spoke again, saying:
"We only pray that you will save us; we shall provide everything our household possesses, as well as our own bodies, wives, and children, to serve you.
Jīvaka replied, "I cannot cure your ailment."
Then the sick people said to one another:
"This man’s mind is set; he will certainly not treat us. We should go to that place where he wishes to treat those he desires."
At that time, various sick people came to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to leave the household life and study the Path.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus immediately ordained them as monks.

At that time, the youth Jīvaka treated the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, administering emetics and purgatives. For those who could be given soup, he prepared it; for those to whom it was not suitable, he did not prepare it. For some, he made soup with the meat of wild birds, providing whatever the patients ate so that they might recover from their illnesses. Once they had recovered, they all returned to secular life and abandoned the path.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka was traveling along a road when he saw a former practitioner of the Way coming toward him. Having seen him, he said to him:
"Did you not previously go forth as a renunciant?"
He replied, "I have gone forth. He asked:
"Why have you ceased your practice of the Way? He replied,
"I previously had an ailment and went to your place seeking treatment, saying:"
"I shall give you such and such wealth," yet you replied to me,
"I am unable to cure it."

"I further entreated you again to treat me, promising to provide everything in my household, as well as my own person, wife, and children, for your service; yet you remained set in your ways and still did not agree to treat me."
We said to one another: "This man’s mind is set;
he will certainly not treat our illnesses for us. We should go instead to that place where he wishes to treat them, and there he will surely treat us."

"Because of this illness, we went to the saṃghārāma and temporarily sought ordination to treat our disease; originally, we had no faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha when we were ordained."
When Jīvaka heard this, he was displeased and immediately went to the World-Honored One. Prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Formerly, because I was treating the illnesses of the Saṃgha, I relinquished my royal duties; yet these bhikṣus have ordained those suffering from five kinds of diseases:
leprosy, abscesses, white leprosy, consumption, and insanity.”

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will take pity on us and command the bhikṣus that from this day forward they shall no longer ordain those with these five kinds of diseases as followers of the Way.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently consented.

At that time, Jīvaka, knowing that the World-Honored One had consented by remaining silent, rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
Then, on account of this matter, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“You should all know!”
Because the youth Jīvaka previously abandoned his royal duties to treat the illnesses and suffering of the Saṃgha, the bhikṣus have now arbitrarily ordained those with five kinds of diseases.
From this day forward, one must not ordain those with five kinds of diseases by bestowing the full precepts (upasaṃpadā); if anyone does so, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
In that city there was a bhikṣu named Nandi, who constantly delighted in sitting meditation and had attained worldly concentration and liberation of mind.

When he arose from the fourth dhyāna, a māra-maiden came and stood before him; the bhikṣu seized her with the intent to violate her, whereupon the māra immediately went outside, and the bhikṣu followed him outside as well.
When that Māra went out from the veranda, the bhikṣu also followed him out from the veranda.
When he went out into the courtyard, the bhikṣu also went into the courtyard.
When Māra further went out to the exterior of the monastery, the bhikṣu also went to the exterior of the monastery.
Outside the monastery there was a dead stallion; whenever Māra went to the place of the dead horse, he would immediately vanish, and his celestial body would not appear.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nandika engaged in unchaste conduct right there at the dead horse. Having committed the unchaste act, he had no intention whatsoever to conceal it and thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu commits unchaste conduct, he commits a pārājika offense and may no longer dwell in the community.'"
"I have now committed an act of impure conduct; yet, I have no intention to conceal it. Will I not have committed a *pārājika* offense? What should I do now?
He then spoke to a friend, a bhikṣu, saying:
“The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: ‘If one commits an impure act, one incurs a pārājika offense and may no longer dwell in the community.
Now, I have committed an impure act of sexual misconduct, yet I have no intention to conceal it; could it be that I have incurred a pārājika offense?’”
"Excellent, Elder!
Please inform the World-Honored One for me.
If there be any instruction, I shall carry it out."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One. On account of this, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"The Saṃgha shall now confer the *pārājika* discipline upon the bhikṣu Nandiya by means of a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."

Having made this grant, he sent the bhikṣu Nandiya to the midst of the Saṃgha. With his right shoulder bared, having removed his leather sandals, prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, and knelt with his right knee on the ground, he joined his palms and made this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
I, the bhikṣu Nandi, have committed an act of impure conduct without any intention to conceal it.
I now beg the Saṃgha for the *pārājika* discipline; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *pārājika* discipline.
In this manner, it is said a second and third time.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!..."
This Bhikṣu Nandiya has committed an act of impure conduct without a mind of concealment; he now requests from the Saṃgha the *pārājika* discipline.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now bestow upon the Bhikṣu Nandiya the *pārājika* discipline.
[The motion] is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Nanda has committed an act of unchastity without any intention to conceal it, and he now begs the Saṃgha for the *pārājika* discipline."
The Saṃgha now confers the Pārājika penalty upon the bhikṣu Nandiya.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s conferring of the Pārājika penalty upon the bhikṣu Nandiya should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the *pārājika* penalty to the bhikṣu Nandi; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus, this matter is upheld as such."
"Having been granted the *pārājika* precepts, you should practice them accordingly in every matter."

One who practices in accordance with the Dharma must not confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; must not provide dependence (*niśraya*) to others; must not keep *śrāmaṇeras*; if appointed to instruct nuns, one must not accept; even if appointed, one should not go to instruct them; one must not recite the precepts for the Saṃgha; one must not engage in questions and answers regarding the Vinaya within the Saṃgha; one must not accept an appointment from the Saṃgha to serve as an administrator (*vaiyāvṛtyakara*); one must not accept a formal judicial decision from the Saṃgha; one must not accept a mission from the Saṃgha; one must not enter a village early or return late; one should associate with bhikṣus and must not associate with non-Buddhists or laypeople; one should comply with the rules of the bhikṣus and must not speak of other worldly matters; one must not recite the Vinaya in the midst of the assembly, though it is permitted if there is no one else capable of reciting it.

You must not commit this offense again, nor should you commit others that are similar to it, derived from it, or worse than it; you must not invalidate the *saṃgha-karman* or those who perform the *karman*;

you must not accept the spreading of seats, the washing of feet, the wiping of leather sandals with water, or the massaging of the body by pure bhikṣus, nor should you accept their prostrations, welcoming, or inquiries after their well-being; you must not accept the holding of robes or alms bowls from pure bhikṣus; you must not bring a pure bhikṣu before the assembly for a formal remembrance (*smṛti-vinaya*) or a confession of fault (*pratijñā-kāraka-vinaya*); you must not testify against a person of integrity; you must not obstruct a pure bhikṣu during the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*); and you must not engage in disputes with pure bhikṣus.

"When a *pārājika* bhikṣu comes or does not come during the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) or its formal procedures (*karmavācanā*), the assembly of monks incurs no offense. The bhikṣus then asked:
"If a bhikṣu who has been given the *pārājika* [exclusion] commits the grave offense of sexual misconduct again, may he receive the *pārājika* exclusion once more?"
The Buddha said, "You should not do so; he should be expelled.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Kapilavastu, the city of the Śākyas.
At that time, when it was the proper hour, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Kapilavastu to beg for food;

having finished his almsround, he returned and left the city. At that moment, Rāhula’s mother, together with Rāhula, saw the Buddha approaching from atop a high pavilion and said to Rāhula, "The one coming there is your father."
At that time, Rāhula quickly descended from the tower and went to where the Tathāgata was; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet and stood to one side.
Then the World-Honored One stroked Rāhula’s head with his hand, and Rāhula thought to himself:
"Since my birth, I have never before experienced such exquisite, smooth, and soft pleasure."
The Buddha asked,
"Are you able to leave the household life to study the Way? He replied:
"I am able to leave the household life.
At that time, the Buddha extended a finger for Rāhula to grasp; leading him into the saṃghārāma, he addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"You shall ordain this youth Rāhula."

He should be ordained in this manner: having shaved his hair and taught him to don the *kāṣāya*, with his right shoulder bared, having removed his leather sandals, and having placed his right knee on the ground with palms joined, he should speak thus:

"I, Rāhula, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha of Bhikṣus. I go forth from home to study the Path under the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is my Truly Realized, Perfectly Awakened One."
Thus he spoke a second and a third time:
"I, Rāhula, have completed my refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; I have gone forth under the Tathāgata to study the Path. The Tathāgata is my Truly Realized, Perfectly Awakened One."
Thus he speaks a second and a third time. He should then instruct him on the reception of the precepts, saying:

"For as long as life lasts, you must not kill; this is called a śrāmaṇera precept. ... [and so on] ... up to: for as long as life lasts, you must not handle gold, silver, or precious objects; this is called a śrāmaṇera precept. These are the ten śrāmaṇera precepts, which must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts."
Then Śāriputra replied, “So be it.
Having received these instructions and ordained the youth Rāhula, he led him to where the Tathāgata was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
Then Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have already ordained Rāhula.
How should I provide him with a room and bedding as a śrāmaṇera?"
The Buddha said, "From this day forward, let them be given in succession starting from the great bhikṣus.
At that time, the young śrāmaṇeras soiled the woven rope beds, seats, and bedding with their excrement, urine, and vomit.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not allow śrāmaṇeras to sit or lie upon these rope-woven beds.
However, if they can protect them from being soiled, their sitting or lying there is permitted."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When the Saṃgha receives offerings, how should a portion be given to the śrāmaṇeras?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"If the Sangha is in harmony, it should be given equally; if they are not in harmony, half should be given.
If they are still not in harmony, one-third should be given."
"If it is not done so, the Sangha shall not divide [the offerings]; if they do divide them, they must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "Regarding the small meal and the large meal, how should these be given to a śrāmaṇera?"
The Buddha said, “He shall be given [ordination] according to the sequence of the Great Sangha.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, hearing that the Buddha had ordained Rāhula and allowed him to go forth, came weeping to the saṃghārāma to the place where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. Once seated to one side, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"When the World-Honored One went forth into homelessness, I had a slight hope that the youth Nanda would take over the family business; yet the World-Honored One has now ordained him as well."

Since Nanda has already left the household life, I still harbored a slight hope that Rāhula would carry on the family business as the successor so that our lineage would not be severed; yet now the World-Honored One has ordained him as well.
Parents provide their children with much benefit, nursing and caring for them until they reach maturity; this is what the people of the world observe.
Yet these bhikṣus, without the parents' permission, arbitrarily ordain them.
"I only pray that from this day forward, the World-Honored One will command all bhikṣus: 'If one's parents do not give permission, one must not be ordained and allowed to leave the household life.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted the king’s words.

When the King saw that the World-Honored One had accepted his words by remaining silent, he immediately rose from his seat, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these circumstances, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“Parents bestow great benefit upon their children; they nourish and breastfeed them, hoping they will grow to maturity—this is what is observed by the people of the world.”
However, there were bhikṣus who would ordain individuals even when their parents had not given permission.

From this day forward, no one shall be ordained or allowed to go forth into homelessness without the permission of their parents; if anyone ordains them, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, while the Buddha was staying at Kausāmbī in the Ghosira Park,
there was the son of a master craftsman who came to the saṃghārāma and requested the bhikṣus to allow him to go forth and practice the Way.
The bhikṣus would arbitrarily grant ordination and allow them to enter the religious life.
At that time, their parents came to the saṃghārāma weeping and asked the bhikṣus,
"Have you seen such a small child coming here?"
The one who had not seen him replied,
"I did not see him. Thereupon,
[the others] searched through the various rooms and found him.
At that time, the householders all criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"The Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
They have no sense of shame and tell lies; yet they claim for themselves: "
"I am practicing the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
Having just rescued my young child, everyone says they saw nothing.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The World-Honored One said: "Listen well!
From this day forward, if you wish to have your hair shaved within the saṃghārāma, you must inform the entire Saṃgha."
If the Saṃgha is not in assembly, one should inform each individual cell by speaking to them, and only then grant the tonsure;
if the Saṃgha is in assembly, one should perform the formal announcement (jñapti), and only after the announcement has been made should one grant the tonsure.
One should make the following formal announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!
This person, so-and-so, wishes to have his hair shaved by so-and-so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let us grant [the hair-cutting ceremony] to so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement.
If one wishes to ordain someone by shaving their hair within a monastery, one must announce this to the entire Saṃgha; once the announcement has been made, they may be granted the going-forth.
One should make the formal motion as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth under so-and-so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let [the name] be granted the going forth.
Thus is the formal motion.

Having made this motion, grant him the going forth. Instruct him to put on the kāṣāya, expose the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak these words:

"I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Sangha. I follow the Tathāgata to leave the household life, with [Name] as my preceptor; the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One."
In this manner, he speaks a second and third time:

“I, [Name], take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Having completed my going forth following the Tathāgata, with [Name] as my preceptor, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, is my World-Honored One.”
Thus it was said a second and a third time. When receiving the precepts, one should say:
"For as long as life lasts, I shall not kill living beings; this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I am able.
"To refrain from stealing for as long as life lasts— this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I am able.
"To refrain from sexual misconduct for as long as life lasts— this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replied, "I am able.
"To refrain from false speech for as long as life lasts— this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replied, "I am able.
"To refrain from drinking alcohol for as long as one lives— this is called a śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, one must not wear flower garlands or smear the body with perfumes; this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, you must not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor go to witness or listen to them; this is called the precept of a śrāmaṇera."
The capable one replies, "I am able.
"For as long as life lasts, one must not sit upon high, wide, or large beds; this is called a śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I am able.
"For as long as life lasts, one must not eat at improper times; this is called a śrāmaṇera precept."
The capable one replies, "I can.
"For as long as life lasts, one must not hold or possess gold, silver, or precious objects, whether raw or wrought; this is called the śrāmaṇera precept."
The one capable of upholding them replies, "I can.
"These are the ten precepts for śrāmaṇeras; they must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts."
The one capable of maintaining it replied, "I can.

At that time, there was a young śrāmaṇera whom the community of monks did not permit to enter and dwell near the village monastery or in an araṇya; consequently, the śrāmaṇera was killed by a leopard.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"One must not obstruct a young śrāmaṇera on both sides.
At that time, in some village monasteries where there was no forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), they obstructed the śrāmaṇeras; the Buddha said:
"It should not be so. In that forest hermitage where there was no monastery near a village, he forbade the śrāmaṇera; the Buddha said: "It should not be so."
He further barred the śrāmaṇera from entering crowded places, the heated bathhouse, the dining hall, and the walking hall; as the śrāmaṇera had no place to stay overnight, the Buddha said:
"One should not bar him from entering crowded places, up to and including the walking hall."

If there are many people staying on the upper floor of a building and many people walking on the lower floor, or if there are many people walking on the lower floor and many people staying on the upper floor, one may say:
"Do not enter my place of rest."

At that time, the śrāmaṇera did not perform services for his upādhyāya or ācārya, nor did he perform services for others; yet they obstructed him, refusing to give him a share of the offerings and requisites within the saṃgha.
The Buddha said, "One should not prevent it; this is the property of the donor.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you should say to a śrāmaṇera:
'You must provide for your upādhyāya, ācārya, and the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma.
If it is the turn of the Saṃgha to perform labor, you should perform it.'"
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who, having caused his son to go forth into homelessness, took him with him into a village to beg for food.
When they arrived before various market stalls and saw cakes and rice, he stretched out his hand and said:
"Give me cake; give me rice."
When the elders saw this, they all reproached him together, saying:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas!
He has no sense of shame; he violates the pure conduct (brahmacarya) while outwardly claiming for himself:..."
"I know the True Dharma.
How can one who has gone forth from the household life thus give birth to a child and carry it about with him? What kind of True Dharma is this?
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One of these circumstances.
The World-Honored One said:
"From this day forward, you must not ordain anyone under twelve years of age.

At that time, Ānanda had a donor’s family whose members had all died, leaving only a small child behind. He brought the child to the Buddha’s presence, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha, knowing this, asked intentionally: "What child is this?
Ānanda then reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One asked,
"For what reason did you not ordain him and let him leave the household life? He replied:
“The World-Honored One has previously established a regulation that one who is less than twelve years of age may not be ordained; for this reason, he was not ordained.
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
“Is this young boy able to drive away crows, able to maintain the precepts, and able to eat only once a day?”
"If one can do as you have said, I grant permission for them to go forth. Ānanda replied,
"This child can drive away crows, can maintain the precepts, and can eat but one meal a day."
The Buddha told Ānanda,
"If these children are all capable of such things, I permit them to receive the full ordination and leave the household life.
At that time, there were two śrāmaṇeras under Baddhālinda:
One was named Keṇa and the other was named Makha.
Shameless and devoid of remorse, they committed impure acts with one another.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and after the Buddha had rebuked Upananda, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, you must not keep two śrāmaṇeras.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu’s son who came to the saṃghārāma to visit.
Then the bhikṣu preached the Dharma for him, saying:

"You should know the suffering of hell, the suffering of animals, and the suffering of hungry ghosts. It is difficult to encounter a Buddha appearing in the world; he appears only once in a great while, like the udumbara flower. Why do you not leave the household life to practice the Way?"
He replied, "If you,
Venerable Sir, will act as my preceptor (upādhyāya), I shall go forth. That bhikṣu,
who already had a śrāmaṇera, thought to himself:
“The World-Honored One has prescribed a precept that one must not keep two śrāmaṇeras.
Because of this, they were hesitant and did not keep two śrāmaṇeras.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"If one is able to teach [them] to uphold the precepts, increase their concentration (*citta*), increase their wisdom (*prajñā*), study, and recite, then it is permitted to keep [such a person].

At that time, there was one who was less than twenty years of age; after receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), he immediately became doubtful. The bhikṣus went to ask the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, if such a doubt arises after receiving full ordination, it is permitted to count the months of gestation, or count the intercalary months, or count the days of the fortnightly *poṣadha* ceremony. If one attains the state of an Arhat, that is then called 'having gone forth and received full ordination.'"
At that time, there were those who wished to receive the precepts who went outside the boundary; the group of six bhikṣus went to obstruct their ordination.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen well, all of you!

From this day forward, it shall not be permitted to confer the precepts by performing the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* and establishing a small boundary (*kṣudra-sīmā*) in haste outside the [original] boundary without first having reached a consensus and exited the boundary.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed to make the following formal motion (*jñapti*) as described above:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha has gathered in one place to establish a small boundary (*sīmā*)."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let us establish a small boundary (*kṣudraka-sīmā*).
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
Now this Saṃgha assembles in one place to establish a small boundary (sīmā).
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s assembly in one place to establish a small boundary should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Saṃgha has already consented to the conclusion of the small boundary. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.

If those who did not agree were outside the boundary when they attempted to obstruct, their obstruction was ineffective; they departed without dissolving the boundary. The remaining bhikṣus were doubtful and informed the Buddha, who said:
“From now on, one should dissolve the boundary before departing; one must not depart without dissolving the boundary.”

To perform the resolution through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one should appoint within the assembly a person capable of performing the *karman* as described above, and make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
Now the assembly of monks has gathered to dissolve the boundary.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent to dissolve the boundary.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Sangha, listen! Now the assembly of monks gathers to dissolve the boundary.
Which elders who consent to the Sangha dissolving the boundary remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak."
“The Sangha has already consented to the dissolution of the boundary; since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, there was one who received full ordination without a preceptor. The Buddha said, “One must not receive the precepts [in such a manner].”
“Can the two Upādhyāyas receive the precepts?
The Buddha said,
“They cannot receive the precepts.”
“Can one receive the precepts with three preceptors?
The Buddha said,
“One cannot receive full ordination.”
“Can one receive the precepts from a multitude of *upādhyāyas*?
The Buddha said,
“One cannot receive full ordination [in such a manner].”
At that time, the preceptor was nine years old when he received the precepts; although he was said to have received full ordination (*upasampadā*), the community of monks incurred an offense.

At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. The land was suffering from famine and scarcity, and grain was extremely expensive; it was difficult to obtain alms, and the people had the appearance of hunger.

At that time, the Buddha and the community of monks received abundant offerings. A certain young non-Buddhist (tīrthika), seeing that the Buddha and the monks were receiving such great offerings, shaved his own head, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, left the household life, and received the precepts. Subsequently, however, the offerings to the monks ceased.
The bhikṣus said to him,
"Go into the village to beg for alms. He asked:
"Is there no food for the Sangha? He replied,
"There is none."
He asked, “What should I do? The bhikṣu replied:
"You should go for alms.
He replied, "If one goes for alms, this person begs and that person begs as well."
"I shall beg for alms in that place.
That person immediately abandoned the path.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, I authorize the prior granting of the four reliances.
At that time, there was another young outsider who came to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
“I wish to go forth.”
The bhikṣus then granted him the going-forth and first gave him the four reliances.
That outsider replied,
"Venerable Sirs!..."
I am capable of undertaking two things:
relying on alms-gathering and relying on sitting at the foot of a tree; I am capable of these two matters.
As for wearing robes made of discarded rags and using medicine that is putrid, I am not capable of these two matters.
"Why is this? For who can touch their own body?
Thereupon, he abandoned the path and did not go forth into homelessness.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"This non-Buddhist did not leave the household life; he has lost a great opportunity.
Had he left the household life, he would have attained the realization of the Path."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, after one has received the precepts, one shall subsequently receive the four reliances.
At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Then, there was a valiant great general who came to the saṃghārāma and spoke to the bhikṣus, saying:
"I wish to leave the household life to practice the Path.
At that time, the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going-forth and the full ordination.

On another occasion, the people within the realm of King Prasenajit rebelled; he immediately dispatched an army to attack them, but was instead defeated by them. He sent an army again, yet was once more defeated by them. The king then asked:
"Where is my capable general so-and-so now? He replied,
"He has left the household life to follow the path as a śramaṇa disciple of the Śākyas."
At that time, the king immediately spoke with reproach:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
They have no sense of shame or modesty; they are full of desire and never satisfied, yet they claim for themselves externally:..."
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be such a True Dharma when even our valiant and heroic generals renounce their homes to follow the Way?
Judging by this, these śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, are all nothing but government officials.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you must not ordain government officials; if anyone should ordain one, they shall be dealt with according to the law."
At that time, he granted ordination and full admission to one who possessed neither robes nor a bowl.
The bhikṣus said to him, "Enter the village to beg for alms. He replied:
"I have no robes or bowl.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, those who lack robes and a bowl shall not receive full ordination."
At that time, there was one who borrowed another’s robes and bowl to receive full ordination; once the ordination was completed, the owner took them back, leaving him naked and crouching in shame.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

“From now on, one must not borrow another’s robes and bowl to receive full ordination. If someone provides the robes, they should be asked for as a gift; if they do not provide them, one should pay their value.”
At that time, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling along the road from the kingdom of Kosala toward the banks of the Kāla-nadī River. One among them said:
"In this very place, there was once a layman who committed sexual misconduct with one who wore the saffron robe."
The crowd asked, "How do you know this? He replied:
"I am one among them. At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If one has violated a bhikṣuṇī, there is no benefit or growth for him within my Dharma and Vinaya; he should not be granted the going forth or the full ordination."
"If one has left the household life and received the full precepts, they should be expelled.

At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; at that moment, rice and grain were extremely scarce within the borders of the country, begging was difficult to accomplish, and all the people had a look of hunger.
At that time, the Buddha and the community of monks received abundant offerings.
There was a young outsider who, seeing the Buddha and the monks receiving such abundant offerings, conceived this thought:
"By what means might I obtain such food without having to leave the household life?"
He immediately shaved his own hair, donned the kāṣāya, took up his bowl, and entered among the assembly to eat.
The bhikṣus asked him, "How many years of seniority do you have? He did not know.
He asked again,
"When did you go forth into homelessness? He replied:
