“I do not know. “Who is your preceptor? Who is your ācārya?”
He also said, "I do not know. He was asked again:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am such-and-such a non-Buddhist ascetic; I have seen the Buddha and the Sangha receiving great offerings."
Having seen this, I immediately thought:
"By what means might I obtain such food without having to leave the household life?
For this reason, I simply shaved off my hair and beard, donned the saffron robes, and entered among the multitude to seek alms.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, those who enter the path with a thieving mind shall derive no benefit within my Dharma; they should not be granted ordination or the full precepts.
If they have already been ordained and received the full precepts, they should be expelled."

Among these, those who have entered the Path with a thief’s mind may go to one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or a community of bhikṣus (saṃgha) where they perform a formal act (karmavācanā) together and recite the precepts; or they may go to one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or a community of bhikṣus where they perform a formal act together but do not recite the precepts; or they may go to one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or a community of bhikṣus where they do not perform a formal act together but recite the precepts; or they may go to one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or three bhikṣus, but not to a community of bhikṣus, and neither perform a formal act together nor recite the precepts.
Or they go to the place of one bhikṣu or two bhikṣus, but do not go to the place of three bhikṣus or the Saṃgha, nor perform the formal act (karmavācanā) or recite the Prātimokṣa together with them.
Or they go to the place of one bhikṣu, but do not go to the place of two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha, nor perform the formal act or recite the Prātimokṣa together with them.

Among these, those who enter the Path with a thieving mind go to the place of a single bhikṣu, but do not go to the places of two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha; they do not participate in the *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the precepts.
If such a person has not yet left the household life to receive full ordination, they should not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, it is permitted that they are indeed considered to have gone forth and received full ordination.

Among these, one who has entered the Path with a thieving mind goes to the place of one bhikṣu or two bhikṣus, but does not go to the place of three bhikṣus or the Saṃgha; they do not perform *karmavācanā* or recite the precepts together with him. If he has not yet left home to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), he must not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if he has already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, it is permitted to recognize him as having indeed left home and received full ordination.

Among these, those who enter the Path with a thieving mind do not go to the presence of one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or three bhikṣus, nor do they go to the presence of the Saṃgha; they do not participate in the *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the precepts. If they have not yet left the household life to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they must not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, it is permitted that they are indeed called "those who have gone forth and received full ordination."

Among these, those who have entered the Path with a thieving mind shall not participate in *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the precepts when they go before one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha. If they have not yet left the household life to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they must not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, it is recognized that they indeed possess the status of having gone forth and received full ordination.

Among these, those who enter the Path with a thieving mind should go before one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or the community of bhikṣus; they may perform the *karmavācanā* together, but they must not recite the *Prātimokṣa* together. If they have not yet left the household life to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), they must not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, they should be expelled.

Among these, one who has entered the Path with a thieving mind—whether they approach a single bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, or the community of bhikṣus for the formal act (karmavācanā) and the recitation of the precepts—if they have not yet left the household life and received full ordination (upasaṃpadā), they must not be granted the going-forth and full ordination;
if they have already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, they should be expelled.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 34;
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 35, Part 2, Section 14.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin Dynasty.

Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others, this is the fifth section of the *Prātimokṣa-vastu* (The Chapter on Receiving Ordination). At that time, there was a eunuch who came to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus:
"I wish to leave the household life and receive full ordination."
The bhikṣus then granted him the going-forth and the full ordination.
Having received the full ordination, he said to the bhikṣus:
"Come and do such and such things with me."
The bhikṣu replied: “Be gone! Perish!”
"What use are you to me?
He then went again to the park keeper and the novice, saying to them:
"Come with me and do such-and-such things."
The novice attendant said to him: "Get out! Begone!"
"What use are you?
That eunuch went outside the monastery and engaged in sexual acts with cowherds and shepherds.
When the lay devotees saw this, they criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, are all eunuchs; among them, those who are males engage in sexual acts together.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Eunuchs provide no benefit or growth within my Dharma; they shall not be permitted to go forth and receive full ordination."
If one has already left the household life and received full ordination, they should be expelled.
Among these, "eunuchs" (pandaka) refers to those who are eunuchs by birth, eunuchs castrated [by surgery], eunuchs through jealousy, eunuchs through transformation, and eunuchs for half the month.
One born [as a eunuch] is one who has been a *pandaka* since birth.
One castrated (*kṛtaka*) is one whose genitals have been entirely cut off, making him a *pandaka*.
One envious (*īrṣyaka*) is one who gives rise to a lustful mind upon seeing another engaged in sexual intercourse.
"Transformation" refers to one who loses the male organ and becomes a eunuch while engaging in sexual intercourse with another.
"The half-month" refers to one who is capable as a male for half the month and incapable for the other half.
At that time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
The Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita had an extremely long lifespan; having conceived a sense of weary detachment, he thought to himself:
"Now that I have been born among these long-lived nāgas, when shall I be able to leave this body?"
He further thought to himself:
"This śramaṇa, son of the Śākyas, practices pure conduct. I should now go to him and seek to leave the household life to follow the Path; thus I may escape this dragon body."
He immediately transformed his body into the form of a young non-Buddhist ascetic and went to the monastery, saying to the bhikṣus:
"I wish to go forth and receive full ordination."
At that time, the bhikṣus, without examining the origins of those they received, granted them the going-forth and the full ordination, and allowed them to dwell in the same room as a single bhikṣu.
Then, while that bhikṣu had gone outside for minor needs, the Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita let his body fall into sleep.
It is the constant nature of dragons that there are two occasions when they do not abandon their original form:
when sleeping and when engaging in sexual intercourse; on these occasions, they do not abandon their original form.
At that time, the body of the Dragon King swelled until it filled the chamber, with his body protruding from the windows, doors, and ventilation holes.
Then that bhikṣu returned and pushed against the door with his hand; his hand touched the dragon’s body, and sensing something unusual within, he immediately cried out in a loud voice, “A snake!”
"A snake!
When the bhikṣu Pippala heard this sound, he asked,
"Why are you crying out so loudly?"
He then related these matters in detail.

At that time, the dragon king also heard the sound of the bhikṣu’s call; he immediately awoke from his sleep, sat cross-legged, straightened his body, set his mind upright, and fixed his attention before him.
Then the bhikṣu entered and asked, "Who are you? She replied:
“I am the nāga king Suprabha. I was born among the long-lived nāgas, and having become weary of this body, I formed this thought:
‘When shall I ever be able to leave behind this nāga body?’”
Again, he had this thought:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas cultivate pure conduct; I should now rather leave the household life to study the Path under them, so as to escape this dragon body."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances. The Buddha said:
"As for animals, they provide no benefit or growth within my Dharma."
If one has not yet left the household life, one must not grant them the full ordination of leaving the household life;
if one has already granted them the full ordination of leaving the household life, they shall be expelled.
At that time, there was a young non-Buddhist ascetic who intentionally killed his mother.
Having committed the murder, he was constantly filled with grief and anxiety, thinking to himself: "Who can remove this sorrow for me?"
He then thought again:
"This śramaṇa, the son of the Śākyas, has cultivated many wholesome dharmas; I should now go forth under him to study the Path so that I may extinguish this sin."
He immediately went to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to leave the household life to study the Path.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they again thought he was the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita and asked him:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am such-and-such a non-Buddhist; I have intentionally killed my mother."
Having already killed them, he constantly harbored sorrow and anxiety, thinking:
"Who can remove this grief and suffering for me? He further thought:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, cultivate many wholesome dharmas; I should now leave the household life under them to study the Path so as to extinguish this sin.
For this reason, he has come seeking to go forth.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"One who has killed his mother gains nothing by way of benefit within my Dharma.
If he has not yet left the household life, he shall not be permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination."
"If you grant him the going forth and the full ordination, he should be expelled.
At that time, there was another non-Buddhist who intentionally killed his father.
Having committed the murder, he constantly harbored grief and anxiety, thinking to himself:
"Who can remove this sorrow and suffering for me?
He then thought to himself:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, cultivate many wholesome dharmas; I should now leave the household life to study the Path under them, so that I may extinguish these transgressions."
He immediately went to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus,
"I wish to leave the household life to practice the Way.
When the bhikṣus saw him, they thought he was the Nāga King Supratiṣṭhita and asked him:
"Who are you? He replied, "I am such-and-such a non-Buddhist ascetic; I have intentionally killed my father."
Having already killed [them], he constantly harbored sorrow and anxiety, thinking:
"Who can remove this grief and suffering for me?
He then further thought:

"The śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, cultivate many wholesome dharmas; I think it would be better for me to leave the household life and study the Path under them, so that I may extinguish this sin.
For this reason, he has come to seek ordination.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"One who has killed his father shall gain no benefit within my Dharma.
If he has not yet left the household life, he must not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination."
"If one has granted him the going-forth and the full ordination, he should be expelled. At that time,
there were many bhikṣus traveling on the road from the kingdom of Kośala who, seeing a forest hermitage, pointed it out to one another, saying,
"This is such-and-such a forest hermitage."
Among those who had killed an arhat, one person said:
"This was indeed an arhat. Why is that?
"At the time of killing, his mind was no different [from that of one who does not kill]. Someone asked:
"How do you know this?"
He replied, "I am one among those very people.
Then the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who has killed an Arhat brings no benefit or growth to my Dharma.
If he has not yet left the household life, he must not be granted the going-forth or the full ordination;
if he has already been granted the going-forth and full ordination, he shall be expelled."
Then the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there should be one who causes a schism in the Saṃgha, what should be done?"
The Buddha said:
"As in the case of Devadatta, if he has not yet left the household life and received full ordination, one must not grant him leave from the household life and full ordination;
if one has already granted him leave from the household life and full ordination, he shall be expelled."
He asked again:
"What should be said regarding one who, with an evil mind, causes the Buddha’s body to bleed? The Buddha said:
"As with Devadatta, if he has not yet left the household life and received full ordination, one must not grant him leave from the household life and full ordination;
if he has already been granted leave from the household life and received full ordination, he should be expelled."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who transformed himself into the form of a woman. The other bhikṣus thought to themselves, "Should he be expelled?
The Buddha said:

"One should not carry out the act of banishment; rather, it is permitted that the preceptor and the ācārya shall immediately place him among the community of bhikṣuṇīs, using his original year of full ordination."
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who transformed herself into the form of a man. The bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves, "Should she be expelled?
The Buddha said:

"One should not carry out the formal act of banishment; rather, it is permitted that he shall use his original year of ordination, and the preceptors and instructors should place him within the community of bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who underwent a transformation into both male and female sexual organs. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should he be subjected to the formal act of banishment?"
The Buddha said, "She should be expelled.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who manifested both male and female sexual organs; the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"Should he be expelled?
The Buddha said,
"He should be expelled."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose male organ and testicles were cut off by bandits. The other bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should he be expelled?
The Buddha said:
"One should not carry out the act of *parivāsa* (banishment).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose male organ and testicles were severed by his enemies. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should he be subjected to *parivāsa*?"
The Buddha said, "He should not be expelled.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose male organ and testicles were bitten by a wild beast; the other bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should he be expelled?
The Buddha said,
"He should not be expelled."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose male organ fell off due to the causal conditions of his karmic retribution. The bhikṣus thought to themselves, "Should he be expelled?
The Buddha said:
"One should not carry out the formal act of banishment.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who cut off his own male organ. The other bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should he be subjected to the formal act of banishment?"
The Buddha said, "He should be expelled.
At that time, there was one who wished to receive full ordination and was about to go outside the boundary; the bhikṣus asked him:
"Who are you? He did not state his own name.
Again he asked:
"Who is your preceptor? He did not, however, state his preceptor's name.
When instructed to request the precepts, he did not do so. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are three kinds of persons who are said to be unable to receive full ordination:

one who does not state their own name; one who is unwilling to state the name of their preceptor; and one who, when instructed to request the precepts, fails to do so. These are the three kinds of persons who cannot receive full ordination."

At that time, there were those who received full ordination while still wearing white lay garments; having received full ordination, they immediately put them on and entered the village to beg for alms.
When the householders saw them, they asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas!
The householder said:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not act in such a manner!
The Buddha said:
“One must not receive full ordination while wearing the clothing of a white-robed layperson.”
At that time, there were others who, wearing the robes of non-Buddhist outsiders, received full ordination. Having received full ordination, they entered a village to beg for food.
When the laypeople saw them, they asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas!
The householder said:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, do not act in this way!
The Buddha said,
“One who wears the robes of an outsider should not be granted full ordination.”
At that time, some who had received full ordination while wearing various bodily ornaments went into the village to beg for alms.
When the laypeople saw them, they asked, "Who are you?"
He replied, “I am a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
The householder said:
“Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya, do not act in this way.
The Buddha said:
“One who wears various ornaments for the body shall not be granted full ordination (upasampadā).”
There are three kinds of persons who are not said to have received full ordination:

one wearing secular clothing, one wearing the robes of an outsider, and one whose body is adorned with various ornaments; these are the three kinds of persons for whom full ordination is not accomplished.
At that time, there was one who conferred full ordination upon a sleeping person; having awakened, the person returned home.
The bhikṣus said, "Stop!"
"Do not return home; you have already received full ordination.
He replied, "I have not received full ordination."
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not confer full ordination upon one who is asleep.
At that time, there was one who conferred full ordination upon a person who was intoxicated; once the intoxication had subsided, the person immediately returned home, and the bhikṣus said:
"You have already received full ordination; stop and do not return home.
He replied, "I have not received full ordination."
The Buddha said:
"One must not confer full ordination upon one who is intoxicated.
At that time, there was one who conferred full ordination upon a person who was insane; once that person regained his sanity, he returned home.
The bhikṣus said: "Stop! Do not go!
You have already received full ordination."
He replied, "I have not received full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"One must not confer the full ordination upon one who is insane.
There are three kinds of persons who may not receive the full ordination:
one who is asleep, one who is intoxicated, and one who is insane; these are called the three types for whom the full ordination must not be conferred."
At that time, there was a naked ascetic who received full ordination; later, having obtained clothing, he returned home.
The bhikṣus said to him, "You have already received full ordination; stop and do not return home!"
He replied, "I have not received full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"One must not confer full ordination upon a naked ascetic.
At that time, there was one who conferred full ordination upon a person prone to anger; later, when his anger subsided, he returned home.
The bhikṣus said to him, "You have already received full ordination; do not return home. He replied:
“I shall not receive the full ordination.
The Buddha said,
“One must not grant the full ordination to one who is possessed by anger.”
At that time, there was a person who received full ordination through forceful bestowal, but subsequently fled and returned home.
The bhikṣus said to him, "You have already received full ordination; stop and do not return home."
He replied, "I have not received full ordination.
The Buddha said:
"One must not forcibly confer the full ordination upon another.
There are three kinds of persons for whom the full ordination is not received:
the naked ascetic, the one who is angry, and the one who is forced to receive the full ordination; these are called the three kinds of persons for whom the full ordination is not received."
"In this way, they have their hands cut off, their feet cut off, both hands and feet cut off; or their ears cut off, or their noses cut off, or both ears and noses cut off;
or their male organs cut off, or their testicles cut off, or both male organs and testicles cut off;
or their upper arms cut off, or their elbows cut off, or their fingers cut off; or they are constantly afflicted with scabies and sores."
The signs of death appear; or the body becomes goitrous, or the body resembles that of a woman;
or there is a registration of one's name, or one evades official taxes; or there are boils and sores, or the body is mottled;
or the head is pointed, or the left arm is withered, or the right arm is withered; or the teeth protrude, or the body is infested with worms, or the head is infested with worms; or...
The hair may be matted, or the fingers may be curved, or there may be six fingers, or webbed fingers;
there may be one testicle, or no testicles, or scrotal hernia; the body may be curved internally, or externally, or both internally and externally;
or there may be the disease of upward breath, or warts, or spitting of foam, or illness.
Or various afflictions and pains; or diseases of the male organ;

or blue eyes, or yellow eyes, or red eyes, or inflamed eyes, or bloodshot eyes, or eyes of a yellowish-red color, or eyes with a blue film, or eyes with a yellow film, or eyes with a white film, or crystalline eyes, or those that are extremely deep.
Their eyes may be protruding, or triangular, or like those of a *mīla*,
or wide-gaping, or bulging, or one-eyed, or squinting, or blind, or jutting out,
or askew, or wrathful, or staring, or afflicted with sores, or mottled.
Some have scabies or sores on their bodies; some have spreading ulcers; some are mute, some are deaf, and some are both mute and deaf;
some have curled toes, some are lame, and some drag their feet; some have only one hand, one foot, or one ear, while others have no hands, no feet, or no ears;
some lack hair on their heads or body hair, and some have no teeth.
Some had blue hair, yellow hair, or white hair; some were very tall, some were very short;
some were women, some were sons of devas, some were sons of asuras, and some were sons of gandharvas;
some had the heads of elephants, some had the heads of horses, some had the heads of camels, some had the heads of oxen, and some had the heads of donkeys.
There were those with the heads of pigs, or the heads of black goats, or the heads of white sheep,
or the heads of deer, or the heads of snakes, or the heads of fish, or the heads of birds; some had two heads,
some three heads, or many heads— all blue, all yellow, all [white].
Some are black; some are entirely red; some are entirely white; some have the color of monkeys.
Some suffer from wind-disorders (*vāta*), some from heat-disorders (*pitta*), some from phlegm-disorders (*kapha*), or from abdominal tumors.
Some have crooked throats, some have hare-lips, some are tongueless, some have their tongues severed, and some are unable to distinguish between the pleasant and the unpleasant.
...or with the chest protruding forward, or protruding backward, or protruding both forward and backward;
or suffering from worm-infestations, or dropsy, or internal diseases, or external diseases, or diseases both internal and external;
or suffering from chronic tumors, or from a condition of constant prostration and inability to turn over, or from perpetual extreme old age, or from consumption (śoṣa); or...
If one has lost their dignified deportment and behaves in such a way as to utterly disgrace the Sangha, such a person shall not be permitted to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, there was one who possessed supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) who received the full ordination while remaining in mid-air; the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination.
When the preceptor was in mid-air while bestowing full ordination upon the candidate below, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination."
When one received full ordination while standing in mid-air through supernormal power, the Buddha said, "This is not called receiving full ordination.
At that time, there were those who received full ordination while remaining invisible and unmanifest; the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination.
Regarding the case where the preceptor has disappeared when one receives full ordination, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination."
When a bhikṣu who had completed the required number of witnesses vanished while receiving full ordination, the Buddha said:
"This does not count as having received full ordination.
At that time, when full ordination was received out of sight and hearing, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination.
When the preceptor receives full ordination while out of sight and hearing, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination."
When one received full ordination with a quorum of monks who were out of earshot and sight, the Buddha said:
"This is not called receiving full ordination.
At that time, when one received full ordination outside the boundary, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination.
When the preceptor was outside the boundary when the full ordination was received, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving full ordination."
When the full number of persons was not present within the boundary and they received the full ordination, the Buddha said:
"It is not called receiving the full ordination.
At that time, there were those who did not receive the śrāmaṇera precepts and yet received the full ordination; the Buddha said:
"One may receive the full ordination, yet the Saṃgha may have committed an offense.
Such was the instruction of the World-Honored One: "No one who brings disgrace upon the Saṃgha shall receive the full ordination."

At that time, there was one who wished to receive the precepts. When he was led outside the boundary and his clothes were removed for inspection, the candidate felt ashamed and this delayed the matter of receiving the precepts.
The bhikṣus then went to inform the World-Honored One of this matter, and the World-Honored One said:
"One must not confer the precepts by thus exposing the body for inspection."
From this time forward, it is permitted to inquire about the thirteen difficult points before conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
During the formal procedure of the motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), one should ask as follows:
"Have you not committed a bordering offense (*antānīka-āpatti*)?"
Have you not committed an offense against a bhikṣuṇī?
Have you not entered the path with a thief’s intent?
Have you not damaged the two paths?
Are you not a eunuch?
Have you not killed your father or your mother?
Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human being?
"Are you not an animal?
Are you not of two sexual organs?
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"From this time forward, it is permitted to first inquire about the thirteen impediments and only then confer the full ordination; one should perform the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, and in this manner the full ordination shall be conferred."
At that time, the candidate who intends to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*) shall be placed in a location where they are within sight but beyond earshot.
Then, the Preceptor (*śikṣādātṛ*) shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
That person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
If the Sangha is ready and the Sangha permits, let [Name] serve as the preceptor for instruction.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
At that time, the preceptor should go to him and say:
"Is this lower robe (antarvāsa), upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), outer robe (saṃghāṭī), and bowl yours? Are these robes and bowl yours?"
If he answers, "Yes," one should say to him:
“Good son, listen attentively!
Now is the time for sincerity. I shall now question you; answer according to my questions.
If it is not true, you should say it is not true; if it is true, you should say it is true.”
"What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor?
Have you reached the age of twenty?"
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given you permission?
Are you not a person burdened by debt?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official? Are you a man?
"A man may have such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption, or insanity; do you now have any of these diseases?"
If there is none, he should answer:
"There is none.
One should then say to him:
"As I have now questioned you, so shall the Saṃgha question you.
As you have just answered me, so shall you answer within the assembly of monks."
Having thus questioned him, that instructor returns to the midst of the Saṃgha.
Standing with the usual deportment at a distance where one can reach the other by stretching out the arms, he should make this announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from such-and-such a person.
If the Saṃgha is ready and the Saṃgha permits, I have finished questioning him; let it be heard that he may be brought forward.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
He calls out, "Come here! Once he has come,

[the preceptor] should take hold of his robe and bowl, instruct him to prostrate at the feet of the Sangha, and then instruct him to stand before the preceptor with his right knee on the ground and palms joined, teaching him to speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, [Name], seek to receive full ordination from [Name].
I, [Name], now request the Saṃgha to grant me full ordination, with [Name] acting as my preceptor."
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, deliver me!
The second and third times, he should speak in this same manner.
At that time, the Preceptor shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*), making the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so.
This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for full ordination, with so-and-so as preceptor."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits me, I shall ask about various difficult matters.
This is my formal announcement (*jñapti*). "Listen, son of good family!
Now is the time for ultimate sincerity and the time for truthful speech. I now question you; you should answer me according to the truth.
What is your name? What is the name of your preceptor?
"Are you twenty years of age?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given their permission?"
Are you not in debt? Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official?
"Are you a man? A man may have such diseases as leprosy, carbuncles, white leprosy, consumption, or insanity; do you now have any such disease?"
If it is said that he has none, then a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations) should be performed, and the motion should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Saṃgha the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] acting as preceptor.
[Name] has personally declared himself pure and free from all obstacles, is twenty years of age, and is fully equipped with the three robes and alms bowl.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Sangha to grant him full ordination, with [Name] acting as preceptor.
So-and-so has declared himself pure and free from obstacles; he is twenty-three years of age and possesses the robes and bowl.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as his preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times, it was said likewise:
"The Sangha has already granted full ordination to [Name], with [Name] as preceptor; the Sangha has consented, for they are silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having received full ordination, was abandoned by the entire community of monks.
The person from whom he had originally received the full ordination lived not far away; she immediately went before him and asked, "What were you doing just now?"
He replied, "I have received full ordination.
The former couple said:
"You should now perform such and such acts together; you may consider this as performing such and such acts for the last time.
At that time, the one receiving full ordination performed unchaste acts with him and subsequently returned to the midst of the assembly.
The bhikṣus asked,
"For what reason were you behind?
He then related the matter in detail to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus said to him: "Depart quickly! Get lost!"
"What use are you?
You should not remain here. The man said:
"Is what I have done not improper? The bhikṣus replied, "It is improper."
The man said, "Why did you not tell me beforehand?
I would have avoided it and not done it."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Blessed One of this matter. The Blessed One said:
"From this day forward, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, you must first recite the four *pārājika* dharmas."
"Listen, noble son!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the four pārājika dharmas.
If a bhikṣu commits any one of these dharmas, he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya. You must never, under any circumstances, commit sexual misconduct or engage in impure acts."
"If a bhikṣu commits an impure act and engages in sexual intercourse, even with an animal, he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a parable:
"It is just as if someone were to have their head cut off; they could never live again."
It is the same for a bhikṣu: once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can no longer restore his status as a bhikṣu.
"In this matter, you must not act for as long as life lasts; can you maintain this?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"One must not steal anything at all, down to even a blade of grass or a leaf."

If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether taking it himself or inciting another to take it, whether breaking it himself or inciting another to break it, whether cutting it himself or inciting another to cut it, or by burning it, burying it, or altering its color—he is no longer a śramaṇa and no longer a son of the Śākya. He is like a tāla tree whose heart has been severed; it will never again grow or flourish.
Monk, it is the same with one who commits a *pārājika* offense; he can never again become one who practices the conduct of a monk.
You must not do this for as long as you live. Can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"Under no circumstances shall you intentionally take the life of any living being, down to even an ant."

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes the life of a human being with his own hand, or seeks out a knife and gives it to another, or instructs another to die, praises death, encourages death, gives another non-medicinal substances, or causes an abortion, or kills through incantations and curses—acting as an agent of such means.
If one instructs another to commit [an offense], they are neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya.
As the parable-tellers say: "It is just like a needle-eye that has been broken; it is no longer fit for use.
The bhikṣu is also like this.
"Monk, one who commits a pārājika offense no longer constitutes a bhikṣu in his practice.
You must not commit this for as long as life lasts; can you maintain this?"
He replied, "I can.
[The Buddha said: "One must not speak falsely, even in jest."
If a bhikṣu, being without truth and without having attained it himself, should say of himself:

"I have attained the state of a superior person; I have attained dhyāna; I have attained liberation; I have attained concentration; I have attained the four formless attainments; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; gods have come to me; nāgas have come to me; spirits have come to me."
"He is neither a śramaṇa nor a son of the Śākya.
As the parable-tellers say: 'Just as a great stone split into two parts can never be joined together again, so it is with a bhikṣu;
having committed a pārājika offense, he cannot return to the practice of a bhikṣu.'"
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you uphold it?
If one is able, they reply, "I can."
“Listen, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances.
By relying upon these, a bhikṣu may go forth, receive full ordination, and fulfill the dharma of a bhikṣu.”
A bhikṣu relies on rag-robes; by relying on these, he is able to go forth and receive full ordination, thereby fulfilling the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"If you obtain long-term benefits, such as robes offered by donors or robes made from scraps of cloth, you may accept them."
"A bhikṣu relies on alms for food; by relying on this, a bhikṣu is able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, and achieve the status of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this throughout your entire life?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:

"If you obtain long-term benefits—such as food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the Saṃgha, or food offered at a donor's invitation—you may accept it."
"By sitting under a tree, a bhikṣu, by relying on this, attains the going-forth and receives full ordination, thereby perfecting the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"If you obtain long-term benefits—such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed house, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door—you may accept them."
"Relying on putrid medicine: by relying on this, a bhikṣu may go forth and receive full ordination, thereby accomplishing the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"If you obtain long-term benefits, such as ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar, you may accept them."

“Now that you have received the precepts, the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished in accordance with the Dharma and the proper place has been attained; your preceptor (*upādhyāya*) is in accordance with the Dharma, your instructors (*ācārya*) are in accordance with the Dharma, and the community of monks is complete and sufficient. You should properly receive the instructions of the teaching.”
"You should exhort others to cultivate merit by repairing stupas and making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, the upādhyāya, and the ācārya.

You must not disobey any teaching that accords with the Dharma; you should study, recite the sutras, and diligently seek skillful means so that, within the Buddha-dharma, you may attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat."
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your efforts will not be in vain and their fruit will never cease.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should ask your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
"From this day forward, let those who have received full ordination go ahead.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having been subject to formal censure by the community, immediately abandoned the path. Later, he came to the saṃghārāma and said to the bhikṣus, "I wish to return to the life of a renunciant."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of these circumstances, and the Buddha said:
“You should ask that person:
‘Do you see your own fault?’”
If they reply, "I do not see my fault," one should not grant them ordination.
If one says,
"I see my transgression," grant them the going forth.
After they have gone forth, one should further ask:
"Do you see your transgression? If they say:
"If he says, 'I do not see my offense,' one should not confer full ordination upon him. If he says:"
"Having seen the offense," one should confer the full ordination (upasampadā) upon them.
Once the full ordination has been conferred, one should say to them:
"Are you able to repent? If he says, "I am unable to repent."
One must not grant the *karmavācanā* for release.
If he says, "I am able to repent," [then one may proceed].
"One should grant him the lifting of the *karmavācanā*.
Having granted the lifting of the *karmavācanā*, one should say to him:
'Confess your offense.'"
"If he repents well, it is fine; otherwise, if the Saṃgha attains harmony, they shall again perform the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) against him.
If the Saṃgha does not attain harmony, they may co-reside with him, and there is no offense."
At that time, Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If one receives full ordination before reaching the age of twenty, should they be said to be a person who has received full ordination?"
The Buddha said,
"This person has received full ordination.
He asked again:
"Is the person who has been granted full ordination well-ordained?
The Buddha said,
"He is well-ordained."
“Is the one who performs the *karmavācanā* performing it correctly?
The Buddha said,
“He is performing the *karmavācanā* correctly.”
"Having already restrained oneself, if one receives full ordination in this manner, it is not called 'properly received full ordination.
He asked again:
"Is receiving full ordination through the three utterances considered receiving full ordination?"
The Buddha said, "This is the conferral of full ordination. [He asked:
"Is that which has been conferred as full ordination properly conferred?"
The Buddha said, “This is a proper bestowal.
[He asked again: “Is this a properly performed *karmavācanā*?”
The Buddha said:
"That was a properly performed *karmavācanā*.
From this point forward, those who receive full ordination in such a manner shall not be said to have received the full precepts."
He asked again:
"If one receives full ordination without being questioned regarding the thirteen grounds for defeat, should it be said that this constitutes receiving full ordination?
The Buddha said:
"This is the proper conferral of full ordination. He asked:
"Is that which has been conferred as full ordination truly a proper conferral of full ordination?"
The Buddha said:
"This person has been fully ordained by Good Bestower. He asked:
"Is the one performing the *karmavācanā* performing it correctly?
The Buddha said,
"He is performing the *karmavācanā* correctly."
"If one has been restrained [from ordination] and then receives full ordination in this manner, it is not called receiving the full precepts.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If a preceptor possesses even one of the thirteen grounds for disqualification and confers the full precepts upon a disciple, should it be said that the full precepts have been properly received?"
The Buddha said,
"You have properly received the full ordination. He asked:
"Is the person to whom full ordination has been conferred said to have been 'well-conferred'?
The Buddha said,
"He is well-conferred."
“Is the one performing the *karmavācanā* performing it correctly?
The Buddha said,
“This is performing the *karmavācanā* correctly.”
"If, after having restrained oneself, one confers the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another in such a manner, the assembly of monks incurs an offense.
At that time, there was one who had received the full ordination from a preceptor (*upādhyāya*) who did not maintain the precepts; later, he became doubtful. The Buddha asked him:
"Did you know that your preceptor did not maintain the precepts?"
He replied, "I do not know. The Buddha said:
"It is said that one receives full ordination by name.
Furthermore, there was another who received full ordination from a preceptor who did not maintain the precepts; later, having doubts, he asked the Buddha:
"Did you know that your preceptor did not maintain the precepts?"
He replied, “I know. [The Buddha asked,] “Do you know that one should not receive full ordination from such a person?”
He replied, "I do not know. The Buddha said:
"This person has received full ordination.

At that time, there was another who had received full ordination from a preceptor who did not maintain the precepts; later, having doubts, he asked: "Did you know that your preceptor did not maintain the precepts? The Buddha asked him:
"Did you know that your preceptor did not maintain the precepts?"
He replied, “I know. [The Buddha asked,] “Do you know that such a person should not be granted full ordination?”
He replied, “I know. The Buddha said:
"Do you know that receiving full ordination from such a person does not result in full ordination?
He replied, "I do not know."
The Buddha said, "He is said to have received full ordination.
At that time, there was one who had received full ordination from a preceptor who did not maintain the precepts; later, he had doubts. The Buddha asked him:
"Do you know whether your preceptor maintains the precepts or not? He replied, "I know."
The Buddha asked,
“Do you know that such a person should not be granted full ordination? He replied:
"I know. The Buddha asked,
"Do you know that receiving full ordination from such a person does not constitute the successful attainment of full ordination?"
He replied, “I know. The Buddha said:
"It is not called the full reception of the *upasampadā*.
The *Upasampadā-khandhaka* is thus completed. 6. The *Poṣadha-khandhaka*, Part One: At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist brahmins within the city gathered on three occasions each month—the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days.

Great crowds would assemble, coming and going and circulating about, acting as mutual friends, providing food and drink, and cherishing one another with great affection as they made offerings throughout the day.

At that time, King Bimbisāra was in his upper chamber on the palace terrace; seeing from afar the great multitude proceeding toward the assembly place of the brahmins, he immediately asked those around him:
"Where are these people intending to go?"

He replied: "Your Majesty, you should know that the brahmins in this city assemble three times each month—on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days. People come and go, moving about together as companions, providing one another with food and drink; they hold one another in great affection. For this reason, the people go to the place where the brahmins gather."
Then King Bimbisāra descended from the palace hall and went to where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, he sat to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“At present, the various brahmins in this city of Rājagṛha assemble three times each month—on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days—traveling back and forth together as companions, providing one another with food and drink.”
Excellent, World-Honored One!
You should now command the bhikṣus to assemble three times each month—
on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days— and you should also cause the multitude to circulate and travel back and forth, acting as companions to one another and providing food and drink.
"I and my ministers shall also assemble there.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently accepted King Bimbisāra’s words.
Seeing that the World-Honored One had silently accepted his request, the king rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"In this city of Rājagṛha, there are various brahmins who hold assemblies three times each month—on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days.
They come and go and circulate among one another, acting as companions and friends, providing food and drink, and cherishing one another deeply."
You, too, shall hold three assemblies each month—
on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days— where you shall cause many people to come and go, circulate, and associate as friends, providing them with food and drink.
"King Bimbisāra and his ministers shall also assemble there. He replied, "So be it."
"World-Honored One!
Then, having received these instructions, the bhikṣus gathered three times each month—on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days.
At those times, the great assembly gathered, moving about and coming and going, acting as mutual friends and providing one another with food and drink.
King Bimbisāra also arrived, bringing with him his ministers and a great assembly.
When the bhikṣus had gathered, they each sat in silence. Then the elders addressed the bhikṣus, saying, "We wish to hear the Dharma being taught."
The bhikṣus did not dare to speak, so they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to preach the Dharma for them.
Having received this permission, they did not know what Dharma they should preach.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, you are permitted to recite the sūtras.

At that time, the bhikṣus wished to explain the meaning in detail; however, while explaining the meaning, they did not fully recite the words and phrases, and each of them gave rise to doubt. The Buddha said:
"It is said that the meaning should not be explained without the corresponding words and phrases.
At that time, two bhikṣus were preaching the Dharma together on a single high seat; the Buddha said, "This should not be done."
Two bhikṣus were preaching the Dharma from the same high seat and fell into dispute. The Buddha said: "You should not do so.
They then arranged high seats close together and preached the meaning of the teachings, while seeking out each other's faults. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done. Because they pressed him closely while discussing the meaning of the doctrine, the Buddha said: "It should not be done."
At that time, several bhikṣus were chanting together with two voices in unison. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
At that time, several bhikṣus wished to preach the Dharma using a melodic, singing style. The Buddha said:
“Listen. At that time, there was a bhikṣu not far from the World-Honored One who was preaching the Dharma with an excessively loud and melodic chanting voice.
Having heard this, the Buddha immediately addressed that bhikṣu:
"Do not teach the Dharma in such a manner. You should teach the Dharma as the Tathāgata teaches it, abiding in the middle way; do not be like ordinary worldly people.
If you wish to teach the Dharma, you should teach it with equanimity, like Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; do not teach the Dharma in the same way as ordinary worldly people."
"Monks! If one preaches the Dharma with a voice that is excessively melodic and singing-like, there are five faults.
What are these five?"
If a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma with an excessive, melodic chant, he himself gives rise to craving and attachment for that sound; this is called the first fault.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma with an excessive, melodic chant, those who hear it give rise to craving and attachment for that sound; this is called the second fault of a bhikṣu.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma using a voice that is excessively melodic like that of a singer, and those who hear it are led to practice and study it, this is called the third fault of a bhikṣu.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma using a singing voice that exceeds the proper measure, the householders who hear it all join in criticizing and disparaging him, saying:
"The bhikṣu preaches the Dharma just like the songs we ourselves practice."
Thus, he gives rise to pride and fails to show respect; this is called the fourth fault of a bhikṣu.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu preaches the Dharma with a faltering or melodic singing voice, or if, while in a place of quietude engaged in contemplation, he recalls and dwells upon such sounds thereby disturbing his meditative concentration, this is called the fifth fault of a bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to assemble in one place at night to preach the Dharma. The Buddha said, "I permit you to preach.
The bhikṣus did not know on which day they should assemble. The Buddha said:
"Listen to [the recitation] on the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, the thirteenth day, or on the tenth, ninth, eighth, fifth, third, second, or even every day."
"If there are few people who preach the Dharma, you should invite them one after another to speak.
When they were unwilling to speak, the Buddha said: "You should not do so."
The listening should be at its minimum, down to the recitation of a single verse.
A single verse is as follows: "Commit no evil; practice all that is good;
purify your own mind—this is the teaching of all Buddhas."
"If you do not consent, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered at night intending to preach the Dharma; some sitting on low seats had doubts. The Buddha said:
"If one gathers to preach the Dharma at night, it matters not whether the seats are high or low."
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered at night, wishing to practice dhyāna. The Buddha said, "I permit it.
At that time, the bhikṣus became drowsy. The Buddha said:
"One sitting nearby should wake him.
If their hands do not reach one another, one should wake him by grasping the door-bolt or the handle of a fly-whisk.
If one is in agreement with him, one may throw his leather sandals at him."
"If you still continue to sleep, you should use a meditation staff to rouse yourself.
Among them, some who were awakened by the meditation staff rebuked it and would not accept it. The Buddha said, "You should not do so."
"If there are those who, when rebuked, do not accept [the correction], they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding those who fall asleep, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to sprinkle water upon them."
If among them there are those who receive water to sprinkle themselves, yet they scold [the giver] and do not accept it, they too shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If they continue to sleep intentionally, the Buddha said:
"One should wipe one's eyes, or wash one's face with water."
At that time, the bhikṣus were still drowsing as before.
The Buddha said:
"You should pluck at your own ears and noses, or rub your foreheads."

If he should again fall asleep, he should spread out his upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*) and rub his body with his hands; or if he should rise and go outside to look toward the four directions and gaze up at the stars, or reach the place for walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), he should restrain his sense faculties so that the mind does not become distracted.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was dwelling in a secluded place, he reflected and thought to himself:

"I have established the precepts for the bhikṣus and recited the Prātimokṣa; yet among them are faithful bhikṣus who have newly received the ordination and have not yet heard the precepts, and thus do not know how they should train in them."
"I should now allow the bhikṣus to assemble in one place to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One emerged from his seclusion and, for this reason, gathered the bhikṣus together, saying:
"Just now, while I was reflecting in seclusion, this thought arose in my mind:"
"I have established the precepts for the bhikṣus and proclaimed the Prātimokṣa rules.
Yet, there are faithful bhikṣus who have newly received the precepts and have not yet heard them; they do not know how they should train in the precepts."
He further thought to himself:
"I would rather now allow the bhikṣus to assemble in one place to recite the Prātimokṣa.
For this reason, he permitted the bhikṣus to gather together in one place to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts.
He spoke thus: "Venerable sirs!
I now wish to recite the Prātimokṣa precepts."
Listen attentively! Keep this well in mind with a virtuous heart.
If you know that you have committed an offense, you should immediately confess it; those who are free from offenses should remain silent.
By remaining silent, it is known that the venerable ones are pure.
If anyone else asks, they should answer in the same way.
Thus, if a bhikṣu remains among the assembly and, even after being asked three times, remembers having committed an offense yet does not confess it, he incurs the offense of intentional lying.
Therefore, the Buddha has declared that false speech is a dharma that obstructs the path.
If a bhikṣu remembers having committed an offense and desires to seek purification, he should confess it; through confession, one attains peace and happiness.
The *Prātimokṣa* refers to the precepts (*śīla*).
By personally maintaining one’s deportment, dwelling, conduct, faculties, countenance, and head, one gathers all wholesome dharmas and achieves meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
I shall speak of it, I shall bind it together, I shall initiate it, I shall proclaim, reveal, and expound it,
and I shall analyze it repeatedly. Therefore, venerable sirs,
I shall now recite the precepts.

"To assemble together in one place" means to gather in one place for the same *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act). Those who ought to convey their consent (*chanda*) must have done so; those who ought to be censured in person must not fail to be censured. For these reasons, it is said that they "should assemble together in one place."
"Listen attentively and maintain a virtuous mind" means to listen to the Dharma with a composed and focused mind; hence it is said, "listen attentively and maintain a virtuous mind.
"One who has committed an offense" refers to one who has performed an act of transgression that has not yet been repented.
There is no offense for one who has not committed it;
or for one who, having committed it, has repented;
or for one who answers in this same manner when questioned by another.
For example, it is like the false speech involved when individual bhikṣus question and answer one another.
When the Buddha speaks of dharmas that obstruct the path, what kind of path do they obstruct?

They obstruct the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; they obstruct emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; and they obstruct the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhatship.
To repent brings peace and happiness.
What kind of peace and happiness is obtained?

One obtains the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; one obtains the fruit of srotāpanna up to the fruit of arhat. Therefore, it is said that to repent brings peace and happiness.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to recite the precepts with a melodic chant.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to recite the precepts with a melodic chant.
At that time, the bhikṣus grew weary from reciting the precepts every day. The Buddha said:
"One should not recite the precepts every day.
From this day forward, it is permitted to recite the precepts on the *poṣadha* day.
At that time, the householders asked the bhikṣus:
"What day is it today? The bhikṣu replied,
"I do not know."
They were all filled with shame.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, you must count the days."
After several days, he forgot much.
The Buddha said:
"You should employ the method of counting."
At that time, the bhikṣus used precious gems to make counting devices. The Buddha said: "You should not do so.
I allow you to make them from bone, ivory, horn, or from copper, iron, lead, tin, white bronze, stone, or clay pellets."
The bhikṣus were troubled by the frequent loss of their items.
The Buddha said:

"I allow you to make holes and pass them through with cords or threads, placing them where the Saṃgha regularly takes its large meals or small meals, at the place for nightly assemblies, or at the place for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa; or you may place them upon a wooden stake or a 'dragon-tooth' stake. If one day passes [without doing so, it is an offense]."
At one time, several householders came and asked the bhikṣus, "Is today the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight?
The bhikṣus did not know and were all filled with shame. They went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to employ the method of counting by thirties:
fifteen days belong to the dark fortnight, and fifteen belong to the bright fortnight.

At that time, the bhikṣus used the method of counting incorrectly; the counting rules for the dark fortnight fell into those for the bright fortnight, and the counting rules for the bright fortnight fell into those for the dark fortnight. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the method of counting by the dark fortnight to dye [the robes] black, and the method of counting by the bright fortnight to dye them white.
If one suffers from the confusion and disorder caused by mixing these methods of counting, the Buddha said:
"I permit the insertion of a separator between them."
At that time, when the bhikṣus wished to recite the precepts on either the fourteenth or the fifteenth day, the Buddha said:
"If the king changes the date, follow the king’s law."
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know whether the *poṣadha* was to be recited on that day or the next; they went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow the *sthavira* to announce on the *poṣadha* day:
'Today the Saṃgha shall recite the precepts.'"
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know when it was [time].
The Buddha said:

"I allow you to signal the time by measuring the shadow, or by making the sound of splitting bamboo, or the sound of striking the ground, or by producing smoke, or by blowing a conch shell, or by beating a drum, or by striking a *gandī*, or by announcing with words:..."
"Venerable sirs! The time has come for the *poṣadha* and the recitation of the precepts.

At that time, having heard that the World-Honored One permitted the recitation of the precepts, the group of six bhikṣus went to gardens or separate rooms and held a separate recitation of the precepts with their own preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), co-preceptors, co-teachers, and close friends and acquaintances.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How can it be that, having heard the World-Honored One permit the recitation of the precepts, you have instead gone to a garden or a separate room to recite the precepts apart from your preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), or those who share the same preceptor or teacher, as well as your close friends and acquaintances?"
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was staying at the Black Rock Mountain in the Abode of the Sages; while meditating in a secluded place, he had this thought:
"Whether I go now to recite the precepts or do not go, I am always foremost in purity."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of the Elder Mahākāśyapa, vanished from Vulture Peak in the instant it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and suddenly appeared beside Mount Kṛṣṇa at the abode of the rishis, where he spread out a seat and sat before Kāśyapa.
Then Kapphiṇa, having prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [his thoughts], asked him intentionally:
"While you were dwelling in this secluded place in meditation, did this thought arise in your mind: [that the Tathāgata is not omniscient]?"
"Whether I go now to recite the precepts or do not go, I am always foremost in purity.
Is this so? He replied:
"Yes," the Buddha said, "it is so!"
"So it is, Kappina! As you have said:
'Whether you go to attend the recitation of the precepts or do not go, you are always foremost in purity.'"

"However, Kappina! The method for reciting the precepts (poṣadha) ought to be practiced with reverence, respect, and service. If you do not revere, respect, and serve the poṣadha, who then shall revere, respect, and serve it?"
Therefore, you should go to recite the precepts; you should not fail to go.
You should go on foot; you should not travel by means of supernormal power. I, too, shall go.
At that time, Kapphiṇa silently accepted the Buddha’s instruction.

Then, having thus addressed Kapphiṇa on this occasion, the World-Honored One—like a strong man bending or extending his arm—vanished from the Black Rock Mountain, the abode of the seer, and returned to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, where he took his seat.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter to the Buddha.
After the Buddha had explained the aforementioned matter in detail, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“I permit the bhikṣus to perform the recitation of the precepts in a harmonious assembly at a single residence.”
"How is it that you, together with your preceptors, ācāryas, co-preceptors, co-ācāryas, and close friends, recite the Prātimokṣa separately from other groups?
If those dwelling in the same monastery do not recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony, they incur a duṣkṛta offense."
"From this day forward, I authorize you to assemble in one place to recite the precepts.

At that time, the bhikṣus, knowing that the World-Honored One had authorized them to recite the precepts in one place, waited for one another at various locations: some waited at the Black Rock on the mountain where the rishis dwell; some waited at the Seven-Leaf Tree Cave on Mount Vihāra; some waited among the graves; some waited by the hot springs; some waited at the Bamboo Grove, the residence of Kalandaka; some waited on Vulture Peak; or they waited in the great hall, the dining hall, the walking-meditation hall, by the river, under trees, or in places where soft grass grew, until they became weary.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, wherever you reside, regardless of the number of people, you shall assemble together in one place to recite the precepts."
The bhikṣus did not know where they should perform the *poṣadha* ceremony.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a *poṣadha* hall by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."

Having made this formal announcement, one should state the name and location: whether it be in the great hall, or on an upper story, or in the walking-hall, or by the side of a river, or under a tree, or beside a rock, or in a place where grass grows.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let a place of confession (*poṣadha-śālā*) be established at such-and-such a location."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Sangha, listen!
Now the community of monks is establishing a hall for the recitation of the precepts at such-and-such a location."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s establishment of a Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a location, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved and authorized the establishment of the Poṣadha hall at such-and-such a location. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter shall be held as decided."
At that time, a *poṣadha* hall had already been established on Vulture Peak Mountain, and they now wished to establish another *poṣadha* hall at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to first dissolve the previous *poṣadha* hall before establishing another; it shall be dissolved by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the *poṣadha* hall at such-and-such a place be dissolved."
[The motion] is thus announced.
"Venerable Sangha, listen! Now the Sangha dissolves the boundary for the place where the *poṣadha* is recited at [place name]."
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha's dissolution of the *poṣadha* hall at such-and-such a place, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to the dissolution of the *poṣadha* hall at such-and-such a place. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, two *poṣadha* halls were established at a single residence. The two administrators disputed with one another, each saying:
"The Saṃgha should first hold the *poṣadha* ceremony in my hall."
Then the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, it is permitted for two people to alternate [in serving], beginning with the senior-most monk."
At that time, there was a monastery where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the great assembly gathered, but the hall for reciting the precepts (*śīla-saṃghāṭa*) was too small to accommodate them all.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has established a rule: if a hall for reciting the precepts has not been formally designated, the *poṣadha* may not be performed."
"What should we do now?
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha has full authority; whether it establishes a boundary or does not establish one, the recitation of the precepts may proceed."

At that time, the senior bhikṣu arrived first at the hall for the recitation of the precepts; he swept and sprinkled water, prepared the seats, provided the pure water pitcher, provided the foot-washing pitcher, lit the lamps, and arranged the voting sticks (śalākā), until he was utterly exhausted.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, young bhikṣus should perform this task.

On the day of the poṣadha, a young bhikṣu should first go to the hall for the recitation of the precepts, sweep and sprinkle it, arrange the seats, prepare the pure water pitcher, the foot-washing pitcher, the lamps and lighting equipment, and the śalākā."
If a junior bhikṣu does not know [the rules], the elder should instruct him.
If the elder does not instruct him, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
If he does not follow the elder’s instruction, it is also a duṣkṛta offense.

When the Elder had finished reciting the precepts, he personally put away the seats, the water jars, the foot-washing jars, the lamps and implements, and the *śalākā* (voting sticks), returning them all to their original places; he was utterly exhausted.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"From now on, after the recitation of the precepts has concluded, the junior bhikṣus should take charge of the water pitcher, the foot-washing pitcher, the lamps, and the śalākā, and return them to their original places."
If a junior monk does not know [the rules], the senior monk should instruct him.
If the senior monk fails to instruct him, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the junior monk does not follow the senior monk’s instruction, he also commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.

At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the group of six bhikṣus engaged in conversation and greetings with laypeople while performing formal acts (*karmavācanā*), reciting the precepts, and preaching the Dharma.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"This is what the elders (*sthavira*) ought to do."

At that time, there was a certain residence where the foolish Andhaka served as the senior elder (upādhyāya). On the day of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), he was unable to converse with laypeople, exchange greetings, perform formal ritual acts (karmavācanā), recite the precepts, or preach the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to invite one who is capable to perform the task; if an elder does not invite one who is capable, it is a duṣkṛta offense."
"If one does not accept the invitation of the elder, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, some laypeople asked the bhikṣus, "How many people are there when the *poṣadha* is recited?
Having asked, they did not know the number and felt ashamed.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to count the bhikṣus.
Although they counted them, they still forgot; the Buddha said:
“One should prepare a *śalākā* (voting stick).
He made it out of precious materials. The Buddha said:
“One must not make it from precious materials; one should instead make it from bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, tin, reed, bamboo, or wood.”
Suffering from the falling off [of the robes], the Buddha said, "You should bind them with cord.
Although they were bound, they still fell off; the Buddha said:
"It should be placed in a casket.
He made a casket out of precious gems, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so."
"One should use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, tin, reed, bamboo, or wood.
When [the water] emerged from the tube, the Buddha said, "One should make a lid."
He used precious gems to make the canopy, whereupon the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so. One should instead use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, tin, reed, bamboo, or wood."
Not knowing where to place the tube, the Buddha said:
"Place it beneath a rope-bed or a wooden bed; or suspend it on a peg, a 'dragon-tooth' peg, or a clothing rack."
At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had permitted them to go to the city of Rājagṛha for the recitation of the precepts,
those who had heard the news from various directions gathered there for the recitation and were utterly exhausted.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, the precepts shall be recited according to the specific location where one resides—whether it be a village or the boundaries of a town."

Listen to the formal motion (*jñapti*) for the binding of the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*); it should be proclaimed as follows when defining the boundaries of the directions: whether it be an open space, or beneath a tree, or a mountain, or a valley, or a rock cave, or an open ground, or a place overgrown with grass, or near the edge of a garden, or among graves, or in a mountain torrent, or at a pile of stones, or at the stump of a tree, or beside thorny bushes, or at a pool of water, or by the side of a canal, or a pond, or at a heap of refuse, or a village, or the boundary of a village.

Once he has proclaimed the characteristics of the four directions, a person capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed from among the assembly; as before, he should make the formal motion (*jñapti*) as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! Regarding the characteristics of the boundary as they have been described, if it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let us establish a single boundary for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa within this one residential area."
"Thus it is announced.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
According to the described boundaries, the Saṃgha now establishes a boundary for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa within this one residential area."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha’s formal act of binding this one residence for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has approved of the formal act of binding this one residence for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit the establishment of a boundary (sīmābandha) as follows: one should arrange the seats, strike the ghaṇṭā, and assemble everyone together in one place; the acceptance of proxy consent (chanda) is not permitted."
