Among these, the resident bhikṣus should proclaim the characteristics of the four boundaries of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā): if there is a mountain in the east, they should call it a mountain; if there is a moat, they should call it a moat; or if it is a village, a city, a field boundary, a garden, a grove, a pond, a tree, a rock, a wall, or a shrine—just as with the characteristics in the east, so it is for the other directions.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu of this residence announces the marks of the great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) in the four directions."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) within these four marks, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident bhikṣu proclaims the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions.
The Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary within these four directional marks, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa."

"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s binding of a great boundary within these four marks for a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa—remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to the formal establishment of a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) within these four directional markers, for a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

At that time, there arose for the bhikṣus matters requiring a formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) involving a group of four; matters involving groups of five, ten, or twenty bhikṣus also arose, and the large assemblies gathered therein became utterly exhausted.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to establish a *sīmā* (boundary).

It should be established by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), declaring the characteristics of the four boundaries, whether by means of a wooden stake, a stone, or a field boundary as the limit."
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident bhikṣu declares the marks of the small boundary (*sīmā*) in the four directions."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now establish a *karmavācanā* boundary (*sīmā*) within these marks of the small four-sided boundary.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣus of this residence have proclaimed the boundary marks of the small four-sided boundary.
Now the Saṃgha shall establish a *sīmābandha* (precept enclosure) within these marks of the small four-sided boundary.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s establishment of the *sīmābandha* within these four-sided marks, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
“The Saṃgha has already consented to the establishment of the boundary for the *sīmā* within these four marks; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, some bhikṣus wished to make the boundary large, while others wished to make it small. The Buddha said:
“From now on, if you wish to alter [the boundary], you must first dissolve the previous one; thereafter, you may make it large or small according to your intention.”
One should perform the resolution through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
Within the assembly, one capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
"Venerable sirs, at this present dwelling place, the bhikṣus share the same residence and perform the same recitation of the precepts.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent to dissolve the boundary.
This is the formal motion."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus residing at this location, who share the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa, now dissolve the boundary.

Those elders who consent to the dissolution of the boundary by the Saṃgha while sharing the same dwelling place and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."

"The Sangha has already consented; the boundary for a common residence and a common recitation of the Prātimokṣa has been dissolved. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, there was a monk who felt weary of the world and, seeing a fine cave in a forest hermitage, thought to himself:
"If I could stay overnight apart from my robes, I might dwell in this cave."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"From now on, you shall establish the *acchinna-cīvara-maryādā* (the boundary for not losing one's robe). It shall be established by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

In this dwelling place, where the residence is the same and the recitation of the *Poṣadha* is the same, if the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let us establish the boundary for not losing one's robes (*akālacīvara-sīmā*)."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

In this residence, which is a single dwelling place and a single place for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, the Saṃgha now establishes a 'boundary for not losing one's robe' (acīvarāsaṃsargaka-sīmā)."

Whichever elders consent to the Saṃgha’s present act of binding the *akālacīvara* boundary—establishing a single dwelling place and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa—let them remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak.

"The Sangha has already consented to this boundary for not losing one's robes, established within this same dwelling place and for the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, the bhikṣus removed their robes and left them in the houses of laypeople; while they were putting on the robes they had removed, their bodies were exposed.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow the bhikṣus to establish a 'boundary for not losing robes' (aśuddhavastra-sīmā), with the exception of villages and the areas outside of villages."

Regarding the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation): from within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
This dwelling place is a single residence with a single *poṣadha* ceremony.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, authorize the establishment of a *acīvarāpattika-sīmā* (the boundary where one does not lose one's robe), excluding villages and the space outside of villages.
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Sangha, listen!

In this dwelling place, which is a single residence with a single recitation of the *Poṣadha*, the Sangha now establishes a boundary for not losing one's robes (*akālacīvara-sīmā*), excluding villages and the areas outside of villages."

"Whichever elders consent to the Sangha’s formal establishment of a non-separation-of-robes boundary (*akathina-sīmā*) within this residence—sharing the same dwelling and the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, excluding villages and the area surrounding them—let them remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to establish a 'boundary for not losing one's robes' within this same dwelling place and this same boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, excluding the village and its surrounding area. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
At that time, the bhikṣus made two boundaries meet at their edges. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; you must establish a marker.
They then allowed the two boundaries to overlap one another. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done; one should leave a space between them.
Those bhikṣus first dissolved the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) and then dissolved the non-separation-of-clothing boundary (acchinna-cīvara-sīmā). The Buddha said: "It should not be done."
"First dissolve the *akathina* boundary, and afterwards dissolve the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*).

At that time, they established an *akathina* boundary on the far side of a swiftly flowing river. A bhikṣu went there to retrieve his robe, but it was swept away by the current. The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, you must not establish an *akathina* boundary on the far side of a swiftly flowing river, except in cases where there is a permanent bridge."

At that time, there were two monastic residences with separate provisions for offerings and separate recitations of the *Poṣadha*. The bhikṣus wished to establish them as a single community with a common recitation of the *Poṣadha* and common provisions for offerings.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I allow you to first dissolve the boundary and then re-establish it; the dissolution is performed by means of a formal motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) as follows."
When each party dissolves their respective boundaries, they must all assemble in one place; the desire for consent (*chanda*) may not be accepted.

One should proclaim the characteristics of the four sides of the boundary: whether it be a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), the foot of a tree, an open space, a mountain, a valley, a rock cave, an open ground, a grassy thicket, a grove, a cemetery, the bank of a river, a stone mound, a stump, a thorn bush, a ditch, a canal, a pond, a heap of refuse, a village, or the boundary of a village.

Having announced the boundaries of the precincts, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* among the assembly should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

As has been described regarding the characteristics of the boundary (*sīmā*): if the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant permission to establish at this place and that place a single area for the sharing of offerings and a single area for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
According to the described boundaries, the Sangha now establishes at these various locations a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single distribution of offerings."

Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha’s delimitation of a boundary at this place and that place for a common recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a common distribution of offerings, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.

“The Saṃgha has already consented to the delimitation of the boundary for a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa and a single distribution of offerings at these various locations. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held as such.”
At that time, there were two monastic residences where the *poṣadha* was observed separately and offerings (*lābha*) were received separately.
Then, the bhikṣus desired to observe the *poṣadha* at one location while receiving offerings separately. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to first dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*) and then establish it again by means of a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*)."
Each of you should understand this for yourselves: you must all assemble in one place and must not engage in sexual desire.

You should announce the boundaries and characteristics of the area—whether it be a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), a secluded place, or even a village boundary as described above—and state the names of the two residences.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Regarding the boundaries and characteristics as they have been declared, if the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha grants its consent, let it be established here that there shall be a common recitation of the precepts (*ekapoṣadha*) and separate offerings (*pṛthag-lābha*)."
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
According to the boundaries and characteristics as described, the Saṃgha now establishes at this place a common recitation of the Prātimokṣa and separate distribution of offerings."

"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha's formal establishment within the boundaries of this four-sided perimeter for a common recitation of the Prātimokṣa but separate distribution of offerings, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to establish, within the four boundaries of this realm, a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa with separate distributions of offerings. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
At that time, there were two monastic residences where the *poṣadha* ceremony was performed separately and offerings (*lābha*) were received separately.
Then, the bhikṣus desired to perform the *poṣadha* separately while sharing the same offerings, for the purpose of protecting their respective residences.
The Buddha said: "I allow you to perform the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) to establish [the boundary].
Within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made: [Insert motion here]"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time for the Saṃgha has come and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let it be established that at this and that residence, the separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa shall be performed with a common distribution of offerings, for the purpose of protecting the residences."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now the Saṃgha shall establish a separate boundary for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa at this and that residence, yet maintain a single distribution of offerings, for the purpose of protecting the residences."

"Which elders consent to the Saṃgha’s formal establishment of a separate recitation of the Prātimokṣa at this and that residence, while sharing the same distribution of offerings, for the sake of protecting the residences? Those who consent, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak."

"The Sangha has already consented to establish a separate *poṣadha* for recitation while sharing the same *lābha* at this and that residence, for the purpose of protecting the residences; the Sangha consents by its silence, and thus this matter shall be so upheld."
At that time, there were two monastic residences that shared the same recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and the same distribution of offerings.
When the bhikṣus wished to recite the *Prātimokṣa* separately and receive offerings separately, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to assemble in one place, dissolve the existing boundary (*sīmā*), and then each, according to their respective residence, re-establish their own boundaries."
At that time, there were two monasteries situated far apart from one another, yet they shared the same recitation of the *Poṣadha* and the same distribution of offerings.
If the [monks] at one monastery received a small amount of food, drink, or requisites for worship, and brought them here, the time for the meal would already have passed.
If one takes the gains and offerings received here to that place, the time for the meal will have already passed.
Then the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not remain at a distant location from another while performing the same *poṣadha* ceremony or sharing the same offerings."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to speak thus:
'If a small amount of food or drink is obtained as an offering at this place, it shall be distributed right here.'"
"If he receives even a small amount of offerings, he shall distribute them right there.
At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a large number of bhikṣus were traveling through a desolate wilderness where no villages were found. They thought to themselves:
"The World-Honored One has established a rule that we must assemble in one place in harmony to recite the precepts (*śīla*)."
"What should we do? They went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣus, listen well!

If, on the day of the *poṣadha*, one is traveling through a wilderness area where there is no village, the community of monks (*saṃgha*) should gather together in one place and recite the precepts collectively.

If the community cannot achieve such harmony, then those who share the same *upādhyāya*, the same *ācārya*, or who are virtuous friends and companions, should gather in one place along the road, establish a minor boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and recite the precepts.

The *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for establishing the boundary should be performed as follows: from within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
"Now there is a gathering of this many bhikṣus. If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant permission to establish a small boundary (sīmā).
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
May the Venerable Saṃgha listen!..."
Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled to establish a small boundary (sīmā).
Those elders who consent to these this many bhikṣus being assembled to establish a small boundary, let them remain silent; those who do not consent, let them speak.

"The Saṃgha has already consented; the assembly of so many bhikṣus has completed the binding of the small boundary (sīmā). Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held as such.

At that time, the bhikṣus departed without unbinding the boundary. Others who were dissatisfied and reproached them went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "One should not depart without unbinding it;
one must perform a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to unbind it."
From among the assembly, one who is capable as described above should be appointed, and he should make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now there are this many bhikṣus assembled. If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the small boundary at this location be dissolved."
The motion is thus made:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
There are now this many bhikṣus assembled; we shall dissolve the small boundary at this location."
"Whichever elders consent to the Sangha's dissolution of this small boundary here, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to the dissolution of this small boundary here. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, there was a heavy rain from the heavens, and the river swelled.

The bhikṣus, being separated by the river, had established a common residence and a common recitation of the precepts; on the fifteenth day, they wished to go to them for the recitation of the precepts, but were unable to cross, and thus the recitation of the precepts was not accomplished.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"One must not combine separate river sections to establish a single boundary for the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), except where there is a boat or a bridge."
At that time, there were two monastic residences far apart from each other that had established a common recitation of the *Poṣadha*.

When the monks wished to go to one another’s location on the fifteenth day to perform the recitation, they were unable to arrive there by that same day, and thus the recitation was not successfully accomplished.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One may not establish a single *poṣadha* recitation for a dwelling place where the locations are far apart. However, if a dwelling place is separated by a river and the distance is great, yet they establish it as a single dwelling place with a single *poṣadha* recitation, then when the bhikṣus are to perform the *poṣadha* on the fifteenth day, they should go there beforehand on the fourteenth day."
"When the *poṣadha* is to be recited on the fourteenth day, one should arrive beforehand on the thirteenth day and must not accept a proxy for the consent (*chanda*).
At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, there was a bhikṣu in a dwelling who entered his room, closed the door, and fell asleep.
When the bhikṣus had finished reciting the precepts, they rose from their seats and departed.
At that time, those who were sleeping heard the sound and immediately arose, asking the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"Where do you wish to go, that you have not recited the precepts? The bhikṣus replied,
"We have already recited the precepts."
He then asked, "Where have you come from just now? He replied:
"I was merely sleeping in my own room with the door closed during the day.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not sleep in one's room on the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony."
From this day forward, those sitting together shall examine one another to ascertain who has arrived and who has not.
From this day forward, it is permitted to recite the precepts only after first making a formal announcement (*jñapti*). The announcement should be made as follows:
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!..."
"Today is the fifteenth day, and the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa. If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen, so that we may recite the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
This is the formal motion (jñapti). Having made this motion, they should then recite the Prātimokṣa.
The Fourth Part of the Vinaya, Volume 35;
The Fourth Part of the Vinaya, Volume 36, Section 15 of the Two Parts,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others.
*Śīlanirdeśa-vastu*, Part Two. At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, there was a bhikṣu residing in a certain place who thought to himself:
"The Buddha has prescribed that the precepts must be recited by assembling together in one place; what shall I do now?"
He then spoke to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen well, all of you!

If on the day of the recitation of the precepts there is a single bhikṣu residing there, that bhikṣu should go to the hall for the recitation of the precepts, sweep and sprinkle it to make it clean, spread out the seating mats, prepare the water pitcher for washing and the foot-washing pitcher, light the lamps, and prepare the śalākā sticks.
If there are visiting bhikṣus who have arrived—whether four or more than four—they should first announce [their presence] and only then recite the precepts.
If there are three persons, they should each say to one another:
"Today is the fifteenth day for the Saṃgha’s recitation of the precepts; I, so-and-so, am pure."
Thus it is said three times.
If there are two persons, they also address each other, saying:
"Today the Saṃgha recites the Prātimokṣa on the fifteenth day; I, so-and-so, am pure."
Thus it is said three times.
If there is one person, they should mentally reflect and verbally declare:
"Today the Sangha recites the precepts on the fifteenth day; I, so-and-so, am pure."
Thus it is said three times.
If there are three persons, they may not receive the desire for purity from a fourth person to recite the *poṣadha*;
if there are two persons, they may not receive the desire for purity from a third person; rather, each should recite it by speaking three times individually.
"If one person cannot receive the *kṣānti* (consent) and purity from a second person, they should recite it three times while reflecting in their mind.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus performed the *kaṭhina* (formal act) and the recitation of the precepts through an illegal separate assembly; they also performed the *kaṭhina* and the recitation of the precepts through an illegal harmonious assembly and a legal separate assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"One must not perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the recitation of the precepts through an illegal separate assembly, nor through an illegal united assembly."
"One must not perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* with an illegal and divided assembly; there are four kinds of such recitations.

At that time, the bhikṣus performed the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* through an illegal and divided assembly, an illegal and harmonious assembly, a legal and divided assembly, and a legal and harmonious assembly.
"If that bhikṣu performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) and recites the precepts through an illegal and divided assembly, the recitation of the precepts is not accomplished.
If he performs a formal act and recites the precepts through an illegal but harmonious assembly, or through a legal but divided assembly, the recitation of the precepts is not accomplished."
"When the Dharma and the harmonious Saṃgha perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts, this is called 'reciting the precepts.
This is how the precepts should be recited; this is my teaching.
At the time of the Uposatha, when the community of monks had gathered for a monastic matter, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Śānta! Now there is business for the Saṃgha.
Then another bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
A sick bhikṣu has not come.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the giving of consent (*chanda*). The person receiving the consent should go and receive it; he should give the consent in this manner:
if he says, 'I give my consent to you.'"
"Thus one gives consent.
Or if one says:
'I speak my consent.'"
"Thus, he gives his consent.
If he says: 'Speak my consent for me.'"
The giving of consent is accomplished.
If one gives consent by manifesting bodily signs, the giving of consent is accomplished.
If one says:
"It is said that 'the formal expression of consent (chanda) must be fully articulated' for the giving of consent to be established.
If one neither manifests the physical signs nor verbally expresses the consent, the giving of consent is not established; one must give the consent again."
If a bhikṣu who has received consent (*chanda*) goes to a sick bhikṣu to convey that consent,
and after having received it, he passes away, or goes elsewhere, or renounces the path, or joins the assembly of non-Buddhists, or joins a separate faction,
or arrives at the boundary of the precept-platform (*sīmā*), or the dawn appears, or he himself declares that he has committed a pārājika offense; [in these cases, the consent is not valid].
If one has violated a bhikṣuṇī; or if one has become a śramaṇa with a thieving mind; or if one has destroyed the two [sexual] organs;
or if one is a eunuch; or if one has killed one's father or mother; or if one has killed an arhat; or if one has caused schism in the Saṃgha;
or if one has, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha; or if one is a non-human, or an animal, or a hermaphrodite; or if...

One who has been formally charged, one who has been expelled, one who should be expelled, one who possesses supernormal powers while in mid-air, or one who is beyond the range of sight and hearing, does not constitute a valid transmission of consent (*chanda*); the consent must be given again by another person.
If one reaches the middle of the assembly or the midst of the Saṃgha, it is also the same.

If a person who has received the *chanda* (consent) falls asleep, enters meditative absorption, or forgets [to convey it], provided they did not do so intentionally, this is called "the giving of consent being accomplished."
If one intentionally does not speak [of this], it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one is able to do so, it is well; if one is unable to do so, that bhikṣu should support the sick bhikṣu—whether on a bed or a rope-cot—and carry him up to the midst of the Saṃgha.

If it is considered that this sick bhikṣu might aggravate his illness or even die, the entire Saṃgha should go to the place where the sick bhikṣu is, surround him, and perform the *karmavācanā* for him.
If there are many sick persons, it is well if they can be gathered in one place.
If this is not possible, the bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā*; there is no other expedient by which a *karmavācanā* may be performed by a separate assembly.
At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, the community of monks gathered in one place, intending to recite the precepts.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Be silent, all of you!"
"Now I wish to recite the precepts.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"There is a sick bhikṣu here who has not come."
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the granting of *pārisuddhi* (purification). I authorize a bhikṣu to go and receive *pārisuddhi*.
He should grant it in this manner."

If one says, "I grant the purification," or "I accomplish the purification," or even if one speaks at length until the words "purification" are reached—just as in the case of granting the formal consent (*chanda*)—this constitutes the granting of purification.

If one does not move the body nor speak the words "purification," it does not constitute the granting of purification; in this case, as with the granting of consent, one must grant the purification once again.
If one who has received the *pārisuddhi* (declaration of purity) goes to the sick bhikṣu and, having received the *pārisuddhi*, passes away;
or if he departs for another path, or ceases his practice of the Way, or enters the assembly of non-Buddhists, or enters the assembly of a separate faction,
or arrives at the boundary of the *sīmā* (ordination ground), or the dawn appears, or he himself declares that he has committed a *pārājika* offense, or commits [a *pārājika* offense]...
A bhikṣuṇī, or one who has joined the saṃgha with a thieving mind, or one who has destroyed the two [sexual] organs,
or a eunuch, or one who has killed his mother, killed his father, or killed an arhat, or one who has caused schism in the Saṃgha,
or one who has maliciously shed the blood of a Buddha, or a non-human, or an animal, or one with both sexual organs, or...

If one has been subject to formal censure, or has been expelled, or is subject to expulsion, or is suspended in mid-air by supernormal power, or is beyond the range of sight and hearing, the granting of purity is not valid; it should be granted again to another.
The same applies if one goes to the middle of the path or into the midst of the assembly.
If the person who has received the purification is asleep, or has entered meditative absorption, or has forgotten, provided it was not done intentionally, it constitutes the granting of purification.
If one intentionally does not speak [of this], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is able to do so, it is well; if one cannot do so, one should support the sick person—whether on a bed, a rope-bed, or a litter—and carry them to the midst of the Saṃgha.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"If we carry the sick bhikṣu here, we fear his illness may be aggravated or he may pass away before arriving; therefore, we should go to him and perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Poṣadha* there."

"If there are many sick persons gathered in one place, it is well; if they cannot be gathered together, the bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*."

If one does not go outside the boundary, one may not perform a *karmavācanā* or recite the *Prātimokṣa* separately from the assembly; there is no other expedient means by which one may perform a *karmavācanā* or recite the *Prātimokṣa* separately from the assembly.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus gave their consent (*chanda*) but did not give their purity (*śauca*). When a matter arose within the Saṃgha, the *poṣadha* ceremony could not be performed.
Then the bhikṣu who had brought the consent said:
"I have brought the consent, but I did not bring the purity."
Because the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) were thus delayed, the bhikṣus all became weary.
The bhikṣus then went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when one is granting one's consent (*chanda*), one should also grant one's purity (*śauca*)."
One should speak thus:
"I give you my consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pārisuddhi*).
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus spoke according to the specific matter at hand.
"I transmit this matter to you for the sake of the *chanda* (consent) and purification.
While other matters arise within the Saṃgha, the bhikṣu holding the *chanda* says:
"I have brought the *chanda* and purification for a specific matter; I have not brought the *chanda* and purification for any other matters."
Because of this matter, there was delay, and the bhikṣus all became weary.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not grant the *chanda* (consent) and *pāriśuddhi* (purity) by citing the specific matter; rather, it is permitted to grant the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* for a formal monastic act (*dharmika saṃghakarma*) in accordance with the Dharma."

At that time, regarding a monk who has received the *chanda* (consent) and *pārisuddhi* (purification), if he dies, or leaves the monastic life, or joins a group of non-Buddhists, or joins a separate faction, or goes to the boundary of the *sīmā*, or if the dawn appears, the monks think:
"Has he lost his granted consent and purification?"
The Buddha said, “It is lost.

At that time, a bhikṣu who had received the *yad-bhūyaḥ* (consent) and the *viśuddhi* (purity) encountered an obstruction on the road, such as the danger of bandits, the danger of wild beasts, or the rising of a river’s flood, preventing him from arriving. He then came from outside the boundary into the midst of the Saṃgha to present his *yad-bhūyaḥ* and *viśuddhi*. The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Is this considered a loss of the desire for purity?
The Buddha said,
"It is not a loss."

From this day forward, it is permitted for a bhikṣu who has granted his consent and purity (*chanda-śuddhi*)—if he faces a danger to life or a danger to the holy life (*brahmacarya*), or if he is unable to reach the assembly within the boundary—to come from outside the boundary into the assembly to grant his consent and purity. In this way, the granting of consent and purity is not lost; this is what I have taught.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having received the *chanda* and purity from one person, were doubtful and did not receive the *chanda* and purity from two persons.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive them."
Having received the *kāyacitta-viśuddhi* (desire for purity) from two persons, he again became doubtful and did not receive the *kāyacitta-viśuddhi* from three persons. The Buddha said:
"I permit you to receive it.
Having received the *kāyacitta-viśuddhi* from three persons, he was doubtful and did not receive the *kāyacitta-viśuddhi* from four persons. The Buddha said:
"Listen and receive it.
The Buddha said,
"If you can fully memorize the characters, you may receive as much as you are able to recall."
If one cannot recall the name, one should state the clan name.
If one cannot remember the clan name, one should state the physical appearance.
If one cannot remember the physical appearance, one should simply say: "Many bhikṣus have granted their consent for the legal monastic business (*dharmasaṃghakārya*) and their purity."
At the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, a great assembly gathered in one place, but the voice of the reciter was too low for the entire assembly to hear.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to stand in the midst of the assembly to recite the *poṣadha*."
If they still do not hear it, one should arrange a high seat within the assembly, making it as lofty and excellent as possible, and recite the precepts from that seat.

If they still do not hear it, one should construct a revolving high seat so that one can stand with hands reaching up to the person on the seat and recite the precepts from above. While reciting, if a mistake or omission occurs, the bhikṣu seated next in order should provide the words.
"If one should intentionally forget, the next second bhikṣu shall speak on his behalf; he shall speak in the proper sequence and must not repeat what has already been said.

At that time, the bhikṣu holding the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* had business arise—whether it be business of the Saṃgha, business of the Buddha, business of the Dharma, or business concerning a sick bhikṣu.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to transmit the *chanda* and *pāriśuddhi* to other bhikṣus."
One should speak as follows:

"I, together with many bhikṣus, transmit my consent and purity; both they and I shall participate in the formal monastic proceedings according to the Dharma through this transmission of consent and purity."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus said:
"Tell us the names of your upādhyāya and ācārya.
When the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"You must not address your upādhyāya or ācārya by their personal names.
At that time, the bhikṣus asked one another:
"What are the names of your upādhyāya and ācārya?"
Fearing and doubting, they did not dare to address him by name.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is someone who asks, you are permitted to address the upādhyāya or ācārya by name."

If a bhikṣu is undergoing parivāsa, mūlāpakarṣa, mānatva, or āvarhaṇa; or at the time of a formal act (karmavācanā), or when establishing a regulation, or when receiving the precepts, or when appointing someone, or when releasing [a penalty], he should address the names of his upādhyāya and ācārya.
At that time, there were certain matters for which a bhikṣu ought to address his preceptor (upādhyāya) or teacher (ācārya) by name; however, being hesitant and fearful, he did not dare to do so.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a matter or circumstance that requires it, I authorize you to address your preceptor or teacher by name."
If a bhikṣu, for the sake of a certain matter, gives his consent and purification (*chandapariśuddhi*); and having given his consent, the matter is subsequently dropped;
yet he then becomes doubtful and dares not go to the place where the *poṣadha* is recited—when the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"If the matter has been dropped, he should go. If he does not go, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If we do not go to the place where the *poṣadha* is being recited, we fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against us to prohibit our recitation."
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so.
They then thought again as follows:

“I shall not go to the place where the *poṣadha* is recited, for fear that [my] close friends and acquaintances might perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against me or obstruct the recitation of the precepts.
The Buddha said: “You should not do so.”
He further thought to himself:
"If I do not sit at the place where the precepts are recited, I fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against me or obstruct the recitation of the precepts."
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
It is likewise if one goes to the place where the precepts are recited for the sake of close friends or acquaintances and does not sit down.

At that time, there was a monastic residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, the community of monks assembled in great numbers. When they were about to recite the precepts, they heard that bandits were approaching; everyone became terrified, rose from their seats, and departed, so that the recitation of the precepts could not be completed.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, when the eight difficult circumstances arise, or if there are other such conditions, I authorize the abbreviated recitation of the precepts."
The eight difficulties are: kings, thieves, fire, water, disease, humans, non-humans, and malevolent insects.
Regarding other circumstances: if a large assembly has gathered but there are insufficient seats, or if many members of the assembly are ill, it is permitted to recite the precepts in brief.
If a large assembly has gathered, but the seating area is not fully covered or it is raining, it is permitted to recite the precepts in brief.

If the *poṣadha* has lasted for many nights—whether due to disputes, or discussions on the Abhidharma or Vinaya, or the preaching of the Dharma—and the night has already passed, from now on it is permitted for the entire assembly, provided they have not yet risen and the dawn-sign (*āloka*) has not yet appeared, to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts; there is no other means by which one may receive the formal act of consent and purity (*chanda-pāriśuddhi*) while staying overnight to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts.
That bhikṣu thought to himself:

"Now, because of these difficult circumstances, the abbreviated recitation of the precepts has been permitted; yet the difficulties are still far off and have not yet arrived, so we may perform the full recitation of the precepts."
At that time, those bhikṣus should recite the precepts in full; if they do not recite them in full, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, those bhikṣus might think:
"This difficult situation is imminent; we cannot recite the precepts in full, so we may recite up to the ninety items."
That bhikṣu should explain up to the ninety matters; if he does not explain them, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"This difficult situation is imminent; we cannot explain extensively up to the ninety matters, but we may explain up to the thirty matters."
"The full exposition should be given up to the thirty matters; those who do not speak thus shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought:
"This difficult situation is imminent; we cannot give the full exposition up to the thirty matters, but we may speak up to the two *aniyata* dharmas."
"A bhikṣu should recite up to the two *aniyata* dharmas; if he does not do so, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought:
"The difficult situation is imminent; we cannot recite extensively up to the two *aniyata* dharmas; we may instead recite the thirteen matters."
He should explain up to thirteen matters; if he does not, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus thought: "This difficult situation is imminent;
we cannot explain extensively up to thirteen matters, but may explain four."
"Those bhikṣus should recite the four matters; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus should think: 'This danger is imminent;
we cannot recite the four matters, so we may recite the introduction to the precepts.'"
"He should recite the *Prātimokṣa* introduction; if he does not, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the bhikṣus thought:
"This danger is imminent; we shall not be able to recite the *Prātimokṣa* introduction."
On account of such difficult circumstances, the bhikṣus should immediately rise from their seats and depart.
There are five ways of reciting the *Prātimokṣa*:
having recited the introduction (*nidāna*), the rest should say:
"The Sangha has already heard.
If the introduction and the four matters have been recited, the rest should say:
"The Sangha has already heard."
If, after the introduction, the four matters, and the thirteen matters have been recited, those remaining should say:
"The Saṃgha has heard it constantly.
If, after the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, and the two matters have been recited, those remaining should say:
“The Saṃgha has heard.
This is the detailed explanation of the fifth; these are called the five types of reciting the precepts.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
When reciting the introduction and the four matters, for the remainder one should say:
"The Sangha has constantly heard this.
When the introduction, the four matters, and the thirteen matters have been recited, for the remainder one should say:
"The Sangha has already heard.
After the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, and the two matters have been recited, those remaining should say:
"The Sangha has already heard."
Having recited the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, the two matters, and the thirty matters, for the remainder one should say:
"The Saṃgha has heard this constantly.
Thus the fifth [section] is explained in detail.
Furthermore, there are five matters:
having recited the introduction, the four matters, and the thirteen matters, for the remainder one should say:
"The Sangha has heard this constantly."
After the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, and the two matters have been recited, the rest should say:
"The Saṃgha has heard it constantly.
After the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, the two matters, and the thirty matters have been recited, the rest should say:
"The Sangha has already heard.
After the introduction, the four matters, the thirteen matters, the two matters, the thirty matters, and the ninety matters have been recited, the remainder should be declared as:
"The Sangha has already heard."
Thus the fifth [type] is explained in detail.
These are called the five kinds of recitation of the precepts (*pātimokkha*).
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Nanayou who was mentally disturbed and insane; sometimes he remembered the recitation of the precepts and sometimes he did not, and sometimes he came and sometimes he did not.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"From now on, perform the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* for the bhikṣu Nanda-yu, declaring him to be mentally deranged and insane."
It should be granted in this manner.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu Nana is mentally deranged and insane; he may remember the recitation of the precepts or not, and he may come or not.

If the Saṃgha’s time has come, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this bhikṣu the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for mental derangement and insanity, so that whether he remembers or does not remember, whether he comes or does not come, the Saṃgha may perform the formal act and recite the precepts.
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Nana-yu is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane; he may or may not remember the recitation of the precepts, and he may or may not come. Now the Saṃgha shall perform the *karmavācanā* for the bhikṣu Nana-yu who is mentally disturbed, deranged, and insane, so that the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts may proceed whether he remembers them or not, and whether he comes or not."

"Whichever elders approve of performing the *karmavācanā* for this monk Nana-yu—to declare him insane and mentally deranged, such that he may or may not remember [the rules], and may or may not come to the assembly—for the purpose of conducting the *karmavācanā* and reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."

"The Sangha has already granted consent to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the monk Nana-yu, who is of a deranged and confused mind—regardless of whether he remembers or not, or whether he comes or not—and the formal act is completed. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
There are three kinds of insanity and delusion:

first, those who, when the *poṣadha* is being recited, are uncertain whether they remember it or not, or whether they will come or not; second, those who, being insane or deluded, remember the *poṣadha* and yet do not come; third, those who, being insane or deluded, do not remember the *poṣadha* and do not come. These are called the three kinds of insanity and delusion.

In this regard, if there are those who remember the recitation of the precepts and those who do not remember the recitation of the precepts, and those who come and those who do not come—if such bhikṣus exist, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one who is insane against them.
If one who remembers the recitation of the precepts comes [to the assembly], the community of monks should not perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one who is insane or deluded.
If one who is insane or deluded neither remembers the recitation of the precepts nor comes [to the assembly], they should not be granted the formal act for one who is insane or deluded.
After that bhikṣu had been subjected to the formal ritual (karmavācanā), his madness and delusion subsequently subsided, and he thought to himself: "What should I do now?
He then informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If one who was insane has been subjected to the formal ritual (karmavācanā), and his insanity and delusion subsequently cease, one should perform a formal ritual of a motion and one proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) to revoke it."
One should understand it in this way.
The *nānāyu* bhikṣu should go before the community of monks, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

I, the bhikṣu Nāman, was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity; when the *poṣadha* was being recited, I sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember, and sometimes came and sometimes did not come. The Saṃgha performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for me regarding the disease of insanity.
"Having performed [the act], I have now returned to composure and seek the *karmavācanā* for the removal of madness and delusion.
Thus he speaks three times.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Nana-yu was previously afflicted with the disease of insanity; when the *poṣadha* was being recited, he sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember, and sometimes came and sometimes did not come."
The community of monks has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for insanity against me.
Now that the insanity and delusion have ceased, I seek the lifting of this formal act for insanity.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent and listen: let the Sangha lift the formal act for insanity.
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Sangha, listen!

This bhikṣu, Nana-yu, was previously afflicted by the disease of insanity. At the time of the recitation of the precepts, he sometimes remembered and sometimes did not remember; sometimes he came and sometimes he did not come. The community of monks has performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for one suffering from the disease of insanity upon him."
Having performed this, his madness and delusion have been brought to rest; he now requests the Saṃgha to grant him the *karmavācanā* for the resolution of his madness and delusion.
Those elders who consent to grant the *karmavācanā* for the resolution of the madness and delusion of the bhikṣu Nana-yu, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.

"The Sangha has already consented to the completion of the *karmavācanā* for the monk Nana-yu, releasing him from the affliction of insanity; because the Sangha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, the bhikṣus each thought to themselves:
"Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed for one suffering from madness and delusion, they may later undergo the cessation and the lifting of that *karmavācanā* for madness and delusion."
"If he becomes insane again, may the *karmavācanā* be performed for him later?
The Buddha said, "From this time forward, whenever he suffers from the illness of insanity, the *karmavācanā* shall be performed for him; once the insanity ceases, it shall be revoked."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying on the banks of the Gaggara River in the kingdom of Campā.
On the fifteenth day, during the time for the recitation of the precepts, the World-Honored One sat in the open air, surrounded by the community of monks before and behind him.

Then Ānanda, when the first watch of the night had passed and it was the beginning of the middle watch, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The first watch has already passed; I pray that the World-Honored One will recite the precepts.”
The World-Honored One remained silent.
Seeing that the World-Honored One was silent, Ānanda returned to his seat.

When the first watch and the middle watch of the night had passed, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The first watch and the middle watch of the night have passed; may the Blessed One please recite the precepts.
The Blessed One remained silent.
Seeing that the Blessed One was silent, Ānanda returned to his seat.

When the first watch of the night had passed, the middle watch had passed, and the last watch had already passed, and the light of dawn appeared as the various birds began to sing, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"The first, middle, and last watches of the night have passed; the light of dawn has appeared and the various birds are singing. The assembly of monks has sat for a long time; may the World-Honored One please recite the precepts."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there is one who is impure among the assembly—if there is one who is impure among the assembly—and yet you wish for the Tathāgata to recite the precepts therein, such a thing is impossible."
At that time, Ānanda returned to his seat in silence.
Then the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"What is impure among this assembly that the Tathāgata has spoken thus?"
"Is it not unreasonable to recite the precepts in the midst of those who are impure?

At that time, Maudgalyāyana surveyed the minds of the assembly and saw an impure person sitting not far from the Tathāgata. This man was not a śramaṇa yet claimed to be a śramaṇa; he did not practice the holy life yet spoke of practicing the holy life. He violated the precepts and was defiled by evil dharmas; his wrong views concealed his evil karma. Internally he was rotten, like a hollow tree. Having seen him, he thought to himself:
"The Buddha spoke these words to Ānanda specifically for this person’s sake:
'It is absolutely impossible that the Tathāgata would preach the precepts in the midst of an assembly where impurity exists.'"
Then Maudgalyāyana went to that person’s place and said to him: “Arise!
The Tathāgata has already seen you!”
"I know you! Arise quickly and depart; there is no need for you to stay here!
At that time, Maudgalyāyana took him by the hand, led him out the door, and returned to the World-Honored One. He prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Saṃgha is already pure; I pray that the World-Honored One will recite the precepts.
The Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
“You should not do this now, nor should you do it hereafter.”
Maudgalyāyana!
From this day forward, I authorize the administration of discipline through one's own confession; if one does not confess, one should not be disciplined.
From this day forward, you yourselves shall perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“This is the Tathāgata’s final recitation of the precepts. Why is this so?”
One who has committed an offense shall not participate in the recitation of the precepts.
One who has committed an offense shall not hear the recitation of the precepts, nor shall they explain the expiation of an offense to one who has committed an offense.
One who has an offense shall not receive the expiation of an offense from another.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“The waters of the ocean possess eight extraordinary qualities; it is for these eight reasons that the asuras dwell there in enjoyment.”
What are these eight?
That all streams of water flow toward and enter it—this is called the first marvel, which the asuras enjoy.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
The seawater remains constant and does not lose its tidal law; this, Maudgalyāyana, is called the second extraordinary quality of the ocean, which is enjoyed by the asuras.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

Now, the five great rivers—the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarayū, Aciravatī, and Mahī—all pour into the ocean and lose their original names, being called simply "the ocean. This, Maudgalyāyana, is the third extraordinary quality of the ocean, which the asuras enjoy.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

These five great rivers and the rain from heaven all flow into the ocean, yet the waters of the sea neither increase nor decrease. This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the fourth extraordinary quality of the ocean’s waters, which the asuras enjoy.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
The waters of the ocean are entirely salty and of a single flavor; this, Maudgalyāyana, is called the fifth marvelous quality of the ocean, which is enjoyed by the asuras.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

The waters of the ocean do not tolerate corpses; if there should be a corpse, the wind blows it out and places it upon the shore. This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the sixth extraordinary marvel of the ocean, which the asuras enjoy.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!
The waters of the sea produce many rare and extraordinary treasures that do not exist on land, all of which emerge from the ocean.
These so-called treasures are gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, conch shells, and agate. Maudgalyāyana, these are the seven wonders of the sea waters, where the asuras take their delight.
Furthermore, Maudgalyāyana!

The great ocean is the dwelling place of those with massive bodies. As for these "massive-bodied" ones, their bodies are one hundred yojanas, two hundred yojanas, three hundred yojanas, and so on, up to seven hundred yojanas in length. Maudgalyāyana, this is called the eighth marvel of the ocean, where the asuras take their delight.
This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the eighth extraordinary marvel of the great ocean waters, which the asuras enjoy.
In this same way, Maudgalyāyana!
Within my Dharma there are also eight extraordinary marvels, by which my disciples, having seen them, find delight therein.
What are these eight?
Just as all streams flow and pour into that great ocean,
so it is, Maudgalyāyana!

"My disciples train in the precepts step by step; they all take refuge in my Dharma and learn various wholesome dharmas therein. This, Maudgalyāyana, is one marvel within my Dharma, which causes my disciples, having seen it, to find joy within themselves."
Maudgalyāyana!
Just as the great ocean remains constant and never loses its law of the tides;
so too do my disciples abide within the precepts, never violating them even unto death. This is called the second marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples to rejoice upon seeing it.
Maudgalyāyana!
Just as the five great rivers all flow into the ocean, losing their original names and being called simply "the ocean";
even so, Maudgalyāyana!

Within my Dharma, there are four castes—Kṣatriyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—who, with firm faith, leave their homes for the homeless life to study the Path; having extinguished their original names, they are all called Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya!
This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the third marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples to rejoice upon seeing it.
Maudgalyāyana!
It is just as the five great rivers and the rain from heaven all flow into the ocean, yet the waters of the ocean neither increase nor decrease.
Thus it is, Maudgalyāyana!

Within my Dharma, those sons of noble family who, with firm faith, renounce the home life for homelessness to study the Path and enter the realm of nirvana without remainder—yet in that realm of nirvana without remainder there is neither increase nor decrease. This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the fourth marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples to rejoice upon seeing it.
"Just as, Maudgalyāyana, the waters of the great ocean are of one single salty taste;
so too within my Dharma there is the single taste of liberation. This, Maudgalyāyana, is the fifth marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples, having seen it, to find joy within themselves."
Maudgalyāyana!
Just as the great ocean does not admit a corpse, and if there should be a corpse, the great winds blow it onto the shore;
so too is it within my Dharma: it does not admit a corpse.

What is called a "corpse" refers to one who is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, who does not practice the holy life yet claims to practice the holy life; who violates the precepts and is defiled by evil dharmas, being impure and obscured by false views that cover over wholesome karma; whose inner nature is rotten like a tree in the midst of the sky. Although he sits among the assembly, he is always far removed from the Saṃgha, and the Saṃgha is likewise far removed from him. Maudgalyāyana, this is the sixth marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples to rejoice upon seeing it.
"It is just as with Maudgalyāyana!

Just as the great ocean produces many rare and extraordinary treasures not found on dry land—namely, the precious gems of gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, coral, giant clam shells, and agate—so too within my Dharma many precious gems are produced.

These precious gems are the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. This, Maudgalyāyana, is called the seventh marvel within my Dharma, which causes all disciples to rejoice upon seeing it."
It is just as with Maudgalyāyana!
The great waters of the ocean are the dwelling place of large-bodied beings; by "large-bodied beings," I mean those whose bodies range from one hundred yojanas up to seven hundred yojanas.
It is even so, Maudgalyāyana!

Within my Dharma, there are also those who assume great forms; by "great forms" is meant those among the Saṃgha who are candidates for the fruit of Srotāpanna and have attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, up to those who are candidates for Arhatship and have attained the fruit of Arhatship. Maudgalyāyana, these are the eight wonders within my Dharma, which cause all my disciples to rejoice upon seeing them.
At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), a large number of ignorant bhikṣus gathered in one place and said to the elder, "Recite the precepts.
He replied, "I have not memorized the precepts."
Next, when the monks in the middle seats and lower seats were told to recite the precepts, they all said they could not recite them, and thus the recitation of the precepts was not accomplished.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"A great number of foolish bhikṣus should not assemble in one place; since they do not know the precepts, they furthermore do not know how to recite the precepts, do not know the poṣadha, and do not know the poṣadha-karman."

"From this day forward, I decree that the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts shall be performed every five years; those who do not perform the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, there were many foolish bhikṣus who gathered together in one place and said to their elders, "We spoke of the recitation of the precepts, but we have now completely forgotten them."
Next, the members of the middle seats and lower seats were questioned, and they all said,
"We previously recited it, but now we have forgotten it entirely. Thus,
the recitation of the precepts was not accomplished.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"A great number of foolish bhikṣus should not assemble in one place; for they neither know the precepts, nor do they know how to recite the precepts, nor do they know the poṣadha, nor do they know the poṣadha-karman."

From this day forward, it is ordained that bhikṣus who have been ordained for five years must recite the Prātimokṣa and the Karmavācanā until they are proficient; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
From this day forward, it is permitted to rely upon a bhikṣu who can recite the Prātimokṣa for the summer retreat (varṣāvāsa).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had entered the summer retreat in dependence upon one who recited the precepts.
During the retreat, the reciter of the precepts passed away. The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "What shall we do?"
He immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"Listen well, all of you!

If there is a bhikṣu who, relying on a bhikṣu who recites the precepts, enters the summer retreat (*varṣā*), and during that retreat the one who recites the precepts passes away, or departs for a distant journey, or abandons the path, or joins the assembly of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or joins the assembly of a separate faction (*nikāya-bheda*), or commits a pārājika offense, or commits an offense with a bhikṣuṇī, or acts as a śramaṇa with a thieving mind, or destroys the two [sexual] organs, or is a eunuch, or kills his father or mother, or kills an arhat, or causes schism in the Saṃgha, or with an evil mind sheds the blood of a Buddha, or is a non-human (*amanuṣya*), or an animal, or a hermaphrodite; if the later retreat has not yet arrived, he should go to a nearby place and enter the later retreat. If he does not do so, he should invite a nearby person capable of reciting the precepts to come and pass the retreat together with him.

If the later retreat (*paścimikā varṣā*) has already been entered, the bhikṣus should go to a nearby place where there is one who recites the *Nidāna*, or the four matters, or the thirteen matters, or the two *aniyata* rules, or the thirty matters, or the ninety matters, or the remaining portion of the Dharma. Once each has recited what they have mastered, they shall return to their original residence and teach it to at least one person.
If one person is unable to recite it all, they may recite according to what they have previously learned, each reciting in sequence without repeating.
If this is done, it is well; otherwise, once the Dharma has been taught and the sutra recited, they should rise from their seats and depart.
At that time, Nanda had a disciple who was intelligent and skilled at managing affairs. Then, Upananda said to him,
"Come with me to travel through the human world."
The man replied, "Wait a moment for me; I shall go ask the Upādhyāya and return.
He then went to Nanda and said:
"Listen, I shall travel through the human world together with Upananda. Nanda replied, "As you wish."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Nanda, saying: "How could you allow your disciple to travel through the countryside with Upananda?"
"This man is deluded; he does not know the precepts, he does not know the recitation of the precepts, he does not know the *poṣadha*, and he does not know the *poṣadha-karman*.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter to the Buddha in detail.
At that time, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter; knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he said to Nanda:
"Is it true that you sent your disciple to travel through the countryside with Upananda?"
"The foolish man, Upananda, does not know the precepts, does not know the recitation of the precepts, does not know the poṣadha,
and does not know the poṣadha-karman. He replied, "It is so."
Then the World-Honored One, using countless skillful means, rebuked Nanda, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, Nanda? Why have you sent your disciple to travel through the countryside with Upananda?
This fool knows neither the precepts, nor the recitation of the precepts, nor the poṣadha, nor the poṣadha-karman."
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Nanda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen well! If there is a disciple who takes leave of his preceptor or teacher to travel to a distant place...”
The Master should ask his disciple:
"For what purpose do you travel?
Who are your companions?"
"To what place are you going?
If the undertaking is improper, or if the companions are improper, or if the person and the destination are improper, one should restrain them and prevent them from going.
If the undertaking to be performed is improper and the destination to be reached is also improper, even if one's companions are excellent, one should still restrain them and prevent them from going.
If the undertaking to be performed is improper but the destination is good, yet the companions are not virtuous, one should likewise restrain them and prevent them from going.
If the undertaking to be performed is improper, even if the destination is excellent and the companions are good, one should still prevent them from going.
If the undertaking to be performed is excellent, but the destination is not good and the companions are also not good, one should likewise prevent them from going.
If the task to be undertaken is good, the destination is good, but the companions are not good, one should still prohibit them from going.
If the task to be undertaken is good, the destination is good, and the companions are also good, one should permit them to go.
At that time, there was a certain residence where a great number of foolish bhikṣus had gathered together.
Then the Venerable Upāli arrived as a guest among this assembly, yet those foolish bhikṣus did not look after him, nor did they rise to welcome or attend to him.
Because Upāli did not look after him, nor welcome him, nor serve him, he departed from that place on that very day.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Listen well!

If there is a residence where many foolish bhikṣus have gathered together in one place, and a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is able to preach the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, uphold the Mātṛkā, and explain the meaning of the Sūtras.

When the bhikṣus hear of this, they shall go half a yojana to meet them, attend to them, look after them, provide them with a place to rest, bathe them, and supply them with whatever food and drink they require; if they do not do so, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, there was a certain residence where a bhikṣu committed an offense on the day the precepts were to be recited. He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess his offense to another who has also committed an offense, and may not accept the confession of another."
"What should I do now?
He then informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen well! On the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), if a bhikṣu commits an offense and thinks to himself:

‘The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not participate in the recitation of the precepts, may not hear the precepts being recited, may not confess his offense to another, and the offender may not accept the confession of another.’”

That bhikṣu should go to a pure bhikṣu, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, and join his palms; if the other is a senior, he should prostrate at his feet, announce his own name as it relates to the offense, and speak these words:
"Venerable sir, please take note!"
I, bhikṣu [name], have committed such-and-such an offense.
I now confess it before the Venerable One, not daring to conceal it; through confession there is peace and happiness, but without confession there is no peace or happiness.
"I recall my transgression and have confessed it; knowing it, I have not concealed it. May the Elder remember that my body of pure precepts is complete and that my *poṣadha* is pure.
Thus one should say three times.
He should say to him:
"You should give rise to a mind of weary detachment. He should then reply:
"Yes. Having said this, one may listen to the recitation of the precepts.
At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, there was a bhikṣu who had doubts regarding an offense he had committed; he thought to himself:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts: one who has committed an offense shall not recite the precepts, shall not hear the precepts, and shall not receive confession from another who has committed an offense; nor shall the offender receive confession from others.”
"What should I do now?
He then informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen well! On the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), if a bhikṣu has doubts regarding an offense, he should think to himself:

'The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that if one has committed an offense, one may not participate in the recitation of the precepts, nor hear the precepts, nor confess toward one who has committed an offense; furthermore, the offender may not accept the confession of another.'"

That bhikṣu should go among the pure bhikṣus, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, placing his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms. Having prostrated at the feet of the elders, he shall state the name of the offense he has committed and speak these words:

"I, [Name], have developed doubt regarding an offense I have committed; I now declare it before you, Venerable Sirs. When I am later free from doubt, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma."
"Thus, one has already heard the precepts.

At that time, on the day for reciting the precepts, the community of monks gathered in one place intending to recite them. As they were about to recite the precepts, there was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense. He then thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not participate in the recitation of the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess his offense to another who has also committed an offense, and may not receive the confession of another."
"What shall I do now?
he said to the person reciting the precepts:
"Please stop for a moment and do not recite the precepts; I have committed such-and-such an offense and wish to confess it before you, Venerable Sir."
While these words were being spoken, the entire assembly fell into a state of commotion.
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter, and the Buddha said:
"Listen well, all of you!
If there is another location where the Saṃgha has gathered in one place intending to recite the Prātimokṣa,
and at the time of the recitation, a bhikṣu commits an offense—

whether that bhikṣu has been formally accused by someone or not, whether he has been reminded of his transgression or not— if he himself remembers the offense and discloses it, knowing within himself that he has this offense, that bhikṣu should say to those nearby:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now repent before the Elder. He further reflects:
"If I were to speak of this to bystanders, I fear it would disturb the assembly of monks and prevent the recitation of the precepts from being accomplished."
That bhikṣu should think to himself:
"Once the sitting has concluded, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma.
Having done this, he may listen to the recitation of the precepts.
At that time, the community of monks gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts.
While the precepts were being recited, there was a bhikṣu who had doubts regarding an offense. He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense is not permitted to recite the precepts, nor permitted to hear the precepts, nor permitted to confess to another who has committed an offense, and the offender is not permitted to accept the confession of another."
"What should I do now? he thought, and immediately said to that person who was reciting the precepts:
"Stop for a moment!"
"I have doubts regarding a certain offense and wish to speak of it to you, Elder.
Having said this, the entire assembly fell into a state of commotion.
The bhikṣus then went to inform the Buddha of these matters, and the Buddha said:
