"Listen well! If the Saṃgha assembles in one place intending to recite the precepts, and at the time of the recitation, there is a bhikṣu who has doubts regarding an offense."

Now, regarding that bhikṣu, there are cases where he is censured and cases where he is not; there are cases where he is reminded of his offense and cases where he is not. If he himself recalls his transgression, he should say to his fellow monks:
"I have doubts concerning my offense; I now speak of it to you, Venerable Sirs. Once the session has concluded and I am free from doubt, I shall perform confession according to the Dharma."
If he further thinks: "I have just spoken with my neighbor;
I fear the assembly will become noisy and confused, and the recitation of the precepts will not be accomplished," he should reflect in his mind:
"Once you have finished sitting, you must perform the ritual confession according to the Dharma when there is no doubt.
Those who act in this manner shall be permitted to hear the recitation of the precepts.
At that time, on the day for the recitation of the precepts, there was a different residence where the entire Saṃgha had committed offenses; they all thought to themselves:

“The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, and may not receive confession from another who has committed an offense; nor may the offender accept the confession of another.”
"What should we do? They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Listen well! Suppose there is another residence where the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense, and each thinks to themselves:

'The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess to another who has also committed an offense, and one who has committed an offense may not accept the confession of another. "

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is pure and free from transgressions, one should go to him, bare the right shoulder, remove the leather sandals, place the right knee on the ground, and join the palms. Having prostrated at the feet of the senior elder, one should personally state the name of the precept violated and say:
"I, [Name], have committed such-and-such an offense; I now confess it before the Venerable One."
He should say to them: "Generate a mind of weary detachment. They will reply:

"Yes. If no visiting bhikṣus have arrived, one should immediately dispatch two or three people to go among a nearby assembly of pure bhikṣus. There, with the right shoulder bared, having removed their leather sandals, and with the right knee touching the ground, they should join their palms, state the name of the precept they have violated, and speak these words:
"I have committed such-and-such an offense; I now confess it before the Venerable Ones."
He should say to him:
"You should give rise to a mind of weary detachment. He replies:
"Yes. This bhikṣu shall return to his place of residence, and the bhikṣus residing there shall inform this bhikṣu of the offense he has committed.
Having done so, they shall then recite the precepts.
At that time, there was a certain separate residence where the entire Saṃgha had doubts regarding an offense. Each of them thought to themselves:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not receive confession from an offender, and an offender may not accept confession from another."
"What should we do? They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Listen well! If, in various different residences, the entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense, each should think:
'The World-Honored One has established the precepts!'"

"One who has committed an offense shall not recite the precepts, shall not hear the precepts, and shall not receive confession from one who has committed an offense; nor shall the offender accept the confession of another.

If a visiting bhikṣu arrives who is pure and free from offenses, one should go to him, bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, and if he is a senior elder, prostrate at his feet. Then, kneeling with the right knee on the ground and joining the palms, one should state the name of the offense committed and speak these words:
"I have developed doubt regarding a certain offense; I now declare it before the Venerable One. When I am later free from doubt, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma."

If there are no visiting bhikṣus present, one should send two or three bhikṣus to a nearby community of pure bhikṣus. There, they should bare their right shoulders, remove their leather sandals, place their right knees on the ground, and join their palms. Having paid homage at the feet of the elders, they should state the name of the precept they have violated and speak these words:
"I have developed doubt regarding a certain offense; I now declare it before the Venerable Ones. When I am later free from doubt, I shall perform the confession according to the Dharma."
That bhikṣu shall return to his original residence, and the bhikṣus there shall inform him of the name of the offense he has committed.
Only after this has been done shall the precepts be recited.

At that time, the community of monks gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts. As they were about to recite the precepts, the entire assembly had committed offenses. Each thought to themselves:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that those who have committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess their offense to another monk who has also committed an offense, and one who has committed an offense may not accept the confession of another."
"What should we do? They immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen well! The Saṃgha has gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts. At the time of the recitation, the entire Saṃgha has committed offenses. Each of them thinks to themselves:

‘The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess toward one who has committed an offense, and one who has committed an offense may not accept another’s confession.’”
Having made this announcement, that bhikṣu shall perform the confession.
He should make the announcement in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This entire assembly of monks has committed an offense.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: this entire Saṃgha now confesses.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
"Having made this announcement, one may then recite the precepts.

At that time, the community of monks gathered in one place intending to recite the precepts. When it was time for the recitation, all the monks had doubts regarding their offenses. Each of them thought:

"The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense is not permitted to recite the precepts, nor hear the precepts, nor confess toward another who has committed an offense; likewise, one who has committed an offense is not permitted to accept the confession of another."
"What should we do? They immediately informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Listen well! If the Saṃgha assembles in one place intending to recite the precepts, and at the time of the recitation all members of the Saṃgha have doubts regarding their offenses, each should think:

'The World-Honored One has established the precepts such that one who has committed an offense may not recite the precepts, may not hear the precepts, may not confess toward one who has committed an offense, and one who has committed an offense may not accept another's confession.'"
After that entire Saṃgha has made the formal motion (jñapti), they should declare their offense, making the motion as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This entire Saṃgha has doubts regarding an offense."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let this assembly of monks confess their own offenses.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Having made this announcement in this manner, one may then recite the precepts.

At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, the entire Saṃgha had committed offenses; however, they did not recognize the names of the offenses nor the characteristics of the offenses. The bhikṣus thought to themselves: "What should we do?"
He immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen well, all of you!
On the day of the recitation of the precepts, the entire Saṃgha has committed an offense, yet they do not recognize the name of the offense nor the characteristics of the offense.

If there is a visiting bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma, upholds the Vinaya, and upholds the Mātṛkā, one should go to him, baring the right shoulder, removing the leather sandals, placing the right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, say:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"If there is a bhikṣu who commits such and such an offense, what has he transgressed?
The one who upholds the Vinaya replied,
"He has committed such and such an offense."

If the visiting bhikṣu knows that the other bhikṣu is easy to instruct, he should lead him to a secluded place and have another bhikṣu stand where they can see him but cannot hear them, and then instruct him to perform repentance according to the Dharma.
Having finished the confession, he returns to that bhikṣu and says:
"The offense committed by this bhikṣu has now been confessed.
If the other bhikṣus believe in the confession of such a bhikṣu, it is well; if they do not believe in the confession, the other bhikṣus must not use force to compel him to confess.
At that time, on the day for the recitation of the precepts, visiting bhikṣus arrived.
Those visiting bhikṣus were to recite the precepts on the fourteenth day, while the resident bhikṣus were to recite them on the fifteenth day.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to report this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Listen well! If there is a residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a few visiting bhikṣus arrive, and the visiting bhikṣus are on the fourteenth day while the resident bhikṣus are on the fifteenth day, the visiting bhikṣus, being fewer, should follow the resident bhikṣus; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."

At that time, there was a residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting monks arrived in numbers equal to those of the resident monks. The visiting monks were to observe the *poṣadha* on the fourteenth day, while the resident monks were to observe it on the fifteenth day. The visiting monks should follow the resident monks; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If on the day of the recitation of the precepts many visiting bhikṣus arrive, and the visiting bhikṣus are scheduled to recite the precepts on the fourteenth day while the resident bhikṣus are scheduled for the fifteenth day, and the resident bhikṣus are few in number, they should seek harmony with the visiting bhikṣus.
If they can achieve harmony with them, it is well; if they cannot achieve harmony, the resident bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.
On the day of the recitation of the precepts, there were few visiting bhikṣus who came from another residence.
If the visiting bhikṣus observe the fifteenth day and the resident bhikṣus observe the fourteenth day,
and the visiting bhikṣus are fewer in number, they should seek reconciliation from the resident bhikṣus.
If they achieve reconciliation, it is well.
If they cannot reach an agreement, the visiting bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.
At the time of the Uposatha day, there were visiting bhikṣus from another residence who arrived at that dwelling place, equal in number to the resident bhikṣus.
If the visiting bhikṣus are on the fifteenth day and the resident bhikṣus are on the fourteenth day, they should seek reconciliation from the resident bhikṣus.
If reconciliation is reached, it is well; if reconciliation is not reached, the visiting bhikṣus should go outside the boundary to recite the precepts.
At the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, there were many visiting bhikṣus arriving at a different residence.
The visiting bhikṣus were on the fifteenth day, while the resident bhikṣus were on the fourteenth day.
Since the resident bhikṣus were few in number, they should seek reconciliation with the visiting bhikṣus.
If they comply, it is well; if they do not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

On the day for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa, if a few visiting bhikṣus arrive—such as when the visiting bhikṣus are on the sixteenth day and the resident bhikṣus are on the fifteenth day—it is also to be treated in this same manner.
At the time of the *poṣadha* ceremony, when the resident monks of a monastery had assembled and were about to recite the precepts, a few visiting monks arrived.
They thought to themselves: "What should we do?"
He immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), resident bhikṣus have assembled at a dwelling place intending to recite the precepts, but few visiting bhikṣus arrive when the time for the recitation comes."
If the resident bhikṣus have already finished reciting the preface of the *Poṣadha*, the visiting bhikṣus should announce their purity (*pārisuddhi*), and the others should listen in due order.

If the recitation of the precepts is finished, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or many have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and the visiting bhikṣus who arrive are few, they must announce their purity; if they do not announce it, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts, if resident bhikṣus wish to recite the precepts and visiting bhikṣus arrive in equal numbers, the resident bhikṣus must recite the precepts again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the precepts has been completed, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and visiting bhikṣus arrive, the resident bhikṣus should recite the precepts again; otherwise, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), there was a community of resident monks gathered at a certain dwelling who intended to recite the precepts.
At that moment, many visiting monks arrived; the resident monks should then have recited the precepts again for them. Otherwise, they were to be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the precepts has been completed, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and many visiting bhikṣus arrive, the resident bhikṣus should recite the precepts again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, at a residence on the day of the *poṣadha*, guest bhikṣus were seated intending to recite the precepts, while few resident bhikṣus had arrived.
If the guest bhikṣus have already finished reciting the introduction (*nidāna*), they should announce their purity (*pārisuddhi*); the others should then listen in due order.

If the recitation of the precepts has been completed, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and a small number of resident bhikṣus arrive, they must announce their purity (*pārisuddhi*); otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, at a residence where the *poṣadha* was to be recited, guest *bhikṣus* were seated intending to recite the precepts when resident *bhikṣus* arrived in equal numbers. The guest *bhikṣus* should have recited the precepts again; if they did not, they were to be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the precepts has been completed, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and a resident bhikṣu arrives, the visiting bhikṣus should recite the precepts again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, at a residence on the day of the *poṣadha*, when guest monks were seated intending to recite the precepts, if resident monks arrived in great numbers, the guest monks should again perform the *poṣadha* with them; otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the precepts has been completed, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and many resident bhikṣus arrive, the visiting bhikṣus should again recite the precepts with them; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
"When resident bhikṣus recite the *poṣadha*, it is the same when resident bhikṣus arrive.
When visiting bhikṣus recite the *poṣadha*, it is the same when visiting bhikṣus arrive.

At that time, there was a different residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrived. Knowing that the resident bhikṣus had not yet arrived, they thought, "If we have four or more than four of us, we may perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *poṣadha* together," and so they immediately performed the *karmavācanā* and recited the *poṣadha* together.
While the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* were being performed, resident bhikṣus arrived. The visiting bhikṣus thought to themselves, "What should we do?
and immediately informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Listen well!

On the day of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha), if there is a residence where visiting bhikṣus arrive and know that resident bhikṣus have not yet arrived, and if we—whether being four or more than four—are present, we may perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) together to recite the precepts; they shall likewise join in performing the ritual and reciting the precepts."

When performing the *karmavācanā* and reciting the *Prātimokṣa*, if newly arrived bhikṣus are few, one should tell those who have already heard the introduction of the precepts to declare their purity, while the others should listen in due order.

If the recitation of the precepts has concluded, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or most have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and few resident bhikṣus arrive, they should announce their purity; otherwise, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, there was a residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting monks arrived and knew that resident monks had not yet come. [They considered: "We have four people, or perhaps more than four; we may perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the *prātimokṣa*. They then proceeded to perform the ritual and recite the *prātimokṣa*.

When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is being performed and the *Poṣadha* (confession of precepts) is being recited, if resident monks arrive, the visiting monks should recite the *Poṣadha* again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the *Poṣadha* has concluded, and the entire assembly has not yet risen, or a majority has not yet risen, or all have already risen, and resident monks arrive, the visiting monks should recite the *Poṣadha* again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, there was a residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrived. Knowing that resident bhikṣus had not yet arrived, they considered themselves to be four or more than four persons and thought, "We may perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *prātimokṣa*"; they then proceeded to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *prātimokṣa*.

When the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is being performed, if many resident monks arrive, the visiting monks should recite the precepts again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

If the recitation of the precepts has concluded, whether the entire assembly has not yet risen, or many have not yet risen, or all have already risen, and many resident monks arrive, the visiting monks should recite the precepts again; if they do not, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, there was a residence where, on the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), resident bhikṣus arrived and knew that visiting bhikṣus had not yet come—whether they were few, equal in number, or many—and it was likewise in these cases.
When visiting bhikṣus recite the precepts, it is the same when visiting bhikṣus arrive.
When resident bhikṣus recite the precepts, it is the same when resident bhikṣus arrive.
Or it is said:
"One should recite the precepts," or one says:
"One should not recite the precepts."
"If he does not come, let him lose it! Let it perish!

Thinking thus, he wishes to employ various means to destroy the other, and proceeds to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*. Since that *karmavācanā* is performed, the ritual is not validly accomplished, and he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a visiting bhikṣu arrived. He saw the dwellings and rooms where resident bhikṣus stayed, and he observed their signs: the arrangement of rope beds, wooden beds, seating mats, woolen rugs, pillows, foot-washing stones, pure water, and water jars. Having seen these signs, he did not inquire further, but proceeded to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts.
While the formal ritual (karmavācanā) and the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) were being performed, an elder bhikṣu arrived. The visiting bhikṣus thought to themselves, "What should we do?
and immediately informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: "Listen well!

If, at a single residence on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrive and see the signs of resident bhikṣus—such as corded beds, wooden beds, bedding, woolen rugs, pillows, foot-washing stones, pure water, and water vessels—and they see these signs yet do not seek them out, they may then perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts."
If one proceeds [with the rite] while [the absentee] is present, the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are not valid; there is an offense.
Upon seeing signs [of his presence], one should seek him out; if he cannot be found after seeking, one should summon him.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* without summoning him, the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are not valid; there is an offense.
Upon seeing the signs, they immediately seek them; seeking them, they do not find them.
Having failed to find them, they say:
"Let them perish!"
"Lost!"; employing various means, he desires to cause it to be destroyed, and thus performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the precepts.
That monk’s *karman* is not valid, and he commits a *sthūlātyaya*.
Having seen the signs, he immediately sought him; not finding him despite his search, he called out to him; having called him, he performed the *karmavācanā* and recited the *Prātimokṣa*.
That bhikṣu’s *karman* was not validly accomplished, yet he did not commit an offense.

If one sees [an offense] and seeks it out, and having sought it, obtains it, then performing the *karmavācanā* and reciting the precepts together constitutes a valid *karmavācanā* and recitation of the precepts; there is no offense.
The same applies when one sees [the offense] but has doubts.
At that time, there was a residence where resident monks arrived; they saw the signs of visiting monks—namely, their robes, bowls, needle-cases, sitting mats, and foot-washing places.
Having seen [the offender], if one does not seek him out and proceeds to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*,
that bhikṣu’s performance of the *karmavācanā* and recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is invalid, and he incurs an offense.
If one sees signs [of his presence] and seeks him out, but cannot find him despite seeking, one should summon him.
If one performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the *Poṣadha* without having summoned [the absent monk], the *karmavācanā* and *Poṣadha* are not valid, and there is an offense.
If one sees signs [of his presence] and seeks him out, but fails to find him, one should say:
"He has lost [his way]!"
"Destroy it! Thinking in various ways to cause another to break [the assembly], he then performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the precepts.
That monk's *karman* is not valid, and he commits a *sthūlātyaya*.

If one sees [a monk] and immediately seeks him out, but cannot find him despite seeking, and then calls out to him; having called him, they perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*, that bhikṣu’s *karmavācanā* and recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are not valid, yet he commits no offense.

If one sees [a person] and seeks them out, and having sought them, they join together to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*, that bhikṣu’s performance of the *karmavācanā* and recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is valid, and he is without offense.
The same applies when there is doubt regarding whether one has seen [the person].

At that time, on the day of the *poṣadha*, there was a certain monastery where visiting monks arrived. Hearing the voices of the resident monks—the sound of their walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), their clearing of throats, the sound of them reciting the scriptures, and the sound of them preaching the Dharma—they did not seek them out, but instead performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and held the *poṣadha*.
While the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* were being performed, an elder bhikṣu arrived.
Not knowing what to do, he informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"Listen well! On the day of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), if there is a monastery where visiting bhikṣus arrive and hear the voices of resident bhikṣus—whether the sound of walking meditation (*caṅkrama*), coughing, chanting the sūtras, or preaching the Dharma—and yet, having heard them, they do not seek them out but proceed to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts."
If that bhikṣu performs the formal act (karmavācanā) and recites the Prātimokṣa, the formal act and the recitation are not valid, and he incurs an offense.

If, after hearing [the summons], he seeks [to attend] but does not find [anyone to summon him], and he performs the formal act and recites the Prātimokṣa without being summoned, that bhikṣu’s formal act and recitation are not valid, and he incurs an offense.
If, having heard [the report], one seeks [the person], and having sought them, does not find them; and not finding them, does not call for them; and since they have not been called, one says:
"They have been lost; they have perished.
Then, by various means, one desires to cause others to break [the harmony] and proceeds to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the *Prātimokṣa*.
That bhikṣu does not accomplish the *karmavācanā* or the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*; he incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

Having heard [the summons], he seeks [the person]; having sought him, he does not find him; not finding him, he calls out; having called out, he performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the *Prātimokṣa*.
That bhikṣu’s formal act (karmavācanā) is not accomplished and he incurs no offense.

Having heard [the announcement], he seeks [to join]; having sought, he obtains [permission]; having obtained it, he joins in harmony with the others to perform the formal act and recite the precepts. That bhikṣu’s formal act and recitation of the precepts are accomplished, and he incurs no offense.
The same applies to hearing [the sound] while being doubtful.

At that time, there was a certain residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, an established monk arrived. Hearing the voices of visiting monks—the sound of walking up and down (*caṅkrama*), the sound of clearing their throats, the sound of reciting scriptures, the sound of preaching the Dharma, and the sound of shaking out their robes—he heard them but did not seek them out; he then performed the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recited the precepts.
That bhikṣu’s formal act (karmavācanā) and recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) are invalid, and he incurs an offense.

Having heard [the summons], he seeks [the person]; having sought him, he does not find him; because he does not find him, he does not summon him, yet he performs the formal act and the recitation of the precepts.
That bhikṣu’s formal ritual (karmavācanā) and recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) are invalid, and he incurs an offense.

Having heard [the summons], he seeks [the person]; having sought him, he does not find him; because he cannot find him, he does not summon him; and having failed to summon him, he then says: "He has vanished!"
"Destroy it!
Thinking thus, he employs various skillful means to cause the other to break [the assembly] and then performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the *Prātimokṣa*.
That monk does not validly perform the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, and incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

Having heard [the announcement], he searches; having searched, he does not find him. Unable to do otherwise, he calls him out; having called him out, the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are performed.
That bhikṣu’s *karmavācanā* and recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* are not valid, yet there is no offense [for those who performed them].

Having heard it, they seek it; having sought it, they obtain it; having obtained it, they perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts together. That bhikṣu completes the formal act and the recitation of the precepts, and is without offense.

"It is the same regarding those who have heard of or have doubts about [the presence of others]. At that time, in a certain other residence, on the day of the *poṣadha*, a visiting bhikṣu arrived. Seeing the resident bhikṣus within the boundary enclosure (*sīmā*), he neither sought them out nor made inquiries, yet proceeded to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves,
"What should we do? and immediately informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said: "Listen well!

If there is another dwelling place where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrive and see resident bhikṣus within the boundary (*sīmā*), yet they neither seek them out nor invite them, but instead perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts, those visiting bhikṣus have validly performed the *karmavācanā* and recited the precepts, but the resident bhikṣus incur an offense."

If, having seen [a person], one seeks them out, and though seeking them, they cannot be summoned, yet one proceeds to perform the formal ritual (kamma) and recite the precepts, that bhikkhu’s performance of the ritual and recitation of the precepts is valid, yet he incurs an offense.

Having seen [the offender], he seeks him out; having sought him out, he calls him; having called him, he performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the *Prātimokṣa*. That bhikṣu completes the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, and there is no offense.
The same applies when one has doubt as to whether he has seen him.

At that time, there was a different residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, resident monks arrived and saw visiting monks within the boundary enclosure. Having seen them, they failed to seek them out and proceeded to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts. Those monks completed the ritual and recited the precepts, yet they were at fault.

If one sees [a monk] and then seeks him out, and having sought him, fails to find him, yet performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the *Prātimokṣa* without summoning him, that *bhikṣu* completes the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, but he incurs an offense.

Having seen [the offender], he seeks him out; having sought him out, he calls him; having called him, he performs the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*. That bhikṣu completes the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and is without offense.
The same applies when there is doubt as to whether he has seen [the offender].
At that time, there was a different residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrived and heard that resident bhikṣus were present within the boundary enclosure (*sīmā*).

Having heard this, they did not seek them out, but proceeded to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the *poṣadha*. Those bhikṣus completed the ritual and recited the *poṣadha*, yet they incurred an offense.

Having heard [the summons], he seeks [to attend]; having sought, he is not called; not being called, he nevertheless performs the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). That bhikṣu completes the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the precepts, yet he incurs an offense.

Having heard it, he seeks [the offender]; having sought him, he calls him; having called him, the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* is performed. That bhikṣu completes the *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* and is without offense.
The same applies when there is hearing and doubt.
"When resident bhikṣus arrive and hear that visiting bhikṣus are likewise on the boundary site, it is the same; when they hear and yet have doubts, it is also the same.

At that time, in a certain other residence, on the day of the *poṣadha*, visiting bhikṣus arrived and saw resident bhikṣus within the boundary. Having seen them, they did not seek [their presence] and proceeded to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts.
While the *karmavācanā* was being performed and the *Poṣadha* recitation was taking place, some resident bhikṣus arrived.
They thought to themselves, "What should we do?
and immediately informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said: “Listen well!

Suppose there is a certain monastic residence where, on the day of the Poṣadha, visiting bhikṣus arrive and see resident bhikṣus within the boundary. If they see them but do not seek them out, and then perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the Prātimokṣa, that [act of] the bhikṣus does not constitute a valid *karmavācanā* for the recitation of the Prātimokṣa; they are at fault.”

If one sees [a monk] and seeks him out, but having sought him does not call him, yet proceeds to perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts, the formal act and the recitation of the precepts are not valid; there is an offense.

If one sees him and seeks him out, and having sought him calls him, and having called him, they act together to perform the formal act and recite the precepts, that bhikṣu’s formal act and recitation of the precepts are valid, and there is no offense.
The same applies to seeing someone and being doubtful.

At that time, there was a residence where, on the day of the *poṣadha* ceremony, an elder monk arrived and saw a visiting monk within the boundary; the same applies to this case, and the same applies to seeing someone and being doubtful.
When a visiting bhikṣu hears that a resident bhikṣu is within the boundary, it is likewise; when he hears it with doubt, it is likewise.
When a resident bhikṣu hears that a visiting bhikṣu is within the boundary, it is likewise; when he hears it with doubt, it is likewise.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:

"From a monastery where there are bhikṣus to a monastery where there are no bhikṣus, we fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (karmavācanā) against us or obstruct our recitation of the Prātimokṣa."
At that time, the bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"You should not entertain such thoughts as:

'From a residence where there are bhikṣus to a residence where there are no bhikṣus, we fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against us or obstruct our recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).'"
That bhikṣu thinks to himself:

"From where there are bhikṣus and monasteries, to where there are no bhikṣus and no monasteries, I fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against us or obstruct our recitation of the precepts."
The Buddha said: "You should not think:

'From a place where there are bhikṣus and a monastery, to a place where there are no bhikṣus and no monastery, we fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (karmavācanā) against us or obstruct our recitation of the precepts.'"
That bhikṣu thinks to himself:

"If I go from a place where there are bhikṣus and a monastery to a place where there are no bhikṣus, or to a place that is not a monastery, or if I go onto the boundary of a bhikṣu's domain, I fear that other bhikṣus will perform a formal act (kamma) against me or obstruct the recitation of the Prātimokṣa."
The Buddha said: "One should not think:

'From a place where there is a bhikṣu and a residence, to a place where there is no bhikṣu and no residence—if I go onto the boundary field of the bhikṣus, I fear that other bhikṣus will perform a *karmavācanā* against me or obstruct my recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.'"
If one goes without the Sangha accompanying them, or if one goes despite there being no obstacles [to doing so], it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
It is likewise when going from a place where there are monks and no dwelling to a place where there are no monks but there is a dwelling.
The same applies from a place where there are monks but no dwelling, up to a place where there are neither monks nor a dwelling.
The same also applies from a place where there are monks but no dwelling, up to a place where there are neither monks nor a dwelling, and a place where there is a dwelling but no monks.
From the case where there are monks and a dwelling place, or no dwelling place, up to the case where there are no monks and yet a dwelling place, it is likewise.
From the case where there are monks and a dwelling place, or no dwelling place, up to the case where there are neither monks nor a dwelling place, it is likewise.
From the case where there is a bhikṣu, whether he has a dwelling place or not, up to the case where there is no bhikṣu, whether he has a dwelling place or not—it is also like this.
If it is for the sake of a close friend or acquaintance, it is also like this.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"We shall go into the monastery and obstruct the other bhikṣus, saying:
'Do not perform a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against the group of six bhikṣus, nor obstruct the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*). "
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not entertain such a thought as:
'I shall go into the monastery to obstruct other bhikṣus by saying...'"
"Do not perform a formal act (kamma) against the group of six bhikkhus to obstruct the recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Nor should one perform a formal act or obstruct the recitation of the Pātimokkha in the presence of bhikkhunīs.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs sent śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerikās into the monastery to block the other bhikṣus, so that they would not perform the *karmavācanā* against the group of six bhikṣus nor obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs should not entertain such thoughts as:

'Send the śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, and śrāmaṇerīs to the monastery to block the other bhikṣus, so that they do not perform a formal act (karmavācanā) against the group of six bhikṣus nor obstruct the recitation of the Prātimokṣa.'"

"Furthermore, one should not perform a *karmavācanā* or obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* in the presence of *śikṣamāṇās*, *śrāmaṇeras*, or *śrāmaṇerīs*. Those bhikṣuṇīs then had this thought:

'Let us send a layperson who is an acquaintance to go inside the monastery and stop the other bhikṣus, so that they do not perform a *karmavācanā* to obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa* for the sake of the group of six bhikṣus.'"
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not entertain such a thought as this:

'Send a lay acquaintance to the monastery to obstruct the other bhikṣus, so that they do not perform a *karmavācanā* against the group of six bhikṣus, nor obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*.'"
"One should not perform *karmavācanā* or obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha* in the presence of laypeople.
At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha, for the sake of the Buddha and the Saṃgha, dispatched various generals to guard the monastery.
Then the bhikṣus said to the generals, "Please step outside for a moment;
we wish to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts.
The generals replied:
“King Bimbisāra has sent us here to protect [the community] for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha.
Since the King’s will is difficult to oppose, we are unable to go outside.
At that time, the bhikṣus went and reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“When you have sent out a messenger with conciliatory words, it is well if they come out; if they do not come out, you yourselves should go together to a place where they cannot see or hear you, perform the *karmavācanā*, and recite the *Prātimokṣa* together. You should not perform the *karmavācanā* or recite the *Prātimokṣa* in the presence of those who have not received the full ordination.”
At that time, there were devas, nāgas, and spirits who came to listen to the recitation of the precepts. A bhikṣu with the divine eye saw them and felt apprehension and caution, thinking to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, forbidding us from performing karmavācanā or reciting the precepts in the presence of those who have not received full ordination."
At that time, the bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha of this matter. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, with the exception of those who have not yet received the full ordination (*upasampadā*), it is permitted for all others to perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts in their presence."
At that time, the Saṃgha of Kauśāmbī was split into two factions. When the bhikṣus wished to achieve reconciliation at Śrāvastī, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to reconcile only after first making a formal announcement (jñapti)."
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Regarding the matter of dispute that has caused the Saṃgha to quarrel and become discordant with one another, that person committed an offense; having been formally accused (*codita*), his offense is now being resolved."
"The dust and defilements of the Saṃgha have been extinguished. If it is the time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha be in harmony.
This is the formal announcement (jñapti).
Having made this announcement in this manner, one should perform the act of harmony.

At that time, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

The matter at hand causes the Saṃgha to engage in strife and contention, preventing harmony and destroying the community; it defiles the Saṃgha and causes division, splitting it into two factions, yet this matter has not been adjudicated, eliminated, or extinguished.
"Is the community of monks in accordance with the Dharma and in harmonious union? The Buddha told Upāli:

"If the matter upon which the community of monks relies causes them to quarrel and dispute, such that they are not in harmony, the community is broken, the community is defiled, and the community becomes divided into two factions."
If one can repent within this assembly and not incite others to raise the matter, this is called the Saṃgha being in harmony through the Dharma.
From this day forward, it is permitted to recite the Prātimokṣa after first making a formal announcement.
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

There is a matter of dispute upon which the Saṃgha has become embroiled in contention; it is not in harmony, the Saṃgha is divided, the Saṃgha is defiled, the Saṃgha is split, and has been separated into two factions."
That person has recognized his own offense and has now repented,
thereby purifying the stain upon the Saṃgha. If the time is right for the Saṃgha,
may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent so that we may perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa in harmony.
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, the Saṃgha shall then perform the recitation of the Prātimokṣa together.
The Khandhaka on the Recitation of the Prātimokṣa concludes here. *The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Volume 36.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume Thirty-Seven, Part Two, Section Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty,
together with Zhu Fonian and others.
7. The Chapter on the Rainy Season Retreat (Varṣā-vastu). At that time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus traveled through the human settlements during all seasons—spring, summer, and winter.

At that time, during the summer months, heavy rains fell from the heavens and the waters swelled, causing [the monks] to lose their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases; they also trampled and killed living plants and trees.
When the lay devotees saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they trample and kill living plants and trees."
Externally, they claim for themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such a case?

At all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter—he wandered among the people; yet in the summer, when torrential rains caused the waters to swell, he lost his robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle-case, and by treading upon living plants and grasses, he cut off the life-force of other beings.
The teachings of the various non-Buddhists still observe a three-month period of retreat during the rains;
yet these sons of the Śākyas wander through human settlements at all times—during spring, summer, and winter alike.

A heavy rain fell from the heavens and the waters swelled, sweeping away his robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case; he trampled and killed living plants and trees, severing the life-force of other beings.
Even insects and birds still have nests and dwellings where they may take refuge.
"O śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
At all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter—you wander through the human world.

When the heavens send down torrential rain and the waters swell, you lose your robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases; furthermore, by treading upon living plants and grasses, you sever the life-faculties of other beings."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They rebuked the group of six bhikṣus, saying:

"How is it that you travel through human settlements at all times—spring, summer, and winter? During the summer, when heavy rains cause the waters to swell, you lose your robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, and you trample and kill living plants and trees."
"Do the laypeople incur an offense because they harbor the notion that grasses and trees possess life-force, thereby causing them to criticize and disparage [the monks]?
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated at his feet with their heads, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the group of six bhikṣus:
"What you have done is improper; it is not dignified conduct, not pure practice, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, and not a compliant course of action—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is this, you group of six bhikṣus!

At all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter—you wander through the human settlements. During the summer, when heavy rains cause the waters to swell, you lose your robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle-cases, and you trample and kill living plants and trees."
"Because the lay devotees perceive life-force in grass and trees, they feel revulsion and thereby cause the lay devotees to incur offense.
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"You should not wander through human settlements at all times—whether in spring, summer, or winter."
From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to observe the three-month summer retreat (varṣā).
One should address the person upon whom one relies, saying:
"I shall observe the summer retreat at this place; Venerable One, please bear this in mind!"

I, the bhikṣu [Name], shall observe the three-month summer retreat (varṣā) in dependence upon the village of [Name], the monastery of [Name], and the cell of [Name], for the purpose of repairing dilapidated dwellings.
"In this manner, it was said a second and third time.
The procedure for the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*) was likewise.
At that time, the bhikṣus residing at the monastery had no one to rely upon and did not know whom to inform.
The bhikṣus had doubts and did not know whether their *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) was valid;
they immediately informed the World-Honored One, who said:
"If one has resolved the intention to enter the *varṣā*, then the *varṣā* is established."
"From this day forward, I authorize the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat through mental resolve (*cittānujñā*) if they have no person upon whom they rely.

At that time, a certain bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat at a residence, but he had no person upon whom to rely and no place to perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*). He forgot to observe the retreat through mental resolve and became doubtful, not knowing whether his rains retreat was valid.
They went and informed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If they have come for the sake of the rains retreat, the rains retreat is thereby established."

At that time, some bhikṣus went to their place of residence for the rains retreat; as they were about to enter the boundary to begin the retreat, the dawn light appeared. They had doubts: "Is the rains retreat validly established?"
He immediately addressed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If one has come for the sake of the rains retreat, then the rains retreat is established."

At that time, a bhikṣu went to a place for the rains retreat with the intention of entering it; having entered the monastery grounds before the appearance of the dawn light, he became doubtful, not knowing whether his formal entry into the retreat (vassa) was valid.
He immediately addressed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If you have come for the sake of the rains retreat, you shall thereby fulfill the requirements for the retreat."

At that time, a bhikṣu was going to his dwelling place intending to enter the rains retreat; with one foot inside the boundary and one foot still outside the boundary when the first light of dawn appeared, he became doubtful, not knowing whether his entry into the retreat was valid.
He immediately addressed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If one has come for the sake of the rains retreat, it constitutes entering the rains retreat."

At that time, some bhikṣus went to their dwelling places intending to enter the rains retreat; with one foot inside the monastery grounds and the other outside the monastery grounds when the dawn light appeared, they had doubts and did not know whether their *varṣā* (rains retreat) was validly established.
He immediately addressed the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"If one has come for the sake of the rains retreat, then the rains retreat is established."
"If, after the *varṣā* retreat has concluded, visiting bhikṣus arrive and displace the resident bhikṣus," the Buddha said,
"They should not be displaced, nor should they depart."

At that time, some bhikṣus, without inspecting the rooms and bedding at their residence, accepted a room and subsequently received an inferior room and poor bedding. They then became angry with the resident bhikṣus who had lived there previously and said:
"Your mind is not impartial; you give fine rooms and good bedding to those you like, while you give inferior rooms and poor bedding to those you do not like."
"Because he does not like me, he has given me a poor room and poor bedding.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to enter the rains retreat at a residence, he should first go there in person to inspect the rooms and bedding before accepting the room."
From this time forward, I authorize the distribution of rooms and bedding; one should appoint a person to distribute rooms and bedding by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
There are five qualities that disqualify one from being appointed to distribute rooms and bedding:
if one is subject to favoritism, hatred, fear, delusion, or lacks knowledge of what may and may not be distributed.
If there are these five qualities, one should not appoint someone to distribute bedding and dwellings.
There are five qualities for which one should be appointed to distribute dwellings and bedding:
if one is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, without delusion, and knows what may be distributed and what may not be distributed.
When these five qualities are present, one should appoint someone to distribute rooms and bedding.

One should appoint someone capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether it be a senior elder (*sthavira*), a junior elder (*anusthavira*), one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya.
One capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let it appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the bedding and lodgings."
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute bedding and dwellings."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha appointing the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the rooms and bedding remain silent; whoever does not approve should speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the rooms and bedding. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
Once the appointment of the person responsible for distributing rooms and bedding is completed, one should count the monks, count the rooms, and count the bedding.
He should then ask:
"How many rooms are occupied by residents?"
How many rooms are empty?
How many rooms have bedding and furniture?
How many rooms lack bedding and furniture?
How many rooms have bedding?
How many rooms lack bedding?
How many rooms receive offerings?
In how many rooms is there no gain or support?
In how many rooms are there utensils?
In how many rooms are there no utensils?
In how many rooms are there donors who provide robes?
In how many rooms are there no donors who provide robes?
In how many rooms is there abundant merit?
Which rooms lack sufficient merit?
Who is the managing owner of these rooms?
If there is a manager, one should ask the elder where he wishes to stay.
"In which room do you not reside?
Having finished counting all the rooms and bedding, they went before the senior elder (sthavira) and spoke as follows:
"Venerable Senior Elder!..."
"In this manner, one may take a dwelling and bedding according to one's own preference.
Having first assigned a room to the senior monk, he next assigns one to the second senior monk.
When the second senior monk has been provided for, he next assigns one to the third senior monk.
When the distribution for the third senior monk is finished, it is next given to the fourth senior monk.
In this manner, it proceeds in succession down to the junior-most monk.
If there are remaining rooms or bedding and furniture, they should be further distributed starting from the senior monks again.
If there are further rooms or quarters, they should again be divided starting from the senior monk (*sthavira*).
If there are still many remaining, one should open up a residence for visiting monks (*āgantuka-bhikṣu*).
If a visiting monk arrives, one should give [a room] to him; if an evil monk arrives, one should not give [one]; if a virtuous monk arrives, one should give [one].
"If there are others who should remain, or if rooms are left vacant, one should not refuse them; if one refuses, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained a dilapidated room and thought to himself:
"I will not accept this room, for fear that I will have to repair it."
The bhikṣus immediately informed the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:
"You should accept [the offerings] and treat them according to your capacity.

At that time, the bhikṣus divided the communal assembly places—whether it be the heated hall (*jantāghara*), the summer hall, or the walking-hall (*caṅkrama*)—and when visiting bhikṣus arrived, they could not obtain rooms and had no place to stay.
The bhikṣus reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:

"One should not divide up places where the Saṃgha assembles, such as a warm-room, a summer hall, a walking-hall, or a hall on the ground floor of a multi-storied building. If these are assembly places, the upper stories should be divided."
"If there is a place where a multitude gathers on the upper terrace, the hall below the terrace should be divided [for use].
At that time, the bhikṣus went throughout the dwellings and saw a forest cave (āraṇyaka-kuṭī). They thought to themselves:
"I shall observe the rains retreat (varṣā) in this place."
Later, there were other bhikṣus who saw a forest cave and spoke thus:
"I shall observe the rains retreat in this place.
On the sixteenth day of the first month, many bhikṣus gathered together inside the cave; because the dwelling was cramped and narrow, many fell ill.
The bhikṣus then addressed the World-Honored One, and the World-Honored One said:

“If a bhikṣu wishes to observe the rains retreat in such a place, he should first go there and establish a sign—whether by making a handprint, or a wheel, or an image of Maheśvara, or an image of Indra, or an image of a grapevine, or a flower, or the five colors, or by writing his name, saying: ‘So-and-so wishes to observe the rains retreat here.’”
The Buddha permitted those who had previously established their markers to remain.
If a bhikṣu departs from this dwelling place without canceling his name [in the register], other bhikṣus, seeing that it has already been occupied, will not dare to stay.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not depart without having extinguished one's name; one should depart only after having extinguished one's name.
At that time, the people of a bordering state rebelled against King Prasenajit, who personally led his army to suppress them.
Some bhikṣus went to a border region where the lodgings were cramped and could not accommodate everyone.
The bhikṣus said to one another:
"The Buddha has commanded us that we should divide the bedding and furniture."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to divide [the space] according to the beds. If it cannot accommodate them, you should divide it equally according to the rope-beds.
If it still cannot accommodate them, you should divide it equally according to the sleeping places."
"If you still do not accept it, you should share the seating area.
That bhikṣu moved the fixed bed, mattress, and bedding to another room. The other bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"You should not move them."
"In some rooms there were many bedding supplies, while in others there were few.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:

'I allow the bhikṣus to speak with those who have long resided there, or the temple master, or the administrator, or whoever has obtained a room for the three-month *varṣā* retreat; only after questioning such persons may the bedding supplies be moved.'"
The bhikṣus did not return the bedding to its original place before departing. Later, other bhikṣus arrived and, thinking the bedding belonged to that room, used it.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"One should not depart without returning the bedding to its original place; one should return the bedding and then depart. If one does not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."

At that time, there were dwellings that were dilapidated and ruined. The bhikṣus became apprehensive, fearing that the Buddha would not permit them to move their bedding and requisites from one room to another. For this reason, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a dwelling is dilapidated, you are permitted to move the bedding and furniture from this room to another.
When those monks moved the bedding but did not use it, and it became infested with insects and rotted away, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It may be used. Since the Buddha had permitted its use, they did not wash their feet or wipe them before using it, but instead wore it as an undergarment against the body.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not go about without having washed one's feet, nor without wiping them, nor while wearing an undergarment.
The bhikṣus, being cautious and apprehensive, reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not use it as an undergarment."
"Therefore, I did not dare to touch it with my hands or feet.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From above the knees to below the armpits, one must not wear [a garment] directly against the body; however, there is no fault in touching it with the hands or feet."
At that time, various donors offered undergarments to the bhikṣus; however, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to accept them, as the Buddha had not permitted the use of undergarments.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to follow the intention of the donor.
If the repair of a dwelling is completed, one must first return the bedding and furniture from this room to their original location before moving them elsewhere.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the repair of the dwelling is completed, one should return the bedding and furniture to their original places; otherwise, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
That bhikṣu moved the fixed bedding and furniture of this monastery to another monastery. The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not move the fixed bedding and furniture of this monastery to another monastery."

"If there is fear, or enemies, or a rebellion among the people, or if the kingdom and its towns are ravaged and ruined, and the population is decimated such that even their dwellings are destroyed—if the bhikṣus are apprehensive and fearful, the Buddha does not permit them to move the fixed bedding and furniture from this monastery to another."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If there is fear of enemies, or if the kingdom is in rebellion, the towns and villages are devastated, the people are perishing, and even one's dwelling place is destroyed, I permit you to move to another location and relocate your bedding and requisites."

At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious; because the Buddha had not permitted the use of monastic bedding as a mattress against the body, they were unable to cover themselves properly.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should move [the bedding] and cover oneself as appropriate."
"If other bhikṣus come to request [bedding], you should neither request it nor give it to them; however, if it can be trusted that it will certainly be recovered later, it should be given.
Subsequently, when the kingdom and its towns returned to tranquility, the population was restored, and the monasteries were rebuilt, yet the bedding and utensils were not returned.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the kingdom and its towns have become peaceful, the people have returned, and the monasteries are completed, one should return the bedding and furniture; if one does not return them, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma."

At that time, there was a monastery where the Saṃgha from the four quarters had received a large quantity of indeterminate bedding—straw mats, rope beds, wooden beds, coarse and fine cushions, pillows, woolen rugs, *kambala* blankets, floor coverings, water jars, staffs, and fans. The bhikṣus did not know how to distribute them.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to give bedding to those whose rooms lack it; if there is any remainder, give it from the senior monks downward.

At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana wished to observe the rains retreat together with the World-Honored One. On the fifteenth day, they set out from their respective residences, but by the seventeenth day they had not yet arrived and did not know what they should do.
He immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the later retreat (paścimā varṣā)."
There are two kinds of *vassa* (rainy-season retreat):
there is the earlier *vassa* and there is the later *vassa*.
If one observes the earlier *vassa*, one should reside for the first three months; if one observes the later *vassa*, one should reside for the latter three months.

Those who had entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early) rains retreat wished to perform the *pravāraṇā*, but those who had entered the *paścimavārṣika* (late) rains retreat did not know whether they were permitted to do so.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive the *pravāraṇā*; remain and wait until the days are complete."

Those who had entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early rains retreat) and completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony were counted as having completed their years [of ordination], but those who had entered the *paścimavārṣika* (later rains retreat) did not know whether they could be so counted.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not count a year until the three months [of the rains retreat] are fully completed."

When those who had entered the prior *anvārambhaṇa* (early retreat) finished the *pravāraṇā* ceremony, they expelled those who had entered the subsequent *anvārambhaṇa*. The monks reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should neither expel them nor depart."

When those who entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer retreat) had completed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony and divided the goods obtained during the rains, those who had entered the *paścimavārṣika* (late summer retreat) were apprehensive and did not dare to accept their share, thinking: "The Buddha has not permitted us to seek or receive goods until the three months [of the retreat] have concluded."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the bhikṣus to accept [the bedding]; they should ensure that the remaining days are sufficient to complete the full term.

Those who had entered the *pūrvavārṣika* (early summer) retreat distributed the bedding after the *pravāraṇā*, while those who had entered the *paścimavārṣika* (late summer) retreat did not dare to accept it out of caution, as the three months of the summer retreat were not yet complete.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “I allow you to accept [these things] for the sake of the future.

At that time, the bhikṣus were dwelling in the open air during the rainy season retreat; being buffeted by the wind and scorched by the sun, their bodies became dark and emaciated, and their skin cracked and peeled. They went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet with their heads to the ground, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"For what reason are your bodies dark and emaciated, and your skin cracked and split?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"It is because you have entered the rains retreat in the open air.
The Buddha said,
"One should not enter the rains retreat in the open air."
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in sheltered places.
At that time, some bhikṣus observed the retreat in trees, and they performed their bodily functions, both great and small, directly upon the trees.
At that time, a tree deity became resentful and, watching for an opportunity, sought to take his life.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"From now on, I do not permit bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in trees, nor should they climb trees."
"Except for when removing a human head, one should not urinate or defecate while circumambulating a tree, nor should one splash or soil the tree with such waste.
At that time, various bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements of the people of Kośala, and there were ferocious beasts along the way.

At that time, the bhikṣus climbed trees higher than a man's height; out of fear and caution, they descended again, thinking, "The Buddha does not permit us to climb trees higher than a man's height," and consequently they were harmed by wild beasts.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From now on, I allow you to climb trees higher than the height of a person for the sake of danger to life or danger to your pure conduct."

When the bhikṣus wished to take dry firewood from trees, [the Buddha] permitted them to use hooks to hook it down, permitted them to use ladders to reach it, or permitted them to use ropes and snares to retrieve it.
Later, the bhikṣus became apprehensive and did not dare to climb onto dry trees. The Buddha said:
"If the entire tree is dry, I permit you to climb it."
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to observe the rains retreat under trees and went to inform the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit you to observe the rains retreat under trees; provided that the tree is taller than a person's head and its branches and leaves are sufficient to provide shade for a single seat."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used wax and honey to coat their curtains and sat within them for the rains retreat. They thought to themselves:
"We shall sleep inside during the night and conceal [the coating] in the morning; whoever sees us will think we are people who have attained supernatural powers."
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, it is not permitted to spend the rainy season retreat inside a tent coated with wax and honey; nor shall one, for the sake of one's own body, practice deceitful behavior by altering one’s usual deportment."
At that time, some bhikṣus wished to observe the rains retreat in small huts. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in small huts, provided that when they stand up their heads are not obstructed, when they sit they have room for their knees, and it is sufficient to shield them from wind and rain."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in a mountain cave. He went at once to inform the Buddha, who said:

"From this day forward, I permit you to observe the rains retreat in a mountain cave; provided that when rising one’s head is not obstructed and when sitting one has room for a knee, it will also suffice to ward off wind and rain."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in a natural mountain cave. The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I allow bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in natural mountain caves; provided that when standing the head is not obstructed and when sitting it accommodates the knees, and it is sufficient to shield against wind and rain."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) in the hollow of a tree. The bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in the hollows of trees; when standing, it does not obstruct the head, and when sitting, there is enough room for the knees. Furthermore, it is sufficient to ward off wind, rain, and water."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat in reliance upon cowherds. He went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to observe the rains retreat in reliance upon cowherds. During the retreat, you should move along wherever the cowherds go."
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to observe the rainy season retreat (varṣā) with oil-pressers who were temporary residents. They went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to observe the rainy season retreat with oil-pressers; during the retreat, you should move and follow wherever the oil-pressers go."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat (*varṣā*) on a boat and went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From now on, I permit the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat on boats; during the retreat, they may move about as the boat travels to wherever it goes."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to observe the rains retreat in dependence upon woodcutters. He went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to observe the rains retreat in dependence upon woodcutters; during the retreat, they may move and follow wherever the woodcutters go."
At that time, a bhikṣu wished to enter the rains retreat in dependence upon a village settlement. He went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize you to enter the rains retreat in dependence upon a village settlement."

If, during the rains retreat (*varṣā*), a village is divided into two parts, one should remain where the provisions and necessities are fully supplied; if one must move during the retreat, one should go wherever one goes.
At that time, there was a donor who invited a bhikṣu, saying:
"I wish to give alms as well as a dwelling.
That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Since that place is far away, one cannot return on the same day; the Buddha has not yet permitted going for such reasons.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From now on, I permit you to go for seven days. You should not accept the seven-day leave solely for the sake of food and drink, except for other causes and conditions—such as for robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, needle cases, or even medicinal herbs. By the seventh day, you must return."
At that time, the bhikṣus invited other elder bhikṣus, saying: "We have incurred a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense;
please perform for us the procedures for concealing it, the *pārivāsika* (probation), the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement to the beginning), the *mānatva* (penance), and the restoration from guilt."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"That place is far away and we cannot return on the same day; yet the Buddha has not yet permitted us to go for such reasons.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to go away for seven days and return within seven days when such a matter arises.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī invited an elder bhikṣu, saying:
"We have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense; please perform the mānatva penance for us to bring about our purification from the offense."
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"That place is far away and I cannot return that very day; furthermore, the Buddha has not yet permitted us to go on such an errand.
He went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“From this day forward, it is permitted that when such circumstances arise, one may receive a seven-day leave and return within seven days.
At that time, there was a śikṣamāṇā who invited a bhikṣu, saying:
“Venerable sir, please come!”
"We have violated the precepts; let us confess our transgressions and receive the precepts again, or receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla).
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"That place is far away and I cannot return that very day; furthermore, the Buddha has not yet permitted such a departure."
He went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, when such circumstances arise, I permit one to go away for seven days and return within seven days.
At that time, a śrāmaṇera invited a bhikṣu.
“Venerable sir, come!
I wish to receive the precepts.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"The destination there is so remote that one could not return on the same day; the Buddha has not yet permitted such a departure.
They went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit those with such business to receive a seven-day leave and return within seven days."
At that time, there was a śrāmaṇerikā who invited a bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable Sir, come!
I wish to receive the six dharmas."
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
"That place is far away; I cannot return on the same day, yet the Buddha has not yet permitted going for such a matter.
He went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted to accept such a matter as departing for seven days and returning within seven days.
At that time, there was a minister who lacked faith and devotion, who invited a bhikṣu, saying:
"Venerable sir, come!"
"I wish to see you.
The bhikṣu thought to himself:
