Thereupon, the elder’s son Śrona immediately spread his robe on the ground and approached the king, prostrating himself with his head at the king's feet.
When the King saw that hair had grown on the soles of his feet, his heart was filled with great joy; having thus bestowed upon him worldly benefits in this very life, he spoke these words:
"I have already granted you worldly benefits in this present life."

"The World-Honored One is at Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha; you should go there to see him, pay homage, and inquire after his well-being, for he will grant you benefits for future lives.
When the lord of Campā and the various elders heard the king’s words, they went together to Vulture Peak Mountain.
At that time, there was an elder named Sājha who served as the Buddha’s attendant; he was sitting on a flat rock in another location.
Then the lord of the city of Campā went to where the elder Sājha was and asked him, "Where is the World-Honored One now?"
"We wish to see the Tathāgata.
Sāketā said, "Wait a moment, householder; I must inform the Buddha."
At that time, the Elder Sāgata vanished from atop the rock and, in the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm, emerged before the Buddha and said:
"The householder of Campā wishes to see the World-Honored One."
The Buddha said, "Go and spread a seat in the shade of a building; I shall go there to sit.

At that time, Sāgata immediately followed these instructions and, having spread the seat, returned to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“I have finished preparing the seats; now is precisely the right time.
Then the World-Honored One emerged from the house, sat down, and addressed Sājha, saying:
“Tell the Elder Campaka to come.”
Then the Elder Sāgata vanished before the Buddha and, in the time it takes a strong man to bend or extend his arm, reappeared atop the rock.
When the elders saw this, they marveled at such an unprecedented marvel, saying:
"If the supernatural power of the World-Honored One’s disciple is thus, how much more so that of the Tathāgata himself!"
Sakṛdāgāmin said, "Householder,
you should know that this is the time.
The Lord of Campā then approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, using various skillful means, preached the Dharma for the sons of the elders and the lord of Campā, exhorting and transforming them until they were filled with great joy. He taught the methods for giving, observing the precepts, and rebirth in heaven; immediately upon these seats, they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, saw the Dharma, realized the Dharma, and attained the fruit of realization, never again to regress. They addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Virtuous One!..."
From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; please accept me as a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
From this day forward, I shall refrain from taking life, and so forth, up to refraining from drinking intoxicants.
At that time, the elder’s son Śrona was seated in the assembly and thought to himself: "I have heard what the Buddha has said:

if I remain at home with my wife and children, I shall not be able to cultivate the pure conduct. It would be better for me now to request from the Buddha the shaving of my hair and beard, to leave the household life, and to become a seeker of the Way."
He intended to cause the assembly to disperse.

At that time, the lord of the city of Campā, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma through various skillful means, felt great joy in his heart; he immediately rose from his seat, paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.

The householder’s son Śrona returned to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“As I have heard the Buddha’s teaching, if I remain at home together with my wife and children, I shall be unable to cultivate the pure conduct.”
"I now wish to request from the World-Honored One permission to shave my hair and beard, leave the household life, and become a seeker of the Way.
The Buddha asked Śoṇa: "Have your parents given you their permission?"
He replied: "World-Honored One,
my parents have not yet given their permission."
The Buddha said,
"If your parents do not permit it, the Tathāgata does not permit you to go forth. He replied:
"I shall now employ skillful means to cause my parents to grant their permission.
The Buddha said,
"Now is precisely the right time."
Then Śrona returned to the city of Campā and went to his parents, saying:

"As I have heard the Buddha teach, if I remain at home together with my wife and children, I shall not be able to cultivate the pure conduct. I now wish to seek from the Buddha the removal of my hair and beard, to leave the household life, and to become a seeker of the Way; I pray that my parents will grant me permission."

The parents replied, "The way of leaving home is extremely difficult; becoming a śramaṇa is also not easy. It would be better to remain at home, delighting in sensual desires and performing meritorious deeds at will, rather than needing to leave home."
When Śrona heard these words from his parents, he still did not desist; even when they spoke thus a second and a third time, he remained as before.
Although Śrona made this request to his parents three times, they still would not grant him permission.
At that time, Śrona immediately rose from his seat, sat upon the ground, and spoke these words:

"From this day forward, I shall cease bathing and no longer anoint my body with perfumes; I shall neither drink nor eat. Whether I die or whether I attain the state of a renunciant, I shall not eat for one day, or even up to five days."

At that time, the kinsmen and acquaintances of Śrona heard that Śrona wished to request from the Buddha the removal of his hair and beard to leave the household life and practice the Way, yet his parents would not permit it, so he did not eat for one day up to five days.
At that time, the relatives and acquaintances of Śrona went to where he was and said to him: "Rise, Śrona!

Bathe your body, anoint it with fragrant perfumes, enjoy food and drink, and freely cultivate merit. It is not easy to leave the household life, and the state of a śramaṇa is difficult; desist, there is no need to renounce the world."
When Śrona heard these words from his kinsmen and acquaintances, he still did not stop; for a second and a third time they spoke likewise, and his friends did the same.
At that time, Śrona’s companions went to where his parents were and spoke to them thus:

"Please allow Śrona to leave the home life to follow the Path; if he delights in leaving the home life, we shall see him constantly; if he does not delight in leaving the home life, he shall return here."
"If Śrona were to die, what then?
His parents immediately replied,
"He may leave the household life as he pleases."
When Śrona heard that his parents had granted their permission, he thought to himself:
"I am currently so emaciated that I cannot endure even a single meal; I should take care of myself for a short while."
At that time, Śrona possessed some measure of strength; he went to his parents and said, "I am now going forth from the household life. His parents said:
"Now is precisely the right time.

Thereupon, Śaila immediately went to Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain in Rājagṛha; arriving at the place where the World-Honored One was, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and said:
"My parents have already granted me permission to leave the home life to practice the Way. I pray that the Buddha will deliver me so that I may receive the full precepts."
The Buddha immediately granted him permission to leave the household life and receive full ordination.
At that time, Śrona’s parents established seven relay stations between the two cities to send hot food for Śrona so that it would arrive at the proper time.
When Śrona had given this food to the Elder, he entered the city himself to beg for alms.
When his parents heard that Śrona had given the food they had sent to the bhikṣus and was begging for alms himself, from that time forward they ceased sending him food.

At that time, Śrona went to dwell in the Śītavana forest by the side of the Warm Water River; he practiced with such diligent effort that the blood flowing from his walking meditation path stained the ground like a place of slaughter.
At that time, Śāṇakavāsin was meditating in a quiet place, and he thought to himself:
"I am now practicing with such diligent effort that among the disciples of the Buddha, there is none who excels me; why is it that I have not yet attained untainted liberation?"
"In my home there is great wealth and treasure; I can enjoy it myself and indulge in making merit as I please.
It would now be better for me to abandon the precepts and return home, rather than continue practicing the Way."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing their thoughts, traveled from Vulture Peak Mountain to the Śītavana forest at his place of walking meditation in the interval it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm; there he saw the ground stained with blood as if it were a place of slaughter.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked the other bhikṣus:
"Whose walking path is this?
The ground is stained with blood as if it were a place of slaughter."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“This bhikṣu Śaila has practiced with such diligent effort that his blood has stained the ground.
The Buddha said:
"Call him here! The bhikṣu,
having received these instructions, went to where Śaila was and said to him,
"The World-Honored One calls you!"
When Dhānañjāni heard the Buddha call him, he immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Knowing [his thoughts], the Buddha asked him intentionally:
“In a secluded place, you had this thought:”
"I have practiced with diligent vigor; among the disciples of the Buddha, there is none superior to me. Why is it that I have not yet attained untainted liberation?
My household possesses great wealth and treasures; I can enjoy them as I please and perform meritorious deeds."
"Is it not better now to abandon the precepts and return home, no longer practicing the Way?
[The other replied: "Indeed, it is so."
“World-Honored One!
The World-Honored One said:
“I shall now question you; answer me as you see fit.”
"When you were living at home, were you able to play the lute? "It was so,
World-Honored One!"
"A householder can indeed play the lute. "Dharmadinna!
What do you think?"
“If the strings of a lute are too tight, is the sound pleasant? “No,
World-Honored One.”
“Kūṭadanta! What do you think?
If the strings of a lute are too loose, is the sound pleasant?”
"No, World-Honored One. "How so, Rāṣṭrapāla?"
“Is the sound of the lute strings good, being neither too loose nor too tight? “It is so,
World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:
“So it is, Śoṇa! If one’s great diligence is restless, or if one’s diligence is too slight and leads to indolence, one should apply balanced diligence and maintain balance among the faculties.”

At that time, having heard the Buddha’s brief instruction and admonition, Śrona retired to a solitary place and practiced with diligent effort, his mind free from negligence. During the first and last watches of the night, he remained vigilant, cultivating the dharmas that aid the path. Before long, he attained the fruit for which he had gone forth; he realized the unsurpassed pure conduct in this very life, realizing: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of being."
It was known that the bhikṣu Śaṇḍaka had attained the path of arhatship.
Having attained the path of arhatship, the bhikṣu Śaṇḍaka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“If there is a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship and exhausted all outflows (āsravas), he delights in the six sense bases, delights in renunciation, delights in non-ill will, delights in tranquility, delights in the exhaustion of craving, delights in the exhaustion of the aggregates of clinging, and delights in the absence of delusion.”
"If there is a bhikṣu who has attained arhatship with the exhaustion of outflows and delights in these six bases,
World-Honored One,
is it possible for such a person to achieve liberation without relying on faith?"
"One should not entertain such a thought as this:

'One attains the path of an Arhat without relying on faith; one exhausts all outflows, exhausting desire and becoming free from desire, exhausting hatred and becoming free from hatred, exhausting delusion and becoming free from delusion, and finds joy in renunciation.'"
“World-Honored One! Is it possible to obtain happiness and freedom from ill-will without relying on the observance of the precepts?
“You should not entertain such a thought.”

"Without relying on the observance of precepts, one attains the path of the Arhat, exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*); exhausting both craving and non-craving, exhausting both anger and non-anger, exhausting both delusion and non-delusion, and delighting in the absence of anger."
“World-Honored One! Is there anyone who, while not severing various gains and offerings, yet delights in tranquility?
“One should not form such a thought.”
"Without severing gain and offerings, one attains the path of Arhatship; one exhausts hatred so as to be without hatred, exhausts delusion so as to be without delusion, and delights in tranquility.

Having exhausted desire so as to be without desire, exhausted hatred so as to be without hatred, and exhausted delusion so as to be without delusion, with craving exhausted and the aggregates of clinging exhausted, one delights in non-delusion."
"Thus it is, bhikṣu!

With the mind liberated from outflows, one sees many forms with the eye; both the liberation through wisdom and the liberation of the mind are undefiled, and consciousness does not become entangled with forms as one dwells in the fourth dhyāna. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind."
“World-Honored One!
It is like a great mountain of rock, entirely a single mass, without deficiency, without holes, and without leaks.
If a great wind and rain were to come from the east, this mountain would not shift and could not be shaken.”
It is likewise in the south, west, and north.
Thus it is, World-Honored One!

If a bhikṣu has attained the path of arhatship, his mind is liberated and his outflows are exhausted; seeing many forms with the eye, he is liberated through wisdom and liberated in mind, and both are undefiled. Consciousness does not mingle with form as he dwells in the fourth dhyāna; it is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Having spoken these words, he further recited these verses:
"The bhikṣu who delights in renunciation, Who delights in tranquility,
Who delights in non-anger, And who has exhausted craving."
Delighting in the exhaustion of the aggregate of sensation, the mind is not deluded;
knowing clearly that [craving] does not arise, one is liberated from this.
Through right liberation, there is then cessation and stillness.
Having attained non-contemplation, there is no further activity.
Just as a great mountain cannot be destroyed by the wind,
so it is with forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.
"Regarding wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, the wise person remains unmoved;
with the mind abiding in liberation, they perceive cessation.
Having spoken this verse, Śoṇakoṭīviṃśa was approved by the Buddha; he rose from his seat, went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and departed.
Not long after he had departed, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"One should declare one's attainment of the Way through such self-recollection as this; however, one should speak only of its meaning and not claim actual attainment. This is unlike other foolish bhikṣus who, out of joy, declare their own attainment only to find nothing gained later, exhausting themselves in vain."
At that time, Śrona went to the Buddha's dwelling at another occasion, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha said to Śrona, "Since your birth you have been accustomed to pleasure and unaccustomed to suffering; therefore, I permit you to wear single-layered leather sandals within the monastery."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have renounced five elephant kings to leave the household life and pursue the Way; this may cause people to laugh and say:
'Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa has renounced five elephant kings to leave the household life and pursue the Way, yet he covets a single pair of leather sandals.'"
“If the World-Honored One permits the bhikṣus to keep them, I too shall keep them.

At that time, the Buddha silently gave his consent. He then assembled the community of bhikṣus for this reason and preached the Dharma to them accordingly, using countless skillful means to praise those who practice the dhūta ascetic virtues, who have few desires and know contentment, and who delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:
“For the sake of protecting the body, protecting the robes, and protecting the bedding, I permit you to wear single-layered leather sandals within the monastery.”
At that time, the bhikṣus wore single-layered leather sandals, which soon became worn through. [The Buddha said:
"I allow you to patch them with tree bark or leather; they should be sewn with thread. If they break or tear, they should be mended with sinew, hair, or leather thread."
At that time, the bhikṣu Xūzhuī addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep awls. *Sifen lü*, fascicle 38.
The Four-Part Vinaya, Volume Thirty-nine; Part Three of the Tripartite [Vinaya].
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian and others.

This is the remainder of the Chapter on Leather (*Carma-vastu*). At that time, Mahākātyāyana was staying in the country of Aparāntaka, dwelling in the bend of Mount Kukkutapāda, together with the lay follower Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and his messenger.
At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself:

"As I have heard the Buddha teach, if I remain at home with my wife and children, I shall not be able to cultivate the pure conduct; it would be better for me to shave off my hair and beard, leave the household life, and become a seeker of the Way."
He then went to where Mahākātyāyana was and spoke to him thus:
"As I have heard the Buddha teach, if I remain at home together with my wife and children, I shall not be able to practice the pure conduct."
"I pray that the Venerable One will grant me ordination and allow me to receive the full precepts.

Kātyāyana said, "The matter of leaving the household life is difficult; the life of a śramaṇa is not easy. You should simply remain at home, uphold the Buddha’s precepts, and constantly practice the Buddha's teachings according to the proper seasons."

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa made this request three times to Mahākātyāyana. Seeing that Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was so earnest as to repeat his plea up to three times, Mahākātyāyana then permitted him to go forth. Ordination is difficult to obtain; it took three years before he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Why is this? Because the number of monks did not yet reach ten.
It was not long after Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa had received the precepts that he attained the path of Arhatship; his recollection of attaining the path was also as described above.

At that time, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa heard of the Buddha’s meritorious qualities, his physical marks and signs of excellence, and how his faculties were tranquil and perfectly subdued—like a king of elephants or a clear, deep pool. Hearing this, he was filled with joy and desired to see the Buddha.
He went to where Kātyāyana was and said to him:
"I have heard that the Buddha’s virtues are such as these; I now wish to go and see the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
Kātyāyana said: "The Buddha’s virtues are as you have described. Kātyāyana said:
"Take my name and go to the Buddha’s presence; bow your head at his feet in salutation and inquire after his well-being, asking whether he is free from illness and living in peace.
Take these five matters and report them to the Buddha:
'In the country of Aśmaka-Avantī, there are few bhikṣus, and it is difficult to receive the full precepts; only after three years can one receive ordination.'"
For what reason?
Because the number of monks does not yet reach ten.
From this day forward, we pray that the World-Honored One will graciously provide a skillful means and permit the reception of the full precepts in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī.

"In the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī, there are many thorns, brambles, tiles, and stones; a single layer of leather sandals cannot endure for long. We pray that the World-Honored One will permit us to wear double-layered leather sandals."

The people of the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī are fond of bathing; may the World-Honored One permit the bhikṣus to bathe frequently. Just as in other regions there are many fine bedding materials—such as eranda, mora, māmora, and kambala.
In the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī, people use skins as bedding—such as the skins of rams, white sheep, and deer; we pray that the World-Honored One will permit us to keep such skin bedding.
There may be a bhikṣu who, after traveling to another region, obtains robes at his place of residence and is unwilling to accept them.
Why is this? He fears committing an offense involving forfeiture (*niḥsargika-pāyattika*). We pray that the World-Honored One will grant permission for a slight expedient means.

At that time, the bhikṣu Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, having heard the words of Mahākātyāyana, accepted them in silence. He immediately rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at [Kātyāyana’s] feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

When Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa heard that the World-Honored One was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in Rājagṛha, he took his three robes and bowl, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha immediately comforted him, saying:
"Are you dwelling in peace and happiness?
Do you not suffer from lack of food and drink?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying, "I am dwelling in peace and comfort; food and drink do not trouble me.
The Buddha instructed Ānanda to prepare a seat for the visiting bhikṣu.
At that time, Ānanda, knowing the established custom, understood that the World-Honored One wished to stay overnight with visiting bhikṣus, and thus had Ānanda prepare a seat.

Having heard the Buddha’s words, Ānanda returned to the Buddha’s chamber and prepared a seat opposite the Buddha’s throne. Once the seat was prepared, he returned to prostrate his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“The seat has been prepared for the visiting bhikṣu; please know that the time is now right.”
At that time, the World-Honored One rose and returned to his chamber, where he took his seat. Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa also entered the Buddha’s chamber and sat opposite him.
After the World-Honored One had sat in silence for a short while, he addressed Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, saying:
“You may preach the Dharma.”

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa spoke the sixteen points of meaning before the Buddha; neither adding nor subtracting anything, his voice was clear and beautiful, and the sequence of the chapters and phrases was perfectly intelligible.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself: "Excellent, bhikṣu!

These sixteen points of meaning neither increase nor decrease, and they do not violate the Dharma; their tone is pure and beautiful, and the sequence of the chapters and phrases is clear and intelligible."
The Buddha asked Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa,
"What did you do in the past? He replied:
"I have long observed the faults of desire; it is difficult to receive the precepts, as three years must pass. Why is this?
Because the number of monks does not yet reach ten."
Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa thought to himself,
"Now is the very time for the five matters sent by my preceptor Kātyāyana.
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Upadhyāya Kātyāyana bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquires after the World-Honored One’s well-being, asking whether he is robust, free from illness, and at ease.
He reports these five matters as previously described."
The Buddha then silently gave his consent.

On the following morning at dawn, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and preached the Dharma to them accordingly. By means of countless skillful methods, he praised the dhūta practices, the proper observance of dignified conduct, having few desires and being content, and delighting in dwelling in seclusion. He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I permit five persons who uphold the Vinaya in the kingdom of Aśmaka-Avantī to receive full ordination."
If there are other regions, those are also permitted.
As for "other regions": to the east there is a country named the Kingdom of White Wood (Pāṭaliputra); beyond that, it is permitted.
To the south there is a stūpa named the Stūpa of Tranquil Virtue (Śāntasādhu); beyond that, it is permitted.
In the west there is a mountain country named Ṛṣigiri, where the mountain is called Ṛṣi-kula; outside of this region, it is permitted.

In the north there is a country named Stambha; outside of this region, it is likewise permitted. Thus, in all such regions outside [the central lands], it is permitted for five persons who maintain the Vinaya to confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

It is permitted for those from the country of Aśmaka-Avantī to wear leather sandals; it is permitted for those from the country of Aśmaka-Avantī to bathe repeatedly; it is permitted to use bedding made of the skins of black sheep, white sheep, or deer; it is permitted for the bhikṣus to accept robes that have come into their hands, provided ten days have not yet elapsed; if more than ten days pass, they must relinquish them, and having relinquished them, they must perform confession.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained some leather to repair his sandals; not far from the Buddha, he tore them apart, fearing he might commit an offense regarding heavy leather sandals.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked the bhikṣu:
"For what reason have you torn apart your sandals?"
He replied, "I fear I may commit an offense regarding heavy leather sandals.
The Buddha said:
"If leather sandals become worn out or torn, I allow them to be reinforced.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained untreated hides; the Buddha said, "I allow you to tan and treat them."
Whether he tans it himself or has someone else tan it, once the leather has been tanned, he cuts it to make a single-layered leather sandal.
He requires a knife; the Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a knife."
He required wooden boards; the Buddha said, "I allow you to keep boards.
He required sinews, or hair, or leather thread, etc.; the Buddha said:
"Listen; you may keep it.
[When they needed] a scraper, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep one."
"If the knife is dull, I allow you to keep a whetstone.
At that time, the monks' knives, awls, sinews, hair, leather, threads, and scrapers were scattered on the ground with no place to rest. The Buddha said:

"I allow you to make bags to contain them; or a woven bamboo basket, or a tree-bark basket. I allow you to wrap them in hair-sacs, and among the ten kinds of robes, I allow you to use any one of them to make a bag."
At that time, the bhikṣus made [sandals] out of leather. The Buddha said:
"I do not permit making them out of leather.
At that time, the bhikṣus wore new garments over their leather sandals while sitting, thereby soiling their robes. The Buddha said:
"One should not sit upon new clothes or leather sandals; nor should a bhikṣu sit upon leather, except in the country of Aśmāpantī.
At that time, some bhikṣus fell asleep while carrying their leather sandals in front of them, and a dog carried them off. The Buddha said:
"One should not fall asleep while carrying leather sandals in front of one; one should cover them with grass."
"If the two soles are joined together, place the *niṣīdana* beneath them.

At that time, a bhikṣu took his leather sandals and placed them at his side while falling asleep; he then turned over and fell upon the sandals. Feeling apprehensive and cautious, he feared he had committed the offense of sleeping on leather.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
At that time, a bhikṣu was walking with leather sandals placed inside his alms bowl; when other bhikṣus saw this, they found it deeply offensive. The Buddha said:
"One should not place leather sandals inside the alms bowl; one should hold the bowl with purity.
At that time, a bhikṣu held his leather sandals and the bowl in one hand, and when the other bhikṣus saw this, they disapproved.
The Buddha said, "It is not permitted to hold a leather sandal and an alms bowl with one hand; rather, you should hold the bowl with one hand and the leather sandal with the other.
At that time, when the bhikṣus were crossing through muddy water, they were unable to lift their robes, and their robes fell into the mud. The Buddha said:
"Listen: hold the finger-ring, the leather sandals, and the bowl in your palms, and with one hand lift up your robe.
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements of Kosala and arrived at a village where no other bhikṣus resided; they stayed overnight in the house of a potter.
At that time, there was a piece of leather by a mud-work site, and a bhikṣu slept upon it.
Seeing it at dawn, he feared he had committed the offense of sleeping on leather. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept large skins—leopard skins, tiger skins, panther skins, otter skins, wildcat skins, *kāra* skins, and fox skins. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"None of these large skins may be kept."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus sat upon high and large beds—whether sitting alone on rope beds, wooden beds, ivory beds, or upon spread horse hides, elephant hides, brocade cushions, multicolored bedding, woolen rugs, or stuffed mattresses made of otter fur. The other bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"One should not sit upon high and large beds, nor even upon stuffed mattresses made of otter fur."
At that time, when the bhikṣus arrived at the house of a layperson, the layperson prepared a fine, high, and large bed for the bhikṣu and invited him to sit upon it.
The bhikṣus said, "The Buddha has not permitted us to sit on high or large beds."
The laypeople said, "Where else shall we obtain beds?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“With the exception of precious couches, you should sit on the remaining types in the houses of laypeople.

At that time, when the bhikṣus arrived at the houses of laypeople, the laypeople prepared leather couches and single-seated couches for the bhikṣus; however, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to sit, thinking to themselves:
“The Buddha has not permitted us to sit upon leather, with the exception of the country of Aśmaka-Avantī.”
The laypeople said, "Where else shall we obtain beds?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to sit within the house of a layperson.

At that time, when the bhikṣus arrived at the house of a layperson, long corded beds and wooden beds were spread out for them; yet the bhikṣus, being cautious and fearful, did not dare to sit, thinking:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to sit on the same bed as a senior elder (upādhyāya or guru)."
The laypeople said,
"Where else could we obtain individual beds for each person?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to sit on [seats] in the houses of laypeople.
At that time, some bhikṣus went to the house of a layperson, and the layperson spread out a leather bag for them. The bhikṣus felt apprehensive and thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to sit upon leather."
The laypeople said,
"Where else could we possibly find separate seating?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; you may sit in the house of a layperson.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda had a cowherd who served as his donor (*dānapati*).
In the early morning, he put on his robes and went to the donor's house, where he spread out a seat and sat down.

At that time, a cowherd came and sat down to listen to the Dharma. The Śākya son Upananda skillfully preached the Dharma to him, using various skillful means to exhort the donor until he was filled with great joy.
He immediately asked,
"Venerable sir, what do you require? Baddhanta replied:
"Please stop!
We require nothing; we have already received sufficient offerings.
He spoke again:
"Please tell us what you require," they said.
Pūraṇa-Kāśyapa replied, "Stop;
there is no need to speak."
"If I were to say so, neither would be given to me. He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I will simply say that I shall give it.
Not far ahead, he saw a calf of variegated color, and Upananda said,
"I require this hide."
He replied, “Wait a moment; I must kill him.
He then killed him and flayed his skin, giving it to Upananda.
Having obtained the hide, Upāli’s brother, Pūraṇa-Kāśyapa (Baddhananda), rose from his seat and took it away.
At that time, the mother cow bellowed loudly and pursued him as far as the gate of the Jetavana.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked him:
"Why does this cow bellow and follow behind you?
He replied, "This is its calf's hide; it is only because I am carrying it that she acts thus."
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not beg for raw hides; if one begs for them, they must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
The bhikṣus were apprehensive and dared not cross water carrying a life-preserving float. The Buddha said:
“Listen. At that time, the bhikṣus grasped the tails of oxen to cross a body of water; only after they had crossed did they realize it was a cow, and they were filled with apprehension.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
From this day forward, you must not cross water by grasping the tail of a cow.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not dare to cross water while sitting on a leather seat; the Buddha said:
“I permit it.
At that time, the bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to board leather boats to cross the water. The Buddha said:
“I permit you to sit or lie down as you please upon a leather boat.”
At that time, the bhikṣus made sheaths for their knives out of leather but did not wrap them with any material, so the blades rusted and were ruined.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wrap the knife with either wool, cotton, or large pieces of leather."
At that time, the bhikṣus possessed double-layered leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"One must not possess double-layered leather sandals.
At that time, the bhikṣus possessed *kaṇapuṭa* leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"One must not permit the possession of *kaṇapuṭa* leather sandals.

At that time, a bhikṣu was traveling along a road in the kingdom of Kosala with some laypeople; his foot was pierced by a wooden splinter, blood flowed profusely, and he suffered so much that he was unable to walk.
At that time, the layperson immediately offered the leather sandals he was wearing to the bhikṣu.
However, the bhikṣu was apprehensive and did not dare to accept them, fearing he might violate the prohibition against *kaṇapuṭa* leather sandals.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to receive [the teaching] through such causes and conditions.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept sandals with curled-up corners; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep sandals made of turned antelope horn.
The bhikṣus kept sandals made of deer horn, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them."
The bhikṣus kept arāli leather sandals; the Buddha said, "You should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus made sandal straps from variegated skins; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus made leather shoe straps out of silk cloth; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them."
The group of six bhikṣus kept *pūralabhadra* leather sandals; the Buddha said, "You should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus wore *candali* leather sandals; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus wore sandals with braided edges; the Buddha said, "One should not keep them."
The group of six bhikṣus wore sandals with many straps; the Buddha said, "You should not keep such.
The group of six bhikṣus wore sandals with curled shapes; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus wore large leather sandals made of lion skin, tiger skin, leopard skin, otter skin, wildcat skin, multicolored skins, and fox skin.
The Buddha said: "None of these may be kept."
The group of six bhikṣus used large leather strips as borders for their sandals, or used them as straps, or for stitching. The Buddha said:
"One must not use borders, straps, or stitching [made of such leather]."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore blue leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"You should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus then used blue trim on their leather sandals, or made straps and stitching from them. The Buddha said:
"One should not use blue materials to trim leather sandals or to make straps for them.
The group of six bhikṣus wore yellow leather sandals, whereupon the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such sandals]."
The group of six bhikṣus wore leather sandals with yellow borders, either with straps or stitched; the Buddha said:
"One should not use leather sandals with yellow borders, nor straps, nor stitching."
The group of six bhikṣus wore red leather sandals;
the Buddha said, "One should not wear red leather sandals; the same applies to the straps and the seams.
The group of six bhikṣus wore white leather sandals; the Buddha said:
"One should not wear white leather sandals; the same applies to those with straps or seams.
The group of six bhikṣus wore leather sandals resembling peacock feathers, and the Buddha said:
"You should not keep them."
The group of six bhikṣus wore leather sandals of variegated brocade color. The Buddha said:
"You should not keep them.
When those bhikṣus obtained leather sandals of variegated brocade color, the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them; however, if they are dyed a discolored color, one is permitted to keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus wore sandals made of coarse wool; the Buddha said, "One should not keep them."
The group of six bhikṣus wore leather sandals with tassels made of cotton cloth;
the Buddha said, "You should not keep such things.
The group of six bhikṣus then wore leather sandals with tassels made of worn-out rags; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such footwear].
The group of six bhikṣus stuffed their leather sandals with *māngaka* grass, *vāsaka* grass, *śara* grass, and *haṃtālaka* grass; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such footwear]."
"You foolish group of six bhikṣus!
What I have prohibited, you instead do as something else.
From this day forward, no one should possess sandals with curled edges."
At that time, as it was raining, the bhikṣus’ feet became muddy, staining their sitting mats, their bodies, and their bedding. The Buddha said:
“In order to protect the body and the sitting mats, I allow you to wear straw sandals or leather shoes within the monastery to wash your feet.”
After he had put on sandals made of *pu* grass and leather and washed his feet, water entered the interior of the sandals, soiling his feet, the seat, his body, and the bedding. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to sew tree bark or leather onto the sole."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus in Śrāvastī were wearing leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"You should not keep them.
Likewise, these four kinds of straw sandals may not be kept."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. The group of six bhikṣus stripped the leaves from tāla trees to make sandals, causing the trees to wither and dry up.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they destroy living beings and yet claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma"—
when one examines it in this way, what True Dharma could there be?
How can one take palmyra leaves to make sandals, thereby causing the tree to wither and dry up?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such things].
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore wooden clogs; their sound was like the trotting of horses and disturbed those engaged in meditation.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep wooden clogs."
At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to step on their sandals with urine or feces, nor did they dare to put on their sandals for washing their feet. The Buddha said:
"Except for those that may be worn while walking, the others should be stepped upon."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vāgṛha.
At that moment, the Vaiśālī Bhadrayānīya bhikṣus were wearing sandals made of gold and silver. The Buddha said:
"One should not keep such things."
He then put on sandals made of lapis lazuli, and the Buddha said,
"You should not keep these.
He then put on sandals made of precious gems, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.
Again, [a monk] wore sandals inlaid with jewels; the Buddha said, "One should not keep them."
The Buddha said: "Such a foolish person!
This is what I have prohibited, yet you willfully perform other matters instead."
"From this day forward, no one shall wear any kind of wooden sandals.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
The group of six bhikṣus were wearing leather sandals while walking back and forth with the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Even the disciples of various external craftsmen show respect toward their teachers.
Yet these six groups of bhikṣus are foolish men!"
He put on leather sandals and walked back and forth together with the Buddha.
The Buddha said,
"From this day forward, no one shall possess any leather sandals."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were in fine places for walking meditation before their upādhyāyas and ācāryas, while the upādhyāyas and ācāryas were in poor places;
they were in high places while the upādhyāyas and ācāryas were in low places;
and they were in front while the upādhyāyas and ācāryas were behind them.

[He] conversed with his preceptor (upādhyāya) and others side-by-side, walked in meditation (caṅkrama) alongside them, tucked up his robe to wrap around his neck and cover his head, wore his robe over both shoulders, and put on leather sandals.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One must not [act thus] with one's preceptor or those equal to a preceptor, nor with an ācārya or those equal to an ācārya; whether it be walking in an improper place for meditation, or even wearing leather sandals, none of these are permitted."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, in the presence of their preceptors and those equal to preceptors, as well as their instructors and those equal to instructors, wore their robes over both shoulders and put on leather sandals; when taking or giving anything, they neither bared their right shoulder nor removed their sandals.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, it is permitted to take or give things while baring the right shoulder and removing leather sandals in the presence of one’s preceptors (upādhyāya) and their equals, or one’s instructors (ācārya) and their equals."

At that time, while the bhikṣus were in the homes of laypeople, they bared their right shoulders and removed their leather sandals before their preceptors (upādhyāya) and those equal to preceptors, as well as their instructors (ācārya) and those equal to instructors; consequently, their private parts were exposed.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I allow [a layperson] in a householder's home to stand before their upādhyāya or those equal to an upādhyāya, or before their ācārya or those equal to an ācārya, without baring the right shoulder and without removing their leather sandals, to take or give things as they please."
At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling along a road with other bhikṣus. One bhikṣu asked another for water, and the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to accept or give anything while wearing leather sandals."
That bhikṣu immediately removed his leather sandals to fetch water, whereupon he lost them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow that if one is traveling on a road, one may wear leather sandals while taking or giving things as one pleases."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, at evening, requested water from another bhikṣu. The latter thought to himself:
"The Buddha has not permitted one to take or give anything while wearing leather sandals."

At that time, the dwelling place was far from water and infested with venomous insects. The bhikṣu removed his leather sandals and went to fetch water; however, the venomous insects bit his feet, causing him pain and distress.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it is after sunset, or if one is far from water, or if one fears venomous insects, one is permitted to wear leather sandals and may take or give them as one pleases."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus did not rise to greet their preceptors (upādhyāya) or those equal to preceptors, nor their instructors (ācārya) or those equal to instructors.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should rise; however, if one is eating in a single sitting, or if one has performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* ritual and does not eat further, or if one is ill, it is permitted to speak as follows:"
"Venerable One, please be patient!
I have a reason for not rising. Regarding the *upādhyāya*:
he is the one from whom one receives and attains the precepts.
Regarding the term "Upādhyāya" (Preceptor) and so forth: they are generally at least ten years senior [to their disciples].
Regarding the term "Ācārya" (Teacher), there are five kinds of Ācāryas:

the Preceptor for Ordination (*pravrajyā-ācārya*), the Preceptor for Receiving the Precepts (*upasaṃpad-ācārya*), the Teacher of Instruction (*śikṣā-ācārya*), the Teacher of the Scriptures (*adhyayana-ācārya*), and the Preceptor of Reliance (*niśraya-ācārya*).
The *upādhyāya* for going forth is the one upon whom one relies to obtain the status of a renunciant.
The *ācārya* for receiving the precepts is the one who performs the *karmavācanā* at the time of receiving the precepts.
The *upādhyāya* is one who instructs in proper deportment (*īryāpatha*).

The *śāstṛ-ācārya* is one from whom one receives the sūtras; that is, the place from which one receives the study of the *sūtras*, or the explanation of their meaning, even down to a single four-line verse.
Regarding the reliance upon an *ācārya*: this extends even to relying on one for the duration of a single night.
As for those such as an *ācārya*, they are generally five years senior [to the disciple].

With the exception of the *ācārya* upon whom one relies, if the room where a bhikṣu dwells requires sweeping, he should sweep it; having swept it, if dust still remains, he is permitted to sprinkle it with muddy water to settle the dust.
Once the mud has been washed away, if there is still dust remaining, it is permitted to spread a ground-cover.
Whether it be *elāyanta*, *maudra*, *maudra-maudra*, *kambala*, or any of the ten kinds of cloth, one may spread whichever is available.
At that time, the bhikṣus went up onto the floor-coverings without having washed their feet. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to place foot-wiping materials by the door; if they are still not clean, you should place a water vessel outside the door to wash your feet."
After the bhikṣus had washed their feet, they ascended onto the floor coverings before their feet were dry; the floor coverings became ruined. The Buddha said:
"One must not ascend onto a floor covering until one's feet are dry."
"If there is an urgent matter, one should wipe the knees with the feet, or wipe the calves, or wipe them with the hands, or wipe them with a worn-out cloth.
At that time, the bhikṣus were fatigued from repeatedly washing their feet when receiving or giving things for their upādhyāyas, upādhyāya-equivalents, ācāryas, and ācārya-equivalents.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"From this day forward, if you have items to receive or give for the sake of your upādhyāya or his equals, or your ācārya or his equals, you are permitted to use a copper tray, a table, or a desk; all necessary items such as food and drink should be placed upon it and given at once."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose foot had become afflicted with a malignant swelling. During a rain shower, other bhikṣus supported him as he went to the latrine; he lay in the mud and suffered extreme pain.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you, for the sake of protecting the body, protecting the robes, and protecting the bedding, to wear single-layered leather sandals within the monastery grounds."

At that time, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, they had to give and receive things from their upādhyāyas and the like, or their ācāryas and the like; consequently, they became utterly exhausted by baring one shoulder and removing their leather sandals.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I allow that if you are traveling on a road, when there is something to be taken or given for the sake of one's upādhyāya or those equal to an upādhyāya, or for one's ācārya or those equal to an ācārya, you may take it or give it from upon the head or over the shoulder."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that moment, the group of six bhikṣus entered a village wearing leather sandals.
When the local householders saw them, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim for themselves:
‘We know the True Dharma.
How can they enter a village wearing leather sandals?”
"Looking at this now, what true Dharma is there?
It is just like a king and his ministers.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not enter a village wearing leather sandals.
At that time, the sick bhikṣus, out of a sense of apprehension and caution, did not dare to enter the village wearing leather sandals. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"I permit sick bhikṣus to enter a village wearing leather sandals."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, feigning illness, entered a village wearing leather sandals. When other bhikṣus saw them, they said to them:
"The Buddha did not say:
'One must not enter a village wearing leather sandals.'"
"Is that so? He replied, "I am ill."
He then asked, "What is your ailment or suffering? She replied:
“Venerable sir!
The Buddha does not speak in such a manner.
If someone were to say:”
“Is it because they are unhappy for even a brief moment that they are called ‘sick’?
We are feigning illness.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not enter a village wearing leather sandals while feigning illness.
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyānī had cracked heels and required sandals with heel-coverings. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to wear sandals with heel-coverings."
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyānī was traveling on a road; his eyesight was dim, and he injured his foot as his toes brushed against the ground.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear leather sandals with toe-covers."

At that time, Pilindavatsa, who had many acquaintances, was traveling on the road and obtained a great deal of large barley, small barley, mottled beans, and non-glutinous rice; the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to accept them.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to receive them.
After the bhikṣus had received them, they did not know where to place them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to store [these] in a bag or a chest.
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyānī was traveling on the road; when he obtained ghee, oil, honey, and rock sugar, he did not dare to accept them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive it.
Having received it, they did not know where to place it.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive [alms] using a *kañcika*, a small bowl, or a medium-sized bowl.
As for the *kañcika*, it is to be placed inside the small bowl."
"The small bowl is for placing inside the intermediate bowl;
the intermediate bowl is for placing inside the large bowl.
The bhikṣus did not know whether they should keep the key, the small bowl, and the intermediate bowl, or whether they should perform the ritual of pure donation (*viśuddha-dāna*) regarding them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “I allow you to keep [the item] without having performed the ritual of pure giving (*viśuddhi-dāna*).
At that time, the Elder Piṅgalavatsa was old and infirm, unable to endure walking; he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to have a handcart, a sedan chair, or a carriage made for walking, with the exception of those for women, heifers, or mares.
At that time, Pilindavatsa was traveling on a road and, having obtained a palanquin, did not dare to accept it; he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is permitted to accept it."
Having obtained a leather palanquin, they did not dare to accept it and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to take it, but having removed the leather, wrap it with any one of the ten kinds of robes."
Furthermore, he obtained a carriage woven from hides but did not dare accept it; he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to remove the leather thongs and hair thongs, and to weave it with other cords; it should be kept."
The bhikṣus required poles for the palanquin and informed the Buddha; the Buddha said, "I allow you to make them.
The bhikṣus required ropes for the palanquin and informed the Buddha; the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep [a carrying device].
If the ropes frequently break, I permit you to make one out of leather.
If the shoulder aches from carrying or being carried, I permit you to install a cushion or mat."
"If one suffers from pain in the feet, it is permitted to make a footstool to serve as a pillow or mat.
At that time, it was not known who should carry it, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"It is permitted for a bhikṣu, or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*), or a lay follower (*upāsaka*), or a novice (*śrāmaṇera*). If a cart is obtained, it is likewise permitted; however, if it is a leather cart, the leather should be removed. One should wrap it with any one of the ten kinds of robes and keep it."
"If one obtains a woven-hide carriage, with the exception of leather thongs and hair thongs, the rest may be kept.
When it was not known who should pull it, they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow a bhikṣu, a monastery attendant, an upāsaka, or a śrāmaṇera to pull it."
At that time, the Elder Piṅgiyānī obtained a person to maintain the monastery; the Buddha said, "He should keep him.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made couches of leather and single-seated chairs of leather; the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.

Furthermore, they made leather mats, leather pillows, leather bedding, and leather floor coverings; these caused the ground to break and breed insects, and the interior of the house became foul and filthy. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them."
At that time, there was a brahmin who had left the household life to practice the Way; he kept a hide from an īśī deer as a foot-wiping cloth inside his door.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep it."
At that time, the bhikṣus frequently broke the ropes of their water buckets. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make ropes from leather.
If a bucket breaks, I allow you to repair it with leather; if a rope breaks, I allow you to make a new rope from leather."
If the cord of the door latch repeatedly breaks, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to make one out of leather. If there is pain in the hand when opening or closing the door, I permit you to wrap it with a large piece of leather."
If the pivot of a door does not turn, it is permitted to cover it with leather.
If the upper pivot is damaged, it is permitted to bind it with leather; the same applies to the lower pivot.
If the legs of a rope bed or a wooden bed are broken, it is permitted to bind them with leather.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose feet were painful.
The Buddha said:
"Wrap your feet with a large hide; once the affliction has been cured, remove it."
If a bhikṣu’s roof-cord breaks while he is repairing the roof, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make it with leather. If the cords for the door-bolt break repeatedly, I allow you to make them with sinew or hair."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept leather alms-bowl bags, leather sandal bags, and needle-and-thread bags.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not keep them."
At that time, there was a monk who had formerly been a carpenter and who kept a leather bag to carry his tools. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not keep it.
A monk who has formerly been a carpenter should not keep any tools whatsoever."
At that time, the community of monks obtained wooden utensils and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep them.
They did not know what material to use for their containers.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make bags from each of the ten kinds of cloth to contain [the items].
At that time, the monks' vessels for ghee and oil were exposed to the elements; the Buddha said:
“If you cover the ear with moist leather, and if insects bite it, you should plaster it with mud.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained an oil vessel shaped like a flower; fearing transgression, he did not dare to keep it. The Buddha said, “I allow you to keep it.”
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a horn-made oil container; fearing transgression, he did not dare to keep it. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep it.
If it leaks from the bottom, leaks from the top, or leaks from the sides, I allow you to wrap and cover it with leather."
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha.
There was a bhikṣu whose foot had been pierced by a wooden splinter and required soft leather sandals. [The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep them."

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling together with Ānanda. Not far from a cemetery in the Śītavana, he saw a pair of expensive, high-quality leather sandals. Knowing the situation, the World-Honored One intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Why do you not take these sandals?"
Ānanda said, "I fear it will cause one to wear heavy leather sandals.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep these discarded refuse-rags.

At that time, some bhikṣus were traveling on a road not far from a cemetery; seeing a corpse impaled on a wooden stake with thick skin, they stripped it off and returned to their quarters to make single-layered leather sandals, which became foul-smelling and filthy inside the rooms.
Other bhikṣus asked,
"Why is it foul-smelling inside the room?
He then answered them with the facts of the matter.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not keep human skin; if one keeps it, it is a sthūlātyaya offense.
Furthermore, one must not keep the skins of other impure or loathsome creatures; if one keeps them, it is a duṣkṛta offense."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had come from a cold, snowy land with his feet frozen and damaged. He went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and sat down to one side.
Knowing the reason, the Buddha nevertheless asked the bhikṣu:
“For what reason are your feet broken?”
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I have come from a place of cold snow, and therefore I am frozen and ruined.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣu:
"What is the dress code of that country?
The bhikṣu replied,
"They wear *pūralāṇḍī* boots."
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to wear it.
If you require a girdle, I permit you to make a girdle."
"If one requests [leather] from a householder or housewife who is not a relative to have it made, it must not be used for any other purpose.
If it is used for another purpose, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made waistbands out of leather; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep it.
Regarding the use of leather for a meditation belt, the Buddha said:
"One should not keep it."
When a bhikṣu kept leather vessels, the Buddha said:
"One should not keep them.
When a bhikṣu kept a leather cap, the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such items].
When a bhikṣu made a leather sandal with a heel-strap, the Buddha said:
"One should not keep it."
The bhikṣus did not wipe their leather sandals, so that their feet and their bedding became soiled. The Buddha said:
"One should not fail to wipe one's leather sandals.
At that time, after washing their feet, the bhikṣus put on their leather sandals before they were dry; the sandals became damp and rotted. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not wash or wipe their foot-wiping cloths frequently; seeing them soiled and filthy, the other bhikṣus were displeased. The Buddha said, "I allow you to wash them."
After he had washed it, he did not wring it out nor did he dry it in the sun, and insects appeared.
The Buddha said:
"One should wash it, wring it out, and dry it in the sun."
The Chapter on Leather is concluded. 3. The Chapter on Robes (Cīvara-vastu). At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Then the five bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The five men said to the Buddha,
"What kind of robes should we wear?
The Buddha said:
“Listen: one may wear rag-robes and ten kinds of garments:
*kusa* cloth, *kapāsa* cloth, *kambala* cloth, *kṣauma* cloth, *carmaka* cloth, *śāṇa* cloth, *māñjiṣṭha* cloth, *kauśeya* cloth, *kauśeya* cloth, and *koṭambaka* cloth.”
"These ten kinds of robes should be dyed the color of a kāṣāya and worn.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a robe from a cemetery; the Buddha said, "I permit you to keep it."
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a garment offered through a formal vow. The Buddha said, "I permit you to keep it.
At that time, while traveling on a road not far from a cemetery, a bhikṣu saw a precious discarded rag-robe; out of fear and caution, he did not dare to take it.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to take it.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a son of a great clan who had gone forth as a monk; he would gather tattered, old rags from the refuse heaps in the market streets and alleyways to make and wear a saṃghāṭī.

When the Queen of King Prasenajit saw him, a heart of compassion arose within her. For the sake of the bhikṣu, she took a garment of high value, tore it apart, smeared it with filth, and discarded it outside.
The bhikṣu was afraid and cautious, and did not dare to take it.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is a bhikṣu, one should take it."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had left the household life from a prominent family; in the marketplaces, alleys, latrines, and among refuse heaps, he gathered tattered and worn-out garments to make and maintain a saṃghāṭī robe.

At that time, the Elder of Śrāvastī felt compassion arise within him; for the sake of the bhikṣus, he discarded many fine garments in the alleys, on the streets, or upon latrines, and had people guard them so that no one would take them.
At that time, there were some bhikṣus who walked straight ahead while entering a village. A person guarding their robes said to them,
"Venerable sirs,
why do you not look to your left and right?"
At that time, the bhikṣu saw it and, out of caution and fear, did not dare to take it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If you are a bhikṣu, I permit you to take it."
At that time, a bhikṣu found a dead person’s garment in a moat and, being apprehensive, reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked him, “With what intention did you take it? He replied:
“I took it as discarded rags; I did not take it with a thieving mind.
The Buddha said, “There is no offense.”
"From this day forward, you should not take the clothes of the dead from within graves or ditches.
At that time, there was a householder who, having washed his clothes, hung them out to dry on a wall.
At that time, some bhikṣus wearing patched robes saw it and, thinking it was discarded refuse-rag clothing (*pāṃśukūla*), took it.
When the layperson saw this, he said to them:
"Do not take it; this is my robe."
The bhikṣu said, "I took this because I thought it was discarded refuse-rag clothing (pāṃśukūla).
He then released him and departed.
That bhikṣu, being fearful and cautious, informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked, "With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"I took discarded rags; I did not take them with a thieving mind.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense."
"From this day forward, you should not take discarded robes from atop a garden, from atop a fence, or from within a moat.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, in front of a magistrate’s court where legal cases were being decided, saw the clothes of a deceased person; the bhikṣu took those clothes.
At that time, the high official commanded a caṇḍāla to take the dead man and discard him.
The caṇḍāla said,
"Why not have the one who took the clothes discard him?"
The high official asked, "Who took the robe? He replied:
"This śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, took it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take the clothes of a dead person from a place where legal matters are being adjudicated."
At that time, a bhikṣu was traveling on a road not far from a cemetery when he saw a dead person who had not yet decomposed and was wearing clothes; he immediately took them and departed.
The dead person then rose up and said:
"Venerable One!..."
"Do not take my robe with you.
The bhikṣu said, "You are a dead man; where would you have a robe?"
Therefore, he continued to carry it away without stopping.
The dead man pursued the bhikṣu until they reached the gate of the Jetavana; there, the man’s feet stumbled and he fell to the ground.
Other bhikṣus saw this and asked the bhikṣu:
"What did he say? The bhikṣu replied, "This is a dead man; I took his robe and brought it here."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not take the robes of a person who has not yet decomposed.
At that time, there was a cowherd who placed his robe upon his head and fell asleep.
At that time, a pāṃśukūlika bhikṣu saw it and thought it was a dead person. He had this thought:
"The World-Honored One does not permit bhikṣus to take the robes of a person who has not yet decayed after death."
He immediately took the arm-bone of a dead man and struck the head of this cowherd until it was split open. The cowherd then rose up and said:
"Venerable Sir!
Why have you beaten me?"
He replied, "I thought you were dead. The cowherd said:
"Do you not distinguish between my death and life?
He then struck the bhikṣu, who died immediately.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not strike a corpse that has not yet decomposed to cause it to decompose.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept items that were not robes, such as bags for alms bowls, bags for leather sandals, and needle cases.
[The monks] kept woollen rugs with brocade patterns, cushions, pillows, woolen carpets, and otter skins.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not use items that are not clothing to make alms-bowl bags or needle-cases."
"One should not keep bedding with brocade patterns, nor woolen rugs, pillows, *karpāsa* cotton, or otter skins.

At that time, some bhikṣus found brocade-patterned bedding, rugs, and pillows among the charnel grounds; fearing transgression and being apprehensive, they did not dare to take them and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to take and use them."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who found in a cemetery a woolen rug made of *elāyanta*, *mora*, and *mora* wool. Fearing and being cautious, he did not dare to take it and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to take it."
"Strip off the leather and the grass; the remainder may be used as a ground-covering for storage.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who found a leather rope-bed, a wooden bed, and a single-seat chair in a cemetery. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to take them."
"Having removed the leather, it is permitted to keep whichever among the ten kinds of robes is used to make it.
At that time, a bhikṣu was in a cemetery and found a rope bed, a wooden bed, and a single-seated chair; being fearful and cautious, he did not dare to take them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take them.
With the exception of two kinds of cords—leather cords and hair cords—you should keep the others."
At that time, a bhikṣu was in a cemetery and found a palanquin, a parasol, and a hand-pulled cart; fearing transgression and out of caution, he did not dare to take them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take and keep them."
At that time, a bhikṣu was among the charnel grounds and found a water jar, a wash-basin, a staff, and a fan; fearing transgression and being cautious, he did not dare to take them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take and keep them."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, while among the burial mounds, found a pickaxe, a hook, a knife, and a sickle; being apprehensive, he did not dare to take them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to take and keep them."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who found money among the graves and brought it back with him.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be accepted."
That bhikṣu required copper and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Smash it so that its characteristics as such are destroyed; only then may you take it with you.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained a garment gnawed by an ox and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“Listen; it is permitted to take and use [it].
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who obtained clothing gnawed by mice. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“It is permitted to take and use [it].”
There was a bhikṣu who obtained some burnt cloth; he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to take it.
There are ten kinds of *pāṃśukūla* (cast-off rags):"

Cloth chewed by oxen, cloth gnawed by rats, burnt cloth, cloth used during menstruation, cloth used by a woman in childbirth, cloth from a shrine, cloth picked up where it has been carried off by birds or blown away by the wind, cloth from a cemetery, cloth obtained through a vow, and cloth received upon assuming royal office—these are called the ten kinds of refuse rags (*pāṃśukūla*).
At that time, King Prasenajit of Kosala and King Ajātaśatru of Magadha were fighting against one another, and many people died.
Then, some bhikṣus wished to go and take the clothes of the dead.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to go there.
If there is anyone who has already spoken to take [it], [you may do so]."
"If there is no one present, you may take them at will.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru and the Licchavis of Vaiśālī fought a battle between them, and many people died.
Then, some bhikṣus wished to go and take the clothes of those dead persons.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should go and inform [the owners] before taking [the items]; if there is no one present, one may take them oneself.
At that time, many lay devotees were removing their clothes at a cemetery, piling them in one place, and burying the dead.
At that time, a bhikṣu who wore rag-robes saw it and, thinking it was a discarded cloth, took it and departed.
When the lay devotees saw this, they said to him:
"This is our robe; do not take it away."
The bhikṣu said, "I thought this was discarded refuse-rag clothing," whereupon he placed it on the ground and departed.
The bhikṣu, being apprehensive and cautious, informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked, "With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"I took it as discarded rags, not with a mind of theft.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One should not take a large heap of robes.

At that time, while many lay devotees were cremating a corpse in a cemetery, a bhikṣu who wore discarded robes (pāṃśukūlika) saw the smoke; he called out to other bhikṣus to go together to the cemetery to collect discarded robes.
He replied,
"So be it," and they immediately went together to that place and remained there in silence.
When the householder saw this, he immediately gave a precious robe to the bhikṣu.
The second bhikṣu said:
"Bring it here; we shall share it together with you."
He said: "With whom would I share it?
He gave it to me of his own accord."
The two men disputed with one another.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should go back and ask the householder."
"To whom shall this robe be given?
If the householder says,
"Whomever it is given to, that is the recipient of the robe."
If he says, "I do not know," or if he says:
"Give it to both;
it should be divided into two portions.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to a cemetery to collect discarded rags (pāṃśukūla). Seeing a discarded rag from afar, another bhikṣu immediately claimed it, saying:
"This is my robe. The second bhikṣu immediately ran to seize it, and the two of them quarreled,
each saying, "This is my robe."
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Pāṃśukūla robes have no owner; they belong to whoever takes them first.
At that time, two bhikṣus went together to a cemetery to collect pāṃśukūla robes. Seeing a robe from afar, they both claimed it, saying: [This is mine! [This is mine!]
"This is my robe. Both men ran together to take the robe, quarreling over it and each saying, "This is my robe.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Regarding these refuse rags which have no owner, let us take them together and divide them into two portions.
At that time, there were many householders who were transporting a corpse and placing it among the burial mounds.
When a pāṃśukūlika bhikṣu saw this, he immediately said to the other bhikṣus, "We should go now to collect discarded rags; we shall obtain many. Those bhikṣus said:
"You all may go; I shall not go.
The bhikṣus then went quickly and obtained a great quantity of discarded robes (pāṃśukūla), which they brought back to the monastery and washed and mended them thoroughly.
That bhikṣu saw him and said to this bhikṣu:
"What were you doing that you did not go with me to fetch the robe?
I went to fetch the robe and obtained a great deal."
That bhikṣu said, "Bring it here; we shall share it together. He replied:
"You did not take it with me; how can we share it?
The two argued together.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"As for those who go to fetch it," at that time there were many pāṃśukūlika bhikṣus who made a mutual agreement to go together to the charnel ground to collect discarded rags.
There was a bhikṣu who obtained a robe of high value;
another bhikṣu said to him, "Bring it here and let us share it together. He replied:
"I have obtained this robe; why should I share it with you?
Thus did many people dispute among themselves.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"According to prior agreements, whatever has been obtained should be divided among all.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then, when various lay devotees’ grandparental and parental ancestors had passed away, they wrapped their ancestral and parental stupas with banners, canopies, and garments.
When the pāṃsukūlika bhikṣu saw it, he stripped it off and took it.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākya, have no sense of shame or remorse; they steal the property of others and yet claim for themselves:..."
"I know the True Dharma.
Looking at it now, what True Dharma is there?
We have erected stupas for our grandparents and parents, wrapping them with banners and canopies as offerings.
"How did they strip it away themselves?
It was as if they were intentionally acting like Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, wrapping the stūpa for the sake of making offerings.
We, however, truly acted out of devotion to our grandparents and parents, wrapping the stūpa with banners and canopies to make offerings."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One must not take such items.
If the wind blows them away and places them elsewhere, or if a bird picks them up and carries them to another place, the bhikṣu, seeing them, may be apprehensive and dare not take them.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it has been blown by the wind, carried away by water, or picked up by birds and deposited elsewhere, you are permitted to take it.
At that time, a bhikṣu saw a robe used for the adornment and offering of a stūpa and took it; having taken it, he was filled with apprehension and hesitation.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"I took it as discarded rags, not with a thieving mind.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One should not accept garments for the purpose of adorning or making offerings to a stūpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

Now, in Vaiśālī, there was a courtesan named Āmrapālī, who was of beautiful appearance; those who wished to stay with her at night would give her fifty *kārsāpaṇas*, and they would give her fifty *kārsāpaṇas* even during the day.
At that time, because of this courtesan, people from the four quarters gathered in Vaiśālī;
according to the laws of the land, it was considered a most excellent spectacle.
