Then, the ministers of Rājagṛha heard that there was a courtesan in Vaiśālī named Āmrapālī, whose physical appearance was exquisite, and that anyone wishing to spend the night with her would be given fifty *niṣkas* of gold, and the same amount by day as well.
At that time, because of a courtesan, people from the four quarters gathered in Vaiśālī, and the spectacle was most magnificent.
Then a high minister went to King Bimbisāra and said:

"Your Majesty should know that in the kingdom of Vaiśālī there is a courtesan named Āmrapālī; she is of upright and beautiful appearance. Those who wish to stay with her for the night must give her fifty ounces of gold, and the same applies during the day."
"Because of this courtesan, people from the four quarters have gathered in Vaiśālī; the spectacle is most excellent.
The king commanded his ministers:
"Why do you not settle a courtesan here?"
At that time, there was a young woman in the city of Rājagṛha named Bhadrā, who was of incomparable beauty, surpassing even Ambapālī.
The minister then established this courtesan such that anyone wishing to stay with her for the night would be given one hundred *niṣkas* of gold; the same applied during the day.
At that time, because of the courtesan, people from all directions gathered in Rājagṛha, and the city was exceedingly beautiful to behold.
Then Prince Abhaya, the son of King Bimbisāra, stayed the night with this courtesan and subsequently became pregnant.
At that time, the courtesan commanded her gatekeeper,
saying, "If anyone comes seeking to see me, you must tell them that I am ill.
Later, when the months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was handsome and upright.
At that time, the courtesan wrapped the child in a white cloth and commanded her maidservant to carry it away and discard it in the alleyway.
The maidservant, having received the command, took up the child and cast him aside.
Meanwhile, Prince Abhaya, at the clear dawn, mounted his chariot intending to go and see the king, and sent men to clear and sweep the roads.
At that time, the prince saw a white object on the road from afar; he immediately stopped his carriage and asked those beside him, "What is this white object? They replied:
"This is a small child. He asked,
"Is it dead?"
"Am I alive?
He replied, "I am indeed alive."
The prince ordered someone to carry the child away; at that time, Prince Abhaya had no son, so he immediately took the child back to his residence and entrusted him to a wet nurse to raise.
Because the child was thus saved, they gave him the name Jīvaka Kumāra.
Because he was taken by the prince, he was named Kumāra.
Later, as he gradually grew up, the prince came to love him very much.
At that time, the prince summoned the youth Jīvaka and said to him:
"If you wish to remain long in the royal household, yet possess no talent or skill, you shall not be able to consume the king's provisions in vain;
you should learn a craft. He replied, "I shall learn it."
Jīva thought to himself:
"What skill should I now learn so that I may acquire great wealth in this present life with little effort?
Having had this thought, he continued:
"I would now rather study the medical arts; thus I may acquire great wealth in this present life with little effort.
He thought to himself, "Who can teach me to study the path of medicine?"
At that time, he heard that in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā there was a physician surnamed Ātreya and named Piṅgala, who was extremely skilled in the medical arts and could teach him.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka went to that country, approached Piṅgala, and said to him:
"I wish to receive instruction in the medical arts from my teacher; please teach me."
He replied, "So be it. Then,
after the youth Jīvaka had studied the medical arts for seven years, he thought to himself:
"I am now practicing the art of medicine; when will it ever come to an end?
He then went to his teacher and said, "I am now practicing the art of medicine; when will it ever come to an end?"
Then the teacher immediately gave him a basket and tools for digging up grass, saying:
"You should search within a yojana around the country of Takṣaśilā for various types of grass; bring back whatever is not medicinal."
Then the youth Jīvaka, following his teacher’s instructions, searched for one *yojana* square around the kingdom of Takṣaśilā for anything that was not medicine.

Having completed the circuit, he found nothing that was not medicine; for among all the plants, trees, and objects he saw, he was well able to distinguish them, knowing that there was not a single thing that could not be used as medicine.
He immediately returned empty-handed and went to his teacher, saying to him:
"Teacher, you should know that I have searched for non-medicinal herbs in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā."
"Within a face one yojana in extent, looking all around, there is nothing that cannot be identified as medicinal.
Every herb and tree seen can be fully distinguished according to its place of application.
The Master replied to Jīvaka:
"You may now depart; you have perfected the path of medicine.
Among those in Jambudvīpa, I am the foremost; after my death, you shall be next."
At that time, Jīvaka thought to himself: "Whom should I treat first?
Since this country is small and located on the frontier, it would be better for me to return to my own country to begin practicing the Way of Medicine."
Thereupon, he immediately returned to the city of Bhagadatta.
In that city of Bhagadatta there was a great elder whose wife had suffered from chronic headaches for twelve years; though many physicians treated her, they were unable to cure her.
Upon hearing this, Jīvaka went to the house and said to the gatekeeper:
"Inform the elder that there is a physician at the gate.
Then the gatekeeper entered and reported it.
“There is a physician outside the gate.
The householder’s wife asked,
“What does the physician look like?”
He replied, "It is a youth. He then thought to himself:
"Even when treated by various veteran physicians, he did not recover; how much less so now that he is young.
He then commanded the gatekeeper, saying, "I have no need for a physician at this time."
The gatekeeper immediately went out and said:
"I have already informed the householder on your behalf; the householder's wife said, 'There is no need for a physician at this time.'"
Jīvaka spoke again: "You may inform your householder’s wife that she should simply allow me to treat her; if she recovers, you may give me whatever you wish."
Then the gatekeeper spoke to him again, saying:
"The physician has said this:
'Simply allow me to treat you; if you are cured, give me whatever you wish.'"
When the householder’s wife heard this, she thought to herself,
"If it is so, there will be no harm done.
She then commanded the gatekeeper to call him in.
Then Jīvaka entered and went to the householder’s wife, asking,
"What is your ailment? She replied:
"I am afflicted in such and such a manner.
He asked again,
"From what does this illness arise?"
He replied, "It arises from such and such.
He asked again:
“How long has it been since you fell ill? He replied,
“It has been this long since I became ill.”
Having been asked thus, he said, "I shall treat your illness.
He then took excellent medicine and boiled it with ghee; he poured it into the nose of the householder’s wife, and from the patient's mouth, both ghee and saliva came out together.
The sick man immediately caught it in a vessel; he took up the ghee but spat out and discarded the rest.
When the youth Jīvaka saw this, his heart was filled with sorrow and distress, thinking:
"If he is so stingy as to begrudge even such a small amount of impure ghee, how could he ever repay me?"
When the patient saw him, he asked Jīvaka, "Are you distressed? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
He asked, "For what reason are you distressed?"
He replied: "I thought to myself:
'This small amount of ghee is impure, yet he still begrudges it; how could he possibly repay me?'"
"It is for this reason that I am sorrowful.
The householder’s wife replied, "It is not easy to maintain a household; what benefit would there be in discarding it?"
"It can be used for lighting lamps; therefore, collect it.
You need only treat the illness—why worry about such things?
He then treated him, and subsequently the illness was cured.
At that time, the elder’s wife gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold, along with male and female slaves, carriages, and horses.
Having received these goods, Jīvaka returned to Rājagṛha and went to the gate of Prince Abhaya, saying to the gatekeeper:
"Go and inform the prince, saying:..."
"Jīva is outside. The gatekeeper immediately went in and informed the king, who commanded the gatekeeper to call him in.
Once Jīva had entered, he prostrated himself at the feet [of the prince], stood to one side, and related the preceding circumstances in detail to Prince Abhaya, saying:
"I shall offer all the goods I have now obtained to Your Majesty.
The prince said, "Stop;
there is no need. Since you have already performed an act of offering, you may use them yourself."
This was the first occasion upon which the youth Jīvaka treated a disease.

Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Zhu Fonian and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
*Cīvaravastu*, Part Two. At that time, King Bimbisāra suffered from blood flowing from his anus; when the female attendants saw this, they all laughed together and said:
"The illness the King now suffers from is like that of my woman.
When King Bimbisāra heard this, he felt ashamed and immediately summoned Prince Abhaya, saying:
"I now have such an illness; you should seek out a physician for me."
He immediately replied to the king, saying, "There is a youth named Jīvaka who is skilled in the art of medicine; he can cure the king's illness.
The king said:
"Summon him! Prince Abhaya summoned Jīvaka and asked him,
"Are you able to cure the King's illness?"
He replied, "I can treat it. [The king said,] "If you can, you may go and treat him."
Then the youth Jīvaka went to King Bimbisāra, prostrated at the king’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and asked the king:
“What ailment do you suffer?”
The king replied, “My illness is such and such.
He asked again:
"From what does illness arise?
The king replied,
"It arises from such and such."
He asked again,
"How long has this ailment been present?
The king replied:
Having been asked, "How long has this ailment been present? he replied,
"I can cure it."
At that moment, he took an iron trough and filled it with warm water, saying to King Bimbisāra,
"Enter this water. The king immediately entered the water.
When he told the king to sit in the water, the king immediately sat;
when he told the king to lie down in the water, the king immediately lay down.

Then Jīvaka sprinkled water upon the king and recited incantations over him, whereupon the king fell asleep. He quickly drew back the water and took a sharp blade to cut open the afflicted area of the king's body. Having thoroughly cleansed the wound, he applied excellent medicinal ointment.
Once the medicine had been applied, the illness was eliminated and the ulcer healed; hair grew back from that spot, indistinguishable from the surrounding healthy skin.
He then immediately filled the trough with water again, sprinkled the water upon the king while reciting incantations, and the king immediately regained consciousness.
The king said,
"Please cure my illness. He replied:
"I have finished treating it.
The king asked,
"Was it treated well?"
He replied, "I am skilled at treating them.
The king then felt him with his hand, yet he could not find the location of the sores.
The King then asked,
"How did you treat the illness so as to leave no trace of a wound? Jīvaka replied:
"Is it not better for me to have a place where there is a wound when I am treated for my illness?
At that time, the king immediately assembled his female attendants and spoke these words:
"The physician Jīvaka has brought me great benefit; whoever thinks of me shall be granted great wealth and treasures."

Then the handmaidens immediately took various necklaces, bracelets, and anklets, as well as concealed precious ornaments for the body and external ornaments such as coins, along with gold, silver, mani-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, and crystal, piling them into a great heap.
At that time, the king summoned Jīvaka and said to him,
"When you have cured my illness, I shall repay your kindness with these items. Jīvaka replied:
"Great King, please stop; you have already made an offering. I shall treat the King's illness for the sake of Prince Abhaya.
The King said, "You may not treat the illnesses of others; you may treat only my own, those of the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, and those within the palace."
"This was the second occasion upon which the youth Jīvaka treated a disease.
At that time, there was an elder in Rājagṛha who constantly suffered from headaches, and there was no physician capable of curing him."
At that time, a physician said to the elder,
"Seven years from now you shall die.
Another said six years, another five, and so on, down to one year, saying that he would die then.
Some physicians said, "He shall die after seven months.
Others said he would die after six months, down to as little as one month; still others said he would die after more than seven days.
Then the elder went in person to Jīvaka Kumārabhṛtya and said,
"Treat my illness, and I shall hire you for one hundred thousand pieces of gold. He replied:
"I cannot. He spoke again, saying:
"I will give you two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred thousand pieces of gold."
He replied, "I cannot. He spoke again:
"I shall become your slave and my household estate; everything shall also belong to you.
Jīvaka replied, "It is not because of a lack of wealth that I am unable to treat you."
For King Bimbisāra previously commanded me, saying:
"You shall treat only my illnesses, those of the Buddha, the community of bhikṣus, and the people within the palace; you must not treat anyone else."
"Therefore, he is unable to do so.
You should now go and inform the king.
At that time, the elder went at once and addressed the king, saying:
"I now have an illness; I pray that Your Majesty will permit Jīvaka to treat my ailment.
At that time, the king immediately summoned Jīvaka and said to him, "There is an elder in the city of Rājagṛha who is ill; are you able to treat him?"
He replied, "I can cure it. [The king said,] "If you are able, you may go and treat him."
At that time, Jīvaka went to the house of the elder and asked, "What is your ailment? He replied:
"The ailment is such and such. He asked again:
"From what does it arise?"
He replied, "It arises from such and such. He asked:
"How long has it been since you arrived? He replied,
"I have been ill for this much time."
Having been questioned thus, he said, "I can cure you.

Then Jīvaka gave him salty food to make him thirsty and wine to make him drunk; he then bound his body to a bed, gathered his kinsmen, took a sharp knife, split open the skull, and showed his kinsmen that the head was filled with worms, saying, "This is the disease."
Jīvaka said to the people:
"As the former physician said:
'Seven years from now, you shall die.'"
He forms this thought: "After seven years, my brain will be exhausted and I shall die.
Such is the unwholesome view held by that physician. Or he says:
Regarding the statement, "In six, five, four, three, two, or one year, death shall come," he forms this thought: "When my brain is exhausted, I shall die."
That too is an incorrect view.
Or, if one says that death shall occur in seven months, or even as late as one month, that too is an incorrect view.
Furthermore, some say:
Regarding the statement, "He shall die in seven days," he forms this thought: "When my brain is exhausted, I shall die.
Thus, he perceives correctly.
"If it is not treated now, after seven days have passed, his brain will be exhausted and he shall die.
Then Jīvaka, having thoroughly cleared the disease from within the head, filled the interior with ghee and honey, rejoined the cranial sutures, and applied excellent medicinal ointment.
Immediately the illness was cured and the flesh filled out again; the hair grew back so that it was no different from the uninjured parts.
Jīvaka said, "Do you remember your previous vow?"
He replied, "I remember! I previously made this vow:
'I shall become your slave, and all my household affairs shall belong entirely to you.'"
Jīva said, "Stop, householder; you have already made an offering.
Return to your original words."

Then that householder immediately gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold; Jīvaka presented one hundred thousand taels to the king, one hundred thousand taels to his father, and two hundred thousand taels for himself.
This was Jīvaka’s third treatment of disease.

At that time, there was the son of a householder in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī who was playing on a wheel when his intestines became knotted within his abdomen; consequently, his food and drink could neither be digested nor pass out. There was no one in that country capable of treating him.
Having heard that there was a great physician in the kingdom of Magadha who was skilled at treating diseases, he immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the king:
"The son of the elder of Kauśāmbī is ill; Jīvaka can cure him. I pray that Your Majesty will send him here."
At that time, King Bimbisāra summoned Jīvaka and asked him, "The son of a householder from Kauśāmbī is ill; are you able to treat him? He replied:
"I can. "If you can, you may go and treat him.
Then the youth Jīvaka mounted a carriage and set out for Kauśāmbī. When Jīvaka first arrived, the son of the elder had already died, and they were escorting him out with music.
Upon hearing the sound, Jīvaka immediately asked,
"What kind of musical drumming is this?
A bystander replied:
"You have come for this reason: the son of the elder has already died; these are the sounds of his musical instruments.
Jīvaka Kumāra, who was skilled in distinguishing all sounds, then said:
"Have him turn back; this is not a dead man."
Having spoken thus, he immediately turned back.
Then the youth Jīvaka descended from his carriage, took a sharp knife, cut open the abdomen, and exposed the constricted intestines to his parents and kinsmen, saying:
"This was caused by playing on the wheel, which led to the constriction of the intestines; it was because food and drink could not be digested in this way, not because of death."

He immediately untied the intestines and restored them to their original positions; he sutured the skin and flesh together and applied excellent medicinal ointment. The wound healed instantly, and hair grew back, no different from the uninjured parts.
At that time, the son of the elder immediately offered Jīvaka four hundred thousand taels of gold; his wife also gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold.
The elder’s parents did likewise, each giving him four hundred thousand taels of gold.
This was the fourth occasion on which the youth Jīvaka cured a disease.
At that time, King Prasenajit of the kingdom of Kośala suffered from a chronic headache for twelve years, and there was no physician capable of curing it.
Hearing that King Bimbisāra had a skilled physician who was well-able to treat diseases, he immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the king:
"I am currently ill; Jīvaka is able to treat me. I pray that you will send him here to treat me."
At that time, the king immediately summoned Jīvaka and asked him,
"Are you able to cure the illness of Prasenajit? He replied:
"Yes," [he replied].
"You may go and treat him. Thus spoke the king.
"That king comes from among the scorpions; you must protect yourself well and do not cut off your own life. He replied, "So be it."
Then the youth Jīvaka went to the kingdom of Udyāna and arrived at the place of Prasenajit. Having prostrated at the king’s feet, he stood to one side and asked the king:
“What is troubling you?”
He replied, "It is such and such an illness. He asked:
"From what does illness arise?
He replied, "It arises from such and such."
He asked, "How long has it been since you fell ill? He replied:
"Your illness has lasted for this long," he said, having questioned him in sequence. Then he spoke:
"I am able to treat it."
The king said,
"If the medicine consists of ghee or is mixed with ghee, I cannot take it.
If you give me medicine mixed with ghee, I shall kill you."
"This illness cannot be cured by other medicines; only ghee will remove it.
The youth Jīvaka then employed a skillful means and said to the king:
"In our medical practice for treating illnesses, we enter and exit at will during the morning, evening, dawn, and night."
The king said to Jīvaka,
"I grant you permission to enter and leave as you please.
Jīvaka then addressed the king again, saying:
"If you require expensive medicine, you shall obtain swift mounts; I pray that Your Majesty grant me this for the sake of the sick.

At that time, the king immediately provided him with camels capable of traveling fifty yojanas in a day. He then gave the king salty food to eat and, in a secluded place, boiled ghee to make it into medicine, transforming it so that it had the color and taste of water. Having prepared it, he took it to the king’s mother and said:
"If the king awakens from sleep and is thirsty for water, you may give him this to drink."
Having given the water to the king’s mother, he immediately mounted a camel that could travel fifty yojanas and departed.
Later, when the king woke from his sleep and was thirsty for water, the mother gave him this medicinal water.
When the medicine was about to be digested, he perceived the scent of ghee;
the king said, "Jīvaka gave me ghee to drink; he is my enemy, so how can he cure me?"
"Go quickly to search for him and bring him back.
He immediately went to Jīvaka’s residence, but could not find him.
He asked the gatekeeper:
"Where is Jīvaka? He replied,
"He has departed on a camel that travels fifty yojanas."
The king became even more terrified and said, "To give me ghee to drink is to provide my enemy with sustenance; how could it possibly cure me?
At that time, the king had a swift-footed man named O, who could travel sixty yojanas in a single day, so he immediately summoned him.
The king said, "Can you pursue the youth Jīvaka? He replied:
"Yes, [I can]. "You may go and summon him," the king said.
“Jīvaka is highly skilled in technical arts; do not eat his food, for he might give you something that is not medicine. He replied, “So be it.”
"I shall obey the King's command.
Having departed, Jīvaka the youth reached the middle of the road; no longer feeling fear, he stopped and prepared food.
At that time, the swift-footed bird caught up with Jīvaka and said to him:
"King Prasenajit summons you," he said,
and [the man] replied, "I shall go."
Jīvaka offered the food to the crow, but the crow refused to eat it.

At that time, Jīvaka himself ate half of an *āmalaka* fruit and set aside the other half; he drank from a vessel of water and set aside half of it. He placed something that was not medicine under his fingernail and dropped it into the fruit and water, saying to the crow:
"I have already eaten half the fruit and drunk half the water; there remains half a fruit and half the water, which you may eat."
The crow then thought to himself:
"He has eaten half a fruit and drunk half the water, leaving the other half for me; there must certainly be nothing in this that is not medicine."
Having immediately eaten half a fruit and drunk half the water, he suffered from sneezing and could no longer go on.
He then took more medicine and placed it before the crow, saying:
"At such and such times, you shall take this medicine and recover."
The youth Jīvaka immediately mounted a camel and traveled fifty yojanas further ahead.
Subsequently, both the king and the crow were cured of their ailments.
King Prasenajit dispatched a messenger to summon Jīvaka, saying:
"You have cured my illness; you may come.
Whatever you obtained while in that country, I shall give to you double. Jīvaka said:
“Stop! Let the King provide the offerings himself; I shall treat the King’s illness for the sake of King Bimbisāra.
At that time, Prasenajit sent a precious garment worth half the kingdom and said to Jīvaka:
"If you are unwilling to come, I shall now give you this robe as a token of my gratitude.
This was Jīvaka’s fifth treatment of illness.
At that time, the World-Honored One suffered from dropsy and said to Ānanda:
"I am suffering from dropsy and wish to have it cured.
At that time, Ānanda, having heard the words of the World-Honored One, went to the city of Rājagṛha and approached Jīvaka, saying:
"The Tathāgata is suffering from dropsy and wishes to have it cured."
At that time, Jīvaka and Ānanda went together to where the Buddha was; they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Does the Tathāgata suffer from dropsy?"
The Buddha said,
"It is so, Jīvaka! I wish to remove it."
He addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How many times do you require [the water] to be poured?
The Buddha replied:
"It requires thirty strokes.

At that time, Jīvaka and Ānanda went together to Rājagṛha, gathered three handfuls of *utpala* flowers, and returned to his house; taking one handful of flowers, he fumigated them with medicinal herbs.
Furthermore, he recited mantras over it; by smelling this, one could obtain ten strokes.
He then took a second handful of flowers and fumigated them with the medicine!
Again, he recited mantras over them; by smelling these, one could likewise obtain ten strokes.
Again, take a third handful of flowers, fumigate them with the medicinal incense, and recite the mantra over them; by smelling them, one may achieve nine downward movements.
Furthermore, drink a palmful of warm water, which will suffice for one downward movement of wind.
He then followed this by placing three handfuls of flowers into Ānanda’s hands.

At that time, Ānanda took the flowers and departed from the city of Rājagṛha, proceeding to where the World-Honored One was. Taking one handful of flowers, he presented them to the World-Honored One; the Tathāgata smelled them, and it was possible to count ten inhalations.
He then gave a second handful, which yielded ten more strokes;
with the third handful, he obtained nine more.
At that time, Jīvaka forgot to tell Ānanda to provide warm water for the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Jīvaka’s mind, immediately called Ānanda and told him to fetch warm water.
Hearing the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda immediately fetched the warm water and gave it to the Buddha.
The Buddha then drank a single palmful of warm water; his ailment was immediately eliminated, and his wind-humor (vāta) was restored to its natural state.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Buddha was unwell, accompanied by eighty-four thousand people as his retinue, went to the World-Honored One’s dwelling. He inquired after the World-Honored One’s health, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, King Udayana, hearing that the World-Honored One was ill,
also set out accompanied by seventy thousand people. King Prasenajit went with sixty thousand people,
and King Brahmadatta went with fifty thousand people.
King Prasenajit, together with forty thousand people; Queen Mallikā, Liśādarśa Purohita, the Four Great Heavenly Kings and their retinues;

Śakra Devendra with the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the Sun God (Āditya) with the gods of the Ābhāsvara Heaven; the Tuṣita God with the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven; the Nirmāṇarati God with the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven; the Paranirmitavaśavartin God with the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; Brahmā with the gods of the Brahma-world; and the Maheśvara God with the gods of the Maheśvara realm—all went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, having heard that the World-Honored One was ill, Śāriputra, together with five hundred bhikṣus, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, having heard that the World-Honored One was ill, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī went to the place where the World-Honored One was, accompanied by five hundred bhikṣuṇīs; Ānanda-Piṇḍola went with five hundred upāsakas; and Viśākhā-mātṛ went with five hundred upāsikās. They prostrated themselves at his feet, touching their heads to them, and inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being.
At that time, Devadatta, hearing that the World-Honored One was ill, went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then, seeing the fourfold assembly gathered before the World-Honored One, Devadatta thought to himself:
"I should now take medicine just as the Buddha does, so that the fourfold assembly will come to inquire after my health."
He immediately went to Jīvaka and said, "I wish to take the medicine that the Buddha takes;
you may give it to me. Jīvaka replied:

“The medicine taken by the World-Honored One is named Nārāyaṇa; this medicine is not for others to take, except for a Wheel-Turning King, an accomplished Bodhisattva, or a Tathāgata who is able to consume it.”
Devadatta said, "If you do not give it to me, I shall kill you.
At that time, Jīvaka, fearing for his life, immediately gave it to him.

Because Devadatta had taken this medicine, he immediately fell gravely ill; his body and mind were both in agony. Being all alone with no one else by his side, and having no relatives or close friends, he thought to himself:
"As I have no savior today, there is only the Tathāgata."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in Devadatta’s mind, emitted from his body on Vulture Peak a light of medicinal herbs to illuminate Devadatta, causing all his pains to be immediately stilled.
At that time, not long after Devadatta had recovered from his illness, he went through the streets and alleys of Rājagṛha and proclaimed:
"The Crown Prince Siddhārtha, having renounced the status of a Wheel-Turning King to leave home and practice the Way, now sustains himself by practicing medicine."
"How do we know this?
We know it because he has just cured my illness.

When the bhikṣus heard this, those who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Devadatta:
“The Tathāgata is compassionate, yet Devadatta remains utterly ungrateful.
At that time, the bhikṣu went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and said to the Buddha:
“It is unprecedented, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata is compassionate, yet Devadatta remains utterly ungrateful.”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"It is not only today that Devadatta has lacked compassion and gratitude. Why is this so?"
In the distant past, there was a king named Sarvadatta who ruled over Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was level and vast, its population was flourishing, and its abundance and joy were beyond compare.
At that time, in Jambudvīpa, there were eighty-four thousand cities, five billion villages, and sixty thousand border towns.
At that moment, there was a sick man who went to King Sarvadada and said to the king:
"I now have no protector or refuge; you alone, O King, are my only hope."
At that time, the king assembled all the physicians of Jambudvīpa and presented this sick man to them. The king asked the physicians:
"What medicine is required for such a patient?"
After the physicians had examined the patient, they said to the king:
"A patient such as this cannot be given medicine by an ordinary person; only a perfected Bodhisattva can provide the medicine."
The king asked,
"What medicine do you require?
The physician replied:
“If this patient can obtain the flesh and blood produced by a Bodhisattva of a compassionate mind and eat them, he will recover in twenty-nine days.
King Sarvamdada thought to himself:

“Birth and death are long and far-reaching, revolving without end as one undergoes various sufferings; whether falling into the hells, the realm of hungry ghosts, or the animal realm, being cut at the feet, cut at the hands, cut at the ears, cut at the nose, having eyes gouged out, or having the head severed—what benefit is there ultimately in all this?”
He immediately entrusted the kingdom to his ministers and entered a quiet place within the palace to contemplate the four immeasurable practices.
At that time, King Sarvamdada took a sharp knife and cut the flesh from his thigh, using the blood as well, and sent it to the sick man by messenger; he continued in this manner for twenty-nine days.
Later, the king asked the messenger,
"How is the patient? The messenger replied to the king:
"It has been cured.
The king said, "Bring it here so that I may see it."
At that time, he immediately bathed the sick man, dressed him in new clothes, and led him to the king’s presence.
The king asked,
"What is your illness like?"
He replied, "It has been cured. The king said:
"You may go as you please.
Then, as that man stepped out the door, his right foot struck the ground and blood flowed forth. Seeing this, the other people asked him, "O man!..."
"Why is there blood coming from your foot? He replied:

"That king is unrighteous, a wicked king, a king who is unrighteously attached to lust, and a king who greedily clings to false views. As he kicked the threshold of that gate with his foot, my foot was thus mangled and bled."
Those people said:
"Never before has there been such an ungrateful person! Having healed the King Sarvamdada by using his own flesh and blood for twenty-nine days, he shows no gratitude whatsoever toward the King."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, the King Sarvada was none other than myself; the sick man was Devadatta."
"In my previous lives, I felt compassion for them with a heart of loving-kindness and never failed them; now it is the same, and I have no failure toward them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the sake of Devadatta:
"All the mountains and seas of the world, I do not consider them heavy; [but the weight of Devadatta’s ingratitude is far greater]."
Those who lack gratitude and reciprocity—I consider them the most grave.
Lacking any return for their kindness, they suffer the agony of leprosy and foul diseases;
or they may contract white leprosy—such is the consequence of lacking gratitude and reciprocity.
"Therefore, monks, you should be mindful of repaying kindness and maintain a sense of gratitude; you should train yourselves in this way.

At that time, the youth Jīvaka attended to the World-Honored One’s illness, preparing decoctions for inducing vomiting and purging as well as the meat of wild birds, through which [the Buddha] recovered. This was the sixth instance of the youth Jīvaka treating an illness.

At another time, the youth Jīvaka took a single garment of great value and went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“If I treat a king, or treat a high minister, or obtain a kingdom, or obtain a village, may the World-Honored One grant me this wish.”
The Buddha said, "I have already transcended all vows; I do not grant vows to others.
Jīvaka spoke again:
“I pray that you grant me a pure vow.
The Buddha said,
“What kind of pure vow do you seek?”
He replied, "This precious robe of mine was obtained from King Prasenajit; its value is equal to half the kingdom. I pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will accept it for my sake."
"From this day forward, I grant that the bhikṣus may, according to their own wishes, wear either robes offered by lay donors or robes made of discarded rags.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.

When the youth Jīvaka had received the World-Honored One’s consent, he immediately took a golden water-pitcher and washed the Buddha’s hands with its water; he then offered this most precious and costly robe to the Buddha, who, out of compassion, accepted it.

The youth Jīvaka prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and the Buddha preached various teachings to him, causing him to rejoice; having bowed before the Buddha, he then departed.

At that time, for this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs. By means of countless skillful expedients, he praised the dhūta practices, the maintenance of dignified deportment, fewness of desires and contentment, and those who possess wisdom and delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:

"This robe is the foremost among expensive robes; it is like the sequence where milk comes from a cow, curd from milk, fresh butter from curd, clarified butter from fresh butter, and the finest essence, *ghṛta*, from clarified butter—it is the most refined and supreme."
"This robe is such that it is the foremost among all robes.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to wear, as they please, robes offered by donors or robes from the refuse heap."

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to accept robes offered by donors, immediately took the expensive *kambala* robe he was wearing and sent it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus would not accept it, saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep robes of high value."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I allow you to keep expensive *kambala* robes.
Later, someone again sent a person to deliver a costly woolen rug (*karpāsa*) worn by the king; the bhikṣus did not dare to accept it.
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep expensive woolen carpets.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to keep them."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept large, long-haired woolen rugs.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not keep them."
The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to possess woolen rugs three cubits wide and five cubits long, with a pile no more than three finger-breadths high; these should be kept after having been formally dedicated through the ritual of *śuddha-dāna*."

At that time, when the youth Jīvaka heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to accept robes offered by donors, he immediately sent someone to deliver a short-pile woolen rug worn by the king to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept it, saying, "The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep short-pile woolen rugs."
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"From this day forward, I permit you to keep [such garments].

At that time, the upāsakas of Rājagṛha, hearing that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to keep robes offered by donors, immediately dispatched men to send various fine garments to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus did not know what they should do with them.
They went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to divide it.
They did not know how to divide it.
The Buddha said:

"One should count the number of people; if there are ten people, divide it into ten parts, and so on up to a hundred people, which would be divided into a hundred parts. When distributing the robes, the good and the bad shall be mixed together."
At that time, the person distributing the robes took a portion for himself.
The Buddha said:
"One should not take a portion for oneself; one should have another person distribute them."
He had another person take his portion while he took his own. The Buddha said, "One should not take one's own portion;
rather, portions should be divided by casting lots.
That bhikṣu cast the lot himself. The Buddha said:
"One should not cast one's own tally; it is permitted for those who do not hear [the count] to cast their tallies.
At that time, there was a king’s robe of great value that could not be divided. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to cut it into pieces and divide them."
"From this day forward, I authorize you to cut cloth with a knife.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a garment that had not yet been washed.
The Buddha said, "I authorize you to wash it yourself or have someone else wash it."
At that time, it was necessary to have a vessel for washing;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a washing vessel. If there is no washing board, I allow you to keep a board. If scissors are required, I allow you to keep them."

At that time, the World-Honored One departed from the city of Rājagṛha and traveled through the human realm toward the south. On the way, he saw a field that was well-tended, with its ridges and furrows perfectly aligned.
Having seen it, he said to Ānanda: "Do you see this field?"
He replied, “I have seen them,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked Ānanda:
"Are you able to establish such a rule for robes for the bhikṣus? He replied:
"Yes," the Buddha said to Ānanda,
"go and instruct the bhikṣus."

Then Ānanda returned from there to Rājagṛha and instructed the bhikṣus to cut and sew their robes in this manner: "This is a long strip; this is a short strip; this is a leaf-shaped piece; this is the first seam; this is the second seam; this is the central seam; and these are the two directions for the strips and leaves."
At that time, in Rājagṛha, many were wearing robes made of cut-and-sewn cloth.
Then, having traveled through the human realm in the southern region, the World-Honored One returned to Rājagṛha; seeing that the bhikṣus there mostly wore robes made of cut-and-sewn cloth, he said:
“Ānanda is clever and possesses great wisdom; though I have explained it only briefly, he is able to understand its meaning in full detail.”
The Tathāgatas, Arhats, and disciples of the Buddhas of the past wore robes such as these, just as I do today;
the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and disciples of the Buddhas of the future will wear robes such as these, just as I do today.
"Cut with a knife to form the robes of a śramaṇa, so that they cannot be stripped away by enemies or thieves.
From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to make the saṃghāṭī, the uttarāsaṅga, and the antarvāsaka by means of cutting."
At that time, the bhikṣus were wearing *antarvāsas* made of cut-and-sewn cloth directly against their bodies; the seams quickly tore and dust and grime entered within the folds.
"From this day forward, I allow you to make *antarvāsas* that are not cut and sewn."

The bhikṣus wore their *uttarāsaṅga* and *saṃghāṭī* robes made of cut pieces; however, the edges of the patches quickly tore, and dust and grime entered the interior, leaving them damp and exposed. The Buddha said:

"From this day forward, I allow you to wear the *uttarāsaṅga* and *saṃghāṭī* robes made of cut pieces, provided that the edges are sewn with 'bird's-foot' stitches, or the edges are braided, or 'horse-tooth' stitches are used."
The bhikṣus did not know how many strips the robe should have.
The Buddha said:
"It should be five strips; it should not be six strips."
It should have seven strips; it should not have eight strips.
It should have nine strips; it should not have ten strips, nor even nineteen strips; it should not have twenty strips.
"If it exceeds these prescribed measurements, one should not keep [such a garment].
At that time, a bhikṣu folded his inner robe (nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī) and entered the house of a layperson, leaving his body exposed.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; I allow you to make and wear one.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept belts of superior color, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such items].
When the bhikṣus made them out of brocade, the Buddha said:
"One should not make them out of brocade."
The bhikṣus wore white waistbands, and the Buddha said:
"One should not make them with white [cloth].
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep a waistband for the *kāṣāya*.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made wide and long waistbands. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not make them."

It is permitted to make it two finger-widths wide and wrap it three times around the waist. If one obtains a pre-made one, it should be folded double, triple, or quadruple; if it becomes disordered after being folded three or four times, it is permitted to sew it together.
"If it is too short, I allow you to join it with cord.
If the belt is thin and soft and breaks quickly after repeated tying, you should attach a buckle or a toggle.
When the bhikṣus made [the belts] out of precious materials, the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials; rather, one should make [the bowl] from bone, or ivory, or horn, or iron, or copper, or white tin, or lead and tin, or thread, or wood, or lacquer."
Not knowing how to secure the amulet,
the Buddha said:
"Sew it with silk, or attach it by piercing a hole."
At that time, the bhikṣus had robes that were torn and damaged, so [the Buddha] said,
"I allow you to mend them. They did not know how to mend them,
so the Buddha said:

"If the heavy stitching comes undone and the edges fray, it is permitted to weave them back together with thread. If the ends of the straps fray, it is permitted to continue them with thread or sew them.
At that time, a bhikṣu entered a village without fastening his saṃkakṣikā, causing the garment to fall and his body to be exposed. The Buddha said:
"One should not enter a village without fastening one's robe; it is permitted to attach a strap or sew it."
At that time, Śāriputra entered the house of a layperson and suffered from his wind-blown, cut-and-sewn robe falling off his shoulder.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to attach hooks and buttons at the shoulders."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha and was traveling through the human realm together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus carried many robes; some wore them on their heads, some carried them on their shoulders, and some fastened them around their waists.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Gavāmpati who went to the bank of the Ganges where the Buddha intended to cross, and immediately cut the water with his supernormal power.
When the Buddha had finished crossing the water, he saw that many of the bhikṣus were carrying numerous robes.
Whether carried on the head, borne on the shoulder, or fastened around the waist, having seen this, he thought:
"These bhikṣus carry so many robes; I should establish a regulation for the bhikṣus regarding the number of robes, setting a limit such that they should not keep more than that."
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm among the people of Vatsa and arrived at Vaiśālī.

When Āmrapālī heard that the Buddha, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, was traveling through the human realm and had arrived at Vaiśālī, she immediately mounted her carriage and proceeded to the place where the World-Honored One was. Seeing from afar that the World-Honored One’s physical marks were upright and majestic, she felt reverence and joy; she immediately alighted from her carriage, went before the Buddha, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for their exhortation and conversion, causing them to attain joy.
Having heard the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, they leaped for joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray, World-Honored One!"
"Please accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow, together with the community of bhikṣus, and stay one night in my park.
At that time, the World-Honored One granted his consent by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had consented, he prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī in the Āmra Park.

When the Licchavis heard that the Buddha, together with twelve hundred and fifty disciples, had been traveling through the human realm and had arrived at Vaiśālī, they donned various garments and ornaments and mounted various carriages to go out and welcome the World-Honored One.

O Licchavis, some wore dark-blue necklaces and garments, rode dark-blue chariots and horses, and had dark-blue attendants; their dark-blue swords, spears, banners, and parasols, as well as their dark-blue jeweled hair-whisks, were likewise adorned. Others had chariots, horses, and attendants that were blue, yellow, red, white, or black, and their magnificent decorations were similarly arranged.
In this manner, five hundred Licchavis approached the place where the World-Honored One was.
At that time, Āmrapālī was returning along the road to meet the Buddha when she encountered the Licchavis; she did not yield the way, and their carriage canopies collided.
At that time, there was an elder among the Licchavis who said to Āmrapālī:
"Why did you not yield the way, so that you might have pressed against one another and our carriage canopies collided?"
Bhaddiya replied, "The reason for this is that I have invited the Buddha and the Sangha to stay overnight in my garden; my mind is fixed solely upon the Buddha, with no other intent."
Liśa said, "I will give you a hundred thousand pieces of gold; please allow the Buddha to accept my invitation for offerings. He replied:
"I have already invited the Buddha and the Sangha to stay overnight in my garden;
how could I now abandon them? Liśa spoke again:
"I will give you two hundred thousand pieces of gold, or even sixteen hundred thousand, so that you may allow the World-Honored One to accept my invitation for food and drink."
He replied, "I cannot. Reṣa spoke again:
"I will give you half the wealth of the kingdom so that you may permit the Buddha to accept my invitation for a meal.
He replied, "Even if you were to give me the entire city of Vaiśālī, I would not relinquish it."
"Why is that? I have already invited the Buddha and the Sangha to be provided for in my garden.
At that time, the five hundred Licchavis shook their hands in anger and resentment toward Āmrapālī, saying:
"Abandon us! they cried, and immediately mounted their carriages and proceeded to the Āmrapālī Grove.

At that time, the World-Honored One was in that grove, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude, preaching the Dharma. Seeing from afar the arrival of the five hundred Licchavis, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"If there is a bhikṣu who does not see the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven when they go forth on excursion, he should observe these Licchavis;
the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven when they wish to go forth on excursion are no different from these."
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Be careful with your thoughts and maintain your dignified deportment; this is my instruction.
What do you think, bhikṣus?"
Be watchful over the thoughts of your mind!

If a bhikṣu contemplates the body within as a station of mindfulness regarding the body, he applies himself with diligence, maintains his mindfulness without distraction, and subdues greed, envy, and the afflictions of the world.

One contemplates the body externally as the application of mindfulness of the body, applying oneself with diligence to maintain mindfulness so that it is not distracted, thereby subduing greed, envy, and the afflictions of the world.
One contemplates the body internally and externally; the contemplation of feelings, mind, and phenomena is likewise.
In this way, a bhikṣu attains right mindfulness.
How does he maintain his deportment?

Whether going out or coming in, bending or stretching, looking down or looking up; whether holding his robes and bowl, drinking, eating, taking medicine, attending to the calls of nature, sleeping or waking, coming or going, sitting or standing, dozing or being awake, speaking or remaining silent—a bhikṣu is always thus single-minded. This is called a bhikṣu maintaining his deportment.

At that time, five hundred Licchavis of Vaiśālī arrived at the place where the chariots were stationed; they alighted from their vehicles, approached the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The five hundred Licchavis were devoid of majestic power in the presence of the Buddha; only the World-Honored One, amidst the great assembly, possessed a radiance and majesty that were supreme and peerless, like the autumn sky free from clouds and mists, where the sun moves through space with incomparable brilliance.
Thus the World-Honored One was among five hundred Licchavis, his spiritual power, renown, and countenance being peerless.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the assembly named Pingiyānī. This brahmin rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to say something."
The Buddha said,
"I grant you leave to speak. Thereupon,
this brahmin spoke a verse in the presence of the Buddha to praise him:
"The King of Magadha has gained a great benefit; the King of Aṅga wears the armor of jewels.
Since a Buddha has appeared in this land, his voice resounds like the Himalayas."
Like the fragrance of a lotus flower, pure and clean, its spreading scent is supreme;
now beholding the Buddha’s radiant light, it is like the sun first rising.
Like the moon moving through the void, free from all clouds and mists.
Thus the Buddha, the World-Honored One, illuminates the world.
Beholding the Buddha’s wisdom is like seeing a great fire blaze in the darkness;
he bestows the clear eye upon all beings and resolves every doubt.
At that time, the Licchavis said to the brahmin,
"You may recite this verse once more.
Then the brahmin immediately repeated this verse two or three times.
At that time, because of his skillful praise in verse, the Licchavis immediately gave him five hundred robes.
Having received these robes, the brahmin offered them to the Buddha, saying:
"May the Buddha, out of compassion, please accept them."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Licchavis:
"There are five kinds of jewels in the world that are difficult to obtain.
What are these five?"
First, it is rare for a Buddha, the World-Honored One, to appear in the world; this treasure is difficult to obtain.
When a Buddha appears in the world, to hear the Buddha’s teaching and explain it for others is a treasure difficult to obtain.
When a Buddha appears in the world and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, those who hear the Dharma and understand it—such a treasure is difficult to find.
When a Buddha appears in the world, those who hear the Buddha preach the Dharma and practice in accordance with that Dharma—such a treasure is difficult to find.
"Those who attain faith and joy find this treasure difficult to obtain.
These are the five treasures that are rare to find in the world.
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s various skillful means of preaching the Dharma for their edification, the five hundred Licchavis were filled with supreme joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“May you accept my invitation for tomorrow morning, together with the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha said,
“I have already accepted the invitation of Āmrapālī.”
Then the five hundred Licchavis shook their hands and said,
"Ambapālī has abandoned us! They immediately rose from their seats,
went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
At that time, Āmrapālī returned home and prepared various kinds of fine food and drink. On the following day, she went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had arrived.

In the early morning, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, proceeded to the house of Āmrapālī and sat down upon the prepared seats.
At that time, Pāṭali provided the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus with various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink.

When they had finished eating and drinking to their satisfaction, he placed his bowl on the ground, took a golden water-vessel, and washed the Buddha’s hands. He then stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“In the kingdom of Vaiśālī there are many gardens and groves; this one is the foremost among them. I now offer it to the World-Honored One, so that you may dwell within it. I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and accept it.”
The Buddha told him:
"You may offer this to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters.
For what reason?

Whether it be the Buddha’s groves and their contents, or his dwellings and their contents, or his alms bowls, robes, sitting mats, or needle cases—just like the stūpas and temples of the Buddha—none among all the gods, nāgas, spirits, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, devas, and humans in the entire world have the power to use them.
Bhadrika said, "I now offer this to the Buddha and the Saṃgha of the four quarters; I pray that you will accept it.
Out of compassion, the Buddha then offered a blessing and accepted it.
"If one builds temples and shrines, plants various fruit trees,
provides bridges and boats to ferry people across, offers water and fruit in the wilderness,
and furthermore bestows houses as gifts."
"For such persons as these, merit increases day and night;
those who are able to maintain the precepts according to the Dharma proceed toward the auspicious path.

At that time, Vādi took a small seat and sat to one side. Then the World-Honored One taught him various Dharmas, causing him great joy; immediately upon his seat, all defilements were eliminated and he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, and having realized the fruit of its fruition, she addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; may I become a female lay follower (upāsikā) of the Buddha."
"From this day forward, you shall not kill living beings, nor shall you drink alcohol.
When Pāṭali heard the Buddha preach the Dharma through various skillful means, he was filled with supreme joy; rising from his seat, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
At that time, while the World-Honored One was reflecting in a quiet place, he thought to himself:
"The bhikṣus traveling on the road carry many garments; some wear them upon their heads, some carry them on their shoulders, and some wear them around their waists."
Having seen this, he thought:
"I should establish for the bhikṣus a regulation regarding the number of robes, so that they may not possess more than the permitted amount.

At that time, during the first watch of the night, the World-Honored One sat in the open air wearing a single robe; when the middle watch arrived and he felt his body grow cold, he immediately put on a second robe.
When the latter part of the night arrived, he felt cold and put on a third robe.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:

"In future generations, there may be sons of good family who cannot endure the cold; I shall permit them to keep three robes as sufficient. I allow the bhikṣus to keep three robes, but they must not exceed this number."
When the night had passed, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this matter and addressed them, saying:

“While I was reflecting in seclusion, I observed that various bhikṣus were traveling on the road carrying heavy loads of robes—some wearing them on their heads, some carrying them on their shoulders, and others fastening them around their waists.”
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"I should now establish for the bhikṣus a limit on the number of robes they may possess; those who exceed it shall not be permitted to keep them.

At first, during the first watch of the night, while sitting in the open air, he wore one robe. When it grew cold at the middle watch, he put on a second robe. When it grew cold again at the final watch, he put on a third robe.
I had this thought: "In the future, there may be sons of good family who cannot endure the cold; for them, three robes will suffice.
I should now establish a rule that the bhikṣus shall possess no more than three robes, and if they exceed this number, they must not keep them."
"From this day forward, I permit the bhikṣus to keep the three robes, but they must not keep more than that.
At that time, the Saṃgha of the four quarters at a different residence obtained a costly saṃghāṭī and made it into bedding. The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should trade it for other goods and use them as appropriate.
He did not know whom to employ to carry out the trade.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I permit bhikṣus to exchange goods. Whether it be through a monastery attendant, a śrāmaṇera, or an upāsaka who acts as an intermediary, or if the donor exchanges them themselves, they may be used according to the circumstances."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vṛji. A certain bhikṣu obtained a kṣauma garment and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep it. Another bhikṣu obtained a rāhurata garment and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“[I] permit you to keep it.
A bhikṣu obtained an *āḍhakavatī* robe and informed the Buddha; the Buddha said, “I permit you to keep it.”
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed robes dyed with superior colors; the Buddha said, "You should not possess them.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus possessed garments of superior brocade; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep brocade garments or white robes; according to the Dharma, they should not be kept. They should be dyed the color of a *kāṣāya* and then kept.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore robes with uncut fringes. The Buddha said:
"They should not be kept."
The group of six bhikṣus made robes with fringes of brocade; the Buddha said, "You should not keep such things.
The group of six bhikṣus kept *pāṇḍu-saṃstara* robes; the Buddha said:
"One must not keep [such things].
Such a foolish person, following my prohibition, has instead made other garments.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī. A donor sent food; it is the constant custom of all Buddhas that if they do not go to eat, they afterwards inspect the dwellings.
While inspecting the dwellings, he saw a bhikṣu spreading his saṃghāṭī on the ground, intending to patch it. Having seen this, he went to where the bhikṣu was and said to him:
"For what reason are you spreading your robe on the ground?"
The bhikṣu said,
"I wish for the inner layer to adhere closely while the outer layer has visible patches.
The Buddha said:
“Excellent, excellent, bhikṣu! It is just as you have done.”
When the bhikṣus returned from their meal, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus for this reason and said to them:
"Bhikṣus, after the meal I went on an inspection tour of the lodgings and saw a bhikṣu spreading his saṃghāṭī robe on the ground, intending to fold it into patches."
Having seen this, he went to where the bhikṣu was and said,
"For what reason have you spread your robe upon the ground?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I wish to have the inner layers adhere to one another, with the outer surface appearing smooth and polished.
I then praised him, saying: "Excellent!"
"It shall be as you have done.
From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to make new robes: one layer for the antarvāsa, one layer for the uttarāsaṅga, and two layers for the saṃghāṭī.
If they are used garments, it is permitted to have two layers for the antaravāsaka, two layers for the uttarāsaṅga, and four layers for the saṃghāṭī.
If they are discarded rags (pāṃsukūla), the number of layers may be as many as one desires.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Āṭavī.
Then the community of monks obtained *sukhābhivyañjana* robes, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep them."
When they obtained brocade robes, the Buddha said:
"I do not permit you to keep them.
When the bhikṣus obtained mosquito nets, the Buddha said:
“Listen, you may keep [it].
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering among the people of the Vṛji country; he went to Mount Vaibhāra and stayed in the Deer Park at the Grove of Fear within the forest.
At that time, there was a prince named Bodhi who had constructed a new hall, which no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, or any other person had yet sat in.

When the prince heard that the Buddha was traveling through the human world among the people of the Vṛji country and was staying at the Deer Park in the Bhīṣaṇavana forest on Mount Vaidehaka, he immediately dispatched a messenger to summon the brāhmaṇa youth Sājja, saying to him:

"Go to the place where the Buddha is, bearing my name; prostrate yourself at his feet and inquire after the World-Honored One’s welfare, asking whether he is light and agile, free from illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace and happiness."
Thus he addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for a meal.

I have constructed a new hall, which has not yet been sat upon by any śramaṇas, brahmins, or common people; I pray that the Buddha sit first, and thereafter Prince Bodhi shall sit, so that immeasurable merit may be obtained."

Then the Brahmin youth Saja, having prostrated at the feet of the prince, went to where the World-Honored One was. After paying his respects and inquiring after His well-being, he withdrew to sit to one side and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Prince Bodhi bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and inquires whether Your Reverence is light and at ease, free from illness and affliction, and dwelling in peace and happiness.”
Thus he addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that the Buddha and the Sangha will accept my invitation for a meal.
I have constructed a new hall where no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, or any person has yet sat; I pray that the Buddha sit first, and then the prince may sit, so that immeasurable merit may be obtained."
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his consent by remaining silent.
Having heard the Buddha’s consent, the brahmin youth Sājja rose from his seat, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed for the residence of Prince Bodhi, where he spoke these words:
“I have finished my petition to the śramaṇa Gautama, and he has granted his consent by remaining silent.”
"Now is precisely the right time.

Thereupon, the prince immediately prepared various kinds of fine foods. When the night had passed, on the following day he swept and sprinkled the hall, and spread new, fine garments from the steps up to the dais.
When the time arrived, he sent someone to inform the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One, having donned his robes and taken up his bowl, went together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus to the house of Prince Bodhi.

Then the prince went to the inner side of the outer gate to welcome the Buddha. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he stepped forward, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and followed behind him in attendance, like a disciple who faithfully follows the teachings.
The World-Honored One entered the prince’s hall and stood silently before it.
The prince said, “I pray that the Buddha will walk upon my clothes to ascend the dais, so that I may obtain merit, peace, and happiness.”
The prince made this request of the World-Honored One a second and a third time, but the World-Honored One remained silent.
Then the World-Honored One looked toward Ānanda; Ānanda understood that the Buddha did not wish to walk upon the new cloth, for the sake of benefiting future sentient beings.
Ānanda said to the prince, "You should gather up this robe;
the Tathāgata does not wish to walk upon it, for the sake of benefiting future sentient beings.
Then the prince quickly withdrew the robe and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"May the Buddha ascend the hall so that I may obtain merit.
Thereupon, the Buddha ascended the hall and took his seat.
Then the prince served the Buddha and the Sangha with various kinds of delicious food and drink. Having finished eating and set aside his bowl, he took a small stool and sat to one side.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had taught the Dharma to the prince through various skillful means, he rose from his seat and departed, returning to his original dwelling. On account of this incident, he assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"If a cloth of great value is spread upon the ground, one should not walk upon it; if one does so, it must be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, the monks' quarters were covered with much dust. The Buddha said, "I allow you to sprinkle water and sweep.
Having sprinkled and swept, dust still remained. The Buddha said:
"Listen: one should sprinkle it with muddy water.
If there is still dust, one should spread upon the ground as a floor-covering any one of these ten kinds of garments: *elāya*, *tāmra*, *māmra*, or woolen cloth."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
King Prasenajit had a stepmother who had faith and devotion in the Buddha-dharma; she took a costly silk robe worn by the king, offered it to the Saṃgha of the four quarters, and then passed away.

At that time, the bhikṣus used it as a ground-covering. Some ministers who lacked faith and devotion went to the saṃghārāma to observe; seeing the bhikṣus using a costly brocade garment worn by the king as a ground-covering, they all spoke in derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya!..."
Lacking knowledge of contentment, they greedily accumulate and store up leftovers, yet claim,
"I know the True Dharma.
Observing them in this way, how can there be any True Dharma?
"The king has used his precious robes as a ground-covering.
Although the donor has made this offering, the recipient must know contentment.
When the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"One should not use the expensive robes worn by kings as floor coverings.
From this day forward, it is permitted to use them as bedding, sitting mats, pillows, or upper garments."
At that time, a bhikṣu wrapped his head and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant permission for it."
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu must not wrap his head; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wraps one's head, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from cold headaches and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make caps out of wool or cotton to wrap around the head.
At that time, the bhikṣu Dhānañjāni put on his robes and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; we pray that the Buddha will grant permission.
The Buddha said, "One must not wear robes in this manner, except within a monastery; this is the practice of laypeople."
"If one wears the robe in this manner, it is in accordance with the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu put on a single robe, went to where the Buddha was, and said:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant his permission."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear only a single garment, except when at the place for defecating or urinating; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a robe with a gathered neck went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant his permission.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear this garment; it is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu wore a padded jacket and went to the World-Honored One, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; we pray that the Buddha will permit it.
The Buddha said, "You should not wear these; this is the practice of laypeople."
"If you wear it, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu wore a garment made of leather and went to the Buddha’s presence, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant permission for it."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a *saṃkakṣikā* went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will permit it.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear these; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears them, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu put on trousers and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; we pray that the Buddha will grant his permission.
The Buddha said, "You should not wear it; this is the practice of laypeople."
"If you wear it, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu wore a loincloth (*kaupīna*) and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta ascetic; I pray that the Buddha will grant permission for it."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear them; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears them, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a gaiter made of *tūla* grass went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the austere and dignified practice of the dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant his permission."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one wears it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
The Buddha said to the bhikṣu:
"You foolish man! You have acted otherwise than what I have prescribed; none of these practices of laypeople may be adopted."
At that time, some bhikṣus, falsely assuming the appearance of matted hair and spiral topknots, came to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the dignified dharma of dhūta asceticism; we pray that the Buddha will permit it."
The Buddha said:
"This should not be done; this is the teaching of the non-Buddhists.
If one acts in such a manner, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who carried a wooden bowl and went to where the Buddha was, saying:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will permit it.
The Buddha said:
"One should not carry such a bowl; this is the practice of the non-Buddhists.
If you possess one, it shall be dealt with according to the law.

At that time, a bhikṣu carrying a *pātraka-śālā* (a bowl-carrying staff) approached a pillar, set his bowl upon the ground, and placed various items upon a horizontal crossbar atop it, slinging the whole over his shoulder as he went. Thus it was called a *pātraka-śālā*. He went to where the Buddha was and said:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; we pray that the Buddha will grant his permission.
The Buddha said, "This is the practice of non-Buddhists; it should not be maintained."
"If you keep one, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a hand-embroidered robe went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the dignified practice of a dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will permit it."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it; this is the dharma of the non-Buddhists.
If you possess one, it shall be dealt with according to the law."
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a garment of grass went to where the Buddha was and said:
"This is the dignified dharma of the dhūta practices; I pray that the Buddha will grant me permission.
The Buddha said:
"One should not be attached to these, for they are the dharmas of the non-Buddhists.
If one is attached, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
Such garments as grass robes, śāṇa-grass robes, tree-bark robes, tree-leaf robes, or pearl-necklace robes—none of these garments may be kept."
"If you keep one, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing an outer-cloth made of animal skin went to the Buddha's presence and said:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will permit it."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it.
If one wears it, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a garment made of vulture feathers went to where the Buddha was and said:
"This is the dhūta practice of dignified decorum; I pray that the Buddha will grant me permission.
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear this; it is the dharma of the non-Buddhists.
If you possess one, you shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing a *kambala* garment made of human hair went to the Buddha’s presence and said:
"This is the dignified practice of the dhūta; we pray that the Buddha will permit it.
The Buddha said, "You should not wear these; they are the practices of non-Buddhists."
"If one wears [such items], it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, a bhikṣu wearing garments made of horsehair, yak-tail hair, and *kambala* wool went to the Buddha's presence and said to the Buddha:
"This is the dignified practice of the *dhūta* asceticism; we pray that the Buddha will permit it."
The Buddha said:
"One should not wear it; this is the practice of non-Buddhists.
If one wears it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, a bhikṣu went naked to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"This is the dignified practice of dhūta; I pray that the Buddha will grant me permission.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; this is the dharma of the non-Buddhists.
If one exposes the body, it is a sthūlātyaya.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Such a foolish person! Having followed my regulations, you have yet committed another transgression.
All such things are the dharmas of external paths; they must not be done."

At that time, there was a residence where the *saṃgha* present there obtained a large quantity of divisible robes and articles. The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they went to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to divide them."
Furthermore, not knowing how to divide it, the Buddha said:

"One should count the number of people—whether ten, twenty, or even up to a hundred—and divide it into a hundred portions. If there are items of superior or inferior quality, they should be distributed by mixing them together."
He then took his own portion for himself. The Buddha said, "One should not take one's own portion; rather, portions should be divided by casting lots.
He then cast the lots himself. The Buddha said:
"One should not cast the voting tally oneself; rather, one who is not present should be asked to cast it.
At the time when the goods were being distributed, some visiting bhikṣus arrived. The Buddha said, "They should be given a share."
