When the distribution of portions is finished, if a guest bhikṣu arrives, he should be given a portion.
If he arrives before the counting sticks have been cast, he should be given a portion.
If he arrives when the counting sticks are being cast, he should be given a portion.
When the voting sticks have been cast and [the distribution] concluded, he does not give a share.
After he has joyfully accepted his share, if a guest bhikṣu arrives, he does not give him a share; if there is any remainder, it is divided further.
"If he arrives after the distribution is finished, one should not give him a share.
If a *śrāmaṇera* has already been given a share, and the person who was sent to distribute it returns, one should not give him a share.
When the monks were dividing the robes, visiting monks arrived repeatedly, and they became utterly exhausted from the task of distributing the robes.

"One person should be appointed to distribute [the items]; this is to be granted through a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*. From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following announcement:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"
Whatever is in this dwelling—whether robes or non-robes—the present Saṃgha should divide.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha consents, let the Saṃgha give [these items] to a certain bhikṣu, who shall then give them to the Saṃgha.
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Whatever robes or non-robes are present at this residence should be distributed by the Saṃgha before its members; the Saṃgha now gives them to the bhikṣu so-and-so, who shall then give them to the Saṃgha."

"Whichever elders approve that these robes, whether they be robes or non-robes, belonging to this residence and now present before the Sangha, should be divided and given by the Sangha to the bhikṣu so-and-so—who shall then give them to the Sangha—let them remain silent.
Whoever does not approve, let them speak."
"The Saṃgha has already consented to grant [this] to the bhikṣu so-and-so; that so-and-so shall now complete the granting to the Saṃgha.
Because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a *vāśuka* robe and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep it.
The bhikṣus suffered from the cold and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Listen to the *cīvarabhāṇaka*.

At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu living in a separate residence. Then, the *saṃmukhībhūta-saṃgha* obtained a large amount of cloth suitable for distribution. The bhikṣus did not know what to do.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a single bhikṣu residing at a dwelling and a large amount of robe-cloth fit for distribution among the *saṃgha* present is obtained,

and if guest bhikṣus arrive— whether four or more than four— one should take that cloth and give it to one bhikṣu to perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation) for its distribution."
If there are three people, they should mutually receive and share [the portion] by means of three utterances;
if there are two people, they should together receive and share it by means of three utterances;
if there is only one person, they should mentally reflect and speak the words aloud:
"This is my portion.
At that time, there was a residence where a monk had the perception that another was a monk, and he wished to divide the robes into separate portions.
The monks did not know whether this constituted a valid division or not.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The distribution is not valid; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a residence where a bhikṣu doubted whether it was appropriate to divide the robes separately.
The bhikṣus did not know whether it was valid or invalid.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is invalid; one incurs a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, there was a residence where a bhikṣu, perceiving himself as not being among the bhikṣus, divided the robes separately.
Did the bhikṣu know whether this constituted a valid division or not?
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The distribution is not valid, yet there is no offense.
At that time, there was a residence where there were no monks, yet [the residents] had the perception that there were monks and proceeded to distribute robes.
The bhikṣus did not know whether it constituted a formal offense or not, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It constitutes a formal offense; one incurs a duṣkṛta."

At that time, there was a residence where there were no bhikṣus present, yet there arose a doubt regarding the distribution of robes; they did not know whether it constituted a valid distribution or not.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It constitutes a valid distribution, [but those who distributed them] incur a duṣkṛta offense."
At that time, in a certain residence, there were no monks present, yet they divided the robes while perceiving them as belonging to monks.
The monks did not know whether this constituted a valid distribution or not, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If it is a portioned robe, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a residence where a monk, perceiving another monk to be a monk, received a robe separately from the group.
The monks did not know whether the receiving of the robe was valid or not.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The acceptance of the robe is not valid; one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a monastery where a bhikṣu doubted whether it was permissible to accept a robe from a separate group.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The acceptance is not valid; one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, there was a monastery where a bhikṣu, perceiving another bhikṣu as not being a bhikṣu, accepted a robe from a separate group.
The bhikṣus did not know whether this constituted a valid acceptance or not, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a valid acceptance, yet there is no offense."
At that time, there was a residence where there were no monks, yet one who perceived them to be monks accepted a robe.
The monks did not know whether the acceptance was valid;
they reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one accepts [the robe], one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
At that time, there was a monastery where no monks were present, and they had doubts regarding the acceptance of robes.
The monks did not know whether the acceptance of the robes was valid or not.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The acceptance is valid; he incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a residence where there were no bhikṣus, yet [a person] accepted a robe while perceiving them to be bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not know whether this constituted a valid acceptance or not, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It constitutes a valid acceptance; there is no offense."
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 40 [and] Volume 41 (Part 5 of 3),
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others.

*Cīvaravastu*, Part Three. At that time, in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there died a bhikṣu of great renown who possessed many monasteries, as well as many gardens, fields, and fruit trees belonging to those monasteries, and many individual cells.
Most of these items belong to individual cells; there are many copper jars, copper basins, axes, chisels, and lampstands, as well as many heavy objects.
There are many rope beds, wooden beds, mattresses for lying down, cushions for sitting, and pillows.
They keep many *elāyanta* rugs, *maudra* rugs, and woolen blankets (*kambala*), and they have many people appointed to guard the monastery.
There were many carriages; many water jars, mendicant staffs, and fans;
many metal utensils, wooden utensils, ceramic utensils, and leather utensils; many hair-shaving razors and bamboo utensils;
and many robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Whether they are well-known or unknown, all such property belongs to the Saṃgha."
The bhikṣus divided the monastery’s gardens, fields, and fruit trees. The Buddha said:
"They should not be divided; they belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
They then divided the cells and the property belonging to individual cells. The Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
They then divided copper jars, copper basins, axes, chisels, and various other heavy objects, and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions."
They divided the rope beds, wooden beds, sitting cushions, bedding, and pillows; the Buddha said, "They should not be divided;
they belong to the Sangha of the four directions.
They divided the *elāyanta*, *maudra*, *maudra-maudra*, and woolen rugs; the Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it belongs to the Saṃgha of the four directions.

From this day forward, I allow the bhikṣus to possess woolen rugs three cubits wide and five cubits long, with a pile no more than three finger-breadths high; these should be distributed among the present Saṃgha."
Regarding those who divide the chariots and carriages belonging to the monastery attendants, the Buddha said:
"They should not be divided; they belong to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
Regarding those who divide the water jars, washing basins, mendicant staffs, and fans, the Buddha said:
"It should not be divided; it belongs to the Sangha of the four directions.
They then divided the iron vessels, wooden vessels, ceramic vessels, leather vessels, and bamboo vessels. The Buddha said:
"They should not be divided; they belong to the Sangha of the four directions."
"From this day forward, I authorize the distribution of razors, robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases.
They then divided the *kuñjara* vessels, saying, "The *saṃgha* present here should divide them."
At that time, there was a different residence where the two assemblies of the Saṃgha had obtained a large quantity of robes and other items to be distributed.
Since the assembly of bhikṣus was large and the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs was small, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be divided into two parts.
At that time, there were no bhikṣuṇīs, only śikṣamāṇās; [the Buddha said: "It should be divided into two parts."
At that time, there were no bhikṣuṇīs and no śikṣamāṇās, only śrāmaṇerikās. The Buddha said:
"They should be divided into two portions.
If there are no śrāmaṇerikās, the Saṃgha itself should divide them."
At that time, there was a residence where the two divisions of the Saṃgha had obtained much property; the bhikṣus were few and the bhikṣuṇīs were many.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be divided into two portions."
"If there are no bhikṣus but there are śrāmaṇeras, it should be divided into two portions.
If there are no śrāmaṇeras, the bhikṣuṇīs should divide it.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human settlements of the Kośala country who arrived at a village where no bhikṣus resided; having arrived, he passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know who should divide these robes and bowls.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a faithful upāsaka or a park-keeper at that place, they should be entrusted with the task."
"If there are members of the fivefold assembly who come forth as renunciants, you should give [it] to them; if none come, you should send it to a nearby monastery.

At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at his residence in Śrāvastī, where there were many bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, various non-Buddhists, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I wish to sit in quiet meditation and contemplate for three months; do not allow outsiders to enter, except for one person who provides offerings."
At that time, the bhikṣus established a regulation among themselves:
"The World-Honored One has spoken thus:
'For three months, remain in quiet meditation and reflection; do not allow outsiders to enter, except for one person who provides offerings.'"
"If there are any who enter [the village], instruct them to perform the *pāyattika* confession.

At that time, the Elder Vāsabhagāmi-putra, together with sixty bhikṣus from the country of Pāṭaliputra—all of whom were forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), alms-seekers (*piṇḍapātika*), wearers of rag-robes (*pāṃśukūlika*), practitioners of the "remaining-food" rule (*khalupaścādbhaktika*), eaters in a single sitting (*aikāsanika*), eaters of a single mouthful (*aikagrāsika*), dwellers among tombs (*śmāśānika*), dwellers in the open air (*abbhokāsika*), dwellers at the foot of trees (*vṛkṣamūlika*), constant-sitters (*naiṣadyika*), followers of whatever seat is available (*yathāsaṃstarika*), and possessors of the three robes (*traicīvarika*)—went to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī and asked the bhikṣus:
"In which room does the Tathāgata reside?"
"I wish to go and see him.
The bhikṣus said, "The Tathāgata has spoken thus:"
"I shall sit in meditation for three months in contemplation; let no outsider enter, except for one person who provides offerings.
If anyone enters, one must perform a *pāyattika* confession.
Upāli first asked,
"Does the World-Honored One speak thus?
The bhikṣu replied:
“The bhikṣus established their own regulation, saying:
‘If anyone enters, it is a pāyattika offense requiring confession. Andhaka said:
"I do not require the regulations established by the elders. Why is this?
For the Buddha has spoken thus:"
"What the Buddha has not prohibited should not be prohibited;
what he has already prohibited should not be transgressed.
One should train in accordance with the rules that have been established."
"We are all forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*), up to those who maintain the three robes (*tricīvara*); we wish to question the World-Honored One at our own convenience.
Then the Elder Upasena, together with those sixty bhikṣus, went directly to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the World-Honored One greeted him, saying:
"Upasena! Are you at ease and well?"
Is your food and drink sufficient?
Is your dwelling peaceful and secure? Ho-xian!
"From where have you come?
Have you not heard what the other bhikṣus said? He replied:
“Living in peace and comfort, we do not suffer for lack of food or drink, and we have also heard the words of other bhikṣus:
‘Venerable sirs!
We, sixty bhikṣus from the country of Pāra, all of whom are forest-dwellers and possessors of the three robes, are traveling through the human settlements of the Kosalans.’”
Upon arriving at the kingdom of Śrāvastī, they asked the bhikṣus of Jetavana:
"In which room does the World-Honored One reside?
We wish to see him."
The bhikṣus spoke thus:
"The World-Honored One shall sit in quiet meditation and contemplation for three months; do not allow outsiders to enter, except for the single person who provides offerings."
"If there is anyone who enters [the order], instruct them to perform the *pāyattika* confession. I then asked:
"Does the World-Honored One truly speak these words regarding the *pāyattika* confession?"
The bhikṣus said: "No;
we have established this regulation ourselves. I then spoke to them:
"I do not require you to restrain me. Why is this?
For the Buddha has spoken these words:"
"What the Buddha has not prohibited should not be prohibited; what he has already prohibited should not be transgressed; one should train in accordance with the prescribed rules.
We are all forest-dwellers (*āraṇyaka*) and even those who maintain the three robes (*tricīvara*); we wish to have the opportunity to inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being as we please.
The Buddha said: “Excellent, excellent, Upatiṣya!”
All of you are forest-dwellers who maintain the three robes; you may freely inquire after his well-being.
If there are others such as yourselves, they too may freely inquire after the World-Honored One’s well-being.

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One had permitted those dwelling in araṇya to inquire after his well-being as they wished, some became practitioners of araṇya, some refused invitations to meals and constantly practiced alms-gathering, some abandoned the robes offered by donors and wore robes made of discarded rags (pāṃśukūla), and some abandoned extra robes and maintained only the three robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus set aside their robes until they formed a great heap. Not knowing what to do, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"They should be bestowed upon the Saṃgha, or given to the Buddha, or given to a stūpa, or given to a single person."
When the bhikṣus heard that it was given to one person and then taken to give to a layperson (avadātavasana), they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not give to a layperson or to a follower of an external path (tīrthika)."

At that time, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and cautious; they did not dare to give bhikṣuṇīs any non-robes, alms-bowl bags, leather sandal bags, needle cases, meditation belts, waistbands, hats, foot-wiping cloths, heat-absorbing cloths, or cloths for wrapping leather sandals.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to give non-robes to bhikṣuṇīs.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should a bhikṣu who is practicing pārivāsika and mānatva be given a share?
The Buddha said,
"He should be given one."
The bhikṣus had this thought:

"Regarding those who have been subjected to acts of censure (tajjaniya-kamma), such as the act of banishment (pabbājaniya-kamma), the act of dependence (niyassa-kamma), the act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople (pāpikāya diṭṭhiyā appaṭinissagge ukkhepanīya-kamma), or the act of formal accusation (ukkhepanīya-kamma)—should a share [of the community's requisites] be given to those persons who have been subjected to such acts?"
The Buddha said, "Give it;
give it by placing it on the ground, or have someone else give it.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained robes from non-Buddhists and wore them without dyeing them.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not wear them immediately; you should dye them before wearing.
At that time, the bhikṣus had laypeople make the robes for them, and the laypeople asked for their share of the cloth.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to calculate the amount of labor performed and provide food or payment accordingly.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Should the monastery attendant and the śrāmaṇera be given an equal share of the robes?
He asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the Saṃgha is in harmony and grants permission, they should be given an equal share with the śrāmaṇeras."
If they do not reach an agreement, one half should be given;
if they do not accept the half, one-third should be given;
if this is not granted, the property should not be divided.
If it is the monastery attendant who guards it, he shall receive one-fourth;
if he does not give it, it should not be divided.
If it is divided, it should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
The bhikṣus were apprehensive and hesitant, not daring to take the robes and give them to their parents. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should give them.
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
The Śākyas of Kapilavastu had newly constructed a hall, but no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, or other person had yet sat upon it.

At that time, Prince Viśvantara was the first to take his seat; all the Śākyas were filled with resentment and indignation, saying, "We have newly built this hall, yet before the Buddha has even sat upon it, this low-born son of a slave-girl has already taken his place within."
At that time, there was a Brahmin attendant who lacked faith and said:
"The Śākyas of the Śākya clan have insulted you, calling you the lowly son of a slave woman; how can you endure this?"
He replied, "I have no power now and am not independent.
When my father passes away and I become king, you may speak to me then."
Later, King Prasenajit lost his throne, and Prince Virūḍhaka ascended the throne himself. A minister who did not have faith said to him:
"Previously, the Śākyas reviled Your Majesty; were you able to endure it?"
"Now you may go forth to punish them.
The King immediately assembled the fourfold army and departed from the city of Śrāvastī for the country of the Śākyas.
At that time, out of compassion, the World-Honored One went ahead to the side of the path where King Virūḍhaka was traveling and sat beneath a withered tree.

When King Virūḍhaka arrived, he saw the Buddha sitting beneath a wretched tree. He immediately alighted from his chariot, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“There are many excellent trees, such as the Aśvattha and others, yet you do not sit beneath them; for what reason do you sit here under this wretched tree?”
The Buddha said,
“Great King! One finds joy under the protection of one’s kinsmen.”
He thought to himself: "The World-Honored One has merely shown compassion for the country of Śrāvastī!
He then turned his army back and returned to Śrāvastī.
The unbelieving and unfaithful ministers and brahmins spoke thus a second and a third time:
"The Śākyas previously insulted the King, calling him the son of a low-born slave woman; you should now go and punish them."
At that time, the king immediately assembled his fourfold army and proceeded toward Śrāvastī; not far from Kapilavastu, he established a small camp to shield himself and remained there.

At that time, the Śākyas of Kapilavastu were all capable of shooting at great distances; there was not one among them who missed the mark. Some could hit a target one *yojana* away, some could hit a target seventy *li* away, and others could hit targets sixty, fifty, forty, or thirty *li* away.

At that time, there were those who shot at King Vairāṭa’s camp; some hit the top of a parasol, the shaft of the parasol, or the parasol-head; some hit the axle of a chariot; some hit the horse's bridle, the bit, or the halter; some hit the finger-seal; and some hit the ear-ornament, the crest-jewel, or merely broke a loose bead—but they never wounded any flesh.
At that time, King Virūḍhaka was greatly terrified and asked,
"How far away from here are the Śākyas?
A minister replied:
"It is seventy *li* from here.
Upon hearing this, the king became even more terrified and said,
"Will I and my army not be harmed by those sons of the Śākyas?"
Then the minister Asraddha addressed the king, saying:
"Those Śākyas all uphold the five precepts as lay devotees (upāsakas); even unto death they never take the life of a living being."
"O King, proceed forward alone; do not be afraid.
He then went and surrounded the city of Kapilavastu.
The bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If he does not grant us entry by opening the gates, we shall never succeed.
At that time, the people within the city were divided among themselves;
some said, "We should give him the city."
Some said, "Do not give it. Then they cast lots;

at that time, the Māra Pāpīyas was among the multitude in the city of Yugaṃdhara and took the lot seven times. Consequently, the lots for the city of King Vairāṭa became numerous, and so they opened the gates to him.

The soldiers immediately entered, closed the city gates behind them, and dug pits in the streets and alleys as deep as a man’s waist; they buried all the members of the Śākya clan—men and women, great and small—intermingled without any gaps between them, and ordered great elephants to trample over them.
At that time, Mahānāman the Śākya, who was the maternal grandfather of King Virūḍhaka, said to the Śākyas:
"You all should not merely look on as King Virūḍhaka releases great elephants to trample people to death; you should rather contemplate the causal conditions of the retribution for past karma."
"The karmic retribution for the fixed deeds committed by the Śākyas in the past must now be experienced.
When King Virūḍhaka heard this, he spoke to Mahānāman, the son of the Śākyas, saying:
"What wish do you desire?"
Mahānāman said: "The Śākyas have already been killed; I am now in such distress that what use is there for a boon?
If you would grant me a boon, let me enter the pool, and during the interval of my being in the water, let the Śākyas emerge without being killed."
King Vairāṭa thought to himself,
"One cannot remain in the water for long.
He said, "I grant you your wish."
Mahānāma immediately entered the pool and tied his hair to the root of a tree, whereupon he passed away beneath the water.
King Virūḍhaka then asked his ministers,
"Why has the Śākya son Mahānāma been in the water for so long?"
A bystander looked at him and replied,
"He is already dead.
The king said:
"Bring it out. He was immediately brought forth and presented to the king.
When King Virūḍhaka saw him, he immediately conceived a heart of compassion and said:
“Mahānāman, for the sake of his kinsmen, he does not spare even his own life.
He then commanded his men to release the Śākyas;
they, having received the instruction, released them.
The Śākyas, having been plundered, stripped, and robbed, arrived at the saṃghārāma with their bodies bare.
The bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to give them robes, thinking:
"The Buddha has not permitted us to give robes to laypeople."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "Borrow some robes;
do not let him come before me in the state of nakedness.
They then immediately borrowed robes for him.
At that time, Śāriputra was traveling with the Buddha through the kingdom of Kośala; while resting at a certain spot, he forgot his saṃghāṭī robe, which he left on the ground before departing.
The Buddha, remembering this, said to Ānanda:
"Take this robe; take it with the intention of a close friend."
Ānanda asked, "In what way does one take [something] with the intention of a close friend?
The Buddha said:
"Accommodate whatever they grasp so as to bring them joy.
[The interlocutor asks: "How does one accommodate whatever they grasp so as to bring them joy? He replied:
“There are seven qualities that constitute a true friend who acts out of benefit and compassion.

What are the seven? They are: giving what is difficult to give; doing what is difficult to do; enduring what is difficult to endure; confiding in one’s secrets; not disclosing them to others; not abandoning one in times of suffering; and not treating one with contempt when one is poor or lowly.”
"It is thus, Ānanda!
These seven qualities constitute what is called a true friend—one who benefits, shows compassion, and brings one joy.
He then spoke these verses:
One who can give what is difficult to give, perform what is difficult to do, and endure what is difficult to endure is a true and virtuous friend;
one who shares secret matters, conceals each other’s faults, does not abandon one in times of suffering, and does not treat one with contempt despite poverty or low status.
"If a person can practice these seven dharmas, they are called a true friend; one should associate with such a person.
The Buddha said, "Such a friend as this should be accepted."
That bhikṣu took [the robe] perceiving one who was not a friend to be a friend. The Buddha said:
"One should not take [it] perceiving one who is not a friend to be a friend.
That bhikṣu took a *pālikara* robe perceiving one who was not a friend to be a friend. The Buddha said:
"One should not take this robe with the intention of making it a personal gift; if it is insufficient, one should not take it.
At that time, the Buddha was in the city of Pāvā. There was a Malla named Lohitya, who had been a close friend of Ānanda during his time as a layman.
Then Ānanda, having dressed and taken his bowl, went to that house and sat down upon the seat;
Lūyī was away and not at home. Ānanda asked his wife, saying, "Is Lūyī here?"
He replied, "He is not here. Ānanda said:
"Bring the robe chest here.
He immediately brought it and placed it before Ānanda.
Then Ānanda took the robes of great value and carried them back to the saṃghārāma, where he prepared face towels and body towels for the senior elders.
At that time, Lūyanamāra returned home, and his wife told her husband about this matter.
Her husband immediately went to the saṃghārāma and approached Ānanda, asking:
"Did you come to my house?"
He replied, "I have. [The other asked,] "Did you take anything?"
He replied, "I have taken some.
[The other asked,] "For what reason did you take the coarse ones and not the fine ones?"
Ānanda said, "I have a specific need for such a robe.
The bhikṣus then thought to themselves:
"Is it appropriate to accept such a robe from a layperson with whom one has a close and intimate relationship?
He asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"It is appropriate to accept it."
"What is meant by 'that which should be accepted from a close friend'?
It is, for example, as Ānanda did regarding Lūṇamāra. The bhikṣus said:
"If the owner is not present, should one take it?
The Buddha said,
"It is permitted for a close friend to take it, whether the owner is present or absent."
At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī and did not accept the invitation for a meal.
It is the constant practice of all Buddhas that, when they do not accept an invitation, they later conduct an inspection of the various quarters.
While making a round through the various quarters, he saw in one place a bhikṣu who was ill; there was no one to attend to him or provide for his needs, and he lay amidst his own excrement and urine.
Having seen this, he went to where the bhikṣu was and, knowing the situation, asked the bhikṣu intentionally:
"For what reason are you lying amidst excrement and urine? Is there anyone to attend to you or provide for your needs?"
He replied, “No. The World-Honored One asked again:
"Why is there none?
He replied, "When I was not ill, I did not look after others' illnesses; therefore, now that I am ill, there is no one to look after me or provide for my needs."
The Buddha said:
"If you do not attend to or provide for the sick, you will gain no benefit and obtain nothing.
If you bhikṣus do not look after one another, who then should attend to the sick?"
Then the World-Honored One immediately assisted the sick bhikṣu in rising, wiped away the bodily impurities, and having wiped them, washed him.

Having washed him, he further laundered his robes and dried them in the sun. He discarded the old, worn-out bedding grass, swept the dwelling place, and smeared it with a coating of mud and water until it was utterly pure. He then spread fresh grass and laid out a robe; once the sick bhikṣu was settled back in bed, he covered him with another robe and departed.

At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished his meal, he assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of these events. Having related in detail what he had previously observed while walking through the rooms—namely, how a sick bhikṣu who had not accepted the invitation was attending to his own affairs—he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, you bhikṣus, you ought to attend to sick bhikṣus; you must not neglect them."
One should act as a caregiver for the sick; one should not fail to do so.
If anyone wishes to make offerings to me, they should make offerings to the sick.
It is permitted that the preceptor (upādhyāya) of that bhikṣu, or one who shares the same preceptor, the ācārya, or one who shares the same ācārya, or a disciple should attend to him.
If there is no one at all who wishes to look after him, the Sangha should assign a caregiver.
If he refuses, they should appoint one in successive order.
If he refuses even when appointed in order, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If there are no bhikṣus, a bhikṣuṇī should perform whatever she is permitted to do, but she must not touch a bhikṣu.
If there are no bhikṣuṇīs, a śikṣamāṇā should perform whatever she is permitted to do, but she must not touch a bhikṣu.
If there is no śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera should perform [the duties].
If there is no śrāmaṇera, a śrāmaṇerī should perform whatever she is capable of doing; however, she must not touch a bhikṣu.
If there is no śrāmaṇerī, an upāsaka should perform [the duties].
If there is no upāsaka, an upāsikā should perform whatever she is capable of doing; however, she must not touch a bhikṣu.

There are five things that make a patient difficult to care for: desiring to eat what one ought not to eat and refusing to take medicine; having a caregiver who possesses sincere intent but does not speak the truth; failing to act when one should act and failing to remain still when one should remain still; being unable to endure physical pain; and having some degree of physical capacity yet refusing to perform tasks oneself while relying on others to do them. These are the five difficulties for a patient.
There are five qualities by which a patient is easy to care for: they do not eat what they ought not to eat;

they take pleasure in taking medicine; they speak the truth to the caregiver; they walk when it is appropriate to walk and do not walk when it is inappropriate; they stay when it is appropriate to stay; they are able to endure physical pain; and they perform whatever slight tasks they are capable of performing. When a patient possesses these five qualities, they are easy to care for.

Furthermore, there are five conditions by which a patient is difficult to attend to: the four matters are as mentioned above; the fifth is being unable to sit quietly and still the inner mind. With these five conditions, one is difficult to attend to.

There are five qualities by which a sick person is easy to care for. Four are as mentioned above; the fifth is that they are able to sit in stillness and quiet the inner mind. A sick person possessing these five qualities is easy to care for.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling on a road in the kingdom of Kośala who arrived at a small dwelling place. There he saw a sick bhikṣu who had no one to attend to him, lying in his own excrement and urine.
He had this thought: "The World-Honored One has given this instruction:
'One should attend to the sick; one should not neglect them.'"
One should act as a caregiver for the sick; one should not fail to act as a caregiver for the sick.
One should provide offerings to the sick; one should not fail to provide offerings to the sick.
Whoever provides offerings to the sick, it is as if they are making offerings to me.
He then attended to the patient.

When the patient died, the bhikṣu took the deceased’s robes and bowl and went to the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī; he approached the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One said:
"Excellent, excellent, bhikṣu!"
That you are able to attend to the sick bhikṣu is precisely what one should do; you should act as a caregiver for the sick bhikṣu.
To provide care for a sick bhikṣu is to provide care for me.
"When someone comes bringing the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case of a deceased bhikṣu, the Saṃgha present at this residence should divide them.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"The robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case of a deceased bhikṣu should be given to the caregiver; they should be granted by performing a formal motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) in this manner."
At that time, the attendant of the sick person should go before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the monks, and announce as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has passed away at that residence; his robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container shall be divided by the Saṃgha present here at this residence.
Thus it was said a second and a third time.

From within the Saṃgha, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether an elder, a junior monk, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya, provided they are capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—should make the following formal motion:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!
A certain bhikṣu has passed away; his robes, alms bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage containers should be divided by the Saṃgha present at this residence.
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha is willing to listen, let the Sangha grant [this] to the bhikṣu who is tending to the sick.
This is the motion. "Venerable Sangha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has passed away; his robes, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and containers for storing clothing should be divided by the Saṃgha present at this residence.
The Saṃgha now grants the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container to this monk who is tending to the sick.

Those elders who consent to granting the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container to this monk who is tending to the sick should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.

"The Sangha has already consented to grant the robe, bowl, sitting mat, needle case, and clothing storage container to the bhikṣu who attended to the sick. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
If, within the Saṃgha, a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed to appoint one person to divide the deceased’s robes and belongings, it is no different from this [procedure].
One adds only a single phrase, saying:
“The Saṃgha gives these robes to monk so-and-so; monk so-and-so shall then return them to the Saṃgha.”
"Thus it was declared.
At that time, many learned bhikṣus died in Śrāvastī, and they left behind many sets of the three robes (*tricīvara*).
The bhikṣus did not know which ones should be given to those who had tended to the sick.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to give [the robes] to those who were the deceased’s regular attendants.

When the Buddha had permitted the giving of robes to those who nursed the sick, there were bhikṣus who attended to the sick only slightly—perhaps helping them rise once, or helping them lie down once, or providing them with a single twig for cleaning teeth or water—and they would immediately take their robes and bowls.
The Buddha said:
“One should not take another’s robes and bowl simply for providing minor nursing care.
There are five conditions under which a caregiver should not take the clothing or bowl of a patient.”
What are the five?
First, not knowing what may or may not be eaten by the patient; giving what may be eaten and withholding what may not be eaten.
Second, treating the patient with contempt and disdain regarding their excrement, urine, saliva, and vomit.
Third, they lack a heart of compassion, acting solely for the sake of food and clothing.
Fourth, they are unable to attend to the sick with medicine and care until they recover or pass away.
Fifth, being unable to preach the Dharma to the sick so as to gladden them, while one’s own practice of wholesome dharmas declines.
Possessing these five qualities, one should not accept the clothing or requisites of a sick person.
There are five qualities for which one should give clothing to a caregiver.
What are the five?
First, knowing what the patient may or may not eat, and being able to provide what they may eat.
Second, not to despise or treat with contempt the excrement, urine, saliva, or vomit of a sick person.
Third, to possess a heart of compassion and kindness, rather than acting for the sake of food or clothing.
Fourth, to be able to manage their medicine and care until they recover or pass away.
Fifth, one is able to preach the Dharma to the sick, causing them to rejoice, while one’s own self increases in wholesome qualities.
Possessing these five qualities, one should accept the clothing and requisites of the sick.
If, when a sick person is about to pass away, they speak these words:
"I give these various possessions of mine to the Buddha, to the Dharma, or to the Sangha; or to a stūpa, or to human beings."
‘If I give it after my death, or if I do not die, let me have it returned.
The Buddha said: “It should not be given in this manner; it should be distributed among the present Saṃgha.”
That sick bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I should accept these inferior three robes, for I fear that those who attend to me will take them away.
The Buddha said:
"One should not think: 'I have received these poor-quality triple robes; I fear the attendant for the sick will take them away.
One should instead receive those that are of good quality."
At that time, the sick person took his robes and bowl and placed them elsewhere, fearing that the attendant would take them; later, when he recovered, there was nothing left for him to wear.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not entertain such a thought."
"I am sending these robes elsewhere, fearing that the one tending to the sick might receive them.
At that time, many learned bhikṣus passed away in Śrāvastī; those bhikṣus possessed many sets of the three robes.
The bhikṣus did not know what kind of robe they should provide for the bhikṣu attending to the sick.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should observe how this attendant behaves."
If one can regard the patient with the highest degree of care, one should provide the three superior robes;
if with a middling degree, the three middling robes;
and if with an inferior degree, the three inferior robes.
At that time, a monk in Śrāvastī who was in debt passed away. The monks did not know who should repay the debt, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use an extra robe (*ātiriktacīvara*) to repay it; if there is no such item, sell the three robes (*tricīvara*) to do so, and give whatever remains to the attendant."
He listened as the attendant examined the sick monk and asked:
"Which are the three robes? Which is the extra robe?"
To whom do you owe? Who owes you?
To whom should you give?
"If one does not inquire, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu whose body was afflicted with sores that defiled his robes and bedding. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep a body-covering robe."
Some had their body hair matted and stuck to their sores, or they suffered from pain at times. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to take a high-priced, fine garment to cover the body, wearing it both inside and out over the *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*."
If one arrives at the house of a layperson, one should say:
"I am suffering from a sore.
If the layperson says:
"Do not suffer; simply sit down.
[The Buddha continued,] "You should lift your *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* (undergarment) and sit.
At that time, a bhikṣu suffered from a prolapsed hemorrhoid; he used a rough wooden stick as a probe and suffered great pain. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to wipe [the bowl] with wool, cotton, or bird feathers.
After using it, they set it aside without washing it; when the bhikṣus saw this, they looked upon it with contempt and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not set it aside without washing after use; it must be washed."
After he had washed it, he did not wring out the water; it became rotten and infested with insects. The Buddha said:
"One should wring out the water and dry it in the sun.
At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu whose body was afflicted with sores, which soiled his robes and bedding. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen: it is permitted to keep a cloth for covering sores.
If one does not have one’s own, it is permitted to take a cloth from among the Sangha to make one.
After it had been made, that bhikṣu did not dare to move the sore-covering cloth from this residence to another place. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen to the transfer.
Later, when the bhikṣu’s wound had healed, he did not take [the robe] back to its original place. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If it has healed, you should wash, dye, and repair it, and then return it to its original place."
"If you do not return it, you shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made a canopy; when the laypeople saw it, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!"
Lacking contentment and shame, they say of themselves,
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such as these?
"It is just like a king or a high minister.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not make canopies."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who defecated and urinated in an open space while naked.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to use grass, or tree leaves, or tree branches, or *elāyanta*, or *mora*, or *mora-mora*, or a woolen rug to make a screen for concealment."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made canopies. When the laypeople saw them, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of moderation and know no shame. They claim for themselves:
'We understand the True Dharma. "
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
It is just like a king and his ministers.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not make a canopy.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the heat while traveling on the road and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use grass or leaves, or any one of the ten kinds of robes, to make a covering for protection."
At that time, the community of monks obtained double-layered robes (*saṃghāṭī*), and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to keep them. At that time,
the bhikṣus did not know how to maintain the three robes (*tricīvara*), and the Buddha said:
"One should maintain them.
If one has doubts, one should relinquish them and receive them again.
If one does not maintain the three robes, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
The Buddha spoke thus:
"One should accept and maintain the three robes.
Yet they would take minor garments and treat them as the three robes—whether they were body-wiping cloths, face-wiping cloths, or bedding mats.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not take such minor garments as one's three robes.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

“Listen: one should make an *antarvāsa* from cloth four cubits long and two cubits wide; an *uttarāsaṅga* from cloth three cubits wide and five cubits long; and the *saṃghāṭī* should be made in the same manner.”
At that time, the robes of the bhikṣus became worn out.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to mend them. They did not know how to mend them.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear the *nāṃsī* (hempen robe) with double-layered borders woven together, and to patch it according to the size and shape—square or round—of each hole.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not enter villages wearing the *khaṇḍa-cīvara* (cut-and-sewn robe). When the laypeople saw them, they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying: [text continues]
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of restraint or contentment and know no shame;
they claim for themselves, 'I know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such as these?"
The monks reported to the Buddha, "They enter the village without wearing robes made of cut cloth, appearing just like the non-Buddhists. The Buddha said,
"One should not enter a village without wearing robes made of cut cloth."
There are five causes and conditions for retaining the saṃghāṭī:
if there is suspicion or fear;
or if it rains, or if there is suspicion of rain.
If one has begun making a *saṃghāṭī* but it is not yet finished;
or if it is being washed, dyed,
discolored, or carefully stored away.
"There are these five reasons for which one may leave the *saṃghāṭī* behind.
At that time, a bhikṣu put on his *saṃghāṭī* backward and entered a village; when the other bhikṣus saw this, they were displeased.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not enter a village wearing one's robes backward.

Out of fear and caution, the bhikṣu did not dare to wear his robes backward outside the village; consequently, he was afflicted by wind and dust, scorched by the sun, and defiled by insects and birds.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to wear your robes in reverse when outside the village.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a seamless robe (*saṃkakṣikā*) that was sufficiently wide and long; he then cut it up to make a patched-leaf robe (*parṇaka*), as he desired few things.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit you to do so.
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a seamless robe (kaṭhina) of sufficient width and length; wishing to make it into a five-patch robe (pañcakaṇḍuka-cīvara), he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted.
At that time, the bhikṣus had committed an offense regarding their robes and reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Permission is granted to relinquish them."

Whether before the Saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual, one should first relinquish [the object] and then perform the pure gift (*śuddhadāna*); it should not be done without relinquishing it.
One should first relinquish it and then send it away; it should not be sent away without having been relinquished.

If that bhikṣu does not relinquish it, but instead accepts it to make the three robes or a *pārikkhārika* robe, or uses it to make something other than a robe—whether it be old, damaged, or burnt—or wears it repeatedly.

"If one does not relinquish [the robe], one should not accept it for use as the three robes or as a *pārikkhāra* robe; rather, when it is worn out or burnt, one may use it to make non-robes, or wear it repeatedly."
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"If the *pārikara* (the requisite) is not present before one, does one incur a *niḥsargika-pāyattika* offense?
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
He put on the robe without first relinquishing it and informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, “One should not put it on without first relinquishing it.”
That bhikṣu was doubtful and did not dare to give away the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* robe, using it instead as a cloak.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to give it to others; I allow you to use it as a cloak."
At that time, the bhikṣus, fearing that their robes might be burned, stolen, or carried away by water, did not dare to wear them. They informed the Buddha, who said, "I allow you to wear them.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not relinquish their robes, but instead bartered them with others.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not trade without first relinquishing the robe;
one must relinquish it and only then exchange it. The bhikṣus thought thus:
"Does one commit an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) if the robe of the Saṃgha exceeds ten days?
He asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
At that time, if a bhikṣu makes a pure gift (*śuddhaka-dāna*) of a robe but does not return it to the owner, he commits a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he obstructs [the owner] and refuses to give it back, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, various bhikṣus did not dye their robes nor alter their color, and they left them in the houses of laypeople; the laypeople then took and wore them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not leave one's robes at the house of a layperson while they are still undyed or have not been altered in color; rather, one should dye them and alter their color to make the robes of a śramaṇa before leaving them at the house of a layperson."
At that time, a bhikṣu obtained a robe that was narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, and he received it to use as a saṃkakṣikā.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to make one."

At that time, the resident Saṃgha at another dwelling place obtained a large quantity of divisible robes and clothing. The group of six bhikṣus went outside the boundary and divided them among themselves.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not go outside the boundary to divide [the property]."

At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu with many acquaintances who was traveling through the human world. He received a large amount of clothing and requisites that were to be distributed by the *saṃgha* present there; however, as they were difficult to divide, he was apprehensive, fearing that the Buddha had not permitted the distribution of robes outside the boundary.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should issue a proclamation as follows:
'Come toward so-and-so; so-and-so shall distribute the robe.'"
"If there are robes that may be distributed, they should be divided.
He did not know when to divide them. [The Buddha said:

"One should make a signal, or measure the time, or measure the shadow, or produce smoke, or blow a conch shell, or beat a drum, or strike a ghaṇṭā, or announce that the time has arrived, or come oneself, or send someone to announce it; then one should give the portion."
Those bhikṣus rearranged the bedding and furniture, whereupon the Buddha said:
"You should not move them about.
There were some rooms with an abundance of bedding and others with a scarcity of bedding; regarding this, the Buddha said:
"From this day forward, it is permitted for a resident monk, or a *māmāte*, or a manager, or one who has received a room in turn, to move after first inquiring [of the occupant]."
After that bhikṣu had moved the bedding, he did not return it to its original place when he departed; other bhikṣus then used it again. The Buddha said:
"One should return the bedding to its original place before departing. If one does not do so, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, as the dwelling was collapsing, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to move their bedding and furniture, thinking:
"The Buddha has spoken thus:
'One should not move bedding and furniture.'"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a dwelling collapses or falls into ruin, one should move the bedding and furniture.
They moved the bedding and furniture to another room, but the other room did not dare to use them, so they became moldy and rotted.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should be used while lying down.

When the Buddha permitted its use for lying down, the bhikṣus did not wash their feet nor wipe their feet, but instead used it as a garment to lie upon. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not use [the robe] as an undergarment without having washed one's feet or wiped them.
Since the Buddha did not permit its use as an undergarment, the bhikṣus were apprehensive and did not dare to bring their hands or feet near it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"From the armpits down to the knees, one should not wear an undergarment directly against the body.
At that time, laypeople offered undergarments to the bhikṣus for use against the body, but the bhikṣus, out of fear and caution, did not dare to accept them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should accept clothing according to what the donor offers.
After he had repaired the ruined dwelling, he did not return the bedding and furniture. The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the quarters have been repaired, one should return the bedding and furniture.
If they are not returned, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus moved their fixed bedding and furniture from that residence to another place and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not move the settled bedding and furniture from this residence to that place.
In a land where the people were in rebellion and in fear, and even the residences were being destroyed, they were apprehensive and did not dare to move the bedding, thinking:
"The Buddha has not permitted moving the settled bedding and furniture from this residence to that place."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If such a situation arises, you are permitted to move [the bedding].
When they were moving the bedding, fearing it might touch their bodies, they did not dare to cover or conceal it, saying:
“The Blessed One does not permit the making of an undergarment.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should move it as best as possible to conceal it; however, if another person urges one to rise, one should not rise, nor should one urge that person to rise.”
"If there are other bhikṣus who can take care of them, they should be given to them; furthermore, if the kingdom is restored, [the bedding] should be returned.
When the people had returned to their peace and the dwellings were finished being repaired, yet the bedding was not returned, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If that is the case and the bedding is not returned, you must deal with it according to the Dharma."
At that time, Śāriputra obtained some fine scraps of cloth and wished to make a five-patch robe.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to make it."
At that time, there was a monastery where the resident Saṃgha obtained a large quantity of divisible clothing and requisites.
The group of six bhikṣus each relied upon one another to avoid taking responsibility for storing them, and consequently, they were lost.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted that those who have witnessed [the theft] should collect and secure the items.
At that time, visiting bhikṣus arrived and moved the clothing and belongings to other rooms, which was not done securely.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to designate a separate room as a storehouse.

Having announced the name of the room—whether it be a heated chamber, a multi-storied building, or a walking-hall—one should appoint a capable person to perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā) as previously described, making the following motion: [Insert the formal motion here]"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha designate this room of so-and-so as a storehouse.
This is the formal motion."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen. The Saṃgha is demarcating a certain room as a storehouse.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha demarcating this certain room as a storehouse remain silent; those who do not consent speak."
“The Saṃgha has already consented to designate the dwelling of so-and-so as a storehouse; the Saṃgha consents, for by its silence it approves. This matter is thus upheld.
At that time, that storehouse was unguarded and not secure.
"A servant or attendant shall be appointed by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
From within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and make the following formal motion:
'Venerable Sangha, listen!'"
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the guardian of goods.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu so-and-so as the guardian of property.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s appointment of the bhikṣu so-and-so as the guardian of property should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so as the guardian of goods; the Sangha consents, for by its silence it approves. This matter is thus upheld.
If a bhikṣu is unwilling to serve as the guardian of goods, one should provide him with an abundance of merit in the form of gruel.
"If you still refuse, then two shares of all the robes, food, and drink you receive should be given to them.
If you still refuse again, they shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ made a large bathing robe and sent someone to deliver it to the monastery.
The bhikṣus did not know what they should do, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Distribute it according to the order of seniority. If there is not enough, you should keep track of the sequence; when more is obtained, you should continue the sequence and give it out."
At that time, he gave a robe of great value in succession. The Buddha said:
"One should not give a robe of great value in succession; rather, one should give starting from the senior-most monk."
"If there is an inequality [in the distribution], one should take divisible robes from among the Sangha to ensure they are divided equally.
At that time, the Sangha obtained an Aṅganāra robe; the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep it."
At that time, a bhikṣu put on the saṃghāṭī robe and went into the heated hall and the dining hall; there, he was splattered with soup and rice, soiled by mud, and covered in smoke and dust.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not put on the saṃghāṭī robe when going into the heated hall or the dining hall."
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the cold during the winter months and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to wear it.
You must protect it with care and ensure it does not become soiled."
At that time, the bhikṣu put it on and went to the latrine; he was defiled by excrement and urine, becoming filthy and foul-smelling.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not put it on and go to the latrine."
At that time, a bhikṣu returned his robe to the room and was urgently pressed by the need to defecate or urinate. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a clothes rack, a peg shaped like a dragon's tooth, a shelter, a tree, some grass, or a stone near the latrine, I allow you to place your robe upon it."

If it rains and one becomes soaked, one should go to a place sheltered from the rain; if the rain comes from the side and soaks one, one should take hold firmly and not let oneself touch the latrine door while entering. One should step onto the stool properly, squatting well so as not to soil one's robes.
That bhikṣu put on his robes and went to the walking path (caṅkrama), where grass, insects, dust, and dew caused his saṃghāṭī robe to become soiled and ruined.
The bhikṣu informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not put on the saṃgha robes while going to the walking path."
At that time, there was an elderly senior monk who was ill; being frail and having traveled a long distance, he suffered from affliction.
[The Buddha said: "I allow you to spread a bedding mat upon it and lie down, protecting yourself."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having entered the rains retreat at one residence, subsequently stayed at another residence.
He did not know from which residence he should take his share of the provisions for the retreat.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to take [the portion] from the place where one has resided for a longer period.
If the duration of residence at both places is equal, it is permitted to take half from each."
Those bhikṣus divided the food for the summer retreat and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "It should not be divided;
one should eat according to what is offered.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had finished accepting the invitation from the brahmin of Veḷuvana, he addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Go and tell the brahmin Verañjā that the Buddha has accepted your invitation for the three-month summer retreat, and now wishes to travel through the human world.
Having received the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda went at once to where Verañjā was and said:
“The World-Honored One speaks thus:”
"Having already accepted your invitation for the three-month summer rains retreat, I now wish to travel through the human world.
When Vairaṇyā heard Ānanda’s words, she finally remembered:
"I invited the śramaṇa Gautama and the community of bhikṣus, yet throughout the ninety days I did not provide them with offerings."
Then Vairaṇyā went to where the Blessed One was, and after paying his respects and exchanging greetings, he withdrew to sit at one side.
At that time, the Blessed One, through countless skillful means, taught him the Dharma so as to bring him joy.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, Vairaṇyā was filled with immense joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will further accept my invitation for ninety days.”
The Buddha replied, "I have already accepted your invitation for ninety days; now I wish to travel through the human realm.
He addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.
The World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When Vairaṇyā heard that the Buddha had accepted her invitation, she rose from her seat, circumambulated the Buddha with joy, and departed.
That very night, he prepared various kinds of food and drink; at dawn the next day, he went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had arrived.
Then the World-Honored One, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and proceeded to the house, where he took his seat.

Then Vairaṇyā provided various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink as an offering to the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. After they had finished eating and set aside their bowls, she offered her three robes to the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus; each person was given two pieces of fine cotton cloth for their summer garments.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive summer robes.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen and receive.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and Upananda, hearing that the Buddha had permitted the acceptance of summer robes, sought and solicited summer robes at all times—during spring, summer, and winter.
While the summer retreat had not yet concluded, he both requested robes and accepted robes.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was observing the summer retreat at a certain residence. Hearing that another residence had obtained a large amount of summer retreat robes, he immediately went to that residence and asked:
"Have you all divided the summer robes yet?"
He replied, "It has not yet been divided.
[The other] said:
"Bring it here; I shall divide it with you.
He then went to another place and asked, "Have you received your share of the summer robes?"
He replied, "It has not yet been divided.
[The other] said:
"Bring it here; let us divide it with you.
At that time, Upananda divided the robes in many places and obtained a large share of robes, which he brought back into the Jetavana.
When the other bhikṣus saw him, they asked:
“The World-Honored One has prescribed that one may keep three robes; as for these many robes, whose robes are they?
He replied, “I divided my robes at various residences, and thus I obtained these many robes.”

Among them were those who had few desires and were content, who practiced the dhūta-austerities, who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame, and who delighted in training in the precepts; they censured the group of six bhikṣus and Pūraṇa-Kāśyapa, saying:
"The World-Honored One has permitted bhikṣus to receive summer robes; why do you seek and demand summer robes at all times—during spring, summer, autumn, and winter?"
"While the summer retreat has not yet concluded, they both beg for robes and receive robes.
Having received their share of robes while residing at this location, they then receive their share of robes at another location.
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was and reported these matters to him in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked Upananda, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Upananda! I have permitted bhikṣus to keep summer robes.
Why do you seek summer robes at all times—during spring, summer, and winter?"
"Can one both beg for robes and receive robes before the *varṣā* (rainy season retreat) has concluded?
Having received one's share of robes at this *varṣā* site, may one also receive a share of robes at another location?
Having rebuked the group of six bhikṣus and Upananda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"From this day forward, one must not at any time—whether in spring, summer, or winter—seek out a robe for the summer; nor should one beg for or receive a robe before the retreat has concluded. Furthermore, having received one's share of robes while observing the retreat in this location, one must not thereafter receive another share of robes in a different location."
"If anyone receives [the robe], they should be dealt with according to the Dharma.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who departed before the summer robes had been distributed. Later, when the other bhikṣus were distributing the summer robes, that bhikṣu returned from his travels and asked:
"Has the distribution of the summer robes been completed?"
He replied, "It has been divided. He asked:
"Will you take my share of the robes?
He replied, "I will not take it."
At that time, that bhikṣu spoke with anger and reproach to the other bhikṣus, saying:
"The robes had not yet been distributed when I went away on a journey; later, when the summer robes were being divided, I was staying here in retreat, yet they did not take my share of the robes."
The bhikṣus had this thought: "Is this sufficient to constitute a formal distribution of robes?
They went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Regarding the distribution of robes:
one should wait for others, and one should also entrust the portion of the summer robe to another person before departing.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who departed before the robes had been distributed; he made a hasty entrustment, saying to another person, "Receive my portion of the robe."
Later, when the bhikṣus were distributing the robes, they asked,
"Who will take the robe-portion for such-and-such a bhikṣu?
At that time, there was no one who would take his portion.
That bhikṣu returned and asked,
"Has the distribution of the robes been completed? They replied:
"It has already been divided. He asked,
"Will you take my share?"
He replied, "I did not take it.
That bhikṣu then spoke with anger and reproach to the other bhikṣus, saying:

“Before the robes had been distributed, I went away on a journey; having entrusted a fellow monk to take the robes for me, I remained here in retreat. Did they not distribute the robes and take a portion for me?”
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Will this suffice for the distribution of the robes?
They went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The components [of the robe] must be returned, and one person must also be formally entrusted with them.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, before the robes had been distributed, set out on a journey and entrusted a certain bhikṣu, saying, "Please take my summer robes for me."
At that time, as the bhikṣus were distributing the robes, they asked,
"Who will take the share of robe-material belonging to such-and-such a bhikṣu?
The one who had received the entrustment forgot and did not take it, and so the bhikṣus proceeded to distribute the robes.
That bhikṣu returned and asked,
"Has the summer robe-cloth been distributed yet? They replied:
"It has already been divided. He asked,
"Will you take my portion?"
He replied, "I did not take it.
That bhikṣu then spoke with anger and reproach to the other bhikṣus, saying:
“Before the robes had been distributed, I went away on a journey and subsequently entrusted a certain bhikṣu to take my share of the robes.
While I was staying here in retreat during the rains, he did not take my share of the robes for me.”
The bhikṣus did not know whether it constituted the distribution of robes or not.
They went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It constitutes the distribution; this was the fault of the one who forgot."
At that time, the bhikṣus set aside food for their summer retreat and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "You should not set it aside;
you should accept it according to what is offered.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana entered parinirvāṇa, leaving behind a great deal of property to be distributed, which the present community of monks (saṃgha) should divide.
That bhikṣu remained beyond the end of the rainy season retreat.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"He should not remain."
"This robe-cloth should be divided among the monks present.

At that time, there was a donor who, wishing to give to the stūpa and the Sangha, provided monastic dwellings and bath-houses; or for the sake of a newborn child, or for one's first tonsure, or for long hair, or for entering a new house, or for a funeral rite—on such occasions, the monks present obtained a great amount of divisible clothing and requisites.
The bhikṣus kept [the robes] until the summer retreat.
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, who said:
"They should not have been kept; these are 'out-of-season' robes (akālacīvara), and the present saṃgha should divide them."
At that time, there was a certain bhikṣu residing in a monastery who obtained a large quantity of robes and requisites for the summer retreat. He thought to himself: "What should I do with these?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"If there is a single bhikṣu who, while observing the rains retreat, receives a large quantity of robes and requisites for the monastic summer retreat, that bhikṣu should form this thought in his mind and say:”
"This is my property.
Whether it has been accepted or not, if another bhikṣu arrives, he should not receive a share.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained a large quantity of divisible clothing and requisites, and the Saṃgha split into two factions.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be divided into two parts.
If the robes and articles to be distributed have not yet been obtained, the Saṃgha shall split into two factions.
The Buddha said:
"One should ask the donor, 'To whom should this be given? If he says:"
"Give it to the Elder so-and-so.
One should then give it to the place where that elder is, following those words. If he says:
"I do not know. Or if one says:
"I gave both."
"It should be divided into two portions.
At that time, among the bhikṣus—both those who had already received robes and those who had not—the Saṃgha was split into two factions.
"Those who had already received robes should divide [their portion] into two parts."
If one has not yet received the robe, one should ask the donor:
"To whom should it be given? If he says:
"Give it to such-and-such an elder, so-and-so.
One should then give it to the place where that elder is, following those words. If he says:
"I do not know. Or if he says:
"I gave them both."
"It should be divided into two portions.
At that time, when the bhikṣus obtained clothing items intended for distribution, there was a bhikṣu who went from this group to that group.
"They should not give him a share," [it was said].
"If no robes or clothing have been obtained, and a bhikṣu goes from this group to that group,
he should not be given a share.
Whether robes or clothing have been obtained or not, if a bhikṣu goes from this group to that group...
"One should not give a share of the robes.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went from this community to that community; before he arrived, he died.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom his robes and bowl should be given.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"It should be given to whichever place he wishes to go.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went from this community to that community, and upon arriving, he died.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom the robes and bowl should be given.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"They should be given to whichever group he has joined."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having been subject to the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma), passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom his robes and bowl should be given, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Wherever the *karmavācanā* is performed in common, the Saṃgha should grant the formal act of suspension (*ukṣepaṇīya-karman*).

At that time, the Saṃgha residing at a certain location split into two factions. A donor invited these two groups of monks to a single location for a meal, and furthermore offered them robes and thread as gifts.
The bhikṣus did not know who should receive the robes and who should receive the thread;
they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should ask the donor:
'To whom is the robe given?
To whom is the thread given?'"
If he says, "Give it to such-and-such an elder," one should give it to whichever elder is located where that person indicates.
If one says, "I do not know," or if one says:
"Give it to both;
it should be divided into two portions.
At that time, the community of monks obtained robes for the summer retreat, and the Sangha split into two factions.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should divide [the robes] according to the number of people.
If the robes for the rainy season retreat have not yet been obtained, and the Saṃgha has split into two factions, [the division should be made accordingly].
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be divided by counting the number of people.
Whether the summer robes have been obtained or not yet obtained, if the Saṃgha has split into two factions, it should be divided by counting the number of people."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having obtained his summer robes, went to another community. The Buddha said:
"He should give them [to the other community].
If he has not yet obtained his summer robes and goes to another community.
The Buddha said:
"It should be given.
If one has not yet received the summer robes, or if one has already received the summer robes and goes to another division, the Buddha said:
"It should be given.
At that time, there was a householder who gathered the monks at their residence and provided them with food and drink from various locations, and offered robes as a gift.

The bhikṣus did not know what to do, so they informed the Buddha.
