The Buddha, employing countless skillful means, preached the Dharma to transform and enlighten him, causing him to attain great joy.
At that time, the brahmin, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, was filled with extreme delight and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow."
The Buddha said,
"Now that the community of bhikṣus is so numerous, you have come to believe in the non-Buddhist paths.
The brāhmaṇa replied:
"Although I have faith in the non-Buddhists and although the community of monks is large, please accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.

The World-Honored One spoke thus to him a second and a third time, and the Brahmin likewise addressed the World-Honored One a second and a third time; at that moment, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
When the brahmin saw that the Buddha had accepted [the invitation], he rose from his seat and returned home, saying to his relatives:
"Tomorrow I shall invite the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for a meal; please assist me in whatever preparations are required."
When his relatives heard this, they were all filled with joy; some began splitting firewood, some prepared the meal, and others fetched water.
Then the brahmin personally adorned the hall and arranged the seats, thinking:
"The Buddha and the community of bhikṣus shall sit upon these seats."
At that time, there was a Brahmin named Śaila in the city of Āmrapālī, who went together with five hundred Brahmins; the Brahmin Śreṇya constantly revered and looked up to him with devotion.

At that time, the brahmin Śaila went to his house accompanied by five hundred brahmins. It was the custom of the brahmin Śreṇya to rise and go out to welcome those who came and invite them into the house to sit; however, on this day, upon seeing them arrive, he neither rose to welcome them nor invited them to sit, but merely saw to it that his hall was decorated and fine seats were spread.
Śilpa asked, "Is it that you wish to take a wife,
or do you wish to give away a daughter?"
"Do you wish to invite the King?
Or do you wish to perform a great sacrifice? He then replied:
"I shall neither take a wife nor even invite the king; I wish to perform a great sacrifice and invite the Buddha and his community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus."

The śramaṇa Gautama possesses great renown as the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, the Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, the Sugata, the Lokavid, the Anuttara, the Puruṣadamyasārathi, the Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Buddha, and the Bhagavat.
Śaila asked Kātyāyana, "Is he truly the Buddha? He replied:
"It is truly the Buddha.
He asked again and again,
"Is it truly the Buddha?"
He replied, “It is indeed so. He asked:
"Where does the Buddha reside?
I now wish to see him.
At that time, Śakra raised his right hand and pointed, saying:
"He is staying there in that green grove. Śaila thought to himself:
"I should not go empty-handed; what should I bring with me when I go to see the śramaṇa Gautama?"
He then thought to himself:
"There are now eight kinds of beverages that were drunk by the ancient desireless sages:
pear juice, jambu fruit juice, jujube juice, sugarcane juice, *kharjūra* fruit juice, *śālukā* fruit juice, *bhallāśa* fruit juice, and grape juice."
At that time, the brahmin Śilpa took these eight kinds of drinks and went to where the Buddha was staying. He paid his respects, inquired after his well-being, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Then the World-Honored One, employing skillful means, preached the Dharma to instruct and transform him, causing him to attain joy.
Śilpa, having heard the Dharma, was filled with supreme joy and immediately offered the eight kinds of fermented liquors to the community of bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not dare to accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive these eight kinds of fermented liquors."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I allow you to drink the eight kinds of syrups; if they do not cause intoxication, they may be drunk outside of the proper time.
If they cause intoxication, they must not be drunk; if one drinks them, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.”
"Furthermore, one should not receive gruel on this day and keep it until the next; if one keeps it, it must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One departed from this dwelling and traveled through the Malla country toward the city of Pāvā.

At that time, the Mallas of Pāvā heard that the World-Honored One, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, was traveling through the human realm from Malla toward Pāvā. They made a mutual regulation among themselves:
"When the World-Honored One arrives, we must all go out together to welcome him; whoever does not welcome him shall be fined one hundred taels of gold."
At that time, there was a Mālava youth named Rūpi, who had no faith or devotion toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he had been a close friend of Ānanda during his days as a layman.
When Ānanda saw Rūpi from afar, he spoke to him, saying: "Excellent, Rūpi!"
"You are able to go out yourself to welcome the Buddha. He replied,
"Venerable Sir!"
I did not go out to welcome him.
In the city of Pāvā, a collective regulation had been established:
"If anyone does not go out to welcome the Buddha, they shall be fined one hundred taels of gold."
"It is for these reasons that he has come; it is not out of faith or reverence that he has come.
When Ānanda heard this, he was displeased and immediately went to where the World-Honored One was, saying to him:
"In this city of Pāvā, there is a son of the Mallas named Rudraka, who was a close friend of mine during my time as a layman."
Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will provide assistance so that they may attain faith and joy.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"What difficulty is there in this?
Even if there were another such person, it would still not be difficult."
At that time, the World-Honored One, through his mind of loving-kindness, moved Rauruka-māra so that he would approach the World-Honored One, just as if someone were leading him there.
Thus Rauruka went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached the Dharma for him to instruct and transform him, causing him to attain joy. Immediately, he became free from dust and defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and attained the Dharma, he realized its fruit and testified to it, saying to the Buddha:
"O Virtuous One!..."

"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, becoming a lay follower (*upāsaka*). I shall refrain from taking life, up to and including refraining from drinking intoxicants.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will constantly accept my offerings of robes, food and drink, medicine, and bedding."
The Buddha told Lu-yi:
"You are now a student who, possessing clear wisdom, has distanced yourself from dust and left behind defilement to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
You have then said:"
"May he always receive from me robes, food and drink, medicine, and bedding.
Furthermore, there will be other disciples who, possessing clear wisdom, have distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement to attain the pure Dharma-eye; they too shall likewise say:
"May he always receive from me robes, food and drink, medicine, and bedding."

At that time, the World-Honored One did not accept invitations from any single individual in the city of Pāvā. Instead, every household within the city gathered food and drink together in one place to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

At that time, Lu-yi went to the place where food was being prepared and saw that there were no cakes. He immediately prepared various kinds of cakes during the night and gave them to the bhikṣus the following day.
The bhikṣus did not accept [the offering], saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to receive cakes before the morning meal.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen and receive [this teaching].
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from the city of Pāvā to Āṭavī.
Now, in the residence at Āṭavī, there were two bhikṣus who were professional barbers by trade; they were father and son who had both gone forth into homelessness.
At that time, two bhikṣus heard that the Buddha had gone from Pāvā to Ātumā, and they thought to themselves:
"What kind of offerings should we prepare for the World-Honored One?"
The father said to his son:

"I shall now seek out a place for shaving the hair; you may go to a place where coins are made and seek employment there. If you obtain anything, you should prepare and provide gruel as an offering to the World-Honored One."

At that time, the father went to serve as a barber for others, while the son went to work for wages; whatever they earned, they spent entirely on preparing rice gruel, which they took to offer to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"Where did you obtain this porridge?
Ānanda then reported the matter to the Buddha in detail, and the Buddha said:
“An ordained person should not shave the hair of a layperson, except for one who wishes to go forth into homelessness.
If a person who has been shaved goes forth, they should not keep a razor; if they do keep one, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.”
At that time, the community of monks obtained hair-cutting razors and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep them.
Then the World-Honored One traveled from Āṭavī to Kāmalā.
When the bhikṣus obtained such medicinal roots as ālūmīna, lumbinī, luptideva, tandu, tandulakalāpa, and śirālū, the bhikṣus did not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept such medicinal roots."
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to accept them.

Among them were the bhikṣus of the country of Kāmala, who obtained such medicines for life as long as they lived— śālmali, mahāśālmali, apricot kernels, *pindīlu*, and *cīnakarīra*— yet the bhikṣus would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to accept such medicines for as long as life lasts.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to accept them."
At that time, the World-Honored One traveled from Kāmarūpa to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Pilindavatsa was residing in that country when he suffered from a cracked foot; a physician instructed him to apply ointment to his foot.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to apply ointment.
He did not know with what medicine he should apply it.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to smear it with ghee, oil, or fat.
When his hand smelled of the ghee and oil, the Buddha said:
"I allow the use of a medicinal applicator.
At that time, as they applied it with their hands, their feet became greasy.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to apply it foot to foot."
When the foot ointment was placed in a shallow vessel and did not remain secure, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a jar.
If it was troublesome because of dust entering it, the Buddha said:
"Listen: one may make a canopy.
At that time, the place where the oil jar was suspended was not secure.
The Buddha said:
“[One may] hang it beneath the bed, or suspend it on a wall, or upon a dragon-tooth peg.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from headaches; the physician instructed them to apply oil to the crown of their heads. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, “I allow you to do so.”
Being fearful and cautious, they did not dare to apply scented oil. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to apply it.
This is the proper method for using oil."

At that time, a bhikṣu suffered from wind-disorder (vāta). A physician instructed him to prepare a medicine to eliminate wind-disorder. Regarding this medicine for eliminating wind-disorder: it consists of steamed rice grains, steamed dregs of wine, or barley; or various herbs that treat wind-disorder; or bran and husks; or boiled urine.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I permit it at the proper time.
Piṅgalavatsa needed a cauldron for boiling; the Buddha said:
"Listen; you may keep it.
The community of monks obtained a large cauldron, and the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted to keep [pots].
Pindola Bharadvāja obtained three kinds of pots:
a copper pot, an iron pot, and an earthenware pot.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep it.
It is likewise permitted for the community of monks to keep it."
Later, when earthenware jars, bronze jars, iron jars, and ceramic jars were obtained, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to keep them.
It is the same for the Saṃgha; I permit them to keep them."
When Pīṅgalavatsa obtained a griddle for frying pancakes, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep it.
It is likewise permitted for the Saṃgha to keep one."
Piliṅgavatsa obtained a copper ladle and a pitcher; the Buddha said, "I permit you to keep them.
It is the same for the Saṃgha; I permit them to keep them."
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 42;
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 43 (Part 7 of the Three-Volume Edition);
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated by Zhu Fonian and others, the second part of the Bhaiṣajyavastu.
At that time, there was a monk who had undergone emesis and purgation, and he sent people from the city of Śrāvastī to cook gruel for him.
Due to certain circumstances, the city gates opened late, and before he could obtain the gruel, he died.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to establish a *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground) within the monastery. It should be established by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.

One should announce the name of the room, the location, the *jentāka* (heating hall), or the *caṅkrama* (walking path). From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman*—whether it be the senior monk (*sthavira*), a monk of intermediate rank, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya but is capable of performing the *karman*—should be appointed. He should then make the following motion (*jñapti*):"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now demarcate a certain place as *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground).
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*)."
"Venerable Sangha, listen! The Sangha now demarcates a certain place to establish it as a pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha’s demarcation of this place as a pure ground, remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to demarcate a certain area as *śuddhasthāna* (pure ground). Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
There are four kinds of pure grounds:
first, when a donor or a supervisor is constructing a monastery (*saṃghārāma*), they designate the area by saying:
"Such-and-such a place is designated as a pure ground for the Saṃgha.
Second, if one constructs a monastery for the Saṃgha but has not yet assigned it to the Saṃgha.
Third, whether it has partial fences, or mostly lacks fences, or is entirely without fences; the same applies to walls or moats.
"The fourth [method] is for the Saṃgha to perform a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) to establish the boundary. The bhikṣus then thought:
"Should the bhikṣus' dwellings also be established as pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*)?"
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be made; the same applies to removing [the markers] from the quarters of bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, śrāmaṇeras, or śrāmaṇerīs."
"If the temple buildings of spirits and deities are also treated in this manner, they may likewise be established as pure ground (*śuddhasthāna*).
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know which places constituted pure ground;
they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should demarcate it.
If one suspects that there was previously a pure ground (śuddhasthāna), one should first release the boundary and then demarcate it again.
At that time, a bhikṣu was repairing an old monastery and did not know whether he could establish it as a pure ground.
The Buddha said, "It may be done.

At that time, a tree grew on impure ground, its branches and leaves casting shade over pure ground. Then, the bhikṣus wished to place pure objects upon it, but they did not know whether it was pure or impure.
The Buddha said, "If the root is in impure ground, the ground itself is impure.

At that time, there was a tree whose roots were in pure ground, yet its branches and leaves covered impure ground. The bhikṣus wished to place pure objects upon it, but they did not know whether it was pure or not.
The Buddha said, "If the roots are in pure ground, it is considered pure.

At that time, there was a tree whose roots were in impure ground, while its branches and leaves covered pure ground, and its fruit fell onto pure ground. The bhikṣus did not know whether this was pure or not.
The Buddha said:
"If it falls of its own accord without being touched by anyone, it is pure. [The monks asked:
"What if it falls because it was blown by the wind or struck by rain? Or if it falls because it was touched by a monkey or various birds? Is this considered pure or not?"
The Buddha said:
"If one does not intentionally intend for it to fall, it is pure.
When the root of a tree is on pure ground and the fruit falls onto impure ground, a bhikṣu wonders whether it is pure or not.
The Buddha said, "It is pure.

At that time, some bhikṣus were planting cucumbers, sugarcane, and vegetables on impure ground, with branches and leaves covering the pure ground; the bhikṣus did not know whether this was considered pure or not.
The Buddha said, "It is impure.

At that time, there were those who planted melons, sugarcane, and vegetables on pure ground, with their branches and leaves covering the impure ground; they did not know whether it was considered pure or not.
The Buddha said, "It is pure.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate fruits that were not pure; when the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are without shame or modesty and know no satiety.
They claim for themselves:
‘I know the True Dharma.’”
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
One does not perform the ritual purification (*parikarma*) for eating fruit.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat fruit that has not been purified; one should eat it only after it has been purified.
One should consume food after performing five kinds of purification methods:

purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by a wound, purification by pecking by a bird, and purification by rendering it unfit for seed. These five kinds of purification should be applied before eating."
Among these, that which is purified by a knife, purified by a wound, or purified by a bird should have the seeds removed before being eaten.
That which is purified by fire or purified by being unfit for sowing may be eaten in its entirety.
Furthermore, there are five other kinds of purification:
"If it has its bark stripped, or its skin peeled, or is rotten, or broken, or withered and shriveled.
At that time, the community of monks obtained a fruit orchard; the Buddha said, "I allow you to accept it."
Furthermore, not knowing who should take charge of it,
the Buddha said:
"It may be a lay attendant of the saṃghārāma, or a śrāmaṇera, or an upāsaka."
The person guarding [the fruit] wished to receive a share. The Buddha said:
"One should calculate the value of the food consumed and pay the price accordingly.
At that time, a bhikṣu ate a fruit whose seeds had not been broken; after he defecated, the seeds sprouted. The bhikṣu, being apprehensive and cautious, said:
"I eat raw seeds," he said to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense; it is pure."
At that time, the bhikṣus grew vegetables; after they themselves had scattered the seeds, they became doubtful and said,
"We ourselves planted these," and did not dare to eat them.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The seeds have already transformed; you are permitted to eat them all.
At that time, a bhikṣu moved some vegetables to another location to plant them and felt doubt, saying:
"Did you grow it yourself?
[The monk] did not dare eat it.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because they are grown anew, their consumption is permitted.

If one has personally cultivated cucumbers, sugarcane, grapes, pears, crabapples, *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, pepper, ginger, or *pippalī*, as well as plants that have been transplanted, these may be eaten."
At that time, there was a young novice who, while carrying pure food across the water, was unable to lift it himself. The Buddha said:
"I allow the great bhikṣus to support the novice so that he may cross over."
At that time, there was a young novice who, carrying pure food, was unable to get onto the bank.
The Buddha said, "I allow a senior bhikṣu to assist him in getting up.

At another time, there was a small novice who could not lift the pure food to hang it on a wall or a peg shaped like a dragon’s tooth, nor could he bring it down. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Allow a bed or a stool to be placed below so that one may go up and down.
At that time, some bhikṣus had butter jars and oil jars that were not covered. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a lay attendant) cover them."
"If there is no *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible), one should hold the lid with one's own hand and suspend it above [the food], but one must not let the hand touch the food.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate impure vegetables; when the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, and never knowing satiety, they take the lives of sentient beings while claiming,
"I know the True Dharma.
How can such people possess the True Dharma?
"If the vegetables are impure, one should eat them [only after purification].
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat impure vegetables; they must be purified."
At that time, he then performed the ritual purification himself. The Buddha said:
"One should not perform the ritual purification oneself; one should have a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle food) perform the purification.
At that time, a bhikṣu took the food with his own hands and then had someone else perform the purification. The Buddha said:

"One should not take food with one's own hand and then have someone else perform the ritual purification (*parikarma*); rather, one should place it on the ground and have someone else perform the purification.
After the purification had been performed, he ate without receiving the food. The Buddha said:
"One should not eat after performing the purification without having received the food; rather, after performing the purification, one should wash one's hands and then receive the food."
After he had washed the vegetables along with their roots and performed the purification again, the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the purification again after having washed them;
this washing itself constitutes the purification."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who previously harbored ill will toward another; he then touched the other’s pure food with the intention:
“May this bhikṣu receive impure food.
Did that bhikṣu know whether it was pure or impure?
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"For one who touches it, it is impure; for one who does not touch it, it is pure.
One who touches it commits a *duṣkṛta* offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, out of resentment toward another bhikṣu, touched that pure food belonging to a young śrāmaṇera with the intention:
"May his preceptor and teacher receive impure food."
That bhikṣu did not know whether it was pure or impure.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"That which has been touched is impure; that which has not been touched is pure."
"To touch it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, the attendants thought to themselves:
"If we force-feed the bhikṣus much food and they do not finish eating so that there is a remainder, we ourselves shall eat it."
That bhikṣu should verbally stop him, saying:
"Do not attach it.
If he does not desist, he should move his food vessel slightly away from the grass.
That bhikṣu did not know whether it was pure or impure.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is pure."
At that time, various lay devotees (gṛhapati) took food and drink vessels to the saṃghārāma to offer them to the bhikṣus.
Later, when the lay devotees returned, they would either eat themselves, take [the food] back home, or give it to the bhikṣus to eat.
The bhikṣus were fearful and cautious, not daring to eat, thinking to themselves:
"We previously handled this with our own hands.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This belongs to the donor; you may wash your hands and receive food for the sake of the donor.
At that time, a sick bhikṣu required gruel, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to cook it."
"If there is no one to listen [to the instructions],
you may cook for yourselves. If they were to cook for one another, not knowing how to do so,
the Buddha said:

"Allow a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person) to wash the vessel, place water and rice inside, and boil it until it bubbles. Then, having washed your hands and received [the vessel], you may cook it yourself until it is done.
At that time, he did not know whether it was cooked or not.
The Buddha said:
"One should stir it with a ladle and observe; if the liquid flows down following the ladle, it is cooked.
If it is cooked, one should pour it into another vessel."
The one pouring out the gruel became exhausted from also having to hold the vessel.
The Buddha said:
"One who pours out the gruel should not also hold the vessel; another person should be assigned to hold the vessel."
"If the hand is burned by the heat, one should grasp tongs, a hot cloth, or grass.
If an insect falls into the porridge, it should be removed.
His hand was burned; the Buddha said:
"One should remove it with a ladle.
When he wished to divide [the food], the Buddha said,
"I allow you to divide it."
Furthermore, not knowing with what vessel to divide [the portion], the Buddha said:
"Whether using a ladle, a small bowl, a medium-sized bowl, or a spoon to make the division; if the bowl is not level, one should make a stand for it; if it is dusty, one should make a lid."
He lifted up his bowl and utensils without having washed them, and other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved.
The Buddha said:
"One should wash them thoroughly before lifting them up."
Having washed them, they did not use ash or bathing beans to cleanse the impurities.
The Buddha said:
"One should use ash and bathing beans to wash."
Having washed them, he did not dry them; as soon as he lifted the vessels, insects appeared. The Buddha said:
"One should not lift them without drying them; one should allow them to become dry before lifting them."
That vessel had a sunken hole; when food entered it, he repeatedly pulled it out and washed it, thereby damaging it by piercing it.
The Buddha said:
"Wash it wherever it can be washed; for the rest, there is no offense."
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"Is it permissible to stay overnight with gruel within the boundary, to cook it within the boundary, or to cook it oneself?
The Buddha said:
"One should not stay overnight within the boundary, cook within the boundary, or cook for oneself.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"If we re-cook the gruel, may we stay overnight within the boundary, cook within the boundary, and cook for ourselves?"
The Buddha said:
"One should not stay overnight within the boundary nor cook within the boundary;
however, I allow you to cook for yourselves. The bhikṣus thought thus:
"May medicines for life-long use be kept overnight within the boundary, cooked within the boundary, and cooked by oneself?
The Buddha said:
"I allow medicines for life-long use to be kept overnight within the boundary, cooked within the boundary, and cooked by oneself."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who intended to receive ghee but mistakenly received oil; he did not know whether this constituted a valid reception.
The Buddha said, "It does not constitute a valid reception."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, wishing to receive oil, mistakenly received ghee; he did not know whether this constituted a valid reception.
The Buddha said:
"It does not constitute a valid reception."
"If one intends to receive this [precept] but instead receives that, does it constitute a valid reception?
The Buddha said,
"It does not constitute a valid reception."
There was a bhikṣu who, having forgotten that he had not formally accepted the food, took it with him while traveling on the road. After crossing a river, he remembered and thought, "What shall I do?
He immediately informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If one thus forgets and does not receive the food, and then carries it while walking on the road, upon seeing a *kappiya-kāraka* (a pure person), one should place the food on the ground, wash one's hands thoroughly, and receive the food again."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, grain was expensive and the people were suffering from famine; it was difficult to obtain almsfood. The bhikṣus placed their food in an open space without covering or storing it away, and cowherds, shepherds, or thieves carried it off.
The bhikṣus thought thus: "The land is suffering from famine;
the World-Honored One should permit us to eat together within the boundary.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When grain is expensive, it is permitted to eat and sleep together within the boundary.
At that time, the bhikṣus cooked their food in the open air without covering or storing it. When cowherds, shepherds, or thieves saw it, they took it away. The bhikṣus thought:
"When grain is expensive, cooking food within the boundary should be permitted."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "During times of high grain prices, I permit cooking within the boundary.
At that time, the bhikṣus had lay attendants (kappiyakāraka) cook the food; they would either take portions for themselves or eat it all up. The bhikṣus then thought to themselves:
"When grain is expensive, one should be permitted to cook it oneself.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"When grain is expensive, I permit you to cook it yourself."

At that time, while traveling on the road, some bhikṣus saw fruit on the ground. While they were seeking a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle allowable things), others had already taken it away.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to cover the fruit with grass or leaves."
Yet people continued to take it away. When this was reported to the Buddha, the Buddha said, "I permit you to take it.
If one sees a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person who makes things permissible), one should place the food on the ground, wash one's hands, and then receive the food. The bhikṣus thought thus:
"When grain is expensive, the World-Honored One should permit us to take food for ourselves.
The Buddha said,
"When grain is expensive, I permit you to take food for yourselves."
At that time, the bhikṣus rose early, received their food, and set it aside as they entered the village.

When those who had accepted the invitation returned, they performed the *khalupaścādbhaktika* (leftover-food) procedure before the other bhikṣus; some shared the food, while others finished it all. The bhikṣus then thought:
"During times of high grain prices, the World-Honored One should permit us to rise early, receive our food, and eat it without performing the *khalupaścādbhaktika* procedure."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to eat food without performing the *kṛtāvadhi* (the ritual of 'leftover food') during times of famine.

At that time, many learned elder bhikṣus entered a village to beg for food. Having obtained food, they took it to a certain place; after eating there, they brought back the remaining food to the monastery and, in the presence of other bhikṣus, performed the *kṛtāvadhi* ritual and ate it again. Those bhikṣus either shared the food among themselves or ate it all up.
The bhikṣus thought thus:

"During times of high grain prices, the World-Honored One should permit us to bring food from the place where we eat and consume it without performing the *yavāgū-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food)."

He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you, when grain is expensive, to bring food from a place where it is being eaten and eat it without performing the *yavāśeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual.

At that time, after the bhikṣus had received their meals, they obtained fruits such as walnuts, jujubes, *pātā*, *āmra*, and *apara*; they performed the *yavāśeṣa* ritual with these before other bhikṣus, and those [other bhikṣus] either shared them or ate them all up.
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"During times of high grain prices, the World-Honored One should permit us to eat such fruits without performing the *atiriktapiṇḍapāta* (remaining food) ritual."
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to eat such fruits when grain is expensive, even without performing the *yavaddhika* (remaining-food) ritual.

At that time, after the bhikṣus had finished their meal, they obtained edible items found in the water—lotus roots, *kapāṭa* (water chestnuts), lotus seeds—and performed the *yavaddhika* ritual before the bhikṣus; they either shared them or ate them all up.
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"The World-Honored One should permit us, when grain is expensive, to eat such edible things found in water after a meal, even without performing the *avasiṣṭa-kriyā* (the ritual for leftover food)."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to eat such edible things found in water without performing the *kṛtya-karaṇīya* (the formal ritual of 'making it non-remainder') when grain is expensive."
At that time, the price of grain returned to its low level. Knowing this, the World-Honored One intentionally asked Ānanda:
"During the period when grain was expensive, out of compassion for the bhikṣus, I permitted eight things:

staying overnight within the boundary; cooking within the boundary; cooking for oneself; taking food with one's own hands; receiving early morning meals; bringing leftover food from the place where it was eaten; eating walnuts, fruits, and the like; eating things edible in water; and eating after having finished a meal without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of declaring a meal finished)."
"Monks, are you now eating stale food?
They replied, "We are eating stale food."
The Buddha said:
"One should not eat it. If one eats it, one shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."

At that time, the kitchen of the Saṃgha was dilapidated, and the bhikṣus propped it up with wooden beams. Since the wood stood upon impure ground, they had doubts and did not know whether it was pure or not.
The Buddha said, "If it is pure, it may be eaten.
At that time, food was moved at night and fell onto impure ground; the bhikṣus did not know whether it was pure or not.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is pure.
At night, while moving the food, some fell onto the ground between the pure and impure areas; the bhikṣus did not know whether it was pure or impure.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is pure.
At that time, a dog took food from a pure place and carried it to an impure place; the bhikṣus did not know whether it was pure or impure.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is pure;
the same applies if it has been carried away by various predatory beasts or birds.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who resented another bhikṣu and moved his food to an impure place, thinking thus:
"May he not attain purity.
A bhikṣu did not know whether it was pure or impure;
he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is contact, it is impure and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if there is no contact, it is pure.
At that time, the bhikṣu felt resentment toward that other bhikṣu and thought to himself:
"By touching pure ground, cause that [person] to become impure.
The bhikṣus did not know what was pure and what was impure, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If one touches [the food], it is impure and constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense;
if one does not touch it, it is pure.
At that time, a visiting bhikṣu arrived, seeking a pure place to set down his food. Before he reached a pure place, the dawn appeared; did he not know whether it was pure or impure?
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is pure.
It is the same even for one who wishes to travel far."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept dry-measure cups, bushels, pecks, and scales. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep these.
Later, when the bhikṣus obtained sesame, non-glutinous rice, black beans, small beans, large wheat, and small wheat, they wished to measure them themselves and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"Listen as I describe the measurements: whether it be the measure of a *kaṭhina*, a bowl, or a small bowl, one shall use the capacity of these vessels, according to their respective sizes, as the standard for *hu* and *dou* measures."
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained ghee, oil, honey, and black rock sugar and wished to weigh them. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to carve wood to make scales with weights like *zhū* and *liǎng*, limited to four or five *liǎng*, using these as the standard for calculating *jīn*."
They consecrated an excellent upper room as a *śuddhasthāna* (pure place), but it became defiled by the smearing of ghee, oil, and mud, or by smoke. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not consecrate an upper room as a pure place; one should consecrate a lower one as a pure place."
When the bhikṣus received fruit, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to distribute it one by one; if there is not enough, you should remember the order, and if more is obtained later, you should continue giving from that."
If one obtains many fruits, one should give four or five pieces to a single person; or a handful; or a small measure; or as much as fits in a bowl; or as much as can be eaten at once.
"If there is still some remaining, you should give it further.
At that time, he gave it to a layperson or a non-Buddhist; the Buddha said:
"One should not give to non-Buddhists or laypeople."

That bhikṣu was later apprehensive and did not dare to give it to his parents, or to the sick, small children, pregnant women, those who were imprisoned, or laypeople who came to the saṃghārāma. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should give it to such people; if there is still a remainder, one should press it to extract the juice and drink it."
At that time, they required pressing equipment. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to keep it.
If the juice has not yet boiled and does not intoxicate a person, one may drink it."
"If one is intoxicated, one should not drink; if one drinks, one shall be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, the Saṃgha received abundant offerings of food and drink, and many bhikṣus suffered from ailments caused by dampness. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to administer emetic and purgative medicines; if gruel is required, give gruel; if the meat of wild birds is required, it should be given.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a headache, and a physician instructed him to perform nasal irrigation. The Buddha said, "It is permitted."
"Unknowing what substance to pour,
the Buddha said:
'Pour clarified butter and oil.'"
Not knowing how to perform the nasal irrigation,
the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to soak sheep's wool, cotton, or bird feathers in oil, and then drip it into the nostril."
It flowed out from all four sides. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a nasal irrigation tube.
They then made the tube out of precious materials. The Buddha said:
"One should not make it using precious gems.
One should instead use bone, or ivory, or horn, or iron, or copper, or white tin, or lead and tin, or reed, or bamboo, or wood."
He set it aside without washing it. The Buddha said:
"One should not set it aside without washing it.
After he had washed it but not dried it, insects appeared; the Buddha said:
"One should not leave [an item] wet after washing it; one should dry it and then set it aside.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a headache; his physician instructed him to irrigate his nose, but the medicine would not enter. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to rub the crown of the head with your hand, or rub the big toe of the foot, or plug the nostrils with solidified butter."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from wind-disorder (vāta), and his physician instructed him to use medicinal smoke.
The Buddha said, "I allow the use of smoke.
At that time, he required a smoking tube, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, it may be made.
He made it out of precious gems; the Buddha said, "One should not use precious gems to make the tube."
It should be made from bone, or ivory, or horn, or iron, or copper, or white tin, or lead and tin, or wood.
If one suffers from burns caused by fire or smoke, it is permitted to attach iron [to the affected area].
"If one suffers from the bamboo tube falling apart," the Buddha said,
"I allow you to make a bag to contain it.
If holding it in the hand was not secure, the Buddha said:
"One should make a strap and fasten it over the shoulder.
He required medicinal pills; the Buddha said, "I allow you to make them."
If one’s hands are not steady enough to hold it, it should be placed inside a smoke-pipe pouch.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a sore; the physician instructed him to prepare an ointment for the sore. The Buddha said:
“I permit you to do so. When the sore has ripened, you should lance it with a knife and apply the medicine.”
From this day forward, it is permitted to cut open an ulcer with a blade; if one suffers from the odor of an ulcer, it should be washed.
When washing with decoctions of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, or fruits, or with urine, if the hand causes pain when washing the affected area, one should wash it with a bird’s feather.
If medicinal broth flows out and is discarded, one should block the four sides with materials.
If suffering from dryness, apply oil; if it is discarded on top, cover it with materials; if the ulcer has a foul odor, apply fragrance.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from malaria. The Buddha said:

"I allow you to cover yourselves with thick clothing; if you are still cold, you should cover yourselves with bedding, woolen rugs, or mattresses. If the cold does not cease, one bhikṣu may lie down together with another."
Out of fear and caution, he did not dare lie down with the sick person.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to lie down with the sick person.
At that time, there was a layperson who fell ill and came to the monastery; a bhikṣu attended to his care. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should use skillful means and parables to dispel [the fear]. If one invokes the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, they will be able to perform the necessary tasks.
When the patient died, the bhikṣus were fearful and hesitant, not daring to abandon him. The World-Honored One spoke thus:
"One should not abandon [the deceased]."
When there was a funeral for a layperson, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "It should be discarded for the sake of the purity of the saṃghārāma.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus shaved the hair from three areas; the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not shave the hair of the three places.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus looked at one another's tails, wondering: "Whose tail is long?
Whose tail is short?"
"What medicine has he applied?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not look at one another's tails, nor ask about their length or what kind of medicine has been applied."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus poured ghee and oil into the anus. The Buddha said, "One should not pour [these things in].
They then instructed others to pour them in. The Buddha said:
"One should not instruct others to perform the ritual bathing.

At that time, a bhikṣu who had completed the rainy season retreat (varṣā) dwelling in the north arrived at the Jetavana Monastery to visit the Buddha. His body was withered and his complexion was haggard; he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The World-Honored One inquired after the visiting bhikṣu:
"Is your dwelling place peaceful and harmonious?
Are you not exhausted by the toil of seeking alms?"

He replied, "The dwelling place is peaceful, harmonious, and free from dispute; however, in that country there is no gruel, and because they cannot obtain gruel, their physical strength has become weak and exhausted.
The Buddha asked:
"What kind of food do they always eat in that country?
He replied, "In that country, they always eat cakes."
The Buddha said, “I permit you to eat flat cakes.

At that time, a horse-dealer from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī came to Śrāvastī, intending to prepare cakes and bean flour for the community of monks. He provided them with flour, flour-sieves, and measuring vessels; salt and salt-caskets; fermented grain (sukta) and jars for it; *mātuluṅga* fruit and cups and spoons; ladles, unguents, and bowls; and food consisting of roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, fruits, oils, sesame, black stone honey, and fine powders. The Buddha said:
"Everyone, listen and receive the food.
The bhikṣus thought thus:
"We do not know whether this gruel is food or not food?"
"Is this an invitation or not an invitation?
Is this sufficient food or not sufficient food?
The Buddha said:
"If one holds grass and leaves no trace [of it], it is neither food, nor an invitation, nor a full meal.
At that time, a bhikṣu had this thought:
"Is drinking rice-gruel considered food or not food?"
"Is this an invitation or not?
Is this sufficient food?
The Buddha said:
"If one drinks it without mixing in the dregs, it is not food, not an invitation, and not a full meal.
At that time, the bhikṣus had this thought:
"We do not know whether these cakes are food or not food; whether this is an invitation or not an invitation; and whether this constitutes a full meal or not?"
The Buddha said,
“It is neither food nor even sufficient food.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate by mixing it with salt that had been kept overnight.
The Buddha said,
"One should not eat salt mixed with food while staying overnight.
At that time, Upāli bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What are the medicines that may be taken for as long as one lives?
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"Those things unfit to be used as food, if a bhikṣu has a cause or condition of illness, may be taken for as long as one lives."
The Bhaiṣajyavastu is complete. 5. The Kaṭhina-vastu, the eighth [chapter]. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were observing the rains retreat in the kingdom of Kośala. When the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day was concluded, they set out on the sixteenth day to see the World-Honored One.

On the road, they encountered rain, and their robes became thoroughly soaked; their *saṃghāṭī* robes were heavy, and they were utterly exhausted. Upon reaching the World-Honored One at Śrāvastī, they prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted the bhikṣus, saying:
"Are you dwelling in harmony and at ease?
Does begging for food not cause you hardship, and are you not exhausted by the journey?"
He replied: "We dwell together in harmony and peace.
We do not consider begging for alms to be suffering."
"Venerable Sir!
There were many bhikṣus who, having completed their summer retreat in various locations in the kingdom of Kosala, performed the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day.

On the sixteenth day, they took up their robes and bowls and came to see the World-Honored One; however, they encountered rain on the road, and their saṃghāṭī robes became wet and heavy, leaving them utterly exhausted."

There were many pāṃśukūlika bhikṣus who had spent the summer retreat in a different location in the Land of Snow and Cold. When their *pravāraṇā* ceremony was completed on the fifteenth day, they took the new and old robes they had obtained on the sixteenth day and went to see the World-Honored One.

While traveling on the road, he encountered rain; his robes became wet and heavy, and he was utterly exhausted. He went to the Jetavana Monastery to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and then withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha comforted the bhikṣus, saying:
"Are you dwelling together in harmony and peace?
Does begging for food not cause you hardship?"
"Are you not exhausted by the journey?
He replied, "We have stayed together in harmony and peace; we do not consider begging for food to be suffering."
"Venerable Sir!

There are many bhikṣus who wear robes made of discarded rags (pāṃsukūla) who have spent the summer retreat in various locations within the Land of Snow. Having completed their *pravāraṇā* on the fifteenth day, they brought their new and old robes and came to see the World-Honored One on the sixteenth day."
"Having encountered rain on the road, my robes became heavy with moisture and I was utterly exhausted.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
"When the summer retreat has concluded, there are four matters that ought to be performed."

What are the four? One should perform the *pravāraṇā*, one should dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*), one should establish the boundary, and one should accept the *kaṭhina* robe. At the conclusion of the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), these four matters should be performed.
There are five causes and conditions for receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.
What are the five?

There is the possession of extra robes, the non-observance of the rules regarding the storage of robes, eating in a separate group, eating from one meal to the next, and entering a village before or after a meal without having informed the bhikṣus. These are the five causes and conditions for receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.
Once the *guṇavat-cīvara* has been received, one obtains five permissions.

What are these five? One may keep extra robes; stay overnight apart from one's robes; eat in a separate group; eat at successive meals; and enter a village before or after a meal without informing the bhikṣus.
Once the *guṇavat-cīvara* has been received, five things may be performed; the Saṃgha should receive the *guṇavat-cīvara* in this manner.
Whether it be a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a rag-robe—whether it be a new garment or an old one—it must be made pure by applying a patch of new material.
If it has already been washed, once washed, one should perform the ritual of purification (*pariśuddhi*).

It must not have been obtained through wrong livelihood, nor obtained by means of signs, nor obtained by incitement, nor obtained after having been kept overnight; it must not be subject to forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) before purification is performed.

From this day forward, it shall be in accordance with the Dharma; it has four borders and is made of five strips with ten divisions. Such a robe the Saṃgha should accept and make into a *kaṭhina* robe, and even if it exceeds these [measurements], it should likewise be accepted.

One should personally wash, dye, stretch, roll, and treat it, then cut it into ten sections and sew them together; it should be received in the presence of the Saṃgha once the monks have finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe.
How is it that the Saṃgha does not validly accept the *kaṭhina* robe? It is not merely by washing that the *kaṭhina* robe is accepted;

nor merely by smoothing it, nor merely by adding borders, nor merely by cutting it into sections, nor merely by stitching the edges, nor merely by attaching fasteners, nor merely by making the flaps, nor merely by installing hooks. If the robe is obtained through wrong livelihood, or obtained through deceit, or obtained through signs, or obtained through incitement, or obtained after having been kept overnight; or if it has been forfeited and not purified, or if it was not brought on that very day and thus is not received in accordance with the Dharma; or if the four sides have no borders added, or if it is not received in the presence of the Saṃgha; or if there is an obstacle and one lacks the *saṃghāṭī*; or if the Saṃgha has duly accepted the *kaṭhina*, yet he remains outside the boundary and accepts the robe for himself—in such cases, the acceptance of the *kaṭhina* robe is not valid.

How is the *kaṭhina* robe (the merit-giving robe) formally accepted? If one obtains a new robe, a robe offered by a donor, or a rag-robe—whether it be a new garment or an old one; whether it has been purified by applying a patch of new material, or has already been washed, or has been washed and then folded and purified; provided it was not obtained through wrong livelihood, nor obtained through flattery or crookedness, nor obtained through hints, nor obtained through incitement; provided it has not been kept overnight, has not been subject to forfeiture, and has been purified; provided it is compliant with the Dharma from the day it was acquired, has borders sewn around its four sides, and consists of five strips with ten sections or more—such a robe may be accepted as a *kaṭhina* robe.
Having washed, dyed, stretched, rolled, and treated it, one should cut it into ten sections and sew them together; then, in the presence of the Saṃgha, one receives it.
Once the Saṃgha has finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, if it is received according to the Dharma within the boundary (*sīmā*), such is the valid reception of the *kaṭhina* robe.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus received dyed robes of bright colors from the Saṃgha to make *kaṭhina* robes. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not make a *kaṭhina* robe out of dyed robes of bright colors."
He used brocade to make it; the Buddha said, "One should not use brocade.
He used white cloth; the Buddha said:
"One should not use white [cloth].
From this day forward, I authorize the use of the color of the *kāṣāya* (monastic robe).
At that time, in another residence, the *saṃgha* present there obtained a highly valuable *kaṭhina* robe; those monks did not know what to do.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a formal announcement (jñapti).
It should be announced in this manner."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the community of monks receives the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the community of monks, being in harmony, receive the *kaṭhina* robe."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one bhikṣu should be appointed to ask:
"Who is able to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha?"
The capable one replied, "I am able.
Then, from among the assembly, one who is competent to perform the *karmavācanā* was selected and made the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe on behalf of the Saṃgha.
This is the formal announcement."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha.
Those elders who consent to the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Saṃgha remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to hold the kaṭhina robe for the Sangha; the Sangha consents, as they remain silent. Thus this matter is upheld."
The Sangha should then perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to give the robe to the monk who holds the *kaṭhina* robe, saying these words:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This resident Sangha has obtained robes that are to be distributed; the present Sangha should divide them."

If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the Saṃgha now bestows this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so; this bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Saṃgha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe to be maintained at this residence.
[The motion is] thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident Saṃgha has obtained clothing that may be distributed; it should be divided among the monks present. The Saṃgha now takes this robe and gives it to the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"This bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Saṃgha, accept it as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha giving this robe to the bhikṣu so-and-so—who shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Saṃgha, accept it as a *kaṭhina* robe and maintain it at this residence—should remain silent;
whoever does not consent should speak."

"The Sangha has consented to bestow this robe upon the bhikṣu so-and-so; that bhikṣu shall take this robe and, for the sake of the Sangha, receive it as a *kaṭhina* robe, and shall maintain it at this residence until its conclusion."
"Since the Saṃgha remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
That bhikṣu should rise and take hold of the robe; when the hands of the various bhikṣus reach the robe and their verbal acknowledgment is clear, he should speak as follows:

"This robe the Saṃgha shall accept to make into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe the Saṃgha now accepts to make into a *kaṭhina* robe; this robe the Saṃgha has already accepted and finished making into a *kaṭhina* robe."
Thus he should speak a second and a third time. Those bhikṣus should then say:
"The recipient has properly received it; whatever merit and renown there is herein belongs to us."
He should answer, "Yes. At that time,
Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Is it by means of the three phrases of the past, or by means of the future, or by means of the present that one receives the *kaṭhina* robe?
The Buddha said to Upāli:

“The nine phrases were spoken for the sake of completeness of expression; yet one does not receive the *kaṭhina* robe by means of the three phrases of the past, nor does one receive the *kaṭhina* robe by means of the three phrases of the future—it is by means of the three phrases of the present that one receives the *kaṭhina* robe.”
Why is this? Upāli!
The past has already ceased and the future has not yet arrived; therefore, one accepts the merit-cloth by means of the three phrases of the present.
"If one obtains cloth that has not yet been made into a robe, one should have a bhikṣu appointed through a *karmavācanā* within the community of monks to make it.
If one obtains what is already made, one should accept it in accordance with the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six, however, accepted the *kaṭhina* robe for the Saṃgha at all times—during spring, summer, and winter.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not receive the *kaṭhina* robe at all times throughout spring, summer, or winter.
From this day forward, it is permitted to refrain from receiving the *kaṭhina* robe for one month after the *pravāraṇā* ceremony has concluded, and to receive the *kaṭhina* robe for five months."
Those six groups of bhikṣus did not put away the *kaṭhina* robe, thinking:
"We have long since obtained the five privileges and shall relinquish them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not entertain such a thought as:
'Because we have long since relinquished the five matters, we shall not bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
From this day forward, it is permitted that at the end of the four months of winter, the Saṃgha should bring forth the *kaṭhina* robe."
One should depart in this manner:
"The Saṃgha is assembled in harmony; those who have not yet received the full ordination should depart, and those who are absent should announce their consent (*chanda*).
What does the Saṃgha intend to do now?"
One should respond, saying:
"The *kaṭhina* robe has been spread.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Today the community of monks is setting forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; let the Saṃgha, being in concord, now set forth the *kaṭhina* robe.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).

One should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe in this manner. If it is not relinquished by the end of the *kaṭhina* period, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
There are eight causes for the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina*:
departure, completion, non-completion, loss, cessation of expectation, hearing [of the end of the period], exiting the boundary, and relinquishing together.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary with the intention of not returning, he loses the *kaṭhina* robe as soon as he departs.
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to make robes, he loses the *kaṭhina* robe as soon as he has finished making those robes.
If a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary and thinks:
"I shall neither make a robe nor return the robe; I shall not complete the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe."
If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary and finishes making the robe, that bhikṣu loses the robe and the *kaṭhina* privileges are also lost.

If a bhikṣu, having finished accepting the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary hoping to obtain a robe, and while he is outside the boundary he reaches the place where he hoped to obtain it, but the bhikṣu sees it and does not get the robe, and his hope is cut off with no further prospect of obtaining it, then with that hope cut off, he has already lost the *kaṭhina* privileges.

If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to make robes, and having finished making them, hears that the Saṃgha has suspended the *kaṭhina*, then upon hearing this, he loses his *kaṭhina* privileges.

If a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to have it made, and while he is still making it, his intention to return remains while he stays outside the boundary; if the Saṃgha then releases the *kaṭhina*, he loses the *kaṭhina* while remaining outside the boundary.

If a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, makes robes outside the boundary, whether that robe-making is finished or unfinished, he returns to his residence; if those bhikṣus assemble and formally relinquish the robe, this constitutes the eighth matter.
"Furthermore, there are six cases:

if a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary with the intention of not returning, and departs before the robe has been obtained, he thereby loses the *kaṭhina* robe."
Excluding the two phrases "losing the robe" and "the hope being cut off" from among the aforementioned eight matters, the rest is as above.
Furthermore, there are six matters:

if a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, takes the robe outside the boundary to make it, and having finished making it, he loses the *kaṭhina* robe—excluding the two phrases "going away" and "the hope being cut off" from among the aforementioned eight matters—the rest is as above.
There are fifteen clauses concerning robes not yet obtained, and likewise fifteen clauses concerning robes already obtained.

There are further fifteen clauses concerning both robes obtained and robes not yet obtained; these are permutations of the eight preceding matters, and as there are no further distinctions, they are not set forth separately.
Furthermore, there are twelve matters:

if a bhikṣu, having accepted the *kaṭhina* robe, goes out and seeks a robe with expectation, obtaining the robe he hoped for, and makes it outside the boundary; if he finishes making the robe and loses the *kaṭhina*, the phrasing regarding not finishing it is also like this, the loss is also like this, and the severance of hope is as stated above.

If a bhikṣu, having accepted a *kaṭhina* robe, goes out with the expectation of obtaining a robe, and without informing anyone that he intends to return, goes beyond the boundary to the place where he expects to obtain the robe, but does not obtain the expected robe and instead obtains a robe other than the one expected, and then makes a robe while outside the boundary—once the robe is made, he loses the *kaṭhina* privileges; the same applies if the robe-making is not completed. The loss is likewise the same, and the severance of the expectation is as described above.

If a bhikṣu, having accepted a *kaṭhina* robe, goes away without informing anyone that he intends to return, and while outside the boundary (*sīmā*) he does not form the intention to return, he reaches the place where he expects to obtain the robe; whether he obtains the expected robe or does not obtain it, if he makes the robe outside the boundary, once the making of the robe is finished, he loses the *kaṭhina* privileges. It is the same if the making is not finished; it is likewise lost in these cases. If his expectation is severed as described above, [the *kaṭhina* is lost].
Furthermore, there are twelve matters:
obtaining the robes one hopes for and not obtaining the robes one hopes for, as in the aforementioned twelve matters.
Furthermore, there are nine matters:
If a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *guṇavat-cīvara*, goes outside the boundary and has not yet obtained the robe, and another bhikṣu asks him:
"Where did you spend the night?"
"Where is the robe?
Why do you not bring it so that we may make a robe for you?
That bhikṣu returned to his dwelling and heard that the community of monks had brought forth the *kaṭhina* robe; he then thought to himself:
"The Sangha now brings forth the *kaṭhina* robe; we shall now prepare the robe.

If he finishes preparing the robe and then loses the *kaṭhina*, or likewise does not prepare the robe after it is lost, or likewise loses the robe itself—these are the three phrases regarding hearing [the announcement] within the boundary. The same applies to the three phrases regarding hearing them while on the road outside the boundary while carrying the robe, and the same applies to the three phrases regarding arriving at the place where that bhikṣu is while carrying the robe. These constitute the nine matters.
Next, the nine cases regarding having already obtained robes are likewise; the nine matters for both obtaining robes and not obtaining robes are likewise.
If a bhikṣu, after receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, goes outside the boundary to another region and thinks to himself:
"If I find good companions, I shall go; if I do not find good companions, I shall return."
When he reaches the halfway point and hears that the community of monks has brought forth the *kaṭhina* robe, he thinks to himself: "I shall make a robe.

Once the robe is finished, he loses the *kaṭhina* privileges; it is the same if it is not finished, the same if the robe is lost, and the same if he goes outside the boundary. These five cases are the same as those mentioned upon hearing the news.
If a bhikṣu, having finished receiving the *kaṭhina* robe, wishes to go to a secluded place for purification— staying there if he finds it agreeable, or returning if he does not—
and while that bhikṣu is at that location, he hears that the Saṃgha has cast out the *kaṭhina*,
he should say: "We must now make robes."

The same applies when the making of robes is finished, or when the relinquishing of the *kaṭhina* robe is not finished; the same applies to the loss of robes, and likewise to being outside the boundary (*sīmā*). These five phrases regarding what has been heard are also the same.

There are two ways to relinquish the *kaṭhina* robe: either the monk who holds the *kaṭhina* robe goes outside the boundary and spends the night there, or the Saṃgha, being in harmony, collectively relinquishes it.
The *kaṭhina* ceremony is thus completed. The Kauśāmbī Khandhaka, the Ninth. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Kauśāmbī.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had violated the precepts; among them,
some said, "He has violated the precepts," while others said:
"He has not committed an offense.
In this regard, a bhikṣu who perceives an offense says to a bhikṣu who does not perceive an offense:
"This bhikṣu has indeed committed an offense; it is not the case that he has not committed one."
Not seeing the offense, that monk’s mind was resolved, and he said: "It is so;
this bhikṣu has indeed broken the precepts; it is not that he has not broken them.
He then brought about a formal assembly to raise the charge against him.
The offending bhikṣu said: "I have committed no offense;
the formal accusation against me is invalid. This illegal accusation renders the *karmavācanā* ineffective.
He then went among the people to seek supporters, saying to other bhikṣus:
"I have not committed an offense, nor has the formal accusation been established; the legal action against me was unlawful, and the *karmavācanā* was invalid.

When that monk perceives it thus—that this monk has not committed an offense, the formal accusation is not established, the legal action was unlawful, and the *karmavācanā* was invalid—[he is considered pure].

The offending bhikṣu, immediately accompanied by his remaining faction and the bhikṣus who had raised the charge, went to the place where the bhikṣu who had previously stated that he did not see the offense was staying, and said to him:
"Venerable sir!..."
"This bhikṣu has not violated the precepts and the formal accusation was not established; he has accused another in an illegal manner, and the *karmavācanā* was not valid.
That bhikṣu, upon returning and seeing that [the other] had indeed not violated them, said:
"He did not violate them; the accusation was not established, it was an illegal accusation, and the *karmavācanā* was not valid."

Those bhikṣus who had been subject to the act of suspension and those who had followed them in that suspension performed the formal ritual of reciting the precepts in a separate assembly from the bhikṣus who recognized their transgression.
At that time, the bhikṣu who had brought the charges went to the World-Honored One, prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“These bhikṣus who were subject to suspension and those who followed them have performed the formal ritual of reciting the precepts in a separate assembly from us.”
The Buddha said:
"This foolish person has caused a schism in the Saṃgha. However, if he performs the *karmavācanā* and recites the precepts as I have taught, his *karman* is valid and he does not commit an offense."
If you perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts as I have instructed, you will achieve success and remain free from transgression. Why is this?
Because there are two types of non-residence.
What are the two?
That bhikṣu either brings about his own exclusion from the community, or the Saṃgha grants him exclusion from the community.
What is meant by a bhikṣu bringing about his own exclusion from the community?
If a bhikṣu causes a schism in the Saṃgha and seeks external allies, this constitutes a bhikṣu’s own act of causing a state of non-residence.
What is it for the Saṃgha to cause one to enter a state of non-residence?

If the Saṃgha performs against him the formal act of *ajñaptikarma* for one who does not acknowledge an offense, the formal act of *apraticchādanakarma* for one who does not repent, or the formal act of *pāpikā-dṛṣṭy-anutsargakarma* for one who does not relinquish evil views, this constitutes the Saṃgha’s imposition of non-cohabitation upon him.
These are the two kinds of non-residence.
There are two kinds of residence:
a monk establishes residence for himself, or the Saṃgha grants him residence.
What is meant by "forming a common residence through one's own initiative"?
When this Saṃgha of bhikṣus is split, a member of that own faction seeks out a virtuous faction from outside; this bhikṣu thus forms a common residence through his own initiative.
What is it for the Saṃgha to grant one the status of living together?

When the Saṃgha is in harmony, they first perform against someone the *ajñāna-karman* (act of not acknowledging), the *apraticchādana-karman* (act of not confessing), or the *akuśala-dṛṣṭy-apatyāga-karman* (act of not relinquishing evil views); subsequently, the harmonious Saṃgha again dissolves these acts. This is what is meant for the Saṃgha to grant one the status of living together.
"These are the two kinds of co-residence.

Then that monk who has been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma*, and the monks who supported his suspension, quarreled with the monks who carried out the suspension; they reviled and slandered one another, seeking out each other's faults.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "Venerable Sir!

Those bhikṣus who have been subject to the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and those who have followed in supporting that act, are quarreling with these bhikṣus who carried out the suspension; they revile and slander one another, seeking out each other's faults."
"What should we do? The Buddha said:

"I permit the Saṃgha to break an illegal concord and sit in such a place so that body and speech do not produce evil; the Saṃgha should break a legal concord and sit with one person's distance between them."
At that time, the World-Honored One went to where the monks who had been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* were staying and spoke these words:
"You should not commit offenses, nor should you claim that you have committed none while refusing to confess them."
Why is this? If a bhikṣu commits an offense, another bhikṣu says to him:
"Venerable sir, you have committed an offense; do you see it yourself?"
He replied, "I did not see him.

That bhikṣu was learned and knew the Āgamas; he upheld the Dharma and the Vinaya and was knowledgeable in the Mātṛkās. He had gained many followers among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists.
That bhikṣu who has committed an offense thinks to himself:

"That bhikṣu is learned, knows the Āgamas, upholds the Dharma, and upholds the Vinaya; he knows the Mātṛkās, and he has many allies among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists."

If I do not now acknowledge my fault, this bhikṣu shall immediately perform against me the formal act of "not acknowledging a fault," the formal act of "refusal to repent," and the formal act of "refusal to relinquish a wrong view."

If that bhikṣu undergoes against me the formal act of *ajñapti-karman* for not seeing an offense, the formal act of *ajñapti-karman* for not confessing an offense, or the formal act of *ajñapti-karman* for not relinquishing a wrong view, then that bhikṣu shall no longer perform formal acts or recite the *Prātimokṣa* together with me; he shall not dwell in the same room as I during the *pravāraṇā*; he shall not sit in the same place, on the same seat, or on the same plank; he shall not eat before or after me; nor shall he, according to seniority, pay homage, prostrate, clasp my hand, or welcome me.

If that bhikṣu does not perform the *karmavācanā* together with me, nor recite the *prātimokṣa* precepts together with me, and even goes so far as not to rise to greet me or take my hand, then disputes will arise among the Saṃgha; they will revile, slander, and seek out each other's faults, whereby the Saṃgha will become divided, defiled by impurities, and dwell in separation.
"If a bhikṣu values this act of schism, he should be told as follows:
'You have committed an offense; you must confess it according to the Dharma. Stop!"
"Cease! Monks, do not engage in quarreling, disputing, or reviling one another; do not slander each other or seek out one another's faults.
All of you should dwell in harmony and assemble together, studying under the same teacher as one body, like water and milk mixed, for the benefit of the Buddha-dharma and to abide in peace."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken thus to the bhikṣu who had been subject to the *ukkhepanīyakamma* (act of suspension) and the bhikṣu who had carried out the suspension, he went to where the bhikṣus who were suspending others were and said to them:
"You must not repeatedly bring up the matters of other bhikṣus."
Why is this? Because in this matter, when a bhikṣu has committed an offense, another bhikṣu asks him:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Do you see yourself as having committed an offense? He replied,
"I do not see it."

That bhikṣu may be learned and knowledgeable of the Āgamas, upholding the Dharma and the Vinaya and knowing the Mātṛkā; he may have many partisans among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists.
That bhikṣu thinks to himself:

"That bhikṣu is learned and knows the Āgamas; he upholds the Dharma and the Vinaya and knows the Mātṛkās. He has many partisans among bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists."

If they say, "I do not see my offense," we shall immediately perform against them the formal act of *karma* for not seeing an offense, the formal act of *karma* for not confessing, and the formal act of *karma* for not relinquishing a wrong view.

If we were to perform against them the formal act of "not seeing one's offense," the formal act of "not confessing," or the formal act of "not relinquishing evil views," we would not perform the *poṣadha* recitation of the precepts with them in a single assembly, nor would we perform the *pravāraṇā*, nor even go out to meet them while holding hands.
