If we do not perform the *karmavācanā* and recite the precepts together, nor even go out to meet one another by taking each other’s hands, the Saṃgha will surely fall into strife, mutually reviling, slandering, and seeking out each other’s faults; this will cause the Saṃgha to be split, to become defiled, and to dwell in separation.
"If a bhikṣu values this matter of schism in the Saṃgha, one should not bring charges against that bhikṣu.
Stop! Stop!"
"Monks, do not engage in strife, nor revile, slander, or seek out the faults of one another.
You should all assemble together in harmony, studying under the same teacher like water and milk mingling, so as to benefit the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and security."

At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken to those bhikṣus, when the night had passed and it was morning, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered Kauśāmbī for alms. Having finished his meal, he returned to the saṃghārāma and, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and said:
"In the distant past, there were King Brahmadatta of Kāśi and King Jīvaka of Kośala, whose ancestors had been enemies."
King Brahmadatta’s army was powerful, heroic, and robust, and his wealth and treasures were likewise abundant.
King Jīvaka’s army was not as powerful, and his wealth and treasures were also meager.

Later, at another time, King Brahmadatta arrived with his fourfold army and marched against the kingdom of Kosala to punish King Jīvaka, seizing all his territories, troops, treasuries, and precious jewels.
At that time, King Jīvaka fled with his first wife and arrived in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; they disguised themselves as śikhin brahmins and lived in the house of a potter.
Later, at another time, the chief queen of King Jīvaka conceived this thought:

"I wish to have that ground leveled and made even, so that at the crossroads when the sun first rises, I may see the fourfold army fighting together and drink the water used for washing their swords."
He immediately went to the king's presence and said:
"Does Your Majesty wish to know?
This is what I am now thinking:"

"If you wish to obtain land that is level and situated at a crossroads where, at the time of sunrise, you may see four divisions of troops fighting and drink the water used for washing their swords," the king said,
"By what means can you now fulfill such a wish?"
"King Brahmadatta has been an enemy of my ancestors; he has seized our kingdom, our army, and our treasuries of precious jewels, leaving nothing behind.
The queen said, "If I am not granted this wish, I shall die."
At that time, King Brahmadatta had a minister named Purohita, who was a companion of King Jīvaka. King Jīvaka said to his wife:
"I must inform my companion."
Then King Jyotiṣprabha went to where Puluṣa was and spoke these words:
"Friend, do you know?
My first wife conceived this thought:"
"If you wish to obtain land that is level and even, at the crossroads of four roads at the time of sunrise, you shall see four divisions of troops fighting; drink the water from washing their swords.
Having thought this, he immediately came and informed me of these matters.
I said to him: "By what means can you now fulfill such a vow?
King Brahmadatta has been an enemy to my ancestors and me; he has seized all our kingdom, army, and treasury, leaving nothing remaining."
The lady then said,
"If I am not permitted to fulfill such a wish, I shall die. I then spoke to her:
"I must use these circumstances to inform my companions. Pūrṇa said,
"Wait a moment!"
"I must examine the interior of her womb.
Then, having gone to examine the womb of the chief consort of King Jīvaka, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa bared his right shoulder, knelt on his right knee, took hold of her hand, and three times proclaimed:
"The King of Kosala is within your womb!"
He said to the lady:

"One must obtain a piece of level ground at a crossroads where, at the time of sunrise, one sees four divisions of troops fighting together and drinking the water used for washing their swords; stay in such a place."
Then Puluhechi went to King Brahmadatta and spoke to him thus:
"Does Your Majesty wish to know?
Such a star has appeared."
"The time should be at dawn, when the sun has just risen, at a crossroads where the four divisions of the army are fighting together and washing their blades.
The King said, "Purūhuta!"
"Now is precisely the right time.
Thereupon, Puḷuñcayā immediately assembled the fourfold army and went to a crossroads to engage in battle and wash their blades.
At that time, the Queen of King Jīvaka, finding the ground level at a crossroads, saw the fourfold army engaged in battle and washing their blades as the sun was rising.

At that time, the lady drank the water used for washing the sword; her womb was thereby fully developed, and she subsequently gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, and who was immediately named Chang.
As he grew up, King Jīvaka loved him dearly.

At that time, King Brahmadatta heard that King Jīvaka of Kosala had fled with his chief queen and was living as a śikhin-brāhmaṇa in the house of a potter. He immediately commanded his attendants, saying:

"Go to the potter’s house, seize King Jīvaka and his chief queen, bind them firmly, and bring them here. Beat the drum of ill omen to manifest the sign of death, then exit through the southern gate and cut them into seven pieces to be placed upon a pointed stake."
When King Jīvadharman heard King Brahmadatta issue such a command, he immediately called his son Jīva and said to him: "Do you know now?
King Brahmadatta of Kāśi is the enemy of my ancestors; he has seized all my kingdoms, armies, and treasures, leaving nothing behind, and has even commanded his followers to kill us."
"You must flee; do not be killed by King Brahmadatta.
At that time, Prince Jyotiṣka immediately fled.
Then King Brahmadatta sent men to arrest Prince Jyotiṣka and the first queen; they bound them and beat the drum of ill omen, manifesting the signs of death as the crowds gathered.
At that time, Prince Changsheng, dressed in humble attire, followed after his parents weeping and shedding tears.
Then King Changsheng looked back and saw his son, and spoke these words:
"No matter how light or heavy an offense may be, none are worth avenging."
"To repay enmity with enmity, the enmity will never cease; only by being without enmity can one put an end to enmity.
He spoke thus a second and a third time.
At that moment, the multitude thought to themselves:
"The King of Kosala is deranged and his mind is disordered; it is only today that he has instructed the Elder Maṇava.
Who, then, is this Elder Maṇava?
At that time, the multitude likewise spoke these words three times.
At that time, King Brahmadatta sent men to lead King Jīvaka out through the right gate and divide him into seven parts, placing them upon pointed stakes.

Thereupon, Prince Jīvaka returned to the city of Vārāṇasī and studied various arts and crafts; he learned writing, the interpretation of physiognomy and astrology, secret prophecies, mathematics, the painting of various images, music, and comedy, becoming the foremost among the multitude in these fields.

At that time, not far from where King Brahmadatta’s court ladies resided, there was an elephant trainer. Then the prince went to the trainer’s place and said, "I wish to learn how to train elephants."
He replied, "You may learn. Then,
when the night was past midnight, the young brahmin student played the lute and sang with playful melody, producing beautiful sounds.
At that time, King Brahmadatta heard the sound of lute-playing, singing, and musical entertainment during the night; the tones were exquisite.
Having heard them, he immediately asked those beside him:
"Who is playing the lute, singing, and performing music past midnight?"
"The tone of its sound is excellent. He replied,
"Does Your Majesty not know this now?"

Not far from the king’s female musicians lived an elephant trainer; he had a disciple named Jīvamjīvaka, who, after midnight had passed, played the lute and sang with such skill that his voice was most melodious.
Having heard this, he immediately said, "Summon him;
I wish to see him. He then received the command and went to summon him.
Once he had arrived and prostrated himself at the king's feet, he stood to one side.
The king asked,
"Is it true that you played the lute and sang songs with such beautiful sounds throughout the night until past midnight? He replied:
"Very well," the king said. "Now, before me, you may play the lute, sing, and perform with beautiful sounds."
Thereupon, he immediately played the lute and sang before the king, producing beautiful sounds; hearing this, the king was filled with great joy.
The king said:
"Stay here, and I shall provide you with food."
He replied, “Yes.
At that time, the chief consort of King Brahmadatta resided in a palace that no one was permitted to enter, except for the king’s wife and the elder Māṇava.
Later, at another time, the queen lost her maṇi jewel. She went to the king's presence and said, "Does Your Majesty know?
I have lost my maṇi jewel."
The king asked, "Who has entered? The queen replied:
"No one else has entered; there is only the King and I, the Elder Maṇava.
Then the King immediately summoned the Elder Maṇava and asked him, "The first wife of my household has lost her pearl; did you take it?"
He thought to himself: "No one else enters the Queen’s chamber; there is only the Queen and myself. If I say:..."
"I will not take it.
Fearing that the king would surely punish me, and thinking that I have been accustomed to pleasure since birth and am unable to endure such bitter suffering,
he then replied to the king:
"I shall take it.
The king asked, "With whom will you take it?"
He replied, "With the Crown Prince.
[The other asked,] "And who else was there?"
He replied: "Furthermore, together with the foremost minister of great wisdom.
[The questioner asked: "Who else was there?"
He replied, "With the foremost great elder in the king's realm.
[The other asked,] "And with whom else?"
He replied, "With the foremost courtesan. Thereupon,
the king immediately had Prince Dīrgha-māṇava, the minister, the elder, and the foremost courtesan arrested and bound.
The prince said to the elder māṇava,
"Do you know that I truly did not take the jewel, yet you falsely claim that I took it?
The elder māṇava replied:
"You truly did not take it, and neither did I.
You are the king's eldest son, dearly beloved by him; he would certainly not have had your life taken for the sake of a pearl. It was for this reason that I led you forward."
The foremost minister of wisdom said to the young brahmin Māṇava:
"Do you truly know that I did not take the jewel, yet you falsely claim that I took it?"
The elder Māṇava said:
"You truly did not take it, nor did I take it.
You are a wise minister capable of finding the jewel; that is why I led you here."
The great householder said to the young brahmin Māṇava:
"Do you truly know that I did not take the jewel, yet you falsely claim that I took it?
The young brahmin replied:
"You truly did not take it, and neither did I.

You are a great elder of this kingdom, possessing immeasurable wealth and treasures; if the King required pearls, you would have been able to give them to him. It was for this reason that I drew you in."
The foremost courtesan said to the young brahmin:
"Do you know that I did not take the pearl, yet you falsely claim that I took it? He replied:
"You truly did not take it, nor did I take it.
You are the foremost courtesan; many people have their hearts set upon you. Those who have not yet obtained you will surely seek you out to find the pearl; for this reason, I merely drew you in."

At that time, the white-robed thieves of the city of Vārāṇasī heard that the King’s first consort had lost her pearl and that the King had imprisoned the crown prince Maṇava, the great ministers, the great elders, and the courtesan.
They immediately went to the elder Maṇava and asked him, "Did the King’s consort truly lose the pearl?"
He replied, "I have lost the pearl. He asked:
"Who has entered the lady's chamber?
She replied, "Only the King, the lady, and I."
He asked, "Who is walking in the middle? He replied:
"A monkey is walking in the midst of them. He said,
"Long Mānava!..."
"Now the jewel can be obtained.
Thereupon, the thief went to King Brahmadatta and said to the king:
"Does Your Majesty not know?"
"Now the jewel can be obtained; Your Majesty may provide ornaments for the women.
The king immediately brought out various ornaments and necklaces, gathered a multitude of monkeys, had them put on the necklaces, and placed them within the palace.
At that time, the monkey who was previously inside saw that all the other monkeys were adorned with necklaces; he then took out the lady’s pearl he had stolen and used it to decorate his own body.
The thieves immediately surrounded him on all four sides to capture the monkey and reported to the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty not know this?"
"I have already obtained the jewel.
Then King Brahmādaśa immediately summoned the elder Māṇava and said to him:
"You did not take the jewel; why did you say that you had taken it?"
He then replied to the king:
"I had this thought: 'In the lady's chamber, no one enters except for the king, the lady, and myself.'"
If I were to say,
"I will not take it," I fear the King would punish me with bitter torment, and I am unable to endure such bitter torment.
"Therefore, I said only that I would take it.
[The king asked: "For what reason, moreover, did you bring the Prince? He replied:
I thought to myself:
"The Prince is dearly beloved by the King; he will certainly not take his life for the sake of a pearl.
For this reason, I led the Prince away.
"Why did you summon the chief minister?
He replied, "I thought to myself:"
"The minister is highly knowledgeable and will surely be able to employ skillful means to recover the jewel.
For this reason, he was brought forward.
"And for what reason did you bring the great elder?"
He replied, "I thought to myself:
'If the King requires jewels, this elder, being so immensely wealthy, will be able to give the King pearls.'"
"Therefore, you drew [the arrow] toward the ear.
"For what reason did you draw [the arrow] toward the courtesan? He replied:
I thought to myself:
"The people of the country and the bandits have set their hearts upon that courtesan.
Those who have not yet obtained her will surely seek out the pearl for her sake."
"Therefore, he drew back his ear.
The King said, "It is unprecedented; the Elder Māṇava possesses such wisdom."
The King then appointed the elder Māṇava as the preeminent official for all affairs.
Later, on another occasion, King Brahmadatta set out on a hunting expedition, arraying his fourfold army.
At that time, the king and the fourfold army each scattered in pursuit of the deer.

As the heat of the day grew intense and they were utterly exhausted, the young brahmin Jīrṇa took the king’s carriage to a secluded spot to rest. The king alighted from the carriage and lay down in its shade, using Jīrṇa’s lap as a pillow to sleep.
Then the brahmin youth Dīrgha thought to himself:

"This king is an enemy of my ancestors; he destroyed my kingdom and plundered all the fourfold army and the treasures of the treasury belonging to my ancestors, leaving nothing behind. He killed my parents and extinguished the royal lineage of the Kosalas."
Recalling his old enmity, he immediately drew his sword, intending to cut off the king’s head.
Then he remembered his father’s former words:
"Enmities have no measure of lightness or gravity; none are worth avenging. To eliminate enmity with enmity will never bring an end to enmity; only through non-enmity does enmity naturally cease."
He immediately withdrew the sword into his inner garment.
At that moment, King Brahmadatta woke up in a startle, and the long-haired Māṇava asked the king,
"For what reason are you startled?"
The king said, "The King of Kosala has a son named Jāṇussoṇi; he has drawn his sword, intending to take my life.
He then replied to the king:
"Where is the prince Jīvaka, the young Māṇava?
There is only the King and I here; Your Majesty may sleep in peace.
The King fell asleep a second time, and it was the same as before.
When the third sleep had passed, Dīrgha Māṇava, reflecting as before, drew his sword once more; the king immediately woke up in alarm.
Then Dīrgha Māṇava seized the king by the head, and the king said:
"Do you wish to kill me?"
He replied, "Yes. [The Buddha asked: "For what reason?"

He replied: "I am Jīvamjīvaka, the son of Prince Dīrgha. The king is my father’s ancestral enemy; he has destroyed my kingdom and plundered all my father’s armies, treasuries, and precious goods until they were exhausted. He killed my parents and severed the lineage of the King of Kosala."
"Because I harbor this enmity, I wished to kill you, O King.
The king then spoke to him, saying:
"I now restore to you your father's and grandfather's army, kingdom, and all precious treasures; do not kill me."
He replied, "I shall save the King's life; may the King likewise not kill me.
The King answered:
"I also grant you your life.
At that time, they together eliminated their ancestral grievances; they immediately reconciled like father and son and returned to the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra together on a single vehicle.
At that time, King Brahmadatta assembled his ministers and addressed them thus:
"If you see the prince Jīvaka, the young Māṇava, what should you do with him? Some said:
"Subdue him so that he is like a conch shell. Or some said:
"Kill him with a sword."
Some said, "The carriage has overturned. Others said:
"Hang his head high. Or some said:
"Then let it be like a torch."
Some said, "Fry it in hot oil. Others said:
"Scrape its body.
Some said: "Hook the flesh with sharp hooks."
Some said: "Boil it with honey. Others said:
"Set fire to his body," some said;
"Wrap him in clothes and burn him," others said.
Some said: "Cut off their hands, cut off their feet, cut off their ears, and cut off their noses. Others said:
"Place a sharp stake through the head," some said; others said,
"Sever the head."
The king then pointed him out to his ministers, saying:
"This is Prince Jīvadatta’s son, Dīrgha-māṇava; from this day forward, no one among the people shall speak ill of him."
"Why is this? Because he sustains my life, and I sustain his life.

At that time, the king immediately returned to his father the troops and soldiers, as well as the entire kingdom, its treasuries, and all precious jewels; he then adorned his daughter and gave her to him.
"O bhikṣus! That long-haired young man who carried a sword and shield had been at enmity with his father and grandfather, yet they have now reconciled and live together like father and son."

You have left the household life for the sake of the Way; you share the same teacher and the same training, blending together like water and milk, benefiting the Buddha-dharma and dwelling in peace and happiness.
Stop! Stop!

"O Bhikṣus! Do not engage in mutual strife, do not revile or slander one another, and do not seek out each other's faults. Be harmonious and do not quarrel; study under the same teacher as one water blends with milk, so as to benefit the Buddha-dharma and dwell in peace and happiness."
Then, another bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Please remain at ease; the Tathāgata is the Lord of Dharma, and he shall naturally know the matters concerning the quarrels among the bhikṣus.”
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke to the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī for a second and a third time:
"Stop! Stop!"

Do not engage in quarrels or disputes, nor in reviling or slandering one another, nor in seeking out each other's faults; dwell in harmony together under the same teacher and study, blending like water and milk, so as to benefit the Buddha-dharma and abide in peace and happiness.
That bhikṣu spoke thus: "World-Honored One! Please remain at ease;
the Tathāgata is the Lord of Dharma, and he himself shall know what to do regarding this matter of dispute among the bhikṣus."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī:
“Evil reports spread abroad, Seeking not the sublime Dharma;
When the Saṃgha is divided, It is never for any other reason.”
Those who break bones and take life, who steal cattle, horses, and wealth,
and those amidst the strife and chaos of nations— even they may yet be reconciled.
But among you, there should be none who engage in various forms of abuse and reviling.
For one who acts in such a manner, that enmity will never be removed.
Even when subjected to various kinds of evil abuse and insults, they do not retaliate;
for those who are able to endure in silence, that enmity shall naturally be dispelled.
One cannot eliminate enmity through enmity; enmity is never thus dispelled.
Only when there is no enmity does enmity naturally subside—this is the Dharma of the brave and the joyful.
One should neither teach others to do it, nor should one do it oneself.
One who can practice in this way is like rain soaking away all dust.
To speak of the firm as being solid is to see solidity where none exists;
failing to understand true solidity, such a person falls into the midst of false recollections.
One who knows the firm as firm, and the unfirm as unfirm—having understood the nature of the firm, such a person enters into right mindfulness.
It is like a person grasping an arrow: if they grasp it loosely, they will wound their own hand.
If a śramaṇa is not good and virtuous, he increases his time in hell.
If one can skillfully grasp the arrow and hold it firmly, the hand will not be injured;
if a śramaṇa is good and virtuous, he shall be born in the happy realms.
Though one may wear the saffron robes, if one harbors the fetters and afflictions,
and is unable to eliminate enmity and harm, such a person is unworthy of the saffron robe.
But when the fetters have been extinguished and one is adorned by the observance of the precepts, [one is truly worthy].
One who has subdued their enemies is truly worthy of the saṃghāṭī robe.
Though one may search everywhere for a companion, none may be found to match oneself;
it is better to remain alone and firm in one's resolve than to dwell with the foolish.
If you seek companions everywhere but find none like yourself,
it is better to practice virtue alone than to associate with the foolish and evil.
Walk alone and do no evil, like a wild elephant on a mountain peak.
If one finds a virtuous companion, one may dwell and travel together with courage and vigor;
moving among the multitude, one’s mind remains ever joyful.
If one does not find a virtuous companion, one should always walk alone with courage and vigor.
"Abandoning the districts, kingdoms, and towns, he remains without concern, like a wild elephant.
At that time, the World-Honored One [observed] that because the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling, slandering one another, and using abusive language, the community of monks was being disturbed.

The World-Honored One was displeased; without informing the assembly of monks or those providing offerings, he himself took up his bedding and placed it back in its original location, then, taking his robes and bowl, returned from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī by means of his supernormal powers.

At that time, the upāsakas of Kauśāmbī heard that the World-Honored One had said that because the bhikṣus were quarreling, slandering, and reviling one another, the Saṃgha was being troubled and disturbed.

The World-Honored One was displeased; he did not inform the assembly of monks or the attendants providing offerings, but instead took up his bedding and placed it back in its original location, took hold of his robes and bowl, and by means of his supernormal power returned from the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the upāsakas made a mutual agreement among themselves:

"None of us should ever see the monks of Kauśāmbī, nor should we rise to greet them, pay them respect, prostrate before them, inquire after their welfare, or speak with them; nor should we provide them with offerings of robes, food and drink, or medicine for the sick."

Those bhikṣus remained as if suspended by formal suspension; bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists all kept their distance, with none speaking to them.
Those monks who were engaged in disputes subsequently found themselves deprived of gains and offerings, and they thought to themselves:
"We should settle this matter of dispute in the presence of the World-Honored One."
He immediately went to Śrāvastī.

At that time, Śāriputra heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling, slandering one another, and reviling each other with mouths like swords; having come from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī, he went with five hundred bhikṣus to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“These bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī have been quarreling, slandering one another, and reviling each other with mouths like swords; having come from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī, what should we do?”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“You should listen to what is spoken by both groups. If there is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, you should accept his words, praise and nurture him, and associate with him as an ally.”
Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does one know whether that bhikṣu speaks in accordance with the Dharma or not?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
“There are eighteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha:

[deeming] the Dharma as non-Dharma, the Vinaya as non-Vinaya; an offense as non-offense; what is light as heavy; what has a remainder as having no remainder; what is grave as not grave; what should be practiced as not to be practiced; what is prescribed as not prescribed; and what is taught as not taught.”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Observe this matter, and you will know whether that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma or not according to the Dharma.
Śāriputra then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How should one provide rooms and bedding for the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī?
The Buddha said:

"One should provide them with rooms and bedding in a private location; if there is no private location, one should create a private location and provide them. They should be distributed according to the method by which the Saṃgha distributes bedding."
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"How should the robes and requisites of the Saṃgha be divided among the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī?
The Buddha said:
"One should give it according to the order of seniority.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When the Kauśāmbī bhikṣus are served gruel during the morning meal, how should they sit?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra: "Did I not previously say this?

When the Saṃgha is split but is united in an unrighteous manner, one should sit in a place that does not produce evil in body or speech; when the Saṃgha is split but the matter has been settled through a righteous union, one should sit in a seat that is vacant by one person."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling and slandering one another, reviling each other, and seeking out each other's faults.

Coming from Kauśāmbī to the kingdom of Śrāvastī, she went together with five hundred bhikṣuṇīs to the place where the World-Honored One was; she bowed her head at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!...”
"These monks from Kauśāmbī have come to Śrāvastī after engaging in quarrels, disputes, and slander, reviling one another and seeking out each other's faults; what should we do?"
The Buddha told Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī:
"You should listen to the speech of both assemblies. If there is a bhikṣu who speaks according to the Dharma, you should accept his words, praise and nurture him, and stand as his ally."
She further addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is one to know whether that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma or not?
The Buddha told Gautamī:
“There are eighteen matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha:
from ‘dharma’ and ‘adharma’ up to ‘speaking’ and ‘not speaking,’ as mentioned above.
By examining these matters, you will know whether that bhikṣu speaks according to the Dharma or speaks contrary to the Dharma.”
“Gautamī Bhikṣuṇī! You should request instruction from the Saṃgha and seek it among the community of bhikṣus who act in accordance with the Dharma.

At that time, Ānanda and Udāyin heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling, slandering one another, reviling each other, and seeking out each other’s faults, their mouths like swords and blades. They came from Kauśāmbī to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and, together with five hundred upāsakas, went to the place where the World-Honored One was. They bowed their heads at his feet in salutation, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The monks of Kauśāmbī are quarreling, slandering, and reviling one another, seeking out each other’s faults with mouths like swords. Having come from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī, what should we do?”
The Buddha said:
"One should listen to the words of both communities as stated above. If there is a donor who makes an offering, it should be divided into two portions.
This group is also the Saṃgha; that group is also the Saṃgha."
"Householder!
Just as when a golden staff is broken into two pieces, both parts are gold;
in the same way, householder, the objects given in charity should be divided into two portions."
"This one is also the Saṃgha; that one is also the Saṃgha.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātā, having heard that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī were quarreling, slandering, reviling one another, and seeking each other's faults with mouths like swords, had come from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī. Together with five hundred upāsikās, she approached the World-Honored One, prostrated herself at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are quarreling, slandering, reviling one another, and seeking each other's faults with mouths like swords. They have come from Kauśāmbī to Śrāvastī; what should we do?"
The Buddha said:
"One should listen to what those two groups have said, as mentioned above.
If there are robes and articles offered as gifts, they should be divided into two portions; for these belong to the Saṃgha, and those also belong to the Saṃgha."
It is like breaking a golden staff into two pieces; both parts are gold.
If one receives a gift of clothing, it should be divided into two portions; this portion is the Saṃgha, and that portion is also the Saṃgha.
At that time, while traveling on the road, the suspended bhikṣu thought to himself in a secluded place:

"Regarding this matter of dispute, I ought to cite the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma to examine whether this legal action of suspension (ukkhepanīyakamma) is in accordance with the Buddha's Dharma or not; whether it is a suspension performed according to the Dharma and thus valid, or whether it is a suspension not in accordance with the Dharma and thus invalid."
At that time, he immediately examined the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, scrutinizing the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya, and reflected thus:

"This is an offense, not a non-offense; this is a formal accusation, not a non-accusation; this is a formal act of accusation performed in accordance with the Dharma and thus accomplished, not one performed contrary to the Dharma and thus unaccomplished."
He then went to the bhikṣu who had raised the issue and spoke to him thus:
"While traveling on the road, I was reflecting in a quiet place and thought to myself:
'Regarding this matter of dispute, is it an offense or not an offense?'"
He then examined the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma, scrutinizing the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya:

what constitutes an offense and what does not; what constitutes a formal accusation and what does not; and whether a formal act of accusation (kamma) was carried out in accordance with the Dharma and thus valid, or whether it was not carried out in accordance with the Dharma and thus invalid.
Then the monk who had initiated the formal act (ukkhepaka) took the monk who was subject to that act to the monk who had brought the charge (codaka), and said to him:
"This monk who is subject to the formal act spoke to me as follows:
'While traveling on the road, while dwelling in a secluded place in meditation, I thought to myself:'"
“As previously stated.

At that time, the bhikṣu who had raised the accusation took the bhikṣu who was following the accusation and the bhikṣu who had been accused to the place where the World-Honored One was. Having prostrated at his feet, they withdrew to sit on one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“This bhikṣu who follows the accusation has brought the bhikṣu who was accused to me and related the circumstances of the accused bhikṣu in full to me; now he likewise relates these same circumstances in full to the World-Honored One.”
The Blessed One told the bhikṣus:
"This is an offense, not a non-offense; this is a formal accusation, not a non-accusation; it is a formal accusation in accordance with the Dharma. This bhikṣu’s *karmavācanā* is valid."

If that bhikṣu complies with the Saṃgha by repenting and reforming his transgressions, and seeks the lifting of the *ajñapti-caturtha-karman* of suspension, he should then be released by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.

It should be understood in this way: that bhikṣu should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, and after prostrating at the feet of the Saṃgha, place his right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

I, bhikṣu [name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of suspension for refusal to see one's offense (*adarśana-utkṣepa-karman*). Now, in accordance with the Saṃgha, I reform my ways and repent; I beg for the lifting of this suspension for refusal to see one's offense. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me its lifting.
Thus it was said a second and a third time.
Among them, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā*—whether an elder, one seated next in rank, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya—should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of suspension for refusal to see [one's offense].
Now, having complied with the Saṃgha and having reformed and repented, he requests the lifting of the formal act of suspension for refusal to see [one's offense].
"If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall lift the *ajñapti-karman* of not-seeing [the offense] for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"

The bhikṣu so-and-so was subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *tarjanīya* (reproval) for not acknowledging [an offense]; he has now complied with the Saṃgha, corrected his ways, and repented, and he now requests the Saṃgha to grant him release from the *tarjanīya* act.

"Whichever elders among you consent to the lifting of the *kamma* for that bhikkhu named so-and-so, who was previously suspended for not seeing [his offense], remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
This is the first motion."
Thus it was said a second and a third time:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to lift the *ajñapti-karman* of not seeing [the offense] for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
The Buddha said: "I authorize you to perform a *jñapti-karman* for reconciliation; it should be announced as follows:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!'"

The matter that caused the Saṃgha to engage in strife, slander, mutual abuse, and seeking out each other's faults has now been resolved; that person who committed the offense has been formally cleared, and the defilement of the Saṃgha has been extinguished.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha perform the act of concord.
This is the formal motion (jñapti).
One should make the formal motion for concord in this manner.
Then Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

“By what causes and conditions do monks engage in strife, quarreling, slandering, and reviling one another, seeking out each other’s faults, causing the Saṃgha to be split, causing the Saṃgha to dwell in separation, and causing the Saṃgha to become defiled?”
"If that matter has not been settled, not been disposed of, and the defilement of the Saṃgha has not been extinguished, can they achieve a legitimate and harmonious assembly?
The Buddha said,
"They cannot achieve a legitimate and harmonious assembly."

Upāli! On account of that matter of dispute, it causes the Saṃgha to engage in contention, slander, and verbal abuse; they seek out each other's faults, causing the Saṃgha to be split, causing the Saṃgha to dwell separately, and causing the Saṃgha to become defiled.
"Since that dispute has been settled, adjudicated, and the defilement of the Saṃgha has been extinguished, the community may attain harmony in accordance with the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the performance of a *jñapti-karman* for reconciliation through the *poṣadha*. It should be performed with the following announcement (*jñapti*):"
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

On account of that matter, the Saṃgha has been embroiled in strife, contention, slander, and abuse; they have sought out each other's faults, causing the Saṃgha to be split, causing the Saṃgha to dwell apart, and causing the Saṃgha to be defiled."
That person has been subject to the formal act of censure by the Saṃgha, which has now been revoked; thus the impurities of the Saṃgha have been extinguished.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha perform the *poṣadha* in harmony.
"Thus it is announced.
Having thus made the announcement, the *poṣadha* should be performed in harmony.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Upāli:
“There are five kinds of persons who have committed an offense. What are the five?
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, another bhikṣu says to him:”
"Did you commit an offense? Do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."
He says to this bhikṣu, "If you see this offense, you should confess it.
This is the first person who commits an offense.
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, another bhikṣu says to him:
"Do you see that you have committed an offense? He replies:
"I do not see it. That bhikṣu said:
"If you see your transgression, you should confess it before the Saṃgha."
This is the second person who commits an offense.
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, another bhikṣu says to him:
"Have you seen that you have committed an offense?"
He replied, "I did not see it. That bhikṣu said:
"If you recognize your offense, you should confess it before this Sangha.
This is the third type of offender.
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, other bhikṣus say to him:
"Did you commit an offense? Do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."
The community of monks should abandon him and not question him, speaking thus:
"Since you do not now see your fault, wherever you go, they too shall raise your offense against you. For you, they shall declare:

'We do not permit you to perform an *aṇuvāda*, nor do we permit you to participate in the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*. Just as a horse-tamer discards a wicked horse that is difficult to tame, once it has been bound to its stake."
"O bhikṣu, you do not see your own faults; furthermore, you have abandoned everything in this manner. Wherever you go, you shall not even be permitted to participate in the poṣadha or the pravāraṇa."
"One should not seek permission from such a person by saying, 'It is so'; this itself constitutes permission.
This is the fourth type of offender.
When a bhikṣu has committed such an offense, another bhikṣu says to him:
"Did you commit an offense? Do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."
"He should undergo the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for suspension due to 'not seeing' (*adarśana*) within the community of monks; this is the fifth type of offender.
Then the Elder Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, removed his leather sandals, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many qualities must one possess to be appointed as a steward?"
The Buddha said:
"There are five things that should be attended to.
What are the five?
A bhikṣu who intends to perform an action should examine whether that matter is true or not; for there may be matters that are untrue.
If that bhikṣu knows that the matter is untrue, he should not perform it.
If that bhikṣu knows that this matter is true, he should further examine whether this matter is beneficial or not beneficial.
If there is a matter that is not beneficial, and that bhikṣu knows that this matter is not beneficial, he should not perform it.

If a bhikṣu knows that a certain matter is beneficial, he should further examine whether that matter is to be done at the proper time or at an improper time; for there are matters that must be done at an improper time.
If that bhikṣu knows that a matter is to be done at an improper time, he should not do it.

If that bhikṣu knows that this matter is to be done at this time, he should further examine it carefully. If doing this matter will cause the Saṃgha to engage in strife, slander, and verbal abuse; if it will cause the Saṃgha to split, cause the Saṃgha to live separately, and cause the Saṃgha to become defiled—then, in order not to cause the Saṃgha to engage in strife, and so forth, up to not causing the Saṃgha to become defiled, that bhikṣu, if he knows that performing the task will cause the Saṃgha to engage in strife, and so forth, up to causing the Saṃgha to become defiled, should not perform it.

If a bhikṣu undertakes a task that does not cause the Saṅgha to quarrel, nor even cause it to become defiled by dust, that bhikṣu should examine the matter again with great care. He should consider whether the undertaking of the task will result in gaining a faction or failing to gain a faction, or whether the undertaking of the task will fail to gain the support of a faction of bhikṣus.
If that bhikṣu knows he cannot obtain the support of fellow bhikṣus for his undertaking, he should not proceed.
If that bhikṣu knows he can obtain the support of fellow bhikṣus, he should know the proper time and, with a virtuous mind and wholesome thoughts, undertake the task.
"Upāli! A bhikṣu who knows these five dharmas should be appointed as an administrator of affairs.
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and spoke this verse:
"Because the benefit for the Saṅgha is certain, he spoke these words;
how can one know of his excellence?
The bhikṣu has attained firm persistence."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse, answering Upāli:
"First, one upholds the precepts without violation; The bhikṣu’s deportment naturally rectifies his body.
Even an enemy cannot reproach him according to the Dharma; He is able to attain such a state that others have nothing to say."
Abiding in such pure morality, he attains fearless speech free from doubt or difficulty;
amidst the assembly he is neither terrified nor perturbed, never failing to provide answers that accord with the meaning of whatever is asked.
Thus, when questioned on the meaning within this assembly, he answers instantly without thought and without anxiety;
whenever the meaning is asked according to the occasion, he is able to answer, responding to all inquiries with an unwavering mind.
Reverently honor the elder bhikṣus—those of the senior, middle, and junior ranks;
being able to explain causes and origins with skillful discernment, one understands the deceptive speech of all enemies.
Enemies cannot gain the upper hand, and one is likewise able to subdue many others;
always acting as a teacher without fail, one is adorned with wisdom and is esteemed by all.
"If one commits such an offense, though not violating [the formal rule], one incurs guilt;
knowing both these stains, one removes them by confessing the stain.
If one does not repent, the assembly shall expel them; if one repents, the assembly shall not drive them away."
Such a person should be exhorted; one should discern them in this way.
If they have faith, they will be able to accept [the task]; they were sent for the sake of the Saṃgha.
If sent by the assembly, they can carry out the instructions; they can perform the work without being self-exalting.
One who shows reverence to elders, To those of superior, middling, and junior seats;
Whose wisdom brings great benefit— Such a person is able to protect the Dharma.
The Kausāmbī-khandhaka is complete. The Fourth Volume of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume Forty-four, Part Three, Section Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī under the Yao Qin dynasty,
together with Zhu Fonian and others.
7. The Cāpāla Varga, Chapter Ten. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the village of Vāsava in the kingdom of Kāśī, near the city of Cāpāla.
At that time, there was an elder monk in another residence who constantly received people like a spring of water, speaking thus:
"If there are visiting monks from elsewhere, I shall provide them with all their necessities, and I will prepare baths, food, and drink as offerings for them."
At that time, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the human settlements of the Kāśī country who arrived at the village of Vāsava.
The residents there immediately provided them with whatever food, drink, and requisites they required as offerings. On another occasion, those bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"I cannot constantly beg from householders for food, drink, provisions, bathing supplies, and porridge as offerings."
"This visiting bhikṣu has come from a great distance and is now weary; he who previously had no acquaintances now has acquaintances. I shall surely not seek anything further from him."
Thereupon, [the host] immediately stopped.
Those visiting bhikṣus thought to themselves:

“This bhikṣu harbors ill will toward us; whereas he formerly provided us with all our necessary food, drink, and bathing requisites, he now stops and no longer gives them to us. Might we not perhaps suspend this bhikṣu?”
They then united to bring this bhikṣu to account.
That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I am now unable to determine for myself whether this is an offense or not an offense."
Is this a formal act of censure (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) or not?
Is the formal act of censure performed in accordance with the Dharma (*dhamma*) and thus valid, or is it contrary to the Dharma and thus invalid?
"I should now go to the World-Honored One at Campā and report this matter in detail to him.
Whatever instructions the World-Honored One may give, I shall carry them out according to his teaching."
At that time, this resident bhikṣu took his robes and bowl, went to Śrāvastī to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at [the Buddha’s] feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
Then the World-Honored One greeted the visiting bhikṣu, saying:
"Was it easy for you to obtain alms?"
"Are you dwelling in harmony?
Are you not exhausted by the journey? He replied:
"The dwellings are harmonious, alms are easily obtained, and the roads are not wearying.
[The other asked: "From where have you come, bhikṣu? That bhikṣu replied:
"I am staying in the village of Vāsava in the kingdom of Kāśī; at a certain dwelling, the resident elder monks constantly provide for the needs of visiting guests, like a spring of water."
"If there should be visiting bhikṣus coming in the future, provide them with whatever they require: food and drink, or rice gruel, or bathing requisites.
Later, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling through the human settlements of the people of Kāśī and arrived at the village of Vāsavagrāmaka.
At that time, I immediately provided him with whatever food and drink he required, as well as gruel and bathing requisites.
Venerable Sir!
At that time, I had this thought:

"I cannot constantly go to the homes of laypeople to beg for food, drink, and necessary requisites; these visiting bhikṣus are now weary from their travels, having previously been strangers but now having become acquainted with us. I think it best that I no longer seek after them."
Thereupon, [the host] immediately desisted.
Those visiting bhikṣus spoke as follows: "The resident bhikṣus harbor ill will toward us;

previously they constantly provided us with whatever food and drink we required, as well as porridge and bathing requisites, but now they no longer provide for us. We should rather bring charges against those bhikṣus for their offenses."
They immediately united and lifted it together.
Venerable Sir! I had this thought:
"Can one not discern whether this is an offense or not an offense?
Whether this is a formal accusation or not an accusation?
Whether this is a formal act of accusation performed in accordance with the Dharma and successfully accomplished?"
"Is it because this formal act of suspension (*karmavācanā*) was not performed in accordance with the Dharma that it is invalid?

I should rather go to the city of Campā and approach the World-Honored One to report these circumstances in detail. Whatever instructions the World-Honored One gives, I shall carry them out according to his teaching."
The Buddha told that bhikṣu:
"O bhikṣu, you have committed no offense, nor is there any offense;
it was not a formal accusation, it did not constitute a formal accusation, and it was an illegal accusation."
"Your bhikṣu-karman was not accomplished; you, bhikṣu, may now return to the village of Vāsavagrāma and once again provide for the needs of the visiting guests, just like a spring of water."
"Monk, I shall be your companion; it shall be according to the Dharma, not otherwise.

Then that visiting monk, wandering among the people from the village of Vāsavagrāma, arrived at the land of Kāśī and went to where the Blessed One was. He prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted the visiting bhikṣus:
"Have you all lived together in harmony?
Have you not been exhausted by the toil of begging for alms?"
That bhikṣu replied:
"I dwell in harmony; I do not consider begging for food to be suffering. He asked:
"From where have you come? He replied,
"I have come from the village of Vaśava."
He asked, "Is there any resident bhikṣu among you who constantly provides for the needs of visiting guests like a spring of water, whom you have expelled?"
He replied, “Indeed, I lifted it up,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha asked,
"For what reason have you raised this matter? They replied:
"Without cause and without condition.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked that bhikṣu:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How can you, foolish men!
While senior bhikṣus provide for visiting bhikṣus like a spring of water, you have raised this issue without cause?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked the visiting bhikṣus, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“There are four types of formal acts (kamma):
an illegal formal act; an illegal formal act performed by a discordant assembly; an illegal formal act performed by a concordant assembly; and a legal formal act performed by a discordant assembly.”
Among these, there are two types of *karmas*:
an illegal *karman* and a *karman* performed by a divided assembly, both of which should not be carried out; if they have been carried out, they must be rectified according to the Dharma.
A legal *karman* and a *karman* performed by a harmonious assembly should be carried out.
There are four cases regarding the fulfillment of the quorum:

there is one who has attained the quorum and should not be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should be censured; there is one who has not attained the quorum and should not be censured; and there is one who has attained the quorum and should be censured.
What kind of person, when reaching the full quorum, should not be censured?

If one has had the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), or *pratisedha-avasa-tirthika-karman* (act of prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople) performed against them, that person, upon reaching the full quorum, may not be censured.
What kind of person does not count toward the full number and should be censured?
If it is a person who wishes to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*), this person does not count toward the full number and may be censured.
What kind of person does not count toward the full number and also should not be censured?

If a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) is being performed for a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī may not count toward the quorum and may not protest. Likewise, if a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī says: "He has committed a pārājika offense; or he has violated a bhikṣuṇī;

or he received the precepts with a thieving intent; or he has damaged the two [sexual] organs; or he is a eunuch; or he has killed his father or mother; or he has killed an arhat; or he has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; or he has maliciously shed the blood of a Buddha; or he is a non-human or an animal; or he is a hermaphrodite; or he has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya*); or he has been expelled (*pabbājaniya*); or he is subject to expulsion; or he is living in seclusion (*parivāsa*); or he is on the boundary of the *sīmā*; or he is in the air by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*); or he is invisible; or he is out of sight or hearing; or he is the very person for whom the *karmavācanā* is being performed. [In these cases, they do not invalidate the ritual.]
Persons such as these do not count toward the required number and should not be censured.
What kind of persons do count toward the number and may be censured?

If they are virtuous bhikṣus dwelling within the same boundary, who do not use supernatural powers to remain in the air, who do not conceal themselves, and who do not depart from the range of sight or hearing—even speaking to those nearby—persons such as these do count toward the number and may be censured.
At that time, among the group of six bhikṣus, one would suspend another; one would suspend two, or three, or even the entire Saṃgha.
Two would suspend one; two would suspend two, or three, or even the entire Saṃgha.
Three people may suspend one person; or two may suspend two; or three may suspend three;
or the Saṃgha may suspend the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One person may not nominate one person, two persons, or three persons; nor may they nominate the Saṃgha.
Two persons may not nominate one person, two persons, or three persons; nor may they nominate the Saṃgha."
It is not permissible for three people to suspend one person, nor for two or three people to suspend a *saṃgha*.
It is also not permissible for a *saṃgha* to suspend a *saṃgha*.
If one person suspends another person, it is an illegal *karmavācanā*, a non-disciplinary *karmavācanā*, and should not be done so.

If one person censures two, three, or the Saṃgha; or if two persons censure one, two, or three, or the Saṃgha; or if three persons censure one, two, or three, or the Saṃgha; or if the Saṃgha censures the Saṃgha—these are illegal *karmas* and non-disciplinary *karmas*, and should not be done in this way.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus performed the *karmavācanā* again; having performed the *tarjanīyakarman*, they further performed the *pravāsanīyakarman*, the *niśrayakarman*, the *pratisaṃharaṇīyakarman*, imposed the *utksepaṇīyakarman*, the *parivāsakarman*, the *mūlāpakarman*, the *mānatvakarman*, the *ābhṛtyakarman*, the *sammukhavinayakarman*, the *smṛtivinayakarman*, the *amūḍhavinayakarman*, the *pratijñākārakakarman*, the *tatsvabhāvaiṣīyakarman*, the *tatsvabhāvānuvartanakarman*, and the *yadbhūyaiṣīyakarman*.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not perform a formal act (karmavācanā) twice; nor, having performed a formal act of censure (tarjanīya-karman), should one subsequently perform a formal act of banishment (pravāsanīya-karman), up to and including the 'covering with grass' (tṛṇaprastāraka)."
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of saṃghas:
the saṃgha of four persons, the saṃgha of five persons, the saṃgha of ten persons, and the saṃgha of twenty persons."

Among these, for a community of four monks, all legal *karmavācanā* (formal acts) should be performed except for the invitation (*pravāraṇā*), the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the rehabilitation from offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
Among these, for a community of five monks in the central lands, all legal *karmavācanā* should be performed except for the conferral of full ordination and the rehabilitation from offenses.
Among these, for a community of ten monks, all legal *karmavācanā* procedures should be performed except for those pertaining to the removal of offenses (*āpattivyutthāna*).
For a community of twenty monks, all *karmavācanā* procedures should be performed; how much more so for one exceeding twenty!
If a formal act (*karmavācanā*) that requires four persons is performed by those who are one person short of the required number, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary formal act.
This is also the case if a *bhikṣuṇī* is made the fourth person; or if a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī* is used; or if one says: "He has committed a bordering offense (*antimāpatti*);

or he has violated a *bhikṣuṇī*; or he received the precepts with a thieving mind; or he has damaged the two [sexual] organs; or he is a eunuch; or he has killed his father or mother, killed an Arhat, or with an evil mind shed the blood of a Buddha; or he is a non-human or an animal; or he is a hermaphrodite; or he has been suspended (*ukkhepaniya*); or he has been expelled (*pabbājaniya*); or he is one for whom expulsion is appropriate—[if such a person] performs the formal act on behalf of another."
If such persons number exactly four, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karmavācanā*;
it should not be done so. The same applies to a community of five, ten, or twenty persons.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus performed illegal and non-vinaya karmas: they performed illegal karmas of a divided assembly, illegal karmas of a harmonious assembly, legal karmas of a divided assembly, legal-but-similar karmas of a divided assembly, legal-but-similar karmas of a harmonious assembly, and karmas of censure that were not brought to a halt.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "One should not perform an illegal and non-vinaya *karma*;

one should not perform an illegal *karma* of a separate assembly; one should not perform an illegal *karma* of a harmonious assembly; one should not perform a legal *karma* of a separate assembly; one should not perform a legal-like *karma* of a separate assembly; one should not perform a legal-like *karma* of a harmonious assembly; and one should not perform a *karma* of censure that is not brought to a stop."
What is a formal act that is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya?

When a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement) is performed such that the motion has been made but the formal act itself is not carried out, this is called a formal act that is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya; it should not be done so.

To perform two *jñaptis* without performing the *karmavācanā*, to perform three *jñaptis* without performing the *karmavācanā*, or to perform many *jñaptis* without performing the *karmavācanā*—such a formal act is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya; it should not be done.

A *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* consisting of one motion and one proclamation is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*; it should not be performed. Likewise, performing one motion and three proclamations, one motion and many proclamations; two motions and one proclamation, two motions and two proclamations, two motions and three proclamations, or two motions and many proclamations; three motions and one proclamation, three motions and two proclamations, three motions and three proclamations, or three motions and many proclamations; or many motions and one proclamation, many motions and two proclamations, many motions and three proclamations, or many motions and many proclamations—these are all illegal and non-disciplinary *karmans* and should not be performed.

To perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) by performing only the single motion without the proclamation is an illegal and non-disciplinary (*adharma-avinaya*) act;

it should not be done so. To perform two motions without the proclamation, three motions without the proclamation, or many motions without the proclamation is an illegal and non-disciplinary act; it should not be done so.
A *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of one motion and two proclamations) that performs one motion and two proclamations is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*;

it should not be done so. To perform one motion and three proclamations; to perform one motion and many proclamations; to perform two motions and one proclamation; to perform two motions and two proclamations; to perform two motions and three proclamations; to perform two motions and many proclamations; to perform three motions and one proclamation; to perform three motions and two proclamations; to perform three motions and three proclamations; to perform three motions and many proclamations; to perform many motions and one proclamation; to perform many motions and two proclamations; to perform many motions and three proclamations; or to perform many motions and many proclamations—these are illegal and non-disciplinary *karmans*; they should not be done so.

If a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* is performed by making the motion (*jñapti*) contrary to the rules for making a motion, or by performing the formal act (*karman*) contrary to the rules for performing a formal act, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*; it should not be done in such a manner.
If one performs the formal motion (*jñapti*) for a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* but does not perform the actual *karman*, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*; it should not be done so.

If one performs two motions but does not perform the *karman*, or performs three motions but does not perform the *karman*, or performs numerous motions but does not perform the *karman*, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*; it should not be done so.

To perform one motion with one *karmavācanā*, one motion with two *karmavācanās*, one motion with many *karmavācanās*; two motions with one *karmavācanā*, two motions with two *karmavācanās*, two motions with three *karmavācanās*, two motions with many *karmavācanās*; three motions with one *karmavācanā*, three motions with two *karmavācanās*, three motions with three *karmavācanās*, three motions with many *karmavācanās*; or many motions with one *karmavācanā*, many motions with two *karmavācanās*, many motions with three *karmavācanās*, or many motions with many *karmavācanās*—these are illegal and contrary to the *vinaya* procedures; they should not be done in this way.

To perform the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) without making the initial motion (*jñapti*) is an illegal and non-disciplinary (*adharma-aviniya*) formal act;

it should not be done so. To perform two formal acts without the motion, three formal acts without the motion, or many formal acts without the motion is an illegal and non-disciplinary formal act; it should not be done so.

To perform one *karmavācanā* with one motion (*jñapti*), to perform one *karmavācanā* with two motions, to perform one *karmavācanā* with three motions, to perform one *karmavācanā* with many motions; or to perform two *karmavācanās* with one motion, to perform two *karmavācanās* with two motions, to perform two *karmavācanās* with three motions, to perform two *karmavācanās* with many motions; or to perform three *karmavācanās* with two motions, to perform three *karmavācanās* with three motions, to perform three *karmavācanās* with many motions; or to perform many *karmavācanās* with one motion, to perform many *karmavācanās* with two motions, to perform many *karmavācanās* with three motions, or to perform many *karmavācanās* with many motions—these are *karmas* that are neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya, and should not be done.

If one performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* by performing the motion (*jñapti*) contrary to the rules for the motion, or performs the three proclamations (*karmavācanā*) contrary to the rules for the proclamations, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary (*adharma-avinaya*) karman; it should not be done in such a manner.
In this situation, there is a bhikṣu who perceives himself as being without offense. Another bhikṣu says to him:
"Have you committed an offense? Do you see it? He replies:
“I did not see it. He was then subjected to the formal act of *karma* for the offense of claiming “I did not see it.
The Buddha said:
"This is an illegal and non-disciplinary *kamma*; it should not be done thus.
In this situation, there is a monk who has committed an offense but has not yet confessed it, and another monk says to him:
"You have committed an offense; you should confess it."
He replied, "I do not repent.
Thereupon, they immediately performed the formal act of *karma* for non-repentance against him.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them was a bhikkhu who held wrong views and would not relinquish them, and the other bhikkhus said to him:
"You hold a wrong view; you should abandon it.
He replied, "I will not abandon it."
He then proceeded to carry out the formal act of *karma* for not relinquishing a wrong view.
The Buddha said:
"That is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such an act should not be performed."
In this situation, there is a bhikṣu who perceives no offense and does not confess an offense, yet another bhikṣu says to him:
"Do you perceive your offense?
You ought to confess it."
He replied, "I do not see my fault; I do not repent.
They thereupon performed the formal act (karmavācanā) of "not seeing the fault and not repenting" against him.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya;
such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed. Among them, there was a bhikkhu who saw no fault and did not relinquish his evil view. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You see that there is an offense; you should abandon this wrong view.
He replied, "I do not see any offense, nor do I have any wrong view that I would not abandon."
He then proceeded to carry out the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of "not seeing the offense" and "not relinquishing evil views.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such a formal act should not be performed."
In this situation, there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense but does not confess it, and who holds an evil view but does not relinquish it. Other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have committed an offense and should confess it; you must relinquish your evil view."
He replied, "I do not repent;
I have no evil view that I would abandon. He was then subjected to the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of non-repentance and non-abandonment of an evil view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them was a bhikkhu who saw that there was no offense, that there was no confession for an offense, and that there was no evil view to be relinquished. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You have seen your fault; you should confess it and abandon this evil view.
He replied, "I do not see my fault, I do not confess it, and I have no evil view that I would abandon."
He then proceeded to carry out a formal act (*karma*) against him for not acknowledging his offense, not confessing it, and not relinquishing his evil view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act should not be performed."
In this case, there is a bhikṣu who perceives no fault where there is no fault. Another bhikṣu asks him, "Do you see your fault? He replies:
“I saw it. That bhikṣu then performed the formal act of *karma* for one who has committed an offense while claiming not to have seen it.
The Buddha said:
"This is an illegal and non-disciplinary *kamma*; it should not have been done.
In this situation, there is a monk who has no offense and does not need to confess, yet other monks say to him:
"You have an offense; you should confess."
He replied, "I shall confess.
That bhikṣu then performed the formal act (kamma) of non-confession against him.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither a legal act nor a disciplinary act; it should not be done.
In this situation, there was a bhikṣu who held wrong views and would not relinquish them, and other bhikṣus spoke to him, saying:
“You possess an evil view that you must abandon.
He replied, “I shall abandon it.”
He then proceeded to carry out the formal act of *karma* for not relinquishing a wrong view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such a *karma* should not be performed."
In this case, there is a bhikṣu who has committed no offense and perceives himself as having committed no offense, yet does not confess it; other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have seen your offense; you should confess it."
He replied, "I see my fault and shall confess it.
He was then subjected to the formal act of *karma* for one who does not acknowledge their fault and does not confess it.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them, there were bhikṣus who had not recognized their offense and who, possessing evil views, did not relinquish them. Other bhikṣus spoke to them, saying:
"You have seen your fault; you should abandon this evil view.
He replied, "I see my fault; I shall abandon this evil view."
He then proceeded to carry out a formal act (*karmavācanā*) against him for not acknowledging his offense and for not relinquishing his evil views.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act should not be performed."
In this case, there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense but does not confess it, and who holds an evil view but does not relinquish it. Other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have committed an offense and should confess it; you hold an evil view and should relinquish it."
He replied, "I shall confess and abandon my evil view. Thereupon,
they immediately performed the formal act (*karma*) of not confessing and not abandoning the evil view against him.
The Buddha said, "This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them, there was a bhikkhu who saw no offense, had repented for what he saw as no offense, and did not relinquish his evil view. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You have seen your fault; you should confess it, and you should abandon this evil view.
He replied, "I have seen my fault; I shall confess it and abandon this evil view."
He then proceeded to carry out a formal act of *karma* against him for not acknowledging his offense, for not repenting of his evil, and for not relinquishing his wrong view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya; such a *karma* should not be performed."
In this situation, there was a bhikṣu who saw that he had committed an offense. Another bhikṣu said to him, "Do you see that you have an offense? He replied:
“I see it. He then proceeded to perform the *karma* for one who has committed the offense of not seeing [the transgression].
The Buddha said:
"This is an illegal and non-disciplinary *kamma*; it should not be done.
In this situation, there was a bhikkhu who had committed an offense and was confessing it, and another bhikkhu said to him:
"You have an offense; you should confess it."
He replied, "I shall confess.
Thereupon, they immediately performed the formal act of *ajñapti-karman* for his refusal to confess.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them was a bhikkhu who held a wrong view and would not relinquish it, and the other bhikkhus said to him:
"You possess evil views which you should abandon.
He replied, "I shall abandon them."
He then proceeded to carry out the formal act (karman) of not relinquishing a wrong view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither according to the Dharma nor according to the Vinaya; such an act should not be performed."
In this assembly, there was a bhikṣu who saw that he had committed an offense and ought to confess it; another bhikṣu said to him:
"You have seen that you have committed an offense and ought to confess it."
He replied, "I see my fault and shall confess it.
The other monks then performed the formal act of *karma* against him for failing to acknowledge his fault and failing to confess it.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them was a bhikkhu who saw that another had committed an offense and held wrong views yet refused to relinquish them. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You see that there is an offense; you should abandon this wrong view.
He replied, "I see the offense; I shall abandon my wrong view."
That bhikṣu then performed the formal act of *karma* for one who does not acknowledge their offense and who does not relinquish evil views.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither Dharma nor Vinaya; such a *karma* should not be performed."
Among them, there was a bhikṣu who had committed an offense and confessed it, yet did not abandon his wrong view. Other bhikṣus said to him:
"You have committed an offense and should confess it; you must abandon your wrong view."
He replied, "I shall confess; I shall abandon my evil views.
They immediately performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not confessing and not abandoning evil views against him.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor the Vinaya; such a formal act (kamma) should not be performed.
Among them was a bhikkhu who saw another bhikkhu confessing his offense yet refusing to abandon his wrong view. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You must see your transgression and confess it; you should abandon this evil view.
He replied, "I see my transgression and shall confess it; I shall abandon this evil view."
He then proceeded to carry out a formal act (*karma*) against him for not acknowledging his offense, not repenting, and not relinquishing his evil view.
The Buddha said:
"This is neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya; such a formal act should not be performed."
This is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karmavācanā*.
What is a legal and disciplinary *karmavācanā*?

In the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, one performs the motion (*jñapti*) according to the rules for making a motion, and one performs the formal act (*karman*) according to the rules for performing a formal act; such is a legal and disciplinary *karmavācanā* that ought to be so.

The *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) should be performed according to the rules for the motion (*jñapti*) when making the motion, and according to the rules for the three proclamations (*karmavācanā*) when performing the proclamation; the karman should be conducted in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
In this regard, there was a bhikṣu who saw that he had committed an offense. Another bhikṣu asked him, "Do you see that you have committed an offense? He replied:
“I did not see it. He was then subjected to the formal act of *karma* for the offense of claiming not to have seen it.
The Buddha said:
"A formal act (kamma) that accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be conducted in this manner.
In this assembly, there was a bhikkhu who had committed an offense and ought to confess it; another bhikkhu said to him:
"You have committed an offense and ought to confess it."
He replied, "I do not repent.
Thereupon, they immediately performed the formal act of *karma* for non-repentance against him.
The Buddha said:
"If it is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, the formal act (kamma) should be performed accordingly.
In this matter, there was a bhikkhu who held a wrong view and would not relinquish it; other bhikkhus said to him:
"You possess a wrong view; you should abandon it.
He replied, "I will not abandon it."
He then performed the *karman* for not relinquishing a wrong view.
The Buddha said:
"The *karman* that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be conducted in this manner."
In this regard, there is a bhikṣu who perceives an offense and confesses that offense; another bhikṣu says to him:
"You perceive an offense and you confess that offense."
He replied, "I do not see [the offense], nor do I repent. Thereupon,
they performed the formal act (karma) of "not seeing the offense" and "not repenting" against him according to his transgression.
The Buddha said:
"It is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya; the formal act (kamma) should be performed in this manner.
In this situation, there was a bhikkhu who saw that another had committed an offense and held an evil view which he did not relinquish. Other bhikkhus said to him:
"You have committed an offense; you must abandon this evil view.
He replied, "I do not see my offense, and I will not abandon this evil view."
He then performed the *karma* of "not seeing the offense" and "not relinquishing evil views" against him according to the offense he had committed.
The Buddha said:
"The *karma* performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be thus."
In this situation, there is a bhikṣu who has committed an offense and confesses it, yet does not relinquish his wrong view. Other bhikṣus say to him:
"You have committed an offense and should confess it; you must relinquish your wrong view."
