He replied, "I do not repent, nor do I relinquish my evil views. Thereupon,
they performed the formal act (*karma*) of non-repentance and non-relinquishment of evil views against him for his offense.
The Buddha said, "It should be done according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya; such is the proper procedure.
Among them was a bhikṣu who saw another bhikṣu confessing his offense yet not relinquishing his evil views. The other bhikṣus said to him:
"You see that you have committed an offense; you should confess it, and you should abandon your wrong view.
He replied, "I do not see any offense, I will not confess, and I will not abandon my wrong view."
He then performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of not recognizing his offense, not confessing it, and not relinquishing his evil view, exactly according to the offense he had committed.
The Buddha said:
"The formal act in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be thus."
This is a formal act (kamma) that is in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya. What is a formal act that is illegal and performed by a separate assembly?

When a formal act is being performed within a single residence, there are those who do not attend; they should have granted their consent (chanda), yet they do not grant it. Those who ought to be censured in the presence of the assembly are indeed censured. He performs a *ñattidutiya-kamma* (a formal act consisting of one motion and one proclamation) or a *ñatticatuttha-kamma* (a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations); having made the motion for this matter, he performs the formal act for that other matter. This is a formal act that is illegal and performed by a separate assembly.
What is an illegal *saṃghakarma* performed by a united assembly?

It is when, within a single residential community, during a *karma* performed in unison, there are those who have not come and whose consent (*chanda*) should have been given, yet they do not give their consent; or there are those present who ought to voice an objection, yet they do not do so; or when one performs a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, one makes the formal motion for this matter but performs the *karman* for that other matter—this is called an illegal *saṃghakarma* performed by a united assembly.
What is the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of a separate assembly that is contrary to the Dharma?

When a formal act is being performed within a single residential community (*sāṃvāsika*), there are those who do not attend; they should have granted their consent (*chanda*), yet they did not grant it. Those present who ought to voice an objection did so. Although he performed the formal acts of a *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* in accordance with the Dharma, this constitutes a formal act of a separate assembly that is contrary to the Dharma.
What is the *dharmasadṛśa-vibhinna-saṃgha-karman* (a formal act that is similar to the Dharma but performed by a divided assembly)?

It refers to performing a formal act within a single residential community when there are those who do not attend; when those who should grant their consent (*chanda*) do not grant it; when those who should be rebuked in the presence of the assembly are rebuked; when a *jñapti-dvitīya* or *jñapti-caturtha* karman is performed; or when the formal act is performed before the motion (*jñapti*) is made. This is called the *dharmasadṛśa-vibhinna-saṃgha-karman*.
What is the legal concordant and harmonious *karmavācanā*?

When performing a *karmavācanā* at a single residence, those who are absent but ought to grant their consent do grant it; those present who ought to voice an objection do not object; and in the case of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*, the formal motion (*jñapti*) is made after the *karman* has been performed. This is called the legal concordant and harmonious *karmavācanā*.
"Which persons, when censuring, constitute a valid censure?
Some, when censuring, constitute a valid censure; others, when censuring, do not constitute a valid censure.
Which censures do not constitute a valid censure?"
When a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is being performed for a bhikṣu, the rebuke by a bhikṣuṇī does not constitute a valid rebuke.
The same applies if a śikṣamāṇā, śrāmaṇera, or śrāmaṇerī says: "He has committed a pārājika offense; he has violated a bhikṣuṇī;

he received the precepts with a thieving mind; he has damaged the two [sexual] organs; he is a eunuch; he has killed his father or mother; he has killed an arhat; he has maliciously shed the blood of a Buddha; he has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; he is a non-human or an animal; he is a hermaphrodite; he has been suspended (*utkṣiptaka*); he has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*); he is subject to expulsion; he is on the boundary of the *sīmā*; he is undergoing the period of separate residence (*parivāsa*); he is in the air by means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*); he is invisible; he is beyond the range of sight or hearing; or he is the very person for whom the formal act is being performed."
"In such cases, the reprimand is not a valid reprimand.
What constitutes a valid reprimand?

If a virtuous bhikṣu resides within the same boundary, is not in the air, is not concealed, is not beyond the range of sight or hearing, and even speaks to his neighbor—such a reprimand is valid; this is known as the formal act of reprimand (karma)."
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:

"If one performs a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) and subsequently performs a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), is this a *karman* performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya?"
The Buddha said to Upāli,
"This is an illegal *karmavācanā*.
Upāli again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Should the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) have been performed against him, yet instead the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) was performed, or the *pratisedha-avasa-samvāsa-karman* (act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople), or even the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) [for reconciliation], is this a legal act in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya?"
The Buddha said:

"This is contrary to the Dharma; you should not perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him, but rather a *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), or even a *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass). These are illegal and non-vinaya acts; you should not do such things."
"In this manner, proceeding by succession even until it reaches the 'grass-covering-the-earth' [method], such an act that is neither *dharma* nor *vinaya* should not be performed.
The Buddha said to Upāli:

"If one performs an act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) when it is appropriate to perform an act of censure, this is an act that is in accordance with the *dharma* and the *vinaya*, and it should be done so."
"In this manner, even up to the *kamma* of 'covering the ground with grass,' a *kamma* that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya should be performed accordingly.

At that time, in another residence, the community of monks performed a *tarjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) against a bhikkhu, yet they did so through an illegal and discordant assembly (*adhamma-vagga-kamma*).
When the other assembly of monks heard that the former assembly had performed an *adharma* (unlawful) and *asāmagrī* (schismatic) *karmavācanā* against the bhikṣu— rendering the *karman* invalid—
they said, "We shall perform the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him."
They then performed a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) that was contrary to the Dharma and lacked concord.

Furthermore, monks in other locations heard that the assembly of monks had performed a *tarjanīya-karman* against a bhikṣu that was contrary to the Dharma and that the *karman* was invalid due to a lack of concord.
"We shall perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him.
They then performed the *tarjanīya-karman*, but it was a formal act performed by a separate assembly (*bhinnasaṃgha*).

When the monks in other locations heard that the community of monks had performed a *tarjanīya-karman* against that bhikṣu—a formal act performed by a separate assembly—the *karman* was not validly accomplished.
"We shall perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him.
They immediately performed the *tarjanīya-karman*, but it was a semblance of the Dharma and a separate assembly (*nānā-saṃgha*).

When the monks in other locations heard that the monks there had performed a *tarjanīya-karman* against a bhikṣu, they declared that because it was a semblance of the Dharma and a separate assembly, the *karman* was not validly accomplished.
"We shall perform a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against him.
This is a formal act that is concordant with the Dharma and performed in harmony.
That bhikṣu then thinks to himself:
"What should I do? he asked the bhikṣus, who in turn informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"Whatever *karmas* are thus contrary to the Dharma are not accomplished; likewise, all such *karmas* are also not accomplished.
At that time, there was a certain residence where the community of monks performed an illegal *karma* of a separate assembly against a bhikṣu.

At that time, the many monks all disputed with one another: some said it was an illegal *karma* performed by a separate assembly; some said it was an illegal *karma* performed by a harmonious assembly; some said it was a legal *karma* performed by a separate assembly; some said it was a legal-like *karma* performed by a separate assembly; some said it was a legal-like *karma* performed by a harmonious assembly; and some said the *karma* was accomplished, while others said it was not accomplished.
The bhikṣus did not know what to do,
so they informed other bhikṣus.
Those bhikṣus went to inform the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In that residence, the community of monks performed a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against a bhikṣu; it was an illegal act by a divided assembly.

Within this community, the monks disputed with one another: some said it was an illegal act by a divided assembly, some said it was an illegal act by a united assembly, and so on, even saying whether it was valid or invalid."
In this context, when the Sangha speaks of "an illegal separate assembly," these are words of Dharma; even up to "a similar-to-Dharma harmonious assembly," these likewise are words of Dharma.
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a bhikṣu to whom the Saṃgha has previously granted a formal act (karmavācanā), and later the assembly of monks grants him release from it, is the release valid or not?"
The Buddha said to Upāli:
"Sometimes it is accomplished; sometimes it is not.
He asked again:
"What constitutes success and what constitutes failure? The Buddha told Upāli:
"There are thirteen kinds of persons for whom the Saṃgha previously performed a *karmavācanā* that did not result in their release."
"Except for these thirteen types of persons, if the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*karmavācanā*) for others and subsequently grants them release, that release is valid.
Upāli again asked the Buddha:
"If the Saṃgha first performs a formal act against someone, and having performed the act of releasing them from that formal act, then expels them—is that expulsion valid or invalid?"
The Buddha said:
"In some cases the expulsion is accomplished; in other cases it is not accomplished.
If the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) has been performed for one of the thirteen types of persons, the expulsion is accomplished."

Apart from these thirteen types of persons, if one performs a *karmavācanā* for others and later dissolves that *karmavācanā*, it is considered dissolved; however, if one expels them, the expulsion is not valid.
The *Campā-khandhaka* is thus completed. The *Tarjanīya-khandhaka*, Chapter Eleven, Part One. At that time, the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
There were two bhikṣus:
one named Prajñā and the other named Rohiṇa. They delighted in quarreling and reviling one another; their mouths issued forth swords and blades as they sought out each other's faults.
While they themselves were engaged in quarreling, disputing, and reviling one another, if there were other bhikṣus who were also quarreling and disputing, he would go to them and urge them, saying:
"You should exert yourselves well and not be inferior to others; you possess much learning and wisdom, your wealth is superior, and you have many acquaintances."
"We shall act as your allies.
Thus, within this community of monks, where no dispute had previously existed, a dispute arose; and once a dispute had arisen, it was not resolved.
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"By what causes and conditions do disputes arise among the Saṃgha where none existed before, and why are existing disputes not extinguished?"

The bhikṣus immediately recognized that these two bhikṣus, Jñāna and Rohiṇa, delighted in quarreling and reviling one another; their mouths were like swords and blades as they sought out each other's faults and engaged in mutual strife and abuse.
If there are other bhikṣus who are quarreling, he immediately goes to them and exhorts them, saying:
"You should exert yourselves well and not be inferior to others; you possess great learning and wisdom, your wealth is superior, and you have many acquaintances."
"We shall act as your allies.
For this reason, there arise disputes in the Saṃgha where none existed before, and those disputes that already exist are not extinguished.

At that time, among the assembly there were bhikṣus who had heard this—those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities and delighted in training in the precepts—and having censured those two bhikṣus, they went to the World-Honored One. Prostrating themselves at his feet and withdrawing to sit to one side, they reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those two bhikṣus:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."

How is it, Wisdom-Lohitaka! that you engage in mutual strife, quarreling, and verbal abuse, letting swords and blades issue from your mouths, and seeking out each other's faults, so that the Sangha, which had no prior dispute, now has a dispute, and the existing dispute is not extinguished?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"I allow the bhikṣus to perform a formal act of censure (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) against Jñāna and Rohiṇa. It should be carried out as follows: assemble the Saṃgha."

Having assembled the Sangha, one should perform the formal act of *ukkhepana* (suspension) against Wisdom and the others; having performed the *ukkhepana*, one should perform the act of *sativinaya* (reinstatement through recollection); having performed the *sativinaya*, one should assign the offense.
Within the assembly, one who is competent to perform the *kamma* should be appointed, and the following motion (*ñatti*) should be made as above:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!..."

These two bhikṣus, Citta and Loṇagiddha, delight in quarreling together, reviling one another, and speaking words like swords and blades as they seek out each other's faults. Having already quarreled among themselves, if there are other bhikṣus who are quarreling, they immediately go to them and urge them, saying:
"Exert yourselves so that you do not fall short of others; you are more learned and wise, your wealth is superior, and you have many acquaintances."
"We shall act as your allies," they said,
thereby causing disputes to arise where none existed before, and preventing existing disputes from being resolved.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, being patient and attentive, perform the *karma* of censure against the two bhikṣus, Wisdom and his companion:
"Should they hereafter again engage in quarreling and mutual abuse, the Saṃgha shall further increase their punishment."
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These two bhikṣus, Jñāna and Rohiṇa, delight in quarreling together, reviling one another, and uttering words like swords and blades, seeking out each other's faults. Having themselves engaged in such quarrels, whenever there are other bhikṣus who quarrel, they immediately go to them and urge them, saying:"
"Exert yourselves and do not be like others; you possess wisdom and great learning, your wealth is superior, and you have many friends.
We shall act as your allies."
Thus, the Saṃgha brought about disputes where none had existed before, and failed to extinguish those disputes already present.
The Saṃgha then performed a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the two bhikṣus, Jñāna and his companion.

"Whichever elders consent to the Saṃgha performing the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against the two bhikṣus, Jñānaka and his equal, [saying]: 'If hereafter they should again engage in strife or revile one another, the Saṃgha shall further increase their punishment.'"
"Those who approve should remain silent; those who do not approve should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā* concluded.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.
"The Sangha has already consented to carry out the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against Wisdom and the others; the Sangha consents by remaining silent, and thus this matter is so upheld.
Once the act of censure has been performed, five things should not be done:
first, one should not confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon others.
2. One should not receive formal dependence (niśraya) from others;
3. One should not keep śrāmaṇeras;
4. One should not accept an appointment by the Saṃgha to instruct bhikṣuṇīs.
Five: If one has been assigned by the Saṃgha to instruct [others], one should not do so; these are the five things one must not do once the *karma* of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*) has been completed.
Furthermore, there are five other things one must not do: one must not recite the precepts;

if questioned on the meaning of the Vinaya within the Saṃgha, one must not answer; if the assembly appoints one to perform a formal act (*karman*), one must not perform it; if the Saṃgha selects and gathers those of wisdom to deliberate on communal affairs, one must not be included in that instance; and if the Saṃgha appoints one to carry out a confidential mission, one must not carry it out. These are the five things one must not do once the *karma* of censure has been completed.
Furthermore, there are five things one should not do:

one must not enter a village too early; one must not return too late in the evening; one should associate with bhikṣus and not associate with non-Buddhists; one should be well-disposed toward and obedient to the instructions of the bhikṣus; and one should not speak contrary words. These are the five things one should not do after having been rebuked.
Furthermore, there are five things one should not do:

after the Saṃgha has performed the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) against someone according to their offense, that person should not commit this same offense again; nor should they commit any other offense similar to it, arising from it, or more serious than it; nor should they harbor resentment toward the *karman* or the person who performed the *karman*. These are the five things one should not do once the act of censure is completed.
Furthermore, there are five things one should not do:

a virtuous bhikṣu should not accept a seat being spread out for him as an offering; he should not accept another’s washing of his feet; he should not accept another’s provision of items for washing his feet; he should not accept another’s wiping of his leather sandals; and he should not accept another’s rubbing or massaging of his body. These five things should not be done after the *karma* of censure has been completed.
Furthermore, there are five things one should not do:

one should not accept the prostrations, the salutation with palms joined, the welcoming reception, or the carrying of the robes and bowl from a virtuous bhikṣu; these five things should not be done after the *karmavācanā* of censure has been completed.
Furthermore, there are five things one should not do: one should not accuse a virtuous bhikṣu;

one should not cause him to be reminded or to make a formal admission; one should not testify to another's matter; one should not obstruct the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*; and one should not dispute with a virtuous bhikṣu. These are the five things one should not do once the censure has been concluded.
"It should be done in this manner.
After the Sangha had completed the formal act (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) of censure against Jñāna and Rohiṇa, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There are three factors for performing a censure *karman*; if these are absent, it is an illegal and non-vinaya *karman* that is not accomplished."
What are the three?
Not performing the formal act of *ukkhepanīya-kamma* (suspension), not performing the formal act of *sativinaya* (reinstatement through mindfulness), and not confessing one's offense.
Furthermore, there are three other matters:
There are three cases where there is no offense, or where an offense should not be confessed, or where an offense has already been committed and the confession is complete:
namely, when no formal accusation has been made,
when the procedure is contrary to the Dharma, or when the assembly is divided.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
not forming a formal recollection, [acting] contrary to the Dharma, and being a separate assembly.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
Not confessing the offense, being contrary to the Dharma, and being a separate assembly.
Furthermore, there are three other matters:
not having committed an offense, being contrary to the Dharma, and being a separate assembly.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
committing an offense that does not require confession, acting contrary to the Dharma, and performing the rite apart from the assembly.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
Having already confessed a transgression, it is *adharma* (unlawful) and a *pṛthag-varga* (separate assembly).
Furthermore, there are three other cases:
[confessing] not in the presence [of the Sangha], which is *adharma* and a *pṛthag-varga*.
When these three factors are employed in performing a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), it is an illegal and non-vinaya act that is not accomplished.
Furthermore, there are three matters by which, when performing a *tarjanīya-karman*, it becomes a legal and vinaya-compliant act that is accomplished.
What are the three? They are:
performing an act of censure (*ukkhepana*), performing an act of recollection (*sāraṇīya*), and making a formal admission (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
Furthermore, there are three other matters:
There are offenses, offenses that are subject to confession, and offenses for which confession has not yet been made.
Furthermore, there are three matters:
formal accusation, the legal procedure, and communal harmony.
The legal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (recollectedness), which is legitimate and in harmony;
the legal act of *pratijñā-vinaya* (acknowledgment), which is legitimate and in harmony; the legal act regarding the commission of an offense, which is legitimate and in harmony.
The offense is one that may be confessed; the legal procedure is in accordance with the Dharma;
the community is in harmony. The offense has not yet been confessed;

the legal procedure is in accordance with the Dharma; the community is in harmony. Being present before the assembly; the legal procedure is in accordance with the Dharma; the community is in harmony. These three factors constitute a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*); such a formal act is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya.
“There are five factors for performing a *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) that render it illegal, contrary to the *vinaya*, and ineffective:

[the accused] is not present; they do not speak for themselves; they are pure; the act is illegal; and the assembly is divided. These five matters constitute a *tarjanīya-karman* that is illegal, contrary to the *vinaya*, and ineffective.”
There are five factors by which a formal act of censure (tarjanīya-karman) is performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and thus becomes valid.
What are these five?

Presence [of the accused], confession [of the offense], impurity, the Dharma, and harmony—these are the five factors by which a formal act of censure is performed in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, and thus becomes valid.

If the Saṃgha is gathered for either the morning meal or the afternoon meal, whether for preaching the Dharma or for the Poṣadha ceremony, the person subject to the *karman* of censure should adjust his robes, remove his leather sandals, stand to one side, kneel with his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
“Accept my confession; from this day forward, I shall reproach myself with a sincere heart and cease [this conduct] forever.
At that time, the bhikṣus Jñāna and Rohiṇa, acting in accordance with the Saṃgha and without opposition, sought the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If one complies with the Saṃgha without opposition and seeks the lifting of the *karma* of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), it is permitted to lift it by means of a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
There are five conditions under which one should not perform the *karma* of releasing a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*):
one should not confer the full precepts upon others, nor should one engage in quarreling with virtuous bhikṣus.
When a person subject to censure possesses these five qualities, one should not perform the *karma* of releasing that censure.

There are five conditions for which a formal act of reconciliation (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*) should be lifted: one has not conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, nor has one engaged in a quarrel with a virtuous bhikṣu.
For one who has been subjected to a formal act of censure (*tarjanīya-karman*), there are likewise these five conditions for which it should be lifted.

It should be understood in this way: the person who has been subjected to the *karma* of censure should go before the community of monks, bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Sangha, please listen!
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the act of formal censure (tarjanīya-karman).
Now, in accordance with the Saṃgha and without opposition, I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this act of formal censure.
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
Thus he should announce a second and a third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed, and he shall make the following announcement as above:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu [Name] has had the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu has complied with the Saṃgha without opposition and now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the *karman* of censure against the bhikṣu so-and-so be lifted.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!”
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has had the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu has complied with the Saṃgha without opposition and now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman*.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha’s lifting of the *tarjanīya-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the first motion."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to the completion of the *karma* of censure for the monk so-and-so. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held as such."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, in the kingdom of Kāpilavastu, there were two resident bhikṣus:
one named Aśvajit and the other named Pūrṇaśa.
In the country of Vajjī, he has committed evil deeds and defiled families; his commission of evil deeds is both seen and heard of, and his defilement of families is both seen and heard of.
He has performed such evil deeds as these:

They themselves plant flowering trees and teach others to plant them; they themselves irrigate and teach others to irrigate; they themselves pluck flowers and teach others to pluck them; they themselves make flower garlands and teach others to make them; they themselves carry various flowers and teach others to carry them to the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*). They sit on the same bed with men or women, eat from the same vessel, and drink from the same vessel; they sing, dance, play, and laugh, performing various musical entertainments. If others perform such acts, they join in by singing along and acting together; they may whistle, play drums or reed organs, blow conch shells, imitate the cries of peacocks, or mimic the calls of cranes; they may run about, pretend to limp, whistle, act as jesters (*bhāṇaka*), or accept wages for their comic performances.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus were traveling through the human realm from the country of Kāśi and arrived at the kingdom of Kuśinagara. In the early morning, they put on their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city to beg for food.

His gait was dignified and his deportment composed; his gaze was steady and his movements—whether bending, stretching, looking down, or looking up—were measured. Carrying his robe and bowl, he walked straight ahead with his eyes fixed forward, his faculties undisturbed, as he went on almsround in the kingdom of Vajjī.
When the householders saw them, they spoke thus:
"Who are these people? They gaze intently without laughing or joking; they do not look to the left or right; they do not draw near one another for amusement, nor do they exchange greetings."

"We should not give food to this man; he is not like our śramaṇas Aśvajit and Pūrṇaśas, who do not gaze intently, nor speak with playful laughter, nor look about to the left and right, nor seek mutual entertainment, but instead offer one another consolation. To such people as these, we should give food."
At that time, while the bhikṣus were begging for alms in the kingdom of Kevaddha and had obtained enough to satisfy themselves, those bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"The bhikṣus who have long resided here are wicked; these wicked bhikṣus dwell among us, keeping the virtuous bhikṣus at a distance."
He committed such evil deeds as planting various flowering trees, even to the point of accepting employment from others.

At that time, the bhikṣus, having traveled through the human world among the people of Veḷudvīpa, returned to the city of Śrāvastī and approached the World-Honored One; they prostrated themselves at his feet and sat down to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One comforted the bhikṣus, saying:
"Do you dwell in harmony and at ease?
Are you not weary from the labor of seeking food and drink?"
He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The community of monks dwells in harmony, peace, and happiness.
We have been traveling through the human realms among the people of the Kāśī country and have arrived at the kingdom of Kīṭāgiri.”
He reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked him, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it, Āśvalāyana and Puṇṇa! That you defile families and engage in evil conduct?
That you are seen and heard to defile families, and seen and heard to engage in evil conduct; that you perform various evil deeds:
planting trees of variegated flowers, even to the point of accepting employment as a servant?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Aśvajit and Pūrṇaśas, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of banishment against Aśvajit and Pūrṇaśas."

It should be done in this manner: assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, perform the formal act of censure against Aśvaka and Punarvasuka; having performed the censure, perform the act of calling to mind; having performed the calling to mind, assign the offense.
In this matter, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

These bhikṣus, Aśvaji and Punabbasu, have defiled families and committed evil deeds in the kingdom of Veḷudvīpa; that they have defiled families has been both seen and heard by us, and that they have committed evil deeds has also been both seen and heard."
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent and perform the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against Aśvabhya and Pūrṇaśobha:
"You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to defile families, and you have been seen and heard to commit evil deeds."
"You should depart from this dwelling place; you need not remain in this dwelling place.
Thus he speaks. "Venerable Sangha, listen!

These bhikṣus, Aśvaka and Punabbasuka, have defiled families and committed evil deeds in the kingdom of Veḷudvīpa; their defiling of families has been both seen and heard of, and their committing of evil deeds has also been both seen and heard of.
The Sangha now performs the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) against Aśvabhū and Pūrṇaśas.
"You have defiled families and committed evil deeds; you have been seen and heard to defile families, and you have been seen and heard to commit evil deeds."
"Depart from this dwelling place; you need not stay here.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) against the bhikṣus Aśvaka and Punabbasu remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
"This is the conclusion of the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise spoken.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to carry out the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīyakarman*) against Aśvabhū-Punarvasu; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter shall be upheld."
Regarding those who perform the formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*), there are five things they must not do:
they must not confer the full precepts upon others, nor may they engage in quarrels with virtuous bhikṣus.

"It should be done in this manner, as in the aforementioned *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure), with the exception that the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) is not performed within the assembly.

After the community of monks had performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) of *pravāsanīya* (act of banishment) against the bhikṣus Aśvaka and Punarvasuka, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There are three factors and five factors by which a *pravāsanīya-karman* is performed; it is illegal, contrary to the *vinaya*, and the karman is not accomplished, as described above."

“There are three dharmas and five dharmas by which a formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīyakarman*) is performed; such a karman is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, as described above.
When the monk who had been banished came into the boundary of the community of his own accord without being summoned, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“He should not come into the boundary without being summoned; it is permitted for him to stay outside.”
He sent a trustworthy messenger to the community of monks to announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, I repent.
From this day forward, I shall reproach myself with a sincere heart and will never do so again."
Those bhikṣus, Aśvabhya and the others, followed the Saṃgha and did not dare to oppose it; they requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pravāsanīyakarman*.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If they follow the Saṃgha without opposition and request from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pravāsanīyakarman*, one should grant them the lifting by means of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman*."

There are five conditions under which one should not be granted the *karma* of revocation of suspension (*abbhāna-kamma*): from having conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, up to having quarreled with virtuous bhikṣus.

Furthermore, there are five conditions under which one should be granted the *karma* of revocation of suspension: from not having conferred the full ordination upon others, up to not having quarreled with virtuous bhikṣus.

A bhikkhu who has been thus understood as having been expelled should go before the Saṃgha, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, placing his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, make this announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, bhikṣu [name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment).
Now, in accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose them, I beg the Saṃgha for the lifting of this *pravāsanīya-karman*.
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, perform for me the *karmavācanā* for the revocation of the suspension.
Thus he should speak a second and a third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of banishment (pravāsanīya-karman).
He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to disobey; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of this act of banishment."

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of revoking the suspension (*pravāsanīya-karman*) for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of suspension (pravāsanīya-karman).
He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of this suspension.
The Sangha now performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the lifting of the suspension from the bhikṣu so-and-so.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha’s lifting of the suspension from the bhikṣu so-and-so should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and third time.
"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent for the *karman* of revoking the suspension for the bhikṣu so-and-so; because the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.

There was a bhikṣu named Saṃgharakṣita who was dull-witted and ignorant, frequently committing many offenses. He lived in close association with laypeople, mingling with them and becoming intimate with them, rather than following the Buddha’s Dharma.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They reproached the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita, saying:

"You are deluded and ignorant, having committed many offenses against the community. Why do you dwell in close association with laypeople, living in their midst, and fail to act in accordance with the Buddha's Dharma?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
"Why do you dwell in association with laypeople, becoming intimate with them, being ignorant and deluded, committing many offenses, and failing to accord with the Buddha's Dharma?
Having thus rebuked him, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita to establish him under formal dependence (*niśraya*)."

It should be done in this manner: assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, perform the formal act of *ukkhepanīyakamma* (suspension); having performed the *ukkhepanīyakamma*, perform the act of *sativinaya* (reinstatement through recollection); having performed the *sativinaya*, impose the penalty.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is foolish and ignorant, having committed many offenses; he dwells in close association with laypeople and is not in accordance with the Buddha-dharma."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of granting dependence to the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita is ignorant and lacks understanding, having committed many offenses; he dwells in close association with laypeople and does not accord with the Buddha-dharma.
The Saṃgha now performs the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) against the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita.
Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Saṃgha performing the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) for the bhikṣu Śramaṇaka remain silent;
those who do not consent speak. This is the first formal act.
The second and third times were spoken in the same manner.

"The Saṃgha has already granted its consent; the formal act (kamma) for making the bhikṣu Saṅgharakṣita have a preceptor has been completed. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held as such."
Once the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman) has been completed, five things must not be done:
one may not confer the full precepts upon others, nor may one engage in a quarrel with a virtuous bhikṣu, and so forth.
"It should be done in this manner.

In this matter, after the community of monks had completed the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to grant the monk Saṅgharakṣita a *niśraya* (dependence/support), the monks informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"There are three factors and five factors [to consider] regarding whether one may or may not perform the *niśraya-karman*, as explained above."
When they performed the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) by specifying a particular direction, the people in that area were destroyed and rose in rebellion. The Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal act of dependence by specifying a particular direction."
They performed the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) by naming a country as the place of dependence. When that country was destroyed and its people were dispersed, the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal act of dependence by naming a country."
They performed the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) by designating a residence. When the people of that residence were dispersed, the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal act of dependence by designating a residence."

If one performs the formal act of *niśraya* (reliance) by designating a person, yet that person has broken the precepts, or broken the view, or broken the proper conduct, or has been subject to suspension (*utkṣepa*), or has been expelled (*pravāsanīya*), or is subject to expulsion, and thus cannot increase the qualities of a śramaṇa—the Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal act of *niśraya* by designating such a person."
They performed the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of designating the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) as the basis for dependence. During that person's retreat, they attained wisdom. The Buddha said:
"One should not perform the formal act of designating the rainy season retreat as the basis for dependence; rather, you should say:
'You should accept dependence and dwell [under it].'"
At that time, the bhikṣu Saṃgharakṣita was on intimate terms with the bhikṣus in the village; he was learned, wise, and skilled in speech.

Saṃgharakṣita went to them to study the Dharma and Vinaya. During the rainy season retreat (varṣā), he attained wisdom and remained in harmony with the community of monks, not daring to act in opposition to them. He then requested from the community of monks the lifting of the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman).
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu who is compliant with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it requests the Saṃgha to revoke the *niśraya-karman*, the Saṃgha should grant the revocation by means of a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
There are five conditions for which the *niśraya-karman* (act of granting dependence) should not be revoked:
from having received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from another person, up to having quarreled with a virtuous bhikṣu.
There are five conditions for which the *niśraya-karman* should be revoked:

From not conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, up to not quarreling with virtuous bhikṣus—if one possesses these five qualities, the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) should be revoked for them.

It should be revoked in this manner: the one subject to the *niśraya-karman* should come before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and make the following formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have had the formal act of dependence (*niśraya-karman*) performed upon me by the Saṃgha.
I now comply with the Saṃgha and request from the Saṃgha the lifting of this formal act of dependence.
"May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the formal act (kamma) for the lifting of dependence.
Thus he should announce a second and third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the formal act should be appointed as above, and he should make the following announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has been granted the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of dependence by the Saṃgha.
He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of this formal act of dependence."
"If it is the time for the Sangha and the Sangha permits, let the Sangha now perform the *karmavācanā* to revoke the *niśraya-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Sangha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has had the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence) performed upon him by the Saṃgha.
In accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose them, he now requests from the Saṃgha the revocation of the *niśraya-karman*.
The Saṃgha now performs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) to release the bhikṣu [Name] from his dependence.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s performance of the formal act to release the bhikṣu [Name] from his dependence should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.
'The Saṃgha has already consented to complete the *niśraya-vimocana-karman* for the bhikṣu so-and-so; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, together with five hundred bhikṣus, were traveling through the human settlements of the land of Kāśi when they arrived at the Ghoṣitārāma forest.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were staying in the Āmalakī Garden.

Then there was a householder named Citta, who heard that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, having been wandering through the human realms among the people of the Kāśī country, had arrived at the Gahvara Forest and were residing in the Āmalakī Garden.
Then that householder went to where Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana were, prostrated himself at their feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana preached the Dharma to him in various ways to instruct and transform him, causing him to attain joy.
At that time, having heard the Dharma taught by Śāriputra and the others, the householder attained understanding and was filled with joy; he then said:
"I pray that the Venerable One, together with the assembly of monks, will accept my invitation for tomorrow."
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana accepted this in silence.
Knowing that Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had consented, the householder rose from his seat, paid his respects, and departed.
He immediately returned to his home and prepared various kinds of food and drink; there was no delicacy in the world that was not present.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Sudharma who had long resided in the Āmalaka Garden, and he thought to himself:
"I should go to the house of the householder Citta to see the food and drink he has prepared."
"What is the manner of preparing food for a visiting bhikṣu?
And what is the manner of preparing food for a resident bhikṣu?

At that time, the bhikṣu Dharmasena went to that house and arrived at the place where the food was being prepared. He inspected it and saw that among all the worldly utensils and provisions for food and drink, there was nothing lacking in flavor. Having seen this, he spoke these words:
"The householder prepares various kinds of food for the visiting bhikṣus, yet he prepares different kinds of food and drink for the resident bhikṣus.
Out of jealousy, they gave rise to anger and spoke these evil words:
"Among all the food and drink prepared by this householder, there is nothing in the world that is not present; there is no flavor lacking, except for sesame dregs."
The householder Citta then said: "Venerable Sādhū,
you who possess such abundant treasures as the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and right attainment, why do you utter such coarse words?"
"Virtuous one!
I have prepared such fine food; what shall I do with the sesame dregs?
She then spoke again:
"I shall now speak a parable, for those of wisdom understand through analogies.
Suppose there is a country where no roosters exist, and a merchant arrives in that land bringing a hen with him."
At that time, there was no rooster for that hen, so she mated with a crow.
The hen subsequently laid eggs from which chicks emerged; they did not crow like chickens nor did they caw like crows, and were thus named "crow-chickens."
Such are these wholesome dharmas!
Possessing such manifold treasures—namely the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, mindfulness, meditative concentrations, and right attainments—you yet utter such coarse words.
"Having prepared such superior delicacies and fine foods, for what purpose do you now seek sesame dregs? He spoke thus:
"The householder reviled me; I wish to depart now."
The householder said,
"Venerable Sādhudharma!
I have not spoken ill of you, nor have I reviled you."
"Virtuous and noble one!
It would be wonderful for you to dwell here in this dense forest; I shall provide you with robes, bedding, food and drink, and medicinal requisites."
He spoke thus: "The householder reviled me; I wish to depart.
He was then asked:
"Venerable sir!
Where do you wish to go? He replied:
"I wish to go to Śrāvastī to the presence of the Blessed One.
The householder said:
"Relate everything we have discussed to the Blessed One exactly as it was, without adding or subtracting anything."
"Why is this? You should return to where I am.
At that time, the bhikṣu Sudharma took his robes and bowl and went to the place of the World-Honored One; having prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, he withdrew and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One inquired after the bhikṣus:
"Are you dwelling in peace and comfort?
Are you not exhausted or distressed by lack of food and drink?"
He replied, "I am dwelling in peace and happiness; I do not find it difficult to obtain food and drink.
He then reported to the World-Honored One, in full detail and without omission or addition, everything that the householder had said.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of countless skillful expedients, rebuked the bhikṣu Dharmadatta, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that ought not to be done."
How is this, Śukradharma!
That householder possesses faith and joy; as a great donor, he provides much benefit by supplying the Saṃgha—how then can you revile him with such base and contemptuous words?
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked Sādhudharma, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I allow the bhikṣus to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against the bhikṣu Sādhudharma to prohibit him from entering the homes of laypeople."
There are five qualities for which a bhikṣu should not have the formal act of *karmavācanā*—the prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople—performed against him:

not honoring one's parents; not respecting śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; and not firmly upholding that which ought to be upheld. If he possesses these five qualities, the Saṃgha should not grant him the formal act of prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople.
There are five qualities for which the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of *karmavācanā* to prohibit [a monk] from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadātavasana*).

These five qualities are: showing reverence to one’s parents; showing reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; and firmly upholding, without abandoning, that which ought to be upheld. When these five qualities are present, the Saṃgha should perform the formal act of prohibiting him from entering the homes of laypeople.
If a bhikṣu possesses ten qualities, a formal act of prohibition (*pratisedha-karman*) against his entering the homes of laypeople should be performed:

he speaks ill of and reviles the families of laypeople; he employs means to cause the decline of the families of laypeople; he acts to their disadvantage; he acts to their detriment; he incites strife among laypeople; he slanders the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in the presence of laypeople; he utters insults regarding lowly matters in the presence of laypeople; and he promises laypeople something according to the Dharma but does not fulfill it.
If a bhikṣu possesses these ten qualities, the formal act of *karmavācanā* for prohibiting him from entering the homes of laypeople (*avadhyāna-karman*) should be performed against him.

Likewise, if he possesses nine qualities, eight qualities, and so on down to a single quality—namely, speaking ill of or reviling laypeople—the formal act of *karmavācanā* for prohibiting him from entering the homes of laypeople should be performed against him.

One should act in this manner: assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, perform the formal act of censure (ukkhepanīyakamma); having performed the censure, perform the act of calling to mind (sativinaya); having performed the calling to mind, bestow the penalty.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This Bhikṣu Saddharma is a donor, the householder Citta, who has faith and devotion; he constantly delights in giving and provides for the community of monks, yet [this monk] reviles him with insults and abuse as if he were lowly."

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of prohibiting the bhikṣu Saddharma from entering the homes of laypeople.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣu Śubhadatta was reviled with insults by the householder Citta, a devoted donor who always delighted in practicing charity and providing for the Saṅgha.
The Sangha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the monk Sādhudharma to prohibit him from entering the homes of laypeople.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha performing the *karmavācanā* to prohibit the monk Sādhudharma from entering the homes of laypeople should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are likewise spoken.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *karmavācanā* for the monk Śubhadharma to prohibit him from entering the homes of laypeople; the Saṃgha consents, because of their silence. This matter is thus upheld."
Once he has performed the *karmavācanā* of prohibiting [the monk] from entering the homes of laypeople, there are five things he must not do:
he must not confer the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon others, nor may he engage in a quarrel with a virtuous bhikṣu.
"It should be done in this manner.

The Saṃgha performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to place the bhikṣu Śubhadharma under the restriction of not being allowed to go to the homes of laypeople. When the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said:

"There are three factors and five factors by which the *karman* of restricting someone from going to the homes of laypeople is performed; if these are present, it is an illegal and non-disciplinary *karman*, and thus it is not accomplished, as explained above."

There are three factors and five factors by which the *karmavācanā* for prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople is performed; it is accomplished through a *karmavācanā* that is in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, as described above.
The Buddha said:

"I permit you to dispatch a messenger to the house of the householder Citta to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* on behalf of the bhikṣu Dharmadinnā, in order to cause the householder Citta to repent."
There are eight qualities by which one should be appointed as a messenger:
first, being learned;
second, being able to speak well.
3. Having already understood it oneself;
4. being able to understand the meaning of others' thoughts;
5. receiving the words of others.
Sixth, the ability to retain what has been learned;
seventh, being free from omissions or errors;
eighth, understanding the meaning of words, whether virtuous or non-virtuous.
"There are eight such qualities by which one should be appointed as an emissary.
He then spoke in verse:
"Standing before the assembly of wise men, His speech shall be free from error;..."
There is neither increase nor decrease, and he does not fail to uphold the teachings spoken.
His words cannot be destroyed, and hearing them, one is not shaken;
such a bhikṣu is capable of serving as an envoy.

“There are these eight qualities, Ānanda, which you are fully able to uphold: hearing them, being able to explain them well, understanding them yourself, being able to understand the minds of others, receiving the words of others, being able to remember and maintain them without omission or loss, and understanding the meaning of both wholesome and unwholesome speech.”
The Buddha said:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to appoint Ānanda as a messenger to offer repentance on behalf of the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma to the householder Citta. Perform the formal act of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."
It should be performed in this manner: from among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let Ānanda be appointed as a messenger to receive the confession of the householder Citta on behalf of the bhikṣu Sudharma."
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now the Saṃgha appoints Ānanda as a messenger to perform repentance on behalf of the bhikṣu Sudharma for the householder Citta."
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to appoint Ānanda as a messenger to cause the bhikṣu Sādhūka to perform repentance before the householder Citta remain silent;
those who do not consent speak."
“The Saṃgha has already consented to appoint Ānanda as the messenger to perform the repentance for the bhikṣu Sādhudharma on behalf of the householder Citta.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.”
Once the Sangha has finished appointing the messenger, he goes to the householder’s home and speaks thus:
"Householder! Repent!
"The Sangha has already imposed a penalty upon the bhikṣu Śubhadharma.
If he accepts the confession, that is well.

If he does not accept it, one should go to a place where he is within sight but beyond hearing, station a *karmakāraka* bhikṣu in that place where he is within sight but beyond hearing, and instruct him to perform the confession according to the Dharma.
They came again and said to the householder: "Householder! Repent!
"That bhikṣu previously committed an offense, but having now repented, the offense has been removed.
If he accepts the repentance, it is well;
if he does not accept it, the bhikṣu who committed the offense should go in person to repent.
Having thus heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda led the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma to the house of the householder Citta and said to him: “Repent!”
"Householder!
That bhikṣu has already been subjected to the censure of the Saṃgha.
Thereupon, the householder Citta immediately repented along with him.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma followed the Saṃgha and did not dare to oppose it; he requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karman* of prohibition against visiting the homes of laypeople.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the bhikṣu Kalyāṇadharma follows the Saṃgha without opposition and requests the lifting of the *karman* of prohibition against visiting the homes of laypeople, you should grant him the lifting through a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
There are five cases in which the *karmavācanā* for revoking the prohibition against entering the homes of laypeople (*avadhyāna-gṛha-pratiṣedha*) should not be granted:
from the time one has conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another person, up to the point of having fought with a virtuous bhikṣu.
There are five conditions for which one should grant the *karmavācanā* for the revocation of the prohibition against entering the homes of laypeople:
from not conferring the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others, up to not engaging in quarrels with virtuous bhikṣus.
If these five conditions exist, one should grant the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the prohibition against entering the homes of laypeople.

It should be lifted in this manner: the person subject to that *karman* should come before the Saṃgha, bare the right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have had the *karmavācanā* for the prohibition against entering the homes of laypeople performed upon me by the Saṃgha.
Now, in accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose them, I beg the Saṃgha to revoke this *karmavācanā* prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople.
"May the Sangha, out of compassion, grant me the lifting of the *karmavācanā* for the prohibition against going to the homes of laypeople.
Thus he should speak a second and a third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the formal act (*karmavācanā*) should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu has had the *karman* of 'prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople' performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu, in accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, requests the Saṃgha to revoke the *karman* of 'prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople.'"
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the *karmavācanā* for the revocation of the prohibition against going to the homes of laypeople.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
That bhikṣu so-and-so has had the *karmavācanā* of "prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople" performed against him by the Saṃgha.
That bhikṣu, being compliant with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of that *karmavācanā* of prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople.
The Saṃgha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the monk so-and-so to revoke the prohibition against entering the homes of laypeople.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha revoking the prohibition against the monk so-and-so entering the homes of laypeople should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.

'The Saṃgha has already consented to complete the *karmavācanā* for the lifting of the prohibition against [this] monk going to the homes of laypeople. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.'"
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 44 [and] Volume 45,
Part 3, Section 9. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others, this is the remainder of the *Kṣudraka-vastu* (Section on Reprimands). At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
Then, the bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense, and other bhikṣus said to him:
"You have committed an offense;
do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:
"How can you commit an offense and yet, when the bhikṣus say to you, 'Have you committed an offense?
Do you see it? [you refuse to acknowledge it]?"
He replied, "I did not see him.
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, stood to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda:
"How is it, bhikṣu Chanda! You have committed an offense, yet when the bhikṣus speak to you, [you do not acknowledge it]?"
"Did you commit an offense? Do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."
After the World-Honored One had rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to suspend the bhikṣu Chanda for failing to acknowledge his offense."

One should act in this manner: one should assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, one should perform the formal accusation (ukkhepana); having performed the accusation, one should grant the formal reminder (sāraṇīya-kamma); having granted the formal reminder, one should impose the offense.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense, and other bhikṣus have said to him:"
"Have you committed an offense?
Do you see it? He replied, "I do not see it."
“If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *karma* of censuring the bhikṣu Chanda for not seeing his own offense.
This is the motion. “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense, and the other bhikṣus said to him:
"Have you seen that you have committed an offense? He replied:
"I did not see it. Now the Saṃgha shall perform the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of the monk Chanda on the ground of his refusal to acknowledge an offense.

Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha performing the formal act of suspension for the monk Chanda on the ground of his refusal to acknowledge an offense, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.

"The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *tajjanīya-karman* for the sake of the bhikṣu Cchanda for not seeing his offense; the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent. This matter is thus upheld."
Once the formal act of *karma* for not seeing one's offense has been performed, there are five things one must not do:
one may not confer the full precepts upon others, nor may one engage in a quarrel with a virtuous bhikṣu, and so forth.
"It should be done in this manner.

After the community of monks had performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) of "reproving for not seeing one's offense" against the bhikṣu Chanda, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"There are three factors and five factors by which the *karman* of reproving for not seeing one's offense is performed; it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and the *karman* is not accomplished, as described above."

Furthermore, there are three dharmas and five dharmas by which the formal act of *karma* for charging a monk with not seeing his own offense is performed; it is a legal and Vinaya-compliant *karma*, accomplished as described above.

When that monk charged with not seeing his offense is present—whether the Saṃgha is at the morning or midday meal, or during the preaching of the Dharma or the *poṣadha*—he should go before the Saṃgha and stand to one side. With his right shoulder bared, his sandals removed, and his right knee touching the ground, he should join his palms and say:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
"I accept my repentance and reproach my own mind; from this day forward, I dare not commit such acts again.
Thus, the bhikṣu Chanda, in accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karma* of suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

“If the bhikṣu Chanda complies with the Saṃgha without opposition and requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karma* for suspension for not acknowledging an offense, the Saṃgha should grant him the lifting through a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).”

There are five conditions for which one should not grant the *karma* of revocation for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of "not seeing one's own fault" (*adarśana-utkṣepa*): from having conferred the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon another, up to fighting with a virtuous bhikṣu.

There are five conditions for which one should grant the *karma* of revocation for the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense of "not seeing one's own fault": from not having conferred the full ordination upon another, up to not fighting with a virtuous bhikṣu.
It should be understood in this way: among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

That bhikṣu so-and-so has been granted by the Saṃgha the formal act of suspension for not seeing his offense (*adarśana-utksepa-karman*). He has complied with the Saṃgha and did not dare to disobey, and now he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of that formal act of suspension for not seeing his offense."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now lift the *karma* of suspension for not seeing one's offense against the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

A certain bhikṣu has had the formal act of *karma* for the suspension for not seeing one's offense performed against him by the Saṃgha. He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it; he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not seeing one's offense.
The Saṃgha now intends to lift the *karma* of suspension for not seeing one’s offense against the bhikṣu [Name].
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha lifting the *karma* of suspension for not seeing one’s offense against the bhikṣu [Name] should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner:
'The Saṃgha has already consented to lift the *karma* of suspension for not seeing one's offense against the monk so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents, because of its silence; thus this matter is upheld.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
Then, the bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense, and the bhikṣus said to him:
"You have committed an offense; you must repent."
He replied, "I will not confess.

When the other bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured the bhikṣu Chanda, saying:
"How does one commit an offense such that another bhikṣu says to him,
'You have committed an offense; you must confess it,' and he replies:..."
"I shall not repent.
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked the bhikṣu Chanda:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."
How does one commit an offense such that another bhikṣu says to him:
"You have committed an offense; confess it"? He replies:
"I do not repent. Having rebuked him thus, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) against the bhikṣu Chanda for the offense of refusing to repent."

It should be done in this manner: one should assemble the Saṃgha; having assembled the Saṃgha, one should perform the formal act of accusation (ukkhepana); having performed the formal act of accusation, one should perform the formal act of recollection (sāraṇīya-kamma); having performed the formal act of recollection, one should impose the offense.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Chanda has committed an offense, and other bhikṣus have said to him:"
"You have committed an offense; you must repent. He replied, "I will not repent."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *karma* to charge Chanda with an offense that does not require confession.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
This bhikṣu Chanda committed an offense, and the other bhikṣus said to him:
"You have committed an offense; confess it. He replied:

"Non-confession. Those elders who consent to the Sangha performing the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of Chanda for the offense of non-confession should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
A second and a third time it is spoken thus:

'The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the formal act of suspension for the offense of non-confession against the bhikṣu Chanda; the Saṃgha consents, because of its silence. Thus this matter is to be maintained.'"
Once he has been dealt with for an offense that was not confessed, there are five things he must not do:
he must not confer the full precepts upon others, and so on, up to he must not engage in quarreling with virtuous bhikṣus.
"It should be done in this manner.

After the Saṃgha had performed the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) to suspend Chanda for failing to repent, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"There are three factors and five factors by which the formal act of suspending one for failing to repent is performed; it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and the karman is not accomplished, as explained above."

There are three factors and five factors by which the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of one who has committed an offense that must not be confessed is performed; it is a formal act in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya, accomplished as described above.

When the person against whom the formal act of suspension for an unconfessed offense has been carried out is present—whether the Sangha is at a small meal or a large meal, or when they are preaching the Dharma or performing the *poṣadha*—he should go before the Sangha and stand to one side, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, placing his right knee on the ground, and joining his palms, saying:
"Venerable Sirs!..."
"I accept my repentance and reproach my own mind; from this day forward, I dare not commit such acts again.
Thus, that bhikṣu Channa, in accordance with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karma* of suspension for his failure to repent.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If the bhikṣu Chanda follows the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it, and requests the lifting of the *karman* of suspension for non-confession of an offense, one should grant him the lifting through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*)."
There are five cases in which the *karman* for suspension for not confessing an offense should not be lifted:
from having conferred the full ordination upon someone, up to having fought with a virtuous bhikṣu.
