There are five cases in which the *karman* for suspension for not confessing an offense should be lifted:
From not bestowing the full precepts upon others to not quarreling with virtuous bhikṣus—this should be understood as follows:

that bhikṣu who has been suspended for failing to repent of his offense should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of one who refuses to repent. I have complied with the Saṃgha and do not dare to oppose it.
Now I beg the Saṃgha to revoke this *karma* of suspension for refusing to repent; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, revoke for me this *karma* of suspension for refusing to repent.
In this manner, it was said a second and third time.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has had the formal act of suspension for not confessing an offense (*āpatti-asthāpana-karman*) performed upon him by the Saṃgha. He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it, and he now requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the formal act of suspension for not confessing an offense.

"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the *karma* of revoking the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*) against the bhikṣu so-and-so for the offense of refusing to confess.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). Listen, venerable Saṃgha!"

The bhikṣu so-and-so has been subjected by the Saṃgha to the formal act of *karma* for the suspension of one who refuses to repent; he has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it, and now he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of this formal act of suspension for refusing to repent.
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha's lifting of the *karma* of suspension for the bhikṣu [Name] for not confessing his offense, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the first motion."
The second and third [announcements] were also made in this manner:

"The Saṃgha has granted its consent; the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for lifting the suspension of the monk so-and-so for the offense of not confessing has been completed. Since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter shall be held as such."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu named Ariṣṭa who conceived such a wrong view as this:
"I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha: committing sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path."

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard that the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa had given rise to wrong views, they went to where the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was. After paying their respects and exchanging greetings, they sat to one side and said to Ariṣṭa:
"Is it true that you know the Dharma taught by the Buddha to be such that engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstacle to the path?"
He replied, “I truly understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha: engaging in sexual misconduct is not an obstructive factor for the path.
At that time, the bhikṣus, wishing to eliminate the evil view of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, earnestly questioned him:
“Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak in such a manner.”

Āḷavaka! With countless skillful means, the Blessed One has taught the Dharma for the severing of desire, the severing of the perception of desire, the extinguishing of thoughts of desire, the dispersal of the fever of desire, and the transcending of the fetters of craving.

The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, has taught that desire is like a great pit of fire, like a torch of grass, and like ripe fruit; it is like a loan, like a dry bone, like a piece of meat, like what is seen in a dream, and like treading upon the edge of a blade. Desire is like a new earthen vessel filled with water placed in the sun, like the head of a venomous snake, like a whirling wheel-blade, and like a sharp halberd.
The Blessed One spoke thus: "Āḷavaka! In this way the Tathāgata has well expounded the Dharma:

it severs desire and is free from desire; it removes defilement and is free from defilement; it subdues craving, destroys the nesting place [of the mind], brings about deliverance from all fetters and bonds, and is the extinction of craving, which is Nirvāṇa."
"The Buddha has taught the Dharma in this way; how can you say, 'Engaging in sensual desire is not an obstacle to the path'?
When the bhikṣus thus questioned the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa with persistence, the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa stubbornly maintained his evil view and spoke with firm determination:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false.

At that time, the bhikṣus were unable to eliminate Ariṣṭa’s evil view, so they went to the World-Honored One, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side, reporting the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Blessed One said to another bhikṣu:
"Take my word and go fetch the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa.
Then that bhikṣu, having received the Blessed One’s instruction, went to where the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa was and spoke to him thus:
“The World-Honored One summons you.
Upon hearing the World-Honored One’s summons, Ariṣṭa went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, and sat down to one side.
The World-Honored One said to Ariṭṭha:
"Is it true that you have spoken these words:
'I understand the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One such that engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path'?"
"Is it so? He replied, "Venerable Sir!"
"It is indeed true that such words were spoken. He asked:
"How do you know that what I have said is thus—that I have not, by means of countless skillful methods, taught the dharma for severing sensual desire as described above?"
At that time, after the Blessed One had rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"I authorize the Saṃgha to perform a formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, in order to issue a reprimand and exhort him to relinquish this matter."

One should admonish him in this manner: among the assembly, a capable person for performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa speaks as follows:"
"Engaging in sexual intercourse is not an obstacle to the path.
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now carry out a formal admonition against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa so that he may relinquish this matter.
“Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak in such a manner; rather, the Blessed One has taught through countless skillful means:”
"Engaging in sexual desire is a dharma that obstructs the Path.
If one commits an act of lust, it constitutes an obstruction to the Path. Thus he spoke.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! This bhikṣu Ariṣṭa has spoken thus:
'I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha that the practice of sensual desire is not an obstacle to the path.'"
"The Saṃgha now grants you this formal admonition to relinquish this matter:
'Āḷavaka! Do not speak such words;
do not slander the Blessed One, for it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.'"
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, the Blessed One has taught through countless skillful means:
"Sensual desire is a dharma that obstructs the path; whoever commits sensual desire immediately obstructs the path."
"Whoever among the elders approves of the Saṃgha’s formal admonition of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa to abandon this matter, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this same manner.
"The Saṃgha has finished its formal admonition and reprimand of the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
After the Saṃgha had formally admonished that bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, he still did not abandon his evil view.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who were of few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, saying:
"How can you, after the Saṃgha has formally admonished you, still refuse to abandon your evil view?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the Blessed One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side. They reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"Why is it that the Saṃgha, having already admonished him with a formal reprimand, still does not cause him to abandon his evil view?
After rebuking him through countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the bhikṣus to perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for not abandoning his evil view."

One should act in this manner: having assembled the Saṃgha, and having assembled the Saṃgha, one should perform the formal charge (ukṣepaṇa); having performed the formal charge, one should perform the formal reminder (smaraṇa); and having performed the formal reminder, one should impose the offense.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa holds evil views; although the Saṃgha has admonished him with a formal reprimand, he does not relinquish his evil views."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience: the Saṃgha now performs the formal act of *karma* for the monk Ariṣṭa regarding his refusal to abandon evil views.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!"
The bhikṣu Ariṣṭa does not relinquish his evil view; although the Saṃgha has admonished him with a formal reprimand, he still does not relinquish it.
The Saṃgha now performs the *karma* of suspension for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa on account of his failure to relinquish his evil view.
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha now performing the formal act (*kamma*) of 'not relinquishing evil views' against the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are to be recited in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the *karmavācanā* for not relinquishing evil views to the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld."
Once one has formed such evil views and does not relinquish them, there are five things one must not do:
from not being permitted to confer the full precepts upon others, up to and including not being permitted to engage in quarrels with virtuous bhikṣus.
"It should be done in this manner.
When the Saṃgha had completed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the bhikṣu Ariṣṭa for the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:

"There are three factors and five factors by which a formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views is performed; such a formal act is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and is not accomplished, as explained above."

Furthermore, there are three factors and five factors by which the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views (*pāpikā-dṛṣṭi-aniḥsarga-utkṣepa-karman*) is accomplished according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya, as described above.

When that bhikṣu who has been suspended for not relinquishing evil views is present—whether the Saṃgha is at the morning meal or the midday meal, during the preaching of the Dharma, or during the *poṣadha* ceremony—he should go before them, stand to one side, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak thus:

Thus, that Ariṣṭa, complying with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *karma* of suspension for not relinquishing his evil view.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

Furthermore, there are five conditions under which one should not grant the *karman* for releasing [a monk] who has not relinquished wrong views:
from the time of conferring the full precepts (*upasampadā*) upon him, up until his engaging in a quarrel with a virtuous bhikṣu.

that bhikṣu who has been subjected to the *karma* of suspension for not relinquishing evil views should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:

Now, being in harmony with the Saṃgha and not daring to oppose it, I beg the Saṃgha to revoke this formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views. Thus it was said a second and a third time.

"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, having committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and not concealing it, has requested from the Saṃgha a six-night mānāpya; the Saṃgha has already granted him a six-night mānāpya."

While he was practicing *mānāpya*, he committed another grave offense and requested from the Saṃgha the *mānāpya-mūlāpakarṣa-karman*; the Saṃgha has already granted him the *mānāpya-mūlāpakarṣa-karman*.

This bhikṣu has completed the *mānatva* and the original-day discipline (*pūrvakalpa-vinaya*). He now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act for the removal of the offense (*āpattivyutthāna-karman*).
The Saṃgha now grants the formal act for the removal of the offense to this bhikṣu [Name].
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha granting the *karmavācanā* for the absolution of the offense to the bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak. This is said a second and a third time.
"The Sangha has already consented to the *karmavācanā* for the removal of offenses for the bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed numerous *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; some had concealed them for one night, some for two nights, and so on, up to ten nights.
That bhikṣu thought to himself, "What should I do?
and informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform for that bhikṣu the formal act of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* regarding the concealment for ten nights of numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses."
It should be granted in this manner:
that bhikṣu should come before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and say:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, some of which were concealed for one night, some for two nights, and so on up to ten nights.

I now request from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for one night up to ten nights; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the formal act of concealment for one night up to ten nights.
In this manner, it is stated a second and third time.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, some of which he concealed for one night up to ten nights; he now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) of concealment for one night up to ten nights.
“If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha grant this bhikṣu so-and-so the *karmavācanā* for concealing [an offense] for one night up to ten nights.
This is the motion (*jñapti*). “Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, some of which he concealed for one night up to ten nights; he now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for one night up to ten nights.
The Sangha now grants this bhikṣu so-and-so the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for concealing [an offense] for one night up to ten nights.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha granting that bhikṣu the formal act for concealing [the offense] for one night up to ten nights should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.

'The Saṃgha has already granted the *karmavācanā* for concealing [the offense] for one night up to ten nights to the bhikṣu so-and-so; the Saṃgha consents, because of its silence; this matter is thus upheld.'"
When that bhikṣu had finished performing the parivāsa, he informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I authorize the Saṃgha to grant that bhikṣu a six-night mānatva through a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman)."

That bhikṣu should come before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and then, with his right knee touching the ground and palms joined, speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, or two nights, up to ten nights. I have requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) of concealment for one night up to ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted me the formal act of concealment.
I, bhikṣu [name], having already completed the period of concealment, now request from the Saṃgha six nights of *mānatva*; may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me six nights of *mānatva*.
In this manner, it is said a second and third time.
From within the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, two nights, or even up to ten nights; he has requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) of concealment for ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted this bhikṣu, so-and-so, the formal act of concealment for ten nights.
This bhikṣu has completed his period of concealment and now requests from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha shall now grant this bhikṣu [named] So-and-so the six-night *mānatva*.
[The motion] is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, two nights, or even up to ten nights. He has already requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted him the formal act of concealment for ten nights."
That bhikṣu has completed ten nights of concealment and now requests from the Saṃgha six nights of *mānāpya*.
The Saṃgha now grants that bhikṣu six nights of *mānāpya*.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha granting that bhikṣu six nights of *mānatva* should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
A second and third time, it was said in the same manner:
"The Saṃgha has granted that bhikṣu the six-night mānāpya; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus shall this matter be upheld."
When he has completed the *mānatva* penance, he informs the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus inform the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to perform the formal act of a fourfold proclamation (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) for that bhikṣu to emerge from his offense."

That bhikṣu should come before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Saṃgha, and with his right knee touching the ground, make this declaration:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

I, Bhikṣu [Name], have committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, two nights, or even up to ten nights. I have requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (karmavācanā) of concealment for ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted me the formal act of concealment for ten nights.
I have completed the period of concealment and have requested from the Saṃgha the six-night *mānatva*; the Saṃgha has already granted me the six-night *mānatva*.

Having completed the six-night *mānatva*, I now request from the Saṃgha the *karma* for the removal of guilt (*āpatti-vyutthāna*). May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *karma* for the removal of guilt.
In this manner, it is said a second and third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu, so-and-so, has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, two nights, or even up to ten nights; he has requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted him the formal act for ten nights.
That bhikṣu so-and-so has completed ten nights of concealment and has requested from the Saṃgha six nights of *mānatva*; the Saṃgha has already granted that bhikṣu six nights of *mānatva*.
That bhikṣu has completed the six-night *mānatva* penance and now requests from the Saṃgha the *karmavācanā* for the removal of his offense.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha shall now confer upon this bhikṣu [named] So-and-so the *karmavācanā* for the removal of his offense.
[The motion] is thus announced. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu so-and-so has committed numerous saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing them for one night, two nights, or up to ten nights. He has requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of concealment for ten nights, and the Saṃgha has already granted him the formal act for ten nights."
That bhikṣu so-and-so has completed ten nights of concealment and has requested from the Saṃgha six nights of *mānāpya*; the Saṃgha has already granted that bhikṣu six nights of *mānāpya*.
That bhikṣu so-and-so has completed the six-night *mānatva* penance and now requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for the removal of his offense.
The Saṃgha now grants that bhikṣu so-and-so the formal act for the removal of his offense.
"Whichever elders among you consent to the *karmavācanā* for the rehabilitation from offense of that bhikṣu so-and-so, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.

"‘The Sangha has already consented to the completion of the *karmavācanā* for the removal of the offense for that bhikṣu so-and-so; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and concealed both of them; he remembered one offense but did not remember the other.
That bhikṣu, according to the offenses he remembers and the number of days they were concealed, requests from the Saṃgha the formal act (karman) for concealing those days.
The Saṃgha grants that bhikṣu the formal act for concealing those days, according to the offenses he remembers and the number of days they were concealed.
While that bhikṣu was practicing the *parivāsa* penance, he recalled a second offense and did not know what to do;
he informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, the Saṃgha shall grant that bhikṣu a *parivāsa* (probation) for the number of days he concealed his second offense, according to his recollection.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and concealed both; one was subject to doubt, while the other was free from doubt.

Regarding those days he concealed while his offense was not yet recognized as such, he requested from the Saṃgha the formal act (kamma) for concealing those days; the Saṃgha then granted that bhikkhu the formal act for concealing those days.
While that bhikṣu was practicing the concealment (parivāsa), he became free from doubt regarding the second offense and thought to himself, "What should I do?
He then informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to grant the *parivāsa* (probation) karmavācanā according to the number of days the offense was concealed.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and concealed both; he recognized one offense but did not recognize the other.
Having recognized the offense he had committed, he requested the *saṃgha* for the *paryuṣitaka-kaṛman*; the *saṃgha* granted him the *kaṛman* according to the number of days he had concealed it.
While he was practicing the *paryuṣitaka*, he immediately recognized a second offense and thought to himself: "What shall I do?"
He immediately informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit the Saṃgha to perform the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* for that bhikṣu according to the number of days he remembers having concealed his second offense."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and concealed both. When he requested the *parivāsa* (probation), he confessed one offense while continuing to conceal the other.
Having requested the *parivāsa-karman* from the Saṃgha regarding the offense he had confessed, the Saṃgha granted him the *parivāsa-karman*.
While he was concealing his offense, a sense of shame and remorse arose within him regarding his second transgression; he thought to himself, "What shall I do?
and informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The Saṃgha should, according to the number of days that the second offense was concealed, grant him the *parivāsa* (probation) through the formal act (*karmavācanā*).
The Buddha said:
"Listen well, all of you!
Suppose a bhikṣu commits two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and conceals both, yet he remembers one offense and does not remember the other.

That bhikṣu requests the *parivāsa* (probation) karmavācanā from the Saṃgha for both the remembered offense and the unremembered offense; the Saṃgha then grants him the *parivāsa* karmavācanā for the concealment of those two offenses."
While he was concealing his offense, a visiting bhikṣu arrived who was learned in the Dharma, learned in the Vinaya, and learned in the Mātṛkā.
That visiting bhikṣu asked the resident bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"What offense has this bhikṣu committed?
For what reason does he practice concealment?
The senior bhikṣu replied:

"Elder! This bhikṣu committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and concealed both. He remembered one offense but did not remember the other; he requested the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* from the Saṃgha for both, and the Saṃgha granted him the *parivāsa* *karmavācanā* for both. Therefore, that bhikṣu undergoes the *parivāsa*."
The visiting bhikṣu said: "Venerable sir!
It is not valid to perform the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* for him."
Why is this? If the bhikṣu remembers the offense for which the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* (act of concealment) was performed, it is valid;
if he does not remember the offense, the *saṃvaraṇa-karman* is invalid, being an illegal (*adharma*) karman that is not accomplished, and the Saṃgha should perform a confession of *duṣkṛta*.
"He should be granted the *mānāpya*.
The same applies whether he is doubtful or not doubtful, or whether he recognizes [the offense] or does not recognize it.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense and concealed it for two months; he remembered one month and did not remember the other month.

He recalled one month that had passed and requested the *saṃgha* for the formal act of concealment (*paryuṣitaka-karman*) for that period; the *saṃgha* granted him the formal act of concealment for one month.
While he was practicing the concealment, he remembered a second month and thought to himself: "What shall I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to grant that bhikṣu the formal act of concealment (praticchādana-karman) for a second month according to his recollection."
The same applies to doubt and lack of doubt, as well as to recognition and lack of recognition.
When requesting the *parivāsa* (probation), the practice of concealing for one month and then confessing for one month is likewise applied.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “Listen well!

If a bhikṣu commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and conceals it for two months—recalling one month and not recalling the other—and he requests from the Saṃgha the *parivāsa* (probation) karmavācanā for both periods, the Saṃgha grants him the two-month *parivāsa* karmavācanā.”
While he was practicing concealment, a visiting bhikṣu arrived who was learned in the Dharma, learned in the Vinaya, and learned in the Mātikā.
That visiting bhikṣu asked the resident bhikṣu:
"Venerable sir!..."
"What offense did he commit?
For what reason does he practice concealment? He replied:
"This bhikṣu committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense and concealed it for two months; he remembers one month and does not remember the other month.

Since he has requested from the Saṃgha concealment for both the remembered and unremembered months, the Saṃgha has granted him the formal act (karmavācanā) of concealment for two months accordingly; therefore, this bhikṣu practices concealment."
That visiting bhikṣu said to the resident bhikṣu:
"It is not right to grant concealment. Why is that?"

It is good for that bhikṣu to remember one month [of concealment] when granting the *parivāsa*; it is not good for him not to remember one month when granting the *parivāsa*. This is an illegal *karmavācanā* that is not accomplished; the Saṃgha should perform a confession of a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"That bhikṣu should be granted *mānāpya*.
It is the same whether there is doubt or no doubt; it is the same whether he recognizes [the offense] or does not recognize it.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, concealed both of them, and then left the monastic order.
Having abandoned the religious life, he returned once more to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
After receiving the full ordination, he concealed two offenses and thought to himself: "What should I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu commits two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and conceals both, he then leaves the monastic order."
Having left the monastic order, he returned and received the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Having received the full ordination, he concealed two offenses.
The Saṃgha should grant him the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā* according to the number of days he previously concealed his offenses and the subsequent days of concealment.
"After the *parivāsa* (probation) has been granted for the concealment, the *mānāpya* (penance) shall be granted.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses and concealed both; he then left the monastic order.
Having left the monastic life and returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*), and having received the full ordination, he confesses his two offenses.
The Sangha should grant him the *parivāsa* (probation) *karmavācanā*, corresponding to the number of days that offense was previously concealed by that bhikṣu.
"After having granted him the *parivāsa* (probation) rite, grant him the *mānāpya* (penance).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, neither of which he concealed; he then left the monastic order.
Having left the monastic life, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Once he had received the full ordination, he concealed two offenses.
He thought to himself, "What should I do? and informed the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu commits two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses and fails to conceal either of them, he then renounces the monastic life.
Having renounced the monastic life, he returns to receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla). Once he has received the full ordination, he conceals both offenses."
“The Saṃgha should grant that bhikṣu the *parivāsa* (probation) for the days he concealed his offenses, following behind him; thereafter, they should grant him the *mānāpya* (rehabilitation).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, neither of which he concealed, and then he left the monastic order.

Having left the monastic life, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Once he had received the full ordination, he confessed his two offenses, and the Saṃgha should immediately grant him *mānāpya* for those two offenses.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses; he concealed one offense and did not conceal the other, and then he left the monastic life.

Having left the monastic life, he returned once more to receive the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). After receiving the full ordination, he first confessed one offense, but subsequently concealed both of them.
He then thought to himself: "What should I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu commits two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses, concealing one offense and not concealing the other, and he then leaves the monastic order..."

Having ceased his practice as a novice, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*). After receiving the full ordination, he first confessed one offense, but subsequently concealed both offenses.

The Saṃgha is permitted to grant that bhikṣu a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) according to the number of days for which each offense was concealed: one offense concealed before and after [the confession], and one offense concealed after [the confession].
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses; he concealed one offense and confessed the other, and then he left the monastic order.

After having left the order, he returned to receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla). Having received the full ordination, he again concealed the offense he had previously concealed, while continuing to confess the one he had previously confessed.

“The Saṃgha should grant the *parivāsa* (probation) for the one offense that was concealed according to its duration, and it should grant the *mānāpya* (act of penance) for the second offense that was not concealed.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses; he concealed one offense and confessed the other, and then he left the monastic order.

Having left the order, he returned and received the full ordination again. Once he had received the full ordination, what he had previously concealed he subsequently confessed, and what he had previously confessed he subsequently concealed.
“The Saṃgha should grant him the *parivāsa* discipline for the first offense previously concealed, and grant the *parivāsa* discipline for the second offense subsequently concealed.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who committed two saṃghāvaśeṣa offenses; he concealed one offense and confessed the other, and then he left the monastic order.
After he had left the order, he returned to receive the full ordination (mahā-śīla). Having received the full ordination, he confessed both offenses, including the one previously concealed.
“The Saṃgha should grant that bhikṣu the parivāsa (probation) for the number of days he concealed his first offense, and grant both of them the mānāpya (penance) for the second offense.”
Regarding "recalling one offense and not recalling another offense," the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are likewise applied.
Regarding "doubting one offense and not doubting another offense," the four permutations are likewise applied.
Regarding the case of being aware of one offense while unaware of another, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are likewise applied.
When requesting concealment (*paryuṣaṇā*), if one conceals one offense while disclosing another, the four permutations are likewise applied.

In this context, from the concealment of one offense and the non-concealment of another, there are five sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Each set consists of four propositions, such as "concealing one and not concealing one," which form twenty propositions in total. It is the same for the twenty propositions during the period of *parivāsa* (probation); it is the same for the twenty propositions once *parivāsa* is completed; it is the same for the twenty propositions during the period of *mānatva* (penance); and it is the same for the twenty propositions once *mānatva* is completed.

The one hundred cases concerning a novice who returns to receive the full precepts are likewise; the one hundred cases concerning those who are insane are likewise; the one hundred cases concerning those with disturbed minds are likewise; the one hundred cases concerning those afflicted by pain are likewise; the one hundred cases concerning those whom the Saṃgha has formally censured for not acknowledging their offense are likewise; the one hundred cases concerning those who do not repent of their offenses are likewise; and the one hundred cases concerning those who do not abandon wrong views are likewise.
At that time, the bhikṣu who had been practicing the parivāsa penance left the monastic order; having left the order, he returned to receive the full ordination (*mahānāma*).
Having received the full ordination, he thought to himself: "What should I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣu who has been practicing the *parivāsa* (probation) leaves the order, and having left the order, returns to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*)."
"Once the full ordination has been received, one should continue to perform the previous day’s sequential practice of concealment.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who should have been subjected to the *mūlāpakarṣa* (reinstatement from the beginning), but that bhikṣu abandoned the path.
Having ceased his practice as a monk, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Once he had received the full ordination, [the rule was that] "the Saṃgha should perform for that bhikṣu the formal act of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the restoration of his original status (*pūrva-paryāya-śuddhi*).
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed the period of concealment (*parivāsa*), ceased his practice as a monk.
Having ceased his practice as a layman, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Once he had received the full ordination, "the Saṃgha should grant that bhikṣu the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for a six-night *mānatva*."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having completed the *mānatva* penance, left the order; after leaving the order, he returned to receive the full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).

Having received the full ordination, [it was said: "That bhikṣu has already completed the days of the *mānatva* and ceased [the practice]; as for the days not yet completed, they should be resumed and continued."
