At that time, the second seer died after seven days and was immediately conceived in the womb of the second queen.
The queen addressed the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty know this?"
"I am now pregnant.
The king immediately increased his offerings as before.
Then the king dispatched a messenger to go and see how many sages were on the banks of the Suraṭṭhā River.
The messenger went immediately to look and saw that the two seers were already dead; he returned at once and informed the king, saying, "The seers are dead.
The king thought to himself:
"Those two rishis, having passed away, were conceived in the wombs of my two queens.
When nine months had been completed, a son was born, handsome and of perfect countenance.
When the King’s first wife gave birth to a son, all manner of good things spontaneously occurred: five hundred merchants arrived;
five hundred merchants returned from the sea having gathered treasures; five hundred hidden treasuries all spontaneously emerged; and five hundred condemned prisoners were released from prison.
At that time, King Candravardhana reflected to himself:
"What name shall I give to this son?
According to the custom of that country, when a male child is born, his parents—or perhaps a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa—bestow a name upon him.
At that time, the king thought to himself:
"What need is there for śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas to bestow a name?
On the day this child was born, many auspicious signs appeared; therefore, he shall be named Śubhakārin (Good Conduct)."
At that time, the king provided him with four types of nurses:
first, one to attend to his physical needs; second, one for bathing and washing; third, one to provide milk; and fourth, one to provide entertainment.
With elephants, horses, and chariots, they performed various musical entertainments and diverse amusements; furthermore, they held peacock feathers behind them as ornaments for such festivities.

When Prince Sudāsa reached the age of eight or nine, he was instructed in various arts: writing, arithmetic, seal-carving, painting, jesting, singing, dancing, and music; he also studied riding elephants, horses, and chariots, as well as archery, charioteering, and the arts of combat. At that time, the prince mastered all of these disciplines.
At that time, the king’s second wife gave birth to a son; simultaneously, many evil omens arose: jackals howled, an asura seized the sun, and five hundred men destined for death arrived.
According to the laws of that country, when a child is first born, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas must be commissioned to give him a name.
The king thought to himself:
"Why must śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas be needed to give a name?"
"On the day this child was born, many evil omens appeared; therefore, he shall be named Duṣkṛta (Evil Conduct).
The king also provided him with four nurses:
first, one to attend to his physical needs; second, one for bathing and washing; third, one to provide milk; and fourth, one to provide entertainment.
There were elephants, horses, and chariots; various musical performances were staged, and there were all kinds of amusements and laughter, even including instruction in the arts of combat.
At that time, Prince Sudāsa was dearly beloved by the King, as were the princes of other minor kingdoms, the queens, the ministers, the attendants, and indeed all the people, who likewise loved him.
As for Prince Duṣkara, the king did not love or cherish him, nor did anyone else at all.
At that time, Prince Duṣkara thought to himself:
"Prince Sukara is dearly loved and cherished by the king and all the people."
"But I alone am thus: the King does not love or care for me, nor does he love or care for any of the others.
I shall seek out a means to take his life.
At that time, the chief queen of the neighboring king, Candraprabhā, gave birth to a daughter and immediately dispatched a messenger to King Candravardhana with these words:
"My first wife has given birth to a daughter; I shall give her as a wife to your son, Sudhana.
At another time, Prince Sudhana had this thought:

"The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are all subject to much poverty and suffering. I should enter the ocean to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi) so that there may be no one among the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa who is poor."
Then, he went at once to the king’s presence and said:

"The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are all largely impoverished and suffering; I wish to enter the ocean to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel so that there shall be no one among the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa who is poor."
The king immediately replied, "I possess vast quantities of gold, silver, and the seven treasures in countless numbers; my treasuries are overflowing. You may take as much as you wish.
He then addressed the king, saying:
"I cannot; yet I must enter the great ocean to fetch the wish-fulfilling jewel, so that no sentient beings in Jambudvīpa shall remain poor.
The king said, "Do as you intend."
At that time, Prince Duṣkṛta thought to himself:
"Now is the very moment; I can find the opportunity to take his life.
He immediately went to the King's presence and said to him:
“Good Conduct is one whom I hold in high esteem; now I wish to enter the sea, and if I do not see him, I fear I shall lose my life. I now wish to accompany him and enter the sea together.”
The king said, "As you wish. Then the prince,
having taken his leave of the king, the queen, and their retinue, went to the city of Śobhāvatī and rang a bell, proclaiming:

"Whoever is able to renounce parents, wife and children, brothers and sisters, as well as all kinsmen and relatives, and who desires gold, silver, precious gems, and priceless jewels, shall follow me into the sea; I shall provide all necessities, including food, drink, and articles of adornment."
At that time, five hundred merchants gathered at his location.
Then, together with those five hundred merchants, Kalyāṇakārin went to the city of Suppāra, where they purchased a ship and sought out a navigator.

The ship's captain, aware of the various perils within the ocean—such as the danger of surging waves, the danger of whirlpools, and the danger of great fish—prepared the vessel and once again proclaimed the aforementioned command; he then set sail and entered the sea.
Because of his meritorious deeds, the wind blew his ship toward the place of the seven treasures. He addressed the merchants, saying:
"We have now arrived at the Isle of Jewels; prepare the ship well and make it firm and sturdy. Take as many jewels as you desire to fill the ship, but do not let it sink."
Then the merchants, having received their instructions, took the treasure.
After the merchant Sucarita had instructed the multitude of merchants, he departed for another place.
Prince Duṣkara then addressed the merchants with these harsh words:
"If Prince Kalyāṇakārin returns safely, he will surely seize your treasures.
Since he has not yet returned, you should push the ship into the sea and depart."
At that time, the prince Duṣkṛta spoke to five hundred merchants; having accepted his words, the merchants pushed their ship into the sea and departed.

Due to the retribution of their meager merit, the wind wrecked their ship, and the five hundred merchants drowned in the sea. Prince Duṣkṛta obtained a single plank, which the wind blew back and forth until he reached the shore. There, on the seashore, he lived by begging for food from house to house in a poor and lowly village.
Then Sudhana returned to his former place; seeing neither the merchants nor the ship, he beat his breast and wept in distress, fearing that the merchants had been harmed by evil spirits or rākṣasas.
Then the deity of the Jewel Island said to Sudhana:

"The five hundred merchants were not harmed by evil spirits or rākṣasas; rather, it was Prince Duṣkara who, through his malicious words, caused the five hundred merchants to destroy their ship and cast it into the sea."
Due to the karmic retribution of his meager merit, a wind wrecked his ship, and five hundred merchants drowned at sea.
Prince Duṣkṛta obtained a plank and was blown by the wind to the shore; he now subsists by begging for alms along the seashore.
The Good Deed thought to himself,
"I would now rather go forward to the palace of the Sea Dragon King to beg for the wish-fulfilling jewel.
He then led the way and departed until they reached the island of the rākṣasīs.
Then five hundred rākṣasīs came out to meet him, and seeing him from afar, they greeted him with comfort:
"Welcome, young man!
Where do you wish to go?"

He replied, "The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are all suffering greatly from poverty; I wish to go to the palace of the Sea Dragon King to beg for a wish-fulfilling jewel, so that the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa may be free from the suffering of poverty."
He then asked again:
"Which vehicle do you wish to take? He replied:
"I wish to take up the Mahāyāna.
The rākṣasī said, "Excellent!"
"If you attain supreme perfect enlightenment, I shall renounce the household life and become your disciple. He replied, "So be it."
From afar he saw a golden bed within the golden city, upon which a nāga sat.
Thereupon, Prince Sudhana went to the golden city and approached the place where the nāga was.
At that time, the Dragon King saw him from afar and greeted him, saying: "Welcome, young man!
Where do you wish to go?"
He replied, "Do you not know, O Dragon King?

The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are all suffering greatly from poverty. I wish to go to the palace of the Dragon King of the Sea to fetch the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), so that the people of Jambudvīpa may be free from poverty and suffering."

He replied: "The palace of the Sea Dragon King is difficult to reach. For seven days one must walk through water that reaches up to the knees; for another seven days, the water reaches the navel; for seven days, it reaches the armpits; for seven days, one must float across; for seven days, one must walk upon lotus flowers; and for seven days, one must walk upon the heads of venomous snakes; only then can one arrive at the palace of the Sea Dragon King."
"You may stop now; I have a precious jewel that can rain down the seven treasures for two thousand yojanas in the eastern direction, and I shall give it to you.
He replied, "I will not take it;
I must go to the palace of the Naga King in the ocean."
He then asked again:
"Which vehicle do you wish to take? He replied:
"I wish to take up the Mahāyāna," he said, adding,
"If you attain supreme perfect enlightenment, I shall leave the household life to become your foremost disciple of wisdom."
He then abandoned the golden city.
From afar, he saw the Dragon King seated upon a silver bed within the silver city.
Prince Sudāsa proceeded to the silver city and approached the Dragon King; seeing him from a distance, the Dragon King greeted him with words of comfort:
"Welcome, young man!
Where do you wish to go? He replied:
"O Dragon King, do you know?

The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa are all suffering greatly from poverty and hardship. I wish to go to the palace of the Sea Dragon King to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi), so that the people of Jambudvīpa may be free from poverty and suffering."

He replied: "The palace of the Sea Dragon King is difficult to reach. For seven days one must walk through water that reaches only the knees; for seven days it reaches the navel; for seven days it reaches the armpits; for seven days one must float across; for seven days one must walk upon lotus flowers; and for seven days one must walk upon the heads of venomous snakes; only then does one arrive at the palace of the Sea Dragon King."
"You should stop now; I have a precious jewel that can rain down the seven treasures over four thousand yojanas in the south, and I shall give it to you.
He replied, "I will not take it; I must go to the palace of the Naga King of the Ocean."
He then asked again:
"Which vehicle do you wish to take? He replied:
"I wish to take up the Mahāyāna," he said, adding,
"If you attain supreme perfect enlightenment, I shall leave the household life to become your foremost disciple endowed with supernormal powers."
He immediately abandoned the silver city and departed.
He then saw a lapis lazuli city where a dragon king sat as before; he gave him a wish-fulfilling jewel capable of raining down treasures over six thousand yojanas in the western direction.
He replied, "I will not take it; I must go to the palace of the Sea Dragon King.
He asked again:
"What vehicle do you wish to take? He replied,
"I wish to take the Mahāyāna."
"If you attain supreme perfect enlightenment, I shall leave the household life and become your foremost disciple of great learning.
At that time, Sudhana continued forward; for seven days the water reached his knees, until he was walking upon lotus flowers, even reaching the place of venomous snakes. He thought to himself:
"By what karma did I receive retribution by being born among venomous snakes? Could this not be the retribution for the poison of anger in a previous life?"
"With what dharma should one subdue them?
Only with a mind of loving-kindness.
He then contemplated the samādhi of loving-kindness.
At that time, all the venomous snakes lowered their heads as he walked over them and proceeded to the palace of the Naga King of the Sea.
When the Naga King saw him from afar, he greeted him with comfort, saying:
"Welcome, young man!"
"What do you desire? He replied,
"I now wish to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel from within your topknot."
He replied: "Your lifespans are short and this jewel is of great value; it is not that I would not give it to you.
I shall give it to you now, but when your life is about to end, you must return the jewel."
He immediately untied the jewel and gave it to him, and sent two nāgas along with him to return with the jewel later.
At that time, Shanxing grasped the jewel and made this aspiration:
"If this is indeed a wish-fulfilling jewel, may it suddenly return to the city of Śobhāvatī."
In the mere instant of such a thought, he returned to the city of Śobhavatī.
At that time, Prince Duṣkara, hearing that Sukara had returned safely from the sea, went immediately to where Sukara was and said to him: "Do you know?"
"I am currently in this poor village, seeking alms from house to house to sustain my life.
You have returned safely from the great ocean; what have you obtained?"
He immediately replied,
"I have come with this wish-fulfilling jewel. Then, Śubhakārin said:
"I am now utterly exhausted and wish to sleep for a short while," he said,
and immediately lay down to sleep with his head resting upon Duṣkṛta’s lap.
At that moment, Duṣkṛta pierced both of his eyes with thorns from a khadira tree and departed with the jewel.
With both eyes wounded and his body stained with flowing blood, he wandered east and west in terror, unable to see the path, until he reached the garden of King Candra.

At that time, there was an old woman guarding the garden who had two young children; seeing him from afar approaching with his body stained by blood and unable to see the path as he wandered in distress, she felt pity for him and asked:
"For what reason are you wandering east and west in this King Candra’s garden, terrified and unable to see the way?"
He then recounted the circumstances in full.
The old woman said, "I have two sons; they may play with you."
"You may now remain here; we shall look after you as if you were our own two children.
At that time, Duṣkṛta returned to the city of Śrāvastī and went to King Candraprabha, saying to the king:
"Does Your Majesty know?"
"While at sea, I encountered a great storm that wrecked my ship; five hundred merchants perished in the ocean, yet I alone returned in safety.
The king said, "Having returned safely from the sea, what have you obtained?"
He replied, "I have obtained this wish-fulfilling jewel.
The king then asked:
"What can this jewel do? He replied, "I do not know."
At that time, the king immediately took the jewels and entrusted them to the treasury, rewarding him.
Then, Duṣkara sent a messenger to tell King Candra of the neighboring kingdom:
"Sukara went with five hundred merchants into the sea to retrieve treasures, but he was swept away by the waters; you should now give me your daughter."
The king replied, "I must speak with my daughter.
He then summoned his daughter and said to her:
"Kalyāṇakārin went to sea with five hundred merchants to retrieve treasures, but was swept away by the waters; Pāpakārin returned safely. Now he wishes to seek you out to be his wife."
She replied, "I cannot;
I wish to go out myself to seek a husband.
Thereupon, the king immediately ordered that everyone within the kingdom be assembled.
Having adorned his daughter, he went outside to seek a husband in the east and west.
At that time, Sudhana immediately tuned his lute and played it, producing beautiful sounds as he stayed within the garden.
At that time, the king’s daughter saw him and immediately went to inform the king, saying:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
I wish to have this man as my husband."
The king said, "This is a blind man.
The woman replied to the king:
"There is no suffering.
Then King Candra immediately summoned Sudhana and asked him: "Young man!"
"Who are you? He replied, "Does Your Majesty not know?
"I am the eldest son of King Candravardhana, named Sukṛti.
The king asked,
"For what reason have you injured your eyes?"
He then related the preceding circumstances in detail to the king.
The king said,
"If you are indeed the son of King Candraprabha, you should now make a vow to restore your eyesight."
Then Shanxing (Good Conduct) made this virtuous vow:

"If, for the sake of the poverty and suffering of the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa, I enter the sea to seek the wish-fulfilling jewel so that the sentient beings of Jambudvīpa may no longer suffer from want—and yet Prince Woxing (Evil Conduct), having destroyed five hundred merchants with his wicked words, abandons me and returns—[then may my vow be fulfilled]."
Furthermore, they pierced both my eyes with thorns from the khadira tree and took my wish-fulfilling jewel back; yet I harbored no ill will toward those people.
If my sincerity is true and without falsehood, may my eyes be restored to their former state.
When he had finished making this vow, his eyes were immediately restored.
The king then adorned his daughter with the finest ornaments and gave her to him in marriage.
The king then dispatched a messenger to King Candravardhana, saying:

"Do you know now? Prince Sudhana has returned safely from the sea; he is now most magnificently adorned, and I shall give my daughter to him in marriage. We shall now proceed to the city of Śūrpāraka."
Then King Candravardhana immediately issued orders for the entire kingdom to be adorned in various ways.
Thereupon, Prince Kalyāṇakārin went to the city of Śūradatta; having prostrated with his head at the king’s feet, he related the circumstances in detail to him.
The king immediately ordered his men to kill Duṣkṛta.
Sukṛta addressed the king, saying:
"I pray that you do not need to kill him."
Then King Candravardhana dispatched Duṣkara out of the country.
Sukara asked the king, "Duṣkara brought the jewel; where is it now?"
The king said,
"It is currently in the treasury.
He addressed the king, saying:
"Bring forth the jewel.
The king immediately brought forth the jewel.
Sudhana then bathed his body thoroughly, put on new, clean white garments, took the jewel and placed it atop a banner on a high and magnificent palace, and made this vow:
"If this is truly a wish-fulfilling jewel, it shall rain down the seven treasures to fill Jambudvīpa, and cause all who are ill to be healed.
At the very moment he made this vow, the seven treasures rained down to fill Jambudvīpa.
"Later, at another time, King Candraprabha passed away, and Sudhana immediately became king.
At that time, Prince Duṣkṛta came to Sudhana and said:
'I am currently outside, begging from house to house for alms to sustain my life.'"
The king replied,
"You may guard my head, and I shall give you what I eat.
He answered the king:
"So be it. Later, at another time, when the king was sleeping lightly, Duṣkṛta thought to himself,
"Now I may take his life."
He immediately drew his sword and struck him.
At that moment, Duṣkṛta’s arm fell off of its own accord, whereupon he cried out, "Cursed be me!
The king then woke up and asked:
"Why, young man, do you call this a calamity?
He replied to the king,
"The heavens themselves have created their own karma."
The king asked,
"For what reason? They informed the king of the circumstances.
The King said,
"Truly, it was you yourself who created that karma.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Was King Candravarman anyone else? He is none other than the present King Śuddhodana.
As for the first queen, she is none other than his present mother, Māyā."
The King Candraprabha of that time was the Śākya youth Yaśoda;
the King Candraprabha’s daughter was Gopī;
and the old woman who guarded the garden was the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī.
The two boys were Nanda and Ānanda in their present lives.
The one who was well-behaved at that time was my own self.
The one who was ill-behaved at that time was Devadatta in his present life.
The five hundred merchants were these five hundred bhikṣus.
Just as he previously destroyed these people with evil teachings, so too does he now destroy them with evil teachings.
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What constitutes the schism of the Saṃgha?"
"How many people, O Śāriputra, are said to have 'broken the Saṃgha'?
Who is it that breaks the harmonious Saṃgha?
The Buddha said:
“Upāli! There are two things that cause a schism in the Saṃgha:
false speech and speech that resembles [the Dharma]. It is by these two things that a schism in the Saṃgha is caused.”
Upāli! Furthermore, there are two matters that cause a schism in the Saṃgha:
performing a formal ritual (karmavācanā) and casting lots (śalākā).

Upāli! A single bhikṣu cannot cause a schism in the Saṃgha; even if he seeks expedient means, he still cannot cause a schism. Nor can a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī cause a schism in the Saṃgha; even if they seek expedient means to cause a schism, they still cannot cause a schism.

Upāli! If one bhikṣu from this assembly and one bhikṣu from that assembly perform the *śalākā* (voting stick) for schism and carry out the *karmavācanā*, they cannot cause a schism in this way; they merely bring defilement upon the Saṃgha. It is the same with two or three people.

Upāli! If this assembly consists of more than four persons and that assembly also consists of more than four persons, they may carry out the *śalākā* (lot-casting) for the schism of the Saṃgha and perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*). Upāli!
"This is what is called 'schism in the Saṃgha'; this is what constitutes a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha. Upāli asked again:
"What does one gain by causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha?"
The Buddha said:
"One who causes a schism in the Saṃgha shall suffer punishment in the hells for one kalpa without remedy.
What is gained by one who, after the Saṃgha has been split, is able to reconcile it?"
The Buddha said:
"One shall obtain the merit of Brahmā and enjoy happiness for one kalpa.
Then he spoke this verse:
“The Saṅgha rejoices in harmony; in harmony, there is no contention.
When there is harmony, the Dharma exists, and one can always diligently cultivate the Path.
One who can bring the Saṅgha into harmony shall enjoy celestial bliss for an eon.”
Upāli asked again: "Do all those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha fall into hell and suffer there for one kalpa?
The Buddha said:
“Upāli! Not all those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha necessarily fall into hell to suffer for one kalpa. Upāli!”

If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Dharma as being Dharma and, firmly adhering to this non-Dharma, causes a schism in the Saṃgha, and he himself knows it is non-Dharma yet maintains the perception of it as such, he then speaks with the perception of it being non-Dharma, saying:
"This is the Dharma; this is the Vinaya; this is the teaching of the Buddha."
"O Upāli! If one who holds different views and different tolerances performs the schism of the Saṃgha,
such a schismatic shall suffer unrelieved pain in the hells for an eon."

If a bhikṣu proclaims as Dharma that which is not Dharma, and persists in this matter, employing means to cause a schism in the Saṃgha, and with the perception of it being non-Dharma speaks with the perception of it being Dharma, saying:
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha."
"Having performed the *śalākā* (voting stick) for the schism of the Saṃgha and carried out the *karmavācanā*, Upāli!
Such a person who has caused a schism shall suffer in the hells for an eon without relief."
The same applies to one who speaks with the perception that the Dharma is non-Dharma. Upāli!

If a bhikṣu speaks what is not the Dharma as if it were the Dharma and persists in this matter, thereby causing a schism in the Saṃgha, he speaks with the perception of the Dharma while perceiving it as non-Dharma.
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha.
Holding no different view and having no different conviction, they carry out the *śalākā* for schism and perform the *karmavācanā*.
In this way, Upāli!
Such a person does not fall into hell to suffer for one kalpa.

The four permutations regarding doubt and non-doubt are likewise; the four permutations regarding the perception of what is not Dharma and doubt are likewise; and so it continues, even up to the four permutations regarding speaking and not speaking.
The *Bhikṣu-saṃghabheda-vastu* (Chapter on Schism in the Saṃgha) is completed.
*The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Scroll 46; *The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Scroll 47; Part 3, Section 11.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Jibin during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others.
13. The Khandhaka on the Settling of Disputes (Adhikaraṇa-samatha-khandhaka), Chapter Sixteen, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Kālodāyin went with the group of six bhikṣus to bathe in the river Ajiravatī.
When Kālodāyin had finished bathing and stepped onto the bank, he put on the robe of one of the group of six bhikṣus, thinking it was his own; without checking, he departed.
After the group of six bhikṣus had finished bathing and stepped onto the shore, they did not see their own robes;
seeing instead the robe of Kālodāyin, they immediately said, "Kālodāyin has stolen our robes!"
While the person was not present, they performed the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment).

Having heard this, Kālodāyin became doubtful and went to the Blessed One; he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported the matter in detail to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you take it? He replied:
"I am taking this robe because it is my own, not with a thieving mind.
The Buddha said, "There is no offense;
however, one should not wear a robe without first inspecting it, nor should one perform a formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) in the absence of the person concerned."

The formal act of censure (tarjanīya-karman), the formal act of banishment (pravāsanīya-karman), the formal act of dependence (niśraya-karman), the formal act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople (pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman), the formal act of suspension (utkṣepanīya-karman), and the formal act of reconciliation after suspension (pratyānayana-karman).
If one performs a *karmavācanā* (formal act) and it is not validly accomplished, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement by presence) for the extinction of disputes; you should explain the *saṃmukhavinaya* in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Trapusa had not committed any grave offenses, such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya.
At that time, all the bhikṣus said,
"He has committed a grave offense.
They then asked him:
"Do you recall committing any grave offenses, such as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*?
Since he did not recall committing a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*, he replied,
"I do not recall committing such offenses."
He then said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sirs!
Do not question me so persistently."
The bhikṣus continued to interrogate him without ceasing.
He thought to himself: "What should I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I authorize the performance of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the purpose of instituting the *smṛti-vinaya* for Ḍabba Mallaputta."
It should be granted in this manner.
Trapusa-māra-putra should go before the Saṃgha, bare his right shoulder, remove his leather sandals, place his right knee on the ground, join his palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"I, Trapusa-māra-putra, have not committed a grave offense, yet the bhikṣus say:
'I have committed a grave offense—a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya.'"
The bhikṣus asked me, saying:
"Do you remember committing a grave offense such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya?
I replied, "I do not remember committing a grave offense such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya."
“I do not recall committing such a grave offense.
Venerable elders!
There is no need to interrogate me repeatedly.”
Yet the bhikṣus continue to press me with their questioning without ceasing.
I do not recall [the matter]; I now request from the Saṃgha the *vinaya* of recollection (*smṛti-vinaya*). May the Saṃgha grant me the *vinaya* of recollection out of compassion.
In this manner, he should request a second and third time.
Among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
"This Trapusa-māra-putra has not committed a grave offense such as a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
Yet all the bhikṣus say:
'He has committed a grave offense, from a *pārājika* down to a *sthūlātyaya*.'"
The bhikṣus asked him,
"Do you remember committing a grave offense, from a pārājika down to a sthūlātyaya?
Since he did not remember committing a grave offense, he replied:
"I have not committed a grave offense.
Venerable elders!
There is no need to interrogate me further."
"Yet the bhikṣus continue to press their accusations without ceasing.
He does not recall committing an offense and now requests from the Saṃgha the *smṛtivinaya* (the verdict based on memory).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant him the *smṛtivinaya*."
It is announced thus:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Tapassu the Malla has not committed a grave offense such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya."
The bhikṣus all said:
“He has committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya.
They then asked him:
"Do you remember committing a grave offense, such as a *pārājika* or even a *sthūlātyaya*?
Since he did not remember committing a grave offense, he replied:
"I do not remember committing a grave offense."
"Elders! There is no need for you to repeatedly challenge and interrogate me.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to challenge and interrogate him again and again without ceasing.
He does not remember his offense and now requests the *saṃgha* for the *smṛtivinaya*.
Now the *saṃgha* shall grant the *smṛtivinaya* to Ḍabba Mallaputta.
Those elders who consent to the *saṃgha* granting the *smṛtivinaya* to Ḍabba Mallaputta remain silent; those who do not consent speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are to be recited in the same manner.
"The Saṃgha has already granted the *smṛti-karman* to Ṭhapassamala; the Saṃgha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter shall be upheld."
"From this day forward, for the sake of settling disputes among the bhikṣus, I shall establish the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection). It should be declared as follows: 'The *smṛtivinaya*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Nandi who was deranged and mentally disturbed; he committed many offenses against the rules and acted contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa, speaking without restraint and moving about or entering and leaving without following the proper decorum.
Later, when he regained his mind, the bhikṣus said:
"He has committed grave offenses: pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, or sthūlātyaya."
The bhikṣus asked, “Nandiya!
Do you remember committing any grave offenses, such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya?”

He replied: "Previously, when I was deranged and my mind was disordered, I committed many offenses; my coming and going, my entering and leaving were not in accordance with the rules of decorum. This was not done intentionally by me, but was merely due to my insanity."
"Elders! There is no need for you to repeatedly challenge me with difficult questions.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to challenge him without ceasing.
That bhikṣu thought to himself, "What should I do?
and informed the other bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow the Saṃgha to grant the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one who is no longer insane) to the bhikṣu Nandiya by means of a formal motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
It should be granted in this manner."
The bhikṣu Nanda should go before the Saṃgha, baring his right shoulder, removing his leather sandals, placing his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

"O monks, while I, the bhikṣu Nanda, was deranged and my mind was disturbed, I committed many offenses and my conduct in coming and going, entering and leaving, did not accord with the rules of decorum.
Later, when I regained my sanity, the bhikṣus asked me:
'Do you remember committing grave offenses such as pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, or sthūlātyaya?'"

I replied: "Previously, when my mind was deranged and confused, I committed many offenses; my coming and going, entering and exiting did not accord with the rules of decorum. This was not done intentionally by me, but because of that deranged state of mind."
"Elders! There is no need for you to continue to interrogate and cross-examine me.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to question him without ceasing.
"I am now no longer deluded; I request the *amūḷhavinaya* from the Saṃgha.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me the *amūḷhavinaya*.
Thus he speaks a second and a third time.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following formal motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Nandika is deranged and mentally disturbed; he has committed many offenses and his speech is unrestrained. His coming and going, and his movements, do not accord with the rules of decorum."
Later, when he regained his mind, the bhikṣus said to him:
"Do you remember committing any grave offenses, such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya?"
He immediately replied:

"When I was previously insane, I committed many offenses; my speech was unrestrained, and my coming and going did not accord with the rules of decorum. This was due to insanity, not intentional action."
"Venerable elders!
Do not continue to interrogate and cross-examine me.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to interrogate him without ceasing.
This bhikṣu is now no longer insane; he requests from the Saṃgha the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the legal procedure for one who is no longer insane).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha bestow the *amūḍha-vinaya* upon the bhikṣu Nandika.
[The motion] is thus stated: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣu Nanda was deranged and mentally disturbed, committing many offenses against the community; his speech was unrestrained, and his coming and going, his movements and conduct, did not accord with the rules of decorum."
Later, when he regained his mind, the bhikṣus said to him:
"Do you remember committing any grave offenses, such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya?"
He immediately replied:
"Previously, I was deranged and my mind was disordered; I committed many offenses and my coming and going did not accord with the rules of decorum.
This was due to my derangement and mental disorder, not something done intentionally."
"Venerable elders!
Do not continue to interrogate and cross-examine me.
Yet the bhikṣus continued to interrogate him without ceasing.
This bhikṣu is now no longer insane; he requests from the Saṃgha the *amūḍha-vinaya* (the discipline for one no longer insane).
The Saṃgha now grants the *amūḍha-vinaya* to the bhikṣu Nandiya.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha granting the *amūḍha-vinaya* to the bhikṣu Nandiya, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.
'The Saṃgha has already granted the *amūḍha-vinaya* to the bhikṣu Nandi; the matter is concluded. Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus.'"

"From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the *amūḷhavinaya* (settlement by way of restoration from insanity) for the resolution of disputes; it should be proclaimed as follows: 'The *amūḷhavinaya*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the city of Campā, by the side of the Gaggarā Pond.
At that time, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the uposatha, the World-Honored One sat in the open air before the assembly of monks, surrounded by his followers.
When the first watch of the night had passed, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"The first watch has passed; may the World-Honored One recite the precepts."
At that time, the World-Honored One remained silent, and Ānanda immediately returned to his seat.

When the middle watch and the latter watch of the night had passed and the dawn light had appeared, Ānanda rose again from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The middle watch and the latter watch have already passed, and the dawn light has appeared."
"The assembly of monks has sat for a long time; we only wish for you to recite the precepts.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The assembly is not pure. It is impossible for the Tathāgata to perform the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) and recite the precepts within an impure assembly."
At that time, Ānanda remained silent and sat down again.
Then the Venerable Maudgalyāyana thought to himself:
"Who among this assembly is impure?"
The Tathāgata has spoken thus:
"There is impurity within the assembly.
It is impossible for the Tathāgata to perform formal acts (*karmavācanā*) or recite the precepts (*śīla*) within an assembly that is not pure."

At that time, Maudgalyāyana reflected and observed the assembly. With his purified divine eye, he saw that bhikṣu sitting not far from the Buddha; though he was not a śramaṇa, he claimed to be a śramaṇa, and though he did not practice pure conduct, he claimed to practice pure conduct. He possessed only broken precepts and various impurities, lacking any wholesome dharmas (śukladharma). His wrong views concealed the many evils he had committed, like a tree in the air which, though having branches and leaves on the outside, has no fruit within.
Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has seen this bhikṣu and therefore spoke these words:
'It is impossible for one to cause the Tathāgata to perform a formal act (karmavācanā) or recite the precepts within an impure assembly.'"
Then Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat, went to where that bhikṣu was, and said to him:
"You should rise now; the World-Honored One knows you and sees you. Depart and vanish; you ought not to remain here."
Then Maudgalyāyana seized that bhikṣu by the arm and led him outside the gate, returning to inform the World-Honored One:
"The assembly is now pure; may the World-Honored One recite the precepts."
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“It should not be so; even at another time, it should not be so, Maudgalyāyana!”
One should cause the person to confess their offense and only then impose the penalty; one should not impose a penalty on someone who has not confessed their own offense.

From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the settlement of disputes through self-accusation (*pātimokkha-thapanā*); it should be declared as follows: "Settlement through self-accusation."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the monks of Śrāvastī were disputing, and the Saṃgha sought to investigate their offenses in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"One should seek out many people who know the Dharma to determine the offense.

From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the legal procedure for settling disputes by means of the 'decision of the majority. This decision of the majority should be declared as follows."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Rājagṛha.
There was a bhikṣu named Hastibala who delighted in debate and engaged in discussions with non-Buddhists; when he encountered pressing questions, his words were inconsistent from beginning to end.
When questioned within the Saṃgha, he likewise contradicted himself with his words from beginning to end, intentionally speaking falsehoods in the midst of the assembly.
At that time, all the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) together reviled and disparaged him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, they utter only false speech, saying of themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is there in such as this?
"When he was questioned with pressing inquiries, his words were inconsistent from beginning to end; therefore, he has uttered a falsehood.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They censured the śrāmaṇera Hastibala, saying:
"How could you debate with the outsiders such that, when questioned with pressing inquiries, your words were inconsistent from beginning to end?"
"When questioned among the assembly of monks, did he also speak with contradictions between what preceded and what followed?
The bhikṣus went to the Buddha, prostrated at his feet, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Hastika-bala, saying:
"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not be done."
"How is it that when you engage in debate with non-Buddhists and are pressed with critical questions, your words contradict one another from beginning to end;
and even when questioned in the midst of the assembly, your words likewise contradict one another from beginning to end? Is this not the act of speaking falsely?"
After the Blessed One had rebuked Elephant Strength with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“You should perform the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a motion followed by three proclamations) against that bhikṣu for the designation of his offense.”
It should be granted in this manner:

having assembled the Sangha, once the Sangha has been assembled, one should perform the formal act of accusation (*ukkhepana*); having performed the accusation, one should perform the act of recollection (*sāraṇīya-kamma*); and having performed the recollection, one should grant the offense.
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and make the following motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This Śākyaputra named Hastibala is fond of debate; when debating with outsiders, his words were contradictory from beginning to end when he was pressed with critical questions."
Even when questioned within the assembly of monks, his words were contradictory from beginning to end; he intentionally uttered falsehoods in the midst of the community.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and hear this: the Saṃgha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the designation of the place of offense against the Śākya son, Khaṇḍadravya.
"O Elephant Power! You have gained nothing beneficial; you have acquired what is unwholesome.
When you were questioned, your words were contradictory from beginning to end."
"If it is likewise when one asks among the assembly of monks, and one intentionally utters a falsehood within that assembly—
this is how it is declared. "Venerable Sangha, listen!
This son of the Śākyas, Hastibala, was fond of debate; when he engaged in discussion with non-Buddhists and was pressed with critical questions, his words were contradictory from beginning to end.
It was likewise when questioned among the community of monks; thus, he deliberately uttered falsehoods in the midst of the assembly.
The Sangha now performs the *karmavācanā* for the establishment of a place of offense against the Śākya son, Khaṇḍadravya. "You, Khaṇḍadravya!

You have gained no benefit and have acted unskillfully; when you were questioned, your words before and after were contradictory. It was likewise when you were questioned in the midst of the assembly, where you deliberately uttered a falsehood."

"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha performing the *karmavācanā* for the place of offense against the elephant-strength Śākyaputra, let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
A second and a third time he spoke thus:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to perform the *karmavācanā* for the place of offense against the Śākya son Khaṇḍadravya; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"From this day forward, for the sake of the bhikṣus, I shall establish the legal procedure for settling disputes by determining the point of offense; it should be formulated as follows.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus of Śrāvastī were disputing among themselves; many of these bhikṣus violated numerous precepts and acted contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa, both practicing such deeds and speaking of them without restraint.
Those bhikṣus formed this thought within themselves:
"We have committed many violations of the various precepts that are contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa; we have both acted and spoken without restraint."

If we were to return and discuss this matter among ourselves, it might cause this dispute to become even more serious and endure for months and years; we would fail to settle the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, thereby preventing the Saṃgha from attaining peace and happiness.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“This dispute should be settled by the method of ‘covering over with grass.
From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the legal procedure for settling disputes by covering over with grass; it should be proclaimed as follows: ‘Covering over with grass.’”
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
There, the monks of Kauśāmbī were disputing with one another; monks were disputing with nuns, nuns were disputing with monks, and nuns were disputing with one another.
There was a bhikṣu named Chanda who abandoned his fellow bhikṣus to assist the bhikṣuṇīs and join their faction.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, those among them who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, rebuked those bhikṣus. They then went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked them:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice; it is something that should not have been done."

Why is it that the bhikṣus of Kauśāmbī are disputing among themselves—bhikṣus disputing with bhikṣus, bhikṣus disputing with bhikṣuṇīs, bhikṣuṇīs disputing with bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs disputing with bhikṣuṇīs—and why does the bhikṣu Chanda abandon the bhikṣus to assist the bhikṣuṇīs and join their faction?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four kinds of disputes:
disputes concerning speech, disputes concerning investigation, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal matters."
What is verbal dispute?
It is when bhikṣus dispute with one another, citing eighteen grounds for dispute:
whether it is Dharma or non-Dharma, Vinaya or non-Vinaya, and so forth, up to what has been spoken and what has not been spoken.
If, by means of such characteristics, they engage in mutual verbal dispute and subsequently fight with one another, this is called a dispute over words (*vāda-vivāda*).
What is a dispute over searching for faults (*anuvāda-vivāda*)? If a bhikṣu seeks out the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of three types of formal accusations:

Regarding those who have violated the precepts, violated the views, or violated the decorum—whether seen, heard, or suspected—one should seek out their offenses based on such signs; one should speak with them without falsehood, seek companions and support for them, and comfort their minds.

If one raises a formal act of *smṛti-vinaya* (reinstatement through recollection), or whether one establishes this matter or does not establish that matter, provided one is neither deluded nor exempted—this is called a dispute for investigation (*anusandhika-adhikaraṇa*).
What is a dispute regarding offenses (*āpattika-adhikaraṇa*)?
To commit the seven kinds of offenses—
ranging from *pārājika* and *saṃghāvaśeṣa* down to *durbhāṣita*— is what constitutes an offense-dispute (*āpatti-araṇa*).
What is a matter-dispute (*adhikaraṇa-araṇa*)?

Matters arising from disputes over speech, matters arising from disputes over seeking [faults], and matters arising from disputes over offenses—these constitute disputes over matters (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
What is the root of disputes over speech?

Greed, hatred, and delusion are roots; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are roots; the Saṃgha is a root; the elements (dhātu) are roots; persons are roots; the six types of disputes are roots; and the eighteen matters of schism are roots—these are the roots of verbal dispute.
What are the roots of the dispute concerning accusations (*paryeṣaṇā-vivāda*)?

Greed, hatred, and delusion are its roots; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are its roots; the Saṃgha is its root; the realm (*dhātu*) is its root; the person is its root; and the three matters of formal accusation (*tri-utkṣepa-karma*) are its roots. These are the roots of the dispute concerning accusations.
What are the roots of disputes arising from offenses? Greed, hatred, and delusion are roots;

the Saṃgha is a root; the realm is a root; the person is a root; the three matters of formal accusation are roots; and the six origins of offenses are roots. These are the roots of disputes arising from offenses.
What are the roots of disputes concerning matters (*adhikaraṇa*)?

Greed, hatred, and delusion are roots; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion are roots; the Saṃgha is a root; the realm (*dhātu*) is a root; and the person (*pudgala*) is a root. These are the roots of disputes concerning matters.
“Verbal dispute is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Verbal dispute may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
In what way is verbal dispute wholesome?

When bhikṣus engage in a dispute with other bhikṣus with a virtuous mind—arguing over what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what should be spoken and what should not be spoken—and they thus engage in mutual dispute with one another in such a manner, this is called a "dispute of speech" that is wholesome.
What is meant by "unwholesome verbal dispute"?

If a bhikṣu, with an unwholesome mind, engages in a verbal dispute with another bhikṣu regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what should be spoken and what should not be spoken—disputing with such characteristics and thereby giving rise to contention—this is called unwholesome verbal dispute.
What is verbal dispute that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

If a bhikṣu engages in verbal dispute with an indeterminate mind, citing the eighteen matters—ranging from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what has been spoken and what has not been spoken—and thus mutually disputes over such matters, this is called verbal dispute that is indeterminate.
Is the dispute over seeking [faults] (paryeṣaṇā-vivāda) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The dispute over seeking may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
In what way is the dispute over seeking wholesome?
In this matter, monks with virtuous minds seek out [the offense] together by means of the three bases for formal accusation (*ukkhepanīyakamma*):

violation of the precepts, violation of views, and violation of conduct—whether seen, heard, or suspected. Internally, there are five qualities that cause this person to be free from transgression, free from stain, pure, and released from the offense; they ensure that no evil reputation spreads concerning this person. Seeking the offense through such characteristics and engaging in communal discourse, they do not falsely seek allies or use power to comfort the mind; they perform the formal accusation and the act of recollection, determining whether a case is settled or unsettled, and ensuring that one who is not deluded is liberated. This is called the excellence of seeking matters related to disputes.
What is the unwholesome nature of seeking out grounds for dispute?

If a bhikṣu, with an unwholesome mind, seeks out the offenses of another bhikṣu by means of the three types of charges—namely, regarding violations of precepts, violations of views, or violations of conduct—based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected;

and if he himself lacks the five internal qualities, desiring that this person be defiled by transgressions and remain impure so that their offense is not cleared away; desiring that an unwholesome reputation spread concerning this person; and thus seeking out offenses through such characteristics while conversing together; not falsely seeking the support of allies, nor comforting the other’s mind; performing formal charges (*ukkhepana*) and reminders (*sāraṇīya*), settling some matters while leaving others unsettled; and being deluded and unable to attain liberation—this is called the unwholesome nature of seeking out grounds for dispute.
What is the neutral (*avyākṛta*) search for the matter of a dispute?

It is when a bhikṣu, with a neutral mind, searches for the offense of another bhikṣu by means of the three grounds for accusation—namely, transgression of the precepts, transgression of views, or transgression of conduct—based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.

By means of such characteristics, he searches for the offense and engages in conversation; he does not falsely seek allies, nor does he exert power to comfort the other’s mind. He performs the formal accusation and the act of recollection, determines whether this matter should be settled or not, and brings about liberation through non-delusion. This is called the neutral search for the matter of a dispute.
"Is an offense (*āpatti*) wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
An offense is either unwholesome or indeterminate.
What kind of offense is unwholesome?"
If an ordinary person or a trainee commits an offense intentionally, this constitutes an unwholesome dispute regarding an offense.
What is a neutral dispute regarding an offense?
If an ordinary person or a trainee commits an offense unintentionally, or if a person free from attachment commits an offense unintentionally, this constitutes a neutral dispute regarding an offense.
“Is a dispute over matters wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate? A dispute over matters may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is a dispute over matters that is wholesome?”

If a bhikṣu, with a virtuous mind, treats a matter arising from a dispute over legal procedures (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) as a dispute over legal procedures, or treats a matter arising from a dispute over accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*) as a dispute over legal procedures, or treats a matter arising from a dispute over offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*) as a dispute over legal procedures, this is called a "virtuous" dispute over legal procedures.
What is a "non-virtuous" dispute over legal procedures?

If one performs matters pertaining to a dispute over offenses (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) with an unwholesome mind, or performs matters pertaining to a dispute over what is to be sought (*anveṣaṇā-adhikaraṇa*), or performs matters pertaining to a dispute over verbal contention (*bhāṣaṇā-adhikaraṇa*), this constitutes an unwholesome *adhikaraṇa*.
If one performs them with a neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind, this constitutes a neutral *adhikaraṇa*.

"Speech, speech-dispute, dispute by speech, and dispute as speech. There may be speech that is itself a speech-dispute; there may be speech that is not a speech-dispute; there may be a speech-dispute that is itself speech; and there may be speech that is itself a dispute."
There are cases where speech is not a dispute, cases where dispute is itself speech, and cases where there is dispute that is not speech.
What is the case where speech is itself a dispute of speech?

If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu through speech, regarding eighteen matters—such as what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, up to what has been spoken and what has not been spoken—and thus disputes through such characteristics, mutually contending and being at odds with one another, this is called the case where speech is itself a dispute of speech.
What is a dispute involving speech but not involving contention?

It is when a father speaks with his son, a son speaks with his father; a son speaks with his mother, a mother speaks with her son; an elder brother speaks with his younger brother, a younger brother speaks with his elder brother; a younger sister speaks with her elder sister, an elder sister speaks with her younger sister; or when others likewise speak together. This is a dispute involving speech but not involving contention.
What is meant by "dispute over speech is itself speech"?

If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu regarding eighteen matters—ranging from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma to what has been spoken and what has not—and they thus dispute with one another according to such characteristics, contending and being at odds with each other, this is called "dispute over speech is itself speech."
What is meant by "speech is itself contention"?

If a bhikṣu engages in contentious speech with another bhikṣu regarding eighteen matters—ranging from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma to what is spoken and what is not spoken—and if they contend with one another according to such characteristics, fighting each other so that there is mutual discord, this is called "speech being itself contention."
What is meant by "speaking without contention"?

When a son speaks with his father, a father with his son; a son with his mother, a mother with her son; a younger brother with his elder brother, an elder brother with his younger brother; a younger sister with her elder sister, an elder sister with her younger sister; or when one speaks with others—this is called speaking without contention.
What is the case where dispute is itself speech?

If a bhikṣu disputes with another bhikṣu regarding eighteen matters—ranging from what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma to what has been spoken and what has not been spoken—and they engage in such mutual verbal dispute, contending with one another until they are at odds, this is called "dispute is itself speech."
What is a dispute that is not verbal?

Excluding verbal disputes, any other matters of dispute—namely, disputes concerning accusations, disputes concerning offenses, and disputes concerning legal matters—these are disputes that are not verbal.

The four phrases—seeking-dispute (*vitandā-vivāda*), dispute-seeking (*vivāda-vitanda*), seeking-dispute (*vitanda-vivāda*), and dispute-seeking (*vivāda-vitanda*)—are explained through their interrelation; as these do not differ from the aforementioned fourfold set regarding verbal disputes (*vāda-vivāda*), they are not repeated here. Here, "seeking" (*vitanda*) is itself "seeking-dispute. The cases of transgression-dispute (*āpatti-vivāda*) and matter-dispute (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*) are also as described above.

"If one bhikṣu, in the presence of another bhikṣu, speaks with kind words and instructs him, yet [the instruction] is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what was taught by the Buddha;
and that [first] bhikṣu says:
'This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is what was taught by the Buddha; you should accept and practice this.'"
In this way, the matter of dispute is settled.
This is called the "unlawful settlement of a dispute by means of a semblance of the *adhiṣṭhāna-vinaya*.
It is the same for one bhikṣu acting on behalf of two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha.
For two bhikṣus, [the procedure] for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, and for the saṃgha is likewise.
For three bhikṣus, [the procedure] for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, and for the saṃgha is likewise.
If it is the Saṃgha, for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, or for three bhikṣus—it is the same for the Saṃgha as well.
If one bhikṣu, in the presence of another bhikṣu, speaks with kind words, teaching in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.
He speaks thus: "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha; you should accept and approve this.
If a dispute is thus settled, this is called the settlement of a dispute according to the Dharma by means of *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of).
In this context, what are the *dharma*, the *vinaya*, and the person that are present?
What is meant by the presence of the *dharma*?
It refers to the *dharma* upheld which serves to settle the dispute.
What is the presence of the *vinaya*?
It is that which settles disputes by means of the *vinaya* as it is upheld.
What is the presence of the person?
This refers to those who engage in mutual debate.
If a monk re-ignites a legal dispute that has already been settled, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If a monk who has arrived later, or one who has newly received the precepts, considers this to be the initial dispute and re-ignites it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
In this same way, one bhikṣu [may act] for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, or for the Saṃgha;
likewise, two bhikṣus [may act] for one bhikṣu, for two bhikṣus, for three bhikṣus, or for the Saṃgha.
The same applies to three bhikṣus for one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, and for the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha may address one bhikṣu with kind words of instruction that are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.
He speaks thus: "This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha; accept this, endure this.
If a dispute is settled in such a manner, it is called the settlement of a dispute according to the Dharma by means of the *saṃmukhavinaya* (the presence of the parties).
What are the presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, and the Saṃgha boundary?
What is the presence of the Dharma?
It is that which consists of the Dharma upheld to settle a dispute.
What is the presence of the *vinaya*?
It is that which settles disputes by means of the *vinaya* as upheld.
What is the presence of persons?
Regarding "the exchange of speech and deliberation":
what is meant by "the Saṃgha being present"?

It refers to those who have gathered together in one place for a collective *karmavācanā*; those who did not attend have entrusted their authority to those present; and those who ought to be censured do not censure [the offender]. This is it.
What is the manifestation of the boundary?
It refers to those who establish restrictions through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*) within the boundary.
If a matter of dispute has been settled, to initiate it again constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣu who arrives later or one who has newly received the precepts claims that this is the initial dispute and further instigates it, it is a pāyattika offense.
If one has already given their consent and later regrets it, it is a pāyattika offense.
“The Sangha [should act] for two bhikṣus; it is the same for a Sangha of three bhikṣus.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“By how many methods of settling is verbal dispute extinguished?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"A dispute over speech is extinguished by two means: by the *pratyakṣa-vinaya* (settlement in the presence) and by the *yadbhūyaś-cīrṇa* (the majority decision).
Ānanda asked again:
“Is there a case where a dispute over speech is settled by a single means of resolution, namely the *saṃmukhavinaya*, without employing the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*?
The Buddha told Ānanda: “There is.”
He asked, "Which ones are they?
The Buddha said:

"If one bhikṣu, in the presence of another bhikṣu, speaks with kind words of instruction that are in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught; and he says:
'This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha; accept this, endure this.'"
"In this way, the matter of dispute is settled. This, Ānanda, is called the settling of a verbal dispute by means of a single method of settlement;
it does not require the 'words of many'."
The meaning of "in the presence of" is as explained above.
It is the same for one bhikṣu [acting] toward two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, or the Saṃgha; it is likewise for two bhikṣus.
It is the same for one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, and the Saṃgha.
It is likewise for three bhikṣus [acting] for one bhikṣu, two bhikṣus, three bhikṣus, and the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha speaks kindly to a certain bhikṣu, instructing him in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught. He speaks thus:
"This is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is what the Buddha has taught; accept this and endure this."
"If a dispute is settled in this manner, Ānanda, it is said that a verbal dispute is settled by a single means of settlement:
the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), and not by the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (majority decision)."
The meaning of "being present" is as explained above.
It is the same for a *saṃgha* acting on behalf of two bhikṣus or three bhikṣus.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If those quarreling bhikṣus do not accept the settlement of the dispute by the Saṃgha in this manner, and they hear that there are virtuous monks and excellent, wise elders at another residence, those quarreling bhikṣus should go to that residence because of this dispute."

Ānanda, if one is on the road and is able to settle a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, this is called the settling of a verbal dispute by means of a single method of settlement:
the *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), without employing the *yebhuyyasika* (decision by majority).
The meaning of "manifest before" (*pratyakṣa*) here is as explained above.

If those disputing bhikṣus are on a journey and are unable to settle the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, those disputing bhikṣus should go before the elders and wise persons within that Saṃgha and speak as follows:

"This matter of dispute arose in such a manner; it arose from such a cause. The Saṃgha attempted to settle it in such a way, but I did not accept it; therefore, I have come to the presence of the Venerable Elders."
"Excellent, Elder!
Please settle this dispute for us in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.

If you, Elder, can settle this dispute for us in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, we shall relinquish this dispute before you."

If you, Venerable One, are unable to settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, we shall ourselves create further disputes and cause the offenses to become even more grave. By failing to settle the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, the bhikṣus will dwell in discomfort.
That disputing bhikṣu should thus relinquish this matter of dispute before the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha should say to that disputing bhikṣu:
"Venerable one!..."

If a dispute arises in this manner, according to its reality and its causes, and if the Saṃgha can settle that dispute by speaking in accordance with the facts, we should consider whether it is possible for us to extinguish this matter of dispute.

"Venerable sir, if a dispute has arisen in this manner, according to its actual facts and its true cause, and if the Saṃgha settles the dispute without speaking in accordance with reality, then, Venerable sir, this dispute will become even more serious;
it will be contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha’s teaching. The dispute will not be settled, and the bhikṣus will not be able to dwell in peace and happiness."
That Saṃgha should accept the dispute in this manner; having accepted it, they should resolve it.
If the bhikṣu involved in the dispute is a junior monk, they should say to him:
"Step aside for a moment!"
"We shall deliberate on this matter among ourselves in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.

If the disputing bhikṣus are elders, the Saṃgha should withdraw to another place and together deliberate and adjudicate this matter in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught.
The community of monks thought to themselves:
"If we were to deliberate on this matter before the assembly, we fear that other matters might arise, causing the discussion of our respective virtues and faults to remain unresolved."
"We would rather gather together in a separate place with those who possess wisdom to collectively deliberate on this matter.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"At that time, the Saṃgha should immediately make a formal announcement (jñapti) and collectively deliberate on this matter."
He makes this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its ear, let the Saṃgha now assemble those who possess wisdom to collectively deliberate and adjudicate this matter."
“Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, one should together deliberate and adjudicate the matter.
If a bhikṣu possesses ten qualities, he should be appointed to deliberate and adjudicate the matter.
What are the ten?
First, the perfection of ethical discipline;
second, extensive learning.
Third, if one recites the Vinaya of both divisions with great fluency;
fourth, if one extensively explains its meaning;
fifth, if one is skillful in speech and possesses clear eloquence, such that one is capable of engaging in dialogue and causing others to rejoice.
6. If a dispute arises, one is able to extinguish it.
7. One is without attachment.
8. One is without aversion.
9. Fearlessness. 10. Absence of delusion.
One who possesses these ten qualities should be appointed to adjudicate matters both collectively and individually.
Those who possess these ten qualities should dwell separately in one place and together deliberate upon this matter.

Among the monks adjudicating the case, there may be those who do not recite the precepts and are ignorant of the Vinaya; they then abandon the correct meaning and speak what is contrary to the Dharma.
The Saṃgha should formally announce the dismissal of this bhikṣu, making the announcement as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so does not recite the precepts and is ignorant of the Vinaya; he has abandoned the correct meaning and uttered what is contrary to the Dharma."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now expel this bhikṣu.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this motion in this manner, he should be expelled.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Among those bhikṣus sitting there who have settled the matter, some recite the Prātimokṣa while others do not recite the Vinaya.
They abandon the correct meaning and speak only a few words of the text."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Saṃgha should make a formal motion (jñapti) to dismiss this bhikṣu who adjudicates the matter.
The motion should be made as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, recites the *Prātimokṣa* but does not recite the Vinaya; he abandons the correct meaning and speaks only a few words of the text.
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha now expels this bhikṣu."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, he dismisses them.
If, among the bhikṣus adjudicating the matter, there is a Dharma-master present in the assembly who abandons the correct meaning and speaks with forceful rhetoric.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"The Saṃgha should perform a formal announcement (*jñapti*) to expel this bhikṣu.
Make the announcement in this manner: [insert formula here]."
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Dharma-master, so-and-so, abandons the meaning of the True Dharma and speaks with the forceful power of mere words.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now expel this bhikṣu."
"Thus it is announced.
Having made this announcement, they should dismiss him.

If a monk who adjudicates the matter is present among those seated, whether he recites the *Prātimokṣa* or the *Vinaya*, he shall speak in accordance with the true meaning and according to the Dharma.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“The Saṃgha should assist this bhikṣu in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions.

If that Saṃgha does not settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, then this [present] Saṃgha should now settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions.”
If that Sangha settles this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, then this Sangha here also approves of this matter.
The Sangha should then say to those monks involved in the dispute:

"If that Sangha has settled this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions, we also approve of this settlement of the dispute in accordance with the Dharma."
"Now we too shall likewise settle this dispute.
Ānanda, if a dispute can be settled in this manner, it is said that a verbal dispute is settled by a single method:
the *saṃmukhavinaya* (settlement in the presence of the parties), and not by the *yadbhūyaḥkṣānti* (the majority decision).
The meaning of "being present," as well as the factors up to the "elements" (*dhātu*), are as explained above.
If a legal dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, yet one subsequently re-ignites it, it is a *pāyattika* offense, as described above.

That disputing monk, unable to accept the settlement of the dispute effected by the second Saṃgha, hears that in another residence there are many monks who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā.
Those disputing bhikṣus should go to where those bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā reside.
If those bhikṣus are able to settle the dispute while on the way, this, Ānanda, is called [a settlement].
A dispute over speech is settled by a single means of resolution; the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence) does not employ the method of "many voices.
Regarding this, what is meant by "in the presence"?
It refers to the presence of the Dharma, the Vinaya, the person, and the monastic boundary (*sīmā*), as described above.
If, after a dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, one should initiate it again, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense as described above.

If those monks involved in the dispute are unable to settle the matter midway in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, those monks involved in the dispute should go to those many monks who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā, and speak to them thus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"This dispute of mine arose in this way; it truly arose from such a cause. The Saṃgha has settled this dispute in this manner, and the second Saṃgha has likewise settled it in this manner."
I do not approve of this, and therefore I have come among you, Venerable Elders.

It would be well, Venerable Elders, if you could settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with what the Buddha has taught; I shall then relinquish this dispute among you.

If the Elder is unable to settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha, we shall then ourselves create further contention, thereby making the offense even more grave.
