"If this dispute is settled in a manner that is not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, and not as taught by the Buddha, the bhikṣus will dwell in discomfort and lack peace.
Those bhikṣus involved in the dispute should then relinquish this dispute before the assembly of many bhikṣus.
Those many bhikṣus should say to the bhikṣu who is disputing:

"If, Elder, this matter of dispute has arisen as it did, according to reality, and according to its cause; and if you speak truthfully regarding how the second Saṃgha extinguished the dispute, and having spoken, you abandon the dispute—then we shall consider whether we are able to extinguish this dispute."

If an elder does not speak according to reality, this dispute will remain unresolved; his offense will become even more grave, and if the dispute is not settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, the bhikṣus will dwell in unhappiness and lack of peace.
"Ānanda! Those many bhikṣus should accept the dispute in this manner, and having accepted it, they should resolve it.
If those bhikṣus who are disputing are of junior standing, one should say to them:"
"Please move aside a little!
We wish to deliberate upon this matter.
If he is a senior elder (*sthavira*), he should himself move to another place and deliberate on this matter together with the others.

If that Sangha settles the dispute not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, nor as taught by the Buddha, and if the second Sangha likewise settles this matter of dispute not in accordance with the Dharma, not in accordance with the Vinaya, nor as taught by the Buddha, then many bhikṣus should settle this dispute in accordance with the Dharma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and as taught by the Buddha.

If that Sangha has settled the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, and the second Sangha has also settled the dispute in accordance with the Dharma, the many bhikṣus should likewise approve of this matter and say to those bhikṣus involved in the dispute:
"Just as that second Sangha has settled the dispute, we also approve; now we shall settle the dispute in this manner."
"Thus it is, Ānanda! A dispute is settled by means of a single resolution;
the *pratyakṣavinaya* (settlement in the presence of) is not used with the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (majority vote)."
Regarding those present herein, the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the persons are as described above.
If, after a dispute has been settled in accordance with the Dharma, one should raise it again, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense as stated above.
The same applies when two bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā go [to another].
The same also applies when one bhikṣu who upholds the Dharma, even up to the Mātṛkā, goes [to another].
At that time, there was a dispute among the bhikṣus in Śrāvastī, and the Saṃgha of Śrāvastī settled the dispute in accordance with the Dharma.
Those bhikṣus who were disputing could not accept the settlement of the dispute by the Saṃgha; they heard that it was also as described above regarding their own residence.
The case of many bhikṣus was as described above;
likewise for two bhikṣus, and for a single bhikṣu.

Those disputing bhikṣus, unable to endure the settlement of the dispute by the Saṃgha of Śrāvastī—down to the level of a single bhikṣu—then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One immediately assembled the community of bhikṣus and, through countless skillful means, rebuked those disputing bhikṣus, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not be done."
"How can you be so foolish!
You do not accept that the Saṃgha of Śrāvastī has settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, nor do you accept it even when a single bhikṣu has settled a dispute?"
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"This dispute should be settled by the method of 'the speech of many. I authorize the distribution of śalākās (voting sticks) and the appointment of a distributor of śalākās through a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
There are five qualities for which one should not be appointed to distribute the *śalākā* (voting sticks):

one who has affection, one who has aversion, one who has fear, one who has delusion, and one who does not know whether they themselves have cast their vote or not. One possessing these five qualities should not be appointed to distribute the *śalākā*.

One who is without attachment, without ill will, without fear, without delusion, and who knows his own conduct and misconduct—possessing these five qualities, one should be appointed to distribute the śalākās.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* as described above should be appointed in this manner:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha appoint the bhikṣu so-and-so to distribute the *śalākā*."
The motion is thus made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now appoints the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the śalākas."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha appointing the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the śalāka remain silent; whoever does not approve should speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of the bhikṣu [Name] to distribute the śalāka. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
There are three ways of drawing lots (*śalākā*):
first, openly; second, in secret; third, by whispering into the ear.
What is meant by "openly"?
Those bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"In this assembly, although there are many bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma, their preceptors and teachers are all in accordance with the Dharma."
One should conduct the *śalākā* (voting sticks) openly. Those monks will then think:
"Although there are many unrighteous persons among the assembly, the elders who are wise and who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā all speak according to the Dharma."
One should conduct the *śalākā* (voting sticks) openly.
The monks should then reflect thus:
"I do not know whether those who speak according to the Dharma are in the majority, or those who speak contrary to the Dharma."
"However, those preceptors and instructors are all in accordance with the Dharma.
That bhikṣu should then openly distribute the śalākā (voting sticks).
The bhikṣus should think as follows:
"I do not know whether this matter of dispute consists mostly of speech in accordance with the Dharma or mostly of speech contrary to the Dharma;
however, those elders who are wise and uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātikā, all speak in accordance with the Dharma."
That bhikṣu should conduct the *śalākā* (voting sticks) openly.
Those bhikṣus should then think: "In this legal dispute, there are many who speak according to the Dharma."
One should then openly distribute the *śalākā* (voting sticks).
They should be distributed in this manner, and two types of *śalākā* should be prepared:
one broken and one whole.
Once the voting sticks (*śalākā*) have been distributed, one should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Those who speak thus shall take the unbroken voting stick;
those who speak thus shall take the broken voting stick."
Once the voting sticks (*śalāka*) have been distributed, they should be counted in a separate place.
If those who speak according to the Dharma are in the majority, he should make a formal motion (*jñapti*):
"The dispute is settled by those who spoke in such a manner."

If the bhikṣus who speak according to the Dharma are few, they should immediately cause a disturbance and then depart; they should send a messenger to the place where the bhikṣus reside and announce to the Saṃgha:
"In that residence, the bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous."
"Excellent, Elder! You should go there;
if there are many bhikṣus who speak according to the Dharma, the dispute will be settled and the merit will be great.
Upon hearing this, that bhikṣu should go; if he does not go, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Ānanda, if a dispute is settled in this manner, it is said that a verbal dispute is extinguished by two means:
through the presence of the *vinaya* (face-to-face settlement) and by the application of the majority decision (*yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*).
Regarding those present herein, the meanings of *dharma*, *vinaya*, person, realm, and saṃgha are as explained above.
How is the "majority decision" (*yadbhūyaḥkṣānti*) applied herein?
It is applied by relying on what is spoken by the majority who uphold the *dharma*, uphold the *vinaya*, and uphold the *mātṛkā*.
If, after having been extinguished in accordance with the Dharma, it is initiated again, it is a *pāyattika* as described above.
"What is the concealment of conduct by means of drawing lots (*śalākā*)? The monks form this thought:"

"In this dispute, although the monks who act according to the Dharma are numerous, their preceptors (upādhyāya) and instructors (ācārya) do not act according to the Dharma. If we were to openly distribute the voting tallies (śalākā), we fear that the monks will follow the lead of their preceptors and instructors and take up the tallies [in favor of them]."
That bhikṣu should conceal his conduct by casting a śalākā.
He should think thus:

"In this dispute, although the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma are numerous, among that assembly there are elders, leaders, and wise men who uphold the Dharma, uphold the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā, yet they abide in what is not the Dharma."

If we were to distribute the voting tickets (*śalākā*) openly, the monks would follow those senior elders and leading wise men among the assembly who abide in what is not the Dharma and seize the voting tickets.
This bhikṣu should perform the *śalākā* (lot) for concealment.
If he is ignorant of two phrases, it is also as described above.

He should perform the *śalākā* in this manner, from two types up until the dispute has been settled according to the Dharma; if he subsequently raises the matter again, he incurs a *pāyattika*, just as when performing the *śalākā* openly as described above.
"What is the practice of whispering while casting the voting tickets?
It is when a bhikṣu thinks to himself:
'Bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma are numerous, yet my preceptor and teacher speak what is contrary to the Dharma.'"
He should distribute the voting tickets (*śalāka*) by whispering them into the ear. That bhikṣu thinks to himself:

"In this legal dispute, although the bhikṣus who act according to the Dharma are numerous, the leading elder and wise bhikṣu at the head of that assembly abides in what is contrary to the Dharma, while upholding what is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the Mātṛkā."
That bhikṣu should conduct the śalākā by whispering into the ear.
If he does not know two phrases, it is also as described above.
He should prepare two kinds of śalākā:
One is broken and the other is whole.
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*): "Those who speak thus shall take the whole *śalākā*;
those who speak thus shall take the broken *śalākā*."

When he distributes the voting tokens (*śalākā*), he should ensure that there is space between the seats for one person’s body, even if it is slightly obstructed; then that monk should whisper, saying:
"Your preceptor (*upādhyāya*), co-preceptor, ācārya, co-ācārya, and close friends have already taken their voting tokens."
"Excellent!
You too should take up the voting tally (*śalākā*), out of compassion.
If the monks who act according to the Dharma are numerous, the dispute will be settled and great merit will be gained.

Once the distribution of the *śalāka* has been completed, they shall count them on one side; from this point until the dispute has been settled according to the Dharma, if they subsequently raise the issue again, they incur a *pāyattika* offense as described above.
There are ten ways of improperly taking *śalākā* (voting sticks): taking the *śalākā* without understanding how to do so;

taking the *śalākā* without being accompanied by virtuous companions; taking the *śalākā* with the intent to cause those who act contrary to the Dharma to be in the majority; knowing that many bhikṣus are acting contrary to the Dharma yet taking the *śalākā*; taking the *śalākā* with the intent to cause a schism in the Saṃgha; knowing that the Saṃgha is about to split yet taking the *śalākā*; taking the *śalākā* in an illegal manner; taking the *śalākā* apart from the assembly; taking the *śalākā* on account of a minor offense; and taking the *śalākā* contrary to what one has perceived.
What is meant by "not understanding how to hold the *śalākā*"?

It refers to not reaching a definitive resolution regarding this matter of dispute, and thus not knowing whether it is according to the Dharma or contrary to the Dharma, and so forth, up to whether it should be spoken or not; this is what is meant by "not understanding how to hold the *śalākā*."
What is meant by not taking up the *śalākā* (voting sticks) with a virtuous companion?

If a monk who is learned, upholds the Dharma, upholds the Vinaya, and upholds the Mātṛkā, does not act as his companion regarding what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma, or even regarding what should and should not be spoken—this is called not taking up the *śalākā* with a virtuous companion.
How can one cause unrighteous bhikṣus to take many śalākās? That bhikṣu thinks thus:
"In this matter of dispute, there are many righteous bhikṣus; I shall now take unrighteous śalākās so that the unrighteous bhikṣus become numerous."
This is how one causes unrighteous bhikṣus to take many śalākās.
How does one know that many unrighteous bhikṣus have taken many śalākās?
That bhikṣu reflects as follows:
"In this matter of dispute, the bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous and, acting as companions in what is contrary to the Dharma, they take up the śalākā.
This is how one knows that the bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma are numerous and have taken up the śalākā.
How is it that one who wishes to cause a schism in the Saṃgha takes up a *śalākā*? He thinks thus:
"In this matter of dispute, the monks who act according to the Dharma are numerous; I shall now take up an *śalākā* that is contrary to the Dharma to cause the Saṃgha to split."
This is for the purpose of causing a schism in the Saṃgha by drawing lots (*śalākā*).
How does one know that the Saṃgha is about to split and thus draw lots?

That bhikṣu knows that there are many bhikṣus who act contrary to the Dharma, and he draws lots as an ally to those who act contrary to the Dharma; this is how one knows that the Saṃgha is about to split and thus draws lots.
What is the illegal taking of a *śalākā* (lot)?
When the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* or the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is performed with a motion (*jñapti*) that differs from the formal act (*karman*), this is the illegal taking of a *śalākā*.
What is the taking of a *śalākā* by a separate assembly?

When the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of a single boundary is not completed by the full assembly, when those who should have been informed have not been informed, and when those present should be censured are indeed censured—this constitutes a separate assembly (*nānāsaṃgha*) taking the voting sticks (*śalākā*).
What is meant by taking up a śalākā (voting stick) for minor offenses?

It refers to taking up a śalākā when one recalls having committed an offense, or when one has committed it unintentionally, or when one has made the resolve to do so; this is called taking up a śalākā for minor offenses.
What is it to take up a śalākā (voting tally) contrary to what one has seen?
To take up a śalākā with a view different from one's own and an acceptance different from one's own—this is taking up a śalākā contrary to what one has seen.
These are the ten kinds of illegal ways of taking up a śalākā.

Furthermore, there are ten ways of drawing lots in accordance with the Dharma, from the way of drawing lots by understanding to the way of drawing lots according to what has been seen; these constitute the ten ways of drawing lots in accordance with the Dharma, which are the opposites of the aforementioned ten ways of drawing lots not in accordance with the Dharma.

There are five kinds of impartial persons: some do not act with the body but act with speech; some do not act with speech but act with the body; some do not act with the body nor act with speech; some act both with the body and with speech; and some are neither driven by attachment, nor by aversion, nor by fear, nor by delusion.
What is meant by a person whose body does not act but whose speech does?
There is a person who does not manifest signs with the body but speaks verbal instructions; this is what is meant by a person whose body does not act but whose speech does.
What is meant by one who does not act with the mouth but acts with the body?
There are those who manifest signs with the body but do not speak verbal instructions; this is what is meant by one who does not act with the mouth but acts with the body.
What is meant by "a person neither acts with the body nor acts with the mouth"?
There is a person who does not manifest signs with the body and does not speak verbal instructions with the mouth; this is what is meant by "neither acting with the body nor acting with the mouth."
What is meant by bodily action and verbal action?
When a person manifests signs with the body and speaks instructions with the mouth, this is called bodily and verbal action.

Among such people, there is one who is without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion; among those people, this person is the most honored, noble, and supreme, just as curd is produced from milk, butter from curd, and ghee from butter—the latter being the most excellent and peerless.
Thus, being without attachment, without aversion, without fear, and without delusion, one is the most honorable, noble, and peerless among those people; these are the five kinds of impartial persons.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 47 [and] Volume 48 (Part 3,
Section 12), translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others, the second part of the *Adhikaraṇa-śamatha-vastu*. At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By how many methods of settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*) are disputes to be settled?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Disputes are settled by means of four methods of resolution:
the Vinaya of presence (sammukhā-vinaya), the Vinaya of recollection (sati-vinaya), the Vinaya of non-insanity (amūḷha-vinaya), and the Vinaya of the locus of the offense (tassapāpiyasika-vinaya)."
Ānanda asked again:

"Is there any case of a legal dispute arising from a search that is settled by two types of extinction (*nirodha*), rather than by the *amūḷhavinaya* (verdict of sanity) or the *tassapāpiyasikā* (verdict of the more serious offense)?"
The Buddha told Ānanda, "There is.
He asked again:
“What is this? The Buddha told Ānanda:

“If a bhikṣu has not committed a grave offense such as a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya, yet other bhikṣus claim he has committed a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a sthūlātyaya, and those bhikṣus say to him:”
"Do you recall committing any pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, or sthūlātyaya offenses?
Since he did not recall them, he replied:
"I do not recall committing any offenses from pārājika down to sthūlātyaya."
"Elder! Do not continue to interrogate and cross-examine me.
Yet that bhikkhu did not cease his interrogation. Ānanda!

"In the kingdom of Uddiyāna. He asked, "Did you go there?"
He replied, "I did not go. [The other asked,] "Did he come?"
He replied, “I have not come. He asked:
“How did you commit the offense? He replied,
“I committed it in a dream.”
Upāli said: "Go; you have not committed even a *duṣkṛta* offense.

The *Kṣudraka-vastu*, the Chapter on the Settlement of Disputes, is thus completed. 14. The Chapter on Bhikṣuṇīs, the seventeenth. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at the Nyagrodha Park in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five hundred Śākya women, went to where the World-Honored One was; she bowed her head at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!
"I pray that you will allow women to go forth from home into the Buddha-dharma to practice the Way.
The Buddha said, "Desist, Gautamī!"
Do not speak these words:
"I wish to allow women to leave the household life to practice the Way. Why is this?
"Gautamī! If women go forth from home into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma to practice the Way, it will cause the Buddha-dharma not to endure for long.
When Mahāprajāpatī heard this instruction from the World-Honored One, she came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

At that time, the World-Honored One, departing from Śrāvastī with twelve hundred and fifty disciples, traveled through the human realm to the kingdom of Kośala; from Kośala, he returned to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Mahāprajāpatī heard that the Buddha was at the Jetavana Monastery; together with five hundred Śākya women, she shaved her head, donned the *kāṣāya*, and traveled to the Jetavana Monastery in Śrāvastī. She stood outside the gate, her feet blistered from walking and her body covered in dust, weeping and shedding tears.
At that time, having seen this, Ānanda went to her and asked:

"Gautamī! For what reason have you and these five hundred Śākya women shaved our heads, donned the saffron robes, and are now standing here weeping with tears streaming down, your feet bleeding from walking and your bodies covered in dust?"
They replied, "We women cannot leave the household life and receive the full precepts within the Buddha's Dharma.
Ānanda said to them:
"Stop! I shall go to the Buddha on your behalf and make this request.
Thereupon, Ānanda went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, stood to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will grant permission for women to leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts.
The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Stop! Do not desire that women go forth from home into the Buddha-dharma to receive the full precepts. Why is this?"
If women go forth from home within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts, they will cause the Buddha-dharma to not endure for long.
For example, Ānanda!
If there are few men and many women in a householder’s family, one knows that the family is in decline.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
If women go forth from home within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts, they will cause the Buddha-dharma not to endure for long.
It is just like a fine rice field that is immediately destroyed by frost and hail.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
If women were to leave the household life and receive the full precepts within the Buddha-dharma, it would cause the Buddha-dharma to not endure for long.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Mahāprajāpatī has rendered great service to the Buddha; after the Buddha’s mother passed away, she nursed the World-Honored One and raised him to adulthood.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: “It is so!”
"It is so! She has shown me great kindness; when my mother passed away, she nurtured me with her milk and raised me until I was grown.

I, too, have shown great kindness to Mahāprajāpatī. If a person comes to know the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha because of another, that kindness is difficult to repay; it cannot be repaid through food, clothing, beds, bedding, or medicine."
"When I appear in the world, I cause Mahāprajāpatī to know the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha;
it is also thus. The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If there is someone who, because of another, gains faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, this kindness is difficult to repay; it cannot be repaid by means of food, clothing, beds, bedding, or medicine."
"When I appear in the world, I cause Mahāprajāpatī to have faith in and delight in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha;
it is just so. The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"If there is a person who, through another, attains refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, upholds the five precepts, knows suffering, knows its origin, knows its cessation, and knows the path, and has no doubt regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—if they attain the fruit of srotāpanna, severing all evil destinies and attaining the certainty of entering the right path, then after seven more births and deaths, they shall reach the end of suffering."
Ānanda! The kindness of such a person as this is difficult to repay; it cannot be repaid through food, clothing, beds, bedding, or medicine.
It is the same for my appearing in the world and causing Mahāprajāpatī to receive the three refuges, up to her certain entry into the right path.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“If women go forth from home into the Buddha’s Dharma and receive the precepts, can they attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the fruit of an arhat?”
The Buddha told Ānanda,
“It can be obtained.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:

"If women may go forth within the Buddha's Dharma and receive the full precepts, attaining the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of an arhat, I pray that the Buddha will grant permission for them to go forth and receive the full precepts."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"I now establish for women eight rules to be observed for as long as life lasts, which must not be transgressed. If they can practice them, this constitutes receiving the precepts."
What are the eight?

Although she may be a bhikṣuṇī of a hundred years’ standing, upon seeing a bhikṣu who has newly received the precepts, she should rise to meet him, pay homage, prepare a pure seat for him, and invite him to sit.
This Dharma should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, one must not transgress it. Ānanda!
A bhikṣuṇī should not revile or scold a bhikṣu, nor should she slander him by saying that he has broken the precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed. Ānanda!

A bhikṣuṇī should not perform an act of formal accusation (*ukkhepana*), a reminder (*sāraṇīya*), or a self-accusation against a bhikṣu; she should not obstruct another’s search for an offense, nor obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, nor obstruct the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*). A bhikṣuṇī should not reprimand a bhikṣu; rather, it is the bhikṣu who should reprimand the bhikṣuṇī.
This Dharma should be respected, revered, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as one lives.
Once the śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts, she shall request the full ordination from the community of bhikṣus.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as one lives.
When a bhikṣuṇī commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, she must undergo the mānatva penance for half a month before both assemblies of the Saṃgha.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
A bhikṣuṇī must request instruction from the saṃgha every half-month.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.
A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (varṣā) in a place where no bhikṣus reside.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; it must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

When the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the rainy season retreat (varṣā), they should seek the three matters—what has been seen, heard, or suspected—for the invitation to admonish (pravāraṇā) from within the Bhikṣu Saṃgha.
This rule should be respected, honored, and praised; for as long as life lasts, it must not be transgressed.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
I have now declared these eight rules that must not be transgressed; if a woman is able to practice them, she has received the precepts.
It is like a person who builds a bridge over a great body of water and crosses over.
"Thus it is, Ānanda!
I have now declared these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women; if they can practice them, this constitutes their reception of the precepts.
At that time, having heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, Ānanda went at once to Mahāprajāpatī and said to her:
“Women may go forth from home into homelessness within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts (mahā-śīla).
The World-Honored One has established for women eight rules that must not be transgressed; if they can practice these, they have received the precepts.”
He then explained the eight matters as above. Mahāprajāpatī said:
"If the World-Honored One has proclaimed these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women, I and the five hundred Śākya women shall together receive them upon our heads."

Ānanda! It is as if there were a man or a woman, young, pure, and elegantly adorned, who had been washed and bathed by someone and was resting upon a terrace; if one were to take a garland of *utpala* flowers, a garland of *ahimudra* flowers, a garland of *campaka* flowers, a garland of *sumana* flowers, or a garland of *vārṣika* flowers and present them to him, he would immediately accept them and fasten them upon his head.
"So be it, Ānanda!
The World-Honored One has taught these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women; I and the five hundred Śākya women shall together receive them upon our heads."
Then Ānanda went at once to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The World-Honored One has spoken the Eight Rules that Women Must Not Transgress. Mahāprajāpatī and the others, having heard them, have received them upon their heads. It is like a man or a woman, young, pure, and beautifully adorned, who, having washed and anointed their hair, stands in a hall; if someone were to bring various flower garlands and give them to her, she would immediately receive them with both hands and fasten them upon her head.”
"Thus it is, Ānanda! Mahāprajāpatī and the five hundred women have received the full ordination.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If women had not gone forth in the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma would have remained for five hundred years.

When Ānanda heard this, he was displeased; harboring regret and distress in his heart, he wept with streaming tears. He went forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

At that time, there was another woman who wished to receive the precepts; the bhikṣuṇī led her toward the Buddha’s dwelling, but on the way they encountered bandits, who then proceeded to humiliate, insult, and mock her.
The bhikṣuṇīs spoke to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, I permit those bhikṣuṇīs to grant ordination and confer the full precepts immediately."
One should grant ordination in this manner.
If one wishes to have the hair shaved within a bhikṣuṇī monastery, one should inform the Saṃgha, or speak to each individual to let them know, and only then have the hair shaved.
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) should be made as follows:
"Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This person, so-and-so, wishes to seek a haircut from so-and-so."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let [the monk] shave the hair of so-and-so.
This is the formal announcement.
Having made this announcement in this manner, he should shave the hair.
If one wishes to receive the going-forth within a bhikṣuṇī monastery, whether by announcing it to the Saṃgha or by informing each individual, one should make the following announcement:
"May the noble sisters of the Saṃgha listen!..."
This person, so-and-so, seeks to go forth from the home life under the guidance of such-and-such a person.
If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and allow so-and-so to go forth.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*), one should grant them the going forth (*pravrajyā*).

The procedure for granting the going forth is as follows: after having the candidate don the saffron robe (*kāṣāya*), have them place their right knee on the ground and join their palms, and instruct them to say these words:
"I, [Name], a certain nun, take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; I now go forth following the Buddha."
"Venerable Sir, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is my World-Honored One.
A second and third time, he spoke thus.
“[My] aunt, [name], has completed her taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha; I have now followed the Buddha into homelessness.
[Name] is my preceptor. The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is my World-Honored One.”
Having spoken thus a second and a third time, one should confer the precepts: "For as long as life lasts, one shall not kill living beings;
this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept. If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not steal; this is a precept for a śrāmaṇerikā.
If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not engage in sexual misconduct;
this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept. If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not speak falsely; this is a precept for śrāmaṇerikās.
If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"Throughout one's entire life, one must not drink alcohol; this is a precept for śrāmaṇerikās.
If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"Throughout one's entire life, one must not wear flower garlands or anoint the body with fragrant oils;
this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept. If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor may one go to witness them;
this is a precept for śrāmaṇerikās. If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not sit upon high or wide beds; this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept.
If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not eat at improper times; this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept.
If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"For as long as life lasts, one must not grasp or possess gold, silver, or precious objects, whether in their raw or refined state;
this is a śrāmaṇerikā precept. If you can uphold it, answer: 'I can.'"
"Thus, these ten precepts for śrāmaṇerikās must not be transgressed for as long as life lasts.

"It is permitted that a girl who is eighteen years old shall train in the precepts for two years; when she has reached twenty, she may receive the full ordination (upasampadā) within the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
If she is ten years of age and has previously been married, she is permitted to train in the precepts for two years; once she has completed twelve years [of age], she shall receive full ordination.
She should be granted this two-year training in the precepts in this manner.

The śrāmaṇerikā should go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs, bare her right shoulder, remove her leather sandals, and after prostrating at the feet of the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, place her right knee on the ground and, with palms joined, speak these words:
"May the venerable saṃgha listen!
I, the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], request the Saṃgha for two years of training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my preceptor.
May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me two years of training in the precepts.
Thus it should be said a second and a third time.

Having led the śrāmaṇerikā away to a place where she cannot hear but can see, one among the assembly who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā, so-and-so, now requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with so-and-so as her preceptress (upādhyāyinī).
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant this śrāmaṇerikā, so-and-so, the two-year training in the precepts, with so-and-so as her preceptress.
[The motion] is thus stated:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now requests from the Sangha the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her preceptor-ni."
The Sangha now grants this śrāmaṇerikā [Name] the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] as her precept-nurse (upādhyāyikā).

Which of you, venerable sisters, approves of the Sangha granting the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name] with [Name] as her precept-nurse? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said a second and a third time.
'The Saṃgha has already granted the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], with [Name] as the *upādhyāyinī*, and this is concluded.'"
“Since the Saṃgha is patient and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld.
One should confer the six rules in this manner: “Listen attentively, [Name]. The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught six rules: one must not commit impure conduct or engage in sexual desire.

If a śikṣamāṇā engages in sexual desire, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan. To touch body to body with a man who possesses a defiled mind constitutes a breach of the precepts; she should be given the precepts again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense.”
If one who is able to uphold them replies, "I can," [the preceptor says]:

"You must not steal, even so much as a blade of grass. If a śikṣamāṇā takes five kārṣāpaṇas or more than five kārṣāpaṇas—whether taking it herself or instructing another to take it, whether cutting it herself or instructing another to cut it, whether breaking it herself or instructing another to break it, or burning it, burying it, or spoiling its color—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan. If she takes less than five kārṣāpaṇas, she commits a transgression of the training rules and should be given the precepts again; for the remainder of her life, she must not violate this."
If she is able, she shall answer, "I am able.

"One must not intentionally take the life of any living being, even so small as an ant. If a *śikṣamāṇā* intentionally takes a human life with her own hand—whether by seeking out a knife and handing it over, teaching death, encouraging death, praising death, giving someone poison, causing an abortion, performing incantations or sorcery, or doing so herself or instructing others to do so—she is no longer a *śikṣamāṇā*, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan. If she takes the life of an animal that cannot transform, she violates the precept; she must receive the precepts again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit such an offense."
If she is able, she shall answer, "I am able. "One must not speak falsely, even in jest.

If a śikṣamāṇā, being untrue and possessing nothing of the sort, claims for herself the attainment of superhuman states (uttarimanuṣyadharma), saying that she has attained dhyāna, liberation, concentration, or meditative absorption; or that she has attained the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat; or that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas have come to make offerings to her—she is not a śikṣamāṇā, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan. If she intentionally speaks a falsehood within the assembly and thus violates the precepts, she must be given the precepts again. Within this, one must not commit an offense as long as life lasts."
If she is able, she should answer, "I am able.

"One must not eat at improper times; if a śikṣamāṇā eats at an improper time, she violates the precepts and should be given the precepts again. Within this, one must not commit such an offense for as long as life lasts."
If she is able, she should answer, "I am able.

"One must not drink alcohol; if a śikṣamāṇā drinks alcohol, she commits a transgression of the precepts and should be given the precepts again. Within this, for as long as life lasts, one must not commit this offense."
If she is able, she shall answer: "I am able.
A śikṣamāṇā should train in all the bhikṣuṇī precepts, except for eating after the prescribed time and taking food for herself to eat.
One should seek out an upādhyāyī and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sister!
I, [Name], now request you, Auntie, to be my upādhyāyī."
"I pray that the Āryā will act as my upādhyāyī; by relying upon the Āryā, I shall receive the full ordination.
Thus he should speak a second and a third time.
The upādhyāyī should respond, saying:

"Very well. "If a śikṣamāṇā has completed her training in the precepts and is either twenty years of age or twelve years [of practice], one should confer the full ordination upon her by means of the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the motion followed by three proclamations)."
The precepts should be conferred in this manner:

the candidate for ordination should be led away from the place where they can hear [the assembly] and placed where they can see it; therein, the preceptor (*śāstr*) should appoint an instructor (*anuśāsaka*).
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!..."
This [name], from the nun preceptor [name], requests to receive the full ordination.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent that [name] shall serve as the instructor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The instructor should go to the person receiving the precepts and say:
"Do these—this *antarvāsa*, this *uttarāsaṅga*, this *saṃghāṭī*, this *saṃkakṣikā* shoulder-covering robe, and this bowl—belong to you as your robes and bowl?"
Listen attentively!
Now is the time for truth; I now question you: if it exists, say it exists; if it does not exist, you should say it does not exist.
What is your name?
"What is the preceptor’s name?
Are you twenty years of age?
Are your robes and bowl complete?"
"Have your parents or husband given their permission for you to do so?
Are you not in debt to anyone?
And are you not a slave?"
Is she a woman? Women may have such various ailments as leprosy, white leprosy, carbuncles,
dry sores, insanity, dual sexual organs, conjoined genitals, narrow genitalia, constant leakage of urine and feces, or constant discharge of urine, feces, mucus, and saliva.
"Do you have any such illnesses? If he answers, "No."
He should say: "Just as I have previously asked, so shall the Saṃgha also ask you within the assembly.
You, too, should answer in this manner."

After the instructor has finished questioning her, he should return to the midst of the Saṃgha and, maintaining his usual dignified demeanor, stand at a place within arm’s reach of the bhikṣuṇī. He should then make the formal announcement (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!..."
This [name], from the preceptor nun [name], requests to receive the full ordination.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; I have finished instructing her and shall now summon her to come forward.
[He] says thus:
"I declare [myself as such]. He should be told: "Come."

Once she has arrived, the preceptor should take her bowl and instruct her to prostrate at the feet of the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha. She should then kneel with her right knee on the ground before the Precept-Master, join her palms, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, please listen!"
I, [Name], having requested the full ordination from the Preceptor Nun [Name], now beg the Sangha for the full ordination, with [Name] as my Preceptor Nun.
"May the Sangha deliver me out of compassion.
Thus he speaks a second and a third time.
Thereupon, the preceptor should make the formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!

This [name], with [name] as her preceptress (upādhyāyī), seeks to receive the full ordination (upasampadā). This [name] now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with [name] as her preceptress."
"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha listen with patience as I inquire about matters of difficulty.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*). Listen attentively!"
This is now a time of sincerity, a time of truthful speech.
I now ask you: if something exists, you should say it exists; if it does not exist, you should say it does not exist.
What is your name?
"What is the Preceptor's name?
Are you twenty years of age?
Are your robes and alms bowl complete?"
"Do your parents or husband permit you?
Are you not in debt to anyone?
Are you not a slave?"
Are you a woman? Women have such diseases as leprosy, white leprosy, carbuncles,

consumption, insanity, hermaphroditism, the fusion of the two orifices, narrowness of the vaginal canal, constant leakage of urine and feces, and the constant discharge of urine, feces, mucus, and saliva.
"Do you have any such illnesses? He replied, "No."
The formal announcement (*jñapti*) should be made as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, please listen!

This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so. This person, so-and-so, now requests the Sangha for the conferral of the full ordination, with the preceptor nun, so-and-so."
So-and-so declares herself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully equipped with robes and bowl.
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent to confer the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as her preceptor-ni.
The announcement is as follows:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This [name], with the nun [name] as her preceptor, seeks to receive the full ordination. This [name] now requests the full ordination from the Sangha, with the nun [name] as her preceptor."
So-and-so has declared herself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully equipped with robes and bowl.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with the Bhikṣuṇī So-and-so as her preceptor.
"Whichever sisters among you approve of the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as the preceptress-nun, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak up.
This is the conclusion of the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already granted that so-and-so receive the full ordination with so-and-so as the preceptress-ni; since the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."

"Then that person receiving the precepts, together with the community of bhikṣuṇīs, goes before the community of bhikṣus; having prostrated at the feet of the Saṃgha, they place their right knee on the ground, join their palms, and speak as follows:
'Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!'"
I, [Name], have requested the full ordination from the preceptor-nun [Name]. I, [Name], now request the Sangha to grant me the full ordination, with [Name] as my preceptor-nun.
"May the Saṃgha deliver me out of compassion.
Thus, for a second and third time, he should speak these words; herein, the Preceptor of the Precepts (Śīlācārya) should ask the aforementioned questions.
Having asked this, one should further ask:
"Have you studied the precepts? Are you pure?"
If she replies, "I have trained in the precepts and am pure," one should ask the other bhikṣuṇīs:
"Have you already studied the precepts? Are you pure? If he answers:
Having declared, "I have studied the precepts and am pure," one should immediately make the formal motion (jñapti):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

This person, [Name], seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun [Name]; this person, [Name], now requests the Sangha to grant her the full ordination, with [Name] as the preceptor nun.
So-and-so has declared herself pure, free from obstacles, of full age, complete with robes and bowl, and has already trained in the purity of the precepts.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent; the Saṃgha now confers the Higher Ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as her Preceptor Nun (upādhyāyinī).
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun so-and-so. This person, so-and-so, now requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with the preceptor nun so-and-so."
So-and-so has declared herself pure, free from obstacles, of full age, complete with robes and bowl, and having trained in the purity of the precepts.
The Sangha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with the Bhikṣuṇī So-and-so as her preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as the preceptor nun should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already consented to confer the full ordination upon so-and-so, with so-and-so as the preceptor nun; because the Saṃgha consents and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
“Listen attentively, virtuous woman!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the eight pārājika rules; if a bhikṣuṇī violates them, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
One must not engage in impure conduct or the practice of sexual desire.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in impure conduct or the practice of sexual desire, even with an animal, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
"You must not violate this for as long as you live; can you maintain it? He replied, "I can."
"One must not steal, even so much as a blade of grass.

If a bhikṣuṇī takes five coins or more than five coins from another person—whether she takes it herself or instructs another to take it, whether she cuts it herself or instructs another to cut it, whether she breaks it herself or instructs another to break it, or whether she burns it, buries it, or alters its color—she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan."
"Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit any transgression;
can you maintain this? He replied, "I can."
"One must not take the life of any living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes the life of a human being, provides a weapon to another, instructs, praises, or encourages death, gives another non-medicinal substances, causes an abortion through incantations or sorcery, or performs such acts herself or instructs others to do so, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan."
"Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit any transgression;
can you uphold this? He replied, "I can."
"One must not utter false speech, even in jest.

If a bhikṣuṇī, being untrue and possessing nothing of the sort herself, claims for herself that she has attained the state of a superior person, or that she has attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, or right reception; or that she has attained the fruit of a srotāpanna up to the fruit of an arhat; or that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas have come to make offerings to her."
"She is not a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
Within this, you must not commit a transgression for as long as life lasts;
can you uphold this? She replied:
"Yes. "One must not touch a body, even down to that of an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, touches the body of a man with a defiled mind—between the armpits and above the knees—whether by rubbing or pressing, stroking upward or downward, pulling or pushing, lifting or lowering, grasping, or pressing firmly."
"She is not a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
Within this, you must not commit any violation for as long as life lasts;
can you uphold this? They replied:
"Yes. "One must not commit any of the eight offenses, even with an animal.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a defiled mind, accepts a man with a defiled mind, and they grasp hands, grasp clothing, go to a secluded place to stay, stand together in seclusion, speak in seclusion, walk together, touch bodies, or make an appointment [to meet]."
"If one commits any of these eight matters, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit them;
can you uphold them? She replied:
"Yes. "One should not conceal another's grave offenses, even down to a *dukkaṭa* (wrong speech).
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a *pārājika* offense, she must not fail to report it herself, nor inform the Saṃgha, nor tell others so that they may know."
At a later time, if this bhikṣuṇī should leave the religious life, or be expelled, or be barred from participating in the communal affairs of the Saṃgha, or enter a non-Buddhist sect, she might say:
"I already knew that this person had committed such and such an offense."
"She is not a bhikṣuṇī, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan, because she conceals another's grave offense.
For as long as life lasts, you must not commit this; can you uphold it?"
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"You must not follow the words of the bhikṣu who has been suspended, nor even those of a śrāmaṇera."

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions, for having violated the rules of decorum and not yet having confessed so as to be excluded from communal residence, nevertheless follows and accords with the words of that bhikṣu.
The bhikṣuṇīs should admonish that bhikṣuṇī, saying:

"Sister! That bhikṣu has been formally accused by the Saṃgha in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions; he has committed an offense regarding deportment and has not yet repented, nor has he performed the act of living together [with the community]. Do not follow the words of that bhikṣu."
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonish this bhikṣuṇī and she persists in her refusal to relinquish [the matter], the bhikṣuṇīs should admonish her up to three times so that she may relinquish this matter.

If she relinquishes [the offense] after up to three admonitions, it is well; if she does not relinquish it, she is no longer a bhikṣuṇī and no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan, having committed the offense of *anuvartana* (following the formal charge).
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such a transgression; can you uphold this?
He replied, "I can.
"Listen attentively, virtuous woman!

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; by relying upon these, a bhikṣuṇī leaves the household life and receives the full ordination. This is the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī. Can you uphold them for as long as you live?
He replied, "I can. [The Buddha said:
"To go forth and receive the full precepts (mahā-śīla) by means of rag-robes (pāṃsukūla) is the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī."
"In this regard, can you maintain [these precepts] for as long as your life lasts? He replied, "I can."
"If one obtains long-term benefits, such as robes offered by donors or cut-and-sewn robes, these should be accepted.
To live by means of alms-gathering and to receive full ordination is the law for bhikṣuṇīs."
"Can you maintain this for as long as your life lasts? He replied, "I can."

"If one obtains long-term benefits—whether it be food assigned by the Sangha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the community of monks, or food offered at a donor's invitation—one should accept it."
"Sitting under a tree for one's seat and receiving the full ordination as a renunciant—this is the dharma of a bhikṣuṇī.
Are you able to uphold this for as long as life lasts? She replied:
"Yes. "If you receive long-term benefits, such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed house, a small room, a stone cell, or two rooms with a single door, you should accept them."
"Taking ordination and receiving the full precepts by relying on the 'rotten medicine' is the rule for bhikṣuṇīs.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts? She replied:
“Yes. “If you obtain long-term benefits—clarified butter, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock honey—you should accept them.

“You have now completed the reception of the precepts; the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished according to the Dharma, the place of ordination is valid, the *upādhyāya* is according to the Dharma, the *ācārya* is according to the Dharma, and both divisions of the Saṃgha are complete.”
You should properly receive the teachings and exhort others to cultivate merit by repairing stupas and making offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

You must not disobey any lawful instructions given by your preceptors (upādhyāya) or teachers (ācārya). You should study, recite the sutras, and diligently seek skillful means so that within the Buddha-dharma you may attain the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), and the fruit of arhatship (arhat).
"Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your merit shall not be in vain and its fruition shall never cease.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should ask your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
Then, he had the person receiving the precepts go forward.
At that time, those who had received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* censured the Śākya and Kauṣṭhila bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"The World-Honored One has spoken thus:
'One should receive full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.'"
"We have received the precepts, but you have not.
When the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī heard this, doubt arose in her mind. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī and the Śākya bhikṣuṇīs have also received the precepts."
At that time, there was one who stood while requesting the precepts. A layperson saw him and immediately said, "This man standing here wishes to seek out a male.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not stand when requesting the precepts; one should kneel on the long seat to request the precepts.

At that time, there was one who squatted while requesting the precepts, which caused the ground to collapse and his private parts to be exposed; feeling ashamed, he was unable to request the precepts.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"Other bhikṣuṇīs should act as proxies to make the formal announcement.
At that time, some Śākya and Kaurika bhikṣuṇīs who were about to receive the full ordination went to a saṃghārāma; on the road, they encountered bandits who violated them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to send a messenger to receive the precepts.
I allow one bhikṣuṇī who is pure and free from obstacles to be appointed as a messenger by the Saṃgha through a formal motion and a second proclamation (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a messenger to request the full ordination on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so from the Bhikṣu Saṃgha."
[The motion] is thus announced.
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
The Sangha now appoints the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a messenger to request the full ordination from the bhikṣu-saṃgha on behalf of the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so."
"Whichever sisters approve of the Sangha appointing the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a messenger to request the full ordination for the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so from the community of bhikṣus, remain silent;
whoever does not approve, speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to appoint the bhikṣuṇī so-and-so as a messenger; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. This matter is thus upheld.
If she travels alone, she lacks protection; therefore, two or three bhikṣuṇīs should be appointed to go together.
The bhikṣuṇī acting as messenger should go before the saṃgha of bhikṣus, prostrate at the feet of the saṃgha, place her right knee on the ground, join her palms, and make this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!..."
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from so-and-so; this so-and-so now requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with so-and-so as her preceptor (upādhyāyī).
"May the Saṃgha rescue me out of compassion.
Thus he should speak a second and a third time.
The Bhikṣu-saṃgha should then ask:
"What is her name? Who is her preceptress (upādhyāyī)?
Has she already completed her training in the precepts?"
"Are you pure? If they answer, "I have trained in the precepts; I am pure."
Furthermore, one should ask the companion bhikṣuṇī:
"Has she already completed her training in the purity of the precepts? If she answers:

Regarding the phrase "The training precepts have been learned and purified," one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed from among the assembly as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, has requested the full ordination from her preceptor bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so; this so-and-so now requests the Sangha for the full ordination, with so-and-so as her preceptor bhikṣuṇī.
So-and-so has already trained in the precepts and is pure; her age is complete, and she is fully equipped with robes and bowl.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen: the Saṃgha shall confer the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as the *upādhyāyī* (preceptor).
[The motion] is thus stated. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This [person], so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptor nun, so-and-so. This so-and-so now requests the Saṃgha for the full ordination, with so-and-so as the preceptor nun."
So-and-so has already trained in the precepts and is pure; her age is complete, and she is fully equipped with robes and bowl.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as the preceptress-ni (upādhyāyī).
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to the Sangha conferring the full ordination upon [Name] with [Name] as the preceptress-ni, please remain silent; those who do not consent, please speak.
This is the first *karmavācanā*."
The second and third times were also spoken in this manner:
"The Saṃgha has already granted full ordination to so-and-so with so-and-so as the preceptress-ni; the Saṃgha consents, for it remains silent; thus this matter is so upheld."
That messenger should return to the bhikṣuṇī monastery and say:
"Sisters! You have already completed the reception of the full ordination."
The World-Honored One gave such an instruction, permitting the dispatch of a messenger to receive the precepts.
Thereupon, people dispatched messengers to receive the precepts based on merely superficial appearances.
The Buddha said:
"One should not dismiss a person from receiving the precepts merely on account of their physical appearance.
He conferred the full ordination upon one who constantly bled; the blood defiled his body and his bedding. The Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full ordination upon one who bleeds."
The Blessed One has given such an instruction: one should not confer the full ordination upon one from whom blood flows.
Yet they conferred the full ordination upon one whose menses do not flow; she was exceedingly negligent in her conduct.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full ordination upon one who does not menstruate.
They then conferred the full ordination upon one who has no milk; the Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full ordination upon one who has no milk.
He conferred the full ordination upon one who had only one breast; the Buddha said, "One should not confer the full ordination upon one who has only one breast."
He conferred the full ordination upon one whose two sexual organs were festering;
the Buddha said, "One should not confer the full ordination upon one whose two sexual organs are festering.
He conferred the full ordination upon one whose two sexual organs were putrid and foul-smelling; the Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full precepts upon one who has two sexual organs and whose body is festering and foul-smelling.
He nevertheless conferred the full precepts upon such a person with two sexual organs. The Buddha said:
"One should not confer the full precepts upon one who possesses two sexual organs."
At that time, while the bhikṣus were gathered in one place reciting the Dharma and the Vinaya together, the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"Should we also recite the Dharma and the Vinaya?"
The Buddha said,
"You should recite it. [The monks] did not know from whom they had received the instruction for the recitation.
The Buddha said:
"One should receive and recite [the precepts] among the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"May we be permitted to recite verses together with the bhikṣuṇīs?
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to recite."
When he was taught while standing in front, he felt ashamed. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to sit behind a bhikṣu and recite; furthermore, I allow you to use any one of the ten kinds of robes as a screen."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, out of anger and displeasure over a minor cause, abandoned the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, saying:
"It is not only among the Śākya-sons that one may practice the holy life; there are other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as well, and I may now practice the holy life under them."
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, renounces the precepts, her renunciation is not valid.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs practiced sorcery and taught others to do so; the Buddha said:

"It should not be so. The group of six bhikṣus performed a formal act (karmavācanā) against the group of six bhikṣuṇīs; those bhikṣuṇīs, complying with their instructions, did not dare to disobey them. They requested the lifting of the formal act, but the bhikṣus refused to lift it.
When the lay devotees saw this, they said:
"Because he did not get his own way, he spoke such words.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not perform a formal ritual (karmavācanā) for a bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs performed the ritual for one another;
the Buddha said, "I allow bhikṣuṇīs to perform a formal ritual for bhikṣuṇīs."
"If you do not know [the procedure], you should listen to a bhikṣu recite the *karmavācanā* and only then perform the *karman*.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to leave the religious life; Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī knew of this, but being uncertain, she did not dare to admonish him or preach the Dharma to him, for the World-Honored One had given such an instruction: "A bhikṣuṇī must not admonish a bhikṣu."
Then the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated herself at his feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Is it the case that no bhikṣuṇī whatsoever may ever reprove a bhikṣu?"
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī is not entirely forbidden from admonishing a bhikṣu;

however, a bhikṣuṇī must not revile a bhikṣu, nor may she reprove him. She must not slander him for having broken his views, broken his precepts, or broken his deportment. She should not admonish him in such a manner."

"Gotamī! If one instructs them to uphold the higher training in morality, the higher training in mind, the higher training in wisdom, or to study and recite the scriptures—such matters should be censured."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs had long hair. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to shave it.

When they were shaving it themselves, there was a young barber who, while shaving the hair of a young bhikṣuṇī, felt her smoothness and lustful thoughts arose; he intended to violate the bhikṣuṇī, whereupon the bhikṣuṇī cried out in a loud voice:
“Do not! Do not! Hearing this, the other bhikṣuṇīs asked:
"Why do you cry out so loudly, 'Mā hā! Mā hā!'?"
He then recounted the matter in full.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When shaving one's hair, it is permitted to have a companion."
"If there are those who possess lustful intentions, they should not be allowed to shave [the hair].
When that male messenger removed the nasal hairs, the Buddha said:
"One should not have a man remove the nasal hairs."
She had a man clip her nails, and the Buddha said:
"One should not have a man clip one's nails.
At that time, while a bhikṣuṇī was inside the house of a layperson, a bhikṣu came there to beg for alms; the bhikṣuṇī did not dare to speak.
Why is this? [It was because] he feared that the bhikṣus might think, "This is food provided through the instruction of a bhikṣuṇī.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen to what the host says and let him know, but do not offer praise.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī inside a layperson's house who did not rise when a bhikṣu arrived.
She informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"She should rise.

If a bhikṣuṇī is eating in one sitting, or if she has not eaten after performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakti* (the ritual of leftover food), or if she is ill, or if she has already finished her meal, she is permitted to speak as follows:"
"Venerable Sir!
It is for such reasons that I do not rise.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who sat down in a layperson's house without having asked the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When bhikṣuṇīs are in the homes of laypeople, they should not sit down without first asking the bhikṣus.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls, went to the home of a layperson. Inside the house was a bhikṣuṇī whom they regularly instructed; seeing the bhikṣus arrive, she rose and asked them:
"Venerable sir! Am I sitting? The bhikṣu said:
"Do not sit. That bhikṣuṇī, being accustomed to comfort and unable to endure standing for long, immediately fell to the ground and became ill.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should look toward those ahead; if it is appropriate to sit, one may sit.

At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were traveling on a road together with bhikṣus. Some walked in front, some walked side-by-side conversing, some walked in front or behind, some tucked up their robes, some wrapped them around their necks, some covered their heads, some wore their robes over both shoulders, and some wore leather sandals.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so. You should bared your right shoulder, remove your leather sandals, and stand behind the bhikṣu."
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs had business concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṃgha, or matters required by a sick bhikṣuṇī, yet they did not dare to go ahead [of the monks]. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to depart after having informed a bhikṣu."
If he encounters a threat to his life or a threat to his holy life, and out of fear and caution does not dare to ask before departing, the Buddha said:
"In the event of such difficulties, whether he asks or does not ask, I permit him to depart."
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī walking on a road who saw a bhikṣu and did not yield the way. The Buddha said:
"One should yield the way.
At another time, there was a bhikṣuṇī walking on a road who saw a bhikṣu yielding the way; it began to rain, she fell to the ground with her feet, and became ill.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because of such causes and conditions, a bhikṣuṇī should slightly bend her body, join her palms, and say:
'Venerable Sir!'"
"Forgive me for saying that the path is narrow.
At that time, there was a donor who invited the two assemblies of monks; he first gave food to the bhikṣuṇīs and afterwards gave food to the bhikṣus.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not first give food to the community of bhikṣuṇīs;
one should first give to the community of bhikṣus, and only then to the community of bhikṣuṇīs."
At that time, there was a donor who invited the two assemblies of monks. He thought to himself:
"The Buddha has given instruction that one should first provide food to the assembly of bhikṣus, and only thereafter provide food to the assembly of bhikṣuṇīs."
He then first gave food to the community of bhikṣus, and by the time he finished, the mealtime had already passed.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the time is about to pass, you should give [the food] all at once."

At that time, there was a householder who invited the community of bhikṣuṇīs for a meal on the following day. Having prepared various kinds of rich and delicious foods at midnight, he went to them at dawn and announced that the time had come.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs dressed in their robes and took up their bowls in the early morning to go to her house; while they were inquiring about each other's seniority and age, the time for their meal passed by.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If the time has passed, it is permitted for eight senior bhikṣuṇīs to sit in order, while the others sit according to their rank."
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs came to the bhikṣu saṃghārāma. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to provide them with beds and seats.
When a bhikṣuṇī’s menstrual flow occurred, she soiled the storage rope-beds, wooden beds, and bedding before departing.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not sit upon a storage-rope bed or a wooden bed.
[When] she had no place to sit while seeking instruction in that monastery, or when receiving an invitation, or while listening to the Dharma, the Buddha said:
“Listen: [he] may sit upon a stone, or sit upon a brick, or sit upon the head of a stump, or sit upon grass or tree leaves, or sit upon a beam.”
The bhikṣuṇī could not endure the hardship and subsequently fell ill.
The Buddha said: "One should say to the bhikṣuṇī:
'If you can take care of the sitting mat, then I shall give it to you.'"
*The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Fascicle 48 [and] Fascicle 49,
Part 3, Section 13. Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others.

This is the latter part of the Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Vārāṇasī; at that time, grain was expensive and the people were famished, making it difficult to obtain food through begging.
After the bhikṣuṇīs had finished eating, there was some food remaining; the bhikṣuṇīs thought to themselves:
"May we give this food to the bhikṣus?"
The Buddha said,
"You may give it.
He then thought again:
"May one give food to a bhikṣu?
The Buddha said,
"One may give it."
“Is it pure for us to give leftover food to a bhikṣu?
The Buddha said,
“It is pure.”
At that time, after the bhikṣus had received their food, there was some left over, and they thought:
"May we give this food to the bhikṣuṇīs?
The Buddha said:
"It may be given.
[The questioner asked: "May one give food on behalf of a bhikṣuṇī?
The Buddha said:
"I may give it. At that time, there was leftover food, and he thought to himself:
"Is it pure for a bhikṣuṇī to receive?"
The Buddha said, “It is pure.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs were dwelling in an araṇya. Later, on another occasion, when an incident arose in that araṇya, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
“A bhikṣuṇī should not dwell in an araṇya.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī dwelling in the house of a layperson who saw the husband together with his wife kissing, caressing their bodies, and grasping and pressing her breasts. Upon seeing this, the young bhikṣuṇī conceived a sense of revulsion toward the Buddha-dharma.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a separate dwelling place for the bhikṣuṇīs.
Those bhikṣuṇīs then engaged in manual labor within that separate dwelling and taught others how to do so. The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not perform arts within her residence.
A bhikṣuṇī sold liquor at a separate residence; the Buddha said:
"She should not sell liquor at a separate residence."
That bhikṣuṇī settled a courtesan in her residence; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
She provided her with perfumes, flowers, and articles for adorning the body; the Buddha said:

"It should not be so. At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs stood near heaps of refuse in alleys, at crossroads, and in marketplaces. When the laypeople saw them, they all criticized, disparaged, and reviled them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame and no pure conduct; yet outwardly they claim for themselves:..."
"I know the True Dharma"— how can there be such a True Dharma?
To stand and dwell in such a place is like being a courtesan.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Bhikṣuṇīs should not stand or stay in such a place.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs used ivory and bone to rub their bodies to create a glossy luster. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
The group of six bhikṣuṇīs polished their bodies with fine medicinal powders to give them a luster. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He curled the hairs on his body; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He then clipped the hairs on his body; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
That bhikṣuṇī wrapped her waist with the robe, wishing to make it appear slender and attractive; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
That bhikṣuṇī wore women’s clothing; the Buddha said, “She should not wear it.
That bhikṣuṇī wore men’s clothing; the Buddha said:
"One should not wear them; it is permitted for bhikṣuṇīs to wear bhikṣuṇī robes.
A bhikṣuṇī wrapped her body with many robes, wishing to make it appear broad and beautiful. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He did not like wearing his robes properly, desiring instead to make his body visible; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He made bird-patterned tassels on the ends of his waistband; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He then made a mandala-style waistband; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He kept a *vīra* waistband; the Buddha said, "One should not keep it.
He kept a *sā* waistband; the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such items].
She then tied a loose thread-belt around her waist. The Buddha said:
