"I allow bhikṣuṇīs to weave and make a belt that encircles the waist once; if it is woven in a circular pattern, I allow it to encircle it twice."
When the bhikṣuṇīs went to the women’s bathing place to bathe, there were some female thieves and courtesans who said to the bhikṣuṇīs:
“You are all young; you have only just begun to grow hair under your arms. How can you already practice the holy life?”

"You should now enjoy sensual pleasures while you have the opportunity; what use is it to regret it later? When you are old, you may practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*); in this way, you will have nothing lost from beginning to end.
When the young bhikṣuṇī heard this, a sense of weary detachment arose within her, and she no longer took pleasure in the Buddha-dharma.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not bathe at a bathing place for women.
Those bhikṣuṇīs bathed beside laymen; when the householders saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī is devoid of shame and remorse and does not cultivate the holy life;
yet she claims, 'I know the True Dharma.
How can she bathe beside a layman?"
"It is no different from a female thief or a prostitute; how can there be the True Dharma in such a case?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not bathe in the presence of a layman."
At that time, there was a woman whose husband had gone away on a journey and was absent. She became pregnant by another man;
having induced an abortion herself, she went and said to the nun who regularly instructed her:
"My husband has gone away on a journey and is not present; I have become pregnant by another man."
"I have already fallen; you may cast it away for me. He replied, "So be it."
That bhikṣuṇī then placed one bowl inside and covered it with another, put them into a carrying net, and set out on the road.
At that time, the elder of Śrāvastī had made this constant vow:
"I shall never eat unless I first give food to those who have left the household life; I must first give, and only then eat."
That householder had some business early in the morning and wished to go elsewhere; he immediately sent a man, saying:
"Go along the roads and streets, and when you see a renunciant coming out, bring him here."
Then, having received these instructions, the messenger immediately went outside to search for her;
seeing the bhikṣuṇī, he said to her, "Auntie, come; I have food for you."
The bhikṣuṇī said: “Stop! Stop!”
"That would already be an offering to me.
He replied, "Not so;
simply come, and I shall give you food."
The bhikṣuṇī said: "Stop! Stop!"
"There is no need.
That messenger then forcibly led the bhikṣuṇī into the house.
A servant inside the house said:
"Pass the bowl here and give me some food.
That bhikṣuṇī said: "Stop, stop!
"Thus you shall have made an offering.
He spoke again:
"Bring forth your bowl; I shall give you food."
He replied again, "There is no need.
He then forcibly seized the bowl and saw that inside it was a recently aborted fetus. Upon seeing this, the elder spoke with reproach:
“Bhikṣuṇīs who lack a sense of shame and modesty and do not cultivate the holy life yet claim to themselves,
‘I know the True Dharma’—
how can there be any True Dharma in such as these?”
"Having caused an abortion, she has cast it away; she is no different from a female thief or a prostitute.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"When there is a death in a layperson's household, a bhikṣuṇī should not dispose of the body for them."
"If a bhikṣuṇī is within a village and sees a bhikṣu seeking alms, she should come out with her bowl and show it to him.
At that time, there was a layperson who was ill and came to the bhikṣuṇīs' residence requiring care. [The bhikṣuṇīs] informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I allow you to employ skillful means to send someone; if he is one who has faith and joy, and praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, then according to what the bhikṣuṇīs are able to do, have him provide care."
After she later passed away, the bhikṣuṇīs were apprehensive and did not dare to discard her body. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to discard it for the sake of purifying the dwelling place."

At that time, King Prasenajit’s border regions were in rebellion and the people were scattered; meanwhile, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs were wandering through the countryside in a place of uncertainty and fear.
When the bandits saw her, they said to one another:
"This bhikṣuṇī is held in high esteem and affection by King Prasenajit; we should surely take her as our wife and toy with her."
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in derision:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; yet outwardly they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what true Dharma is there?
How can you wander among humans in a place of doubt and terror, no different from a female thief or a prostitute?"
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs should not wander among people in border regions where there is suspicion or fear.
At that time, there were bhikṣuṇīs residing in forest hermitages (āraṇyaka-vihāra) and bhikṣus residing in villages, and they wished to exchange goods with one another.
She informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow you to exchange [them].
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had a dwelling in an araṇya, while a layperson had a dwelling within a village; they wished to trade with one another.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "I allow lay attendants (*karmadāna*) to engage in trade.
At that time, two householders disputed over a dwelling place; one of them offered it as a gift to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, and the bhikṣuṇīs accepted it immediately.
A certain householder immediately spoke with derision, saying:
"This bhikṣuṇī has no sense of shame or modesty; she accepts much and is never satisfied.
Yet outwardly she claims for herself:"
"I know the True Dharma. How can there be True Dharma now?
He accepts a dwelling place while others are disputing over it; though the donor has no weariness, the recipient ought to know contentment.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not accept a dwelling that is subject to communal dispute.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī wished to observe the summer retreat within a bhikṣuṇī dwelling in the royal park, but she was apprehensive and did not dare to do so. She recalled the World-Honored One’s instruction that bhikṣuṇīs should not reside in *araṇya* (forest) dwellings; however, the bhikṣuṇī dwelling in the royal park was secure and well-established.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"With the exception of the bhikṣuṇī dwelling places within the royal gardens, one should not reside in other āraṇya locations.
At that time, there were bhikṣuṇīs who did not go to the place where instruction was given.
She informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should go.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had business concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, as well as needs for a sick bhikṣuṇī; she informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen, give your consent for me to depart.

At that time, Kāḷudāyin reviled and beat the bhikṣuṇīs; he spat on them, threw flowers at them, or splashed water upon them; he spoke coarse words, deceitful words, and used persuasion and abuse, saying:
"May your path be destroyed, may you rot, may you be burned, and may you have intercourse with donkeys!"
"Striking" refers to using the hand, a staff, or a stone.
"Harsh speech" refers to speaking of the two sexual organs as being either good or bad.

"Deceptive speech" refers to saying: "If a man has bathed until clean, anointed his body with fine perfumes, combed and groomed his beard and hair, adorned himself with beautiful flower garlands and necklaces, and holds a peacock-feather parasol—could there be anything more excellent than this?"
If it is a woman, it is also like this.
The one who exhorts her says: "Sister!..."

"You are still young, with hair only just beginning to grow beneath your arms; why must you thus destroy yourself by practicing the holy life? It would be better to enjoy the five desires while you have the time, and wait until old age before practicing the holy life."
At that time, the young bhikṣuṇī conceived a sense of weary detachment and took no pleasure in the Buddha-dharma.

When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, those who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured Kālodāyin, saying:
"How can you revile and strike a bhikṣuṇī, even going so far as to use deceptive speech to entice her?"
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha then assembled the community of bhikṣus and, employing countless skillful means, rebuked Kālodāyin:
"How could you revile and strike a bhikṣuṇī, even going so far as to use deceptive words to persuade her?"
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I authorize the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to perform a formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* against Kālodāyin, declaring that he is not to be saluted."
It should be performed in this manner.
From within the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This Kāḷudāyin has reviled and beaten bhikṣuṇīs, even resorting to deceitful speech and persuasion.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of its forbearance, grant the *akalana-karman* (the act of non-prostration) against Kāḷudāyin.
The motion is thus stated:
"Venerable Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This Kāḷudāyin has reviled and beaten bhikṣuṇīs, even resorting to deceitful speech and persuasion."
The Sangha now performs the *akṛta-vandana-karman* (the formal act of not requiring salutation) against him.
Any of you, Venerable Sisters, who consent to the Sangha performing the *akṛta-vandana-karman* against Kālodāyin, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to perform the *akaraṇīya-karman* (act of non-prostration) against Kālodāyin; the Sangha consents, as it remains silent. Thus this matter is upheld."

At that time, Kāḷudāyin, complying with the community of bhikṣuṇīs and not daring to oppose them, requested from the community of bhikṣuṇīs the formal act (*karmavācanā*) of being exempted from performing prostrations.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu complies with the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs and does not dare to oppose them, and requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the lifting of the *akaraṇīya-ānāmantiya-karman* (the formal act of not being required to pay respects), the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs should lift it for him by means of a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*."
It should be understood in this way.
From among the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the venerable Saṃgha listen!..."

This Kāḷudāyin has had the *akaraṇīya-karman* (the formal act of not being required to pay respects) performed against him by the community of bhikṣuṇīs; he has complied with the community of bhikṣuṇīs and did not dare to oppose them.
Now he requests the community of bhikṣuṇīs to revoke this *akaraṇīya-karman*.
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now revoke the *karman* of not performing prostrations.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Listen, sisters of the Saṃgha!"

This Kāḷudāyin has had the *akaraṇīya-karman* (act of non-salutation) performed against him by the community of bhikṣuṇīs; he has complied with the community of bhikṣuṇīs and does not dare to oppose them, and he now requests from the community of bhikṣuṇīs the lifting of the *akaraṇīya-karman*.
The Sangha now lifts the *akaraṇīya-karman* (the formal act of not requiring salutation) against Kālodāyin.
Which of you, sisters, approves of the Sangha lifting the *akaraṇīya-karman* against Kālodāyin? Those who approve remain silent; those who do not approve speak.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to revoke the *akaraṇīya-karman* (the formal act of not being saluted) against Kālodāyin; since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs and lived together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs; they teased one another, or sang hymns together, or wailed together, or laughed and joked together, thereby disturbing the bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing meditation.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to prohibit him.
Thereupon they prohibited him entirely, not even allowing him entry into the nuns' quarters. The Buddha said:
"One should not prohibit everything; one should prohibit according to the degree of disturbance.
If it is a place where everyone lives in total disorder, then everything should be prohibited.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs came to the dwelling place of the bhikṣu-saṃgha and, together with the group of six bhikṣus, teased one another, or sang hymns together, or wailed together, or laughed and joked together. They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen and prohibit them.
Thereupon, he prohibited everything. The Buddha said:
"One should not prohibit everything; one should prohibit [only] according to the place of disorder and noise."
"If they reside together in total disorder, they must all be prohibited.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras came to the residence of the bhikṣuṇīs and lived together with the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās, teasing one another, or chanting together, or wailing together, or laughing and playing together, thereby disturbing the bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing dhyāna.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to summon him and inflict punishment.
If he does not reform, you should perform the *akaraṇīya-karman* (act of non-prostration) against his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and teacher (*ācārya*)."

At that time, the group of six bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās came to the monastery and stayed together with the group of six bhikṣus and śrāmaṇeras; they teased one another, or sang hymns together, or wailed together, or laughed and joked together, thereby disturbing the bhikṣus who were engaged in meditation.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"She should be summoned and punished.
If she does not reform, a formal act of relinquishing instruction (śikṣā-deśanā-karman) should be performed against her preceptors and teachers."

At that time, not far from the dwelling place of the bhikṣuṇīs, there was a channel carrying flowing water. A bhikṣuṇī, because her path was situated below, received the flow and experienced pleasure; she felt doubt. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"She does not commit a pārājika offense, but she commits a sthūlātyaya offense."
"A bhikṣuṇī should not position her private parts against the flow of water.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Nandā went to a walking path beneath a flowering tree, where a thief took her away to sexually assault her. She had doubts regarding this matter and reported the circumstances to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked,
"Nanda! Do you perceive pleasure?"
He replied, "It was as if red-hot iron had entered my body.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense;
however, a bhikṣuṇī should not go alone to such a place for walking meditation.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was walking in meditation at an araṇya. This bhikṣuṇī was of upright and beautiful countenance, and a young brahmin, seeing her, became infatuated with her. He immediately seized her, intending to violate her.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Release me;
I shall go to such-and-such a place.

He released her immediately. Upon arriving at that location, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā smeared her body with excrement. The brāhmaṇa became enraged and struck her on the head with a stone, causing both eyes to fall out.

Utpalavarṇā did not remember this, but when she later realized it through her supernormal powers, she immediately flew by means of those powers to where the Buddha was. Having prostrated with her head at his feet, she stood to one side.
The Buddha said, "This bhikṣuṇī has faith and joy; her eyes shall be restored."
Immediately, as she had spoken, it returned to its original state.
That bhikṣuṇī felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
"A bhikṣuṇī should not go to an araṇya (forest hermitage).

At that time, a bhikṣuṇī who had violated the precepts became pregnant; while on a hanging latrine, she defecated and urinated and caused an abortion, which fell into the latrine. When a scavenger saw it, he reviled and cursed her, saying:
"Bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame or remorse and do not cultivate pure conduct, yet they claim for themselves externally:"
"I know the True Dharma"—
how can there be such a thing as the True Dharma?
How is it that you cause an abortion and cast it into a latrine, no different from a female thief or a prostitute?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not defecate or urinate on a suspended latrine.
Those bhikṣuṇīs were doubtful and did not dare to defecate or urinate on a water latrine; the Buddha said:

"Listen. At that time, a bhikṣuṇī sat with her legs crossed in the paryaṅka posture when blood and impurities issued forth, staining the spaces between her heels and toes. While she was walking for alms, insects and grass clung to her feet; when the laypeople saw this, they all mocked her.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
She was hesitant and did not dare to sit in the half-lotus posture, so the Buddha said:
"Listen; sit on half [the seat].
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Śrāvastī.
There were six groups of bhikṣuṇīs who, while inside the homes of laypeople, looked through holes in the walls.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke together in derision, saying:
"The bhikṣuṇīs have no sense of shame; though they claim for themselves, 'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what is there of the True Dharma?
How can one peer through a hole in another's house like a female thief or a prostitute? It is no different.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not look through a hole in the wall at the house of a layperson.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Rājagṛha.
Then Ānanda, together with a great saṃgha of five hundred bhikṣus, was wandering among the people of Magadha.
At that time, Ānanda had sixty disciples, all of whom were young and wished to return their precepts.
When Ānanda arrived at Rājagṛha, Mahākāśyapa saw him coming from afar and said to him:
"This assembly is about to lose [its members]; you, being young, do not know contentment."
Ānanda said, "Venerable Sir!
My hair has already turned white; how can it be that I am still not exempt from being called 'young' in the presence of Kāśyapa?"

Kāśyapa replied, "You are with young bhikṣus who do not properly guard their sense faculties, who do not know moderation in eating, and who cannot apply themselves diligently during the first and last watches of the night; you go from house to house merely to break the grain. Your assembly shall suffer loss, for these young bhikṣus of yours lack contentment."
When the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā heard those words, she became angry and displeased, saying:
"Mahākāśyapa is merely a heretic; why does he repeatedly insult Ānanda by calling him a 'young man,' causing him such displeasure?"
Then Mahākāśyapa said to Ānanda: “Look at this bhikṣuṇī; out of anger she reviles me in such a manner. Ānanda!”
"Except for the World-Honored One,
I do not recall any other matter more venerable than the Buddha's Dharma. Ānanda said:
“Venerable sir! We repent;
women are ignorant.”
Kāśyapa spoke these words a second and a third time, and Ānanda likewise spoke thus a second and a third time:
“I repent! When the night had passed, Kāśyapa dressed in the morning, took up his bowl, and went to Rājagṛha to beg for food; at that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā saw him and spat upon him.

When the bhikṣuṇīs heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse;
they censured Sthūlanandā, saying: "How could you spit upon the Venerable Kāśyapa?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus for this matter and rebuked the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, saying:
"How could you have spat upon the Venerable Kāśyapa?"
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I allow you to summon her to come and undergo punishment.
If one bhikṣu summons one bhikṣuṇī, she should go."
If one does not go, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If a single bhikṣu summons two bhikṣuṇīs, three bhikṣuṇīs, or the Saṃgha, he must go;
if he does not go, he should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
When two bhikṣus summon one bhikṣuṇī, she should go;
if she does not go, she should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
When two bhikṣus summon two bhikṣuṇīs, or three bhikṣuṇīs, or the Saṃgha, she should go.
If one does not go, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
Three bhikṣus may summon one bhikṣuṇī; she should go;
if she does not go, she should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If three bhikṣus summon two bhikṣuṇīs, three bhikṣuṇīs, or the Saṃgha, they should go;
if they do not go, they should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If the Saṃgha summons one bhikṣuṇī, she should go.
If one does not go, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
When the Saṃgha summons two bhikṣuṇīs, three bhikṣuṇīs, or the entire Saṃgha, one must go;
if one does not go, one should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
When the group of six bhikṣus heard this, they spoke thus:
"If we wish to summon a bhikṣuṇī, we shall summon her; if we wish to do something, we shall do it."
Why is this? For the World-Honored One has spoken these words:
"If one bhikṣu calls for a bhikṣuṇī, she should go;..."
"If you do not go, you should be dealt with according to the Dharma.
This applies even to the Saṃgha.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should compare oneself with others; one must not go where one should not go.
This concludes the *Nikāya-saṃgraha* (Niganthipada). Chapter 18: The *Dharma-skandha*. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a visiting bhikṣu who, without asking the resident bhikṣus, entered an empty room; a snake fell upon him, whereupon he cried out in a loud voice:
"A snake! A snake!"
A monk standing nearby heard this and asked,
"Why are you making such a loud noise?
He then explained the circumstances to him.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. Having censured the visiting bhikṣu, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, stood to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the visiting bhikṣu:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper deportment, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not a practice in accordance with the teaching—it is something that should not have been done."
"How is it that he does not speak? The senior bhikṣu, knowing [the situation], entered an empty room where a snake had fallen upon him; he cried out loudly:
"Snake! Snake!"
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I authorize the establishment of rules for visiting bhikṣus."
That visiting bhikṣu should conform to the rules for visiting bhikṣus; he should conform in this manner.

If a visiting bhikṣu wishes to enter the monastery, he should recognize whether there is a Buddha-stūpa, a Śrāvaka-stūpa, or a senior elder (sthavira), and he should remove his leather sandals and hold them in his hand.
He did not shake out his leather sandals and then took hold of them with soiled hands.
The Buddha said, "One should not take hold of them without shaking them out; one should shake them out.
Once the World-Honored One had said they should be shaken out, he shook them against a tree. The tree deity felt resentment and reproached him. The Buddha said:

"One should not shake one's leather sandals against a tree; rather, one should shake them against a stone, or against a wooden stump, or against a fence, or by shaking the two sandals against each other."
"He should go to the gate and push it with his hand; if there is a bolt or lock, he should open it.
If he cannot open it, he should knock gently so that those inside hear him."

If they do not hear you, you should strike loudly; if they do not open, you should take your robes and bowl and hand them to a second bhikṣu to hold, then go to the base of the fence or wall, leap over it, and enter to open the door.
At that time, as he passed by the side of the stūpa walking to the left, the guardian deity of the stūpa became angry.
The Buddha said:
"One should not pass by walking to the left; one should pass by circumambulating the stūpa to the right."

"Having arrived inside the monastery, if there is a peg, a dragon-tooth peg, a clothes rack, or if by a canal, a tree, a stone, or a patch of grass, he should place his robe and bowl upon it; then, going to the place for washing feet, he washes his feet."
If there is no water, one asks, "Where is there water?
and then proceeds to fetch it from wherever they say there is water.
One should ask:
"Are there insects? Are there no insects? If he says:
"There are insects.
If it was a large beast that had touched the water and departed, he would then take water in his jar.
He did not wash his hands before grasping the jar to fetch water, and the other bhikṣus all detested this. The Buddha said:

"One should not grasp a water jar without having washed one's hands; it is permitted to embrace the belly of the jar with both arms, or to pass the cord through the handle using a corner of one's robe.

When he arrived at the place where there was water, he should have washed his hands thoroughly and filled the vessel with water to wash his feet. However, as soon as he grasped the water with his feet still unwashed, the other bhikṣus looked upon this with distaste.
The Buddha said, "You should not do it that way; you should hold water with one hand and wash your feet with the other.
He first washed his right foot and then his left foot, whereupon the Buddha said:
"One should first wash the left foot and afterwards wash the right foot.
He then put on his soiled robe without wiping his leather sandals.
The Buddha said:
"One should not put them on without wiping them; one should wipe them and then put them on.
Because he did not drain the water from his feet before putting on his leather sandals, they became rotten and damaged. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should drain the water from one's feet and then put on the leather sandals."
He should be asked: "Do you have this many rooms for me for so many years?
If he replies:
"Yes. One should further ask:
"Is this room occupied by someone or unoccupied?"
If they say, "No person dwells," one should ask:
"Are there bedding and seats,
or not? If he says, "There are."
One should ask: "Is there a covering, or is there no covering? If he says:
"If there is," one should ask:
"Is there profit, or is there no profit?"
If he says, "There is a benefit," one should ask:
"Are there vessels or no vessels? If one says, "There are."
He asked again:
"Is there a robe for the dwelling, or no robe for the dwelling? If he says:
"There is. One should further ask:
"Is there abundance of merit, or is there lack of merit?"
If he says, "There is," and you wish to take it, you should say to him:
"I shall take it.
He should go to the room and push open the door; if it is locked, he should unlock it.

Having opened the door, he should grasp both sides of the door frame with his hands and put his head inside to inspect the interior of the room, ensuring there are no snakes or venomous insects; if there are any, he should drive them out.

Having entered the room, he should remove the beds, mattresses, bedding, pillows, floor coverings, woolen blankets, or [items placed] upon wooden planks or boards. As for the floor coverings, one should distinguish their inner and outer sides;
having thoroughly swept the room and removed the dirt and soil, one should first look for a place where they may be discarded and then discard them.
If one obtains needles, thread, knives, or even worn-out items down to a single pill of medicine, and places them in one spot, whoever owns them and recognizes them shall take them.
He should sweep and clear away [debris] such as stakes, antelope-horn pegs, clothes-racks, or broken walls; if there are mouse holes, he should plaster them with mud.

If the ground is uneven, one should level it, smear it with mud, and coat it to make it clean; then take the floor-covering, shake it out, dry it in the sun, and bring it into the room. If what was previously spread is of poor quality, one should spread something better;

if what was previously spread is good, one should spread it back as it was before. Take the bed-legs and related items, wipe and treat them cleanly, and bring them in; one should sweep the area around the bed, shake out the bedding, bring it in, and place it upon the legs. Take the bedding, pillows, mats, and blankets, shake them out cleanly, and spread them upon the corded bed.
He kept his usual robes and those he did not wear in the same place, and when taking the robes he usually wore, the other garments became disordered. The Buddha said:
"The robes you usually wear should be kept in a separate place."
He placed his alms-bag, leather sandal bag, needle-case, and oil-container all together in one spot. Other monks disapproved of this, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; they should each be kept in their own separate places."
"One should first enter the room and check whether the door-latch is high or low before closing it.
Upon leaving the room, one should look at the four walls to see if there is any dust."
If there is anything that should be swept or sprinkled away, one should take a stool and wash it clean; one should prepare a pure water jar, a washing jar, and a drinking vessel; and one should ask:
"Where is the place for the great evacuation?"
Where is the small place for walking? Where is the pure ground?
Where is the impure ground?
What is a stūpa of the Buddha?
What is a stūpa of a śrāvaka?
And what is the dwelling of the foremost elder?
"What are the second, third, and fourth senior monks' quarters?
He should first pay homage to the Buddha stūpa and then to the śrāvaka stūpas; the four senior monks should then pay homage in their respective order.
He grasped his feet and ankles to pay homage, [whereupon the Buddha said], "One should not grasp the ankles to pay homage.
He grasped his knees to pay homage, [whereupon the Buddha said], "One should not grasp the knees to pay homage.
He paid homage while wearing his robe tucked up, wrapped around his neck, covering his head, draped over both shoulders, or while wearing leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"None of this should be done.
From this day forward, one should bare the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, place the right knee on the ground, grasp both feet, and speak thus:
'Venerable Sir, I pay homage.'"
If the four senior elders are meditating within the hall, one should pay respects to the hall according to the order of seating.
They should then ask:
"Where is the place for the community's main meal, the place for the light meal, the place for the night assembly, and the place for the recitation of the precepts?"
What are the food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, and food on the first day of the month?
To what places does the meal invited by a donor proceed in succession?
He asked again:
"Tomorrow, which donor has invited the assembly of monks for the morning meal and the midday meal?
Which donor has had the saṃgha perform the 'turning over of the bowl' (pātrāvavartana) against them?"
Whose house is a household of practitioners?
Where are the dogs vicious?
Where are there good people?
"Where are the wicked people?
From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for visiting bhikṣus; visiting bhikṣus should comply with it.
If they do not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
"From this day forward, a rule shall be established for resident bhikṣus; resident bhikṣus should comply with it, and they should act in accordance with it as follows.

Upon hearing that visiting bhikṣus have arrived, resident bhikṣus should go outside to welcome them and take their robes and bowls. They should place them in the heated bathhouse, the multi-storied pavilion, or the walking path. They should provide seats for the visiting bhikṣus, as well as water and a vessel for washing the feet, a towel for drying the feet, and take up their leather sandals, placing them on the left side so that they are not stained by mud or water."
If it becomes soiled by mud or water, it should be moved to another location.
After the guest bhikṣu has washed his feet, he should return the foot-washing implements to their original place.
One should ask:
"Venerable sir, would you like some water? If he says:
“Drink. He should then hold the flask to fetch water.

If he does not wash his hands while holding the flask, other bhikṣus will find it offensive; therefore, he should embrace the flask with both arms, or hook the corner of his robe behind his ear, and only then go to the water’s edge to wash his hands thoroughly.
"If it is a pool or flowing water, one should clear away the surface with the hand and take the pure water from below.
When he was carrying water and the water became hot while walking in the midday sun, the Buddha said:
"One should cover it with grass or tree leaves to create a shade and carry it away."
He did not wash the vessel and passed it over with water still in it. The Buddha said:
"It should be washed thoroughly.
After he had drunk, he did not wash the vessel before passing it to others; other bhikṣus detested this, and the Buddha said:
"One should wash [the hands] and then give it.
When he was giving water, he spoke with his mouth open, causing saliva to fall into the water. The Buddha said:
"One should not speak while [giving water]."
"If you have something to say, you should turn your face toward them and speak.
When he lifted the vessel without washing it first, the other bhikṣus saw this and all loathed it. The Buddha said: "You should not do so."
"He should ask: 'Venerable Elder, how many years of seniority do you have? If he says:"
[If asked], "For how many years? one should say: "This is the room;

these are the rope-couch, the wooden bed, the mattress and pillow, the woolen blanket, and the floor-covering; this is the spittoon; this is the vessel for urination; this is the place for defecation; this is the place for urination; this is the clean area; this is the impure area; this is the stūpa of the Buddha; this is the stūpa of the śrāvakas; this is the room of the first senior elder; these are the rooms of the second, third, and fourth senior elders; this is the assembly hall for the main meal, the minor meal, the night gathering, and the *poṣadha*; this is the place where the Saṃgha is assigned meals, even down to such-and-such a location; and the donor so-and-so has invited the Saṃgha tomorrow for the minor and main meals."
The Saṃgha has performed the *pātra-āvartana* (turning-over of the bowl) karmavācanā against such-and-such a household.
The Saṃgha has performed the *śikṣādattaka* (disciplinary) karmavācanā against such-and-such a household.
At such-and-such a place, there are vicious dogs.
"Such-and-such a place is good; such-and-such a place is bad.
I now establish a rule for the senior bhikṣus: the senior bhikṣus should comply with it; if they do not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had formerly been a brahmin living in Śrāvastī; he was excessively filthy and loathed his own excrement and urine. Using sharp toilet grass, he injured his body, causing sores from which pus and blood flowed, defiling his person, his robes, his bedding, and his couch.
The bhikṣus asked,
"Venerable sir, what ailment do you have?
He then explained the circumstances in detail.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta-austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse. They reproached the brahmin renunciant bhikṣu, saying:

"How can you defile yourself so much with your own excrement, using sharp toilet grass to injure your body until pus and blood flow out, defiling your person, your robes, your bedding, and your couch?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus, saying:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified decorum, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not a pure practice, and not a compliant practice—it is something that should not have been done."

How is it that you, a renunciant bhikṣu who has left the household life as a brāhmaṇa, are so foul and impure that you discharge your own excrement with such force that it wounds your body, causing pus and blood to flow, thereby defiling your person, your robes, your bedding, and your couch?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for the latrines for the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should comply with this rule, and they should comply in this manner."
"One should not delay for long in suppressing the urge to defecate or urinate; when going to relieve oneself, one should take up toilet grass.

He went before the senior monk while seated below him, or spoke and walked alongside him, or went ahead or behind with his robe tucked over one shoulder, or wrapped it around his neck, or covered his head, or wore leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; however, if one goes ahead, it is permitted to go ahead."
“Upon reaching the exterior of the latrine, one should snap one’s fingers or cough to alert anyone or any non-human being.

Having entered the interior of the latrine, one should place one’s robes upon a peg, a dragon-tooth peg, a clothes rack, a cloth-shed, by the water’s edge, under a tree, on a stone, or among the grass. If one fears the rain will soak them, they should be placed in a place sheltered from the rain.”

If the wind blows or the rain soaks one's robes, it is permitted to wear them while holding them firmly with the hands so that they do not touch the latrine. One should place both feet firmly on either side. Before ascending the latrine, one must first look to see if there are snakes, scorpions, centipedes, or millipedes, and drive them out.
Before he had even finished squatting, his robes were lifted and his body was exposed. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
You should squat with both legs together and gradually lift your robes."

"Once you have squatted, you should look [at the toilet] so as not to let [the excrement] move forward or backward, nor to let it come near the two sides, thereby defiling the toilet hole with feces, urine, mucus, or spittle.
He made a loud noise while defecating; when the other bhikṣus heard it, they found it loathsome. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
While he was defecating, he involuntarily made a sound without realizing it and felt doubt. The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
While on the latrine, he chewed a tooth-stick, or slept, or entered meditative concentration. The Buddha said: [there is no offense].
"It should not be done thus.
Because he was doubtful, he did not dare to defecate or urinate in a latrine situated upon the water. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
He rose from the latrine without using toilet grass to wipe his body, thereby soiling his person, his robes, and his sitting mat. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use toilet grass before rising."
The Blessed One gave such an instruction, permitting the use of toilet grass, yet they used long pieces of toilet grass.
The Buddha said:
"One should not use long toilet grass; at most, it should be the length of one span."
He used a toilet brush made of various leaves, or tree bark, or a ball of grass and cow dung; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He used a short toilet brush and soiled his hands; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done; it must be exactly four finger-widths in length.
When he used the toilet grass without shaking it out and discarded the feces upon the grass, other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said: "It should not be done."
He placed the used and unused toilet grass together in one place; when he took some, his hands became soiled. The Buddha said, "It should be kept in a separate place.
Having finished using the toilet grass, he stood up and his body was exposed. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
One should rise slowly and gradually lower one's robes.
When he reaches the washing place, one should snap one's fingers so that whether he is a human or a non-human, he may take notice."
"When he arrives at the washing place, he should first look around; if there are snakes, centipedes, or venomous insects, he should drive them out.
He first lifted his robes and then squatted, exposing his body. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He washed [the bowl] in the water vessel; other bhikṣus disapproved of this, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
When he washed it with water, there was a sound; other bhikṣus heard it and disapproved, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When they used up all the water, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should leave enough for at least one person to wash."
After washing, he did not remove the water from his body, leaving it to soil his clothes and his person. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you must remove the water by wiping with your hand, a leaf, or a piece of cloth."
If the hands have an odor, they should be washed using salt earth, ash, mud, or cow dung; if they still smell, they should be scrubbed with a stone, a brick, or soap powder.
As he rose without lowering his lower garment, his body was exposed. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should rise while gradually lowering your garment.
He saw that the washing vessel was empty and had no water in it. The Buddha said:
"One who needs to see [the water] should pour it.

He stood before the latrine to receive the scriptures, recite them, practice walking meditation, and sew robes, thereby obstructing other bhikṣus from using the latrines for defecation or urination. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He recited the sūtras, received instruction, performed walking meditation, and made robes while at the side of the latrine; other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He saw excrement on the latrine but did not remove it. The Buddha said:
"One who sees it should remove it. I shall now teach the rules for defecating and urinating for the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should comply with them."
"If one does not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a certain bhikṣu who went on almsround; he was young and had much that he did not understand, so he entered a house without observing the signs of the door.

There was a woman sleeping in a house; she lay on her back naked, and impurity issued forth, defiling her female organ. When that bhikṣu saw this, he felt ashamed and afraid, and immediately hurried out from the house.
Just as the bhikṣu had gone out, her husband entered the house and saw his wife lying on her back, naked, with her body defiled by impurities. Having seen this, he thought to himself:
"My wife lies here on her back, naked and her body defiled by impurities; that bhikṣu must have rushed out of the house only after violating my wife."
He immediately went after him and asked,
"Did you commit an offense against my wife and then flee? The bhikṣu said:
“Householder, do not speak such words; we ought not to do such a thing.
The householder said:
“You have come out from my house; how can you say you will not do it?”
He then struck the bhikṣu, who died immediately.

When the other bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those who had few desires, were contented, practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame and remorse;

they censured that alms-seeking bhikṣu, saying: "How can an alms-seeking bhikṣu, being young and ignorant of much, enter the sleeping quarters of another woman without first observing the signs at the door?"
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat to one side. They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of this matter and rebuked the bhikṣu who had gone for alms:

"What you have done is improper; it is not in accordance with dignified conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not the practice of compliance. It is something that ought not to be done."
"How can a bhikṣu who begs for alms, being young and lacking much understanding, enter the bedchamber of another woman without first observing the signs of the door?
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for bhikṣus who beg for alms; bhikṣus who beg for alms should comply with it in this manner."

If a bhikṣu who lives on almsfood enters a village to beg for food, he should, early in the morning, wash his hands clean and go to the side of the robe-rack. With one hand he lifts a robe and with the other he pulls it out; he spreads it out and shakes it to inspect it, ensuring there are no snakes or insects, and only then does he fasten his waistband. He then spreads out and shakes the saṃkakṣikā and the uttarāsaṅga to inspect them. He folds the saṃghāṭī and places it upon his head or over his shoulder. Having washed the bowl clean, he places it in a carrying net, or wraps it in a hand-towel, or stores it in a bowl-bag. He then takes up his undergarment, his foot-washing sandals, his felt blanket, and his walking sandals.
He should take the key, leave the room, close the door, and push it to test it. If it is not secure, he should install a bolt.
If it is secure, he should pull the cord inside, then look around in all four directions; if no one sees him, he may conceal and lift the door-latch.
If one sees anything that is not durable, one should take it away or place it in a more secure location.
While traveling on the road, one should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas.
If one encounters others, one should greet them, saying:
"Welcome. If one wishes to go to a village, one should step slightly off the path, place the bowl on the ground, take up the saṃghāṭī, spread it out, shake it, and inspect it before putting it on.
If there is a place in the vicinity of the village where utensils are sold, or a house, or a craftsman, one should take off one's leather sandals while walking on the road and entrust them there.
When entering the village, one should observe the alleys, look for an open space, observe the marketplace, observe the gates, and observe the heaps of refuse.
"When entering the home of a layperson, one should observe the characteristics of the first gate up to the seventh gate.
At that time, while a bhikṣu on alms-round was inside another's house, the wind blew his robe off his shoulder. He turned toward a woman to adjust it. The Buddha said:
"One should not adjust one's robe toward a woman; one should face a wall."
When that alms-collecting bhikṣu held his bowl with his right hand and his staff with his left hand, his private parts were exposed. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus; one should hold the staff with the right hand and the bowl with the left hand."
That alms-seeking bhikṣu stood in the middle of the road, causing men and women to avoid the path; when the laypeople saw this, they all spoke with derision, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking a sense of shame and never knowing satisfaction, they claim, "I know the True Dharma.
Yet, when walking on the road, they force men and women to clear the way for them; how can such a person possess the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who goes for alms should not stand in the middle of the road.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
"One should not stand on the path.
He stood in a secluded place, whereupon the Buddha said:
"That should not be done; one should stand in a visible place."
When that bhikṣu who begs for alms went forward to meet and take food as others were carrying it out, the laypeople saw this and all reviled him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Without knowing contentment, they say of themselves,
"I know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such a case?
They hurriedly went ahead to take food as if grain were scarce.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu who begs for alms should not go ahead to take food."

"If it be a woman, or if one is ill, or pregnant, or carrying a child, or if it is raining, or if one's hands are occupied with objects, or if the ground is muddy, and she calls for the bhikṣu—if the bhikṣu hesitates and does not dare go forward to receive her, the Buddha said:
'If she calls, you should go.'"
When a bhikṣu seeking alms obtained rice, parched rice, flour, fish, and meat, he placed them all together in one spot. Other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said:
"One should not place these mixed together in one spot."
If there is only one alms bowl, it should be separated from others by means of an object—
such as a tree leaf, bark, a metal vessel, a secondary bowl, or a small bowl.
Flour should be wrapped in a hand-towel.
That alms-collecting bhikṣu went to a great household to beg for food, and when the householder saw him, he spoke with derision:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
You know no contentment, yet you say of yourselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
Even to the point where householders beg for alms as if grain were scarce—how can there be True Dharma in such a case?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not select households to beg for alms; if one does not obtain anything by begging in regular order, then one may select.
Yet that bhikṣu who begs for alms insisted on begging until he obtained it before departing. When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking a sense of shame and never knowing contentment, they say of themselves, "I know the True Dharma.
Yet they beg insistently from others, only departing once they have obtained what they want; this is like a time of grain scarcity—how can such behavior be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; if you know that [the time] will arrive, you should wait.
"When he goes out, you should observe the signs of the first gate, up to the signs of the heap of refuse."

If he leaves the village, he should return to the path and proceed wearing his leather sandals; when he leaves the path, he should set down his bowl on the ground, fold his saṃghāṭī robe and place it upon his shoulder or head, and while walking, he should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas.
If one sees someone, one should first greet them, saying: "Welcome.

At the place where that bhikṣu who begs for alms habitually eats, one should go and sweep it clean, sprinkle water, and prepare the vessels for water and for leftover food; furthermore, one should provide a seat, a foot-stone, a water-vessel, and a towel for wiping the feet.
"If you see another bhikṣu coming for alms, you should rise to meet him from afar and receive his bowl.
If there is a bowl-stand or a head-rest for bowls, take up your robe, spread it out, and examine it to ensure it is not stained with grease, dust, mud, or bird droppings."

If it is soiled in this way, one should wipe what should be wiped, knead what should be kneaded, shake out what should be shaken out, and wash what should be washed; having washed it, one should wring out the water and spread it upon a rope bed or a wooden bed.

He should provide a seat for the bhikṣu who has come for alms, offer him a water vessel, water, a foot-stone, and a towel for wiping the feet; he should take up the leather sandals and place them to the left, watching over them so that they are not stained by mud or water, and if they become wet with water, he should move them.

Having washed the feet of that bhikṣu seeking alms, he should take the water vessel, the foot-washing stone, and all other items and return them to their original places; then, having thoroughly cleansed his own hands with soap powder, he should offer water to that bhikṣu seeking alms.
Next, one should give food to that person.
While they are eating, one should observe their needs and provide whatever is required; if there is curd-milk, clear curd-milk, fermented grain juice, salt, or vegetables, one should give them.
If it is hot, one should provide a fan; if water is needed, one should give it.
If the time for the meal is about to pass, they should eat together.
Once the bhikṣu who has gone begging for food has finished eating, one should take his bowl and provide him with water for washing his hands.

If, after having eaten, there is food remaining, one should give it to a human or a non-human; or one should place it on ground without grass or in water without insects. One should wash the vessel containing the leftover food and return it to its original place, and likewise restore the seat, the foot-washing stone, and the water vessel to their proper positions.
"Return all items to their original places and sweep the dining area.
He then used his alms bowl to remove the filth, and when the other bhikṣus saw this, they all loathed it.
The Buddha said:
"One should not use the alms bowl to remove filth; rather, one should use a washbasin or a broom. The alms bowl should be kept clean.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus seeking alms who ate together in one place. A pregnant dog watched them eat but could not eat herself; due to her hunger, she subsequently miscarried.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"At the time of eating, whether it be a human or a non-human, one should give food, even as much as a single morsel.
I now establish a rule for bhikṣus who beg for alms; you should comply with it. If you do not comply, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was an araṇya bhikṣu who was indolent and failed to provide anything at all; he did not possess water vessels or items for washing his feet, nor did he set aside any leftover food.
Not far from this dwelling, a large band of robbers passed by. At that time, one robber said to the others, "The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, always have this custom:
they keep water vessels and items for washing their feet, and they also leave behind leftover food. We should go there; if we obtain food, we shall eat it together."
Then the bandits arrived there and asked,
"Do you have water? He replied:
"No. "Is there anything for washing the feet? He replied:
"No. "Is there any food remaining? He replied:
"No," the thief said. "You live in an araṇya;
you do not possess a vessel for washing your feet, nor do you have any leftover food."
He then beat him until he died.

When the monks heard of this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they reproached that forest-dwelling bhikṣu, saying:
"You are indolent and negligent! How can you dwell in a forest hermitage without providing water vessels, even to the point of not setting aside any leftover food?"
Then the bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked that forest-dwelling bhikṣu:

"What you have done is improper; it is not the proper demeanor, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure conduct, and not conduct in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done."
“What is this laziness and indolence, that you dwell in an araṇya while lacking water vessels, even to the point of not setting aside any leftover food?
Having rebuked the araṇya bhikṣu with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
“From this day forward, I shall establish a rule for araṇya bhikṣus which they must follow; an araṇya bhikṣu should comply with the araṇya dharma in this manner.”

If an araṇyaka bhikṣu enters a village for alms, he should wash his hands clean at dawn and go to the clothing rack. With one hand he lifts the robe and with the other he pulls it out; he then spreads it out, shakes it, and inspects it to ensure there are no snakes or insects before putting it on. He fastens his waistband, and having spread out and shaken the saṃkakṣikā and the uttarāsaṅga and inspected them, he folds the saṃghāṭī and places it upon his head or shoulder. Having washed the bowl clean, he places it in its net bag—either wrapped in a hand-towel or contained within a bowl-sack—and then takes up his undergarment, his foot-washing sandals, his felt blanket, and his staff with its protective covering and walking shoes for the road.
He should take the key, leave the room, and upon returning, close the door and push it to see if it is secure.
If it is not secure, he should install a bolt.
If it is secure, he should pull the cord and fasten it inside.

Looking around in the four directions, if no one sees you, you should hide it by placing the door-bolt inside; if someone sees it and it is not secure, you should take it away and place it in a more secure location.
While traveling on the road, one should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas. If one encounters people, one should first greet them, saying: "Welcome.

If one intends to enter a village, one should step slightly off the path, set down the bowl upon the ground, take up the saṃghāṭī, spread it out, shake it, and inspect it before putting it on. If there is a place where utensils are sold by the village, or a house, or a worker, one should take off one's leather sandals and walking staff, beat them clean, and leave them there.
When entering a village, he should observe the characteristics of the streets, or the characteristics of open spaces, marketplaces, gateways, or heaps of refuse.
Upon entering the house of a layperson, he should observe the first gateway characteristic through to the seventh gateway characteristic.
At that time, an araṇyaka bhikṣu was inside another’s house when the wind blew his robe off his shoulder. He turned toward a woman to adjust it. The Buddha said:
“One should not adjust one’s robe while facing a woman; one should face a wall.”
When that forest-dwelling bhikṣu held his bowl in his right hand and his staff in his left, his body was exposed. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should hold the staff in your right hand and carry the bowl in your left."
That forest-dwelling bhikṣu stood in the middle of the road, causing men and women to avoid the path; when the householders saw this, they all reviled him together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!..."
Lacking a sense of shame and never feeling satiated, they say of themselves, "I know the True Dharma.
Yet they stand in the path and force men and women to avoid it; how can such a person possess the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“An araṇya bhikṣu should not stand on the road.
Since the World-Honored One had stated that one should not stand on the road, they stayed in a secluded place; the Buddha then said:
"One should not do so; one should remain within sight.
When food was brought out by others, that forest-dwelling bhikṣu would go forward to meet and receive it.
Seeing this, the laypeople all criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are shameless and lack contentment;
they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.
How can there be any True Dharma in such as these?"
They hurried forward to receive food as if grain were scarce.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“An araṇya bhikṣu should not hurry forward to receive food.”

If it is a woman who is pregnant, or carrying a child, or if it is raining, or if she is holding something in both hands, or if she calls out to the bhikṣu while standing in muddy water on the ground, and the bhikṣu hesitates and does not dare to go forward.
The Buddha said, "If you are summoned, you should go.
When an araṇya bhikṣu received rice, or cooked grain, parched flour, fish, or meat, and placed them all together in one spot, other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said:
"One should not mix these together in one place.
If they are in a single bowl, they should be separated by an object—such as a tree leaf, bark, a key-ring, a secondary bowl, or a small bowl; or the parched grain should be wrapped in a hand-towel."
That forest-dwelling bhikṣu went to a great household to beg for food, and when the laypeople saw him, they all reviled him together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
They have no sense of shame and lack contentment; yet they say of themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma," he said, yet he chose a great family to beg from as if grain were scarce; how can such a thing be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not select specific great families for alms; if one does not receive anything by begging in regular order, then one may select them.
Yet that forest-dwelling bhikṣu insisted on begging until he had obtained food before departing.
At that time, all the lay devotees saw this and together reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and are never satisfied; they claim for themselves:
'We know the True Dharma.'"
"To beg from others by force until one's demands are met before departing—this is like a time when grain is scarce. How can such a thing be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; if you know that you will receive it, you should wait."
When he was about to eat, he thought to himself:
"This is for the thief; this is for myself.
As he went out, he should observe the signs of the first gate, continuing even to the sign of the heap of excrement.

If he leaves the village, he should take up his walking sandals and staff, step slightly off the path to set down his bowl on the ground, and fold his saṃghāṭī robe to place it upon his shoulder or head. While walking, he should constantly contemplate wholesome dharmas; if he sees someone, he should first greet them, saying: "Welcome."
At the place where that forest-dwelling bhikṣu usually eats, he should go there to sweep and sprinkle it clean, and prepare water vessels,
vessels for leftover food, as well as a seat, a foot-stone, a water vessel, and a towel for wiping the feet.
"If you see another forest-dweller (āraṇyaka) approaching, you should rise to meet him from afar and receive his bowl for him, placing it on the bowl-stand or supporting it upon your head.
You should take up his robe, spread it out, and examine it to ensure it is not stained with grease, dust, mud, or bird droppings."

If it is soiled in this way, one should wipe it if it should be wiped, rub it if it should be rubbed, shake it out if it should be shaken out; if it is to be washed, once washed, one should wring out the water and spread it to dry upon a rope bed or a wooden bed.

He should provide a seat for the forest-dwelling bhikṣu, as well as a water vessel and water; he should provide a foot-stone and a foot-wiping cloth; he should take up the leather sandals and place them to the left; he should watch over them so that they are not stained by mud or dirty water, and if they become soiled with mud, he should move them away.
Having washed the feet of that forest-dwelling bhikṣu, he should take the water vessel, the foot-washing stone, and all other items and return them to their original places.
Having thoroughly washed his own hands with cleansing powder (kaṣāya), he should set aside a portion of the remaining food in a clean place; if any thieves should come, he should give it to them.
He should give water to that forest-dwelling bhikṣu, and then give him food.
During the mealtime, he should look after his needs and provide whatever is required; if there is curd-milk, clear curd-milk, fermented grain-liquor, salt, or vegetables, he should give them to him.
If it is hot, one should fan him; if he needs water, one should give it to him.
If the time for the meal is about to pass, they should eat together.

After the forest-dwelling bhikṣu has eaten, one should take his bowl and provide him with water for washing his hands. Having finished eating oneself, if there is any leftover food, one should give it to humans or non-humans, or place it on ground free of grass or in water free of insects.
"One should wash the vessels containing leftover food, and return the beds, seats, foot-washing stones, water jars, and all other items to their original places;
one should then sweep the dining area. He used his alms bowl to remove the filth, and when the other bhikṣus saw this, they all detested it. The Buddha said:
"One should not use the alms bowl to remove filth; one should instead use a washbasin or a broom."
The alms bowl should be kept clean.
If bandits should come, one should say:
"This is water; this is for washing the feet; this is food. It has been set aside specifically for you as something pure and clean; if you wish to eat, then eat."
Then the bandits asked the āraṇyaka, “What time is it tonight?
That bhikṣu was unable to answer and felt ashamed.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A forest-dwelling bhikṣu should be well-acquainted with the divisions of the night.
At that time, a thief questioned the forest-dweller, saying:
“What direction is this?
The araṇyaka bhikṣu did not know how to answer and felt ashamed.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“A forest-dwelling bhikṣu should be well-acquainted with the characteristics of the directions.
A bandit asked the bhikṣu:
“What constellation is it today?”
The forest-dwelling bhikṣu was unable to answer. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A forest-dwelling bhikṣu should be well-versed in the stars."
That forest-dwelling bhikṣu spread out fine bedding and slept soundly. At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"A forest-dwelling bhikṣu should not act in this way; he should remain vigilant in mind during the first and last watches of the night for contemplation."
I now establish the rules for forest-dwelling bhikṣus; forest-dwelling bhikṣus should comply with these rules in accordance with the Dharma.
If they do not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.

A householder invited the community of monks for a meal on the following day; that very night, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, and at dawn, he went to inform them that the time had arrived.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were receiving the invited meal, there was confusion: some were already seated while others were just sitting down; some had already been given food while others were just being given it; some had already eaten while others were just eating; some had already departed while others were just about to leave; and some had already gone out while others were just about to go out. Thus, the donor did not know who had already eaten.
"Who has not yet eaten?
At that time, the lay devotees all became resentful and disparaging, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or modesty; they know no satiety."
They say of themselves:
"I know the True Dharma.

Yet, when accepting an invitation from a donor, they go about in a confused manner; there are those who have already sat and those who are just sitting, those to whom food has already been given and those to whom it is just being given, and even those who have already departed and those who are just about to depart.
In this way, what true Dharma could there be that would allow us not to know with whom it has already been shared and with whom it has not yet been shared?
"Who has already eaten?
Who has not yet eaten?

When the bhikṣus heard this, those who were of few desires and contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse, censured those bhikṣus who had accepted the invitation, saying:

"What is it to go to a donor's invitation in a confused manner—where some have already sat, some are just sitting, and others are about to leave—causing the donor not to know with whom he has actually shared [the meal]?"
With whom has it not been shared?
Who has already eaten?
Who has not yet eaten?
Then the bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, sat to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this incident, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked those bhikṣus who had accepted the invitation:

"How is it that you accepted a donor's invitation and went about in such a confused manner—some already seated, some just about to sit, and others just about to leave—causing the donor not to know with whom he had shared [the meal]?"
With whom has it not been shared?
Who has already eaten?
And who has not yet eaten?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, I shall establish for the bhikṣus the rules regarding the serving of food. The bhikṣus should comply with these rules; they should comply in this manner."
If a bhikṣu wishes to go to accept an invitation, he should go to where the Saṃgha regularly takes its light meal or its main meal, or stay in a place from which it is visible.
When the donor announces that the time has arrived, the elder (upādhyāya) should walk in front like an elephant and proceed.
"If the senior monk is going to the place for defecation or urination, he should wait.

Yet the junior monks walked ahead of him, spoke while walking side-by-side, or walked either in front or behind; some had their robes tucked up, some wrapped them around their necks, some covered their heads, some wore their robes over both shoulders, or some wore leather sandals. The Buddha said:
"You should not act in this way."
"One should bared the right shoulder, remove one's leather sandals, and walk behind.
If there are matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, the Sangha, or matters involving a sick bhikṣu, the Buddha said:
"One should inform the senior monk and go before him."
If he faces threats to his life or threats to his holy life (*brahmacarya*), and out of fear and caution does not dare to go without asking, the Buddha said:
"In the event of such difficulties, whether he asks or does not ask, it is permitted for him to depart."
They went to the place where food was served and sat down in a disorderly heap. The Buddha said: "You should not do so.

You should sit according to the order of seniority. Once the elder has sat down, you should look toward those of middle and junior rank to ensure they are not sitting improperly or have failed to properly cover their bodies."

If there is anyone sitting improperly or failing to properly cover their body, one should snap one's fingers to alert them, or send someone to speak to them, so that they may know to sit properly and in accordance with the Dharma.
Once the middle seat has been taken, one should observe the senior and junior monks to ensure they are not sitting improperly or failing to properly cover their bodies.

If there are those sitting improperly or failing to properly cover their bodies, one should snap one's fingers to alert them or send someone to speak to them, so that they may understand and sit properly and correctly.
"When one has descended from their seat and is seated, it is also like this.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to the meal without a bowl; his fellow monks should have lent him a bowl.
There was another bhikṣu who went to the meal without having washed his bowl; a snake was inside the bowl and spat [upon the food]. After the bhikṣu had eaten, he fell ill. The Buddha said:
"One should not take one's bowl to the meal site without having washed it; rather, one should eat only after washing it thoroughly.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, out of greed for honor and respect, went to the meal site last, intending to make the other bhikṣus see them and rise up.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not, out of greed for profit or honor, go to the place where food is being served last and cause the other bhikṣus to rise."
If it is for those who have not yet arrived, one may permit those sitting nearby to open up their seating space.
If a donor offers fruit to the senior monk (upādhyāya), he should ask:
"Is the fruit pure?"
If he says, "It is not pure," the Elder should instruct him to make it pure.
If it has already been purified, one should ask:
"For whom was this sent?
If it was sent for the Elder, one may take it as one pleases.
If one says,
"For the Saṃgha," one should tell them to pass the message so that it reaches everyone.
If a donor gives various kinds of soup to the Elder, he should ask:
"For whom was this sent?
If [the donor] says:
"Take as you wish, for you are the Elder. If he says:
"If it is for the Saṃgha," one should say, "and instruct that the message be passed on until it reaches everyone.
At that time, there were bhikṣus who could not obtain food; [the Buddha] permitted those sitting nearby to request it on their behalf.
"If there is no one else to sit with you, you should reduce your portion by half and give it to them.
At that time, the bhikṣus would eat as soon as they received food. When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame and lack contentment."
He says of himself, "I know the True Dharma.
Yet he seizes the opportunity to obtain food and eats as if during a time of famine when grain is precious; if this is so, how can there be True Dharma?
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not do so;
you should announce that you have received an equal portion before eating.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were eating while propping their elbows on the table, thereby obstructing those sitting beside them. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat with the elbows thrust out; one should eat with the elbows drawn in.
At the time of eating, the group of six bhikṣus coughed and spat excessively, causing their spittle to fly and fall upon those sitting beside them.
Other bhikṣus disapproved of this and reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You should not do so; you should spit slowly.
When they were eating, the remains of fruit or the roots of vegetables were scattered about and defiled the ground, and they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. Items that are unfit for consumption should be gathered and placed at the side of one's feet; when departing, one should take them away and discard them.
He discarded the water used for washing the bowl here and there, causing the ground to become muddy. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so;
one should receive it in a basin and discard it outside.
At that time, many bhikṣus were sitting together with the group of six bhikṣus on a single table inside the house of a layperson to eat their meal.
A certain bhikṣu from the group of six rose up without informing his neighbor; as he did so, the bench tilted and fell over, causing the others to fall down and their bodies to be exposed.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be done. One should inform [the neighbor] so that they may sit properly."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having finished his meal, departed in silence. The donor did not know whether the food was good or not, nor whether it had been sufficient. The laypeople all criticized and disparaged him, saying: [They spoke thus: "How can he eat and then leave so abruptly? He does not even wait for us to express our appreciation. They said, "He eats as much as he likes and then departs without a word. This is not the way of a śramaṇa; this is not the Dharma of the Buddha.
