"All the followers of other paths praise giving and extol the donors, yet the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, depart in silence after eating; this leaves us wondering whether the food was good or not."
"Was it sufficient or not?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not depart in silence after having eaten; one should recite a *dakṣiṇā* for the donor, even if it is only a single verse."
"If one gives for the sake of profit, that profit will surely be obtained;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will surely obtain happiness in the future.
Thus spoke the World-Honored One.
"One should recite the *dakṣiṇā*.
At that time, everyone spoke at once, resulting in a great clamor.
The Buddha said, "One should not speak in such a chaotic manner; the *sthavira* (elder) should be instructed to recite it."
If the Elder is unable to speak, one should tell someone capable to speak.
If the Elder does not speak, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If the Elder speaks but does not explain [the matter], it is also a *duṣkṛta* offense.

While he was pronouncing the *dakṣiṇā*, the others all departed; he then sat down, or sat in a secluded place, or sat in a covered place, or preached the Dharma to women in a place where no man capable of understanding was present, exceeding five or six words and engaging in lewd conversation.
The people of the time all complained and rebuked them, speaking of the matter to the bhikṣus, who then informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"At the time of the *dakṣiṇā*, other bhikṣus should not depart; they should leave the *sthavira* behind, with four remaining to wait for him, while the rest are permitted to go."
If it is for the sake of the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha, or for the sake of a sick bhikṣu, one should inform them so they may know before departing.
If one tells another bhikṣu to go, or if a donor wishes to hear a discourse on giving, one should praise the virtue of giving.
If they wish to hear a discourse on the dharma of the donor, one should praise the dharma of the donor.
If they wish to hear about the devas, one should praise the devas.
If they wish to hear about their deceased ancestors, one should praise their deceased ancestors; one should praise the donor’s generosity, praise the donor, and praise the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
"I shall teach the rules for meals to the bhikṣus; the bhikṣus should comply with them.
If they do not comply, they shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the robes of the bhikṣus became stained with grease.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to wash them using salt-earth, or ash, or soil, or cow dung.
They used coarse and abrasive stones to wash the robes, causing the robes to be ruined. The Buddha said:
"One should not use coarse or rough grinding stones; rather, one should use fine grinding stones.

If the color fades, it should be dyed again—either with clay, or with the bark of the dhava tree, or the bark of the pāṭala tree, or with *kandhara*, or *pippalī*, or *āmalaka*, or with tree roots, or with madder."
When he soaked the dyeing liquid in the midday sun, the color did not last long.
The Buddha said, "You should not do it that way;
you should boil it. He did not know where to boil it.
The Buddha said:
"One should boil it in a cauldron, or in a full jar, or in a copper vessel or pot.
When they were boiling it, the pieces of bark were too large to fit; the Buddha said:
"One should mince it finely with an axe; if it boils up, one should press it down with a wooden stick.
Not knowing whether it was cooked or not, the Buddha said:
"One should take two or three drops of the broth and place them in cold water. If they sink, it is cooked; one should then strain out the broth."
He did not know where to place the strained liquid; the Buddha said:
"Place it in a large jar. If both the liquid and the dregs flow through, you should cover it with a broom."
"If the broom is weak, it should be supported with wood.
When they were straining the juice, they grew exhausted from having to hold the basin as well; the Buddha said, "It should not be done that way.
One person should hold the basin and another should strain the juice. If it is hot, one should use tongs to handle the hot object."
The dye spoiled because the cold and hot liquids were mixed together.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus. Cold and hot liquids should be kept in separate places; once the hot liquid has been cooled by fanning, they may then be blended."
He went to dye it in the dye solution, but the dye was ruined. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should take a small amount and dye it in another vessel."
Having dyed it, he spread it on the ground and the color was ruined. The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He then spread it on grass and ruined the grass; he spread it on grass and leaves and the color became uneven. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; one should spread it upon an *elāyanta-mora*, *mora-mora*, or a woolen rug (*kūrpa*).

From among the ten kinds of robes, take each individual robe and spread it on the ground, then place the dyed robe upon it or hang it on a cord. If he requires a cord, he is permitted to keep one; if he requires pins, he is permitted to have them made."
"For those who require a fastening for their robes, I allow you to make a toggle. If the dye runs unevenly, you should turn the robe over.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having finished drying his dyed robe, turned his back toward the boiling vat; consequently, the dye and the liquid ran down the robe unevenly.
There was a certain bhikṣu who had previously been in conflict with another; seeing him, he did not speak to let the other know that the color of his robe had become spoiled.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not act in this way. Upon seeing it, one should either exchange it for another or speak to him so that he may be made aware."

When that bhikṣu had finished dyeing the robes, he departed without putting away the cauldron, the *jinman*, the copper pitcher, the jars, the pot, the axe, the rope and pegs, the *elīyanta-mora* and *mora-mora*.
The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should store it away before departing, and if others ask for it, you should give it to them.
After he had finished dyeing the robes, he did not sweep the dyeing area, leaving the ground unclean. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus; you should sweep and then depart.
He put on a new robe while sweeping, and the dust and dirt defiled it. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear a new robe; one should wear an old one."
"If you have no private robes, you should wear the robes of the Saṃgha.
He swept against the wind so that the dust came and covered his body. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should sweep with the wind."
There are five ways of sweeping the ground that do not yield great merit:

sweeping against the wind or with the wind without knowing the proper direction; failing to erase footprints; failing to remove filth; and failing to return the broom to its original place. One who sweeps the ground with these five methods does not obtain great merit.
There are five things by which one gains great merit:
sweeping against the wind, sweeping with the wind, erasing footprints, removing filth, and returning the broom to its original place. By possessing these five things, one gains great merit.
If the senior monk is downwind, one should say to him:
"Please move aside a little;
I wish to sweep the ground."
"I now teach the method for dyeing robes for the bhikṣus; you should comply with it.
If you do not comply, you shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.

The Fourth Part: 1. The Khandhaka on Dwellings (Vihāra-khandhaka) 1. The First Section of the Khandhaka on Dwellings. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Bārāṇasī.
Then five persons rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed him, saying:
“Blessed One!”
"What kind of dwellings and bedding should we occupy? The Buddha said,

"It is permitted for you to stay in forest hermitages (āraṇya), at the foot of trees, in empty rooms, in mountain valleys or caves, in the open air, on straw mats, beside heaps of grass, in groves, among graves, by the water's edge, or upon spread grass or leaves."
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from ailments because they slept without pillows.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to use stones, brick, or wood to make them, or to use the arm as a pillow; or, among the ten kinds of robes, you may use any one of them to make a pillow."
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha. King Bimbisāra of Magadha thought to himself:
"If the World-Honored One enters whichever park first upon his arrival, I shall offer it as a gift to be established as a saṃghārāma."
At that time, there was the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha, which was the most preeminent.
Then the World-Honored One, knowing the king’s thoughts, proceeded immediately to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

When the King saw the World-Honored One approaching from afar, he immediately dismounted from his elephant, took the rug from atop the elephant, folded it into four layers, and having spread it out, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will sit upon this seat."
The World-Honored One then proceeded to the seat and sat down.
At that time, King Bimbisāra took a golden water-pitcher, offered water to the Buddha, and said:
"This Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in the city of Rājagṛha is the most excellent; I now offer it as a gift to the World-Honored One. I pray that out of compassion you will graciously accept it."
The Buddha said to the king:
"Now you should offer this park to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters.
For what reason?"

Whether it be that which belongs to the Buddha, or the property of a garden, or the property of a dwelling, or items such as robes, alms bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases—if none of these can be used by any devas, worldlings, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, or brahmins, they should be revered as if they were a stūpa.
The King then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable One!
I offer this Kalandaka Bamboo Grove to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters; out of compassion, please accept it for my sake."
Then the World-Honored One spoke these verses to exhort him:
“Those who give gardens and fruit trees, Who provide bridges and boats to ferry people across;
Who offer wells and springs along desolate roads, And likewise bestow dwellings and houses—”
"Such people as these increase their merit day and night;
those who uphold the precepts and delight in the Dharma will be born in the good realms.

At that time, King Bimbisāra prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side. The World-Honored One, for the sake of the king, preached the Dharma through various skillful means, causing him to attain great joy.
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the king rejoiced; he rose from his seat, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were coming down from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain into the city of Rājagṛha at early dawn, a great householder saw them and asked:
"Virtuous ones, where did you spend the night?"
He replied, "In mountain caves, by the water's edge, beneath trees, beside rocks, or upon the grass.
The householder asked:
“Is there no dwelling? He replied,
“There is none.”
"If one were to build a room, would that be permissible?
The bhikṣu replied:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted the building of rooms."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to build dwellings. At that time,

when the elder heard that the Buddha had permitted the bhikṣus to build dwellings, he immediately constructed sixty separate rooms on Vulture Peak Mountain, providing everything they required in full.

He invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal on the following day and offered them lodgings; that very night he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, and on the next day went to inform them that the time had arrived.

In the early morning, the World-Honored One dressed himself, took up his bowl, and together with one thousand two hundred and fifty great bhikṣus, went to the house of the great elder and sat down upon the prepared seat.

Then the householder personally served various kinds of delicious food and drink until everyone was fully satisfied. Having finished eating, he set aside his bowl and took a golden pitcher of water to offer to the World-Honored One, saying to the Buddha:

"I have built sixty dwellings on Vulture Peak Mountain, providing everything necessary for their complete fulfillment. For the sake of merit, for the sake of a great sacrifice, and for the sake of rebirth in the good realms, I now offer them to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters; I pray that you will compassionately accept them."
Then the World-Honored One accepted it and exhorted him with these words of counsel:
"To ward off cold and heat, And likewise from various fierce beasts;
From mosquitoes, gadflies, and venomous insects, And also to shield against torrential rain."
Violent and sudden evil winds may thus cause obstructions and cataracts;
yet by maintaining the precepts without flaw and diligently practicing the Buddha-dharma,
one attains firmness and joy through the analytical contemplation of meditative concentration.
"To give dwellings to the community of monks—this the World-Honored One has declared the foremost.

At that time, the elder of Rājagṛha took a low seat and sat before the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, taught and transformed him with the Dharma, causing him to attain joy.
Having instructed and exhorted the elder with a discourse on the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the World-Honored One had permitted the community of monks to build dwellings, wished to construct a great lecture hall in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove modeled after the royal palace, providing all necessary supplies and furnishings in full.
The Buddha said, "I permit you to build it."
At that time, there was a donor who wished to build a multi-storied pavilion for the Sangha; the Buddha said, "I permit its construction.
At that time, there was another donor who wished to build a *vimāna* chamber for the Sangha; the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted to build.
At that time, there was a donor who wished to construct for the Saṃgha a dwelling shaped like an elephant. The Buddha said, "Permission is granted to build it."
There was a donor who wished to build various kinds of dwellings for the Saṃgha; the Buddha said, "I permit you to build them.
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to build dwellings; the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to act; everything required by the procedure for constructing a hut is permitted to be provided.
Once the hut is finished, if there is dust on the ground, it should be plastered with mud. If one falls ill because there is no bedding, the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to use *elāyanta-mora*, *mora-mora*, or woolen blankets; from among the ten kinds of robes, one may use any single robe as a ground-covering."
"If one has an illness, it is permitted to make a bed; there are five kinds of beds as mentioned above.
When they wished to weave a bed, the Buddha said:
"We allow you to weave it."
With the exception of two kinds of cords—
leather cords and hair cords— one should use other types of cords to make them.
If the cords are insufficient, one should string them through the lattice-work of the bed frame and weave them loosely.
He lay down on that bed without any bedding and fell ill; the Buddha permitted him to make a mattress.
He did not know with what material to make it, so the Buddha said:
"One should listen [to the instructions]: if a storage bag is made of grass, wool, or cotton, or if it is a small mat, it should be stretched and sewn along the four sides of the bed.
If the border of the mat is torn or frayed, it should be repaired."
If they are stored in one place, they should be sewn together with cords.
If a mattress becomes greasy and soiled, one should make a double-layered mattress.
If it becomes excessively greasy, one should make a bedding mat to cover it.
At that time, the bhikṣus had no pillows. The Buddha said, "I allow you to make them.
They did not know how to make them.
The Buddha said:
“Whether square, circular, or triangular.
At that time, the community of monks in Rājagṛha obtained much śaṇa-hemp; the bhikṣus were hesitant and did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said:
"I have heard and received it.

It may be used as a cord for a bed, a cord for a wooden bed, or woven to make the outer and inner layers of a mattress; or it may be made into a floor covering, or into a cord, or into stuffing for a mattress."
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained cords of *vāmaka* grass and wove them into beds. The Buddha said, "I allow you to accept them.
At that time, snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and various venomous insects entered the dwellings. Bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire were startled upon seeing them. The Buddha said:
"Listen to the instructions regarding bed supports.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made high supports. The Buddha said:
"One should not make high supports; they should be no more than one and a half cubits or one span in height."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose robe was not sturdy and did not provide a secure resting place. The Buddha said:
"It should be folded and placed at the side of the head or behind the back.
When he turned over while lying down and fell onto the robe, the Buddha said:
“Listen: [the robes] should be hung on a cord, or on a dragon-tooth peg, or hung on a robe-rack.
When the robes he habitually wears and those he does not wear were kept in one place, there was confusion when taking the habitually worn robes. The Buddha said:
“One should not keep the habitually worn robes and the unworn robes together in one place.”
He placed his alms bowl, leather sandal bag, needle case, and oil container in one spot; when other bhikṣus saw this, they disapproved. The Buddha said:
"Place the alms bowl bag and the needle case in one place, and put the leather sandal bag and the oil container together in another."
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from darkness inside their rooms.
The Buddha said: "I allow you to light lamps. If you need oil, give them oil; if you need lamp wicks, give them wicks; if you need oil containers, give them containers."
Not knowing where to place the lamp, the Buddha said:

"I allow you to place it on the corner of a wooden bed, a rope bed, or upon a jar; or place it within a wall niche. However, if there is concern that ants might drink the oil, you should provide a barrier."
"If the lamp is not bright, one should pull out the wick to make it higher. If the hands are soiled with oil, it is permitted to use chopsticks;

if one fears burning the chopsticks, it is permitted to make them of iron. That room had no door and was not secure; thieves, cowherds, and shepherds took the bhikṣus' robes, bowls, needle-cases, and sitting mats and departed.

The Buddha said: "It is permitted to make a door; if a door pivot is required, it is permitted to make one. If one fears foul odors inside the door, it is permitted to pierce the door panel to make a hole for the air to escape."
Fearing that venomous creatures such as snakes and centipedes might enter through the openings, he permitted the use of curtains and wooden panels to screen the doors.
However, there were no locks or keys; consequently, thieves and those who let out cattle and sheep took the bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, needle-case, and sitting mat and carried them away.
The Buddha said,
"I allow you to make locks and keys.
[The monks] did not know where to install them.
The Buddha said:
"Whether it is on the side, above, or below.
[The questioner] did not know how to open it.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to cut holes [in the walls] to make curved bars or hooks; if you suffer from darkness, I allow you to open windows.
Since those windows were unobstructed, thieves and cowherds took the monks' robes, bowls, needle-cases, and bedding. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make screens and wooden partitions.
Not knowing how to make them,
the Buddha said:
"Whether made square, or made round, or made in the shape of an elephant's ear.
At night they were troubled by bats, and during the day by swallows entering; the Buddha said:
"I allow you to weave a screen with a coarse mesh, or to make lattice windows."
At that time, the doors were not bolted; thieves and cowherds took the bhikṣus’ robes, bowls, needle-cases, and sitting mats and departed. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to bolt the doors."
That precept-breaking bhikṣu pulled the rope to open the door and took away the other bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, needle case, and sitting mat.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to install a bolt and a horizontal bar."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus privately used the bedding and furniture belonging to the Saṃgha. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not privately use the bedding and furniture belonging to the Saṃgha."
"I allow you to make a mark.
[The monks] did not know what kind of mark to make.
The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to fashion an image of Maheśvara, or an image of a basket, or an image of a grapevine, or to depict it in five colors, or as a lotus flower, or by means of its name."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus placed the monastic insignia upon their private property. When the other bhikṣus saw this, they said to them:
"Venerable sirs!
The World-Honored One has not spoken in such a manner."
"Is it not forbidden to privately use the property of the Sangha?
He replied, "This is not the property of the Sangha; it is my own possession."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not apply the monastic insignia to one's private property; however, I permit that private items be dyed to serve as insignia."
Those six groups of bhikṣus were then making various marks: some made crescent-moon shapes, others made circular marks;
some made marks like the sun, some made marks like barley roots, some made marks like a piece of ginger, and some made marks in the shape of an ox. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. I allow you to make marks like water droplets sprinkled on the ground, marks like balls of cow dung, or wheel-shaped marks."
He moved the bedding and mats from his room and placed them elsewhere. The Buddha said:
"You should not move them; you should assign them a name, saying:
'This is the bedding and mats of so-and-so.'"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a young śrāmaṇera; he wished to install a partition inside his room. The Buddha said, "I permit you to do so.
At another time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to open a curved passage in front of his room. The Buddha said:
"I permit you to build.
When they wished to build an inner chamber behind it, the Buddha said:
"I permit you to build."
If one needs a door, it is permitted to make one; if one needs a wall, it is permitted to make a wall; if one needs half a wall, it is permitted to make one.
If one needs to make a large bed, the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make one."

"If a small chair is required, it is permitted to make one; if a rope chair is required, it is permitted to make one; if a small rope chair is required, it is permitted to make one; if a single-seated chair is required, it is permitted to make one; if boards and planks are required, they are permitted; if floor coverings are required, they are permitted."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to build a dwelling with eaves extending on all four sides and railings installed above; permission was granted for him to do so.
Permission was also granted to provide everything necessary for the construction of such dwellings.
At that time, on the day of the poṣadha, many members of the Saṃgha gathered, and the hall was too small to accommodate them all.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to make it large.
They did not know how to make it.
The Buddha said:
"Whether it be square, circular, or rectangular; whether it be two-winged, three-winged, or four-winged—such constructions are permitted.
Whatever is required for the construction of the great hall should all be provided."
At that time, the people within the hall each occupied a single bed, so that they could not accommodate one another. The Buddha said:
"I allow those who have been ordained for three years or more to sit together on a single bed. If they still cannot fit while sitting, one should make a long bed or a long board."
"If he still does not accept it, you should bind grass together to make a seat.
After binding grass to make a seat, he then tore his robe. The Buddha said:

"You should wrap the edges with soft grass. If he still does not accept it, you should sprinkle the ground with muddy water, or spread sand, or spread grass and tree leaves upon the ground to sit on."
He was together with a woman upon grass or leaves; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He spread out a robe together with a woman; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When he was together with a woman upon a garment, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He climbed onto a stone together with a woman. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; however, if one person is unable to move the stone when climbing it, then climbing is permitted."
When he was in doubt about boarding a boat with a woman, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to cross directly, whether sitting, standing, or lying down.
At that time, the bhikṣus were practicing walking meditation in the open air; suffering from wind, rain, and sun exposure, they fell ill. The Buddha said:
"Listen, you are to construct a hall for walking meditation (caṅkrama).
Not knowing how it should be constructed,
the Buddha said:
"Listen; for the construction of the hall, I shall provide everything that is required.
At that time, an elder who was old, sick, and frail fell to the ground while walking in meditation. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to tie ropes at both ends and walk along the rope."
When they held onto the rope to walk, their hands became soft and chafed. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a loop or a bamboo tube, pass a cord through the tube, and grasp it with the hand while walking.
When they grew exhausted from walking, he allowed beds to be placed at both ends.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were washing their feet, it rained; the rain soaked their newly dyed robes, ruining their color.
The Buddha said: "A separate place for washing feet should be established.

They required water basins, so water basins were provided; they required water jars, so water jars were provided; they required foot-washing stones, so stones were provided; they required sitting mats, so sitting mats were provided.
When that deity washed his feet, rain fell as mud, soiling his feet, his robes, and his sitting mat. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a path using stone, brick, or wood.
At that time, the distance from Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain to water was great; the Buddha said:
“[The Buddha] permitted the construction of a channel. While it was being made, there was concern that the channel might collapse or burst. The Buddha said:
“I permit you to block both sides with stones, bricks, or wood.”

If a pond is to be constructed within the monastery, and its banks should collapse or break, one is permitted to shore up the four sides with stone, brick, or wood; above this, a roof should be constructed to cover it.
"If there is a problem with mud at the edge of the pond, one should install stones, bricks, wooden planks, or gravel.
Regarding the problem of small children falling into the water, the Buddha said:
"I allow the construction of a railing."
The water in that pond was hot. The Buddha said:

"I permit you to fill a jar with it during the day and place it inside the house at night, or outside at night; if there is a problem with mud inside the house, I permit you to build a separate water-house."
"If the ground is muddy and soils the feet, it is permitted to place stones, bricks, or gravel there; one who requires a water vessel should be given one.
They used vessels made of precious materials. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials; they should be made of iron, copper, or clay."
The water vessel had no place to rest and was breaking;
the Buddha said, "One should construct a separate rack within the water-house to place it.
At that time, the community of monks obtained a conch shell; the Buddha said:
“Permit you to keep it.
Since there was no place to store it, the Buddha said:
“Permit you to store it together with the water vessel in one place.”
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha and the kingdom of Śrāvastī.

There was a householder named Sudatta, who always delighted in providing alms to the solitary, the destitute, and beggars; consequently, because of this practice, he became known by the name "Giver of Food to the Solitary" (Anāthapiṇḍada).
He possessed landed estates within Rājagṛha, and every year he would travel from Śrāvastī to Rājagṛha to inspect them.
In Rājagṛha there was an elder who was his close friend; this elder had personally decorated his hall and intended to invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada went to the house of the elder. It was the elder’s custom that whenever Anāthapiṇḍada arrived, he would immediately rise to greet him and invite him to take a seat.
On this day as well, he neither rose to welcome him nor invited him to sit; instead, he merely adorned the hall for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha.
When it was time for the meal, Anāthapiṇḍada arrived and asked the householder, "Why have you adorned the hall? What do you intend to do?"
Is it because you wish to arrange a marriage?
Or do you wish to invite the King?
Or do you wish to perform a great sacrificial rite?

The householder replied, "I am neither marrying nor inviting the king; I wish to establish a great sacrificial feast and invite the Buddha along with one thousand two hundred and fifty members of the Sangha."
That ascetic Gautama possesses such a great reputation, being designated as:
Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.
Anāthapiṇḍika asked, "Is this truly the Buddha? He replied:
"Is this truly the Buddha?
He asked this twice more, and each time he received the same answer:
"This is truly the Buddha."
After Anāthapiṇḍika had asked this twice or thrice, he asked again:
"Where is the Buddha?
I wish now to go and pay my respects."
The householder replied,
"The Buddha is currently staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada looked up at the sun and thought to himself:
"I have seen the World-Honored One today, but it was not the proper time; I shall go tomorrow.
Thereupon, Anāthapiṇḍada returned home and fell asleep with mindfulness of the Buddha in his heart.
At that time, there was a certain deva who had been a kinsman of Anāthapiṇḍada in a former life; out of compassion and for his benefit, he thought to himself: "Anāthapiṇḍada!..."
"If you wish to see the World-Honored One, let there be no obstacle that prevents you from seeing the Buddha.
He then used his supernormal power to extinguish the darkness, and suddenly it became bright.
At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada woke from his sleep; seeing the light, he thought it was daytime and immediately set out for the gate of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the gatekeeper deity, seeing that Anāthapiṇḍada desired to see the World-Honored One without hindrance, thought:
"I should now open the gate.
He then opened the gate immediately.
When Anāthapiṇḍada had passed through the Śīghra gate, that deity withdrew his supernormal power; at dawn, the light vanished and it suddenly became dark.
Anāthapiṇḍada was seized with terror and his hair stood on end, thinking:
"Could it be that an enemy has come to harm me?"
At that time, the gate deity saw Anāthapiṇḍada eating and was struck with fear; he immediately comforted him, saying:
"Do not be afraid! Do not be afraid!"
He then spoke in verse:
"Even if one were to offer a hundred horses, along with a hundred golden ornaments,
a hundred chariots drawn by horses, and a hundred young maidens."
Necklaces made of the seven treasures, A hundred white elephants from the Snowy Mountains,
each with six tusks, Along with great heaps of gold and purple-gold sand, The king and all the royal regalia—
The well-trained elephant upon which the king rides—by giving such a gift, the merit of walking a single step [is greater]; one-sixteenth part of that merit does not equal it.
"Householder, simply proceed forward; proceeding forward brings benefit."
Anāthapiṇḍika asked, "Who are you? He replied:
"I am the deity Āśīviṣa. He thought to himself:
"How extraordinary! A celestial deity has come to comfort me."
Then Anāthapiṇḍada went to the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove. At that time, the World-Honored One was walking back and forth in the open air;
seeing Anāthapiṇḍada approaching from afar, he returned to his seat, spread out his mat, and sat down. It is the constant law of all Buddhas that a halo of light illuminates their bodies.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada saw from afar that the World-Honored One’s countenance was upright and handsome, his faculties were tranquil, and he had attained the supreme and foremost self-mastery; his faculties were as firm as a great dragon, and like a clear, deep pool, pure and free from defilement.
Having seen him, a sense of reverence arose within him; with a heart of faith and respect, he approached the Buddha and asked, "Are you sleeping peacefully?
The World-Honored One replied:
"While the world sleeps in peace, I am different from them.
Then he spoke this verse:
"All sleep in peace; The holy life has attained Nirvāṇa."
If one does not transgress in desire, one attains liberation from all bonds.
When all craving has been exhausted and the feverish afflictions are subdued, one attains peaceful rest through their cessation; both body and mind are utterly stilled.
Then Anāthapiṇḍada approached before his meal, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for the sake of Anāthapiṇḍada, used various skillful means to instruct and transform him through the teaching of the Dharma, causing him to attain joy.

Immediately upon sitting there, he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; having seen the Dharma and realized the Dharma, he attained the superior fruit, and a sense of weary detachment arose within him. He addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and become a lay follower (upāsaka) of the Buddha."
"From this day forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall refrain from taking life, up to and including refraining from drinking intoxicants.
I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of monks, will accept my invitation for the ninety-day summer retreat."
The Buddha said,
"I have already accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation.
He then spoke again, saying:
“I pray that you accept my invitation for next year.
The Buddha said,
“I have already accepted King Bimbisāra’s invitation.”
He spoke again, saying:
"Virtuous One! I pray that you will accept my invitation for the following year."
The Buddha replied:
"If there is such a place—pure, free from clamor, devoid of wild beasts, and a secluded forest where one may practice seated meditation—the Tathāgata shall dwell in such a place."
He then addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I have already understood this; I shall know the proper time myself."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of monks, will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Then, Anāthapiṇḍada rose from his seat, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.
At that time, King Bimbisāra heard that Anāthapiṇḍika had invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal the following day. He immediately sent a messenger with these words:

"You are but a guest staying here; since this assembly of monks is so large—numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty—it would not be necessary for you to provide the offerings. I shall provide the food on your behalf."
Thereupon, he immediately sent a messenger to reply to the king, saying:
"This shall suffice as an offering.
There is no need for further gifts; I shall provide them myself."
At that time, the great householder of Magadha heard that Anāthapiṇḍada had invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal the following day. He went to him and said:
"You are merely a guest; since this assembly of monks is so large, you need not provide the offerings yourself. I shall arrange them for you."
He replied: "Householder! This shall suffice as an offering."
"No need! I shall provide it myself.

Anāthapiṇḍada immediately returned home and prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink throughout the night. When the night had passed, at dawn, he went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had come.
The World-Honored One, having dressed and taken his bowl, went together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus to the home of Anāthapiṇḍada and took his seat.

Then Anāthapiṇḍada personally served various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks until they were fully satisfied. Having finished eating and set aside his bowl, he took a low stool and sat before the Buddha.
Then the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, taught the Dharma to Anāthapiṇḍada, transforming and enlightening him until he attained joy.
Having finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat and departed.
Then, as Anāthapiṇḍika was returning from Rājagṛha to Śrāvastī, he reached various villages and towns and issued proclamations everywhere, saying:

"In open spaces, plant orchards and fruit trees, and provide ponds, wells, bridges, and boats. A Buddha has appeared in the world and has now accepted my invitation to observe the summer rains retreat in Śrāvastī; He shall travel by this path to Śrāvastī, enabling you all to obtain immeasurable merit."
Having arrived at Śrāvastī, he thought to himself:

"Where now is there a place that is neither too near nor too far, where one may come and go and wander about, where the ground is level and vast, which is free from crowds during the day and free from noise at night, and where there are no mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, bees, or other stinging insects?"
"I shall purchase it to establish a saṃghārāma for the sake of the Buddha. He then thought:

"Prince Jeta has a fine garden that is neither too near nor too far from Śrāvastī; it is level and spacious for traveling and sightseeing, with no crowds during the day and no noise at night, and it is free from mosquitoes, gadflies, and stinging insects."
"I should now go to Prince Jeta's place and request to purchase it.
He immediately went to the prince's location and said, "The Buddha has appeared in the world; does your majesty know this?"
"He has already accepted my invitation to observe the summer retreat in Śrāvastī; you may sell this park to me, and I shall give you one hundred thousand gold coins.
He replied, "I will not sell it."
Again, he spoke as before:
"I pray you grant me the garden; I shall give you two hundred, three hundred, or four hundred thousand pieces of gold. He replied:
"If you were to cover the ground with gold coins laid side by side until there was no space left between them,
I still would not give it to you," said Anāthapiṇḍada, breaking his word:
"You have already fixed the price."
"You may accept it. The prince asked,
"What is the fixed price?"
He replied, "When you previously said that gold coins should be spread out across the ground so as to leave no space between them, was that not a definitive statement regarding the price?
Your Majesty may now examine the ancient regulations established by your ancestors."
He then consulted the king’s established precedent; having done so, he settled the price and said:
"Householder! It is as you wish."

Then, Anāthapiṇḍada returned home and commanded his men to take out a great quantity of gold coins and spread them across the ground of Jeta’s Grove; however, there was a small remaining area where the gold had not yet been spread.
Having seen this, Jeta thought to himself:
"This is no ordinary person, nor is he an ordinary field of merit, for he has caused me to disregard my precious treasures so much for the sake of feeding the *Gṛhapati* (Anāthapiṇḍada)."
He then said, "Householder, stop!
Do not spread any more gold; I myself wish to offer the remaining ground to the World-Honored One."
Anāthapiṇḍika said, "You may proceed as you please.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled through the human realm from Rājagṛha to the country of Vajji, and subsequently proceeded on to Vaiśālī.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went before the Buddha to take possession of dwellings for the sake of their preceptors, co-preceptors, teachers, and co-teachers, as well as for the sake of their close friends and acquaintances.
At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana arrived together later.
The Buddha asked,
"Whose room is this?"
The group of six bhikṣus said:
"This is the room of our preceptors, co-preceptors, ācāryas, co-ācāryas, and our close friends and relatives."
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana did not obtain rooms for lodging and stayed overnight on the outer terrace.
When the night had passed, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
The World-Honored One, knowing [the answer], asked intentionally:
"Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, are you resting and rising in peace and comfort?
They replied:
"Are you at ease?
the World-Honored One asked.
"Where did you spend the night?"
He replied, “On the outer edge. [The other asked,] “For what reason is it so?”
He then related the circumstances in full to the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them:
“Whom do you consider worthy of receiving the first seat, the first water, and the first food; of being met with rising to greet, prostrating with reverence, and being greeted with kind words?”
Some said: "One who has gone forth from a great clan.
Others said: [and so forth].
"One with a handsome countenance," some say;
"one who dwells in an araṇya," others say.
Some said, "The one who begs for alms. Others said:
"Regarding 'pamsukūla robes' (rag-patch robes):
some say it refers to those who do not eat food for which the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (prepared-food) ritual has been performed."
Some said, "Those who eat in a single sitting. Others said:
"Regarding 'one who eats a single morsel of food,' some say:
'One who dwells among burial mounds.'"
Some said, "Those who sit in the open air. Others said:
"Under a tree" means:
some say it refers to "one who always sits."
Some said, "According to the order of seating. Others said:
"Regarding the 'three robes':
some say it refers to one who is capable of chanting."
Some said, "The one who is learned"; others said:
[The one who is virtuous].
"Regarding the 'Dharma Master,' some say:
'One who upholds the Vinaya.'"
Or some said: "One who practices dhyāna.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen well! Regarding what should and should not be given:
Long ago, in a past age, there were three friends."
An elephant, a monkey, and a francolin partridge lived together in a single nyagrodha tree.
They thought to themselves:
"We dwell together; it is not right that we fail to show respect and instead treat one another with contempt. It would be better for us to honor one another according to our relative ages."
"If you are the eldest, you should respect, revere, and provide for them.
Having performed such duties, we shall dwell together in the forest.
Then the monkey and the francolin partridge asked the elephant:
"Do you remember how long ago this occurred?
The elephant replied,
"I remember that when I was small, this nyagrodha tree touched my navel as I walked past it."
The elephant and the francolin asked the monkey,
"How far back do you remember events?
The monkey replied:
"I recall that when I was small, this nyagrodha tree reached up to my raised hand and head.
The elephant said to the monkey,
"You have lived for more years than I."
The elephant and the monkey asked the partridge together:
"How far back do you remember events? He replied:
"I recall that on the right side of the King of Snowy Mountains there was a great nyagrodha tree; I ate its fruit there, and upon coming here, it immediately sprouted from my excrement."
He thought to himself, "The partridge has lived more years than I. Thereupon,
the elephant placed the monkey on its head, and the monkey placed the partridge on its shoulder, and they traveled together through the human world.
Traveling from village to village and city to city, he preached the Dharma, saying:
"Those who revere their elders are able to abide in the Dharma;
they will attain renown in the present life and be reborn in the good realms in the future."
At that time, when the francolin had preached such a Dharma, all people followed it and the teachings spread.
You who have gone forth within my Dharma and Vinaya should likewise show mutual respect; in this way, the Buddha-Dharma may continue to spread.
"From this day forward, I authorize you to pay respect, prostrate, welcome, and inquire after the health of the senior monks according to their age.

When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha’s instruction, they arranged themselves in order of seniority and showed reverence to the elders; yet when those [junior] bhikṣus prostrated before laypeople, they would say:
"You are older than I by birth."
The Buddha said:
"One should not pay homage to laypeople; among yourselves, there are those to whom you should pay homage and those to whom you should not. One should not pay homage to any woman.
Furthermore, one who has received the full ordination earlier should not pay homage to one who received it later."

Those who have committed an offense against the boundaries, those who have violated a bhikṣuṇī, those who received the precepts with a thieving mind, those who have damaged the two organs, eunuchs, those who have killed their father, killed their mother, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or have shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil intent; non-humans, animals, those with dual sexual organs; those who have been suspended, those who have been expelled, or those who ought to be expelled—all such as speak what is contrary to the Dharma should not be saluted.
Who should be paid homage?
A junior śrāmaṇerī should pay homage to senior śrāmaṇerīs, śrāmaṇeras, śikṣamāṇās, bhikṣuṇīs, and bhikṣus; likewise, one should pay homage to all such persons and their stūpas.
If a young śrāmaṇera, he should pay homage to senior śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, śikṣamāṇās, and even bhikṣus, as well as to all stūpas; he should pay homage to them all.
A junior śikṣamāṇā should pay homage to senior śikṣamāṇās, bhikṣuṇīs, and bhikṣus, as well as to stūpas; she should pay homage to them.
A junior bhikṣuṇī should pay homage to senior bhikṣuṇīs and bhikṣus, and she should also pay homage to stūpas.
A junior bhikṣu should pay homage to a senior bhikṣu, and he should also pay homage to the stūpa of a senior bhikṣu.
All devas, worldlings, māras, Brahmā kings, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas should all pay homage to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and they should also pay homage to his stūpa.
Since the Blessed One has given this instruction, one should pay homage to the stūpas.
They then proceeded to pay homage to the stūpas and shrines of laypeople. The Buddha said:
"One should not pay homage to the stūpas and shrines of laypeople."
Since he was unable to pay homage to the stūpas and shrines of laypeople, he circumambulated them by keeping them to his left; the deities who protect these shrines became angry.
The Buddha said:
"One should proceed according to the direction from which one originally came; one should not intentionally circumambulate by keeping [the object] to the left."
The bhikṣus had this thought:
"Should śrāmaṇeras be ranked according to their year of birth, or according to their year of ordination?
The Buddha said:
"Seniority should be determined by the year of birth.
If the years of birth are equal, seniority should be determined by the year of ordination.
Thus, a certain bhikṣu arrived first, and later a senior bhikṣu arrived.
One night they moved forward to where the bhikṣus were;
the Buddha said, "You should neither move nor rise; I allow you to sit in the middle.
Once they were sitting in the middle, they moved about again, causing a noisy commotion among the assembly. The Buddha said:
"Let those who arrive later sit in the lower seats.
Once they had sat in the lower seats, they were actually sitting below the laypeople (*avadātavasana*). The Buddha said: "This should not be done."
He further sat below the śrāmaṇeras; the Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you should sit below the mahābhikṣus.
He did not participate in the later *varṣā* (rainy season retreat), yet he received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and counted that as a year of seniority; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
The preceptor and the ācārya should instruct [the candidate] regarding the proper time for receiving the precepts, giving instruction such as this:

'Whether it be winter, spring, or summer; whether you obtain [the opportunity] for several days, one month, half a month, one day, during the morning meal, or the afternoon meal, or even at the time of measuring the shadow.'"
The group of six bhikṣus, seeing a senior elder approaching at the home of a layperson, did not rise; this was not the practice of the Saṃgha. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so; you ought to rise."
Standing by the water, under a tree, by a rock, upon the grass, or on a boat, he did not rise; instead, he avoided the senior monk, saying, "This is not the property of the Saṃgha."
The Buddha said, "You should rise.
At that time, there was a householder who had built a dwelling for the Sangha, yet no one lived in it. He spoke these words:

"A wealthy householder with abundant riches and treasures has built a dwelling for the Saṃgha, and the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are now living within it. We are poor; who would allow us to dwell here?"
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“The Saṃgha should grant this bhikṣu the formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman). It should be granted in this manner.
Having appointed from among the assembly a capable person to perform the formal act as described above, he should make the following announcement:”
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
Now the Saṃgha intends to assign this room belonging to so-and-so to the bhikṣu so-and-so for maintenance.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen."
The motion is as follows: "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This room, [named] so-and-so, is assigned for the care and maintenance of the bhikṣu so-and-so."
"Whichever elders approve of the Saṃgha assigning this room, [belonging to] so-and-so, for such-and-so to manage, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved assigning the room of so-and-so to the bhikṣu so-and-so to manage. Since the Saṃgha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, the bhikṣus wished to build a dwelling. The Buddha said, "I permit it.
They wished to level the ground. The Buddha said:
"Listen. If there are stones, tree roots, or thorns, they should be removed;
if there are pits, ditches, or low-lying areas, they should be filled level."
If there is concern regarding water, one should construct embankments and barriers;
if there is fear that the land has an owner or might lead to further disputes, one should resolve the matter with absolute clarity;
if there are large tree stumps or stones, they should be excavated and removed.
If it cannot be removed, burn it away;
if it cannot be removed even after burning, douse it with water or sour vinegar once burned;
or break it out by striking it with a stone mallet.
"If it is difficult to remove, break it out with an iron hammer.
If it still cannot be removed, dig a large pit at the edge and bury it deep.
He wished to level the ground; "one should plow it and then grind it smooth."
"Who should be appointed to act as the arbitrator?
The Buddha said:
"It may be a bhikṣu, a śrāmaṇera, a monastery attendant, or an upāsaka."
"If he requires bricks, it is permitted for him to have them made, whether by himself or by instructing others to do so.
If he requires brick molds, it is permitted to give them to him.
If mud is applied to the brick molds," the Buddha said:
"One should place a piece of refuse inside the water and then wipe the four edges.
When there was grass at the site where the bricks were being made, the Buddha said:
"One should do so in a place free of grass; if the bricks are not dry, they should be turned over."
If one cuts grass when returning [from work], there is no offense.
If the bricks are uneven, they should be scraped level.
If they are dry, they should be stacked.
If it rains and the covering becomes soaked, one should cover it over again.
If the wind blows the upper covering away, one should weigh it down with wood or stones.
If one fears that cattle, sheep, or other livestock will eat the straw used for the covering, one should plaster it with mud.
"Upon the mud, he should provide a door for that [wall].
He drew images of dragons and snakes beside the door. The Buddha said:
"One should not make such images; I allow you to make images of grapevines or lotus flowers."
He wished to make an image of a flower above the door; [the Buddha] permitted him to do so.
He made an image of an army; the Buddha said:
"One should not make such [images]; one should use purple, vermilion, or five kinds of colors."
He relied upon the liberation from form.
The Buddha said:
"One should not rely [upon it]."
Those elder monks who were aged and ill, as well as those who had traveled from afar, found themselves unable to lean against anything and were physically distressed. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to use grass, leaves, tree bark, or any one of the ten types of robes to place behind your back and lean against it."
That bhikṣu slept during the day with his side pressed to the ground in a place where many people were present. When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized him together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, claim to be awakened, yet they sleep during the day with their sides pressed to the ground?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
Regarding those elder bhikṣus who were aged, infirm, and had traveled from afar, who did not sleep during the day and were utterly exhausted, the Buddha said:
"Listen: enter the room, close the door, and sleep.
He then sent the sick person away. The Buddha said:
"One should not send away a sick person, nor should one depart [from them]."
Those monks of the group of six, feigning illness, did not yield their places to the senior monks. When the other monks reported this to the Buddha, the Buddha said, "One should not act in this way.
Those sick monks resided in large upper chambers on the upper stories, defiling them with excrement, urine, spittle, filth, and foul odors.
The Buddha said:
"A sick bhikṣu should not dwell in a large room on an upper story; he should dwell in a small room, or have a separate small hut built."
That sick bhikṣu was unable to go to the place for defecation and urination. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to dig a pit near [the dwelling] to establish a place for defecation and urination.
If he is unable to leave the room, I allow him to place a toilet vessel within the house."
If he was unable to rise and leave the bed, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to bore a hole in the bed so that the vessel may be placed beneath it.
He spat in the room, defiling the floor; the Buddha said:
"It should not be so. As that senior, elderly, and sick bhikṣu frequently rose up and became exhausted, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a spittoon."
He picked lice from a place where many people were staying and threw them on the ground.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
Because that senior, elderly, and sick bhikṣu rose repeatedly to discard the lice and became utterly exhausted, the Buddha said:
"When listening [to the sound], one should place inside [the ear] an object such as a piece of felt, cotton cloth, a worn-out rag, or cotton wool.
If lice crawl out, one should make a tube to contain them."
He used precious gems to make the tube. The Buddha said:

"One should not use precious gems to make a tube. It is permitted to use ivory, bone, iron, copper, lead and tin, sugarcane, bamboo, reed, or wood to make a tube. If lice emerge, one should make a lid to block them."
He used precious gems to make the stopper. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems; one should use ivory, bone, or even wood.
If there is no place to fix it, one should tie it to the interior of the bed leg with thread."
At that time, when the monks were assigning rooms, a certain monk received a dilapidated room.
He thought to himself, "Perhaps I will have to repair it," and so he did not take possession of it. The Buddha said:
"It should be accepted; it should be repaired according to one's capacity.
When he wished to repair the room, the Buddha said:
"I allow that all necessary implements for the repair be provided."

At that time, the World-Honored One traveled through the human realm from Vaiśālī, passing through the country of Vatsa and arriving at Śrāvastī, accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada heard that the World-Honored One had come from there to Śrāvastī; he immediately mounted his carriage to go out and welcome him. Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, he alighted from the carriage and proceeded forward to where the Buddha was, prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet and then withdrawing to stand to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached various teachings to the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada to instruct and transform him, causing him to attain great joy. Having done so, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation for tomorrow's meal and stay overnight at the Jetavana."
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation, Anāthapiṇḍada paid homage and departed for his home. That very night, he prepared various kinds of rich and delicious food and drink; at dawn, he went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had arrived.
The World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the refectory where he took a seat.
Anāthapiṇḍada personally served various kinds of exquisite foods, making offerings to the Buddha and the assembly of monks until they were fully satisfied.
Having set aside his bowl, taken a golden pitcher, and offered water, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I offer this Jeta Grove to the World-Honored One; I only pray that you will accept it."
The Buddha said,
"Householder! You may take this garden and offer it to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four directions."
Why is this so? Householder!

If these—the garden of the World-Honored One, the garden’s property; the dwellings, the dwellings’ property; the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case—are indeed a stūpa and temple, then no one among all the devas, worldlings, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, Māras, or Brahmās can make use of them.
He then offered the garden to the Buddha and the Sangha of the four quarters according to those instructions, saying:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion, will accept it.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a verse of exhortation:
"Those who plant orchards and fruit trees, or provide bridges and boats,
who give springs and wells in the wilderness, as well as gifts of dwellings—
for such people as these, merit increases day and night."
"By always maintaining the precepts according to the Dharma, one will later be reborn in a good realm.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍada prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew, and sat to one side. The World-Honored One, through countless skillful means, preached the Dharma in various ways to instruct and transform him, causing him to attain joy. Having heard the Dharma and being filled with joy, Anāthapiṇḍada prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and departed.
At that time, oxen and sheep entered the Jeta Grove without any restriction.
The Buddha said, "Dig a moat to form a barrier.
When the elder bhikṣus who were old and sick were unable to cross it while walking, the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted to build a bridge.
But they did not know how it should be made. [The Buddha said:
"It should be made with planks or wood, or by installing ropes and cords to connect them."
When an elder bhikṣu who was old and infirm fell to the ground while crossing a bridge, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to install ropes on both sides so that he may hold them and cross safely. If he still falls to the ground despite holding the ropes, you should install railings on both sides."
If the moat is not secure, one should construct a double-layered fence.

If there is no gate, a gate is permitted; if the fence is not sturdy, one should build a wall. All materials required for constructing the wall should be provided, and if it remains insecure, a multi-storied pavilion should be built.
At that time, Prince Jeta wished to construct a grand and costly main gate for the Jetavana; the Buddha said, "I permit you to build it.
At that time, the trees in the Jetavana grove were not fine; the Buddha said:
"I allow you to plant three kinds of trees:
flowering trees, fruit trees, and leafy trees.
At that time, a bhikṣu well-known among the senior monks returned to the Jetavana after eating at Śrāvastī and suffered from the heat; the Buddha said:

"It is permitted to use grass or tree leaves as a screen; among the ten kinds of robes, it is permitted to use any one of them as a screen to provide shade. If it remains hot despite this, one should plant three kinds of trees along the sides of the stairways and paths, as described above."
At that time, the Jetavana was far from water, so [the Buddha] said, "I allow you to construct canals to channel water.
Concerned that the canals might collapse, the Buddha said, "I allow you to protect them with grass; if the grass rots and decays, you should further protect them with bricks, stones, or wood."
If one further constructs a well, everything necessary for constructing the well is permitted to be given.
If the vessel used for drawing water from the well breaks, it is permitted to press wood around the four sides to hold the vessel within it.
If it is intentionally damaged, it is permitted to store it in a bag made of woolen cloth.
If it is intentionally damaged again, it is permitted to make one out of leather.
If the cord breaks, it is permitted to make one out of leather.
If a bhikṣu is unaccustomed to working and suffers from hand pain, he is permitted to turn the wheel by pulling it.
If the holes in the wheel are damaged, he is permitted to make them with iron.
If he suffers because water flows back into the well, he should block the four sides with stones, bricks, or wood.
If one is troubled by mud at the washing place, one should install bricks or stones.
If one is troubled by small children falling into the well, one should construct a railing or barrier using wood, tiles, bricks, or stones.
"If the rope of a water-drawing vessel breaks and it falls into the well, one should retrieve it with a hook.
Since there was no place to secure the rope for the well, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct a frame near the edge of the well and place [the vessel] upon it."
At that time, there was no bathhouse at Jetavana. The Buddha said, "I allow you to build one.
They did not know how to construct it.
The Buddha said:
"I permit it to be square, circular, or octagonal.
He built it in front of his house; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so; it should be made in a secluded corner.
They complained that the bathhouse was cold, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a door."
Concerned about the smoke, [the Buddha said,] "I allow you to open a hole at the top.
Concerned about the darkness, [he said,] "One should open windows.
Concerned about the mud, [he said,] "One should make a bathing platform using stone bricks or wood."
Being troubled by mud staining his feet, [the Buddha said,] "The ground should be paved with stone bricks.
If the wooden floorboards are uneven, they should be chiseled into a 'dog-tooth' pattern so that they press against one another.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus acted such that when the Elder desired coolness, he would close the door, and when he desired warmth, he would open it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should be given according to what the Saṃgha desires.
Those six groups of bhikṣus entered the bathhouse first and sat in the best places; when the elders arrived later, they found no place to sit.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"They should sit according to their respective places.
When that senior monk did not enter his place because it was empty, the Buddha said:
“The next person in the seat should sit.
[If] smoke burns the face, “one may use a screen.
If one suffers from heat in the head, “one may cover it.”
Suffering from heat on his back, [the Buddha] said, "I permit you to cover it.
If the body is foul-smelling, he said, "I permit you to wash it with mud.
That bhikṣu was hesitant and did not dare to put perfume into the mud; the Buddha said:
"Listen. The ground in the bathhouse is hot; you should sprinkle it with water to cool it.
He bathed with a layperson and they looked at each other's backsides, saying, "So-and-so’s is long," or "So-and-so’s is coarse."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not bathe together with laypeople; however, if one praises the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha, bathing is permitted.
At that time, the bhikṣus placed their robes on the open ground, and they were soaked by the rain. The Buddha said:
“Listen: [the robes] may be hung on the wall, on pegs shaped like dragon’s teeth, or on a clothes rack.
They were troubled by the smoke blackening and soiling the robes;
the Buddha said, “I allow you to construct a separate room for the robes.”
When those who were naked rubbed their bodies against one another who were also naked, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When those who were naked rubbed their bodies against those who were not naked, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done. Those who do not go naked were apprehensive and hesitant, and did not dare to rub their bodies against those who go naked. The Buddha said, "I permit it."
Those naked ascetics shaved the hair of other naked ascetics; the Buddha said, "This should not be done.
Those naked ascetics shaved the hair of those who were not naked; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When those who were not naked shaved the hair of those who were naked, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He chewed a tooth-stick while naked; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He washed his hands, feet, and face while naked; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He ate while naked; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
They defecated and urinated while naked; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
They paid homage to one who was naked; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When those who were naked prostrated to those who were not naked, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
When those who do not go naked prostrated to those who go naked, the Buddha said,
"This should not be done. When they traveled on the road while going naked, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He walked back and forth naked; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
At that time, the bathhouse at Jetavana was far from water. [The Buddha said: “I allow you to dig a well by opening a channel, as described above.
If the water is scarce, one should construct a large channel.
They suffered hand pain while drawing water; [the Buddha said: “I allow you to install a waterwheel (*ārgha*)."
He did not know where to store the water.
[The Buddha said,] "I allow you to place it in a jar.
When it rained, he suffered from his clothes becoming soaked. [The Buddha said,] "I allow you to build a shelter over the well."
At that time, a bhikṣu was drawing water while naked; seeing a woman approaching, he felt ashamed and sat down. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."

At that time, some bhikṣus were bathing in the water of springs, canals, or ponds. The nāga girls became angry and resentful. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so."

It is permitted to bathe while covered by four kinds of obstructions: if there is an obstruction of walls, an obstruction of trees or grass, an obstruction of water over the body, or an obstruction of clothing over the body.
Regarding those who bathe in the three upper locations, if there is anything required, they are permitted to take and give to one another.
As for covering the body with clothing, everything must be in accordance with the Dharma.
One may undertake the management of bathing facilities; if the water is scarce, one should enlarge the openings for water flow.
If one fears that too much water leaks out below, one should construct a smaller leakage outlet at the side.
The bhikṣus fell ill from bathing in the open air. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct separate small bathhouses.
If you suffer from mud on the ground, I allow you to install bricks, stones, wood, gravel, or sand. If there is old mud, you should drain away the water."
At that time, the bhikṣus were warming water in an open area when rain fell and soaked their robes.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to build a house for warming water.
At that time, the bhikṣus placed firewood on the bare ground, and it was soaked by the rain. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to build a firewood shed.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who watched over food being cooked in the open air; when it rained, his robes became wet and he soaked the lay assistants' food, utensils, and vessels. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to build a kitchen for pure food."
At that time, when the bhikṣus were invited by laypeople to receive food and drink and went accordingly, they encountered rain on the road which soaked their robes. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to establish separate monasteries within the vicinity of a village."

At that time, some bhikṣus were defecating or urinating in an open area. A woman saw them, and the bhikṣus rose in haste; because they had not finished defecating, they subsequently suffered from illness.
The Buddha said, "I permit the construction of latrines.
They established one large place for defecation, and many people would stand waiting there when it was in use. The Buddha said:
"One should construct many separate areas.
If one can see through the doorway, a screen should be made; if they look at one another, a partition should be erected.
When those senior, elderly, or infirm bhikṣus fell to the ground upon rising from defecation or urination, it was permitted to install railings and supports along the sides.
In various places, he would wipe away excrement—whether on a corner of a wall, upon a stone, or upon grass. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; I allow you to construct a separate place for washing."
He urinated here and there, defiling the ground with mud. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
One should urinate in a single spot at the edge."
"If you still have concerns about being defiled by mud, you should construct a separate place for urination.
[The monks] did not know how to construct it.
The Buddha said:

"Listen: dig a pit in the ground, place stones at the bottom, and set a jar upon them. Open the bottom of the jar so that it leaks downward, and fix wooden supports on both sides of the jar. If you are concerned about foul odors, cover it with a lid."

At that time, the bhikṣus were walking in meditation in the open air. There were snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes; those bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire became terrified upon seeing them. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct elevated walkways for walking in meditation."
Not knowing how to construct it,
the Buddha said:
"Erect pillars below and install wooden planks above to form a walkway."
"If you suffer from wind, rain, or exposure to the sun, you are permitted to build a roofed shelter.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
The group of six bhikṣus lit fires to warm themselves inside a well-painted and finely decorated room, causing smoke to blacken the room and defile the bedding. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done. At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the cold during the winter months. [The Buddha said: "I permit you to light a fire on the open ground to warm yourselves.

They suffered from the cold on their backs while sitting on the open ground. [The Buddha said: "I permit you to light a fire outside until the smoke has vanished, then bring the charcoal inside the house."
"If it cannot be accommodated there, you should build a separate hall for lighting fires.
[The monks] did not know how to construct it.
The Buddha said:
“They made it square, or they made it round, or they made it long.
They installed the *hu-dian* (fire-hearth) in various places. The Buddha said:
“One should not do so.”
"It is permitted that a fire-pit be placed in the center of the hall.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained fire-pits with wheels; the Buddha said, "It is permitted to keep them."
"Who should be responsible for carrying this out?
The Buddha said,
"A śrāmaṇera, or a bhikṣu, or a monastery attendant."
That bhikṣu was not accustomed to blowing on a fire; by blowing on it, he became ill. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to blow with a tube.
He made a tube out of precious materials. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems.
It is permitted to use ivory, horn, bone, or [vessels] made of copper, iron, śara-grass tubes, bamboo, reeds, or wood."
If the mouth of the tube is scorched, it is permitted to affix an iron plate.
If firewood or embers fall into the stove, one should reach up to retrieve them;
if one fears scorching the hands, one should make tongs.
He used precious gems to make the tongs. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
I allow [tongs] to be made from bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, or wood."
"If one suffers from a burning sensation in the head, it is permitted to apply copper or iron plates.
If one wishes to collect fire to form a braid or to kindle a fire, "one should prepare a fire-pit and place the fire therein."
"If you fear the fire will go out, cover it with ashes.
At that time, the bhikṣus washed their faces, hands, and feet with cold water and suffered from the chill.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to wash with warm water."
Not knowing what "warmth" meant,
the Buddha said:
"A water jar filled with water is placed beside a fire."
If there are many *karakas* (water jars) or if they cannot fit near the fire, one should place three *tri-kaṭaka* (tripods) and set a jar filled with water upon them to warm it.
If the jar is large and obstructs the fire, one should suspend it by means of a rope.
"If the cord burns, place the cord in a tube; if the tube burns, coat it with clay.
When pouring water, the tube broke. The Buddha said, "One should take the water using another vessel."
When pouring water from a water flask, one often suffers from spilling the water; therefore, a water-spout tube should be made.
If the hanging cord breaks, an iron ring or button should be fixed at the top.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the cold while washing their feet during the winter months; the Buddha said:
"One should place the foot-basin and foot-washing vessel inside the house to wash one's feet, and one should provide whatever is required for washing the feet.

At that time, a bhikṣu rose early, anointed his feet with oil, and entered a village to beg for food. A woman received him by prostrating at his feet; her hands were smeared with oil as she took the bhikṣu’s bowl. When other bhikṣus saw this, they looked upon it with disapproval.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not rise early and enter a village to beg for alms with oil smeared on one's feet.
When the bhikṣus' feet became cracked and split, [the Buddha] said: "I allow you to smear oil on the heels and the soles of the feet, extending it to the toes and their digits."
At that time, the community of monks obtained a single-story dwelling, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to reside there.
Then the World-Honored One traveled from the kingdom of Magadha to the city of Khaṇḍava.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus had halls decorated with embroidered images of male and female figures for the World-Honored One. The Buddha said, "This should not be done.
It is permitted to use other various colors featuring the patterns of birds and beasts."
At that time, the community of monks obtained a two-storied building with two rooms and a single door; the Buddha said, "I permit you to dwell there.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Ānanda obtained a separate room, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to keep it.
At that time, Rāhula was staying in the Nāḷika grove.
At that time, there was a householder in Nāḍika who, without being exhorted by anyone, spontaneously resolved to build a dwelling to offer to Rāhula.

After Rāhula had stayed in this dwelling, he traveled abroad. When the householder heard that Rāhula had stayed in the dwelling and was now traveling abroad, he then offered the dwelling to the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm in Magadha and arrived at the Nāḷikera Grove, where he spread his seat and sat down.

Then Rāhula, hearing that a householder had offered a dwelling to the community of monks, went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In Nāḷikera there is a householder who, without anyone encouraging or exhorting him, has spontaneously resolved to build a dwelling and offer it to me.”
"After I have stayed in this room and departed to wander among the people, the householder will subsequently offer the room to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha told Rāhula:
