"I permit you to go to that householder and say to him:"
"Have you perhaps seen me do anything blameworthy—anything impure or contrary to the dharma of a śramaṇa, whether in speech or in bodily conduct?
Then Rāhula, having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, went to the householder and related the above words to him in detail. The householder replied:
"I do not see in you anything that should be censured, nor any conduct unbecoming of a śramaṇa, whether in speech or in physical action, that is impure.
Then Rāhula went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"I have fully explained to the householder what was previously commanded.
The householder replied to me, saying:
'I do not see any matter in you that is worthy of reproach; nor do I see any lack of purity in your śramaṇa-dharma, whether in your speech or in your physical conduct.'"
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:
"Listen well! This is an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous abiding."

There is giving according to the Dharma, receiving according to the Dharma, and dwelling according to the Dharma. What is giving not according to the Dharma, receiving not according to the Dharma, and dwelling not according to the Dharma?

Suppose there is a person who, out of personal delight, builds a dwelling and gives it first to one person and then to many people; this is giving not according to the Dharma, receiving not according to the Dharma, and dwelling not according to the Dharma.
Having given to one person, to give again to the Saṃgha is likewise.
Having given to one person, if the Saṃgha has split into two factions, to give to the faction with which one belongs is likewise.
Having given to one person, giving to another group is likewise [unlawful].

Or if there is someone who, out of personal preference, builds a dwelling and gives it first to many individuals and then to the Saṃgha, this constitutes an unlawful gift, an unlawful acceptance, and an unlawful residence.
If, after giving to many people, the Saṃgha has split into two factions, the same applies to what is given to those within one's own faction.
Likewise, it is the same when, after giving to many people, one gives to a different faction.
Having given to many people, one gives to a single person in the same way.
Having constructed a dwelling and given it to the Saṃgha, one then transfers it to others in the same way.
Having constructed a dwelling and given it, one gives it to those of the same faction in the same way.
It is likewise when, having constructed a dwelling, one gives it to another sect;
this is an unrighteous gift, an unrighteous acceptance, and an unrighteous residence.
What is a righteous gift, a righteous acceptance, and a righteous residence?

Suppose there is someone who delights in building a dwelling for himself; giving it to one person constitutes a gift according to the Dharma, a reception according to the Dharma, and a residence according to the Dharma.
It is the same when giving to many people, to the Saṃgha, or to both divisions of the Saṃgha.
"This is what it means to give according to the Dharma, to receive according to the Dharma, and to abide according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering among the people of Kāśī together with five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, there were four elder bhikṣus in the kingdom of Kevaddha: Aśvajit, Punabbasu, Baṇḍu, and Rohaṇa.

When these four bhikṣus heard that the World-Honored One, accompanied by five hundred followers, was traveling through the human realm and would soon arrive at Kevaddha, they thought, "The World-Honored One has two disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana; when they come here, we fear they will drive us out of this dwelling place."
"We would rather select the superior rooms for the World-Honored One, while dividing the remainder into four parts as our private property.
The monastery buildings and their furnishings shall constitute the portion for the first bhikṣu;
the jars, pots, cauldrons, axes, chisels, lampstands, and various other heavy items shall constitute the portion for the second bhikṣu."
The rope beds, wooden beds, large cushions, small cushions, bedding, and miscellaneous items constitute the share for the third monk;
the remaining timber, bamboo, grass, flowers, fruits, and leaves constitute the share for the fourth monk.
Then the four bhikṣus selected the superior room for the World-Honored One and remained there, while the rest were divided into four groups as described above.

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm among the people of Kāśī and arrived at Veṇugrāma, where he spread out his seat and sat down. He addressed Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana:
"Go and tell those resident bhikṣus: 'The World-Honored One has come to the kingdom of Kāśī together with five hundred bhikṣus; you should now prepare bedding and seating for the bhikṣus.'"
Having received the instruction of the World-Honored One, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to where the resident bhikṣus were and prepared bedding as they had been commanded.
Those bhikṣus replied:

"The World-Honored One is the Master of the Dharma; you may stay and reside as you please. We have already selected the superior rooms for the World-Honored One, and the remainder has been divided into four parts as mentioned above; there are no extra bedding materials for visiting bhikṣus."
Then Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
For this reason, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and addressed them, saying:

"These four portions of goods are the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters; they should not be divided, they should not be taken for personal use, and they should not be bought or sold. Furthermore, they are not to be sold by the Saṃgha, nor by a multitude of people, nor even by a single individual."

If that monk, whether as a community, a group of many, or a single person, takes it for himself, divides it, or sells or buys it, it does not constitute taking for oneself, it does not constitute division, and it does not constitute selling or buying; he commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
What are the goods belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters?

These include the monastery and its appurtenances, as well as the furnishings of each individual cell; this is the first category of goods belonging to the Sangha of the four quarters. They must not be divided, they must not be appropriated for personal use, and they must not be sold or purchased. Whether by the Sangha, by a large group of people, or by a single individual, these may not be divided, may not be taken for private use, and may not be sold or purchased.

Whether it be the Saṃgha, a group of many people, or a single individual; whether by partitioning, taking for oneself, or buying and selling—if the partition is not effected, the taking for oneself is not effected, or the buying and selling is not effected, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
The second and third [divisions] are also like this.
In the fourth division, the fruits and leaves may be shared; however, if the flowers are offered to the Buddha, the remainder is as stated above.
*Sifen lü*, Fascicle 50.
The Four-Part Vinaya, Scroll Fifty-one; Part Two of the Fourth Division.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian and others.
This is the remainder of the *Vihāra-vastu*. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.
There was a bhikṣu who had constructed a private dwelling on the communal grounds of the Saṃgha. When a visiting elder bhikṣu arrived, he said to him:
"Arise and make way for the elder."
He replied, "It does not arise. He asked:
"Why is that? He replied, "It is my private chamber."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should tell him to get up.
If he gets up, that is well; if he does not get up, you should say to him:"
"To return the land to the Saṃgha is the only principle; there is no reason to incorporate monastic land into one's own possession.
A bhikṣu had completed a house that was not sturdy, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so."
He then spent his entire life working on a single dwelling, yet it was not completed in a timely manner. The Buddha said:

"This should not be done. If one is building an exceptionally grand and magnificent multi-storied hall, twelve years of work are permitted; for other buildings, the duration should be adjusted according to their size and scale."
That administrator always received the monastery’s permanent administrative quarters throughout the spring, summer, and winter. The Buddha said: "This should not be done.
It is permitted that at the conclusion of the three months of the summer retreat, they shall receive them according to the distribution for the senior monks."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was in charge of managing the monastery; he then took up residence in various quarters. The Buddha said: "You should not do so.
You should stay in one place for ninety days."
That administrator resided in the dwellings of many people—namely, the dining hall, the heated hall, and the walking hall—thereby leaving no place for visiting bhikṣus to stay. The Buddha said:
"This should not be done."
If the lower hall is a dwelling where many people reside, one should stay in the upper hall.
If the upper hall is a dwelling where many people reside, one should stay in the lower hall.
He performed minor maintenance tasks on the mud walls, such as patching cracks or leveling the surface, and then sought out the room of the administrator. The Buddha said: "You should not do so."
He appointed a novice (śrāmaṇera) as a monastery attendant (saṃghārāmika), who then served as a construction supervisor (karmadāna). The Buddha said:
"This should not be done. He then built a small hut and requested a room from the construction supervisor. The Buddha said: [This should not be done].
"It should not be so. If one constructs a dwelling that accepts rope beds and wooden beds, it is permitted to grant it to the *karmadāna* (the overseer of works).
He constructed a poor-quality dwelling and then demanded the room of the *karmadāna*. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. If a cell has been constructed that is well-adorned, perfumed with incense, and fully equipped with all necessities, it is permitted to give it as a cell.
At that time, there was a *karmadāna* bhikṣu who, having received a cell, passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom this room belonged and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It belongs to the Saṃgha."
At that time, there was an administrator monk who sent someone to inform the Saṃgha, requesting a cell.
After that monk had gone before the Saṃgha and requested a cell, the administrator monk passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom this room belonged.
The Buddha said:
"It belongs to the Saṃgha."
After the *karmadāna* bhikṣu had sent a messenger to the Saṃgha to request a cell, that messenger bhikṣu passed away.
The bhikṣus did not know to whom this cell should be given.
The Buddha said,
"It should be given to that person who was managing the affairs.
At that time, the person managing the affairs passed away during the summer retreat (varṣā), and the bhikṣus did not know to whom this room should be given.
The Buddha said, "It depends on the Saṃgha.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had built a hut but left it unfinished and departed. Then, a visiting bhikṣu spoke to the resident bhikṣu, saying:
"You may roof this room.
The senior bhikṣu replied,
"The one who built it should roof it."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"I allow you to construct a very large and heavy multi-storied gabled room, provided it is completed with a roof within six years; for smaller ones, act according to the circumstances and what is appropriate."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was building a hut, and another bhikṣu covered it over them.
Those two bhikṣus disputed with one another regarding who had first or last repaired the dwelling.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The one who acts first should be the first to be disciplined.
At that time, two bhikṣus were building a dwelling together and disputed over who should work first or later. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to alternate; the senior monk shall take the lead."
At that time, a *karmadāna* bhikṣu accepted a room under formal assignment during the summer retreat and then accepted another room as well. The Buddha said:
"This should not be done. One should treat the very room one is currently occupying as one's retreat dwelling."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
King Udayana was on intimate terms with Baddhālī, and the king invited him to stay in Kauśāmbī for the summer retreat.

At that time, after Upāli (Baddhalita) had accepted an invitation to observe the rains retreat, he heard that the monks observing the retreat at another location had obtained a great quantity of robes and requisites. He immediately went there, stayed for a short while, and then returned to Kauśāmbī.
When King Udayana heard this, he criticized him with disdain:

"How is it that after Bāḷananda accepted my invitation for the summer retreat, he heard that monks at another location had obtained a great abundance of summer retreat requisites, went there to stay, and only later returned here?"
When the bhikṣus heard this, they went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and rebuked the Śākya son Upananda, saying:

"How could you, having accepted an invitation to observe the summer rains retreat at Kauśāmbī, hear that the Saṃgha in another place had obtained a great quantity of requisites for the summer retreat, and then go there to stay before returning here again?"
Having rebuked him with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu observes the rains retreat in this place, and hears that the Saṃgha in another place has obtained a large quantity of robes and requisites for the summer retreat, and goes there to stay, he thereby loses his status in this place. If he stays there only briefly and then returns to this place, he likewise loses his status in that place."
At that time, the dwellings of the community of monks were old and dilapidated.
A certain householder said, "If you give these to me, I shall repair them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* should be performed as follows.
Within the assembly, one who is capable of performing the *karman* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its approval, let the Saṃgha now bestow this room upon the layperson [Name] for repair, with the bhikṣu [Name] acting as the overseer."
[The motion] is thus stated.
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
The Sangha now bestows this room upon the layperson [Name] for repair, with the bhikṣu [Name] acting as the overseer."
"Whichever elders among you consent to the Sangha granting this room for a certain layperson to repair and for a certain bhikṣu to oversee the work, remain silent; whoever does not consent, speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to allow the householder so-and-so to repair the dwelling and the bhikṣu so-and-so to oversee the construction.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, a *karmadāna* bhikṣu departed before the lodgings had been assigned. The other bhikṣus subsequently assigned the lodgings.
When the *karmadāna* bhikṣu returned, he asked, "Was my *karmadāna* lodging reserved for me?"
He replied, "No," and immediately censured the bhikṣus, saying:
"I had not yet been assigned a room when I went out, but later the rooms were assigned.
This would have been beneficial for me; why was no room given to me?
The bhikṣus did not know whether this constituted a valid assignment or not.
The Buddha said:
"It shall be accomplished.
You should wait for him to return; he, in turn, should entrust someone else to take it."

At that time, a bhikṣu in charge of monastery affairs was about to depart on a journey before the rooms had been assigned; he entrusted another bhikṣu with taking a room for him, but did not specify the location of the room.
Since that bhikṣu had many duties to attend to, the other bhikṣu did not know which room he should take for him.
After the bhikṣus had finished distributing the rooms, he returned from that place and asked the bhikṣus,
"Have the rooms been distributed yet? They replied:
"It has already been divided.
"Will you take a room for me? He replied:
"No. He then reproached him, saying:
"Before the rooms had been assigned, I went abroad and entrusted another bhikṣu to take a room for me."
"I am of benefit to him, yet he does not give me a room.
The bhikṣus did not know whether this constituted a valid [assignment] or not.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding the constituent parts:
one should wait for the return [of the assigner], and he too should point it out, saying:
'Take such-and-such a room.'"
After that monk in charge of construction affairs had taken a room, he later received a superior room during the distribution of rooms and consequently abandoned his previous one.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
"It should be divided further from the senior monk; if there is no one to take it, it should be given.
That bhikṣu was doubtful and did not dare to take hold of the community's door-bolt or key, nor a staff, a ring, a peg, a horn ladle, a copper ladle, or a bathing bench. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to take them."
He did not dare move these items from this dwelling place to that one. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to move them.
There are five qualities by which one should not be appointed to distribute rice porridge for the Saṃgha; even if appointed, one should not distribute it:

If there are those who possess attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion, and who do not know what has already been distributed and what remains undistributed—possessing these five qualities, one should not be appointed to distribute rice gruel for the Sangha; nor, if already appointed, should they perform the distribution.
There are five qualities by which one should be appointed to distribute rice gruel for the Saṃgha:
being without attachment, without aversion, without fear, without delusion, and knowing what has already been distributed and what has not yet been distributed.

One who possesses these five qualities should be appointed to distribute rice gruel for the Saṃgha; once appointed, they should cause the distribution of rice gruel, the distribution of light meals, and the distribution of *khajjaka* (solid foods). They may also be appointed to invite assemblies, to lay out bedding, to distribute bedding, to distribute bathing robes, and to distribute robes—both those that may be taken and those that may be given.
The appointment of bhikṣus as messengers and the appointment of śrāmaṇeras as messengers are all likewise.
There are five qualities by which one who distributes porridge for the Saṃgha enters hell as swiftly as a shot arrow:
having attachment, having aversion, having fear, having delusion, and not knowing what has been distributed and what remains undistributed.
If one divides the rice porridge with these five qualities, one enters hell as swiftly as an arrow shot.

There are five qualities for dividing the rice porridge by which one is born in heaven as swiftly as an arrow shot: being without attachment, without hatred, without fear, without delusion, and knowing what has been divided and what has not yet been divided.
If one possesses these five qualities while serving as the distributor of rice gruel for the Saṃgha, rebirth in heaven will be as swift as shooting an arrow;

this applies even to the appointment of a śrāmaṇera as an attendant, and so forth. The *Vastu on Dwellings* is thus completed. 2. The *Miscellaneous Vastu*, Part One. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vārāṇasī.
The five bhikṣus came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What kind of alms bowls should we carry?"
The Buddha said, "I allow you to use *kāra* bowls and *śāra* bowls.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who entered the midst of the Saṃgha for a meal but had no bowl. The Buddha said:
"Listen, let those sitting nearby hear this:
if there is such a bowl among the Sangha, lend it to him.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took a bowl into which a snake had spat venom; he used it for food without washing it, and after eating, he fell ill.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat without having washed one's bowl; it is permitted to eat after having washed it.
At that time, the hair of the bhikṣus had grown long, and the Buddha said:
"Listen: shaving is permitted, whether one shaves oneself or causes another to shave.
He required a razor, and [the Buddha] said, "Its manufacture is permitted.
He used precious materials to make the handle, and the Buddha said:
"It is not permitted to use precious materials; copper and iron are permitted.
Since it was difficult to grasp and protect a blade held bare-handed, the Buddha said:
"I permit the making of a sheath for the blade."
They used precious gems to make it. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems; I allow you to make it from bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, *śara* grass, bamboo, reeds, or wood."

He made a sheath for the knife, but he was troubled by its movement damaging the blade. [The Buddha said: "One should use an object to shield it—whether wool, cotton, or dog skin. If it falls, it should be sewn together with thread. If it is difficult to protect while holding it in the hand, one should place it in a pouch."
"If it comes out of the mouth of the bag, it should be tied with a cord.
If you fear losing it while carrying it by hand, tie it with a cord and sling it over your shoulder.
At that time, a bhikṣu’s knife blade was curled; [the Buddha] said, "I allow you to sharpen it on your hand."
If the blade becomes dull, it should be ground on a stone.
Fearing that the hand might slip while grasping the stone, one should place it within a knife-sheath.
If the blade is blunt, it should be scraped.
"If one scrapes oneself or instructs another to scrape," [the monks] required a scraping knife. The Buddha said,
"Its use is permitted."
At that time, a bhikṣu who had shaved his hair found it inconvenient as the loose hairs stuck to his robes.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to keep a hair-receptacle.
He did not know how to make one.

"I allow [the use of] a hair-comb made by weaving bamboo, or by bending wood into a coil and covering it with tree bark; or, among the ten kinds of robes, I allow each individual robe to be used as a hair-comb."
He placed his hair-keeping cloth on the ground and, when using it, laid it upon his knees; as mud soiled his robes, the Buddha said:
"You should not do this. I allow you to hang it with a cord or place it upon a peg."
At that time, a bhikṣu suffered from long nasal hairs. The Buddha said,
"I allow you to pull them out—
either pulling them out yourself or having someone else pull them out."
He required tweezers; the Buddha said, "Their use is permitted.
He made them out of precious materials; the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems to make them.
It is permitted to use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, or pewter to make them.
If one is troubled by the head of the tweezers breaking, it is permitted to attach iron to the head."
"It is difficult to protect with one's hands; I allow you to keep it in a razor case.
At that time, the monks' fingernails were long, so the Buddha said, "I allow you to clip them."
"Whether one cuts them oneself or has another cut them.
They required nail clippers; the Buddha said, "Their use is permitted."
They made them out of precious gems. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems; I allow the use of copper or iron.
Since it is difficult to hold and protect by hand, I allow making a tube to contain it."
He used precious gems to make the tube; the Buddha said, "One should not use precious gems.
It is permitted to use copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, bamboo, or wood."
"Since there is the problem of [the contents] leaking from the tube, you should make a lid to seal it.
He made the lid out of precious materials; the Buddha said, "One should not use precious materials."
It is permitted to use copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, bamboo, or wood.
If it becomes troublesome because it falls apart when kept in one place, it is permitted to place it inside a knife-sheath.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu with long nails who went to the house of a layperson. This bhikṣu was handsome in appearance; when the laywoman saw him, she became infatuated with him and said to the bhikṣu:
"Do such and such a thing with me."
The bhikṣu said: "Sister! Do not speak such words;
it is not according to our Dharma that we should do so."
The woman said: "If you do not comply with me, I shall tear open my own body and face with my fingernails.
When my husband returns, I shall say to him:"
“That bhikṣu summoned me and commanded me to do such a thing; I did not comply with him, so he then used his fingernails to scratch and tear my body and face like this.
When that bhikṣu heard this, he was filled with shame and fear, and immediately fled from that house in great haste.
The bhikṣu also went out, and her husband likewise entered from outside. The wife immediately scratched and tore at her own body and face, saying to her husband:
"The bhikṣu called me and urged me to do such-and-such a thing; when I would not comply, he scratched and tore at my body and face."
Her husband immediately pursued the bhikṣu in haste, saying:
"You wished to violate my wife; when she would not comply, did you then tear at her body and face?"
The bhikṣu replied, "Householder, do not speak such words; according to our Dharma, it should not be so. He then said:
"How can you say, 'It should not be so,' when your fingernails are as long as this?"
He then struck the bhikṣu, who died immediately.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep long nails."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus trimmed their nails until they bled; the Buddha said, "You should not do so.
They then trimmed their nails into the shape of a half-moon; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He trimmed his nails so that their tips were pointed; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He polished his nails until they shone, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so.
He dyed his nails with colors, and the Buddha said:
"You must not do so," the Buddha said to the bhikṣus.
"You are deluded people!"
They avoided what was prescribed by me and instead performed other tasks.
[I] permitted the bhikṣus to trim their nails using a leather whetstone.
[The monks] did not know how long or short they should be trimmed. How much should be trimmed?
The Buddha said:
"They should be trimmed to a maximum length of one barley grain.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used scissors to trim their beards and hair. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He shaved his hair but did not shave his beard. The Buddha said, "One should shave both the hair and the beard."
He shaved his beard but did not shave his hair; the Buddha said, "One should shave both the beard and the hair.
He then plucked out his hair; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He kept his hair long, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so."
He twisted his mustache and made it stand up; the Buddha said, "You should not do so.
You foolish people!"
They avoided what was prescribed by me and instead performed other tasks.
From this day forward, you must shave off all hair and beard.
Those bhikṣus did not know how long the hair had to be before it should be shaved.
The Buddha said:
"The maximum length is two finger-breadths; if one shaves once every two months, this is the maximum length.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were combing their beards and hair, so the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He then smeared oil on his hair, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
The group of six bhikṣus painted their eyelids.
When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have many desires and are never satisfied; yet they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma"—
how can there be such a True Dharma?
It would be just like that of a layperson.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not paint the eyelids in this manner.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from eye pain, and the Buddha said:
"Listen to the various medicines.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus looked at their faces in a mirror, or looked at their faces in water, or rubbed objects against a wall to make it shine and reflect their faces.
At that time, the householders saw this and all together reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have many desires and are never satisfied.
They claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma"—
how can there be such a True Dharma?
It is like looking at one's face in a mirror, as if it were a white cloth.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so.
At that time, a bhikṣu suffered from facial sores, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted for other bhikṣus to apply medicinal ointment.
If one is alone in a room, it is permitted to use water or a mirror to reflect one's face while applying the ointment.
Regarding that bhikṣu’s grooming of his body and hair, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
That bhikṣu spat on his body and rubbed it; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He bathed in an open space, and when the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have many desires and are never satisfied;
yet they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, what true Dharma is there?
Bathing in the open air is just like those who wear white robes.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who thought to himself:
"I shall strike my own shoulders and arms to make them coarse and well-formed."
The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
He then formed this thought:
“[They] smear their bodies with incense for the sake of its fragrance.
The Buddha said, “You should not do so.”
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from the foul odor of their perspiration.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a scraper for removing sweat.
They made one out of precious materials; the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials.
It is permitted to use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, lead, tin, śara grass, bamboo, or wood to make them."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus fashioned a sweat-scraping blade with a head shaped like a razor, using it to scrape away sweat as well as body hair.
The Buddha said: "You should not do so."
"Furthermore, one should not keep such a knife.
At that time, a monk suffering from an ulcer washed the painful sore with coarse medicinal powder.
The Buddha said:

"It is permitted to use fine medicinal powders, fine mud, or leaves, flowers, and fruits as appropriate for the illness of a bhikṣu. It is also permitted to wash the various sores of a sick person, even those suffering from the stench of perspiration."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore earrings. The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus placed beads upon their earlobes. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When the group of six bhikṣus wore earrings, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
The group of six bhikṣus used palmyra leaves or lead and tin to fashion rings that stretched their earlobes wide; the Buddha said, "You should not do so.
Those same group of six bhikṣus then wrapped their earlobes; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
They then made waistbands of lead and tin; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He put a necklace around his neck; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He put bracelets on his arms and legs; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He then put on a finger-ring, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so."
He used five-colored threads to bind his armpits, waist, and arms;
the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He then wore finger-seals; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the city of Rājagṛha.
There were at that time six heterodox teachers who lived together with their disciples.
At that time, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa was accompanied by ninety thousand disciples;
Maskarin Gośālīputra was accompanied by eighty thousand disciples;
and so on, decreasing in this manner until Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta, who was accompanied by forty thousand disciples.

At that time, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha who was a disciple of the six teachers. Having obtained a large piece of sandalwood, he immediately fashioned it into a bowl, placed it inside a precious netted bag, erected a tall pole in the middle of his courtyard, and set it upon the top, proclaiming:
"If there is any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa in this city of Rājagṛha who is an arhat possessing supernatural powers, let him take this bowl and depart."
Then Pūraṇa Kāśyapa went to the householder’s place and said, “I am an arhat possessed of great supernormal powers; you may give this bowl along with its bag to me.”
The householder said, "If you are an arhat possessed of great supernatural power, I shall give it to you; you may go and take it.
He wished to take it, but had no means by which he could do so.
At that time, Makkhali Gosāla, Ajita Keśakambalin, Pakudha Kaccāyana, Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, and Nirgrantha Jñātiputra went to the householder’s place and spoke these words:
“We are arhats possessed of supernormal powers; you may give this bowl along with its bag to us.”
The householder said, "If you are an arhat possessing great supernormal powers, I shall give it to you; you may go and take it.
He wished to take it, but had no means by which he could do so.
At that time, Piṇḍola and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were sitting together upon a large rock. Piṇḍola said to Maudgalyāyana, "You are an Arhat;
the World-Honored One has prophesied that you are foremost in supernormal powers. You should go and fetch it."
Maudgalyāyana said, "I have never manifested supernatural powers before a layperson.
You are also an arhat possessed of great supernormal power; the World-Honored One has declared you to be foremost in the lion's roar. You should go and fetch it."

When Piṇḍola heard Maudgalyāyana’s words, he immediately joined the rocks together, leaped into the air, and circled the city of Rājagṛha seven times. The people of the country all fled east and west, crying out, "The rock is about to fall!"
At that time, the elder was in his upper chamber when he saw Piṇḍola from afar in the midst of the air; he immediately joined his palms in prostration and spoke these words:
"Take this bowl."
“Pindola! Pindola immediately took up his bowl. The elder spoke again:
“Stop for a moment.”
“Pindola! Pindola immediately lowered himself slightly and stood there.
Then the householder took the bowl from his hand, filled it with excellent food, and gave it to him.
At that time, Piṇḍola took the bowl and, using his supernormal power, departed through the air.

When the bhikṣus heard of this, among them were those with few desires and contentment, who practiced the dhūta austerities, delighted in training in the precepts, and possessed a sense of shame; they reproached Piṇḍola, saying:
"How could you manifest supernormal powers in the presence of laypeople?"
Then the bhikṣus went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and sat down to one side. They reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus; knowing [the answer] yet asking deliberately, he addressed Piṇḍola:
"Did you manifest supernatural powers before the layperson?"
He replied, "It is indeed so. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One rebuked Piṇḍola with countless skillful means:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not proper conduct, not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, not pure practice, and not a practice in accordance with the path—it is something that should not have been done.
Why did you manifest supernatural powers before laypeople, like a courtesan who displays herself before the multitude for the sake of half a coin?"
"You are just like this; for the sake of a wretched wooden bowl, you display supernormal powers before a layperson.
One should not display supernormal powers before a layperson; if one does so, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense."
A bhikṣu should not keep a sandalwood bowl; if he keeps one, he must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
If he obtains one that is already finished, it is permitted to break it up and distribute it among the other bhikṣus to be used as eye medicine.

At that time, when the various non-Buddhist practitioners heard that the śramaṇa Gautama had prohibited the bhikṣus from manifesting supernatural powers before laypeople, they concluded that the śramaṇa’s prohibition would never again be transgressed.
"We should now go to that place and say to him:
'You, Śramaṇa Gautama, claim for yourself to have attained Arhatship; we too are Arhats.
You claim for yourself to possess supernormal powers; we too possess supernormal powers.'"
"You claim to possess great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom.
Now let us together manifest superhuman powers; if the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one superhuman power, I shall manifest two;
if he manifests two, I shall manifest four."
If the śramaṇa Gautama manifests four superhuman states, I shall manifest eight;
if he manifests eight, I shall manifest sixteen;
if he manifests sixteen, I shall manifest thirty-two.
"If you manifest thirty-two [marks], I shall manifest sixty-four.
If what you manifest increases further, my manifestation shall likewise increase by double.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners proclaimed these words everywhere throughout the streets and alleys of the city:
“The śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess supernormal powers, yet I too possess supernormal powers;
he claims to possess great wisdom, yet I too possess great wisdom.”
"We now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in manifesting supernormal powers and superhuman dharmas.
If the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, whatever the śramaṇa Gautama manifests, we shall manifest double that amount."
At that time, there was a certain place within the city of Rājagṛha, a vast and level expanse of land.

Then that householder, taking with him many flowers, incense, necklaces, musical instruments, banners, food and drink, clothing, medicines, and bedding, intended to make offerings there to the non-Buddhist *Bhagavān*.

At that time, when the elder wished to take flowers to offer to the non-Buddhists, his hand entered the vessel but could not emerge. Whether he wished to take incense, flowers, necklaces, banners, streamers, music, food, drink, clothing, medicine, or bedding, as soon as he reached for them, his hand became stuck in the vessel and could not be withdrawn.
At that time, when the elder wished to take flowers to make an offering to the Buddha, whatever he took with his hand encountered no obstruction.
In this manner, whatever he took with his hand—even down to medicines and bedding—met with no obstruction.
He thought to himself:
"It is marvelous that the World-Honored One possesses such great supernormal power.
Then the householder addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One, together with the great assembly of bhikṣus, will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Seeing that the World-Honored One had granted his consent through silence, the elder came forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

Having returned to his home, he prepared various kinds of rich and delicious food throughout the night; then, at the clear dawn of the following day, he went to inform [the Buddha] that the time had arrived.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, proceeded to the house of that elder.

At that time, wherever the World-Honored One moved his feet, great powerful devas in the void scattered celestial māndārava flowers, sandalwood powder, and celestial *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses upon the traces of the Buddha’s path, while performing celestial music and singing praises to the Buddha.
At that time, as he followed the World-Honored One, the elder thought to himself:
"From where does this sound come? Does it emerge from the earth, or does it come from above?"
Looking up into the air, he saw from afar celestial *mandārava* flowers, even unto *puṇḍarīka* flowers, as well as celestial music remaining suspended in the sky; he then thought to himself:
"This sound does not emerge from the earth, but comes from above."
At that time, the World-Honored One arrived at the house of the elder and took his seat. When the various non-Buddhist practitioners heard of this, they thought to themselves:
"That elder has always supported us non-Buddhists; why is it that he now invites the Buddha and the Sangha for a meal?"
"I should now go there myself so that their provisions will become insufficient.
He then went to the house of the elder together with his retinue.
When the gatekeeper saw the various non-Buddhist practitioners arriving with their retinue, he immediately went to inform the elder, saying:
"Do you know? Now these various non-Buddhist practitioners have come with their retinues; should they be permitted to enter?
The householder replied:
"Do not allow him to enter.
The Buddha said,
"Elder, you may allow him to enter."
The householder addressed the Buddha, saying, "There are many followers of other paths; this place is narrow and cramped, and I fear it will not be sufficient to accommodate them.
The Buddha said:
"Please enter; there is sufficient space to accommodate you.
The elder spoke again:
"The number of outsiders is great, the seating is cramped, and the food and drink are limited."
"I originally prepared this offering for one thousand two hundred and fifty people; now I fear it will not suffice.
The Buddha told the elder, "Let him enter;
there is sufficient space to accommodate him, and the food and drink will be enough."
At that time, by means of his supernormal power, the World-Honored One caused the ground to become level, even, and vast, extending far to the east and west.
Then, countless hundreds of thousands of high seats appeared spontaneously; it was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
At that time, the World-Honored One was seated together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus as well as various non-Buddhists.

Then, that householder prepared various kinds of fine food to offer to the Buddha, the assembly of bhikṣus, and the non-Buddhists; when everyone had been fully satisfied and had set aside their bowls, he took a low seat and sat before the Buddha.

Then the World-Honored One, for the sake of the householder, taught the Dharma through countless skillful means, instructing and transforming him so that he attained joy. Having finished preaching the Dharma to the householder, he rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist teachers, together with their retinues, went to King Bimbisāra, joined their palms above their heads, and said:
"May the King always be victorious.
They addressed him, saying:
“The śramaṇa Gautama claims to be an arhat, and I too am an arhat;
the śramaṇa Gautama claims to possess supernormal powers, and I too possess supernormal powers;
the śramaṇa Gautama claims to have great wisdom, and I too have great wisdom.”
"We now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in the display of supernormal powers and superhuman attainments.
If the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, whatever the śramaṇa Gautama manifests, whether much or little, we shall double it all."
"Great King!
I now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in manifesting supernormal powers and superhuman dharmas.

At that time, King Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
“May the World-Honored One deign to compete with the non-Buddhists in manifesting supernormal powers and superhuman attainments!
The World-Honored One addressed the king, saying:
"Cease! I know the proper time myself; what should be manifested shall be manifested when the time is right.
Tomorrow I shall depart, according to the King's wishes."
On the following day, the World-Honored One departed from Rājagṛha together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
At that time, King Bimbisāra followed behind the World-Honored One, leading five hundred chariots laden with various kinds of fine foods.
At that time, when the various non-Buddhists heard that the World-Honored One had departed from Rājagṛha early in the morning, they said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has departed without being able to compete with us in supernormal powers."
"King Bimbisāra has provided five hundred wagons laden with various kinds of fine food for us, not for that Gautama Śramaṇa.
We should now follow him to wherever he goes, and call upon him there to compete with him in supernatural powers and superhuman feats."
He then followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, King Bimbisāra heard that early in the morning the Buddha had departed from Rājagṛha with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. The king followed behind the World-Honored One together with eighty-four thousand people; the Brahmakāyika devas, Śakra Devānām Indra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and countless hundreds of thousands of other celestial beings also followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One went to the city of Ujjayinī. The king of Ujjayinī was named Prasenajit. The various non-Buddhist practitioners from the kingdom of Magadha and those from Ujjayinī all went together to King Prasenajit’s residence, joined their palms above their heads, and praised him, saying:
“May Your Majesty be ever victorious!”
The śramaṇa Gautama claims for himself that he is an arhat, yet I too am an arhat;
he claims for himself that he possesses supernormal powers, yet I too possess supernormal powers;
he claims for himself that he possesses great wisdom, yet I too possess great wisdom.

"In the city of Rājagṛha, we sought to compete with him in supernatural powers and superhuman states, yet the śramaṇa Gautama was unable to compete with us in supernatural powers and superhuman states."
"We now wish to compete together in supernatural powers and superhuman feats; if the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, whatever the śramaṇa Gautama manifests, we shall double it all."
Then King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
"You may display supernatural powers and superhuman feats together with the various non-Buddhists.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to King Prasenajit:
"Stop! Do not do so!"
"I know the proper time; when it is appropriate to manifest [myself], I shall manifest.
Tomorrow I shall depart, according to the King's wish.
Then, at dawn the following day, the World-Honored One departed from Ujjayinī. King Prasenajit followed behind the World-Honored One with five hundred chariots, carrying various kinds of fine food.
When the various non-Buddhists heard that the World-Honored One had departed, they said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama was unable to compete with us in the supernormal powers and superhuman dharmas, and so he has gone away."
"The King has prepared five hundred chariots laden with food and drink for us, not for them; we shall follow you wherever you go and compete with him in supernatural powers and superhuman feats."
He immediately followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the World-Honored One was departing, set out together with eighty-four thousand people; King Prasenajit of Vārāṇasī set out together with seventy thousand people; and the great assembly of devas, including Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, surrounded by countless hundreds of thousands of attendants, followed behind the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One traveled to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī and stayed in the Gośṛṅga Park.

At that time, King Udayana was reigning. The non-Buddhist practitioners from the kingdom of Magadha, those from the kingdom of Ujjayinī, and those from Kauśāmbī all went to King Udayana, joined their palms above their heads, and praised him, saying:
"May the King always be victorious!"
He spoke these words: "Śramaṇa Gautama!
You claim for yourself that you are an arhat, and I too am an arhat."
They claim for themselves that they possess great supernormal powers, and I too possess great supernormal powers;
they claim for themselves that they possess great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom.

In the kingdoms of Magadha and Ujjayinī, we sought to compete with him in supernormal powers and superhuman attainments; however, the śramaṇa Gautama was unable to compete with me in supernormal powers and superhuman attainments and departed.
"We now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in supernatural powers and superhuman dharmas: if the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, according to however many he manifests, we shall double them all."
Then King Udayana went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"You may compete with those non-Buddhists in a contest of supernatural powers and superhuman feats.
The Buddha said to the king, "Stop!"
"Stop! I know the proper time myself; I shall manifest it when it is appropriate.
I shall depart tomorrow; let it be as the King wishes. Then, at dawn the following day, he departed.
At that time, King Udayana followed behind the World-Honored One with five hundred chariots carrying various kinds of food and drink.
When the non-Buddhist practitioners heard that the World-Honored One was departing, they said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has fled because he was unable to compete with us in supernormal powers and superhuman dharmas."
"King Udayana has provided five hundred chariots laden with food and drink for us, not for them.
We shall now follow wherever he goes and together demonstrate our supernormal powers and superhuman feats."
He then followed behind the World-Honored One.

At that time, King Bimbisāra was accompanied by eighty-four thousand people; King Ujjayinī was accompanied by seventy thousand people; and King Udayana was accompanied by sixty thousand people, all following behind the World-Honored One.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and a great assembly of hundreds of thousands of devas followed behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One proceeded to the Nyagrodha Grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and stayed there.

At that time, King Brahmadatta of Kapilavastu, who was the Buddha’s half-brother, was visited by various non-Buddhist practitioners from the kingdom of Magadha, those from Ujjayinī, those from Kauśāmbī, and those from the kingdom of Kapilavastu. They all went together to King Brahmadatta’s presence and, placing their palms together above their heads, said:
"May the King always be victorious!"
He addressed King Brahmadatta, saying:
"The śramaṇa Gautama claims for himself that he is an arhat, and I am also an arhat;
he claims for himself that he possesses great supernormal powers, and I also possess great supernormal powers."
"You claim to possess great wisdom, and I too possess great wisdom.

In the kingdoms of Magadha, Ujjayinī, and Kauśāmbī, I contended with the śramaṇa Gautama regarding supernormal powers and states beyond the human; yet the śramaṇa Gautama was unable to contend with me regarding supernormal powers and states beyond the human, and so he departed."
"We now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in the manifestation of supernormal powers and dharmas that transcend those of men; if the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, whatever the śramaṇa Gautama manifests, whether much or little, we shall double it all."
Then King Brahmadatta went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, sat to one side, and said to the Buddha:
“I pray, World-Honored One,
that you will manifest supernatural powers and the dharmas that transcend those of men.”
The Buddha said to the king: "Stop! Stop!"
"I know the time when it is appropriate to manifest; I shall manifest it when the time comes.
Tomorrow I shall depart from the kingdom of Kapilavastu; you may act according to the King's wishes.
At dawn the following day, the World-Honored One departed.
At that time, King Brahmadatta immediately loaded five hundred chariots with various kinds of food and drink and followed behind the World-Honored One.
When the various non-Buddhist practitioners heard that the World-Honored One was departing, they spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa Gautama!..."
Unable to compete with me in supernormal powers or in qualities surpassing those of men, he abandoned us and departed.
King Brahmadatta loaded five hundred wagons with food and drink for our sake, not for the śramaṇa Gautama.
"Now we shall follow wherever he goes and challenge him to compete in supernatural powers and superhuman feats.
He then followed behind the World-Honored One with his retinue.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Buddha was departing, immediately set out with eighty-four thousand people; King Prasenajit with seventy thousand; King Udayana with sixty thousand; and King Brahmadatta with fifty thousand, all following behind the World-Honored One.
Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings, together with their retinues of countless hundreds of thousands of devas, followed behind the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm from Kapilavastu and arrived at the Jeta Grove in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, where he took up residence.

At that time, King Prasenajit was ruling in Śrāvastī. Then the non-Buddhist practitioners from the kingdom of Magadha, the non-Buddhist practitioners from the city of Ujjayinī, the non-Buddhist practitioners from Kauśāmbī, the non-Buddhist practitioners from Kapilavastu, and the non-Buddhist practitioners from Śrāvastī all went to King Prasenajit, joined their palms above their heads, and said to him:
"May Your Majesty be ever victorious!"
He spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa Gautama claims for himself that he is an arhat, yet I too am an arhat;
he claims for himself that he possesses great supernormal powers, yet I too possess great supernormal powers."
They claimed for themselves, "We possess great wisdom; we too possess great wisdom.

We wished to compete with them in supernormal powers and states beyond the human realm in the kingdoms of Magadha, Ujjayinī, Kauśāmbī, and Kapilavastu, yet they departed without being able to compete with us in supernormal powers and states beyond the human realm.
"We now wish to compete with the śramaṇa Gautama in supernormal powers and states beyond the human realm; if the śramaṇa Gautama manifests one, we shall manifest two;
in this manner, according to the number he manifests, we shall double it all."

King Prasenajit went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and reported the circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!”
"I pray that you will manifest supernatural powers and the qualities that transcend those of ordinary men. The Buddha said to the king: "Stop!
"Stop! I myself know the proper time; when it is appropriate to manifest [these powers], I shall manifest them.
During the fifteenth day of the winter month, from the first day until the fifteenth, the Tathāgata shall manifest supernormal powers that transcend the human state."
"Great King!
If you wish to behold the Tathāgata manifesting supernormal powers and qualities surpassing those of men, then come.
At that time, there was a certain place in Śrāvastī where the ground was level, even, and vast; the World-Honored One went there, prepared his seat, and sat down.
At that time, Brahmā, King of Devas, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee upon the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, the World-Honored One, saying:
"I shall prepare a high seat for the World-Honored One."
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"Cease! I myself know the proper time."
Śakra, Lord of the Devas; the Four Great Kings; King Bimbisāra; King Prasenajit; King Udayana; King Brahmadatta; King Prasenajit; Queen Mallikā; the householder Liśataka; and Pūraṇa each spoke thus:
“I shall prepare a high seat for the World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told them: "Cease for now!
I myself know the proper time."

At that time, among the householders, those who had faith in the non-Buddhist outsiders prepared seats for them worth hundreds of thousands of coins; meanwhile, those who had faith in, delighted in, and respectfully made offerings to the World-Honored One prepared seats in succession from the first day until the fifteenth day.
At that time, when the World-Honored One looked toward the east, countless hundreds of thousands of seats appeared spontaneously; it was likewise so in the south, west, and north.
In the center was a natural lion throne made of the seven treasures, upon which the Tathāgata sat.

At that time, the entire great assembly took their seats. Then, a donor whose turn it was to provide offerings presented a *yōji* (tooth-stick) to the Buddha. After the World-Honored One accepted and chewed it, he discarded it behind him; it immediately became a great tree, its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves spreading out luxuriantly and flourishing.

At that time, when the great assembly witnessed such supernatural power of the World-Honored One, they all rejoiced greatly at this unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

Then, observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state and conceived a mind of weary detachment, the World-Honored One immediately employed countless skillful means to preach the Dharma in various ways, causing them to attain great joy.
At that time, hundreds of thousands of people on the seats were distanced from dust and freed from defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the first day upon which the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers and transformations.

On the second day, these tree flowers blossomed, endowed with perfect color and fragrance; the tree blossoms scattered everywhere among the great assembly, accumulating up to the knees. The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the rest of the great assembly all smelled this fragrance.

At that time, when the great assembly witnessed such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, they all rejoiced greatly at this unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

Observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state and given rise to a mind of weary detachment, the World-Honored One immediately employed countless skillful means to preach the Dharma in various ways so that they might attain joy. At that moment, hundreds of thousands of people seated there distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
This was the second day on which the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers and transformations.

On the third day, the fruits of the trees spontaneously produced color, fragrance, and flavor; these fruits fell to the ground of their own accord without being shaken and remained unbroken. The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the great assembly all partook of them together.

When this great assembly saw such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, they were all filled with great joy at having experienced what they had never before; a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state of weary detachment, immediately preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the third day on which the World-Honored One manifested supernatural powers and transformations.

At that time, there was a donor who had prepared offerings for the fourth day; he presented water to the World-Honored One, who then took a handful of water and cast it upon the ground. By the Buddha’s supernatural power, it immediately became a great pond.

The water is pure and free from all dust and impurities; drinking it brings no harm. It is adorned with various flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), night-blooming lilies (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka)—and with diverse kinds of birds such as ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, tortoises, turtles, fish, and otters, all creatures of the aquatic realm.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such miraculous transformations through the World-Honored One’s supernormal powers, they all rejoiced greatly at this unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) arose within them.

Then, observing that the great assembly had experienced this unprecedented state and developed a mind of weary detachment, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣur-viśuddhi*).

At that time, on the fifth day, a river emerged from each of the four sides of the pond, flowing straight without deviation. The water was serene and pure, free of waves, and adorned with various extraordinary flowers. The sound of the flowing water was the voice of the Dharma, proclaiming that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, and empty, and that all dharmas are non-self and extinguished in nirvana.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such miraculous transformations through the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, they were all filled with great joy at having experienced what they had never before; a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

Then, observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state and developed a mind of weary detachment, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the fifth day of the World-Honored One’s miraculous transformations.
On the sixth day, the World-Honored One transformed the great assembly so that they were all of one and the same kind, without any distinction or gradation.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, they were all filled with great joy at having experienced what they had never known before; a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

Then, observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state and that a spirit of weary detachment had been born in them, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the sixth day of the World-Honored One’s miraculous transformations.
On the seventh day, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to the great assembly while suspended in mid-air; they heard the sound of the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma, but did not see his form.

At that time, when the great assembly witnessed such miraculous transformations through the World-Honored One’s supernatural power, they all rejoiced greatly at this unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.

Observing that the great assembly had attained this unprecedented state and that a sense of weary detachment had arisen, the World-Honored One immediately preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
On the eighth day, the lay devotees who followed non-Buddhist paths sent a messenger to summon the various non-Buddhists, saying: "Do you not know?
The śramaṇa Gautama has already manifested his supernatural powers; it is now the eighth day, so why have you all not come?"
He desired to come, yet he was unable to do so.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"If Pūraṇa Kāśyapa were bound by a firm leather thong and led along by an ox, even if the leather thong were to snap and his body be torn apart, he would still be unable to come to my presence for the sake of engaging in debate without abandoning his own views; this is likewise true for the Nirgranthas and others."
Then Brahmā Śakra addressed Śakra, the Lord of Devas, saying:
"The various non-Buddhist practitioners claim to be equal to the World-Honored One, yet they are unable to come and compete with the World-Honored One in manifesting supernormal powers."
"Now you may destroy their high seats.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, addressed the Four Heavenly Kings:
"The various non-Buddhists claim to be equal to the World-Honored One, yet they cannot come to compete with the World-Honored One in supernatural power."
"Now you may destroy their high seats.
At that time, the Four Heavenly Kings immediately summoned the Wind Deity, the Cloud and Rain Deities, and the Thunder Deity, and addressed them thus:
"The various non-Buddhists claim to be equal to the World-Honored One, yet they cannot come to compete with the World-Honored One in supernatural power."
"Now you may destroy that high seat, reducing it to nothingness without remainder.
When the wind deities and others heard the instruction of the Four Heavenly Kings, they immediately seized the heretics' high seat, breaking and scattering it until not a trace remained.
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners, drenched by the wind and rain, entered thickets of grass and trees, mountain valleys, and caves to hide themselves.
Then there were the naked ascetics, the Nirgrantha followers of Pārśva, such as Pāṭaliputra and Pauṣpaja, who tied large stones to their necks and threw themselves into deep abysses.

At that time, the great assembly, witnessing the supernatural transformations and miraculous powers of the World-Honored One, all rejoiced greatly at such an unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for them, until they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, as described above.
This was the Blessed One’s eighth day of miraculous manifestation.
On the ninth day, the Blessed One preached the Dharma to the great assembly atop the summit of Mount Sumeru; they heard his voice, but could not see his form.
When the great assembly saw such a transformation by the World-Honored One, they all rejoiced greatly at this unprecedented occurrence, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the Blessed One’s ninth-day transformation.
On the tenth day, the Blessed One preached the Dharma in the Brahma Heaven; at that time, the great assembly heard his voice but did not see his form.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such a miraculous transformation by the World-Honored One, they were all filled with great joy at having experienced something unprecedented, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the Tathāgata’s tenth daily transformation. On the eleventh day, the World-Honored One manifested supernatural transformations before the great assembly:

he made one body into many bodies and many bodies into one; he appeared nearby or remained invisible at a distance; his body passed unimpeded through mountain obstructions and stone walls; he traveled through the air like a bird in flight; he emerged from and sank into the earth as easily as waves in water; he walked upon the water as if treading on solid ground; smoke and flames issued from his body like a great fire; and with his hand he touched the sun and moon, reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such a miraculous transformation by the World-Honored One, they were all filled with great joy at having attained what they had never experienced before, and a sense of weary detachment arose within them.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the Blessed One’s tenth day of miraculous transformation.

On the twelfth day, the Blessed One, amidst the great assembly, reflected in his mind upon the teaching of the Dharma: what should be recollected and what should not be recollected; what should be contemplated and what should not be contemplated; what should be abandoned and what should be cultivated.

At that time, when the great assembly saw such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s supernormal powers, they were all filled with great joy at having experienced what they had never before; a sense of weary detachment from the world arose within them.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for them, until—as described above—they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
This was the Blessed One’s twelfth supernormal transformation on the day of the deity.
On the thirteenth day, the Blessed One taught the Dharma and gave instructions to the great assembly; as for that teaching of the Dharma and those instructions, everything was ablaze.
In what way are all things ablaze?
The eye is ablaze, forms are ablaze, consciousness is ablaze, and eye-contact is ablaze.
The feeling—whether painful, pleasant, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises conditioned by eye-contact is also ablaze.
What is it that burns?
The fires of greed, hatred, and delusion burn; birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction burn.
Suffering has birth as its condition.
It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; all are ablaze.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard the World-Honored One preach the Dharma in this way, were all taught and converted, and they rejoiced greatly at such an unprecedented experience.
He immediately preached the Dharma for them until they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, as described above.
This was the thirteenth day of the Tathāgata’s miraculous transformations.

On the fourteenth day, next, a donor offered a handful of flowers to the World-Honored One; having smelled them, the World-Honored One cast them into the air. By the Buddha's supernatural power, they were transformed into fourteen thousand flower-pavilion towers, within each of which sat a Buddha. To the left and right, Śakra, Brahmā, and the other devas joined their palms in reverent salutation and spoke these verses:
"Homage to the King of Men, the Great Being, the Unsurpassed;
none can know the meditative absorption upon which the World-Honored One relies.
At that time, the great assembly, seeing such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s supernormal power, all rejoiced greatly, having attained what they had never experienced before.
The World-Honored One then preached the Dharma for him, until he attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, as described above.

At that time, King Bimbisāra of Magadha prepared a sacrificial offering on the fifteenth day; having prepared various kinds of fine foods during the night, when the night had passed and the next morning arrived, he served the Buddha and the Saṅgha with many kinds of delicious food and drink. He likewise provided full offerings to King Prasenajit of Kosala, King Udayana, King Brahmadatta, King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī, Queen Mallikā, the elder Ṛṣidatta, Pūraṇa, and the entire great assembly.
Having finished eating, the World-Honored One set aside his bowl. King Bimbisāra took another low seat and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One broke his cross-legged posture and extended his feet onto the table; as his feet reached the table, the earth shook in six ways and eighteen manners.

At that time, on the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet were the marks of wheels; each wheel had a thousand spokes, its rim was perfectly formed, and its characteristics were complete. A brilliant radiance shone forth from the wheels, and this light illuminated the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system.

At that time, King Magadha, seeing such wheel-marks upon the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet, immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What merit did you perform in the past to obtain these marks of a thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of your feet—marks that are brilliantly radiant, from which light issues forth from within the wheels, and whose light illuminates the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system?
At that time, the Buddha said to King Bimbisāra:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Hitajanaka who reigned as the sovereign of Jambudvīpa."

At that time, the land of Jambudvīpa was abundant in resources, its population was flourishing and happy, with eighty-four thousand cities and settlements, numbering five billion five hundred million.

At that time, the city where King Benefactor of Sentient Beings resided was named Wisdom Light; it measured twelve yojanas from east to west and seven yojanas from south to north. That city was vast, its population flourishing, its wealth and goods limitless, and it was adorned with every joy.
The king’s first wife was named Hui-shi (Wisdom-Deed), and she had no children.

For the sake of a son, she performed rites and made offerings to various deities: to the rivers and lakes, to Pūrṇabhadra, to Ratnabhadra, to the gods of the sun and moon, to Śakra and Brahmā, to the spirits of earth, water, fire, and wind, to Maheśvara, to the deities of gardens and forests, to the spirits of streets and alleys, to Hārītī, and to the various spirits of villages; everywhere she made offerings, praying for a son.
Later, at another time, the king’s first queen became pregnant. Women possess three kinds of wisdom:
they know when a man has looked upon them with desire, they know the moment of conception, and they know from whom the child was conceived.
Then the lady went at once to the king's presence and said:
"Does Your Majesty know?
I am now pregnant."
The King said, "Excellent!
He then redoubled his offerings for the lady, increasing by one fold all her requirements, including the finest food and drink, clothing, medicine, bedding, and everything else she needed.
When the ten months were complete, he gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome.
On the day of the boy’s birth, eighty-four thousand treasures spontaneously emerged from beneath the earth in eighty-four thousand cities.
Wherever there was a storehouse of silver, silver trees sprang forth, with roots, trunks, branches, and leaves all made of white silver.
Wherever there was a storehouse of gold, gold trees sprang forth, with roots, trunks, flowers, and leaves all made of gold.
There were those containing lapis lazuli, those containing crystal, those containing red pearls, those containing agate, and those containing musaragalva; all were likewise so.
At that time, according to the laws of the land, when a child was first born, his name would be given either by his parents or by śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Then King Benefactor of Beings thought to himself:
"Why must śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas be the ones to give him a name?"
"The mother of this child is named Prajñāvatī; I shall now name the child Prajñādīpa. He then named him Prajñādīpa.
At that time, the king appointed four types of nurses for the child: [the wet-nurse, the nurse for bathing, the nurse for play, and the nurse for adornment].
First is the tending of the body; second is the washing of clothes; third is the nursing of the infant; and fourth is playful amusement.
Regarding the mother who tends the body, she attends to the physical form and its various limbs and joints.
The washerwoman attends to the washing of clothes and the bathing of the body.
The wet-nurse is in charge of providing milk.

The playmate attends to the prince when he plays upon elephants, horses, or carriages; she provides flowers, incense, precious objects, and various toys for him to dally with, holds a peacock-feather parasol behind him, and entertains the prince so that he may find joy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"All things must come to an end; That which is high shall surely fall.
Those who are born do not fail to die; All who possess life are impermanent."
Sentient beings fall into the realm of existence; all things are conditioned.
In all worlds, there is none who does not age and die.
Sentient beings are subject to the law of permanence [in flux]; as they are born again and again, they all return to death.
According to the karma one has created, there are retributions for both sin and merit.
Evil karma leads to falling into hell; good karma leads to birth in the heavens.
Noble conduct leads to birth in the happy realms, and one attains the outflow-free nirvana.

At that time, King Benefactor of Sentient Beings passed away. When the prince grew up to the age of eight or nine, his mother taught him various arts and skills: calligraphy, painting, arithmetic, comedy, song, dance, instrumental music, elephant riding, horseback riding, charioteering, archery, and martial prowess; he became thoroughly proficient and well-versed in all these arts.
