When he reached the age of fourteen or fifteen, the various ministers went to the prince’s residence and said to him:
"Do you know? The King has passed away; it is now your turn to ascend the throne as king and issue your commands."
The prince replied:
"I cannot carry out the royal commands for the sake of the king. Why is this?"
In a previous life, I was once a king for six years; because of these causes and conditions, I fell into hell for sixty thousand years.
For this reason, I am currently unable to act as a king or carry out royal commands.
The ministers said,
"Is there any expedient means by which one might become king and issue royal commands? He replied:
"There is. "What is it? He replied:
"If I can cause all men and women in Jambudvīpa who are capable of speech to practice the ten wholesome actions—from not killing to not holding wrong views—then I shall become king."
When the ministers had heard the prince’s instruction, they immediately dispatched messengers carrying letters to the four directions to proclaim this command, saying: "Do you all know?..."
When King Benefactor of Sentient Beings had passed away, Prince Wisdom-Lamp was next in line to become king, whereupon he spoke these words: "I shall not be king;
rather, when all men and women of Jambudvīpa who are able to speak practice the ten wholesome paths—from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views—I will then become king."
When the people of the land heard this instruction, they all practiced the ten wholesome paths of action, from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views.
The ministers then went to Prince Prajñāpradīpa and said to him:
"Does the Prince know?"

"Whether male or female, all those among the people of Jambudvīpa who are able to speak shall practice the ten wholesome actions, from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views; you may now ascend the royal throne and carry out the king's commands."
The prince said, "Bring the silk.
He then gave him the first piece of white silk and tied it upon his own head, speaking these words:
"Was there such a king at that time? Was he good or not?
The ministers replied, "He was most excellent."
Then the ministers addressed the king, saying:
"When Your Majesty was first born, eighty-four thousand treasuries spontaneously emerged; these may now be taken and deposited in the royal treasury."
The king said: "What need is there to enter the treasury?
You may simply give alms at that crossroads to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the orphaned, and the elderly, bestowing everything according to whatever they seek."

When the ministers had heard King Prajñāpradīpa’s instruction, they immediately went to the treasuries located throughout the eighty-four thousand cities. At the four city gates and at the crossroads, they bestowed gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the orphaned, the elderly, and the infirm, giving them everything they requested.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"King Prajñāpradīpa has placed [his treasures] in all the treasuries throughout the eighty-four thousand cities, at the four crossroads within each of the four city gates."
"I give to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the orphaned, and the elderly, bestowing everything they ask for.

I fear they may come to seize my throne; therefore, I should now go to test King Jñānapradīpa: whether he gives with the aim of non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path, or with the aim of retrogression."
They immediately transformed themselves into men and said to one another:
"King Prajñāpradīpa instructs us to practice the ten unwholesome deeds, from killing up to wrong view."
At that time, all the ministers went to the king’s presence and said to him:
“Did Your Majesty truly instruct the people of the country to practice the ten unwholesome actions, from killing up to wrong view?
The king replied:
"No. Why is this? For I have previously said this:"

"If I do not become king, but instead cause all sentient beings capable of speech in Jambudvīpa to practice the ten wholesome paths—from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views—then I shall become king."
"Therefore, I do not speak such words.
You all should now prepare the elephant carriages; I wish to go myself to teach and transform the people of the country.
(From the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Volume 51)
The Four-Part Vinaya, Volume Fifty-Two, Part Three of the Fourth Division,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty,
together with Zhu Fonian and others.
From the *Kṣudraka-vastu*, Part Two: At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself, "I must not allow the King to ride upon an ordinary worldly mount.
He immediately prepared his celestial elephant, which had six tusks, each of which was thick and massive, and stationed it outside the gate.
At that time, King Prajñāpradīpa, seeing such an elephant carriage, asked his ministers, "Whose elephant is this?
The ministers replied:
"I do not know whose elephant this is;
it must certainly be the King’s elephant, for no one else possesses such a one.
May Your Majesty please mount it."
The king immediately mounted [the vehicle], and the king said:
"Go and show me that man who said I taught the people of the kingdom to practice the ten unwholesome deeds.
He then pointed him out to the king.
The king asked,
"Did King Prajñāpradīpa instruct you to practice the ten unwholesome actions? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The king asked again:
"Is there any expedient means by which one may practice the ten wholesome paths of action?"
He replied, “There is. He asked:

"What is this? he asked. He replied, "If one attains the state of a bodhisattva and eats their flesh and drinks their blood, only then can one practice the ten wholesome actions, from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views."
At that time, King Jñānapradīpa thought to himself:

"Since beginningless time, I have undergone manifold sufferings and transmigrated through the five realms of existence; whether I have had my hands cut off, my feet cut off, my ears or nose cut off, my eyes gouged out, or my head severed, what benefit has there ever been in all this?"
He immediately took a sharp knife and cut flesh from his own thigh, placing it in a vessel and pouring blood into it to give to that person, saying to him:
"O man! You may eat this flesh and drink this blood, and you shall be able to practice the ten wholesome deeds."
At that time, the man, unable to withstand the majestic power of King Jñānapradīpa, immediately vanished and was no longer seen.
Suddenly, a deva-king stood before the king and asked him:
"For which realm do you now give this gift: for one world-system, or two, three, or four?"
"Are you the sun or moon, Śakra Devendra, Māra the King,
or Brahmā the King? The king replied,
"I practice giving not for the sake of one world-system, nor two, three, or four world-systems, nor even for the sake of Māra or Brahmā."
I formed this intention:

"Practicing giving, I desire to seek unexcelled, perfect, and true all-knowledge; to deliver those not yet delivered, to liberate those not yet liberated, to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa, and to deliver them from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction, and so forth."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, thought to himself:
"It would be most improper for me to cause King Prajñāpradīpa to die from this wound; I shall instead pour the celestial nectar (amṛta) over his body."
He then poured it upon him, and the wound was immediately healed as it had been before.
The Buddha said to King Bimbisāra:
“As for that King Benefactor of Sentient Beings at that time, could he have been anyone else?”
The King, his father, is none other than Śuddhodana.
The King’s first consort at that time was my mother, Māyā. The King Prajñādīpa was myself.

In a previous life, I taught and transformed countless people throughout Jambudvīpa—whether men or women who were able to speak—causing them all to practice the ten wholesome paths of action, from refraining from killing up to refraining from wrong views.
"For this reason, the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet is fully perfected, its radiance shining brilliantly to illuminate the trichiliocosm.

At that time, the great assembly, witnessing such miraculous transformations of the World-Honored One’s spiritual power, all rejoiced greatly at having experienced what they had never before; a sense of weary detachment from the world arose within them.

The World-Honored One observed that the great assembly was filled with immense joy and had developed a sense of weary detachment; he preached the Dharma through countless skillful means, causing hundreds of thousands of people to immediately, while still on their seats, distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.
This was the fifteenth-day transformation of the Blessed One.
At that time, the Blessed One was in Rājagṛha.
King Bimbisāra had granted permission for the bhikṣus to enter and leave the palace gates without any hindrance or difficulty.
At that time, the King’s consort was listening from behind a screen; she said, "If the bhikṣus have anything to say, come and tell me.
The palace chambers were lined with expensive śiṃśapā wood for their pillars.
When the bhikṣus saw this, they remarked, "To use such precious timber for pillars—would it not be better to use it to make alms bowls for the bhikṣus?"
When the person who had been in that secluded place heard this, he immediately went and informed the king.
The king then commanded his men to fashion new pillars to replace the old ones, taking the [old] wood to make alms bowls which he bestowed upon the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep bowls made of śiṃśapā wood.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep wooden bowls; this is the practice of non-Buddhists.
If one keeps one, it must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, King Bimbisāra offered stone bowls to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep stone alms bowls.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"You should not keep them."
"This is the Dharma bowl of the Tathāgata; if one keeps it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, King Bimbisāra offered a golden bowl to the bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu would not accept it, saying:
"The World-Honored One has not yet permitted us to keep golden bowls."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not possess a golden bowl. This is the practice of laypeople;
if one possesses one, it must be dealt with according to the Dharma."
Then King Bimbisāra further had silver bowls made, lapis lazuli bowls made, jeweled bowls made, and bowls made of various precious gems, which he offered to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus did not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep such a bowl.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep such bowls as these; this is the practice of laypeople.
If one keeps them, one must be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Bhagga.
The Bhikṣus of the Vajjiputtaka school of Vaiśālī possessed gold bowls; the Buddha said, "One should not possess them.
They then possessed silver bowls, lapis lazuli bowls, precious bowls, and bowls made of various jewels; the Buddha said:
"You must not keep them.
You foolish people!
You avoid what I have prohibited and instead engage in other matters."
"From this day forward, no one shall possess any precious bowl; if anyone does possess one, it shall be dealt with according to the Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.
The Licchavis obtained a precious maṇi bowl of great value and, filling it with powdered sandalwood incense, offered it to the World-Honored One.
“Venerable One!
Out of compassion, please accept this maṇi bowl.
The Buddha said:
“Reverend Liśa!
I ought not to keep this bowl.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Out of compassion, we pray that you will accept this sandalwood powder incense.
The World-Honored One then accepted it.
At that time, the Licchavis thought to themselves:
"To whom should this bowl be given?
One among them said,
"Give it to Pūraṇa Kāśyapa."
Some said: "With Makakalagosiya, Ajita Keśakambala, Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra, Nirgrantha Jñātiputra, and Saccaka Nigaṇṭhaputra."
He then took the bowl and gave it to Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha.

At that time, Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha heard that the Licchavis of Vaiśālī had first offered a precious maṇi bowl to the śramaṇa Gautama, who had not accepted it, and that they were now offering it to him. Conceiving a mind of arrogance, pride, and envy, filled with resentment and displeasure, and failing to exercise self-restraint, he spoke these evil words:
"If you would cut off the tongues of all the Licchavi youths and fill this bowl with them, only then shall I accept it."
He thought to himself: "Saccaka the Nigaṇṭha!
He greatly desires to destroy and ruin our lineage."
He immediately struck and killed him with a stone.
Although the other wished to explain himself and resolve their previous harsh words, he would not listen to his speech and instead struck and killed him.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If one is able to speak, one's purpose will surely be understood.
The Buddha said:
"There are five qualities that govern speech, by which one may present one's own case without being reproached, causing others to rejoice and have no regrets later."
What are the five?
One speaks what is wholesome and does not speak what is unwholesome;
one speaks in accordance with the Dharma and does not speak contrary to the Dharma.
One speaks words that are pleasing, not those that are displeasing;
one speaks with truth, not with falsehood or deceit;
one speaks for the sake of benefit, not for what is unbeneficial.
"When one possesses these five qualities of speech, one can present one's own case without being reproached, causing others to rejoice and later feel no regret.
He then spoke in verse:
"The eloquent speaker is near to victory; He speaks according to the Dharma, never what is not Dharma."
Kind speech is truthful speech; it benefits and does no harm.
One who speaks words well brings no burning affliction to themselves, nor do they infringe upon others—such speech is called well-spoken.
Speak words of loving-kindness, and you will not be rebuked by others;
when speaking, let there be nothing unloving, and no evils shall gather around you.
Speak with sincerity as the nectar of truth; truthful speech is the supreme.
In accordance with the true Dharma, one abides in nirvāṇa.
Whatever the Buddha has taught leads to peace and reaches nirvāṇa;
that which can bring an end to the limits of suffering—this is the most excellent teaching.
At that time, King Bimbisāra offered an iron bowl to a bhikṣu, but the bhikṣu would not accept it, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep iron bowls.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Listen, you are permitted to possess iron alms bowls.
At that time, there was an ironworker who had gone forth; wishing to make bowls for the bhikṣus, he informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I permit you to make them.”
He required a brazier; the Buddha said, "Its use is permitted.
He required a hammer and tongs; the Buddha said:
"Permission is granted to make it.
He required bellows; "Permission is granted to make them.
He required a whetstone; the Buddha said:
"I permit you to make it.
He required a lathe; the Buddha said, "I permit you to make it."
He had trouble with various items in his spinning-lathe kit falling and scattering. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a bag to contain them and hang it on a peg or a 'dragon-tooth' peg.
He kept his bowl without fumigating it, which led to the problem of dirt and odor. The Buddha said:
"Listen to the instructions for fumigation. He did not know how to perform the fumigation.

[The Buddha said: "Listen: construct a furnace, or a cauldron, or a jar; coat it variously with clay, and plaster the interior with a mixture of apricot kernels and hemp seeds. Level the ground with ash to create the site for the fumigation bowl, set up a support, and place the bowl upon it."

Place the bowl over the incense burner and cover it; fill the four sides with ash and press down with the hands to make it firm. Then, using either firewood or cow dung, fill the four sides and burn it; one should perform the fumigation in this manner.
At that time, the World-Honored One was wandering among the people in the country of Soma.
There was a potter who had faith and devotion, to whom the World-Honored One pointed out a place for clay and said:
"Take earth from this spot; beat it in such a manner, dry it in such a manner, make the mud in such a manner, and temper it in such a manner."
Having fashioned the bowl in this manner and polished it in this manner,
and having dried it in the sun, one constructs a large, sturdy furnace, places the bowl inside, covers it with a lid, and coats it with clay.
If one uses khadira wood, or jujube wood, or śiṃśapā wood, or āmalaka wood, one should place them at the four sides and burn them.
He then acted exactly as the Buddha had instructed; having completed it in due order, he took a particularly precious and fine *sumana* bowl and offered it to the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus would not accept it, saying, "The World-Honored One has not yet permitted us to possess such a bowl."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to keep [them].
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the village of Ugga.
At that time, the bhikṣus obtained *uyyāna* bowls but would not accept them, saying:
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep such bowls.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; you may keep it.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Ukkaṭṭhā.
The bhikṣus obtained Ukkaṭṭhā bowls but did not accept them, saying:
"We have not yet been permitted by the Buddha to keep such bowls," they said to the Buddha. The Buddha said,
"I permit you to receive them."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.
Some bhikṣus obtained black alms-bowls but would not accept them, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep black alms-bowls."
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to keep [it].
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus received red bowls but did not accept them, saying,
"The Buddha has not yet permitted us to keep such bowls.
They informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to keep them.
There are six kinds of bowls:
iron bowls, *sumana* bowls, *uyagara* bowls, *uyagasa* bowls, black bowls, and red bowls."
Generally speaking, there are two kinds of almsbowls:
iron bowls and clay bowls.
There are those that hold one and a half *dō* and those that hold three *dō*; these are what should be accepted and maintained.
He placed the bowl on a brick that was about to fall; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He placed the bowl on a stone that was about to fall; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He placed the bowl on a shelf; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He placed the bowl on the path; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He placed the bowl on a stone; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done. He placed his bowl under a fruit tree; the Buddha said: "It should not be done."
He placed his bowl on an uneven spot; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He held two bowls with one hand; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done. Except when the bowls are separated by a finger.
He then held two bowls with one hand and opened the door. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done, except when using one's mind.
After he had placed the bowl behind the door-panel, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He placed the bowl before the door; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He placed the bowl beneath a rope bed or a wooden bed; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He placed the bowl between a rope bed and a wooden bed; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done, except for a brief moment.
He placed his bowl on the corner of a rope bed or a wooden bed; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so, except for a brief moment.
While he was standing there washing his bowl, it fell to the ground and broke. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
Because he nevertheless lost his bowl, broke it, and made a new one, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He placed long items inside his bowl. The Buddha said:
"No items whatsoever should be placed inside a bowl.
He then drew images of grapevines and lotus flowers inside the bowl. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He drew a swastika on the bowl; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He painted his own name on the bowl; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He wrapped the four sides or the rim of the bowl; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He then wrapped his bowl with a single continuous cloth; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
"One should wrap two parts and leave one part open; if there are many holes from stars, one should wrap it entirely.
He placed the bowl on the ground, which damaged its luster. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
One should sprinkle the ground with mud to settle it. If it nevertheless continues to smell, one should place it upon leaves or grass.
If it still smells, one should provide a bowl-rest; if it continues to smell even then, one should cover the bottom with a piece of cloth.
He used a jeweled base for it; the Buddha said, "One should not use jewels;
one should use white tin, lead, or pewter.
He was troubled by its falling off.
The Buddha said:
"One should use resin from the *hu* tree or wax as glue.
When a monk lifted his bowl without first washing it, other monks saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus;
it should be washed and lifted.
He did not wash it with soap powder, and the oiliness did not depart. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
One should wash it using soap powder, or earth, or ash, or cow dung, or mud.
He washed the bowl with a mixture of sand and cow dung and thereby damaged the bowl. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.

One should fill a vessel with water, soak cow dung in it until it settles, and then use the clear liquid to wash the bowl; or one may wash it with fine powder, fine mud, leaves, flowers, or fruit, taking care to remove all grease."

If the alms bowl has star-shaped or mortar-like holes, and food enters within them, one should pick it out; if it can be picked out, one should pick it out, but for the remainder that cannot be removed, there is no fault.
He washed his bowl and set it aside before it was dry; as a result, grime formed. The Buddha said:
"You should not do so. You must set it aside only after it has been dried."
Holding the bowl in his hand, he found it difficult to protect and maintain;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to make a bowl bag to contain it.
When the bowl fell out because the mouth of the bag was not tied, the Buddha said:
"It should be tied with a cord.
As it was difficult to protect and hold while grasping the bowl bag with one's hand, the Buddha said:
"One should make a strap to sling over the shoulder."

At that time, a bhikṣu carried his bowl under his arm with the opening of the bowl facing his side. While traveling on the road, he encountered rain; he tripped and fell to the ground, and the bowl pressed against his side, resulting in an ailment. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
"The mouth of the bowl should face outward.
Because the *sumana* bowl was damaged when being inserted into or removed from its bag, the Buddha said:
"One should place it in a box or a chest."
He used precious materials to make a chest or a box. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials; one should instead use śara grass, bamboo, or wood."
"If the bowls clash against one another, you should use grass, tree leaves, or any one of the ten types of robes to create a barrier between them.
When they were taken out from the mouth of the box, the Buddha said:
"You should make a lid."
He used jewels to make the canopy, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus. One should use śara grass, bamboo, or wood to make it."
"If it is placed in an unstable location, it should be secured with a strap to a peg shaped like a dragon's tooth.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha.
King Bimbisāra had granted permission for the bhikṣus to enter and leave the Āmrapālī Garden without any restriction or difficulty.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went to the park keeper and said,
"We need mangoes. He immediately gave them to them.
He requested it again and was given it once more; in this manner, he eventually ate all of those fruits.
Later, at another time, the king required *āmra* fruits and commanded an attendant minister to fetch some.
The minister immediately received the imperial decree and went to where the garden keeper was to request fruit;
the latter replied, "The fruit is exhausted. He asked:
"Why is it finished?
He replied, "The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas have eaten it all."
That minister then spoke with derision:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and have many desires;
yet they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
Although the donor may never grow weary of giving, the recipient ought to know contentment.
Why, then, have you eaten all of the king's fruit?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not eat amra fruit.
At that time, while the bhikṣus were begging for alms, they obtained the juice of amra fruit; the Buddha said:
“Drinking is permitted.
He obtained boiled *āmra* fruits; the Buddha said, “Eating is permitted.”
He obtained mango juice, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to drink it.
If it has not yet fermented into wine, it may be drunk even at improper times; if it has fermented into wine, it should not be drunk. If one drinks it, one shall be dealt with according to the law."

Later, at another time, when the mangoes were ripening in abundance, Ānanda, who delighted in eating this fruit, went to where the World-Honored One was. He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The mangoes are ripening in abundance.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, on account of these causes and conditions, assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma to them in accordance with their needs. By means of countless skillful expedients, he praised those who practice *dhūta* austerities, who are dignified, have few desires, are content, and possess wisdom.
He addressed the bhikṣus: "From this day forward, I permit you to eat *āmra* fruit."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
Then the group of six bhikṣus turned their robes backward and wore them as if they were being arrested, frightening and mocking one another.
When the lay devotees saw this, they all joined together in reproaching and disparaging them:
“The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment.
They claim of themselves:
‘We know the True Dharma.’”
"Instead of being restrained, they further terrify and mock one another; like kings and great ministers, what kind of true Dharma is this?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not be restrained in such a manner, nor should one further terrify or mock another."
At that time, a sick bhikṣu was being seized; as the hair was on the inside, it irritated his wound and caused him pain. The Buddha said:
"Wrap him in an undergarment; if he suffers from heat, he should instead wear his kāṣāya over it as a covering."
At that time, a bhikṣu’s robe was torn. The Buddha said, “It should be repaired.
He did not know how to repair it.
The Buddha said:
"If it is sewn with thread, or sewn with double threads, any place where there is a hole should be patched with material.
If the hole is large, one should patch it with small material to cause the robe to shrink. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
One should repair it by patching the hole with cloth twice the width of two fingers.
If the cloth shrinks while being patched, one should weigh down the four corners with stones while patching."
"If it still shrinks, drive stakes into the four corners and stretch it out;
if it still shrinks, one should construct a frame to stretch it.
[The monk] did not know how to make such a frame.
The Buddha said,
"It should be made of wood.
He required cords for stretching it out, and the Buddha said:
"Listen; sew it with cord.
Not knowing with what material to sew it, the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to sew with bird feathers or a hairpin; if one's fine or soft garment has become damaged, it is permitted to sew it with a needle.
He made a needle out of precious materials, and the Buddha said, "It should not be done so."
"It is permitted to make them from copper or iron.
Regarding the pain in the fingers caused by sewing with needles, the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make a thimble."
They made finger-rings out of precious gems; the Buddha said, "You should not do so.
I allow [rings] to be made of copper, iron, bone, ivory, horn, lead, tin, white tin, lacquer, or wood."
When he was sewing the robe, he suffered from crookedness; [the Buddha] permitted him to use a string-line to mark it straight.
He required thread for the marking; the Buddha said:
"It should be given."
If he wishes to use dyed threads to mark his robes, "Whether it be lime, red ochre, white clay, ink, or yellow arsenic—everything is permitted to be given."
"If the center is not fixed, it should be measured with a scale.
He made the scale out of precious materials, whereupon the Buddha said:
"One should not make it out of precious materials; I allow it to be made of copper, iron, or even wood."
He spread the robe on the ground to sew it, and dust settled upon the cloth.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to sprinkle the ground with mud-water before spreading the robe.
While he was sewing the robe, the needle pricked the ground and damaged it. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done. He spread his robe upon śābara grass and sewed it while the grass remained attached to the robe; the Buddha said, "It should not be done."
He spread grass upon the ground and sewed the seams of the cloth upon the leaves; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
It is permitted to sew each of the ten kinds of robes upon an īriyāna, a tāmra, a māmra, or a woolen rug."
That bhikṣu suffered from the loss of his ink-line, measuring cord, scale, thread, needle, knife, and miscellaneous items for mending robes.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make a bag to contain them."
He did not lift the clothes rack, and it became soaked by the rain.
The Buddha said, "It should be taken up and stored. [The monks] did not know where to store it.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to place [the robes] in the walking hall, the warm room, or the dining hall.
If the robe-hangers are too large for the door to admit them, they should be placed outside in a place sheltered from the rain."
"If it is rained upon or soaked by wind and rain, you should hang it high.
After he had finished mending the robe, he untied it to take it away but did not lift the remaining wood. The Buddha said, "You should lift it."
Not knowing where to place it,
the Buddha said:
"Place it beneath a pavilion or upon a bed."
He did not lift it by means of a rope; the Buddha said, "It should be rolled up and tied, then lifted using a bamboo rack for robes.
At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by the scattering of needles; the Buddha said:
"Allow the making of needle-cushions.
Because they were previously troubled by their falling apart, allow the making of cases.
They used precious materials to make them; the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials to make it;
it is permitted to use copper, iron, or even bamboo and wood.
Concerned that the needle would protrude from the mouth of the tube, the Buddha said:
"It should be fitted with a stopper.
He made it out of precious gems.
The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials to make it.
It is permitted to use copper, iron, or even bamboo and wood.
If the needle is rusty, one should place it among roasted flour; if it is still troubled by rust, one should attach it to other objects to take away the rust so that it does not remain."
At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by the scattering and loss of their needle cases, knives, and scraps of cloth, thread, and yarn.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make bags to contain them; if these various items fall out from the mouth [of the bag], they should be tied with a cord."
"If it is difficult to protect while holding it in the hand, one should make a strap and wear it over the shoulder.
At that time, a bhikṣu’s iron bowl was cracked and broken;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to repair it—whether by driving in nails, using red clay, or using tree resin as glue."
The *sumana* bowl became cracked and broken;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to seal it with lacquer, or with lime, or with white clay.
When the *kāla* black bowl broke, [the Buddha said], "One should drill holes and sew them together with needle and thread."
He required a drill; the Buddha said, "Its use is permitted.
He made one out of precious materials; the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials; it is permitted to use copper or iron.
If one fears that the thread will break, one should use sinew or the tail hair of an ox or horse.
If one fears that insects will eat the sinew or thread, one should apply lacquer over it."
"If one suffers from food or water entering [the wound], it should likewise be sealed with *hugu* (hemp resin).
If it further suffers from damage, it should be secured with iron clamps.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣus produced fire by means of a fire-gem at their forest hermitage. Some thieves came to harass the bhikṣus because of that gem. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not produce fire by means of a fire-gem in a forest hermitage."
At that time, the bhikṣus required fire. The Buddha said:
"I permit the bhikṣus to produce fire by means of fire-magic in an araṇya.
If they require fire-drilling wood (arani), I permit them to make it."
"If one requires a fire-drill, it is permitted to make one.
Whatever cords or other necessary items are required, all are permitted to be given.
He was troubled that the components of the fire-drill were falling apart, so [the Buddha] said, "It is permitted to make a bag to contain them."
"There is the danger of dampness where there is no secure place. [The Buddha said: "I allow you to hang it beneath the bed or upon a peg shaped like a dragon's tooth.
They did not know with what material to support the fire. [The Buddha said: "One should take fire using grass, or leaves, or *kusha* grass, or *śyāmāka* grass, or cow or horse dung."
At that time, a bhikṣu repeatedly drilled for fire and injured his hand, suffering from pain.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to produce fire by means of a fire-gem in a secluded place.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
The group of six bhikṣus used water containing living creatures; when the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, lack a heart of compassion and take the lives of sentient beings, yet they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not use water containing insects; I allow you to make a water-strainer."
Not knowing how to make it, the Buddha said:
"It may be made in the shape of a ladle, or triangular, or with a horizontal rim, or as a straining jar. If one fears that small insects will escape, it is permitted to place a sand bag inside."
He discarded the insects and sand onto dry land; the Buddha said, "You should not do so;
I allow you to return them and place them back into the water.
At that time, two bhikṣus were quarreling as they were traveling through the kingdom of Kośala; one bhikṣu was carrying a water-strainer to filter water for drinking.
One of his companions borrowed a water-strainer from him, but he would not give it; consequently, the monk was unable to obtain water to drink and suffered greatly.
The monks reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One who has one should give it. A bhikṣu should not travel even half a yojana without a water-strainer."
"If there is none, one should strain the water using a corner of the saṃghāṭī.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vajjī.

Then, two monks from the group of six lay together on a single bed. When other monks saw them, they thought they were lying with women; it was only when they rose later that they realized they were not women.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Two persons should not sleep on the same bed.
They were uncertain and did not allow a sick person to share a bed with them; the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to lie on the same bed as a sick person.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Vṛji.

Two monks from the group of six lay together upon a single bedding; when other monks saw them, they thought they were lying with a woman, but only later, upon rising, did they realize it was not a woman.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Two persons should not lie down together on the same bedding.
At that time, the bhikṣus happened to have only a single spread, whether of grass or leaves; the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to spread separate bedding mats for each person to lie upon.
During the cold season, when there is only one blanket, it is permitted for each person to have their own inner garment to cover the body while using the blanket as a common outer covering."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus ate from a single bowl. When the lay devotees saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma.
What kind of True Dharma is this?
Two people eating from the same bowl, just like a king and his great minister.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Two persons should not eat from the same bowl.
At that time, the bhikṣus were using a single vessel to hold their rice; the Buddha said:
"One should divide the remaining food from other vessels and eat separately.
If there are no separate bowls, it is permitted to set aside half of one's portion at the time of eating and give it to that person.
If the time for the meal is about to expire, it is permitted for one person to take a single morsel of food, hand it to the other person, and have them take and eat it."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus lay propped up on their elbows with their heads resting on a table while eating. When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized them together, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame. They claim for themselves, 'We know the True Dharma. [Yet they act like this!]"
"What kind of true Dharma is this?
To eat while lying half-prostrate, like a king or a great minister.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus.

At that time, there were elder monks who were aged and ill and unable to hold their bowls with their own hands while eating; [the Buddha] permitted them to place [their bowls] in the corner of a rope-bed or a wooden bed, or to set them upon a water-jar.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stood upon rope beds and wooden beds; the ropes of the beds broke, causing the mattresses to be ruined.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said: "You should not do so."
"If a bhikṣu wishes to take something up or lift something, he is permitted to stand upon the crossbars of his bed.

At that time, the various non-Buddhists kept large rope beds by making them into small rope beds; the group of six bhikṣus followed the example of these non-Buddhists and kept their rope beds in such a manner.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not do so.

Kālodāyin was large in stature, and the bed in the bathhouse was too small for him to fit upon; he was uncertain and did not dare to take a large bed from outside to fashion it into a smaller one for bathing. He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to place beds of various sizes within the bathhouse for the purpose of bathing.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept householders' implements, such as plows or nets; they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not keep them."
He kept precious water-pots and basins; the Buddha said, "One should not keep such things.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Yavatu who paid homage and served various non-Buddhist practitioners, whether it be fire, the sun and moon, or the various non-Buddhist doctrines such as the path of silence.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should not practice various other heterodox dharmas.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who was chewing his food while staying in an araṇya; another bhikṣu said to him:
“You have committed the offense of eating at the improper time!
He replied, “I have not committed the offense of eating at the improper time; I am merely chewing my cud.”
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This bhikṣu has just recently come from among cattle to be born here; were it not so, he would not have lived for long."
"If other bhikṣus have such illnesses, they may act in this way so as to relieve themselves without suffering.
If food is spat out before it has left the mouth, it may be swallowed back.
At that time, there were crows and parrots in the Jeta Grove making noise and disturbing the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation. The Buddha said:
"One should make a noise to startle them away, or use a bow to strike wood so they will leave.
At that time, the bhikṣus gathered at night to go to the place for the poṣadha ceremony and were troubled by the darkness;
the Buddha said, "I allow you to carry a torch."
"If the place where one sits is dark, lighting a lamp is permitted.
If they require a lamp vessel, "giving one is permitted.
If they require oil or a wick, "giving them is permitted."
If it is not clear, raise the wick high.
If the hands are soiled by oil, the use of chopsticks is permitted.
If one suffers from burns from the fire caused by the chopsticks, the use of iron chopsticks is permitted.
If one suffers from the lamp wick lying down, it is permitted to fix an iron pillar at the center of the wick.
If it is still not bright, it is permitted to make the wick large.
If it is still dark, one should place lamps in the four corners of the room.
If it is still not bright, one should fashion a revolving lamp.

If it is still not bright, one should place lamps around the four sides of the room, or set up lamp-stands, or fill a jar with water and place oil upon it, then wrap mustard seeds in cloth to serve as wicks and light them.

At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ sent someone to deliver six kinds of items: a single-seated rope bed, a brazier, a lantern, a broom, a fan, and a bushel measure. The bhikṣus did not accept them and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept the others, but the bushel measure should not be accepted."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Vīra, who had gone forth from the brahmin caste. He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable Sir!

"These monks come from various clans and have different names; they subvert the meaning of the Buddha’s sūtras. We pray that the World-Honored One will allow us to use the elegant discourses of the world to repair the Buddha’s sūtras."
The Buddha said, "You foolish people! This is indeed a corruption;
you seek to adulterate the Buddhist scriptures with the doctrines of non-Buddhists."
The Buddha said, "I permit you to recite and study the Buddhist sūtras according to the local dialects and linguistic conventions of the country.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling on a road in the kingdom of Kośala who reached a secluded spot and wished to relieve himself. At that moment, a woman also arrived at the secluded spot wishing to relieve herself.
Not far from this place there was a pond. At that time, a bhikṣu went to that pond to wash, and a woman also came to that pond to wash.
When the laypeople saw them, they said:
"This bhikṣu has come out from that direction to wash, and the woman has done the same; the bhikṣu must have violated this woman."
When the bhikṣus heard this, they reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not defecate or urinate in such places as to cause people to harbor doubts, nor should one wash in the water of a pond."
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda arrived at the house of a lay follower toward evening and sat inside; after a short while, he departed without informing the host.
At that time, bandits were watching his house during the day; when they encountered the gate opening at dusk, they immediately entered and plundered the house.
The head of the household asked, "Who opened the gate and went out at night?"
The family members replied,
"This is the Śākya son, Upananda.
Then all the lay devotees spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or remorse;
they claim for themselves, 'I know the True Dharma,' yet they conspire with bandits to come and plunder my house. How can such as these possess the True Dharma?"
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“One should not go to the homes of laypeople at twilight.

At that time, there were matters concerning the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṃgha, the stūpas, or a sick bhikṣu; or if a donor summoned them and it was already near dusk, the bhikṣus hesitated and did not dare to go. The Buddha said:
"If there is such a matter, you should go.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda intended to preach the Dharma for a woman; the woman, perceiving his intention, said to him:
"Why do you not preach the Dharma for yourself?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not preach the Dharma with a lustful mind.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus practiced divination for women; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He then consulted a person for divination, and the Buddha said,
"One should not do so."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus made a wager with others for goods. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
When they obtained the goods, they took them. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. Six groups of bhikṣus walked along the road holding hands together, pushing others aside until they fell to the ground.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are shameless and lack contentment; yet they claim,
'We know the True Dharma,' walking hand-in-hand along the road like royal ministers."
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should not be so."
At that time, while the bhikṣus were traveling on the road, someone offered them leather sandals and oil-flasks filled with flowers. The bhikṣus hesitated and did not dare to accept them.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to accept them."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus lent goods on interest; they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus borrowed goods on interest from others; they informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were engaged in a quarrel with others; they had their robes tucked up, wrapped them around their necks, covered their heads, draped their robes over both shoulders, and were wearing leather sandals as they spoke with the elders.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not do so. You should bare your right shoulder, remove your leather sandals, go before the senior monk (upādhyāya), slightly bend your body, join your palms, and speak as follows:"
"I wish to make a report. The Elder should reply:
"Speak according to the Dharma and according to the Vinaya."

At that time, as Baddhananda was traveling on the road carrying a fine, large, round parasol, the lay devotees saw him from afar and, thinking he was either a king or a high minister, they became terrified and moved aside to clear the path.
Not looking closely from afar, they realized it was Baddhananda, whereupon they all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have many desires and no satiety; yet they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"Yet he walks along the road carrying a magnificent, large, round parasol, just like a royal minister, causing us to be terrified and forced to clear the way.
What kind of true Dharma is this?"
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not carry a round umbrella while walking on a road, nor should he keep one.

At that time, when it rained, the bhikṣus went to the great meal, the small meal, or to the night assembly for the poṣadha; the rain soaked their robes and the fresh dye was ruined. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Listen: for the purpose of protecting one's robes, it is permitted to make a canopy within the monastery using tree bark, leaves, or bamboo.
He required a pole for the canopy, and the Buddha said, "It is permitted to make one."
They made it using precious gems. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems.
It is permitted to make it from bone, ivory, horn, white tin, lead, pewter, or wood."
He required a canopy; the Buddha said, "Its making is permitted.
He made it using precious gems; the Buddha said:
"One should not use jewels to make it; it is permitted to use bone, or even wood.
He required a large canopy, and the Buddha said, "It is permitted to give one."
They made it out of precious gems. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems; I allow you to make it from bone, or even from wood.
They wished to cover the top [of the stupa]. [The Buddha] said: "I allow you to cover it with *tāla* leaves, *mālūra* leaves, or bark."
"If it suffers from deterioration at its four edges, I permit it to be layered.
He required a pole for the canopy; the Buddha said, "I permit you to make one."
They made it out of precious gems. The Buddha said:
"One should not use precious gems to make it.
It is permitted to make it from bone, ivory, horn, or even wood."
Because the staff of his parasol was too long, he was unable to enter or exit through the doorway. The Buddha said:
"It should be made detachable.
If you are concerned that the staff might slip out, you should make a hole and install a crossbar."
"If they are broken or bent, permission is granted to have them made with iron handles and to fasten them with chains.

At that time, the Śākya son Upananda placed his alms bowl inside a carrying net, threaded it onto the end of a staff, and walked along carrying it on his shoulder. When the lay devotees saw him, they thought, "The king's attendants are coming," and they fled from the road in terror.
Before long, they recognized him as Upananda, and they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and lack a sense of shame; yet they claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.'"
"In this way, how can there be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It should not be so."
"Furthermore, you should not keep such staffs or carrying-bags.
At that time, an elderly and infirm bhikṣu fell to the ground while traveling on the road.
The Buddha said, "For those who are old or infirm, I permit the use of a staff."
"Because there was concern that the ends would wear out under the staff, I permitted the making of ferrules.
They used precious materials to make them, so the Buddha said:
"Precious materials should not be used; I permit their use of bone, ivory, horn, white tin, lead, and pewter."
"If the top is broken, it is also permitted to use such materials to repair it.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept walking sticks with hollows. Then all the lay devotees (gṛhapati) collectively reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and lack a sense of shame. They claim for themselves:"
"To claim, 'I know the True Dharma,' while holding a staff in mid-air like a royal minister—
how can such a thing be the True Dharma?"
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "You should not do so.

While traveling on the road, the bhikṣus encountered snakes, scorpions, centipedes, and millipedes; those bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire were all terrified by the sight and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"It is permitted to hold a *khakkhara* staff and shake it, or to place small stones in a tube and shake it to make a sound, or to shake a split bamboo to make a sound.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus held large, round royal fans. When the laypeople saw this, they all criticized and disparaged them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and have no sense of shame; they claim for themselves:"
"I know the True Dharma," he said, while holding a large round fan like a royal minister. "In such a manner, how can there be True Dharma?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus.
Those who had already received [the items] were hesitant to accept them due to their doubts, so they informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to receive them for the sake of the stūpa."
At that time, the bhikṣus were traveling on the road and suffered from the heat; they informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to make fans out of tree leaves, branches, or grass, using each of the ten kinds of robes."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus carried leather fans. The Buddha said, "You should not keep them.
The group of six bhikṣus then made fans by stretching leather over a frame of ten pieces of wood arranged lengthwise and crosswise. The Buddha said:
"One should not keep [such fans].
At that time, the fans of the bhikṣus became worn out, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to repair them with tree bark, or to patch them with leaves, or to patch them with leather."
"If it falls apart, you should sew it with thread; if the thread breaks, you should sew it with sinew-thread; if the edges fray, you should wrap them with leather.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from heat during the morning and midday meals, or when assembled at night, or during the recitation of the precepts. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to make large fans, or to make revolving-fan machines."
"Who pushed it? he asked.
The Buddha said, "It is permitted for a bhikṣu, a śrāmaṇera, a park-keeper, or an upāsaka to push it."
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were weaving woolen fans, killing many small insects and grasses. When the laypeople saw this, they all reviled them, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or remorse; they harm the lives of living beings, yet they claim, 'We know the True Dharma.'"
"By grasping a whisk-fan and harming the lives of sentient beings, how can there be the True Dharma?
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep such a whisk-fan."
At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by insects, dust, and dew falling upon their bodies.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a whisk.
They did not know how to make one, so the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to make [a whisk] from grass, or from tree bark and leaves using thread, or by cutting scraps of silk.
At that time, a certain bhikṣu obtained a tail-whisk (*vālavyajana*). The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "It is permitted to keep it."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.

Then Upāli was discussing the Dharma and Vinaya with the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus came together to listen to the precepts; however, the seating area was so cramped that they could not accommodate one another. The Buddha said:
"Those who are three years junior [in seniority] may sit together on wooden benches; those who are two years junior may sit together on small corded benches."
The newly ordained young bhikṣus did not understand how to manage numerical records and their interrelations; they were permitted to use counting sticks (*śalākā*) to keep track of numbers.
They used precious materials to make them, whereupon the Buddha said:
"One should not use precious materials."
"It is permitted to use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, lead, tin, white brass, or wood.
When he placed it on the ground with soiled hands, the Buddha said:
"One should not place it on the ground; it should be set upon a wooden board."
After he had placed the board on the ground and then placed his soiled robe upon his knees, the Buddha said:
"You should not do it that way.
You should place your feet [underneath] to serve as a stool."
As the counting sticks suffered from falling out, he said, "I allow you to make a bag to hold them.
When they were not tied and fell out of the mouth [of the bag], he said, "I allow you to tie them with a cord and place them upon a peg or a dragon-tooth peg."
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Jeta Grove, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of myriads of followers as he preached the Dharma.

There was a bhikṣu who, having eaten garlic, stayed at a distance from the Buddha. Knowing this, the World-Honored One intentionally asked Ānanda, "For what reason does this bhikṣu stay at a distance?"
Ānanda said, “This bhikṣu has eaten garlic.
The Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Would you rather crave such flavors and fail to listen to the Dharma?
From this day forward, no one should ever eat garlic."
At that time, Śāriputra suffered from a wind-disorder (vāta), and his physician instructed him to consume garlic. The Buddha said, "I permit its consumption.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu walking along carrying a load on his back; when the laypeople saw this, they all reviled and disparaged him.
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, are just like white-robed laypeople, walking along with burdens on their backs.
Thus they all gave rise to a sense of contempt.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not travel carrying loads on one's back.
At that time, the bhikṣus required firewood, dye-herbs, cow dung, or woolen and hemp fibers, and wished to carry them themselves.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to carry them in uninhabited places."
"If one sees a layperson (avadātavasana), one should lower the robe to the ground or shift it onto the shoulder.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Elāra who wore his robe [in this manner]; when the laypeople saw him, they all reviled and disparaged him, saying:
"He wears his robe and carries his belongings just like we laypeople do."
They all gave rise to conceit and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear one's robes in such a manner, nor should one walk about carrying things on one's back."

At that time, the bhikṣus gathered bricks, stones, timber, and other materials within the monastery; fearing transgression and being cautious, they did not dare to carry them on their backs to transport them. They informed the Buddha, who said:
"I allow you to carry items on your backs within the monastery."
At that time, after Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a donor who spoke as follows:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to erect a stūpa for them, we shall do so."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to make it.
They did not know how to make it.
The Buddha said:
"It may be made square, or circular, or with eight corners.
[The monks] did not know with what materials it should be made.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct them with stone, brick, or wood, and then plaster them.
He did not know what kind of plaster to use.
The Buddha said:
"I allow the use of black mud, or clay from a riverbank, or cow-dung mud, or white mud, or lime, or white chalk soil."
When he wished to construct a foundation for a stūpa, the Buddha said,
"I permit you to do so.
When he wished to offer flowers and incense, the Buddha said:
“Listen; railings may be constructed on all four sides, and flowers and incense may be placed upon them.
When they wished to hang banners and canopies above, the Buddha said:
“It is permitted to install objects for suspending banners and canopies.”
When he climbed up onto the stupa, the deity who protects the stupa became angry. The Buddha said:
"One should not climb up.
However, if one must climb up for the purpose of taking something, climbing is permitted."
When he climbed onto the upper railing, the deity who protects the stūpa became angry. The Buddha said:
"One should not climb up.
However, if one must climb up for the purpose of taking something, climbing is permitted."
He climbed onto a wooden peg and then onto a "dragon-tooth" peg. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
If it is necessary to go up to take or give something, I permit you to climb."
He placed a canopy upon the upper image as an offering. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
One should instead employ another expedient means by placing the canopy upon a pedestal."

The flowers, incense, oil for lamps, banners, canopies, music, and other articles of offering at that stupa were being ruined by rain, scattered by the wind, scorched by the sun, covered in dust and dirt, and defiled by the impurities of crows and birds. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to construct various kinds of roofs to cover them."

All necessities for building a house should be provided: if the ground is dusty, it should be smeared with mud—either black mud or cow-dung mud; if white is required, it should be smeared with lime or white clay.
He required a foot-washing vessel; [the Buddha said,] "It should be given.
He required a stone for walking upon; the Buddha said, "Its use is permitted."
He requested ground-covering materials, and [the Buddha] said, "I allow you to give them.
At that time, there were no outer walls as enclosures, so oxen and horses entered without restraint.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to build walls."
"If a door is required, you are permitted to build one.
At that time, the donors of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana thought to themselves:
"While those two were alive, we constantly provided them with food and drink."
"Now that he has entered parinirvāṇa, if the World-Honored One permits us to offer superior and delicious food as an offering to the stūpa, we shall deliver it.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I permit you to make such offerings."
Not knowing what kind of vessel to use for holding food,
the Buddha said:
"I permit the use of gold and silver bowls, precious vessels, and vessels made of various jewels."
Not knowing how to carry it away, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to transport it by means of elephants, horses, or carriages; or by carrying it on a litter, or bearing it on the head, or slung over the shoulder."
At that time, the bhikṣus themselves performed music or blew conch shells as an offering. The Buddha said, "You should not do so.
They were apprehensive and did not dare to have laypeople perform music as an offering. The Buddha said:
"Listen. He did not know who should eat the food and drink offered to the stūpa.
The Buddha said:
“Bhikṣus, śrāmaṇeras, upāsakas, or those who manage the construction work should eat.
At that time, the donors of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana thought:
“If the Buddha permits us to adorn and make offerings to the stūpa, we shall do so.”
The Buddha said, "It is permitted.
They required flowers, incense, necklaces, music, banners and streamers, lamp oil, and high-platformed vehicles; the Buddha said:
"I permit you to make them.
He wished to make images; the Buddha said, "I permit you to make them."
Not knowing how to enshrine the śarīra, he was told:

"They should be enshrined within a golden stūpa, or a silver stūpa, or a jeweled stūpa, or a stūpa made of various gems; or they should be wrapped in fine silk, or in *pāṭaśilinda* cloth, or in *dukūla* cloth."
Furthermore, not knowing how to maintain their conduct, the Buddha said:
"I permit the use of elephants, horses, chariots, palanquins, and vehicles for carrying loads; whether borne on the shoulders or on the head, if they are about to tip over, one should support them."
He himself performed musical offerings, and the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
Fearing and being cautious, he did not dare to have laypeople perform musical offerings; the Buddha said:
“Listen. He wished to sweep the stūpa of a śrāvaka, and the Buddha said:
“One should sweep it with tala leaves, mālūra leaves, or a peacock’s tail feather.”
"There is that great flower; you are permitted to place it upon the base of a stūpa, or on a railing, or on a dragon-tooth peg, or within a niche, or suspended from a cord hanging before the eaves."

If there is much fragrant clay, it is permitted to fashion hand-images, wheel-images, images of Maheśvara, or images of *vīra*, or images of grapevines, or images of lotuses; or if there is any remaining [clay], it should be used for plastering the ground.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the city of Rājagṛha.

Because of his profound reverence for the World-Honored One, no one dared to shave the Buddha’s hair; there was only a young child, who being ignorant and having nothing to fear, shaved the Buddha’s hair.
At that time, there was a young boy named Upāli who was shaving the Buddha’s hair. His parents stood before the World-Honored One, joined their palms, and said:
“This young boy Upāli is shaving the World-Honored One’s hair; does it look well?”
The Buddha said,
"You have shaved the hair well, which brings comfort to the body, yet you are bending too far.
His parents then spoke to him, saying:
"Do not bend your body too much and cause the World-Honored One discomfort.
He then asked the Buddha again,
"Is it good for a small child to have their hair shaved?"
The Buddha said,
"You have shaved your hair well, but your body is too straight.
His parents said to him:
"Do not stand with your body too straight, causing the World-Honored One discomfort.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"Is it good for a small child to have his hair shaved?"
The Buddha said,
“You have shaved your hair well, but your inhalation is too coarse.
His parents then spoke to him, saying:
"Do not breathe in so roughly as to cause the Buddha discomfort.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying,
"Is it well for a child to have his hair shaved?"
The Buddha said,
“You have shaved your hair well, but your exhalations are too coarse.
His parents then spoke, saying:
"Do not exhale so roughly as to disturb the Buddha.
At that moment, the young boy Upāli, having brought both inhalation and exhalation to a halt, entered the fourth dhyāna.
Then the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Upāli has already entered the fourth dhyāna; you take the knife from his hand.
Ānanda, having received these instructions, immediately took the knife.
At that time, Ānanda used his old hair-receptacle to collect the World-Honored One’s hair.
The Buddha said:

"One should not use an old vessel to hold the Tathāgata’s hair; one should instead use a new vessel, or wrap it in a new cloth, or in silk, or in a *pāṃśukūla* robe, or in a *tūṭūla* robe to contain it."
At that time, there was a prince, General Kokālika, who intended to go to the western regions to wage war and came to request the World-Honored One’s hair and beard.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to give them to him."
Having received it, he did not know how to store it.
The Buddha said:

"It is permitted to place it inside a golden stūpa, or a silver stūpa, or a jeweled stūpa, or a stūpa made of various gems; or it may be wrapped in silk, or in *pāṃśukūla* cloth, or in *tūṇaka* cloth."
Not knowing how to carry it, the Buddha said:
"I allow you to carry it on an elephant, a horse, or a carriage; or on a palanquin; or to bear it upon the head or upon the shoulder."
At that time, the prince took the World-Honored One’s hair and went forth to wage war, where he achieved victory.
Upon returning to his kingdom, the prince erected a hair-stūpa for the World-Honored One; this was a stūpa from the time when the World-Honored One was still in the world.
The bhikṣus spoke thus:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to carry the World-Honored One’s hair as we travel, we shall indeed carry it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I shall listen.
Not knowing how to settle himself,
the Buddha said:

"Listen: [the relics] should be placed securely within a golden stūpa, or a silver stūpa, or a jeweled stūpa, or a stūpa made of various gems; or they should be wrapped in a *pāṭaśilindrika* cloth, or a *tūṇḍivela* cloth."
Not knowing how to carry and transport them, the Buddha said:
"One may carry them on elephants, horses, carriages, or litters; or one may bear them upon the shoulders or upon the head."
He carried the stupa of the Blessed One tucked under his arm; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He then carried it with his robe hitched up, wrapped around his neck, wrapped around his head, or draped over both shoulders, or while wearing leather sandals; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus.
One should go with the right shoulder bared, having removed one's leather sandals, carrying the World-Honored One’s stūpa either on the head or borne upon the shoulder.
He then carried the World-Honored One’s stūpa to the place for defecation and urination; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus;
it should be maintained with purity.
When he carried the World-Honored One’s stūpa without having washed his anus or penis, the Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus;
it should be made for one who is pure to hold.
He then placed the Tathāgata’s stūpa in an inferior room while he himself stayed overnight in a superior room. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. One should place the Tathāgata’s stūpa in a superior room and stay oneself in an inferior room.
They placed the Tathāgata’s stūpa in a lower room and stayed themselves in an upper room; the Buddha said:
"It should not be so. You should place the Tathāgata’s stūpa in the upper room and stay for the night in the lower room yourself.
They stayed in the same room as the Tathāgata’s stūpa, whereupon the Buddha said:
"It should not be done. Because he was guarding it securely, he remained fearful and cautious, not daring to sleep with it. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to place it upon a peg, or upon a 'dragon-tooth' peg, or to sleep with it at the head of your bed."
At that time, the upāsakas thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One permits us to erect a stūpa for the World-Honored One while he is still alive, we shall build one."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to make one.
They did not know how to make it.
The Buddha said,
"It should be made square, or with eight corners, or circular.
Again, they did not know with what materials it should be made.
The Buddha said:
"It should be made of brick, stone, or wood; everything is according to the aforementioned rules, even the ground covering is as previously described.
Regarding the need for a banner-pole, the Buddha said:
"It is permitted to erect a banner—whether it be a lion banner, a dragon banner, or a banner of a humped ox.
Since there were no fences or enclosures on the four sides of those stupas, cattle and sheep trampled them without restraint; "a fence should be constructed as described above."
At that time, the various non-Buddhist practitioners were constantly making offerings of food and drink at their shrines and temples. The upāsakas thought to themselves:
"If the World-Honored One would permit us to present excellent food as an offering, we shall do so."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I permit you to act as described above.
They did not know who should eat this food.
The Buddha said,
"Those who build stūpas should eat [the offerings].
At that time, the various non-Buddhists were constantly adorning and making offerings at their own non-Buddhist shrines and temples, and the upāsakas thought to themselves:
“If the Blessed One would permit us to adorn and make offerings to the stūpa of the Blessed One, we shall do so.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“I permit you to do as described above.”
He stayed overnight inside the stūpa of the World-Honored One. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
Because he was guarding the stūpa, he was apprehensive and did not dare to stay overnight inside it. The Buddha said:
"If there is someone to guard and watch over it, one may allow it to remain overnight inside.
He then hid items within the stūpa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
Because he wished to store items within the stūpa for the sake of its preservation, yet feared and hesitated to do so, the Buddha said:
"I permit it.
He then entered the interior of the stūpa wearing leather sandals; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He entered the stūpa holding his leather sandals; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He walked around the stupa wearing leather sandals; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He entered the interior of the stupa wearing *puṭa* boots; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He entered the interior of the stupa while holding his leather boots;
the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
Out of fear and caution, he did not dare to put on his *puṭa* sandals while walking around the outside of the stūpa.
The Buddha said:
"I permit it."
Because they ate beneath the stupa and defiled it, the Buddha said, "One should not eat beneath a stupa.

At that time, when the bhikṣus were circumambulating the stupa, or visiting their quarters, or at the bathing pool, large assemblies of the Saṃgha gathered; as the space was narrow and could not accommodate them all, they were apprehensive and did not dare to sit and eat beneath the stupa, for the World-Honored One had not permitted sitting beneath a stupa.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to sit and eat beneath the stūpa, but you must not cause it to become defiled or impure.
At that time, the bhikṣus did not know what to do.
The Buddha said:
"I allow you to place impure communal items by your side and carry them out after eating.
He then passed beneath a stūpa containing a corpse; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He buried a dead person beneath the stupa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He burned a corpse beneath the stūpa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He burned a corpse in front of the stūpa; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
They burned corpses on all four sides of the stūpa, causing a foul odor to enter; the deity who protects the stūpa became angry. The Buddha said:
"One should not burn corpses on all four sides of the stūpa, causing a foul odor to enter."
When he passed beneath the stupa carrying a shroud or a bed, the guardian deity of the stupa became angry.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
Thereupon, the bhikṣu who wore rag-robes (pāṃśukūla) was apprehensive and did not dare to pass beneath the stupa carrying his rag-robes.
“The World-Honored One has given this instruction: ‘It is not permitted to pass beneath a stupa carrying the clothes of a deceased person.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“If they have been washed clean, dyed, and perfumed with incense, it is permitted.”
He defecated and urinated beneath the stupa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He defecated and urinated in front of the stupa; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
They then defecated and urinated on all four sides of the stūpa, causing a foul odor to enter; the deity who protects the stūpa became angry, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
He chewed a tooth-stick beneath the stupa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He chewed a tooth-stick in front of the stupa; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He chewed the tooth-stick around the four sides of the stūpa;
the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
He spat beneath the stūpa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
He spat before the stūpa; the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He sat with his legs extended before the stūpa; the Buddha said, "One should not do so."
"If there is a partition of a stupa within a monastery, it is permitted to sit with one's feet extended in the space between them.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the kingdom of Kosala, traveling through the human world with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, proceeding toward the brahmin village of Tundiya.
Having arrived at another place, the World-Honored One smiled.
At that time, Ānanda thought to himself:
"For what reason and by what cause does the World-Honored One smile now?"
"The World-Honored One does not smile without cause or condition.
With his right shoulder bared, having removed his leather sandals and placed his right knee upon the ground, he joined his palms and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"One does not smile without cause and condition; for what reason did you smile just now?
I wish to know this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

“In the distant past, after the Buddha Kāśyapa had entered parinirvāṇa, there was a king of the Śibi kingdom who, at this very spot, erected a great stūpa over the course of seven years, seven months, and seven days. Having completed it, he performed a great offering for seven years, seven months, and seven days, seating the monks of both orders beneath the shade of an elephant tree and providing them with their first meal.”
At that time, not far from this place, there was a farmer plowing a field. The Buddha went to him and took a clod of earth, brought it back here, and spoke this verse:
"Even if one were to offer hundreds of thousands of necklaces, All made of Jāmbūnada gold, It would not equal the merit of taking a single clod of earth To erect a stupa for the Buddha."
Even if one were to offer a hundred thousand lumps of Jambūnada gold,
it would not be as meritorious as using a single lump of clay to erect a stūpa for the Buddha.
Even if one were to offer hundreds of thousands of loads of gold— all of it Jambūnada gold—
it would not equal the superior merit of using a single lump of clay to erect a stupa for the Buddha.
