Even if one were to carry a hundred thousand pieces of gold— all of it Jambūnada gold—
it would not be as meritorious as taking a single lump of clay to erect a stupa for the Buddha.
Even if one were to use hundreds of thousands of walls made entirely of Jambūnada gold,
it would not be as meritorious as using a single lump of clay to erect a stūpa for the Buddha.
Even if one were to provide hundreds of thousands of mountain crags, all made of Jambūnada gold,
it would not equal the excellence of using a single lump of clay to erect a stupa for the Buddha.
Even if one were to offer a hundred thousand mountains of gold— all of it Jambūnada gold—
it would not be as meritorious as using a single lump of clay to erect a stūpa for the Buddha.
At that time, the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās all took a single lump of clay and placed it at this spot; immediately, a great stūpa was formed.
At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by the foul odor inside their dwellings. The Buddha said:
"You should sprinkle water and sweep.
If it still smells, plaster it with fragrant mud. If it continues to smell, you should hang incense at the four corners of the building."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.
At that time, the community of monks received a great abundance of food and drink offerings; the bhikṣus did not exercise moderation and consequently fell ill. The Buddha said:
"You should take medicine."
If he requires emetics or purgatives, one should give him emetics or purgatives.
If he requires rice gruel, give him rice gruel.
If he requires the flesh of wild birds, one should give it to him.

At that time, the youth Jīvaka was treating the illnesses of the Saṃgha; he prepared emetic and purgative medicines, as well as congee and broth made from the meat of wild birds for the Buddha and the Saṃgha, but it was not sufficient. He went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, stood to one side, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“Venerable Sir!...”
"The bhikṣus have fallen ill; if you permit the bhikṣus to build a bathhouse for bathing, their illnesses may be alleviated.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave his silent assent.
At that time, knowing that the Buddha had granted permission, the youth Jīvaka rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed.

Then the World-Honored One, on account of this matter, assembled the community of bhikṣus and, employing skillful means, preached the Dharma in accordance with their needs. He praised those who practice the dhūta austerities, who are upright and dignified, who have few desires and are content, and who delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:
“I allow the bhikṣus to construct bathhouses for bathing.”

translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.

At that time, the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra arrived in the kingdom of Vaiśālī. He was a close friend and acquaintance of the Licchavis; when the great Licchavis heard that the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra had arrived in Vaiśālī, they went at once to pay their respects, but the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra did not respond to them.
He said, "Venerable sir!
What have I committed?"
Therefore, we have come to inquire after you,
yet you do not answer us. He replied,
“Why should I speak with people like you?”
“Ṭhapassī the son of Māra has treated me with contempt and caused me distress,
yet you did not come to my aid. He then said,
“What skillful means should I employ so that Ṭhapassī the son of Māra will no longer trouble you?”
He replied: "If you go while the Buddha and the great assembly of monks are gathered together, go there and speak these words:
'Venerable Sir!'"

That such a thing has occurred is unwholesome, contrary to the Dharma, improper, and untimely; we who considered this place pure, peaceful, and free from fear, have instead given rise to distress, like fire arising from water.
"Why is this? Because the monk Ṭhapassamala has violated my wife, the Saṃgha should act in harmony to carry out his *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment).
If this is done, he will not come to trouble me again."
He immediately replied,
"What difficulty is there in this?
That Mahāliśa went to where the Buddha and the great assembly were and spoke as he had said above.
At that time, Trapusa Māra-putra was sitting not far from the Buddha. Knowing this, the Buddha intentionally asked Trapusa Māra-putra:
"Did you hear those words spoken by Viśākha?"
He replied, “I have heard it; only the Buddha knows it.
The Buddha said to Trapusa Māra-putra:
“You should not answer in such a manner.
You must speak truth when it is true, and speak falsehood when it is false.

When Trapusa the Malla had heard these words of the Buddha, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Since my birth, I have never committed sexual misconduct even in a dream, let alone while awake.
The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Excellent! Trapuṣabhadra, this is a good answer.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should ask that Mahāliṣa:
'Do not slander this pure bhikṣu, Ṭhapassamallaputta, with groundless charges of unchastity.
To slander a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges of unchastity incurs a grave and heavy offense.'"
When the bhikṣus heard the World-Honored One’s instruction, they immediately began to cross-examine Mahāliṣa:
“You should speak the truth.
How did this matter occur?”
Do not slander Dharmaruci with groundless charges of impurity; to slander a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges of impurity incurs a grave and heavy offense.
When the Mahāliṣas had been thus interrogated by the bhikṣus, they spoke as follows:
“Tapassamallaputta is pure; he has committed no impure act.”
"This was merely what the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra taught me.

When the other bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and dread of blame.
They censured Mahāliśa, saying: "The son of Ṭhapaka truly has no impure conduct; why do you slander him with groundless charges of impurity?"
The bhikṣus went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One assembled the community of bhikṣus and, using countless skillful means, rebuked Mahāliśa, saying:
"What you have done is wrong; it is not a practice in accordance with the Dharma, nor is it a pure practice."
"How could you defame the son of Taṭṭhāma with groundless charges of impurity?
Having rebuked them with countless skillful means, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"From this day forward, perform the *karmavācanā* of the second motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) against Mahāliśa: overturn his alms-bowl and cease all verbal exchange with him."
There are five conditions in a household of white-robed laypeople for which one should perform the ritual of overturning the bowl:
being unfilial toward one's father, being unfilial toward one's mother, not revering śramaṇas, not revering brāhmaṇas, and not serving bhikṣus.
There are five such qualities for which one should perform the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa* (the formal act of overturning the bowl).
There are five qualities for which one should not perform the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa*.
What are these five?
Filial toward one’s father, filial toward one’s mother, respectful toward śramaṇas, respectful toward brāhmaṇas, and honoring and serving bhikṣus—
one who possesses these five qualities should not have the *pātrābhyuddhāra* (the bowl-covering) performed against them.
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas for which the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl):

reviling and slandering a bhikṣu; acting to the detriment and disadvantage of a bhikṣu; employing means to deprive him of a dwelling place; inciting strife among bhikṣus; speaking ill of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha in the presence of a bhikṣu; slandering a bhikṣu with groundless charges of impure conduct; or committing an offense against a bhikṣuṇī. If one possesses such ten dharmas, the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* against him.

In this manner, if one reviles or slanders a bhikṣu by means of nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or even one such factor, the Saṃgha should perform the *pātra-nyāsa* (turning over the bowl).
There is such a case where the Saṃgha should perform the "turning over of the bowl" (pātra-pratigrahaṇa) against someone.

It should be performed in this manner: from within the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and he should make the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"May the virtuous Saṃgha listen!
This Mahāliśa, though pure, has slandered the Venerable Dharmaruci with groundless charges of a *pārājika* offense.

If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now perform the "bowl-covering" (*pātra-āvartana*) against this Mahāliśa, such that he shall no longer have dealings with us.
[The motion] is thus stated:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
This Mahāliśa, son of Tapassu, is pure, yet he has slandered [another] with a groundless charge of a *pārājika* offense."
The Sangha now performs the *pātrāvakṣepa* (turning over of the bowl) against [him], such that there shall be no mutual interaction.
Those elders who consent to the Sangha performing the *pātrāvakṣepa* against Mahāliśa so that there shall be no mutual interaction, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.

"The Sangha has already consented to perform the 'bowl-covering' rite against Mahāliṣa, prohibiting further association with him. Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter shall be held thus."
"Listen: the Saṃgha has appointed a messenger to go to Mahāliśa and speak these words to him:
'The Saṃgha has performed the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* against you, imposing the *pātra-nyubja* (inversion of the bowl) so that there shall be no further social interaction.'"

"One who possesses eight qualities should be appointed to go: one who is able to listen, able to speak, understands for oneself, can cause others to understand, is able to receive [the teaching], able to memorize and retain it, is free from error or loss, and can distinguish between the good and bad meanings."
"One who possesses these eight qualities should be appointed as a messenger for the Saṃgha.
Then he spoke in verse:
"If one is in the midst of the great assembly, Their mind is free from timidity;..."
What is spoken is neither increased nor diminished; in receiving the teaching there is no loss or reduction.
His words are free from confusion, and he does not waver when questioned.
A bhikṣu such as this is fit to serve as an envoy for the Saṃgha.
“Ānanda! There are these eight matters; you should authorize [a messenger] to act as a monk’s envoy and speak thus to that Mahāliśa:
‘The Saṃgha now performs for you the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* of overturning the alms-bowl (*pātra-āvartana*) and prohibiting social interaction.’”
From among the assembly, those capable of performing the *karmavācanā* were selected as described above, and they made the following formal motion (*jñapti*):
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now appoint Ānanda as an emissary of the Saṃgha to go to Mahāliśa and say to him:"
"Now the Saṃgha performs for you the ritual of overturning the bowl so that there shall be no mutual association.
Thus is the formal announcement.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Sangha now appoints Ānanda as its messenger to go to Mahāliśa and speak these words:
"The Sangha has now performed the *pātrāvarṣaṇa* rite against you, such that there shall be no mutual interaction."
"Whoever among the elders approves of the Saṃgha appointing Ānanda as its messenger, let him remain silent; whoever does not approve, let him speak.
"The Saṃgha has approved the appointment of Ānanda as its messenger to go to that Mahāliśa and say:
'The Saṃgha has performed the *pātrāvakarṣaṇa* (the overturning of the bowl) against you, such that there shall be no mutual coming and going.'"
“[The motion] is concluded.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
At that time, Ānanda put on his robes, took up his bowl, and went to the house of Mahā-leṣa.
At that time, Mahāliśa was combing his hair under the eaves of the outer gatehouse when he saw Ānanda approaching from afar. He quickly gathered up his hair and went forward to meet him, saying:
"It is well, Venerable One!"
"I pray that you will enter my house. Ānanda replied,
"I ought not to enter your house to accept offerings of beds, seats, food, or drink."
Vimala said: "Venerable Ānanda!
For what reason?"
He replied, "The Saṃgha has already performed the *pātra-nyubja* rite against you, so that we shall no longer associate with one another. Viśākha said:
"For what reason? Ānanda then explained the causes and conditions in detail for him. He then said:
“Venerable Ānanda! Is this how you would kill me?
He immediately fainted and fell to the ground;
after a long time he regained consciousness, rose up, rubbed his eyes with his hands, and said to Ānanda:
"What skillful means should I employ to resolve my overturned bowl so that we may resume our mutual visits?
Ānanda said, "You should go and confess before the community of monks."

At that time, Mahāliṣa conformed to the Saṃgha and did not dare to oppose it; he requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nigraha* (the bowl-banishment) so that they might once again interact with one another.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"If Mahāliṣa conforms to the Saṃgha and does not dare to oppose it, and requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-nigraha* so that they may once again interact with one another, you should perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to lift it."
From among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* shall be appointed as described above, and make the following formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

Now the Saṃgha intends to lift the *pātrānāmiṣa* (the bowl-banishment) and the *na-samvāsa* (exclusion from communal life) for Mahāliśa. He has complied with the Saṃgha and does not dare to disobey; he requests from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātrānāmiṣa* and *na-samvāsa* *karmavācanā*."

"If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent; let the Saṃgha now lift the *pātra-āvṛti* against Mahāliśa so that they may once again go and come between one another.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Listen, venerable Saṃgha!"

The Saṃgha imposed the *pātra-āvṛti* (the bowl-covering) and the suspension of mutual interaction upon Mahālīśa; he conformed to the Saṃgha and did not dare to oppose it, and thus he requested from the Saṃgha the lifting of the *pātra-āvṛti* and the suspension of mutual interaction through formal ritual action (*karmavācanā*).
Now the Saṃgha intends to lift the *pātra-nikubjana* (the bowl-inversion) for Mahāliśa and restore mutual social interaction with him.
Those elders who consent to the Saṃgha’s lifting of the *pātra-nikubjana* for Mahāliśa and restoring mutual interaction, remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has already consented to lift the *pātra-nikṣepa* for that Mahāliśa and restore mutual social interaction with him; the Sangha consents by remaining silent. Thus it shall be held."

At that time, Kālodāyin was staying in an araṇya hermitage. While he was on the road, he burned some grass; the fire spread and蔓延 (extended) until it eventually set fire to King Prasenajit’s Deer Park.
At that time, the householders all spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame; they take the lives of living beings.
They themselves claim:"
"I know the True Dharma.
Having burned the King’s Deer Park, how can there be any True Dharma here?
The bhikṣus went and informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, as the bhikṣus were traveling on a road, there was grass obstructing their way. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to press down the grass with bamboo, or to weigh it down with stones or wood."
At that time, a wild fire outside the Jetavana Monastery spread its flames toward it. The bhikṣus did not know what to do and immediately informed the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to clear the grass in between by cutting it back, or to block it with ditches and moats, or to extinguish it with earth, or to burn it back."
There was a bhikṣu who was frail and old; he could not walk without a carrying bag for his bowl and without a staff.
He thought to himself: "What shall I do?"
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said,
"I allow the Saṃgha to grant that elderly bhikṣu a staff and a bag for his alms-bowl by means of a formal act consisting of one motion and one announcement (jñapti-dvitīya-karman)."
It should be granted in this manner: from among the assembly, one capable of performing the *karmavācanā* should be appointed as described above, and the following motion (*jñapti*) should be made:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu so-and-so is weak and aged; he is unable to walk without a staff and without carrying his bowl in a bag. He has requested a staff and a bowl-bag from the Saṃgha."
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha bestow a staff and a pouch upon the bhikṣu so-and-so.
This is the motion. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu, so-and-so, is infirm and aged; he is unable to walk without a staff and a bag for his bowl. He now requests a staff and a bag from the Saṃgha.
The Saṃgha now grants this bhikṣu a staff and a bag for his bowl.
"Whichever elders approve of the Sangha's granting of a staff and a pouch to the bhikṣu [Name], let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak.
The Sangha has already approved the granting of the staff and pouch to the bhikṣu [Name]. Since the Sangha approves and remains silent, this matter is thus upheld."
At that time, Śāriputra saw the assembly of monks performing an illegal *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical act) and, finding no one who agreed with him, wished to remain silent and let it proceed.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to remain silent."
There are five cases in which one should not remain silent:
if a formal act (*karmavācanā*) is performed according to the Dharma but one’s mind does not agree with it, yet one remains silent and acquiesces;
or if one finds companions who agree with one’s view, yet one still remains silent and acquiesces.
If one sees a minor offense and remains silent;
if one remains silent while another is undergoing the *parivāsa* (probation);
or if one remains silent on the boundary of the *sīmā* (monastic precinct).
To remain silent regarding these five matters is contrary to the Dharma.
There are five matters for which one should remain silent:
remaining silent when seeing another person act contrary to the Dharma;
One must not remain silent when it is improper to do so;
one must not remain silent when having committed a grave offense; and one must not remain silent while living in communal residence.
One should remain silent while dwelling together;
these are the five matters for which one should remain silent.
There are five matters for which one should act in harmony.
What are the five?
If one acts in accordance with the Dharma through harmony;
or if one remains silent and leaves the matter as it is.
If one has granted consent;
or if one has heard it from a trustworthy person;
or if one was previously sitting silently among them.
"In this way, these five matters should be brought into harmony.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in the Jeta Grove preaching the Dharma to a multitude of countless beings.
Then, as the World-Honored One sneezed, the bhikṣus uttered words of blessing, saying:
"Long life! The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās also said: "Long life."
The great assembly then became noisy and chaotic, so the Buddha said, "You should not do this.
At that time, there was a lay devotee who sneezed; the bhikṣus, being fearful and cautious, did not dare say, "Long life! The lay devotees all spoke with derision and resentment, saying:
"When we sneeze, the bhikṣus do not recite the blessing for long life.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I allow you to recite the blessing for long life."

At that time, the lay devotees prostrated to the bhikṣus, but the bhikṣus, being cautious and fearful, did not dare say, "May you live long," for the World-Honored One had not permitted them to offer such blessings.
The lay devotees all complained,
saying, "We prostrate to the bhikṣus, yet the bhikṣus do not bless us with longevity."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
“I allow you to recite benedictions for long life.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, upon having a minor dispute, uttered curses, saying:
"If I were to do such a thing, I would fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, and would not be born within the Buddha-dharma.
If others were to do such a thing, they too would fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, and would not be born within the Buddha-dharma."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be done so. You are permitted to speak as follows:"
"If I perform such an act, I take refuge in the Buddha.
If you perform such an act, you too shall say:
'I take refuge in the Buddha.'"
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus wore waistbands with tassels attached to the ends.
The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
They then wore leather belts. The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. The group of six bhikṣus kept jaṭīna-bands; the Buddha said: "It should not be so."
They wore belts made of loose threads; the Buddha said, "You must not do so.
You foolish people!"
Avoiding what I have prohibited, they instead perform other actions.
From this day forward, none of these kinds of long, wide sashes should be kept.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus kept long, wide sashes, whereupon the Buddha said:
"It should not be so. It is permitted to make a waistband three finger-widths wide, wrapped three times around the waist.
Those bhikṣus of the group of six dyed the band with a deep, true color; the Buddha said:
"It should not be done. He made a brocade sash; the Buddha said, "It should not be done."
He made a white sash; the Buddha said, "It should not be done so.
I allow you to make a sash in the color of a kāṣāya."

At that time, there was a potter of faith and devotion who made various kinds of vessels and gave them to the bhikṣus. The bhikṣus did not dare to accept them and informed the Buddha. The Buddha said, "I allow you to accept them."
"There are two kinds of vessels that should not be kept: sitting benches made of earthenware, and earthenware measures such as *hu*, *dou*, *sheng*, and *he*.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda went to the potter's house and sat with his thighs resting upon earthenware vessels; the vessels broke, and he fell backward, exposing the ground.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not sit upon earthenware vessels, nor should one sit with the thighs crossed in the home of a layperson.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus recited the heterodox texts on the auspicious and inauspicious placement of houses, incantations for the joints of the limbs, incantations for the kṣatriyas, incantations for the śivaras, incantations for knowing the auspiciousness and misfortune of birth and death, and incantations for interpreting all sounds.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
When they instructed others to do it, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
He lived his life by this means, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
At that time, the bhikṣus had foul breath. The Buddha said:
"You should chew a willow twig.
There are five faults in not chewing a willow twig: [the list follows]."

If one does not chew the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick), there are these five faults: foul breath, inability to distinguish flavors, an increase in heat and phlegm, loss of appetite, and lack of clarity in the eyes.
There are five benefits to chewing a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*):
first, the breath does not become foul;
second, one distinguishes flavors.
Third, it eliminates heat and phlegm.
Fourth, it induces appetite for food.
Fifth, it clarifies the eyesight.
"There are five such benefits to chewing the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick).
After the Blessed One had permitted the chewing of the *dantakāṣṭha*, they chewed long tooth-sticks. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
"The maximum length for a *karamada* (a span) is one *vitasti* (the distance between the thumb and the middle finger). Regarding those who chewed tooth-sticks that were too long, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
Regarding those who chewed on various leaves, the Buddha said,
"One should not do so.
Regarding those who chewed only on bark, the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who chewed a short tooth-stick; because he saw the Buddha with reverence, he swallowed it immediately, which caused him distress.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
The shortest length is four finger-breadths.
He chewed the tooth-stick in places frequented by many people—whether in the heated hall, the dining hall, or the walking hall.
The bhikṣus saw this and disapproved, going to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "One should not do so.
There are three matters that ought to be done in a secluded place: defecating, urinating, and chewing a tooth-stick. These three matters should be performed in a secluded place."
At that time, the bhikṣus had much plaque on their tongues.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a tongue-scraper.
They made one out of precious materials, and the Buddha said:
"It should not be so. It is permitted to use bone, ivory, horn, copper, iron, white tin, lead, tin, *śara* grass, bamboo, reeds, and wood."
He lifted it up without washing it; other bhikṣus saw this and disapproved. The Buddha said: "You should not do so; you ought to wash it.
He washed it but did not dry it in the sun before lifting it up; it became damaged. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done. At that time, the bhikṣus were troubled by food particles entering between their teeth.
The Buddha said, "I allow you to make a toothpick."
They made it out of precious gems. The Buddha said, "One should not use precious gems;
I allow you to make it from bone, ivory, horn, or even bamboo and wood.
Having made it, they failed to wash it before setting it aside. When the other bhikṣus saw this, they all disapproved. The Buddha said:
"It should not be done thus;
it should be washed.
After he had washed it, he lifted it up without drying it in the sun, and it became spoiled. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so;
one should have it dried and then removed.
At that time, the bhikṣus suffered from having impurities in their ears, and the Buddha said:
"Allow the making of ear-pickers.
He made one out of precious materials, and the Buddha said, "It should not be so."
"It is permitted to use bone, ivory, horn, or even bamboo and wood to make them.
After using them, he failed to wash them before setting them aside. When the other bhikṣus saw this, they disapproved. The Buddha said, "You should not do so."
"One should lift it after washing.
He lifted it without drying it, and it became damaged. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
"You should lift it only after it has been dried.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.

At that time, the bhikṣus kept many parrots, mynas, and starlings; their chirping and calling during the first and last watches of the night disturbed the bhikṣus who were practicing dhyāna. The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep such birds.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Kauśāmbī.
Then the Śākya son Upananda kept a puppy, which barked when it saw the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not keep [it].
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vṛji.
At that time, the Vajjiputtaka bhikṣus of Vaiśālī kept a young bear; it tore through their robes, bowls, sitting mats, and needle cases, and furthermore injured the bodies of the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not keep [them].
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, various Licchavis, riding on elephants, horses, chariots, and litters, and carrying swords and staves, came wishing to see the World-Honored One.
They left their weapons outside the monastery and entered within to pay their respects.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went outside and would frequently ride upon those elephants, horses, carriages, and litters, or carry swords and blades while playing together.
When the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in reproach and disdain, saying:

"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, do not know contentment and have no sense of shame; they ride upon those elephants, horses, carriages, and litters, and carry swords and blades while playing together, just like kings and great ministers."
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"A bhikṣu should not ride upon elephants, horses, carriages, or litters while engaging in playful laughter; nor should a bhikṣu carry swords or blades."
At that time, there were senior bhikṣus who were elderly and infirm; unable to travel from this dwelling place to that one, they feared and hesitated to ride in vehicles. The Buddha said:
"I permit you to ride in a carriage drawn by men."
"If it is a man who rides, all animal mounts are likewise male.
He had fears for his life and for his pure conduct; out of apprehension and caution, he did not dare to ride and fled on foot. The Buddha said:
"If there are such dangers as these, I permit you to ride an elephant or a horse to escape."

At that time, some laypeople came with swords and blades to entrust them to the bhikṣus for safekeeping. The bhikṣus, being fearful and cautious, did not dare to accept them, as the World-Honored One had given such an instruction that they were not permitted to carry swords or blades.
He informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I allow you to store and keep [the items] for the sake of making the donor's provisions secure.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
King Udayana was a close friend of Piṇḍola; every morning and evening, the king would go to visit him.
At that time, an unfaithful Brahmin minister followed the king and said to him:
"Why does Your Majesty go to pay your respects every morning and evening to this man of lowly occupation, yet when he sees the King, he does not rise?"
The king replied, "I shall go tomorrow at dawn; if you still do not rise, I shall take your life.
At dawn the following day, the king went to where Piṇḍola was. Seeing the king approaching from afar, Piṇḍola thought to himself:
"This king has now come with an evil mind; if I do not rise, he will take my life.
If I rise now, he will lose his royal throne; if I do not rise, he will take my life and I shall fall into hell."
"Will this king cause me to fall into hell?
Will I lose my royal throne?
He then further thought to himself:
"It would be better for him to lose his throne than to fall into hell.
He then rose to welcome him from afar and, taking the initiative, inquired after his welfare, saying:
"Welcome, Great King!"
The king asked,
"For what reason do you now rise to welcome me? He replied:
"I have risen for your sake.
The king asked,
"Why did you not rise yesterday?"
He replied, "It is also for your sake. The king asked:
"What is this so-called 'self'?
He replied, "Yesterday you came with a virtuous mind; today you come harboring an evil mind."
"If I do not rise, he will take my life; if he takes my life, I will surely fall into hell.
I thought to myself:
"This king comes with an evil intent; if I do not rise, he will take my life, but if I rise, I will certainly lose my royal throne."
"If my life were taken, I would surely fall into hell; it would be better to cause me to lose my royal throne than to cause me to fall into hell.
For this reason, he raised his ear. The King asked:
"I shall lose my position? He replied, "You will."
The king asked again,
"In how many days will it be lost? He replied:
"In seven days' time.

Thereupon, the king immediately returned to Kauśāmbī, repaired the city walls and moats, gathered provisions of grain, firewood, and fodder, assembled his troops, and established defensive guard over the city.
After several days had passed, he said: "Today is the first day.
In this manner, it continued until the seventh day, at which point he spoke these words:
"The ascetic speaks falsehood," he said, and proceeded to sport upon a boat with his court ladies in the Ganges River.

At that time, King Udena’s kingdom had not seen rain for seven years. Having heard that King Bimbisāra of Magadha possessed a "water-jewel" such that if this jewel were brought forth, the heavens would immediately send down rain, he raised a fourfold army and marched toward Rājagṛha, surrounding the city and remaining there.
That city was so secure that it could not be taken by any other means; it could only be captured once its water, grain, and food supplies were completely exhausted.

At that time, there was within the city a minister of great skill and wisdom who instructed them to place bamboo and reeds into the ponds, causing lotus flowers to grow up through the holes in the stalks.
Then that minister went to King Bimbisāra and said:
"Does Your Majesty not know?
The city of Rājagṛha is secure and cannot be taken by any other means; it can only be taken once its water and grain are exhausted."
Now you should dispatch a messenger to speak these words to King Prasenajit:
"Please desist for now!
There is no need to fight with elephants, horses, chariots, swords, or spears."
"You may now use various flowers—blue lotuses (utpala), red lotuses (padma), yellow lotuses (kumuda), and white lotuses (puṇḍarīka)—to fight; I, too, shall use such flowers to fight."
"You may also form balls of rice and fight with them; I too shall form balls of rice and fight with them. The king said, "So be it."
Thereupon, he immediately dispatched a messenger to King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī to convey the aforementioned message in full.
The king thought to himself:
"The city of Rājagṛha is well-fortified; it can only be taken once its water, grain, and food supplies are exhausted, yet within the city, water, grain, and food are abundant."
He replied to the messenger, saying:

"I have not come for the sake of the city. For seven years there has been no rain in my kingdom, and I heard that in your country there is a water-jewel; when this jewel is brought forth, the heavens immediately send down rain. For this reason, I have come."
The messenger replied:
"Great King! Why did you not say at the outset that you required the pearl?"
"If you say you require the pearl, I shall give it to you immediately.
Your Majesty may depart now; the pearl shall be sent shortly.
The king then withdrew his army and headed toward the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
Hearing the sound of King Udayana sporting with his court ladies, he immediately asked those nearby,
"Whose sound of play is this?
The ministers replied:
"Does Your Majesty know?
King Udayana, together with his court ladies, is sporting on a boat upon the Ganges River; that is the sound of their play.
The king immediately commanded his attendants not to make a sound and released the elephant near the bank of the Ganges, dispatching the foremost white elephant along with its keepers.
At that time, King Udayana’s minister went out and saw a white elephant, and said to the king:
"There is a wild elephant.
The king immediately commanded his men, saying:
"Do not make a sound; pull the boat close to the shore.
He immediately drew near the shore.
King Udayana was well-versed in the arts of taming elephants; he then recited the incantation, played the lute, and went forward to seize the elephant.
At that time, the elephant-keeper immediately seized the king, who was filled with great terror.
The keeper asked the king,
"Are you afraid?"
The king said, "I am afraid. He replied:
"Do not fear, O King. King Prasenajit summons you.
The king became even more terrified and thought to himself:
"Will Paraśuṣṭi kill me along with my attendants?
Thinking this, they immediately bound him and escorted him under guard to the presence of King Paraśuṣṭi.
He asked, "Are you afraid? and she replied:
"I am afraid. The king said,
"Do not be afraid!"
"You may teach my son Gopāla the art of taming elephants, and you may also teach my daughter to play the lute.
He then took him to the kingdom of Uddiyāna and kept his feet shackled there for seven years.
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda came from the lady Sāmāvatī in Kauśāmbī to Udāyin in the kingdom of Vairantī; carrying a letter from King Udāyin, he went to the lady’s residence.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, who said:
"A bhikṣu should not perform services for laypeople; if he does so, it is a duṣkṛta offense.
At that time, he taught the king’s son the art of training elephants and taught his daughter how to play the lute.
Later, at another time, he had an illicit affair with the king’s daughter.
When Prince Kūbara learned of this, he thought to himself:
"If I report this to the king, he will surely take my life."
"He was my teacher and instructed me with great hardship;
she is the king's daughter and he is the king—it is only fitting that this should be so.
Thus, he concealed it and did not tell anyone.
Later, when King Udayana wished to flee, he immediately prepared a swift female elephant for himself.
Kuvalaya, becoming aware of this, thought to himself:
"He has prepared a swift elephant; he surely intends to escape."
"If I inform the King, he will surely take his life; he is my teacher who taught me with such hardship.
Thus she hid him and said nothing to anyone.

She placed the King’s daughter upon the elephant and drank from it while atop the animal; before the glass vessel had even hit the ground, they had already traveled from Vairañjā to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī.
The king then went to Queen Śyāmāvatī and spoke these words to her:
"While I was bound there, I made a vow:
'I shall provide for eight brahmins, ensuring that all their needs are fully satisfied.'"
"Now that you wish to give it to him, you may prepare everything.

The Queen said, "If it is so, then all the elephants, horses, chariots, gold, silver, and the seven treasures, as well as the King, myself, and everything else we possess— all such things combined and given to a single person— would still not satisfy him even if he were to receive them all."
The king said, "What should we do now? The lady replied:
"This Mahākātyāyana is of the great Brahmin caste.
You should now invite him along with seven other bhikṣus of the Brahmin caste, and provide these royal provisions for these eight men."
"He does not accept those teachings; even if you were to offer them to him, he would still not accept them. The King said, "So be it."

Then King Udayana went to where Kātyāyana was, prostrated himself at his feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. At that time, Kātyāyana, through various skillful means, preached the Dharma to the king, causing him to attain joy.
When the king had heard the Dharma and was filled with joy, he spoke these words:
"I pray that you will accept my invitation for a meal tomorrow, for eight people including yourself.
At that time, Kātyāyana accepted by remaining silent.
When the king saw that Kātyāyana had silently accepted his invitation, he rose from his seat, bowed his head at the master’s feet in salutation, and departed with joy.
Returning to his home, the king prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink; then, early the next morning, he went to inform him that the time had arrived.
At that time, Mahākātyāyana, having dressed in the early morning and taken up his bowl, went with eight others to the palace of King Udayana and sat upon the prepared seat.

King Udayana personally served them various kinds of delicious food and drink until they were fully satisfied. When the meal was finished and they had set aside their bowls, he took a golden pitcher, filled it with water, and offered it to them, along with an elephant as a gift.
Kātyāyana said, "Stop! Stop!"
"O King, this already constitutes sufficient offering; we ought not to accept such an offering.
He then offered chariots, horses, men, along with gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, pearls, musaragalva, and agate—the seven treasures—as alms.
Kātyāyana said: "Stop!"
"Stop! This itself constitutes an offering; we should not accept such an offering.
Then King Udayana, having prostrated at the feet of Kātyāyana, took a low seat and sat down.

At that time, Kātyāyana preached the Dharma to the king in various ways until he was filled with joy; having done so, he rose from his seat and departed, returning to the monastery to inform the bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha.
At that time, for this reason, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, for their sake, taught the *Khandhaka* on the observance of the precepts, both major and minor:

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world—one who is worthy of offerings, perfectly and fully awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, Buddha, World-Honored One—he awakens to and realizes truth for himself amidst the assembly of all devas, humans, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, celestial Māras, and Brahmā kings, and he teaches the Dharma to others."
The discourse is excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end; it is complete in both letter and meaning, revealing and clarifying the pure conduct.
If householders or their sons, or those born of other lineages, hear this, they will give rise to faith and joy upon hearing the True Dharma.
With a mind of faith and joy, he formed this thought:
"I am currently bound by the household life and my wife and children; I cannot purely practice the holy life (brahmacarya).
I would rather now shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron robes, and with faith renounce the home for the homeless life."

At another time, he renounced all his wealth, whether much or little, and likewise abandoned all his kinsmen, whether many or few; he shaved off his hair and beard, donned the saṃghāṭī robe, and left the household life to enter the homeless path.

He has discarded ornaments and finery just like those who have left the household life; he observes the same precepts as the bhikṣus; he refrains from taking life and lays aside the sword and staff; he is always possessed of shame and remorse, and maintains thoughts of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings—this is what constitutes non-killing.
Abandoning theft—taking only what is given and not taking what is not given—with a mind that is pure and free from any intent to steal, this is non-stealing.
Abandoning unchaste conduct, practicing the holy life with diligent effort, remaining unattached to sensual desire, and dwelling in purity and fragrance; this is the abandonment of unchaste conduct.
To abandon false speech, being truthful and not deceiving the world, is non-false speech. To abandon divisive speech:
if one hears something here, one does not transmit it there; if one hears something there, one does not transmit it here; thus, one does not cause discord or disruption.

If there are those who are separated, one brings them into harmony; for those already in harmony and affection, one constantly causes them joy; and in uttering words of reconciliation, one speaks with an awareness of the proper time—this is what constitutes the absence of divisive speech.

To abstain from harsh speech: that which is coarse and violent, causing distress to others, giving rise to anger and displeasure—such harsh speech is severed. One’s words are gentle, producing no resentment or harm; they are beneficial and loved by all, such that people delight in hearing them. Constantly uttering such beneficial and virtuous words is what is meant by "not using harsh speech."

To abstain from unbeneficial speech means to speak at the proper time, to speak truthfully, to speak beneficially, to speak in accordance with the Dharma, to speak in accordance with the Vinaya, and to speak in order to settle disputes; to speak only when there is a relevant purpose and to know the proper timing for what is said—this is what it means to abstain from unbeneficial speech.
One shall not drink intoxicants and shall remain far from states of heedlessness;

one shall not wear flowers, perfumes, or necklaces; one shall not engage in singing, dancing, or theatrical performances, nor go to witness them; one shall not sit upon high or broad beds; and one shall not eat at improper times.

If one eats but a single meal a day, does not handle gold, silver, or the seven treasures; does not take a wife, concubines, or maidens; does not keep slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, chickens, dogs, pigs, sheep, fields, houses, gardens, or pavilions; and does not accumulate or hoard any such things; does not practice deception with light scales or small measures; does not adulterate goods with inferior substances; does not engage in trade for profit; and refrains from maiming others’ limbs, killing, imprisoning, seizing their wealth, or forcing them into labor.
He refrains from speaking with falsehood or deceit that incites litigation and disputes; he abandons others' affairs and eliminates all such unwholesome deeds.

In his conduct, he knows the proper time and does not act at an improper time; he eats according to the capacity of his stomach and wears clothing according to the needs of his body, taking only what is sufficient.
The robes and alms bowl follow him of their own accord, just as the wings and body of a flying bird are together.
In this way, wherever the bhikṣu goes, his robes and bowl follow his person.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, having received the faithful offerings of others, seek various accumulations of food, drink, clothing, fragrances, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects; [the bhikṣu does not do so].
He is free from such insatiable practices;
unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, collect seeds and plant trees for the sake of spirit villages—
he is free from such activities.
Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful,

employ various expedients to seek gain and sustenance— such as high, wide, and large beds made of ivory and various jewels, quilts and bedding embroidered with diverse patterns, and skins of various colors—
he has distanced himself from such methods of seeking gain.

Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, employ various expedients merely to adorn their own bodies—rubbing their bodies with ghee and oil, bathing in scented water, anointing themselves with perfumes, grooming their hair with fragrant pomades, wearing fine flower garlands, dyeing their eyes a deep blue, adorning their faces and heads in various ways, binding colored threads around their arms, carrying walking sticks with hollows, wielding swords and spears along with peacock-feather parasols, using pearls for fans, and looking at themselves in mirrors.
They wear sandals of variegated leather and don pure white robes;
they are able to abandon such forms of adornment.

Like other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful, they devote themselves solely to amusements: chess, dice, backgammon, *chupulu*, the eight-path game, the ten-path game, or even stone-clapping.

He abandons such various diversions as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas do when consuming the offerings of the faithful—namely, speaking of matters that obstruct the Path: matters of kings, matters of thieves, matters of warfare, armies, and horses; matters of ministers, matters of riding and vehicles, matters of entering and leaving gardens and parks, matters of lying down and rising, matters of women, matters of clothing and food and drink, matters of kinsmen, matters of the state, and thoughts of entering the great ocean to explore the world;
he abandons all such activities that obstruct the Path.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful, employing countless expedient means of flattery and sweet words, manifesting signs and disparaging others to seek profit through profit;
he abandons such wrong livelihoods and flattery.

Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, constantly engage in debate and contention—whether in gardens and groves, at bathing pools, or in lecture halls—saying:
"I know such a doctrine and discipline; you know nothing! You have entered a wrong path, whereas I am on the right path," thus placing their own prior words after those of others.
The latter statement contradicts the former.
I am able to endure what you cannot endure; I am superior to you. Your words are merely delusions. Having now gained the victory in our debate with you, ask whatever you wish to ask.
He completely abandons all such matters of dispute.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, employ various means to seek out missions— acting as messengers for kings, royal ministers, brāhmaṇas, or householders, traveling from here to there and from there back here, carrying messages from this place to that and from that place to this,
doing so themselves or instructing others to do so— he is able to remain far removed from such mission work.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in various forms of competitive games—whether wrestling with bows, fighting with swords, or clashing with staves; or pitting cocks against each other, dogs against dogs, pigs against pigs, rams against rams, goats against goats, deer against deer, elephants against elephants, horses against horses, camels against camels, oxen against oxen, hump-backed cattle against hump-backed cattle, or water buffaloes against water buffaloes;
or even staging contests between women, men, boys, and girls—he has completely eliminated all such playful and combative activities.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in practices that obstruct the Path and live by wrong livelihood— such as divining the good and bad fortune of men and women, or seeking gain and support through various means involving animals—
he has utterly eliminated all such practices that obstruct the Path.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful while practicing obstructive dharmas and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood— such as summoning or exorcising spirits, or performing various rites of suppression—
he has completely severed such obstructive dharmas.

Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in practices that obstruct the path and live by wrong livelihood—whether by casting spells for others' illnesses, reciting malevolent incantations, or reciting auspicious mantras; whether by treating back ailments or inducing perspiration, by applying acupuncture to cure diseases, or by treating ailments of the nose or the lower body—he has completely abandoned such wrong livelihoods and practices that obstruct the path.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who consume the offerings of the faithful while practicing obstructive dharmas and sustaining themselves through wrong livelihood— such as administering medicines to treat human illnesses by inducing vomiting or purging, or treating men and women—
he has completely eliminated such obstructive dharmas.

He has abandoned such obstructive practices that lead to wrong livelihood, which other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas perform while consuming the offerings of the faithful: such as reciting incantations over fire; or reciting incantations for safe travel to ensure good fortune; or reciting the *kṣatriya-mantras*; or reciting bird-mantras; or reciting mantras for the joints and limbs; or reciting talismanic incantations for consecrating dwellings; or performing incantations to counteract objects burned by fire or gnawed by rats; or reciting books on the timing of death and rebirth; or reciting books on the interpretation of dreams; or reading the palms and shoulders of others; or reciting the *devapraśna* (questions of the gods); or reciting books on the cries of birds and beasts. He has completely severed all such obstructive dharmas.

Just as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, maintain themselves through wrong livelihood by observing celestial omens—some saying it will rain, others saying it will not; some saying grain will be expensive, others saying it will be cheap; some saying there will be much illness, others saying there will be little; some saying there will be terror, others saying there will be peace; some saying there will be an earthquake, others saying a comet has appeared; some saying there will be a lunar eclipse, others saying there will be none; some saying there will be a solar eclipse, others saying there will be none; some saying there will be a stellar eclipse, others saying there will be none; or predicting that a lunar eclipse brings such-and-such a favorable result or such-and-such an unfavorable result, and likewise for solar and stellar eclipses—he has completely abandoned such modes of wrong livelihood.

Unlike other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, while consuming the offerings of the faithful, engage in practices that obstruct the path and sustain themselves through wrong livelihood—such as claiming "this country will surpass that country" or "that country is superior to this one," or "this is better than that" or "that is better than this"—and thus divining such matters of fortune, misfortune, good, and evil;
[he] has completely severed such practices that obstruct the path.

In these matters, he cultivates and accumulates noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*); being inwardly unattached, his mind is peaceful and blissful. Although his eyes behold forms, he does not grasp at their signs; he is not carried away by the eye and its objects. His faculty of sight is firm and dwells in tranquility; free from craving and desire, he is without sorrow or affliction. He does not leak out any evil or unwholesome states, firmly upholding the categories of precepts and being able to well protect the faculty of sight.
It is the same for the ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Having well trained in, guarded, sustained, and disciplined these six bases of contact so that they are brought to rest, it is like a well-trained driver at a crossroads on level ground, holding the reins in his left hand and the whip in his right.

It is the same for a bhikṣu who trains well in guarding, training, and calming: he trains well in guarding, training, and calming within the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*). Possessing such noble ethical discipline (*ārya-śīla*) and attaining the noble faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*), he knows moderation in eating and does not crave flavors to nourish his body. Without arrogance or conceit, he takes only what is necessary to sustain himself so as to remain free from suffering and affliction. Thus, he is able to cultivate pure conduct; consequently, existing suffering is extinguished and new suffering does not arise. There is neither increase nor decrease, and being capable and free from worldly concerns, he dwells in physical ease and happiness.
It is just as when a man or a woman suffers from a wound and applies medicine to it so that the wound may heal;
in the same way, a bhikṣu eats with contentment, taking only what is necessary to bring peace to his body.
It is just as when a person greases a cart with oil for the sake of wealth and goods, desiring that it may carry them further to their destination.
It is likewise with a bhikṣu who knows moderation in eating, taking only what is necessary to sustain the body.

A bhikṣu who possesses such noble ethical discipline and has attained noble faculties knows moderation regarding food; he practices diligent wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night; whether by day, walking or sitting, he is always thus single-mindedly mindful to eliminate the hindrances.
During the first watch of the night, whether walking or sitting, he remains constantly and single-mindedly mindful of removing the hindrances.

During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side with one foot upon the other, mindful that he shall rise at the appointed time, maintaining a focused perception of light with an undisturbed mind. Upon reaching the last watch of the night, he rises and reflects; whether walking or sitting, he remains constantly and single-mindedly mindful of removing the hindrances.
A bhikṣu possesses such noble precepts and has attained the noble faculties; he knows moderation in eating.
During the first and last watches of the night, he remains diligent and awake, always maintaining a single-minded mindfulness without confusion.
“How is it, bhikkhu, that mindfulness is not confused?

A bhikkhu thus contemplates the body as a body within himself; with diligence and without slackening, his mindfulness is not confused, and he subdues stinginess, greed, and the worldly afflictions of sorrow.”
Contemplating the body as an external body, one dwells with diligence and without indolence, with mindfulness undisturbed, subduing stinginess, greed, and the afflictions of the world;
contemplating the body as both internal and external, one dwells with diligence and without indolence, with mindfulness undisturbed, subduing stinginess, greed, and the afflictions of the world.
Feeling, mind, and mental phenomena are also like this;
this, bhikṣu, is called mindfulness without confusion. How so, bhikṣu?
What is single-mindedness?

Whether walking, entering or exiting, looking left or right, bending or stretching, bowing or raising oneself, holding the robe and bowl, receiving food, attending to the needs of nature, sleeping or waking, sitting or standing, speaking or remaining silent—in all such circumstances, one is always thus single-minded; this is called single-mindedness.
For example, it is like a person traveling with a great multitude; whether in front, in the middle, or at the rear, they always attain peace and happiness and are free from fear.
So too is it with a bhikṣu: whether walking, entering, or exiting, even up to remaining silent, he is always thus single-minded.
A bhikṣu possesses such noble ethical discipline and attains the noble faculties;
he knows moderation in eating, practices diligence and wakefulness during the first and last watches of the night, and is always thus single-minded and undisturbed.
He delights in dwelling in an araṇya, at the foot of a tree, or he delights in staying in mountain caves, in the open air, or by a heap of refuse.
If he is among the burial mounds or by the water’s edge, that alms-collector, having returned, washes his feet, sets aside his robes and bowl,
and sits cross-legged with body straight and mind upright, binding his mindfulness before him; he eliminates stinginess and greed so that the mind does not dwell with them,
eliminates ill-will so that there is no resentment or envy, and the mind abides in non-ill-will, pure and stainless.

While harboring anger, one should always maintain loving-kindness and compassion; having eliminated sloth and torpor, one does not dwell with them; by fixing the mind on clarity, mindfulness remains undisturbed;
having severed restlessness and remorse, one does not dwell with them, for the inner mind is tranquil and the mind of one free from restlessness and remorse is pure.
Having severed doubt and crossed beyond doubt, his mind is single-mindedly directed toward wholesome dharmas.
It is like a slave who, having been granted security by his master, is released from slavery.
He thought to himself:
"Formerly I was a slave, but now I am liberated and at peace; I have attained self-mastery and shall no longer be subject to others.
For this reason, he experienced joy, and his mind became tranquil and blissful.

Furthermore, it is like a person who borrows another's wealth to engage in trade and thereby earns interest; once the principal has been repaid, there remains a surplus sufficient to support his wife and children. He thinks to himself:
"I previously borrowed this debt to engage in trade and have now earned interest upon it."
"Having recovered what was returned to me, there remains enough to support my wife and children.
I am now truly free and no longer fear others.
For these reasons, he attained great joy, and his mind became peaceful and at ease.
It is like a person who has long been ill and recovers from that illness; when his food and drink are digested and his body possesses color and strength, he thinks to himself:
"I previously had this illness, but now I have recovered; my food and drink are digested, and my body possesses color and strength."
By this cause and condition, he immediately attains joy and his mind becomes peaceful and happy.
It is like a person who has been long confined in a prison and is safely released from it; that person thinks to himself:
"I was previously bound and imprisoned, but now I have attained liberation; I have nothing further to fear."
By these causes and conditions, he immediately attains joy and his mind becomes peaceful and secure.
It is like a person who, carrying much wealth and treasure, crosses a vast wilderness without encountering bandits or robbers and passes through it safely; that person thinks to himself:
"I have previously crossed this wilderness while carrying much wealth and treasure, and now I have nothing further to fear."
By these causes and conditions, one attains joy and the mind becomes peaceful and at ease.

It is the same for a bhikṣu who possesses the five hindrances: like a slave, a debtor, one with a chronic illness, one in prison, or one traveling through a vast wilderness; seeing for himself that the various fetters are not yet severed, he causes his mind to be defiled and his power of wisdom to be unclear.
He then abandons sensual desires and unwholesome states, and accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, he experiences joy and happiness, attaining the first dhyāna.

With that joy and happiness, he moistens and saturates his body; it is filled to overflowing, pervading every part without exception. It is like a skilled bath-attendant who places fine medicinal powder in a vessel and pours water over it, so that the water and the powder are blended and harmonized; the water moistens and saturates it all, leaving no spot untouched and none of it spilling away.
It is likewise for a bhikṣu who attains the first dhyāna: joy and bliss pervade his entire body without any empty space; this is the first time he experiences bliss in his present body. Why is this?
Because of heedfulness, diligence, and tirelessness, and because mindfulness is undisturbed and he delights in dwelling in tranquility, he abandons applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Thereupon, inner confidence arises; his mind becomes one-pointed, free from applied and sustained thought, and with mental concentration, joy, and bliss, he enters the second dhyāna.
With his mind concentrated, he moistens and saturates his body with joy and bliss; it pervades and overflows him, leaving no part untouched.

It is just as when a spring at the summit of a mountain gushes forth from within itself—not from the east, west, south, north, or from above—but rather clear, cool water emerges from that very pool, moistening and saturating the entire pond until it is completely filled and overflowing, with no empty space remaining.
It is likewise for a bhikṣu entering the second dhyāna: his mind is concentrated, and joy and bliss pervade and overflow him; this is the second instance of attaining happiness in the present body.

He relinquishes the state of joy and dwells in the bliss of mindful equanimity, experiencing physical pleasure as the noble ones describe it—the bliss of mindful equanimity—and thus enters the third dhyāna.
He is without rapture regarding the body, but is saturated, permeated, filled, and overflowing with bliss, such that there is no part of him that is not suffused.

It is just as when blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses have emerged from the earth but have not yet risen above the water; their roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves are saturated within the water, such that there is no part of them that is not moistened.

It is likewise for a bhikṣu entering the third dhyāna: free from joy, he dwells in bliss, saturating and permeating the body so that there is no part of it not reached. This is the third dhyāna, the attainment of bodily happiness where one sports.
Abandoning both suffering and pleasure, as well as prior sorrow and joy, and having first eliminated neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, he enters the fourth dhyāna with pure mindfulness and equanimity.
His body and mind are pure, fully suffused and overflowing, such that there is no place where this purity does not pervade.

Just as when a man or woman bathes and purifies themselves, putting on new, clean white garments so that there is no part of the body not covered, so too it is with a bhikṣu who has entered the fourth dhyāna:
his mind is pure and pervades his entire body, leaving no space uncovered.
He enters the fourth dhyāna; his mind is neither agitated nor lax, and it is not associated with craving or aversion, abiding in the stage of immovability.

It is like a well-sealed house, plastered inside and out, with doors and windows firmly closed, free from wind and dust; within it a lamp is lit, undisturbed by humans, non-humans, wind, or birds fanning it, its flame rising straight up without wavering, burning in tranquil stillness.

It is likewise for a bhikṣu entering the fourth dhyāna: there is no agitation, the mind is free from indolence, it is not associated with craving or aversion, and one has already established oneself in the unmoving ground; this is the fourth dhyāna, the realm where one sports in the bliss attained in the present body.
Why is this? Because, through heedfulness, diligence, tirelessness, mindfulness without confusion, and delighting in dwelling in tranquility,
he attains a concentrated mind that is pure and free from defilement, supple and subdued, abiding on the stage of immovability.
From within his own body, he gives rise to a mind capable of manifesting a different body, complete with all limbs and joints and lacking no sense faculties.
He then observes that this body is a composite of the four great elements of form, whereas that body is a manifestation produced through transformation.

The physical form of these four great elements is distinct, and the physical form of that emanated body produced by the four great elements is also distinct; from within this physical form of the four great elements, the mind arises and performs an emanation, such that that body is fully endowed with all sense faculties, limbs, and joints.
It is, for example, as if a person were to draw a sword from its scabbard and think:
"This is the scabbard; this is the sword; the sword is one thing and the scabbard is another.
Having drawn the sword out from that scabbard, he reflects thus.
It is also like a person who takes a snake out from within a basket and thinks:
"This is the basket; this is the snake; the basket is one thing and the snake is another.
Thus, the snake has emerged from this basket.
It is, for example, like a person taking a garment out of a chest, who thinks:
"This is the chest; this is the garment; the chest is one thing, the garment is another.
Thus he takes the garment out from within the chest.
The bhikṣu is likewise so.
This is the first superior quality of a bhikṣu. Why is this?

Because through non-negligence, diligence, and tirelessness, his mindfulness is undisturbed and he delights in tranquility; thus, with a concentrated mind purified, he even enters the stage of immovability.

From within his own physical body composed of the four great elements, he gives rise to a mind that transforms and creates an emanation-body, complete with all sense faculties and limbs. He then thinks:
"This body is a composite of the four great elements, whereas that body exists as a transformation."

"This physical body composed of the four great elements is one thing, and that transformed body composed of the four great elements is another; this mind resides in this body, depends upon this body, and is bound to this body."

It is like a lapis lazuli maṇi jewel that has been polished until it is exceedingly bright, clear, and free from stain; if one were to thread it with blue, yellow, or red cords, a man with sight would hold it in his palm and observe:
"This is the jewel, this is the cord; the jewel is distinct from the cord, and this jewel is strung upon this cord."

In the same way, a bhikṣu likewise arises from this physical body composed of the four great elements and, by means of the mind, manifests a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) complete with all sense faculties and limbs.
He then forms this thought: "This body is a composite of the four great elements; that body exists as a manifestation."
‘This four-element physical body is one thing, and that transformed four-element physical body is another.
This mind dwells in this body, depends upon this body, and is bound to this body.
This is the second superior dharma of a bhikṣu.
Why is this? Because they are characterized by non-negligence, diligence, tirelessness, mindfulness without confusion, and a delight in tranquility.
With a concentrated mind thus purified, they enter the stage of immovability (*aniñjya-bhūmi*) and single-mindedly cultivate the realization of the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-jñāna*).
He is then able to perform various transformations: from a single body he becomes countless bodies, and from countless bodies he returns to a single body.

His body can fly, passing through stone walls and barriers without obstruction as if moving through empty space; he walks and stands in mid-air like a bird in flight; he emerges from and sinks into the earth as if it were water surging with waves; he may appear as smoke or flame, or like a mass of great fire; with his hand he can touch the sun and moon, and his body reaches as far as the Brahma Heaven.
It is like a potter who skillfully prepares the clay; whatever vessel he wishes to create according to his intent, he can bring it to completion so that it serves a useful purpose.
It is like a master craftsman who is skilled at working wood; whatever he creates according to his intent, he can accomplish with ease so that it serves a useful purpose.
It is like a master ivory-worker who is skilled at treating ivory; whatever he fashions according to his will is accomplished with ease and brings benefit.
It is like a goldsmith who skillfully refines pure gold; whatever he fashions according to his will is accomplished with ease and brings benefit.

The bhikṣu is also like this: with a concentrated mind that is pure and has reached the stage of immovability, he acts according to his will even as far as the Brahma-heaven; this is the third superior quality of a bhikṣu.

With a mind purified through meditative concentration, he enters the stage of immovability and, practicing with single-minded devotion, realizes the knowledge of the divine ear. His divine ear is purified and surpasses that of the human ear; he hears two kinds of sounds:
those of humans and those of non-humans.

For example, suppose there were a lecture hall within a city or town that was vast, lofty, and prominent; a person with keen hearing standing therein would hear various sounds without exerting any effort of the auditory faculty.
The bhikṣu is likewise; because his mind is concentrated, his divine ear becomes purified, and he is able to hear the various sounds of humans and non-humans.
This is the fourth superior quality of a bhikṣu.

With a mind purified by meditative concentration and having entered the stage of immovability, he cultivates with single-mindedness to realize the knowledge of others' minds. He knows the minds of external sentient beings—whether they possess desire or are free from desire, whether they have defilement or are free from defilement, whether they have delusion or are free from delusion; he knows whether their minds are expansive or contracted, small or great, concentrated or distracted, bound or liberated, superior or unsurpassed, knowing them all completely.
Just as a man or woman who delights in their own appearance will invariably see their reflection when looking into water or a mirror, so too it is with a bhikṣu:
because his mind is purified through concentration, he knows the thoughts and mental activities of all external sentient beings.
This is the fifth supreme quality of a bhikṣu.

With a mind purified by concentration, he enters the stage of imperturbability and, practicing with single-minded devotion, realizes the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*). He is then able to remember various kinds of countless past lives: he can recall one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, and countless hundreds of thousands of births. He recalls how, when the kalpa-fire had consumed everything and the world-system was reborn, he was born there with such a name, such a caste, such a clan, such food, such a lifespan, such a duration of stay, such an end to his life, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure.

Passing away from there, they were reborn again in that same place; thus, through such successive cycles, they came to be born here, and they fully remember and recognize all their various forms, colors, and appearances, numbering in the infinite.

For example, suppose there is a person who departs from his own village and travels to another country; while there, whether walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent, he then departs from that country for yet another country, again whether walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent. Continuing in this manner until he returns to his original country, he does not require great effort to recall and recognize all the countries he traversed, thinking:
"From this country I went to that country, and within that country I walked thus, stood thus, spoke thus, and remained silent;
from that country I went to another country, and within that country I walked thus, stood thus, spoke thus, and remained silent."
"In this manner, passing from one stage to another, he returns to his own country.

So too it is with the bhikṣu: being able to purify the mind through meditative concentration up to the immovable stage, he realizes it through the knowledge of past lives and can recollect the various events of countless hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
This is the bhikṣu’s attainment of the foremost clarity:

ignorance is severed and extinguished; the dharma of clarity arises and darkness has departed; the dharma of luminous understanding remains. This is the bhikṣu’s realization through the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
Why is this? Because, through heedfulness, diligence, and tirelessness, their minds are free from confusion and they delight in dwelling in tranquility.

With a concentrated mind purified up to the stage of immovability (*āneñjya-bhūmi*), they practice single-mindedly and perceive beings dying here and being born there. Through the realization of knowledge, they attain the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and see beings dying here and being born there; they discern their forms as beautiful or ugly, their natures as good or evil, and their status as noble or base across all realms of existence. They are able to know all this according to the causes and conditions of the karmic retributions created by those beings.
Thus, this person engages in bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct; they revile the noble ones and hold wrong views.
Due to the retribution for these wrong views, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Such beings, having practiced virtue in body, virtue in speech, and virtuous thoughts in mind, do not revile the noble ones; possessing right view and cultivating right action, they are reborn among gods or humans after the death of the body.
Thus, with the purified divine eye, he sees beings dying here and being born there; according to the karmic causes created by those beings, he knows them all.

It is like a vast level plain at a crossroads where there is a high and prominent great hall; a person with clear vision standing therein sees beings coming from the east to the west, going from the west to the east, going from the south to the north, and going from the north to the south.

In this way, a bhikṣu, with a mind purified by concentration up to the stage of imperturbability, perceives beings passing away from this life and being reborn in that life; through the realization of knowledge and with the purified divine eye, he perceives beings passing away from this life and being reborn in that life, and he knows all things, even down to the causes and conditions of the karmic retribution created by those beings.
This is the second clear knowledge attained by a bhikṣu:

ignorance is abandoned, the dharma of clarity arises, darkness has departed, and the dharma of illumination remains; this is the knowledge and realization that witnesses beings dying here and being born there.
Why is this? Because, through heedfulness, diligence, and tirelessness, their minds are not distracted and they delight in tranquility.
With a concentrated mind that is pure, up to the stage of immovability, they single-mindedly cultivate and realize untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).

He knows, as it truly is, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; he knows, as they truly are, the outflows, the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of the outflows.
Knowing thus and seeing thus, his mind is liberated from the outflow of sensual desire (*kāśrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhavāśrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyāśrava*).
