Having attained the knowledge of liberation, he realizes: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence."
For example, suppose there are pieces of wood, stones, fish, turtles, and other aquatic creatures moving back and forth in clear water.
A person with sight observes them and sees the wood, stones, fish, and turtles, thinking:
"This is wood or stone; these are fish and turtles moving back and forth."

In the same way, the bhikṣu likewise, with a concentrated mind purified to the stage of immovability, attains the realization of untainted wisdom and reaches the point where he is no longer subject to rebirth.
This is the third clear knowledge attained by a bhikṣu:
ignorance is abandoned, the dharma of clarity arises, the dharma of darkness departs, and the dharma of luminous understanding remains; this is the light of untainted wisdom.
"For what reason?
Because they are heedful, diligent, and untiring; because their mindfulness is unconfused and they delight in dwelling in tranquility.
The *Saṃyukta-khaṇḍa* (Miscellaneous Section) is thus completed. *The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, Fascicle 53.
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Scroll 54; Part Five of the Fourth Division.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī under the Yao Qin dynasty, together with Zhu Fonian and others.
3. The Compilation of the Dharma and Vinaya by Five Hundred Monks. At that time, the World-Honored One had entered parinirvāṇa among the śāla trees in the Malla Garden at Kuśinagara.

After the Mallas had washed the Buddha’s relics, they wrapped them in pure *karpāsa* cloth; they then further enshrouded them with five hundred layers of fine cotton fabric. They prepared an iron coffin, filled it with fragrant oil, placed the relics within it, and covered it with a lid.
Furthermore, they constructed a wooden outer coffin and placed an iron inner coffin within it, piling up various fragrant woods beneath.
Then, the foremost among the Malla youths held fire to ignite it, but the devas immediately extinguished the flames.
The other Mallas passed the great torches one to another and lit them all, but the devas extinguished them all as well.
Anuruddha said to the Mallas:
"There is no need for such exhaustion; the devas are extinguishing your fires."
He then asked Aniruddha, "Venerable One!
For what reason have the devas extinguished the fire?"
He replied, "Mahākāśyapa is traveling on the road between the two cities of Pāvā and Kuśinagara, accompanied by a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus."
He thought to himself:
"Shall I be able to see the Buddha’s relics before they have been cremated?
Knowing that Kāśyapa was thinking thus, the devas extinguished the fire for this reason.
The Malla son said, "Venerable Aniruddha!
Please pause for a moment now, to fulfill the wishes of those devas."
At that time, Mahākāśyapa was traveling on the road between those two countries together with a great community of five hundred bhikṣus.
Then there were certain Nirgrantha followers who were carrying *mandārava* flowers from the time of the World-Honored One’s parinirvāṇa as they traveled along the road.
Seeing them from afar, Kāśyapa asked: "From where have you come?"
He replied, "I have come from the city of Kuśinagara. He asked again:
"Do you recognize me, World-Honored One? He replied, "I do."
He asked again:
"Are you still in the world now? He replied:
"He is no longer in this world; it has already been seven days since his parinirvāṇa. I have brought these flowers from him.
When Kāśyapa heard this, he was displeased.

Among them were bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire; upon hearing that the World-Honored One had already entered parinirvāṇa, they threw themselves to the ground. Just as a tree falls when its roots are severed, so it was with these bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire; weeping, they said:
"The Sugata’s parinirvāṇa—how could it have come so soon!"
"How has the Eye of the World so quickly perished?
How can the Dharma we have revered come to an end so soon?
Some rolled about on the ground like logs; these bhikṣus who had not yet abandoned desire were likewise, weeping in grief and distress, saying:
"How premature is the Parinirvāṇa of the Sugata!
At that time, the Śākya son Upananda was among the assembly, and he said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable ones, please desist!
Do not grieve or weep excessively; we have attained liberation from that mahallaka.
While he was alive, he constantly instructed us as to what should and should not be done, and what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
"We shall now be able to act according to our own will; we may do whatever we wish to do, or not do whatever we wish not to do.
When Mahākāśyapa heard this, he was displeased and immediately addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Arise quickly and take up your robes and bowls; let us go at once so that we may see the World-Honored One’s relics before they have been cremated."
Upon hearing Kāśyapa’s words, the bhikṣus immediately and swiftly took up their robes and bowls.
Thereupon, Mahākāśyapa, together with five hundred people, went to the city of Kuśinagara.
He left the city, crossed the Hiraṇyavatī River, and went to Devadaha Monastery, where he approached Ānanda and said: "Ānanda!
I wish to see the World-Honored One’s relics before they have been cremated."
Ānanda replied: "If one wishes to see the World-Honored One before his relics have been cremated, it will be difficult to obtain such a sight. Why is this?"

The World-Honored One’s relics have already been washed and wrapped in new *karpāsa* cloth; they were further encased in five hundred layers of fine cotton fabric, placed within an iron coffin filled with fragrant oil, and set inside a wooden outer casket. A great quantity of fragrant wood has now been piled beneath it, and as it is about to be cremated, it will be difficult to behold them again.
Then Mahākāśyapa gradually approached the place where the Buddha’s relics were piled. The outer and inner coffins opened of their own accord, and the World-Honored One revealed his feet.
When Mahākāśyapa saw that the wheel-marks on the soles of the World-Honored One’s feet were stained and defiled, he asked Ānanda:
“The World-Honored One’s countenance is upright and handsome, and his body is the color of gold; who has defiled the wheel-marks on his feet?”
Ānanda replied: "Venerable Kāśyapa!
The minds of women are tender;
when she previously prostrated before the Buddha, tears fell upon his feet, and as she grasped them with her hands, they defiled the World-Honored One’s feet."
Upon hearing this, Mahākāśyapa was displeased and immediately prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One.
The bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and the great assembly of devas likewise all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
Then the World-Honored One’s feet returned into the coffin and were no longer visible.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa sighed with grief and spoke a verse while circumambulating the coffin seven times; the fire did not burn it, as it was naturally extinguished.
At that time, after Mahākāśyapa had cremated the relics, he assembled the community of bhikṣus on account of these events and addressed them, saying:
"Previously, while I was traveling on the road, I heard Upananda say to the bhikṣus:
'Venerable ones, please stop!'"
"Do not grieve or weep any longer; we have now attained liberation from that mahallaka.
While he was alive, he would scold and instruct us, saying, 'This should be done and this should not be done; this ought to be performed and this ought not to be performed.'"
"Now that we have attained mastery, we may do as we wish, or not do it at all.
We should now discuss the Dharma and Vinaya together so that non-Buddhists do not find cause for further criticism and reproach, saying:

"The law and discipline of the Śramaṇa Gautama are like smoke; while the World-Honored One was alive, everyone studied the precepts together, but now that he has passed away, there is no one who studies the precepts."
"Venerable elders!
You may now select and assign those bhikṣus who are learned, wise, and are arhats.
At that time, four hundred and ninety-nine individuals were selected, all of whom were arhats possessed of great learning and wisdom.
At that time, the bhikṣus said,
"Ānanda should be appointed to be included among the number. Mahākāśyapa said:
"Do not include Ānanda among the number. Why?
Because Ānanda possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; since he possesses attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion, he should not be allowed to be included among the number."
Then the bhikṣus spoke again:
"This Ānanda is one who makes offerings to the Buddha; he constantly follows the Buddha's movements and has personally received the teachings from the World-Honored One."
"He will surely inquire about various matters with the Blessed One; therefore, he should now be included in the count.
They then included him in the count.
All the bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"In what place should we assemble to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya, where food, drink, and bedding are abundant and lacking nothing?
They all replied, "Only in Rājagṛha are dwellings, food, drink, and bedding so numerous; we should now go together there to assemble and discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya."
Then Mahākāśyapa made the formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

These bhikṣus have been appointed by the Saṃgha. If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now proceed to Rājagṛha to assemble and discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya."
"Thus it was announced.
Having made this announcement, they all proceeded together toward Vaiśālī.
While Ānanda was traveling on the road, he reflected to himself in a quiet place:
"Just as a newborn calf, though it still drinks milk, walks together with five hundred great oxen;
so too am I now, a practitioner who still has work to do, walking together with five hundred arhats."
At that time, all the elders went to Vaiśālī, and Ānanda resided there in Vaiśālī.
Many bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists came to pay their respects, and a great multitude gathered.
At that time, there was a Vatsiputriya bhikṣu who possessed great supernormal powers; having attained the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds, he thought to himself:

"Now Ānanda is at Vaiśālī, where bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, kings, ministers, and various śramaṇas and non-Buddhists have all come to pay their respects, and a great multitude has gathered."
"I shall now examine Ānanda to see whether he possesses desire or is free from desire.
He then examined Ānanda and perceived that he possessed desire and was not free from it; he further thought:
"I shall now cause him to give rise to a mind of weary detachment."
Desiring to inspire in Ānanda a sense of weary detachment, he spoke these verses:
“Dwell in tranquility beneath the empty tree, With your mind intent upon Nirvāṇa;
Practice meditation without negligence— What is the use of speaking much?”

When Ānanda heard the Vajjiputta bhikṣu speak of disenchantment, he immediately dwelt alone, practicing with diligence and heedfulness, remaining tranquil and undisturbed; this was an unprecedented quality in Ānanda.

At that time, Ānanda was in an open space where he had spread out a rope bed; having spent much of the night walking in meditation, as the night passed and the signs of dawn were about to appear, his body was utterly exhausted, and he thought to himself:
"I am now completely fatigued; it would be well for me to sit for a short while."

Having thought thus, he sat down; having sat down, just as he was about to recline, in the brief interval before his head reached the pillow, his mind attained the untainted liberation (anāsrava-vimukti). This is an unprecedented quality (abhūtapūrva-dharma) of Ānanda.
At that time, having attained arhatship, Ānanda spoke this verse:
"Though I have heard many various teachings And have constantly made offerings to the World-Honored One, I have already severed birth and death; Gautama now wishes to lie down."
Then the bhikṣus traveling from Vaiśālī to Rājagṛha spoke thus:
"What should we do first? Should we first repair the dwellings and prepare the bedding?"
"Shall we first discuss the Dharma and Vinaya?
They all replied,
"We should first attend to the treatment of the dwellings and bedding."
He then immediately prepared the rooms and bedding.

At that time, Mahākāśyapa convened the community of bhikṣus for this purpose; among them, Dhitarakāśyapa served as the presiding elder (upādhyāya), the Elder Vappa as the second elder, Mahākāśyapa as the third elder, and the Elder Mahācunda as the fourth elder.
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, being in charge of the monastic affairs, made the formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its ear, let the Saṃgha now assemble to discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya."
“Thus it was stated.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed Mahākāśyapa, saying:
“I have heard this directly from the Buddha and remember the words of the Buddha:”
"From this day forward, for the sake of all bhikṣus, I relinquish the minor and miscellaneous precepts. Kāśyapa asked: "Ānanda!..."
"Did you not ask the World-Honored One what constitutes the minor precepts? Ānanda replied:
"At that time, I was distressed and helpless, having failed to ask the World-Honored One which were the minor precepts (kṣudrānukṣudra-śikṣāpada). Then all the bhikṣus said:
"Come, we shall tell you which are the minor precepts."
Among them, some said:
"With the exception of the four *pārājika* offenses, the rest are miscellaneous minor precepts (*khuddānukhuddaka-sikkhāpada*). Others said:
"Except for the four *pārājika* offenses and the thirteen matters, all others are miscellaneous minor precepts. Or some say:
"Except for the four *pārājika* offenses, the thirteen matters, and the two *aniyata* rules, all others are miscellaneous minor precepts."
Some said: "Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses, the thirteen matters, the two *aniyata* rules, and the thirty matters, all the rest are minor precepts (*khuddaka-śikṣāpada*)."
Some said: "Excluding the four *pārājika* offenses up to the ninety matters, all others are merely minor precepts.
Then Mahākāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“Venerable Elders! At present, the various people’s words are inconsistent, and we do not know which of these are the minor precepts (*kṣudrānukṣudra-śikṣāpada*).
From this day forward, we should establish a collective regulation: that which was not previously established by the Buddha shall not be established now.”
"What the Buddha previously ordained should not now be set aside; you should train in accordance with what the Buddha has ordained.
Thereupon, they immediately established such a regulation together.
Mahākāśyapa then said to Ānanda:
"You previously sought to ordain women within the Buddha-dharma; you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You must now perform repentance. Ānanda replied:
"Venerable Sir!
This was not done by me intentionally; Mahāprajāpatī had great kindness toward the Buddha, for she nurtured the World-Honored One after his mother passed away."
"Venerable Kāśyapa!
I do not see any fault in myself regarding this matter; however, out of faith in you, Venerable One, I now offer my confession.
Mahākāśyapa spoke again:
"You have caused the World-Honored One to entreat you three times to act as his provider of offerings, yet you said you would not; for this you have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You must now perform repentance."
Ānanda replied to Kāśyapa: "I did not do this intentionally;
it was because honoring the Buddha is a difficult task that I merely said I could not.
I do not see any fault in myself regarding this matter, yet out of faith in your great virtue, I now offer my confession."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"When you sewed the saṃghāṭī for the Buddha, you stepped on it with your foot while sewing; this constitutes a duṣkṛta offense.
You must now perform repentance."
Ānanda replied, "Venerable Kāśyapa!
It was not done out of pride; it is simply because there is no one else to hold it."
"I do not see any fault in myself regarding this; however, out of faith in the Venerable One, I now offer my confession.
Kāśyapa spoke again:

"The World-Honored One has thrice declared his desire to enter parinirvāṇa to you. You did not entreat the World-Honored One to remain in the world for an eon or more than an eon, so that countless people might obtain benefit, and out of compassion for the devas and humans of the world, they might attain peace and happiness. You have committed a duṣkṛta offense."
"Now you should perform confession.
Ānanda replied, "Venerable Kāśyapa!"
"This was not done by me intentionally; it was Māra within my heart who caused me not to request the Buddha to remain in the world.
Within this matter, I do not see any fault in myself, yet out of faith in your reverence, I now offer this confession."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
“When the World-Honored One was alive, he asked you for water; because you did not give it to him, you incurred a *duṣkṛta* offense.
You should now perform repentance.”
Ānanda replied, “It was not that I acted intentionally;
rather, five hundred chariots had recently passed through the water, making it very turbid.
Fearing that the World-Honored One might drink it and fall ill, I did not offer it.”
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"You should simply give it; perhaps through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, or perhaps through the gods, the water will become pure. Ānanda said:
"I do not see any fault within myself regarding this matter; however, out of faith in the Venerable One, I now offer my confession.
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"You did not ask the World-Honored One which rules constitute the minor precepts."
"You have committed a *duṣkṛta* offense;
you should now perform repentance. Ānanda said:
"I did not do this intentionally; at that time, I was distressed and despondent, and I failed to ask the World-Honored One which were the minor precepts (*kṣudrānukṣudra-śikṣāpada*).
Within these matters, I did not see myself as having committed an offense, but because I trusted the Venerable One, I now offer my confession."
Kāśyapa spoke again:
"Since you did not prevent women from defiling the Buddha’s feet, you have incurred the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
You must now perform confession."
Ānanda replied: "It was not done intentionally by me;
rather, the hearts of women are tender, and as she prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, her tears defiled them.
I do not see any fault in this matter myself, but out of faith in the Venerable One, I now offer my confession."
Then Mahākāśyapa made this formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its attention, let the Saṃgha now question Upāli regarding the Dharma and Vinaya."
The motion is as follows.
At that time, Upāli made the formal motion to the Saṃgha:
“Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now have the Elder Mahākāśyapa ask the questions and me answer.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Then, Mahākāśyapa immediately asked:
"Where did the first *pārājika* originally arise?
Who was the first to commit it? Upāli replied:
"In Vaiśālī, Sūdena Kalandakaputra first committed [the offense].
Where did the second original occurrence take place? He replied:
"In Rājagṛha, the bhikṣu Kumbhakāra-putra, Dhaniya, first committed [this offense].
He asked again:
"Where did the third nidāna originate?"
He replied, "It was at Vaiśālī,
by the side of the Vālukārāma River, where a bhikṣu first committed the offense.
He asked again:
"Where did the fourth *pūrvakalpa* (introductory narrative) take place?
He replied, "It was at Vaiśālī,
by the side of the Vārāṇā river, where a bhikṣu first committed an offense."
He asked again:
"Where did the first *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense originally arise? He replied:
"In Śrāvastī, Kāḷudāyin was the first to commit [the offense].
Thus it is recounted in succession according to the place where each arose, as explained in the first section.
Again, he asked:
"Where did the first *aniyata-dharma* (undetermined offense) originally arise?
He replied, "In Śrāvastī; Kālodāyin was the first to commit it."
The second case is likewise.
He asked again:
"Where did the origin of the *niḥsargika* [offenses] arise?"
He replied, "It was in Śrāvastī,
committed by the group of six bhikṣus for the first time.
This was repeated in succession, just as described in the first section.
He asked again:
"Where did the first *pāyattika* offense originally arise? He replied:
"In Śrāvastī, the bhikṣu Hastikaśipu, son of a Śākya, was the first to commit [an offense].
Thus it was transmitted in succession as explained in the first section.
Again, he asked:
"Where did the Prātimokṣa-saṃvaraṇīya originate? He replied,
"It originated in Śrāvastī, concerning the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā."
The second, third, and fourth [sections] are as explained in the first part.
He asked again:
"Where did the first *śaikṣa-dharma* (training rule) originate?"
He replied: "It was in Śrāvastī; the group of six bhikṣus were the first to commit it.
Thus it was related in succession, as explained in the first section.
The specific precepts for bhikṣuṇīs are as explained in the Vinaya.
He asked again:
"Where did the original institution of receiving the full ordination (mahā-śīla) first arise?"
He replied, "In Vārāṇasī, among the five bhikṣus.
He asked again:
"Where was the precept first heard? He replied,
"In Rājagṛha, for the sake of the young bhikṣus."
He asked again:
"Where did the original account of the first hearing of the *varṣā* (rainy-season retreat) originate? He replied:
"It originated in Śrāvastī due to the group of six bhikṣus.
He asked again:
"Where did the original institution of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony originate?"
He replied: "It was in Śrāvastī, arising because of the group of six bhikṣus.
Thus it was asked in succession until reaching the *Vinayottaragrantha*.
At that time, he immediately gathered all matters concerning bhikṣus into one place to form the Bhikṣu-vinaya;
he gathered all matters concerning bhikṣuṇīs into one place to form the Bhikṣuṇī-vinaya.
All the rules for receiving the precepts are collected in one place to form the *Upasampadā-khandhaka*.
All the rules for the *poṣadha* ceremony are collected in one place to form the *Poṣadha-khandhaka*.
All the rules concerning the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*) are collected in one place to form the *Varṣā-khaṇḍaka*.
All the rules concerning the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) are collected in one place to form the *Pravāraṇā-khaṇḍaka*.
All rules concerning leather are collected in one place as the Leather Khandhaka.
All rules concerning robes are collected in one place as the Robes Khandhaka.
All rules concerning medicine are collected in one place as the Medicine Khandhaka.
All the rules concerning the *kaṭhina* robe are collected in one place to form the *Kaṭhina-khandhaka*.
The two *vinayas*, together with all the *khandhakas*, the *Skandhaka-vinaya*, and the *Ekottara-vinaya*, are collectively gathered to form the *Vinaya-piṭaka*.
Then Mahākāśyapa made the formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now question Ānanda regarding the Dharma and the Vinaya."
"Thus it is announced.
At that time, Ānanda again made the formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now authorize Mahākāśyapa to question and me to answer.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Mahākāśyapa then questioned Ānanda, saying:
"In what place was the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* spoken?
In what place was the *Ekottarika Āgama* spoken?
In what place was the *Daśottara Sūtra* spoken?"
Where was the *Lokadhātu-saṃvarta-vivarta-sūtra* spoken?
Where was the *Saṃgīti-sūtra* spoken? Where was the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* spoken?
"In what place was the *Sūtra on the Questions of Śakra Devendra* spoken?
Ānanda answered all these questions as they are recounted in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
He then compiled all the long sūtras into the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
Among all the sūtras, those of medium length constitute the *Madhyama Āgama*.
Those ranging from one matter to ten matters, and from ten matters to eleven matters, constitute the *Ekottara Āgama*.
The various bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, upāsikās, and devas, together with Śakra, Māra, and Brahmā, were gathered as the *Saṃyuktāgama*.

Thus, the Jātaka-sūtras, Itivṛttaka-sūtras, Kāraṇavibhaṅga-sūtras, Vaipulya-sūtras, Adbhutadharma-sūtras, Avadāna-sūtras, Upadeśa-sūtras, Geya-sūtras, Dharmapada-sūtras, Pārāyaṇa-sūtras, Praśna-vyākaraṇa-sūtras, and Āryagāthā-sūtras—these, when collected together, constitute the *Kṣudraka-piṭaka*.

Regarding the sections on difficulties and ease, as well as those concerning bonds and associations, these were compiled into the *Abhidharma Piṭaka*. At that time, they were thus compiled as the Three Piṭakas.

Then, the Elder Pūrṇa, hearing that five hundred Arhats at Rājagṛha were collectively compiling the Dharma and the Vinaya, immediately set out for Rājagṛha with five hundred bhikṣus. Upon arriving at the place where Mahākāśyapa was, he spoke these words:
"I have heard that the Great Virtuous One, together with five hundred Arhats, is collectively compiling the Dharma and the Vinaya; I also wish to join their ranks and hear the Dharma."

At that time, Mahākāśyapa, on account of these circumstances, assembled the community of bhikṣus and questioned Upāli again regarding this bhikṣu; thus, as previously described, they compiled [the teachings] into the Tripiṭaka.
He said, "Venerable Kāśyapa! I accept all of this,
with the sole exception of eight matters."
"Venerable Sir!
I have personally heard this from the Buddha and remember it without forgetting.

The Buddha has permitted eating food that was stored overnight, cooked indoors, cooked by oneself, taken by oneself, or received early in the morning; as well as food brought from elsewhere, such as various fruits or edible things produced from pond water—all such items he permits one to eat without having to perform the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the formal ritual for leftover food)."
Mahākāśyapa replied, “It is indeed as you have said.
Because the World-Honored One had compassion for the bhikṣus during a time of famine when people were devouring one another and it was difficult to obtain alms, he permitted these eight matters.”
"At that time, the world was once again prosperous and food and drink were abundant; the Buddha then revoked his prohibition and permitted it.
They spoke further, saying: "Venerable Kāśyapa!..."
“The World-Honored One possesses all-knowing vision; it would not be fitting for him to prohibit something and then permit it again, or to permit something and then prohibit it again.

Kāśyapa replied, “Precisely because the World-Honored One possesses all-knowing vision, it is appropriate for him to prohibit something and then permit it again, or to permit something and then prohibit it again.”
Pūrṇa! We have established this regulation:
that which was not prohibited by the Buddha should not be prohibited, and that which was prohibited by the Buddha should not be rescinded.
"One should learn in accordance with the precepts as established by the Buddha.
Thus, five hundred arhats gathered together at Rājagṛha to compile the Dharma and Vinaya; for this reason, it is said that there were five hundred people who compiled the Dharma and Vinaya.

4. The Council of Seven Hundred on the Dharma and Vinaya. At that time, one hundred years after the Parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, the Bhikṣus of the Vajjiputtaka school in Vaiśālī practiced ten matters, saying:

"These things are pure, permitted by the Buddha: one may take food with two fingers; one may [store food] between villages; one may [store food] within the monastery; one may accept subsequent approval; one may follow established custom; one may act in harmony; one may keep salt overnight; one may drink *jaḷauka* liquor; one may possess an uncut sitting mat; and one may receive gold and silver."
On the day of the *poṣadha*, donors offered gold and silver, which they divided among themselves.

At that time, Yaśakaṇa’s son heard that the Vaiśālī bhikṣus were conducting such affairs; he went to the Vātsīputrīya bhikṣus and saw them encouraging the donors to give gold and silver to the Saṃgha during the *poṣadha*. When it was announced within the assembly that [the gift] was to be given to the bhikṣu Kaṇa’s son, he immediately said:
"I do not accept it."
"Why is this? A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept gold or silver; a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, renounces jewels and does not wear ornaments.
On another day, having divided [the property], he sent it to the bhikṣu Gaṇaka-putra.
The bhikṣu Kātyāyanīputra said:
"I do not need it.
I have already said:..."
"The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, have cast aside their precious jewels and do not wear ornaments.
He then said, "The upāsakas of Vaiśālī are angry; go and teach them so that they may be reconciled."
At that time, a messenger was immediately dispatched to go together with him.
The bhikṣu Yaśakāṇaputra went to the lay follower of Vaiśālī and spoke these words:
"Did you truly speak to me in anger?"
I said: "Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas!
You do not accept gold or silver; you have cast aside precious jewels and do not wear ornaments."
He spoke to the upāsaka, saying:
"When the World-Honored One was in Rājagṛha, the king and his ministers were assembled in the royal palace, and they spoke these words:
'The śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ought to accept gold and silver; they do not renounce precious treasures, nor do they refrain from wearing fine ornaments.'"
At that time, there was a great elder in the assembly named Muktika who said to the ministers:
"Do not speak such words as:
'The śramaṇa sons of the Śākyas accept gold and silver and do not renounce jewels; they are not without attachment to fine ornaments.'"
"Why is this? A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, ought not to accept gold or silver; he renounces jewels and gems, and does not wear ornaments.
At that time, the elder Muktaka explained this to the various ministers, causing each of them to understand and rejoice.

At a later time, the householder Maṇicūḍa went to the place where the World-Honored One was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and related the previous circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, saying:
"I then explained it for each of them, causing them all to rejoice."
“World-Honored One!
In speaking these words, would I not be contravening the holy intent or failing to accord with the Dharma teachings?
The Buddha said:
“Householder! What you have said is in accordance with the Dharma and reality, and does not contradict the teaching of the World-Honored One. Why is this?

A śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept gold or silver; setting aside jewels and gems, he should not wear ornaments. Should one who accepts gold or silver then experience the five desires, if he experiences the five desires, it is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas.
"Householder!
If you see a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, handling gold and silver, you should certainly know that this is not the dharma of a śramaṇa.
I say this: one may seek and beg for gold and silver for the sake of bamboo, reeds, grass, or wood, but one must never personally accept or take hold of gold and silver."
"Therefore, O Vimala!
For this reason, a śramaṇa, a son of the Śākyas, should not accept gold or silver; he should renounce jewels and gems, and not wear ornaments."
After leaving Vaisali, at another time, while the World-Honored One was at Jetavana, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are four things that cause the sun and moon to lose their brilliance."
What are these four? They are asuras, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist; these are the four things that cause the sun and moon to lose their brilliance.
In the same way, there are four things that defile and pollute śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, causing them to lack radiance and distinction.
What are the four?
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who drink alcohol and are unable to abandon it; this is the first defilement.
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who engage in the practice of sensual desire and are unable to relinquish it; this is the second defilement.
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who accept gold and silver and do not relinquish their finery; this is the third defilement.
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain themselves through wrong livelihood and are unable to abandon it; this is the fourth defilement.
"These are the four matters.
Because of these four matters, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas become defiled and obscure, lacking any radiance.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“Defiled by the stain of greed, these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are shrouded by ignorance and attached to beautiful forms.”
Drinking alcohol with a distracted mind, And further practicing the ways of sensual desire;
Accepting gold, jewels, and necklaces— These are the characteristics of the unwise.
Whether as śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, They sustain themselves through wrong livelihood.
The Buddha has declared these to be fetters, like the sun obscured by clouds and mist.
Lacking light, they fail to manifest its majestic brilliance; they are impure and utterly defiled.
Shuttered by the darkness of blindness, one is driven as a slave by craving.
"Having committed evil and unwholesome deeds, how can one who is deluded practice the Path?
Hatred and enmity increase greatly, and one receives yet another body in the future. "Therefore, O Laisa!"
For this reason, you should know that the śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, ought not to accept gold or silver, and should discard all ornaments.
When I have spoken these words, do you still not believe me on this account?
Vaiśravaṇa replied: "It is not that I lack faith;
I have faith and devotion toward you. You may remain here in Vaiśālī, and I shall provide you with whatever you require: clothing, food and drink, medicine, and other necessities."
Then, having instructed and gladdened the Licchavis, the bhikṣu Gaṇaka joined with that messenger bhikṣu and returned to the place where the bhikṣu Vāseṭṭha was.
Seeing from afar that the bhikṣu Gaṇaka was approaching, he immediately asked the messenger bhikṣu:
"Bhikṣu Gaṇaka, has he already understood the parable and gained faith among the Licchavis?"
He replied, "Yes," and then said:
"He has already placed his faith and delight in the son of Gaṇa, and he treats us as if we were not śramaṇas or sons of the Śākya!
The bhikṣu Vātsīputra asked, "For what reason?"
He then related the preceding circumstances in detail.
Those bhikṣus of Vaiśālī said to the bhikṣu Gaṇaka:
"Did you not see your fault when you previously reviled the Saṃgha?"
He replied, "I did not revile the Saṃgha.
They then united and performed the formal act of suspension against him.
The bhikṣu Gaṇaka thought to himself:
"If this elder Revata would become my companion in this dispute of mine, then it could be settled in accordance with the Dharma."
He then asked another person, "Where is Revata? The other replied:
"I heard that he was by the side of the Vāhī river.
He immediately went to the side of the Vāhī river. Revata was not there, so he asked:
“Where is Revata? He replied, “I have heard he is in the kingdom of Kaṇauj.”
He immediately went to that country.
Upon his arrival, Revata was again not there, so he asked once more: "Where is Revata?"
He replied, "In the country of Āgālura. He then went to that country.
Since he was not there either, [Upāli] asked: "Where is Revata? He replied:
"In the kingdom of Saṃkāsya. He then went to that country.
Seeing Revata amidst a gathering of monks, he asked Revata about his disciple who was making offerings:
"Venerable Elder Revata, will you go among the community of monks?
He replied, "I shall go."
At that time, Revata went to the assembly of monks; having listened to the Dharma teaching, he took his sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) and returned to his quarters after midnight.

At that same time, Yaśakāṇa’s son was also in the assembly of monks; having listened to the Dharma teaching, he too took his sitting mat and went to Revata’s place after midnight, thinking to himself:
"Now is the very time when I should fully explain the prior circumstances so that he may hear them."
He then asked Revata: "Venerable Elder!
Is it permissible to take food with two fingers?"
He asked in return:
"What is meant by 'picking up food with two fingers'? He replied:

"Venerable Elder! Having finished eating and having relinquished the formal posture, if one does not perform the *kṛtānyodana-vidhi* (the rite for leftover food), is it permissible to eat by taking morsels with two fingers? Revata replied:
"One should not do so.
He asked: "Where was this prescribed?"
He replied, “It was at Śrāvastī;
because they ate without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of remaining food), it was for this reason that the rule was established.
He asked again:
"Venerable Elder! Is it possible to reach the village?
He replied in turn:
“How does one obtain the village interval?
He replied: “Venerable Elder!...”
"Having finished eating and abandoned the formal posture, if one goes into the midst of a village to obtain food without performing the *khalupaścādbhakti* (the rite of not taking more food),
it is not permissible," said Revata.
"One should not do so."
He asked, "Where was it prescribed? He replied:
"In Śrāvastī, [the Buddha] ate without having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* rite;
for this reason, it was prescribed. He asked: "Venerable Elder!..."
"Is it permissible to enter the monastery?
He replied, asking in turn:
"In what way is it permissible to enter the monastery?"
He replied, "Venerable Elder! Within the monastery,
one may perform a *karmavācanā* for a separate assembly."
Revata said, "One should not do so. He asked:
"In what place was it established? He replied,
"It was established in Rājagṛha, within the Poṣadha-khandhaka."
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to receive [the precepts] later? He replied in turn:
"In what way is it permissible to receive them later?"
He replied: "Venerable Elder!
Once the *karmavācanā* has been performed by a separate assembly within the boundary, it is subsequently permitted."
Revata said, "It should not be done. He asked:
"In what place was it established? He replied,
"It was established in Rājagṛha, within the Poṣadha-khaṇḍaka."
He asked again:
"Have you attained the eternal Dharma?
He replied: "I have. The other asked in turn:
"How does one attain the eternal Dharma? He replied, "Venerable Elder!"
Having done this, he said, "This was originally what I was supposed to do. He replied,
"Does the bhikṣu know?"
One should examine the sūtras and vinaya to verify the legal codes.

If one does not examine the vinaya and fails to verify the legal codes, thereby violating the Dharma—whether it concerns what has already been done that should not have been done, or what has not yet been done that should not be done.

If one examines the Sūtras and Vinaya, scrutinizing the laws and regulations, and finds that they correspond with the Sūtras, correspond with the legal codes, and do not contradict the fundamental Dharma—whether an action has already been performed or has not yet been performed—it should be carried out.
He asked again: "Venerable Elder! Have you reached a reconciliation?"
He asked in return: "How can harmony be attained? He replied:
"Venerable Elder! Having finished eating and abandoned the formal posture, if one mixes ghee, oil, honey, fresh butter, rock sugar, and curd together in one place, may it be eaten?"
He replied, "One should not do so. He asked:
"Where was it established?
He replied, "In Śrāvastī;
because they ate without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of remaining food), it was established for that reason."
He asked again:
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible for salt to remain overnight?"
He asked in return:
"How can one allow salt to remain overnight? He replied:
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to use preserved salt (saṃvāsaka-lavaṇa) and put it into food before eating? He replied:
"One should not do so.
He asked, "Where was this prescribed?"
He replied, "It was established in Śrāvastī, within the Bhaiṣajyavastu. He asked again:
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to drink *śāloruṇa* liquor? He replied:
"One should not do so.
He asked, "Where was this prescribed?"
He replied, "It was in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, established by the Elder Bhikṣu Sāgata.
He asked again:
“Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to possess an uncut sitting mat? He replied:
"One should not keep [it].
He asked: "Where was this prescribed?"
He replied, "It was at Śrāvastī, due to the Six Group of Monks.
He asked again:
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to accept gold and silver? He replied:
"One should not do so.
He asked, "Where was this prescribed?"
He replied: "It was at Rājagṛha, established because of the Śākya son Upananda. He said:
"Venerable Elder! The Bhikṣus of Vaiśālī, the Vajjiputtas, practice these ten matters, saying:
'These are pure and in accordance with the Dharma; they are permitted by the Buddha.'"
He exhorted the donor to give gold and silver to the community of monks during the *poṣadha* ceremony, instructing that the person distributing the goods should divide them.
He said: "Do not tell this to anyone else."
Why is this? I fear that the bhikṣus there may hold differing views and thus refuse to associate with you.

You should go to Mount Aḍakavatī on the banks of the Ganges; there dwells the bhikṣu Trapusa, who is my preceptor and lives together with sixty Bhāradvāja bhikṣus. They are all courageous and diligent in their practice, possessing the crossing over of fearlessness.
Having explained these matters in full to him, they made an appointment by the banks of the Vāhīkā River, saying, "I too shall go there.
Then the bhikṣu Yaśakāṇa-putra went to that mountain and approached Subhadra, explaining all these matters to him in detail.
"At the side of the Kakutthā River, the Venerable Revata will also arrive.
At that time, the Bhikṣu Vajjiputtaka of Vaiśālī heard that the Bhikṣu Yasakanni-putta had gone among the people to seek out companions.
He then took a fine robe from Vaiśālī and went to the disciples of Revata, saying:
"I have brought this fine robe for the sake of the Venerable Revata; I offer it to him."
"I shall now stop and no longer give it to him; instead, I shall turn it over to you, so you may take it.
He replied, "Stop!
"Stop! I will not accept it.
Yet he pressed him repeatedly and insistently until he finally accepted it.
Having accepted it, he spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!
The bhikṣus of the two countries of Pāveyya and Pāṭaliputra are disputing; the World-Honored One has gone forth and is currently in the country of Pāveyya."
"Excellent, Elder! You should speak on my behalf to the Venerable Sthavira:
'The bhikṣus of the two kingdoms of Pāveyya and Pāṭaliputra are disputing, and the World-Honored One has gone forth to the kingdom of Pāveyya.'"
"Excellent, Great Virtue!
You should assist the bhikṣu Pāyāsi. He then replied:
“Venerable sir! The Elder Revata is so highly esteemed that I did not dare speak out of fear.
He pressed him insistently until he finally went to Revata’s place and spoke to him thus:
“Venerable Sir!
The bhikṣus of the two countries of Pāvā and Pāṭaliputra are disputing with one another, and the World-Honored One has gone forth to Pāvā.
We pray that the Venerable Sir will [go there as well].”
"You are assisting the bhikṣu Pāyana.
He immediately replied: "You fool!"
"Keep me among the impure classes!
Begone! You are no longer needed."
Having sent him away, he went to the Vajjiputtaka bhikkhus at Vesālī and spoke to them thus:
"Venerable sirs!
I previously said to you:..."
"The Venerable Revata is highly esteemed and difficult to address; I was unable to speak with him.
"Now you have been severely rebuked," he asked.
"What did he say? He replied, "He has already dismissed me."
He asked again, "How many years of seniority do you have? He replied:
"Twelve years. He asked, "Even though you are twelve years old,
do you still feel fear regarding being sent away?"
He replied, "If they do not accept my offerings, why should I not be afraid?
Then Upatiṣya and the other bhikṣus spoke thus:
"We should now go to the place where the dispute arose.
They immediately boarded their boat and traveled along the Ganges River.
At that time, being exhausted by the heat of the day, they stayed the boat on the bank and rested in the shade.
At that time, there was an elder traveling along the road in the village of Vaso who thought to himself:
"Regarding this present dispute, I shall examine the Sūtras and the Vinaya to determine whose words accord with the Dharma."
"Who speaks according to the Dharma?

He then examined the Sūtras and the Vinaya, scrutinizing the legal codes, and immediately knew that the bhikṣus of the country of Pāri were speakers of the Dharma, while the bhikṣus of Vairaṇyā were not speakers of the Dharma.
At that time, a deity, without manifesting their form, praised him, saying: "Excellent, noble son!
Just as you have observed, the bhikṣu Pāli speaks according to the Dharma, while the bhikṣu Pāyana speaks contrary to the Dharma."
Then the elders went together to Vaiśālī.
In Vaiśālī there was an elder named Sarvakāmin, who was the most senior monk (sthavira) in Jambudvīpa.
Then Sambhūta said to Revata:
"Let us go now to the dwelling of the Elder Sarvakāmin to stay the night, and explain this matter in detail so that he may hear it."
Then the two men followed each other and went to that house.
At that time, the Elder Sarvakāmin had been sitting in meditation and reflecting through the night for a long duration. Revata thought to himself:
"This senior elder is already old and his physical strength is weak; yet he has sat for such a long time. How much more so should I not sit in this manner?"
At that time, Revata sat down and remained in contemplation until late at night.
The Elder Sarvakāmin thought to himself:
"This visiting bhikṣu has come from afar and is utterly exhausted, yet he still sits thus in meditative contemplation; how much more so should I remain seated for a long time?"
Then that elder sat for a long time again in contemplation.
When much of the night had passed, he said to Revata: "Elder!..."
"What dharma have you been contemplating this night?
He replied, "When I was formerly a layman, I practiced the mind of loving-kindness; this night, I have contemplated and entered the samādhi of loving-kindness."
He then said: "You have entered a minor meditative concentration this very night. Why is that?
"The Samādhi of Loving-kindness is a minor concentration. He then asked again:
"Venerable Sarvakāmin, what dharma did you contemplate during this night?"
He replied, "When I was formerly a layperson, I practiced the dharma of emptiness; this night, I have entered the samādhi of emptiness many times. He said:
“Venerable sir, tonight I have contemplated the dharma of the Great Man.
Why is this? Because the dharma of the Great Man enters the samādhi of emptiness.”
He thought to himself:
"Now is the right time; I should explain the prior causal conditions so that he may understand. He then asked:
"Venerable Elder! Is it permissible to take food with two fingers? He asked.
“How does one eat by pinching food with two fingers?
He replied, “Venerable sir!”
"If one has finished eating, discarded the formal posture, and has not performed the *kṛtānyodana-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food), may one eat by picking up food with two fingers? He replied,
"One should not do so."
He asked, "Where was it prescribed? He replied:
"In Śrāvastī, [the Buddha] ate food without having performed the *kṛtāvakāśa* (remaining-food) rite; for this reason, he established the rule.
Thus it was stated one by one, up until the case where, during the *poṣadha* ceremony, one accepted gold and silver and had the distributor of goods divide them, as described above.
He then said: "Do not speak of this to others; I fear that people’s minds may differ and they will be unable to reach harmony.
Aśvajit was the first elder, Svāgata the second elder, Revata the third elder, and Vatsa the fourth elder; Ānanda served as the preceptor for them all.
At that time, when the Elder Sarvakāmin was presiding over the affairs of the Saṃgha, the Elder immediately made the formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent, let the Saṃgha now discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya."
"Thus it was stated.
At that time, the bhikṣu Pāyana said to the bhikṣu Pāli:
"You should now bring forth impartial and upright persons."
He replied, "The Elder Sabbakāmī, Revata, Yasas, and Sumana are impartial men.
Then the bhikkhu Pārileyyaka spoke to the bhikkhu of Pāṭaliputta, saying:
"You all should also produce an impartial person. They then said:
"The Elder Subhūti, the Elder Vāṣpa, the Elder Śāriputra, and the Elder Aniruddha are impartial persons."
"Among them is the bhikṣu Āyīthū, who is capable of exhorting and transforming others. Those bhikṣus said,
"Include this bhikṣu among our number."
"Why is this? Wherever he may be, he shall exhort and transform us.
Thus, he was included among their number.
Those elders thought to themselves:
"If we were to inquire into this matter in the midst of the assembly, we fear it would give rise to further disputes; we do not know whose words are correct."
"Whose words are incorrect?
Might we now rather appoint a sequence and deliberate together in a separate location?
Those elders had this thought:
"In what other place shall we settle this matter?
they asked, and then said,
"It shall be in the Pāri forest."
Then the Elder Sarvakāmin made the formal motion:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!

Regarding this bhikṣu who has been formally accused by the Sangha, if the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha grant its consent to discuss the Dharma and Vinaya within the Pārileyyaka forest, while other bhikṣus are not present therein."
"Thus it is announced.
Having thus made the announcement, he should, by means of a formal act (*karmavācanā*), appoint two or three bhikṣus to go with other bhikṣus to the Pārileyyaka forest.
Then the Elder Sarvakāmin, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; thus all the elders gathered.
Then the Elder Sarvakāmin made the formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*). Then Upāli made the formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen. The Saṃgha now questions the Elder Sarvakāmin regarding the Dharma and Vinaya.
Thus is the formal motion (jñapti)."
Then the Elder Sarvakāmin again made this formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now direct Revata to question and me to answer regarding the Dharma and Vinaya."
"Thus it is stated. Revata asked, "Venerable Elder!"
"Is it pure with two fingers?
He then asked in return:
"What is meant by 'pure with two fingers'?"
He replied, "Venerable Elder!
Having finished eating and abandoned the formal posture, is it permissible to eat by picking up food with two fingers?"
He replied, "One should not do so. He asked:
“Where was it established?
He replied: “In Śrāvastī;
because they ate without having performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (the ritual of leaving food remaining), it was established on that account.”
"This is the first matter: it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what was taught by the Buddha. Having deliberated on the matter separately, cast down one śalāka;

in this manner, examine each point individually until reaching the tenth matter—all being contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to what was taught by the Buddha—and cast down a śalāka for each."
Those elders spoke thus:
"Just as we have now settled this matter in another place, we now wish to investigate it likewise within the Saṃgha."
"Why is this? So that all people may know.

If the time is right for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now discuss the Dharma and the Vinaya.

The Elder Revata then made the formal motion:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits, let the Saṃgha now question the Elder Sarvakāmin regarding the Dharma and Vinaya."
"Let it be announced thus.
At that time, the Elder Sarvakāmin immediately made the formal announcement:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
"If it is the time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, let the Saṃgha now direct Upāli to question the Dharma and Vinaya while I provide the answers.
Having made this motion, Upāli then asked:

therefore, this was prescribed. This is the first matter: it is not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha. Having investigated this within the Saṃgha, one casts down a *śalākā* (voting tally).

In this manner, each of the ten matters is investigated one by one; as they are all not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and not the teaching of the Buddha, once investigated within the Saṃgha, a *śalākā* is cast down for each.

Section 5: The Section on Discipline (Vinayavastu), Part 1. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Vaiśālī.
Then Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, engaged in unchaste conduct with his former wife; does this constitute an offense of pārājika?"
The Buddha said,
“Upāli! At the very beginning,
before the precepts had been established, there was no offense.”

"There is no offense.
However, if there is a large quantity of gathered cloth, one should not take it as *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) material."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu walking not far from a cemetery who saw from a distance many discarded rags; he immediately gathered them up and departed, saying, "I shall take them back later."
Other monks who wear rag-robes saw it and, thinking it was a discarded rag-robe, took it away.
When that monk returned and did not see his robe, he went to the monastery and saw another monk washing and mending it. He immediately said to him:
"You have stolen my robe; you have committed theft."
He replied, "I did not steal it; it was merely discarded rags (pāṃśukūla)!
Because of this doubt, the Buddha said:
"With what intention did you do this?
He replied, "I took it with the intention of making it into a *pāṃsukūla* (rag-robe)."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not take up a heap of discarded rags."

At that time, there was a householder walking not far from a cemetery who saw from afar a highly valuable discarded robe (pāṃsukūla). He immediately went to take it, placed it among the grass, and departed, saying, "I shall return to take this and give it to a certain bhikṣu."
At that time, there was a pāṃśukūlika bhikṣu who saw it and took it away immediately.
When the lay devotee returned and did not see his robe, he went to the monastery and saw the bhikṣu washing and mending it.
He then said to him: "You have stolen my robe!"
The bhikṣu replied, "I did not steal your robe; I took only a discarded rag.
Being in doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you do this?
He replied, "I took it with the thought of making it into a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe)."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not take discarded robes from such places."
At that time, there was a cowherd who took off his garment, placed it before his head, and fell asleep.
A bhikṣu who wore discarded rags (pāṃśukūlika) saw him and, thinking he was a dead man, had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has not permitted bhikṣus to take the garments of a complete corpse."
He immediately took the arm bone of a dead man and struck him on the head.
The man woke up and said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"Why did you strike me?
The bhikṣu replied,
"I thought you were a dead man."
The cowherd said, "How could you not even distinguish my death from my life?
and he struck the bhikṣu with his skilled hand.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"One should not kill a person and break their body open to take the clothing.
At that time, there were many young children who had taken off their clothes, placed them in one spot, and were playing with a mound of earth.
A bhikṣu who wore rag-robes saw them and immediately took them away.
When the children saw this, they said to him,
"Do not take our clothes away!"
The bhikṣu replied,
"I thought this was a discarded rag-robe," and having set it down, he departed.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"I took it as discarded rags.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One should not take up a rag-robe from a heap of refuse.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus used rock honey to entice and deceive small children, intending to take them to the marketplace to sell them.
When his parents saw this, they immediately asked the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, what have you said? He replied:
"I have said nothing.
Having left the child behind, he departed.
The man was suspicious, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind?
He replied, "With a mind of theft."
The Buddha said:
“If it is worth five coins and is moved from its original place, it is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a thieving mind, swapped the counting sticks belonging to another’s portion; that person became doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"If one raises the tally, it is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another's tally for his share and felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"If its value is five *māṣakas* and it is moved from its original place, it is a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who turned another’s counting-stick; he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
“If one employs a means to take five coins, but they have not yet left their original place, it is a sthūlātyaya.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who twice stole items, each time for less than five coins. He thought to himself:
"Since my thefts before and after do not total five coins, I have not committed a pārājika offense."
The Buddha said,
"If the total amount reaches five coins, whether taken before or after, it is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, not far from the Jetavana, there was a householder plowing a field.
A visiting bhikṣu saw this and said to him, "This is the property of the Saṃgha;
do not plow it. He replied:
"This is not the Saṃgha's land; it is my land," he said.
The bhikṣu spoke again, saying, "This is the Saṃgha's land; do not plow it."
The householder immediately released his plow and departed, saying:
"I have my own land, yet I am unable to cultivate it.
Then that visiting bhikṣu entered Jetavana and questioned the resident bhikṣus.
"A householder is plowing not far from here.
Whose land is this? He replied:
"This is the layperson's ground," said the senior bhikṣu. "Why do you ask?"
He then related the circumstances in detail and became doubtful. The Buddha asked him, "With what intention did you do this?
He related the circumstances in full, and the Buddha said:
"You have committed no offense, yet you should not have done such a thing.
At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If one acts with the intent to devalue, and takes five coins or more than five coins—whether taking them oneself or instructing another to take them; whether cutting or breaking them oneself or instructing another to cut or break them; whether shattering them oneself or instructing another to shatter them; or whether burning them, burying them, or spoiling their color—is this an offense?"
The Buddha said:
"All such acts constitute a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who divided land and moved another person's boundary markers.
He was doubtful, and the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"By means of a thieving mind.
The Buddha said:
"If one shifts the boundary markers and the value is five coins or more, it is a *pārājika* offense."

At that time, the monastery garden of the Saṃgha was waterless and falling into ruin. The group of six bhikṣus diverted water from another’s field into the monastery garden. Feeling doubtful, they asked the Buddha:
“With what intention did you do this?”
He replied, "With a mind of theft.
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose donor’s field was ruined for lack of water. He diverted water from another source into the donor’s field and felt doubt.
The Buddha said: "Pārājika."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a grudge against a lay family; he diverted the water from another's field and abandoned it so that the field was ruined and left fallow.
He felt doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"It is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another’s water. He felt doubtful, and the Buddha said:
“If its value is five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is a *pārājika* offense.
The bhikṣus were doubtful and did not dare to take water from canals, springs, or ponds; the Buddha said:
"If it is not protected by a human being, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Caṇḍāla who had a dispute; he possessed a precious *sumana* bowl.
Because of that dispute, he was constantly filled with sorrow and spoke these words:
"If there is anyone who can settle this dispute of mine, I shall give him this bowl."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Āyītóu, who was wise, discerning, and skilled in settling disputes. Having settled the dispute for them, he took his bowl and departed.
This bhikṣu, thinking he had lost his bowl, went out to search for it; seeing Āyītó holding it in his hand, he immediately said to him:
"You have stolen my bowl."
He replied: "I did not steal your bowl; you yourself made this solemn promise:
'If there is anyone who can settle my dispute, I shall give this bowl to them.'"
"Therefore, I took it. He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?"
He fully explained the circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"You have committed no offense;
however, you should not have accepted such an object."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Yaśoda who possessed a saṃghāṭī robe.
There was also another bhikṣu named Vāsavadatta who, without being told, took it and put it on, then entered a village to beg for alms.
Thinking he had lost his robe, he went out to search for it; seeing that Vāsavadatta was wearing it, he immediately seized him and said, "You have committed theft. He replied:
“I did not steal your robe; I took it only out of a sense of intimacy and affection!
He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him:
“With what state of mind did you take it?”
He replied, "I took it with a sense of intimacy and affection, not with a mind of theft.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense;
however, one should not take [a robe] from one who is not a close friend while harboring the intention that they are a close friend.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Śuddha who possessed a saṃghāṭī. The bhikṣu Sūpananda, without asking its owner, put it on and entered a village to beg for alms.
The master, believing his robe had been lost, went out to search for it. Seeing that Sūdayin was wearing it, he immediately seized him and said:
"You have taken my robe; you have committed theft."
He replied, "I did not steal; I was merely wearing it on loan!
The Buddha, being suspicious, asked him:
"With what state of mind did you do this?
He replied, "I borrowed it; it was not with the intent to steal."
The Buddha said, “There is no offense. However,
one should not enter a village and put on [the robes] without first asking the owner.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took another's pear fruit and felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"If it is worth five coins and is removed from its original place, it is a pārājika offense.
Whether it be jambu fruit, pālevata fruit, grapes, or various other fruits, if they are worth five coins, in all such cases it is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who shook a pear tree with the intent of causing damage and loss. The Buddha said:
"If the value is five coins, it is a pārājika offense.
If one shakes down jambu fruits, pālevata fruits, grapes, or various other fruits with the intent of causing damage and loss, in all such cases it is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another’s melon; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"If its value is five māsakas, it is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole sugarcane; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"If [the value] is five māsakas, it is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took another's vegetables and felt doubt; the Buddha said:
"If [the value] is five māsakas, it is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took another’s lotus flower and felt doubt. The Buddha said:
“If it is worth five coins, it is a pārājika offense.
Whether it be a padma, a utpala, a kuvalaya, or a puṇḍarīka flower, if it is worth five coins, in all such cases it is a pārājika offense.”
"If one further breaks or destroys it with the intent to cause loss to another, and the value is five *kārsāpaṇas* or more, it is in every case a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a person guarding the property and a thief who gave *khajjaka* food to a bhikṣu. The bhikṣu thought to himself: "This is not their food."
They did not accept it.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This is the food of a donor; I allow you to wash your hands clean and receive it to eat."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took another’s lotus root; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
“If it is worth five coins, it is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who gathered wood in a forest protected by others; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
“Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a mind of theft, took another’s food without a valid basis; being doubtful, the Buddha said: “Pārājika.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took another’s food without a valid basis; being doubtful, he questioned by the Buddha:
“With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If there was no intent to steal," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"Because of speaking falsely, it is a *pāyattika*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who sent another bhikṣu to steal a rope bed.
The messenger bhikṣu thought it was not theft and took the bed back; being doubtful, he reported this to the Buddha, who said:
"In the case of one who instructs by means of a stratagem, it is a *pārājika* offense; for the messenger, there is no offense.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who sent another bhikṣu to fetch a rope bed. The messenger, thinking he was stealing it, took the bed and brought it back. Feeling doubt, [the sender] asked the Buddha, who said:
"The one who took it is guilty of a *pārājika* offense; the one who instructed him is without offense."
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who possessed litters traveling together with the group of six bhikṣus.
The group of six bhikṣus thought to themselves:
"When we arrive at our destination, we shall steal those litters."
The Buddha said:
"If one steals from this place, it is a pārājika offense.
If one steals while on the road, or upon arriving at a dwelling, it is likewise a pārājika offense."
At that time, there were six groups of bhikṣus who saw a boat drifting on the Ganges River and thought to themselves:
"We could steal this boat without exerting our own physical strength."
He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him,
"With what intention did you do this?
He then fully explained the circumstances, and the Buddha said:
"But, O mind, there is no offense;
however, you should not give rise to such a thought.
A bhikṣu stole another's boat, taking it from this shore to the other shore, and felt doubt. The Buddha said:

"Pārājika. Whether from the far shore to this shore, whether with the current or against the current, whether by sinking in the water, or by pulling onto dry land, or by unmooring another's boat from its place—these are all pārājika."
"If one attempts to resolve [the matter] through expedient means but does not leave the spot, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, two bhikṣus went to bathe in the river Aciravatī and saw a basket containing expensive clothes being carried down by the current. Upon seeing it, one bhikṣu said:
"This basket belongs to me."
The second bhikṣu said, "The items in the basket belong to me.
They then took the expensive garments together, whereupon they became doubtful. The Buddha said:
"With what state of mind?
He replied, "With the perception of it as discarded rags (pāṃśukūla)."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not take discarded robes from within the water."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole a golden flower garland; being doubtful about his offense, he asked the Buddha, who said: "It is a pārājika.
At that time, there were many bird nests dwelling within the Jetavana Monastery; when the night had advanced, the birds cried out and disturbed the bhikṣus who were practicing meditation.
There was an elder bhikṣu who sent a park keeper to remove a bird’s nest.
Inside that bird’s nest, he saw gold and scraps of silk; he brought these back and gave them to the elder bhikṣu.
Regarding that doubt, the Buddha said:
"Wild birds and beasts have no utility; there is no offense in taking them, yet one should not accept such things.

At that time, there was a mouse hole in the Jeta Grove. A bhikṣu had a gardener destroy it, and from within that mouse hole, the gardener found medicinal herbs and scraps of cloth, which he brought and gave to the bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus were doubtful. The Buddha said:
"Animals have no use for it; there is no offense, yet one should not accept such things.
At that time, there was a village not far from the monastery, and various rats went into the village to fetch walnuts, which they brought back and formed a great heap inside the monastery.
The group of six bhikṣus took food with the intent to steal.
They were doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"It is a pārājika offense."
At that time, not far from the Jetavana, there was a hunter who had set a trap to catch deer; inside the trap lay a dead deer.
The group of six bhikṣus took it with the intent to steal and eat it, and they felt doubt.
The Buddha said, "It is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to an araṇya during the day.
There was a thief who had tied up an ox at a tree; when the ox saw the bhikṣu, it wept.
Moved by compassion, the bhikṣu released it and let it go.
A bhikṣu was doubtful; the Buddha asked him, "With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"Because he acted with a mind of loving-kindness and had no intent to steal," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"One should not do such a thing.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to an araṇya during the day; there, some thieves had tied up oxen and placed them therein.
Seeing no one to the left or right, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"This will be beneficial for me," he thought,
and immediately untied the ox and led it away.
Before they had gone far, he felt regret and said:
"What use have I for this ox?
he said, and immediately released it.
The bhikṣu was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention?
He replied, "With the intention of theft."
The Buddha said:
"If it is worth five coins and is removed from its place, it is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a leopard that had caught a deer; the deer, wounded, entered the monastery and died.
When the bhikṣus took food, they were doubtful; the Buddha said, "There is no offense.
At that time, there was a hunter who had captured deer, and a deer entered the monastery. The hunter, searching for the deer, arrived and asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you see such-and-such a deer?
Those bhikṣus who had not seen it said they had not seen it; the hunter then searched for it everywhere and found it.
At that time, the hunter became angry and resentful toward the bhikṣus, saying:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, have no sense of shame or remorse; they deceive with false speech, yet claim for themselves:
'I know the True Dharma.
Seeing a deer, they say they do not see it—how can there be any True Dharma in such a case?"
The bhikṣus were doubtful and reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said, "There is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole a pārihārika-cīvara (a robe for wearing while traveling). Being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a mind of theft, lifted another's pārikāra robe from its place; being doubtful, the Buddha said: "Pārājika."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a thieving mind, turned over a pālicara robe; he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"If one seeks five coins by means of a stratagem, but has not yet moved it from its place, it is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole a rope bed, a wooden bed, large or small cushions, pillows, woolen blankets, or else a water jar, a washing vessel, a staff, or a fan. The Buddha said:
"If the value is five coins, it is in all cases a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, while rearranging a rope bed, said:
"This too belongs to the Saṃgha; that too belongs to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
"One must not exchange them upside down.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who exchanged wooden beds, large or small mats, or pillows upside down; these too belong to the Saṃgha, and those also belong to the Saṃgha.
Regarding the woolen blanket, the water jar, the bathing vessel, the staff, and the fan, he said:
"This too belongs to the Saṃgha; that too belongs to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another's stone; he felt doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"If its value is five coins, it is a pārājika offense."

If one steals timber for a moat, bamboo, reeds, *manjaka* grass, *parpaṭa* grass, or tree bark; or if one steals leaves, flowers, or fruits from a tree guarded by another; and if one has doubt regarding these, the Buddha said:
"If the value is five *kārsāpaṇas*, it is in all cases a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole a robe from another’s robe-rack; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
“It is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a mind of theft, lifted a robe on another’s robe-rack and moved it away from the rack; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with a thieving mind, shifted a garment from another shelf; he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"If one seeks five coins through such means but has not yet removed it from its place, it is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took both the strap and the frame from another person’s clothing rack. Feeling doubtful, he questioned the Buddha, who asked:
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"By means of a thieving mind.
The Buddha said:
"If the value is five coins and it is removed from its place, it is a *pārājika* offense."

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, together with the group of six bhikṣus, were sitting and eating inside the house of a layperson; the layperson had spread out a garment of great value as a seat for them.
Among them was a group of six bhikṣus who, with a thieving mind, turned [the object] over with their feet; they were doubtful, and the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you do this? They replied:
"With the intent to steal.
The Buddha said:
"If one seeks five coins by means of an expedient, but has not yet moved them from their place, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense."
The Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 55 [and] Volume 56, Part 7 of the Fourth Division;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Zhu Fonian and others;
Part Two of the *Vinayavibhaṅga*. At one time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kṣemā who had a lay donor’s family. A disciple of hers went to that family and said to the donor:
“The Venerable Kṣemā requires five pecks of sesame seeds.”
The donor said, "It can be obtained!
and immediately gave it to him.
That disciple obtained some sesame seeds and ate them herself.
Later, on another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī Khemā dressed in the morning, took her bowl, went to the house of a donor, arranged her seat, and sat down.
The donor asked,
"Is sesame seed delicious? He replied:
"What kind of sesame seeds are these?
The donor then explained the matter from beginning to end.
When Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā returned, she spoke to her disciple bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"You stole my five pecks of sesame.
The disciple replied, "I did not steal it;
I took it out of a sense of intimacy and affection."
Being suspicious, the Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
“I took it with a friendly and affectionate intention.
The Buddha said,
“There is no offense.”
"One should not, with an intention that is not one of intimacy, take [something] with an intention of intimacy; because of such false speech, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Cāmā had a family of donors. Her disciple went to that family and said:
"The elder Cāmā requires a gruel made of three kinds of medicinal herbs."
He replied, "It can be obtained!
and immediately gave it to him; having received it, he ate it himself.
Later, at dawn, the bhikṣuṇī Khemā dressed herself, took up her bowl, and went to that house where she spread out a seat and sat down.
The donor asked, “Ayye!
[What brings you here?]”
"Are these three kinds of medicinal gruel delicious? He replied,
"What are the three kinds of medicinal gruel?"
The donor then related the matter from beginning to end.
Kṣema returned and said to that bhikṣuṇī’s disciple:
"You stole my three kinds of medicinal gruel."
He replied, "I did not steal; I took it out of a sense of intimacy.
He was uncertain, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
He replied, "I took it with a sense of intimacy and affection."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not take [an item] from someone who is not a close friend while intending them to be a close friend; because of the lie, one incurs a *pāyattika*."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took his preceptor’s portion of solid food (khādanīya).
The preceptor said to him, “If you eat my portion, you commit the offense of theft. He replied:
