"I did not steal; I took it with the intention of a close friend.
He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied, "I took it out of affection.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense; however, one should not take [something] with the intention of a close friend when one does not have the intention of a close friend.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose potter served as his donor (dānapati).
The donor said to him:
“Venerable sir, when you require a vessel, please let me know. He replied, “So be it.”
After the donor had risen and returned home, another person came to the shop to sell vessels.
Later, when a bhikṣu required a jar, he took that other man’s jar and departed with it.
He said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, do not take my flask away.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is the jar belonging to so-and-so; so-and-so previously said to me, 'If you need a vessel, take it.
Therefore, I have taken it."
He replied, "This is not so-and-so’s jar.
The bhikṣu immediately set down the jar and departed. Feeling doubtful, the Buddha asked him:
“What was your intention?
He then explained the circumstances in detail. The Buddha said, “There is no offense;
however, one should not take anything without first asking the owner.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose patron (dānapati) was a wine-seller.
The patron said to the bhikṣu,
"Venerable sir, if you require a steamer, take one."
He replied, "So be it.
Thereupon, the donor returned home, while another person took up residence at the place where wine was being sold.
Later, a bhikṣu came seeking a steamer to take it away.
The owner said to him, "Venerable sir, do not take my steamer.
The bhikṣu replied:
"This is the steamer belonging to so-and-so; previously, so-and-so told me, 'If you need a steamer, take one. That is why I took it."
He replied, "This is not so-and-so’s steamer.
The bhikṣu set down the steamer and departed, feeling doubtful. The Buddha asked him:
"What was your intention?
[The monk] answered fully regarding the causes and conditions, and the Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One should not take another's property without asking the owner.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose patrons were merchants, who said to him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"If you have anything you need, simply take it. He replied, "So be it."
After those merchants returned home, another person later came to this place to sell goods.
Later, when a bhikṣu required rice, he simply took some rice and departed with it.
He said, "Venerable sir, do not take my rice away."
The bhikṣu said:
"This is such-and-such a person’s rice; he previously told me:
'If you have any need, take it.'"
"Therefore, I took it.
He replied, "This is not someone else's rice."
The bhikṣu then set aside the rice and departed. Feeling doubtful, he was questioned by the Buddha:
"With what intention did you do this?
He related the circumstances in full, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense;
however, one should not take [an item] without first asking the owner.
At that time, there was a cloth merchant who acted as a donor (*dānapati*), and the donor said:
"Venerable sir, please take whatever robes you require. He replied, "So be it."
That donor passed away, leaving behind a son.
When the bhikṣu required a robe, he took the robe and departed.
The son said:
"Venerable sir!
Do not take my robe with you.
The bhikṣu said:
"This is a certain robe; previously he said to me:
'When you need a robe, take it. He replied:
"Such-and-such has already died.
The bhikṣu left his robes and departed. Being doubtful, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you leave?"
He related the circumstances in full, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not take [an item] without first asking the owner."
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Vaiśālī.

There was a Licchavi who lacked faith and devotion; he wrapped five coins in a piece of tattered cloth, placed them among a heap of refuse, and sent someone to watch closely, instructing him to bring anyone who saw and took them back to him.
At that time, a *pāṃśukūlika* (rag-robe monk) saw it and, thinking it was a discarded rag, immediately took it and placed it in his bag.
When the messenger saw this, he said:
"So-and-so, the Licchavi, calls for you."
The bhikṣu replied,
"I am going. He went to where Liśa was, and Liśa asked:
"Venerable sir, should one handle money and precious gems?
The bhikṣu replied, "One should not."
"Why did you take it? He replied, "I did not take it."
He said, "Bring it out and show it.
He immediately brought it out from the bag and showed it to him.
This bhikṣu felt shame and remorse, and the other bhikṣus did likewise; they reported this matter in full to the World-Honored One, who said:
"Listen well, all you bhikṣus!

If there is a bhikṣu who wishes to take such discarded rags (pāṃśukūla), he should step on them with the toes of his left foot and pull them loose with the toes of his right foot to examine them; if anything impure is found, he should remove it, and only then take away what is clean.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Śrāvastī.
Kāḷudāyin and the group of six bhikṣus were bathing in the river Ajiravatī.
Kāḷudāyin emerged from the water first onto the bank and, by mistake, put on the robes of the group of six bhikṣus before departing.
The group of six bhikṣus came out later; not seeing their own robes on the riverbank, they saw Kālodāyin’s robe and said, "He has committed theft; he has taken our robes."
He did not, therefore, carry out the formal act of banishment in his presence.

At that time, Kāḷudāyin heard of this and became doubtful; he went to the Blessed One, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit at one side, and reported these circumstances in detail to the Blessed One.
The World-Honored One asked,
"With what state of mind [did you do this]? He replied:
"If it is one's own robe and not taken with a thieving mind," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."

Furthermore, one should not put on the robes without first inspecting them; nor should one carry out a formal act of censure, or of banishment, or of dependence, or of prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople, or of suspension, or of the revocation of banishment (*pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman*) without the person being present.
"If it is not completed, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who found a garment blown by the wind; he was uncertain about it, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?"
He replied, "I took it as discarded rags (pāṃsukūla), not with a mind of theft.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense, but one should not take clothing blown by the wind or discarded rags.

At that time, there was a householder who, having washed his clothes, hung them on a wall to dry. A bhikṣu seeking discarded rags saw them, took them to be discarded rags, and immediately carried them away.
At that time, the householder saw him and said,
"Venerable sir!
Do not take my robe away."
The bhikṣu said, "I thought this was a discarded rag-robe (pāṃśukūla).
He immediately set the robe down and departed. Being doubtful, the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you take it?
He replied, "I took it as discarded rags (pāṃśukūla)."
The Buddha said, "There is no offense,
yet one should not take discarded robes from atop a wall, a fence, or from within a moat.
At that time, there was a householder who, having finished washing his clothes, hung them upon a grain-bin to dry.
There was a bhikkhu of the group of six who, with a thieving mind, took [an object] away.
He felt doubtful about it, and the Buddha said:
"It is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there were many bandits who left the city of Śrāvastī and, not far from the Jetavana Grove, drank liquor during the day.
When the sun had set, they placed their remaining liquor among the trees and entered the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus went out from Jetavana and, with a thieving mind, took some [oil] to drink. Feeling doubtful, they asked the Buddha, who said:
"You have committed a pārājika offense.

At another time, there was a bhikṣu seeking alms who, having dressed in his robes and taken up his bowl in the morning, went to the house of a donor. He encountered a torrential rain, and the water washed various kinds of fat away. He thought to himself:
"This was obtained without seeking; it can serve as medicine.
He immediately took and consumed it, but felt doubtful. The Buddha asked him, "With what state of mind did you do this?"
He replied, "I took it as discarded refuse; it was not with a mind of theft.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
One should not take discarded items from within water and consume them without having formally received them; [if one does so], it is a *pāyattika*.
At that time, there was a donor family of a certain bhikṣu, and another bhikṣu said to him:
"I wish to go to your donor's house; what should I say there?
He replied, "Say whatever you please."
That bhikṣu required fifty *liang* of rock honey; he went to the house of a lay donor (*dānapati*) and said, "A certain bhikṣu requires fifty *liang* of rock honey."
The donor said, "It may be so," and immediately gave it to him.
This bhikṣu, having obtained it, ate it himself and did not give it to that other bhikṣu.
Later, at another time, that bhikṣu went to the house of a donor, and the donor said to him:
"Venerable One!..."
“Is candied sugar good?
The bhikṣu asked, “What kind of candied sugar?”
"For whom is this rock honey?
The lay devotee then gave a full account of the matter from beginning to end.
That bhikṣu returned and said to this bhikṣu:
"You have committed theft by taking my rock honey.
He replied, "I have not committed theft; you said to me:..."
"Speak as you wish.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"You should not speak in such a manner; you should say, 'This is the teaching, this is the word.'"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another’s palanquin; he felt doubt.
The Buddha said, “It is a pārājika offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who stole another’s firewood; he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"If [the value] is exactly five coins, it is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, Pilindavatsa had a donor who had two young children; they were clever and did not fear people.
When Pilindavatsa arrived at his home, the young children would embrace his feet and play with them as he moved about.
Later, on another occasion, these two children were stolen away by bandits.
At that time, Pilindavatsa, having dressed in the morning and taken up his bowl, went to the house of a donor and sat upon the seat prepared for him.
The child’s parents, weeping and shedding tears, said:
"Our child has been stolen away by a thief."
"If he were here now, he would come to grab the Venerable's feet as a joke. He then replied,
"You may search for him everywhere within the house."
The parents searched for him but could not find him.

At that time, Pilindavatsa returned, entered his cell within the monastery, and entered meditative concentration, focusing his mindfulness upon the body. With his pure, supramundane divine eye, he saw that the child had been stolen by bandits and was being carried away on a boat upon the Ganges River.
Having seen him, in the time it takes for a person to bend and extend their arm, he vanished from within the monastery and appeared upon the thief’s boat on the Ganges River.

When the boy saw him, he immediately rejoiced and came to embrace his feet. Vatsa then used his supernormal power to take the boy with him and placed him in a room on the upper story of the pavilion; he then went to where the donor was prepared and sat upon the seat.
At that time, the parents wept and said,
"If our son were here, he would now embrace the feet of the Great Virtuous One to play. He replied:
"You may search for it in the room on the upper story.
He replied, "I have already searched, but could not find it."
Pilindavatsa said, "Just search further.
He then searched again in a room on the upper story of the pavilion and found it.
At that time, the child’s parents were greatly delighted and said, "Our son was stolen by a thief, yet now Pilindavatsa has brought him back for us.

When the bhikṣus heard this, among them were those who had few desires and were contented, who practiced the dhūta austerities, who delighted in training in the precepts, and who possessed a sense of shame and remorse; they censured Pilindavatsa, saying:
"How did the thieves steal another's child and bring it back to me?

Having heard this, Pilindavatsa was filled with doubt; he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported these circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One, knowing this, asked intentionally:
"With what intention did you take it? He replied:
"Taking with a mind of loving-kindness, there is no intention to steal.
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense."
"One should not perform such an act.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Ghoṣila who had a lay donor family; the donor fell ill, and the bhikṣu came to inquire after his health.
He had two sons who were clever and perceptive. After the donor had shown them the treasure store, he said to the bhikṣu regarding the location:
"When these two boys have grown up, if one of them is superior, show him this place of treasure."
Thereupon, he passed away.
Later, when the bhikṣu Ghoṣila visited the two children, he pointed out the location of the treasure to the elder one.
Then, one of the younger children came weeping into the monastery and spoke to Ānanda, saying:
"Venerable sir!
Look at this monk, Koṣṭhila; he has taken the paternal inheritance left by my father and divided it between two people, yet bestowed it all upon one.
Then Ānanda spoke to the monk Koṣṭhila, saying:
"How can you divide the paternal inheritance left by another between two people and give it to one?
Go away, Upananda; you should not perform the *poṣadha* together with us."
At that time, Ānanda did not participate in the poṣadha ceremony for six consecutive sessions.
Meanwhile, the bhikṣu Utkṣiptaka formed a faction with Rāhula.
Then, in the morning, Rāhula dressed himself, took up his bowl, and went to the Śākya women and Koliya women of the kingdom of Kapilavastu, where he spoke to them as follows:
"You all may take the boys and girls before Ānanda; if a small child cries, Ānanda shall say:
'Take the small child away.'"
"You all should speak these words:
'We cannot take the young child away; even Ānanda must listen to the words of the bhikṣu Ghoṣila.'"
At that time, the women sent Rāhula away and brought their sons and daughters before Ānanda.
As the children cried, Ānanda said,
"Take these children away."
Then the women said, "We cannot take the young child away, even at the request of the venerable Bhikṣu Gośṛṅga.
Ānanda, with a heart of compassion, immediately spoke:
"Uttara, what is your situation?
Uttara then related the circumstances in detail, and Ānanda said, "Go!
"...down to not committing even a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Vaiśālī.
Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
There were bhikṣus by the side of the Vālukā River who practiced the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), became weary of their bodies, and committed suicide.
Is this an offense? The Buddha said:
“Before the precept was first established, there was no offense. [The questioner asked:
“If one perceives a human being as a human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“An *pārājika*. If one suspects it is a human, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“Thullaccaya. “If one perceives a human being as a non-human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“A *sthūlātyaya*. If one perceives a non-human being as a human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“Thullaccaya. “If one suspects it is a non-human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“Thullaccaya. “Venerable Sir,
if one kills a male life while perceiving him as female, is this an offense?”
The Buddha said:
"It is a pārājika offense.
[He asked: "Venerable Sir!"
"If one kills a woman while perceiving her as a man, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha said,
"It is a *pārājika*."
“If one perceives her as a woman and takes her life, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha said,
“It is a *pārājika*.”
“Venerable Sir! If one forms the perception of this being as a man and takes his life, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. "If one seeks out a person carrying a knife, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
"If one takes a life, one commits an offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to a donor's household to inquire after a sick person.
The donor’s wife was of upright and beautiful countenance; having seen her, the bhikṣu became bound by lustful desire and said to her:
"You should do such-and-such a thing with me. His wife said,
"Venerable Sir!..."
"Do not speak such words; my husband is still alive, and I do not wish to commit such an evil deed.
The bhikṣu then praised the happiness of death to her husband, and the husband died immediately. Being in doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to visit a lay donor who was ill.
The donor’s wife was beautiful; having seen her, the bhikṣu became bound by lustful desire and said to her:
"Let us do such a thing together.
His wife said, "While my husband is still alive, I do not wish to do such a thing."
The bhikṣu then gave medicine to the husband to cause his death; being filled with doubt, the Buddha asked him, "With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"Because of the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"it is a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to visit a lay donor who was ill.
The donor’s wife was beautiful; having seen her, the bhikṣu became bound by lustful desire and said to her, “Do such-and-such a thing with me.”
His wife said, "My husband is still alive; I do not wish to do such a thing.
The bhikṣu then gave his husband an emetic and purgative to end his life. Being in doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"With the intent to kill."
The Buddha said,
"It is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to inquire after a donor who was ill.
The donor’s wife was beautiful; having seen her, a bhikṣu became bound by lustful desire and said to her, “Do such-and-such a thing with me.
His wife replied:
"My husband is still alive; I do not wish to do such a thing.
The bhikṣu then gave her unsuitable food that caused her death. Feeling doubt, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you act?"
He replied, "With a murderous intent.
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to visit a lay donor who was ill.
The donor’s wife was beautiful; having seen her, the bhikṣu became bound by lustful desire and said to her:
"Perform such an act with me. His wife said,
"While my husband is still alive, I do not wish to perform such an act."
The bhikṣu then gave her husband non-medicinal substances to end his life; being doubtful, the Buddha asked him, "With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said,
"This constitutes a *pārājika* offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who went to inquire after a donor who was ill.
The bhikṣu’s appearance was handsome and upright; when his wife saw him, her mind became bound by desire for the bhikṣu, and she said to him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"You may do such a thing with me.
The bhikṣu replied, "Sister!"
"Do not speak such words; it is improper for me.
While your husband is still alive, how could you commit such an evil deed?
The wife then spoke as follows:
"While my husband is still alive, I may not live in harmony with you.
She then gave her husband medicine to end his life.
Once he had died, she spoke to the bhikṣu, saying:
"My husband has already died; you may do such things with me.
The bhikṣu said, "Sister!..."
"Do not speak such words; it is not appropriate for me.
The wife replied, "It was for your sake that I took my husband's life."
"Why did you not do such a thing?
When the bhikṣu heard this, doubt arose within him, and he reported it to the Buddha. The Buddha asked him, "With what intention did you act?"
He then related the circumstances in detail, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
Medicines for inducing vomiting or purging are not things that should be eaten; the same applies to non-medicinal substances."

At that time, there was a woman whose husband was away on a journey. Having conceived by another man, she went to a bhikṣu whom her family habitually supported and said to him, "My husband is not here, and I have conceived by another; give me medicine to cause an abortion."
The bhikṣu then recited a spell over the food and gave it to her to eat, whereby she caused an abortion.
The bhikṣu felt doubt, and the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a woman whose husband was away on a journey; having conceived by another man, she went to the bhikṣu whom her family habitually supported and said to him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
“My husband is away on a journey, and I have conceived by another man; give me medicine to cause an abortion.
The bhikṣu then recited a spell over the medicine and gave it to her so that the fetus would fall.
The bhikṣu felt doubt, and the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind?
He replied, "With the intent to kill."
The Buddha said: “It is a pārājika.
To consecrate fine medicinal powders, to consecrate flower garlands, to consecrate incense and clothing, and likewise to consecrate a fetus—all such acts constitute a pārājika.”
At that time, there was a woman whose husband was away on a journey; having conceived through another man, she went to the bhikṣuṇī whom she had previously supported and said, "Auntie!..."
"My husband is away on a journey; I have conceived by another man, so I gave myself medicine to cause an abortion.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Sister!..."
"I do not know medicine; come here and I will press your abdomen for you.
He then pressed it for her, causing the fetus to fall.
Being suspicious, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind?
He replied, "With the intent to kill."
The Buddha said, "It is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a woman whose husband was away on a journey; having conceived through another man, she went to the bhikṣuṇī whom she had previously supported and said:
“Āyuṣmatī! My husband is away on a journey; I have conceived by another man, so give me medicine to cause an abortion.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"I do not know medicine; come, I shall bite it for you.
He then bit the fetus where it was located, causing it to fall. The Buddha asked, "Was there doubt? [The monk replied: "Yes. The Buddha said: [This is an offense].
"With what state of mind? He replied,
"With a murderous intent."
The Buddha said, "It is a *pārājika* offense.
At that time, there was a woman whose husband was away on a journey; having conceived by another man, she went to where a bhikṣu whom she regularly supported was staying and said to him:
"Venerable Sir!
My husband is away on a journey; I have conceived by another man, so give me medicine to cause an abortion.
The bhikṣu then gave her an excessive emetic and purgative, whereby the mother died and the child lived.
Regarding that doubt, the Buddha said:
"If the mother dies, there is no offense;
if she does not die while one employs means to cause an abortion, it is a *sthūlātyaya*."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who helped a sick person rise; the patient passed away.
Being in doubt, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"There is no offense."
"If one passes away while being assisted to sit, there is no offense; if one passes away while being bathed, there is no offense; if one passes away while taking medicine, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been long ill, and his caregiver, becoming weary and distressed, gave him food that was unsuitable for him, thereby causing him to end his life.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said,
"It is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time. His caregiver, becoming weary and disgusted with him, gave him what was not medicine and caused him to pass away.
Feeling doubtful, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:

"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been long ill and possessed many articles. Those who attended to him, coveting his property, gave him food that was unfit for consumption, causing him to pass away.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said,
"This is a pārājika offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been ill for a long time and possessed much wealth. Those attending him were greedy for profit, so they gave him non-medicinal substances, causing his death.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had an abscess under his armpit; another bhikṣu pressed upon it for him, whereupon the first one said:
"Do not press!"
"Do not press!
[The monk replied,] "But I pressed it intentionally and could not stop," whereupon he passed away.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with a murderous intent."
The Buddha said, “There is no offense; however,
one should not press down with such force.”
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose entire body was swollen. Another bhikṣu applied an irritant ointment to him, whereupon he said:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Do not apply it; I am suffering from a burning pain.
He replied, "Be patient for a moment!"
"He shall surely recover.
Although they applied it incessantly, he nevertheless passed away.
Being uncertain, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with a murderous intent."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense;
however, one should not apply it by force in such a manner."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who moved a sick bhikṣu from the shade into the sunlight; that patient passed away.
Being in doubt, the Buddha said:
"There is no offense."
"Moving from the sun to a shaded place is also not an offense.
If a sick person wishes to go from the shade to the sun, or from the sun to the shade, and the sick person passes away [during this movement], [there is no offense].
He was doubtful about supporting [the patient]. The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
If, while supporting a sick person out of or into a room, the patient passes away, he is doubtful. The Buddha said: [There is no offense.]
"There is no offense.

If a sick person wishes to go out of the house and is supported out, or wishes to enter the house and is supported in, and passes away while being supported, there is no offense for those who support him."
If a patient dies while being assisted to the place for defecation, or if they die upon being assisted back to the dwelling, there is no offense in any case.
If a patient dies while being assisted to the place for urination, or if they die upon returning to the dwelling, there is no offense in any case.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu suffering from malaria. Another bhikṣu pressed down heavily upon him, whereupon the sick man said:
"Do not press! Do not press!"
He pressed him repeatedly until he passed away.
Suspecting [the monk's intent], the Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this?"
He replied, “It was not with a murderous intent.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense;
however, one should not exert such force.
At that time, there was a sick bhikṣu, and another bhikṣu went to inquire after him; he pushed aside the robe to look at his face and asked:
“Venerable sir, has your illness slightly improved?
He replied, “Do not disturb me!”
"Do not shake it!
Yet he shook it incessantly and consequently passed away.
Feeling doubt, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with a murderous intent."
The Buddha said, "There is no offense. However,
one should not forcibly brush it away."
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, through a stratagem, dispatched one person to take another's life; that person then went and took the life.
The [instigator] felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
"In all cases, this is a pārājika offense."

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, through various means, dispatched one person to take another's life. Among them was one who, harboring doubt, did not prevent him; that person then went and took the life.
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"It is a *pārājika* offense for all of them.

At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, through various means, conspired together to take another's life. Among them was one person who felt doubt and immediately tried to stop them, yet they proceeded to go and take the life anyway.
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"If he restrained him, it is a *sthūlātyaya*; if he did not restrain him, it is a *pārājika*.
At that time, there was a thief who stole a bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, needle case, and sitting mat. The bhikṣu immediately seized the thief and suppressed him, whereupon the thief passed away.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"And you should not suppress or punish him.

At that time, there was a thief who stole a bhikṣu’s robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case. When the bhikṣu caught the thief, he placed him inside an underground cellar, whereupon the thief subsequently passed away.
He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"And it should not be so. At that time, there was an evil bhikṣu who stole the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case of another bhikṣu. The other bhikṣus said:
"This evil bhikṣu has stolen the robes, bowl, sitting mat, and needle case of a bhikṣu; we should seize him and speak the Dharma to him."
He immediately seized him and beat him until his hands were broken, after which he died.
Being filled with doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you do this?"
He replied, “It was not with an intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense [for the former], but to strike one who has received the full ordination is a *pāyattika* offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who disputed with a layperson; the bhikṣu then went to the authorities and spoke [on the matter].
At that time, there was a high minister who ordered him to be seized, bound, and imprisoned; consequently, he died in prison.
The minister felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied, "Not with the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense. However, to speak of another person [as having committed an offense] constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who killed a macaque; he suspected that he had committed a *pārājika* offense by taking human life.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
To take the life of an animal constitutes a pāyattika."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had been disputing with that other bhikṣu.
When the latter became ill, this bhikṣu went to inquire after his health.
Other bhikṣus observed him and thought: "This bhikṣu previously harbored a grudge against the sick bhikṣu; his coming now to inquire must surely have some ulterior motive."
At that time, this bhikṣu gave what was not medicine to the sick person, and the person passed away.
Feeling doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"Parājika. At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a dispute with another bhikṣu; that bhikṣu went among the people and fell ill, whereupon this bhikṣu said:
"Even though you have gone among the people, you still cannot escape [the offense]."
He immediately went to pay his respects.
Other bhikṣus observed him and thought: "This bhikṣu previously had a grudge against this sick bhikṣu; his coming now to pay his respects must surely have some ulterior motive."
This bhikṣu gave what was not medicine to the sick person, and the person passed away.
Feeling doubt, the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you act?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
“A *pārājika*. It is the same for the two kinds of non-food.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having dressed and taken her bowl in the morning, went to the house of a layperson. A young child was sleeping inside a mortar-house; Thullanandā went and touched the pestle of a foot-operated mortar, and the pestle fell upon the child, who immediately passed away.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"One must not touch another's pestle and mortar.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having dressed in the morning and taken her bowl, went to the home of a layperson; there was a small child sleeping beside a pestle and mortar.
Thullanandā touched another’s mortar and pestle; as the mortar rolled, it crushed a small child to death.
Feeling doubt, the Buddha asked her, “With what intention did you do this?”
He replied, "Not with the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense;
however, one should not touch another's mortar and pestle.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, having dressed in the morning and taken her bowl, went to the home of a layperson. On the bed there was a small child sleeping; Thullanandā sat down without looking, whereupon the female donor said:
“Sister! Do not sit upon the child!
She did not hear him and sat down anyway; the child died immediately.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"Furthermore, one should not sit upon a seat in the house of a layperson without first inspecting it.

At that time, there was a donor in Śrāvastī who invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for a meal the following day. That very night, he prepared various kinds of abundant and delicious food and drink, and went in the morning to inform them that the time had arrived.
The World-Honored One, having donned his robes and taken up his alms bowl, went together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus to the house of a donor and sat upon the prepared seat.
It is the constant rule of all Buddhas not to accept food or drink until the assembly has gathered.
At that time, there was a monk who had entered the order late in life; having ordained his son, he went to the home of another layperson during the morning meal.
The monks asked the boy, "Where has your father gone?"
He then ordered the World-Honored One to wait and not eat. He replied,
“I do not know.”
The bhikṣu said, "Go and search for it.
He searched and found it, and the son said to his father:
“Where have you come from?
By waiting for your father, you have caused the Buddha and the Sangha to be unable to receive their meal.
His father, filled with rage, seized his son; the son released himself and pushed his father down until he fell to the ground and died instantly.
He was doubtful, so the Buddha asked him,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"One should not push one's father.
At that time, there was a mother who seized a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu freed himself and pushed her away, whereupon she fell to the ground and died.
He was filled with doubt, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with the intent to kill."
The Buddha said, “There is no offense. However,
one should not push or shove one’s mother.”
At that time, there was a father who seized a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu freed himself and pushed him away, causing the father to fall to the ground and die immediately.
The bhikṣu was filled with doubt, so the Buddha asked him:
"With what state of mind did you act?"
He replied, "Not with the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense;
however, one should not push him away.
It is the same when a brother seizes a bhikṣu, a sister seizes a bhikṣu, or when both together seize a bhikṣu.”
At that time, there were two elder sisters who said to their younger sister,
"Why do you not ask the bhikṣu for food and clothing? She replied:
“Since one who has gone forth does not wish to seek anything from others,
if you show me the place where the bhikṣu is, I shall seek it for you.
He then showed him the place.
He said to the bhikṣu, "Why do you not give my wife food and clothing?
He then stepped forward and seized the bhikṣu; the bhikṣu pushed him away to free himself, and he fell to the ground and died.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"One should not push them away.
At that time, there were men and women who seized a bhikṣu; the bhikṣu pushed them away to free himself, and they fell to the ground and died.
Being in doubt, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with a murderous intent."
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense;
however, one should not push him."
At that time, not far from the bhikṣuṇī monastery, there was a man whose hands and feet had been severed.
A bhikṣuṇī was walking nearby carrying *sūvīra* juice; having seen him, she said: "Auntie!..."
"Give me some drink.
The bhikṣuṇī gave it to him immediately; he drank it and died.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with a murderous intent."
The Buddha said,
"There is no offense.
At that time, not far from the bhikṣuṇī monastery, there was a person whose hands and feet had been severed.
A bhikṣuṇī was carrying water and walking not far from him; having seen her, he said: "Auntie!
Give me some water to drink."
He then gave it to him to drink, and he died immediately.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked:
"With what intention did you do this?"
He replied, "Not with a murderous intent.
The Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
At that time, not far from the bhikṣuṇī monastery, there was a person whose hands and feet had been severed.
A bhikṣuṇī was walking along, carrying *sūvīra* (sour gruel), not far from him. Having seen her, he spoke to her:
“Sister! I must wash my wound with *suvīra* [sour gruel] so that it may perhaps recover slightly.
She gave it to him to wash; once he had washed it, he died.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"One should not provide her with water for washing;
the same applies to holding water for her to wash herself.
At that time, not far from the bhikṣuṇī monastery, there was a person whose hands and feet had been severed.
There was a bhikṣuṇī who, carrying some *sūvīra*, was walking not far from him. The bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If I wash his wound with this *sūvīra*, it might cause him to die prematurely."
He immediately washed it for him, and the man died.
The Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this?"
He replied, "With the intent to kill.
The Buddha said:
“A *pārājika*. It is likewise when one holds water and gives it for washing.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus who, together with the group of six bhikṣus, were on Vulture Peak Mountain breaking pieces of wood to cover their dwellings.
There was a bhikkhu of the group of six who took a pointed wooden splinter and threw it directly at a person; the wood entered his body and passed through, and the man died immediately.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked him:
"With what intention did you do this?"
He replied, “It was not with a murderous intent.
The Buddha said:
"There is no offense.
However, one should not throw a wooden beam directly at a person; it should be thrown crosswise.
At that time, a bhikṣu engaged in construction work for a new dwelling; by mistake he dropped a stone, which fell upon another bhikṣu, who died immediately.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"If a brick, or a wooden beam, a rafter, a cross-beam, a ridgepole, or any other kind of timber falls, it is likewise.

At that time, there was a cowherd tending cattle on Vulture Peak Mountain; one of the group of six bhikṣus struck the cow's horn with a stone, and the stone flew up and fell upon the cowherd, who died instantly.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
"If it was not with the intent to kill," the Buddha said,
"there is no offense."
"Striking an animal that cannot undergo transformation constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu on Vulture Peak Mountain who caused a rock to collapse and fall, striking a traveler on the road and killing him.
Suspecting him, the Buddha asked,
"With what intention did you do this? He replied:
“I did not do so with the intent to kill.
The Buddha said,
“There is no offense.”
"One should not cause the rocks to collapse.
If there is a reason one wishes to take a rock, one should tell people to move away.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to abandon the precepts and engage in inferior activities; he had this thought:
"I ought not to have committed such an evil deed after having gone forth in the Buddha’s Dharma.
He then went to the summit of Mount Mātaṅga, threw himself down upon the bamboo-worker, and the bhikṣu survived while that man died.
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"If that person dies, there is no offense; however, if one employs the means to attempt suicide, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who wished to abandon the path and engage in lowly occupations, and he thought to himself:
"I have gone forth in the Buddha's Dharma; I ought not to commit such an evil deed.
He went to the summit of Mount Upavāhana and threw himself down upon the man who was cutting bamboo; that man died, while the bhikṣu survived.
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"If that person has died, there is no offense; however, if one employs the means to attempt suicide, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, carrying *suvīra* juice, was walking not far from a cemetery when a person with a pointed stake through his head spoke to him.
"Give me this drink. The bhikṣu gave it to him, and having drunk it, he died.
Being doubtful, the Buddha asked:
"With what state of mind did you do this? He replied,
"Not with the intent to kill."
The Buddha said, “There is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, carrying water, walked not far from a cemetery. A person with a pointed stake on his head said:
"Give me water to drink.
He gave it to him, and having drunk it, he died immediately.
Being doubtful, the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.
At that time, there was a mad bhikṣu who, after killing a person, regained his senses; he felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
“There is no offense.”
"If the mind is deranged or one is afflicted by pain, there is no offense in any case.
At that time, the World-Honored One was in Vaiśālī.
Then Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!

If monks on the banks of the Vaggumudā River, for the sake of food, falsely and without basis claim before laypeople that they have attained superhuman states (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), does this constitute an offense?"
The Buddha said, "Since the precept had not yet been established at that time, there was no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, out of overweening pride, made a self-assertion; later, through diligent and unremitting effort, he realized the superior, exalted Dharma.
He thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One has established a precept for the bhikṣus: 'If a bhikṣu, not knowing it himself, claims to have attained the state of a superior person, saying, "I know this; I see this," [he commits an offense]. "
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, for the sake of seeking purification, one says:
"I neither knew nor saw, yet I said that I knew and saw; this was a false and deceptive lie."
"A bhikṣu who commits a pārājika offense is not to live in communion.
Since I falsely claimed realization out of overweening pride, but later applied myself with diligence and unwearied effort until I attained the superior and sublime Dharma, what should I do now?"
He then related the matter in detail to a bhikṣu who was in agreement with him, saying:
"Excellent, Elder! Please inform the World-Honored One on my behalf."
"We shall practice according to the instructions taught by the World-Honored One.
The bhikṣus went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and reported the matter in detail to the World-Honored One.

At that time, the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus and preached the Dharma accordingly, using countless skillful means to praise the head-dhuta practices, dignified conduct, fewness of desires, contentment, and delight in renunciation. He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those with overweening pride are not guilty of an offense."
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha, “Venerable Sir!
If one claims to have attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*) before an animal that lacks the power of transformation (*vikurvaṇa*), does this constitute an offense?”
The Buddha said, "It is a duṣkṛta.
[The monk asked: "Venerable Sir!"
“If one perceives a human being as a human being,
is this an offense? The Buddha said, “It is a *pārājika*.”
“If one suspects it, is this an offense?
The Buddha said,
“It is a sthūlātyaya.”
“If one perceives a human being as a non-human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said,
“It is a sthūlātyaya.”
"If one perceives a non-human being as a human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said,
"It is a sthūlātyaya."
“If one suspects it is a non-human being, is this an offense?
The Buddha said,
“It is a sthūlātyaya.”
“Venerable Sir! If one perceives a man as a woman, does this constitute an offense?
The Buddha said:
"Pārājika. If one perceives a woman as a man, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
“Pārājika. [The questioner asked:
“If one perceives this woman as being that other woman, is this an offense?
The Buddha said:
"If one speaks clearly, it is a *pārājika*;
if one does not speak clearly, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
"If one perceives another man before this man, is there an offense?"
The Buddha said:
"If one speaks and makes it clear, it is a pārājika offense;
if one speaks but does not make it clear, it is a sthūlātyaya offense."
If one causes [the victim] to understand clearly through hand gestures, messengers, writing, or signs, it is a pārājika offense.
If one does not cause them to understand clearly, it is a thullaccaya offense.

“Venerable Sir! If one claims to have attained the state of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma) before those capable of transformation—such as devas, nāgas, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, pretas, or animals—is this an offense?”
The Buddha said:
"If one speaks and makes it clear, it is a sthūlātyaya;
if one does not make it clear, it is a duṣkṛta."
If one causes [another] to understand through hand gestures, written messages, or signs, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
If they do not understand, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, in the presence of others, claimed for himself the attainment of superhuman states (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*).
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"If one speaks clearly and distinctly, it is a pārājika offense;
if one does not speak clearly and distinctly, it is a sthūlātyaya offense."
"To speak toward this when one intends to speak toward that constitutes a *pārājika* offense in every case.
At that time, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the kingdom of Kośala.
At that time, a brahmin named Naimittika, who was full of faith and devotion, saw him and said,
"The Great Virtuous Arhat has arrived! The bhikṣu asked:
"What do you say? he asked. He replied, "Venerable sir, you should accept food, clothing, medicine, and all other necessary requisites."
The bhikṣu said, "There is such a principle.
The bhikṣu was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"There is no offense.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who claimed for himself that he had attained the faculties (indriya), powers (bala), factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), mindfulness (smṛti), meditative concentrations (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), samādhis, and right attainments (samāpatti). Another bhikṣu doubted this, and the Buddha said: "Pārājika."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who explained to others the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, bases of power, meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and right attainments, yet he did not claim to have attained them himself.
The bhikṣus were doubtful; the Buddha said, "There is no offense.
At that time, a bhikṣu had a donor (dānapati), and the bhikṣu spoke to him, saying:
"The one who constantly preaches the Dharma for you is an Arhat.
The donor then asked, "What does the Venerable One preach?"
He then remained silent.
The bhikṣu was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"It was not clear; it is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, a bhikṣu had a donor who said to him,
"Those who frequently come to your house are arhats. The donor then asked:
"Venerable sir, what have you said?
He remained silent.
The bhikṣus were doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"If it is not clear, it is a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
At that time, a bhikṣu had a donor who said to him:
"Those who sit frequently upon your seat are arhats."
He then asked, "Venerable sir, what did you say?
but he remained silent.
A bhikṣu was doubtful; the Buddha said:
"If it is not clear, it is a sthūlātyaya.
At that time, a bhikṣu had a donor (dānapati), and the bhikṣu said to him:
"The one who has received food from you many times is an Arhat.
The donor asked, "Venerable Sir, what do you mean by this?"
He remained silent. Being doubtful, the Buddha said:
"If it was not clear, it is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, a donor said to a bhikṣu whom he regularly supported,
"If you, Venerable One, are an arhat, please take off your saṃghāṭī.
The bhikṣu immediately took it off, displaying the sign but remaining silent.
Regarding doubt, the Buddha said:
"It is a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, there was a donor who spoke to a bhikṣu whom he regularly supported, saying:
“If the Venerable One is an Arhat, he shall put on the saṃghāṭī.
The bhikṣu immediately put it on, displaying his state without speaking.
Being in doubt, the Buddha said:
“Thullaccaya. At that time, a donor said to a bhikkhu whom he regularly supported:
“Venerable sir, if you are an arahant, you may sit upon this corded bed.”
He then sat down, manifesting his intent without speaking.
Being in doubt, the Buddha said:
"It is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, a donor said to a bhikṣu whom he regularly supported,
"Venerable sir, if you are an arhat, please stand up.
He immediately stood up, manifesting the sign without speaking.
Regarding doubt, the Buddha said:
"It is a *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, there was a donor who asked a bhikṣu whom he regularly supported:
"Venerable sir, if you are an Arhat, please go up to the upper story of the house.
He immediately went up, manifesting his state without speaking.
[The monks] were doubtful, so the Buddha said:
“Thullaccaya. At that time, a donor said to a bhikkhu whom he regularly supported:
“Venerable sir, if you are an Arhat, you may descend.”
The bhikṣu immediately descended, manifested his physical form, but remained silent.
Being doubtful, the Buddha said:
"It is a sthūlātyaya."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had a donor.
The bhikṣu said to him, "The one who frequently preaches the Dharma for you is a śrāvaka disciple of the Buddha. The donor asked:
“Venerable sir, what have you said?
He remained silent.
Regarding doubt, the Buddha said:
"If it is not clear, it is a sthūlātyaya.
Entering the house of a donor repeatedly, whether to accept a seat or to accept food, is likewise."
At that time, a donor said to a bhikṣu whom he regularly supported, "If you, Venerable One, are a disciple of the Buddha and a śrāvaka, then remove your saṃghāṭī.
He immediately removed it; [the donor] displayed his signs but did not speak.
Regarding this doubt, the Buddha said:
"It is a *sthūlātyaya*.
It is the same whether one is wearing the *saṃghāṭī*, sitting, rising, ascending to an upper chamber, or descending from it."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"It is through the causal conditions of karmic retribution that one attains the supernormal powers (ṛddhi). The bhikṣus said:
“Maudgalyāyana!
You said: ‘One attains supernormal powers through the causal conditions of karmic retribution.’”
"Such a thing is impossible.
To falsely claim to have attained the state of a superior person (uttaramanuṣyadharma) constitutes a pārājika offense;
he is no longer a bhikṣu. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
“Because of the causal conditions of this karmic retribution, one attains the supernormal power of the divine feet;
Maudgalyāyana has committed no offense. Then Maudgalyāyana told the bhikṣus:
“By the causal conditions of karmic retribution, one attains the divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of others' minds, and the divine eye.”
The bhikṣus said: "Maudgalyāyana! You say:..."
"It is impossible that one could obtain the divine ear or even the divine eye through the causal conditions of karmic retribution.
To falsely claim to have attained the qualities of a superior person (uttara-manuṣya-dharma) constitutes a pārājika offense; such a person is no longer a bhikṣu."
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"There are karmic causes and conditions through which one attains the divine ear and even the divine eye; Maudgalyāyana has committed no offense."
Then Maudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus: "Venerable elders!
There are such beings passing through the void that one hears the sound of their skeletal bones clashing against one another."
The bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana,
"Venerable sir!
You have said:..."
"It is impossible that there could be such beings passing through the air, from whose bodies the sound of bones clashing could be heard.
To falsely claim to have attained the state of a superior person (uttarimanussa-dhamma) is a *pārājika* offense; he is no longer a bhikṣu.
The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "There are such beings; Maudgalyāyana has committed no offense.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:
"I see sentient beings whose entire bodies have needles for hair; from their own bodies, they repeatedly emerge and re-enter, undergoing immeasurable suffering and wailing with loud cries."
Then the bhikṣus said to Maudgalyāyana:

At that time, Maudgalyāyana addressed the bhikṣus:

he is no longer a bhikṣu. The bhikṣus reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

Maudgalyāyana is without offense.

The bhikṣus said: "Maudgalyāyana!
There is such a pond as you have described."
"That is impossible.
Then, by means of his supernormal power, Mahāmaudgalyāyana went to that place and took the flowers; returning to the monastery, he placed them inside the building and called to the bhikṣus, saying:

"Maudgalyāyana has committed no offense. Then Maudgalyāyana told the bhikṣus:

Being doubtful, the Buddha said:
"If one hears [a secret] and speaks it to another without returning with the words [to inform the original speaker], it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
It is the same for a woman who grinds incense.
At that time, there was a householder who went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus:
"Venerable sir, please speak for me.
The bhikṣus said, "Householder, what do you wish to say?"
He said, "Speak for me to such-and-such a householder, saying, 'Give me your daughter to be my wife. The bhikṣu said:
“Householder! We shall speak for you.
Thereupon, they appointed one bhikṣu to perform the formal act of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a motion followed by one proclamation), sending him to that householder’s place to say:
"Householder! I shall speak to you concerning the words of the Saṃgha. He replied:
"Venerable Saṃgha, what command have you seen?
The bhikṣu said: "The community of monks says:"
"Give your daughter to such-and-such a layman to be his wife. He replied,
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I shall give it when I have received the Sangha's command.
At that time, the messenger bhikṣu returned to the saṃghārāma and informed the Sangha; the Sangha then immediately notified the lay devotee so that he would know.
The bhikṣu was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"Every *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. At that time,
there was a donor who went to the monastery and said to the bhikṣus,
"Venerable Saṃgha, please speak for me."
The bhikṣu asked:
"Householder, what do you wish to say? He replied:
"Speak for me to the householder so-and-so, saying: 'Take your daughter to be my wife.
The bhikṣu said: "I shall speak for you."
He immediately appointed one bhikṣu to perform the formal motion (jñapti-dvitīya-karman) and sent him to that householder’s place, saying: “Householder!
I shall speak the words of the Saṃgha to you.”
The householder said, "Venerable Sir,
what has the Saṃgha seen that it commands?"
The bhikṣu said: "The Saṃgha has told you:
'Give your daughter to such-and-such a layman to be his wife.'"
He replied, "Venerable sir! I shall give it in accordance with the Sangha's command."
The messenger thought to himself:
"If I were now to return and inform the Saṃgha, the credit for this would not belong to me.
He then went directly to speak with that householder. Being in doubt, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"If the community of monks commits a *sthūlātyaya*, it causes the bhikṣu-saṃgha to incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
At that time, there was a donor who went to where a regularly supported bhikṣu was staying and said to him:
"Speak for me to such-and-such a layman, saying: 'Give your daughter to me to be my wife.'"
The bhikṣu said: "Householder, I shall speak for you."
The bhikṣu then went to that householder’s place and said:
“You may give your daughter to that certain householder to be his wife.
The householder replied:
"I have already given my daughter to another. Or if he says:
"Another has already taken her away."
If one says, "He has died," or if one says:
"The thieves stole it.
If one says, "There is none."
The bhikṣu returned to the layperson’s place and spoke these words:
“It is all *sthūlātyaya*.
At that time, there was a donor who said to the bhikṣu whom he regularly supported:
"Speak for me to the householder so-and-so, saying: 'You may give your daughter to me to be my wife.
The bhikṣu said: "I shall speak for you."
The bhikṣu then went to that householder and said,
"You may give your daughter to that certain householder to be his wife.
The householder replied:

"My daughter has leprosy; or it is said she has an ulcer, or white leprosy, or a wasting disease, or madness, or hemorrhoids, or a constant discharge of blood, or a chronic heat in the soles of her feet."
After the bhikṣu had returned and spoken thus to the householder, he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"In all such cases, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
At that time, there was a householder who, having quarreled with his wife, drove her out; he then went to the bhikṣu whom he regularly supported and spoke to him, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
He who fought with me and was driven out—I now wish to reconcile and perform confession with him.
The bhikṣu then brought about their reconciliation and had him perform confession. [The other bhikṣu] felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
"Because it was for the sake of repentance, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a woman who, having quarreled with her husband, went out and approached a bhikṣu whom she had previously supported, saying:
"I have quarreled with my husband and come outside; I now wish to repent."
The bhikṣu then went and brought about reconciliation so that she would repent; he was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"For the sake of repentance, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a woman who quarreled with her husband, saying:
"If you do not require me as your wife, you should say so.
The husband said,
"I do not require you as my wife."
She immediately drove him out.
She went to where the bhikṣu she usually made offerings to was staying and said to him:
"I had a quarrel with my husband; I said this to my husband:"
"If you do not require me as your wife, you should say so.
The husband said,
"I do not require you."
"He immediately drove me out.
Now I wish to perform repentance.
The bhikṣus then brought them together to perform the repentance. Being in doubt, they asked the Buddha, who said:
"Because it was for the sake of repentance, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a householder who took a courtesan as his wife. A man who had previously been in frequent contact with this woman saw him and said:
"I wish to do such-and-such a thing with you."
Others said to him, "She is no longer a courtesan; she has now become the wife of a certain layman.
That man then forcibly took her and committed sexual intercourse with her.
Upon hearing this, the husband immediately drove her out. She then went to the bhikṣu whom she had long supported and said to him:
"Venerable Sir!

Since I became your wife as a householder, I have never committed an offense with another man; only this thief has forcibly dragged me away and violated me. I now wish to confess this together with my husband."
The bhikṣu then went and brought about reconciliation so that she would repent together with her husband; he was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"Because it was for the sake of repentance, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a lay devotee who provided for the needs of a courtesan and went to the place where a bhikṣu he regularly supported was staying, saying:
"Please tell that courtesan for me: 'Wait for me at such-and-such a place. The bhikṣu said: "So be it."
He immediately went to the courtesan’s place and said,
“A certain householder told you to wait for him at such-and-such a location.
The bhikṣu felt doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"First, there was no offense because they were in harmony;
however, acting as a messenger for a layperson constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.
At that time, there was a householder who had betrothed a young girl; since he did not take her as his wife, nor did he permit her to marry anyone else.
Then the woman said to the bhikṣu whom she regularly supported,
"Venerable Sir,
please speak to a certain householder on my behalf:"
"My parents wish to take you away and give me to another man.
You must either come to meet me or release me. The bhikṣu said:
"So be it. That bhikṣu then went to the householder's place and said:
"A certain young girl says:..."
‘My parents wish to take you away to give you to another; you should now either go to meet them or let them go.
He was doubtful, so the Buddha said:
‘Since he has already made a vow previously, there is no offense.’”
"To act as a messenger for a layperson constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
At that time, there was a householder who had betrothed a young girl; he neither welcomed a wife for her nor permitted her to marry anyone else.
The parents said, "We do not know who was told to have this young woman go to such-and-such a lay devotee; we would rather allow her to marry someone else.
At that time, a bhikṣu whom their family regularly supported became insane and spoke as follows:
"I shall speak for you.
The bhikṣu then went to that householder's place, seized him by the head, and said:
"You must either welcome such-and-such a young girl or release her."
Later, having regained his mind, he felt doubt. The Buddha said:
"One who is deranged, whose mind is disordered, and who is beset by intense pain and affliction commits no offense whatsoever.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in Rājagṛha.
Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!
The Venerable Trapusa was pure, yet the bhikṣu Maitrāyaṇīputra slandered him with baseless charges. Is this an offense?"
The Buddha said,
“Since the precept had not yet been established at that time, there is no offense.
[He asked,] “Venerable Sir!”
"If one slanders a pure bhikṣu with groundless charges, is this an offense?
The Buddha said,
"It is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu sitting under a tree with a woman. Another bhikṣu said to him, "You have committed the offense of sexual misconduct with a woman. He replied:
"I have committed no offense; I was merely sitting under a tree with him.
The slanderer felt doubt, and the Buddha said:
"Since you spoke the truth and did not intend to defame him, there is no offense."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had sexual intercourse with his former wife.
Another bhikṣu who resembled him was told by other bhikṣus:
"You have committed an offense with your former wife."
He said, "I have committed no offense.
It is because that [other] monk has committed an offense that those two bhikṣus resemble me."
He was doubtful about this, and the Buddha said:
"Since it was for the sake of the truth and not out of malice, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose patron was a courtesan; another bhikṣu said to him:
"You have committed an offense with a courtesan.
He replied, "She is my patron; I have not committed an offense."
He was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"Because it was for the sake of the truth and not out of malice, there is no offense.
It is the same if [the object] is a woman, a girl, a paṇḍaka, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, or a śrāmaṇerikā."
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who took hold of a novice monk (śrāmaṇera) and fondled him, making a sound.
Another bhikṣu said to him, "You have committed an offense against a śrāmaṇera. He replied:
“I did not commit an offense; I merely touched it with my hand.
He remained doubtful, so the Buddha said:
“Since you spoke the truth and did not slander [me], there is no offense.”
At that time, a bhikṣu took another bhikṣu’s waistband.
The latter said,
“You have stolen my belt.”
He said, "I did not steal; I took it out of a sense of intimacy.
He was doubtful, and the Buddha said:
"If one does not slander for the sake of speaking the truth, there is no offense.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, with groundless charges of *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, slandered another; being doubtful, he asked the Buddha, who said:
"It is a *pāyattika*."
6. Ekottarika Āgama on the Vinaya, Part One. Thus have I heard:
At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.

If a bhikṣu speaks words that merely resemble the text while obstructing the Dharma and the Vinaya, this bhikṣu causes many people to fail to obtain benefit and creates various karmic sufferings that destroy the True Dharma."

If a bhikṣu conforms to the words and phrases and does not violate the Dharma or the Vinaya, such a bhikṣu benefits many people, prevents them from performing deeds that lead to suffering, and causes the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
"Therefore, O bhikṣus, you should follow these words and phrases; do not add to or subtract from them so as to contravene the Dharma and the Vinaya. You should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it with joy, and they faithfully accepted and upheld it.
The Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣu speaks what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, or speaks the Dharma as not the Dharma, such a bhikṣu causes many people to fail to obtain benefit and performs deeds of manifold suffering that extinguish the True Dharma."

If there is a bhikṣu who declares what is not Dharma to be "not Dharma" and what is Dharma to be "Dharma," such a bhikṣu benefits many people, performs manifold wholesome deeds, and causes the True Dharma to endure for a long time. Therefore, you all should follow this teaching: declare what is not Dharma to be "not Dharma" and what is Dharma to be "Dharma"; you should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and rejoiced, believing, delighting in, and upholding it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Vinaya as being Vinaya, or speaks of what is Vinaya as not being Vinaya, he causes many people to fail to obtain benefit and creates manifold karmic suffering that extinguishes the True Dharma."

If a bhikṣu speaks of what is not Vinaya as "not Vinaya," and speaks of what is Vinaya as "Vinaya," he benefits many people, does not create karma of suffering, and causes the True Dharma to endure for a long time.
Therefore, you all should follow this instruction: "This is not the Vinaya" means it is not the Vinaya; "this is the Vinaya" means it is the Vinaya. You should train yourselves in this manner.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and rejoiced, believing, delighting in, and upholding it.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

“If a bhikṣu enforces what has not been prescribed and abandons what has been prescribed, he will in this way gradually cause the precepts to be ruined. He will cause many people to fail to obtain benefit and will create a multitude of karmic sufferings that extinguish the True Dharma.”

If a bhikṣu does not establish what has not been established, does not abolish what has been established, and thus gradually brings the precepts to fulfillment, benefiting many people so they do not perform painful deeds and causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time.

"Therefore, you should not establish what has not been established, nor should you abolish what has been established; you should train yourselves in accordance with the precepts as they have been laid down.
When the bhikṣus heard this, they rejoiced, and with faith and delight, they accepted and upheld it.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, because he perceives the faults of the multitude, he establishes a precept for the bhikṣus based on a single principle in order to gather and sustain the Saṃgha."
"For this single reason, the Tathāgata has established the precepts for the bhikṣus.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
This applies to every sentence until the end of the period during which the True Dharma remains.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The Tathāgata appears in the world for one purpose: to establish the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the bhikṣus, thereby bringing them into harmony with the Saṃgha."
"For this reason, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world and established the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the bhikṣus.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it with joy, and with faith and delight, they accepted and upheld it.
This applies to every sentence up until the long endurance of the True Dharma.

Likewise for the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment), the *niśraya-karman* (act of dependence), the *apratisaṃkramaṇīya-śrāmaṇeraka-karman* (act of prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople),

the *adarśana-utksepaṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not seeing an offense), the *apratikarmāraṇīya-karman* (act of suspension for not making amends), and the *akuśaladṛṣṭy-anutsarga-karman* (act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views).

Examining the regulations established by the Vinaya: there are rules for receiving dependence (*niśraya*), rules for the *brahmadaṇḍa* penalty, rules for formal accusation (*codanā*), rules for calling to mind (*smṛti*), rules for requesting permission (*śravaṇam anujñāpayati*), rules for self-accusation (*svavāda*), rules for obstructing the *ānuvartana*, rules for obstructing the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, and rules for obstructing the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*).
There are also rules for the precepts, rules for the recitation of the precepts, and rules for the *poṣadha*.
He established the formal procedure for the Poṣadha; he established the invitation (Pravāraṇā); he established the formal procedure for the invitation;

he established the *jñapti* formal procedure; he established the *jñapti-dvitīya* formal procedure; he established the *jñapti-caturtha* formal procedure; he established the granting of concealment (*parivāsa*);

he established the granting of the *mūlāpakarṣa*; he established the granting of the *manatta*; he established the granting of rehabilitation from offenses (*ābṛti-āpatti*); he established the four *pārājika* rules; he established...
The thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules, the two *aniyata* rules, the thirty *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules,
the ninety *pāyattika* rules, the four *pratideśanīya* rules, the *śaikṣaka* rules, and the seven methods for settling disputes—
each individual item is to be treated according to the *tarjanīya-karman*.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"The utterance of a single word constitutes the relinquishing of the precepts; one speaks thus:
'I renounce the Buddha.'"
"Having spoken these words, one has thereby abandoned the precepts.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it with joy, and with faith and delight, they accepted and upheld it.

"I renounce the Dharma; I renounce the Saṃgha; I renounce my preceptor; I renounce those who share a preceptor with me; I renounce my teacher; I renounce those who share a teacher with me; I renounce all bhikṣus of pure conduct; I renounce the precepts; I renounce the Vinaya; I renounce the matters of training. I am a white-robed layman; remember me as a park-keeper; remember me as an upāsaka; remember me as a śrāmaṇera; remember me as a follower of an external path or a disciple of an external path; remember that I do not follow the Dharma of the Śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākya. Each phrase is to be recited in this same manner.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two kinds of offenses:
the first is light, and the second is grave; these are the two kinds of offenses."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and rejoiced, believing, delighting in, and upholding it.
Furthermore, there are two matters:
first, that which is light yet remains [to be dealt with]; second, that for one who is light, a *karmavācanā* may be performed.
Furthermore, there are two matters: pārājika and saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Furthermore, there are two matters:
Pārājika and sthūlātyaya. Furthermore, there are two matters: pārājika and pāyattika.
Furthermore, there are two matters:
pārājika and pāyattika. Furthermore, there are two matters: [pārājika and] pratideśanīya.
Pārājika and duṣkṛta. Furthermore, there are two cases:
pārājika and dukkaṭa; from saṃghāvaśeṣa down to dukkaṭa, it is likewise.
The same applies from *sthūlātyaya* down to *durbhāṣita*.
The same applies from *pāyattika* down to *durbhāṣita*.
The same applies from *pratideśanīya* down to *durbhāṣita*.
The same applies to the *duṣkṛta* offense of evil speech.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"There are two views that those who have left the household life should not practice:"
To view what is not the Dharma as the Dharma, and to view the Dharma as not the Dharma;
furthermore, there are two views:
to say that the Vinaya is not the Vinaya, and to say that what is not the Vinaya is the Vinaya.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is not an offense as an offense, and viewing what is an offense as not an offense.
Furthermore, there are two views:
What is light is seen as heavy, and what is heavy is seen as light.
Furthermore, there are two views:
seeing the state with remainder as being without remainder, and seeing the state without remainder as being with remainder.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is coarse and evil as not coarse and evil, and viewing what is not coarse and evil as coarse and evil.
Again, there are two views:
The ancient rules are viewed as not being ancient rules, and what are not ancient rules are viewed as ancient rules.
Furthermore, there are two views:
that which is prescribed is viewed as not prescribed, and that which is not prescribed is viewed as prescribed.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what has been taught as not taught, and viewing what has not been taught as taught.
Furthermore, there are two views:
One perceives alcohol as non-alcohol, and perceives non-alcohol as alcohol.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
one perceives drinking as non-drinking, and perceives non-drinking as drinking.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is food as non-food, and viewing what is non-food as food.
Again, there are two views:
At that time, one perceives what is not the proper time as the proper time, and perceives what is not the proper time as the proper time.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
perceiving the pure as impure, and perceiving the impure as pure.
Furthermore, there are two views:
regarding what is grave as not grave, and regarding what is not grave as grave.
Furthermore, there are two views:
What is difficult to see is not difficult to criticize; what is not difficult to criticize is difficult to see.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of views:
seeing insects where there are none, and seeing no insects where there are insects.
Furthermore, there are two views:
the view that destroys [the object] but does not destroy [the subject], and the view that does not destroy [the object] but destroys [the subject].
Again, there are two views:
One views what is not a seed as a seed, and views what is a seed as not a seed.
Furthermore, there are two other views:
viewing what has already been understood as not yet understood, and viewing what has not yet been understood as already understood.
Furthermore, there are two views:
viewing what is worthy of intimacy as unworthy of intimacy, and viewing what is unworthy of intimacy as worthy of intimacy.
Again, there are two views:
There are those who see what is fearful as not fearful, and those who see what is not fearful as fearful.
Furthermore, there are two views:
seeing the path as not the path, and seeing what is not the path as the path.
Furthermore, there are two views:
