relinquishing the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha; relinquishing the upādhyāya, relinquishing those who share the same upādhyāya; relinquishing the ācārya, and relinquishing those who share the same ācārya—these are the seven. This applies even to the statement that one is no longer a śramaṇa or a son of the Śākya, and so forth.
For seven reasons, the Tathāgata appears in the world and establishes the precepts for the bhikṣus:

to gather the Saṅgha, to bring joy to the Saṅgha, to bring peace and happiness to the Saṅgha, to inspire faith in those who lack it, to increase the faith of those who already have it, to discipline those who are difficult to tame, and to provide peace and happiness to those who possess a sense of shame and remorse. These are the seven.
In this manner, there are seven sets of seven phrases; even up to "the True Dharma shall long endure," it is the same.
For these seven reasons, the Tathāgata appeared in the world and established the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the bhikṣus:
from "for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha," there are seven sets of seven phrases, even up to "the True Dharma shall long endure," it is the same.
This applies likewise up to the seven methods for settling disputes, with the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) serving as the paradigmatic case.

"There are eight illegal ways of obstructing the *poṣadha*: obstructing [the claim that] one has committed an unfounded breach of the precepts, or obstructing [the claim that] one has not committed it;..."
To refute [the views of] what has been done and what has not been done; to refute [the views of] what has been done and what has not been done regarding deportment;
to refute [the views of] what has been done and what has not been done regarding right livelihood—these constitute the eight.

There are eight ways in which the *poṣadha* (confession of precepts) may be lawfully obstructed; these are the opposites of the aforementioned points. There are eight qualities by which one should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs:

being fully observant of the two hundred and fifty precepts; being learned; having recited the Vinaya of both divisions; being skilled in speech and clearly understanding the meaning, phrases, and syllables; being of noble lineage—such as a kṣatriya, brāhmaṇa, or householder; being of handsome appearance; not having committed a grave offense despite having left the household life for the sake of the Buddha; and having twenty years of seniority or more. These are the eight.
There are eight things that must not be transgressed, as explained in the Bhikṣuṇī-khandhaka.
There are eight conditions under which a layperson’s bowl should be turned upside down (the *pātra-parivartana*):

reviling and slandering bhikṣus; causing their decline; acting without benefit to them; depriving them of a place of residence; inciting strife among bhikṣus; and disparaging the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha in the presence of bhikṣus. These are the eight.
There are eight things that cause laypeople to lose faith in a bhikṣu:

reviling and slandering laypeople; causing them loss and harm; acting without benefit to them; creating a lack of dwelling places for them; inciting strife and discord among laypeople; and disparaging the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha in the presence of laypeople. These are the eight.
If a bhikṣu possesses these eight qualities, a *karmavācanā* for the formal act of "prohibiting him from entering the homes of laypeople" should be performed against him, as described above.
There are eight qualities by which one should be appointed as a companion to serve as a messenger:

being able to listen, being able to speak, understanding it oneself and causing others to understand, being able to receive [the message], being able to retain it, not losing it, knowing what is good and bad, and explaining the meaning and intent; these are the eight.

At that time, the World-Honored One was at the side of the Gaggarā Pond in the city of Campā; on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the recitation of the precepts, he sat in the open air, surrounded by the community of monks before and behind him.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who charged another bhikṣu with an offense based on what he had seen, heard, or suspected.
While the charge was being made, that bhikṣu instead gave evasive answers and then gave rise to anger.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should interrogate that person with thorough scrutiny; he has no capacity for the Buddha-dharma and makes no progress therein.

It is like a farmer's field where seedlings and tares grow together; their stalks and leaves are so similar that they cannot be distinguished until they cause harm, and only when the grain matures do one realize the difference between them and the worthless weeds."
Once it is known that they are not grain, one weeds them out by their roots. Why?
For fear of harming the sprouts of goodness.

It is the same for a bhikṣu: if there is an evil bhikṣu whose coming, going, sitting, and rising, as well as his holding of robes and bowl, are indistinguishable from those of a virtuous bhikṣu, he does not even reveal his offense.
Once their offenses have been exposed, one will finally recognize the difference between the true bhikṣus and the tares and weeds among them.
Having recognized this difference, the community should act in harmony to perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) to remove them.
Why is this? For fear of obstructing virtuous bhikṣus.
It is like a farmer processing grain who winnows it against the wind; the good grain remains gathered, while the chaff and husks are blown away by the wind.
Why is this? For fear of defiling good grain.
In the same way, when evil bhikṣus come and go, enter and exit, they are not distinguished from virtuous bhikṣus, even to the point that their offenses are not exposed.
Once their offenses have been brought forth, one will then know that among the bhikṣus there are chaff, husks, and those who are corrupt and evil.
Having known this, the community should act in harmony to carry out their formal expulsion and removal.
For example, suppose there is a person who needs wood to make a well-railing; he leaves the city, takes a sharp axe in his hand, and goes into that forest, striking all the trees.
If they are solid, their sound is firm and real; if they are hollow, their sound is empty and rattling.
Yet that hollow tree—its roots, trunk, branches, and leaves—is no different from one that is solid and full.
It is only when struck that one knows it is empty within.

Once the internal emptiness is known, one immediately cuts and fells it, stripping away the branches and leaves first to remove the coarse exterior; thereafter, one planes and pares it until it is finely refined, with both the interior and exterior made pure, so as to fashion it into a well-railing.

Such evil bhikṣus, whether walking, coming, going, or entering and exiting, carry their robes and bowls with deportment no different from that of virtuous bhikṣus, even to the point of not revealing their offenses.

Once their offenses have been exposed, one will then recognize those among the śramaṇas who are defiled, like weeds, tares, or hollow trees; having recognized them, one should immediately act in unison to carry out their formal expulsion (pravāsanīya-karman). Why is this?
"Fearing that it might cause harm to virtuous bhikṣus," he spoke this verse:
"Living together, one knows their character and conduct: They are envious and prone to anger."
One who speaks kind words among people, yet commits unrighteous acts in private,
and employs skillful means to utter falsehoods— such a person the wise are able to perceive;
they should be cast out like weeds and tares, or like trees growing in mid-air.
One who calls himself a śramaṇa should be expelled from the void;
having already been expelled for practicing evil and what is contrary to the Dharma,
one should know that living together with those who are pure is what brings true illumination.
"Through harmony, one is expelled together; through harmony, one reaches the end of suffering.
Thus spoke the Buddha. Having heard this, the bhikṣus rejoiced, placed their faith in it with gladness, and received it for practice.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now explain to you eight kinds of evil horses and eight kinds of evil persons.
Listen attentively!
What are the eight?
There may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent that it should go, yet it instead bucks and stumbles and does not move;
or there may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent that it should go, yet it instead leans against both shafts and does not advance.

There may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent that it should go forward, yet it stumbles and falls to the ground; having injured its knees, it further breaks the axle and the shafts.
Or there may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent that it should go forward, yet it instead moves backward and does not advance.
Or there may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent that it should go forward, yet it instead gallops onto a wrong path, breaking its wheels and snapping its axle.

There may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent to make it go, yet it neither fears the driver nor the whip; through its stratagems, it bites the bit and butts forward, being impossible to restrain.
There may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent to make it go, yet it stands on its hind legs with its forefeet and spits foam.
There may be a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given with the intent to make it go, yet it either crouches down or lies prostrate.
These are the eight.
What are these eight kinds of evil persons?
There may be a bhikṣu who raises a charge against another for an offense seen, heard, or suspected, and that bhikṣu then says:
"I do not recall! I do not recall!
Just as a wicked horse, when given a bridle and a whip with the intent to make it go, instead bucks and stumbles and refuses to move, I say that this person is just like that.

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who points out a fault based on what he has seen, heard, or suspected, yet that bhikṣu neither admits to having committed an offense nor denies it, but remains silent. He is like a stubborn horse to which a bridle and whip have been given; though one wishes to make it go, it merely leans against the two shafts of the carriage and does not move forward. I say that such a person is just like this.
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who points out a fault—whether seen, heard, or suspected—in another, and that person says:
"Venerable sir, you yourself have committed this same offense; how can you remove the offenses of others?"

"It is just as when one gives a bridle and whip to a wicked horse, intending for it to go forward, yet it instead stumbles and falls to the ground, injuring its knees and breaking its axle-pole; I say that such a person is exactly like this."
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who points out a fault—whether seen, heard, or suspected—to another bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu says:
"Venerable sir, you are yourself deluded!
You still require instruction from others, yet you wish to instruct me."
"It is just as when a wicked horse is given a bridle and a whip with the intent to make it go forward, yet it instead walks backward; I say that such a person is also like this.

Or, there may be a bhikṣu who brings up a charge against another regarding what was seen, heard, or suspected, and the other person instead speaks of other matters in response and gives rise to anger; just as when a wicked horse is given a bridle and a whip with the intent to make it go forward, yet it gallops onto a wrong path, breaking the axle and shattering the wheels—I say that such a person is also like this."

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who brings up the charges of another bhikṣu regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected; yet that bhikṣu neither fears the Saṃgha nor fears committing an offense, and refusing to accept the words of the one who has charged him, he takes his sitting mat, places it upon his shoulder, and departs, being impossible to rebuke or restrain. He is just like a wicked horse to which a bridle and whip are given in order to make it go, yet it neither fears the driver nor the whip, and with its mouth agape and snorting, it charges headlong, impossible to control. I say that such a person is exactly like this.

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who points out a fault—whether seen, heard, or suspected—in another bhikṣu, and that other bhikṣu, having tucked his upper robe (uttarāsaṅga) over his left shoulder, raises his hand in the midst of the Saṃgha and speaks loudly:
"Do you really intend to instruct me?"

"Just as when a wicked horse is given a bridle and a whip with the intent to make it go, yet it stands on its hind legs with both feet, foaming at the mouth—I say that such a person is exactly like this."
Suppose there is a bhikṣu who points out a fault—whether seen, heard, or suspected—in another bhikṣu, and that bhikṣu says:
"Venerable sir, you have not even given me robes, a bowl, bedding, or medicine; why then do you instruct me?"
He immediately renounced the precepts and took up the lower path, going to where the bhikṣus were and saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I have abandoned the holy life; is this not a source of joy to you?"
"Just as when a wicked horse is given a bridle and a whip with the intent that it should go forward, yet it instead crouches and lies down, I say that such a person is exactly like this.
These are the eight kinds of evil persons."

I have already described the eight kinds of evil horses and the eight kinds of evil persons; I have fully explained that which the World-Honored One should compassionately teach his disciples. You should now dwell in empty places or beneath trees to practice meditative concentration; do not be negligent, lest you later come to regret it. This is my instruction.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, filled with joy, faith, and delight, they received and upheld it.

At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realms together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus in the kingdom of Kośala. On the way, he saw a great mass of fire blazing intensely. Having seen it, he immediately left the road, sat down on a seat prepared beneath a tree, and addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see that great mass of fire blazing there?”
If someone were to seize that fire, grasp it, and rub it, it would immediately burn their skin, flesh, sinews, and bones until they were completely consumed.

On the other hand, if another person were to seize a woman of the Kṣatriya caste, a woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste, a woman of the Vaiśya caste, or a woman of the Śūdra caste, and grasp her, rub her, and kiss her—of these two matters, which one would be considered better?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
“Venerable Sir,
if one were to seize a woman of the Kṣatriya caste or others, caress her, and kiss her, would this be considered virtuous?”
"Why is this? If one were to grasp fire, it would immediately burn and scorch the skin, flesh, sinews, and bones until they are completely consumed, resulting in great agony that cannot be endured.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“I now tell you this:
it would be better for you to seize this fire, grasp it, and rub it against yourself until your skin, flesh, sinews, and bones are completely consumed. Why is that? Because—”
One shall not fall into the three evil realms because of these causes.

If one is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, or does not practice pure conduct yet claims to practice pure conduct; if one breaks the precepts and performs evil deeds, lacking entirely the observance of discipline and dignified deportment; if one commits offenses while shrouded by false views; if one is empty and rotten within while appearing complete and pure without; and if one consumes the faithful offerings of others but, because of being unable to digest such offerings, falls into the three evil realms to undergo suffering for a long night.

Therefore, one should maintain pure precepts while consuming the offerings of the faithful—food, drink, clothing, bedding, medicine, and all other necessities—which enables the donor to obtain a great karmic reward and ensures that the purpose for which one has left the household life to become a śramaṇa is fully accomplished.

“O bhikṣus! Would you rather have your feet pierced by a red-hot iron spear, or would you rather receive the prostrations at your feet from faithful sons and daughters of good family who delight in the Dharma?
Between these two matters, which is the better?”
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"We would rather receive the prostrations at our feet from faithful sons and daughters of good family. Why is that?"
"Because one suffers great agony when a heated spear pierces the foot.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I now tell you: it would be better to have a heated spear pierce your foot."
Why is this? Because one does not fall into the three evil realms on account of this cause.
If one is not a śramaṇa yet claims to be a śramaṇa, or if one does not practice pure conduct yet claims to practice pure conduct.

Violating the precepts and performing evil deeds, they utterly lack the majestic deportment of one who upholds the discipline; obscured by false views, they commit offenses while appearing outwardly pure, though inwardly they are empty and putrid. Consuming the faithful offerings of others, because they cannot digest such offerings, they fall into the three evil realms and suffer for a long night.

Therefore, one should maintain pure precepts while consuming the offerings of the faithful, as well as all other necessities mentioned above, so that the donor may obtain a great reward and the purpose for which one has left the household life to become a śramaṇa may also be fulfilled.
“O bhikṣus, would you rather have your own heads severed by a hot axe, or would you prefer to receive the touch of the hands of faithful sons and daughters of good family?”
"Of these two matters, which is the better?
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
It would be better for a son or daughter of good family to have their body touched by the hands of one who enjoys faith and music. Why is this?
Because being beheaded with a heated axe brings about great suffering.
“I now tell you this:
it would be better for you to take a heated axe and cut off your own head; why is that? Because—”
One shall not fall into the three evil realms because of this cause; the rest is as stated in the preceding passage.

"O bhikṣus, you would rather wear garments of hot iron that burn and consume your bodies until they are completely destroyed than accept and wear the various fine robes offered by faithful sons and daughters of good family."
"Of these two matters, which is the better?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"Venerable Sir, it would be better for you to accept those various fine robes."
"Why is this? Because they wear garments of glowing iron that burn their bodies, causing them great suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I now tell you: it would be better to take glowing iron as clothing to burn the body. Why is this?
One shall not fall into the three evil realms because of this cause; the rest is as stated in the preceding passage.

"O bhikṣus, would you rather swallow glowing iron balls that burn and rot your five viscera as they pass out from below, or would you accept the offerings of food and drink from faithful sons and daughters of good family?"
"Between these two matters, which is the better?
The bhikṣus replied,
"It would be better to accept that offering of food and drink."
"Why is this? Because they must swallow glowing iron balls and endure great suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I now tell you: it would be better to swallow glowing iron balls.
Why? Because one will not fall into the three evil realms on account of this cause. The rest is as stated in the preceding passage."
Receiving various kinds of gruel is also like this.

"O bhikṣus, would you rather sit upon a bed of hot iron, burning and scorching your own bodies until they are withered and putrefied, than receive various fine beds and bedding from faithful sons and daughters of good family?"
"Of these two matters, which is the better?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"It would be better to accept those various fine beds and bedding."
"Why is this? Because they burn their own bodies upon beds of glowing iron until they are scorched and withered, undergoing great agony.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I now tell you: it would be better for you to sit or lie down upon a red-hot iron bed and burn your body.
Why? Because by this cause you will not fall into the three evil realms. The rest is as stated in the preceding passage."
"O bhikṣus, would you rather dwell within a house of glowing iron that burns your bodies, or would you accept the lodging of faithful sons and daughters of good family to stay overnight therein?"
"Of these two matters, which is the better?
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha,
"It would be better to accept that dwelling and stay there overnight."
Why is this? Because they undergo great suffering within those heated iron chambers. "I now tell you!
It would be better to have one's body burned and completely withered away within that hot iron chamber. Why?
Because by reason of this, one will not fall into the three evil realms; the rest is as stated in the preceding passage.

When the World-Honored One had spoken these words, sixty bhikṣus had boiling blood gush forth from their mouths and faces; sixty bhikṣus abandoned the precepts and ceased their practice of the Way; and sixty bhikṣus attained the untainted liberation of mind.
There were many bhikṣus who, having distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attained the pure Dharma-eye.
"There are nine things that members of the white-robed laity should not do if they have not yet become *dānapati* (patrons), nor should one sit in their home when visiting them."

What are the nine? Seeing a bhikṣu, they do not delight in rising to greet him; they do not delight in paying him homage; they do not delight in inviting the bhikṣu to sit; they do not delight in his sitting; even if there is something to be said, they do not accept it; if they have clothing, food, drink, or necessary requisites, they treat the bhikṣu with contempt and do not give them; or if they have much, they give little; or if they have fine things, they give coarse and inferior ones; or they give without respect. These are the nine things for which one should not go to the homes of laypeople.

Furthermore, there are nine cases where one who has not yet become a *dānapati* should become a *dānapati*, and nine cases where one who has already become a *dānapati* should go and sit [in the assembly]; the latter part of the previous phrase refers to this.
There are nine unrighteous ways of obstructing the *poṣadha*:

obstructing by means of groundless charges of broken precepts—whether one does not obstruct when one should, or obstructs when one should not—and the same applies to obstructing on account of broken views or broken conduct; these constitute the nine.
There are nine ways in which the *poṣadha* is obstructed according to the Dharma; these are the opposites of the aforementioned phrases.
There are nine statements by which the precepts are relinquished:

relinquishing the Buddha, relinquishing the Dharma, relinquishing the Saṃgha, relinquishing the upādhyāya, relinquishing the co-upādhyāya, relinquishing the ācārya, relinquishing the co-ācārya, relinquishing all fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and relinquishing the precepts—these constitute the nine.
Thus, nine times nine constitute the sections, and this applies even to those who are not Śramaṇas or sons of the Śākya clan.
"The Tathāgata, having appeared in the world, saw that there were transgressions; therefore, for the sake of the nine benefits, he established the precepts for the bhikṣus:
to uphold the Saṃgha, and so on, up to the cessation of future outflows—these are the nine."
When the Tathāgata appears in the world, seeing that there are faults, he establishes the *tarjanīya-karman* (act of censure) for the bhikṣus based on nine beneficial purposes:

from "restraining [a monk] who has joined the Saṃgha" up to "severing future outflows (*āsrava*). These constitute the nine; the same applies up to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
"There are ten kinds of robes:

*kusa* cloth, *kappāsa* cloth, *kambala* cloth, *cīra* cloth, *chamā* cloth, *śaṇa* cloth, *māṣa* cloth, *koseyya* cloth, *kauśeya* cloth, and *dūṣya* cloth. These ten kinds of robes should be dyed the color of a *kāṣāya*."
"There are ten kinds of robes:

rag-robes, robes gnawed by oxen, robes gnawed by rats, burnt robes, robes from menstrual stains, robes from childbirth, robes from a shrine, robes from a cemetery, robes obtained through a vow, robes given by a consecrated king, and robes received while traveling—these are the ten."

“There are ten unrighteous things that obstruct the recitation of the *Poṣadha*: that which is not a *pārājika* offense, that which does not enter into the discourse on *pārājika* offenses; that which is not a forfeiture (*naiḥsargika*) offense, that which does not enter into the discourse on forfeiture offenses; that which accords with the requirements of a righteous Saṃgha, that which is not censured by the requirements of a righteous Saṃgha; that which is not included in the discourse on censure according to the requirements of a righteous Saṃgha; not having seen, heard, or suspected a breach of the precepts; not having seen, heard, or suspected a breach of views; and not having seen, heard, or suspected a breach of conduct. These are the ten.”
There are ten lawful grounds for obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*, which are the opposites of the aforementioned [unlawful] points.
Furthermore, there are ten unlawful grounds for obstructing the recitation of the *Poṣadha*:

one who has not committed a border offense (*antāpatti*) is not included among those who have committed a border offense; one who has not committed an offense against a bhikṣuṇī is not included among those who have committed an offense against a bhikṣuṇī; one who did not receive the precepts with a thieving mind is not included among those who received the precepts with a thieving mind; one who has not violated the two [sexual] organs is not included among those who have violated the two organs; and one who is not a eunuch is not included among those who are eunuchs—these constitute the ten.

There are ten [cases] where, according to the Dharma, the *poṣadha* (recitation of the precepts) must be suspended; these are the opposites of the aforementioned points. "There are ten qualities by which one should be appointed to instruct the bhikṣuṇīs:

one who fully maintains the two hundred and fifty precepts; one who is learned; one who has extensively recited the Vinaya of both divisions; one who is skillful in speech and whose exposition is clear and distinct; one who has gone forth from a noble family—whether a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa, or a householder; one who is handsome in appearance; one who is respected by the bhikṣuṇīs; one who is capable of preaching the Dharma to the bhikṣuṇīs so as to bring them joy; one who has not committed a grave offense despite having gone forth and donned the saffron robe for the sake of the Buddha; and one who has twenty years of seniority or more than twenty years of seniority. These are the ten."
At that time, the Buddha told Upāli:
"You all must not repeatedly point out the offenses of other bhikṣus. Why is this?"
If one’s own bodily deportment is not pure, yet they raise the offense of another bhikṣu, they should immediately say to him:
"Venerable sir, first purify your own bodily deportment."
"Upāli! If a bhikṣu’s bodily deportment is pure, others will not speak ill of him.

The same applies if his speech is impure, his livelihood is impure, he is not learned, or he has not extensively recited the two divisions of the Vinaya—as explained above in the five sets of five dharmas."
Furthermore, Upāli! When accusing another bhikṣu, one should further cultivate five qualities:

at the proper time and not at an improper time; with truth and not with untruth; for the benefit of the other and not for their detriment; with gentleness and not with harshness; and with a mind of loving-kindness and not with anger.
Upāli! One should suspend another bhikṣu only after these ten conditions are met.
There are ten unlawful ways of taking the voting tickets:

There are ten [cases] of taking a tally: taking a tally without understanding the matter; taking a tally together with one who does not act according to the Dharma; taking a tally with the intention of causing those who act contrary to the Dharma to receive many tallies; taking a tally while knowing there are many who act contrary to the Dharma; taking a tally with the intention of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; taking a tally while knowing the Saṃgha intends to split; taking a tally for a minor offense; taking a tally contrary to what one has perceived; taking a tally in an illegal manner; and taking a tally as a separate faction. These are the ten.
There are ten ways of receiving the voting tally in accordance with the Dharma;

these are the opposites of the preceding [ten] phrases. "The Tathāgata appeared in the world and, seeing that there were transgressions, established the precepts for the bhikṣus based on ten principles:
from 'for the sake of gathering the Saṃgha' up to 'for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dharma'—these constitute the ten."
"There are ten kinds of persons who should not be saluted: one who claims to have committed an offense against the boundaries;

one who has violated a bhikṣuṇī; one who received the precepts with a thieving mind; one who has destroyed the two paths; a eunuch; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; and one who has maliciously shed the blood of a Buddha—these are the ten."
“There are ten modes of conduct in which a bhikṣu should not be saluted:

when he is urinating, when he is defecating, when he is naked, when he is shaving his head, when he is preaching the Dharma, when he is chewing a tooth-stick, when he is rinsing his mouth, when he is drinking, when he is eating, and when he is consuming fruit—these are the ten.”
“There are ten faults in drinking alcohol:

it makes one’s complexion ugly, diminishes strength, impairs the clarity of the eyes, leads to frequent displays of anger, causes the loss of wealth, increases illness, gives rise to quarrels and disputes, results in the spread of an evil reputation, destroys wisdom, and leads to rebirth in hell after death—these are the ten.”
"When a renunciant enters a royal palace and goes among the women of the court, there are ten faults:
if the king and his consort are in union when the bhikṣu enters the palace and goes among the women, the consort may see the bhikṣu and smile, and the bhikṣu may see the consort and likewise smile."
The king forms this thought:
"Whether the bhikṣu has already done this, or whether he is about to do this.
This is the first transgression of an ordained person entering the royal palace among the ladies of the court.
Furthermore, if a king, while intoxicated, engages in union with his consort but does not remember it, and the consort subsequently becomes pregnant, the king thinks to himself:
"A bhikṣu entered the palace; this must have been done by that bhikṣu."
This is the second fault. Furthermore, suppose the crown prince intends to rebel and kill the king, and the king thinks to himself:
"The bhikṣu has entered my palace; this must have been his teaching."
This is the third fault.
Furthermore, when the king is within, secret words are heard outside; the king then thinks:
"A bhikṣu has entered my inner palace; this is what he has transmitted."
This is the fourth fault.
Furthermore, if the king loses a treasure or something resembling a treasure, the king thinks:
"A bhikṣu entered my palace; he must have taken it."
This is the fifth fault.
Furthermore, if the king places a person of low status in a high position, those who are displeased with this outwardly say:
"It was the monk's doing that he entered the palace."
This is the sixth fault. Furthermore, if the king appoints those of high rank to lower positions, those who are displeased at this will say:
"The reason monks enter the palace is because of what they have done."
This is the seventh fault.
Furthermore, without any cause or reason, the king assembles the fourfold army at an improper time; those who are displeased say:
"The monk has entered the palace; this is his doing."
This is the eighth fault.
Furthermore, if the king gathers his troops and then returns midway, those who are displeased will say:
"The bhikṣu entered the palace; this was his doing."
This is the ninth fault.
Furthermore, if a king stays among his palace ladies and sees fine elephants, horses, or beautiful women, his mind will give rise to attachment; this is not the dharma of a bhikṣu.
This is the tenth fault. There are ten qualities by which one should not confer the full ordination upon another:

being unable to instruct a disciple in the training of higher morality, higher mind, and higher wisdom; being unable to instruct them in higher deportment, higher purity of conduct, and higher training in the *prātimokṣa*; being unable to instruct them to abandon evil views and establish them in right views; being unable to move a disciple from an unpleasant dwelling to a pleasant one; being unable to provide a resolution and decision according to the Dharma and the Vinaya when doubt or regret arises; and if one has not yet reached ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). These are the ten.
There are ten qualities by which one should confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; the opposite of these [ten] is as follows.
There are ten qualities by which one should not confer the full ordination upon others:

not fully observing the two hundred and fifty precepts, not being well-versed in the teachings, being unable to instruct disciples in the *Abhidharma* and *Vinaya*, being unable to instruct them to abandon evil views and abide in right views, not knowing the *Prātimokṣa*, not knowing the exposition of the *Prātimokṣa*, not knowing the *Poṣadha*, not knowing the *Poṣadha-karman*, or having less than ten years of seniority (*daśavarṣa*). These are the ten.
There are ten qualities by which one should confer the full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon others; these are the opposites of the aforementioned points.
There are ten qualities by which one should not adjudicate legal matters in a particular location:

not fully observing the two hundred and fifty precepts, not being widely learned, not having extensively recited both divisions of the Vinaya, not being skillful in speech to enable others to understand, being unable to engage in question-and-answer sessions or provide instruction and reprimand in accordance with the Dharma to effect a formal exclusion (*pravāsanīya-karman*) so that the person may attain joy, being unable to effectively settle disputes when they arise, not knowing the *Prātimokṣa*, not knowing the exposition of the *Prātimokṣa*, not knowing the *Poṣadha*, and not knowing the *Poṣadha-karman*. These are the ten.
There are ten qualities for which legal matters should be settled through differentiation; these are the opposites of the preceding points.
There are ten qualities for which legal matters should not be settled through differentiation:

six points are as above, plus not understanding how to settle a dispute, not knowing how a dispute arises, not knowing how a dispute is extinguished, and not knowing the path leading to the extinction of a dispute—these constitute the ten.
There are ten qualities by which a legal case should be decided according to its specific circumstances; these are the opposites of the aforementioned [ten] qualities.
There are ten qualities by which a legal case should not be decided according to its specific circumstances:
six are as listed above, plus being influenced by affection, being influenced by hatred, being influenced by fear, and being influenced by delusion.
"These are the ten. There are ten further dharmas for which legal cases should be decided by distinction; these are the opposites of the preceding phrases.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
By what causes and conditions do disputes arise in the Saṃgha where none previously existed, and why do existing disputes fail to be extinguished?
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"To bring a formal charge against another bhikṣu by claiming he has committed an offense when he has not, or that he has not committed an offense when he has; by claiming an offense is light when it is heavy, or heavy when it is light; by declaring what is not Dharma to be Dharma, or what is Dharma to be non-Dharma; by declaring what is not Vinaya to be Vinaya, or what is Vinaya to be non-Vinaya; or by enacting what was not prescribed as prescribed, or abolishing what was prescribed."
"By these causes and conditions, disputes that have not yet arisen among the Saṃgha will arise, and disputes that already exist will not be extinguished.
Ānanda again asked the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
“By what causes and conditions can it be that the Saṃgha has no disputes and does not give rise to them, and that existing disputes are eliminated?
The Buddha answered Ānanda by reversing the previous statement.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"There are ten roots of dispute that you should know; apply skillful means well to bring them to cessation.
What are these ten?..."
The preceding sentence was reversed. At that time, Upāli rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
Regarding the statement "to cause a schism in the Saṃgha," to what extent is one said to have caused a schism?
Who is it that breaks the harmonious Saṃgha?
The Buddha replied:

"The ten matters are as stated above; by seeking a faction through these ten matters, or by instructing others to seek one, and then performing separate *poṣadha*, *karmavācanā*, and *saṃghakarma*—this constitutes a schism in the Saṃgha, which is called 'breaking the harmonious Saṃgha.'"
Upāli asked about the Sangha being in harmony, which is the reverse of the preceding phrase.
There are eleven statements:

renouncing the precepts, renouncing the Buddha, renouncing the Dharma, renouncing the Sangha, renouncing the upādhyāya, renouncing the co-upādhyāya, renouncing the ācārya, renouncing the co-ācārya, renouncing a bhikṣu of pure conduct, renouncing the Prātimokṣa, renouncing the Vinaya, and renouncing the training matters—these constitute the eleven.
"These eleven points constitute the categories; this applies even to those who are not śramaṇas or sons of the Śākyas.
At that time, the World-Honored One was staying in a grove in the city of Acyuta and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"Wherever a bhikṣu may be, do not engage in strife, do not revile one another, do not let swords and blades issue from your mouths, and do not seek out each other's faults. Even to remember such a place would be unpleasant; how much less could one dwell there?"
You should definitely know that three things are quickly extinguished and you should know that three things increase.
What are these three?
Mindfulness of renunciation, mindfulness of non-ill will, and mindfulness of non-envy—these three matters are quickly cut off and extinguished.
What three dharmas increase?
The thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of envy—these three dharmas increase.
Therefore, wherever there is strife, mutual abuse, words like swords and blades, or the seeking of others' faults, one finds no joy even in recollecting it, much less being able to dwell there.
Therefore, you should definitely understand that there is the decline of three factors and the increase of three factors.
If a bhikṣu, wherever he may be, does not engage in mutual strife—this is the opposite of the aforementioned case.

When there is conflict, both parties are unable to endure it; harboring defilement in their hearts, they harbor mutual hatred and harm, increasing their anger. Being ill-disciplined, they do not accept instruction, and they also lose their sense of reverence.
You should know that this dispute will only grow more intense and solidified, and it cannot be settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Buddha’s instructions.

If bhikṣus engage in quarreling, yet both sides exercise forbearance, harbor no defilement in their hearts, do not feel mutual hatred or malice, refrain from increasing their anger, and instead skillfully subdue themselves, accepting one another's instruction without losing their respect; [only then can the dispute be resolved].
It should be known that this dispute is not firm and can be settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Buddha’s instructions.

If monks engage in a dispute where both parties are intolerant, harboring impurities in their hearts, hating and harming one another, increasing their anger, and failing to discipline themselves properly—neither accepting instruction nor showing respect—[the dispute will persist].

If, when a dispute arises, one does not settle that dispute by means of each of the seven methods for settling disputes, it should be known that this dispute will further increase and become more entrenched, and it cannot be settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Buddha’s instructions.
If a dispute is settled in accordance with the Dharma, it is the opposite of the preceding statement.

If monks engage in quarreling and do not resolve the matter through conciliation with those of superior, middling, or inferior rank, then it does not enter into the Sūtras and Vinaya, nor is it in accord with the legal code.

If, when a dispute arises, it is not settled one by one through the seven methods for settling disputes, you should know that this dispute will increase and become firmly established, and it cannot be settled in accordance with the Dharma, the Vinaya, or the Buddha’s teachings.
If a matter of dispute is settled in accordance with the Dharma, it is the opposite of the preceding case.
If one does not consult with those who uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātikā to settle the matter of dispute, the dispute will increase, as described in the preceding case.
"If a legal dispute is settled in accordance with the Dharma, it is as stated in the preceding passage.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Upāli:
"You should not repeatedly bring up the offenses of other bhikṣus."
Why is this? If one raises the faults of others while one’s own body is impure and one’s speech is impure, another will say:
"Venerable sir!..."
"First, one must purify one's own physical and verbal conduct. Upāli!
If a bhikṣu’s body and speech are pure, he will not give rise to talk about others.
Furthermore, Upāli!

If one who has been accused of being impure in livelihood, of having little learning, or of not reciting the Sūtras, should accuse another of an offense, that person will immediately respond with these words:
"Venerable sir!..."
"First, one must purify one's own livelihood and recite the sūtras.
"If, Upāli, one censures another bhikṣu who has purified his livelihood and is learned in the recitation of the sūtras, no further words shall arise [against him]."
Furthermore, Upāli!
If one accuses another bhikṣu who is not learned, does not know the Vinaya, and whose speech is indistinct—like a white sheep—and yet accuses him of an offense, then the other will speak these words:
"Venerable sir!..."
"First one must study the Vinaya and learn its terminology. Upāli,
if one censures another bhikṣu who is learned, recites the Vinaya, and speaks with clarity, then no further dispute will arise.
Therefore, Upāli! A bhikṣu should understand this:

if a bhikṣu has both affection and respect for me, he should charge him with his faults; if he has no affection but has respect, he should charge him; if he has no respect but has affection, he should charge him; and if he has neither affection nor respect, yet is able to cause him to abandon evil and turn toward the good, he should charge him.

If one lacks both affection and reverence, they will likewise be unable to cause others to abandon evil and practice good; however, those bhikṣus whom he holds in high esteem, who respect, revere, and have faith in him, can cause others to abandon evil and practice good—such persons should be appointed.

If there is neither affection nor reverence, one cannot cause them to abandon evil and practice good; furthermore, if there is no bhikṣu whom they hold in high esteem, respect, and trust, one cannot cause them to abandon evil and practice good.
Upāli! The Saṃgha should immediately set him aside and expel him, saying:
"Venerable one!..."

Wherever you go, they shall perform *ukkhepana* (formal suspension) against you, remind you of your offenses, cause you to confess them, obstruct your *ānupāda* (acceptance of alms), obstruct the recitation of the *Prātimokṣa*, and obstruct the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism).
"Just as a horse trainer, when a wild horse is difficult to tame, immediately unfastens the halter and pegs and casts it away;
so too is this bhikṣu. One should not first seek permission from such a person; this itself constitutes permission."
When the Buddha had spoken thus, Upāli heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
Upāli then asked the Buddha:
"Venerable Sir!"
"By how many factors does one initiate legal proceedings against a bhikṣu?
The Buddha replied,
"One initiates legal proceedings against a bhikṣu by means of three factors:"
"Breach of precepts, breach of views, and breach of decorum. Upāli asked again:
"When these three matters give rise to a formal charge, by how many further factors is the formal act of censure (ukkhepanīyakamma) carried out?"
The Buddha said:
"One may raise [a formal charge] on three grounds:
what has been seen, what has been heard, and what is suspected."

Upāli asked again: "If one initiates a formal act through three matters and performs a formal censure through three dharmas, how many internal qualities must one possess before such a censure may be carried out?
The Buddha said:
“There are five internal qualities that one should employ when performing a formal reprimand (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), as previously explained: acting at the proper time and not at an improper time;
[the other three being] such-and-such—these are the five qualities. At that time, the Blessed One was staying by a pond in the Vajji country and addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you think that I teach the Dharma for the sake of robes, alms-food, medicine for the sick, or bedding and seats?”
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
We would not dare to give rise to such a thought as that the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma for the sake of robes, or even down to bedding and seats.”
The Buddha asked,
"If you do not do so, with what state of mind would you act? The bhikṣus replied:
“We have formed this thought:
‘The World-Honored One preaches the Dharma out of his compassionate concern for sentient beings. The Buddha said:
“If you truly possess such a mind, then regarding the dharmas I have awakened to and realized—

the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path— you should joyfully unite in their practice and study.”

If you joyfully practice in harmony with others and a fellow bhikṣu commits an offense against the precepts, you should not raise the matter hastily; rather, you should examine yourself to ensure that you do not cause yourself distress, nor harm others.

If that offender does not harbor resentment or anger, does not harbor enmity or malice, and is not difficult to awaken, he can personally eliminate his offense, abandon what is unwholesome, and abide in wholesome dharmas.
If one acts in this way, one must further weigh what is appropriate;

even if it causes oneself distress, provided it does not harm that person, then that offender—who finds no joy in anger and is difficult to enlighten—will be able to swiftly eliminate their transgressions, abandon unwholesome states, and abide in wholesome dharmas.
That bhikṣu should reflect thus:
"I have incurred a slight affliction; it causes no harm to them, but brings about beneficial affection, enabling me to abandon what is unwholesome and abide in wholesome dharmas."
"Then one should charge him with the offense. A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"If I charge another with an offense, I shall bring suffering upon myself, yet it will not harm him."
"Those who have committed offenses are prone to anger yet easily attain understanding, and are able to swiftly abandon their transgressions.
The rest is as stated above.
The bhikṣu further reflects thus:
"If one brings up another's transgression, it will cause me distress and harm.
That person who possesses such faults is prone to anger and difficult to enlighten; they will not quickly abandon their transgressions."
‘If I raise a charge against him to remind him of his transgression, he will answer me with irrelevant talk and give rise to anger.
Such a person should be set aside and need not be charged again.
In this way, monks who are harmonious and joyful, when encountering various points of dispute within the Abhidharma, should say:
"Venerable sirs! What you have spoken accords with both the letter and the meaning; we should not dispute it together."
If there are other bhikṣus whose words are trusted by others, one should say to them:
"The meaning of what the Elder has spoken accords with the text; you should not dispute it."
Furthermore, there are other bhikṣus whose words are trusted by others; they too should speak these same words and say:
"The Elder’s words differ in phrasing but are identical in meaning. This is but a minor matter; do not engage in dispute."
"If there are many people who trust him and credit his words, one should speak to them in this way.
Furthermore, if there are yet more people who trust him and credit his words, one should likewise speak to them in this way."
Again he said: "The Elder’s statement is likewise one where the phrasing is identical but the meaning differs.
He further spoke these words:
"Elder! The words and meanings you have spoken are both inconsistent; do not engage in mutual strife.
This should be said to those many people who place their trust in such speech.
Furthermore, there are those who speak with credibility; they too should speak in this manner.
If such a dispute arises within a harmonious Saṃgha, they should gather together in harmony.
Having assembled together, you should conduct such an investigation: "Does this mutual quarreling create an obstacle to the Dharma of a śramaṇa?
What do you think?
Those other bhikṣus who perceive the correct principle should speak as follows:
"Contention is an obstacle to the Dharma of a śramaṇa. He asked again:
"If one holds such a view, is it not censurable?"
He said: "In my opinion, to create obstacles for the dharma of a śramaṇa is precisely what is censurable.
He asked again:
"If one creates obstacles for the dharma of a śramaṇa, which is a censurable act, can one advance in roots of goodness and attain the fruits of a śramaṇa?
A bhikṣu who perceives correct principle replied:
"In my view, that which is censurable cannot advance one in roots of goodness, nor can it lead to the attainment of the fruits of a śramaṇa."
If the dispute is settled in such a manner, one should say to that bhikṣu:
"You have settled this dispute for us.
That bhikṣu should respond, saying:

"I do not know his mind; however, I have faith and devotion in the Buddha. The World-Honored One has taught me the Dharma at the proper time, providing the most supreme and sublime exposition of good and evil. Just as I have heard such a Dharma from the World-Honored One, I shall now speak it for you."

If that bhikṣu, having heard this, then abandons the matter of contention, then when the bhikṣu speaks in such a manner, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others; thus, no other bhikṣus will be able to reproach him.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy and faith, received and upheld it.

"There are thirteen kinds of persons who, having not yet received the full ordination (upasampadā), should not receive it; if they have already received it, they should be subject to expulsion (pravāsanīya): one who confesses to having committed a pārājika offense;

one who has violated a bhikṣuṇī; one who received the precepts with a thieving mind; one who has damaged both sexual organs; a eunuch; one who has killed his father; one who has killed his mother; one who has killed an arhat; one who has caused a schism in the Saṃgha; one who, with malicious intent, has shed the blood of a Buddha; a non-human; an animal; and one who possesses two sexual organs."
"These are the thirteen kinds of persons who, having not received the full ordination, should not receive it; if they have received it, they should be expelled.
At that time, the Buddha told Upāli:
"You all must not repeatedly bring up the offenses of other bhikṣus."
Why is this? If a bhikṣu frequently points out the faults of others while his own person is not pure, others will say:
"Venerable sir, first purify your own body."
If one exposes another bhikṣu who is pure in body, it does not give rise to further talk from others.

Likewise, if one is impure in speech, impure in livelihood, lacks extensive learning, does not recite the Vinaya, does not contemplate the Sūtras, speaks without clarity like a white sheep, and likewise lacks compassion for the bodily actions of virtuous bhikṣus—it is the same.

Furthermore, Upāli! If a bhikṣu wishes to bring forth the offenses of another so that their guilt is not concealed, he shall raise up those who have committed an offense and not raise up those who have not.
He takes the word of that bhikṣu himself and proceeds according to his own admission (*svavacanena*), being well-versed in speech, eloquent, and capable of making it beneficial.

Furthermore, Upāli! In accusing another bhikṣu, one should likewise possess five qualities: acting at the proper time and not at an improper time; [the remaining four] as described above for these five qualities.
"Upāli! If a bhikṣu possesses these seventeen qualities, he should be allowed to point out another's offense.
There are twenty-two qualities by which one should not confer the full ordination upon others: [text continues]"

Not knowing what is Dharma and not knowing what is non-Dharma, up to not knowing what should be spoken and what should not be spoken; not knowing which offenses may be confessed and not knowing which offenses may not be confessed; not knowing how to perform confession and not knowing how to achieve purification through confession—possessing these twenty-two qualities, one should not confer the full precepts upon others.
“There are twenty-two qualities by which one should confer the full ordination upon others; the opposite of these [qualities] is as stated above.
At that time, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“By means of twenty-two kinds of conduct, one may know whether a person is fit to adjudicate legal cases:”
One who fully upholds the two hundred and fifty precepts, is learned and well-versed in the Abhidharma and Vinaya, does not dispute with others nor stubbornly cling to these matters;
one who, when there is need for censure, censures them and then remains settled; when there is need for instruction, instructs them and then remains settled;
and when there is need for formal suspension, suspends them and then remains settled—one who is without attachment, without aversion, and without fear.
Out of delusion, one does not accept food or drink from this group, nor does one accept food or drink from that group;
one does not accept robes, bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases from this group, nor does one accept robes, bowls, sitting mats, or needle-cases from that group;
one does not provide for this group, nor does one provide for that group; and one does not enter a village together with this group.
Furthermore, one does not enter a village together with that faction, nor does one make an appointment or agreement with them;
nor does one go there later or sit down later. One who possesses these twenty-two qualities is known as a person capable of adjudicating a legal case fairly.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.
The Ekottarika of the Vinaya is complete. The Fourth Part of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya, Volume 60.
